Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa

Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Fully Enlightened One.

Khuddakanikāye

In the Khuddaka Nikāya

Udāna-aṭṭhakathā

Commentary on the Udāna

Ganthārambhakathā

Introduction to the Text

Mahākāruṇikaṃ [M 0.0001][V 0.0001][P 0.0001] nāthaṃ, ñeyyasāgarapāraguṃ;

Vande nipuṇagambhīra-vicitranayadesanaṃ.

I pay homage to the Greatly Compassionate Lord, who has crossed to the far shore of the ocean of knowables, whose teaching is subtle, profound, and of diverse methods.

Vijjācaraṇasampannā, yena nīyanti lokato;

Vande tamuttamaṃ dhammaṃ, sammāsambuddhapūjitaṃ.

I pay homage to that supreme Dhamma, revered by the Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas, by which those endowed with knowledge and conduct are led forth from the world.

Sīlādiguṇasampanno, ṭhito maggaphalesu yo;

Vande ariyasaṅghaṃ taṃ, puññakkhettaṃ anuttaraṃ.

Endowed with virtues such as morality, established in the paths and fruits, I pay homage to that noble Sangha, the unsurpassed field of merit.

Vandanājanitaṃ puññaṃ, iti yaṃ ratanattaye;

Hatantarāyo sabbattha, hutvāhaṃ tassa tejasā.

By the power of the merit generated by this homage to the Triple Gem, may I, with all obstacles destroyed, be safe everywhere.

Tena [V 0.0002] tena nidānena, desitāni hitesinā;

Yāni suddhāpadānena, udānāni mahesinā.

Those inspired utterances which were taught by the Great Seer, the Seeker of Welfare, on various occasions and with a pure cause.

Tāni sabbāni ekajjhaṃ, āropentehi saṅgahaṃ;

Udānaṃ nāma saṅgītaṃ, dhammasaṅgāhakehi yaṃ.

All of those utterances were brought together into one collection and compiled by the Dhamma-compilers as that which is named the Udāna.

Jinassa dhammasaṃvega-pāmojjaparidīpanaṃ;

Somanassasamuṭṭhāna-gāthāhi paṭimaṇḍitaṃ.

An illumination of the Conqueror's Dhamma, inspiring spiritual urgency and joy, adorned with verses that arise from gladness.

Tassa gambhīrañāṇehi, ogāhetabbabhāvato;

Kiñcāpi dukkarā kātuṃ, atthasaṃvaṇṇanā mayā.

Although it is difficult for me to compose a commentary on its meaning, because it must be fathomed by profound wisdom.

Sahasaṃvaṇṇanaṃ [M 0.0002][P 0.0002] yasmā, dharate satthusāsanaṃ;

Pubbācariyasīhānaṃ, tiṭṭhateva vinicchayo.

Yet, because the Teacher's Dispensation still exists together with its commentary, and because the definitive interpretation of the ancient teachers, who were like lions, still stands.

Tasmā taṃ avalambitvā, ogāhetvāna pañcapi;

Nikāye upanissāya, porāṇaṭṭhakathānayaṃ.

Therefore, relying on that, having penetrated the five Nikāyas, and depending on the method of the ancient commentaries,

Suvisuddhaṃ asaṃkiṇṇaṃ, nipuṇatthavinicchayaṃ;

Mahāvihāravāsīnaṃ, samayaṃ avilomayaṃ.

Not contradicting the doctrine of the residents of the Mahāvihāra, which is utterly pure, unadulterated, and contains definitive interpretations of subtle meanings,

Punappunāgataṃ atthaṃ, vajjayitvāna sādhukaṃ;

Yathābalaṃ karissāmi, udānassatthavaṇṇanaṃ.

Having carefully avoided repetitive explanations, I will compose the commentary on the Udāna to the best of my ability.

Iti ākaṅkhamānassa, saddhammassa ciraṭṭhitiṃ;

Vibhajantassa tassatthaṃ, sādhu gaṇhantu sādhavoti.

Thus, from me, who desires the long endurance of the True Dhamma and is analyzing its meaning, may the virtuous receive this explanation well.

Tattha udānanti kenaṭṭhena udānaṃ? Udānanaṭṭhena. Kimidaṃ udānaṃ nāma? Pītivegasamuṭṭhāpito udāhāro. Yathā hi yaṃ telādi minitabbavatthu mānaṃ gahetuṃ na sakkoti, vissanditvā gacchati, taṃ “avaseko”ti vuccati. Yañca jalaṃ taḷākaṃ gahetuṃ na sakkoti, ajjhottharitvā [V 0.0003] gacchati, taṃ “ogho”ti vuccati. Evameva yaṃ pītivegasamuṭṭhāpitaṃ vitakkavipphāraṃ antohadayaṃ sandhāretuṃ na sakkoti, so adhiko hutvā anto asaṇṭhahitvā bahi vacīdvārena nikkhanto paṭiggāhakanirapekkho udāhāraviseso “udāna”nti vuccati. Dhammasaṃvegavasenapi ayamākāro labbhateva.

Therein, in what sense is it an udāna? In the sense of an inspired utterance. What is this thing called an udāna? It is an exclamation produced by the force of rapture. For just as a substance to be measured, like oil, cannot be held by the measure but spills over and flows away, and is called an 'overflow'; and just as water cannot be held by a lake but overflows and streams away, and is called a 'flood'; even so, a particular kind of exclamation—which is an expansion of thought produced by the force of rapture that cannot be contained within the heart, but, becoming excessive and not remaining inside, issues forth through the door of speech, irrespective of a listener—is called an udāna. This form can also be found by way of spiritual urgency regarding the Dhamma.

Tayidaṃ katthaci gāthābandhavasena katthaci vākyavasena pavattaṃ. Yaṃ pana aṭṭhakathāsu “somanassañāṇamayikagāthāpaṭisaṃyuttā”ti udānalakkhaṇaṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ yebhuyyavasena vuttaṃ. Yebhuyyena hi udānaṃ gāthābandhavasena bhāsitaṃ pītisomanassasamuṭṭhāpitañca. Itarampi pana “atthi, bhikkhave, tadāyatanaṃ, yattha neva pathavī na āpo”tiādīsu (udā. 71) “sukhakāmāni bhūtāni, yo daṇḍena vihiṃsatī”ti (dha. pa. 131), “sace bhāyatha dukkhassa, sace vo dukkhamappiya”nti evamādīsu (udā. 44; netti. 91) ca labbhati.

This udāna occurs in some places in the form of verse and in others in the form of prose. As for the characteristic of an udāna given in the commentaries as 'connected with verses comprised of joy and knowledge,' that was stated as a generalization. For an udāna is generally spoken in the form of verse and is produced by rapture and joy. However, the other form, prose, is also found, for instance, in passages such as: 'There is, monks, that sphere where there is neither earth nor water...'; 'Beings desire happiness; one who harms them with a rod...'; and 'If you fear suffering, if suffering is displeasing to you...'

Evaṃ tayidaṃ sabbaññubuddhabhāsitaṃ, paccekabuddhabhāsitaṃ, sāvakabhāsitanti tividhaṃ hoti. Tattha paccekabuddhabhāsitaṃ – “sabbesu [P 0.0003] bhūtesu nidhāya daṇḍaṃ, aviheṭhayaṃ [M 0.0003] aññatarampi tesa”ntiādinā (su. ni. 35; cūḷani. khaggavisāṇasuttaniddesa 121) khaggavisāṇasutte āgatameva. Sāvakabhāsitānipi –

Thus, this udāna is threefold: that spoken by an Omniscient Buddha, that spoken by a Paccekabuddha, and that spoken by a disciple. Among these, that spoken by a Paccekabuddha is found in the Khaggavisāṇa Sutta, for instance: 'Having laid aside the rod toward all beings, not harming any one of them...' And those spoken by disciples—

“Sabbo rāgo pahīno me, sabbo doso samūhato;

Sabbo me vihato moho, sītibhūtosmi nibbuto”ti. (theragā. 79) –

'All my lust is abandoned, all my hatred is uprooted, all my delusion is destroyed; I have become cool, quenched.'

Ādinā theragāthāsu –

and so forth, in the Theragāthā.

“Kāyena saṃvutā āsiṃ, vācāya uda cetasā;

Samūlaṃ taṇhamabbuyha, sītibhūtāsmi nibbutā”ti. (therīgā. 15) –

'I was restrained in body, and in speech and mind. Having pulled out craving with its root, I have become cool, quenched.'

Ādinā therīgāthāsu ca āgatāni. Tāni pana tesaṃ therānaṃ therīnañca na kevalaṃ udānāni eva, atha kho sīhanādāpi honti. Sakkādīhi devehi bhāsitāni “aho dānaṃ paramadānaṃ, kassape suppatiṭṭhita”ntiādīni (udā. 27), ārāmadaṇḍabrāhmaṇādīhi manussehi ca bhāsitāni “namo tassa bhagavato”tiādīni (a. ni. 2.38) tisso saṅgītiyo ārūḷhāni udānāni santi eva, na tāni idha adhippetāni. Yāni pana sammāsambuddhena sāmaṃ [V 0.0004] āhacca bhāsitāni jinavacanabhūtāni, yāni sandhāya bhagavatā pariyattidhammaṃ navadhā vibhajitvā uddisantena udānanti vuttāni, tāneva dhammasaṅgāhakehi “udāna”nti saṅgītanti tadevettha saṃvaṇṇetabbabhāvena gahitaṃ.

And so forth, they are also found in the Therīgāthā. However, those of the elders and elder nuns are not merely utterances, but indeed lion's roars as well. There are utterances spoken by deities such as Sakka, saying, "Ah, the supreme gift, well-established in Kassapa!" and so on (Ud. 27), as well as those spoken by humans like the Ārāmadaṇḍa brahmin, saying, "Homage to that Blessed One!" and so on (AN 2.38). Though such utterances, included in the three councils, exist, they are not what is intended here. Only those words spoken directly by the Perfectly Enlightened One himself, being the words of the Conqueror, which the Blessed One, dividing the Teaching into nine parts and designating them, called "Udāna"—these alone were collected as "Udāna" by the compilers of the Dhamma. Thus, it is precisely these that are intended here as the subject for explanation.

Yā pana “anekajātisaṃsāra”ntiādigāthāya dīpitā bhagavatā bodhimūle udānavasena pavattitā anekasatasahassānaṃ sammāsambuddhānaṃ avijahitaudānagāthā ca, etā aparabhāge pana dhammabhaṇḍāgārikassa bhagavatā desitattā dhammasaṅgāhakehi udānapāḷiyaṃ saṅgahaṃ anāropetvā dhammapade saṅgītā. Yañca “aññāsi vata, bho koṇḍañño, aññāsi vata, bho koṇḍañño”ti (mahāva. 17; saṃ. ni. 5.1081; paṭi. ma. 2.30) udānavacanaṃ dasasahassilokadhātuyā devamanussānaṃ pavedanasamatthanigghosavipphāraṃ bhagavatā bhāsitaṃ, tadapi dhammacakkappavattanasuttantadesanāpariyosāne attanā [M 0.0004] adhigatadhammekadesassa yathādesitassa ariyamaggassa [P 0.0004] sāvakesu sabbapaṭhamaṃ therena adhigatattā attano parissamassa saphalabhāvapaccavekkhaṇahetukaṃ paṭhamabodhiyaṃ sabbesaṃ eva bhikkhūnaṃ sammāpaṭipattipaccavekkhaṇahetukaṃ “ārādhayiṃsu vata maṃ bhikkhū ekaṃ samaya”ntiādivacanaṃ (ma. ni. 1.225) viya pītisomanassajanitaṃ udāhāramattaṃ, “yadā have pātubhavanti dhammā”tiādivacanaṃ (mahāva. 1-3; udā. 1-3) viya pavattiyā nivattiyā vā na pakāsananti, na dhammasaṅgāhakehi udānapāḷiyaṃ saṅgītanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

And that verse beginning with “anekajātisaṃsāra,” which was set forth by the Blessed One at the foot of the Bodhi tree and proclaimed as an inspired utterance, and which is the unabandoned inspired utterance of many hundreds of thousands of perfectly enlightened Buddhas—this, in a later period, was not included in the Udāna collection by the compilers of the Dhamma, but was instead incorporated into the Dhammapada because it was taught by the Blessed One to the Treasurer of the Dhamma. And that inspired utterance, “Indeed, Koṇḍañña has understood! Indeed, Koṇḍañña has understood!” (Mahāvagga 17; Saṃyutta Nikāya 5.1081; Paṭisambhidāmagga 2.30), proclaimed by the Blessed One with a resounding echo capable of being made known to gods and humans in the ten-thousandfold world-system—this too, spoken at the conclusion of the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta’s teaching, was merely an exclamation born of joy and gladness, like the statement, “Indeed, the monks pleased me at one time” (Majjhima Nikāya 1.225). It was occasioned by the Elder's attainment, as the very first among the disciples, of the Noble Path as it had been taught—a portion of the Dhamma realized by the Buddha himself—and by his reflection on the fruitfulness of his own effort, and, at the first enlightenment, by reflection on the correct practice of all the monks. Like the statement, “When, indeed, phenomena become manifest” (Mahāvagga 1-3; Udāna 1-3), it does not indicate either arising or ceasing, and thus was not included in the Udāna collection by the compilers of the Dhamma. This should be understood.

Taṃ panetaṃ udānaṃ vinayapiṭakaṃ, suttantapiṭakaṃ, abhidhammapiṭakanti tīsu piṭakesu suttantapiṭakapariyāpannaṃ, dīghanikāyo, majjhimanikāyo, saṃyuttanikāyo, aṅguttaranikāyo, khuddakanikāyoti pañcasu nikāyesu khuddakanikāyapariyāpannaṃ, suttaṃ, geyyaṃ, veyyākaraṇaṃ, gāthā, udānaṃ, itivuttakaṃ, jātakaṃ, abbhutadhammaṃ, vedallanti navasu sāsanaṅgesu udānasaṅgahaṃ.

This inspired utterance is comprised within the Suttanta Piṭaka among the three Piṭakas—the Vinaya Piṭaka, the Suttanta Piṭaka, and the Abhidhamma Piṭaka. Within the five Nikāyas—the Dīgha Nikāya, the Majjhima Nikāya, the Saṃyutta Nikāya, the Aṅguttara Nikāya, and the Khuddaka Nikāya—it is comprised within the Khuddaka Nikāya. Among the nine limbs of the teaching—sutta, geyya, veyyākaraṇa, gāthā, udāna, itivuttaka, jātaka, abbhutadhamma, and vedalla—it is included in the Udāna.

“Dvāsīti buddhato gaṇhiṃ, dve sahassāni bhikkhuto;

Caturāsīti sahassāni, ye me dhammā pavattino”ti. (theragā. 1027) –

Eighty-two thousand I received from the Buddha,

Two thousand from the monk;

Eighty-four thousand are these Dhammas that are current for me.

Evaṃ dhammabhaṇḍāgārikena paṭiññātesu caturāsītiyā dhammakkhandhasahassesu katipayadhammakkhandhasaṅgahaṃ. Bodhivaggo, mucalindavaggo, nandavaggo, meghiyavaggo, soṇavaggo, jaccandhavaggo, cūḷavaggo, pāṭaligāmiyavaggoti vaggato aṭṭhavaggaṃ; suttato asītisuttasaṅgahaṃ, gāthāto pañcanavutiudānagāthāsaṅgahaṃ. Bhāṇavārato aḍḍhūnanavamattā bhāṇavārā. Anusandhito bodhisutte [V 0.0005] pucchānusandhivasena ekānusandhi, suppavāsāsutte pucchānusandhiyathānusandhivasena dve anusandhī, sesesu yathānusandhivasena ekekova anusandhi, ajjhāsayānusandhi panettha natthi. Evaṃ sabbathāpi ekāsītianusandhisaṅgahaṃ. Padato satādhikāni ekavīsa padasahassāni, gāthāpādato tevīsati catussatādhikāni aṭṭha sahassāni[P 0.0005], akkharato sattasahassādhikāni saṭṭhi sahassāni tīṇi ca satāni dvāsīti ca akkharāni. Tenetaṃ vuccati –

Thus, it is a compilation of a certain number of Dhamma aggregates among the eighty-four thousand Dhamma aggregates acknowledged by the Treasurer of the Dhamma. By way of chapters, there are eight: the Bodhi Chapter, the Mucalinda Chapter, the Nanda Chapter, the Meghiya Chapter, the Soṇa Chapter, the Jaccandha Chapter, the Cūḷa Chapter, and the Pāṭaligāmiya Chapter. By way of suttas, it is a collection of eighty suttas. By way of verses, it is a collection of ninety-five Udāna verses. By way of recitation sections, there are eight and a half recitation sections. By way of connections, in the Bodhisutta there is one connection in the manner of inquiry; in the Suppavāsāsutta, there are two connections in the manner of inquiry and in due order; in the remaining suttas, there is only one connection each in due order; here, there is no connection based on inclination. Thus, in all, it is a collection of eighty-one connections. By way of words, there are twenty-one thousand, one hundred words. By way of verse lines, there are eight thousand, four hundred and twenty-three. By way of syllables, there are sixty-seven thousand, three hundred and eighty-two syllables. Therefore, it is said:

“Asīti eva suttantā, vaggā aṭṭha samāsato;

Gāthā ca pañcanavuti, udānassa pakāsitā.

Eighty suttas in all, and eight chapters in brief;

And ninety-five verses are declared for the Udāna.

“Aḍḍhūnanavamattā [M 0.0005] ca, bhāṇavārā pamāṇato;

Ekādhikā tathāsīti, udānassānusandhiyo.

And eight and a half recitation sections by measure;

Likewise, eighty-one are the connections of the Udāna.

“Ekavīsasahassāni, satañceva vicakkhaṇo;

Padānetānudānassa, gaṇitāni viniddise”.

Twenty-one thousand and one hundred—

the discerning one should declare

these counted words of the Udāna.

Gāthāpādato pana –

But by way of verse lines:

“Aṭṭhasahassamattāni, cattāreva satāni ca;

Pādānetānudānassa, tevīsati ca niddise.

Eight thousand, and four hundred,

and twenty-three—these lines of the Udāna

one should declare.

“Akkharānaṃ sahassāni, saṭṭhi satta satāni ca;

Tīṇi dvāsīti ca tathā, udānassa paveditā”ti.

Sixty-seven thousand syllables,

and three hundred and eighty-two as well,

are proclaimed for the Udāna.

Tassa aṭṭhasu vaggesu bodhivaggo ādi, suttesu paṭhamaṃ bodhisuttaṃ, tassāpi evaṃ me sutantiādikaṃ āyasmatā ānandena paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikāle vuttanidānamādi. Sā panāyaṃ paṭhamamahāsaṅgīti vinayapiṭake (cūḷava. 437) tantimārūḷhā eva. Yo panettha nidānakosallatthaṃ vattabbo kathāmaggo sopi sumaṅgalavilāsiniyaṃ dīghanikāyaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.nidānakathā) vutto evāti tattha vuttanayeneva veditabbo.

Among its eight chapters, the Bodhi Chapter is the beginning; among the suttas, the Bodhi Sutta is the first. Of that sutta also, the beginning is the introduction starting with ‘Thus I have heard,’ which was spoken by the Venerable Ānanda at the time of the First Great Council. This First Great Council has indeed been established in the textual tradition of the Vinaya Piṭaka (Cūḷavagga 437). And whatever path of discourse is spoken here for the sake of skill in the introduction, that too is indeed spoken in the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī, the commentary on the Dīgha Nikāya (Dī. Ni. Aṭṭha. 1, Nidānakathā), and should thus be understood according to the method explained therein.

1. Bodhivaggo

1. The Chapter on Awakening

1. Paṭhamabodhisuttavaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the First Discourse on Awakening

1. Yaṃ [V 0.0006][M 0.0006][P 0.0006] panettha “evaṃ me suta”ntiādikaṃ nidānaṃ, tattha evanti nipātapadaṃ. Metiādīni nāmapadāni. Uruvelāyaṃ viharatīti ettha vīti upasaggapadaṃ, haratīti ākhyātapadanti imināva nayena sabbattha padavibhāgo veditabbo.

1. In the introduction here, which begins with “Thus have I heard,” the word “Thus” (evaṃ) is a particle. The words beginning with “I” (me) are nominal words. In the phrase “dwelling at Uruvelā” (Uruvelāyaṃ viharati), “vi-” is a prefix, and “harati” is a verbal word. In this way, the division of words should be understood everywhere.

Atthato pana evaṃsaddo tāva upamūpadesasampahaṃsanagarahaṇavacanasampaṭiggahākāra- nidassanāvadhāraṇapucchāidamatthaparimāṇādi anekatthappabhedo. Tathā hesa “evaṃ jātena maccena, kattabbaṃ kusalaṃ bahu”nti evamādīsu (dha. pa. 53) upamāyaṃ āgato. “Evaṃ te abhikkamitabbaṃ, evaṃ te paṭikkamitabba”ntiādīsu (a. ni. 4.122) upadese. “Evametaṃ bhagavā, evametaṃ sugatā”tiādīsu (a. ni. 3.66) sampahaṃsane. “Evamevaṃ panāyaṃ vasalī yasmiṃ vā tasmiṃ vā tassa muṇḍakassa samaṇakassa vaṇṇaṃ bhāsatī”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 1.187) garahaṇe. “Evaṃ, bhanteti kho te bhikkhū bhagavato paccassosu”ntiādīsu (dī. ni. 2.3; ma. ni. 1.1) vacanasampaṭiggahe. “Evaṃ byā kho ahaṃ, bhante, bhagavatā dhammaṃ desitaṃ ājānāmī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.398) ākāre. “Ehi tvaṃ, māṇavaka, yena samaṇo ānando tenupasaṅkama, upasaṅkamitvā mama vacanena samaṇaṃ ānandaṃ appābādhaṃ appātaṅkaṃ lahuṭṭhānaṃ balaṃ phāsuvihāraṃ puccha ‘subho māṇavo todeyyaputto bhavantaṃ ānandaṃ appābādhaṃ appātaṅkaṃ lahuṭṭhānaṃ balaṃ phāsuvihāraṃ pucchatī’ti, evañca vadehi ‘sādhu kira bhavaṃ ānando yena subhassa māṇavassa todeyyaputtassa nivesanaṃ, tenupasaṅkamatu anukampaṃ [P 0.0007] upādāyā’ti”ādīsu (dī. ni. 1.445) nidassane. “‘Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, kālāmā, ime dhammā kusalā vā akusalā vā’ti? ‘Akusalā, bhante’. ‘Sāvajjā vā anavajjā vā’ti? ‘Sāvajjā, bhante’. ‘Viññūgarahitā vā viññuppasatthā vā’ti? ‘Viññūgarahitā, bhante’. ‘Samattā samādinnā ahitāya dukkhāya saṃvattanti, no’vā? ‘Kathaṃ vo ettha hotī’ti? ‘Samattā, bhante, samādinnā ahitāya dukkhāya saṃvattanti, evaṃ no ettha hotīti’”ādīsu [V 0.0007] (a. ni. 3.66) avadhāraṇe. “Evamete sunhātā suvilittā kappitakesamassū āmuttamālābharaṇā”tiādīsu [M 0.0007] (dī. ni. 1.286) pucchāyaṃ. “Evaṃgatāni puthusippāyatanāni (dī. ni. 1.182), evaṃvidho evamākāro”tiādīsu idaṃsaddassa atthe. Gatasaddo hi pakārapariyāyo, tathā vidhākārasaddā. Tathā hi vidhayuttagatasadde lokiyā pakāratthe vadanti. “Evaṃ lahuparivattaṃ evamāyupariyanto”tiādīsu (a. ni. 1.48) parimāṇe.

In meaning, however, the word `evaṃ` has many different applications, such as simile, instruction, praise, blame, acceptance of speech, manner, indication, ascertainment, questioning, the meaning of 'this,' measure, and so on. For example, in simile: "Thus, by one born as a mortal, much good should be done" (Dhp. 53). In instruction: "Thus should you advance, thus should you retreat" (AN 4.122). In praise: "Thus it is, Blessed One, thus it is, Fortunate One" (AN 3.66). In blame: "Just so, this outcaste woman praises the shaven-headed ascetic in this or that way" (SN 1.187). In acceptance of speech: "‘Yes, venerable sir,’ those monks replied to the Blessed One" (DN 2.3; MN 1.1). In manner: "Thus, venerable sir, I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One" (MN 1.398). In indication: "Come, young man, approach the ascetic Ānanda... and say thus: ‘May the venerable Ānanda, out of compassion, come to the residence of the young man Subha, son of Todeyya’" (DN 1.445). In ascertainment: "‘What do you think, Kālāmas? Are these things wholesome or unwholesome?’ ‘Unwholesome, venerable sir.’ ... ‘Undertaken and practiced, they lead to harm and suffering. That is how it appears to us here’" (AN 3.66). In questioning: "Are they thus well-bathed, well-anointed, with hair and beard trimmed, adorned with garlands and ornaments?" (DN 1.286). In the meaning of the word 'this' (`idaṃ`): "Thus varied (`evaṃgatāni`) are the fields of skill" (DN 1.182), and "of such a kind (`evaṃvidho`), of such a nature (`evamākāro`)." For the word `gata` is a synonym for `pakāra` (manner), as are the words `vidha` and `ākāra`. Indeed, worldly people use words conjoined with `vidha` and `gata` in the sense of `pakāra`. In measure: "Thus quickly changing, thus limited is the lifespan" (AN 1.48).

Nanu ca “evaṃ vitakkitaṃ no tumhehi, evamāyupariyanto”ti cettha evaṃsaddena pucchanākāraparimāṇākārānaṃ vuttattā ākārattho eva evaṃsaddoti. Na, visesasabbhāvato. Ākāramattavācako hettha evaṃsaddo ākāratthoti adhippeto. “Evaṃ byā kho”tiādīsu pana ākāravisesavacano. Ākāravisesavācino cete evaṃsaddā pucchanākāraparimāṇākārānaṃ vācakattā. Evañca katvā “evaṃ jātena maccenā”tiādīni upamānaudāharaṇāni yujjanti. Tattha hi –

But is it not the case that here, in the phrases ‘Have you thought thus?’ and ‘thus the lifespan ends,’ since the word ‘evaṃ’ has expressed the manner of questioning and the manner of measure, the word ‘evaṃ’ is only in the sense of ‘manner’? No, because a distinction exists. Here, the word ‘evaṃ,’ which expresses mere manner, is intended in the sense of ‘manner.’ However, in phrases like ‘Thus indeed,’ it denotes a specific manner. And these words ‘evaṃ’ denote a specific manner, for they denote the manner of questioning and the manner of measure. This being so, the examples of simile, such as ‘Thus, by one born as a mortal,’ are justified. For there—

“Yathāpi puppharāsimhā, kayirā mālāguṇe bahū;

Evaṃ jātena maccena, kattabbaṃ kusalaṃ bahu”nti. –

Just as from a heap of flowers many garlands can be made, even so by one born as a mortal much good should be done.

Ettha puppharāsiṭṭhānīyato manussuppatti sappurisūpanissayasaddhammassavanayonisomanasikārabhogasampattiādito [P 0.0008] dānādipuññakiriyāhetusamudāyato sobhāsugandhatādiguṇavisesayogato mālāguṇasadisiyo bahukā puññakiriyā maritabbasabhāvatāya maccena kattabbāti abhedatāya puppharāsi mālāguṇā ca upamā, tesaṃ upamānākāro yathāsaddena aniyamato vutto. Puna evaṃsaddena niyamanavasena vutto. So pana upamākāro niyamiyamāno atthato upamā eva hotīti vuttaṃ “upamāyaṃ āgato”ti.

Here, by a mortal, due to the nature of being subject to death, many meritorious actions, resembling garlands, are to be done. These actions arise from a collection of causes for meritorious actions such as giving, which are based on human birth, association with the virtuous, hearing the true Dhamma, wise attention, abundance of wealth, and so forth—all of which stand in the place of a heap of flowers. And they resemble garlands due to their possession of special qualities like beauty and fragrance. Thus, because of this application, the heap of flowers and the garlands constitute the simile. The manner of comparison for these is stated without restriction by the word `yathā`. Again, it is stated with restriction by the word `evaṃ`. But when that manner of comparison is restricted, in meaning it is indeed a simile. Thus it is said, 'it is used in simile.'

Tathā “evaṃ iminā ākārena abhikkamitabba”ntiādinā upadisiyamānāya samaṇasāruppāya ākappasampattiyā yo tattha upadesākāro, so atthato upadesoyevāti vuttaṃ – “evaṃ te abhikkamitabbaṃ, evaṃ te paṭikkamitabbantiādīsu upadese”ti.

Similarly, with regard to the perfection of deportment befitting a recluse, which is taught by means of phrases such as ‘one should proceed thus, in this manner,’ the manner of instruction that is present there is, in essence, instruction itself. Thus it is said: 'in instruction, in passages such as, “you should proceed thus, you should retreat thus.”'

“Evametaṃ bhagavā, evametaṃ sugatā”ti ettha bhagavatā yathāvuttamatthaṃ aviparītato jānantehi kataṃ yaṃ tattha vijjamānaguṇānaṃ pakārehi [M 0.0008] haṃsanaṃ udaggatākaraṇaṃ sampahaṃsanaṃ, so tattha pahaṃsanākāroti vuttanayena yojetabbaṃ.

In the phrase, "Thus it is, Blessed One, thus it is, Fortunate One," the praising, uplifting, and rejoicing in the existing qualities by means of their various aspects—done by those who know the meaning spoken by the Blessed One without distortion—is the manner of praise. This should be connected in the way that has been stated.

“Evamevaṃ [V 0.0008] panāya”nti ettha garahaṇākāroti vuttanayena yojetabbaṃ. So ca garahaṇākāro “vasalī”tiādikhuṃsanasaddasannidhānato idha evaṃsaddena pakāsitoti viññāyati. Yathā cettha, evaṃ upamākārādayopi upamādivasena vuttānaṃ puppharāsiādisaddānaṃ sannidhānato vuttāti veditabbaṃ.

In 'Evamevaṃ panāyaṃ,' the manner of censure should be connected in the way stated. And that manner of censure, by reason of the proximity of deprecatory words such as 'outcaste,' is understood to be revealed here by the word 'evaṃ.' Just as here, so too the manners of comparison and so forth should be understood as being stated because of the proximity of words like 'heap of flowers' and so on, which are mentioned by way of simile and so forth.

“Evaṃ no”ti etthāpi tesaṃ yathāvuttadhammānaṃ ahitadukkhāvahabhāvena sanniṭṭhānajananatthaṃ anumatiggahaṇavasena “no vā kathaṃ vo ettha hotī”ti pucchāya katāya “evaṃ no ettha hotī”ti vuttattā tadākārasanniṭṭhānaṃ evaṃsaddena āvikataṃ. So pana tesaṃ dhammānaṃ ahitāya dukkhāya saṃvattanākāro niyamiyamāno avadhāraṇattho hotīti vuttaṃ – “evaṃ no ettha hotītiādīsu avadhāraṇe”ti.

Here too, in the phrase 'Evaṃ no' ('Thus for us'), for the purpose of generating a conclusion about the state of those aforementioned things as being conducive to what is unbeneficial and to suffering, by way of seeking assent, when the question 'No vā kathaṃ vo ettha hoti?' ('Or how is it for you in this matter?') was asked, and because it was said, 'Evaṃ no ettha hoti' ('Thus it is for us in this matter'), the conclusion of that manner was made manifest by the word 'evaṃ'. Furthermore, that manner of conducing to what is unbeneficial and to suffering, being specified, has the meaning of determination. Thus it is said: 'In such phrases as "Evaṃ no ettha hoti," it is in the sense of determination.'

“Evañca vadehī”ti yathāhaṃ vadāmi evaṃ samaṇaṃ ānandaṃ vadehīti vadanākāro idāni vattabbo evaṃsaddena nidassīyatīti “nidassanattho”ti vuttaṃ.

In the phrase 'Evañca vadehī' ('And speak thus'), the manner of speaking, 'Speak to the ascetic Ānanda in the way that I speak,' which is now about to be stated, is indicated by the word 'evaṃ'. Therefore, it was said that it has the meaning of indication.

Evamākāravisesavācīnampi etesaṃ evaṃsaddānaṃ [P 0.0009] upamādivisesatthavuttitāya upamādiatthatā vuttā. “Evaṃ, bhante”ti pana dhammassa sādhukaṃ savanamanasikāre niyojitehi bhikkhūhi tattha patiṭṭhitabhāvassa paṭijānanavasena vuttattā tattha evaṃsaddo vacanasampaṭiggahattho. Tena evaṃ, bhanteti sādhu, bhante, suṭṭhu, bhanteti vuttaṃ hoti. Svāyamidha ākāranidassanāvadhāraṇesu daṭṭhabbo.

Thus, even for these words 'evaṃ' that denote specific modes, their meaning as simile and so forth is stated by virtue of their being used in the special sense of simile and so on. In the phrase 'Evaṃ, bhante' ('Thus, venerable sir'), however, because it is spoken by the monks—who are engaged in properly listening to and attending to the Dhamma—by way of acknowledging their state of being established therein, the word 'evaṃ' there has the meaning of accepting the utterance. By this, 'Evaṃ, bhante' is said to mean 'Sādhu, bhante' ('Good, venerable sir'), 'Suṭṭhu, bhante' ('Excellent, venerable sir'). This very word 'evaṃ' should be understood here in the senses of manner, indication, and determination.

Tattha ākāratthena evaṃsaddena etamatthaṃ dīpeti – nānānayanipuṇamanekajjhāsayasamuṭṭhānaṃ atthabyañjanasampannaṃ vividhapāṭihāriyaṃ dhammatthadesanāpaṭivedhagambhīraṃ sabbasattānaṃ sakasakabhāsānurūpato sotapathamāgacchantaṃ tassa bhagavato vacanaṃ sabbappakārena ko samattho viññātuṃ, sabbathāmena pana sotukāmataṃ janetvāpi evaṃ me sutaṃ, mayāpi ekenākārena sutanti.

Therein, in the sense of manner, the word 'evaṃ' indicates this meaning: Who is able to understand in every way the word of that Blessed One—which is skillful in various methods, arises from manifold dispositions, is complete in meaning and phrasing, possesses various marvels, is profound in its text, meaning, teaching, and penetration, and comes into the range of hearing of all beings according to their respective languages? However, even after generating the desire to listen with all one's strength, one says, 'Evaṃ me sutaṃ' ('Thus have I heard'), meaning, 'By me also it has been heard in one particular manner.'

Ettha [M 0.0009] ca ekattanānattaabyāpāraevaṃdhammatāsaṅkhātā nandiyāvattatipukkhalasīhavikkīḷitadisālocanaaṅkusasaṅkhātā ca assādādivisayādibhedena nānāvidhā nayā nānānayā. Nayā vā pāḷigatiyo, tā ca paññattianupaññattādivasena saṃkilesabhāgiyādilokiyāditadubhayavomissakādivasena kusalādivasena khandhādivasena, saṅgahādivasena, samayavimuttādivasena, ṭhapanādivasena[V 0.0009], kusalamūlādivasena, tikapaṭṭhānādivasena ca nānappakārāti nānānayā, tehi nipuṇaṃ saṇhaṃ sukhumanti nānānayanipuṇaṃ.

And here, the 'various methods' (nānānayā) are methods of many kinds, differentiated by way of gratification, objects, and so forth: those designated as the method of unity, the method of diversity, the method of non-activity, and the method of suchness; and those designated as the Nandiyāvaṭṭa method, the Tipukkhala method, the Sīhavikkīḷita method, the Disālocana method, and the Aṅkusa method. Or, the methods are the ways of the Pāli text, and these are of various kinds: by way of designation, subsidiary designation, etc.; by way of that which partakes of defilement, the mundane, etc., and a mixture of both, etc.; by way of the wholesome, etc.; by way of the aggregates, etc.; by way of inclusion, etc.; by way of the temporally liberated, etc.; by way of setting aside, etc.; by way of the wholesome roots, etc.; and by way of the triple conditional relations of the Paṭṭhāna, etc. Thus they are 'various methods'. Because of these, it is skillful, fine, and subtle; hence it is 'skillful in various methods' (nānānayanipuṇaṃ).

Āsayova ajjhāsayo, so ca sassatādibhedena apparajakkhatādibhedena ca anekavidho. Attajjhāsayādiko eva vā aneko ajjhāsayo anekajjhāsayo. So samuṭṭhānaṃ uppattihetu etassāti anekajjhāsayasamuṭṭhānaṃ.

Inclination (āsaya) itself is disposition (ajjhāsaya), and it is of many kinds, distinguished by way of eternalism, etc., and by way of the state of having little dust, etc. Or, the many dispositions, such as the disposition for the goal (atthajjhāsaya), are themselves 'manifold dispositions' (anekajjhāsayo). That is the origin (samuṭṭhāna), the cause of arising, for this teaching; hence it is 'arising from manifold dispositions' (anekajjhāsayasamuṭṭhānaṃ).

Sīlādiatthasampattiyā tabbibhāvanabyañjanasampattiyā saṅkāsanapakāsanavivaraṇavibhajanauttānīkaraṇapaññattivasena chahi atthapadehi akkharapadabyañjanākāraniruttiniddesavasena chahi byañjanapadehi ca samannāgatattā atthabyañjanasampannaṃ.

It is 'complete in meaning and phrasing' (atthabyañjanasampannaṃ) because it is endowed with the accomplishment of meaning, such as virtue, etc., and with the six terms of meaning—concise exposition, detailed exposition, elucidation, analysis, clarification, and designation; and because it is endowed with the accomplishment of phrasing that clarifies that meaning, and with the six terms of phrasing—letters, words, phrases, forms, etymology, and detailed explanation.

Iddhiādesanānusāsanībhedena tesu ca ekekassa visayādibhedena [P 0.0010] vividhaṃ bahuvidhaṃ vā pāṭihāriyaṃ etassāti vividhapāṭihāriyaṃ. Tattha paṭipakkhaharaṇato rāgādikilesāpanayanato pāṭihāriyanti atthe sati bhagavato na paṭipakkhā rāgādayo santi ye haritabbā, puthujjanānampi vigatūpakkilese aṭṭhaguṇasamannāgate citte hatapaṭipakkhe iddhividhaṃ pavattati, tasmā tattha pavattavohārena ca na sakkā idha pāṭihāriyanti vattuṃ. Sace pana mahākāruṇikassa bhagavato veneyyagatā ca kilesā paṭipakkhā, tesaṃ haraṇato pāṭihāriyanti vuttaṃ, evaṃ sati yuttametaṃ. Atha vā bhagavato ceva sāsanassa ca paṭipakkhā titthiyā, tesaṃ haraṇato pāṭihāriyaṃ. Te hi diṭṭhiharaṇavasena diṭṭhippakāsane asamatthabhāvena ca iddhiādesanānusāsanīhi haritā apanītā honti. Paṭīti vā ayaṃ saddo pacchāti etassa atthaṃ bodheti “tasmiṃ paṭipaviṭṭhamhi, añño āgañchi brāhmaṇo”tiādīsu (cūḷani. pārāyanavagga, vatthugāthā 4) viya. Tasmā samāhite [M 0.0010] citte vigatūpakkilese katakiccena pacchā haritabbaṃ pavattetabbanti paṭihāriyaṃ. Attano vā upakkilesesu catutthajjhānamaggehi haritesu pacchā haraṇaṃ paṭihāriyaṃ. Iddhiādesanānusāsaniyo vigatūpakkilesena katakiccena sattahitatthaṃ puna pavattetabbā, haritesu ca attano upakkilesesu parasattānaṃ upakkilesaharaṇāni hontīti paṭihāriyāni bhavanti. Paṭihāriyameva pāṭihāriyaṃ, paṭihāriye vā iddhiādesanānusāsanīsamudāye bhavaṃ ekekaṃ pāṭihāriyanti vuccati. Paṭihāriyaṃ vā catutthajjhānaṃ maggo ca paṭipakkhaharaṇato. Tattha jātaṃ nimittabhūtato tato vā āgatanti pāṭihāriyanti attho veditabbo.

It possesses 'various marvels' (vividhapāṭihāriyaṃ) because it has marvels (pāṭihāriyaṃ) that are diverse or of many kinds, distinguished by psychic power, mind-reading, and instruction, and within these, by the distinctions of their respective objects and so forth. Therein, in the sense that a marvel (pāṭihāriya) is so called from 'removing opposition' (paṭipakkhaharaṇato) by dispelling defilements such as passion, it should be noted that the Blessed One has no opposing defilements like passion that are to be removed. And even for worldlings, in a mind free from corruptions, endowed with eight qualities, and with opposition destroyed, the power of psychic feats arises. Therefore, it cannot be said that 'marvel' here refers to that common usage. However, if it is said that for the greatly compassionate Blessed One, the defilements present in those to be trained are also 'opposition', and 'marvel' is so called from removing them, then this is fitting. Or, the heretics are the opposition to the Blessed One and his Dispensation, and 'marvel' is so called from removing them. For they are indeed removed, dispelled, by the marvels of psychic power, mind-reading, and instruction, by way of removing their wrong views and rendering them incapable of proclaiming their views. Alternatively, the word 'paṭi' indicates the meaning 'after', as in such passages as 'After he had entered, another brahmin came.' Therefore, a 'marvel' (pāṭihāriya) is so called because it is to be brought forth (haritabbaṃ) or made to occur afterwards, by one who has accomplished his task with a concentrated mind free from corruptions. Or, after one's own corruptions have been removed (haritesu) by the fourth jhāna and the path, the subsequent bringing forth (haraṇaṃ) is a 'marvel'. The marvels of psychic power, mind-reading, and instruction are to be made to occur again for the welfare of beings by one who is free from corruptions and has accomplished his task. And when one's own corruptions have been removed, they become removers of the corruptions of other beings; thus they are 'marvels' (pāṭihāriyāni). 'Marvel' (paṭihāriya) is simply 'marvel' (pāṭihāriya). Or, each individual marvel arising in the collection of marvels—psychic power, mind-reading, and instruction—is called a 'marvel'. Or, the fourth jhāna and the path are a 'marvel' because they remove opposition. The meaning should be understood thus: it is a 'marvel' because it is born therein, or because it has that as its basis, or because it comes from that.

Yasmā [V 0.0010] pana tantiatthadesanā tabbohārābhisamayasaṅkhātā hetuhetuphalatadubhayapaññattipaṭivedhasaṅkhātā vā dhammatthadesanāpaṭivedhā gambhīrā, sasādīhi viya mahāsamuddo anupacitakusalasambhārehi alabbhaneyyappatiṭṭhā duppariyogāhā ca, tasmā tehi catūhi gambhīrabhāvehi yuttanti bhagavato vacanaṃ dhammatthadesanāpaṭivedhagambhīraṃ.

Furthermore, because the Dhamma, its meaning, its teaching, and its penetration are profound—whether reckoned as the text, its meaning, its teaching, and the full understanding thereof, or as the penetration of the concepts of cause and the fruit of the cause—and because, like the great ocean for hares and other such creatures, they are for those who have not accumulated the provisions of the wholesome a place where a footing is unobtainable and which is difficult to fathom, therefore the Blessed One’s word, being endowed with these four kinds of profundity, is profound in its Dhamma, meaning, teaching, and penetration.

Eko eva bhagavato dhammadesanāghoso, ekasmiṃ khaṇe pavattamāno nānābhāsānaṃ sattānaṃ attano attano bhāsāvasena [P 0.0011] apubbaṃ acarimaṃ gahaṇūpago hoti. Acinteyyo hi buddhānaṃ buddhānubhāvoti sabbasattānaṃ sakasakabhāsānurūpato sotapathaṃ āgacchatīti veditabbaṃ.

The Blessed One’s voice in teaching the Dhamma is but a single sound; yet, occurring in a single moment, it becomes comprehensible to beings of various languages simultaneously, according to their own respective tongues. For truly, the spiritual power of the Buddhas is inconceivable; thus it should be understood that it comes into the range of hearing for all beings in accordance with their own individual languages.

Nidassanatthena “nāhaṃ sayambhū, na mayā idaṃ sacchikata”nti attānaṃ parimocento “evaṃ me sutaṃ, mayāpi evaṃ suta”nti idāni vattabbaṃ sakalaṃ suttaṃ nidasseti.

By way of illustration, in order to absolve himself of the claim, 'I am self-become; this was not realized by me,' he points to the entire sutta that is now to be recited, saying: 'Thus have I heard; by me also it was heard thus.'

Avadhāraṇatthena “etadaggaṃ, bhikkhave, mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ bahussutānaṃ yadidaṃ ānando, gatimantānaṃ, satimantānaṃ, dhitimantānaṃ, upaṭṭhākānaṃ yadidaṃ ānando”ti (a. ni. 1.219-223) evaṃ bhagavatā, “āyasmā ānando atthakusalo, dhammakusalo, byañjanakusalo, niruttikusalo, pubbāparakusalo”ti (a. ni. 5.169) evaṃ dhammasenāpatinā ca pasatthabhāvānurūpaṃ attano dhāraṇabalaṃ dassento sattānaṃ [M 0.0011] sotukāmataṃ janeti. “Evaṃ me sutaṃ, tañca kho atthato vā byañjanato vā anūnamanadhikaṃ, evameva na aññathā daṭṭhabba”nti. Aññathāti bhagavato sammukhā sutākārato aññathā na pana bhagavatā desitākārato. Acinteyyānubhāvā hi bhagavato desanā, sā neva sabbākārena sakkā viññātunti vuttovāyamattho. Sutākārāvirujjhanameva hi dhāraṇabalaṃ.

By way of emphasis, the Blessed One declared, “Monks, among my monk disciples who are learned, Ānanda is foremost; among those who are quick-witted, who are mindful, who are resolute, and who attend on others, Ānanda is foremost.” Similarly, the General of the Dhamma praised him, saying, “Venerable Ānanda is skilled in meaning, skilled in the Dhamma, skilled in phrasing, skilled in etymology, and skilled in what precedes and what follows.” Demonstrating his own power of retention in accordance with this praise, he inspires in beings an eagerness to listen. “Thus have I heard, and it should be regarded as neither deficient nor excessive in meaning or wording, just so and not otherwise.” “Otherwise” here means otherwise than how it was heard in the presence of the Blessed One, not otherwise than how the Blessed One taught it. For the teaching of the Blessed One has inconceivable power; it is not possible to fully understand it in every aspect. The power of retention lies precisely in not contradicting how it was heard.

Mesaddo tīsu atthesu dissati. Tathā hissa “gāthābhigītaṃ me abhojaneyya”ntiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 1.194; su. ni. 81) mayāti attho. “Sādhu me, bhante, bhagavā saṃkhittena dhammaṃ desetū”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 4.88; 5.382; a. ni. 4.257) mayhanti attho. “Dhammadāyādā me, bhikkhave, bhavathā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.29) mamāti attho. Idha pana “mayā sutaṃ, mama suta”nti ca atthadvaye yujjati.

The word 'me' is seen in three senses. For instance, in 'Food obtained by singing verses is not to be eaten by me,' it has the meaning of 'mayā' (by me). In 'Good, venerable sir, may the Blessed One teach the Dhamma to me in brief,' it has the meaning of 'mayhaṃ' (to me). In 'Monks, be heirs of my Dhamma,' it has the meaning of 'mama' (my). Here, however, it is suitable in two senses: 'heard by me' and 'my hearing'.

Ettha ca yo paro na hoti, so attāti evaṃ vattabbe niyakajjhattasaṅkhāte sasantāne vattanato tividhopi mesaddo kiñcāpi ekasmiṃyeva atthe dissati, karaṇasampadānādivisesasaṅkhāto [V 0.0011] pana viññāyatevāyaṃ atthabhedoti “me-saddo tīsu atthesu dissatī”ti vuttoti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Here, although the word 'me', in all three instances, is seen in only one sense—that which is not another, but one's own self, existing in one's own continuum—yet this distinction of meaning is understood to arise from the particularities of the instrumental, dative, and other cases. Therefore, it should be understood that it is said, 'The term 'me' is seen in three meanings.'

Sutanti ayaṃ sutasaddo saupasaggo anupasaggo ca gamanavissutakilinnūpacitānuyogasotaviññeyya sotadvārānusāra [P 0.0012] viññātādianekatthappabhedo. Kiñcāpi hi upasaggo kiriyaṃ viseseti, jotakabhāvato pana satipi tasmiṃ sutasaddo eva taṃ tamatthaṃ vadatīti anupasaggassa sutasaddassa atthuddhāre saupasaggassa gahaṇaṃ na virujjhati.

The word 'suta' here, whether with or without a prefix, has many distinctions of meaning, such as 'going,' 'fame,' 'defiled,' 'accumulated,' 'applied,' 'knowable by hearing,' and 'understood through the ear-door.' Although a prefix specifies an action, nevertheless, by virtue of its illuminating nature, the word 'suta' itself conveys that particular meaning even when a prefix is present. Therefore, in extracting the meaning of the word 'suta' when it is without a prefix, the inclusion of its prefixed forms is not contradictory.

Tattha “senāya pasuto”tiādīsu gacchantoti attho. “Sutadhammassa passato”tiādīsu (udā. 11) vissutadhammassāti attho. “Avassutā avassutassā”tiādīsu (pāci. 657) kilesena kilinnā kilinnassāti attho. “Tumhehi puññaṃ pasutaṃ anappaka”ntiādīsu (khu. pā. 7.12) upacitanti attho. “Ye jhānappasutā dhīrā”tiādīsu (dha. pa. 181) jhānānuyuttāti attho. “Diṭṭhaṃ sutaṃ muta”ntiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.241) sotaviññeyyanti attho. “Sutadharo sutasannicayo”tiādīsu [M 0.0012] (ma. ni. 1.339) sotadvārānusāraviññātadharoti attho. Idha panassa “sotadvārānusārena upadhārita”nti vā “upadhāraṇa”nti vā attho. Me-saddassa hi mayāti atthe sati “evaṃ mayā sutaṃ sotadvārānusārena upadhārita”nti yujjati. Mamāti atthe sati “evaṃ mama sutaṃ sotadvārānusārena upadhāraṇa”nti yujjati.

Therein, in such phrases as 'senāya pasuto,' it has the meaning of 'going.' In 'sutadhammassa passato,' it means 'of one with a well-known Dhamma.' In 'avassutā avassutassā,' it means 'soiled by defilements to one who is soiled.' In 'tumhehi puññaṃ pasutaṃ anappakaṃ,' it means 'accumulated.' In 'ye jhānappasutā dhīrā,' it means 'devoted to jhāna.' In 'diṭṭhaṃ sutaṃ mutaṃ,' it means 'knowable by ear-consciousness.' In 'sutadharo sutasannicayo,' it means 'one who retains what is known by following the ear-door.' Here, however, its meaning is either 'ascertained by following the ear-door' or 'the act of ascertaining.' For when the word 'me' has the meaning of 'mayā' (by me), it is suitable as: 'Thus was it heard by me, that is, ascertained by following the ear-door.' When it has the meaning of 'mama' (my), it is suitable as: 'Thus, my hearing is an ascertainment by following the ear-door.'

Evametesu tīsu padesu yasmā sutasaddasannidhāne payuttena evaṃsaddena savanakiriyājotakena bhavitabbaṃ, tasmā evanti sotaviññāṇasampaṭicchanādisotadvārikaviññāṇānantaraṃ uppannamanodvārikaviññāṇakiccanidassanaṃ. Meti vuttaviññāṇasamaṅgīpuggalanidassanaṃ. Sabbāni hi vākyāni evakāratthasahitāniyeva avadhāraṇaphalattā tesaṃ. Sutanti assavanabhāvappaṭikkhepato anūnānadhikāviparītaggahaṇanidassanaṃ. Yathā hi sutaṃ sutamevāti vattabbataṃ arahati tathā taṃ sammā sutaṃ anūnaggahaṇaṃ anadhikaggahaṇaṃ aviparītaggahaṇañca hotīti. Atha vā saddantaratthāpohanavasena saddo atthaṃ vadatīti etasmiṃ pakkhe yasmā sutanti [P 0.0013] etassa asutaṃ na hotīti ayamattho vutto, tasmā sutanti assavanabhāvappaṭikkhepato anūnānadhikāviparītaggahaṇanidassanaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – evaṃ me sutaṃ, na mayā idaṃ diṭṭhaṃ, na sayambhūñāṇena sacchikataṃ, na aññathā vā upaladdhaṃ. Api ca sutaṃva, tañca kho sammadevāti. Avadhāraṇatthe vā evaṃsadde ayamatthayojanā, tadapekkhassa sutasaddassa niyamattho sambhavatīti [V 0.0012] tadapekkhassa sutasaddassa assavanabhāvappaṭikkhepo anūnānadhikāviparītaggahaṇanidassanatā ca veditabbā. Iti savanahetusavanavisesavasenapi sutasaddassa atthayojanā katāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Since in these three words, the word 'evaṃ', employed in the proximity of the word 'sutaṃ', must indicate the act of hearing, therefore 'evaṃ' indicates the function of the mind-door consciousness that arises immediately after the ear-door consciousnesses, such as ear-consciousness and receiving consciousness. 'Me' indicates the person endowed with the aforementioned consciousness. For all statements, as their result is affirmation, are indeed accompanied by the meaning of the affirmative particle 'eva'. 'Sutaṃ' indicates the grasping without deficiency, excess, or perversion, by way of rejecting the state of not hearing. For just as what is heard deserves to be called 'just as it was heard', so too it is rightly heard—a grasping without deficiency, without excess, and without perversion. Or alternatively, in the view that a word conveys meaning by excluding the meaning of other words, since the meaning 'it was not unheard' is stated for 'sutaṃ', therefore 'sutaṃ' indicates the grasping without deficiency, excess, or perversion, by way of rejecting the state of not hearing. This is what is meant: 'Thus have I heard'—it was not seen by me, nor realized by self-originated knowledge, nor obtained in any other way. But it was indeed heard, and heard correctly. Or, if the word 'evaṃ' is taken in the sense of affirmation, this is the interpretation of the meaning: the determined meaning of the word 'sutaṃ' which is dependent on it becomes possible, and thus the rejection of the state of not hearing for the word 'sutaṃ' dependent on it, and its indication of grasping without deficiency, excess, or perversion, should be understood. Thus, it should be understood that the interpretation of the meaning of the word 'sutaṃ' has also been made in terms of the cause of hearing and the specific nature of hearing.

Tathā evanti tassā sotadvārānusārena pavattāya viññāṇavīthiyā nānatthabyañjanaggahaṇato nānappakārena ārammaṇe pavattibhāvappakāsanaṃ ākārattho evaṃsaddoti karitvā. Meti attappakāsanaṃ. Sutanti dhammappakāsanaṃ yathāvuttāya viññāṇavīthiyā pariyattidhammārammaṇattā. Ayañhettha saṅkhepo – nānappakārena ārammaṇe pavattāya viññāṇavīthiyā karaṇabhūtāya mayā na aññaṃ kataṃ, idaṃ pana kataṃ, ayaṃ dhammo sutoti.

Similarly, 'evaṃ' reveals the state of occurring in various ways in the object, due to the grasping of various meanings and expressions by that consciousness-process which proceeds in accordance with the ear-door, this being because the word 'evaṃ' has the meaning of 'mode'. 'Me' reveals the self. 'Sutaṃ' reveals the Dhamma, because the aforementioned consciousness-process has the scriptural Dhamma as its object. Herein, this is the summary: By me, with the consciousness-process that proceeds in various ways regarding the object as the instrument, nothing else was done; rather, this Dhamma was heard.

Tathā [M 0.0013] evanti nidassitabbappakāsanaṃ nidassanattho evaṃsaddoti katvā nidassetabbassa niddisitabbabhāvato. Tasmā evaṃsaddena sakalampi suttaṃ paccāmaṭṭhanti veditabbaṃ. Meti puggalappakāsanaṃ. Sutanti puggalakiccappakāsanaṃ. Sutasaddena hi labbhamānā savanakiriyā savanaviññāṇappabandhappaṭibaddhā, tattha ca puggalavohāro, na ca puggalavohārarahite dhammappabandhe savanakiriyā labbhati. Tassāyaṃ saṅkhepattho – yaṃ suttaṃ niddisissāmi, taṃ mayā evaṃ sutanti.

Similarly, 'evaṃ' reveals that which is to be indicated, this being because the word 'evaṃ' has the meaning of indication, and because that which is to be indicated has the nature of being pointed out. Therefore, it should be understood that the entire sutta is referred to by the word 'evaṃ'. 'Me' reveals the person. 'Sutaṃ' reveals the person's function. For the act of hearing obtained through the word 'sutaṃ' is connected with the continuity of auditory consciousness, and therein lies the conventional designation of a person; nor is the act of hearing found in a continuity of phenomena devoid of the conventional designation of a person. Its concise meaning is this: 'The sutta which I shall point out, that I have heard thus'.

Tathā evanti yassa cittasantānassa nānārammaṇappavattiyā nānatthabyañjanaggahaṇaṃ hoti, tassa nānākāraniddeso ākārattho eva evaṃsaddoti katvā. Evanti hi ayamākārapaññatti dhammānaṃ taṃ taṃ pavattiākāraṃ upādāya paññapetabbasabhāvattā. Meti kattuniddeso. Sutanti visayaniddeso, sotabbo hi dhammo savanakiriyākattupuggalassa [P 0.0014] savanakiriyāvasena pavattiṭṭhānaṃ hoti. Ettāvatā nānappakārena pavattena cittasantānena taṃsamaṅgino kattu visaye gahaṇasanniṭṭhānaṃ dassitaṃ hoti.

Similarly, 'evaṃ' is a designation of various modes for that mental continuum in which there is the grasping of various meanings and expressions due to its proceeding with various objects, this being because the word 'evaṃ' has the meaning of 'mode'. For 'evaṃ' is a designation of mode, because it has the nature of being designated by taking up the respective modes of occurrence of phenomena. 'Me' is a designation of the agent. 'Sutaṃ' is a designation of the object, for the Dhamma to be heard is the sphere of occurrence for the person who is the agent of the act of hearing, by way of the act of hearing. To this extent, for one endowed with that mental continuum, the firm establishment of the grasping of the object by the agent is shown by means of the mental continuum that has proceeded in various ways.

Atha vā evanti puggalakiccaniddeso, sutānañhi dhammānaṃ gahitākārassa nidassanassa avadhāraṇassa vā pakāsanasabhāvena evaṃsaddena tadākārādidhāraṇassa puggalavohārupādānadhammabyāpārabhāvato puggalakiccaṃnāma niddiṭṭhaṃ hotīti. Sutanti viññāṇakiccaniddeso, puggalavādinopi hi savanakiriyā viññāṇanirapekkhā na hotīti. Meti ubhayakiccayuttapuggalaniddeso. Meti hi saddappavatti ekanteneva sattavisesavisayā viññāṇakiccañca tattheva samodahitabbanti. Ayaṃ panettha saṅkhepo – mayā savanakiccaviññāṇasamaṅginā puggalena viññāṇavasena laddhasavanakiccavohārena sutanti.

Alternatively, 'evaṃ' is a designation of the person's function; for by the word 'evaṃ', which by its nature reveals the indication or affirmation of the grasped mode of the heard teachings, the so-called 'person's function' is designated, because the bearing of that mode, etc., is an activity of the phenomena that are the basis for the conventional designation of a person. 'Sutaṃ' is a designation of the function of consciousness, for even for those who assert a person, the act of hearing is not independent of consciousness. 'Me' is a designation of the person connected with both functions. For the application of the word 'me' relates exclusively to a specific being as its domain, and the function of consciousness should be integrated therein. Herein, this is the summary: 'Heard' by me, a person endowed with consciousness whose function is hearing, and who has obtained the conventional designation of 'one whose function is hearing' by way of that consciousness.

Tathā [V 0.0013] evanti ca meti ca saccikaṭṭhaparamatthavasena avijjamānapaññatti. Sabbassa hi saddādhigamanīyassa atthassa paññattimukheneva paṭipajjitabbattā sabbapaññattīnañca vijjamānādīsu chasu paññattīsu avarodho, tasmā yo māyāmarīciādayo viya abhūtattho anussavādīhi gahetabbo viya anuttamatthopi [M 0.0014] na hoti. So rūpasaddādiko ruppanānubhavanādiko ca paramatthasabhāvo saccikaṭṭhaparamatthavasena vijjati. Yo pana evanti ca meti ca vuccamāno ākārattho, so aparamatthasabhāvo saccikaṭṭhaparamatthavasena anupalabbhamāno avijjamānapaññatti nāma. Tasmā kiñhettha taṃ paramatthato atthi, yaṃ evanti vā meti vā niddesaṃ labhetha? Sutanti vijjamānapaññatti, yañhi taṃ ettha sotena upaladdhaṃ, taṃ paramatthato vijjamānanti.

Similarly, both 'evaṃ' and 'me' are designations of what is non-existent, in the sense of ultimate reality in the true sense. For since every meaning accessible through words must be understood only through the medium of designation, and since all designations are included in the six designations beginning with 'existent', therefore that unreal meaning, which is like an illusion or a mirage and is as if to be grasped through tradition and so on, is not even the highest meaning. That ultimate nature, such as form and sound, characterized by being affected, experienced, and so on, exists in the sense of ultimate reality in the true sense. But that meaning of 'mode' which is spoken of as 'evaṃ' and 'me', being a non-ultimate nature and unapprehendable in the sense of ultimate reality in the true sense, is called a designation of what is non-existent. Therefore, what is there here that ultimately exists, which could obtain the designation 'evaṃ' or 'me'? 'Sutaṃ' is a designation of what is existent, for that which is apprehended here by the ear, that ultimately exists.

Tathā evanti sotapathamāgate dhamme upādāya tesaṃ upadhāritākārādīnaṃ paccāmasanavasena. Meti sasantatipariyāpanne khandhe [P 0.0015] karaṇādivisesavisiṭṭhe upādāya vattabbato upādāpaññatti. Sutanti diṭṭhādīni upanidhāya vattabbato upanidhāpaññatti. Diṭṭhādisabhāvarahite saddāyatane pavattamānopi sutavohāro dutiyaṃ tatiyantiādiko viya paṭhamādīni, diṭṭhamutaviññāte apekkhitvā sutanti viññeyyattā diṭṭhādīni upanidhāya vattabbo hoti. Asutaṃ na hotīti hi sutanti pakāsitoyamatthoti.

Furthermore, 'evaṃ' is said by way of repeatedly considering the discerned modes, etc., of phenomena that have entered the ear-path. 'Me' is an 'upādāya paññatti' (designation based on appropriation), because it is spoken by taking the aggregates that are included within one's own continuum and are distinguished by specific actions, etc. 'Sutaṃ' is an 'upanidhā paññatti' (designation by comparison), because it is spoken by comparing it with the seen, etc. Even though the conventional usage of 'heard' operates in the sound-base, which is devoid of the nature of the seen, etc., just as 'second', 'third', and so on, depend on 'first' and so on, it is spoken by comparing it with the seen, etc., because 'heard' is knowable by referring to the seen, the perceived, and the cognized. For indeed, this meaning is revealed by 'sutaṃ': 'it is not unheard'.

Ettha ca evantivacanena asammohaṃ dīpeti. Paṭividdhā hi attanā sutassa pakāravisesā evanti idha āyasmatā ānandena paccāmaṭṭhā, tenassa asammoho dīpito hoti. Na hi sammūḷho nānappakārapaṭivedhasamattho hoti, paccayākāravasena nānappakārā duppaṭividdhā ca suttantāti dīpitanti. Sutantivacanena sutassa asammosaṃ dīpeti, sutākārassa yāthāvato dassiyamānattā. Yassa hi sutaṃ sammuṭṭhaṃ hoti, na so kālantare mayā sutanti paṭijānāti. Iccassa asammohena paññāsiddhi, sammohābhāvena paññāya eva vā savanakālasambhūtāya taduttarikālapaññāsiddhi, tathā asammosena satisiddhi. Tattha paññāpubbaṅgamāya satiyā byañjanāvadhāraṇasamatthatā. Byañjanānañhi paṭivijjhitabbo ākāro nātigambhīro, yathāsutaṃ dhāraṇameva tattha karaṇīyanti satiyā byāpāro adhiko, paññā tattha guṇībhūtā hoti paññāya pubbaṅgamāti katvā. Satipubbaṅgamāya paññāya atthappaṭivedhasamatthatā. Atthassa hi paṭivijjhitabbo ākāro gambhīroti paññāya byāpāro adhiko, sati tattha guṇībhūtāyevāti satiyā pubbaṅgamāyāti [M 0.0015] katvā. Tadubhayasamatthatāyogena atthabyañjanasampannassa dhammakosassa anupālanasamatthatāya dhammabhaṇḍāgārikattasiddhi.

Here, by the word 'evaṃ', the absence of confusion is indicated. For the specific aspects of what was heard were penetrated and reviewed by the Venerable Ānanda himself as 'thus,' and thereby his absence of confusion is demonstrated. For one who is confused is incapable of penetrating diverse aspects, and it is indicated that the suttas are diverse and difficult to penetrate by way of conditions. By the word 'sutaṃ', the absence of forgetfulness regarding what was heard is indicated, as the manner of hearing is presented accurately. For one whose hearing has become forgotten does not later declare, 'I heard it.' Thus, by his absence of confusion, the accomplishment of wisdom is established; or, by the absence of confusion, the wisdom that arose at the time of hearing leads to the accomplishment of subsequent wisdom. Similarly, by the absence of forgetfulness, the accomplishment of mindfulness is established. Herein, with mindfulness that is preceded by wisdom, there is the capacity to grasp the wording. For the aspect of the wording to be penetrated is not very profound; simply retaining what was heard is the task there. Thus, the function of mindfulness is predominant, while wisdom is secondary, as it is a case of being preceded by wisdom. With wisdom that is preceded by mindfulness, there is the capacity to penetrate the meaning. For the aspect of the meaning to be penetrated is profound; thus, the function of wisdom is predominant, while mindfulness is secondary, as it is a case of being preceded by mindfulness. Through the capacity for both, the accomplishment of the status of Treasurer of the Dhamma is achieved, by the ability to preserve the Dhamma-store complete in meaning and wording.

Aparo [V 0.0014] nayo – evantivacanena yonisomanasikāraṃ dīpeti, tena ca vuccamānānaṃ ākāranidassanāvadhāraṇatthānaṃ upari vakkhamānānaṃ nānappakārappaṭivedhajotakānaṃ aviparītasiddhi dhammavisayattā. Na hi ayoniso manasikaroto [P 0.0016] nānappakārappaṭivedho sambhavati. Sutantivacanena avikkhepaṃ dīpeti, “paṭhamabodhisuttaṃ kattha bhāsita”ntiādipucchāvasena pakaraṇapattassa vakkhamānassa suttassa savanaṃ samādhānamantarena na sambhavati vikkhittacittassa savanābhāvato. Tathā hi vikkhittacitto puggalo sabbasampattiyā vuccamānopi “na mayā sutaṃ, puna bhaṇathā”ti bhaṇati. Yonisomanasikārena cettha attasammāpaṇidhiṃ pubbe ca katapuññataṃ sādheti sammā appaṇihitattassa pubbe akatapuññassa vā tadabhāvato. Avikkhepena saddhammassavanaṃ sappurisūpanissayañca sādheti assutavato sappurisūpanissayavirahitassa ca tadabhāvato. Na hi vikkhitto sotuṃ sakkoti, na ca sappurise anupanissayamānassa savanaṃ atthīti.

Another approach: by the word 'evaṃ', it indicates wise attention. And through this, the unerring accomplishment of various kinds of penetration, which illuminate the modes, examples, and determinations to be explained later, is due to their being objects of the true Dhamma. For penetration of various kinds does not arise for one who attends unwisely. By the word 'sutaṃ', it indicates non-distraction. For listening to the sutta, which pertains to the context and will be explained—as when a question arises like, 'Where was the first discourse on awakening delivered?'—cannot occur without composure, since a distracted mind is unable to listen. Indeed, a distracted person, even when spoken to with complete detail, says, 'I did not hear; please speak again.' Here, by wise attention, one accomplishes proper self-aspiration and past meritorious deeds, for these are absent in one whose self is not rightly directed or who has not performed meritorious deeds previously. By non-distraction, one accomplishes listening to the true Dhamma and association with the virtuous, for these are absent in one who has not heard or who lacks association with the virtuous. For a distracted person cannot listen, nor is there listening for one who does not associate with the virtuous.

Aparo nayo – “yassa cittasantānassa nānappakārappavattiyā nānatthabyañjanaggahaṇaṃ hoti, tassa nānākāraniddeso”ti vuttaṃ. Yasmā ca so bhagavato vacanassa atthabyañjanappabhedaparicchedavasena sakalasāsanasampattiogāhanena niravasesaṃ parahitapāripūrīkaraṇabhūto evaṃ bhaddako ākāro na sammā appaṇihitattassa pubbe akatapuññassa vā hoti. Tasmā evanti iminā bhaddakena ākārena pacchimacakkadvayasampattimattano dīpeti, sutanti savanayogena purimacakkadvayasampattiṃ. Na hi appatirūpe dese vasato sappurisūpanissayavirahitassa ca savanaṃ atthi. Iccassa pacchimacakkadvayasiddhiyā āsayasuddhi siddhā hoti. Sammā paṇihitacitto pubbe ca katapuñño visuddhāsayo hoti tadasuddhihetūnaṃ kilesānaṃ dūrībhāvato. Tathā hi vuttaṃ “sammā paṇihitaṃ cittaṃ, seyyaso naṃ tato kare”ti (dha. pa. 43) “katapuññosi tvaṃ, ānanda, padhānamanuyuñja, khippaṃ hohisi anāsavo”ti (dī. ni. 2.207) ca. Purimacakkadvayasiddhiyā [P 0.0017] payogasuddhi. Patirūpadesavāsena hi sappurisūpanissayena ca sādhūnaṃ diṭṭhānugatiāpajjanena [M 0.0016] parisuddhappayogo hoti. Tāya ca āsayasuddhiyā adhigamabyattisiddhi, pubbeyeva taṇhādiṭṭhisaṃkilesānaṃ visodhitattā payogasuddhiyā āgamabyattisiddhi. Suparisuddhakāyavacīpayogo hi vippaṭisārābhāvato avikkhittacitto pariyattiyaṃ visārado hoti. Iti payogāsayasuddhassa āgamādhigamasampannassa vacanaṃ aruṇuggamanaṃ viya sūriyassa udayato yonisomanasikāro viya ca kusalakammassa arahati bhagavato vacanassa pubbaṅgamaṃ bhavitunti ṭhāne nidānaṃ ṭhapento evaṃ me sutantiādimāha.

Another approach: It has been said: 'For one whose mental continuum functions in various ways, grasping diverse meanings and expressions, there is a varied explanation of modes.' And because such an excellent mode—which constitutes the complete fulfillment of others' welfare without remainder by way of distinguishing the meanings and expressions of the Blessed One's words and by immersing oneself in the entire dispensation—does not belong to one whose self is not rightly directed or who has not previously performed merit. Therefore, by 'evaṃ', this excellent mode, he indicates his own attainment of the latter two wheels; and by 'sutaṃ', through the connection with hearing, he indicates the attainment of the former two wheels. For there is no hearing for one dwelling in an unsuitable place or lacking reliance on the virtuous. Thus, by the accomplishment of the latter two wheels, purity of disposition is established. One whose mind is rightly directed and who has previously performed merit has a purified disposition due to the removal of defilements, which are the causes of its impurity. As it is said: 'A rightly directed mind will do one greater good' (Dhp 43), and 'You are one who has performed merit, Ānanda; apply yourself to exertion; you will quickly be taintless' (DN 16). By the accomplishment of the former two wheels, purity of practice is established. For by dwelling in a suitable place, by relying on the virtuous, and by following the example of the good, one's practice becomes thoroughly purified. Through that purity of disposition, mastery in realization is accomplished, since craving, wrong views, and defilements have been previously purified. Through purity of practice, mastery in learning is accomplished. For one whose bodily and verbal practice is thoroughly purified, being free from remorse and having an unscattered mind, becomes confident in the scriptures. Thus, the words of one whose practice and disposition are pure, and who is endowed with learning and realization, are worthy to be the forerunner of the Blessed One’s teaching—like the dawn preceding the sunrise or wise attention preceding wholesome action. Therefore, establishing the introduction in its proper place, he began with 'Thus have I heard.'

Aparo [V 0.0015] nayo – evanti iminā pubbe vuttanayeneva nānappakārappaṭivedhadīpakena vacanena attano atthapaṭibhānapaṭisambhidāsampattisabbhāvaṃ dīpeti. Sutanti iminā evaṃsaddasannidhānato vakkhamānāpekkhāya vā sotabbabhedappaṭivedhadīpakena dhammaniruttipaṭisambhidāsampattisabbhāvaṃ dīpeti. Evanti ca idaṃ vuttanayeneva yonisomanasikāradīpakavacanaṃ bhāsamāno “ete dhammā mayā manasānupekkhitā diṭṭhiyā suppaṭividdhā”ti dīpeti. Pariyattidhammo hi “idha sīlaṃ kathitaṃ, idha samādhi, idha paññā, ettakā ettha anusandhiyo”tiādinā nayena manasā anupekkhito anussavākāraparivitakkasahitāya dhammanijjhānakkhantibhūtāya ñātapariññāsaṅkhātāya vā diṭṭhiyā tattha tattha vuttarūpārūpadhamme “iti rūpaṃ, ettakaṃ rūpa”ntiādinā nayena suṭṭhu vavatthapetvā paṭividdho attano ca paresañca hitasukhāvaho hotīti. Sutanti idaṃ savanayogadīpakavacanaṃ bhāsamāno “bahū mayā dhammā sutā dhātā vacasā paricitā”ti dīpeti. Sotāvadhānappaṭibaddhā hi pariyattidhammassa savanadhāraṇaparicayā. Tadubhayenapi dhammassa svākkhātabhāvena, atthabyañjanapāripūriṃ dīpento savane ādaraṃ janeti. Atthabyañjanaparipuṇṇañhi dhammaṃ ādarena assuṇanto mahatā hitā paribāhiro hotīti ādaraṃ janetvā sakkaccaṃ dhammo sotabbo.

Another method: With the word 'evaṃ' (thus), in the way previously stated, through this statement that reveals penetration of various kinds, he reveals the reality of his own attainment of the analytical knowledge of meaning and of spontaneous exposition. With the word 'sutaṃ' (heard), through this statement that reveals penetration of the different things to be heard—either due to the proximity of the word 'evaṃ' or in anticipation of what is to be said—he reveals the reality of his attainment of the analytical knowledge of the Dhamma and of language. And by speaking this word 'evaṃ', which indicates wise attention as explained, he declares: 'These teachings have been repeatedly contemplated by my mind and well penetrated by my view.' For the Dhamma of the scriptures, when repeatedly contemplated by the mind in ways such as, 'Here virtue is taught, here concentration, here wisdom; here are so many connections,' and so on, is penetrated by the view—which is knowledge of full understanding, supported by reflection in the manner of tradition and by patient endurance born of contemplation of the Dhamma. By thoroughly establishing the teachings of material and immaterial states spoken of here and there in ways such as, 'Such is material form, this much is material form,' and so on, one penetrates them, bringing welfare and happiness to oneself and others. By speaking this word 'sutaṃ', which indicates the application of listening, he declares: 'Many teachings have been heard by me, borne in mind, and practiced with speech.' For listening, retention, and practice concerning the Dhamma of the scriptures are dependent on attentive hearing. By both these means, by revealing the well-proclaimed nature of the Dhamma and its completeness in meaning and phrasing, he generates reverence in listening. For one who listens without reverence to the Dhamma, which is complete in meaning and phrasing, is excluded from great benefit. Therefore, having generated reverence, the Dhamma should be listened to attentively.

“Evaṃ [P 0.0018] me suta”nti iminā pana sakalena vacanena āyasmā ānando tathāgatappaveditaṃ dhammaṃ attano adahanto asappurisabhūmiṃ atikkamati, sāvakattaṃ paṭijānanto sappurisabhūmiṃ okkamati. Tathā asaddhammā cittaṃ [M 0.0017] vuṭṭhāpeti, saddhamme cittaṃ patiṭṭhāpeti. “Kevalaṃ sutamevetaṃ mayā, tasseva pana bhagavato vacana”nti dīpento attānaṃ parimoceti, satthāraṃ apadisati, jinavacanaṃ appeti, dhammanettiṃ patiṭṭhāpeti.

With this entire utterance, 'Thus have I heard,' Venerable Ānanda, by not claiming the Dhamma proclaimed by the Tathāgata as his own, transcends the plane of the ignoble; by acknowledging his status as a disciple, he enters the plane of the noble. Thus he raises his mind from the false Dhamma and establishes his mind in the true Dhamma. By declaring, 'This was merely heard by me; it is indeed the word of that Blessed One,' he frees himself, points to the Teacher, ascribes the Conqueror's word, and establishes the guideline of the Dhamma.

Apica “evaṃ me suta”nti attanā uppāditabhāvaṃ appaṭijānanto purimassavanaṃ vivaranto “sammukhā paṭiggahitamidaṃ mayā tassa bhagavato catuvesārajjavisāradassa dasabaladharassa āsabhaṭṭhānaṭṭhāyino sīhanādanādino sabbasattuttamassa dhammissarassa dhammarājassa dhammādhipatino dhammadīpassa dhammasaraṇassa saddhammavaracakkavattino sammāsambuddhassa, na ettha atthe vā dhamme vā pade vā byañjane vā kaṅkhā vā vimati vā kattabbā”ti sabbadevamanussānaṃ imasmiṃ dhamme assaddhiyaṃ vināseti, saddhāsampadaṃ uppādeti. Tenetaṃ vuccati –

Moreover, with 'Thus have I heard,' by not acknowledging that he himself had produced it and by disclosing the prior hearing, he dispels the lack of faith in this Dhamma among all gods and humans and generates the accomplishment of faith, implying: 'This was received by me in person from that Blessed One—the one skilled in the four kinds of fearlessness, possessor of the ten powers, standing in the position of the chief bull, roaring the lion's roar, the supreme among all beings, the Lord of the Dhamma, the King of the Dhamma, the Master of the Dhamma, the Lamp of the Dhamma, the Refuge of the Dhamma, the Supreme Wheel-turning Monarch of the True Dhamma, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. Here, no doubt or uncertainty should be entertained regarding the meaning or the teaching.' For this reason, it is said:

“Vināsayati assaddhaṃ, saddhaṃ vaḍḍheti sāsane;

Evaṃ me sutamiccevaṃ, vadaṃ gotamasāvako”ti.

Saying, 'Thus have I heard,' the disciple of Gotama dispels faithlessness and increases faith in the Dispensation.

Ekanti [V 0.0016] gaṇanaparicchedaniddeso. Ayañhi ekasaddo aññaseṭṭhāsahāyasaṅkhyādīsu dissati. Tathā hi ayaṃ “sassato attā ca loko ca, idameva saccaṃ moghamaññanti ittheke abhivadantī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 3.27; udā. 55) aññe dissati. “Cetaso ekodibhāva”ntiādīsu (pārā. 11; dī. ni. 1.228) seṭṭhe. “Eko vūpakaṭṭho”tiādīsu (cūḷava. 445; dī. ni. 1.405) asahāye. “Ekova kho, bhikkhave, khaṇo ca samayo ca brahmacariyavāsāyā”tiādīsu (a. ni. 8.29) saṅkhyāyaṃ, idhāpi saṅkhyāyameva daṭṭhabbo. Tena vuttaṃ – “ekanti gaṇanaparicchedaniddeso”ti.

The word 'ekaṃ' is an indication of demarcation by counting. For this word 'eka' is seen in such senses as other, best, without a companion, and number. Indeed, it is seen as 'other' in passages such as: 'Some declare, "The self and the world are eternal; this alone is true, all else is false."' It is seen as 'best' in passages such as: 'The unification of the mind.' It is seen as 'without a companion' in passages such as: 'Alone, secluded.' It is seen as 'number' in passages such as: 'Monks, there is only one moment, one opportunity for living the holy life.' Here too, it should be understood only as 'number.' Therefore, it was said: 'The word "ekaṃ" is an indication of demarcation by counting.'

Samayanti paricchinnaniddeso. Ekaṃ samayanti aniyamitaparidīpanaṃ. Tattha samayasaddo –

The word 'samayaṃ' indicates a specific occasion. The phrase 'ekaṃ samayaṃ' is an indefinite indication. In this context, the word 'samaya'—

“Samavāye [P 0.0019] khaṇe kāle, samūhe hetudiṭṭhisu;

Paṭilābhe pahāne ca, paṭivedhe ca dissati”.

Is seen in the sense of concurrence, moment, time, collection, cause, views, acquisition, abandonment, and penetration.

Tathā hissa “appeva nāma svepi upasaṅkameyyāma kālañca samayañca upādāyā”ti evamādīsu (dī. ni. 1.447) samavāyo attho, yuttakālañca paccayasāmaggiñca labhitvāti hi adhippāyo, tasmā paccayasamavāyoti veditabbo[M 0.0018]. “Ekova kho, bhikkhave, khaṇo ca samayo ca brahmacariyavāsāyā”tiādīsu (a. ni. 8.29) khaṇo, okāsoti attho. Tathāgatuppādādiko hi maggabrahmacariyassa okāso tappaccayappaṭilābhahetuttā, khaṇo eva ca samayo, yo khaṇoti ca samayoti ca vuccati, so eko yevāti hi attho. “Uṇhasamayo pariḷāhasamayo”tiādīsu (pāci. 358) kālo. “Mahāsamayo pavanasmi”ntiādīsu (dī. ni. 2.332) samūho. Mahāsamayoti hi bhikkhūnaṃ devatānañca mahāsannipātoti attho. “Samayopi kho te, bhaddāli, appaṭividdho ahosi, bhagavā kho sāvatthiyaṃ viharati, bhagavāpi maṃ jānissati ‘bhaddāli nāma bhikkhu satthusāsane sikkhāya na paripūrakārī’ti, ayampi kho te, bhaddāli, samayo appaṭividdho ahosī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 2.135) hetu. Sikkhāpadassa kāraṇañhi idha samayoti adhippetaṃ. “Tena kho pana samayena uggāhamāno paribbājako samaṇamuṇḍikāputto samayappavādake tindukācīre ekasālake mallikāya ārāme paṭivasatī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 2.260) diṭṭhi. Tattha hi nisinnā titthiyā attano attano diṭṭhisaṅkhātaṃ samayaṃ pavadantīti so paribbājakārāmo “samayappavādako”ti vuccati.

For in such cases, the meaning is concurrence, as in the phrase, “Perhaps tomorrow we may approach at the proper time and occasion” (Dī. Ni. 1.447). The intention is that one obtains both the suitable time and the full assembly of conditions; therefore, it should be understood as the concurrence of conditions. In passages like, “Monks, there is only one moment and one occasion for living the holy life” (A. Ni. 8.29), it means moment, that is, opportunity. For the arising of the Tathāgata, etc., is the opportunity for the path of the holy life because it is the cause for obtaining its conditions. And ‘moment’ is the same as ‘occasion’—what is called ‘moment’ and ‘occasion’ is one and the same. In phrases like, “The time of heat, the time of scorching” (Pāc. 358), it means time. In passages like, “A great gathering in the grove” (Dī. Ni. 2.332), it means an assembly. For ‘great gathering’ here refers to the great assembly of monks and deities. In statements like, “But for you, Bhaddāli, the cause was not penetrated. The Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī, and the Blessed One would know of me, ‘The monk named Bhaddāli does not fully apply himself to training in the Teacher’s dispensation.’ This too, Bhaddāli, was a cause you did not penetrate” (Ma. Ni. 2.135), it means cause. Here, ‘samaya’ is intended to mean the reason for a training rule. In passages like, “Now at that time, the wanderer Uggāhamāna, son of Samaṇamuṇḍikā, was dwelling at Tindukācīra, the place for proclaiming views, in a single hall in Mallikā's park” (Ma. Ni. 2.260), it means view. For there, the sectarians who were seated proclaimed their own so-called views; thus, that wanderer’s dwelling was called ‘the place for proclaiming views.’”

“Diṭṭhe [V 0.0017] dhamme ca yo attho, yo cattho samparāyiko;

Atthābhisamayā dhīro, paṇḍitoti pavuccatī”ti. (saṃ. ni. 1.129) –

“One who has comprehended the benefit in this very life and the benefit in the life to come—that steadfast one is called a wise person.”

Ādīsu paṭilābho. Atthābhisamayāti hi atthassa adhigamāti attho. “Sammā mānābhisamayā antamakāsi dukkhassā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.28) pahānaṃ. Adhikaraṇaṃ samayaṃ vūpasamanaṃ apagamoti abhisamayo pahānaṃ. “Dukkhassa pīḷanaṭṭho saṅkhataṭṭho santāpaṭṭho vipariṇāmaṭṭho abhisamayaṭṭho”tiādīsu (paṭi. ma. 2.8) paṭivedho[P 0.0020]. Paṭivedhoti hi abhisametabbato abhisamayo, abhisamayova attho abhisamayaṭṭhoti pīḷanādīni abhisametabbabhāvena ekībhāvaṃ upanetvā vuttāni, abhisamayassa vā paṭivedhassa visayabhūto attho abhisamayaṭṭhoti tāneva tathā ekantena vuttāni. Tattha pīḷanaṃ dukkhasaccassa taṃsamaṅgino hiṃsanaṃ avipphārikatākaraṇaṃ. Santāpo dukkhadukkhatādivasena santappanaṃ paridahanaṃ.

In these and other passages, it means acquisition. For the meaning of ‘atthābhisamaya’ is the attainment of the benefit. In passages like, “Through the right overcoming of conceit, he made an end of suffering” (MN 1.28), it refers to abandonment. Superior calming, pacification, and removal is abhisamaya, which is abandonment. In passages like, “Suffering has the meaning of oppression, the meaning of being conditioned, the meaning of burning, the meaning of change, and the meaning of penetration” (Patis. 2.8), it refers to realization. For realization is indeed abhisamaya because it is to be penetrated; abhisamaya itself is the meaning of ‘to be penetrated,’ and thus oppression and the like are spoken of, having been brought into unity by virtue of their nature as objects to be penetrated. Alternatively, the meaning that is the object of abhisamaya or realization is called ‘the meaning of penetration,’ and those very things are then spoken of exclusively as such. Therein, oppression, with regard to the truth of suffering, is the harming and the causing of constriction for one endowed with it. Burning is the scorching and tormenting in the sense of suffering as suffering, and so on.

Ettha [M 0.0019] ca sahakārīkāraṇasannijjhaṃ sameti samavetīti samavāyo samayo. Sameti samāgacchati ettha maggabrahmacariyaṃ tadādhārapuggalehīti khaṇo samayo. Sameti ettha etena vā saṃgacchati satto sabhāvadhammo vā uppādādīhi sahajātādīhi vāti kālo samayo. Dhammappavattimattatāya atthato abhūtopi hi kālo dhammappavattiyā adhikaraṇaṃ karaṇaṃ viya ca kappanāmattasiddhenānurūpena voharīyatīti. Samaṃ, saha vā avayavānaṃ ayanaṃ pavatti avaṭṭhānanti samūho samayo yathā samudāyoti. Avayavasahāvaṭṭhānameva hi samūho. Avasesapaccayānaṃ samāgame sati eti phalametasmā uppajjati pavattatīti samayo hetu yathā samudayoti. Sameti saṃyojanabhāvato sambandho eti attano visaye pavattati, daḷhaggahaṇabhāvato vā saṃyuttā ayanti pavattanti sattā yathābhinivesaṃ etenāti samayo diṭṭhi. Diṭṭhisaṃyojanena hi sattā ativiya bajjhantīti. Samiti saṅgati samodhānanti samayo paṭilābho. Samayanaṃ upasamayanaṃ apagamoti samayo pahānaṃ. Samucchedappahānabhāvato pana adhiko samayoti abhisamayo yathā abhidhammoti. Abhimukhaṃ ñāṇena sammā etabbo abhisametabboti abhisamayo, dhammānaṃ aviparītasabhāvo. Abhimukhabhāvena sammā eti gacchati bujjhatīti abhisamayo, dhammānaṃ yathābhūtasabhāvāvabodho. Evaṃ tasmiṃ tasmiṃ atthe samayasaddassa pavatti veditabbā.

Herein, samaya is samavāya (concurrence), because it ‘comes together’ (sameti) or ‘concurs’ (samaveti) with the presence of cooperative causes. It is a moment (khaṇa) because the path and the holy life ‘come together’ (sameti samāgacchati) herein with the individuals who are their support. It is time (kāla) because a being or a natural phenomenon ‘comes together’ (sameti) or ‘meets with’ (saṃgacchati) arising, etc., or co-nascence, etc., herein or herewith. For although time is not substantially existent, being merely the process of phenomena, it is conventionally spoken of as if it were a location or an instrument for the process of phenomena, by means of a suitable designation established by mere convention. It is a collection (samūha) because it is the ‘coming’ (ayanaṃ) or process and establishment of parts ‘together’ (samaṃ or saha), as in samudāya (arising). For a collection is simply the co-establishment of parts. It is a cause (hetu) because when the remaining conditions have come together, the fruit ‘proceeds’ (eti) from this, arises, and occurs, as in samudaya (origin). It is a view (diṭṭhi) because a connection ‘comes together’ (sameti) by way of being a fetter and ‘proceeds’ (eti) or occurs in its own domain; or because beings, bound by firm grasping, ‘proceed’ (ayanti) according to their attachment by means of this. For beings are greatly bound by the fetter of views. It is acquisition (paṭilābha) because it is a meeting (samiti), a coming together (saṅgati), a combination (samodhāna). It is abandonment (pahāna) because it is a ‘calming’ (samayanaṃ), a pacifying (upasamayanaṃ), a removal (apagamo). But because it is abandonment by cutting off, abhisamaya is a ‘superior’ (adhiko) samaya, as in abhidhamma. It is abhisamaya because it is to be rightly gone to or penetrated ‘face-to-face’ (abhimukhaṃ) with knowledge; it is the undistorted nature of phenomena. It is abhisamaya because one rightly ‘goes to’ (eti), proceeds, and awakens ‘face-to-face’ (abhimukhabhāvena); it is the awakening to the true nature of phenomena as they really are. Thus, the occurrence of the term samaya in these various meanings should be understood.

Samayasaddassa atthuddhāre abhisamayasaddassa gahaṇe kāraṇaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Idha [P 0.0021] panassa kālo attho samavāyādīnaṃ asambhavato. Desadesakaparisā viya hi desanāya nidānabhāve [V 0.0018] kālo eva icchitabboti.
