Yasmā panettha samayoti kālo adhippeto, tasmā saṃvaccharautumāsaddhamāsarattidivasapubbaṇhamajjhanhikasāyanhapaṭhamayāma- majjhimayāmapacchimayāmamuhuttādīsu kālabhedabhūtesu samayesu ekaṃ samayanti dīpeti.

The reason for the inclusion of the word ‘abhisamaya’ in the elucidation of the meaning of the word ‘samaya’ should be understood in the way already stated. Here, however, its meaning is time, because concurrence and the like are not applicable. For just as place, teacher, and assembly are the basis of the teaching, so too time alone is to be intended. Since in this context ‘samaya’ is intended as time, it indicates ‘a time’ among the divisions of time, such as years, seasons, months, half-months, nights, days, forenoon, midday, afternoon, first watch, middle watch, last watch, moments, and so on.

Kasmā panettha aniyamitavaseneva kālo niddiṭṭho, na utusaṃvaccharādivasena niyametvā niddiṭṭhoti ce? Kiñcāpi etesu saṃvaccharādīsu samayesu yaṃ yaṃ suttaṃ yasmiṃ yasmiṃ saṃvacchare utumhi [M 0.0020] māse pakkhe rattibhāge divasabhāge vā vuttaṃ, sabbampi taṃ therassa suviditaṃ suvavatthāpitaṃ paññāya. Yasmā pana “evaṃ me sutaṃ asukasaṃvacchare asukautumhi asukamāse asukapakkhe asukarattibhāge asukadivasabhāge vā”ti evaṃ vutte na sakkā sukhena dhāretuṃ vā uddisituṃ vā uddisāpetuṃ vā, bahu ca vattabbaṃ hoti, tasmā ekeneva padena tamatthaṃ samodhānetvā “ekaṃ samaya”nti āha.

If it is asked: Why is the time here indicated only indefinitely, and not specified by defining it according to season, year, and so on? Although the Elder knew well and clearly ascertained with wisdom every discourse spoken in any given year, season, month, fortnight, part of the night, or part of the day, yet because it would not be possible to easily remember, recite, or have others recite if it were said, 'Thus have I heard—in such a year, in such a season, in such a month, in such a fortnight, in such a part of the night, or in such a part of the day,' and much would have to be said, therefore, summarizing the meaning into a single phrase, he said, 'At one time.'

Ye vā ime gabbhokkantisamayo jātisamayo saṃvegasamayo abhinikkhamanasamayo dukkarakārikasamayo māravijayasamayo abhisambodhisamayo diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārasamayo desanāsamayo parinibbānasamayoti evamādayo bhagavato devamanussesu ativiya pakāsā anekakālappabhedā eva samayā, tesu samayesu desanāsamayasaṅkhātaṃ ekaṃ samayanti dīpeti. Yo vāyaṃ ñāṇakaruṇākiccasamayesu karuṇākiccasamayo, attahitaparahitappaṭipattisamayesu parahitappaṭipattisamayo, sannipatitānaṃ karaṇīyadvayasamayesu dhammakathāsamayo, desanāpaṭipattisamayesu desanāsamayo, tesu samayesu aññatarasamayaṃ sandhāya “ekaṃ samaya”nti āha.

Alternatively, there are these occasions in the Blessed One’s life, of many different periods and exceedingly renowned among gods and humans: the occasion of descent into the womb, the occasion of birth, the occasion of spiritual urgency, the occasion of renunciation, the occasion of practicing austerities, the occasion of conquering Māra, the occasion of perfect enlightenment, the occasion of abiding in bliss in this very life, the occasion of teaching, and the occasion of final Nibbāna. Among these occasions, 'at one time' indicates the one designated as the occasion of teaching. Or again, among the occasions of the duties of knowledge and compassion, it was the occasion of the duty of compassion; among the occasions of practicing for one’s own welfare and for the welfare of others, it was the occasion of practicing for the welfare of others; among the occasions of the twofold duty for those assembled, it was the occasion of the Dhamma discourse; among the occasions of teaching and practice, it was the occasion of teaching. In reference to one or another of these occasions, he said, 'at one time.'

Kasmā panettha yathā abhidhamme “yasmiṃ samaye kāmāvacaraṃ kusalaṃ cittaṃ uppannaṃ hotī”ti (dha. sa. 1) ca ito aññesu suttapadesu “yasmiṃ samaye, bhikkhave, bhikkhu vivicceva kāmehi vivicca akusalehi dhammehī”ti [P 0.0022] (a. ni. 4.200) ca bhummavacanena niddeso kato, vinaye ca “tena samayena buddho bhagavā”ti (pārā. 1) karaṇavacanena niddeso kato, tathā akatvā “ekaṃ samaya”nti accantasaṃyogatthe upayogavacanena niddeso katoti? Tattha tathā, idha ca aññathā atthasambhavato. Tattha hi abhidhamme ito aññesu ca suttantesu ādhāravisayasaṅkhāto adhikaraṇattho kiriyāya kiriyantaralakkhaṇasaṅkhāto bhāvenabhāvalakkhaṇattho ca sambhavatīti. Adhikaraṇañhi kālattho samūhattho ca samayo tattha vuttānaṃ phassādidhammānaṃ, tathā kālo sabhāvadhammappavattimattatāya paramatthato avijjamānopi ādhārabhāvena paññāto taṅkhaṇappavattānaṃ tato [M 0.0021] pubbe parato ca abhāvato yathā “pubbaṇhe [V 0.0019] jāto sāyanhe jāto”tiādīsu. Samūhotipi avayavavinimutto paramatthato avijjamānopi kappanāmattasiddhena rūpena avayavānaṃ ādhārabhāvena paññāpīyati, yathā “rukkhe sākhā, yavo yavarāsimhi samuṭṭhito”tiādīsu. Yasmiṃ kāle dhammapuñje ca kāmāvacaraṃ kusalaṃ cittaṃ uppannaṃ hoti, tasmiṃyeva kāle dhammapuñje ca phassādayopi hontīti ayañhi tattha attho. Tathā khaṇasamavāyahetusaṅkhātassa samayassa bhāvena tattha vuttānaṃ phassādidhammānaṃ bhāvo lakkhīyati. Yathā hi “gāvīsu duyhamānāsu gato, duddhāsu āgato”ti ettha gāvīnaṃ dohanakiriyāya gamanakiriyā lakkhīyati, evaṃ idhāpi yasmiṃ samayeti vutte ca padatthassa sattāvirahābhāvato satīti ayamattho viññāyamāno eva hotīti samayassa sattākiriyāya cittassa uppādakiriyā phassādīnaṃ bhavanakiriyā ca lakkhīyati. Tathā yasmiṃ samaye yasmiṃ navame khaṇe yasmiṃ yonisomanasikārādihetumhi paccayasamavāye vā sati kāmāvacaraṃ kusalaṃ cittaṃ uppannaṃ hoti, tasmiṃ samaye khaṇe hetumhi paccayasamavāye ca phassādayopi hontīti. Tasmā tadatthajotanatthaṃ bhummavacanena niddeso kato.

Why here, unlike in the Abhidhamma where the indication is made with the locative case, as in: 'At the time when a wholesome mind pertaining to the sense-sphere arises,' and in other Sutta passages, as in: 'At the time, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu, quite secluded from sensual pleasures…,' and in the Vinaya where the indication is made with the instrumental case, as in: 'At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One…'—why, instead of following these, is the indication made with the accusative case in the sense of continuous connection, as in 'at one time'? Because the possibility of meaning is different there and here. For in the Abhidhamma and in other Suttas, the meaning of location (adhikaraṇa), designated as basis and domain, is possible; and also the meaning of 'the marking of one state by another' (bhāvenabhāvalakkhaṇa), designated as the marking of one action by another. For 'occasion' (samayo), meaning time and collection, is the location for the phenomena such as contact mentioned there. Time, though ultimately non-existent, is designated as a basis for the mere occurrence of natural phenomena, since they do not exist before or after that moment, as in 'born in the morning.' A collection, too, though ultimately non-existent as distinct from its parts, is designated as a basis for the parts by a conventional form, as in 'a branch on the tree.' At whatever time and in whatever collection of phenomena a wholesome mind pertaining to the sense-sphere arises, at that very time and in that collection, contact and other states also arise. This is the meaning there. Likewise, by the state of the occasion—designated as moment, conjunction, and cause—the state of the phenomena such as contact is marked. Just as in 'He went while the cows were being milked,' the action of going is marked by the action of milking, so too here, by the action of the occasion's existence, the action of the mind's arising and the being of contact and other states are marked. Similarly, when there is an occasion, a ninth moment, a cause such as wise attention, or a conjunction of conditions, a wholesome mind pertaining to the sense-sphere arises; and on that occasion, in that moment, in that cause, and in that conjunction of conditions, contact and other states also arise. Therefore, to illuminate that meaning, the indication is made with the locative case.

Vinaye ca “annena vasati, ajjhenena vasatī”tiādīsu [P 0.0023] viya hetuattho, “pharasunā chindati, kudālena khaṇatī”tiādīsu viya karaṇattho ca sambhavati. Yo hi sikkhāpadapaññattisamayo dhammasenāpatiādīhipi dubbiññeyyo, tena samayena karaṇabhūtena hetubhūtena ca vītikkamaṃ sutvā bhikkhusaṅghaṃ sannipātāpetvā otiṇṇavatthukaṃ puggalaṃ paṭipucchitvā vigarahitvā ca taṃ taṃ vatthuṃ otiṇṇasamayasaṅkhātaṃ kālaṃ anatikkamitvā sikkhāpadāni paññāpento tatiyapārājikādīnaṃ viya sikkhāpadapaññattiyā hetuṃ apekkhamāno tattha tattha vihāsi, tasmā tadatthajotanatthaṃ vinaye karaṇavacanena niddeso kato.

And in the Vinaya, the meaning of cause is possible, as in 'he lives by means of food' or 'he lives by means of study'; and the meaning of instrument is possible, as in 'he cuts with an axe' or 'he digs with a spade.' For the occasion for promulgating a training rule is difficult to discern even for the General of the Dhamma and others. By means of that occasion, which served as both cause and instrument, the Blessed One—having heard of a transgression, assembled the Sangha of bhikkhus, questioned the individual involved in the incident, and rebuked him—dwelt there, laying down the training rules without letting the time designated as the 'occasion of the incident' pass, while looking for a cause for the rule's promulgation, as in the case of the third pārājika and others. Therefore, to illuminate that meaning, the indication in the Vinaya is made with the instrumental case.

Idha pana aññasmiñca evaṃjātike accantasaṃyogattho sambhavati. Yasmiñhi samaye saha samuṭṭhānahetunā idaṃ udānaṃ uppannaṃ, accantameva taṃ samayaṃ ariyavihārapubbaṅgamāya dhammapaccavekkhaṇāya bhagavā vihāsi, tasmā “māsaṃ [M 0.0022] ajjhetī”tiādīsu viya upayogatthajotanatthaṃ idha upayogavacanena niddeso kato. Tenetaṃ vuccati –

Here, however, and in other similar texts, the meaning of continuous connection is possible. For, at the time when this inspired utterance arose together with its originating cause, the Blessed One dwelt throughout that entire period engaged in reflection on the Dhamma, which was preceded by a noble abiding. Therefore, just as in instances such as 'he studies for a month,' the indication here is made with the accusative case to illuminate this meaning of duration. Hence, it is said:

“Taṃ taṃ atthamapekkhitvā, bhummena karaṇena ca;

Aññatra samayo vutto, upayogena so idhā”ti.

“Having regarded that particular meaning, by the locative and by the instrumental case, elsewhere the word ‘samaya’ is spoken; here, it is by the accusative case.”

Porāṇā pana vaṇṇayanti – “yasmiṃ samaye”ti vā “tena samayenā”ti vā “ekaṃ samaya”nti [V 0.0020] vā abhilāpamattabhedo esa niddeso, sabbattha bhummameva atthoti. Tasmā “ekaṃ samaya”nti vuttepi ekasmiṃ samayeti attho veditabbo.

The ancients, however, explain that whether it is said “at which time,” or “by that time,” or “on one occasion,” this indication is merely a difference in expression; the meaning is everywhere only that of the locative case. Therefore, even when it is said “on one occasion,” the meaning should be understood as “at one time.”

Bhagavāti garu. Garuñhi loke “bhagavā”ti vadanti. Ayañca sabbaguṇavisiṭṭhatāya sabbasattānaṃ garu, tasmā bhagavāti veditabbo. Porāṇehipi vuttaṃ –

Bhagavā means venerable. Indeed, in the world, they call a venerable one ‘Bhagavā.’ And this one, due to his distinction in all virtues, is venerable to all beings; therefore, he is to be known as ‘Bhagavā.’ It has also been said by the ancients:

“Bhagavāti [P 0.0024] vacanaṃ seṭṭhaṃ, bhagavāti vacanamuttamaṃ;

Garu gāravayutto so, bhagavā tena vuccatī”ti.

“‘Bhagavā’ is an excellent word, ‘Bhagavā’ is a supreme word; He is venerable, endowed with that which is worthy of reverence; for that reason he is called ‘Bhagavā.’”

Tattha seṭṭhavācakavacanaṃ seṭṭhanti vuttaṃ seṭṭhaguṇasahacaraṇato. Atha vā vuccatīti vacanaṃ, attho. Bhagavāti vacanaṃ seṭṭhanti bhagavāti iminā vacanena vacanīyo yo attho, so seṭṭhoti attho. Bhagavāti vacanamuttamanti etthāpi vuttanayeneva attho veditabbo. Gāravayuttoti garubhāvayutto garuguṇayogato visesagarukaraṇārahatāya vā gāravayutto. Evaṃ guṇavisiṭṭhasattuttamagarugāravādhivacanaṃ bhagavāti idaṃ vacananti veditabbaṃ. Apica –

Therein, the word that denotes excellence is said to be 'excellent' because it accompanies excellent qualities. Or alternatively, the meaning of 'The word Bhagavā is excellent' is that the meaning to be conveyed by this word 'Bhagavā' is excellent. In 'The word Bhagavā is supreme' also, the meaning should be understood in the same way as stated. 'Endowed with that which is worthy of reverence' means endowed with the state of being venerable due to possessing venerable qualities, or endowed with that which is worthy of reverence because he is worthy of being specially venerated. Thus, it should be understood that this word 'Bhagavā' is a designation for one who is venerable and worthy of reverence, the supreme among beings, distinguished by virtues. Furthermore—

“Bhagī bhajī bhāgī vibhattavā iti,

Akāsi bhagganti garūti bhāgyavā;

Bahūhi ñāyehi subhāvitattano,

Bhavantago so bhagavāti vuccatī”ti. –

“He had fortunes (bhagī), he resorted (bhajī), he was a partaker (bhāgī), and he analyzed (vibhattavā); He effected the breaking (bhaggaṃ akāsi) [of defilements], he is venerable (garu), and he is fortunate (bhāgyavā); His mind is well-developed by many methods, He has gone to the end of becoming (bhavantago); thus he is called ‘Bhagavā.’”

Niddese (mahāni. 84) āgatanayena –

According to the method that comes in the Niddesa (Mahāni. 84):

“Bhāgyavā bhaggavā yutto, bhagehi ca vibhattavā;

Bhattavā vantagamano, bhavesu bhagavā tato”ti. –

“He is fortunate (bhāgyavā), a breaker (bhaggavā), endowed with fortunes (bhagehi yutto), and an analyzer (vibhattavā); He has resorted (bhattavā) [to noble states], and has abandoned going (vantagamano) in the modes of existence (bhavesu); therefore (tato), he is ‘Bhagavā.’”

Imāya [M 0.0023] gāthāya ca vasena bhagavāti padassa attho veditabbo. So panāyaṃ attho sabbākārena visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.142) vutto, tasmā tattha vuttanayeneva vivaritabbo.

And by means of this verse, the meaning of the word ‘Bhagavā’ is to be understood. Now, this meaning has been stated in all its aspects in the Visuddhimagga; therefore, it should be explained only according to the method stated there.

Apica bhāge vani, bhage vā vamīti bhagavā. Tathāgato hi dānasīlādipāramidhamme jhānavimokkhādiuttarimanussadhamme vani bhaji sevi bahulamakāsi, tasmā bhagavā. Atha vā teyeva [V 0.0021] “veneyyasattasantānesu kathaṃ nu kho uppajjeyyu”nti vani abhipatthayīti bhagavā. Atha vā bhagasaṅkhātaṃ issariyaṃ yasañca vami uggiri kheḷapiṇḍaṃ viya anapekkho chaḍḍayīti bhagavā. Tathā hi tathāgato hatthagataṃ cakkavattisiriṃ devalokādhipaccasadisaṃ cātuddīpissariyaṃ, cakkavattisampattisannissayañca sattaratanasamujjalaṃ yasaṃ tiṇāyapi amaññamāno nirapekkho pahāya abhinikkhamitvā sammāsambodhiṃ abhisambuddho, tasmā ime siriādike bhage vamīti bhagavā. Atha vā bhāni nāma nakkhattāni, tehi samaṃ [P 0.0025] gacchanti pavattantīti bhagā. Sineruyugandharauttarakuruhimavantādibhājanalokavisesasannissayasobhā kappaṭṭhitibhāvato, tepi bhage vami, tannivāsisattāvāsasamatikkamanato tappaṭibaddhachandarāgappahānena pajahīti. Evampi bhage vamīti bhagavāti evamādinā nayena bhagavāti padassa attho veditabbo.

Furthermore, he is Bhagavā because he partook of (vani) portions (bhage), or because he vomited (vami) portions (bhage). For the Tathāgata partook of, resorted to, and cultivated (vani bhaji sevi) abundantly the perfections such as giving and morality, and the transcendent human states such as the meditative absorptions and liberations; therefore, he is Bhagavā. Or, he desired (vani), that is, he yearned, 'How might these very states arise in the mental continuities of trainable beings?'; therefore, he is Bhagavā. Or, he vomited (vami), that is, he spat out, he discarded without attachment like a lump of phlegm, the portions (bhaga) known as sovereignty and fame; therefore, he is Bhagavā. For indeed, the Tathāgata, regarding the sovereignty of a wheel-turning monarch that had come into his hands—a sovereignty over the four continents equal to the lordship of the deva world—and the fame, resplendent with the seven treasures, that is the basis for the fortune of a wheel-turning monarch, as not even worth a blade of grass, renounced it without attachment, went forth, and fully awakened to perfect self-enlightenment. Therefore, because he vomited these portions of glory and so on, he is Bhagavā. Or, ‘bhāni’ is a name for the constellations; things that go or proceed in accordance with them are ‘bhagā’. These are the splendors of the special abodes of the receptacle world, such as Sineru, Yugandhara, Uttarakuru, and Himavanta, which are established for an eon. These portions (bhage) too he vomited (vami), that is, he abandoned them by transcending the abodes of the beings dwelling there and by abandoning the desire and passion connected with them. In this way too, because he vomited the portions, he is Bhagavā. By this and other such methods, the meaning of the word 'Bhagavā' is to be understood.

Ettāvatā cettha evaṃ me sutanti vacanena yathāsutaṃ dhammaṃ savanavasena bhāsanto bhagavato dhammasarīraṃ paccakkhaṃ karoti, tena “nayidaṃ atikkantasatthukaṃ pāvacanaṃ, ayaṃ vo satthā”ti satthu adassanena ukkaṇṭhitaṃ janaṃ samassāseti. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā “yo kho, ānanda, mayā dhammo ca vinayo ca desito paññatto, so vo mamaccayena satthā”ti (dī. ni. 2.216; mi. pa. 4.1.1). Ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavāti vacanena tasmiṃ samaye bhagavato avijjamānabhāvaṃ dassento rūpakāyaparinibbānaṃ sādheti, tena “evaṃvidhassa nāma dhammassa desetā dasabaladharo vajirasaṅghātasamānakāyo sopi bhagavā parinibbuto, kenaññena jīvite āsā janetabbā”ti jīvitamadamattaṃ janaṃ saṃvejeti, saddhamme cassa ussāhaṃ janeti.

Thus far in this context, by the words “Thus have I heard,” he who speaks the Dhamma as he heard it makes the Dhamma-body of the Blessed One present. Thereby, he reassures the people who are distressed by the Teacher’s absence, saying, “This teaching does not have a Teacher who has passed away; this is your Teacher.” For this was said by the Blessed One: “Ānanda, the Dhamma and the Vinaya that I have taught and laid down for you will be your Teacher after I am gone.” By the words “On one occasion, the Blessed One,” while showing the Blessed One’s non-existence at that time, he establishes the parinibbāna of the physical body. Thereby, he inspires a sense of urgency in people intoxicated with the pride of life, thinking: “Even the Blessed One—the teacher of such a Dhamma, the bearer of the ten powers, whose body was like a mass of diamond—has attained parinibbāna. Who else should generate a desire for life?” And he generates enthusiasm in them for the good Dhamma.

Evanti [M 0.0024] ca bhaṇanto desanāsampattiṃ niddisati, vakkhamānassa sakalasuttassa evanti nidassanato. Me sutanti sāvakasampattiṃ savanasampattiñca niddisati, paṭisambhidāpattena pañcasu ṭhānesu bhagavatā etadagge ṭhapitena dhammabhaṇḍāgārikena sutabhāvadīpanato “tañca kho mayāva sutaṃ, na anussutikaṃ, na paramparābhata”nti imassa catthassa dīpanato. Ekaṃ samayanti kālasampattiṃ niddisati bhagavato uruvelāyaṃ viharaṇasamayabhāvena buddhuppādappaṭimaṇḍitabhāvadīpanato. Buddhuppādaparamā hi kālasampadā. Bhagavāti desakasampattiṃ niddisati guṇavisiṭṭhasattuttamagarubhāvadīpanato.

And by saying ‘Thus,’ he indicates the accomplishment of the teaching, because the entire sutta that is about to be spoken is indicated by ‘Thus.’ By saying ‘heard by me,’ he indicates the accomplishment of the disciple and the accomplishment of the hearing, by showing that it was heard by the Treasurer of the Dhamma, who had attained the analytical knowledges and had been placed by the Blessed One at the head of those in five respects, and by showing the meaning that “it was heard by me myself, it is not from hearsay, it is not handed down in tradition.” By saying ‘on one occasion,’ he indicates the accomplishment of the time, by showing that it was adorned with the arising of a Buddha, being the time when the Blessed One was dwelling at Uruvelā. For the supreme accomplishment of time is the arising of a Buddha. By the word ‘Bhagavā,’ he indicates the accomplishment of the teacher, by showing his state of being venerable, the supreme among beings, distinguished by his qualities.

Uruvelāyanti [P 0.0026] mahāvelāyaṃ, mahante vālukārāsimhīti attho. Atha vā urūti vālukā vuccati, velāti mariyādā. Velātikkamanahetu ābhatā uru uruvelāti evampettha attho daṭṭhabbo.

‘At Uruvelā’ means on the great sandbank, that is, on the great heap of sand. Or alternatively, ‘uru’ is a term for sand, and ‘velā’ is a term for a boundary. Sand (uru) brought (ābhatā) due to the overstepping of the boundary (velā) is ‘Uruvelā.’ Thus the meaning should be seen here.

Atīte [V 0.0022] kira anuppanne buddhe dasasahassatāpasā tasmiṃ padese viharantā “kāyakammavacīkammāni paresampi pākaṭāni honti, manokammaṃ pana apākaṭaṃ. Tasmā yo micchāvitakkaṃ vitakketi, so attanāva attānaṃ codetvā pattapuṭena vālukaṃ āharitvā imasmiṃ ṭhāne ākiratu, idamassa daṇḍakamma”nti katikavattaṃ katvā tato paṭṭhāya yo tādisaṃ vitakkaṃ vitakketi, so tattha pattapuṭena vālukaṃ āharitvā ākirati. Evaṃ tattha anukkamena mahāvālukārāsi jāto, tato naṃ pacchimā janatā parikkhipitvā cetiyaṭṭhānamakāsi. Taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ – “uruvelāyanti mahāvelāyaṃ, mahante vālukārāsimhīti attho daṭṭhabbo”ti.

In the past, it is said, when a Buddha had not arisen, ten thousand ascetics dwelling in that region established an agreement: 'Bodily and verbal actions are evident to others, but mental action is not. Therefore, whoever thinks a wrong thought should, having reproached themselves, bring sand in a leaf-bowl and scatter it in this place. This shall be their penance.' Having made this agreement, from then on, whoever thought such a thought would bring sand in a leaf-bowl and scatter it there. Thus, in that place, a great heap of sand was gradually formed. Later, the people who came after enclosed it and made it a place for a shrine. In reference to that, it was said: 'At Uruvelā means at the great sandy expanse, that is, at the great heap of sand—this is the meaning that should be understood.'

Viharatīti avisesena iriyāpathadibbabrahmaariyavihāresu aññataravihārasamaṅgitāparidīpanaṃ. Idha pana ṭhānanisajjāgamanasayanappabhedesu iriyāpathesu āsanasaṅkhātairiyāpathasamāyogaparidīpanaṃ ariyavihārasamaṅgitāparidīpanañcāti veditabbaṃ. Tattha yasmā ekaṃ iriyāpathabādhanaṃ aññena iriyāpathena vicchinditvā aparipatantaṃ attabhāvaṃ harati pavatteti, tasmā viharatīti padassa iriyāpathavihāravasenettha attho veditabbo. Yasmā pana bhagavā dibbavihārādīhi sattānaṃ vividhaṃ hitaṃ harati upaharati upaneti uppādeti, tasmā tesampi vasena vividhaṃ haratīti evamattho veditabbo.

The word 'viharati' (he dwells) is a term that, in a general sense, indicates the state of being endowed with one of the abidings, namely, abiding in postures, divine abiding, brahma-abiding, or noble abiding. Here, however, among the postures which are divided into standing, sitting, walking, and lying down, it should be understood as indicating engagement with the posture known as sitting, and also as indicating the state of being endowed with noble abiding. Therein, since one carries on and maintains the body without it collapsing by cutting off the affliction of one posture with another posture, the meaning of the word 'viharati' should be understood here by way of abiding in postures. Furthermore, since the Blessed One brings, conveys, leads to, and produces various kinds of welfare for beings by means of divine abidings and so forth, the meaning should also be understood in this way: 'he brings various kinds'—by way of those abidings as well.

Najjāti [M 0.0025] nadati sandatīti nadī, tassā najjā, nadiyā ninnagāyāti attho. Nerañjarāyāti nelaṃ jalamassāti “nelañjalāyā”ti vattabbe lakārassa rakāraṃ katvā “nerañjarāyā”ti vuttaṃ, kaddamasevālapaṇakādidosarahitasalilāyāti attho. Keci “nīlajalāyāti [P 0.0027] vattabbe nerañjarāyāti vutta”nti vadanti. Nāmameva vā etaṃ etissā nadiyāti veditabbaṃ. Tassā nadiyā tīre yattha bhagavā vihāsi, taṃ dassetuṃ “bodhirukkhamūle”ti vuttaṃ. Tattha “bodhi vuccati catūsu maggesu ñāṇa”nti ettha (cūḷani. khaggavisāṇasuttaniddesa 121) maggañāṇaṃ bodhīti vuttaṃ. “Pappoti bodhiṃ varabhūrimedhaso”ti ettha (dī. ni. 3.217) sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ. Tadubhayampi bodhiṃ bhagavā ettha pattoti rukkhopi bodhirukkhotveva nāmaṃ labhi. Atha vā satta bojjhaṅge bujjhīti bhagavā bodhi, tena bujjhantena sannissitattā so rukkhopi bodhirukkhoti nāmaṃ labhi, tassa bodhirukkhassa. Mūleti samīpe. Ayañhi mūlasaddo “mūlāni uddhareyya antamaso usīranāḷamattānipī”tiādīsu (a. ni. 4.195) mūlamūle dissati. “Lobho akusalamūla”ntiādīsu (dī. ni. 3.305) asādhāraṇahetumhi. “Yāvatā majjhanhike kāle chāyā pharati, nivāte paṇṇāni [V 0.0023] patanti, ettāvatā rukkhamūla”ntiādīsu samīpe. Idhāpi samīpe adhippeto, tasmā bodhirukkhassa mūle samīpeti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo.

Regarding 'najjā' (of the river): because it flows (nadati) and streams (sandati), it is called a 'nadī' (river). Thus, 'of that river' (tassā najjā) means of the river that flows to a low place. Regarding 'Nerañjarāya': when 'nelañjalāya' should have been said—meaning 'of that which has faultless water'—the word 'nerañjarāya' is stated, having changed the letter 'la' to 'ra'. The meaning is: 'of that with water free from faults such as mud, moss, and water-plants.' Some say that when 'nīlajalāya' (of that with blue water) should have been said, 'nerañjarāya' was stated. Or, it should be understood that this is simply the name of that river. To show where on the bank of that river the Blessed One dwelt, it was said, 'at the foot of the Bodhi tree.' Therein, in the passage 'Bodhi is said to be the knowledge in the four paths,' the knowledge of the path is called 'bodhi.' In the passage 'The one of great wisdom attains the supreme Bodhi,' omniscience is called 'bodhi.' Because the Blessed One attained both these kinds of Bodhi at this place, the tree also received the name 'Bodhi tree.' Or, because the Blessed One awakened (bujjhi) to the seven factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga), the Blessed One is 'bodhi'; because it was his support while he was awakening, that tree also received the name 'Bodhi tree.' 'At the foot' (mūle) means 'nearby' (samīpe). For this word 'mūla' is seen to mean the root of a plant in passages such as 'one should pull up the roots, even so much as a blade of usīra grass.' In passages such as 'Greed is an unwholesome root,' it is seen to mean a primary cause. In passages such as 'As far as the shade spreads at midday, and as far as the leaves fall when there is no wind, that much is the foot of the tree,' it is seen to mean 'nearby.' Here too, 'nearby' is intended. Therefore, the meaning here should be understood thus: 'at the foot of the Bodhi tree' means 'near the Bodhi tree.'

Paṭhamābhisambuddhoti paṭhamaṃ abhisambuddho hutvā, sabbapaṭhamaṃyevāti attho. Ettāvatā dhammabhaṇḍāgārikena udānadesanāya nidānaṃ ṭhapentena kāladesadesakāpadesā saha visesena pakāsitā honti.

'Newly awakened' means having become fully awakened for the first time, that is, before all others. By this much, the Treasurer of the Dhamma, in establishing the introduction to the discourse of the inspired utterance, has declared the time, place, and speaker, together with their particular attributes.

Etthāha “kasmā dhammavinayasaṅgahe kayiramāne nidānavacanaṃ vuttaṃ, nanu bhagavatā bhāsitavacanasseva saṅgaho kātabbo”ti? Vuccate – desanāya ciraṭṭhitiasammosasaddheyyabhāvasampādanatthaṃ. Kāladesadesakavatthuādīhi upanibandhitvā ṭhapitā hi desanā ciraṭṭhitikā hoti asammosā saddheyyā ca desakālakattuhetunimittehi upanibaddho viya vohāravinicchayo. Teneva ca āyasmatā mahākassapena “paṭhamaṃ, āvuso ānanda, udānaṃ kattha bhāsita”ntiādinā desādīsu pucchāya katāya [M 0.0026] vissajjanaṃ karontena dhammabhaṇḍāgārikena “evaṃ me suta”ntiādinā udānassa nidānaṃ bhāsitanti.

Here, one asks: 'Why, when the Dhamma and Vinaya were being compiled, was the introductory passage spoken? Should not only the words spoken by the Blessed One have been compiled?' The reply is given: For the purpose of endowing the teaching with long-lastingness, non-confusion, and credibility. For a teaching that is established by being linked to time, place, speaker, subject matter, and so on, becomes long-lasting, free from confusion, and credible, like a legal decision that is linked to the speaker, time, agent, reason, and grounds. It was for this very reason that when the Venerable Mahākassapa asked questions about the place and so on, beginning with, 'Friend Ānanda, where was the first inspired utterance spoken?', the Treasurer of the Dhamma, in giving his reply, spoke the introduction to the Udāna, beginning with, 'Thus have I heard.'

Apica satthu sampattipakāsanatthaṃ nidānavacanaṃ. Tathāgatassa hi bhagavato pubbaracanānumānāgamatakkābhāvato [P 0.0028] sambuddhattasiddhi. Na hi sammāsambuddhassa pubbaracanādīhi attho atthi sabbattha appaṭihatañāṇacāratāya ekappamāṇattā ñeyyadhammesu. Tathā ācariyamuṭṭhidhammamacchariyasāsanasāvakānurāgābhāvato khīṇāsavattasiddhi. Na hi sabbaso parikkhīṇāsavassa katthacipi ācariyamuṭṭhiādīnaṃ sambhavoti suvisuddhassa parānuggahappavatti. Iti desakadosabhūtānaṃ diṭṭhisīlasampattidūsakānaṃ accantaṃ avijjātaṇhānaṃ abhāvasaṃsūcakehi ñāṇasampadāpahānasampadābhibyañjakehi ca sambuddhavisuddhabhāvehi purimavesārajjadvayasiddhi, tato ca antarāyikaniyyānikadhammesu sammohābhāvasiddhito pacchimavesārajjadvayasiddhīti bhagavato catuvesārajjasamannāgamo attahitaparahitappaṭipatti ca nidānavacanena pakāsitā honti, tattha tattha sampattaparisāya ajjhāsayānurūpaṃ ṭhānuppattikappaṭibhānena dhammadesanādīpanato. Idha pana vimuttisukhappaṭisaṃvedanapaṭiccasamuppādamanasikārapakāsanenāti yojetabbaṃ. Tena vuttaṃ – “satthu sampattipakāsanatthaṃ nidānavacana”nti.

Furthermore, the introductory word serves to proclaim the Teacher's accomplishment. For the Tathāgata, the Blessed One, the state of a Perfectly Enlightened One is accomplished due to the absence of prior composition, inference, tradition, and reasoning. Indeed, for a Perfectly Enlightened One, there is no need for prior composition and the like, since his knowledge operates unimpeded everywhere and is of a uniform measure regarding all knowable phenomena. Similarly, due to the absence of a teacher's fist, stinginess with the Dhamma, and affection for disciples of the teaching, the state of one whose cankers are destroyed is accomplished. For one whose cankers are utterly destroyed, there is no possibility anywhere of a teacher's fist and the like; for the completely pure one, the teaching of the Dhamma proceeds for the benefit of others. Thus, through the states of a Buddha's purity—which indicate the complete absence of ignorance and craving (these being the speaker's faults that corrupt the accomplishment of view and virtue) and which demonstrate the accomplishment of knowledge and abandonment—the first two grounds of confidence are accomplished. And from that, due to the accomplishment of the absence of delusion regarding obstructive and emancipating phenomena, the latter two grounds of confidence are accomplished. Therefore, the Blessed One's possession of the four grounds of confidence, and his practice for his own welfare and the welfare of others, are revealed by the introductory word, through elucidating the Dhamma here and there to the assembled congregation in accordance with their disposition, with spontaneous, situational eloquence. Here, however, it should be connected with showing the experience of the bliss of liberation and the contemplation of dependent origination. Therefore, it is said: 'The introductory word is for the purpose of proclaiming the Teacher’s accomplishment.'

Tathā sāsanasampattipakāsanatthaṃ nidānavacanaṃ. Ñāṇakaruṇāpariggahitasabbakiriyassa hi bhagavato natthi niratthakā paṭipatti attahitā vā. Tasmā paresaṃyeva atthāya pavattasabbakiriyassa [V 0.0024] sammāsambuddhassa sakalampi kāyavacīmanokammaṃ yathāpavattaṃ vuccamānaṃ diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikaparamatthehi yathārahaṃ sattānaṃ anusāsanaṭṭhena sāsanaṃ, na kabbaracanā. Tayidaṃ satthu caritaṃ kāladesadesakaparisāpadesādīhi saddhiṃ tattha tattha nidānavacanena yathārahaṃ pakāsīyati, idha pana abhisambodhivimuttisukhappaṭisaṃvedanapaṭiccasamuppādamanasikārenāti yojetabbaṃ. Tena vuttaṃ – “sāsanasampattipakāsanatthaṃ nidānavacana”nti.

Similarly, the introductory word serves to proclaim the accomplishment of the Dispensation. Indeed, for the Blessed One, whose every action is embraced by knowledge and compassion, there is no practice that is fruitless, nor one for his own welfare. Therefore, for the Perfectly Enlightened One, whose every action proceeds only for the welfare of others, all bodily, verbal, and mental action, when described as it occurred, is the Dispensation—by way of instructing beings according to their due with benefits in the present life, in future lives, and the ultimate benefit—and not poetic composition. This conduct of the Teacher, together with time, place, speaker, assembly, and so on, is appropriately revealed here and there through the introductory word. Here, however, it should be connected with supreme enlightenment, the experience of the bliss of liberation, and the contemplation of dependent origination. Therefore, it is said: 'The introductory word is for the purpose of proclaiming the accomplishment of the Dispensation.'

Apica satthuno pamāṇabhāvappakāsanena sāsanassa pamāṇabhāvadassanatthaṃ nidānavacanaṃ. Sā cassa pamāṇabhāvadassanatā [P 0.0029] heṭṭhā vuttanayānusārena veditabbā. Bhagavāti hi iminā tathāgatassa rāgadosamohādisabbakilesamaladuccaritādidosappahānadīpanena[M 0.0027], sabbasattuttamabhāvadīpanena ca anaññasādhāraṇañāṇakaruṇādiguṇavisesayogaparidīpanena, ayamattho sabbathā pakāsito hotīti idamettha nidānavacanappayojanassa mukhamattadassanaṃ.

Furthermore, by proclaiming the Teacher's status as the authority, the introductory word serves to show the Dispensation's status as the authority. And this demonstration of its status as the authority should be understood according to the method stated above. For by this word 'Bhagavā', this meaning is fully revealed in every way: by showing the Tathāgata's abandonment of all faults such as defilements, stains, and misconduct like greed, hatred, and delusion; by showing his state as supreme among all beings; and by illuminating his connection with special qualities not shared with others, such as knowledge and compassion. This here is but a brief indication of the purpose of the introductory word.

Taṃ panetaṃ “evaṃ me suta”nti ārabhitvā yāva “imaṃ udānaṃ udānesī”ti padaṃ, tāva imassa udānassa nidānanti veditabbaṃ. Tathā hi taṃ yathā paṭipanno bhagavā imaṃ udānaṃ udānesi, ādito paṭṭhāya tassa kāyikacetasikappaṭipattiyā pakāsanatthaṃ saṅgītikārehi saṅgītikāle bhāsitavacanaṃ.

Now, that which begins with 'Thus have I heard' and extends as far as the phrase 'uttered this inspired utterance,' should be understood as the introduction to this Udāna. For that is the word spoken by the compilers at the time of the compilation in order to show, from the beginning, the Blessed One's bodily and mental practice and the manner in which he, having so practiced, uttered this inspired utterance.

Nanu ca “imasmiṃ sati idaṃ hotī”tiādi bhagavato eva vacanaṃ bhavituṃ arahati, na hi satthāraṃ muñcitvā añño paṭiccasamuppādaṃ desetuṃ samattho hotīti? Saccametaṃ, yathā pana bhagavā bodhirukkhamūle dhammasabhāvapaccavekkhaṇavasena paṭiccasamuppādaṃ manasākāsi, tatheva naṃ bodhaneyyabandhavānaṃ bodhanatthaṃ paṭiccasamuppādasīhanādasuttādīsu desitassa ca vacanānaṃ desitākārassa anukaraṇavasena paṭiccasamuppādassa manasikāraṃ aṭṭhuppattiṃ katvā bhagavatā bhāsitassa imassa udānassa dhammasaṅgāhakā mahātherā nidānaṃ saṅgāyiṃsūti yathāvuttavacanaṃ saṅgītikārānameva vacananti niṭṭhamettha gantabbaṃ. Ito paresupi suttantesu eseva nayo.

But should not the words 'When this exists, that comes to be,' and so on, rightly be the Blessed One’s alone? For indeed, apart from the Teacher, no one else is capable of expounding dependent origination. This is true. However, just as the Blessed One, at the foot of the Bodhi tree, contemplated dependent origination by way of reviewing the nature of phenomena, so too, for the purpose of awakening his kinsmen who were capable of being awakened, the great elders who compiled the Dhamma recited the introduction to this Udāna spoken by the Blessed One, making the contemplation of dependent origination the occasion and imitating the manner of teaching and the words taught in discourses such as the Dependent Origination Lion’s Roar Sutta and others. Therefore, it should be concluded here that the aforesaid words are the words of the compilers themselves. In the suttas that follow this one, this is the same method.

Ettha ca attajjhāsayo parajjhāsayo pucchāvasiko aṭṭhuppattikoti cattāro suttanikkhepā veditabbā. Yathā hi anekasataanekasahassabhedānipi suttāni saṃkilesabhāgiyādipaṭṭhānanayena soḷasavidhataṃ nātivattanti, evaṃ tāni sabbānipi attajjhāsayādisuttanikkhepavasena catubbidhabhāvaṃ nātivattanti. Kāmañcettha attajjhāsayassa aṭṭhuppattiyā ca parajjhāsayapucchāvasikehi saddhiṃ saṃsaggabhedo sambhavati ajjhāsayānusandhipucchānusandhisambhavato, attajjhāsayaaṭṭhuppattīnaṃ aññamaññaṃ [V 0.0025] saṃsaggo natthīti niravaseso paṭṭhānanayo na [P 0.0030] sambhavati. Tadantogadhattā vā sambhavantānaṃ sesanikkhepānaṃ mūlanikkhepavasena cattāro suttanikkhepāti vuttaṃ.

And here, four ways of setting forth a sutta should be known: based on personal inclination, based on others’ inclination, prompted by a question, and arising from an occasion. For just as the suttas, though of countless hundreds and thousands of divisions, do not go beyond sixteen kinds by the method of the Paṭṭhāna beginning with the 'corruptible section,' so too all of them do not go beyond this fourfold state by way of the ways of setting forth a sutta beginning with 'based on personal inclination.' And although it is certainly possible for a mixed division to occur for 'based on personal inclination' and 'arising from an occasion' together with 'based on others' inclination' and 'prompted by a question'—due to the possibility of a connection of inclination and a connection of question—there is no mutual mixing between 'based on personal inclination' and 'arising from an occasion'. Therefore, a complete Paṭṭhāna-style method is not possible. Or, because any other possible expositions are included within them, it is said that there are four ways of setting forth a sutta by way of being root expositions.

Tatrāyaṃ [M 0.0028] vacanattho – nikkhipanaṃ nikkhepo, suttassa nikkhepo suttanikkhepo, suttadesanāti attho. Nikkhipīyatīti vā nikkhepo, suttaṃ eva nikkhepo suttanikkhepo. Attano ajjhāsayo attajjhāsayo, so assa atthi kāraṇabhūtoti attajjhāsayo, attano ajjhāsayo etassāti vā attajjhāsayo. Parajjhāsayepi eseva nayo. Pucchāya vaso pucchāvaso, so etassa atthīti pucchāvasiko. Suttadesanāya vatthubhūtassa atthassa uppatti atthuppatti, atthuppatti eva aṭṭhuppatti, sā etassa atthīti aṭṭhuppattiko. Atha vā nikkhipīyati suttaṃ etenāti nikkhepo, attajjhāsayādi eva. Etasmiṃ pana atthavikappe attano ajjhāsayo attajjhāsayo. Paresaṃ ajjhāsayo parajjhāsayo. Pucchīyatīti pucchā, pucchitabbo attho. Pucchanavasena pavattaṃ dhammappaṭiggāhakānaṃ vacanaṃ pucchāvasaṃ, tadeva nikkhepasaddāpekkhāya pucchāvasikoti pulliṅgavasena vuttaṃ. Tathā atthuppattiyeva aṭṭhuppattikoti evamettha attho veditabbo.

Herein, this is the meaning of the terms: 'Laying down' (nikkhepana) is a 'laying down' (nikkhepo). The laying down of a discourse is a 'discourse-laying-down' (suttanikkhepo), meaning the exposition of a discourse. Or, because it is laid down, it is a 'laying down'; the discourse itself is the 'laying down', hence a 'discourse-laying-down'. 'One's own inclination' (attano ajjhāsayo) is 'self-inclination' (attajjhāsayo); it is called 'self-inclination' because that inclination exists for it as a cause, or because its own inclination belongs to it. The same method applies to 'others' inclination'. The sway of a question (pucchāya vaso) is 'question-sway' (pucchāvaso); it is called 'question-prompted' (pucchāvasiko) because that sway exists for it. The arising of a matter (atthassa uppatti) that serves as the basis for the exposition of a discourse is 'matter-arising' (atthuppatti); 'matter-arising' itself is 'occasion-arising' (aṭṭhuppatti); it is called 'occasion-arisen' (aṭṭhuppattiko) because that occasion exists for it. Alternatively, that by which a discourse is laid down is a 'laying down'; this refers to 'self-inclination' and so on. In this alternative analysis of meaning, 'one's own inclination' is 'self-inclination'. 'The inclination of others' is 'others' inclination'. Because it is questioned, it is a 'question' (pucchā), meaning the matter to be questioned. The statement of those who receive the Dhamma, proceeding by way of questioning, is 'question-sway' (pucchāvasaṃ); that very thing, with reference to the word 'laying down', is stated in the masculine form as 'question-prompted' (pucchāvasiko). Similarly, 'occasion-arising' itself is 'occasion-arisen' (aṭṭhuppattiko). Thus should the meaning here be understood.

Ettha ca paresaṃ indriyaparipākādikāraṇanirapekkhattā attajjhāsayassa visuṃ suttanikkhepabhāvo yutto kevalaṃ attano ajjhāsayeneva dhammatantiṭhapanatthaṃ pavattitadesanattā, parajjhāsayapucchāvasikānaṃ pana paresaṃ ajjhāsayapucchānaṃ desanāpavattihetubhūtānaṃ uppattiyaṃ pavattitānaṃ kathamaṭṭhuppattiyā anavarodho, pucchāvasikaaṭṭhuppattipubbakānaṃ vā parajjhāsayānurodhena pavattitānaṃ kathaṃ parajjhāsaye anavarodhoti? Na codetabbametaṃ. Paresañhi abhinīhāraparipucchādivinicchayādivinimuttasseva suttantadesanākāraṇuppādassa aṭṭhuppattibhāvena gahitattā parajjhāsayapucchāvasikānaṃ visuṃ gahaṇaṃ. Tathā hi brahmajāladhammadāyādasuttādīnaṃ vaṇṇāvaṇṇaāmisuppādādidesanānimittaṃ aṭṭhuppatti vuccati, paresaṃ pucchāya vinā ajjhāsayameva nimittaṃ katvā desito parajjhāsayo, pucchāvasena desito pucchāvasikoti [P 0.0031] pākaṭoyamatthoti.

Herein, the separate status of 'self-inclination' as a type of discourse-laying-down is justified, because it is independent of causes such as the maturing of others' faculties, and because the teaching is set forth for the purpose of establishing the lineage of the Dhamma solely through one's own inclination. But for 'others' inclination' and 'question-prompted'—which are set forth upon the arising of others' inclinations and questions that are the cause for the teaching to proceed—how is there no conflict with 'occasion-arising'? Or for those teachings preceded by 'question-prompted' and 'occasion-arising', which are set forth in accordance with others' inclinations, how is there no conflict with 'others' inclination'? This objection should not be raised. For it is because the arising of a cause for the exposition of a discourse that is free from others' aspirations, questions, and so on, is taken as being 'occasion-arising', that 'others' inclination' and 'question-prompted' are taken separately. Indeed, in the Brahmajāla Sutta, the Dhammadāyāda Sutta, and others, the cause for the teaching—such as praise, blame, or the arising of material gain—is called 'occasion-arising'. A discourse taught having taken only another's inclination as the cause, without a question, is 'others' inclination'. A discourse taught by way of a question is 'question-prompted'. This meaning is evident.

Tattha paṭhamādīni tīṇi bodhisuttāni mucalindasuttaṃ, āyusaṅkhārossajjanasuttaṃ, paccavekkhaṇasuttaṃ, papañcasaññāsuttanti imesaṃ udānānaṃ attajjhāsayo nikkhepo. Huhuṅkasuttaṃ, brāhmaṇajātikasuttaṃ, bāhiyasuttanti imesaṃ udānānaṃ pucchāvasiko nikkhepo. Rājasuttaṃ, sakkārasuttaṃ, ucchādanasuttaṃ, piṇḍapātikasuttaṃ, sippasuttaṃ, gopālasuttaṃ, sundarikasuttaṃ[M 0.0029], mātusuttaṃ, saṅghabhedakasuttaṃ, udapānasuttaṃ, tathāgatuppādasuttaṃ, moneyyasuttaṃ, pāṭaligāmiyasuttaṃ, dvepi [V 0.0026] dabbasuttānīti etesaṃ udānānaṃ aṭṭhuppattiko nikkhepo. Pālileyyasuttaṃ, piyasuttaṃ, nāgasamālasuttaṃ, visākhāsuttañcāti imesaṃ udānānaṃ attajjhāsayo parajjhāsayo ca nikkhepo. Sesānaṃ ekapaññāsāya suttānaṃ parajjhāsayo nikkhepo. Evametesaṃ udānānaṃ attajjhāsayādivasena nikkhepaviseso veditabbo.

Herein, for the first three Bodhi suttas, the Mucalinda Sutta, the Āyusaṅkhārossajjana Sutta, the Paccavekkhaṇa Sutta, and the Papañcasaññā Sutta—for these udānas, the laying down is 'self-inclination'. For the Huhuṅka Sutta, the Brāhmaṇajātika Sutta, and the Bāhiya Sutta—for these udānas, the laying down is 'question-prompted'. For the Rāja Sutta, the Sakkāra Sutta, the Ucchādana Sutta, the Piṇḍapātika Sutta, the Sippa Sutta, the Gopāla Sutta, the Sundarika Sutta, the Mātā Sutta, the Saṅghabhedaka Sutta, the Udapāna Sutta, the Tathāgatuppāda Sutta, the Moneyya Sutta, the Pāṭaligāmiya Sutta, and both Dabba suttas—for these udānas, the laying down is 'occasion-arisen'. For the Pālileyya Sutta, the Piya Sutta, the Nāgasamāla Sutta, and the Visākhā Sutta—for these udānas, the laying down is both 'self-inclination' and 'others' inclination'. For the remaining fifty-one suttas, the laying down is 'others' inclination'. Thus, the specific type of laying down for these udānas, by way of 'self-inclination' and so on, should be understood.

Ettha ca yāni udānāni bhagavatā bhikkhūnaṃ sammukhā bhāsitāni, tāni tehi yathābhāsitasuttāni vacasā paricitāni manasānupekkhitāni dhammabhaṇḍāgārikassa kathitāni. Yāni pana bhagavatā bhikkhūnaṃ asammukhā bhāsitāni, tānipi aparabhāge bhagavatā dhammabhaṇḍāgārikassa puna bhāsitāni. Evaṃ sabbānipi tāni āyasmā ānando ekajjhaṃ katvā dhārento bhikkhūnañca vācento aparabhāge paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikāle udānantveva saṅgahaṃ āropesīti veditabbaṃ.

And herein, those udānas that were spoken by the Blessed One in the presence of the bhikkhus, those suttas were practiced verbally by them just as they were spoken, reflected upon mentally, and recounted to the Treasurer of the Dhamma. As for those udānas spoken by the Blessed One not in the presence of the bhikkhus, those too were later spoken again by the Blessed One to the Treasurer of the Dhamma. Thus, the Venerable Ānanda, having gathered all of them together, bearing them in mind and teaching them to the bhikkhus, later, at the time of the First Great Council, placed them in the collection as the Udāna. So it should be understood.

Tena kho pana samayenātiādīsu tena samayenāti ca bhummatthe karaṇavacanaṃ, kho panāti nipāto, tasmiṃ samayeti attho. Kasmiṃ pana samaye? Yaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā uruvelāyaṃ viharati najjā nerañjarāya tīre bodhirukkhamūle paṭhamābhisambuddho. Tasmiṃ samaye. Sattāhanti satta ahāni sattāhaṃ, accantasaṃyogatthe etaṃ upayogavacanaṃ. Yasmā bhagavā taṃ sattāhaṃ nirantaratāya accantameva phalasamāpattisukhena vihāsi, tasmā sattāhanti accantasaṃyogavasena upayogavacanaṃ vuttaṃ. Ekapallaṅkenāti visākhāpuṇṇamāya anatthaṅgateyeva sūriye aparājitapallaṅkavare vajirāsane nisinnakālato paṭṭhāya sakimpi anuṭṭhahitvā yathāābhujitena ekeneva pallaṅkena[P 0.0032].

In phrases such as 'Tena kho pana samayena', the phrase 'tena samayena' is an instrumental expression used in the sense of the locative. 'Kho pana' are particles. The meaning is 'at that time' (tasmiṃ samaye). But at what time? At the time when the Blessed One was dwelling at Uruvelā, on the bank of the river Nerañjarā, at the foot of the Bodhi tree, having newly attained supreme enlightenment. At that time. 'Sattāhaṃ' means seven days, a week. This is an accusative expression in the sense of continuous connection. Because the Blessed One dwelt for that week uninterruptedly, with the bliss of the attainment of fruition, therefore 'sattāhaṃ' is stated as an accusative expression by way of continuous connection. 'Ekapallaṅkena' means: from the time he sat on the excellent, unconquered diamond seat on the full moon day of Visākha, before the sun had set, without rising even once, in that single cross-legged posture just as it had been assumed.

Vimuttisukhapaṭisaṃvedīti vimuttisukhaṃ phalasamāpattisukhaṃ paṭisaṃvediyamāno nisinno hotīti attho. Tattha vimuttīti tadaṅgavimutti, vikkhambhanavimutti, samucchedavimutti, paṭippassaddhivimutti, nissaraṇavimuttīti pañca vimuttiyo. Tāsu yaṃ deyyadhammapariccāgādīhi tehi tehi guṇaṅgehi nāmarūpaparicchedādīhi vipassanaṅgehi ca yāva tassa tassa aṅgassa aparihānivasena pavatti, tāva taṃtaṃpaṭipakkhato vimuccanato vimuccanaṃ pahānaṃ. Seyyathidaṃ[M 0.0030]? Dānena macchariyalobhādito, sīlena pāṇātipātādito, nāmarūpavavatthānena sakkāyadiṭṭhito, paccayapariggahena ahetuvisamahetudiṭṭhīhi, tasseva aparabhāgena kaṅkhāvitaraṇena kathaṃkathībhāvato, kalāpasammasanena “ahaṃ mamā”ti gāhato, maggāmaggavavatthānena amagge maggasaññāya, udayadassanena ucchedadiṭṭhiyā, vayadassanena sassatadiṭṭhiyā, bhayadassanena sabhaye abhayasaññāya, ādīnavadassanena [V 0.0027] assādasaññāya, nibbidānupassanena abhiratisaññāya, muccitukamyatāñāṇena amuccitukamyatāya, upekkhāñāṇena anupekkhāya, anulomena dhammaṭṭhitiyaṃ nibbāne ca paṭilomabhāvato, gotrabhunā saṅkhāranimittabhāvato vimuccanaṃ, ayaṃ tadaṅgavimutti nāma. Yaṃ pana upacārappanābhedena samādhinā yāvassa aparihānivasena pavatti, tāva kāmacchandādīnaṃ nīvaraṇānañceva, vitakkādīnañca paccanīkadhammānaṃ, anuppattisaññitaṃ vimuccanaṃ, ayaṃ vikkhambhanavimutti nāma. Yaṃ catunnaṃ ariyamaggānaṃ bhāvitattā taṃtaṃmaggavato ariyassa santāne yathārahaṃ “diṭṭhigatānaṃ pahānāyā”tiādinā (dha. sa. 277; vibha. 628) nayena vuttassa samudayapakkhiyassa kilesagaṇassa puna accantaṃ appavattibhāvena samucchedappahānavasena vimuccanaṃ, ayaṃ samucchedavimutti nāma. Yaṃ pana phalakkhaṇe paṭippassaddhattaṃ kilesānaṃ, ayaṃ paṭippassaddhivimutti nāma. Sabbasaṅkhatanissaṭattā [P 0.0033] pana sabbasaṅkhāravimuttaṃ nibbānaṃ, ayaṃ nissaraṇavimutti nāma. Idha pana bhagavato nibbānārammaṇā phalavimutti adhippetā. Tena vuttaṃ – “vimuttisukhapaṭisaṃvedīti vimuttisukhaṃ phalasamāpattisukhaṃ paṭisaṃvediyamāno nisinno hotīti attho”ti.

Experiencing the bliss of liberation means sitting while experiencing the bliss of liberation, the happiness of fruition attainment—this is the meaning. Herein, “liberation” refers to five types of liberation: liberation by substitution of opposites, liberation by suppression, liberation by cutting off, liberation by tranquilization, and liberation by escape. Among these, whatever liberation occurs through the relinquishment of gifts and other virtuous qualities, and through insight factors such as the determination of name-and-form—as long as those factors remain unweakened—that liberation, by virtue of its freeing from this or that opposing state, is called liberation or abandonment. For example: Through generosity, one is liberated from stinginess and greed; through virtue, from killing and so on; through the determination of name-and-form, from identity view; through the examination of conditions, from wrong views of causelessness and distorted causes; in the subsequent stage, through the overcoming of doubt, from the state of uncertainty; through the contemplation of aggregates, from the grasping of “I” and “mine”; through distinguishing the path from the non-path, from the perception of the non-path as the path; through seeing arising, from the annihilationist view; through seeing passing away, from the eternalist view; through seeing danger, from the perception of safety in what is dangerous; through seeing drawbacks, from the perception of gratification; through disenchantment, from the perception of delight; through the knowledge of the desire for release, from the lack of desire for release; through the knowledge of equanimity, from lack of equanimity; through conformity knowledge, from being contrary to the stable nature of phenomena, that is, Nibbāna; through the change-of-lineage knowledge, from taking formations as an object. This is called liberation by substitution of opposites. Whatever liberation through concentration, whether access or absorption, as long as it remains unweakened—that liberation, designated as the non-arising of the hindrances of sensual desire and so on, and of opposing states such as applied thought—is called liberation by suppression. Whatever liberation occurs through the development of the four noble paths, whereby in the continuum of the noble one, as is appropriate, the group of defilements belonging to the side of arising—as stated in the words “for the abandoning of wrong views” (Dhs. 277; Vibh. 628)—is utterly cut off and ceases permanently by way of abandonment through cutting off, this is called liberation by cutting off. Whatever is the tranquilization of defilements at the moment of fruition, this is called liberation by tranquilization. Nibbāna, however, is called liberation by escape because it has escaped from all conditioned phenomena and is liberated from all formations. Here, however, the fruition-liberation with Nibbāna as its object is intended for the Blessed One. Therefore, it is said: “Experiencing the bliss of liberation means sitting while experiencing the bliss of liberation, the happiness of fruition attainment—this is the meaning.”

Vimuttīti ca upakkilesehi paṭippassaddhivasena cittassa vimuttabhāvo, cittameva vā tathā vimuttaṃ veditabbaṃ, tāya vimuttiyā jātaṃ sampayuttaṃ vā sukhaṃ vimuttisukhaṃ. “Yāyaṃ, bhante, upekkhā sante sukhe vuttā bhagavatā”ti (ma. ni. 2.88) vacanato upekkhāpi cettha sukhamicceva veditabbā. Tathā ca vuttaṃ sammohavinodaniyaṃ “upekkhā pana santattā, sukhamicceva bhāsitā”ti (vibha. aṭṭha. 232). Bhagavā hi catutthajjhānikaṃ arahattasamāpattiṃ samāpajjati, na itaraṃ. Atha vā “tesaṃ vūpasamo sukho”tiādīsu yathā saṅkhāradukkhūpasamo sukhoti vuccati, evaṃ sakalakilesadukkhūpasamabhāvato aggaphale labbhamānā paṭippassaddhivimutti eva idha sukhanti veditabbā. Tayidaṃ vimuttisukhaṃ maggavīthiyaṃ [M 0.0031] kālantareti phalacittassa pavattivibhāgena duvidhaṃ hoti. Ekekassa hi ariyamaggassa anantarā tassa tasseva vipākabhūtāni nibbānārammaṇāni tīṇi dve vā phalacittāni uppajjanti anantaravipākattā lokuttarakusalānaṃ. Yasmiñhi javanavāre ariyamaggo uppajjati, tattha yadā dve anulomāni, tadā tatiyaṃ gotrabhu, catutthaṃ maggacittaṃ, tato paraṃ tīṇi phalacittāni honti. Yadā pana tīṇi anulomāni, tadā catutthaṃ gotrabhu, pañcamaṃ maggacittaṃ, tato paraṃ dve phalacittāni honti. Evaṃ catutthaṃ pañcamaṃ appanāvasena pavattati, na tato paraṃ bhavaṅgassa āsannattā. Keci pana “chaṭṭhampi cittaṃ appetī”ti vadanti, taṃ aṭṭhakathāsu (visuddhi. 2.811) paṭikkhittaṃ. Evaṃ maggavīthiyaṃ phalaṃ veditabbaṃ. Kālantare phalaṃ [V 0.0028] pana phalasamāpattivasena pavattaṃ, nirodhā vuṭṭhahantassa [P 0.0034] uppajjamānañca eteneva saṅgahitaṃ. Sā panāyaṃ phalasamāpatti atthato lokuttarakusalānaṃ vipākabhūtā nibbānārammaṇā appanāti daṭṭhabbā.

“Liberation” refers to the state of the mind being freed through the pacification of defilements, or the mind itself should be understood as thus liberated. The happiness born of or associated with that liberation is the bliss of liberation. Since it is said, “Venerable sir, this equanimity is spoken of by the Blessed One as peaceful happiness” (MN ii 88), here too equanimity should be understood as happiness. Similarly, it is said in the Sammohavinodanī: “Equanimity, being peaceful, is indeed spoken of as happiness” (VibhA 232). For the Blessed One enters the arahant attainment based on the fourth jhāna, not another. Alternatively, just as in such texts as, “Blissful is the cessation of those things,” the cessation of the suffering due to formations is called bliss, so too here the liberation by tranquilization attained in the supreme fruition—being the cessation of all the suffering due to defilements—should be understood as bliss. This bliss of liberation is twofold, according to the division in the occurrence of fruition consciousness: in the path process and in a subsequent period. For immediately after each noble path, three or two resultant fruition consciousnesses arise, having Nibbāna as their object, since supramundane wholesome states have immediate resultants. In the impulsion series where the noble path arises, when there are two conformity moments, the third is change-of-lineage, the fourth is path consciousness, and after that three fruition consciousnesses occur. But when there are three conformity moments, the fourth is change-of-lineage, the fifth is path consciousness, and after that two fruition consciousnesses occur. Thus, the fourth or fifth moment occurs as absorption, but no moment beyond that, owing to the proximity of the life-continuum. Some, however, say that a sixth moment also occurs as absorption, but this is refuted in the commentaries (Vism ii 811). Thus should fruition in the path process be understood. Fruition in a subsequent period, however, is that which occurs through fruition attainment, and the fruition that arises upon emerging from cessation is also included in this. This fruition attainment, in essence, should be seen as absorption that is the resultant of the supramundane wholesome states, having Nibbāna as its object.

Ke taṃ samāpajjanti, ke na samāpajjantīti? Sabbepi puthujjanā na samāpajjanti anadhigatattā. Tathā heṭṭhimā ariyā uparimaṃ, uparimāpi ariyā heṭṭhimaṃ na samāpajjantiyeva puggalantarabhāvūpagamanena paṭippassaddhabhāvato. Attano eva phalaṃ te te ariyā samāpajjanti. Keci pana “sotāpannasakadāgāmino phalasamāpattiṃ na samāpajjanti, uparimā dveyeva samāpajjanti samādhismiṃ paripūrakāribhāvato”ti vadanti. Taṃ akāraṇaṃ puthujjanassāpi attanā paṭiladdhalokiyasamādhisamāpajjanato. Kiṃ vā ettha kāraṇacintāya? Vuttañhetaṃ paṭisambhidāyaṃ “katamā dasa saṅkhārupekkhā vipassanāvasena uppajjanti (paṭi. ma. 1.57), katame dasa gotrabhudhammā vipassanāvasena uppajjantī”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.60) imesaṃ pañhānaṃ vissajjane sotāpattiphalasamāpattatthāya sakadāgāmiphalasamāpattatthāyāti tesampi ariyānaṃ phalasamāpattisamāpajjanaṃ vuttaṃ. Tasmā sabbepi ariyā yathāsakaṃ phalaṃ samāpajjantīti niṭṭhamettha gantabbaṃ.

Who attains it, and who does not? All ordinary people do not attain it because they have not realized it. Similarly, the lower noble ones do not attain the higher, and the higher noble ones do not attain the lower, because they have passed on to another personal state, whereby the former has been tranquillized. Those noble ones attain only their own fruition. However, some say, “Stream-enterers and once-returners do not attain fruition attainment; only the two higher ones attain it because they are fulfillers of concentration.” This is groundless, since even an ordinary person attains the mundane concentration that they have personally gained. Or what is the use of reasoning here? For it was said in the Paṭisambhidāmagga: “Which ten kinds of equanimity towards formations arise through insight? Which ten change-of-lineage factors arise through insight?” In the explanation of these questions, the attainment of fruition attainment by even those noble ones is stated, for the sake of the fruition attainment of stream-entry and for the sake of the fruition attainment of once-returning. Therefore, it should be concluded here that all noble ones attain their respective fruitions.

Kasmā pana te samāpajjantīti? Diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāratthaṃ. Yathā hi rājāno rajjasukhaṃ, devatā dibbasukhaṃ anubhavanti, evaṃ ariyā “lokuttarasukhaṃ [M 0.0032] anubhavissāmā”ti addhānaparicchedaṃ katvā icchitakkhaṇe phalasamāpattiṃ samāpajjanti.

Why do they attain it? For the sake of dwelling happily in this very life. Just as kings enjoy royal happiness and deities enjoy divine happiness, so too do noble ones, having made a determination of the duration, attain fruition attainment at the desired moment, thinking, “We will experience supramundane happiness.”

Kathañcassā samāpajjanaṃ, kathaṃ ṭhānaṃ, kathaṃ vuṭṭhānanti? Dvīhi tāva ākārehi assā samāpajjanaṃ hoti nibbānato aññassa ārammaṇassa amanasikārā, nibbānassa ca manasikārā. Yathāha –

How is its attainment, how is its abiding, and how is the emergence from it? Firstly, its attainment occurs in two ways: by not attending to any object other than Nibbāna, and by attending to Nibbāna. As it is said:

“Dve kho, āvuso, paccayā animittāya cetovimuttiyā samāpattiyā, sabbanimittānañca amanasikāro, animittāya [P 0.0035] ca dhātuyā manasikāro”ti (ma. ni. 1.458).

“Friend, there are two conditions for the attainment of the signless liberation of mind: non-attention to all signs, and attention to the signless element.”

Ayaṃ panettha samāpajjanakkamo – phalasamāpattitthikena ariyasāvakena rahogatena paṭisallīnena udayabbayādivasena saṅkhārā vipassitabbā. Tassevaṃ pavattānupubbavipassanasseva saṅkhārārammaṇagotrabhuñāṇānantaraṃ [V 0.0029] phalasamāpattivasena nirodhe cittamappeti, phalasamāpattininnabhāvena ca sekkhassāpi phalameva uppajjati, na maggo. Ye pana vadanti “sotāpanno attano phalasamāpattiṃ samāpajjissāmīti vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā sakadāgāmī hoti, sakadāgāmī ca anāgāmī”ti. Te vattabbā – evaṃ sante anāgāmī arahā bhavissati, arahā ca paccekabuddho, paccekabuddho ca sambuddhoti āpajjeyya, tasmā yathābhinivesaṃ yathājjhāsayaṃ vipassanā atthaṃ sādhetīti sekkhassāpi phalameva uppajjati, na maggo. Phalampi tassa sace anena paṭhamajjhāniko maggo adhigato, paṭhamajjhānikameva uppajjati. Sace dutiyādīsu aññatarajjhāniko, dutiyādīsu aññatarajjhānikamevāti.

Here is the procedure for attainment: A noble disciple desirous of fruition attainment, having gone to a secluded place and being in solitude, should contemplate formations by way of their arising and passing away, and so forth. For one whose insight thus proceeds in sequence, immediately after the change-of-lineage knowledge which has formations as its object, the mind is directed to cessation by way of fruition attainment. And due to its inclination towards fruition attainment, even for a trainee, only fruition arises, not the path. But as for those who say, “A stream-enterer, intending to attain his own fruition attainment, develops insight and becomes a once-returner; and a once-returner becomes a non-returner,” they should be told: “If that were so, then a non-returner would become an Arahant, an Arahant a Paccekabuddha, and a Paccekabuddha a Sambuddha—this would follow.” Therefore, since insight accomplishes its purpose according to one’s resolve and disposition, even for a trainee, only fruition arises, not the path. And as for that fruition, if the path associated with the first jhāna was attained by this person, then only the fruition associated with the first jhāna arises. If the path associated with one of the other jhānas, from the second onwards, was attained, then only the fruition associated with one of those jhānas arises.

Kasmā panettha gotrabhuñāṇaṃ maggañāṇapurecārikaṃ viya nibbānārammaṇaṃ na hotīti? Phalañāṇānaṃ aniyyānikabhāvato. Ariyamaggadhammāyeva hi niyyānikā. Vuttañhetaṃ “katame dhammā niyyānikā? Cattāro ariyamaggā apariyāpannā”ti (dha. sa. 1295). Tasmā ekanteneva niyyānikabhāvassa ubhato vuṭṭhānabhāvena pavattamānassa anantarapaccayabhūtena ñāṇena nimittato vuṭṭhiteneva bhavitabbanti tassa nibbānārammaṇatā yuttā, na pana ariyamaggassa [M 0.0033] bhāvitattā tassa vipākabhāvena pavattamānānaṃ kilesānaṃ asamucchindanato aniyyānikattā avuṭṭhānasabhāvānaṃ phalañāṇānaṃ purecārikañāṇassa kadācipi nibbānārammaṇatā ubhayattha anulomañāṇānaṃ atulyākārato. Ariyamaggavīthiyañhi anulomañāṇāni anibbiddhapubbānaṃ thūlathūlānaṃ lobhakkhandhādīnaṃ sātisayaṃ padālanena lokiyañāṇena ukkaṃsapāramippattāni maggañāṇānukūlāni uppajjanti, phalasamāpattivīthiyaṃ pana [P 0.0036] tāni tāni tena tena maggena tesaṃ tesaṃ kilesānaṃ samucchinnattā tattha nirussukkāni kevalaṃ ariyānaṃ phalasamāpattisukhasamaṅgibhāvassa parikammamattāni hutvā uppajjantīti na tesaṃ kutoci vuṭṭhānasambhavo, yato tesaṃ pariyosāne ñāṇaṃ saṅkhāranimittaṃ vuṭṭhānato nibbānārammaṇaṃ siyā. Evañca katvā sekkhassa attano phalasamāpattivaḷañjanatthāya udayabbayādivasena saṅkhāre sammasantassa vipassanāñāṇānupubbāya phalameva uppajjati, na maggoti ayañca attho samatthito hoti. Evaṃ tāva phalasamāpattiyā samāpajjanaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Why is it that here the change-of-lineage knowledge, unlike the one that precedes path-knowledge, does not have Nibbāna as its object? Because fruition-knowledges are not of a nature to lead out. For only the dhammas of the noble path are of a nature to lead out. As it is said: "Which dhammas are of a nature to lead out? The four noble paths, which are supramundane" (Dhs. §1295). Therefore, with regard to the knowledge that is the proximate condition for the state of leading-out—which proceeds by emerging from both [formations and defilements]—it must have emerged from the sign [of formations]; thus, its having Nibbāna as its object is proper. However, the fruition-knowledges, because they arise as the result of the developed noble path, do not eradicate defilements, are not of a nature to lead out, and have a nature that does not emerge. Hence, the knowledge that precedes them never has Nibbāna as its object, because the conforming knowledges are dissimilar in nature in the two cases. In the process of the noble path, the conforming knowledges arise having reached the peak of excellence through mundane knowledge, by exceptionally breaking through the gross aggregates of greed and other defilements, which have not been previously penetrated, and are favorable to path-knowledge. But in the process of fruition attainment, since those defilements have already been cut off by the respective paths, these knowledges arise without any exertion, merely as preparatory factors for the noble ones’ partaking of the happiness of fruition attainment. Thus, there is no possibility of their emerging from anything, such that the knowledge at their conclusion could have Nibbāna as its object by emerging from the sign of formations. And thus, for a trainee contemplating formations by way of arising and passing away and so on for the purpose of enjoying their own fruition attainment, through the sequence of insight knowledges only fruition arises, not the path. This meaning is thus established. So far, the way of attaining fruition should be understood in this way.

“Tayo kho, āvuso, paccayā animittāya cetovimuttiyā ṭhitiyā, sabbanimittānaṃ amanasikāro, animittāya ca dhātuyā manasikāro, pubbe ca abhisaṅkhāro”ti (ma. ni. 1.458) –

“Friend, there are three conditions for the stability of the signless liberation of mind: not attending to all signs, attending to the signless element, and prior determination.”

Vacanato [V 0.0030] panassā tīhākārehi ṭhānaṃ hoti. Tattha pubbe ca abhisaṅkhāroti samāpattito pubbe kālaparicchedo. “Asukasmiṃ nāma kāle vuṭṭhahissāmī”ti paricchinnattā hissā yāva so kālo nāgacchati, tāva vuṭṭhānaṃ na hoti.

However, because of the utterance, for this attainment there is stability in three ways. Therein, 'preliminary preparation' means the determination of time before the attainment. Because it is determined for this attainment, 'I will emerge at such-and-such a time,' as long as that time does not arrive, there is no emergence.

“Dve kho, āvuso, paccayā animittāya cetovimuttiyā vuṭṭhānassa, sabbanimittānañca manasikāro, animittāya ca dhātuyā amanasikāro”ti (ma. ni. 1.458) –

"Friends, there are two conditions for emerging from the signless liberation of mind: attention to all signs and non-attention to the signless element."

Vacanato panassā dvīhākārehi vuṭṭhānaṃ hoti. Tattha sabbanimittānanti rūpanimittavedanāsaññāsaṅkhāraviññāṇanimittānaṃ. Kāmañca na sabbānevetāni ekato manasi karoti, sabbasaṅgāhikavasena panevaṃ vuttaṃ. Tasmā yaṃ bhavaṅgassa ārammaṇaṃ, tassa manasikaraṇena phalasamāpattito [M 0.0034] vuṭṭhānaṃ hotīti evaṃ assā vuṭṭhānaṃ veditabbaṃ. Tayidaṃ evamidha samāpajjanavuṭṭhānaṃ arahattaphalabhūtaṃ –

However, because of the utterance, emergence from it occurs in two ways. Therein, 'of all signs' refers to the signs of form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness. And although one does not attend to all these at once, it is said thus by way of complete inclusion. Therefore, emergence from the fruition attainment occurs by attending to the object of the life-continuum—thus, its emergence should be understood. This entering into attainment and emerging from it here is what has become the fruit of Arahantship:

“Paṭippassaddhadarathaṃ, amatārammaṇaṃ subhaṃ;

Vantalokāmisaṃ santaṃ, sāmaññaphalamuttamaṃ”.

"With distress pacified, having the deathless as its object, auspicious, having relinquished the world's bait, peaceful, the supreme fruit of the contemplative life."

Iti vuttaṃ sātātisātaṃ vimuttisukhaṃ paṭisaṃvedesi. Tena vuttaṃ – “vimuttisukhapaṭisaṃvedīti vimuttisukhaṃ phalasamāpattisukhaṃ paṭisaṃvediyamāno nisinno hotīti attho”ti.

Thus it is said, he experienced the bliss of liberation, a pleasure surpassing pleasure. Therefore it was said: 'Experiencing the bliss of liberation' means 'he sits experiencing the bliss of liberation, which is the bliss of the fruition attainment'—this is the meaning.

Athāti adhikāratthe nipāto. Khoti padapūraṇe. Tesu adhikāratthena [P 0.0037] athāti iminā vimuttisukhapaṭisaṃvedanato aññaṃ adhikāraṃ dasseti. Ko panesoti? Paṭiccasamuppādamanasikāro. Athāti vā pacchāti etasmiṃ atthe nipāto, tena “tassa sattāhassa accayenā”ti vakkhamānameva atthaṃ joteti. Tassa sattāhassāti pallaṅkasattāhassa. Accayenāti apagamena. Tamhā samādhimhāti arahattaphalasamādhito. Idha pana ṭhatvā paṭipāṭiyā satta sattāhāni dassetabbānīti keci tāni vitthārayiṃsu. Mayaṃ pana tāni khandhakapāṭhena imissā udānapāḷiyā avirodhadassanamukhena parato vaṇṇayissāma. Rattiyāti avayavasambandhe sāmivacanaṃ. Paṭhamanti accantasaṃyogatthe upayogavacanaṃ. Bhagavā hi tassā rattiyā sakalampi paṭhamaṃ yāmaṃ teneva manasikārena yutto ahosīti.

The word 'atha' is a particle in the sense of a new topic. 'Kho' is a particle for filling out the meter. Among these, by the word 'atha' with the meaning of a new topic, it indicates a matter other than the experiencing of the bliss of liberation. And what is this? Attention to dependent origination. Or, 'atha' is a particle in the sense of 'after'; by this, it illuminates the meaning about to be spoken, namely 'after the passing of that week.' 'Of that week' means of the week of the cross-legged posture. 'By the passing' means by the departure. 'From that concentration' means from the concentration of the fruition of Arahantship. Here, however, some have elaborated that seven weeks should be shown in sequence. But we will explain them later by means of the recitation from the Khandhaka, in a way that does not contradict this Udāna Pāḷi. 'Of the night' (rattiyā) is the genitive case in the sense of a partial relationship. 'The first' (paṭhamaṃ) is the accusative case in the sense of continuous duration. For the Blessed One was engaged in that very attention throughout the entire first watch of that night.

Paṭiccasamuppādanti [V 0.0031] paccayadhammaṃ. Avijjādayo hi paccayadhammā paṭiccasamuppādo. Kathamidaṃ jānitabbanti ce? Bhagavato vacanena. Bhagavatā hi “tasmātihānanda, eseva hetu, etaṃ nidānaṃ, esa samudayo, esa paccayo jarāmaraṇassa, yadidaṃ jāti…pe… saṅkhārānaṃ, yadidaṃ avijjā”ti (dī. ni. 2.105 ādayo) evaṃ avijjādayo hetūti vuttā. Yathā dvādasa paccayā dvādasa paṭiccasamuppādāti.

'Dependent origination' means the phenomena that are conditions. For ignorance and so on, which are the phenomena that are conditions, are 'dependent origination'. If it is asked, 'How is this to be known?' By the word of the Blessed One. For by the Blessed One it was said: 'Therefore, Ānanda, this is the cause, this is the source, this is the origin, this is the condition for aging and death, that is to say, birth… (etc.) …for formations, that is to say, ignorance.' Thus ignorance and so on are said to be causes. As it is said: 'Twelve conditions, twelve dependent originations'.

Tatrāyaṃ vacanattho – aññamaññaṃ paṭicca paṭimukhaṃ katvā kāraṇasamavāyaṃ appaṭikkhipitvā sahite uppādetīti paṭiccasamuppādo. Atha vā paṭicca paccetabbaṃ paccayārahataṃ paccayaṃ paṭigantvā na vinā tena sambandhassa uppādo paṭiccasamuppādo[M 0.0035]. Paṭiccasamuppādoti cettha samuppādapadaṭṭhānavacanaviññeyyo phalassa uppādanasamatthatāyutto hetu, na paṭiccasamuppattimattaṃ veditabbaṃ. Atha vā paccetuṃ arahanti naṃ paṇḍitāti paṭicco, sammā sayameva vā uppādetīti samuppādo, paṭicco ca so samuppādo cāti paṭiccasamuppādoti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo.

Herein, this is the word-analysis: Because it produces effects dependently on one another, having faced each other, without rejecting the conjunction of causes, it is 'dependent origination' (paṭiccasamuppāda). Or, having approached a condition that is fit to be a condition and should be approached, the arising of a related effect, not without that condition, is 'dependent origination'. And here, in 'paṭiccasamuppāda', the cause endowed with the capacity to produce the fruit should be understood by the word 'origination' (samuppāda), not merely the dependent occurrence. Or, because the wise are worthy of approaching it (paccetuṃ arahanti), it is 'dependent' (paṭicca); and because it produces (uppādeti) rightly (sammā) or together (saha), it is 'origination' (samuppāda). Because it is both 'dependent' and an 'origination', it is 'dependent origination'. Thus the meaning should be seen here.

Anulomanti “avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā”tiādinā nayena vutto avijjādiko paccayākāro attanā kattabbakiccakaraṇato anulomoti [P 0.0038] vuccati. Atha vā ādito paṭṭhāya antaṃ pāpetvā vuttattā pavattiyā vā anulomato anulomo, taṃ anulomaṃ. Sādhukaṃ manasākāsīti sakkaccaṃ manasi akāsi. Yo yo paccayadhammo yassa yassa paccayuppannadhammassa yathā yathā hetupaccayādinā paccayabhāvena paccayo hoti, taṃ sabbaṃ aviparītaṃ aparihāpetvā anavasesato paccavekkhaṇavasena citte akāsīti attho. Yathā pana bhagavā paṭiccasamuppādānulomaṃ manasākāsi, taṃ saṅkhepena tāva dassetuṃ “iti imasmiṃ sati idaṃ hoti, imassuppādā idaṃ uppajjatī”ti vuttaṃ.

'Forward order' (anuloma) refers to the sequence of conditions beginning with ignorance, spoken in the manner of 'with ignorance as a condition, formations come to be,' etc. It is called 'forward order' because it performs the task that ought to be done by it. Or, it is 'forward order' because it is spoken starting from the beginning and brought to the end, or because it is in accordance with the process of occurrence. That is the 'forward order'. 'He attended carefully' means he applied his mind respectfully. The meaning is this: he placed in his mind, by way of reflection, the whole matter—without distortion, without omission, and completely—of how each conditioning phenomenon is a condition for each conditioned phenomenon by way of being a condition such as a root condition, etc. But to show briefly how the Blessed One attended to the dependent origination in forward order, it was said: 'This being, that is; from the arising of this, that arises.'

Tattha itīti evaṃ, anena pakārenāti attho. Imasmiṃ sati idaṃ hotīti imasmiṃ avijjādike paccaye sati idaṃ saṅkhārādikaṃ phalaṃ hoti. Imassuppādā idaṃ uppajjatīti imassa avijjādikassa paccayassa uppādā idaṃ saṅkhārādikaṃ phalaṃ uppajjatīti attho. Imasmiṃ asati idaṃ na hoti, imassa nirodhā idaṃ nirujjhatīti avijjādīnaṃ abhāve saṅkhārādīnaṃ abhāvassa avijjādīnaṃ nirodhe saṅkhārādīnaṃ nirodhassa ca dutiyatatiyasuttavacanena etasmiṃ paccayalakkhaṇe niyamo dassito hoti – imasmiṃ sati eva, nāsati. Imassuppādā eva, nānuppādā. Anirodhā eva, na nirodhāti. Tenetaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ antogadhaniyamaṃ idha paṭiccasamuppādassa [V 0.0032] vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Nirodhoti ca avijjādīnaṃ virāgādhigamena āyatiṃ anuppādo appavatti. Tathā hi vuttaṃ – “avijjāya tveva asesavirāganirodhā saṅkhāranirodho”tiādi. Nirodhanirodhī ca uppādanirodhībhāvena vutto “imassa nirodhā idaṃ nirujjhatī”ti.

Herein, iti means 'thus,' that is, 'in this manner.' 'When this exists, that comes to be' means: when this condition, beginning with ignorance, exists, this result, beginning with formations, comes to be. 'With the arising of this, that arises' means: with the arising of this condition, beginning with ignorance, this result, beginning with formations, arises. This is the meaning. 'When this does not exist, that does not come to be; with the cessation of this, that ceases' means: in the absence of things beginning with ignorance, there is the absence of things beginning with formations; and with the cessation of things beginning with ignorance, there is the cessation of things beginning with formations. By the words of the second and third suttas, the fixed nature in this characteristic of a condition is shown: only when this exists, not when it does not exist; only from its arising, not from its non-arising. By this, it should be understood that this characteristic, with its inherent fixed nature, is here spoken of as dependent origination. And 'cessation' is the non-arising, the non-occurrence in the future of things beginning with ignorance, through the attainment of dispassion. For so it is said: 'With the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of formations,' and so on. And cessation is spoken of as being opposed to arising in the phrase 'with the cessation of this, that ceases'.

Tenetaṃ [M 0.0036] dasseti – anirodho uppādo nāma, so cettha atthibhāvotipi vuccatīti. “Imasmiṃ sati idaṃ hotī”ti idameva hi lakkhaṇaṃ pariyāyantarena “imassa uppādā idaṃ uppajjatī”ti vadantena parena purimaṃ visesitaṃ hoti. Tasmā na dharamānataṃyeva sandhāya “imasmiṃ satī”ti vuttaṃ, atha kho maggena aniruddhabhāvañcāti viññāyati. Yasmā ca “imasmiṃ asati idaṃ na hoti, imassa nirodhā idaṃ nirujjhatī”ti [P 0.0039] dvidhāpi uddiṭṭhassa lakkhaṇassa niddesaṃ vadantena “avijjāya tveva asesavirāganirodhā saṅkhāranirodho”tiādinā nirodho eva vutto, tasmā natthibhāvopi nirodho evāti natthibhāvaviruddho atthibhāvo anirodhoti dassitaṃ hoti. Tena anirodhasaṅkhātena atthibhāvena uppādaṃ viseseti. Tato na idha atthibhāvamattaṃ uppādoti attho adhippeto, atha kho anirodhasaṅkhāto atthibhāvo cāti ayamattho vibhāvitoti. Evametaṃ lakkhaṇadvayavacanaṃ aññamaññavisesanavisesitabbabhāvena sātthakanti veditabbaṃ.

By this, it is shown that non-cessation is called arising, and that herein is also called existence. For this very characteristic, 'When this exists, that comes to be,' is specified by the latter statement when expressed in another way as 'with the arising of this, that arises.' Therefore, 'when this exists' is not said referring only to a present state, but rather, it is understood as referring also to the state of not having been ceased by the path. And because, when explaining the characteristic stated in two ways—'when this does not exist, that does not come to be; with the cessation of this, that ceases'—cessation alone is spoken of in the passage beginning, 'With the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of formations,' therefore it is shown that non-existence is also cessation, and that existence, which is the opposite of non-existence, is non-cessation. By that existence, designated as non-cessation, it specifies 'arising.' From this it follows that the intended meaning here is not that arising is mere existence, but rather that it is existence designated as non-cessation—this meaning is clarified. Thus, this pair of statements about the characteristics should be understood as meaningful through their mutual relationship of qualifying and being qualified.

Ko panāyaṃ anirodho nāma, yo “atthibhāvo, uppādo”ti ca vuccatīti? Appahīnabhāvo ca, anibbattitaphalārahatāpahānehi phalānuppādanārahatā ca.
