Ye hi pahātabbā akusalā dhammā, tesaṃ ariyamaggena asamugghāṭitabhāvo ca. Ye pana na pahātabbā kusalābyākatā dhammā, yāni tesu saṃyojanāni akhīṇāsavānaṃ tesaṃ aparikkhīṇatā ca. Asamugghāṭitānusayatāya hi sasaṃyojanā khandhappavatti paṭiccasamuppādo. Tathā ca vuttaṃ –

And what is this called 'non-cessation,' which is also referred to as 'existence' and 'arising'? It is the state of not being abandoned, and the capability of producing a fruit, a capability that is not removed through the non-abandonment of its conditions. For those unwholesome states that are to be abandoned, it is their state of not having been uprooted by the noble path. As for those wholesome and indeterminate states that are not to be abandoned, it is the non-exhaustion of the fetters related to them in those whose taints are not destroyed. For, due to the non-uprooting of the latent tendencies, the continuation of the aggregates together with the fetters is dependent origination. And so it is said:

“Yāya ca, bhikkhave, avijjāya nivutassa bālassa yāya ca taṇhāya sampayuttassa ayaṃ kāyo samudāgato, sā ceva avijjā bālassa appahīnā, sā ca taṇhā aparikkhīṇā. Taṃ kissa hetu? Na, bhikkhave, bālo acari brahmacariyaṃ sammā dukkhakkhayāya, tasmā bālo kāyassa bhedā kāyūpago hoti, so kāyūpago samāno na parimuccati jātiyā jarāmaraṇenā”tiādi (saṃ. ni. 2.19).

'Bhikkhus, for the fool who is shrouded by that ignorance and bound to that craving, this body has come to be. That ignorance has not been abandoned by the fool, and that craving has not been exhausted. For what reason? Because, bhikkhus, the fool has not lived the holy life rightly for the complete destruction of suffering. Therefore, upon the breakup of the body, the fool goes to another body. Having gone to another body, he is not freed from birth, aging, and death,' and so on (Saṃyutta Nikāya 2.19).

Khīṇasaṃyojanānaṃ [M 0.0037][V 0.0033] pana avijjāya abhāvato saṅkhārānaṃ, taṇhupādānānaṃ abhāvato upādānabhavānaṃ asambhavoti vaṭṭassa upacchedo paññāyissatīti. Tenevāha –

But for those whose fetters are destroyed, due to the absence of ignorance, there is an absence of formations; and due to the absence of craving and clinging, there is no possibility of clinging and becoming. Thus, the cutting off of the round is made known. Therefore, he said:

“Channaṃ tveva, phagguṇa, phassāyatanānaṃ asesavirāganirodhā phassanirodho, phassanirodhā vedanānirodho”tiādi (saṃ. ni. 2.12).

'Indeed, Phagguna, with the remainderless fading away and cessation of the six contact-bases, there is the cessation of contact. With the cessation of contact, there is the cessation of feeling,' and so on (Saṃyutta Nikāya 2.12).

Na hi aggamaggādhigamato uddhaṃ yāva parinibbānā saḷāyatanādīnaṃ appavatti. Atha kho natthitā nirodhasaddavacanīyatā khīṇasaṃyojanatāti nirodho vutto. Apica cirakatampi kammaṃ anibbattitaphalatāya appahīnāhāratāya ca phalārahaṃ santaṃ eva nāma hoti, na nibbattitaphalaṃ[P 0.0040], nāpi pahīnāhāranti. Phaluppattipaccayānaṃ avijjāsaṅkhārādīnaṃ vuttanayeneva phalārahabhāvo anirodhoti veditabbo. Evaṃ aniruddhabhāveneva hi yena vinā phalaṃ na sambhavati, taṃ kāraṇaṃ atītantipi imasmiṃ satīti iminā vacanena vuttaṃ. Tatoyeva ca avusitabrahmacariyassa appavattidhammataṃ anāpanno paccayuppādo kālabhedaṃ anāmasitvā anivattanāya eva imassa uppādāti vutto. Atha vā avasesapaccayasamavāye avijjamānassapi vijjamānassa viya pageva vijjamānassa yā phaluppattiabhimukhatā, sā imassa uppādāti vuttā. Tathā hi tato phalaṃ uppajjatīti tadavatthaṃ kāraṇaṃ phalassa uppādanabhāvena uṭṭhitaṃ uppatitaṃ nāma hoti, na vijjamānampi atadavatthanti tadavatthatā uppādoti veditabbo.

For there is no non-occurrence of the six sense-bases and so on from the attainment of the highest path up until final Nibbāna. Rather, 'cessation' is spoken of because the state of having destroyed the fetters is a state of non-existence and is fit to be expressed by the word 'cessation.' Moreover, even kamma done long ago, because its fruit has not been produced and its nutriment has not been abandoned, is indeed capable of fruiting and is considered existent; its fruit has not been produced, nor has its nutriment been abandoned. The state of being capable of fruiting should be understood as 'non-cessation' in the manner explained for the conditions for the arising of a result, such as ignorance, formations, and so on. For it is precisely by reason of this state of non-cessation that the cause, without which the result cannot come to be, is spoken of with the words 'when this exists,' even if it is past. And for this very reason, for one who has not lived the holy life to completion, the arising of a condition that has not attained a state of non-occurrence is spoken of as 'the arising of this' for the sake of its irreversibility, without regard to distinctions of time. Alternatively, when the remaining conditions converge, that orientation towards the arising of a fruit—even of a condition that is not present, as if it were present, and all the more so when it is present—is what is called 'the arising of this.' For since the result arises from that, the cause in that state is said to have arisen, to have sprung up, by virtue of its being in the state of producing the result. It is not that it exists in another state. Therefore, 'arising' should be understood as being in that very state.

Tattha satīti iminā vijjamānatāmattena paccayabhāvaṃ vadanto abyāpārataṃ paṭiccasamuppādassa dasseti. Uppādāti uppattidhammataṃ asabbakālabhāvitaṃ phaluppattiabhimukhatañca dīpento aniccataṃ paṭiccasamuppādassa dasseti. “Sati, nāsati, uppādā, na nirodhā”ti pana hetuatthehi bhummanissakkavacanehi samatthitaṃ nidānasamudayajātipabhavabhāvaṃ paṭiccasamuppādassa dasseti. Hetuatthatā cettha bhummavacane yassa bhāve tadavinābhāviphalassa bhāvo lakkhīyati, tattha pavattiyā veditabbā yathā “adhanānaṃ dhane ananuppadīyamāne dāliddiyaṃ vepullaṃ agamāsī”ti (dī. ni. 3.91) ca “nipphannesu sassesu subhikkhaṃ jāyatī”ti ca. Nissakkavacanassāpi hetuatthatā phalassa pabhave pakatiyañca pavattito yathā “kalalā hoti [M 0.0038] abbudaṃ, abbudā jāyatī pesī”ti (saṃ. ni. 1.235) ca “himavatā gaṅgā pabhavanti, siṅgato saro jāyatī”ti ca. Avijjādibhāve ca tadavinābhāvena saṅkhārādibhāvo lakkhīyati, avijjādīhi ca saṅkhārādayo pabhavanti pakariyanti [V 0.0034] cāti te tesaṃ pabhavo pakati ca, tasmā tadatthadīpanatthaṃ “imasmiṃ sati imassa uppādā”ti hetuatthe bhummanissakkaniddesā katāti.

Herein, by 'when there is' (sati), in speaking of conditionality through mere presence, He shows the non-active nature of dependent origination. By 'from arising' (uppādā), in illuminating its nature of arising, its not being constantly existent, and its orientation towards the arising of a result, He reveals the impermanence of dependent origination. Moreover, by means of locative and ablative expressions with causal meaning—'when there is,' 'when there is not,' 'from arising,' 'not from cessation'—He demonstrates the well-established nature of dependent origination as being a source, an origin, a birth, and a producer. Herein, the causal meaning in the locative expression is understood where the presence of one thing signifies the presence of its inseparable result, and its occurrence is to be known as in: 'When wealth is not provided for the poor, poverty became widespread' and 'When crops are harvested, there is abundance.' The causal meaning of the ablative expression is also due to its operating in the production and nature of the result, as in: 'From the first embryonic stage comes the second; from the second, the lump of flesh is born' and 'From the Himalayas the Ganges originates; from the peak a lake is born.' And when ignorance and other factors are present, formations and other states are discerned as inseparable from them; and from ignorance and the rest, formations and the like arise and are produced, thus they are their origin and nature. Therefore, to clarify this meaning, the locative and ablative indications with causal meaning—'when this is... from the arising of this...'—were made.

Yasmā [P 0.0041] cettha “imasmiṃ sati idaṃ hoti, imassuppādā idaṃ uppajjatī”ti saṅkhepena uddiṭṭhassa paṭiccasamuppādassa “avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā”tiādiko niddeso, tasmā yathāvutto atthibhāvo uppādo ca tesaṃ tesaṃ paccayuppannadhammānaṃ paccayabhāvoti viññāyati. Na hi aniruddhatāsaṅkhātaṃ atthibhāvaṃ uppādañca anivattasabhāvatāsaṅkhātaṃ udayāvatthatāsaṅkhātaṃ vā “sati eva, nāsati, uppādā eva, na nirodhā”ti antogadhaniyamehi vacanehi abhihitaṃ muñcitvā añño paccayabhāvo nāma atthi, tasmā yathāvutto atthibhāvo uppādo ca paccayabhāvoti veditabbaṃ. Yepi paṭṭhāne āgatā hetuādayo catuvīsati paccayā, tepi etasseva paccayabhāvassa visesāti veditabbā. Iti yathā vitthārena anulomaṃ paṭiccasamuppādaṃ manasi akāsi, taṃ dassetuṃ, “yadidaṃ avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

Since herein, for the dependent origination briefly stated as 'when this is, that is; with the arising of this, that arises,' the exposition beginning with 'with ignorance as condition, formations' is given, therefore, the aforementioned presence and arising are understood to be the conditionality of those respective conditionally arisen phenomena. For there is no other conditionality apart from that which is expressed by statements with inherent restrictions—such as, 'only when there is, not when there is not; only from arising, not from cessation'—referring to presence designated as non-cessation, and arising designated as having a non-reversing nature or as the state of coming into being. Thus, the aforementioned presence and arising should be understood as conditionality. Even the twenty-four conditions, such as root-condition and others, which come in the Paṭṭhāna, should be understood as specific aspects of this very conditionality. Thus, to show how He mentally attended to dependent origination in detail and in forward order, it was said, 'that is, with ignorance as condition, formations,' and so on.

Tattha yadidanti nipāto, tassa yo ayanti attho. Avijjāpaccayātiādīsu avindiyaṃ kāyaduccaritādiṃ vindatīti avijjā, vindiyaṃ kāyasucaritādiṃ na vindatīti avijjā, dhammānaṃ aviparītasabhāvaṃ aviditaṃ karotīti avijjā, antavirahite saṃsāre bhavādīsu satte javāpetīti avijjā, avijjamānesu javati vijjamānesu na javatīti avijjā, vijjāya paṭipakkhāti avijjā, sā “dukkhe aññāṇa”ntiādinā catubbidhā veditabbā. Paṭicca na vinā phalaṃ eti uppajjati ceva pavattati cāti paccayo, upakārakattho vā paccayo. Avijjā ca sā paccayo cāti avijjāpaccayo, tasmā avijjāpaccayā. Saṅkharontīti saṅkhārā, lokiyakusalākusalacetanā, sā puññāpuññāneñjābhisaṅkhāravasena tividhā veditabbā. Vijānātīti viññāṇaṃ, taṃ lokiyavipākaviññāṇavasena dvattiṃsavidhaṃ. Namatīti nāmaṃ, vedanādikkhandhattayaṃ. Ruppatīti rūpaṃ, bhūtarūpaṃ cakkhādiupādārūpañca. Āyatati āyatañca [M 0.0039] saṃsāradukkhaṃ nayatīti āyatanaṃ[P 0.0042]. Phusatīti phasso. Vedayatīti vedanā. Idampi dvayaṃ dvāravasena chabbidhaṃ, vipākavasena gahaṇe chattiṃsavidhaṃ. Paritassatīti taṇhā, sā kāmataṇhādivasena saṅkhepato tividhā, vitthārato aṭṭhuttarasatavidhā ca. Upādīyatīti upādānaṃ, taṃ kāmupādānādivasena catubbidhaṃ. Bhavati bhāvayati cāti bhavo, so kammūpapattibhedato duvidho. Jananaṃ jāti. Jīraṇaṃ jarā. Maranti tenāti maraṇaṃ. Socanaṃ soko. Paridevanaṃ paridevo. Dukkhayatīti dukkhaṃ, uppādaṭṭhitivasena dvedhā khaṇatīti dukkhaṃ. Dumanassa bhāvo domanassaṃ. Bhuso āyāso upāyāso[V 0.0035]. Sambhavantīti nibbattanti. Na kevalañca sokādīhiyeva, atha kho sabbapadehi “sambhavantī”ti padassa yojanā kātabbā. Evañhi “avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā sambhavantī”ti paccayapaccayuppannavavatthānaṃ dassitaṃ hoti. Esa nayo sabbattha.

Herein, 'that is' (yadidaṃ) is a particle, and its meaning is 'which is this' (yo ayaṃ). In 'with ignorance as condition,' etc.: Ignorance (avijjā) is that which finds (vindati) what is not to be found (avindiyaṃ), such as bodily misconduct; and does not find (na vindati) what is to be found (vindiyaṃ), such as bodily good conduct. It makes the unperverted nature of phenomena unknown. It causes beings to run on (javāpeti) in the endless cycle of existence, in states of becoming, etc. It runs on (javati) in what is non-existent and does not run on in what is existent. It is the opposite of knowledge (vijjā). It should be understood as fourfold, beginning with 'ignorance concerning suffering.' A condition (paccayo) is so called because dependent upon it (paṭicca), a result comes to be (eti), arises, and continues, and not without it; or, a condition has the meaning of being supportive. Ignorance is itself a condition, thus 'ignorance-condition' (avijjāpaccayo); therefore, 'from ignorance as condition' (avijjāpaccayā). 'They form' (saṅkharonti), thus they are formations (saṅkhārā); these are worldly wholesome and unwholesome volitions. They should be understood as threefold by way of meritorious, demeritorious, and imperturbable formations. 'It cognizes' (vijānāti), thus it is consciousness (viññāṇaṃ); this is thirty-twofold by way of mundane resultant consciousness. 'It inclines' (namati), thus it is name (nāmaṃ); this is the triad of aggregates beginning with feeling. 'It is afflicted' (ruppati), thus it is form (rūpaṃ); this is material form, both primary elements and derived form beginning with the eye. It extends (āyatati) and leads (nayati) to long (āyataṃ) suffering in saṃsāra, thus it is a base (āyatanaṃ). 'It contacts' (phusati), thus it is contact (phasso). 'It feels' (vedayati), thus it is feeling (vedanā). This pair is sixfold by way of the sense doors; when taken by way of result, it is thirty-sixfold. 'It thirsts' (paritassati), thus it is craving (taṇhā); this is threefold in brief by way of sensual craving, etc., and one hundred and eightfold in detail. 'It clings' (upādīyati), thus it is clinging (upādānaṃ); this is fourfold by way of clinging to sensual pleasures, etc. 'It becomes and brings into being' (bhavati bhāvayati), thus it is becoming (bhavo); this is twofold by the distinction of kamma-becoming and rebirth-becoming. Generating (jananaṃ) is birth (jāti). Ageing (jīraṇaṃ) is old age (jarā). 'Beings die by means of it' (maranti tena), thus it is death (maraṇaṃ). Grieving (socanaṃ) is sorrow (soko). Lamenting (paridevanaṃ) is lamentation (paridevo). 'It causes suffering' (dukkhayati), thus it is suffering (dukkhaṃ); or, it destroys (khaṇati) in two ways, by arising and by presence, thus it is suffering. The state of a troubled mind (dumanassa bhāvo) is dejection (domanassaṃ). Intense fatigue (bhuso āyāso) is despair (upāyāso). 'They come into being' (sambhavanti) means they are produced (nibbattanti). The word 'come into being' should be connected not only with sorrow and the rest, but with all the terms. For in this way, by saying 'from ignorance as condition, formations come into being,' the distinction between condition and conditioned phenomena is shown. This is the method in all cases.

Tattha aññāṇalakkhaṇā avijjā, sammohanarasā, chādanapaccupaṭṭhānā, āsavapadaṭṭhānā. Abhisaṅkharaṇalakkhaṇā saṅkhārā, āyūhanarasā, saṃvidahanapaccupaṭṭhānā, avijjāpadaṭṭhānā. Vijānanalakkhaṇaṃ viññāṇaṃ, pubbaṅgamarasaṃ, paṭisandhipaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, saṅkhārapadaṭṭhānaṃ, vatthārammaṇapadaṭṭhānaṃ vā. Namanalakkhaṇaṃ nāmaṃ, sampayogarasaṃ, avinibbhogapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, viññāṇapadaṭṭhānaṃ. Ruppanalakkhaṇaṃ rūpaṃ, vikiraṇarasaṃ, appaheyyabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, viññāṇapadaṭṭhānaṃ. Āyatanalakkhaṇaṃ saḷāyatanaṃ, dassanādirasaṃ, vatthudvārabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, nāmarūpapadaṭṭhānaṃ. Phusanalakkhaṇo phasso, saṅghaṭṭanaraso, saṅgatipaccupaṭṭhāno, saḷāyatanapadaṭṭhāno. Anubhavanalakkhaṇā [P 0.0043] vedanā, visayarasasambhogarasā, sukhadukkhapaccupaṭṭhānā, phassapadaṭṭhānā. Hetubhāvalakkhaṇā taṇhā, abhinandanarasā, atittibhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā, vedanāpadaṭṭhānā. Gahaṇalakkhaṇaṃ upādānaṃ, amuñcanarasaṃ, taṇhādaḷhattadiṭṭhipaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, taṇhāpadaṭṭhānaṃ. Kammakammaphalalakkhaṇo bhavo, bhavanabhāvanaraso, kusalākusalābyākatapaccupaṭṭhāno, upādānapadaṭṭhāno. Tattha tattha bhave paṭhamābhinibbattilakkhaṇā jāti, niyyātanarasā, atītabhavato idhuppannapaccupaṭṭhānā, dukkhavicittatāpaccupaṭṭhānā vā. Khandhaparipākalakkhaṇā jarā, maraṇūpanayanarasā, yobbanavināsapaccupaṭṭhānā. Cutilakkhaṇaṃ maraṇaṃ[M 0.0040], visaṃyogarasaṃ, gativippavāsapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ. Antonijjhānalakkhaṇo soko, cetaso nijjhānaraso, anusocanapaccupaṭṭhāno. Lālappanalakkhaṇo paridevo, guṇadosaparikittanaraso, sambhamapaccupaṭṭhāno. Kāyapīḷanalakkhaṇaṃ dukkhaṃ, duppaññānaṃ domanassakaraṇarasaṃ, kāyikābādhapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ. Cittapīḷanalakkhaṇaṃ domanassaṃ, manovighātanarasaṃ, mānasabyādhipaccupaṭṭhānaṃ. Cittaparidahanalakkhaṇo upāyāso, nitthunanaraso, visādapaccupaṭṭhāno. Evamete avijjādayo lakkhaṇāditopi veditabbāti. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthāro pana sabbākārasampannaṃ vinicchayaṃ icchantena sammohavinodaniyā (vibha. aṭṭha. 225) vibhaṅgaṭṭhakathāya gahetabbo.

Herein, ignorance has the characteristic of unknowing, the function of delusion, the manifestation of concealing, and the taints as its proximate cause. Formations have the characteristic of fabrication, the function of accumulating, the manifestation of arranging, and ignorance as their proximate cause. Consciousness has the characteristic of cognizing, the function of being the forerunner, the manifestation of rebirth-linking, and formations as its proximate cause, or alternatively, the base and object. Name has the characteristic of bending, the function of association, the manifestation of inseparability, and consciousness as its proximate cause. Form has the characteristic of being afflicted, the function of being dispersed, the manifestation of being unabandonable, and consciousness as its proximate cause. The six sense bases have the characteristic of a sphere, the function of seeing and so on, the manifestation as base and door, and name-and-form as their proximate cause. Contact has the characteristic of touching, the function of impacting, the manifestation of meeting, and the six sense bases as its proximate cause. Feeling has the characteristic of experiencing, the function of enjoying the flavour of the object, the manifestation of pleasure and pain, and contact as its proximate cause. Craving has the characteristic of being a cause, the function of delighting, the manifestation of insatiability, and feeling as its proximate cause. Clinging has the characteristic of grasping, the function of not letting go, the manifestation of the strengthening of craving and views, and craving as its proximate cause. Becoming has the characteristic of kamma and its result, the function of being and causing to be, the manifestation of wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate states, and clinging as its proximate cause. Birth has the characteristic of first arising in such and such an existence, the function of issuing forth, the manifestation of arising here from a past existence, or alternatively, the manifestation of the diversity of suffering. Ageing has the characteristic of the maturing of the aggregates, the function of leading towards death, the manifestation of the destruction of youth. Death has the characteristic of passing away, the function of separation, the manifestation of departure from a state of existence. Sorrow has the characteristic of internal burning, the function of mental burning, the manifestation of grieving. Lamentation has the characteristic of wailing, the function of proclaiming virtues and faults, the manifestation of agitation. Pain has the characteristic of bodily affliction, the function of causing mental distress for those of little wisdom, the manifestation of bodily ailment. Grief has the characteristic of mental affliction, the function of mental vexation, the manifestation of mental disorder. Despair has the characteristic of mental scorching, the function of groaning, the manifestation of despondency. Thus, these factors beginning with ignorance should be understood in terms of their characteristics and so on. This is the summary here. As for the detailed exposition, one who desires a complete analysis should consult the Vibhaṅga Commentary, the Sammohavinodanī (The Dispeller of Delusion).

Evanti niddiṭṭhassa nidassanaṃ, tena avijjādīheva kāraṇehi, na issaranimmānādīhīti dasseti. Etassāti yathāvuttassa. Kevalassāti asammissassa sakalassa vā. Dukkhakkhandhassāti [V 0.0036] dukkhasamūhassa, na sattassa, nāpi jīvassa, nāpi subhasukhādīnaṃ. Samudayo hotīti nibbatti sambhavati.

Thus (evaṃ) is an illustration of what has been pointed out, thereby showing that it is by causes such as ignorance, and not by creation by a lord, etc. 'Of this' (etassa), that is, of what has been stated. 'Of the whole' (kevalassa), that is, of what is unmixed or complete. 'Of the mass of suffering' (dukkhakkhandhassa), that is, of the aggregate of suffering, not of a being, nor of a life, nor of pleasant happiness, etc. 'Arising' (samudayo) occurs, that is, production (nibbatti) comes to be (sambhavati).

Etamatthaṃ [P 0.0044] viditvāti yvāyaṃ avijjādivasena saṅkhārādikassa dukkhakkhandhassa samudayo hotīti vutto, sabbākārena etamatthaṃ viditvā. Tāyaṃ velāyanti tāyaṃ tassa atthassa viditavelāyaṃ. Imaṃ udānaṃ udānesīti imaṃ tasmiṃ atthe vidite hetuno ca hetusamuppannadhammassa ca pajānanāya ānubhāvadīpakaṃ “yadā have pātubhavantī”tiādikaṃ somanassasampayuttañāṇasamuṭṭhānaṃ udānaṃ udānesi, attamanavācaṃ nicchāresīti vuttaṃ hoti.

Having understood this matter (etamatthaṃ viditvā), that is, having understood in every way this matter which has been stated as the arising of the mass of suffering, beginning with formations, by way of ignorance, etc. 'At that time' (tāyaṃ velāyaṃ), that is, at the time of understanding that matter. 'He uttered this inspired utterance' (imaṃ udānaṃ udānesi), it is said that when that matter was understood, he uttered this inspired utterance, beginning with 'When indeed phenomena appear,' which illuminates the power of understanding both the cause and the phenomena arisen from the cause, arising from knowledge accompanied by joy, and he expressed a gladdened speech.

Tassattho – yadāti yasmiṃ kāle. Haveti byattanti imasmiṃ atthe nipāto. Keci pana “haveti āhave yuddhe”ti atthaṃ vadanti, “yodhetha māraṃ paññāvudhenā”ti (dha. pa. 40) vacanato kilesamārena yujjhanasamayeti tesaṃ adhippāyo. Pātubhavantīti uppajjanti. Dhammāti anulomapaccayākārapaṭivedhasādhakā bodhipakkhiyadhammā. Atha vā pātubhavantīti pakāsenti, abhisamayavasena byattā pākaṭā honti. Dhammāti catuariyasaccadhammā, ātāpo vuccati kilesasantāpanaṭṭhena vīriyaṃ. Ātāpinoti sammappadhānavīriyavato. Jhāyatoti ārammaṇūpanijjhānena [M 0.0041] lakkhaṇūpanijjhānena jhāyantassa. Brāhmaṇassāti bāhitapāpassa khīṇāsavassa. Athassa kaṅkhā vapayanti sabbāti athassa evaṃ pātubhūtadhammassa yā etā “ko nu kho, bhante, phusatīti. No kallo pañhoti bhagavā avocā”tiādinā (saṃ. ni. 2.12) nayena, “katamaṃ nu kho, bhante, jarāmaraṇaṃ, kassa ca panidaṃ jarāmaraṇanti. No kallo pañhoti bhagavā avocā”tiādinā (saṃ. ni. 2.35) nayena paccayākāre kaṅkhā vuttā, yā ca paccayākārasseva appaṭividdhattā “ahosiṃ nu kho ahaṃ atītamaddhāna”ntiādinā (ma. ni. 1.18; saṃ. ni. 2.20) soḷasa kaṅkhā āgatā. Tā sabbā vapayanti apagacchanti nirujjhanti. Kasmā? Yato pajānāti sahetudhammaṃ, yasmā avijjādikena hetunā sahetukaṃ imaṃ saṅkhārādikaṃ kevalaṃ dukkhakkhandhadhammaṃ pajānāti aññāsi paṭivijjhīti.

The meaning of that is: 'When' (yadā) means at what time. 'Indeed' (have) is a particle in the sense of 'manifestly.' Some, however, say the meaning is 'in battle, in war' (āhave yuddhe), their intention being that it refers to the time of fighting the defilement-Māra, according to the saying, 'One should fight Māra with the weapon of wisdom' (Dhp 40). 'Appear' (pātubhavanti) means they arise. 'Phenomena' (dhammā) refers to the factors of enlightenment that facilitate the penetration of the conditional pattern in conformity with the truth. Alternatively, 'appear' (pātubhavanti) means they become manifest; through direct realization, they become evident and clear. 'Phenomena' (dhammā) refers to the Four Noble Truths. 'Ardent' (ātāpo) refers to energy (vīriya) in the sense of burning up the defilements. 'Of one who is ardent' (ātāpino) means of one who possesses the energy of the right strivings. 'Meditating' (jhāyato) means of one who meditates by means of focusing on the object and focusing on the characteristics. 'Of the brahmin' (brāhmaṇassa) refers to one who has banished evil, a destroyer of the taints. 'Then all his doubts vanish' (athassa kaṅkhā vapayanti sabbā): for one in whom these phenomena have thus manifested, all those doubts concerning the conditional pattern, such as those expressed in the questions: 'Venerable sir, who contacts?' 'The question is not proper,' the Blessed One said (SN 2.12), and 'Venerable sir, what is ageing-and-death, and for whom is this ageing-and-death?' 'The question is not proper,' the Blessed One said (SN 2.35), as well as the sixteen doubts that arise from not having penetrated the conditional pattern itself, such as 'Did I exist in the past?' (MN 1.18; SN 2.20)—all these vanish, depart, and cease. Why? 'Because he understands the phenomenon with its cause' (yato pajānāti sahetudhammaṃ). Because he understands, has understood, and has penetrated this entire phenomenon of the mass of suffering, of formations and so on, together with its cause, which is conditioned by the cause of ignorance and so on.

Kadā panassa bodhipakkhiyadhammā catusaccadhammā vā pātubhavanti uppajjanti pakāsenti vā? Vipassanāmaggañāṇesu[P 0.0045]. Tattha vipassanāñāṇasampayuttā satiādayo vipassanāñāṇañca yathārahaṃ attano visayesu tadaṅgappahānavasena subhasaññādike pajahantā kāyānupassanādivasena visuṃ visuṃ uppajjanti, maggakkhaṇe pana te nibbānamālambitvā samucchedavasena paṭipakkhe pajahantā [V 0.0037] catūsupi ariyasaccesu asammohappaṭivedhasādhanavasena sakideva uppajjanti. Evaṃ tāvettha bodhipakkhiyadhammānaṃ uppajjanaṭṭhena pātubhāvo veditabbo.

When, for the Blessed One, do the factors of enlightenment or the four truths become manifest, arise, or appear? In the insight-knowledge and path-knowledge. Therein, mindfulness and other factors associated with insight-knowledge, along with insight-knowledge itself, arise separately in their respective objects—such as in the contemplation of the body and so on—abandoning perceptions of beauty and the like by way of abandonment by substitution. However, at the moment of the path, they arise all at once, taking Nibbāna as their object, abandoning their opposites by way of eradication, and serving as the means for penetrating the Four Noble Truths without delusion. Thus, the manifestation of the factors of enlightenment should be understood herein in the sense of their arising.

Ariyasaccadhammānaṃ pana lokiyānaṃ vipassanākkhaṇe vipassanāya ārammaṇakaraṇavasena, lokuttarānaṃ tadadhimuttatāvasena, maggakkhaṇe nirodhasaccassa ārammaṇābhisamayavasena, sabbesampi kiccābhisamayavasena pākaṭabhāvato pakāsanaṭṭhena pātubhāvo veditabbo.

As for the Noble Truths, their manifestation should be understood in the sense of making manifest, because they are apparent: for the mundane truths, at the moment of insight, by way of making them an object for insight; for the supramundane truths, by way of being inclined towards them; at the moment of the path, for the truth of cessation, by way of penetrating it as an object, and for all of them, by way of penetrating their respective functions.

Iti bhagavā satipi sabbākārena sabbadhammānaṃ attano ñāṇassa pākaṭabhāve paṭiccasamuppādamukhena vipassanābhinivesassa katattā nipuṇagambhīrasududdasatāya paccayākārassa taṃ paccavekkhitvā uppannabalavasomanasso paṭipakkhasamucchedavibhāvanena saddhiṃ attano tadabhisamayānubhāvadīpakamevettha udānaṃ udānesīti.

Thus, the Blessed One—although all phenomena were in every way manifest to his own knowledge—because he had made the application to insight by way of dependent origination, and because of the subtle, profound, and very difficult to see nature of the causal pattern, having reviewed it, with strong joy having arisen, uttered this inspired utterance, which, together with the explanation of the eradication of opposing factors, reveals the very power of his own penetration of that.

Ayampi [M 0.0042] udāno vutto bhagavatā iti me sutanti ayaṃ pāḷi kesuciyeva potthakesu dissati. Tattha ayampīti pisaddo “idampi buddhe ratanaṃ paṇītaṃ, ayampi pārājiko hotī”tiādīsu viya sampiṇḍanattho, tena uparimaṃ sampiṇḍeti. Vuttoti ayaṃ vuttasaddo kesohāraṇavappanavāpasamīkaraṇajīvitavuttipamuttabhāvapāvacanabhāvena pavattana ajjhenakathanādīsu dissati. Tathā hesa “kāpaṭiko māṇavo daharo vuttasiro”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 2.426) kesohāraṇe āgato.

'This inspired utterance, too, was spoken by the Blessed One—thus have I heard.' This Pāḷi text is found in only some manuscripts. Therein, in 'ayampi,' the particle 'pi' has the meaning of collecting together, as in 'This, too, is a precious gem in the Buddha,' and 'This one, too, commits a pārājika offense.' By this, it collects together what is to come. The word 'vutta' is seen in meanings such as hair-cutting, sowing, smoothing the ground, livelihood, being freed, utterance as a noble statement, recitation, and speaking. For instance, it appears in the sense of hair-cutting in 'the young brahmin Kāpaṭika, a youth with a shaven head' (MN 2.426).

“Gāvo tassa pajāyanti, khette vuttaṃ virūhati;

Vuttānaṃ phalamasnāti, yo mittānaṃ na dubbhatī”ti. –

For him who is not treacherous to friends, cows multiply, what is sown in the field sprouts, and he enjoys the fruit of what is sown.

Ādīsu [P 0.0046] (jā. 2.22.19) vappane. “No ca kho paṭivutta”ntiādīsu (pārā. 289) aṭṭhadaṇḍakādīhi vāpasamīkaraṇe. “Pannalomo paradattavutto migabhūtena cetasā viharāmī”tiādīsu (cūḷava. 332) jīvitavuttiyaṃ. “Paṇḍupalāso bandhanā pavutto abhabbo haritattāyā”tiādīsu (pārā. 92) bandhanato pamuttabhāve. “Gītaṃ vuttaṃ samīhita”ntiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.285) pāvacanabhāvena pavattite. “Vutto pārāyaṇo”tiādīsu ajjhene. “Vuttaṃ kho panetaṃ bhagavatā ‘dhammadāyādā me, bhikkhave, bhavatha, mā āmisadāyādā’”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.30) kathane. Idhāpi kathane eva daṭṭhabbo, tena ayampi udāno bhāsitoti attho. Itīti evaṃ. Me sutanti padadvayassa attho nidānavaṇṇanāyaṃ [V 0.0038] sabbākārato vuttoyeva. Pubbe “evaṃ me suta”nti nidānavasena vuttoyeva hi attho idha nigamanavasena “iti me suta”nti puna vutto. Vuttasseva hi atthassa puna vacanaṃ nigamananti. Itisaddassa atthuddhāro evaṃ-saddena samānatthatāya “evaṃ me suta”nti ettha viya, atthayojanā ca itivuttakavaṇṇanāya amhehi pakāsitāyevāti tattha vuttanayeneva veditabboti.

In passages such as the preceding (Jā. 2.22.19), it is used in the sense of sowing. In 'but it has not been levelled back' (Pārā. 289) and so on, it is used in the sense of smoothing the ground with an eight-pronged harrow and the like. In 'With body-hair fallen, living on what is given by others, I dwell with a mind like a wild deer' (Cūḷava. 332) and so on, it is used in the sense of livelihood. In 'A yellow leaf released from its stalk is incapable of becoming green again' (Pārā. 92) and so on, it is used in the sense of being freed from its bond. In 'Song, speech, and intention' (DN 1.285) and so on, it is used in the sense of being uttered as a noble statement. In 'The Pārāyana has been recited' and so on, it is used in the sense of recitation. In 'This was said by the Blessed One: "Bhikkhus, be my heirs in the Dhamma, not my heirs in material things"' (MN 1.30) and so on, it is used in the sense of speaking. Here, too, it should be understood in the sense of speaking. Therefore, the meaning is: 'This inspired utterance, too, was spoken.' The word 'iti' means 'thus.' The meaning of the two words 'me sutaṃ' has already been explained in every way in the commentary on the introduction. Indeed, the meaning previously stated by way of introduction as 'evaṃ me sutaṃ' is here stated again by way of conclusion as 'iti me sutaṃ.' For the repetition of a meaning already stated is called a conclusion. The extraction of the meaning of the word 'iti' is due to its having the same meaning as the word 'evaṃ,' as in 'evaṃ me sutaṃ.' The application of the meaning has also been shown by us in the commentary on the Itivuttaka, so it should be understood in accordance with the method stated there.

Paramatthadīpaniyā khuddakanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

Of the Paramatthadīpanī, the Commentary on the Khuddaka Nikāya,

Udānasaṃvaṇṇanāpaṭhamabodhisuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

Here ends the commentary on the First Bodhi Sutta in the Exposition of the Udāna.

2. Dutiyabodhisuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Second Bodhi Sutta

2. Dutiye [M 0.0043] paṭilomanti “avijjānirodhā saṅkhāranirodho”tiādinā nayena vutto avijjādikoyeva paccayākāro anuppādanirodhena nirujjhamāno attano kattabbakiccassa akaraṇato paṭilomoti vuccati. Pavattiyā vā vilomanato paṭilomo, antato [P 0.0047] pana majjhato vā paṭṭhāya ādiṃ pāpetvā avuttattā ito aññenatthenettha paṭilomatā na yujjati. Paṭilomanti ca “visamaṃ candasūriyā parivattantī”tiādīsu viya bhāvanapuṃsakaniddeso. Imasmiṃ asati idaṃ na hotīti imasmiṃ avijjādike paccaye asati maggena pahīne idaṃ saṅkhārādikaṃ phalaṃ na hoti nappavattati. Imassa nirodhā idaṃ nirujjhatīti imassa avijjādikassa paccayassa nirodhā maggena anuppattidhammataṃ āpāditattā idaṃ saṅkhārādikaṃ phalaṃ nirujjhati, nappavattatīti attho. Idhāpi yathā “imasmiṃ sati idaṃ hoti, imassuppādā idaṃ uppajjatī”ti ettha “imasmiṃ satiyeva, nāsati, imassa uppādā eva, na nirodhā”ti antogadhaniyamatā dassitā. Evaṃ imasmiṃ asatiyeva, na sati, imassa nirodhā eva, na uppādāti antogadhaniyamatālakkhaṇā dassitāti veditabbaṃ. Sesamettha yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ paṭhamabodhisuttavaṇṇanāya vuttanayānusārena veditabbaṃ.

2. In the second sutta, regarding 'in reverse order' (paṭiloma): the causal pattern of ignorance and so forth, which is stated according to the method beginning with 'with the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of formations,' is called 'reverse' because, ceasing through cessation by non-arising, it does not perform its own function. Or, it is 'reverse' because it is contrary to the process of existence. However, since it is not stated by starting from the end or the middle and proceeding to the beginning, the state of being 'reverse' here is not appropriate in any other sense. And 'paṭilomaṃ' is a neuter designation of state, as in 'the sun and moon revolve irregularly.' 'When this is not, this does not come to be' means: when this condition, such as ignorance, is not present—having been abandoned by the path—this result, such as formations, does not come to be, does not proceed. 'With the cessation of this, this ceases' means: with the cessation of this condition, such as ignorance—because it has been brought to a state of non-arising by the path—this result, such as formations, ceases, it does not proceed. This is the meaning. Here too, just as in the passage 'When this is, this comes to be; with the arising of this, this arises,' an implicit rule is shown, namely: 'only when this is, not when it is not; only from the arising of this, not from its cessation.' So too here, the characteristic of an implicit rule is shown, namely: 'only when this is not, not when it is; only from the cessation of this, not from its arising.' This should be understood. Whatever else needs to be said here should be understood in accordance with the method stated in the commentary on the First Bodhi Sutta.

Evaṃ yathā bhagavā paṭilomapaṭiccasamuppādaṃ manasi akāsi, taṃ saṅkhepena dassetvā idāni vitthārena dassetuṃ “avijjānirodhā saṅkhāranirodho”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha avijjānirodhāti ariyamaggena avijjāya anavasesanirodhā, anusayappahānavasena aggamaggena avijjāya [V 0.0039] accantasamugghāṭatoti attho. Yadipi heṭṭhimamaggehi pahīyamānā avijjā accantasamugghāṭavaseneva pahīyati, tathāpi na anavasesato pahīyati. Apāyagāminiyā hi avijjā paṭhamamaggena pahīyati. Tathā sakideva imasmiṃ loke sabbattha ca anariyabhūmiyaṃ upapattipaccayabhūtā avijjā yathākkamaṃ dutiyatatiyamaggehi pahīyati, na itarāti. Arahattamaggeneva hi sā anavasesaṃ pahīyatīti. Saṅkhāranirodhoti saṅkhārānaṃ anuppādanirodho hoti. Evaṃ niruddhānaṃ pana saṅkhārānaṃ nirodhā viññāṇaṃ, viññāṇādīnañca nirodhā nāmarūpādīni niruddhāni eva hontīti dassetuṃ “saṅkhāranirodhā viññāṇanirodho”tiādiṃ vatvā “evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa nirodho hotī”ti vuttaṃ. Tattha yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayameva.

Thus, having briefly shown how the Blessed One contemplated dependent origination in reverse order, now to show it in detail, it is said: 'With the cessation of ignorance, formations cease,' and so on. Here, 'with the cessation of ignorance' means the remainderless cessation of ignorance by the noble path, the utter uprooting of ignorance by the supreme path through the abandonment of underlying tendencies. For although ignorance is abandoned by the lower paths by way of utter uprooting, it is nevertheless not abandoned without remainder. The ignorance leading to the plane of misery is abandoned by the first path. Similarly, the ignorance that is the condition for rebirth just once more in this world and everywhere in the non-noble plane is abandoned by the second and third paths respectively, but not the other kinds. For only by the path of arahantship is it abandoned without remainder. 'The cessation of formations' means the non-arising cessation of formations. Thus, to show that from the cessation of formations that have thus ceased, consciousness ceases, and with the cessation of consciousness and so on, name-and-form and so on are indeed ceased, it is said: 'With the cessation of formations, consciousness ceases,' and so on, concluding with: 'Thus is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.' Here, what needs to be said is in the same manner as was stated previously.

Apicettha [M 0.0044] kiñcāpi “avijjānirodhā saṅkhāranirodho, saṅkhāranirodhā viññāṇanirodho”ti [P 0.0048] ettāvatāpi sakalassa dukkhakkhandhassa anavasesato nirodho vutto hoti, tathāpi yathā anulome yassa yassa paccayadhammassa atthitāya yo yo paccayuppannadhammo na nirujjhati pavattati evāti imassa atthassa dassanatthaṃ “avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā…pe… samudayo hotī”ti vuttaṃ. Evaṃ tappaṭipakkhato tassa tassa paccayadhammassa abhāve so so paccayuppannadhammo nirujjhati nappavattatīti dassanatthaṃ idha “avijjānirodhā saṅkhāranirodho, saṅkhāranirodhā viññāṇanirodho…pe… dukkhakkhandhassa nirodho hotī”ti vuttaṃ, na pana anulome viya kālattayapariyāpannassa dukkhakkhandhassa nirodhadassanatthaṃ. Anāgatasseva hi ariyamaggabhāvanāya asati uppajjanārahassa dukkhakkhandhassa ariyamaggabhāvanāya nirodho icchitoti ayampi viseso veditabbo.

Moreover, although here, with just the statement, 'With the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of formations; with the cessation of formations, there is the cessation of consciousness,' the remainderless cessation of the entire mass of suffering is spoken of; nevertheless, just as in the forward order, to show the meaning that 'due to the existence of each particular causal factor, each particular conditionally arisen phenomenon does not cease but continues to occur,' it is said, 'With ignorance as condition, formations... this is the origination'; so too, by way of its opposite, to show that 'in the absence of each particular causal factor, each particular conditionally arisen phenomenon ceases and does not continue to occur,' it is said here, 'With the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of formations; with the cessation of formations, there is the cessation of consciousness... this is the cessation of the mass of suffering.' This is not, however, as in the forward order, for the purpose of showing the cessation of the mass of suffering as it is comprised in the three periods of time. For it is the cessation of only the future mass of suffering—which is liable to arise in the absence of the cultivation of the noble path—that is intended through the cultivation of the noble path. This distinction, too, should be understood.

Etamatthaṃ viditvāti yvāyaṃ “avijjānirodhādivasena saṅkhārādikassa dukkhakkhandhassa nirodho hotī”ti vutto, sabbākārena etamatthaṃ viditvā. Imaṃ udānaṃ udānesīti imasmiṃ atthe vidite “avijjānirodhā saṅkhāranirodho”ti evaṃ pakāsitassa avijjādīnaṃ paccayānaṃ khayassa avabodhānubhāvadīpakaṃ udānaṃ udānesīti attho.

`Having understood this matter` means: having understood in every way this meaning that was spoken thus: 'By way of the cessation of ignorance and so on, there is the cessation of the mass of suffering beginning with formations.' `He uttered this inspired utterance` means: when this meaning was understood, he uttered an inspired utterance that illuminates the power of awakening to the destruction of the conditions beginning with ignorance, a destruction declared thus: 'With the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of formations.' The meaning is this.

Tatrāyaṃ saṅkhepattho – yasmā avijjādīnaṃ paccayānaṃ anuppādanirodhasaṅkhātaṃ khayaṃ avedi aññāsi paṭivijjhi, tasmā etassa vuttanayena ātāpino jhāyato brāhmaṇassa vuttappakārā bodhipakkhiyadhammā catusaccadhammā vā pātubhavanti uppajjanti pakāsenti vā. Atha yā paccayanirodhassa [V 0.0040] sammā aviditattā uppajjeyyuṃ pubbe vuttappabhedā kaṅkhā, tā sabbāpi vapayanti nirujjhantīti. Sesaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayameva.

Herein, this is the summary meaning: Because he knew, understood, and penetrated the destruction of the conditions beginning with ignorance—a destruction designated as non-arising cessation—therefore, for that ardent, meditating brahmin, the factors of enlightenment of the kinds described, or the truths of the four noble truths, become manifest, arise, or are revealed. Then, whatever doubts of the kinds previously mentioned that might arise from not having properly understood the cessation of conditions, all of them are dispelled and cease. The rest is in the same manner as was stated previously.

Dutiyabodhisuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Second Bodhi Sutta is finished.

3. Tatiyabodhisuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Third Bodhi Sutta

3. Tatiye [P 0.0049] anulomapaṭilomanti anulomañca paṭilomañca, yathāvuttaanulomavasena ceva paṭilomavasena cāti attho. Nanu ca pubbepi [M 0.0045] anulomavasena paṭilomavasena ca paṭiccasamuppāde manasikārappavatti suttadvaye vuttā, idha kasmā punapi tadubhayavasena manasikārappavatti vuccatīti? Tadubhayavasena tatiyavāraṃ tattha manasikārassa pavattitattā. Kathaṃ pana tadubhayavasena manasikāro pavattito? Na hi sakkā apubbaṃ acarimaṃ anulomapaṭilomaṃ paṭiccasamuppādassa manasikāraṃ pavattetunti? Na kho panetaṃ evaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ “tadubhayaṃ ekajjhaṃ manasākāsī”ti, atha kho vārena. Bhagavā hi paṭhamaṃ anulomavasena paṭiccasamuppādaṃ manasi karitvā tadanurūpaṃ paṭhamaṃ udānaṃ udānesi. Dutiyampi paṭilomavasena taṃ manasi karitvā tadanurūpameva udānaṃ udānesi. Tatiyavāre pana kālena anulomaṃ kālena paṭilomaṃ manasikaraṇavasena anulomapaṭilomaṃ manasi akāsi. Tena vuttaṃ – “anulomapaṭilomanti anulomañca paṭilomañca, yathāvuttaanulomavasena ceva paṭilomavasena cā”ti. Iminā manasikārassa paguṇabalavabhāvo ca vasībhāvo ca pakāsito hoti. Ettha ca “anulomaṃ manasi karissāmi, paṭilomaṃ manasi karissāmi, anulomapaṭilomaṃ manasi karissāmī”ti evaṃ pavattānaṃ pubbābhogānaṃ vasena nesaṃ vibhāgo veditabbo.

3. In the third sutta, ‘in forward and reverse order’ means both forward and reverse, that is, in the manner of the forward order as well as the reverse order as previously explained. But was not the practice of attention to dependent origination in both forward and reverse order already mentioned in two suttas? Why then is the practice of attention in both ways mentioned again here? Because this is the third time attention was directed to it in both ways. But how was attention directed in both ways? Surely, one cannot attend to dependent origination in both forward and reverse order simultaneously, without a prior instance and a final one? However, this should not be seen as “He attended to both at once,” but rather in turns. First, the Blessed One attended to dependent origination in the forward order and then uttered an inspired utterance in accordance with that. Next, he attended to it in the reverse order and uttered another inspired utterance accordingly. Then, on the third occasion, he attended to the forward order at one time and the reverse order at another time—thus practicing attention in forward and reverse order. Therefore, it is said: ‘in forward and reverse order’ means both forward and reverse, that is, in the manner of the forward order as well as the reverse order as previously explained. By this, the proficient strength and mastery of his attention are demonstrated. Moreover, in this context, the distinction should be understood based on the preliminary advertences arising thus: “I will attend in the forward order; I will attend in the reverse order; I will attend in the forward and reverse order.”

Tattha avijjāya tvevāti avijjāya tu eva. Asesavirāganirodhāti virāgasaṅkhātena maggena asesanirodhā, aggamaggena anavasesaanuppādappahānāti attho. Saṅkhāranirodhoti sabbesaṃ saṅkhārānaṃ anavasesaṃ anuppādanirodho. Heṭṭhimena hi maggattayena keci saṅkhārā nirujjhanti, keci na nirujjhanti avijjāya sāvasesanirodhā. Aggamaggena panassā anavasesanirodhā na keci saṅkhārā na nirujjhantīti.

Herein, ‘avijjāya tveva’ is ‘avijjāya tu eva.’ ‘Asesavirāganirodhā’ means: because of the remainderless cessation through the path known as dispassion, the meaning is the abandonment of non-arising without remainder through the supreme path. ‘Saṅkhāranirodho’ means the cessation of future arising, without remainder, of all formations. For by the lower three paths, some formations cease and some do not cease, because of the cessation of ignorance with remainder. But by the supreme path, due to the remainderless cessation of that ignorance, no formations fail to cease.

Etamatthaṃ [V 0.0041] viditvāti yvāyaṃ avijjādivasena saṅkhārādikassa dukkhakkhandhassa samudayo nirodho ca avijjādīnaṃ samudayā nirodhā ca hotīti vutto, sabbākārena etamatthaṃ viditvā. Imaṃ udānaṃ udānesīti idaṃ yena maggena yo [P 0.0050] dukkhakkhandhassa samudayanirodhasaṅkhāto attho kiccavasena ārammaṇakiriyāya ca vidito, tassa ariyamaggassa ānubhāvadīpakaṃ vuttappakāraṃ udānaṃ udānesīti attho.

‘Having understood this meaning’ means: having understood in all its aspects this meaning, which has been stated thus: ‘Whatever is the origin and cessation of this mass of suffering, beginning with formations, occurs by way of the origin and cessation of ignorance and so on.’ ‘He uttered this inspired utterance’ means: he uttered this inspired utterance of the aforementioned kind, which illuminates the power of that noble path by which the meaning, known as the origin and cessation of the mass of suffering, was known by way of its function and by way of making it an object.

Tatrāyaṃ saṅkhepattho – yadā have pātubhavanti dhammā ātāpino jhāyato brāhmaṇassa, tadā so brāhmaṇo tehi uppannehi bodhipakkhiyadhammehi yassa vā ariyamaggassa catusaccadhammā pātubhūtā[M 0.0046], tena ariyamaggena vidhūpayaṃ tiṭṭhati mārasenaṃ, “kāmā te paṭhamā senā”tiādinā (su. ni. 438; mahāni. 28; cūḷani. nandamāṇavapucchāniddesa 47) nayena vuttappakāraṃ mārasenaṃ vidhūpayanto vidhamento viddhaṃsento tiṭṭhati. Kathaṃ? Sūriyova obhāsayamantalikkhaṃ, yathā sūriyo abbhuggato attano pabhāya antalikkhaṃ obhāsentova andhakāraṃ vidhamento tiṭṭhati, evaṃ sopi khīṇāsavabrāhmaṇo tehi dhammehi tena vā ariyamaggena saccāni paṭivijjhantova mārasenaṃ vidhūpayanto tiṭṭhatīti.

Herein, this is the summary meaning: When the dhammas truly become manifest for the ardent, meditating brahmin, then that brahmin—with those arisen factors of enlightenment, or with that noble path for which the four truths have become manifest—stands dispelling Māra’s army. He stands dispelling, shaking, and destroying Māra’s army of the kind described in the method beginning, ‘Sensual pleasures are your first army.’ How? Like the sun illuminating the sky. Just as the risen sun, while illuminating the sky with its own radiance, stands dispelling the darkness, so too that brahmin whose cankers are destroyed, while penetrating the truths with those dhammas or with that noble path, stands dispelling Māra’s army.

Evaṃ bhagavatā paṭhamaṃ paccayākārapajānanassa, dutiyaṃ paccayakkhayādhigamassa, tatiyaṃ ariyamaggassa ānubhāvappakāsanāni imāni tīṇi udānāni tīsu yāmesu bhāsitāni. Katarāya rattiyā? Abhisambodhito sattamāya rattiyā. Bhagavā hi visākhapuṇṇamāya rattiyā paṭhamayāme pubbenivāsaṃ anussaritvā majjhimayāme dibbacakkhuṃ visodhetvā pacchimayāme paṭiccasamuppāde ñāṇaṃ otāretvā nānānayehi tebhūmakasaṅkhāre sammasitvā “idāni aruṇo uggamissatī”ti sammāsambodhiṃ pāpuṇi, sabbaññutappattisamanantarameva ca aruṇo uggacchīti. Tato teneva pallaṅkena bodhirukkhamūle sattāhaṃ vītināmento sampattāya pāṭipadarattiyā tīsu yāmesu vuttanayena paṭiccasamuppādaṃ manasi karitvā yathākkamaṃ imāni udānāni udānesi.

Thus, these three inspired utterances—the first concerning the understanding of the structure of conditions, the second the attainment of the destruction of conditions, and the third the proclamation of the power of the noble path—were spoken by the Blessed One during the three watches of the night. On which night? On the seventh night from his full enlightenment. For the Blessed One, on the night of the full moon of Visākha, recollected his past lives in the first watch, purified the divine eye in the middle watch, and in the last watch, directed his knowledge to dependent origination. Having contemplated the formations of the three realms through various methods, at the point when he knew, ‘Now the dawn will break,’ he attained perfect enlightenment. And immediately upon attaining omniscience, the dawn arose. Thereafter, while spending seven days at the foot of the Bodhi tree on that very seat, on the seventh night, he attended to dependent origination in the three watches in the manner described and uttered these inspired utterances in sequence.

Khandhake pana tīsupi vāresu “paṭiccasamuppādaṃ anulomapaṭilomaṃ manasākāsī”ti (mahāva. 1) āgatattā khandhakaṭṭhakathāyaṃ “tīsupi yāmesu evaṃ manasi katvā paṭhamaṃ udānaṃ paccayākārapaccavekkhaṇavasena, dutiyaṃ nibbānapaccavekkhaṇavasena, tatiyaṃ maggapaccavekkhaṇavasenāti evaṃ imāni bhagavā udānāni udānesī”ti vuttaṃ, tampi na virujjhati. Bhagavā [P 0.0051] hi ṭhapetvā ratanagharasattāhaṃ sesesu chasu sattāhesu antarantarā dhammaṃ paccavekkhitvā [V 0.0042] yebhuyyena vimuttisukhapaṭisaṃvedī vihāsi, ratanagharasattāhe pana abhidhammaparicayavaseneva vihāsīti.

However, in the Khandhaka, since it is stated for all three occasions, ‘He attended to dependent origination in forward and reverse order’ (Mahāva. 1), it is said in the commentary to the Khandhaka: ‘Having thus attended in all three watches, the Blessed One uttered these inspired utterances: the first by way of reflecting on the structure of conditions, the second by way of reflecting on Nibbāna, and the third by way of reflecting on the path.’ That too is not in contradiction. For the Blessed One, setting aside the week of the Jewelled House, dwelt during the remaining six weeks mostly experiencing the bliss of liberation, reflecting on the Dhamma from time to time. But during the week of the Jewelled House, he dwelt solely by way of investigating the Abhidhamma.

Tatiyabodhisuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Third Bodhi Sutta is concluded.

4. Huṃhuṅkasuttavaṇṇanā

4. 1. The Chapter on Awakening. 4. The Nigrodha Sutta.

4. Catutthe [M 0.0047] ajapālanigrodheti tassa kira chāyāyaṃ ajapālā gantvā nisīdanti, tenassa “ajapālanigrodho”tveva nāmaṃ udapādi. Keci pana “yasmā tattha vede sajjhāyituṃ asamatthā mahallakabrāhmaṇā pākāraparikkhepayuttāni nivesanāni katvā sabbe vasiṃsu, tasmā ajapālanigrodhoti nāmaṃ jāta”nti vadanti. Tatrāyaṃ vacanattho – na japantīti ajapā, mantānaṃ anajjhāyakāti attho, ajapā lanti ādiyanti nivāsaṃ etthāti ajapāloti. Yasmā vā majjhanhike samaye anto paviṭṭhe aje attano chāyāya pāleti rakkhati, tasmā ‘ajapālo’tissa nāmaṃ rūḷhanti apare. Sabbathāpi nāmametaṃ tassa rukkhassa, tassa samīpe. Samīpatthe hi etaṃ bhummaṃ “ajapālanigrodhe”ti.

4. In the fourth sutta, regarding ‘at the Ajapāla banyan tree’: It is said that goatherds would go and sit in its shade; hence, its name ‘Ajapāla Banyan’ arose. Some, however, say: ‘Because elderly brahmins, unable to recite the Vedas, built dwellings enclosed by walls and all resided there, the name “Ajapāla Banyan” arose.’ Herein, this is the word analysis: ‘They do not chant’ (na japanti), thus ‘ajapā’; the meaning is ‘non-reciters of the sacred texts.’ ‘The ajapā take up residence here,’ thus ‘ajapālo.’ Or, because at midday it protects and guards with its shade the goats that have come within, others hold that its conventional name is ‘Ajapāla’ (goat-protector). In any case, this is the name of that tree, and the phrase means ‘in the vicinity of it.’ For this locative case in ‘ajapālanigrodhe’ is used in the sense of proximity.

Vimuttisukhapaṭisaṃvedīti tatrapi dhammaṃ vicinanto vimuttisukhañca paṭisaṃvedento nisīdi. Bodhirukkhato puratthimadisābhāge esa rukkho hoti. Sattāhanti ca idaṃ na pallaṅkasattāhato anantarasattāhaṃ. Bhagavā hi pallaṅkasattāhato aparānipi tīṇi sattāhāni bodhisamīpeyeva vītināmesi.

Regarding ‘experiencing the bliss of liberation’: There too he sat, investigating the Dhamma and experiencing the bliss of liberation. This tree is in the eastern direction from the Bodhi tree. And this ‘week’ is not the week immediately following the week on the seat. For the Blessed One, after the week on the seat, spent another three weeks in the vicinity of the Bodhi tree itself.

Tatrāyaṃ anupubbikathā – bhagavati kira sammāsambodhiṃ patvā sattāhaṃ ekapallaṅkena nisinne “na bhagavā vuṭṭhāti, kinnu kho aññepi [P 0.0052] buddhattakarā dhammā atthī”ti ekaccānaṃ devatānaṃ kaṅkhā udapādi. Atha bhagavā aṭṭhame divase samāpattito vuṭṭhāya devatānaṃ kaṅkhaṃ ñatvā kaṅkhāvidhamanatthaṃ ākāse uppatitvā yamakapāṭihāriyaṃ dassetvā tāsaṃ kaṅkhaṃ vidhametvā pallaṅkato īsakaṃ pācīnanissite uttaradisābhāge ṭhatvā cattāri asaṅkhyeyyāni kappasatasahassañca upacitānaṃ pāramīnaṃ balādhigamaṭṭhānaṃ pallaṅkaṃ bodhirukkhañca animisehi cakkhūhi olokayamāno sattāhaṃ vītināmesi, taṃ ṭhānaṃ animisacetiyaṃ nāma jātaṃ. Atha pallaṅkassa [V 0.0043] ca ṭhitaṭṭhānassa ca antarā puratthimato ca pacchimato ca āyate ratanacaṅkame caṅkamanto sattāhaṃ vītināmesi, taṃ ratanacaṅkamacetiyaṃ nāma jātaṃ. Tato pacchimadisābhāge devatā ratanagharaṃ māpayiṃsu[M 0.0048], tattha pallaṅkena nisīditvā abhidhammapiṭakaṃ visesato anantanayaṃ samantapaṭṭhānaṃ vicinanto sattāhaṃ vītināmesi, taṃ ṭhānaṃ ratanagharacetiyaṃ nāma jātaṃ. Evaṃ bodhisamīpeyeva cattāri sattāhāni vītināmetvā pañcame sattāhe bodhirukkhato ajapālanigrodhaṃ upasaṅkamitvā tassa mūle pallaṅkena nisīdi.

Here is the sequential account: It is said that after attaining perfect enlightenment, the Blessed One sat for seven days in a single cross-legged posture. A doubt arose for some devas: 'The Blessed One does not rise. Are there perhaps other qualities that bring about Buddhahood?' On the eighth day, emerging from his meditative attainment, the Blessed One, aware of the devas' doubt, rose into the sky to dispel their uncertainty, performed the Twin Miracle, and having removed their doubt, he stood in the northern quarter, slightly inclined to the east of the throne. For seven days he passed the time gazing with unblinking eyes at the throne and the Bodhi tree, the place for the attainment of the fruit of the perfections accumulated over four incalculable aeons and one hundred thousand aeons. That place became known as the Unblinking Shrine. Then, he spent seven days walking on the long Jeweled Walkway between the throne and the place where he had stood, extending from east to west; that place became known as the Jeweled Walk Shrine. Next, devas constructed a jeweled house in the western quarter, where he sat cross-legged and spent seven days thoroughly examining the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, especially the Samantapaṭṭhāna with its infinite methods. That place became known as the Jeweled House Shrine. Thus, he spent four weeks in the vicinity of the Bodhi tree. In the fifth week, he went from the Bodhi tree to the Ajapāla Banyan tree and sat cross-legged at its base.

Tamhā samādhimhā vuṭṭhāsīti tato phalasamāpattisamādhito yathākālaparicchedaṃ vuṭṭhahi, vuṭṭhahitvā ca pana tattha evaṃ nisinne bhagavati eko brāhmaṇo taṃ gantvā pañhaṃ pucchi. Tena vuttaṃ “atha kho aññataro”tiādi. Tattha aññataroti nāmagottavasena anabhiññāto apākaṭo eko. Huṃhuṅkajātikoti so kira diṭṭhamaṅgaliko mānathaddho mānavasena kodhavasena ca sabbaṃ avokkhajātikaṃ passitvā jigucchanto “huṃhu”nti karonto vicarati, tasmā “huṃhuṅkajātiko”ti vuccati, “huhukkajātiko”tipi pāṭho. Brāhmaṇoti jātiyā brāhmaṇo.

Regarding 'having emerged from that meditation': from that concentration of the attainment of fruition, he arose after the determined period of time. And having arisen, while the Blessed One was seated there, a certain brahmin approached him and asked a question. Hence it is said, 'Then a certain one,' and so on. Here, 'a certain one' means someone unknown and unrenowned by name or clan. Regarding 'of the Huṃhuṅka type': It is said that he was one who held to auspicious signs, was stiff with pride, and went about saying 'huṃ huṃ' because, out of pride and anger, he would become disgusted upon seeing any person of a lower caste; therefore he is called 'of the Huṃhuṅka type.' There is also the reading 'Huhukkajātiko.' Regarding 'a brahmin': he was a brahmin by birth.

Yena bhagavāti yassaṃ disāyaṃ bhagavā nisinno. Bhummatthe hi etaṃ karaṇavacanaṃ[P 0.0053]. Yena vā disābhāgena bhagavā upasaṅkamitabbo, tena disābhāgena upasaṅkami. Atha vā yenāti hetuatthe karaṇavacanaṃ, yena kāraṇena bhagavā devamanussehi upasaṅkamitabbo, tena kāraṇena upasaṅkamīti attho. Kena ca kāraṇena bhagavā upasaṅkamitabbo? Nānappakārarogadukkhābhipīḷitattā āturakāyehi mahājanehi mahānubhāvo bhisakko viya rogatikicchanatthaṃ, nānāvidhakilesabyādhipīḷitattā āturacittehi devamanussehi kilesabyādhitikicchanatthaṃ dhammassavanapañhapucchanādikāraṇehi bhagavā upasaṅkamitabbo. Tena ayampi brāhmaṇo attano kaṅkhaṃ chinditukāmo upasaṅkami.

Regarding the phrase 'to where the Blessed One was': this means in whatever direction the Blessed One was seated. For this is an instrumental word used in the sense of the locative. Or, he approached from that direction, from whatever direction the Blessed One should be approached. Alternatively, 'yena' is an instrumental word in the sense of cause; the meaning is that by whatever reason the Blessed One should be approached by gods and humans, by that reason he approached. And for what reason should the Blessed One be approached? Just as a physician of great power is approached by the populace, whose bodies are afflicted and oppressed by various kinds of illness and suffering, for the treatment of their diseases, so too the Blessed One should be approached by gods and humans, whose minds are afflicted and oppressed by the various diseases of the defilements, for the treatment of the disease of the defilements, for reasons such as listening to the Dhamma and asking questions. Thus, this brahmin too, wishing to cut off his own doubt, approached.

Upasaṅkamitvāti upasaṅkamanapariyosānadīpanaṃ. Atha vā yaṃ ṭhānaṃ upasaṅkami, tatopi bhagavato samīpabhūtaṃ āsannataraṃ ṭhānaṃ upagantvāti attho. Sammodīti samaṃ sammā vā modi, bhagavā cānena, sopi bhagavatā “kacci bhoto khamanīyaṃ kacci yāpanīya”ntiādinā paṭisanthārakaraṇavasena samappavattamodo ahosi. Sammodanīyanti sammodanārahaṃ sammodajananayoggaṃ. Kathanti kathāsallāpaṃ. Sāraṇīyanti saritabbayuttaṃ [M 0.0049] sādhujanehi pavattetabbaṃ, kālantare vā cintetabbaṃ. Vītisāretvāti niṭṭhāpetvā. Ekamantanti bhāvanapuṃsakaniddeso. Ekasmiṃ [V 0.0044] ṭhāne, atisammukhādike cha nisajjadose vajjetvā ekasmiṃ padeseti attho. Etadavocāti etaṃ idāni vattabbaṃ “kittāvatā nu kho”tiādivacanaṃ avoca.

Regarding 'having approached': this indicates the completion of the act of approaching. Alternatively, the meaning is that having reached the place to which he approached, he then went to a spot even closer to the Blessed One. Regarding 'exchanged greetings': he rejoiced together or well; the Blessed One with him, and he with the Blessed One. A joy proceeding in equal measure arose by way of making polite conversation, as in 'I hope you are well, sir, I hope you are keeping comfortable,' and so on. Regarding 'worthy of greeting': worthy of being greeted, suitable for generating rejoicing. Regarding 'conversation': talk, polite conversation. Regarding 'memorable': worthy of being remembered, to be engaged in by good people, or to be reflected upon at another time. Regarding 'having concluded': having finished. Regarding 'to one side': this is an adverbial expression in the neuter gender. The meaning is: in one spot, in one place, having avoided the six faults of sitting, such as sitting too directly in front. Regarding 'he said this': he spoke these words, 'To what extent, indeed...' and so on, which are now to be spoken.

Tattha kittāvatāti kittakena pamāṇena. Nūti saṃsayatthe nipāto. Khoti padapūraṇe. Bhoti brāhmaṇānaṃ jātisamudāgataṃ ālapanaṃ. Tathā hi vuttaṃ – “bhovādi nāma so hoti, sace hoti sakiñcano”ti (ma. ni. 2.457; dha. pa. 396). Gotamāti bhagavantaṃ gottena ālapati. Kathaṃ panāyaṃ brāhmaṇo sampatisamāgato bhagavato gottaṃ [P 0.0054] jānātīti? Nāyaṃ sampatisamāgato, chabbassāni padhānakaraṇakāle upaṭṭhahantehi pañcavaggiyehi saddhiṃ caramānopi, aparabhāge taṃ vataṃ chaḍḍetvā uruvelāyaṃ senanigame eko adutiyo hutvā piṇḍāya caramānopi tena brāhmaṇena diṭṭhapubbo ceva sallapitapubbo ca. Tena so pubbe pañcavaggiyehi gayhamānaṃ bhagavato gottaṃ anussaranto, “bho gotamā”ti bhagavantaṃ gottena ālapati. Yato paṭṭhāya vā bhagavā mahābhinikkhamanaṃ nikkhamanto anomanadītīre pabbajito, tato pabhuti “samaṇo gotamo”ti cando viya sūriyo viya ca pākaṭo paññāto, na tassa gottajānane kāraṇaṃ gavesitabbaṃ.

Here, regarding 'kittāvatā': it means 'by what measure.' Regarding 'nu': it is a particle in the sense of doubt. Regarding 'kho': it is a filler particle. Regarding 'bho': it is a form of address traditional to the brahmin caste. For so it is said: 'He is one who says "bho" by name, if he has any possessions.' Regarding 'Gotama': he addresses the Blessed One by his clan name. But how did this brahmin, being a new acquaintance, know the Blessed One’s clan name? He was not a new acquaintance. For when the Blessed One was wandering for six years during the time of his great striving, together with the group of five who were attending upon him, and also in a later period, after having abandoned that practice and wandering for alms alone, without a companion, in Uruvelā near the village of Senā, he had been seen and spoken with before by that brahmin. Therefore, recalling the Blessed One’s clan name, which was used by the group of five previously, he addressed the Blessed One by his clan name, saying 'Gotama.' Alternatively, from the time the Blessed One went forth, making the great renunciation, and was ordained on the bank of the Anomā River, from that time onwards he became as renowned and well-known as the moon and the sun by the name 'the ascetic Gotama.' The reason for his knowing the clan name need not be sought.

Brāhmaṇakaraṇāti brāhmaṇaṃ karontīti brāhmaṇakaraṇā, brāhmaṇabhāvakarāti attho. Ettha ca kittāvatāti etena yehi dhammehi brāhmaṇo hoti, tesaṃ dhammānaṃ parimāṇaṃ pucchati. Katame ca panāti iminā tesaṃ sarūpaṃ pucchati.

Regarding 'brahmin-making qualities': 'they make a brahmin' (brāhmaṇaṃ karonti), thus they are 'brahmin-making qualities' (brāhmaṇakaraṇā); the meaning is 'qualities that make the state of a brahmin.' And here, by the phrase 'to what extent,' he asks for the measure of those qualities by which one becomes a brahmin. And by the phrase 'and what are they,' he asks for their intrinsic nature.

Etamatthaṃ viditvāti etaṃ tena puṭṭhassa pañhassa sikhāpattaṃ atthaṃ viditvā tāyaṃ velāyaṃ imaṃ udānaṃ udānesi, na pana tassa brāhmaṇassa dhammaṃ desesi. Kasmā? Dhammadesanāya abhājanabhāvato. Tathā hi tassa brāhmaṇassa imaṃ gāthaṃ sutvā na saccābhisamayo ahosi. Yathā ca imassa, evaṃ upakassa ājīvakassa buddhaguṇappakāsanaṃ. Dhammacakkappavattanato hi [M 0.0050] pubbabhāge bhagavatā bhāsitaṃ paresaṃ suṇantānampi tapussabhallikānaṃ saraṇadānaṃ viya vāsanābhāgiyameva jātaṃ, na sekkhabhāgiyaṃ, na nibbedhabhāgiyaṃ. Esā hi dhammatāti.

Regarding 'having understood this meaning': having understood this meaning, which was the pinnacle of the question asked by that brahmin, at that time He uttered this inspired utterance, but He did not teach the Dhamma to that brahmin. Why? Because he was not a suitable vessel for the teaching of the Dhamma. Indeed, for that brahmin, having heard this verse, there was no realization of the truths. And just as for this one, so for Upaka the Ājīvaka was the declaration of the Buddha’s virtues. For, in the period before the setting in motion of the Wheel of Dhamma, what was spoken by the Blessed One, even when others heard it—like the giving of refuge to Tapussa and Bhallika—became only a portion related to latent tendencies, not a portion related to training, not a portion related to penetration. For such is the nature of things.

Tattha yo brāhmaṇoti yo bāhitapāpadhammatāya brāhmaṇo, na diṭṭhamaṅgalikatāya huṃhuṅkārakasāvādipāpadhammayutto hutvā kevalaṃ jātimattakena brahmaññaṃ paṭijānāti. So brāhmaṇo bāhitapāpadhammattā huṃhuṅkārappahānena nihuṃhuṅko, rāgādikasāvābhāvena nikkasāvo, bhāvanānuyogayuttacittatāya [P 0.0055] yatatto, sīlasaṃyamena vā saṃyatacittatāya yatatto, catumaggañāṇasaṅkhātehi [V 0.0045] vedehi antaṃ saṅkhārapariyosānaṃ nibbānaṃ, vedānaṃ vā antaṃ gatattā vedantagū. Maggabrahmacariyassa vusitattā vusitabrahmacariyo, dhammena so brahmavādaṃ vadeyya “brāhmaṇo aha”nti etaṃ vādaṃ dhammena ñāyena vadeyya. Yassa sakalalokasannivāsepi kuhiñci ekārammaṇepi rāgussado, dosussado, mohussado, mānussado, diṭṭhussadoti ime ussadā natthi, anavasesaṃ pahīnāti attho.

Here, 'who is a brahmin' means one who is a brahmin by virtue of having banished evil qualities, not one who, being endowed with evil qualities such as holding to auspicious signs, the 'hum-hum' sound, and stains, claims brahminhood merely by birth alone. That brahmin, because he has banished evil qualities, is without the 'hum-hum' sound through having abandoned it (nihuṃhuṅko); due to the absence of stains such as lust, he is stainless (nikkasāvo); due to a mind yoked to the practice of development, he is self-restrained (yatatto), or due to a mind restrained by moral discipline, he is self-restrained. He is one who has gone to the end (vedantagū), having reached Nibbāna, the cessation of formations, which is the end, by means of the knowledges called 'vedas,' namely the four path-knowledges; or because he has gone to the end of the Vedas. Because he has lived the holy life of the path, he is one who has lived the holy life (vusitabrahmacariyo). Righteously may he make the brahmin-claim; he may make this claim, 'I am a brahmin,' righteously and with justice. For whom, in the entire congregation of the world, in regard to any single object, there is no surge of lust, no surge of hatred, no surge of delusion, no surge of pride, and no surge of wrong view—these surges do not exist; the meaning is they are abandoned without remainder.

Catutthasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the fourth discourse is completed.

5. Brāhmaṇasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Brahmin Discourse

5. Pañcame sāvatthiyanti evaṃnāmake nagare. Tañhi savatthassa nāma isino nivāsaṭṭhāne māpitattā sāvatthīti vuccati, yathā kākandī, mākandīti. Evaṃ tāva akkharacintakā. Aṭṭhakathācariyā pana bhaṇanti – yaṃkiñci manussānaṃ upabhogaparibhogaṃ sabbamettha atthīti sāvatthi. Satthasamāyoge ca kimettha bhaṇḍamatthīti pucchite sabbamatthītipi vacanaṃ upādāya sāvatthīti.

5. In the fifth discourse, 'in Sāvatthī' means in the city of that name. For it is called Sāvatthī because it was founded on the dwelling place of the sage named Savattha, just as are Kākandī and Mākandī. Thus say the grammarians. The commentary teachers, however, say: 'Whatever is for people's use and enjoyment, all is here,' hence Sāvatthī. And, in a caravan assembly, when asked, 'What merchandise is here?' taking up the reply, 'Everything is here,' it is called Sāvatthī.

“Sabbadā sabbūpakaraṇaṃ, sāvatthiyaṃ samohitaṃ;

Tasmā sabbamupādāya, sāvatthīti pavuccatī”ti. (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.14);

All requisites are always assembled in Sāvatthī; therefore, on account of everything, it is called Sāvatthī.

Tassaṃ [M 0.0051] sāvatthiyaṃ, samīpatthe cetaṃ bhummavacanaṃ. Jetavaneti attano paccatthike jinātīti jeto, raññā vā paccatthikajane jite jātoti jeto, maṅgalakamyatāya vā tassa evaṃ nāmameva katanti jeto. Vanayatīti [P 0.0056] vanaṃ, attano sampattiyā sattānaṃ attani bhattiṃ karoti uppādetīti attho. Vanuke iti vā vanaṃ, nānāvidhakusumagandhasammodamattakokilādivihaṅgavirutālāpehi mandamārutacalitarukkhasākhāpallavahatthehi ca “etha maṃ paribhuñjathā”ti pāṇino yācati viyāti attho. Jetassa vanaṃ jetavanaṃ. Tañhi jetena kumārena ropitaṃ saṃvaddhitaṃ paripālitaṃ. Sova tassa sāmī ahosi, tasmā jetavananti vuccati, tasmiṃ jetavane.

In that Sāvatthī: this is a locative expression in the sense of proximity. Regarding Jetavana: because 'he conquers (jināti) his enemies,' he is Jeta; or because 'he was born (jāto) when the enemy people were conquered by the king,' he is Jeta; or because this name was simply given to him out of a desire for auspiciousness, he is Jeta. It is a 'grove' (vana) because it inspires devotion (vanayati); the meaning is that through its own accomplishment, it creates and produces devotion for itself in beings. Or, it is a 'grove' (vana) because it entreats (vanute); the meaning is that with the melodious calls of various birds like cuckoos intoxicated by the fragrance of many kinds of flowers, and with its tree branches and new leaves stirred by the gentle breeze like hands, it seems to entreat living beings, saying, 'Come and enjoy me.' The grove of Jeta is Jetavana. For it was planted, nurtured, and protected by Prince Jeta. He was its owner; therefore, it is called Jetavana. In that Jetavana...

Anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāmeti mātāpitūhi gahitanāmavasena sudatto nāma so mahāseṭṭhi, sabbakāmasamiddhitāya [V 0.0046] pana vigatamalamaccheratāya karuṇādiguṇasamaṅgitāya ca niccakālaṃ anāthānaṃ piṇḍaṃ deti, tasmā anāthapiṇḍikoti vuccati. Āramanti ettha pāṇino visesena pabbajitāti ārāmo, pupphaphalādisobhāya nātidūranāccāsannatādipañcavidhasenāsanaṅgasampattiyā ca tato tato āgamma ramanti abhiramanti anukkaṇṭhitā hutvā vasantīti attho. Vuttappakārāya vā sampattiyā tattha tattha gatepi attano abbhantaraṃyeva ānetvā rametīti ārāmo. So hi anāthapiṇḍikena gahapatinā jetassa rājakumārassa hatthato aṭṭhārasahi hiraññakoṭīhi koṭisanthārena kiṇitvā aṭṭhārasahi hiraññakoṭīhi senāsanāni kārāpetvā aṭṭhārasahi hiraññakoṭīhi vihāramahaṃ niṭṭhāpetvā evaṃ catupaññāsahiraññakoṭipariccāgena buddhappamukhassa saṅghassa niyyātito, tasmā “anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāmo”ti vuccati. Tasmiṃ anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme.

Regarding 'Anāthapiṇḍika's Park': By the name given by his parents, that great merchant was named Sudatta. But because he was fulfilled in all desires, free from the stain of stinginess, endowed with qualities such as compassion, and constantly gave alms (piṇḍa) to the destitute (anātha), he was called Anāthapiṇḍika. It is called a 'park' (ārāma) because beings, especially the ordained, delight (āramanti) there. The meaning is that because of its beauty with flowers and fruits, and its possession of the fivefold qualities of a suitable lodging—such as being neither too far nor too near—they come from various places and dwell there, delighting and taking great joy, free from discontent. Alternatively, it is called a 'park' (ārāma) because, by means of the aforesaid accomplishment, it brings even those who have gone to other places back into its fold and causes them to delight. For it was bought by the householder Anāthapiṇḍika from Prince Jeta for eighteen crores of gold coins, laid edge to edge; he had dwellings built for another eighteen crores, and he completed the monastery dedication festival for a further eighteen crores. Thus, with a total expenditure of fifty-four crores of gold, it was dedicated to the Sangha with the Buddha at its head. Therefore, it is called 'Anāthapiṇḍika's Park.' In that park of Anāthapiṇḍika...

Ettha ca “jetavane”ti vacanaṃ purimasāmiparikittanaṃ, “anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme”ti pacchimasāmiparikittanaṃ. Ubhayampi dvinnaṃ pariccāgavisesaparidīpanena puññakāmānaṃ [P 0.0057] āyatiṃ diṭṭhānugatiāpajjanatthaṃ. Tattha hi dvārakoṭṭhakapāsādakaraṇavasena bhūmivikkayaladdhā aṭṭhārasa hiraññakoṭiyo anekakoṭiagghanakā rukkhā ca jetassa pariccāgo, catupaññāsa koṭiyo [M 0.0052] anāthapiṇḍikassa. Iti tesaṃ pariccāgaparikittanena “evaṃ puññakāmā puññāni karontī”ti dassento dhammabhaṇḍāgāriko aññepi puññakāme tesaṃ diṭṭhānugatiāpajjane niyojetīti.

Herein, the phrase 'in Jetavana' is a proclamation of the former owner, while 'in Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park' is a proclamation of the later owner. Both are stated for the purpose of revealing the exceptional nature of their donations, so that those desiring merit may follow their example in the future. For in this matter, the donation of Jeta was eighteen crores of gold obtained from the sale of the land for the construction of gatehouses and mansions, and trees worth countless crores; the donation of Anāthapiṇḍika was fifty-four crores. Thus, by proclaiming their donations, the Treasurer of the Dhamma, showing that 'thus do those who desire merit perform meritorious deeds,' encourages other merit-seekers to follow their example.

Tattha siyā – yadi tāva bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati, “jetavane”ti na vattabbaṃ. Atha jetavane viharati, “sāvatthiya”nti na vattabbaṃ. Na hi sakkā ubhayattha ekaṃ samayaṃ viharitunti. Na kho panetaṃ evaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, nanu avocumhā “samīpatthe etaṃ bhummavacana”nti. Tasmā yadidaṃ sāvatthiyā samīpe jetavanaṃ, tattha viharanto “sāvatthiyaṃ viharati jetavane”ti vutto. Gocaragāmanidassanatthaṃ hissa sāvatthivacanaṃ, pabbajitānurūpanivāsaṭṭhānadassanatthaṃ sesavacananti.

Therein, it might be argued: 'If the Blessed One is dwelling in Sāvatthī, then it should not be said, "in Jetavana." But if dwelling in Jetavana, then it should not be said, "in Sāvatthī." For it is not possible to dwell in both places at the same time.' However, this should not be viewed in that way. Did we not say, 'This is a locative case used in the sense of proximity'? Therefore, since Jetavana is near Sāvatthī, one dwelling there is said to be 'dwelling in Sāvatthī, in Jetavana.' The mention of Sāvatthī is to indicate his alms-resort village, while the remaining phrase is to show a dwelling place suitable for renunciants.

Āyasmā ca sāriputtotiādīsu āyasmāti piyavacanaṃ. Casaddo samuccayattho. Rūpasāriyā nāma brāhmaṇiyā puttoti sāriputto. Mahāmoggallānoti pūjāvacanaṃ. Guṇavisesehi mahanto moggallānoti hi mahāmoggallāno. Revatoti khadiravanikarevato, na kaṅkhārevato. Ekasmiñhi divase bhagavā rattasāṇiparikkhitto viya suvaṇṇayūpo, pavāḷadhajaparivārito viya suvaṇṇapabbato, navutihaṃsasahassaparivārito viya dhataraṭṭho haṃsarājā, sattaratanasamujjalāya caturaṅginiyā [V 0.0047] senāya parivārito viya cakkavatti rājā, mahābhikkhusaṅghaparivuto gaganamajjhe candaṃ uṭṭhāpento viya catunnaṃ parisānaṃ majjhe dhammaṃ desento nisinno hoti. Tasmiṃ samaye ime aggasāvakā mahāsāvakā ca bhagavato pāde vandanatthāya upasaṅkamiṃsu.

In phrases like 'the Venerable Sāriputta and others,' 'Venerable' (āyasmā) is a term of endearment. The word 'ca' (and) has the meaning of conjunction. Sāriputta means 'son of the brahmin woman named Rūpasārī.' Mahāmoggallāna is a term of veneration, for he is called Mahāmoggallāna because he was 'Moggallāna who is great (mahā) in special qualities.' Revata refers to Revata of the Acacia Wood (Khadiravaniya), not Kaṅkhārevata. On one occasion, the Blessed One—like a golden pillar wrapped in red cloth, like a golden mountain surrounded by coral banners, like Dhataraṭṭha the swan-king attended by ninety thousand swans, like a wheel-turning monarch encircled by a fourfold army radiant with the seven treasures, surrounded by a great assembly of monks, like the moon rising in the middle of the sky—was seated teaching the Dhamma in the midst of the four assemblies. At that time, these chief disciples and great disciples approached the Blessed One to pay homage at his feet.

Bhikkhū āmantesīti attānaṃ parivāretvā nisinnabhikkhū te āgacchante dassetvā abhāsi. Bhagavā hi te āyasmante sīlasamādhipaññādiguṇasampanne paramena upasamena samannāgate paramāya ākappasampattiyā yutte upasaṅkamante passitvā pasannamānaso tesaṃ guṇavisesaparikittanatthaṃ bhikkhū āmantesi [P 0.0058] “ete, bhikkhave, brāhmaṇā āgacchanti, ete, bhikkhave, brāhmaṇā āgacchantī”ti. Pasādavasena etaṃ āmeḍitaṃ, pasaṃsāvasenātipi vattuṃ yuttaṃ. Evaṃ vutteti evaṃ bhagavatā te [M 0.0053] āyasmante “brāhmaṇā”ti vutte. Aññataroti nāmagottena apākaṭo, tassaṃ parisāyaṃ nisinno eko bhikkhu. Brāhmaṇajātikoti brāhmaṇakule jāto. So hi uḷārabhogā brāhmaṇamahāsālakulā pabbajito. Tassa kira evaṃ ahosi “ime lokiyā ubhatosujātiyā brāhmaṇasikkhānipphattiyā ca brāhmaṇo hoti, na aññathāti vadanti, bhagavā ca ete āyasmante brāhmaṇāti vadati, handāhaṃ bhagavantaṃ brāhmaṇalakkhaṇaṃ puccheyya”nti etadatthameva hi bhagavā tadā te there “brāhmaṇā”ti abhāsi. Brahmaṃ aṇatīti brāhmaṇoti hi jātibrāhmaṇānaṃ nibbacanaṃ. Ariyā pana bāhitapāpatāya brāhmaṇā. Vuttañhetaṃ – “bāhitapāpoti brāhmaṇo, samacariyā samaṇoti vuccatī”ti (dha. pa. 388). Vakkhati ca “bāhitvā pāpake dhamme”ti.

Regarding 'He addressed the bhikkhus': Pointing out to the bhikkhus seated around him those who were approaching, he spoke. Indeed, the Blessed One, seeing those venerable ones approaching—endowed with virtues such as morality, concentration, and wisdom, possessed of the highest peace, and endowed with the highest accomplishment in deportment—his mind filled with faith, addressed the bhikkhus to proclaim their special virtues, saying, 'Behold, bhikkhus, these brahmins are coming; behold, bhikkhus, these brahmins are coming.' This repetition was due to faith; it is also fitting to say it was due to praise. Regarding 'When this was said': When the Blessed One had thus referred to those venerable ones as 'brahmins,' a certain bhikkhu of brahmin birth, who was not prominent by name or clan and was seated in that assembly, thought: 'These worldly people say that one is a brahmin by reason of pure birth on both sides and accomplishment in the brahminical training, and not otherwise. Yet the Blessed One calls these venerable ones "brahmins." Come now, I shall ask the Blessed One about the characteristics of a brahmin.' For this very purpose, the Blessed One had at that time called those elders 'brahmins.' For 'one who recites the Veda (brahma) is a brahmin' is the derivation for brahmins by birth. The noble ones, however, are brahmins because they have barred out evil. And this has been said: 'Because he has barred out evil, he is a brahmin; because of his peaceful conduct, he is called a recluse' (Dhp. 388). And He will say: 'Having barred out evil states...'

Etamatthaṃ viditvāti etaṃ brāhmaṇasaddassa paramatthato sikhāpattamatthaṃ jānitvā. Imaṃ udānanti imaṃ paramatthabrāhmaṇabhāvadīpakaṃ udānaṃ udānesi.

Regarding 'Having known this meaning': this means having known the ultimate meaning of the word 'brahmin,' the meaning that has reached its pinnacle. Regarding 'This inspired utterance': he uttered this inspired utterance that reveals the state of being a true brahmin in the ultimate sense.

Tattha bāhitvāti bahi katvā, attano santānato nīharitvā samucchedappahānavasena pajahitvāti attho.
