Pāpake dhammeti lāmake dhamme, duccaritavasena tividhaduccaritadhamme, cittuppādavasena dvādasākusalacittuppāde, kammapathavasena dasākusalakammapathe, pavattibhedavasena anekabhedabhinne sabbepi akusaladhammeti attho. Ye caranti sadā satāti ye sativepullappattatāya sabbakālaṃ rūpādīsu chasupi ārammaṇesu satatavihāravasena satā satimanto hutvā catūhi iriyāpathehi caranti. Satiggahaṇeneva cettha sampajaññampi gahitanti veditabbaṃ. Khīṇasaṃyojanāti catūhipi ariyamaggehi dasavidhassa saṃyojanassa samucchinnattā parikkhīṇasaṃyojanā. Buddhāti catusaccasambodhena buddhā. Te ca pana sāvakabuddhā, paccekabuddhā[V 0.0048], sammāsambuddhāti tividhā, tesu idha sāvakabuddhā adhippetā. Te [P 0.0059] ve lokasmi brāhmaṇāti te seṭṭhatthena brāhmaṇasaṅkhāte dhamme ariyāya jātiyā jātā, brāhmaṇabhūtassa vā bhagavato orasaputtāti imasmiṃ sattaloke paramatthato brāhmaṇā nāma, na jātigottamattehi, na jaṭādhāraṇādimattena vāti attho. Evaṃ imesu dvīsu suttesu brāhmaṇakarā [M 0.0054] dhammā arahattaṃ pāpetvā kathitā, nānajjhāsayatāya pana sattānaṃ desanāvilāsena abhilāpanānattena desanānānattaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Therein, regarding 'bāhitvā': having cast out, having removed from one's own continuity, having abandoned by way of cutting off and eradication—this is the meaning. Regarding 'pāpake dhamme': base qualities, the threefold unwholesome conduct by way of misconduct, the twelve unwholesome thought-arisings by way of mental activity, the ten unwholesome courses of action by way of kammic paths, and all the various unwholesome states by way of diverse manifestations—this is the meaning. Regarding 'Ye caranti sadā satā': those who, having attained the fullness of mindfulness, always dwell with constant mindfulness in the six objects such as forms, and move about in the four postures. Here, by the term 'sati' (mindfulness), 'sampajañña' (clear comprehension) should also be understood as included. Regarding 'Khīṇasaṃyojanā': those whose tenfold fetters have been completely destroyed by the four noble paths, thus they are 'khīṇasaṃyojanā' (those with destroyed fetters). Regarding 'Buddhā': those awakened by the realization of the four truths. They are of three kinds: disciple-buddhas (sāvakabuddhā), solitary buddhas (paccekabuddhā), and Perfectly Self-Enlightened Buddhas (sammāsambuddhā). Here, disciple-buddhas are intended. Regarding 'Te ve lokasmiṃ brāhmaṇā': They are named brahmins in this world of beings in the ultimate sense because they are born of the noble birth into the states designated as 'brahmin' in the highest sense, or because they are the legitimate sons of the Blessed One who has become a brahmin; not by mere birth or clan, nor by wearing matted hair and the like—this is the meaning. Thus, in these two discourses, the qualities that make one a brahmin are explained as leading to arahantship. However, due to the diverse inclinations of beings, the variety of teachings should be understood as a diversity of expressions in the manner of teaching.

Pañcamasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the fifth discourse is concluded.

6. Mahākassapasuttavaṇṇanā

6. The Explanation of the Mahākassapa Sutta

6. Chaṭṭhe rājagaheti evaṃnāmake nagare. Tañhi mahāmandhātumahāgovindādīhi pariggahitattā “rājagaha”nti vuccati. “Durabhibhavanīyattā paṭirājūnaṃ gahabhūtanti rājagaha”ntiādinā aññenettha pakārena vaṇṇayanti. Kintehi? Nāmametaṃ tassa nagarassa. Taṃ panetaṃ buddhakāle cakkavattikāle ca nagaraṃ hoti, sesakāle suññaṃ yakkhapariggahitaṃ tesaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ hutvā tiṭṭhati. Veḷuvane kalandakanivāpeti veḷuvananti tassa vihārassa nāmaṃ. Taṃ kira aṭṭhārasahatthubbedhena pākārena parikkhittaṃ buddhassa bhagavato vasanānucchavikāya mahatiyā gandhakuṭiyā aññehi ca pāsādakuṭileṇamaṇḍapacaṅkamadvārakoṭṭhakādīhi paṭimaṇḍitaṃ bahi veḷūhi parikkhittaṃ ahosi nīlobhāsaṃ manoramaṃ, tena “veḷuvana”nti [P 0.0060] vuccati. Kalandakānañcettha nivāpaṃ adaṃsu, tasmā “kalandakanivāpo”ti vuccati. Pubbe kira aññataro rājā taṃ uyyānaṃ kīḷanatthaṃ paviṭṭho surāmadamatto divāseyyaṃ upagato supi, parijanopissa “sutto rājā”ti pupphaphalādīhi palobhiyamāno ito cito ca pakkāmi. Atha surāgandhena aññatarasmā rukkhasusirā kaṇhasappo nikkhamitvā rañño abhimukho āgacchati. Taṃ disvā rukkhadevatā “rañño jīvitaṃ dassāmī”ti kalandakavesena gantvā kaṇṇamūle saddamakāsi. Rājā paṭibujjhi, kaṇhasappo nivatto. So taṃ disvā “imāya kāḷakāya mama jīvitaṃ dinna”nti kāḷakānaṃ nivāpaṃ tattha paṭṭhapesi, abhayaghosañca ghosāpesi. Tasmā tato paṭṭhāya taṃ “kalandakanivāpa”nti saṅkhaṃ gataṃ. Kalandakāti hi kāḷakānaṃ nāmaṃ, tasmiṃ veḷuvane kalandakanivāpe.

6. In the sixth (sutta), at a city named Rājagaha. It is called 'Rājagaha' because it was occupied by great kings such as Mahāmandhātu and Mahāgovinda. Some explain it in another way, saying, 'Because it was difficult for rival kings to overcome and served as their stronghold, it is called Rājagaha,' and so on. But what is the point of these explanations? That is simply the name of that city. This city was indeed a city during the time of the Buddhas and the wheel-turning monarchs, but at other times, it was empty, inhabited by yakkhas, serving as their dwelling place. At Veḷuvana, the Kalandakanivāpa: 'Veḷuvana' is the name of that monastery. It is said to have been surrounded by a wall eighteen cubits high, adorned with a large fragrant chamber suitable for the Blessed Buddha’s residence, along with other structures like palaces, huts, caves, pavilions, walking paths, gates, and towers. Outside, it was enclosed by bamboo, shimmering blue and delightful; hence it was called 'Veḷuvana.' And they provided a feeding ground for the kalandakas there; therefore, it was called 'Kalandakanivāpa.' Long ago, it is said, a certain king entered that grove for amusement. Intoxicated with liquor, he lay down for a midday nap and fell asleep. His attendants, thinking, 'The king is asleep,' wandered here and there, enticed by flowers and fruits and such. Then, drawn by the scent of liquor, a black snake emerged from a hollow in a tree and approached the king. Seeing this, the tree deity, wishing to give the king his life, took the form of a kalandaka and made a noise near his ear. The king awoke, and the black snake retreated. Seeing this, the king thought, 'This black creature has given me my life,' and established a feeding ground for the black creatures there, proclaiming safety for them. From then on, that place came to be known as 'Kalandakanivāpa.' 'Kalandaka' is, indeed, the name for black creatures. Thus, in that Bamboo Grove, at the Kalandakanivāpa.

Mahākassapoti [V 0.0049] mahantehi sīlakkhandhādīhi samannāgatattā mahanto kassapoti mahākassapo, apica kumārakassapattheraṃ upādāya ayaṃ mahāthero [M 0.0055] “mahākassapo”ti vuccati. Pippaliguhāyanti tassā kira guhāya dvārasamīpe eko pippalirukkho ahosi, tena sā “pippaliguhā”ti paññāyittha. Tassaṃ pippaliguhāyaṃ. Ābādhikoti ābādho assa atthīti ābādhiko, byādhikoti attho. Dukkhitoti kāyasannissitaṃ dukkhaṃ sañjātaṃ assāti dukkhito, dukkhappattoti attho. Bāḷhagilānoti adhimattagelañño, taṃ pana gelaññaṃ sato sampajāno hutvā adhivāsesi. Athassa bhagavā taṃ pavattiṃ ñatvā tattha gantvā bojjhaṅgaparittaṃ abhāsi, teneva therassa so ābādho vūpasami. Vuttañhetaṃ bojjhaṅgasaṃyutte –

Mahākassapa: He is called 'Mahākassapa' because he was endowed with great aggregates of virtue, etc., and was thus a great Kassapa; moreover, with reference to the Elder Kumārakassapa, this great elder is called 'Mahākassapa.' Pippaliguhā: It is said that near the entrance of that cave, there was a pippali tree, which is why it became known as 'Pippaliguhā.' In that Pippaliguhā. Ābādhiko: 'He has an illness,' thus he is 'ābādhiko'; the meaning is 'sick.' Dukkhito: 'Bodily suffering has arisen for him,' thus he is 'dukkhito'; the meaning is 'afflicted with suffering.' Bāḷhagilāno: Extremely ill. He endured that illness being mindful and clearly comprehending. Then, the Blessed One, knowing of his condition, went there and recited the Bojjhaṅga Paritta. Through that alone, the elder's illness subsided. And this was stated in the Bojjhaṅga Saṃyutta:

“Tena kho pana samayena āyasmā mahākassapo pippaliguhāyaṃ viharati ābādhiko dukkhito bāḷhagilāno. Atha kho bhagavā sāyanhasamayaṃ paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito yenāyasmā mahākassapo tenupasaṅkami, upasaṅkamitvā paññatte āsane nisīdi. Nisajja kho bhagavā…pe… etadavoca – ‘kacci te, kassapa, khamanīyaṃ, kacci yāpanīyaṃ, kacci dukkhā vedanā [P 0.0061] paṭikkamanti, no abhikkamanti, paṭikkamosānaṃ paññāyati no abhikkamo’ti? ‘Na me, bhante, khamanīyaṃ, na yāpanīyaṃ, bāḷhā me bhante, dukkhā vedanā abhikkamanti no paṭikkamanti, abhikkamosānaṃ paññāyati no paṭikkamo’ti.

At that time, the Venerable Mahākassapa was dwelling in the Pippali Cave, afflicted, suffering, severely ill. Then, in the evening, the Blessed One arose from seclusion and approached the Venerable Mahākassapa. Having approached, he sat down on the appointed seat. Sitting there, the Blessed One said this: 'I hope you are bearing up, Kassapa; I hope you are managing. I hope your painful feelings are subsiding and not increasing, that their subsiding is apparent and not their increase?' 'No, venerable sir, I am not bearing up, I am not managing. My painful feelings are severe, venerable sir; they are increasing, not subsiding. Their increase is apparent, not their subsiding.'

“‘Sattime, kassapa, bojjhaṅgā mayā sammadakkhātā bhāvitā bahulīkatā abhiññāya sambodhāya nibbānāya saṃvattanti. Katame satta? Satisambojjhaṅgo kho, kassapa, mayā sammadakkhāto bhāvito bahulīkato abhiññāya sambodhāya nibbānāya saṃvattati…pe… upekkhāsambojjhaṅgo kho, kassapa, mayā sammadakkhāto bhāvito bahulīkato abhiññāya sambodhāya nibbānāya saṃvattati. Ime kho, kassapa, satta bojjhaṅgā mayā sammadakkhātā bhāvitā bahūlīkatā abhiññāya sambodhāya nibbānāya saṃvattantī’ti. ‘Taggha bhagavā bojjhaṅgā, taggha, sugata, bojjhaṅgā’”ti.

'Kassapa, these seven factors of enlightenment are well-expounded by me, developed and cultivated, and they lead to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, and to Nibbāna. What seven? The enlightenment factor of mindfulness, Kassapa, is well-expounded by me, developed and cultivated, and it leads to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, and to Nibbāna... the enlightenment factor of equanimity, Kassapa, is well-expounded by me, developed and cultivated, and it leads to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, and to Nibbāna. These, Kassapa, are the seven factors of enlightenment well-expounded by me, developed and cultivated, and they lead to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, and to Nibbāna.' 'Truly, Blessed One, they are factors of enlightenment; truly, Sugata, they are factors of enlightenment.'

“Idamavoca bhagavā. Attamano āyasmā mahākassapo bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinandi. Vuṭṭhahi cāyasmā mahākassapo tamhā [M 0.0056] ābādhā, tathā pahīno cāyasmato mahākassapassa so ābādho ahosī”ti.

The Blessed One said this. Pleased, the Venerable Mahākassapa rejoiced in the Blessed One's words. And the Venerable Mahākassapa recovered from that illness; thus that illness of the Venerable Mahākassapa was dispelled.

Tena [V 0.0050] vuttaṃ – “atha kho āyasmā mahākassapo aparena samayena tamhā ābādhā vuṭṭhāsī”ti.

Therefore it was said: "Then, at a later time, the Venerable Mahākassapa recovered from that illness."

Etadahosīti pubbe gelaññadivasesu saddhivihārikehi upanītaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ paribhuñjitvā vihāre eva ahosi. Athassa tamhā ābādhā vuṭṭhitassa etaṃ “yaṃnūnāhaṃ rājagahaṃ piṇḍāya paviseyya”nti parivitakko ahosi. Pañcamattāni devatāsatānīti sakkassa devarañño paricārikā pañcasatā kakuṭapādiniyo accharāyo. Ussukkaṃ āpannāni hontīti therassa piṇḍapātaṃ dassāmāti pañcapiṇḍapātasatāni sajjetvā suvaṇṇabhājanehi ādāya antarāmagge ṭhatvā, “bhante, imaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ gaṇhatha, saṅgahaṃ no karothā”ti vadamānā piṇḍapātadāne yuttappayuttāni honti. Tena vuttaṃ “āyasmato mahākassapassa piṇḍapātappaṭilābhāyā”ti.

'This occurred to him' means that previously, on the days of his illness, he had consumed the almsfood brought by his co-resident disciples and remained in the monastery. Then, when he had recovered from that illness, this thought occurred to him: 'What if I were to enter Rājagaha for alms?' 'Five hundred deities' refers to five hundred Kakuṭapādiniyo nymphs who were attendants of Sakka, the king of the gods. 'They became eager' means that, thinking, 'We will give almsfood to the elder,' they prepared five hundred portions of almsfood, and taking them in golden vessels, they stood along the road, saying, 'Venerable sir, accept this almsfood; grant us your favor,' thus they were diligently engaged in the giving of almsfood. Therefore it was said, 'for the Venerable Mahākassapa’s obtaining of almsfood.'

Sakko kira devarājā therassa cittappavattiṃ ñatvā tā accharāyo uyyojesi “gacchatha tumhe ayyassa mahākassapattherassa piṇḍapātaṃ datvā attano patiṭṭhaṃ karothā”ti. Evaṃ hissa ahosi “imāsu sabbāsu gatāsu kadāci ekissāpi hatthato piṇḍapātaṃ thero paṭiggaṇheyya, taṃ tassā bhavissati dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāyā”ti. Paṭikkhipi thero, “bhante[P 0.0062], mayhaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ gaṇhatha, mayhaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ gaṇhathā”ti vadantiyo “gacchatha tumhe katapuññā mahābhogā, ahaṃ duggatānaṃ saṅgahaṃ karissāmī”ti vatvā, “bhante, mā no nāsetha, saṅgahaṃ no karothā”ti vadantiyo punapi paṭikkhipitvā punapi apagantuṃ anicchamānā yācantiyo “na attano pamāṇaṃ jānātha, apagacchathā”ti vatvā accharaṃ pahari. Tā therassa accharāsaddaṃ sutvā santajjitā ṭhātuṃ asakkontiyo palāyitvā devalokameva gatā. Tena vuttaṃ – “pañcamattāni devatāsatāni paṭikkhipitvā”ti.

It is said that Sakka, the king of the gods, knowing the elder's train of thought, dispatched those nymphs, saying, "Go, give almsfood to the noble elder Mahākassapa and establish a foundation of merit for yourselves." For this thought had occurred to him: "Among all these who have gone, should the elder accept almsfood from the hand of even one, it will be for her long-term welfare and happiness." The elder refused them. As they were saying, "Venerable sir, accept my almsfood, accept my almsfood," he said, "Go away. You have already made merit and possess great wealth. I will extend my support to the destitute." When they said, "Venerable sir, do not ruin our opportunity; grant us your favor," he refused them again. As they were unwilling to depart and continued begging, he said, "You do not know your own measure; go away!" and snapped his fingers. Hearing the sound of the elder's finger-snap, they were startled and, unable to remain, they fled and went back to the world of the gods. Therefore it was said: "having refused five hundred deities."

Pubbaṇhasamayanti [M 0.0057] pubbaṇhe ekaṃ samayaṃ, ekasmiṃ kāle. Nivāsetvāti vihāranivāsanaparivattanavasena nivāsanaṃ daḷhaṃ nivāsetvā. Pattacīvaramādāyāti cīvaraṃ pārupitvā pattaṃ hatthena gahetvā. Piṇḍāya pāvisīti piṇḍapātatthāya pāvisi. Daliddavisikhāti duggatamanussānaṃ vasanokāso. Kapaṇavisikhāti bhogapārijuññappattiyā dīnamanussānaṃ vāso. Pesakāravisikhāti tantavāyavāso. Addasā kho bhagavāti kathaṃ addasa? “Ābādhā vuṭṭhito mama putto kassapo kinnu kho karotī”ti āvajjento veḷuvane nisinno eva bhagavā dibbacakkhunā addasa.

'In the morning time' means at a certain time in the morning. 'Having dressed' means having firmly put on his lower robe, by way of changing from the one worn in the monastery. 'Taking his bowl and robe' means having put on his outer robe and taken the bowl in his hand. 'He entered for alms' means he entered for the purpose of almsfood. 'The street of the destitute' is the dwelling place of poor people. 'The street of the impoverished' is the residence of people in distress due to the loss of their possessions. 'The weavers' street' is the dwelling place of weavers. 'The Blessed One saw'—how did he see? While seated in the Bamboo Grove, the Blessed One reflected, "My son Kassapa has recovered from his illness. What is he doing now?" and he saw with his divine eye.

Etamatthaṃ [V 0.0051] viditvāti yāyaṃ āyasmato mahākassapassa pañcahi accharāsatehi upanītaṃ anekasūpaṃ anekabyañjanaṃ dibbapiṇḍapātaṃ paṭikkhipitvā kapaṇajanānuggahappaṭipatti vuttā, etamatthaṃ jānitvā. Imaṃ udānanti imaṃ paramappicchatādassanamukhena khīṇāsavassa tādībhāvānubhāvadīpakaṃ udānaṃ udānesi.

'Having understood this matter' means knowing this matter which has been told: the practice of the Venerable Mahākassapa in supporting the impoverished people by refusing the divine almsfood with its many soups and curries, brought by five hundred nymphs. 'This inspired utterance' means he uttered this inspired utterance, which reveals the steadfast nature and power of one whose cankers are destroyed, by way of demonstrating supreme contentment.

Tattha anaññaposinti aññaṃ posetīti aññaposī, na aññaposī anaññaposī, attanā posetabbassa aññassa abhāvena adutiyo, ekakoti attho. Tena therassa subharataṃ dasseti. Thero hi kāyaparihārikena cīvarena kucchiparihārikena ca piṇḍapātena attānameva posento paramappiccho hutvā viharati, aññaṃ ñātimittādīsu kañci na poseti katthaci alaggabhāvato. Atha vā aññena aññatarena posetabbatāya abhāvato anaññaposī. Yo hi ekasmiṃyeva paccayadāyake paṭibaddhacatupaccayo so anaññaposī nāma na hoti ekāyattavuttito[P 0.0063]. Thero pana “yathāpi bhamaro puppha”nti (dha. pa. 49) gāthāya vuttanayena jaṅghābalaṃ nissāya piṇḍāya caranto kulesu niccanavo hutvā missakabhattena yāpeti. Tathā hi naṃ bhagavā candūpamappaṭipadāya thomesi. Aññātanti abhiññātaṃ, yathābhuccaguṇehi patthaṭayasaṃ, teneva vā anaññaposibhāvena appicchatāsantuṭṭhitāhi ñātaṃ. Atha vā aññātanti sabbaso pahīnataṇhatāya lābhasakkārasilokanikāmanahetu attānaṃ jānāpanavasena na ñātaṃ. Avītataṇho [M 0.0058] hi pāpiccho kuhakatāya sambhāvanādhippāyena attānaṃ jānāpeti. Dantanti chaḷaṅgupekkhāvasena indriyesu uttamadamanena dantaṃ. Sāre patiṭṭhitanti vimuttisāre avaṭṭhitaṃ, asekkhasīlakkhandhādike vā sīlādisāre patiṭṭhitaṃ. Khīṇāsavaṃ vantadosanti kāmāsavādīnaṃ catunnaṃ āsavānaṃ anavasesaṃ pahīnattā khīṇāsavaṃ. Tato eva rāgādidosānaṃ sabbaso vantattā vantadosaṃ. Tamahaṃ brūmi brāhmaṇanti taṃ yathāvuttaguṇaṃ paramatthabrāhmaṇaṃ ahaṃ brāhmaṇanti vadāmīti. Idhāpi heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva desanānānattaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Herein, regarding anaññaposiṃ (not supporting another): one who supports another is an aññaposī; one who is not an aññaposī is an anaññaposī. Because there is no other to be supported by oneself, he is without a second, meaning he is alone. By this, the elder’s quality of being easy to support is shown. For the elder, supporting only himself with the robes that are carried on his body and the almsfood that is carried in his belly, dwells as one with the fewest of wishes. He does not support any other among relatives, friends, and so on, because of his non-attachment to anything whatsoever. Or alternatively, he is an anaññaposī because of the absence of being one who is to be supported by any other person. For one whose four requisites are dependent on a single supporter is not called an anaññaposī, because his livelihood depends on one person. The elder, however, in the manner stated in the verse, 'Just as a bee from a flower...' (Dhp. 49), wanders for alms relying on the strength of his legs, and being ever new among families, he maintains himself with mixed almsfood. For this reason, the Blessed One praised him for his practice comparable to the moon. Aññātaṃ means well-known, one whose fame is spread because of his true qualities; or, he is known for his fewness of wishes and contentment precisely because of his state of not supporting others. Alternatively, aññātaṃ means 'not known' in the sense of not making oneself known for the sake of gain, honor, and fame, due to having entirely abandoned craving. For one who has not abandoned craving, being of evil wishes, makes himself known for the sake of deception and with the intention of being esteemed. Dantaṃ (tamed) means tamed in the sense faculties through supreme self-control by means of the six-factored equanimity. Sāre patiṭṭhitaṃ (established in the essence) means established in the essence of liberation, or established in the essence of virtue and so on, such as the aggregate of the adept's virtue. Khīṇāsavaṃ vantadosaṃ (whose taints are destroyed, who has vomited forth faults): because the four taints, beginning with the taint of sensual pleasure, have been abandoned without remainder, he is one 'whose taints are destroyed.' For that very reason, because faults such as greed have been entirely vomited forth, he is one 'who has vomited forth faults.' Tamahaṃ brūmi brāhmaṇaṃ (him I call a brahmin) means: 'That person endowed with the aforementioned qualities, a brahmin in the ultimate sense, I call a brahmin.' Here too, the diversity of the teaching should be understood in the way explained below.

Chaṭṭhasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the sixth discourse is concluded.

7. Ajakalāpakasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Ajakalāpaka Sutta.

7. Sattame pāvāyanti evaṃnāmake mallarājūnaṃ nagare. Ajakalāpake cetiyeti ajakalāpakena [V 0.0052] nāma yakkhena pariggahitattā “ajakalāpaka”nti laddhanāme manussānaṃ cittīkataṭṭhāne[P 0.0064]. So kira yakkho aje kalāpe katvā bandhanena ajakoṭṭhāsena saddhiṃ baliṃ paṭicchati, na aññathā, tasmā “ajakalāpako”ti paññāyittha. Keci panāhu – ajake viya satte lāpetīti ajakalāpakoti. Tassa kira sattā baliṃ upanetvā yadā ajasaddaṃ katvā baliṃ upaharanti, tadā so tussati, tasmā “ajakalāpako”ti vuccatīti. So pana yakkho ānubhāvasampanno kakkhaḷo pharuso tattha ca sannihito, tasmā taṃ ṭhānaṃ manussā cittiṃ karonti, kālena kālaṃ baliṃ upaharanti. Tena vuttaṃ “ajakalāpake cetiye”ti. Ajakalāpakassa yakkhassa bhavaneti tassa yakkhassa vimāne.

7. In the seventh sutta: at Pāvā means in the city of the Malla kings of that name. At the Ajakalāpaka Shrine: at a place revered by people, which received the name 'Ajakalāpaka' because it was possessed by a yakkha named Ajakalāpaka. It is said that this yakkha accepts an offering of goats made into bundles and tied up, together with a portion of goat, and not otherwise; therefore, he became known as 'Ajakalāpaka.' Some, however, say he is called 'Ajakalāpaka' because he causes beings to cry out like goats. It is said that when beings bring an offering and present it while making the sound of a goat, he is pleased; therefore, he is called 'Ajakalāpaka.' That yakkha is endowed with power, is harsh and fierce, and is always present there. Therefore, people revere that place and from time to time bring offerings. For that reason it is said, 'at the Ajakalāpaka Shrine.' In the dwelling of the yakkha Ajakalāpaka means in that yakkha's mansion.

Tadā kira satthā taṃ yakkhaṃ dametukāmo sāyanhasamaye eko adutiyo pattacīvaraṃ ādāya ajakalāpakassa yakkhassa bhavanadvāraṃ gantvā tassa dovārikaṃ bhavanapavisanatthāya yāci. So “kakkhaḷo, bhante, ajakalāpako yakkho, samaṇoti vā brāhmaṇoti vā gāravaṃ na karoti, tasmā tumhe eva jānātha, mayhaṃ pana tassa anārocanaṃ na yutta”nti tāvadeva yakkhasamāgamaṃ gatassa ajakalāpakassa santikaṃ [M 0.0059] vātavegena agamāsi. Satthā antobhavanaṃ pavisitvā ajakalāpakassa nisīdanamaṇḍape paññattāsane nisīdi. Yakkhassa orodhā satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhaṃsu. Satthā tāsaṃ kālayuttaṃ dhammiṃ kathaṃ kathesi. Tena vuttaṃ – “pāvāyaṃ viharati ajakalāpake cetiye ajakalāpakassa yakkhassa bhavane”ti.

At that time, it is said, the Teacher, wishing to tame that yakkha, went alone and without a companion in the evening, taking his bowl and robes, to the door of the dwelling of the yakkha Ajakalāpaka and asked his doorkeeper for entry into the dwelling. The doorkeeper replied, 'Venerable sir, the yakkha Ajakalāpaka is harsh; he shows no respect to ascetics or brahmins. Therefore, you yourself should know best. For my part, it is not proper for me not to inform him.' And at that very moment, he went with the speed of the wind to Ajakalāpaka, who had gone to an assembly of yakkhas. The Teacher entered the dwelling and sat on the prepared seat in Ajakalāpaka's sitting pavilion. The yakkha's female attendants approached the Teacher, paid homage, and stood to one side. The Teacher gave them a timely talk on the Dhamma. For that reason it is said: 'He was dwelling at Pāvā, in the Ajakalāpaka shrine, in the dwelling of the yakkha Ajakalāpaka.'

Tasmiṃ samaye sātāgirahemavatā ajakalāpakassa bhavanamatthakena yakkhasamāgamaṃ gacchantā attano gamane asampajjamāne “kiṃ nu kho kāraṇa”nti āvajjentā satthāraṃ ajakalāpakassa bhavane nisinnaṃ disvā tattha gantvā bhagavantaṃ vanditvā “mayaṃ, bhante, yakkhasamāgamaṃ gamissāmā”ti āpucchitvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā gatā yakkhasannipāte ajakalāpakaṃ disvā tuṭṭhiṃ pavedayiṃsu “lābhā te, āvuso, ajakalāpaka, yassa te bhavane sadevake loke aggapuggalo bhagavā nisinno, upasaṅkamitvā [P 0.0065] bhagavantaṃ payirupāsassu, dhammañca suṇāhī”ti. So tesaṃ kathaṃ sutvā “ime tassa muṇḍakassa samaṇakassa mama bhavane nisinnabhāvaṃ kathentī”ti kodhābhibhūto hutvā “ajja mayhaṃ tena samaṇena saddhiṃ saṅgāmo bhavissatī”ti cintetvā yakkhasannipātato uṭṭhahitvā dakkhiṇaṃ pādaṃ ukkhipitvā saṭṭhiyojanamattaṃ pabbatakūṭaṃ akkami, taṃ bhijjitvā dvidhā ahosi. Sesaṃ ettha yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ āḷavakasuttavaṇṇanāyaṃ (saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.246) āgatanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

At that time, Sātāgira and Hemavata, while going to the assembly of yakkhas over Ajakalāpaka’s mansion, found their journey impeded. Reflecting, 'What could be the reason?' they saw the Teacher seated in Ajakalāpaka’s mansion. They went there, paid homage to the Blessed One, and, taking their leave by saying, 'Venerable sir, we will go to the assembly of yakkhas,' they circumambulated him and departed. At the assembly of yakkhas, upon seeing Ajakalāpaka, they joyfully informed him, saying: 'It is a great gain for you, friend Ajakalāpaka, that the Blessed One, the supreme person in the world with its gods, is seated in your mansion! Go and attend upon the Blessed One, and listen to the Dhamma.' Hearing their words, he was overcome with anger, thinking, 'These two are talking about that shaveling ascetic sitting in my mansion!' He thought, 'Today I will have a battle with that ascetic!' Rising from the assembly of yakkhas, he lifted his right foot and stamped on a mountain peak sixty yojanas in size, which split and became twofold. The remainder of what is to be said here should be understood in the manner that has come down in the commentary on the Āḷavaka Sutta.

Ajakalāpakassa [V 0.0053] samāgamo hi āḷavakasamāgamasadisova ṭhapetvā pañhakaraṇaṃ vissajjanaṃ bhavanato tikkhattuṃ nikkhamanaṃ pavesanañca. Ajakalāpako hi āgacchantoyeva “etehiyeva taṃ samaṇaṃ palāpessāmī”ti vātamaṇḍalādike navavasse samuṭṭhāpetvā tehi bhagavato calanamattampi kātuṃ asakkonto nānāvidhappaharaṇahatthe ativiya bhayānakarūpe bhūtagaṇe nimminitvā tehi saddhiṃ bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā antanteneva caranto sabbarattiṃ nānappakāraṃ vippakāraṃ katvāpi bhagavato kiñci kesaggamattampi nisinnaṭṭhānato calanaṃ kātuṃ nāsakkhi. Kevalaṃ pana “ayaṃ samaṇo maṃ anāpucchā mayhaṃ bhavanaṃ pavisitvā nisīdatī”ti kodhavasena pajjali. Athassa bhagavā cittappavattiṃ ñatvā “seyyathāpi nāma caṇḍassa kukkurassa nāsāya pittaṃ bhindeyya, evaṃ so bhiyyosomattāya [M 0.0060] caṇḍataro assa, evamevāyaṃ yakkho mayi idha nisinne cittaṃ padūseti, yaṃnūnāhaṃ bahi nikkhameyya”nti sayameva bhavanato nikkhamitvā abbhokāse nisīdi. Tena [P 0.0066] vuttaṃ – “tena kho pana samayena bhagavā rattandhakāratimisāyaṃ abbhokāse nisinno hotī”ti.

Indeed, the encounter with Ajakalāpaka was similar to the encounter with Āḷavaka, except for the asking of questions, the answering, and the threefold exiting from and entering into the dwelling. For Ajakalāpaka, upon his very arrival, thinking, 'I will drive away this ascetic with these very things,' created whirlwinds and rain showers, but with these he was unable to make the Blessed One move in the slightest. Then, with hands holding various weapons and having conjured up a host of spirits of exceedingly frightening appearance, he approached the Blessed One with them. Though he roamed about nearby all night, perpetrating all kinds of disturbances, he could not make the Blessed One move even a hair's breadth from his seated position. He merely burned with anger, thinking, 'This ascetic has entered my dwelling without asking me and sits here!' Then the Blessed One, knowing the state of his mind, reflected, 'Just as if one were to break bile on the nose of a fierce dog, it would become even fiercer, so too does this yakkha’s mind become corrupted while I am sitting here. What if I were to go outside?' So, of his own accord, the Blessed One left the dwelling and sat in the open air. Thus it is said: 'At that time, the Blessed One was sitting in the open air in the pitch-black darkness of the night.'

Tattha rattandhakāratimisāyanti rattiyaṃ andhakaraṇatamasi, cakkhuviññāṇuppattivirahite bahalandhakāreti attho. Caturaṅgasamannāgato kira tadā andhakāro pavattīti. Devoti megho ekamekaṃ phusitakaṃ udakabinduṃ pāteti. Atha yakkho “iminā saddena tāsetvā imaṃ samaṇaṃ palāpessāmī”ti bhagavato samīpaṃ gantvā “akkulo”tiādinā taṃ bhiṃsanaṃ akāsi. Tena vuttaṃ “atha kho ajakalāpako”tiādi. Tattha bhayanti cittutrāsaṃ, chambhitattanti ūrutthambhakasarīrassa chambhitabhāvaṃ. Lomahaṃsanti lomānaṃ pahaṭṭhabhāvaṃ, tīhipi padehi bhayuppattimeva dasseti. Upasaṅkamīti kasmā panāyaṃ evamadhippāyo upasaṅkami, nanu pubbe attanā kātabbaṃ vippakāraṃ akāsīti? Saccamakāsi, taṃ panesa “antobhavane khemaṭṭhāne thirabhūmiyaṃ ṭhitassa na kiñci kātuṃ asakkhi, idāni bahi ṭhitaṃ evaṃ bhiṃsāpetvā palāpetuṃ sakkā”ti maññamāno upasaṅkami. Ayañhi yakkho attano bhavanaṃ “thirabhūmī”ti maññati, “tattha ṭhitattā ayaṃ samaṇo na bhāyatī”ti ca.

Herein, 'in the pitch-black darkness of the night' means in the blinding darkness of the night, in a thick darkness where eye-consciousness cannot arise. It is said that at that time, a darkness endowed with four aspects prevailed. 'The deva' means the cloud; it lets fall a single raindrop at a time. Then the yakkha, thinking, 'With this sound I will frighten this ascetic and make him flee,' went near the Blessed One and made that terrifying sound, beginning with 'Akkulo.' Hence it is said: 'Then Ajakalāpaka…' and so on. Herein, 'fear' means terror of the mind; 'being stunned' means the state of the body being paralyzed, as if the thighs had become pillars; 'horripilation' means the state of the body’s hairs standing on end. With all three terms, only the arising of fear is shown. Regarding the word 'approached': why did he approach with such an intention? Had he not already perpetrated the harm he was capable of? Truly, he had. But he approached again, thinking, 'When he was standing inside the dwelling, in a safe place on firm ground, I was unable to do anything to him. Now that he is standing outside, it should be possible to frighten him in this way and make him flee.' For this yakkha considers his own dwelling to be 'firm ground,' and thinks, 'Because he was standing there, this ascetic was not afraid.'

Tikkhattuṃ “akkulo pakkulo”ti akkulapakkulikaṃ akāsīti tayo vāre “akkulo pakkulo”ti bhiṃsāpetukāmatāya evarūpaṃ saddaṃ akāsi. Anukaraṇasaddo hi ayaṃ. Tadā hi so yakkho sineruṃ ukkhipanto viya mahāpathaviṃ parivattento viya ca mahatā ussāhena asanisatasaddasaṅghāṭaṃ viya ekasmiṃ ṭhāne puñjīkataṃ hutvā viniccharantaṃ disāgajānaṃ hatthigajjitaṃ, kesarasīhānaṃ sīhaninnādaṃ[P 0.0067], yakkhānaṃ hiṃkārasaddaṃ, bhūtānaṃ aṭṭahāsaṃ, asurānaṃ apphoṭanaghosaṃ[V 0.0054], indassa devarañño vajiranigghātanigghosaṃ, attano gambhīratāya vipphārikatāya bhayānakatāya ca avasesasaddaṃ avahasantamiva abhibhavantamiva ca kappavuṭṭhānamahāvātamaṇḍalikāya vinigghosaṃ puthujjanānaṃ hadayaṃ phālentaṃ viya mahantaṃ paṭibhayanigghosaṃ abyattakkharaṃ tikkhattuṃ attano yakkhagajjitaṃ gajji [M 0.0061] “etena imaṃ samaṇaṃ bhiṃsāpetvā palāpessāmī”ti. Yaṃ yaṃ niccharati, tena tena pabbatā papaṭikaṃ muñciṃsu, vanappatijeṭṭhake upādāya sabbesu rukkhalatāgumbesu pattaphalapupphāni sīdayiṃsu, tiyojanasahassavitthatopi himavantapabbatarājā saṅkampi sampakampi sampavedhi, bhummadevatā ādiṃ katvā yebhuyyena devatānampi ahudeva bhayaṃ chambhitattaṃ lomahaṃso, pageva manussānaṃ. Aññesañca apadadvipadacatuppadānaṃ mahāpathaviyā undriyanakālo viya mahatī vibhiṃsanakā ahosi, sakalasmiṃ jambudīpatale mahantaṃ kolāhalaṃ udapādi. Bhagavā pana taṃ saddaṃ “kimī”ti amaññamāno niccalo nisīdi, “mā kassaci iminā antarāyo hotū”ti adhiṭṭhāsi.

Three times he made the sound 'Akkulo Pakkulo,' which is to say that three times, desiring to frighten him, he made a sound of that nature. For this is an onomatopoeic sound. At that moment, the yakkha—as if lifting Mount Sineru, as if turning over the great earth, with a mighty effort—roared his yakkha-roar three times. It was a great, terrifying roar with indistinct syllables, like the clash of a hundred thunderbolts gathered in one place and bursting forth; like the trumpeting of the elephants of the directions, the roar of maned lions, the snarling of yakkhas, the loud laughter of spirits, the clapping sound of asuras, and the crashing of the vajra of Indra, king of the devas. It was a sound that, due to its own depth, vastness, and terror, seemed to mock and overwhelm all other sounds, like the roar of the great whirlwind at the dissolution of the aeon, a sound that seemed to split the hearts of ordinary people. He roared thinking, 'With this I will frighten this ascetic and make him flee.' Wherever the sound went forth, mountains crumbled into layers. In all the trees, vines, and bushes, beginning with the great forest trees, the leaves, fruits, and flowers withered. Even the Himavant, king of mountains, spanning three thousand yojanas, trembled, shook, and quaked. Beginning with the earth-deities, for most of the devas, too, there arose fear, paralysis, and horripilation—how much more so for humans! And for other beings—footless, two-footed, and four-footed—there was a great terror, as if it were the time of the great earth's destruction. A great uproar arose over the entire surface of Jambudīpa. The Blessed One, however, paying the sound no heed, sat motionless. He made a resolution: 'May no one come to harm because of this.'

Yasmā pana so saddo “akkula pakkula” iti iminā ākārena sattānaṃ sotapathaṃ agamāsi, tasmā tassa anukaraṇavasena “akkulo pakkulo”ti, yakkhassa ca tassaṃ nigghosanicchāraṇāyaṃ akkulapakkulakaraṇaṃ atthīti katvā “akkulapakkulikaṃ akāsī”ti saṅgahaṃ āropayiṃsu. Keci pana “ākulabyākula iti padadvayassa pariyāyābhidhānavasena akkulo bakkuloti ayaṃ saddo vutto”ti vadanti yathā “ekaṃ ekaka”nti. Yasmā ekavāraṃ jāto paṭhamuppattivaseneva nibbattattā ākuloti ādiattho ākāro, tassa ca [P 0.0068] kakārāgamaṃ katvā rassattaṃ katanti. Dve vāre pana jāto bakkulo, kulasaddo cettha jātipariyāyo kolaṃkolotiādīsu viya. Vuttaadhippāyānuvidhāyī ca saddappayogoti paṭhamena padena jalābujasīhabyagghādayo, dutiyena aṇḍajaāsīvisakaṇhasappādayo vuccanti, tasmā sīhādiko viya āsīvisādiko viya ca “ahaṃ te jīvitahārako”ti imaṃ atthaṃ yakkho padadvayena dassetīti aññe. Apare pana “akkhulo bhakkhulo”ti pāḷiṃ vatvā “akkhetuṃ khepetuṃ vināsetuṃ ulati pavattetīti akkhulo, bhakkhituṃ khādituṃ ulatīti bhakkhulo. Ko paneso? Yakkharakkhasapisācasīhabyagghādīsu aññataro yo koci manussānaṃ anatthāvaho”ti tassa atthaṃ vadanti. Idhāpi pubbe vuttanayeneva adhippāyayojanā veditabbā.

Since that sound reached the ears of beings in the form of 'akkula pakkula,' therefore, by imitating it, the phrase 'akkulo pakkulo' arose. And because that yakkha made the sound 'akkula pakkula' while roaring and uttering, they concluded, 'He made the sound akkulapakkulikaṃ,' and thus included it in the collection. Some, however, say that the sound 'akkulo bakkulo' is a synonymous expression for the word-pair 'ākulabyākula,' just as 'ekaṃ' is expressed as 'ekaka.' Because a being born once is called 'ākula'—with the initial 'ā' having the meaning of arising—and by adding a 'k' sound and shortening it, it becomes 'akkula.' A being born twice is called 'bakkula,' where the word 'kula' here refers to birth, as in 'kolaṃkola,' etc. The usage of words follows the intended meaning; thus, with the first word, womb-born beings, like lions and tigers, are meant, and with the second word, egg-born beings like venomous snakes, black serpents, etc., are meant. Therefore, others say that the yakkha conveys this meaning through the two words, just as a lion or a venomous snake might: 'I am the taker of your life.' Still others say the Pāli is 'akkhulo bhakkhulo,' explaining it as: 'one who is able to destroy, eliminate, and annihilate is an akkhulo; one who is able to devour and eat is a bhakkhulo. And who is this? Any one of the yakkhas, rakshasas, pisācas, lions, tigers, etc., who brings harm to humans.' Here too, the application of the intended meaning should be understood in the way previously stated.

Eso [M 0.0062] te, samaṇa, pisācoti “ambho, samaṇa, tava pisitāsano pisāco upaṭṭhito”ti mahantaṃ bheravarūpaṃ abhinimminitvā bhagavato purato ṭhatvā attānaṃ sandhāya yakkho vadati.

'This is your pisāca, ascetic.' Thus, having magically created a great and terrifying form, the yakkha stood before the Blessed One and said, referring to himself: 'O ascetic, your flesh-eating pisāca has appeared before you!'

Etamatthaṃ [V 0.0055] viditvāti etaṃ tena yakkhena kāyavācāhi pavattiyamānaṃ vippakāraṃ. Tena ca attano anabhibhavanīyassa hetubhūtaṃ lokadhammesu nirupakkilesataṃ sabbākārato viditvā. Tāyaṃ velāyanti tassaṃ vippakārakaraṇavelāyaṃ. Imaṃ udānanti taṃ vippakāraṃ agaṇetvā assa agaṇanahetubhūtaṃ dhammānubhāvadīpakaṃ imaṃ udānaṃ udānesi.

'Having understood this matter'—that is, having recognized in every way this disturbance being caused by the yakkha through body and speech, and also his own untaintedness by worldly conditions, which was the cause of his invincibility—'at that time' means at the time that disturbance was being made. 'This inspired utterance' means that, disregarding that disturbance, he uttered this inspired utterance which reveals the power of the Dhamma, the very cause for disregarding it.

Tattha yadā sakesu dhammesūti yasmiṃ kāle sakaattabhāvasaṅkhātesu pañcasu upādānakkhandhadhammesu. Pāragūti pariññābhisamayapāripūrivasena pāraṅgato, tatoyeva tesaṃ hetubhūte samudaye, tadappavattilakkhaṇe nirodhe, nirodhagāminiyā paṭipadāya ca pahānasacchikiriyābhāvanābhisamayapāripūrivasena pāragato. Hoti brāhmaṇoti evaṃ sabbaso bāhitapāpattā brāhmaṇo nāma hoti, sabbaso sakaattabhāvāvabodhanepi catusaccābhisamayo [P 0.0069] hoti. Vuttañcetaṃ – “imasmiṃyeva byāmamatte kaḷevare sasaññimhi samanake lokañca lokasamudayañca paññapemī”tiādi (saṃ. ni. 1.107; a. ni. 4.45). Atha vā sakesu dhammesūti attano dhammesu, attano dhammā nāma atthakāmassa puggalassa sīlādidhammā. Sīlasamādhipaññāvimuttiādayo hi vodānadhammā ekantahitasukhasampādanena purisassa attano dhammā nāma, na anatthāvahā saṃkilesadhammā viya asakadhammā. Pāragūti tesaṃ sīlādīnaṃ pāripūriyā pāraṃ pariyantaṃ gato.

Therein, 'when in his own dhammas' refers to the time when, with regard to the five aggregates of clinging designated as one's own being, one has gone beyond. 'Gone beyond' means having reached the far shore by way of the full completion of comprehension and penetration; and for that very reason, with regard to their cause, the origin; with regard to cessation, characterized by their non-arising; and with regard to the path leading to cessation, one has gone beyond by way of the full completion of abandoning, realizing, developing, and penetrating. 'He is a brahmin'—thus, having entirely cast out evil, one is called a brahmin. Moreover, through the complete understanding of one's own being, there is the penetration of the four truths. And this was stated: 'In this very fathom-long body, with its perceptions and mind, I make known the world, the origin of the world...' and so on. Alternatively, 'in his own dhammas' means in the dhammas pertaining to oneself. The dhammas pertaining to oneself are the dhammas such as virtue for a person who desires what is beneficial. For purifying dhammas such as virtue, concentration, wisdom, and liberation, by bringing about ultimate welfare and happiness, are called a person's 'own dhammas,' not like the defiling dhammas that bring harm, which are not one's own. 'Gone beyond' means having reached the far shore, the limit, by fulfilling those dhammas such as virtue.

Tattha sīlaṃ tāva lokiyalokuttaravasena duvidhaṃ. Tesu lokiyaṃ pubbabhāgasīlaṃ. Taṃ saṅkhepato pātimokkhasaṃvarādivasena catubbidhaṃ, vitthārato pana anekappabhedaṃ. Lokuttaraṃ maggaphalavasena duvidhaṃ, atthato sammāvācāsammākammantasammāājīvā. Yathā ca sīlaṃ, tathā samādhipaññā ca lokiyalokuttaravasena duvidhā. Tattha lokiyasamādhi saha upacārena aṭṭha samāpattiyo, lokuttarasamādhi maggapariyāpanno[M 0.0063]. Paññāpi lokiyā sutamayā, cintāmayā, bhāvanāmayā ca sāsavā, lokuttarā pana maggasampayuttā phalasampayuttā ca. Vimutti nāma phalavimutti nibbānañca, tasmā sā lokuttarāva. Vimuttiñāṇadassanaṃ lokiyameva, taṃ ekūnavīsatividhaṃ paccavekkhaṇañāṇabhāvato. Evaṃ etesaṃ sīlādidhammānaṃ attano santāne arahattaphalādhigamena anavasesato nibbattapāripūriyā pāraṃ pariyantaṃ gatoti sakesu dhammesu pāragū.

Therein, virtue is, in the first place, twofold by way of the mundane and the supramundane. Of these, the mundane is the virtue of the preliminary part. In brief, this is fourfold by way of the restraint of the Pātimokkha and so on; in detail, however, it has many divisions. The supramundane is twofold by way of path and fruit; in essence, it is right speech, right action, and right livelihood. Just as with virtue, so too concentration and wisdom are twofold by way of the mundane and the supramundane. Therein, mundane concentration comprises the eight attainments together with access concentration; supramundane concentration is that which is included in the path. Mundane wisdom, which is accompanied by taints, arises from learning, reflection, and meditation; supramundane wisdom, however, is that which is associated with the path and with the fruit. Liberation refers to the liberation of the fruit and Nibbāna; therefore, it is solely supramundane. The knowledge and vision of liberation is only mundane, as it is nineteenfold, being of the nature of reviewing knowledge. Thus, because these dhammas—virtue and so forth—have been brought to fulfillment in his own continuum without remainder through the attainment of the fruit of arahantship, he has gone to the far shore, the limit; thus he is 'one who has gone beyond in his own dhammas.'

Atha vā sotāpattiphalādhigamena sīlasmiṃ pāragū. So hi “sīlesu paripūrakārī”ti vutto, sotāpannaggahaṇeneva cettha sakadāgāmīpi gahito hoti. Anāgāmiphalādhigamena samādhismiṃ [V 0.0056] pāragū. So hi “samādhismiṃ paripūrakārī”ti vutto. Arahattaphalādhigamena itaresu tīsu pāragū. Arahā hi paññāvepullappattiyā aggabhūtāya akuppāya cetovimuttiyā adhigatattā paccavekkhaṇañāṇassa ca pariyosānagamanato paññāvimuttivimuttiñāṇadassanesu pāragū nāma hoti. Evaṃ sabbathāpi catūsu ariyasaccesu catumaggavasena pariññādisoḷasavidhāya [P 0.0070] kiccanipphattiyā yathāvuttesu tasmiṃ tasmiṃ kāle sakesu dhammesu pāragato.

Alternatively, through the attainment of the fruit of stream-entry, one has gone beyond in virtue. For such a one is called 'one who fulfills the virtues,' and here, by the inclusion of the stream-enterer, the once-returner is also included. Through the attainment of the fruit of non-returning, one has gone beyond in concentration. For such a one is called 'one who fulfills concentration.' Through the attainment of the fruit of arahantship, one has gone beyond in the other three. For an Arahant, by having attained the supreme, unshakable liberation of mind through the attainment of the fullness of wisdom, and because the reviewing knowledge has reached its culmination, is called one who has gone beyond in wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation. Thus, in every way, with regard to the Four Noble Truths, by means of the four paths, through the accomplishment of the sixteen kinds of functions beginning with full understanding, one has, at that particular time, gone beyond in one's own dhammas as they have been described.

Hoti brāhmaṇoti tadā so bāhitapāpadhammatāya paramatthabrāhmaṇo hoti. Atha etaṃ pisācañca, pakkulañcātivattatīti tato yathāvuttapāragamanato atha pacchā, ajakalāpaka, etaṃ tayā dassitaṃ pisitāsanatthamāgataṃ pisācaṃ bhayajananatthaṃ samuṭṭhāpitaṃ akkulapakkulikañca ativattati, atikkamati, abhibhavati, taṃ na bhāyatīti attho.

He is then a brahmin in the ultimate sense because of having banished evil things. Then, as for the phrase 'he overcomes this goblin and the `pakkula`,' it means that after having gone to the further shore as stated, O Ajakaḷāpaka, he overcomes, surpasses, and subdues this goblin shown by you, which came to devour flesh, and the terrifying clamor stirred up to generate fear. The meaning is that he is not afraid of it.

Ayampi gāthā arahattameva ullapitvā kathitā. Atha ajakalāpako attanā katena tathārūpenapi paṭibhayarūpena vibhiṃsanena akampanīyassa bhagavato taṃ tādibhāvaṃ disvā “aho acchariyamanussovatāya”nti pasannamānaso pothujjanikāya saddhāya attani niviṭṭhabhāvaṃ vibhāvento satthu sammukhā upāsakattaṃ pavedesi.

This verse too was spoken extolling only Arahantship. Then Ajakaḷāpaka, seeing that very quality of the unshakable Blessed One even when confronted by the terrifying and frightening manifestation he himself had created, with a confident mind exclaimed, 'Oh, what a wonderful man!' Then, revealing that the faith of a worldling was established in him, he declared himself a lay follower in the presence of the Teacher.

Sattamasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Seventh Sutta is concluded.

8. Saṅgāmajisuttavaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Saṅgāmaji Sutta

8. Aṭṭhame [M 0.0064] saṅgāmajīti evaṃnāmo. Ayañhi āyasmā sāvatthiyaṃ aññatarassa mahāvibhavassa seṭṭhino putto, vayappattakāle mātāpitūhi patirūpena dārena niyojetvā sāpateyyaṃ niyyātetvā gharabandhanena baddho hoti. So ekadivasaṃ sāvatthivāsino upāsake pubbaṇhasamayaṃ dānaṃ datvā sīlaṃ samādiyitvā sāyanhasamaye suddhavatthe suddhuttarāsaṅge gandhamālādihatthe dhammassavanatthaṃ jetavanābhimukhe gacchante disvā “kattha tumhe gacchathā”ti pucchitvā “dhammassavanatthaṃ jetavane satthu santika”nti vutte “tena hi ahampi gamissāmī”ti tehi saddhiṃ jetavanaṃ agamāsi. Tena ca samayena bhagavā [P 0.0071] kañcanaguhāyaṃ sīhanādaṃ nadanto kesarasīho viya saddhammamaṇḍape paññattavarabuddhāsane nisīditvā catuparisamajjhe dhammaṃ deseti.

8. In the eighth sutta, Saṅgāmaji was his name. This venerable one was the son of a very wealthy merchant in Sāvatthī. When he came of age, his parents joined him with a suitable wife, handed over the family wealth, and he was bound by the ties of household life. One day, seeing the lay followers of Sāvatthī who in the forenoon had given alms and undertaken the precepts, and in the evening were going towards Jetavana to hear the Dhamma—dressed in clean clothes with clean upper robes, carrying perfumes and garlands in their hands—he asked, 'Where are you going?' When they replied, 'To the Teacher's presence at Jetavana to hear the Dhamma,' he said, 'In that case, I too shall go,' and he went with them to Jetavana. At that time, the Blessed One, like a maned lion roaring its lion's roar in a golden cave, was seated on the excellent Buddha-seat prepared in the Dhamma pavilion, teaching the Dhamma amidst the fourfold assembly.

Atha [V 0.0057] kho te upāsakā bhagavantaṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu, saṅgāmajipi kulaputto tassā parisāya pariyante dhammaṃ suṇanto nisīdi. Bhagavā anupubbikathaṃ kathetvā cattāri saccāni pakāsesi, saccapariyosāne anekesaṃ pāṇasahassānaṃ dhammābhisamayo ahosi. Saṅgāmajipi kulaputto sotāpattiphalaṃ patvā parisāya vuṭṭhitāya bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā pabbajjaṃ yāci “pabbājetha maṃ bhagavā”ti. “Anuññātosi pana tvaṃ mātāpitūhi pabbajjāyā”ti? “Nāhaṃ, bhante, anuññāto”ti. “Na kho, saṅgāmaji, tathāgatā mātāpitūhi ananuññātaṃ puttaṃ pabbājentī”ti. “Sohaṃ, bhante, tathā karissāmi, yathā maṃ mātāpitaro pabbajituṃ anujānantī”ti. So bhagavantaṃ vanditvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā mātāpitaro upasaṅkamitvā, “ammatātā, anujānātha maṃ pabbajitu”nti āha. Tato paraṃ raṭṭhapālasutte (ma. ni. 2.293 ādayo) āgatanayena veditabbaṃ.

Then those lay followers paid homage to the Blessed One and sat to one side. The clansman Saṅgāmaji also sat at the edge of the assembly, listening to the Dhamma. The Blessed One gave a gradual discourse and revealed the Four Noble Truths. At the conclusion of the discourse on the truths, many thousands of beings had a breakthrough to the Dhamma. The clansman Saṅgāmaji, having attained the fruit of stream-entry, approached the Blessed One after the assembly had risen, paid homage, and requested the going forth, saying, 'Blessed One, let me go forth.' 'But have you been permitted by your mother and father to go forth?' 'Venerable sir, I have not been permitted.' 'Saṅgāmaji, the Tathāgatas do not give the going forth to a son who has not been permitted by his mother and father.' 'Venerable sir, I will act in such a way that my mother and father will permit me to go forth.' He paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him respectfully, and approached his parents, saying, 'Mother, father, permit me to go forth.' From this point on, it should be understood according to the method given in the Raṭṭhapāla Sutta.

Atha so “pabbajitvā attānaṃ dassessāmī”ti paṭiññaṃ datvā anuññāto mātāpitūhi bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā pabbajjaṃ yāci. Alattha kho ca bhagavato santike pabbajjaṃ upasampadañca, acirūpasampanno ca pana so uparimaggatthāya ghaṭento vāyamanto aññatarasmiṃ araññāvāse vassaṃ vasitvā chaḷabhiñño hutvā vutthavasso bhagavantaṃ dassanāya mātāpitūnañca [M 0.0065] paṭissavamocanatthaṃ sāvatthiṃ agamāsi. Tena vuttaṃ – “tena kho pana samayena āyasmā saṅgāmaji sāvatthiṃ anuppatto hotī”ti.

Then, having given the promise, 'I will show myself after I have gone forth,' and having been permitted by his parents, he approached the Blessed One and requested the going forth. He obtained both the going forth and the higher ordination in the presence of the Blessed One. Not long after his higher ordination, striving and making an effort for the sake of the higher paths, he spent the rains-residence in a certain forest dwelling. Having attained the six supernormal knowledges and having completed the rains-residence, he went to Sāvatthī to see the Blessed One and to be released from the promise made to his parents. Hence it was said: 'At that time, the Venerable Saṅgāmaji had arrived in Sāvatthī.'

So hāyasmā dhuragāme piṇḍāya caritvā pacchābhattaṃ piṇḍapātapaṭikkanto jetavanaṃ pavisitvā bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā bhagavatā saddhiṃ katapaṭisanthāro aññaṃ byākaritvā puna bhagavantaṃ vanditvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā nikkhamitvā aññatarasmiṃ rukkhamūle divāvihāraṃ nisīdi. Athassa mātāpitaro ñātimittā cassa āgamanaṃ sutvā, “saṅgāmaji, kira idhāgato”ti haṭṭhatuṭṭhā turitaturitā vihāraṃ gantvā pariyesantā naṃ tattha nisinnaṃ disvā upasaṅkamitvā [P 0.0072] paṭisanthāraṃ katvā “mā aputtakaṃ sāpateyyaṃ rājāno hareyyuṃ, appiyā dāyādā vā gaṇheyyuṃ, nālaṃ pabbajjāya, ehi, tāta, vibbhamā”ti yāciṃsu. Taṃ sutvā thero “ime mayhaṃ kāmehi anatthikabhāvaṃ na jānanti, gūthadhārī viya gūthapiṇḍe kāmesuyeva allīyanaṃ icchanti, nayime sakkā dhammakathāya saññāpetu”nti assuṇanto viya nisīdi. Te nānappakāraṃ yācitvā attano vacanaṃ aggaṇhantaṃ disvā gharaṃ pavisitvā puttena saddhiṃ tassa bhariyaṃ saparivāraṃ uyyojesuṃ “mayaṃ nānappakāraṃ taṃ yācantāpi tassa manaṃ alabhitvā āgatā, gaccha tvaṃ, bhadde, tava bhattāraṃ puttasandassanena yācitvā saññāpehī”ti. Tāya kira āpannasattāya [V 0.0058] ayamāyasmā pabbajito. Sā “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā dārakamādāya mahatā parivārena jetavanaṃ agamāsi. Taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ – “assosi kho āyasmato saṅgāmajissā”tiādi.

That venerable one, having walked for alms in the first village of his round and returned from his alms round after the meal, entered Jetavana and approached the Blessed One. Having exchanged courteous greetings with the Blessed One, he declared final knowledge. Then, after venerating the Blessed One and circumambulating him, he departed and sat down at the foot of a certain tree for the day's abiding. Then his parents, relatives, and friends, hearing of his arrival, said, 'Saṅgāmaji, they say, has come here!' Delighted and overjoyed, they went hastily to the monastery. Searching for him and seeing him seated there, they approached, greeted him, and pleaded: 'Dear son, do not let the kings take your property for lack of an heir, nor let unloved heirs seize it. The homeless life is not for you. Come, dear son, disrobe!' Hearing this, the elder thought, 'They do not understand my lack of interest in sensual pleasures. Like dung-eaters for a ball of dung, they only desire to cling to sensual pleasures. It is impossible to make them understand with a Dhamma talk,' and he remained seated as if not hearing. Seeing that he did not accept their words after they had pleaded in various ways, they returned home and sent his wife with their son and a large retinue, saying, 'We have returned after pleading with him in various ways but failed to win his mind. Go, good lady, persuade your husband by showing him his son.' It is said that this venerable one had gone forth when she was pregnant. She agreed, saying, 'Very well,' and, taking the child, went to Jetavana with a large retinue. Regarding this, it is said: 'The venerable Saṅgāmaji’s wife heard...' and so on.

Tattha purāṇadutiyikāti pubbe gihikāle pādaparicaraṇavasena dutiyikā, bhariyāti attho. Ayyoti “ayyaputto”ti vattabbe pabbajitānaṃ anucchavikavohārena vadati. Kirāti anussavanatthe nipāto, tassa anuppatto kirāti sambandho veditabbo. Khuddaputtañhi samaṇa, posa manti āpannasattameva maṃ chaḍḍetvā pabbajito, sāhaṃ etarahi khuddaputtā, tādisaṃ maṃ chaḍḍetvāva tava samaṇadhammakaraṇaṃ ayuttaṃ, tasmā, samaṇa, puttadutiyaṃ maṃ ghāsacchādanādīhi bharassūti. Āyasmā pana, saṅgāmaji, indriyāni ukkhipitvā taṃ neva oloketi, nāpi ālapati. Tena vuttaṃ – “evaṃ vutte āyasmā saṅgāmaji tuṇhī ahosī”ti.

Herein, purāṇadutiyikā means a former companion from his household life, one who was his second by way of serving at his feet; that is, his wife. As for Ayya, when 'ayyaputta' (noble son) should have been said, she addresses him with a term suitable for monastics. Kirā is a particle in the sense of hearsay; its connection should be understood as 'it is said that he has arrived.' She says: 'Monk, support this little son!' For she thinks: 'You went forth having abandoned me when I was just pregnant. Now I have a little son. It is not proper for you to practice the monastic life having abandoned me in such a state. Therefore, monk, you must support me, who am now with my son, with food, clothing, and so on.' The Venerable Saṅgāmaji, however, having cast down his senses, neither looked at her nor spoke to her. Therefore it is said: 'When this was said, the Venerable Saṅgāmaji remained silent.'

Sā [M 0.0066] tikkhattuṃ tatheva vatvā tuṇhībhūtameva taṃ disvā “purisā nāma bhariyāsu nirapekkhāpi puttesu sāpekkhā honti, puttasineho pitu aṭṭhimiñjaṃ āhacca tiṭṭhati, tasmā puttapemenāpi mayhaṃ vase vatteyyā”ti maññamānā puttaṃ [P 0.0073] therassa aṅke nikkhipitvā ekamantaṃ apakkamma “eso te, samaṇa, putto, posa na”nti vatvā thokaṃ agamāsi. Sā kira samaṇatejenassa sammukhe ṭhātuṃ nāsakkhi. Thero dārakampi neva oloketi nāpi ālapati. Atha sā itthī avidūre ṭhatvā mukhaṃ parivattetvā olokentī therassa ākāraṃ ñatvā paṭinivattitvā “puttenapi ayaṃ samaṇo anatthiko”ti dārakaṃ gahetvā pakkāmi. Tena vuttaṃ – “atha kho āyasmato saṅgāmajissa purāṇadutiyikā”tiādi.

Having said the same thing three times and seeing that he remained silent, she thought: 'Men may be unconcerned about their wives, but they are concerned about their sons. A father's love for his son penetrates to the very marrow of his bones. Therefore, through affection for his son, he might come under my influence.' Thinking thus, she placed the child on the elder's lap, stepped aside, and said, 'This is your son, monk; support him!' Then she walked a short distance away. It is said that due to the monk's spiritual power, she was unable to stand long in his presence. The elder neither looked at the child nor spoke to him. Then the woman, standing not far away, turned her face and, observing the elder's disposition, understood. Turning back, she thought, 'This monk has no need even for his son.' She then took the child and departed. Therefore it is said: 'Then the former wife of the Venerable Saṅgāmaji…' and so on.

Tattha puttenapīti ayaṃ samaṇo attano orasaputtenapi anatthiko, pageva aññehīti adhippāyo. Dibbenāti ettha dibbasadisattā dibbaṃ. Devatānañhi sucaritakammanibbattaṃ pittasemharuhirādīhi apalibuddhaṃ dūrepi ārammaṇasampaṭicchanasamatthaṃ dibbaṃ pasādacakkhu hoti. Idampi catutthajjhānasamādhinibbattaṃ abhiññācakkhuṃ tādisanti dibbaṃ viyāti dibbaṃ, dibbavihārasannissayena laddhattā vā dibbaṃ, mahājutikattā mahāgatikattā vā dibbaṃ, tena dibbena. Visuddhenāti nīvaraṇādisaṃkilesavigamena suparisuddhena. Atikkantamānusakenāti manussānaṃ visayātītena. Imaṃ evarūpaṃ vippakāranti imaṃ evaṃ vippakāraṃ yathāvuttaṃ pabbajitesu asāruppaṃ aṅke puttaṭṭhapanasaṅkhātaṃ virūpakiriyaṃ.

Herein, puttenapi (even by his son) has the intended meaning: 'This monk has no need even for his own breast-born son, how much more so for others.' Regarding dibbena (by the divine eye): it is 'divine' because it is similar to the divine. For the divine eye of deities, produced by wholesome deeds, is unobstructed by bile, phlegm, blood, and so on, and is capable of receiving objects even from afar. This knowledge-eye, too, produced by the concentration of the fourth jhāna, is like that; thus, being like the divine, it is 'divine.' Alternatively, it is 'divine' because it is obtained through reliance on a divine abiding, or because of its great radiance and great pervasiveness. By that divine eye. Visuddhena (purified) means thoroughly pure through the removal of defilements such as the hindrances. Atikkantamānusakena (surpassing the human) means having surpassed the range of humans. Imaṃ evarūpaṃ vippakāraṃ (this kind of misconduct) refers to this very misconduct as described, which is unsuitable for the ordained—namely, the improper action designated as placing a child on his lap.

Etamatthanti [V 0.0059] etaṃ āyasmato saṅgāmajissa puttadārādīsu sabbattha nirapekkhabhāvasaṅkhātaṃ atthaṃ sabbākārato viditvā. Imaṃ udānanti imaṃ tassa iṭṭhāniṭṭhādīsu tādibhāvadīpakaṃ udānaṃ udānesi.

Regarding etam atthaṃ (this matter): having understood in every way this matter concerning the Venerable Saṅgāmaji, designated as the state of non-attachment towards all things, such as his son and wife. Regarding imaṃ udānaṃ (this inspired utterance): he uttered this inspired utterance, which reveals his state of equanimity with regard to desirable and undesirable things.

Tattha āyantinti āgacchantiṃ, purāṇadutiyikanti adhippāyo. Nābhinandatīti daṭṭhuṃ maṃ āgatāti na nandati na tussati. Pakkamantinti sā ayaṃ mayā asammoditāva gacchatīti gacchantiṃ. Na socatīti na cittasantāpamāpajjati. Yena pana kāraṇena thero evaṃ nābhinandati na socati, taṃ dassetuṃ “saṅgā saṅgāmajiṃ mutta”nti vuttaṃ. Tattha saṅgāti rāgasaṅgo dosamohamānadiṭṭhisaṅgoti pañcavidhāpi saṅgā samucchedappaṭipassaddhivimuttīhi [M 0.0067] vimuttaṃ saṅgāmajiṃ bhikkhuṃ. Tamahaṃ [P 0.0074] brūmi brāhmaṇanti taṃ tādibhāvappattaṃ khīṇāsavaṃ ahaṃ sabbaso bāhitapāpattā brāhmaṇanti vadāmīti.

Herein, āyantiṃ (coming) refers to the arriving former wife; this is the intended meaning. Nābhinandati (he does not delight) means he does not rejoice or feel pleased, thinking, 'She has come to see me.' Regarding pakkamantiṃ (departing): he does not grieve for her who is departing, thinking, 'She is going away unwelcomed by me.' Na socati (he does not grieve) means he does not fall into mental affliction. To show the reason why the elder neither delights nor grieves, it is said: 'Freed from attachments, Saṅgāmaji.' Herein, saṅgā (attachments) refers to the five kinds of attachment: the attachment of lust, and the attachments of hatred, delusion, pride, and wrong view. It refers to the monk Saṅgāmaji, freed from these five attachments by the liberations of cutting off and of tranquillization. Regarding tam ahaṃ brūmi brāhmaṇaṃ (him I call a brahmin): him, that one with taints destroyed who has attained such a state of equanimity, I call a brahmin because he has cast out all evil.

Aṭṭhamasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Eighth Sutta is finished.

9. Jaṭilasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Jaṭila Sutta

9. Navame gayāyanti ettha gayāti gāmopi titthampi vuccati. Gayāgāmassa hi avidūre viharanto bhagavā “gayāyaṃ viharatī”ti vuccati, tathā gayātitthassa. Gayātitthanti hi gayāgāmassa avidūre ekā pokkharaṇī atthi nadīpi, tadubhayaṃ “pāpapavāhanatittha”nti lokiyamahājano samudācarati. Gayāsīseti gajasīsasadisasikharo tattha eko pabbato gayāsīsanāmako, yattha hatthikumbhasadiso piṭṭhipāsāṇo bhikkhusahassassa okāso pahoti, tatra bhagavā viharati. Tena vuttaṃ – “gayāyaṃ viharati gayāsīse”ti.

9. In the ninth sutta, regarding gayāyaṃ (at Gayā): here 'Gayā' refers to both a village and a ford. For the Blessed One, dwelling not far from the village of Gayā, is said to be 'dwelling at Gayā,' and similarly with regard to the ford of Gayā. As for the ford of Gayā, not far from the village of Gayā there is a pond and also a river; the common people refer to both as the 'ford for washing away evil.' Regarding gayāsīse (at Gayāsīsa): there is a mountain there named Gayāsīsa, whose peak resembles an elephant's head. There, a flat rock like an elephant's frontal globe provides space for a thousand monks, and it is there the Blessed One dwells. Therefore it is said: 'He dwells at Gayā, at Gayāsīsa.'

Jaṭilāti tāpasā. Te hi jaṭādhāritāya idha “jaṭilā”ti vuttā. Antaraṭṭhake himapātasamayeti hemantassa utuno abbhantarabhūte māghamāsassa avasāne cattāro phagguṇamāsassa ādimhi cattāroti aṭṭhadivasaparimāṇe himassa patanakāle. Gayāyaṃ ummujjantīti keci tasmiṃ titthasammate udake paṭhamaṃ nimuggasakalasarīrā tato ummujjanti vuṭṭhahanti uppilavanti. Nimujjantīti [V 0.0060] sasīsaṃ udake osīdanti. Ummujjanimujjampi karontīti punappunaṃ ummujjananimujjanānipi karonti.

Jaṭilā refers to ascetics. They are called 'jaṭilas' here because they wear matted hair. Antaraṭṭhake himapātasamaye (during the eight-day interval in the time of snowfall) means during the period of snowfall lasting eight days, namely, the last four days of the month of Māgha and the first four days of the month of Phagguṇa, which falls within the winter season. Gayāyaṃ ummujjanti (they emerge at Gayā) means that some, having first submerged their entire bodies in that water esteemed as a ford, then emerge, rise up, and float. Nimujjanti (they submerge) means they sink into the water including their heads. Ummujjanimujjampi karonti (they also perform emerging and submerging) means they repeatedly perform acts of emerging and submerging.

Tattha hi keci “ekummujjaneneva pāpasuddhi hotī”ti evaṃdiṭṭhikā, te ummujjanameva katvā gacchanti. Ummujjanaṃ pana nimujjanamantarena natthīti avinābhāvato nimujjanampi te karontiyeva. Yepi “ekanimujjaneneva pāpasuddhi hotī”ti evaṃdiṭṭhikā, tepi ekavārameva nimujjitvā vuttanayena avinābhāvato ummujjanampi katvā pakkamanti. Ye pana “tasmiṃ titthe nimujjaneneva pāpasuddhi hotī”ti [P 0.0075] evaṃdiṭṭhikā, te tattha nimujjitvā assāse sannirumbhitvā maruppapātapatitā viya tattheva jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpuṇanti[M 0.0068]. Apare “punappunaṃ ummujjananimujjanāni katvā nhāte pāpasuddhi hotī”ti evaṃdiṭṭhikā, te kālena kālaṃ ummujjananimujjanāni karonti. Te sabbepi sandhāya vuttaṃ – “ummujjantipi nimujjantipi ummujjanimujjampi karontī”ti. Ettha ca kiñcāpi nimujjanapubbakaṃ ummujjanaṃ, nimujjanameva pana karontā katipayā, ummujjanaṃ tadubhayañca karontā bahūti tesaṃ yebhuyyabhāvadassanatthaṃ ummujjanaṃ paṭhamaṃ vuttaṃ. Tathā sambahulā jaṭilāti jaṭilānaṃ yebhuyyatāya vuttaṃ, muṇḍasikhaṇḍinopi ca brāhmaṇā udakasuddhikā tasmiṃ kāle tattha tathā karonti.

There, some, holding the view that 'purification from evil is achieved merely by emerging once,' perform only emerging and then depart. However, since emerging does not exist without submerging, by its inseparability, they also perform submerging. And those who hold the view that 'purification from evil is achieved merely by submerging once,' they too submerge just once, but in the manner stated, by its inseparability, they also perform emerging and then depart. As for those who hold the view that 'purification from evil is achieved by submerging in that very bathing-place,' they submerge there, restrain their breathing, and like those who have fallen from a precipice, they meet their end right there. Others, holding the view that 'purification from evil is achieved by bathing while repeatedly emerging and submerging,' perform emerging and submerging from time to time. All these are referred to by the statement: 'They emerge, they submerge, and they perform both emerging and submerging.' Here, although emerging is preceded by submerging, only a few perform merely submerging, while many perform emerging and both. To show the predominance of the latter, emerging is mentioned first. Similarly, 'many matted-hair ascetics' is said to indicate the majority of ascetics, though even shaven-headed and top-knotted brahmins who believe in water-purification also act in the same way there at that time.

Osiñcantīti keci gayāya udakaṃ hatthena gahetvā attano sīse ca sarīre ca osiñcanti, apare ghaṭehi udakaṃ gahetvā tīre ṭhatvā tathā karonti. Aggiṃ juhantīti keci gayātīre vediṃ sajjetvā dhūmadabbhipūjādike upakaraṇe upanetvā aggihutaṃ juhanti aggihutaṃ paricaranti. Iminā suddhīti iminā gayāyaṃ ummujjanādinā aggiparicaraṇena ca pāpamalato suddhi pāpapavāhanā saṃsārasuddhi eva vā hotīti evaṃdiṭṭhikā hutvāti attho.

'Pouring water' (osiñcanti) means some take water from Gayā in their hands and sprinkle it on their own heads and bodies, while others take water in pots and, standing on the bank, do the same. 'Offering to the fire' (aggiṃ juhanti) means some prepare an altar on the bank of Gayā, bring implements such as firewood, ladles, and offerings, and perform fire sacrifices, tending the fire. 'By this, purity' (iminā suddhi) means that, holding the view that 'by this, namely, by emerging in Gayā and so forth and by tending the fire, there is purification from the stain of evil, a washing away of evil, or even purification from the cycle of existence'—this is the meaning.

Ummujjanādi cettha nidassanamattaṃ vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tesu hi keci udakavāsaṃ vasanti, keci udakassañjaliṃ denti, keci tasmiṃ udake ṭhatvā candimasūriye anuparivattanti, keci anekasahassavāraṃ sāvittiādike japanti, keci “inda āgacchā”tiādinā vijjājapaṃ avhāyanti, keci mahatupaṭṭhānaṃ karonti, evañca karontā keci otaranti, keci uttaranti keci uttaritvā suddhikaācamanaṃ karonti, keci antoudake ṭhitā tantī vādenti, vīṇaṃ vādentīti evamādikā nānappakārakiriyā [P 0.0076] dassenti. Yasmā vā te evarūpā vikārakiriyā karontāpi tasmiṃ udake nimujjanaummujjanapubbakameva karonti, tasmā taṃ sabbaṃ nimujjanummujjanantogadhameva katvā “ummujjantī”tipiādi vuttaṃ. Evaṃ tattha ākulabyākule vattamāne [V 0.0061] uparipabbate ṭhito bhagavā tesaṃ taṃ kolāhalaṃ sutvā “kinnu kho eta”nti olokento taṃ kiriyavikāraṃ addasa, taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ – “addasā kho bhagavā…pe… iminā suddhī”ti, taṃ vuttatthameva.

Here, emerging and the like should be understood as mentioned by way of mere illustration. Among them, some dwell in the water, some offer handfuls of water, some stand in that water and follow the course of the moon and sun, some recite the Sāvittī and other chants thousands of times, some invoke deities with incantations like 'Come, Indra,' and some perform great acts of reverence. And while doing so, some descend, some ascend, some ascend and perform a purificatory rinsing, some stand in the middle of the water playing stringed instruments or lutes—thus they display various kinds of activities. Or, because even while engaging in such varied activities, they perform them only after first submerging and emerging in that water, therefore all that is included within submerging and emerging, and thus it is said, 'they emerge,' and so on. Thus, while such a confused commotion was occurring there, the Blessed One, standing on the upper mountain, heard their uproar and, wondering, 'What is this?', looked and saw those distorted activities. Referring to that, it is said: 'The Blessed One saw... by this purity'; that is the meaning already stated.

Etamatthaṃ [M 0.0069] viditvāti etaṃ atthaṃ udakorohanādiasuddhimagge tesaṃ suddhimaggaparāmasanaṃ saccādike ca suddhimagge attano aviparītāvabodhaṃ sabbākārato viditvā. Imaṃ udānanti imaṃ udakasuddhiyā asuddhimaggabhāvadīpakaṃ saccādidhammānañca yāthāvato suddhimaggabhāvadīpakaṃ udānaṃ udānesi.

'Having understood this meaning' (etamatthaṃ viditvā) means having fully known in every way this matter: their grasping at a path of purification which is in fact an impure path of descending into water and so forth, and his own undistorted understanding of the true path of purification regarding the truths and so forth. 'This inspired utterance' (imaṃ udānaṃ) means he uttered this inspired utterance which reveals the nature of water-purification as an impure path and reveals the nature of the truths and other doctrines as the path of purification, just as they are.

Tattha na udakena sucī hotīti ettha udakenāti udakummujjanādinā. Udakummujjanādi hi idha uttarapadalopena “udaka”nti vuttaṃ yathā rūpabhavo rūpanti. Atha vā udakenāti ummujjanādikiriyāya sādhanabhūtena udakena suci sattassa suddhi nāma na hoti, natthīti attho. Atha vā sucīti tena yathāvuttena udakena suci pāpamalato suddho nāma satto na hoti. Kasmā? Bahvettha nhāyatī jano. Yadi hi udakorohanādinā yathāvuttena pāpasuddhi nāma siyā, bahu ettha udake jano nhāyati, mātughātādipāpakammakārī añño ca gomahiṃsādiko antamaso macchakacchape upādāya, tassa sabbassāpi pāpasuddhi siyā, na panevaṃ hoti. Kasmā? Nhānassa pāpahetūnaṃ appaṭipakkhabhāvato. Yañhi yaṃ vināseti, so tassa paṭipakkho yathā āloko andhakārassa, vijjā ca avijjāya, na evaṃ nhānaṃ pāpassa. Tasmā niṭṭhamettha gantabbaṃ “na udakena suci hotī”ti.

Here, in 'one is not purified by water' (na udakena sucī hoti), 'by water' (udakena) means by emerging from water and so forth. For 'emerging from water and so forth' (udakummujjanādi) is here called 'water' (udaka) by eliding the latter part of the compound, just as 'form-existence' (rūpabhava) is called 'form' (rūpa). Alternatively, 'by water' (udakena) means that so-called purification for a being does not occur—that is, it does not exist—by water that is the means for actions like emerging and so forth. Or, 'purified' (sucī) means that a so-called being is not purified from the stain of evil by that aforementioned water. Why? Because many people bathe here. For if so-called purification from evil were to occur by the aforementioned descending into water and so forth, many people bathe in this water—those who commit evil deeds like matricide, and others such as cattle and buffaloes, down to the fish and turtles—for that entire multitude of beings, purification from evil would occur. But this is not the case. Why? Because bathing is not the antidote to the causes of evil. For that which destroys something is its antidote, just as light is the antidote to darkness, and knowledge to ignorance; but bathing is not thus the antidote to evil. Therefore, the conclusion to be reached here is: 'One is not purified by water.'

Yena pana suci hoti, taṃ dassetuṃ “yamhi saccañcā”tiādimāha. Tattha yamhīti yasmiṃ puggale[P 0.0077]. Saccanti vacīsaccañceva viratisaccañca. Atha vā saccanti ñāṇasaccañceva paramatthasaccañca. Dhammoti ariyamaggadhammo, phaladhammo ca, so sabbopi yasmiṃ puggale upalabbhati, so sucī so ca brāhmaṇoti so ariyapuggalo visesato khīṇāsavo accantasuddhiyā suci ca brāhmaṇo cāti. Kasmā panettha saccaṃ dhammato visuṃ katvā gahitaṃ? Saccassa bahūpakārattā. Tathā hi “saccaṃ ve amatā vācā (su. ni. 455), saccaṃ have sādutaraṃ rasānaṃ (saṃ. ni. 1.246; su. ni. 184), sacce atthe ca dhamme ca, āhu santo patiṭṭhitā (su. ni. 455), sacce ṭhitā samaṇabrāhmaṇā cā”tiādinā (jā. 2.21.433) anekesu suttapadesu saccaguṇā pakāsitā. Saccavipariyassa [V 0.0062] ca “ekaṃ dhammaṃ atītassa, musāvādissa jantuno (dha. pa. 176), abhūtavādī nirayaṃ upetī”ti (dha. pa. 306) ca ādinā pakāsitāti.

To explain by what one is purified, he said: 'In whom there is truth and Dhamma,' and so forth. Herein, 'in whom' (yamhi) refers to the person. 'Truth' (saccaṃ) means both verbal truth and the truth of abstinence. Alternatively, 'truth' means both the truth of knowledge and the ultimate truth. 'Dhamma' (dhammo) refers to the Noble Path Dhamma and the Fruit Dhamma; all of these are found in that person. Thus, he is pure, and he is a brahmin—meaning that noble individual, especially one whose cankers are destroyed, is pure through ultimate purity and is also a brahmin. But why is truth mentioned separately from Dhamma here? Because truth is of great benefit. For it is said: 'Truth is indeed the deathless speech' (Su. Ni. 455), 'Of all flavors, truth is the sweetest' (Saṃ. Ni. 1.246; Su. Ni. 184), 'The good are established in truth, meaning, and Dhamma' (Su. Ni. 455), and 'Ascetics and brahmins stand firm in truth' (Jā. 2.21.433)—thus, in many suttas, the virtues of truth are declared. And the opposite of truth is declared by such statements as: 'For one who has transgressed one thing, a person who speaks falsehood' (Dhp. 176), and 'A speaker of falsehood goes to hell' (Dhp. 306).

Navamasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the ninth discourse is concluded.

10. Bāhiyasuttavaṇṇanā

10. The Explanation of the Bāhiya Sutta

10. Dasame [M 0.0070] bāhiyoti tassa nāmaṃ. Dārucīriyoti dārumayacīro. Suppāraketi evaṃnāmake paṭṭane vasati. Ko panāyaṃ bāhiyo, kathañca dārucīriyo ahosi, kathaṃ suppārake paṭṭane paṭivasatīti?

10. In the tenth discourse, his name was Bāhiya. Dārucīriya means 'the bark-clad one'. He lived in a port town called Suppāraka. But who was this Bāhiya? How did he come to be Dārucīriya, and how did he come to dwell in the port town of Suppāraka?

Tatrāyaṃ anupubbīkathā – ito kira kappasatasahassamatthake padumuttarasammāsambuddhakāle eko kulaputto haṃsavatīnagare dasabalassa dhammadesanaṃ suṇanto satthāraṃ ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ khippābhiññānaṃ etadagge ṭhapentaṃ disvā “mahā vatāyaṃ [P 0.0078] bhikkhu, yo satthārā evaṃ etadagge ṭhapīyati, aho vatāhampi anāgate evarūpassa sammāsambuddhassa sāsane pabbajitvā satthārā edise ṭhāne etadagge ṭhapetabbo bhaveyyaṃ yathāyaṃ bhikkhū”ti taṃ ṭhānantaraṃ patthetvā tadanurūpaṃ adhikārakammaṃ katvā yāvajīvaṃ puññaṃ katvā saggaparāyaṇo hutvā devamanussesu saṃsaranto kassapadasabalassa sāsane pabbajitvā paripuṇṇasīlo samaṇadhammaṃ karontova jīvitakkhayaṃ patvā devaloke nibbatti. So ekaṃ buddhantaraṃ devaloke vasitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde bāhiyaraṭṭhe kulagehe paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhi, taṃ bāhiyaraṭṭhe jātattā bāhiyoti sañjāniṃsu. So vayappatto gharāvāsaṃ vasanto vaṇijjatthāya bahūnaṃ bhaṇḍānaṃ nāvaṃ pūretvā samuddaṃ pavisitvā aparāparaṃ sañcaranto satta vāre saddhiṃyeva parisāya attano nagaraṃ upagañchi.

Here is the gradual account: A hundred thousand eons ago, during the time of the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One named Padumuttara, a clansman in the city of Haṃsavatī, while listening to the Dhamma discourse of the Ten-Powered One, saw the Teacher placing a certain monk foremost among those of quick understanding. Reflecting, "Great indeed is this monk, who is thus placed foremost by the Teacher! Oh, may I too in the future, having gone forth in the dispensation of such a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, be placed by the Teacher in such a foremost position as this monk!" he aspired to that position, performed deeds in accordance with that aspiration, and made merit throughout his life. Destined for heaven, he wandered among gods and humans until, in the dispensation of the Ten-Powered One Kassapa, he went forth, perfected in virtue, and practiced the ascetic duties until the end of his life. Then he was reborn in the heavenly world. After dwelling in the heavenly world for an entire Buddha-interval, at the arising of this Buddha, he took rebirth in a respectable household in the Bāhiya country. Because he was born in the Bāhiya country, they knew him as Bāhiya. Having come of age, while still living the household life, he filled a ship with many goods for trade and set sail upon the ocean. Traveling back and forth, he reached his own city seven times together with his company.

Aṭṭhame vāre pana “suvaṇṇabhūmiṃ gamissāmī”ti āropitabhaṇḍo nāvaṃ abhiruhi. Nāvā mahāsamuddaṃ ajjhogāhetvā icchitadesaṃ apatvāva samuddamajjhe vipannā. Mahājano macchakacchapabhakkho ahosi. Bāhiyo pana ekaṃ nāvāphalakaṃ gahetvā taranto ūmivegena mandamandaṃ khipamāno bhassitvā samudde patitattā jātarūpeneva samuddatīre nipanno. Parissamaṃ vinodetvā assāsamattaṃ labhitvā uṭṭhāya lajjāya gumbantaraṃ pavisitvā acchādanaṃ aññaṃ kiñci [V 0.0063] apassanto akkanāḷāni chinditvā vākehi paliveṭhetvā [M 0.0071] nivāsanapāvuraṇāni katvā acchādesi. Keci pana “dāruphalakāni vijjhitvā vākena āvuṇitvā nivāsanapāvuraṇaṃ katvā acchādesī”ti vadanti. Evaṃ [P 0.0079] sabbathāpi dārumayacīradhāritāya “dārucīriyo”ti purimavohārena “bāhiyo”ti ca paññāyittha.

On the eighth occasion, intending to go to Suvaṇṇabhūmi, he boarded a ship loaded with goods. The ship entered the great ocean but, before reaching its desired destination, was wrecked in the middle of the sea. The great crowd of people became food for fish and turtles. Bāhiya, however, grabbed a plank from the ship and floated. While being tossed slowly by the force of the waves, his clothes slipped off into the sea, so he lay on the seashore naked as at birth. After recovering from his exhaustion and catching his breath, he rose and, out of shame, entered a thicket. Finding no other covering, he cut stems of the akka plant, wove them together with bark-strips, and fashioned a lower and an upper garment to cover himself. Some, however, say that he pierced planks of wood, strung them together with bark-strips, and made a lower and an upper garment to cover himself. Thus, in any case, from wearing a robe made of wood, he became known as 'Dārucīriya,' and by his former designation, as 'Bāhiya.'

Taṃ ekaṃ kapālaṃ gahetvā vuttaniyāmena suppārakapaṭṭane piṇḍāya carantaṃ disvā manussā cintesuṃ “sace loke arahanto nāma honti, evaṃvidhehi bhavitabbaṃ, kinnu kho ayaṃ ayyo vatthaṃ diyyamānaṃ gaṇheyya, udāhu appicchatāya na gaṇheyyā”ti vīmaṃsantā nānādisāhi vatthāni upanesuṃ. So cintesi – “sacāhaṃ iminā niyāmena nāgamissaṃ, nayime evaṃ mayi pasīdeyyuṃ, yaṃnūnāhaṃ imāni paṭikkhipitvā imināva nīhārena vihareyyaṃ, evaṃ me lābhasakkāro uppajjissatī”ti. So evaṃ cintetvā kohaññe ṭhatvā vatthāni na paṭiggaṇhi. Manussā “aho appiccho vatāyaṃ ayyo”ti bhiyyosomattāya pasannamānasā mahantaṃ sakkārasammānaṃ kariṃsu.

When the people saw him take a single potsherd and wander for alms in the port town of Suppāraka in the aforesaid manner, they thought: 'If there are indeed Arahants in the world, they must be like this. Would this venerable one accept cloth if it were offered, or would he decline out of contentment?' Investigating thus, they brought pieces of cloth from various directions. He reflected: 'If I do not proceed in this manner, these people will not be so pleased with me. Let me refuse these and continue living in this very way. In this way, gain and honor will arise for me.' Having thought thus, standing in deceit, he did not accept the cloth. The people, thinking, 'Ah, how content this venerable one is!' became exceedingly pleased in their minds and paid him great honor and respect.
