Sopi bhattakiccaṃ katvā avidūraṭṭhāne ekaṃ devāyatanaṃ agamāsi. Mahājano tena saddhiṃ eva gantvā taṃ devāyatanaṃ paṭijaggitvā adāsi. So “ime mayhaṃ cīradhāraṇamatte pasīditvā evaṃvidhaṃ sakkārasammānaṃ karonti, etesaṃ mayā ukkaṭṭhavuttinā bhavituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti sallahukaparikkhāro appicchova hutvā vihāsi. “Arahā”ti pana tehi sambhāvīyamāno “arahā”ti attānaṃ amaññi, uparūpari cassa sakkāragarukāro abhivaḍḍhi, lābhī ca ahosi uḷārānaṃ paccayānaṃ. Tena vuttaṃ – “tena kho pana samayena bāhiyo dārucīriyo suppārake paṭivasati samuddatīre sakkato garukato”tiādi.

He too, after completing his meal, went to a nearby shrine. A large crowd went with him, tended to the shrine, and gave it to him. He thought: 'Merely because I wear this bark-cloth robe, they are pleased and show such honor and respect. It is fitting that I live with heightened conduct for their sake.' Thus, being of light requisites and content, he lived there. Being esteemed by them as an 'Arahant,' he came to consider himself an 'Arahant.' The honor and respect for him grew ever greater, and he became a recipient of abundant requisites. Therefore it is said: 'At that time, Bāhiya Dārucīriya was dwelling in Suppāraka on the seashore, honored and respected,' and so forth.

Tattha sakkatoti sakkaccaṃ ādarena upaṭṭhānavasena sakkato. Garukatoti guṇavisesena yuttoti adhippāyena pāsāṇacchattaṃ viya garukaraṇavasena garukato. Mānitoti manasā sambhāvanavasena mānito. Pūjitoti pupphagandhādīhi pūjāvasena pūjito. Apacitoti abhippasannacittehi maggadānaāsanābhiharaṇādivasena apacito. Lābhī cīvara…pe… parikkhārānanti paṇītapaṇītānaṃ uparūpari [P 0.0080] upanīyamānānaṃ cīvarādīnaṃ catunnaṃ paccayānaṃ labhanavasena lābhī.

Here, "honored" means honored with care and attention through service. "Respected" means respected as worthy due to special qualities, like a stone parasol, thus held in high esteem. "Revered" means revered in mind through esteem. "Venerated" means venerated with flowers, incense, and such. "Esteemed" means esteemed by devoted hearts by way of offering paths, bringing seats, and so on. "A recipient of robes… and other requisites" means a recipient of the four requisites—robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines—as increasingly excellent offerings were brought to him.

Aparo [M 0.0072] nayo – sakkatoti sakkārappatto. Garukatoti garukārappatto. Mānitoti bahumānito [V 0.0064] manasā piyāyito ca. Pūjitoti catupaccayābhipūjāya pūjito. Apacitoti apacāyanappatto. Yassa hi cattāro paccaye sakkatvā suabhisaṅkhate paṇītapaṇīte denti, so sakkato. Yasmiṃ garubhāvaṃ paccupaṭṭhapetvā denti, so garukato. Yaṃ manasā piyāyanti bahumaññanti ca, so mānito. Yassa sabbampetaṃ pūjanavasena karonti, so pūjito. Yassa abhivādanapaccuṭṭhānañjalikammādivasena paramanipaccakāraṃ karonti, so apacito. Bāhiyassa pana te sabbametaṃ akaṃsu. Tena vuttaṃ – “bāhiyo dārucīriyo suppārake paṭivasati sakkato”tiādi. Ettha ca cīvaraṃ so aggaṇhantopi “ehi, bhante, imaṃ vatthaṃ paṭiggaṇhāhī”ti upanāmanavasena cīvarassāpi “lābhī”tveva vutto.

Another explanation – "honored" means one who receives honor. "Respected" means one who receives respect. "Esteemed" means highly regarded and cherished in the mind. "Worshipped" means worshipped with offerings of the four requisites. "Revered" means one who receives reverence. For one to whom they give carefully prepared, excellent requisites, honoring them, that person is honored. One to whom they give, establishing a sense of reverence, that person is respected. One whom they cherish in the mind and highly regard, that person is esteemed. For one to whom they do all this in the manner of worship, that person is worshipped. For one to whom they show the highest deference through bowing, rising, joining palms, and so on, that person is revered. But in Bāhiya’s case, they did all this. Therefore, it is said: "Bāhiya of the Bark Robe dwells at Suppāraka, honored," and so on. Here, even though he did not accept the robe, he is still said to be "a recipient" of robes because they offered it to him saying, "Come, venerable sir, accept this cloth."

Rahogatassāti rahasi gatassa. Paṭisallīnassāti ekībhūtassa bahūhi manussehi “arahā”ti vuccamānassa tassa idāni vuccamānākārena cetaso parivitakko udapādi cittassa micchāsaṅkappo uppajji. Kathaṃ? Ye kho keci loke arahanto vā arahattamaggaṃ vā samāpannā, ahaṃ tesaṃ aññataroti. Tassattho – ye imasmiṃ sattaloke kilesārīnaṃ hatattā pūjāsakkārādīnañca arahabhāvena arahanto, ye kilesārīnaṃ hananena arahattamaggaṃ samāpannā, tesu ahaṃ ekoti.

"Secluded" means gone into solitude. "Withdrawn" means being solitary. Though many people called him an arahant, a thought arose in his mind in the manner now being stated, a wrong intention of the mind arose. How so? "Whatever arahants there are in the world, or those who have attained the path to arahantship, I am one of them." The meaning of this is: "Those in this world of beings who are arahants because of having destroyed the enemies that are the defilements and because of being worthy of offerings and honor, or those who have attained the path to arahantship by destroying the enemies that are the defilements—among them, I am one."

Purāṇasālohitāti purimasmiṃ bhavesālohitā bandhusadisā ekato katasamaṇadhammā devatā. Keci pana “purāṇasālohitāti purāṇakāle bhavantare sālohitā mātubhūtā ekā devatā”ti vadanti, taṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ paṭikkhipitvā purimoyevattho gahito.

`A former blood relative` means a deity who was a blood relation in a previous existence, like a kinsman, and who had practiced the ascetic life together. Some say, "`A former blood relative` means one deity who was a blood relation in a past existence, having been his mother," but this is rejected in the commentary, and the former meaning is accepted.

Pubbe kira kassapadasabalassa sāsane osakkamāne sāmaṇerādīnaṃ vippakāraṃ disvā satta bhikkhū saṃvegappattā “yāva sāsanaṃ na antaradhāyati, tāva attano patiṭṭhaṃ karissāmā”ti suvaṇṇacetiyaṃ vanditvā araññaṃ paviṭṭhā ekaṃ pabbataṃ disvā “jīvite sālayā nivattantu, nirālayā imaṃ pabbataṃ [M 0.0073] abhiruhantū”ti vatvā nisseṇiṃ bandhitvā sabbe taṃ pabbataṃ abhiruyha nisseṇiṃ pātetvā samaṇadhammaṃ [P 0.0081] kariṃsu. Tesu saṅghatthero ekarattātikkameneva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. So uttarakuruto piṇḍapātaṃ ānetvā te bhikkhū, “āvuso, ito piṇḍapātaṃ paribhuñjathā”ti āha. Te “tumhe, bhante, attano ānubhāvena evaṃ akattha, mayampi sace tumhe viya visesaṃ nibbattessāma, sayameva āharitvā bhuñjissāmā”ti bhuñjituṃ na icchiṃsu. Tato dutiyadivase dutiyatthero anāgāmiphalaṃ pāpuṇi, sopi tatheva piṇḍapātaṃ ādāya tattha gantvā itare nimantesi, tepi tatheva paṭikkhipiṃsu. Tesu arahattappatto [V 0.0065] parinibbāyi, anāgāmī suddhāvāsabhūmiyaṃ nibbatti. Itare pana pañca janā ghaṭentā vāyamantāpi visesaṃ nibbattetuṃ nāsakkhiṃsu. Te asakkontā tattheva parisussitvā devaloke nibbattā. Ekaṃ buddhantaraṃ devesuyeva saṃsaritvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde devalokato cavitvā tattha tattha kulaghare nibbattiṃsu. Tesu hi eko pakkusāti rājā ahosi, eko kumārakassapo, eko dabbo mallaputto, eko sabhiyo paribbājako, eko bāhiyo dārucīriyo. Tattha yo so anāgāmī brahmaloke nibbatto, taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ “purāṇasālohitā devatā”ti. Devaputtopi hi devadhītā viya devo eva devatāti katvā devatāti vuccati “atha kho aññatarā devatā”tiādīsu viya. Idha pana brahmā devatāti adhippeto.

In the past, it is said, during the decline of the dispensation of Kassapa the Buddha, seven monks, seeing the misconduct of novices and others, were seized by a sense of urgency. They thought, "Before the dispensation disappears, we will establish ourselves firmly." After paying homage to the Golden Stupa, they entered the forest. Seeing a mountain, they declared, "Let those with attachment to life return; those without attachment, let them ascend this mountain." They set up a ladder, climbed the mountain, threw down the ladder, and practiced the duties of a recluse. Among them, the elder of the Sangha attained Arahantship in just one night. He brought almsfood from Uttarakuru and said to the other monks, "Friends, partake of this almsfood!" But they replied, "Venerable sir, you have done this through your own power. If we too attain such a distinction, we will fetch our own food and eat." They refused to eat. The next day, the second elder attained the fruit of non-returning. He too brought almsfood and invited the others, but they similarly declined. The Arahant passed away into final Nibbāna, while the non-returner was reborn in the Pure Abodes. The remaining five, though striving and exerting themselves, could not achieve any distinction. Unable to succeed, they withered away right there and were reborn in the deva world. They wandered in the deva worlds for an entire Buddha-interval and, after passing away from the deva world at the arising of the present Buddha, were reborn in various noble families. Among them, one became King Pakkusāti, another Kumārakassapa, another Dabba the Mallaputta, another Sabhiya the wanderer, and another Bāhiya Dārucīriya. As for that non-returner who was reborn in the brahmā world, it is with reference to him that this was said: 'a former blood-relative deity.' For a male deity (devaputta), like a female deity (devadhītā), is also called a 'devatā', as in such phrases as 'then a certain deity...'. Here, however, a Brahmā is intended by the term 'deity'.

Tassa hi brahmuno tattha nibbattasamanantarameva attano brahmasampattiṃ oloketvā āgataṭṭhānaṃ āvajjentassa sattannaṃ janānaṃ pabbataṃ āruyha samaṇadhammakaraṇaṃ, tatthekassa parinibbutabhāvo, anāgāmiphalaṃ patvā attano ca ettha nibbattabhāvo upaṭṭhāsi. So “kattha nu kho itare pañca janā”ti āvajjento kāmāvacaradevaloke tesaṃ nibbattabhāvaṃ ñatvā aparabhāge kālānukālaṃ “kinnu kho karontī”ti tesaṃ pavattiṃ oloketiyeva. Imasmiṃ pana kāle “kahaṃ nu kho”ti āvajjento bāhiyaṃ suppārakapaṭṭanaṃ upanissāya dārucīradhāriṃ kohaññena jīvikaṃ kappentaṃ disvā “ayaṃ mayā saddhiṃ pubbe nisseṇiṃ bandhitvā pabbataṃ abhiruhitvā samaṇadhammaṃ karonto atisallekhavuttiyā jīvite anapekkho [M 0.0074] arahatāpi ābhataṃ [P 0.0082] piṇḍapātaṃ aparibhuñjitvā idāni sambhāvanādhippāyo anarahāva arahattaṃ paṭijānitvā vicarati lābhasakkārasilokaṃ nikāmayamāno, dasabalassa ca nibbattabhāvaṃ na jānāti, handa naṃ saṃvejetvā buddhuppādaṃ jānāpessāmī”ti tāvadeva brahmalokato otaritvā rattibhāge suppārakapaṭṭane dārucīriyassa sammukhe pāturahosi. Bāhiyo attano vasanaṭṭhāne uḷāraṃ obhāsaṃ disvā “kiṃ nu kho eta”nti bahi nikkhamitvā olokento ākāse ṭhitaṃ mahābrahmānaṃ disvā añjaliṃ paggayha “ke tumhe”ti pucchi. Athassa so brahmā “ahaṃ te porāṇakasahāyo tadā anāgāmiphalaṃ patvā brahmaloke nibbatto, tvaṃ pana kiñci visesaṃ nibbattetuṃ asakkonto tadā puthujjanakālakiriyaṃ katvā saṃsaranto idāni titthiyavesadhārī anarahāva samāno ‘arahā aha’nti imaṃ laddhiṃ gahetvā vicarasīti ñatvā āgato, neva kho tvaṃ, bāhiya, arahā, paṭinissajjetaṃ pāpakaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ, mā te ahosi dīgharattaṃ ahitāya dukkhāya, sammāsambuddho loke uppanno. So hi bhagavā arahā, gaccha naṃ payirupāsassū”ti [V 0.0066] āha. Tena vuttaṃ – “atha kho bāhiyassa dārucīriyassa purāṇasālohitā devatā”tiādi.

For, immediately upon being born there, that Brahmā, having surveyed his own brahmā-attainment and reflecting on the place from which he had come, recalled the seven persons climbing the mountain and practicing the recluse's duties, the final Nibbāna of one of them, and his own attainment of the fruit of non-returning and rebirth there. He wondered, "Where now are the other five?" and, knowing they had been reborn in the desire-realm deva worlds, he would later observe their activities from time to time, thinking, "What are they doing now?" But at this time, as he reflected, "Where now?" he saw Bāhiya, wearing bark garments near the port of Suppāraka, making a living through pretense. He thought, "This man once fastened a ladder with me, climbed the mountain, and practiced the recluse's duties. Though he lived with extreme austerity, indifferent to life, and did not even partake of the almsfood brought by an Arahant, now, with the intention of being esteemed, though not an Arahant, he wanders about professing Arahantship, desiring gain, honor, and fame. He does not know that the Ten-Powered One has arisen. Let me stir him up and make him aware of the Buddha’s arising." Instantly descending from the brahmā-world, he appeared before Bāhiya Dārucīriya during the night in the port of Suppāraka. Seeing a resplendent light in his dwelling, Bāhiya wondered, "What is this?" Stepping outside, he looked up and saw the Great Brahmā standing in the sky. Raising his joined hands in salutation, he asked, "Who are you?" The Brahmā replied, "I am your old companion. Back then, I attained the fruit of non-returning and was reborn in the brahmā-world. But you, unable to achieve any distinction, died as a worldling and have been wandering in saṃsāra. Now, though you are not an Arahant, you wear the guise of an external ascetic and wander about holding the view, 'I am an Arahant.' Knowing this, I have come. You, Bāhiya, are certainly not an Arahant. Abandon this evil view, lest it be for your harm and suffering for a long time. A Perfectly Enlightened One has arisen in the world. That Blessed One is an Arahant. Go and attend upon him." Thus it was said: "Then, a deity who was a former blood-relative of Bāhiya Dārucīriya…" and so on.

Tattha anukampikāti anuggahasīlā karuṇādhikā. Atthakāmāti hitakāmā mettādhikā. Purimapadena cettha bāhiyassa dukkhāpanayanakāmataṃ tassā devatāya dasseti, pacchimena hitūpasaṃhāraṃ. Cetasāti attano cittena, cetosīsena cettha cetopariyañāṇaṃ gahitanti veditabbaṃ. Cetoparivitakkanti tassa cittappavattiṃ. Aññāyāti jānitvā. Tenupasaṅkamīti seyyathāpi nāma balavā puriso samiñjitaṃ vā bāhaṃ pasāreyya, pasāritaṃ vā bāhaṃ samiñjeyya, evameva brahmaloke antarahito bāhiyassa purato pātubhavanavasena upasaṅkami. Etadavocāti “ye kho keci loke arahanto vā”tiādipavattamicchāparivitakkaṃ bāhiyaṃ sahoḍhaṃ coraṃ gaṇhanto viya “neva kho tvaṃ, bāhiya, arahā”tiādikaṃ etaṃ [P 0.0083] idāni vuccamānavacanaṃ brahmā avoca. Neva kho tvaṃ, bāhiya, arahāti etena tadā bāhiyassa asekkhabhāvaṃ paṭikkhipati, nāpi arahattamaggaṃ vā samāpannoti etena [M 0.0075] sekkhabhāvaṃ, ubhayenapissa anariyabhāvameva dīpeti. Sāpi te paṭipadā natthi, yāya tvaṃ arahā vā assa arahattamaggaṃ vā samāpannoti iminā panassa kalyāṇaputhujjanabhāvampi paṭikkhipati. Tattha paṭipadāti sīlavisuddhiādayo cha visuddhiyo. Paṭipajjati etāya ariyamaggeti paṭipadā. Assāti bhaveyyāsi.

Herein, 'compassionate' means inclined to help, abounding in compassion. 'Desiring his welfare' means desiring his benefit, abounding in loving-kindness. By the first phrase, the deity shows his desire to relieve Bāhiya’s suffering; by the latter, his intention to bestow benefit. 'With the mind' means with one's own mind; here, by 'mind' as the principal factor, it should be understood that the knowledge of others' minds (cetopariyañāṇa) is meant. 'The thought of his mind' means the process of his thought. 'Having known' means having understood. 'He approached him' means just as a strong man might stretch out his bent arm or bend his outstretched arm, so the deity, vanishing from the brahmā-world, approached by appearing before Bāhiya. 'He said this to him' means the Brahmā spoke these words now being spoken, beginning with 'Indeed, Bāhiya, you are not an Arahant,' and so on, as if seizing Bāhiya—who was entertaining the wrong thought that began, 'Whatever Arahants there are in the world...'—like a thief caught with the stolen goods. By 'Indeed, Bāhiya, you are not an Arahant,' he rejects Bāhiya’s state of being a non-learner (asekkha) at that time. By 'nor have you entered upon the path to Arahantship,' he rejects his state of being a learner (sekkha). By both, he reveals only his non-noble state. By 'Nor do you have that practice by which you might become an Arahant or enter upon the path to Arahantship,' he also rejects his status as a virtuous worldling (kalyāṇaputhujjana). In this context, 'practice' (paṭipadā) refers to the six purifications, beginning with purification of virtue. 'Paṭipadā' is so called because one proceeds along the noble path by means of it. 'Might be' means 'you might be.'

Ayañcassa arahattādhimāno kiṃ nissāya uppannoti? “Appicchatāya santuṭṭhitāya sallekhatāya dīgharattaṃ katādhikārattā tadaṅgappahānavasena kilesānaṃ vihatattā arahattādhimāno uppanno”ti keci vadanti. Apare panāhu “bāhiyo paṭhamādijhānacatukkalābhī, tasmāssa vikkhambhanappahānena kilesānaṃ asamudācārato arahattādhimāno uppajjatī”ti. Tadubhayampi tesaṃ matimattameva “sambhāvanādhippāyo lābhasakkārasilokaṃ nikāmayamāno”ti ca aṭṭhakathāyaṃ āgatattā. Tasmā vuttanayenevettha attho veditabbo.

And on what basis did this conceit of Arahantship arise in him? Some say: "The conceit of Arahantship arose due to his having few wants, contentment, austerity, having made aspirations for a long time, and by having the defilements suppressed by way of temporary abandonment." Others say: "Bāhiya was one who had attained the four jhānas beginning with the first; therefore, the conceit of Arahantship arose in him through the suppression-abandonment of defilements, owing to their non-occurrence." Both these views are merely their opinions, for it is stated in the commentary: 'with the intention of being esteemed, desiring gain, honor, and fame.' Therefore, the meaning here should be understood according to the method already stated.

Atha bāhiyo ākāse ṭhatvā kathentaṃ mahābrahmānaṃ oloketvā cintesi – “aho bhāriyaṃ vata kammaṃ, yamahaṃ arahāti cintesiṃ, ayañca ‘arahattagāminī paṭipadāpi te natthī’ti vadati, atthi nu kho loke koci arahā”ti? Atha naṃ pucchi. Tena vuttaṃ – “atha ke carahi devate loke arahanto vā arahattamaggaṃ vā samāpannā”ti.

Then Bāhiya, observing the Great Brahmā speaking while standing in the sky, thought: "Oh, what a grave deed, that I considered myself an Arahant, yet this one says, 'You do not even have the practice leading to Arahantship.' Is there, I wonder, any Arahant in the world?" Then he asked him. Therefore it was said: "Who now then, O deity, are there in the world who are Arahants or who have entered upon the path to Arahantship?"

Tattha [V 0.0067] athāti pucchārambhe nipāto. Ke carahīti ke etarahi. Loketi [P 0.0084] okāsaloke. Ayañhettha adhippāyo – bhājanalokabhūte sakalasmiṃ jambudīpatale kasmiṃ ṭhāne arahanto vā arahattamaggaṃ vā samāpannā etarahi viharanti, yattha mayaṃ te upasaṅkamitvā tesaṃ ovāde ṭhatvā vaṭṭadukkhato muccissāmāti. Uttaresūti suppārakapaṭṭanato pubbuttaradisābhāgaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ.

Herein, atha is a particle in the sense of commencing a question. Ke carahi means 'who now...'. Loke means in the world of space. Herein, this is the intended meaning: In the entire continent of Jambudīpa, which is the receptacle-world, in what place do Arahants or those who have attained the path to Arahantship now dwell, so that we, having approached them and become established in their instruction, might be freed from the suffering of the round of existence? Uttaresu is said in reference to the northeastern direction from the port of Suppāraka.

Arahanti ārakattā arahaṃ. Ārakā hi so sabbakilesehi suvidūravidūre ṭhito maggena savāsanānaṃ kilesānaṃ viddhaṃsitattā. Arīnaṃ vā hatattā arahaṃ. Bhagavatā hi kilesārayo anavasesato ariyamaggena hatā samucchinnāti. Arānaṃ vā hatattā arahaṃ. Yañca avijjābhavataṇhāmayanābhi [M 0.0076] puññādiabhisaṅkhārāraṃ jarāmaraṇanemi āsavasamudayamayena akkhena vijjhitvā tibhavarathe samāyojitaṃ anādikālappavattaṃ saṃsāracakkaṃ. Tassānena bodhimaṇḍe vīriyapādehi sīlapathaviyaṃ patiṭṭhāya saddhāhatthena kammakkhayakarañāṇapharasuṃ gahetvā sabbepi arā hatā vihatā viddhaṃsitāti. Arahatīti vā arahaṃ. Bhagavā hi sadevake loke aggadakkhiṇeyyattā uḷāre cīvarādipaccaye pūjāvisesañca arahati. Rahābhāvato vā arahaṃ. Tathāgato hi sabbaso samucchinnarāgādikilesattā pāpakilesassāpi asambhavato pāpakaraṇe rahābhāvatopi arahanti vuccati.

He is an Arahant because he is far (āraka). For he stands very far, utterly distant from all defilements, having destroyed them along with their latent tendencies by means of the path. Or, he is an Arahant because he has slain (hata) the enemies (ari). For by the Blessed One the defilement-enemies have been slain and cut off without remainder by the noble path. Or, he is an Arahant because he has destroyed (hata) the spokes (arā). The wheel of saṃsāra, revolving since beginningless time—which has a hub made of ignorance and craving for existence, spokes of meritorious and other formations, and a rim of aging and death, and is pierced by an axle made of the origin of taints and yoked to the chariot of the three modes of existence—of this wheel, he, standing on the ground of virtue with the feet of energy at the seat of enlightenment, and taking up with the hand of faith the axe of knowledge that brings about the destruction of kamma, has slain, destroyed, and demolished all the spokes. Or, he is an Arahant because he is worthy (arahati). For the Blessed One, being the foremost recipient of offerings in the world with its devas, is worthy of excellent requisites such as robes and of special veneration. Or, he is an Arahant because of the absence of secrecy (rahābhāva). For the Tathāgata, because he has utterly cut off defilements such as lust, and because even an evil defilement is impossible for him, and also because of the absence of secrecy in the doing of evil, is called an Arahant.

Sammā sāmañca sabbadhammānaṃ buddhattā sammāsambuddho. Bhagavā hi abhiññeyye dhamme abhiññeyyato, pariññeyye dhamme pariññeyyato, pahātabbe dhamme pahātabbato, sacchikātabbe dhamme sacchikātabbato, bhāvetabbe dhamme bhāvetabbato abhisambujjhi. Vuttañhetaṃ –

He is the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddho) because he has correctly and by himself awakened to all phenomena. For the Blessed One indeed fully awakened to phenomena to be directly known by directly knowing them, to phenomena to be fully understood by fully understanding them, to phenomena to be abandoned by abandoning them, to phenomena to be realized by realizing them, and to phenomena to be developed by developing them. For this has been said:

“Abhiññeyyaṃ abhiññātaṃ, bhāvetabbañca bhāvitaṃ;

Pahātabbaṃ pahīnaṃ me, tasmā buddhosmi brāhmaṇā”ti. (su. ni. 563; ma. ni. 2.399; visuddhi. 1.131);

What should be directly known has been directly known; what should be developed has been developed; what should be abandoned has been abandoned by me; therefore, O brahmin, I am the Buddha.

Apica [P 0.0085] kusale dhamme anavajjasukhavipākato, akusale dhamme sāvajjadukkhavipākatotiādinā sabbattikadukādivasena ayamattho netabbo. Iti aviparītaṃ sayambhuñāṇena sabbākārato sabbadhammānaṃ abhisambuddhattā sammāsambuddhoti ayamettha saṅkhepo. Vitthāro pana visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.129-131) āgatanayeneva veditabbo. Arahattāyāti aggaphalappaṭilābhāya. Dhammaṃ desetīti ādikalyāṇādiguṇavisesayuttaṃ sīlādipaṭipadādhammaṃ samathavipassanādhammameva vā veneyyajjhāsayānurūpaṃ upadisati katheti.

Furthermore, this meaning should be understood by way of all the triads, dyads, and so on; for instance: wholesome phenomena, due to their blameless and happy results; unwholesome phenomena, due to their blameworthy and painful results. Thus, because of having unerringly and in every way fully awakened to all phenomena by his self-arisen knowledge, he is the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One—this is the summary here. The detailed explanation, however, should be understood according to the method presented in the Visuddhimagga. Arahattāya means for the attainment of the supreme fruit. Dhammaṃ deseti means he instructs and speaks the Dhamma of the practice beginning with virtue, endowed with excellent qualities such as being beautiful in the beginning, or the Dhamma of serenity and insight itself, in accordance with the disposition of those to be trained.

Saṃvejitoti [V 0.0068] “dhiratthu vata, bho, puthujjanabhāvassa, yenāhaṃ anarahāva samāno arahāti amaññiṃ, sammāsambuddhañca loke uppajjitvā dhammaṃ desentaṃ na jāniṃ, dujjānaṃ kho panidaṃ jīvitaṃ, dujjānaṃ maraṇa”nti saṃvegamāpādito, devatāvacanena yathāvuttenākārena saṃviggamānasoti attho. Tāvadevāti tasmiṃyeva khaṇe. Suppārakā pakkāmīti buddhoti nāmamapi savanena uppannāya buddhārammaṇāya pītiyā saṃvegena [M 0.0077] ca codiyamānahadayo suppārakapaṭṭanato sāvatthiṃ uddissa pakkanto. Sabbattha ekarattiparivāsenāti sabbasmiṃ magge ekarattivāseneva agamāsi. Suppārakapaṭṭanato hi sāvatthi vīsayojanasate hoti, tañcāyaṃ ettakaṃ addhānaṃ ekarattivāsena agamāsi. Yadā suppārakato nikkhanto, tadaheva sāvatthiṃ sampattoti.

Saṃvejito means he was stirred to urgency, thinking: 'Fie upon this state of an ordinary person, whereby I, being no Arahant, considered myself an Arahant, and did not know of the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One who had arisen in the world and was teaching the Dhamma. Hard to know indeed is this life, hard to know is death.' The meaning is that his mind was stirred with urgency by the words of the deity in the manner described. Tāvadeva means at that very moment. Suppārakā pakkāmi means that, his heart urged on by the joy that arose from merely hearing the name 'Buddha' and took the Buddha as its object, and by his sense of urgency, he departed from the port of Suppāraka, heading for Sāvatthī. Sabbattha ekarattiparivāsena means he traveled the entire way by staying only one night at each place. For Sāvatthī is one hundred and twenty yojanas from the port of Suppāraka, and he traveled this great distance with a stay of one night. Some say that when he left Suppāraka, he arrived in Sāvatthī that very day.

Kathaṃ panāyaṃ evaṃ agamāsīti? Devatānubhāvena, “buddhānubhāvenā”tipi vadanti. “Sabbattha ekarattiparivāsenā”ti pana vuttattā maggassa ca vīsayojanasatikattā antarāmagge gāmanigamarājadhānīsu yattha yattha rattiyaṃ vasati, tattha tattha dutiyaṃ aruṇaṃ anuṭṭhāpetvā sabbattha ekarattivāseneva sāvatthiṃ upasaṅkamīti ayamattho dīpito hotīti. Nayidaṃ evaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Sabbasmiṃ vīsayojanasatike magge ekarattivāsenāti imassa atthassa adhippetattā. Ekarattimattaṃ so sakalasmiṃ tasmiṃ magge [P 0.0086] vasitvā pacchimadivase pubbaṇhasamaye sāvatthiṃ anuppattoti.

But how did he travel in this way? Some say it was by the power of the devas and by the power of the Buddha. However, since it was said, 'With one night's stay everywhere,' and since the road was one hundred and twenty yojanas long, the meaning explained is this: wherever he stayed for the night along the way—in villages, towns, or royal cities—he did not let a second dawn arise there, and thus he approached Sāvatthī by staying only one night in each place. But this should not be understood in that way. For the intended meaning of 'with one night's stay on the entire one-hundred-and-twenty-yojana road' is this: having stayed for just a single night on that entire road, he arrived in Sāvatthī on the final day in the forenoon.

Bhagavāpi bāhiyassa āgamanaṃ ñatvā “na tāvassa indriyāni paripākaṃ gatāni, khaṇantare pana paripākaṃ gamissantī”ti tassa indriyānaṃ paripākaṃ āgamayamāno mahābhikkhusaṅghaparivuto tasmiṃ khaṇe sāvatthiṃ piṇḍāya pāvisi. So ca jetavanaṃ pavisitvā bhuttapātarāse kāyālasiyavimocanatthaṃ abbhokāse caṅkamante sambahule bhikkhū passitvā “kahaṃ nu kho etarahi bhagavā”ti pucchi. Bhikkhū “bhagavā sāvatthiṃ piṇḍāya paviṭṭho”ti vatvā pucchiṃsu “tvaṃ pana kuto āgato”ti? “Suppārakapaṭṭanato āgatomhī”ti. “Dūrato āgatosi, nisīda, tāva pāde dhovitvā makkhetvā thokaṃ vissamāhi, āgatakāle satthāraṃ dakkhasī”ti. “Ahaṃ, bhante, attano jīvitantarāyaṃ na jānāmi, ekarattenevamhi katthacipi ciraṃ aṭṭhatvā anisīditvā vīsayojanasatikaṃ maggaṃ āgato, satthāraṃ passitvāva vissamissāmī”ti vatvā taramānarūpo sāvatthiṃ pavisitvā anopamāya buddhasiriyā virocamānaṃ bhagavantaṃ passi. Tena vuttaṃ “tena kho pana samayena sambahulā bhikkhū abbhokāse caṅkamanti. Atha kho bāhiyo dārucīriyo yena te bhikkhū tenupasaṅkamī”tiādi.

The Blessed One, knowing of Bāhiya's arrival, thought, 'His faculties have not yet matured, but they will mature in a short while.' Awaiting the maturity of his faculties, surrounded by a great assembly of monks, the Blessed One entered Sāvatthī for alms at that moment. Having entered Jetavana, Bāhiya, after the morning meal, seeking relief from bodily fatigue, saw many monks walking in the open air. He asked, 'Where is the Blessed One now?' The monks replied, 'The Blessed One has entered Sāvatthī for alms.' They then asked him, 'But where have you come from?' 'From the port town of Suppāraka,' he answered. 'You have come from afar. Sit down, wash your feet, anoint them, and rest awhile. You will see the Teacher when he returns.' 'Venerable sirs, I do not know the danger to my life. I have traveled a hundred and twenty yojanas in a single night without stopping or sitting anywhere. Only after seeing the Teacher will I rest,' he said. Hastening, he entered Sāvatthī and saw the Blessed One shining with incomparable Buddha-splendor. Thus it is said: 'Now at that time, several monks were walking in the open air. Then Bāhiya the bark-clad ascetic approached those monks...' and so on.

Tattha [V 0.0069] kahanti kattha. Nūti saṃsaye, khoti padapūraṇe, kasmiṃ nu kho padeseti attho. Dassanakāmamhāti daṭṭhukāmā amha. Mayañhi taṃ bhagavantaṃ [M 0.0078] andho viya cakkhuṃ, badhiro viya sotaṃ, mūgo viya kalyāṇavākkaraṇaṃ, hatthapādavikalo viya hatthapāde, daliddo viya dhanasampadaṃ, kantāraddhānappaṭipanno viya khemantabhūmiṃ, rogābhibhūto viya ārogyaṃ, mahāsamudde bhinnanāvo viya mahākullaṃ passituṃ [P 0.0087] upasaṅkamituñca icchāmāti dasseti. Taramānarūpoti taramānākāro.

Here 'kahaṃ' means 'where'. 'Nu' expresses doubt, 'kho' is a particle for filling out the phrase, meaning 'in what place indeed?' 'Dassanakāmamhā' means 'we wish to see'. This shows the meaning: 'For we wish to see and approach the Blessed One, just as the blind wishes for an eye, the deaf for an ear, the mute for eloquent speech, the crippled for hands and feet, the poor for wealth, the traveler in the wilderness for a safe land, the sick for health, and those whose boat is wrecked in the great ocean for a great raft.' 'Taramānarūpo' means 'having the appearance of haste'.

Pāsādikanti bāttiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇaasītianubyañjanabyāmappabhāketumālālaṅkatāya samantapāsādikāya attano sarīrasobhāsampattiyā rūpakāyadassanabyāvaṭassa janassa sabbabhāgato pasādāvahaṃ. Pasādanīyanti dasabalacatuvesārajjachaasādhāraṇañāṇaaṭṭhārasāveṇika- buddhadhammappabhutiaparimāṇaguṇagaṇasamannāgatāya dhammakāyasampattiyā sarikkhakajanassa pasādanīyaṃ pasīditabbayuttaṃ pasādārahaṃ vā. Santindriyanti cakkhādipañcindriyalolabhāvāpagamanena vūpasantapañcindriyaṃ. Santamānasanti chaṭṭhassa manindriyassa nibbisevanabhāvūpagamanena vūpasantamānasaṃ. Uttamadamathasamathamanuppattanti lokuttarapaññāvimutticetovimuttisaṅkhātaṃ uttamaṃ damathaṃ samathañca anuppatvā adhigantvā ṭhitaṃ. Dantanti suparisuddhakāyasamācāratāya ceva hatthapādakukkuccābhāvato davādiabhāvato ca kāyena dantaṃ. Guttanti suparisuddhavacīsamācāratāya ceva niratthakavācābhāvato davādiabhāvato ca vācāya guttaṃ. Yatindriyanti suparisuddhamanosamācāratāya ariyiddhiyogena abyāvaṭaappaṭisaṅkhānupekkhābhāvato ca manindriyavasena yatindriyaṃ. Nāganti chandādivasena agamanato, pahīnānaṃ rāgādikilesānaṃ punānāgamanato, kassacipi āgussa sabbathāpi akaraṇato, punabbhavassa ca agamanatoti imehi kāraṇehi nāgaṃ. Ettha ca pāsādikanti iminā rūpakāyena bhagavato pamāṇabhūtataṃ [P 0.0088] dīpeti, pasādanīyanti iminā dhammakāyena, santindriyantiādinā sesehi pamāṇabhūtataṃ dīpeti. Tena catuppamāṇike lokasannivāse anavasesato sattānaṃ bhagavato pamāṇabhāvo pakāsitoti veditabbo.

“Pāsādika” means that, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man, the eighty minor characteristics, a fathom-wide aura, and a radiant halo, his body is supremely beautiful in every way, inspiring faith in all who are intent on seeing his physical form. “Pasādanīya” means that, endowed with the ten powers, the four kinds of confidence, the six uncommon knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and countless other virtues, his Dhamma body is worthy of inspiring faith, suitable to be revered, and deserving of faith for those who are receptive. “Santindriya” means that the five faculties, beginning with the eye, are calmed, having departed from a state of fickleness. “Santamānasa” means that the sixth faculty, the mind, is calmed, having approached a state of non-indulgence. “Uttamadamathasamathamanuppatta” means having attained and abided in the supreme taming and calming, known as liberation through transcendent wisdom and liberation of mind. “Danta” means tamed in body, due to perfectly pure bodily conduct, absence of fidgeting of hands and feet, and absence of frivolity. “Gutta” means guarded in speech, due to perfectly pure verbal conduct, absence of useless speech, and absence of frivolity. “Yatindriya” means restrained in faculties, by the power of the mind-faculty, due to perfectly pure mental conduct, the practice of noble power, and the absence of both busyness and unreflective equanimity. “Nāga” means one who is called a Nāga for these reasons: because he does not go by way of desire and so on; because of the non-return of the defilements, such as passion, that have been abandoned; because of not committing any evil whatsoever; and because of not going to a future existence. Here, 'Pāsādika' reveals the Blessed One’s status as the standard in terms of his physical body; 'Pasādanīya' reveals this in terms of his Dhamma body; and the remaining terms, beginning with 'Santindriya,' reveal this in other aspects. Thus, it should be understood that in this world of beings who judge by four standards, the Blessed One’s status as the standard for all beings without exception is made manifest.

Evaṃbhūtañca bhagavantaṃ antaravīthiyaṃ gacchantaṃ disvā “cirassaṃ vata me sammāsambuddho diṭṭho”ti haṭṭhatuṭṭho pañcavaṇṇāya pītiyā nirantaraṃ phuṭasarīro [M 0.0079] pītivipphāritavivaṭaniccalalocano diṭṭhaṭṭhānato paṭṭhāya oṇatasarīro bhagavato sarīrappabhāvemajjhaṃ ajjhogāhetvā tattha nimujjanto bhagavato samīpaṃ upasaṅkamitvā pañcapatiṭṭhitena vanditvā bhagavato pāde sambāhanto paricumbanto “desetu me, bhante, bhagavā dhamma”nti āha. Tena vuttaṃ – “bhagavato pāde [V 0.0070] sirasā nipatitvā bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – ‘desetu me, bhante, bhagavā dhammaṃ, desetu sugato dhammaṃ, yaṃ mamassa dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāyā’”ti.

Seeing the Blessed One, who was of such a nature, walking in the street, he thought, “After so long, I have seen the Perfectly Enlightened One!” Filled with joy and delight, his body continuously pervaded with five-colored rapture, his eyes wide with rapture, open, and motionless, he bowed from the very spot where he saw him, his body bent in reverence. Plunging into the midst of the Blessed One’s bodily radiance and immersing himself therein, he approached the Blessed One, paid homage with the five-point prostration, and, massaging and kissing the Blessed One’s feet, pleaded, “Venerable sir, may the Blessed One teach me the Dhamma.” Thus it was said—having fallen with his head at the Blessed One’s feet, he said this to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, may the Blessed One teach me the Dhamma, may the Sugata teach me the Dhamma, that which would be for my long-term welfare and happiness.”

Tattha sugatoti sobhanagamanattā, sundaraṃ ṭhānaṃ gatattā, sammā gatattā, sammā gadattā sugato. Gamanampi hi gatanti vuccati, tañca bhagavato sobhanaṃ parisuddhaṃ anavajjaṃ. Kiṃ pana tanti? Ariyamaggo. Tena hesa gamanena khemaṃ disaṃ asajjamāno gato, aññepi gametīti sobhanagamanattā sugato. Sundarañcesa ṭhānaṃ amataṃ nibbānaṃ gatoti sundaraṃ ṭhānaṃ gatattā sugato. Sammā ca gatattā sugato tena tena maggena pahīne kilese puna apaccāgamanato. Vuttañhetaṃ –

There, ‘Sugata’ means ‘well-gone’ because of his excellent going, because he has gone to a beautiful place, because he has gone rightly, and because he speaks rightly. For ‘going’ is also called ‘gata’, and that of the Blessed One is excellent, pure, and blameless. What is that? The Noble Path. By that going, he has gone to the safe destination without attachment, and he leads others there as well—thus, because of his excellent going, he is Sugata. And because he has gone to the beautiful place, the deathless Nibbāna, he is Sugata as one who has gone to a beautiful place. And because he has gone rightly, he is Sugata, since the defilements abandoned by means of that path do not return again. For it is said—

“Sotāpattimaggena ye kilesā pahīnā, te kilese na puneti na pacceti na paccāgacchatīti sugato. Sakadāgāmi…pe… arahattamaggena…pe… na paccāgacchatīti sugato”ti (cūḷani. mettagūmāṇavapucchāniddesa 27).

He is the Well-Gone because he does not return to, does not revert to, does not come back to those defilements that are abandoned by the path of stream-entry. He is the Well-Gone because he does not come back to those defilements abandoned by the path of the once-returner... and by the path of Arahantship.

Atha vā sammā gatattāti tīsupi avatthāsu sammāpaṭipattiyā gatattā, suppaṭipannattāti attho. Dīpaṅkarapādamūlato hi paṭṭhāya yāva mahābodhimaṇḍā [P 0.0089] tāva samatiṃsapāramipūritāya sammāpaṭipattiyā ñātatthacariyāya lokatthacariyāya buddhatthacariyāya koṭiṃ pāpuṇitvā sabbalokassa hitasukhameva paribrūhanto sassataṃ ucchedaṃ kāmasukhaṃ attakilamathanti ime ante anupagacchantiyā anuttarāya bojjhaṅgabhāvanāsaṅkhātāya majjhimāya paṭipadāya ariyasaccesu tato paraṃ samadhigatadhammādhipateyyo sabbasattesu avisayāya sammāpaṭipattiyā ca gato paṭipannoti evampi sammā gatattā sugato. Sammā cesa gadati yuttaṭṭhāne yuttameva vācaṃ bhāsatīti sugato. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

Or alternatively, 'because of having gone rightly' means because of having gone by right practice in all three states; the meaning is 'because of being well-practiced.' For, starting from the feet of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara up to the seat of great awakening, having reached the pinnacle through the right practice of fulfilling the thirty perfections—the practice for the welfare of his kinsmen and the practice for the welfare of the world—and promoting only the welfare and happiness of the entire world, not approaching the extremes of eternalism, annihilationism, sensual indulgence, and self-mortification; by means of the unsurpassed middle way, known as the development of the factors of awakening, and thereafter, with the Dhamma as his sovereign master through the realization of the noble truths, he has gone and proceeds with a right practice that is beyond the range of all beings. In this way too, because of having gone rightly, he is the Well-Gone. And he speaks rightly, uttering only fitting speech in a fitting place; thus he is the Well-Gone. And this has been said:

“Kālavādī[M 0.0080], bhūtavādī, atthavādī, dhammavādī, vinayavādī, nidhānavatiṃ vācaṃ bhāsitā kālena sāpadesaṃ pariyantavatiṃ atthasaṃhita”nti (dī. ni. 1.9; ma. ni. 3.14).

“He is one who speaks at the proper time, one who speaks what is factual, one who speaks what is beneficial, one who speaks on the Dhamma, one who speaks on the Discipline. He speaks speech that is well-grounded, reasoned, delimited, and connected with benefit.”

Aparampi vuttaṃ –

Furthermore, it has been said:

“Yā [V 0.0071] sā vācā abhūtā atacchā anatthasaṃhitā, yā ca paresaṃ appiyā amanāpā, na taṃ tathāgato vācaṃ bhāsatī”tiādi (ma. ni. 2.86).

“That speech which is unfactual, untrue, and unbeneficial, and which is also unpleasing and disagreeable to others—the Tathāgata does not speak such speech.”

Evaṃ sammā gadattāpi sugato.

Thus, also because of speaking rightly, he is the Well-Gone.

Yaṃ mamassa dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāyāti yaṃ dhammassa upadisanaṃ cirakālaṃ mama jhānavimokkhādihitāya tadadhigantabbasukhāya ca siyā. Akālo kho tāva bāhiyāti tava dhammadesanāya na tāva kāloti attho. Kiṃ pana bhagavato sattahitapaṭipattiyā akālopi nāma atthi, yato bhagavā kālavādīti? Vuccate – kāloti cettha veneyyānaṃ indriyaparipākakālo adhippeto. Yasmā pana tadā bāhiyassa attano indriyānaṃ paripakkāparipakkabhāvo dubbiññeyyo, tasmā bhagavā taṃ avatvā attano antaravīthiyaṃ ṭhitabhāvamassa kāraṇaṃ apadisanto āha “antaragharaṃ paviṭṭhamhā”ti. Dujjānanti dubbiññeyyaṃ. Jīvitantarāyānanti jīvitassa antarāyakaradhammānaṃ vattanaṃ avattanaṃ vāti vattukāmo sambhamavasena “jīvitantarāyāna”nti āha. Tathā hi anekapaccayappaṭibaddhavuttijīvitaṃ anekarūpā ca tadantarāyā. Vuttañhi –

The phrase 'That which would be for my long-term welfare and happiness' means: 'Whatever instruction of the Dhamma would be for my long-term benefit regarding jhāna, liberation, and so on, and for the happiness to be attained thereby.' The phrase 'Now is not the time, Bāhiya' means: 'It is not yet time for a Dhamma teaching for you.' But is there indeed any unsuitable time for the Blessed One, who is practicing for the welfare of beings, since the Blessed One is one who speaks at the right time? It is said: Here, by 'time' is meant the time of the maturing of the faculties of those to be trained. Since at that time it was difficult for Bāhiya himself to discern the mature or immature state of his own faculties, the Blessed One, without mentioning that, indicated the fact of his being in the middle of the street as the reason, saying, 'We have entered among the houses.' 'Hard to know' means difficult to discern. Regarding 'dangers to life': wishing to speak of the occurrence or non-occurrence of things that endanger life, he said 'dangers to life' out of agitation. For life, which proceeds bound to many conditions, has dangers of many kinds. For it has been said:

“Ajjeva kiccamātappaṃ, ko jaññā maraṇaṃ suve;

Na hi no saṅgaraṃ tena, mahāsenena maccunā”ti. (ma. ni. 3.272; netti. 103);

“Striving should be done today itself; who knows if death will come tomorrow? For we have no agreement with Death and his great army.”

Kasmā [P 0.0090] panāyaṃ jīvitantarāyameva tāva purakkharoti? “Nimittaññutāya adiṭṭhakosallena vā”ti keci. Apare “devatāya santike jīvitantarāyassa sutattā”ti vadanti. Antimabhavikattā pana upanissayasampattiyā codiyamāno evamāha. Na hi tesaṃ appattaarahattānaṃ jīvitakkhayo hoti. Kiṃ pana kāraṇā bhagavā tassa dhammaṃ desetukāmova dvikkhattuṃ paṭikkhipi? Evaṃ kirassa ahosi “imassa maṃ diṭṭhakālato paṭṭhāya [M 0.0081] sakalasarīraṃ pītiyā nirantaraṃ phuṭaṃ, atibalavā pītivego, dhammaṃ sutvāpi na tāva sakkhissati paṭivijjhituṃ. Yāva pana majjhattupekkhā saṇṭhāti, tāva tiṭṭhatu, vīsayojanasataṃ maggaṃ āgatattā darathopissa kāye balavā, sopi tāva paṭippassambhatū”ti. Tasmā dvikkhattuṃ paṭikkhipi. Keci pana “dhammassavane ādarajananatthaṃ bhagavā evamakāsī”ti vadanti. Tatiyavāraṃ yācito pana majjhattupekkhaṃ darathappaṭipassaddhiṃ paccupaṭṭhitañcassa jīvitantarāyaṃ disvā [V 0.0072] “idāni dhammadesanāya kālo”ti cintetvā “tasmā tihā”tiādinā dhammadesanaṃ ārabhi.

But why does he give such priority to this danger to life? Some say, 'Because of his knowledge of omens or his skill in the unperceived.' Others say, 'Because he had heard about the danger to his life from a deity.' However, being one in his final existence and being urged on by the maturity of his supporting conditions, he spoke thus. For such beings, the end of life does not occur before they have attained Arahantship. But for what reason did the Blessed One, though wishing to teach him the Dhamma, refuse him twice? It is said that this occurred to him: 'From the time he saw me, his entire body has been continuously pervaded by joy. The force of this joy is exceedingly strong, and even after hearing the Dhamma, he will not yet be able to penetrate it. Let the situation stand until equanimity is established. Moreover, having come a distance of one hundred and twenty yojanas, the fatigue in his body is strong; let that too subside.' Therefore, he refused him twice. Some, however, say, 'The Blessed One did so to generate reverence for hearing the Dhamma.' But when requested a third time, seeing that equanimity was established, his fatigue had subsided, and the danger to his life was imminent, he thought, 'Now is the time for the Dhamma teaching,' and began the teaching with the words, 'Therefore, Bāhiya...'

Tattha tasmāti yasmā tvaṃ ussukkajāto hutvā ativiya maṃ yācasi, yasmā vā jīvitantarāyānaṃ dujjānataṃ vadasi, indriyāni ca te paripākaṃ gatāni, tasmā. Tihāti nipātamattaṃ. Teti tayā evanti idāni vattabbākāraṃ vadati.

Therein, 'therefore' (tasmā) is used because you, having become eager, request me so insistently; or because you speak of the difficulty in knowing the dangers to life, and because your faculties have reached maturity. 'Tiha' is merely a particle. 'Te' means 'by you.' 'Evaṃ' (thus) indicates the manner of what is now to be said.

Sikkhitabbanti adhisīlasikkhādīnaṃ tissannampi sikkhānaṃ vasena sikkhanaṃ kātabbaṃ. Yathā pana sikkhitabbaṃ, taṃ dassento “diṭṭhe diṭṭhamattaṃ bhavissatī”tiādimāha.

'One should train' (sikkhitabbaṃ) means that the training should be undertaken by way of the three trainings, beginning with the training in higher virtue. And showing how one should train, he said, 'In the seen, there will be only the seen,' and so on.

Tattha diṭṭhe diṭṭhamattanti rūpāyatane cakkhuviññāṇena diṭṭhamattaṃ. Yathā hi cakkhuviññāṇaṃ rūpe rūpamattameva passati, na aniccādisabhāvaṃ, evameva sesaṃ. Cakkhudvārikaviññāṇena hi me diṭṭhamattameva bhavissatīti sikkhitabbanti attho. Atha vā diṭṭhe diṭṭhaṃ nāma [P 0.0091] cakkhuviññāṇena rūpavijānananti attho. Mattanti pamāṇaṃ. Diṭṭhā mattā etassāti diṭṭhamattaṃ, cakkhuviññāṇamattameva cittaṃ bhavissatīti attho. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yathā āpāthagate rūpe cakkhuviññāṇaṃ na rajjati, na dussati, na muyhati, evaṃ rāgādivirahena cakkhuviññāṇamattameva me javanaṃ bhavissati, cakkhuviññāṇappamāṇeneva javanaṃ ṭhapessāmīti.

Herein, 'in the seen, there will be only the seen' means, in the visible-form base, there is merely what is seen by eye-consciousness. For just as eye-consciousness sees only the form itself in a form, not its nature as impermanent and so on, so it is with the rest. The meaning is: 'For me, there will be merely what is seen by eye-door consciousness'—thus should one train. Alternatively, in 'the seen,' 'the seen' means the knowing of form by eye-consciousness. 'Matta' means measure. 'Diṭṭhamatta' means that of which the measure is the seen, meaning the mind will be merely eye-consciousness. This is what is meant: just as eye-consciousness does not become lustful, averse, or deluded when a form comes into its range, so too, free from lust and so forth, my impulsion will be merely eye-consciousness. I will establish the impulsion only by the measure of eye-consciousness.

Atha vā diṭṭhaṃ nāma cakkhuviññāṇena diṭṭhaṃ rūpaṃ, diṭṭhamattaṃ nāma tattheva uppannaṃ sampaṭicchanasantīraṇavoṭṭhabbanasaṅkhātaṃ cittattayaṃ. Yathā taṃ na rajjati, na dussati, na muyhati, evaṃ āpāthagate rūpe teneva sampaṭicchanādippamāṇena javanaṃ uppādessāmi, nāhaṃ taṃ pamāṇaṃ atikkamitvā rajjanādivasena uppajjituṃ dassāmīti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Eseva nayo sutamute[M 0.0082]. Mutanti tadārammaṇaviññāṇehi saddhiṃ gandharasaphoṭṭhabbāyatanaṃ veditabbaṃ. Viññāte viññātamattanti ettha pana viññātaṃ nāma manodvārāvajjanena viññātārammaṇaṃ. Tasmiṃ viññāte viññātamattanti āvajjanappamāṇaṃ. Yathā āvajjanaṃ na rajjati, na dussati, na muyhati, evaṃ rajjanādivasena ca uppajjituṃ adatvā āvajjanappamāṇeneva cittaṃ ṭhapessāmīti ayamettha attho. Evañhi te, bāhiya, sikkhitabbanti evaṃ imāya paṭipadāya tayā, bāhiya, tissannaṃ sikkhānaṃ anuvattanavasena sikkhitabbaṃ.

Alternatively, 'the seen' means the form seen by eye-consciousness; 'only the seen' means the triad of consciousnesses called receiving, investigating, and determining that has arisen right there. Just as that does not become lustful, averse, or deluded, so too, when a form comes into range, I will cause impulsion to arise only by that measure of receiving and so forth. I will not allow it to arise by way of lust and so forth, having transgressed that measure—this is the meaning to be understood here. This same method applies to the heard and the sensed. 'The sensed' should be understood as the bases of smell, taste, and touch, together with the consciousnesses that have those as their object. In 'in the cognized, there will be only the cognized,' 'the cognized' means the object cognized by mind-door adverting. In that cognized, 'only the cognized' means the measure of adverting. Just as adverting does not become lustful, averse, or deluded, so too, not allowing the mind to arise by way of lust and so on, I will establish the mind only by the measure of adverting—this is the meaning here. 'Thus, Bāhiya, should you train' means: Bāhiya, by this practice, you should train by way of following the three trainings.

Iti bhagavā bāhiyassa saṃkhittarucitāya chahi viññāṇakāyehi saddhiṃ chaḷārammaṇabhedabhinnaṃ [V 0.0073] vipassanāya visayaṃ diṭṭhādīhi catūhi koṭṭhāsehi vibhajitvā tatthassa ñātatīraṇapariññaṃ dasseti. Kathaṃ? Ettha hi rūpāyatanaṃ passitabbaṭṭhena diṭṭhaṃ nāma, cakkhuviññāṇaṃ pana saddhiṃ taṃdvārikaviññāṇehi dassanaṭṭhena, tadubhayampi yathāpaccayaṃ pavattamānaṃ dhammamattameva, na ettha koci kattā vā kāretā vā, yato taṃ hutvā abhāvaṭṭhena aniccaṃ, udayabbayappaṭipīḷanaṭṭhena dukkhaṃ, avasavattanaṭṭhena [P 0.0092] anattāti kuto tattha paṇḍitassa rajjanādīnaṃ okāsoti? Ayamettha adhippāyo sutādīsupi.

Thus, on account of Bāhiya's preference for conciseness, the Blessed One, having divided the domain of insight—which is differentiated by the six sense objects together with the six groups of consciousness—into four portions, namely the seen and so forth, shows him the full understanding of knowing and scrutinizing therein. How so? Herein, the visible-form base is called 'the seen' in the sense of being something to be seen; eye-consciousness, however, together with the consciousnesses of that door, is so in the sense of seeing. Both of these are merely phenomena that proceed according to conditions; there is no doer or instigator herein. Since that, having come to be, is impermanent in the sense of non-existence, suffering in the sense of oppression by arising and passing away, and not-self in the sense of being beyond control, whence could there be an opportunity therein for lust and so forth for a wise person? This is the intended meaning here, and also in the case of the heard and so forth.

Idāni ñātatīraṇapariññāsu patiṭṭhitassa upari saha maggaphalena pahānapariññaṃ dassetuṃ, “yato kho te, bāhiyā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha yatoti yadā, yasmā vā. Teti tava. Tatoti tadā, tasmā vā. Tenāti tena diṭṭhādinā, diṭṭhādipaṭibaddhena rāgādinā vā. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – bāhiya, tava yasmiṃ kāle yena vā kāraṇena diṭṭhādīsu mayā vuttavidhiṃ paṭipajjantassa aviparītasabhāvāvabodhena diṭṭhādimattaṃ bhavissati, tasmiṃ kāle tena vā kāraṇena diṭṭhādipaṭibaddhena rāgādinā saha na bhavissasi, ratto vā duṭṭho vā mūḷho vā na bhavissasi, pahīnarāgādikattā tena vā diṭṭhādinā saha paṭibaddho na bhavissasīti. Tato tvaṃ, bāhiya, na tatthāti yadā yasmā vā tvaṃ tena rāgena vā ratto dosena vā duṭṭho mohena vā mūḷho na bhavissasi, tadā tasmā vā tvaṃ tattha diṭṭhādike na bhavissasi, tasmiṃ diṭṭhe vā sutamutaviññāte vā “etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā”ti taṇhāmānadiṭṭhīhi allīno patiṭṭhito na bhavissasi. Ettāvatā pahānapariññaṃ matthakaṃ pāpetvā khīṇāsavabhūmi dassitā.

Now, for one established in the full understandings of knowing and scrutinizing, in order to show the full understanding of abandoning above that, together with the path and fruition, the passage beginning, 'When, Bāhiya...' was begun. Therein, 'yato' means 'when' or 'because.' 'Te' means 'your.' 'Tato' means 'then' or 'therefore.' 'Tena' means 'by that seen and so forth,' or 'by lust and so forth connected with the seen and so forth.' This is what is meant: Bāhiya, at whatever time or for whatever reason, for you who are practicing the method taught by me regarding the seen and so forth, through awakening to their non-distorted nature, there will be merely the seen and so forth. At that time or for that reason, you will not be together with lust and so forth connected with the seen and so forth. You will not be lustful, or hateful, or deluded. Because lust and so forth have been abandoned, you will not be bound together with that seen and so forth. 'Then you, Bāhiya, are not therein' means: when or because you are not lustful with that lust, or hateful with that hate, or deluded with that delusion, then or therefore you will not be in that seen and so forth. You will not be clinging and established by way of craving, conceit, and views in that which is seen, heard, sensed, or cognized, thinking, 'This is mine, this I am, this is my self.' By this much, having brought the full understanding of abandoning to its culmination, the state of one whose cankers are destroyed is shown.

Tato [M 0.0083] tvaṃ, bāhiya, nevidha na huraṃ na ubhayamantarenāti yadā tvaṃ, bāhiya, tena rāgādinā tattha diṭṭhādīsu paṭibaddho na bhavissasi, tadā tvaṃ neva idhaloke na paraloke na ubhayatthāpi. Esevanto dukkhassāti kilesadukkhassa ca vaṭṭadukkhassa ca ayameva hi anto ayaṃ parivaṭumabhāvoti ayameva hi ettha attho. Ye pana “ubhayamantarenā”ti padaṃ gahetvā antarābhavaṃ nāma icchanti, tesaṃ taṃ micchā. Antarābhavassa hi bhāvo abhidhamme paṭikkhittoyeva. Antarenāti vacanaṃ pana vikappantaradīpanaṃ, tasmā ayamettha attho – “neva idha na huraṃ, aparo vikappo na ubhaya”nti.

‘Then you, Bāhiya, are neither here nor beyond nor in between’ means: when you, Bāhiya, are not bound by that lust and so forth to the seen and so forth therein, then you are neither in this world, nor in the next world, nor in both. ‘This is the very end of suffering’ means: this indeed is the end of both the suffering of defilements and the suffering of the round; this is the state of not revolving again. This is indeed the meaning here. As for those who, taking the phrase ‘nor in between,’ desire what is called an intermediate existence, that is wrong for them. For the existence of an intermediate state is indeed rejected in the Abhidhamma. The word ‘antarena,’ however, indicates another alternative. Therefore, this is the meaning here: ‘neither here nor beyond; another alternative is: not in both.’

Atha vā antarenāti vacanaṃ pana vikappantarābhāvadīpanaṃ. Tassattho – “neva idha na huraṃ, ubhayamantare pana na [P 0.0093] aññaṭṭhānaṃ atthī”ti. Yepi ca “antarāparinibbāyī sambhavesī”ti [V 0.0074] ca imesaṃ suttapadānaṃ atthaṃ ayoniso gahetvā “atthiyeva antarābhavo”ti vadanti, tepi yasmā avihādīsu tattha tattha āyuvemajjhaṃ anatikkamitvā antarā aggamaggādhigamena anavasesakilesaparinibbānena parinibbāyatīti antarāparinibbāyī, na antarābhavabhūtoti purimassa suttapadassa attho. Pacchimassa ca ye bhūtā eva, na bhavissanti, te khīṇāsavā purimapade bhūtāti vuttā. Tabbiruddhatāya sambhavamesantīti sambhavesino, appahīnabhavasaṃyojanattā sekhā puthujjanā ca. Catūsu vā yonīsu aṇḍajajalābujasattā yāva aṇḍakosaṃ vatthikosañca na bhindanti, tāva sambhavesī nāma, aṇḍakosato vatthikosato ca bahi nikkhantā bhūtā nāma. Saṃsedajā opapātikā ca paṭhamacittakkhaṇe sambhavesī nāma, dutiyacittakkhaṇato paṭṭhāya bhūtā nāma. Yena vā iriyāpathena jāyanti, yāva tato aññaṃ na pāpuṇanti, tāva sambhavesino, tato paraṃ bhūtāti attho. Tasmā natthīti paṭikkhipitabbā. Sati hi ujuke pāḷianugate atthe kiṃ aniddhāritasāmatthiyena antarābhavena parikappitena payojananti.

Or, the term 'antarena' indicates the absence of an alternative. Its meaning is: 'Neither here nor in the next world, and there is no other place in between.' Those who, having improperly grasped the meaning of the sutta passages 'antarāparinibbāyī' and 'sambhavesī,' claim, 'There is indeed an intermediate existence,' are mistaken. For the meaning of the former sutta term, 'antarāparinibbāyī,' is that one attains Nibbāna by realizing the highest path and completely eradicating defilements in the interim, without exceeding the middle of the lifespan in the Aviha and other realms; it does not mean one exists as an intermediate being. And as for the latter term, those who are already 'bhūtā' (existent), not those who will become, are the ones with taints destroyed, called 'bhūtā' in the former passage. Contrary to that, 'sambhavesino' are those who seek becoming, namely, trainees and ordinary people, because they have not abandoned the fetter of existence. Alternatively, among the four types of birth, egg-born and womb-born beings are called 'sambhavesī' as long as they have not broken the eggshell or the membrane of the womb. Once they emerge from the eggshell or the membrane of the womb, they are called 'bhūtā.' Moisture-born and spontaneously-born beings are called 'sambhavesī' at the moment of their first consciousness. From the second moment of consciousness onward, they are called 'bhūtā.' Or, 'sambhavesino' refers to beings who, from the moment they are born through whatever mode of deportment, have not yet attained a different mode. After that, they are called 'bhūtā.' Therefore, the claim that it exists must be rejected. For when there is a straightforward meaning that follows the Pāli, what is the use of a speculated intermediate existence whose capacity has not been ascertained?

Ye pana “santānavasena pavattamānānaṃ dhammānaṃ avicchedena desantaresu pātubhāvo diṭṭho, yathā taṃ vīhiādiaviññāṇakasantāne, evaṃ saviññāṇakasantānepi avicchedena desantaresu pātubhāvena bhavitabbaṃ. Ayañca nayo sati antarābhave yujjati, na aññathā”ti yuttiṃ vadanti. Tena hi iddhimato cetovasippattassa cittānugatikaṃ kāyaṃ [M 0.0084] adhiṭṭhahantassa khaṇena brahmalokato idhūpasaṅkamane ito vā brahmalokagamane yutti vattabbā. Yadi sabbattheva avicchinnadese dhammānaṃ pavatti icchitā, yadipi siyā iddhimantānaṃ iddhivisayo acinteyyoti. Taṃ idhāpi samānaṃ “kammavipāko [P 0.0094] acinteyyo”ti vacanato. Tasmā taṃ tesaṃ matimattameva. Acinteyyasabhāvā hi sabhāvadhammā, te katthaci paccayavasena vicchinnadese pātubhavanti, katthaci avicchinnadese. Tathā hi mukhaghosādīhi paccayehi aññasmiṃ dese ādāsapabbatappadesādike paṭibimbapaṭighosādikaṃ paccayuppannaṃ nibbattamānaṃ dissati, tasmā na sabbaṃ sabbattha upanetabbanti ayamettha saṅkhepo. Vitthāro pana paṭibimbassa udāharaṇabhāvasādhanādiko antarābhavakathāvicāro kathāvatthupakaraṇassa (kathā. 505; kathā. aṭṭha. 505) ṭīkāyaṃ gahetabbo.

Some argue, 'The uninterrupted manifestation of phenomena that proceed by way of a continuum is observed in other places, as seen in the continuum of non-conscious things like rice seeds. Similarly, in a conscious continuum, there must also be an uninterrupted manifestation in other places. This principle is logical if there is an intermediate existence, but not otherwise.' If so, then the logic should be stated for the instantaneous travel here from the Brahma-world, or the going from here to the Brahma-world, of one with psychic power who has attained mastery of mind and resolves for the body to follow the mind. If the occurrence of phenomena is desired in an uninterrupted location everywhere, then it might be said that the domain of psychic power of those with psychic power is inconceivable. That is the same here too, because it is said, 'The result of kamma is inconceivable.' Therefore, that is merely their opinion. For inherent phenomena are by nature inconceivable; due to conditions, they manifest in some places in a discontinuous location, and in other places in a continuous location. For, due to conditions such as a face or a sound, a conditionally arisen phenomenon such as a reflection or an echo is seen arising in another place, such as on a mirror or a mountainside. Therefore, not everything can be applied to everything—this is the summary here. The detailed account, however, the discussion and examination of the intermediate existence, including the demonstration of the reflection as an example, should be taken from the subcommentary on the Kathāvatthupakaraṇa.

Apare pana “idhāti kāmabhavo, huranti arūpabhavo, ubhayamantarenāti rūpabhavo vutto”ti. Aññe “idhāti ajjhattikāyatanāni, huranti bāhirāyatanāni, ubhayamantarenāti cittacetasikā”ti. “Idhāti vā paccayadhammā, huranti paccayuppannadhammā, ubhayamantarenāti paṇṇattidhammā [V 0.0075] vuttā”ti vadanti. Taṃ sabbaṃ aṭṭhakathāsu natthi. Evaṃ tāva “diṭṭhe diṭṭhamattaṃ bhavissatī”tiādinā diṭṭhādivasena catudhā tebhūmakadhammā saṅgahetabbā. Tattha subhasukhaniccaattaggāhaparivajjanamukhena asubhadukkhāniccānattānupassanā dassitāti heṭṭhimāhi visuddhīhi saddhiṃ saṅkhepeneva vipassanā kathitā. “Tato tvaṃ, bāhiya, na tenā”ti iminā rāgādīnaṃ samucchedassa adhippetattā maggo. “Tato tvaṃ, bāhiya, na tatthā”ti iminā phalaṃ. “Nevidhā”tiādinā anupādisesā parinibbānadhātu kathitāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tena vuttaṃ – “atha kho bāhiyassa…pe… āsavehi cittaṃ vimuccī”ti.

Others, however, say: '"Here" refers to the sense-sphere existence, "there" to the formless existence, and "between the two" refers to the form existence.' Others say: '"Here" means the internal sense bases, "there" the external sense bases, and "between the two" means mind and mental factors.' Still others say: '"Here" refers to conditioned phenomena, "there" to their conditioning phenomena, and "between the two" refers to conceptual phenomena.' All of this is not found in the commentaries. Thus, for now, the phenomena of the three realms are to be included in four ways—by way of the seen, and so on—through the statement, 'In the seen, there will be merely the seen,' and so on. Herein, the contemplation of the unattractive, suffering, impermanence, and non-self is shown by way of abandoning the grasping of the attractive, pleasure, permanence, and self. Thus, insight is briefly explained along with the preceding purifications. By the words, 'Then, Bāhiya, you are not thereby,' the path is intended, on account of its aim being the eradication of lust and so on. By the words, 'Then, Bāhiya, you are not therein,' the fruit is intended. By the words, 'Neither here…' and so on, the Nibbāna-element without residue of aggregates is explained. Thus it is said: 'Then Bāhiya’s… mind was liberated from the taints...'

Imāya saṃkhittapadāya desanāya tāvadevāti tasmiṃyeva khaṇe, na kālantare. Anupādāyāti aggahetvā. Āsavehīti ābhavaggaṃ āgotrabhuṃ savanato pavattanato cirapārivāsiyaṭṭhena madirādiāsavasadisatāya ca “āsavā”ti [P 0.0095] laddhanāmehi kāmarāgādīhi. Vimuccīti samucchedavimuttiyā paṭippassaddhivimuttiyā ca vimucci nissajji. So hi satthu dhammaṃ suṇanto eva sīlāni sodhetvā yathāladdhaṃ cittasamādhiṃ nissāya vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā khippābhiññatāya tāvadeva sabbāsave khepetvā [M 0.0085] saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. So saṃsārasotaṃ chinditvā katavaṭṭapariyanto antimadehadharo hutvā ekūnavīsatiyā paccavekkhaṇāsu pavattāsu dhammatāya codiyamāno bhagavantaṃ pabbajjaṃ yāci. “Paripuṇṇaṃ te pattacīvara”nti puṭṭho “na paripuṇṇa”nti āha. Atha naṃ satthā “tena hi pattacīvaraṃ pariyesā”ti vatvā pakkāmi. Tena vuttaṃ – “atha kho bhagavā…pe… pakkāmī”ti.

By this teaching in brief terms, 'at that very moment' means in that same instant, not at another time. 'Without grasping' means without taking up. 'From the taints' means from sensual desire and so on, which have received the name 'āsavā' because they flow and proceed up to the peak of existence and up to the change-of-lineage consciousness, and because of their long-standing infusion and their similarity to intoxicants like liquor. 'Was liberated' means he was liberated and released through liberation by cutting off and liberation by tranquilization. For, while listening to the Teacher's Dhamma, he purified his moral conduct, and relying on the mental concentration he had attained, he established insight, and due to his swift direct knowledge, he at that very moment exhausted all the taints and attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges. Having cut off the stream of saṃsāra, he became one for whom the round of existence was ended, bearing his final body. While the nineteen kinds of reviewing knowledge were occurring, being urged by the nature of things, he requested ordination from the Blessed One. When asked, 'Are your bowl and robes complete?' he replied, 'They are not complete.' Then the Teacher, having said to him, 'In that case, search for a bowl and robes,' departed. Therefore it is said: 'Then the Blessed One… departed.'

So kira kassapadasabalassa sāsane vīsavassasahassāni samaṇadhammaṃ karonto “bhikkhunā nāma attanā paccaye labhitvā yathādānaṃ karontena attanāva paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti ekassa bhikkhussapi pattena vā cīvarena vā saṅgahaṃ nākāsi, tenassa ehibhikkhuupasampadāya upanissayo nāhosi. Keci panāhu – “so kira buddhasuññe loke coro hutvā dhanukalāpaṃ sannayhitvā araññe corikaṃ karonto ekaṃ paccekabuddhaṃ disvā pattacīvaralobhena taṃ usunā vijjhitvā pattacīvaraṃ gaṇhi, tenassa iddhimayapattacīvaraṃ na uppajjissatīti, satthā taṃ ñatvā ehibhikkhubhāvena pabbajjaṃ na adāsī”ti. Tampi pattacīvarapariyesanaṃ caramānaṃ ekā dhenu vegena āpatantī paharitvā jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpesi. Taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “atha kho acirapakkantassa bhagavato bāhiyaṃ dārucīriyaṃ gāvī taruṇavacchā adhipatitvā jīvitā voropesī”ti.

It is said that for twenty thousand years he practiced the duties of a monk in the dispensation of Kassapa, the Ten-Powered One. Thinking, 'It is proper for a monk, having obtained requisites himself, to consume them himself without giving gifts,' he did not offer support to even a single monk with a bowl or a robe. For that reason, the supporting condition for the 'Come, monk' ordination did not exist for him. Some, however, say: 'It is said that in a world devoid of Buddhas, he became a thief and, having armed himself with a bow and quiver, committed theft in the forest. Seeing a Paccekabuddha, out of greed for his bowl and robe, he shot him with an arrow and took the bowl and robe. For that reason, a bowl and robe created by psychic power would not arise for him. The Teacher, knowing this, did not grant him the going forth with the words, "Come, monk."' While he was searching for a bowl and robe, a cow, rushing swiftly, gored him and brought his life to an end. In reference to this, it was said: 'Then, not long after the Blessed One had departed, a cow with a young calf attacked Bāhiya Dārucīriya and deprived him of life.'

Tattha [V 0.0076] acirapakkantassāti na ciraṃ pakkantassa bhagavato. Gāvī taruṇavacchāti ekā yakkhinī taruṇavacchadhenurūpā. Adhipatitvāti abhibhavitvā madditvā. Jīvitā voropesīti purimasmiṃ attabhāve laddhāghātatāya diṭṭhamatteneva [P 0.0096] vericittaṃ uppādetvā siṅgena paharitvā jīvitā voropesi.

Herein, not long after... had departed means: not long after the Blessed One had departed. A cow with a young calf means: a certain yakkhiṇī in the form of a cow with a young calf. Having attacked means: having overwhelmed and crushed. Deprived him of life means: because of a past deed of killing committed in a previous existence, upon the mere sight of him, a mind filled with enmity arose, and goring him with her horn, she deprived him of his life-faculty.

Satthā piṇḍāya caritvā katabhattakicco sambahulehi bhikkhūhi saddhiṃ nagarato nikkhamanto bāhiyassa sarīraṃ saṅkāraṭṭhāne patitaṃ disvā bhikkhū āṇāpesi – “bhikkhave, ekasmiṃ gharadvāre ṭhatvā mañcakaṃ āharāpetvā idaṃ sarīraṃ nagarato nīharitvā jhāpetvā thūpaṃ karothā”ti, bhikkhū tathā akaṃsu. Katvā ca pana vihāraṃ gantvā satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā attanā katakiccaṃ ārocetvā tassa abhisamparāyaṃ pucchiṃsu. Atha nesaṃ bhagavā tassa parinibbutabhāvaṃ ācikkhi. Bhikkhū “tumhe, bhante, ‘bāhiyo dārucīriyo arahattaṃ patto’ti vadatha, kadā so arahattaṃ patto”ti [M 0.0086] pucchiṃsu. “Mama dhammaṃ sutakāle”ti ca vutte “kadā panassa tumhehi dhammo kathito”ti? “Piṇḍāya carantena ajjeva antaravīthiyaṃ ṭhatvā”ti. “Appamattako so, bhante, tumhehi antaravīthiyaṃ ṭhatvā kathitadhammo, kathaṃ so tāvatakena visesaṃ nibbattesī”ti? “Kiṃ, bhikkhave, mama dhammaṃ ‘appaṃ vā bahuṃ vā’ti pamiṇatha, anekāni gāthāsahassānipi anatthasaṃhitāni na seyyo, atthanissitaṃ pana ekampi gāthāpadaṃ seyyo”ti dassento –

The Teacher, having gone for alms and completed his meal, was leaving the city with many monks when he saw Bāhiya’s body lying on a rubbish heap. He commanded the monks: 'Monks, go to a house, have a bier brought, take this body out of the city, cremate it, and build a stūpa.' The monks did so. Having done this, they went to the monastery, approached the Teacher, reported what they had done, and asked about his future state. Then the Blessed One told them of his attainment of final extinguishment. The monks asked, 'Venerable sir, you say that Bāhiya Dārucīriya attained arahantship. When did he attain arahantship?' 'At the time he heard my Dhamma.' And when it was said thus, they asked, 'But when was the Dhamma taught to him by you?' 'Just today, while I was standing in the middle of the street on my alms round.' 'Venerable sir, the Dhamma taught by you while standing in the middle of the street was so brief. How did he realize such a special attainment with so little?' 'Why, monks, do you measure my Dhamma as "little" or "much"? Even thousands of verses unconnected with what is beneficial are not excellent. But one verse connected with what is beneficial is excellent.' To show this, he said:

“Sahassamapi ce gāthā, anatthapadasañhitā;

Ekaṃ gāthāpadaṃ seyyo, yaṃ sutvā upasammatī”ti. (dha. pa. 101) –

“Though there be a thousand verses composed of meaningless phrases, better is a single line of a verse, hearing which one becomes tranquil.”

Dhammapade imaṃ gāthaṃ vatvā “na kevalaṃ so parinibbānamattena, atha kho mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ khippābhiññānaṃ aggabhāvenapi pūjāraho”ti dassento “etadaggaṃ, bhikkhave, mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ khippābhiññānaṃ, yadidaṃ bāhiyo dārucīriyo”ti (a. ni. 1.216) taṃ āyasmantaṃ etadagge ṭhapesi. Taṃ [P 0.0097] sandhāya vuttaṃ – “atha kho bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ piṇḍāya caritvā…pe… parinibbuto, bhikkhave, bāhiyo dārucīriyo”ti.

Having spoken this verse in the Dhammapada, to show that 'He is worthy of honor not only on account of his final extinguishment, but also for being the foremost among my monk disciples in swift insight,' the Teacher declared: 'Monks, the foremost among my monk disciples who are of swift insight is this one, namely, Bāhiya Dārucīriya.' He thus placed the venerable one in that foremost position. In reference to this, it was said: 'Then the Blessed One, having gone for alms in Sāvatthī… and so on… Monks, Bāhiya Dārucīriya has attained final extinguishment.'

Tattha pacchābhattanti bhattakiccato pacchā. Piṇḍapātapaṭikkantoti piṇḍapātapariyesanato paṭinivatto. Padadvayenāpi katabhattakiccoti vuttaṃ hoti. Nīharitvāti nagarato bahi netvā. Jhāpethāti dahatha. Thūpañcassa karothāti assa bāhiyassa sarīradhātuyo gahetvā cetiyañca karotha[V 0.0077]. Tattha kāraṇamāha – “sabrahmacārī vo, bhikkhave, kālakato”ti. Tassattho – yaṃ tumhe seṭṭhaṭṭhena brahmaṃ adhisīlādipaṭipattidhammaṃ sandiṭṭhaṃ caratha, taṃ so tumhehi samānaṃ brahmaṃ acarīti sabrahmacārī maraṇakālassa pattiyāva kālakato, tasmā taṃ mañcakena nīharitvā jhāpetha, thūpañcassa karothāti.

Herein, after the meal means: after the business of the meal. Returned from the alms round means: returned from the search for alms-food. By both phrases, 'having completed the business of the meal' is what is meant. Having taken out means: having taken outside the city. You should cremate means: you should burn. And you should make a stūpa for him means: taking the bodily relics of this Bāhiya, you should also make a cetiya. Therein, he states the reason: 'Monks, one who shares the holy life with you has passed away.' The meaning of this is: that same holy life—the practice of higher virtue and so on, which is supreme in the highest sense—that you practice, he too practiced in the same way as you; thus he is one who shares the holy life. Having reached the time of death, he has passed away. Therefore, taking him out on a bier, you should cremate him, and you should make a stūpa for his relics.

Tassa kā gatīti pañcasu gatīsu tassa katamā gati upapatti bhavabhūtā, gatīti nipphatti, ariyo puthujjano vāti kā niṭṭhāti attho. Abhisamparāyoti pecca bhavuppatti bhavanirodho vā. Kiñcāpi tassa thūpakaraṇāṇattiyāva parinibbutabhāvo atthato pakāsito hoti, ye pana bhikkhū tattakena na jāniṃsu, te “tassa kā gatī”ti [M 0.0087] pucchiṃsu. Pākaṭataraṃ vā kārāpetukāmā tathā bhagavantaṃ pucchiṃsu.

What is his destination? means: among the five destinations, which destination, which state of rebirth, has he attained? Or, destination means accomplishment; was he a noble one or a worldling? What was his final state? This is the meaning. Future state means rebirth after death or the cessation of becoming. Although the fact of his final extinguishment was already revealed in principle by the command to build a stūpa, those monks who did not understand from just that much asked, 'What is his destination?' Or, desiring to have it made more manifest, they questioned the Blessed One in that way.

Paṇḍitoti aggamaggapaññāya adhigatattā paṇḍena ito gato pavattoti paṇḍito. Paccapādīti paṭipajji. Dhammassāti lokuttaradhammassa. Anudhammanti sīlavisuddhiādipaṭipadādhammaṃ. Atha vā dhammassāti nibbānadhammassa. Anudhammanti ariyamaggaphaladhammaṃ. Na ca maṃ dhammādhikaraṇanti dhammadesanāhetu na ca maṃ vihesesi yathānusiṭṭhaṃ paṭipannattā. Yo hi satthu santike dhammaṃ sutvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ vā gahetvā yathānusiṭṭhaṃ na paṭipajjati, so satthāraṃ viheseti nāma. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ – “vihiṃsasaññī paguṇaṃ na bhāsiṃ, dhammaṃ paṇītaṃ manujesu brahme”ti (mahāva. 9; ma. ni. 1.283; 2.339). Atha vā na ca maṃ dhammādhikaraṇanti na ca imaṃ dhammādhikaraṇaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – vaṭṭadukkhato niyyānahetubhūtaṃ imaṃ mama sāsanadhammaṃ suppaṭipannattā na viheseti. Duppaṭipanno hi sāsanaṃ bhindanto satthu [P 0.0098] dhammasarīre pahāraṃ deti nāma. Ayaṃ pana sammāpaṭipattiṃ matthakaṃ pāpetvā anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā parinibbāyi. Tena vuttaṃ – “parinibbuto, bhikkhave, bāhiyo dārucīriyo”ti.

“Wise” means one who has attained by the wisdom of the highest path, one who has gone or proceeded from here by wisdom; thus, he is wise. “Practiced” means he undertook the practice. “Of the Dhamma” means of the supramundane Dhamma. “In accordance with the Dhamma” means the practice-Dhamma beginning with purity of virtue. Alternatively, “of the Dhamma” means of the Dhamma of Nibbāna; “in accordance with the Dhamma” means the Dhamma of the noble path and fruition. “Nor did he trouble me on account of the Dhamma” means he did not trouble me for the sake of teaching the Dhamma, because he practiced as instructed. For one who, having heard the Dhamma from the Teacher or taken up a meditation subject, does not practice as instructed, is said to trouble the Teacher. Referring to this, it is said: “Perceiving harm, I did not speak what was familiar, the sublime Dhamma among humans, O Brahmā.” Alternatively, “nor did he trouble me on account of the Dhamma” means he did not trouble me regarding this Dhamma-matter. This is what is meant: he did not trouble me, because he practiced well this Dhamma of my teaching, which is the cause for release from the suffering of the cycle of rebirths. For one who practices wrongly, by breaking the dispensation, is said to strike the Teacher’s Dhamma-body. But this one, having brought right practice to its summit, attained final Nibbāna in the Nibbāna-element without residue. Therefore, it is said: “Monks, Bāhiya of the Bark Cloth has attained final Nibbāna.”

Etamatthaṃ viditvāti etaṃ therassa bāhiyassa anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā parinibbutabhāvaṃ, tathā parinibbutānañca khīṇāsavānaṃ gatiyā pacurajanehi dubbiññeyyabhāvaṃ sabbākārato viditvā. Imaṃ udānanti imaṃ appatiṭṭhitaparinibbānānubhāvadīpakaṃ udānaṃ udānesi.

“Having understood this matter”: that is, having understood in all aspects the fact of the Elder Bāhiya's attainment of final Nibbāna in the Nibbāna-element without residue, and also the fact that the destiny of the taintless ones who have thus attained final Nibbāna is difficult for many people to discern, he uttered this inspired utterance. “This inspired utterance” means he uttered this inspired utterance that illuminates the power of unestablished final Nibbāna.

Tattha yatthāti yasmiṃ nibbāne āpo ca na gādhati, pathavī ca tejo ca vāyo ca na gādhati, na patiṭṭhāti. Kasmā? Nibbānassa asaṅkhatasabhāvattā. Na hi tattha saṅkhatadhammānaṃ lesopi [V 0.0078] sambhavati. Sukkāti sukkavaṇṇatāya sukkāti laddhanāmā gahanakkhattatārakā. Na jotantīti na bhāsanti. Ādicco nappakāsatīti tīsu dīpesu ekasmiṃ khaṇe ālokapharaṇasamattho ādiccopi ābhāvasena na dibbati. Na tattha candimā bhātīti satipi bhāsurabhāve kantasītalakiraṇo candopi tasmiṃ nibbāne abhāvato eva attano juṇhāvibhāsanena na virocati. Yadi tattha candimasūriyādayo natthi, lokantaro viya niccandhakārameva [M 0.0088] taṃ bhaveyyāti āsaṅkaṃ sandhāyāha “tamo tattha na vijjatī”ti. Sati hi rūpābhāve tamo nāma na siyā.

Therein, “where” refers to that Nibbāna in which water does not find footing, nor do earth, fire, or wind find footing or become established. Why? Because Nibbāna is unconditioned by nature. Indeed, not even a trace of conditioned phenomena can exist there. “The bright ones” (sukkā) refers to the planets, constellations, and stars, so named because of their bright color. “They do not shine” means they do not give light. “The sun does not illuminate”: even the sun, capable of spreading light across the three continents in a single moment, does not shine there, simply due to its non-existence. “Nor does the moon gleam there”: even the moon, with its radiant, cool, and pleasant rays, does not shine with its moonlight in that Nibbāna, simply due to its non-existence. Anticipating the doubt, “If the moon, sun, and so on are not there, might that place be perpetually dark like the space between worlds?” he said, “Darkness is not found there.” For when there is an absence of form, there can be no such thing as darkness.

Yadā ca attanā vedi, muni monena brāhmaṇoti catusaccamunanato monanti laddhanāmena maggañāṇena kāyamoneyyādīhi ca samannāgatattā “munī”ti laddhanāmo ariyasāvakabrāhmaṇo teneva monasaṅkhātena paṭivedhañāṇena yadā yasmiṃ kāle aggamaggakkhaṇe attanā sayameva anussavādike pahāya attapaccakkhaṃ katvā nibbānaṃ vedi paṭivijjhi. “Avedī”tipi pāṭho, aññāsīti attho. Atha rūpā arūpā ca, sukhadukkhā pamuccatīti athāti tassa nibbānassa jānanato pacchā. Rūpāti rūpadhammā, tena pañcavokārabhavo ekavokārabhavo ca gahito hoti. Arūpāti arūpadhammā, tena rūpenāmissīkato [P 0.0099] arūpabhavo gahito hoti. So “catuvokārabhavo”tipi vuccati. Sukhadukkhāti sabbattha uppajjanakasukhadukkhatopi vaṭṭato. Atha vā rūpāti rūpalokapaṭisandhito. Arūpāti arūpalokapaṭisandhito. Sukhadukkhāti kāmāvacarapaṭisandhito. Kāmabhavo hi byāmissasukhadukkho. Evametasmā sakalatopi vaṭṭato accantameva muccatīti gāthādvayenapi bhagavā “mayhaṃ puttassa bāhiyassa evarūpā nibbānagatī”ti dasseti.

“And when a sage, a brahmin, has known for himself by means of wisdom”: Here, a noble disciple, a brahmin, is called a ‘sage’ (muni) because he is endowed with bodily sagacity and so on. By that very penetration-knowledge called ‘wisdom’ (mona)—so called from knowing the four truths—when, at the moment of the highest path, he himself, having abandoned hearsay and the like and having made it directly evident, knew and penetrated Nibbāna. There is also the reading `avedi` (‘he knew’); the meaning is ‘he understood’ (`aññāsi`). “Then from form and the formless, from pleasure and pain, he is freed”: “Then” means after knowing that Nibbāna. “Form” means the phenomena of form; by this, the five-constituent existence and the one-constituent existence are included. “The formless” means formless phenomena; by this, the formless existence, which is unmixed with form, is included. This is also called the “four-constituent existence.” “Pleasure and pain” means from the pleasure and pain that arise everywhere in the cycle of existence.
