Alternatively, “form” means from rebirth in the form realm; “the formless” means from rebirth in the formless realm; and “pleasure and pain” means from rebirth in the sensual realm, for sensual existence is a mixture of pleasure and pain. Thus, he is completely freed from this entire cycle of existence. Through these two verses, the Blessed One shows: “Such is the destiny of my son Bāhiya, which is Nibbāna.”

Dasamasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the tenth sutta is concluded.

Niṭṭhitā ca bodhivaggavaṇṇanā.

And the commentary on the Bodhi Chapter is concluded.

2. Mucalindavaggo

2. The Mucalinda Chapter

1. Mucalindasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Mucalinda Sutta

11. Mucalindavaggassa [M 0.0089][V 0.0079][P 0.0100] paṭhame mucalindamūleti ettha mucalindo vuccati nīparukkho. So “niculo”tipi vuccati, tassa samīpe. Keci pana “mucaloti tassa rukkhassa nāmaṃ, taṃ vanajeṭṭhakatāya pana mucalindoti vutta”nti vadanti. Mahā akālameghoti asampatte vassakāle uppannamahāmegho. So hi gimhānaṃ pacchime māse sakalacakkavāḷagabbhaṃ pūrento udapādi. Sattāhavaddalikāti tasmiṃ uppanne sattāhaṃ avicchinnavuṭṭhikā ahosi. Sītavātaduddinīti sā ca sattāhavaddalikā udakaphusitasammissena sītavātena samantato paribbhamantena dusitadivasattā duddinī nāma ahosi. Mucalindo nāma nāgarājāti tasseva mucalindarukkhassa samīpe pokkharaṇiyā heṭṭhā nāgabhavanaṃ atthi, tattha nibbatto mahānubhāvo nāgarājā. Sakabhavanāti attano nāgabhavanato. Sattakkhattuṃ bhogehi parikkhipitvāti sattavāre attano sarīrabhogehi bhagavato kāyaṃ parivāretvā. Uparimuddhani mahantaṃ phaṇaṃ vihaccāti bhagavato muddhappadesassa upari attano mahantaṃ phaṇaṃ pasāretvā. “Phaṇaṃ karitvā”tipi pāṭho, so evattho.

11. In the first sutta of the Mucalinda Chapter, regarding the phrase “at the root of the Mucalinda tree”: here, Mucalinda refers to the Nipa tree. It is also called the Nicula tree. Some, however, say: “Mucala is the name of that tree, but it is called Mucalinda due to its being the chief of the forest.” “A great untimely cloud”: a great cloud that arose when the rainy season had not yet arrived. Indeed, it appeared in the last month of the hot season, filling the entire interior of the world-system. “A seven-day downpour”: when that cloud arose, there was uninterrupted rain for seven days. “Cold winds and a stormy day”: that seven-day downpour, with its cold wind mixed with the touch of water swirling all around, became what is called a stormy day because the days were spoiled. “Mucalinda, the Nāga king”: near that very Mucalinda tree, there is a Nāga abode beneath a pond. A Nāga king of great power was reborn there. “From his own abode”: from his Nāga abode. “Having encircled him seven times with his coils”: having surrounded the Blessed One’s body seven times with the coils of his own body. “Holding his great hood over his head”: having spread his own great hood above the region of the Blessed One’s head. There is also the reading, “having made a hood,” which has the same meaning.

Tassa kira nāgarājassa etadahosi “bhagavā ca mayhaṃ bhavanasamīpe rukkhamūle nisinno, ayañca sattāhavaddalikā vattati, vāsāgāramassa laddhuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. So sattaratanamayaṃ pāsādaṃ nimminituṃ sakkontopi “evaṃ kate kāyasāro gahito na bhavissati, dasabalassa kāyaveyyāvaccaṃ karissāmī”ti mahantaṃ attabhāvaṃ katvā [P 0.0101] satthāraṃ sattakkhattuṃ bhogehi parikkhipitvā upari phaṇaṃ katvā dhāresi. “Parikkhepabbhantaraṃ lohapāsāde bhaṇḍāgāragabbhappamāṇaṃ ahosī”ti khandhakaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (mahāva. aṭṭha. 5) vuttaṃ. Majjhimaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “heṭṭhālohapāsādappamāṇa”nti (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.284). “Icchiticchitena iriyāpathena satthā viharissatī”ti kira nāgarājassa ajjhāsayo. Bhagavā pana yathānisinnova sattāhaṃ vītināmesi. Tañca ṭhānaṃ supihitavātapānaṃ suphusitaaggaḷadvāraṃ kūṭāgāraṃ viya ahosi. Mā [V 0.0080] bhagavantaṃ sītantiādi tassa tathā karitvā ṭhānakāraṇaparidīpanaṃ. So hi [M 0.0090] “mā bhagavantaṃ sītaṃ bādhayittha, mā uṇhaṃ, mā ḍaṃsādisamphasso bādhayitthā”ti tathā karitvā aṭṭhāsi.

It is said that this thought occurred to the nāga king: “The Blessed One is seated at the foot of a tree near my dwelling, and this seven-day rain is occurring—it is fitting to provide him with a dwelling.” Though he was capable of creating a palace made of seven kinds of jewels, he thought, “If I do so, the value of this physical act will not be realized; I will perform bodily service for the One of Ten Powers.” Thus, he manifested a large body, encircled the Teacher seven times with his coils, and held a hood above him. It is said in the Khandhaka Commentary that “the space within the coils was the size of a storeroom in the Lohapāsāda.” In the Majjhima Commentary, however, it is said to be “the size of the lower Lohapāsāda.” It is said the nāga king’s intention was: “The Teacher will dwell in whatever posture he wishes.” The Blessed One, however, passed the seven days just as he was seated. And that place was like a gabled chamber with well-closed windows and well-bolted doors. The phrase beginning with 'May the Blessed One not be cold' explains the reason for his acting in that way. For he stood there, having acted thus with the thought: “May cold not afflict the Blessed One, nor heat, nor the touch of gadflies and the like.”

Tattha kiñcāpi sattāhavaddalikāya uṇhameva natthi, sace pana antarantarā megho vigaccheyya, uṇhaṃ bhaveyya, tampi mā bādhayitthāti evaṃ tassa cintetuṃ yuttaṃ. Keci panettha vadanti “uṇhaggahaṇaṃ bhogaparikkhepassa vipulabhāvakaraṇe kāraṇakittanaṃ. Khuddake hi tasmiṃ bhagavantaṃ nāgassa sarīrasambhūtā usmā bādheyya, vipulabhāvakaraṇena pana tādisaṃ ‘mā uṇhaṃ bādhayitthā’ti tathā karitvā aṭṭhāsī”ti.

In this regard, although there is no heat at all during the seven-day great rain, it was fitting for him to think that if the clouds were to disperse intermittently, heat would arise, and 'May that too not afflict him.' Some, however, say in this matter: 'The inclusion of "heat" serves to state the reason for making the coil-enclosure vast. For if it were made small, the heat generated from the nāga’s body would afflict the Blessed One in that confined space; but by making it vast, he stood there having acted thus with the thought, "May such heat not afflict him."'

Viddhanti ubbiddhaṃ, meghavigamena dūrībhūtanti attho. Vigatavalāhakanti apagatameghaṃ. Devanti ākāsaṃ. Viditvāti “idāni vigatavalāhako ākāso, natthi bhagavato sītādiupaddavo”ti ñatvā. Viniveṭhetvāti apanetvā. Sakavaṇṇanti attano nāgarūpaṃ. Paṭisaṃharitvāti antaradhāpetvā. Māṇavakavaṇṇanti kumārakarūpaṃ.

'Viddhaṃ' means cleared; the meaning is 'made distant by the departure of the clouds.' 'Vigatavalāhakaṃ' means 'devoid of clouds.' 'Devaṃ' means 'the sky.' 'Viditvā' means having known thus: 'Now the sky is devoid of clouds; there is no danger of cold and so on for the Blessed One.' 'Viniveṭhetvā' means 'having unwound.' 'Sakavaṇṇaṃ' means 'his own nāga form.' 'Paṭisaṃharitvā' means 'having made it disappear.' 'Māṇavakavaṇṇaṃ' means 'the form of a youth.'

Etamatthanti vivekasukhappaṭisaṃvedino yattha katthaci sukhameva hotīti etamatthaṃ sabbākārena jānitvā. Imaṃ udānanti imaṃ vivekasukhānubhāvadīpakaṃ udānaṃ udānesi.

'Etamatthaṃ' means having known this meaning in all its aspects: for one who experiences the bliss of seclusion, there is only happiness anywhere whatsoever. 'Imaṃ udānaṃ' means he uttered this inspired utterance, which illuminates the power of the bliss of seclusion.

Tattha sukho vivekoti nibbānasaṅkhāto upadhiviveko sukho. Tuṭṭhassāti catumaggañāṇasantosena tuṭṭhassa. Sutadhammassāti pakāsitadhammassa vissutadhammassa. Passatoti taṃ vivekaṃ, yaṃ vā kiñci passitabbaṃ nāma, taṃ sabbaṃ [P 0.0102] attano vīriyabalādhigatena ñāṇacakkhunā passantassa. Abyāpajjanti akuppanabhāvo, etena mettāpubbabhāgo dassito. Pāṇabhūtesu saṃyamoti sattesu ca saṃyamo avihiṃsanabhāvo sukhoti attho. Etena karuṇāpubbabhāgo dassito.

Therein, 'sukho viveko' means: the seclusion from substrates, known as Nibbāna, is happiness. 'Tuṭṭhassa' means: for one who is content through the contentment of the knowledge of the four paths. 'Sutadhammassa' means: for one who has heard the Dhamma, that is, one for whom the Dhamma has been made manifest. 'Passato' means: for one who sees that seclusion—or whatever is to be seen—seeing all of it with the eye of wisdom acquired through the power of one's own effort. 'Abyāpajjaṃ' is the state of non-agitation; by this, the preliminary part of loving-kindness is shown. 'Pāṇabhūtesu saṃyamo' means: restraint towards living beings, the state of non-harming, is happiness; this is the meaning. By this, the preliminary part of compassion is shown.

Sukhā virāgatā loketi vigatarāgatāpi loke sukhā. Kīdisī? Kāmānaṃ samatikkamoti, yā kāmānaṃ samatikkamoti vuccati, sā vigatarāgatāpi sukhāti attho, etena anāgāmimaggo kathito. Asmimānassa yo vinayoti iminā pana arahattaṃ kathitaṃ. Arahattañhi asmimānassa paṭippassaddhivinayoti vuccati, ito parañca sukhaṃ nāma natthi, tenāha “etaṃ ve paramaṃ sukha”nti. Evaṃ arahattena desanāya kūṭaṃ gaṇhīti.

'Sukhā virāgatā loke' means: being without lust in the world is happiness. What kind of being without lust? That which is called 'kāmānaṃ samatikkamo,' 'the overcoming of sensual pleasures'—that very state of being without lust is happiness; this is the meaning. By this, the path of the non-returner is stated. By the phrase 'asmimānassa vinayo,' however, Arahantship is stated. Indeed, Arahantship is called the calming and removal of the conceit 'I am.' And beyond this, there is no happiness whatsoever; therefore, He said, 'etaṃ ve paramaṃ sukhaṃ,' 'This truly is the supreme happiness.' Thus, with Arahantship, He brought the discourse to its pinnacle.

Paṭhamasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the first sutta is concluded.

2. Rājasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Rājasutta

12. Dutiye [V 0.0081][M 0.0091] sambahulānanti vinayapariyāyena tayo janā “sambahulā”ti vuccanti, tato paraṃ saṅgho. Suttantapariyāyena pana tayo tayo eva, tato uddhaṃ sambahulā. Tasmā idhāpi suttantapariyāyena sambahulāti veditabbā. Upaṭṭhānasālāyanti dhammasabhāmaṇḍape. Sā hi dhammaṃ desetuṃ āgatassa tathāgatassa bhikkhūnaṃ upaṭṭhānakaraṇaṭṭhānanti “upaṭṭhānasālā”ti vuccati. Atha vā yattha bhikkhū vinayaṃ vinicchinanti, dhammaṃ kathenti, sākacchaṃ samāpajjanti, sannipatanavasena pakatiyā upatiṭṭhanti, sā sālāpi maṇḍapopi “upaṭṭhānasālā”tveva vuccati. Tatthāpi hi buddhāsanaṃ niccaṃ paññattameva hoti. Idañhi buddhānaṃ dharamānakāle [P 0.0103] bhikkhūnaṃ cārittaṃ. Sannisinnānanti nisajjanavasena saṅgamma nisinnānaṃ. Sannipatitānanti tato tato āgantvā sannipatanavasena sannipatitānaṃ. Atha vā buddhāsanaṃ purato katvā satthu sammukhe viya ādaruppattiyā sakkaccaṃ nisīdanavasena sannisinnānaṃ, samānajjhāsayattā aññamaññasmiṃ ajjhāsayena suṭṭhu sammā ca nipatanavasena sannipatitānaṃ. Ayanti idāni vuccamānaṃ niddisati. Antarākathāti kammaṭṭhānamanasikārauddesaparipucchādīnaṃ antarā aññā ekā kathā, atha vā majjhanhike laddhassa sugatovādassa, sāyaṃ labhitabbassa dhammassavanassa ca antarā pavattattā antarākathā, samaṇasamācārasseva vā antarā pavattā aññā ekā kathāti antarākathā. Udapādīti uppannā.

12. In the second sutta, 'many' (sambahulā) refers to three persons according to the Vinaya method; beyond that is the Saṅgha. According to the Suttanta method, however, three are just three, and beyond that is 'many'. Therefore, here too, 'many' should be understood according to the Suttanta method. 'In the assembly hall' (upaṭṭhānasālāyaṃ) means in the Dhamma assembly pavilion. For it is called the 'assembly hall' because it is the place where monks attend upon the Tathāgata when he comes to teach the Dhamma. Alternatively, wherever monks decide upon the Vinaya, speak on the Dhamma, engage in discussion, or naturally gather for attendance, that hall or pavilion is called the 'assembly hall'. There, the Buddha’s seat is always prepared. This, indeed, is the custom of monks during the time when the Buddhas are present. 'Of those seated together' (sannisinnānaṃ) means of those who have gathered and are seated. 'Of those assembled' (sannipatitānaṃ) means of those who have come from various places and gathered in an assembly. Alternatively, 'of those seated together' means of those sitting respectfully as if in the presence of the Teacher, with the Buddha’s seat placed before them, due to the arising of reverence; and 'of those assembled' means of those who, because of their shared intentions, are well and properly gathered with mutual goodwill. 'This' (ayaṃ) indicates what is now being said. 'Incidental talk' (antarākathā) means another, single conversation in between matters such as the cultivation of a meditation subject, recitation, and inquiry. Alternatively, it is 'incidental talk' because it occurs between the instruction from the Sugata received at midday and the hearing of the Dhamma to be received in the evening; or it is another, single conversation that occurs in between the proper conduct of an ascetic, thus it is 'incidental talk'. 'Arose' (udapādi) means it arose (uppannā).

Imesaṃ dvinnaṃ rājūnanti niddhāraṇe sāmivacanaṃ. Mahaddhanataro vātiādīsu pathaviyaṃ nikhaṇitvā ṭhapitaṃ sattaratananicayasaṅkhātaṃ mahantaṃ dhanaṃ etassāti mahaddhano, dvīsu ayaṃ atisayena mahaddhanoti mahaddhanataro. Vāsaddo vikappattho. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Ayaṃ pana viseso – niccaparibbayavasena mahanto bhogo etassāti mahābhogo. Devasikaṃ pavisanaāyabhūto mahanto koso etassāti mahākoso. Apare pana “devasikaṃ pavisanaāyabhūtaṃ maṇisārapheggugumbādibhedabhinnaṃ pariggahavatthu dhanaṃ, tadeva sāragabbhādīsu nihitaṃ koso”ti vadanti. Vajiro, mahānīlo, indanīlo, marakato, veḷuriyo, padumarāgo, phussarāgo, kakketano, pulāko, vimalo, lohitaṅko[M 0.0092], phaliko, pavāḷo, jotiraso, gomuttako, gomedako, sogandhiko, muttā, saṅkho, añjanamūlo, rājapaṭṭo, amataṃsako, piyako, brāhmaṇī cāti catubbīsati maṇi nāma. Satta [P 0.0104] lohāni kahāpaṇo ca sāro nāma. Sayanacchādanapāvuraṇagajadantasilādīni pheggu nāma. Candanāgarukuṅkumatagarakappūrādi gumbā nāma. Tattha purimena ādisaddena sālivīhiādimuggamāsādipubbaṇṇāparaṇṇabhedaṃ dhaññavikatiṃ ādiṃ [V 0.0082] katvā yaṃ sattānaṃ upabhogaparibhogabhūtaṃ vatthu, taṃ sabbaṃ saṅgayhati. Mahantaṃ vijitaṃ raṭṭhaṃ etassāti mahāvijito. Mahanto hatthiassādivāhano etassāti mahāvāhano. Mahantaṃ senābalañceva thāmabalañca etassāti mahabbalo. Icchitanibbattisaṅkhātā puññakammanipphannā mahatī iddhi etassāti mahiddhiko. Tejasaṅkhāto ussāhamantapabhusattisaṅkhāto vā mahanto ānubhāvo etassāti mahānubhāvo.

'Of these two kings' (imesaṃ dvinnaṃ rājūnaṃ) is a genitive expression used for specification. In phrases such as 'or wealthier' (mahaddhanataro vā), 'one with great wealth' (mahaddhano) means one who has great wealth, described as an accumulation of the seven kinds of gems, buried and stored in the earth; 'wealthier' (mahaddhanataro) means one who is exceedingly wealthy between the two. The word 'vā' is used in the sense of an option. This same method applies to the remaining phrases. This, however, is the specific meaning: 'one with great possessions' (mahābhogo) means one who has great possessions for constant use. 'One with a great treasury' (mahākoso) means one who has a great treasury that is a source of daily incoming revenue. Others, however, say: 'Wealth is property for daily use, comprising various kinds such as gems, core valuables, non-essentials, and aromatics; and that same wealth, deposited in strongrooms and so on, is the treasury.' The twenty-four kinds of gems are: diamond, great sapphire, indra-sapphire, emerald, beryl, ruby, topaz, cat’s-eye, pulāka, vimala, red quartz, crystal, coral, jotirasa, gomuttaka, gomedaka, sogandhika, pearl, conch, añjanamūla, rājapaṭṭa, amataṃsaka, piyaka, and brāhmaṇī. The seven metals and coins are called 'core valuables' (sāra). Beds, coverings, cloaks, ivory, stone, and so on are called 'non-essentials' (pheggu). Sandalwood, aloe wood, saffron, tagara, camphor, and so on are called 'aromatics' (gumbā). Here, by the first 'etc.' (ādisaddena), all objects used for the enjoyment and consumption of beings are included, starting with various kinds of grains such as different types of early and late crops like sāli-rice, vīhi-rice, mung beans, and other beans. 'One with a great conquered territory' (mahāvijito) means one who has a vast conquered kingdom. 'One with great transport' (mahāvāhano) means one who has many vehicles such as elephants and horses. 'One with great strength' (mahabbalo) means one who has both a great army and great physical strength. 'One with great psychic power' (mahiddhiko) means one who has great psychic power, produced by meritorious deeds, which is described as the fulfillment of wishes. 'One with great influence' (mahānubhāvo) means one who has great influence, described as majesty, or as great power consisting of energy, counsel, lordship, and ability.

Ettha ca paṭhamena āyasampadā, dutiyena vittūpakaraṇasampadā, tatiyena vibhavasampadā, catutthena janapadasampadā, pañcamena yānasampadā, chaṭṭhena parivārasampadāya saddhiṃ attasampadā, sattamena puññakammasampadā, aṭṭhamena pabhāvasampadā tesaṃ rājūnaṃ pakāsitā hoti. Tena yā sā sāmisampatti, amaccasampatti, senāsampatti, raṭṭhasampatti, vibhavasampatti, mittasampatti, duggasampattīti satta pakatisampadā rājūnaṃ icchitabbā. Tā sabbā yathārahaṃ paridīpitāti veditabbā.

Herein, for those kings, the attainment of income (āyasampadā) is shown by the first term; the attainment of wealth and equipment (vittūpakaraṇasampadā) by the second; the attainment of opulence (vibhavasampadā) by the third; the attainment of a territory (janapadasampadā) by the fourth; the attainment of vehicles (yānasampadā) by the fifth; the attainment of self-accomplishment (attasampadā) together with the attainment of a retinue (parivārasampadā) by the sixth; the attainment of merit from past deeds (puññakammasampadā) by the seventh; and the attainment of power (pabhāvasampadā) by the eighth. By this, those seven natural endowments desirable for kings—namely, the endowment of the sovereign (sāmisampatti), the endowment of ministers (amaccasampatti), the endowment of an army (senāsampatti), the endowment of a country (raṭṭhasampatti), the endowment of wealth (vibhavasampatti), the endowment of friends (mittasampatti), and the endowment of fortifications (duggasampatti)—all these should be understood as having been explained as is appropriate.

Dānādīhi catūhi saṅgahavatthūhi parisaṃ rañjetīti rājā. Magadhānaṃ issaroti māgadho. Mahatiyā senāya samannāgatattā seniyagottattā vā seniyo. Bimbi vuccati suvaṇṇaṃ, tasmā sārabimbivaṇṇatāya bimbisāro. Keci pana “nāmamevetaṃ tassa rañño”ti vadanti. Paccāmittaṃ parasenaṃ jinātīti pasenadi. Kosalaraṭṭhassa adhipatīti kosalo. Ayañcarahīti ettha carahīti nipātamattaṃ. Vippakatāti apariyositā. Ayaṃ tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ antarākathā aniṭṭhitāti [P 0.0105] attho.

He gladdens (rañjeti) the assembly with the four bases of sympathy, such as giving, thus he is a king (rājā). He is the lord (issaro) of the Magadhans, thus he is Māgadha. He is called Seniya either because he is endowed with a great army (mahāsenā) or because he is of the Seniya clan (seniyagotta). Gold (suvaṇṇa) is called 'bimbi'; therefore, because his complexion is the color of pure gold, he is Bimbisāra. Some, however, say, 'This is merely the name of that king.' He conquers (jināti) the opposing enemy army (parasenaṃ), thus he is Pasenadi. He is the ruler (adhipati) of the Kosala kingdom, thus he is Kosala. In the phrase 'ayañcarahi', 'carahi' is merely a particle. 'Unfinished' (vippakatā) means not concluded (apariyositā). The meaning is that this incidental talk of those monks was not completed (aniṭṭhitā).

Sāyanhasamayanti sāyanhe ekaṃ samayaṃ. Paṭisallānā vuṭṭhitoti tato tato rūpādiārammaṇato cittassa paṭisaṃharaṇato paṭisallānasaṅkhātāya [M 0.0093] phalasamāpattito yathākālaparicchedaṃ vuṭṭhito. Bhagavā hi pubbaṇhasamayaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaparivuto sāvatthiṃ pavisitvā bhikkhūnaṃ sulabhapiṇḍapātaṃ katvā katabhattakicco bhikkhūhi saddhiṃ sāvatthito nikkhamitvā vihāraṃ pavisitvā gandhakuṭippamukhe ṭhatvā vattaṃ dassetvā ṭhitānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ yathāsamuṭṭhitaṃ sugatovādaṃ datvā tesu araññarukkhamūlādidivāṭṭhānaṃ uddissa gatesu gandhakuṭiṃ pavisitvā phalasamāpattisukhena divasabhāgaṃ vītināmetvā yathākālaparicchede samāpattito vuṭṭhāya, “mayhaṃ upagamanaṃ āgamayamānā catasso parisā sakalavihāraṃ paripūrentiyo nisinnā, idāni me dhammadesanatthaṃ dhammasabhāmaṇḍalaṃ upagantuṃ kālo”ti āsanato vuṭṭhāya, kesarasīho viya kañcanaguhāya surabhigandhakuṭito nikkhamitvā yūthaṃ upasaṅkamanto mattavaravāraṇo viya akāyacāpallena [V 0.0083] cāruvikkantagamano asītianubyañjanappaṭimaṇḍitabāttiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇasamujjalāya byāmappabhāya parikkhepavilāsasampannāya pabhassaraketumālālaṅkatāya nīlapītalohitodātamañjiṭṭhapabhassarānaṃ vasena chabbaṇṇabuddharaṃsiyo vissajjentiyā acinteyyānubhāvāya anupamāya buddhalīlāya samannāgatāya rūpakāyasampattiyā sakalavihāraṃ ekālokaṃ kurumāno upaṭṭhānasālaṃ upasaṅkami. Tena vuttaṃ – “atha kho bhagavā…pe… tenupasaṅkamī”ti.

'Evening time' (sāyanhasamayaṃ) means at evening time. 'Having risen from seclusion' (paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito)—that is, having risen at the appropriate time from the attainment of fruition, which is called 'seclusion' (paṭisallāna) because it is a withdrawing of the mind from objects such as forms and so on. For in the morning the Blessed One, surrounded by the Saṅgha of monks, entered Sāvatthī, made almsfood easily available to the monks, finished his meal duties, and left Sāvatthī with the monks. Entering the monastery, he stood before the Fragrant Cottage, gave the monks who were standing there the customary instruction, and having given the Sugata’s advice to them according to what had arisen, when they had gone to their daytime resting places—such as the roots of trees in the forest—he entered the Fragrant Cottage and spent the day in the bliss of fruition attainment. Emerging at the appropriate time, he thought, 'The four assemblies, awaiting my arrival, are seated, filling the entire monastery. Now is the time for me to go to the Dhamma hall for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma.' Rising from his seat, like a maned lion from a golden cave, he emerged from the fragrant cottage. Approaching the assembly like a majestic elephant, with a graceful gait free of bodily restlessness, he made the entire monastery a single light and approached the attendance hall by means of the perfection of his physical form, which was radiant with the thirty-two major marks of a great man adorned with the eighty minor characteristics, endowed with the splendor of a surrounding fathom-wide radiance, decorated with a brilliant flame-like aureole, possessed of unthinkable power and incomparable grace, and emitting the six-colored Buddha rays: blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, and brilliant. Thus it is said: 'Then the Blessed One... approached.'

Evaṃ upasaṅkamitvā vattaṃ dassetvā nisinne te bhikkhū tuṇhībhūte disvā “mayi akathente ime bhikkhū buddhagāravena kappampi na kathessantī”ti kathāsamuṭṭhāpanatthaṃ “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave”tiādimāha. Tattha kāya nutthāti katamāya nu bhavatha. “Kāya notthā”tipi pāḷi, so evattho, “kāya nvetthā”tipi paṭhanti, tassa katamāya nu etthāti attho. Tatrāyaṃ saṅkhepattho – bhikkhave, katamāya [P 0.0106] nāma kathāya idha sannisinnā bhavatha, katamā ca tumhākaṃ kathā mamāgamanapaccayā aniṭṭhitā, taṃ niṭṭhāpessāmīti evaṃ sabbaññupavāraṇāya pavāresi.

Having thus approached and explained the observances, seeing those monks sitting silently, he thought, 'If I do not speak, these monks, out of reverence for the Buddha, will not speak even for an eon.' To initiate conversation, he said, 'For what now, monks...?' and so on. Here, 'For what now?' (kāya nuttha) means, 'For what are you assembled?' 'Kāya notthā' is also a reading, with the same meaning. Others read it as 'kāya nvetthā', meaning 'For what are you here?' The concise meaning here is: 'Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here? And what conversation of yours was unfinished on account of my arrival? I will conclude it.' Thus, he invited them with the invitation of the Omniscient One.

Na khvetanti na kho etaṃ, ayameva vā pāṭho. “Na khota”ntipi paṭhanti, na kho etaṃ icceva padavibhāgo. Kulaputtānanti jātiācārakulaputtānaṃ. Saddhāti saddhāya, kammaphalasaddhāya ratanattayasaddhāya ca. Agārasmāti gharato, gahaṭṭhabhāvāti attho. Anagāriyanti pabbajjaṃ. Pabbajitānanti upagatānaṃ[M 0.0094]. Yanti kiriyāparāmasanaṃ. Tatthāyaṃ padayojanā – “bhikkhave, tumhe neva rājābhinītā na corābhinītā na iṇaṭṭā na jīvitapakatā pabbajitā, atha kho saddhāya agārato nikkhamitvā mama sāsane pabbajitā, tumhe etarahi evarūpiṃ rājappaṭisaṃyuttaṃ tiracchānakathaṃ katheyyātha, yaṃ evarūpāya kathāya kathanaṃ, etaṃ tumhākaṃ na kho patirūpaṃ na yuttamevā”ti.

‘Na khvetaṃ’ is ‘na kho etaṃ’; or this itself is the reading. Some also read ‘na khotaṃ’; the word division is simply ‘na kho etaṃ.’ ‘Kulaputtānaṃ’ (of sons of good families) means of sons of good families by birth and conduct. ‘Saddhā’ stands for `saddhāya` (by faith): by faith in kamma and its fruit, and by faith in the Triple Gem. ‘Agārasmā’ (from home) means from the house, that is, from the state of a householder. ‘Anagāriyaṃ’ (homelessness) means the going forth (pabbajjā). ‘Pabbajitānaṃ’ (of those who have gone forth) means of those who have undertaken it. ‘Yaṃ’ (which) is a reference to the action. Here is the sentence construction: ‘Bhikkhus, you have gone forth neither because you were hounded by kings, nor hounded by thieves, nor due to debt, nor for a livelihood; rather, out of faith, having left the home life, you went forth into my dispensation. Would you now engage in such animalistic talk connected with kings? Such talk, the speaking of such, is surely not proper for you, not fitting at all.’

Evaṃ sannipatitānaṃ pabbajitānaṃ appatirūpaṃ paṭikkhipitvā idāni nesaṃ patirūpaṃ paṭipattiṃ anujānanto “sannipatitānaṃ vo, bhikkhave, dvayaṃ karaṇīyaṃ dhammī vā kathā ariyo vā tuṇhībhāvo”ti āha. Tattha voti tumhākaṃ. Karaṇīyanti hi padaṃ apekkhitvā kattari sāmivacanametaṃ, tasmā tumhehīti attho. Dvayaṃ karaṇīyanti dve kātabbā. Dhammī kathāti catusaccadhammato anapetā kathā, pavattinivattiparidīpinī dhammadesanāti attho. Dasakathāvatthusaṅkhātāpi hi dhammakathā tadekadesā evāti. Ariyoti ekantahitāvahattā ariyo, visuddho uttamoti vā ariyo. Tuṇhībhāvoti samathavipassanābhāvanābhūtaṃ akathanaṃ. Keci pana “vacīsaṅkhārapaṭipakkhabhāvato dutiyajjhānaṃ ariyo tuṇhībhāvo”ti vadanti. Apare “catutthajjhānaṃ [V 0.0084] ariyo tuṇhībhāvo”ti [P 0.0107] vadanti. Ayaṃ panettha attho – “bhikkhave, cittavivekassa paribrūhanatthaṃ vivekaṭṭhakāyā suññāgāre viharantā sace kadāci sannipatatha, evaṃ sannipatitehi tumhehi ‘assutaṃ sāveti sutaṃ vā pariyodapetī’ti vuttanayena aññamaññassūpakārāya khandhādīnaṃ aniccatādipaṭisaṃyuttā dhammakathā vā pavattetabbā, aññamaññaṃ abyābādhanatthaṃ jhānasamāpattiyā vā viharitabba”nti.

Thus, after rejecting what was improper for the assembled monastics, the Blessed One now authorized for them a proper practice, saying: "Monks, when you have gathered, two things are to be done by you: either a Dhamma talk or noble silence." Here, 'vo' means 'by you'. The word 'karaṇīyaṃ' is a gerundive, and when construed with 'vo', it means 'to be done by you'. 'Dvayaṃ karaṇīyaṃ' means 'two things are to be done'. 'Dhammī kathā' refers to a discussion not deviating from the Four Noble Truths—that is, a teaching of Dhamma that clarifies what leads to continuation in saṃsāra and what leads to its cessation. For even the Dhamma talk comprised of the ten topics of conversation is just a part of those very truths. 'Ariyo' means 'noble' because it leads entirely to welfare, or because it is pure and supreme. 'Tuṇhībhāvo' means refraining from speech, which is the cultivation of serenity and insight. Some, however, say that 'noble silence' refers to the second jhāna, as it counteracts verbal formations. Others say it refers to the fourth jhāna. But the meaning here is this: 'Monks, for the sake of developing mental seclusion, when you dwell in empty dwellings dedicated to seclusion, if you occasionally gather, then having gathered, you should either engage in Dhamma discussion—as stated, 'it makes the unheard heard or clarifies what has been heard'—for mutual benefit, connected to the impermanence of the aggregates, etc., or you should dwell in jhāna attainment for the sake of not disturbing one another.'

Tattha purimena karaṇīyavacanena anotiṇṇānaṃ sāsane otaraṇūpāyaṃ dasseti, pacchimena otiṇṇānaṃ saṃsārato nissaraṇūpāyaṃ. Purimena vā āgamaveyyattiye niyojeti, pacchimena adhigamaveyyattiye. Atha vā purimena sammādiṭṭhiyā paṭhamaṃ uppattihetuṃ dīpeti, dutiyena dutiyaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ –

There, by the first statement regarding what should be done, he shows the means of entering the Dispensation for those who have not yet entered, while by the latter, he shows the means of escape from the round of existence for those who have entered. Or, the first enjoins one to proficiency in scriptural knowledge, the latter to proficiency in realization. Furthermore, the first reveals the primary cause for the arising of right view, and the second, the secondary cause. For it was said:

“Dveme, bhikkhave, hetū dve paccayā sammādiṭṭhiyā uppādāya parato ca ghoso, paccattañca yoniso manasikāro”ti (a. ni. 2.127).

‘Monks, there are these two causes, these two conditions for the arising of right view: the voice of another, and appropriate attention within oneself.’

Purimena [M 0.0095] vā lokiyasammādiṭṭhiyā mūlakāraṇaṃ vibhāveti, pacchimena lokuttarasammādiṭṭhiyā mūlakāraṇanti evamādinā ettha yojanā veditabbā.

Alternatively, by the former, he makes clear the root cause of mundane right view; by the latter, the root cause of supramundane right view. In this way and so forth, the application of meaning here should be understood.

Etamatthaṃ viditvāti tehi bhikkhūhi kittitakāmasampattito jhānādisampatti santatarā ceva paṇītatarā cāti etamatthaṃ sabbākārato viditvā. Imaṃ udānanti imaṃ ariyavihārasukhānubhāvadīpakaṃ udānaṃ udānesi.

‘Having understood this meaning’ means having understood in every way that the attainments of jhāna and the like are more peaceful and more sublime than the accomplishment in sensual pleasures praised by those monks. ‘This inspired utterance’ means he uttered this inspired utterance, which illuminates the power of the bliss of the noble abiding.

Tattha yañca kāmasukhaṃ loketi lokasaddo “khandhaloko āyatanaloko dhātuloko”tiādīsu (mahāni. 3, 7; cūḷani. ajitamāṇavapucchāniddesa 2) saṅkhāresu āgato.

Therein, regarding ‘whatever sensual pleasure in the world,’ the word ‘world’ appears in such contexts as ‘the world of aggregates, the world of sense bases, the world of elements,’ etc., with reference to conditioned phenomena.

“Yāvatā candimasūriyā pariharanti,

Disā bhanti virocanā;

Tāva sahassadhā loko,

Ettha te vattatī vaso”ti. –

‘As far as the moon and sun revolve, illuminating the directions, shining brightly, so far extends the thousandfold world; therein your power prevails.’

Ādīsu (ma. ni. 1.503) okāse āgato. “Addasā kho bhagavā buddhacakkhunā lokaṃ volokento”tiādīsu [V 0.0085] (mahāva. 9; ma. ni. 1.283) sattesu. Idha pana [P 0.0108] sattaloke okāsaloke ca veditabbo. Tasmā avīcito paṭṭhāya upari brahmalokato heṭṭhā etasmiṃ loke yaṃ vatthukāme paṭicca kilesakāmavasena uppajjanato kāmasahagataṃ sukhaṃ. Yañcidaṃ diviyaṃ sukhanti yañca idaṃ divi bhavaṃ dibbavihāravasena ca laddhabbaṃ brahmānaṃ manussānañca rūpasamāpattisukhaṃ. Taṇhakkhayasukhassāti yaṃ āgamma taṇhā khīyati, taṃ nibbānaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā taṇhāya ca paṭipassambhanavasena pavattaphalasamāpattisukhaṃ taṇhakkhayasukhaṃ nāma, tassa taṇhakkhayasukhassa. Eteti liṅgavipallāsena niddeso, etāni sukhānīti attho. Keci ubhayampi sukhasāmaññena gahetvā “eta”nti paṭhanti, tesaṃ “kalaṃ nāgghatī”ti pāṭhena bhavitabbaṃ.

In these and other passages, it refers to space. In such contexts as ‘Indeed, the Blessed One, surveying the world with the Buddha-eye, saw…,’ it refers to beings. Here, however, it should be understood as referring to the world of beings and the world of space. Therefore, in this world, from Avīci upwards and below the Brahma-world, there is the happiness associated with sensuality, which arises dependent on the objects of sensual pleasure, by way of the defilements of sensual pleasure. ‘And this which is divine happiness’ refers to the happiness of the attainment of form for brahmās and humans, which is to be obtained by way of divine abidings, being happiness that occurs in the divine realm. ‘Of the happiness of the destruction of craving’: the happiness of the attainment of fruition that proceeds by way of the calming of craving, taking as its object that Nibbāna on account of which craving is destroyed, is called ‘the happiness of the destruction of craving’. Of that happiness of the destruction of craving. ‘Ete’ is a designation by reversal of gender; the meaning is ‘these happinesses’. Some, taking both under the general term of happiness, read ‘etaṃ’; for them, the reading should be ‘kalaṃ nāgghati’.

Soḷasinti soḷasannaṃ pūraṇiṃ. Ayañhettha saṅkhepattho – cakkavattisukhaṃ ādiṃ katvā sabbasmiṃ manussaloke manussasukhaṃ, nāgasupaṇṇādiloke nāgādīhi anubhavitabbaṃ sukhaṃ, cātumahārājikādidevaloke chabbidhaṃ kāmasukhanti yaṃ ekādasavidhe kāmaloke uppajjantaṃ kāmasukhaṃ, yañca idaṃ rūpārūpadevesu dibbavihārabhūtesu rūpārūpajjhānesu ca uppannattā “diviya”nti [M 0.0096] laddhanāmaṃ lokiyajjhānasukhaṃ, sakalampi tadubhayaṃ taṇhakkhayasukhasaṅkhātaṃ phalasamāpattisukhaṃ soḷasa bhāge katvā tato ekabhāgaṃ soḷasabhāgaguṇe laddhaṃ ekabhāgasaṅkhātaṃ kalaṃ na agghatīti.

‘Sixteenth’ means the sixteenth part. Here is the summary meaning: human happiness in the entire human world, beginning with the happiness of a wheel-turning monarch; the happiness experienced by nāgas, supaṇṇas, and others in their respective worlds; the six kinds of sensual pleasures in the Cātumahārājika and other deva worlds—that is, the sensual pleasure arising in the eleven kinds of sense-sphere worlds; and that worldly jhāna happiness, which, having arisen in the form and formless divine abodes and in the form and formless jhānas, has obtained the name ‘divine’—all of that combined is not worth a sixteenth part of the happiness of the attainment of fruition, which is known as the happiness of the destruction of craving; that is, not even one part out of sixteen parts.

Ayañca atthavaṇṇanā phalasamāpattisāmaññena vuttā. Pāḷiyaṃ avisesena taṇhakkhayassa āgatattā paṭhamaphalasamāpattisukhassāpi kalaṃ lokiyaṃ na agghati eva. Tathā hi vuttaṃ –

This explanation of the meaning is given in terms of the attainment of fruition in general. Since in the Pāli the destruction of craving is mentioned without specification, worldly happiness is not worth even a fraction of the happiness of the first attainment of fruition. For so it has been said:

“Pathabyā ekarajjena, saggassa gamanena vā;

Sabbalokādhipaccena, sotāpattiphalaṃ vara”nti. (dha. pa. 178);

‘Better than sole sovereignty over the earth, or going to heaven, or lordship over all the worlds, is the fruit of stream-entry.’

Sotāpattisaṃyuttepi vuttaṃ –

In the Connected Discourses on Stream-Entry it is also said:

“Kiñcāpi, bhikkhave, rājā cakkavattī catunnaṃ dīpānaṃ issariyādhipaccaṃ rajjaṃ kāretvā kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjati devānaṃ tāvatiṃsānaṃ sahabyataṃ, so tattha nandane vane accharāsaṅghaparivuto dibbehi ca pañcahi kāmaguṇehi samappito samaṅgībhūto paricāreti, so catūhi dhammehi asamannāgato. Atha kho so aparimuttova [V 0.0086] nirayā, aparimutto [P 0.0109] tiracchānayoniyā, aparimutto pettivisayā, aparimutto apāyaduggativinipātā. Kiñcāpi, bhikkhave, ariyasāvako piṇḍiyālopena yāpeti, nantakāni ca dhāreti, so catūhi dhammehi samannāgato, atha kho so parimutto nirayā, parimutto tiracchānayoniyā, parimutto pettivisayā, parimutto apāyaduggativinipātā.

‘Even though, monks, a wheel-turning king, after ruling and exercising sovereignty and lordship over the four continents, with the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world, in companionship with the Tāvatiṃsa gods, and there, in the Nandana Grove, surrounded by a host of nymphs, enjoys himself, furnished and endowed with the five divine strands of sensual pleasure, he is not endowed with four qualities. He is therefore not freed from hell, not freed from the animal realm, not freed from the realm of ghosts, not freed from the planes of misery, bad destinations, and downfall. But though, monks, a noble disciple lives on almsfood and wears rag-robes, he is endowed with four qualities. He is therefore freed from hell, freed from the animal realm, freed from the realm of ghosts, freed from the planes of misery, bad destinations, and downfall.’

“Katamehi catūhi? Idha, bhikkhave, ariyasāvako buddhe aveccappasādena samannāgato hoti ‘itipi so bhagavā arahaṃ…pe... buddho bhagavā’ti. Dhamme aveccappasādena…pe… viññūhī’ti. Saṅghe aveccappasādena…pe… puññakkhettaṃ lokassā’ti. Ariyakantehi sīlehi samannāgato hoti akhaṇḍehi…pe… samādhisaṃvattanikehi. Imehi catūhi dhammehi samannāgato hoti. Yo ca, bhikkhave, catunnaṃ dīpānaṃ paṭilābho, yo catunnaṃ [M 0.0097] dhammānaṃ paṭilābho, catunnaṃ dīpānaṃ paṭilābho catunnaṃ dhammānaṃ paṭilābhassa kalaṃ nāgghati soḷasi”nti (saṃ. ni. 5.997).

‘By what four? Here, monks, a noble disciple possesses unwavering faith in the Buddha: “Indeed, the Blessed One is an Arahant… the Buddha, the Blessed One.” He possesses unwavering faith in the Dhamma… to be experienced by the wise.” He possesses unwavering faith in the Sangha… the unsurpassed field of merit for the world.” He possesses virtues dear to the noble ones, unbroken… conducive to concentration. He is endowed with these four qualities. And, monks, the gain of the four continents is not worth a sixteenth part of the gain of these four qualities.’

Evaṃ bhagavā sabbattha lokiyasukhaṃ sauttaraṃ sātisayaṃ, lokuttarasukhameva anuttaranti atisayanti bhājesīti.

Thus the Blessed One everywhere analyzed worldly happiness as being with a superior and surpassable, and supramundane happiness alone as being unsurpassed and supreme.

Dutiyasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the second discourse is concluded.

3. Daṇḍasuttavaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Daṇḍa Sutta

13. Tatiye kumārakāti dārakā. Antarā ca sāvatthiṃ antarā ca jetavananti antarāsaddo “tadantaraṃ ko jāneyya, aññatra tathāgatā”ti (a. ni. 6.44; 10.75), “janā saṅgamma mantenti, mañca tvañca kimantara”ntiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 1.228) kāraṇe āgato. “Addasā maṃ, bhante, aññatarā itthī vijjantarikāya bhājanaṃ dhovantī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 2.149) khaṇe. “Yassantarato na santi kopā”tiādīsu (udā. 20) citte. “Antarā vosānamāpādī”tiādīsu [P 0.0110] vemajjhe. “Apicāyaṃ, bhikkhave, tapodā dvinnaṃ mahānirayānaṃ antarikāya āgacchatī”tiādīsu (pārā. 231) vivare[V 0.0087]. Svāyamidhāpi vivare veditabbo. Tasmā sāvatthiyā ca jetavanassa ca vivareti, evamettha attho veditabbo. Antarāsaddayogato cettha upayogavacanaṃ “antarā ca sāvatthiṃ antarā ca jetavana”nti. Īdisesu ṭhānesu akkharacintakā “antarā gāmañca nadiñca gacchatī”ti ekameva antarāsaddaṃ payujjanti, so dutiyapadenapi yojetabbo hoti. Idha pana yojetvā vutto.

13. In the third sutta, `kumārakā` means young boys. In the phrase `antarā ca sāvatthiṃ antarā ca jetavanaṃ` (between Sāvatthī and Jetavana), the word `antarā` has come in the sense of ‘reason’ in passages such as: “Who could know the reason for that, other than a Tathāgata?” and “People gather and deliberate; what is the reason concerning you and me?” In passages such as “Venerable sir, a certain woman saw me washing a pot during a flash of lightning,” it has come in the sense of a ‘moment.’ In passages such as “In whom there are no angers from within,” it has come in the sense of the ‘mind.’ In passages such as “He came to an end in the middle,” it has come in the sense of ‘in the middle.’ In passages such as “Moreover, monks, this Tapodā river flows from the opening between two great hells,” it has come in the sense of an ‘opening.’ Here, too, it should be understood in the sense of an ‘opening.’ Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as “the opening between Sāvatthī and Jetavana.” And here, due to its connection with the word `antarā`, the accusative case is used: `antarā ca sāvatthiṃ antarā ca jetavanaṃ`. In such places, grammarians use the word `antarā` only once, as in `antarā gāmañca nadiñca gacchati` (he goes between the village and the river), and it should be connected with the second term as well. Here, however, it is stated after being connected with both.

Ahiṃ daṇḍena hanantīti bilato nikkhamitvā gocarāya gacchantaṃ kaṇhasappaṃ chātajjhattaṃ anubandhitvā yaṭṭhīhi pothenti. Tena ca samayena bhagavā sāvatthiṃ piṇḍāya gacchanto antarāmagge te dārake ahiṃ daṇḍena hanante disvā “kasmā kumārakā imaṃ ahiṃ daṇḍena hanathā”ti pucchitvā “ḍaṃsanabhayena, bhante”ti ca vutte “ime attano sukhaṃ karissāmāti imaṃ paharantā nibbattaṭṭhāne dukkhaṃ anubhavissanti, aho avijjāya nikatikosalla”nti dhammasaṃvegaṃ uppādesi. Teneva ca dhammasaṃvegena udānaṃ udānesi. Tena vuttaṃ “atha kho bhagavā”tiādi.

Regarding the phrase, `Ahiṃ daṇḍena hananti` (They are striking a snake with a stick): they were pursuing and beating with sticks a black cobra that was inwardly famished, which had come out of its hole and was going in search of food. At that time, the Blessed One, while going to Sāvatthī for alms, saw those boys on the road beating the snake with a stick. Having asked, “Why, young boys, are you striking this snake with a stick?” and upon being told, “Out of fear of being bitten, venerable sir,” he gave rise to a sense of spiritual urgency, reflecting: “These boys, striking this snake thinking, ‘We will create our own happiness,’ will experience suffering in their place of rebirth. Oh, the cunning skill of ignorance!” And with that very sense of spiritual urgency, he uttered an inspired utterance. Therefore, it is said: “Then, the Blessed One…” and so forth.

Tattha [M 0.0098] etamatthaṃ viditvāti “ime dārakā attasukhāya paradukkhaṃ karontā sayaṃ parattha sukhaṃ na labhissantī”ti etamatthaṃ jānitvāti evameke vaṇṇenti. Aññesaṃ duppaṭipannānaṃ sukhapariyesanaṃ āyatiṃ dukkhāya saṃvattati, suppaṭipannānaṃ ekantena sukhāya saṃvattati. Tasmā “paravihesāvinimuttā accantameva sukhabhāgino vata mayhaṃ ovādappaṭikarā”ti somanassavasenevetampi satthā udānaṃ udānesīti vadanti. Apare pana bhaṇanti “evaṃ tehi kumārakehi pavattitaṃ paraviheṭhanaṃ sabbākārena ādīnavato viditvā paravihesāya [P 0.0111] parānukampāya ca yathākkamaṃ ādīnavānisaṃsavibhāvanaṃ imaṃ udānaṃ udānesī”ti.

Therein, regarding `etamatthaṃ viditvā` (having understood this matter): some explain it thus, as “having known this matter: ‘These boys, by causing suffering to others for their own happiness, will not themselves obtain happiness in the next world.’” Others say that the Teacher uttered this inspired utterance out of gladness, reflecting: “For those who practice wrongly, the search for happiness leads to future suffering, whereas for those who practice rightly, it leads exclusively to happiness. Therefore, those freed from harming others, who act in accordance with my instruction, are indeed partakers of ultimate happiness.” Still others, however, say that having seen in every way the danger in the tormenting of others initiated by those boys, he uttered this inspired utterance to demonstrate, in due order, the danger of harming others and the benefit of compassion for others.

Tattha sukhakāmānīti ekanteneva attano sukhassa icchanato sukhānugiddhāni. Bhūtānīti pāṇino. Yo daṇḍena vihiṃsatīti ettha daṇḍenāti desanāmattaṃ, daṇḍena vā leḍḍusatthapāṇippahārādīhi vāti attho. Atha vā daṇḍenāti daṇḍanena. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yo sukhakāmāni sabbabhūtāni jātiādinā ghaṭṭanavasena vacīdaṇḍena vā pāṇimuggarasatthādīhi pothanatāḷanacchedanādivasena sarīradaṇḍena vā sataṃ vā sahassaṃ vā ṭhāpanavasena dhanadaṇḍena vāti imesu daṇḍesu yena kenaci daṇḍena vihiṃsati viheṭheti dukkhaṃ pāpeti, attano sukhamesāno, pecca so na labhate sukhanti so puggalo attano sukhaṃ esanto gavesanto patthento [V 0.0088] pecca paraloke manussasukhaṃ dibbasukhaṃ nibbānasukhanti tividhampi sukhaṃ na labhati, aññadatthu tena daṇḍena dukkhameva labhatīti attho.

Therein, `sukhakāmāni` (desirous of happiness) means being greedy for pleasure, due to desiring one’s own happiness exclusively. `Bhūtāni` (beings) means living creatures. In the phrase `yo daṇḍena vihiṃsati` (whoever harms with a stick), `daṇḍena` (with a stick) is merely an illustrative term; the meaning is “with a stick, or with clods of earth, weapons, blows from the hand, and so on.” Alternatively, `daṇḍena` means by punishment. This is what is said: whoever harms, torments, or causes suffering to any beings who are desirous of happiness, by any of these punishments—whether by verbal punishment, by way of insults concerning their birth and so on; or by bodily punishment, by way of beating, striking, or cutting with the hand, a club, a weapon, and so on; or by punishment of wealth, by way of imposing a fine of a hundred or a thousand—that person, `attano sukhamesāno, pecca so na labhate sukhaṃ` (seeking one’s own happiness, one does not obtain happiness after death). The meaning is that this person, while seeking, searching for, and aspiring to their own happiness, does not, after death, in the next world, obtain the threefold happiness of human happiness, divine happiness, and the happiness of Nibbāna. On the contrary, through that punishment, they obtain only suffering.

Pecca so labhate sukhanti yo khantimettānuddayasampanno “yathāhaṃ sukhakāmo dukkhappaṭikūlo, evaṃ sabbepī”ti cintetvā sampattaviratiādīsu ṭhito vuttanayena kenaci daṇḍena sabbānipi bhūtāni na hiṃsati na bādhati, so puggalo paraloke manussabhūto manussasukhaṃ, devabhūto dibbasukhaṃ, ubhayaṃ atikkamanto nibbānasukhaṃ labhatīti. Ettha ca tādisassa puggalassa avassaṃbhāvitāya taṃ sukhaṃ paccuppannaṃ viya hotīti dassanatthaṃ “labhate”ti vuttaṃ. Purimagāthāyapi eseva nayo.

Regarding `pecca so labhate sukhaṃ` (after death, one obtains happiness): one who is endowed with patience, loving-kindness, and compassion, having reflected, “Just as I am desirous of happiness and averse to suffering, so too are all beings,” and being established in refraining when the opportunity arises and so forth, does not, in the manner stated, harm or oppress any beings with any kind of punishment. That person, in the next world, having become a human, obtains human happiness; having become a deva, obtains divine happiness; and transcending both, obtains the happiness of Nibbāna. And here, to show that for such a person, because of the inevitability of the result, that happiness is as if it were present, it is said `labhate` (obtains). The same method applies to the previous verse as well.

Tatiyasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Third Sutta is concluded.

4. Sakkārasuttavaṇṇanā

4. The Commentary on the Sutta on Honour

14. Catutthe [M 0.0099][P 0.0112] tena kho pana samayena bhagavā sakkato hotīti kappānaṃ satasahassādhikesu catūsu asaṅkhyeyyesu paripūritassa puññasambhāravisesassa phalabhūtena “ito paraṃ mayhaṃ okāso natthī”ti ussahajātena viya uparūpari vaḍḍhamānena sakkārādinā bhagavā sakkato hoti. Sabbadisāsu hi yamakamahāmegho vuṭṭhahitvā mahoghaṃ viya sabbapāramiyo “ekasmiṃ attabhāve vipākaṃ dassāmā”ti sampiṇḍitā viya bhagavato lābhasakkāramahoghaṃ nibbattayiṃsu. Tato annapānavatthayānamālāgandhavilepanādihatthā khattiyabrāhmaṇādayo āgantvā “kahaṃ buddho, kahaṃ bhagavā, kahaṃ devadevo, kahaṃ narāsabho, kahaṃ purisasīho”ti bhagavantaṃ pariyesanti. Sakaṭasatehi paccaye āharitvā okāsaṃ alabhamānā samantā gāvutappamāṇepi sakaṭadhurena sakaṭadhuraṃ āhacca tiṭṭhanti ceva anubandhanti ca andhakavindabrāhmaṇādayo viya. Sabbaṃ taṃ khandhake (mahāva. 282) tesu tesu ca suttesu āgatanayena veditabbaṃ. Yathā ca bhagavato, evaṃ bhikkhusaṅghassāti. Vuttañhetaṃ –

14. In the fourth discourse, the phrase ‘at that time the Blessed One was honored’ means this: The Blessed One was honored by honors and the like that grew ever greater, as if driven by an eagerness declaring, “Beyond this, there is no opportunity for me,” this being the fruit of the special accumulation of merit fulfilled during four incalculable aeons plus a hundred thousand aeons. For, from all directions, all the perfections, like great twin rain clouds rising up and creating a mighty flood, converged as if having resolved, “We will give our fruit in this single existence,” and thus generated a great flood of gains and honors for the Blessed One. Then, from here and there, nobles, brahmins, and others came with food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, perfumes, and ointments in hand, searching for the Blessed One and asking, “Where is the Buddha? Where is the Blessed One? Where is the god of gods? Where is the bull among men? Where is the lion among men?” Unable to find an opportunity to offer even after bringing requisites by the hundreds of carts, they stood pressing cart-yoke against cart-yoke for a distance of a league all around, and they followed closely, like the brahmins of Andhakavinda and others. All this should be understood in the way it is related in the Khandhaka (Mahāvagga 282) and in various suttas. And as it was for the Blessed One, so it was for the community of monks. For it has been said:

“Yāvatā kho, cunda, etarahi saṅghā vā gaṇā vā loke uppannā, nāhaṃ, cunda, aññaṃ [V 0.0089] ekasaṅghampi samanupassāmi evaṃ lābhaggayasaggappattaṃ, yatharivāyaṃ, cunda, bhikkhusaṅgho”ti (dī. ni. 3.176).

“Cunda, among all the communities or groups that have arisen in the world at this time, I do not see even a single other community that has attained such a pinnacle of gain and honor as this community of monks.”

Svāyaṃ bhagavato ca bhikkhusaṅghassa ca uppanno lābhasakkāro ekato hutvā dvinnaṃ mahānadīnaṃ udakogho viya appameyyo ahosi. Tena vuttaṃ – “tena kho pana samayena bhagavā sakkato hoti…pe… parikkhārānaṃ, bhikkhusaṅghopi sakkato…pe… parikkhārāna”nti.

This gain and honor that arose for the Blessed One and the community of monks, having become one, was immeasurable, like the flood of water from two great rivers. Therefore it was said: “At that time, the Blessed One was honored… with requisites, and the community of monks was also honored… with requisites.”

Titthiyā pana pubbe akatapuññatāya ca duppaṭipannatāya ca asakkatā agarukatā, buddhuppādena pana visesato vipannasobhā sūriyuggamane khajjopanakā viya nippabhā [P 0.0113] nittejā hatalābhasakkārā ahesuṃ. Te tādisaṃ bhagavato saṅghassa ca lābhasakkāraṃ asahamānā issāpakatā “evaṃ ime pharusāhi vācāhi ghaṭṭetvāva palāpessāmā”ti usūyā visuggāraṃ uggirantā tattha tattha bhikkhū akkosantā paribhāsantā vicariṃsu[M 0.0100]. Tena vuttaṃ – “aññatitthiyā pana paribbājakā asakkatā honti…pe… parikkhārānaṃ. Atha kho te aññatitthiyā paribbājakā bhagavato sakkāraṃ asahamānā bhikkhusaṅghassa ca gāme ca araññe ca bhikkhū disvā asabbhāhi pharusāhi vācāhi akkosanti paribhāsanti rosenti vihesentī”ti.

The sectarians, however, due to their lack of past merit and their wrong practice, were unhonored and unrespected. But with the arising of the Buddha, their splendor was especially ruined; like fireflies at sunrise, they became devoid of radiance, lacking in power, and their gains and honors were destroyed. Unable to bear such gains and honors for the Blessed One and the Sangha, they became filled with envy and, spewing the venomous vomit of jealousy, they wandered about here and there abusing and reviling the monks, thinking, “Thus we will harass them with harsh words and make them flee.” Therefore it was said: “The wanderers of other sects, however, are unhonored… with regard to requisites. Then those wanderers of other sects, unable to endure the honor shown to the Blessed One and the community of monks, upon seeing monks in a village or in the wilderness, abuse, revile, provoke, and vex them with uncivil and harsh words.”

Tattha asabbhāhīti asabhāyoggāhi sabhāyaṃ sādhujanasamūhe vattuṃ ayuttāhi, duṭṭhullāhīti attho. Pharusāhīti kakkhaḷāhi mammacchedikāhi. Akkosantīti jātiādīhi akkosavatthūhi khuṃsenti. Paribhāsantīti bhaṇḍanavasena bhayaṃ uppādentā tajjenti. Rosentīti yathā parassa roso hoti, evaṃ anuddhaṃsanavasena rosaṃ uppādenti. Vihesentīti viheṭhenti, vividhehi ākārehi aphāsuṃ karonti.

Therein, ‘with uncivil words’ (asabbhāhi) means with words unfit for an assembly, unsuitable to be spoken in an assembly or a gathering of good people; that is, with coarse words. ‘With harsh words’ (pharusāhi) means with rough, heart-piercing words. ‘They abuse’ (akkosanti) means they revile them with the grounds for abuse, such as birth and so on. ‘They revile’ (paribhāsanti) means they threaten them, creating fear by way of quarreling. ‘They provoke’ (rosenti) means they create anger by way of severe censure, such that another person becomes angry. ‘They vex’ (vihesenti) means they harass; they cause discomfort in various ways.

Kathaṃ panete samantapāsādike bhagavati bhikkhusaṅghe ca akkosādīni pavattesunti? Bhagavato uppādato pahīnalābhasakkāratāya upahatacittā pathaviṃ khaṇitvā pakkhalantā viya avaṇe veḷuriyamaṇimhi vaṇaṃ uppādentā viya ca sundarikaṃ nāma paribbājikaṃ saññāpetvā tāya satthu bhikkhūnañca avaṇṇaṃ vuṭṭhāpetvā akkosādīni pavattesuṃ. Taṃ panetaṃ sundarīvatthu parato sundarīsutte (udā. 38) pāḷiyaṃyeva āgamissati, tasmā yamettha vattabbaṃ, taṃ tattheva vaṇṇayissāma.

But how did they direct these abuses and so forth at the Blessed One and the community of monks, who are inspiring from all sides? With their minds afflicted by the loss of gain and honor since the Buddha’s arising, they acted like those who stumble while digging the earth, or like those creating a flaw on a flawless beryl gem. Having persuaded a female wanderer named Sundarikā, they instigated dispraise of the Teacher and the monks through her, thus engaging in abuse and the like. This story of Sundarī will appear later in the Pāli canon itself, in the Sundarī Sutta (Ud 4.8); therefore, whatever should be said here, we will explain there.

Bhikkhū [V 0.0090] bhagavato santikaṃ upasaṅkamitvā taṃ pavattimārocesuṃ. Tena vuttaṃ – “atha kho sambahulā bhikkhū yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṃsu…pe… vihesentī”ti. Taṃ vuttatthameva.

The monks approached the Blessed One and reported this matter. Therefore it was said: “Then a number of monks approached the Blessed One… (and so on, down to) …they vex.” The meaning of this has already been stated.

Etamatthaṃ [P 0.0114] viditvāti etaṃ issāpakatānaṃ titthiyānaṃ vippaṭipattiṃ sabbākārato viditvā. Imaṃ udānanti imaṃ tehi kate vippakāre pasannacittehi ca parehi kate upakāre tādibhāvānubhāvadīpakaṃ udānaṃ udānesi.

‘Having understood this matter’ means having understood in every way this wrong practice of the envious sectarians. ‘This inspired utterance’ means that he uttered this inspired utterance—one that illuminates the power of the state of being unshaken—in response to the harm done by them and the help done by others with serene minds.

Tattha gāme araññe sukhadukkhaphuṭṭhoti gāme vā araññe vā yattha katthaci sukhena dukkhena ca phuṭṭho sukhadukkhāni anubhavanto, tesaṃ vā paccayehi samaṅgībhūto. Nevattato no parato dahethāti “ahaṃ sukhito[M 0.0101], ahaṃ dukkhito, mama sukhaṃ, mama dukkhaṃ, parenidaṃ mayhaṃ sukhadukkhaṃ uppādita”nti ca neva attato na parato taṃ sukhadukkhaṃ ṭhapetha. Kasmā? Na hettha khandhapañcake ahanti vā mamanti vā paroti vā parassāti vā passitabbayuttakaṃ kiñci atthi, kevalaṃ saṅkhārā eva pana yathāpaccayaṃ uppajjitvā khaṇe khaṇe bhijjantīti. Sukhadukkhaggahaṇañcettha desanāsīsaṃ, sabbassāpi lokadhammassa vasena attho veditabbo. Iti bhagavā “nāhaṃ kvacani, kassaci kiñcanatasmiṃ, na ca mama kvacani, katthaci kiñcanatatthī”ti catukoṭikaṃ suññataṃ vibhāvesi.

Herein, 'touched by pleasure and pain in a village or in a forest' means: whether in a village, in a forest, or anywhere whatsoever, being touched by pleasure and pain, experiencing pleasure and pain, or being endowed with their conditions. 'One should not posit it from self or from another' means: one should not establish that pleasure and pain from the perspective of self or from the perspective of another, thinking: 'I am happy, I am unhappy; my happiness, my unhappiness; this pleasure and pain of mine was produced by another.' Why is that? Because in this fivefold aggregate, there is nothing whatsoever fit to be seen as 'I,' 'mine,' 'another,' or 'another's.' There are only formations, which, having arisen according to conditions, break up moment by moment. And herein, the taking up of pleasure and pain is the principal topic of the discourse; the meaning should be understood in terms of all worldly phenomena. Thus, the Blessed One made plain the four-limbed emptiness: 'I am not anyone's possession in any way, nor does anything of mine exist anywhere in any way.'

Idāni tassa attato parato ca adahanassa kāraṇaṃ dasseti “phusanti phassā upadhiṃ paṭiccā”ti. Ete sukhavedanīyā dukkhavedanīyā ca phassā nāma khandhapañcakasaṅkhātaṃ upadhiṃ paṭicca tasmiṃ sati yathāsakaṃ visayaṃ phusanti, tattha pavattantiyeva. Adukkhamasukhā hi vedanā santasabhāvatāya sukhe eva saṅgahaṃ gacchatīti duvidhasamphassavasenevāyaṃ atthavaṇṇanā katā.

Now, he shows the reason for not positing it from self or from another: 'Contacts impinge, dependent on the substrate.' These contacts, associated with pleasant and painful feeling, impinge on their respective objects dependent on the substrate called the five aggregates, when that is present; they just occur there. Indeed, since neutral feeling, due to its peaceful nature, is included under pleasure, this explanation of the meaning is made in terms of the two kinds of contact.

Yathā pana te phassā na phusanti, taṃ dassetuṃ “nirupadhiṃ kena phuseyyuṃ phassā”ti vuttaṃ. Sabbaso hi khandhūpadhiyā asati kena kāraṇena te phassā phuseyyuṃ, na taṃ kāraṇaṃ atthi. Yadi hi tumhe akkosādivasena uppajjanasukhadukkhaṃ na icchatha, sabbaso nirupadhibhāveyeva [P 0.0115] yogaṃ kareyyāthāti anupādisesanibbānadhātuyā gāthaṃ niṭṭhapesi. Evaṃ iminā udānena vaṭṭavivaṭṭaṃ kathitaṃ.

But as to how those contacts do not impinge, to show that, it was said: 'With no substrate, by what could contacts impinge?' For when the substrate of the aggregates is entirely absent, by what reason could those contacts impinge? That reason does not exist. If you do not wish for the pleasure and pain that arises through abuse and so on, you should apply effort entirely in the state of being without substrate—thus he concluded the verse with the element of Nibbāna without residue remaining. In this way, by this inspired utterance, the round of existence and that which is not the round were explained.

Catutthasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Fourth Sutta is concluded.

5. Upāsakasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Sutta on the Lay Follower

15. Pañcame [V 0.0091] icchānaṅgalakoti icchānaṅgalanāmako kosalesu eko brāhmaṇagāmo, taṃnivāsitāya tattha vā jāto bhavoti vā icchānaṅgalako. Upāsakoti tīhi saraṇagamanehi bhagavato santike upāsakabhāvassa paveditattā upāsako pañcasikkhāpadiko buddhamāmako, dhammamāmako, saṅghamāmako. Kenacideva karaṇīyenāti uddhārasodhāpanādinā [M 0.0102] kenacideva kattabbena. Tīretvāti niṭṭhāpetvā. Ayaṃ kira upāsako pubbe abhiṇhaṃ bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā payirupāsati, so katipayaṃ kālaṃ bahukaraṇīyatāya satthu dassanaṃ nābhisambhosi. Tenāha bhagavā – “cirassaṃ kho tvaṃ, upāsaka, imaṃ pariyāyamakāsi, yadidaṃ idhāgamanāyā”ti.

15. In the fifth, 'Icchānaṅgalaka' refers to a Brahmin village named Icchānaṅgala in the Kosala country; one is called an Icchānaṅgalaka either for residing there, or for being born or prosperous there. 'Lay follower' means one who, having declared his status as a lay follower in the presence of the Blessed One by taking the three refuges, is an observer of the five precepts, devoted to the Buddha, devoted to the Dhamma, and devoted to the Saṅgha. 'For some reason or other' means by some duty that had to be done, such as collecting or clearing debts. 'Having settled' means having finished. It is said that this lay follower formerly used to frequently approach and attend upon the Blessed One, but for some time, due to many duties, he was unable to obtain a sight of the Teacher. Therefore the Blessed One said: 'It has been a long time, lay follower, since you made this occasion, that is, for coming here.'

Tattha cirassanti cirena. Pariyāyanti vāraṃ. Yadidanti nipāto, yo ayanti attho. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – idha mama santike āgamanāya yo ayaṃ ajja kato vāro, taṃ imaṃ cirena papañcaṃ katvā akāsīti. Cirapaṭikāhanti cirapaṭiko ahaṃ, cirakālato paṭṭhāya ahaṃ upasaṅkamitukāmoti sambandho. Kehici kehicīti ekaccehi ekaccehi. Atha vā kehici kehicīti yehi vā tehi vā. Tattha gāravaṃ dasseti. Satthari abhippasannassa hi satthudassanadhammassavanesu viya na aññattha ādaro hoti. Kiccakaraṇīyehīti [P 0.0116] ettha avassaṃ kātabbaṃ kiccaṃ, itaraṃ karaṇīyaṃ. Paṭhamaṃ vā kātabbaṃ kiccaṃ, pacchā kātabbaṃ karaṇīyaṃ. Khuddakaṃ vā kiccaṃ, mahantaṃ karaṇīyaṃ. Byāvaṭoti ussukko. Evāhanti evaṃ iminā pakārena ahaṃ nāsakkhiṃ upasaṅkamituṃ, na agāravādināti adhippāyo.

Therein, 'for a long time' means after a long time. 'Occasion' means a turn. 'Yadidaṃ' is a particle, meaning 'that which is this.' This is what is said: 'This turn for coming into my presence, which was made today, you have made it after a long time, having created a proliferation of things to do.' 'Long-expectant' is parsed as 'I am long-expectant'; the connection is 'I have been desiring to approach for a long time.' 'By some things or other' means by certain things. Alternatively, 'by some things or other' means by whatever things. Therein, he shows disrespect. For one who is deeply devoted to the Teacher, there is no respect for other things as there is for seeing the Teacher and hearing the Dhamma. Regarding 'duties and obligations': herein, what must be done is a 'duty' (kicca), the other is an 'obligation' (karaṇīya). Or, what is to be done first is a 'duty,' what is to be done later is an 'obligation.' Or, a minor task is a 'duty,' a major one is an 'obligation.' 'Engaged' means busy. 'Thus I' means: 'In this way I was unable to approach, not out of disrespect and so on'—this is the intention.

Etamatthaṃ viditvāti dullabhe buddhuppāde manussattalābhe ca sattānaṃ sakiñcanabhāvena kiccapasutatāya kusalantarāyo hoti, na akiñcanassāti etamatthaṃ sabbākārato viditvā. Imaṃ udānanti tadatthaparidīpanameva imaṃ udānaṃ udānesi.

'Having understood this matter' means: having understood in all its aspects this meaning—that when the arising of a Buddha and the attainment of a human state are rare, for beings, through having impediments and being engrossed in duties, there is an obstacle to the wholesome, but not so for one without impediments. 'This inspired utterance' means: he uttered this inspired utterance which is precisely for the purpose of elucidating that meaning.

Tattha sukhaṃ vata tassa na hoti kiñcīti yassa puggalassa kiñci rūpādīsu ekavatthumpi “mameta”nti taṇhāya pariggahitabhāvena na hoti natthi na vijjati, sukhaṃ vata tassa puggalassa, aho sukhamevāti attho. “Na hosī”tipi pāṭho, tassa atītakālavasena attho veditabbo. Keci pana na hoti kiñcīti padassa “rāgādikiñcanaṃ yassa na hotī”ti atthaṃ vaṇṇenti, taṃ na sundaraṃ pariggahadhammavasena desanāya āgatattā. Rāgādikiñcananti pariggahetabbassāpi saṅgahe sati yuttameva vuttaṃ siyā atha vā yassa puggalassa [V 0.0092] kiñci appampi kiñcanaṃ palibodhajātaṃ rāgādikiñcanābhāvato eva na hoti, taṃ tassa akiñcanattaṃ sukhassa paccayabhāvato [M 0.0103] sukhaṃ vataṃ, aho sukhanti attho. Kassa pana na hoti kiñcananti ce, āha “saṅkhātadhammassa bahussutassā”ti. Yo catūhipi maggasaṅkhāhi soḷasakiccanipphattiyā saṅkhātadhammo katakicco, tato eva paṭivedhabāhusaccena bahussuto, tassa.

Herein, 'Indeed, happiness is for him who has nothing' means: for the person for whom not even a single thing among forms and so on does not exist, is not present, is not found, in the sense of being grasped by craving as 'this is mine'—for that person, happiness indeed! The meaning is, 'Oh, what happiness!' There is also the reading 'there was not,' the meaning of which should be understood in terms of past time. Some, however, explain the meaning of the phrase 'there is nothing' as 'one for whom there is no impediment such as lust,' but that is not sound, because the teaching is presented in terms of things that are grasped. If impediments such as lust were included among things to be grasped, it would be rightly said. Alternatively, for the person for whom not even the slightest impediment arises as an obstruction, precisely because of the absence of impediments such as lust—that state of having nothing, being a condition for his happiness, means 'happiness indeed, oh, what happiness!' If it is asked, 'But for whom is there nothing?', he said: 'For one who has comprehended the Dhamma, for one of great learning.' For him who, through the accomplishment of the sixteen functions by means of the four paths, has comprehended the Dhamma and has done what was to be done, and is thereby of great learning through the abundance of penetration.

Iti bhagavā akiñcanabhāve ānisaṃsaṃ dassetvā sakiñcanabhāve ādīnavaṃ dassetuṃ “sakiñcanaṃ passā”tiādimāha. Tassattho – rāgādikiñcanānaṃ āmisakiñcanānañca atthitāya sakiñcanaṃ, sakiñcanattā eva aladdhānañca laddhānañca kāmānaṃ pariyesanārakkhaṇahetu kiccakaraṇīyavasena “ahaṃ mamā”ti gahaṇavasena ca vihaññamānaṃ vighātaṃ āpajjamānaṃ passāti dhammasaṃvegappatto satthā attano [P 0.0117] cittaṃ vadati. Jano janasmiṃ paṭibandharūpoti sayaṃ añño jano samāno aññasmiṃ jane “ahaṃ imassa, mama aya”nti taṇhāvasena paṭibandhasabhāvo hutvā vihaññati vighātaṃ āpajjati. “Paṭibaddhacitto”tipi pāṭho. Ayañca attho –

Thus, the Blessed One, having shown the benefit in the state of having no impediments, said, beginning with ‘See the one with impediments,’ in order to show the danger in the state of having impediments. Its meaning is: one is ‘with impediments’ due to the existence of impediments such as lust and material impediments; and because of being with impediments, one is vexed and falls into distress on account of the duties and obligations of seeking and guarding sensual pleasures, whether unobtained or obtained, and through the grasping of ‘I’ and ‘mine.’ ‘See’ such a person—thus the Teacher, having attained a sense of spiritual urgency regarding the Dhamma, speaks to his own mind. ‘A person is of the nature of being bound to a person’ means that one person, being distinct, becomes bound in nature to another person through craving, thinking, ‘I am for this one, this one is mine,’ and is thereby vexed and falls into distress. The reading ‘with a bound mind’ is also found. And this is the meaning:

“Puttā matthi dhanammatthi, iti bālo vihaññati;

Attā hi attano natthi, kuto puttā kuto dhana”nti. (dha. pa. 62) –

“Sons are mine, wealth is mine”—thus the fool is tormented. Indeed, oneself is not one’s own—how then sons? How then wealth?

Ādīhi suttapadehi dīpetabboti.

This is to be elucidated by these and other Sutta passages.

Pañcamasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the fifth discourse is concluded.

6. Gabbhinīsuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Discourse concerning the Pregnant Woman

16. Chaṭṭhe aññatarassa paribbājakassāti ekassa kuṭumbikassa paribbājakassa. Daharāti taruṇī. Māṇavikāti brāhmaṇadhītāya vohāro. Pajāpatīti bhariyā. Gabbhinīti āpannasattā. Upavijaññāti ajja suveti paccupaṭṭhitavijāyanakālā hotīti sambandho. So kira brāhmaṇajātiko sabhariyo vādapatthassame ṭhito, tena naṃ sapajāpatikaṃ paribbājakavohārena [V 0.0093] samudācaranti. Bhariyā panassa brāhmaṇajātikattā brāhmaṇāti ālapati. Telanti tilatelaṃ. Telasīsena cettha yaṃ yaṃ vijātāya pasavadukkhappaṭikāratthaṃ icchitabbaṃ, taṃ sabbaṃ sappiloṇādiṃ āharāti āṇāpeti. Yaṃ me vijātāya bhavissatīti [M 0.0104] yaṃ telādi mayhaṃ vijātāya bahinikkhantagabbhāya upakārāya bhavissati. “Paribbājikāyā”tipi pāṭho. Kutoti kasmā ṭhānā, yato ñātikulā vā mittakulā vā telādiṃ āhareyyaṃ, taṃ ṭhānaṃ me natthīti adhippāyo. Telaṃ [P 0.0118] āharāmīti vattamānasamīpatāya vattamānaṃ katvā vuttaṃ, telaṃ āharissāmīti attho. Samaṇassa vā brāhmaṇassa vā sappissa vā telassa vāti ca samuccayattho vā-saddo “aggito vā udakato vā mithubhedā vā”tiādīsu (mahāva. 286; dī. ni. 2.152; udā. 76) viya. Sappissa vā telassa vāti paccatte sāmivacanaṃ, sappi ca telañca yāvadatthaṃ pātuṃ pivituṃ dīyatīti attho. Apare pana “sappissa vā telassa vāti avayavasambandhe sāmivacanaṃ. Sappitelasamudāyassa hi avayavo idha yāvadatthasaddena vuccatī”ti vadanti. No nīharitunti bhājanena vā hatthena vā bahi netuṃ no dīyati, ucchadditvānāti vamitvā, yaṃnūna dadeyyanti sambandho. Evaṃ kirassa ahosi “ahaṃ rañño koṭṭhāgāraṃ gantvā telaṃ kaṇṭhamattaṃ pivitvā tāvadeva gharaṃ āgantvā ekasmiṃ bhājane yathāpītaṃ vamitvā uddhanaṃ āropetvā pacissāmi, yaṃ pittasemhādimissitaṃ, taṃ agginā jhāyissati, telaṃ pana gahetvā imissā paribbājikāya kamme upanessāmī”ti.

16. Regarding the sixth, 'a certain wanderer' refers to a certain householder who had become a wanderer. 'Young' means a young woman. 'Māṇavikā' is a term for a brahmin’s daughter. 'Pajāpatī' means wife. 'Gabbhinī' means pregnant. 'Upavijaññā' is connected thus: the time of her delivery is imminent, today or tomorrow. It is said that he was of brahmin birth and, together with his wife, was dwelling at a place for settling disputes. Therefore, they were addressed with the designation 'wanderer' and 'female wanderer.' His wife, however, being of brahmin birth, he addresses as 'brahmin lady.' 'Oil' means sesame oil. With oil as the chief item, he gives the order: 'Bring ghee, salt, and everything else that is needed to counteract the suffering of childbirth.' 'What will be for my wife in labor' means 'whatever oil and so forth will be of use for my wife who is giving birth, whose child has come out.' There is also the reading 'for the female wanderer.' 'From where?' means from what place? The intention is: 'There is no place for me, no family of relatives or friends, from which I might bring oil and so forth.' 'I bring oil' is said using the present tense because of its proximity to the future; the meaning is 'I shall bring oil.' In the phrase 'for an ascetic or a brahmin, of ghee or of oil,' the word 'or' has a collective sense, as in such phrases as 'from fire or from water or from discord.' 'Of ghee or of oil' is the genitive case used for the object, meaning: 'ghee and oil are given to drink as much as one desires.' But others say: 'In "of ghee or of oil," the genitive case is used in the sense of a part-whole relationship. For here a part of the whole of ghee and oil is expressed by the words "as much as one desires."' 'Not to be taken out' means it is not given to be taken out, whether by a vessel or by hand. 'Having thrown it up' means having vomited. The connection is to 'what if I were to give it?' It is said that this thought occurred to him: 'What if I go to the king’s storeroom, drink oil up to my throat, come home right away, vomit it just as I drank it into a vessel, put it on the stove and cook it? Whatever is mixed with bile, phlegm, and so on, will be burned away by the fire. Then, taking the oil, I will apply it to the task of this female wanderer.'

Uddhaṃ kātunti vamanavasena uddhaṃ nīharituṃ. Na pana adhoti viriñcanavasena heṭṭhā nīharituṃ na pana sakkoti. So hi “adhikaṃ pītaṃ sayameva mukhato niggamissatī”ti pivitvā āsayassa arittatāya aniggate vamanavirecanayogaṃ ajānanto alabhanto vā kevalaṃ dukkhāhi vedanāhi phuṭṭho āvaṭṭati ca parivaṭṭati ca. Dukkhāhīti dukkhamāhi. Tibbāhīti bahalāhi tikhiṇāhi vā. Kharāhīti kakkhaḷāhi. Kaṭukāhīti ativiya aniṭṭhabhāvena dāruṇāhi. Āvaṭṭatīti ekasmiṃyeva ṭhāne anipajjitvā attano sarīraṃ ito cito ākaḍḍhanto āvaṭṭati. Parivaṭṭatīti ekasmiṃ padese nipannopi aṅgapaccaṅgāni parito khipanto vaṭṭati, abhimukhaṃ vā vaṭṭanto āvaṭṭati, samantato vaṭṭanto parivaṭṭati.

'To make go upwards' means to expel upwards by means of vomiting. 'But not downwards' means he is unable to expel downwards by means of purging. For he drank, thinking, 'The excess I have drunk will come out of my mouth by itself.' But because his stomach was not empty and it did not come out, and because he did not know of or could not obtain a means for vomiting or purging, he was afflicted by purely painful feelings and rolled about and tossed about. 'Painful' means hard to bear. 'Sharp' means intense or piercing. 'Harsh' means rough. 'Bitter' means extremely unpleasant and severe. 'He rolls about' means, not lying down in one place, he drags his body here and there and rolls. 'He tosses about' means, even when lying in one place, he thrashes his limbs about; or, rolling forwards is 'rolling about,' while rolling all around is 'tossing about.'

Etamatthaṃ viditvāti “sakiñcanassa appaṭisaṅkhāparibhogahetukā ayaṃ dukkhuppatti, akiñcanassa [P 0.0119] pana sabbaso ayaṃ natthī”ti etamatthaṃ sabbākārato jānitvā tadatthappakāsanaṃ imaṃ udānaṃ udānesi.

Having understood this meaning—namely, that 'for one with impediments, this arising of suffering is caused by unreflective consumption, whereas for one without impediments, this does not exist at all'—having known this matter in all its aspects, he uttered this inspired utterance which makes that meaning clear.

Tattha [V 0.0094][M 0.0105] sukhino vatāti sukhino vata sappurisā. Ke pana teti? Ye akiñcanā, ye rāgādikiñcanassa pariggahakiñcanassa ca abhāvena akiñcanā, kesaṃ panidaṃ kiñcanaṃ natthīti āha – “vedaguno hi janā akiñcanā”ti, ye ariyamaggañāṇasaṅkhātaṃ vedaṃ gatā adhigatā, tena vā vedena nibbānaṃ gatāti vedaguno, te ariyajanā khīṇāsavapuggalā anavasesarāgādikiñcanānaṃ aggamaggena samucchinnattā akiñcanā nāma. Asati hi rāgādikiñcane kuto pariggahakiñcanassa sambhavo. Evaṃ gāthāya purimabhāgena arahante pasaṃsitvā aparabhāgena andhaputhujjane garahanto “sakiñcanaṃ passā”tiādimāha. Taṃ purimasutte vuttatthameva. Evaṃ imāyapi gāthāya vaṭṭavivaṭṭaṃ kathitaṃ.

Herein, 'Happy indeed!' means 'Happy indeed are the good people!' Who then are they? Those who are without impediments. They are without impediments due to the absence of the impediment of lust and so forth and the impediment of possessions. To the question, 'For whom does this impediment not exist?' he said: 'For people who are knowers of the Veda are without impediments.' 'Knowers of the Veda' (vedagū) are those who have gone to, have attained, the 'Veda' known as the knowledge of the noble path, or who by that Veda have gone to Nibbāna. Those noble people, individuals whose corruptions are destroyed, are called 'without impediments' because the impediments of lust and so forth have been cut off without remainder by the highest path. For when the impediment of lust and so forth does not exist, whence could the impediment of possessions arise? Thus, having praised the Arahants with the first half of the verse, and censuring the blind worldlings with the latter half, he said, 'See the one with impediments,' and so on. That has the same meaning as was stated in the previous discourse. In this way, by this verse also, the round of existence and its cessation have been explained.

Chaṭṭhasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the sixth discourse is finished.

7. Ekaputtakasuttavaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Discourse of the Only Son

17. Sattame ekaputtakoti eko putto, so ca anukampitabbaṭṭhena ekaputtako, piyāyitabbaṭṭhena piyo, manassa vaḍḍhanaṭṭhena manāpo. Sarīrasobhāsampattiyā vā dassanīyaṭṭhena piyo, sīlācārasampattiyā kalyāṇadhammatāya manāpo. Kaleti satte khepetīti kālo, maraṇaṃ. Taṃ kato pattoti kālaṅkato, kālena vā maccunā kato naṭṭho adassanaṃ gatoti kālaṅkato, matoti attho.

17. In the seventh discourse, 'an only son' means one son. And he is called 'an only son' in the sense that he is to be compassionated; 'dear' in the sense that he is to be loved; and 'pleasing' in the sense that he causes the mind to grow. Or, he is 'dear' in the sense of being pleasant to behold due to the perfection of his bodily beauty; he is 'pleasing' due to the perfection of his virtue and conduct, by his possession of virtuous qualities. 'Time' (kāla) is that which consumes beings; it is death. 'Kālaṅkato' means one who has gone to or reached that (death). Or, 'kālaṅkato' means one who has been brought to ruin, gone to invisibility, by time, that is, by death; the meaning is 'dead'.

Sambahulā upāsakāti sāvatthivāsino bahū upāsakā mataputtaupāsakassa sahasokībhāvena yāva āḷāhanā pacchato gantvā matasarīrassa kattabbaṃ kāretvā paṭinivattā yathānivatthāva udakaṃ otaritvā sīsaṃnhātā vatthāni pīḷetvā anotāpetvāva ekaṃ nivāsetvā [P 0.0120] ekaṃ uttarāsaṅgaṃ katvā upāsakaṃ purato katvā “sokavinodanaṃ dhammaṃ satthu santike sossāmā”ti bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamiṃsu. Tena vuttaṃ “allakesā”tiādi.

Regarding 'many lay followers': many lay followers who were residents of Sāvatthī, sharing in the grief for the lay follower whose son had died, went behind him as far as the cremation ground. Having performed the necessary rites for the dead body, they returned. Still in their clothes, they entered the water, bathed their heads, and wrung out their garments. Without drying them, they put on one as a lower garment and made another an upper robe. Placing that lay follower before them, they approached the Blessed One, thinking, 'We shall hear a teaching for dispelling sorrow in the Teacher's presence.' Therefore, it was said, 'with wet hair,' and so forth.

Tattha allavatthāti udakena tintavatthā. Divā divassāti divasassapi divā, majjhanhike kāleti attho. Yasmā jānantāpi tathāgatā pucchanti[M 0.0106], jānantāpi na pucchanti. Kālaṃ viditvā pucchanti, kālaṃ viditvā na pucchanti, tasmā jānantoyeva bhagavā kathāsamuṭṭhāpanatthaṃ pucchanto [V 0.0095] “kiṃ nu kho tumhe upāsakā”tiādimāha. Tassattho – tumhe upāsakā aññesu divasesu mama santikaṃ āgacchantā otāpitasuddhavatthā sāyanhe āgacchatha, ajja pana allavatthā allakesā ṭhitamajjhanhike kāle idhāgatā, taṃ kiṃ kāraṇanti. Tena mayanti tena puttaviyogajanitacittasantāpena balavasokābhibhūtatāya evaṃbhūtā mayaṃ idhūpasaṅkamantāti.

Therein, 'with wet clothes' means clothes soaked with water. 'By day, during the day' means during the day of the day, that is, at midday; this is the meaning. Since Tathāgatas, though knowing, sometimes ask, and though knowing, sometimes do not ask—they ask having known the time, and they do not ask having known the time—therefore the Blessed One, though knowing, asked in order to initiate a conversation, saying, 'Why now, lay followers?' and so forth. The meaning of this is: 'Lay followers, on other days when you come to my presence, you come in the evening with dried, clean clothes. But today you have come here at midday with wet clothes and wet hair. What is the reason for that?' 'It is because of that' means: 'It is because we are overwhelmed by powerful sorrow, by the mental anguish born from separation from a son, that we, being in such a state, have approached this place.'

Etamatthaṃ viditvāti piyavatthusambhavā sokadukkhadomanassādayo, asati piyavatthusmiṃ sabbaso ete na santīti etamatthaṃ sabbākārato jānitvā tadatthappakāsanaṃ imaṃ udānaṃ udānesi.

Having understood this matter: knowing in all its aspects this meaning—that from the existence of a dear object arise sorrow, pain, dejection, and so forth, and that when a dear object does not exist, these do not exist at all—he uttered this inspired utterance which illuminates that meaning.

Tattha piyarūpassādagadhitāseti piyasabhāvesu rūpakkhandhādīsu sukhavedanassādena gadhitā paṭibaddhacittā. Gadhitāseti hi gadhitāiccevattho. Seti vā nipātamattaṃ.
