Piyarūpā nāma cakkhādayo puttadārādayo ca. Vuttañhetaṃ – “kiñca loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ cakkhu loke …pe… dhammataṇhā loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpa”nti (cūḷani. hemakamāṇavapucchāniddesa 55).

Therein, regarding 'greedy for the taste of what is dear and appears as form': this means having a mind that is bound and greedy, through the taste of pleasant feeling, for things of a dear nature, such as the form aggregate and so on. For 'gadhitāse' has the meaning of 'gadhitā' (greedy). Or, 'se' is merely a particle. 'Things that are dear and appear as form' refers to the eye and so on, and to sons, wives, and so on. For this has been said: 'And what in the world is a dear form and an agreeable form? The eye in the world... craving for mental objects in the world is a dear form and an agreeable form.'

“Khettaṃ vatthuṃ hiraññaṃ vā, gavassaṃ dāsaporisaṃ;

Thiyo bandhū puthu kāme, yo naro anugijjhatī”ti ca. (su. ni. 775);

And: 'A field, a plot of land, or gold, cattle and horses, slaves and servants, women, relatives—whatever man is greedy for these manifold sensual pleasures.'

Tasmā tesu piyarūpesu assādena giddhā mucchitā ajjhāpannāti attho. Ke pana te piyarūpassādagadhitāti te dasseti “devakāyā [P 0.0121] puthumanussā cā”ti, cātumahārājikādayo bahudevasamūhā ceva jambudīpakādikā bahumanussā ca. Aghāvinoti kāyikacetasikadukkhena dukkhitā. Parijunnāti jarārogādivipattiyā yobbanārogyādisampattito parihīnā. Yathālābhavasena vāyamattho devamanussesu veditabbo. Atha vā kāmañcekantasukhasamappitānaṃ devānaṃ dukkhajarārogā na sambhavanti, tadanativattasabhāvatāya pana tepi “aghāvino”ti “parijunnā”ti ca vuttā. Tesampi vā pubbanimittuppattiyā paṭicchannajarāya cetasikarogassa ca vasena dukkhādīnaṃ sambhavo veditabbo. Maccurājassa vasaṃ gacchantīti piyavatthuvisayāya taṇhāya appahīnattā punappunaṃ gabbhūpagamanato [M 0.0107] dhātuttayissaratāya maccurājasaṅkhātassa maraṇassa vasaṃ hatthameva gacchanti.

Therefore, the meaning is that they are greedy, infatuated, and overcome by those dear forms due to their taste. But who are those who are greedy for the taste of what is dear and appears as form? He indicates them thus: 'hosts of devas and many humans'—that is, the many assemblies of devas beginning with those of the Four Great Kings, and the many humans of Jambudīpa and so on. 'Afflicted' means pained by bodily and mental suffering. 'Worn out' means they have declined from the perfection of youth, health, and so on, due to the calamity of aging, sickness, and so forth. Or, this meaning should be understood in relation to devas and humans according to their respective conditions. Alternatively, although it is true that suffering, aging, and sickness do not occur for devas who are endowed with exclusive pleasure, yet because their nature is not to overcome these things, they too are called 'afflicted' and 'worn out.' Or, for them too, the arising of suffering and the like should be understood by way of the arising of the preliminary signs, of hidden aging, and of mental disease. 'They come under the sway of the King of Death' means: because craving for dear objects has not been abandoned, they repeatedly enter the womb; and due to their lack of mastery over the three realms, they come into the very hand, under the sway, of death, which is known as the King of Death.

Ettāvatā vaṭṭaṃ dassetvā idāni “ye ve divā”tiādinā vivaṭṭaṃ dasseti. Tattha ye ve divā ca ratto ca appamattāti “divasaṃ caṅkamena nisajjāya āvaraṇīyehi dhammehi cittaṃ parisodhetī”tiādinā [V 0.0096] vuttanayena divasabhāge rattibhāge ca daḷhaṃ appamattā appamādappaṭipadaṃ pūrenti. Jahanti piyarūpanti catusaccakammaṭṭhānabhāvanaṃ ussukkāpetvā ariyamaggādhigamena piyarūpaṃ piyajātikaṃ cakkhādipiyavatthuṃ tappaṭibaddhachandarāgajahanena jahanti. Te ve khaṇanti aghamūlaṃ, maccuno āmisaṃ durativattanti te ariyapuggalā aghassa vaṭṭadukkhassa mūlabhūtaṃ, maccunā maraṇena āmasitabbato āmisaṃ, ito bahiddhā kehicipi samaṇabrāhmaṇehi nivattituṃ asakkuṇeyyatāya durativattaṃ, saha avijjāya taṇhaṃ ariyamaggañāṇakudālena khaṇanti, lesamattampi anavasesantā ummūlayantīti. Svāyamattho –

Having shown the round of existence to this extent, he now shows the path beyond the round with the words beginning, 'Those who indeed by day...' and so forth. Therein, 'those who indeed by day and by night are heedful' means: in the manner described by such passages as, 'During the day, by walking meditation and sitting, one purifies the mind from obstructive states,' they fulfill the practice of heedfulness, being firmly heedful in the daytime and in the nighttime. 'They abandon what is dear and appears as form' means: having striven in the development of the meditation subject of the Four Noble Truths, through the attainment of the noble path they abandon what is dear and appears as form—that is, dear objects such as the eye—by abandoning the desire and lust connected with them. 'They indeed dig up the root of affliction, the bait of Death, hard to overcome' means: those noble individuals, with the spade that is the knowledge of the noble path, dig up craving together with ignorance—which is the root of affliction, that is, of the suffering of the round; which is the bait of Death, because it is to be consumed by death; and which is hard to overcome, because it cannot be averted by any ascetics or brahmins outside this Dispensation—uprooting it without leaving even a trace. This is the meaning:

“Appamādo [P 0.0122] amatapadaṃ, pamādo maccuno padaṃ;

Appamattā na mīyanti, ye pamattā yathā matā”ti. (dha. pa. 21) –

'Heedfulness is the path to the Deathless; heedlessness is the path to death. The heedful do not die; the heedless are as if already dead.'

Ādīhi suttapadehi vitthāretabboti.

This should be elaborated upon with these and other such passages from the discourses.

Sattamasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Seventh Discourse is finished.

8. Suppavāsāsuttavaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Discourse concerning Suppavāsā

18. Aṭṭhame kuṇḍikāyanti evaṃnāmake koliyānaṃ nagare. Kuṇḍadhānavaneti tassa nagarassa avidūre kuṇḍadhānasaṅkhāte vane.

18. In the eighth discourse: 'At Kuṇḍiyā' means in the city of the Koliyans so named. 'In the Kuṇḍadhāna Wood' means in the wood known as Kuṇḍadhāna, not far from that city.

Pubbe kira kuṇḍo nāma eko yakkho tasmiṃ vanasaṇḍe vāsaṃ kappesi, kuṇḍadhānamissakena ca balikammena tussatīti tassa tathā tattha baliṃ upaharanti, tenetaṃ vanasaṇḍaṃ kuṇḍadhānavanantveva paññāyittha. Tassa avidūre ekā gāmapatikā ahosi, sāpi tassa yakkhassa āṇāpavattiṭṭhāne niviṭṭhattā teneva paripālitattā kuṇḍikāti voharīyittha[M 0.0108]. Aparabhāge tattha koliyarājāno nagaraṃ kāresuṃ, tampi purimavohārena kuṇḍikātveva vuccati. Tasmiñca vanasaṇḍe koliyarājāno bhagavato bhikkhusaṅghassa ca vasanatthāya vihāraṃ patiṭṭhāpesuṃ, tampi kuṇḍadhānavanantveva paññāyittha. Atha bhagavā janapadacārikaṃ caranto anukkamena taṃ vihāraṃ [V 0.0097] patvā tattha vihāsi. Tena vuttaṃ – “ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā kuṇḍikāyaṃ viharati kuṇḍadhānavane”ti.

Long ago, it is said, a yakkha named Kuṇḍa made his dwelling in that grove. He was pleased with offerings made that included kuṇḍadhāna, so they made such offerings to him there. Thus, that grove became known as Kuṇḍadhāna Forest. Not far from it was a village settlement, and because it was located within the yakkha's sphere of influence and protected by him, it too came to be called Kuṇḍikā. Later, the Koliyan kings built a city there, and it was called Kuṇḍikā, retaining the former name. And in that same grove, the Koliyan kings established a monastery for the Blessed One and the community of monks to reside in. This too became known as Kuṇḍadhāna Forest. Then, while traveling through the countryside, the Blessed One gradually arrived at that monastery and stayed there. Hence it is said: "At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Kuṇḍikā in Kuṇḍadhāna Forest."

Suppavāsāti tassā upāsikāya nāmaṃ. Koliyadhītāti koliyarājaputtī. Sā hi bhagavato aggupaṭṭhāyikā paṇītadāyikānaṃ sāvikānaṃ etadagge ṭhapitā sotāpannā ariyasāvikā. Yañhi kiñci bhagavato yuttarūpaṃ khādanīyaṃ bhojanīyaṃ bhesajjaṃ vā na tattha aññāhi saṃvidhātabbaṃ atthi, sabbaṃ taṃ sayameva attano paññāya vicāretvā sakkaccaṃ sampādetvā [P 0.0123] upaneti. Devasikañca aṭṭhasataṃ saṅghabhattapāṭipuggalikabhattāni deti. Yo koci bhikkhu vā bhikkhunī vā taṃ kulaṃ piṇḍāya paviṭṭho rittahattho na gacchati. Evaṃ muttacāgā payatapāṇī vossaggaratā yācayogā dānasaṃvibhāgaratā. Assā kucchiyaṃ purimabuddhesu katādhikāro pacchimabhaviko sāvakabodhisatto paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhi. Sā taṃ gabbhaṃ kenacideva pāpakammena satta vassāni kucchinā parihari, sattāhañca mūḷhagabbhā ahosi. Tena vuttaṃ – “satta vassāni gabbhaṃ dhāreti sattāhaṃ mūḷhagabbhā”ti.

Suppavāsā was the name of that female lay follower. A Koliyan daughter, she was a princess of the Koliyan clan. Indeed, she was the foremost attendant of the Blessed One, ranked highest among the female disciples who were givers of excellent offerings. She was a stream-enterer, a noble female disciple. Whatever hard food, soft food, or medicine suitable for the Blessed One was needed, there was no need for others to arrange it; she herself, with her own wisdom, carefully considered, prepared, and presented it with diligence. And daily, she gave one hundred and eight meals: meals for the Saṅgha and individual meals. Any monk or nun who entered that family's house for alms never left empty-handed. Thus, she was generous, open-handed, delighting in relinquishment, ready to be asked for anything, and fond of sharing gifts. In her womb, a disciple-bodhisatta, who had accumulated merit in the time of previous Buddhas and was destined for his final existence, took rebirth. She carried that fetus in her womb for seven years due to some evil kamma, and was in obstructed labor for seven days. Hence it is said: "She bore the fetus for seven years and was in obstructed labor for seven days."

Tattha satta vassānīti satta saṃvaccharāni, accantasaṃyoge ca idaṃ upayogavacanaṃ. Gabbhaṃ dhāretīti gabbhaṃ vahati, gabbhinī hotīti attho. Sattāhaṃ mūḷhagabbhāti satta ahāni byākulagabbhā. Gabbho hi paripakko sampajjamāno vijāyanakāle kammajavātehi sañcāletvā parivattito uddhaṃpādo adhosiro hutvā yonimukhābhimukho hoti, evaṃ so katthaci alaggo bahi nikkhamati. Vipajjamāno pana viparivattanavasena yonimaggaṃ pidahitvā tiriyaṃ nipajjati, sayameva vā yonimaggo pidahati, so tattha kammajavātehi aparāparaṃ parivattamāno byākulo mūḷhagabbhoti vuccati. Tassāpi satta divase evaṃ ahosi, tena vuttaṃ “sattāhaṃ mūḷhagabbhā”ti.

Here, 'seven years' means seven years, and this is in the accusative case in the sense of continuous duration. 'She carries the fetus' means she bears the fetus, that is, she is pregnant. 'For seven days with an obstructed fetus' means for seven days with a disordered fetus. For when the fetus is fully matured and about to be born, it is moved and turned by the kamma-born winds so that, with feet upwards and head downwards, it faces the opening of the womb; and in this way, being unattached, it emerges outside. But if it goes wrong, due to a faulty turning, it blocks the birth passage by lying across it, or the birth passage itself closes up. There, being repeatedly turned around by the kamma-born winds, it is called an 'obstructed fetus'. For her too, it was like this for seven days, hence it is said, 'for seven days with an obstructed fetus.'

Ayañca gabbho sīvalitthero. Tassa kathaṃ satta vassāni gabbhavāsadukkhaṃ, sattāhaṃ mūḷhagabbhabhāvappatti, mātu cassāpi sotāpannāya ariyasāvikāya [M 0.0109] tathā dukkhānubhavanaṃ jātanti? Vuccate – atīte kāsikarāje bārāṇasiyaṃ rajjaṃ kārente eko kosalarājā mahantena balenāgantvā bārāṇasiṃ gahetvā taṃ rājānaṃ māretvā tassa aggamahesiṃ attano aggamahesiṃ akāsi. Bārāṇasirañño pana putto pitu maraṇakāle niddhamanadvārena palāyitvā attano ñātimittabandhave ekajjhaṃ katvā anukkamena balaṃ saṃharitvā bārāṇasiṃ āgantvā avidūre mahantaṃ khandhāvāraṃ bandhitvā tassa rañño paṇṇaṃ pesesi “rajjaṃ vā detu, yuddhaṃ vā”ti[V 0.0098]. Rājakumārassa [P 0.0124] mātā sāsanaṃ sutvā “yuddhena kammaṃ natthi, sabbadisāsu sañcāraṃ pacchinditvā bārāṇasinagaraṃ parivāretu, tato dārūdakabhattaparikkhayena kilantā nagare manussā vināva yuddhena rājānaṃ gahetvā dassantī”ti paṇṇaṃ pesesi. So mātu sāsanaṃ sutvā cattāri mahādvārāni rakkhanto satta vassāni nagaraṃ uparundhi, nagare manussā cūḷadvārena nikkhamitvā dārūdakāni āharanti, sabbakiccāni karonti.

And this fetus was the elder Sīvali. How could he have experienced the suffering of dwelling in the womb for seven years, the state of an obstructed fetus for seven days, and how could his mother, a stream-enterer and noble female disciple, also have undergone such suffering? It is said: In the past, when the king of Kāsi was ruling in Bārāṇasī, a king of Kosala came with a large army, captured Bārāṇasī, killed that king, and made his chief queen his own chief queen. But the son of the king of Bārāṇasī, at the time of his father’s death, escaped through a drainage gate, gathered his relatives and friends, gradually assembled an army, returned to Bārāṇasī, and set up a large encampment not far away. He sent a message to that king: 'Either surrender the kingdom, or let there be war.' Hearing the message, the prince’s mother sent a reply: 'There is no need for war. Cut off passage in all directions and surround the city of Bārāṇasī. Then, when the people in the city are exhausted from lack of firewood, water, and food, they will seize the king and hand him over, without a fight.' Hearing his mother’s advice, he guarded the four great gates and besieged the city for seven years. The people in the city went out through the small gates to fetch firewood and water and performed all their duties.

Atha rājakumārassa mātā taṃ pavattiṃ sutvā “bālo mama putto upāyaṃ na jānāti, gacchatha, assa cūḷadvārāni pidhāya nagaraṃ uparundhatūti vadethā”ti puttassa gūḷhasāsanaṃ pahiṇi. So mātu sāsanaṃ sutvā satta divase tathā akāsi. Nāgarā bahi nikkhamituṃ alabhantā sattame divase tassa rañño sīsaṃ gahetvā kumārassa adaṃsu. Kumāro nagaraṃ pavisitvā rajjaṃ aggahesi. So tadā satta vassāni nagararundhanakammanissandena etarahi satta vassāni mātukucchisaṅkhātāya lohitakumbhiyā vasi, avasesato pana sattāhaṃ nagarūparundhanena sattāhaṃ mūḷhagabbhabhāvaṃ āpajji. Jātakaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “satta divasāni nagaraṃ rundhitvā gahitakammanissandena sattavassāni lohitakumbhiyaṃ vasitvā sattāhaṃ mūḷhagabbhabhāvaṃ āpajjī”ti vuttaṃ. Yaṃ pana so padumuttarasammāsambuddhapādamūle “lābhīnaṃ aggo bhaveyya”nti mahādānaṃ datvā patthanaṃ akāsi, yañca vipassissa bhagavato kāle nāgarehi saddhiṃ sahassagghanikaṃ guḷadadhiṃ datvā patthanaṃ akāsi, tassānubhāvena lābhīnaṃ aggo jāto. Suppavāsāpi “nagaraṃ rundhitvā gaṇha, tātā”ti pesitabhāvena satta vassāni kucchinā gabbhaṃ pariharitvā sattāhaṃ mūḷhagabbhājātā[M 0.0110]. Evaṃ te mātāputtā attano kammassa anurūpaṃ īdisaṃ dukkhaṃ paṭisaṃvediṃsu.

Then the prince's mother, hearing of the situation, thought, "My foolish son does not know the right means. Go, tell him to close the small gates and blockade the city." She sent a secret message to her son. Hearing his mother’s message, he acted accordingly for seven days. The citizens, unable to leave, on the seventh day seized that king’s head and gave it to the prince. The prince entered the city and took the kingdom. Thus, due to the karmic result of blockading the city for seven days at that time, he now dwelt for seven years in what is called a 'blood-filled jar,' namely his mother's womb; and as for the remaining part, due to the seven days of blockading the city, he experienced the state of an obstructed fetus for seven days. However, in the Jātaka commentary, it is said: "As a result of the action of having blockaded the city for seven days, he dwelt for seven years in a blood-filled jar and then experienced the state of an obstructed fetus for seven days." Moreover, because he had made a great offering at the feet of the Perfectly Self-Enlightened Buddha Padumuttara, wishing, "May I become the foremost among those who receive offerings," and because he had offered jaggery and curd worth a thousand together with the citizens during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī, making a similar aspiration, by the power of those deeds, he was born as the foremost among recipients of offerings. Suppavāsā too, because she had sent the message, "Blockade the city and seize it, my son," carried the fetus in her womb for seven years and for seven days had an obstructed fetus. Thus, both mother and son experienced such suffering in accordance with their own kamma.

Tīhi [P 0.0125] vitakkehīti ratanattayaguṇānussatipaṭisaṃyuttehi tīhi sammāvitakkehi. Adhivāsetīti mūḷhagabbhatāya uppannadukkhaṃ sahati. Sā hi bhagavato sambuddhabhāvaṃ, ariyasaṅghassa suppaṭipattiṃ, nibbānassa ca dukkhanissaraṇabhāvaṃ anussarantī attano uppajjamānadukkhaṃ amanasikaraṇeneva abhibhavitvā khamati. Tena vuttaṃ “tīhi vitakkehi adhivāsetī”ti.

By three thoughts: this means by the three right thoughts connected with the recollection of the qualities of the Triple Gem. Endures: she bears the suffering that arises due to the state of an obstructed fetus. For she, recollecting the Blessed One’s state of perfect enlightenment, the good practice of the Noble Saṅgha, and Nibbāna as the escape from suffering, overcomes the suffering arising in her by simply not attending to it, and thus she tolerates it. Therefore, it is said: "She endures with three thoughts."

Sammāsambuddho vatātiādi tesaṃ vitakkānaṃ pavattiākāradassanaṃ. Tassattho – yo bhagyavantatādīhi kāraṇehi bhagavā lokanātho sammā aviparītaṃ sāmaṃ sayameva sabbadhamme aho vata buddho, so bhagavā evarūpassa etarahi mayā anubhaviyamānassa aññassa ca evaṃjātikassa [V 0.0099] sakalassa vaṭṭadukkhassa pahānāya accantaṃ anuppādanirodhāya dhammaṃ katheti, aviparītadhammaṃ katheti. Aviparītadhammadesanatāya hi satthu sammāsambodhisiddhi. Tassa yathāvuttaguṇassa bhagavato dhammassavanante jātattā sīladiṭṭhisāmaññena saṃhatattā ca sāvakasaṅghoti laddhanāmo aṭṭhaariyapuggalasamūho suppaṭipanno vata aho vata sammā paṭipanno, yo ariyasaṅgho evarūpassa īdisassa vaṭṭadukkhassa pahānāya anuppādanirodhāya anivattipaṭipadaṃ paṭipanno. Susukhaṃ vata aho vata suṭṭhu sukhaṃ sabbasaṅkhatanissaṭaṃ nibbānaṃ, yasmiṃ nibbāne īdisaṃ vaṭṭadukkhaṃ na upalabbhatīti. Ettha ca paṭipajjamānāpi paṭipannā icceva vuttā paṭipattiyā anivattibhāvato. Atha vā uppannasaddo viya paṭipannasaddo vattamānatthopi veditabbo. Tenevāha “sotāpattiphalasacchikiriyāya paṭipanno”ti.

“Truly, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One!” and so forth shows the manner in which these thoughts arose. The meaning of this is: The Blessed One, the Lord of the world, who, for reasons such as being fortunate, is called ‘Bhagavā,’ has, by himself, rightly and without distortion, awakened to all phenomena—ah, truly a Buddha! That Blessed One teaches the Dhamma for the abandonment of all such suffering of the cycle of rebirth—which is now being experienced by me and by others of this kind—and for its final cessation without re-arising; he teaches the undistorted Dhamma. For it is by teaching the undistorted Dhamma that the Teacher’s perfect self-enlightenment is accomplished. The assembly of the eight noble individuals, which has received the name ‘the Saṅgha of disciples’ because it arose at the end of hearing the Dhamma from that Blessed One who possesses the aforementioned qualities, and because it is united in virtue and view, is truly of good practice—ah, truly of right practice! That Noble Saṅgha has entered upon the irreversible path for the abandonment of such suffering of the cycle of rebirth and for its cessation without re-arising. Nibbāna, which is the escape from all that is conditioned, is truly supreme happiness—ah, truly well and happy!—that Nibbāna in which such suffering of the cycle of rebirth is not found. And here, even those who are still practicing are called ‘those who have practiced’ because their practice is irreversible. Alternatively, like the word ‘arisen,’ the word ‘practiced’ should be understood as having a present tense meaning. Therefore, he said, “one who is practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry.”

Sāmikanti attano patiṃ koliyarājaputtaṃ. Āmantesīti abhāsi. Mama vacanena bhagavato pāde sirasā vandāhīti mayhaṃ vacanena cakkalakkhaṇappaṭimaṇḍitāni vikasitapadumasassirīkāni bhagavato caraṇāni tava sirasā vandāhi, uttamaṅgena abhivādanaṃ karohīti attho. Appābādhantiādīsu ābādhoti visabhāgavedanā vuccati, yā ekadese uppajjitvāpi sakalasarīraṃ ayapaṭṭena ābandhitvā [P 0.0126] viya gaṇhati. Ātaṅkoti kicchajīvitakaro rogo. Atha vā yāpetabbarogo ātaṅko, itaro ābādho. Khuddako vā rogo ātaṅko, balavā [M 0.0111] ābādho. Keci pana “ajjhattasamuṭṭhāno ābādho, bahiddhāsamuṭṭhāno ātaṅko”ti vadanti. Tadubhayassāpi abhāvaṃ pucchāti vadati. Gilānasseva ca uṭṭhānaṃ nāma garukaṃ hoti, kāye balaṃ na hoti, tasmā niggelaññatāya lahuparivattisaṅkhātaṃ kāyassa lahuṭṭhānaṃ sarīrabalañca pucchāti vadati. Phāsuvihāranti ṭhānanisinnagamanasayanasaṅkhātesu catūsu iriyāpathesu sukhavihārañca pucchāti vadati. Athassa pucchitabbākāraṃ dassentī “suppavāsā, bhante”tiādimāha. Evañca vadehīti idāni vattabbākāraṃ nidasseti.

Her husband: her own husband, the Koliyan prince. She addressed: she spoke. “At my word, bow your head to the Blessed One’s feet”: the meaning is, “At my word, bow your head to the Blessed One’s feet, which are adorned with the marks of wheels and possess the splendor of a blooming lotus; perform this act of veneration with your head, the highest part of the body.” Regarding “freedom from affliction” and so forth: “affliction” (ābādha) refers to a discordant feeling, which, even when arising in one part, seizes the entire body as if bound by an iron band. “Ailment” (ātaṅka) is a disease that makes it difficult to live. Alternatively, an ailment is a disease that must be endured, while the other is an affliction. Or, an ailment is a minor disease, while an affliction is a severe one. Some, however, say, “An affliction is one that arises internally, while an ailment is one that arises externally.” She says to ask about the absence of both of these. For a sick person, rising is difficult; there is no strength in the body. Therefore, she says to ask about the lightness of rising, which is called ease of movement due to the absence of sickness, and also about bodily strength. Regarding “dwelling in comfort” (phāsuvihāra), she says to ask about dwelling in comfort in the four postures—standing, sitting, walking, and lying down. Then, indicating the manner in which he should ask, she says, “Suppavāsā, venerable sir,” and so forth. “And thus you should speak”: now she indicates the manner in which he should speak.

Paramanti vacanasampaṭicchanaṃ. Tena sādhu, bhadde, yathā vuttaṃ, tathā paṭipajjāmīti dasseti. Koliyaputtoti suppavāsāya sāmiko koliyarājaputto. Sukhinī hotūti sadevake loke aggadakkhiṇeyyo satthā suppavāsāya pesitavandanaṃ sampaṭicchitvā tadanantaraṃ attano mettāvihārasaṃsūcakaṃ buddhāciṇṇaṃ sukhūpasaṃhāraṃ tassā sāmaññato pakāsetvā puna tassā puttassa ca gabbhavipattimūlakadukkhuppattipaṭikkhepamukhena sukhūpasaṃhāraṃ nidassento “sukhinī…pe… arogā, arogaṃ puttaṃ vijāyatū”ti āha.

'Paramam' means the acceptance of the words. By this, it is shown: 'Good, lady, as it has been said, so shall I practice.' 'Son of the Koliyans' means the Koliyan prince, Suppavāsā’s husband. 'May she be happy'—the Teacher, the foremost worthy of offerings in the world with its deities, having accepted the veneration sent by Suppavāsā, immediately thereafter, having generally shown to her the bringing of happiness, which is the customary practice of the Buddhas and indicative of His own dwelling in loving-kindness, and again, for her and her son, by way of rejecting the arising of suffering rooted in the misfortune of the pregnancy, while pointing out the bringing of happiness, said: 'May she be happy… may she be free from disease, may she give birth to a healthy son.'

Saha [V 0.0100] vacanāti bhagavato vacanena saheva. Yasmiṃ kāle bhagavā tathā avoca, tasmiṃyeva kāle tampi kammaṃ parikkhayaṃ agamāsi. Tassa parikkhīṇabhāvaṃ oloketvā satthā tathā abhāsi. Apare pana vadanti – sace tathā satthā nācikkhissā, tato parampi kiñci kālaṃ tassā taṃ dukkhaṃ anubandhissā. Yasmā pana bhagavatā “sukhinī arogā arogañca puttaṃ vijāyatū”ti vuttaṃ, tasmā tassa vacanasamakālameva so gabbho byākulabhāvaṃ vijahitvā sukheneva bahi nikkhami, evaṃ tesaṃ mātāputtānaṃ sotthi ahosi. Acinteyyo hi buddhānaṃ [P 0.0127] buddhānubhāvo. Yathā hi paṭācārāya piyavippayogasambhūtena sokena ummādaṃ patvā –

'Together with the words' means simultaneously with the Blessed One’s words. At the very moment the Blessed One spoke thus, at that same moment that kamma reached its exhaustion. Seeing its complete exhaustion, the Teacher spoke in that way. But others say: If the Teacher had not declared it, then for some time longer that suffering would have pursued her. However, because the Blessed One said, 'May she be happy, free from illness, and give birth to a healthy son,' at that very moment the fetus, having abandoned its disturbed state, emerged easily. Thus, there was well-being for that mother and son. Indeed, the spiritual power of the Buddhas is inconceivable. Just as in the case of Paṭācārā, who, overwhelmed by grief arising from the loss of her loved ones, fell into madness—

“Ubho puttā kālakatā, panthe mayhaṃ patī mato;

Mātā pitā ca bhātā ca, ekacitakamhi jhāyare”ti. (apa. therī 2.2.498) –

“Both my sons are dead, my husband died on the road; Mother, father, and brother too, all burn on a single pyre.”

Vatvā [M 0.0112] jātarūpeneva carantiyā “satiṃ paṭilabhāhi bhaginī”ti bhagavato vacanasamanantarameva ummādo vūpasami, tathā suppiyāpi upāsikā attanāva attano ūruyaṃ katena mahāvaṇena vuṭṭhātuṃ asakkontī sayanapiṭṭhe nipannā “āgantvā maṃ vandatū”ti vacanasamanantarameva vaṇe pākatike jāte sayameva gantvā bhagavantaṃ vandīti evamādīni vatthūni idha udāharitabbānīti.

Having spoken, as she was wandering about in her natural state, immediately after the Blessed One’s words, 'Sister, regain your mindfulness,' her madness subsided. Similarly, the laywoman Suppiyā, unable to rise from the great wound she had inflicted on her own thigh and lying on her bed, immediately after the words 'Let her come and pay homage to me,' the wound having been healed, she herself went and paid homage to the Blessed One. Such stories as these should be cited here.

Evaṃ, bhanteti, bhante, yathā bhagavā saputtāya mātuyā arogabhāvaṃ āsīsanto āha – “sukhinī arogā arogaṃ puttaṃ vijāyatū”ti, taṃ evameva. Na hi kadāci buddhānaṃ bhagavantānaṃ vacanassa aññathābhāvoti adhippāyo. Keci pana “evamatthū”ti vadanti, apare “hotū”ti padassa atthaṃ ānetvā vaṇṇayanti. Abhinanditvāti karavīkarutamañjunā brahmassarena bhagavatā vuccamāne tasmiṃ vacane pītisomanassapaṭilābhato abhimukhabhāvena nanditvā. Anumoditvāti tato pacchāpi sammodanaṃ uppādetvā, cittena vā abhinanditvā vācāya anumoditvā, vacanasampattiyā vā abhinanditvā atthasampattiyā anumoditvā. Sakaṃ gharaṃ paccāyāsīti attano gharaṃ paṭigacchi. Ye pana “yena sakaṃ ghara”nti paṭhanti, tesaṃ yadipi ya-ta-saddānaṃ sambandhabhāvato “tenā”ti padaṃ vuttameva hoti, tathāpi “paṭiyāyitvā”ti pāṭhaseso yojetabbo hoti.

'Indeed, venerable sir'—this means, venerable sir, as the Blessed One, wishing good health for the mother with her son, said, 'May she be happy and free from illness, may she give birth to a healthy son,' so it is. For never do the words of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, turn out otherwise—this is the intended meaning. Some, however, say, 'May it be thus,' while others explain it by supplying the meaning of the word 'hotu' (may it be). 'Having rejoiced'—he rejoiced in His presence due to the joy and gladness gained upon hearing those words spoken by the Blessed One with a voice as sweet as the karavīka bird’s, a divine voice. 'Having expressed approval'—afterwards, having generated mutual joy, either by rejoicing with the mind and expressing approval with speech, or by rejoicing in the excellence of the words and approving the excellence of the meaning. 'Returned to his own home' means he went back to his own dwelling. For those, however, who read 'yena sakaṃ gharaṃ' (to where his own home was), although the word 'tena' (by that way) is already implied due to the correlative nature of the words 'ya' and 'ta,' the remainder of the reading, 'paṭiyāyitvā' (having returned), should be supplied.

Vijātanti pajātaṃ, pasutanti attho. Acchariyanti andhassa pabbatārohanaṃ viya niccaṃ na [V 0.0101] hotīti acchariyaṃ, ayaṃ tāva saddanayo. Aṭṭhakathāsu pana “accharāyoggaṃ acchariya”nti vuttaṃ[P 0.0128], accharaṃ paharituṃ yuttanti attho. Vatāti sambhāvane, aho acchariyanti attho. Bhoti dhammālapanaṃ. Abhūtapubbaṃ bhūtanti abbhutaṃ.

'Vijātaṃ' means 'pajātaṃ' (born); 'pasutaṃ' (delivered) is the meaning. 'Acchariyaṃ' (marvelous)—like a blind man climbing a mountain, it is not something that happens constantly, hence it is 'acchariyaṃ'. This, to begin with, is the grammatical explanation. In the commentaries, however, it is said: 'Acchariyaṃ is that which is worthy of a finger-snap' (accharāyoggaṃ), meaning it is fit to snap the fingers at. 'Vata' (indeed) is a particle used in the sense of wonder, meaning 'Oh, how marvelous!' 'Bho' (sir) is a respectful form of address. 'Abbhutaṃ' (unprecedented) is that which has come to be, not having been before.

Tathāgatassāti aṭṭhahi kāraṇehi bhagavā tathāgato – tathā āgatoti tathāgato, tathā gatoti tathāgato, tathalakkhaṇaṃ āgatoti tathāgato, tathadhamme yāthāvato abhisambuddhoti tathāgato, tathadassitāya tathāgato, tathavāditāya tathāgato, tathākāritāya tathāgato, abhibhavanaṭṭhena tathāgato.

'Of the Tathāgata'—the Blessed One is called Tathāgata for eight reasons: because he has come thus (tathā āgato); because he has gone thus (tathā gato); because he has arrived at the true characteristic (tathalakkhaṇaṃ āgato); because he has fully awakened to things as they actually are (tathadhamme yāthāvato abhisambuddho); because of seeing truly (tathadassitāya); because of speaking truly (tathavāditāya); because of acting truly (tathākāritāya); and in the sense of having overcome all (abhibhavanaṭṭhena).

Kathaṃ [M 0.0113] bhagavā tathā āgatoti tathāgato? Yathā sabbalokahitāya ussukkamāpannā purimakā sammāsambuddhā āgatāti. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Yena abhinīhārena te bhagavanto āgatā, tena aṭṭhaguṇasamannāgatena ayampi bhagavā āgato. Yathā ca te bhagavanto dānapāramiṃ pūretvā sīlanekkhammapaññāvīriyakhantisaccaadhiṭṭhānamettāupekkhāpāramīti imā dasa pāramiyo, dasa upapāramiyo, dasa paramatthapāramiyoti samatiṃsa pāramiyo pūretvā pañca mahāpariccāge pariccajitvā pubbayogapubbacariyadhammakkhānañātatthacariyādayo pūretvā buddhicariyāya koṭiṃ patvā āgatā, tathā ayampi bhagavā āgato. Yathā ca te bhagavanto cattāro satipaṭṭhāne…pe… ariyaṃ aṭṭhaṅgikaṃ maggaṃ bhāvetvā brūhetvā āgatā, tathā ayampi bhagavā āgato. Evaṃ tathā āgatoti tathāgato.

How is the Blessed One called Tathāgata because he has thus come (tathā āgato)? Just as the previous Perfectly Self-Enlightened Ones came, having undertaken the endeavor for the welfare of the whole world. What is meant by this? By whichever aspiration endowed with eight qualities those Blessed Ones came, by that same aspiration this Blessed One has also come. And just as those Blessed Ones came, having fulfilled the ten perfections—giving, morality, renunciation, wisdom, energy, patience, truthfulness, determination, loving-kindness, and equanimity—along with the ten subsidiary perfections and the ten ultimate perfections, making thirty perfections in total; having made the five great relinquishments; having fulfilled prior endeavors, prior conduct, the expounding of the Dhamma, conduct for the welfare of relatives, and so forth; and having reached the culmination of the conduct for Buddhahood, so too has this Blessed One come. And just as those Blessed Ones came, having developed and cultivated the four foundations of mindfulness... and the Noble Eightfold Path, so too has this Blessed One come. In this way, he is the Tathāgata because he has thus come.

Kathaṃ tathā gatoti tathāgato? Yathā sampatijātā te bhagavanto samehi pādehi pathaviyaṃ patiṭṭhāya uttarābhimukhā sattapadavītihārena gatā, setacchatte dhāriyamāne sabbāva disā anuvilokesuṃ, āsabhiñca [P 0.0129] vācaṃ bhāsiṃsu loke attano jeṭṭhaseṭṭhabhāvaṃ pakāsentā, tañca nesaṃ gamanaṃ tathaṃ ahosi avitathaṃ anekesaṃ visesādhigamānaṃ pubbanimittabhāvena, tathā ayampi bhagavā gato, tañcassa gamanaṃ kathaṃ ahosi avitathaṃ tesaññeva visesādhigamānaṃ pubbanimittabhāvena. Evaṃ tathā gatoti tathāgato.

How is he the Tathāgata because he has 'thus gone' (tathā gato)? Just as those Blessed Ones, immediately after birth, having stood firmly on the ground with even feet, went forward seven steps facing north, while a white parasol was held over them, surveyed all directions, and uttered the bull-like utterance proclaiming their state as chief and best in the world—and that going of theirs was true, not false, serving as a premonitory sign for the attainment of many distinctions—so too has this Blessed One gone. And his going was likewise true, not false, serving as a premonitory sign for the attainment of those very distinctions. Thus, he is the Tathāgata because he has 'thus gone'.

Yathā vā te bhagavanto nekkhammena kāmacchandaṃ pahāya gatā, abyāpādena byāpādaṃ, ālokasaññāya thinamiddhaṃ, avikkhepena uddhaccakukkuccaṃ, dhammavavatthānena vicikicchaṃ pahāya gatā, ñāṇena avijjaṃ padāletvā, pāmojjena aratiṃ vinodetvā, aṭṭhasamāpattīhi aṭṭhārasahi mahāvipassanāhi [V 0.0102] catūhi ca ariyamaggehi taṃ taṃ paṭipakkhaṃ pahāya gatā, evaṃ ayampi bhagavā gato. Evampi tathā gatoti tathāgato.

Or, just as those Blessed Ones went, having abandoned sensual desire through renunciation, ill will through non-ill will, sloth and torpor through the perception of light, restlessness and remorse through non-distraction, and doubt through the discrimination of phenomena; having pierced ignorance by means of knowledge, having dispelled discontent by means of joy; and having abandoned each respective opposing state by means of the eight attainments, the eighteen great insights, and the four Noble Paths—so too has this Blessed One gone. In this way also, he is the Tathāgata because he has 'thus gone'.

Kathaṃ tathalakkhaṇaṃ āgatoti tathāgato? Pathavīdhātuyā kakkhaḷalakkhaṇaṃ, āpodhātuyā paggharaṇalakkhaṇaṃ, tejodhātuyā uṇhattalakkhaṇaṃ, vāyodhātuyā vitthambhanalakkhaṇaṃ, ākāsadhātuyā asamphuṭṭhalakkhaṇaṃ, rūpassa ruppanalakkhaṇaṃ, vedanāya vedayitalakkhaṇaṃ, saññāya sañjānanalakkhaṇaṃ, saṅkhārānaṃ abhisaṅkharaṇalakkhaṇaṃ, viññāṇassa vijānanalakkhaṇanti [M 0.0114] evaṃ pañcannaṃ khandhānaṃ, dvādasannaṃ āyatanānaṃ, aṭṭhārasannaṃ dhātūnaṃ, bāvīsatiyā indriyānaṃ, catunnaṃ saccānaṃ, dvādasapadikassa paccayākārassa, catunnaṃ satipaṭṭhānānaṃ, catunnaṃ sammappadhānānaṃ, catunnaṃ iddhipādānaṃ, pañcannaṃ indriyānaṃ, pañcannaṃ balānaṃ, sattannaṃ bojjhaṅgānaṃ, ariyassa aṭṭhaṅgikassa maggassa, sattannaṃ visuddhīnaṃ, amatogadhassa nibbānassāti evaṃ tassa tassa dhammassa yaṃ sabhāvasarasalakkhaṇaṃ, taṃ tathaṃ avitathaṃ anaññathaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ ñāṇagatiyā āgato avirajjhitvā patto adhigatoti tathāgato. Evaṃ tathalakkhaṇaṃ āgatoti tathāgato.

How is he the Tathāgata because he has 'arrived at the true characteristic' (tathalakkhaṇaṃ āgato)? The characteristic of hardness for the earth element, the characteristic of flowing for the water element, the characteristic of heat for the fire element, the characteristic of supporting for the wind element, the characteristic of non-impingement for the space element; the characteristic of being afflicted for form, the characteristic of being felt for feeling, the characteristic of perceiving for perception, the characteristic of compounding for formations, the characteristic of cognizing for consciousness—thus, for each and every phenomenon, whether the five aggregates, the twelve sense bases, the eighteen elements, the twenty-two faculties, the four truths, the twelve-linked dependent origination, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right exertions, the four bases of spiritual power, the five spiritual faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, the Noble Eightfold Path, the seven stages of purification, or the Deathless Nibbāna—whatever its intrinsic and essential characteristic may be, that true, unerring, and unmistakable characteristic he has arrived at by the path of knowledge, attained it without deviation, and realized it. Thus, he is the Tathāgata because he has 'arrived at the true characteristic'.

Kathaṃ tathadhamme yāthāvato abhisambuddhoti tathāgato? Tathadhammā nāma cattāri ariyasaccāni. Yathāha [P 0.0130] – “cattārimāni, bhikkhave, tathāni avitathāni anaññathāni. Katamāni cattāri? Idaṃ dukkhanti, bhikkhave, tathametaṃ avitathametaṃ anaññathameta”nti (saṃ. ni. 5.1090) vitthāro. Tāni ca bhagavā abhisambuddho, tasmā tathānaṃ abhisambuddhattā tathāgato.

How is he the Tathāgata because he has 'fully awakened to the true phenomena as they really are' (tathadhamme yāthāvato abhisambuddho)? The true phenomena are the Four Noble Truths. As it is said: “Monks, these four things are true, unerring, not otherwise. What four? ‘This is suffering,’ monks, this is true, this is unerring, this is not otherwise…” (SN 5.430) and so on in detail. And the Blessed One has fully awakened to these truths. Therefore, because of having fully awakened to these true phenomena, he is the Tathāgata.

Apica jarāmaraṇassa jātipaccayasambhūtasamudāgataṭṭho tatho avitatho anaññatho…pe… saṅkhārānaṃ avijjāpaccayasambhūtasamudāgataṭṭho tatho avitatho anaññatho, tathā avijjāya saṅkhārānaṃ paccayaṭṭho…pe... jātiyā jarāmaraṇassa paccayaṭṭho tatho avitatho anaññatho, taṃ sabbaṃ bhagavā abhisambuddho, tasmāpi tathānaṃ abhisambuddhattā tathāgato. Abhisambuddhattho hi ettha gatasaddoti. Evaṃ tathadhamme yāthāvato abhisambuddhoti tathāgato.

Moreover, the fact that aging and death are produced and have come to be from birth as their condition is true, unerring, not otherwise... (and so on)... the fact that formations are produced and have come to be from ignorance as their condition is true, unerring, not otherwise. Likewise, the fact that ignorance is a condition for formations... (and so on)... the fact that birth is a condition for aging and death is true, unerring, not otherwise. The Blessed One has fully awakened to all of this. Therefore, also because of having fully awakened to these true phenomena, he is the Tathāgata. For in this context, the word 'gata' has the meaning of 'fully awakened'. Thus, he is the Tathāgata because he has 'fully awakened to the true phenomena as they really are'.

Kathaṃ tathadassitāya tathāgato? Yaṃ sadevake…pe… sadevamanussāya pajāya aparimāṇāsu lokadhātūsu aparimāṇānaṃ sattānaṃ cakkhudvāre āpāthamāgacchantaṃ rūpārammaṇaṃ nāma atthi, taṃ bhagavā sabbākārato jānāti passati. Evaṃ jānatā passatā ca tena taṃ iṭṭhāniṭṭhādivasena vā diṭṭhasutamutaviññātesu labbhamānakapadavasena vā “katamaṃ taṃ rūpaṃ rūpāyatanaṃ[V 0.0103], yaṃ rūpaṃ catunnaṃ mahābhūtānaṃ upādāya vaṇṇanibhā sanidassanaṃ sappaṭighaṃ nīlaṃ pītaka”ntiādinā (dha. sa. 616) nayena anekehi nāmehi terasahi vārehi dvipaññāsāya nayehi vibhajjamānaṃ tathameva hoti, vitathaṃ natthi. Esa nayo sotadvārādīsu āpāthamāgacchantesu saddādīsu. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā –

How is he the Tathāgata by virtue of 'seeing what is true' (tathadassitāya)? Whatever visible object there is that comes into the range of the eye-door of countless beings in infinite world-systems, in the world with its devas... with its devas and humans, the Blessed One knows and sees it in all its aspects. And as he thus knows and sees, that object—whether in terms of being agreeable or disagreeable, or in terms of the designations obtainable in what is seen, heard, sensed, and cognized—when analyzed as “What is that form, that form-base? The form which is derived from the four great elements, has color and appearance, is visible and resistant, such as blue, yellow,” and so forth (Dhs § 585), by means of numerous names, thirteen sections, and fifty-two methods, is just so (tatha), it is not otherwise (vitatha). This same method applies to sounds and other objects that come into the range of the ear-door and so on. For this has been said by the Blessed One:

“Yaṃ[M 0.0115], bhikkhave, sadevakassa lokassa…pe… sadevamanussāya diṭṭhaṃ sutaṃ mutaṃ viññātaṃ pattaṃ pariyesitaṃ anuvicaritaṃ manasā, tamahaṃ jānāmi, tamahaṃ abbhaññāsiṃ, taṃ tathāgatassa viditaṃ, taṃ tathāgato na upaṭṭhāsī”ti (a. ni. 4.24).

“Monks, whatever in the world with its devas... with its devas and humans, is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought, and mentally investigated—that I know, that I have directly known. That is known to the Tathāgata; it is present to the Tathāgata.” (cf. AN 4.24)

Evaṃ tathadassitāya tathāgato[P 0.0131]. Tattha tathadassīatthe tathāgatoti padasambhavo veditabbo.

Thus, he is the Tathāgata by virtue of 'seeing what is true' (tathadassitāya). Herein, the formation of the word 'Tathāgata' should be understood in the sense of 'one who sees thus' (tathadassī).

Kathaṃ tathavāditāya tathāgato? Yaṃ rattiṃ bhagavā anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ abhisambuddho, yañca rattiṃ anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā parinibbāyi, etthantare pañcacattālīsavassaparimāṇakālaṃ yaṃ bhagavatā bhāsitaṃ lapitaṃ suttageyyādi, sabbaṃ taṃ parisuddhaṃ paripuṇṇaṃ rāgamadādinimmathanaṃ ekasadisaṃ tathaṃ avitathaṃ. Tenāha –

How is he the Tathāgata by virtue of 'speaking what is true' (tathavāditāya)? In the interval between the night the Blessed One fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment and the night he passed into the Nibbāna-element without residue remaining—during this period of forty-five years—whatever was spoken and uttered by the Blessed One, such as suttas, geyyas, and so on, all of it is completely pure, complete, a crusher of passion, intoxication, and the like, of a single uniform nature, true, and unerring. Therefore, he said:

“Yañca, cunda, rattiṃ tathāgato anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ abhisambujjhati, yañca rattiṃ anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā parinibbāyati, yaṃ etasmiṃ antare bhāsati lapati niddisati, sabbaṃ taṃ tatheva hoti, no aññathā, tasmā ‘tathāgato’ti vuccatī”ti (dī. ni. 3.188).

“Cunda, on the night the Tathāgata fully awakens to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, and on the night he attains final Nibbāna through the Nibbāna-element without remainder—whatever he speaks, utters, and declares in the interim is just so and not otherwise. Therefore, he is called ‘Tathāgata.’”

Gadaattho ettha gatasaddo. Evaṃ tathavāditāya tathāgato.

Here, the word ‘gata’ has the meaning of ‘gada’ (spoken). Thus, he is the Tathāgata by virtue of speaking what is true.

Apica āgadanaṃ āgado, vacananti attho. Tatho avitatho aviparīto āgado assāti dakārassa takāraṃ katvā tathāgatoti evamettha padasiddhi veditabbā.

Furthermore, ‘āgadanaṃ’ is ‘āgado,’ meaning ‘speech.’ Because his speech (āgada) is true (tatha), unfailing, and not contrary, by changing the letter ‘d’ to ‘t,’ the term ‘Tathāgata’ is formed. Thus should the derivation of the word be understood here.

Kathaṃ tathākāritāya tathāgato? Bhagavato hi vācāya kāyo anulometi, kāyassapi vācā, tasmā yathāvādī tathākārī, yathākārī tathāvādī ca hoti. Evaṃbhūtassa cassa yathāvācā, kāyopi tathā gato pavattoti attho. Yathā ca kāyo, vācāpi tathā gatā pavattāti tathāgato. Tenāha –

How is he the Tathāgata by virtue of acting accordingly? Indeed, for the Blessed One, the body conforms to his speech, and the speech to his body. Therefore, as he speaks, so he acts; and as he acts, so he speaks. For one who is such, his body proceeds (gato) in accordance with his speech, and his speech proceeds (gatā) in accordance with his body; thus, he is the Tathāgata. Therefore, he said:

“Yathāvādī[V 0.0104], bhikkhave, tathāgato tathākārī, yathākārī tathāvādī. Iti yathāvādī tathākārī, yathākārī tathāvādī. Tasmā ‘tathāgato’ti vuccatī”ti (a. ni. 4.23).

“Monks, as the Tathāgata speaks, so he acts; as he acts, so he speaks. Thus, as he speaks, so he acts; as he acts, so he speaks. Therefore, he is called ‘Tathāgata.’”

Evaṃ [M 0.0116] tathākāritāya tathāgato.

Thus, he is the Tathāgata by virtue of acting accordingly.

Kathaṃ abhibhavanaṭṭhena tathāgato? Yasmā upari bhavaggaṃ heṭṭhā avīciṃ pariyantaṃ karitvā tiriyaṃ aparimāṇāsu lokadhātūsu sabbasatte abhibhavati sīlenapi samādhināpi paññāyapi vimuttiyāpi vimuttiñāṇadassanenapi[P 0.0132], na tassa tulā vā pamāṇaṃ vā atthi, atha kho atulo appameyyo anuttaro devadevo sakkānaṃ atisakko, brahmānaṃ atibrahmā sabbasattuttamo, tasmā tathāgato. Tenāha –

How is he the Tathāgata in the sense of overcoming? Because, from the peak of existence above to the Avīci hell below, and across the immeasurable world-systems, he overcomes all beings through virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation. There is no one equal to him or any measure of him. Indeed, he is unequaled, immeasurable, unsurpassed, the god of gods, beyond Sakka, beyond Brahmā, the highest of all beings. Therefore, he is the Tathāgata. Therefore, he said:

“Sadevake, bhikkhave, loke…pe… sadevamanussāya tathāgato abhibhū anabhibhūto aññadatthudaso vasavatti, tasmā ‘tathāgato’ti vuccatī”ti (a. ni. 4.23).

“Monks, in the world with its gods… the Tathāgata is the overcomer, unovercome, the all-seeing, the wielder of power. Therefore, he is called ‘Tathāgata.’”

Tatrāyaṃ padasiddhi – agado viya agado, desanāvilāso ceva puññussayo ca. Tena so mahānubhāvo bhisakko viya dibbāgadena sappe sabbaparappavādino sadevakañca lokaṃ abhibhavati. Iti sabbalokābhibhavane tatho avitatho aviparīto yathāvuttova agado etassāti dakārassa takāraṃ katvā tathāgatoti veditabbo. Evaṃ abhibhavanaṭṭhena tathāgato.

Herein, this is the derivation of the term: ‘agado’ (a medicine), like a medicine. This ‘agado’ is both the elegance of his teaching and the excellence of his merit. With this, like a greatly powerful physician with divine medicine overcomes snakes, he overcomes all who hold other doctrines and the world with its gods. Thus, because in overcoming all the world he possesses this ‘agada’ which is ‘tatha’ (true), unfailing, and not contrary, as has been said, by changing the letter ‘d’ to ‘t,’ he should be understood as ‘Tathāgata.’ Thus, he is the Tathāgata in the sense of overcoming.

Apica tathāya gatoti tathāgato, tathaṃ gatoti tathāgato. Tattha sakalalokaṃ tīraṇapariññāya tathāya gato avagatoti tathāgato. Lokasamudayaṃ pahānapariññāya tathāya gato atītoti tathāgato. Lokanirodhaṃ sacchikiriyāya tathāya gato adhigatoti tathāgato. Lokanirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadaṃ tathaṃ gato paṭipannoti tathāgato. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā –

Furthermore, he is the Tathāgata because he has ‘gone by way of truth’ (tathāya gato), and because he has ‘gone in such a way’ (tathaṃ gato). Herein, he is the Tathāgata because he has truly understood the entire world through the full understanding of judgment. He is the Tathāgata because he has truly transcended the origin of the world through the full understanding of abandoning. He is the Tathāgata because he has truly attained the cessation of the world through realization. He is the Tathāgata because he has practiced the path leading to the cessation of the world in such a way. This was said by the Blessed One:

“Loko, bhikkhave, tathāgatena abhisambuddho, lokasmā tathāgato visaṃyutto. Lokasamudayo, bhikkhave, tathāgatena abhisambuddho, lokasamudayo tathāgatassa pahīno, lokanirodho, bhikkhave, tathāgatena abhisambuddho, lokanirodho tathāgatassa sacchikato. Lokanirodhagāminī paṭipadā[V 0.0105], bhikkhave, tathāgatena abhisambuddhā[P 0.0133], lokanirodhagāminī paṭipadā tathāgatassa bhāvitā. Yaṃ, bhikkhave[M 0.0117], sadevakassa lokassa…pe… sabbaṃ taṃ tathāgatena abhisambuddhaṃ. Tasmā ‘tathāgato’ti vuccatī”ti (a. ni. 4.23).

“Monks, the world has been fully understood by the Tathāgata; the Tathāgata is disengaged from the world. The origin of the world, monks, has been fully understood by the Tathāgata; the origin of the world has been abandoned by the Tathāgata. The cessation of the world, monks, has been fully understood by the Tathāgata; the cessation of the world has been realized by the Tathāgata. The path leading to the cessation of the world, monks, has been fully understood by the Tathāgata; the path leading to the cessation of the world has been developed by the Tathāgata. Monks, whatever there is in the world with its gods… all that has been fully understood by the Tathāgata. Therefore, he is called ‘Tathāgata.’”

Aparehipi aṭṭhahi kāraṇehi bhagavā tathāgato – tathāya āgatoti tathāgato, tathāya gatoti tathāgato, tathāni āgatoti tathāgato, tathā gatoti tathāgato, tathāvidhoti tathāgato, tathā pavattitoti tathāgato, tathehi agatoti tathāgato, tathā gatabhāvena tathāgato.

The Blessed One is also the Tathāgata for eight other reasons: because he has come by way of truth (tathāya āgato); because he has gone by way of truth (tathāya gato); because he has come to the truths (tathāni āgato); because he has gone in such a way (tathā gato); because he is of such a nature (tathāvidho); because he proceeds in such a way (tathā pavattito); because he has not gone from the truths (tathehi agato); and because of the state of having gone in such a way (tathā gatabhāvena).

Kathaṃ tathāya āgatoti tathāgato? Yā sā bhagavatā sumedhabhūtena dīpaṅkaradasabalassa pādamūle –

How is he the Tathāgata because he has ‘come by way of truth’? When the Blessed One, as the wise Sumedha, was at the feet of Dīpaṅkara, the one with the ten powers—

“Manussattaṃ liṅgasampatti, hetu satthāradassanaṃ,

Pabbajjā guṇasampatti, adhikāro ca chandatā;

Aṭṭhadhammasamodhānā, abhinīhāro samijjhatī”ti. (bu. vaṃ. 2.59) –

“Human existence, perfection of gender, a cause, the sight of the Teacher, renunciation, accomplishment of virtues, a meritorious deed, and aspiration; with the convergence of these eight conditions, the resolution is fulfilled.”

Evaṃ vuttaṃ aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgataṃ abhinīhāraṃ sampādentena “ahaṃ sadevakaṃ lokaṃ tiṇṇo tāressāmi, mutto mocessāmi, danto damessāmi, santo samessāmi, assattho assāsessāmi, parinibbuto parinibbāpessāmi, buddho bodhessāmī”ti mahāpaṭiññā pavattitā. Vuttañhetaṃ –

Having fulfilled this eight-factored aspiration, he made the great proclamation: “Having crossed over, I will lead the world with its gods across. Freed, I will free them. Tamed, I will tame them. Pacified, I will pacify them. Comforted, I will comfort them. Fully extinguished, I will lead them to full extinguishment. Awakened, I will awaken them.” This was said:

“Kiṃ me ekena tiṇṇena, purisena thāmadassinā;

Sabbaññutaṃ pāpuṇitvā, santāressaṃ sadevakaṃ.

“What use is it for me, a man of strength and vision, to cross over alone? Having attained omniscience, I will lead the world with its gods across.”

“Iminā me adhikārena, katena purisuttame;

Sabbaññutaṃ pāpuṇitvā, tāremi janataṃ bahuṃ.

“By this meritorious deed of mine, performed before the Supreme Man, may I, attaining omniscience, lead many people across.”

“Saṃsārasotaṃ chinditvā, viddhaṃsetvā tayo bhave;

Dhammanāvaṃ samāruyha, santāressaṃ sadevakaṃ.

“Having cut the stream of saṃsāra, having shattered the three planes of existence, I will board the ship of the Dhamma and lead the world with its gods across.”

“Kiṃ me aññātavesena, dhammaṃ sacchikatenidha;

Sabbaññutaṃ pāpuṇitvā, buddho hessaṃ sadevake”ti. (bu. vaṃ. 2.55-58);

“What use is it for me to realize the Dhamma here in an unknown guise? Having attained omniscience, I will become a Buddha in the world with its gods.”

Taṃ [V 0.0106] panetaṃ mahāpaṭiññaṃ sakalassāpi buddhakaradhammasamudāyassa pavicaya paccavekkhaṇasamādānānaṃ kāraṇabhūtaṃ [P 0.0134] avisaṃvādetvā lokanāyako yasmā mahākappānaṃ satasahassādhikāni cattāri asaṅkhyeyyāni sakkaccaṃ [M 0.0118] nirantaraṃ niravasesato dānapāramiādayo samatiṃsapāramiyo pūretvā, aṅgapariccāgādayo pañca mahāpariccāge pariccajitvā, saccādhiṭṭhānādīni cattāri adhiṭṭhānāni paribrūhetvā, puññañāṇasambhāre sambharitvā, pubbayogapubbacariyadhammakkhānañātatthacariyādayo ukkaṃsāpetvā, buddhicariyaṃ paramakoṭiṃ pāpetvā, anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ abhisambujjhi, tasmā tasseva sā mahāpaṭiññā tathā avitathā anaññathā, na tassa vālaggamattampi vitathaṃ atthi. Tathā hi dīpaṅkaradasabalo koṇḍañño maṅgalo…pe… kassapo bhagavāti ime catuvīsati sammāsambuddhā paṭipāṭiyā uppannā “buddho bhavissatī”ti byākariṃsu. Evaṃ catuvīsatiyā buddhānaṃ santike laddhabyākaraṇo ye te katābhinīhārehi bodhisattehi laddhabbā ānisaṃsā, te labhitvāva āgatoti tāya yathāvuttāya mahāpaṭiññāya tathāya abhisambuddhabhāvaṃ āgato adhigatoti tathāgato. Evaṃ tathāya āgatoti tathāgato.

This great vow, which serves as the foundation for the entire collection of qualities that bring about Buddhahood—examining, reflecting, and undertaking them—the Leader of the World fulfilled without fail. For four incalculables and a hundred thousand great eons, he diligently, continuously, and completely perfected the thirty perfections, beginning with the perfection of generosity. He relinquished the five great sacrifices, such as giving up limbs. He fully developed the four resolutions, including the resolve on truth. He accumulated the stores of merit and wisdom. He exalted previous efforts, past conduct, the declaration of the Dhamma, and conduct for the welfare of relatives. He brought the conduct for Buddhahood to its ultimate peak. Thus, he attained unsurpassed perfect enlightenment. Therefore, this great vow of his was true, not false, not otherwise—not even a hair’s breadth of falsehood exists in it. Indeed, the twenty-four Perfectly Enlightened Ones—from Dīpaṅkara, the Ten-Powered One, Koṇḍañña, Maṅgala, up to Kassapa, the Blessed One—arose in succession and prophesied, “He will become a Buddha.” Having received such prophecies from these twenty-four Buddhas, he attained all the benefits that should be gained by Bodhisattas who have made their resolve. Having thus come to and attained the state of perfect enlightenment in accordance with that aforesaid true, great vow, he is called the Tathāgata. In this way, because he has come in accordance with truth, he is the Tathāgata.

Kathaṃ tathāya gatoti tathāgato? Yāya mahākaruṇāya lokanātho mahādukkhasambādhappaṭipannaṃ sattanikāyaṃ disvā “tassa natthañño koci paṭissaraṇaṃ, ahameva namito saṃsāradukkhato mutto mocessāmī”ti samussāhitamānaso mahābhinīhāramakāsi. Katvā ca yathāpaṇidhānaṃ sakalalokahitasampādanāya ussukkamāpanno attano kāyajīvitanirapekkho paresaṃ sotapathāgamanamattenapi cittutrāsasamuppādikā atidukkarā dukkaracariyā samācaranto yathā mahābodhiyā paṭipatti hānabhāgiyā saṃkilesabhāgiyā ṭhitibhāgiyā vā na hoti, atha kho uttaruttari visesabhāgiyāva hoti, tathā paṭipajjamāno anupubbena niravasese bodhisambhāre sampādetvā abhisambodhiṃ pāpuṇi. Tato parañca tāyeva mahākaruṇāya sañcoditamānaso pavivekaratiṃ paramañca santaṃ vimokkhasukhaṃ pahāya bālajanabahule loke tehi samuppāditaṃ sammānāvamānavippakāraṃ agaṇetvā vineyyajanassa vinayanena niravasesaṃ buddhakiccaṃ [P 0.0135] niṭṭhapesi. Tattha yo bhagavato sattesu mahākaruṇāya samokkamanākāro, so parato āvibhavissati. Yathā ca buddhabhūtassa [M 0.0119] lokanāthassa sattesu mahākaruṇā, evaṃ bodhisattabhūtassapi mahābhinīhārakālādīsūti sabbattha sabbadā ca ekasadisatāya tathā avitathā anaññathā, tasmā tīsupi avatthāsu sabbasattesu samānarasāya tathāya mahākaruṇāya sakalalokahitāya gato paṭipannoti tathāgato. Evaṃ tathāya gatoti tathāgato.

How is he the Tathāgata, in the sense that he has practiced truthfully? It is because the Lord of the World, with that great compassion, seeing the multitude of beings fallen into great suffering and distress, with a mind uplifted, made the great resolve, thinking, “There is no other refuge for them; I alone, having first been freed from this suffering of saṃsāra, will free them.” Having made this resolve, in accordance with his aspiration, he devoted himself to accomplishing the welfare of the entire world. Disregarding his own body and life, he performed extremely difficult and arduous practices, such that even the mere hearing of them would arouse terror in the minds of others. Just as the practice for great enlightenment is not of a nature that partakes of decline, defilement, or stagnation, but rather partakes of ever-increasing distinction, so did he practice. Gradually fulfilling all the requisites for enlightenment without remainder, he attained full enlightenment. Thereafter, moved by that same great compassion, abandoning the delight of solitude and the supreme, peaceful bliss of liberation, and disregarding the various kinds of honor, dishonor, and mistreatment produced by the multitude of foolish people in the world, he fully accomplished the entire task of a Buddha by training those who could be trained. Herein, the manner in which the Blessed One's great compassion deeply pervaded beings will become clear later. Just as the great compassion of the Lord of the World for beings when he became a Buddha, so too was it for him as a Bodhisatta from the time of his great resolve onwards. In all circumstances and at all times, it was uniform, true, unfailing, and unalterable. Therefore, in all three states, with that true compassion of equal essence towards all beings, he has gone forth and practiced for the welfare of the entire world; thus he is the Tathāgata. Thus, because he has practiced truthfully, he is the Tathāgata.

Kathaṃ tathāni āgatoti tathāgato? Tathāni nāma cattāri ariyamaggañāṇāni. Tāni hi [V 0.0107] idaṃ dukkhaṃ, ayaṃ dukkhasamudayo, ayaṃ dukkhanirodho, ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadāti evaṃ sabbañeyyadhammasaṅgāhakānaṃ pavattinivattitadubhayahetubhūtānaṃ catunnaṃ ariyasaccānaṃ dukkhassa pīḷanaṭṭho saṅkhataṭṭho santāpaṭṭho vipariṇāmaṭṭho, samudayassa āyūhanaṭṭho nidānaṭṭho saṃyogaṭṭho palibodhaṭṭho, nirodhassa nissaraṇaṭṭho vivekaṭṭho asaṅkhataṭṭho amataṭṭho, maggassa niyyānaṭṭho hetvaṭṭho dassanaṭṭho ādhipateyyaṭṭhotiādīnaṃ tabbibhāgānañca yathābhūtasabhāvāvabodhavibandhakassa saṃkilesapakkhassa samucchindanena paṭiladdhāya tattha asammohābhisamayasaṅkhātāya aviparītākārappavattiyā dhammānaṃ sabhāvasarasalakkhaṇassa avisaṃvādanato tathāni avitathāni anaññathāni, tāni bhagavā anaññaneyyo sayameva āgato adhigato, tasmā tathāni āgatoti tathāgato.

How is he the Tathāgata, in the sense that he has come to the truths? ‘The truths’ (tathāni) refers to the four knowledges of the noble path. For these—namely, ‘This is suffering,’ ‘This is the origin of suffering,’ ‘This is the cessation of suffering,’ ‘This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering’—are the four Noble Truths which encompass all knowable phenomena, being the cause of both arising and ceasing. Regarding these, suffering has the characteristic of oppression, of being conditioned, of torment, of change; the origin has the characteristic of accumulation, of being a cause, of connection, of obstruction; cessation has the characteristic of escape, of seclusion, of being unconditioned, of deathlessness; the path has the characteristic of leading out, of being a cause, of seeing, of sovereignty—and so on with their specific distinctions. Because they do not deviate from the inherent nature, function, and essential characteristic of phenomena—which is realized through a non-perverted mode of operation designated as the comprehension of non-delusion, attained by eradicating the faction of defilements that obstructs the understanding of the true nature of things—they are true, unfailing, and unalterable. The Blessed One, not being led by another, came to and attained these truths by himself. Therefore, because he has come to the truths, he is the Tathāgata.

Yathā ca maggañāṇāni, evaṃ bhagavato tīsu kālesu appaṭihatañāṇāni catupaṭisambhidāñāṇāni catuvesārajjañāṇāni pañcagatiparicchedañāṇāni chaasādhāraṇañāṇāni sattabojjhaṅgavibhāvanañāṇāni aṭṭhamaggaṅgavibhāvanañāṇāni navānupubbavihārasamāpattiñāṇāni dasabalañāṇāni ca tathabhāve veditabbāni.

And just as the knowledges of the path, so too should the Blessed One’s unobstructed knowledges concerning the three times, the four analytical knowledges, the four kinds of intrepidity, the knowledge of discerning the five destinations, the six uncommon knowledges, the knowledge of the analysis of the seven factors of enlightenment, the knowledge of the analysis of the eight factors of the path, the knowledges of the nine successive meditative attainments, and the knowledges of the ten powers, be understood as being true.

Tatrāyaṃ vibhāvanā – yañhi kiñci aparimāṇāsu lokadhātūsu aparimāṇānaṃ sattānaṃ hīnādibhedabhinnāsu atītāsu khandhāyatanadhātūsu sabhāvakiccādi [P 0.0136] avatthāvisesādi khandhappaṭibaddhanāmagottādi ca jānitabbaṃ. Anindriyabaddhesu ca atisukhumatirohitavidūradesesupi rūpadhammesu yo taṃtaṃpaccayavisesehi saddhiṃ paccayuppannānaṃ vaṇṇasaṇṭhānagandharasaphassādiviseso, tattha sabbattheva hatthatale ṭhapitaāmalake viya [M 0.0120] paccakkhato appaṭihataṃ bhagavato ñāṇaṃ pavattati, tathā anāgatāsu paccuppannāsu cāti imāni tīsu kālesu appaṭihatañāṇāni nāma. Yathāha –

Herein, this is the detailed explanation: Whatever is to be known in the immeasurable world systems concerning the past aggregates, sense bases, and elements of immeasurable beings, who are differentiated by distinctions such as inferior and so forth—their inherent nature, function, specific states, and the names, clans, and so on connected with the aggregates; and whatever specific distinctions of color, shape, smell, taste, touch, and so on, of conditioned phenomena that arise together with their respective particular conditions, even in material phenomena not bound to the sense faculties that are extremely subtle, hidden, or in distant regions—in all these, the Blessed One’s knowledge operates directly and unimpededly, like a myrobalan fruit placed in the palm of the hand. So too concerning the future and the present. These are called the unimpeded knowledges concerning the three times. As it is said:

“Atītaṃse buddhassa bhagavato appaṭihataṃ ñāṇaṃ, anāgataṃse buddhassa bhagavato appaṭihataṃ ñāṇaṃ, paccuppannaṃse buddhassa bhagavato appaṭihataṃ ñāṇa”nti (paṭi. ma. 3.5).

“Regarding the past, the Blessed One, the Buddha, has unimpeded knowledge; regarding the future, the Blessed One, the Buddha, has unimpeded knowledge; regarding the present, the Blessed One, the Buddha, has unimpeded knowledge.”

Tāni panetāni tattha tattha dhammānaṃ sabhāvasarasalakkhaṇassa avisaṃvādanato tathāni avitathāni anaññathāni, tāni bhagavā sayambhūñāṇena adhigañchīti. Evampi tathāni āgatoti tathāgato.

Moreover, these knowledges are true, unfailing, and unalterable, because of their non-deviation from the inherent nature, function, and characteristic of phenomena in their respective spheres. The Blessed One attained them through his self-originated knowledge. In this way too, because he has come to that which is true, he is the Tathāgata.

Tathā [V 0.0108] atthappaṭisambhidā dhammappaṭisambhidā niruttippaṭisambhidā paṭibhānappaṭisambhidāti catasso paṭisambhidā. Tattha atthappabhedassa sallakkhaṇavibhāvanavavatthānakaraṇasamatthaṃ atthappabhedagataṃ ñāṇaṃ atthappaṭisambhidā. Dhammappabhedassa sallakkhaṇavibhāvanavavatthānakaraṇasamatthaṃ dhammappabhedagataṃ ñāṇaṃ dhammappaṭisambhidā. Niruttippabhedassa sallakkhaṇavibhāvanavavatthānakaraṇasamatthaṃ niruttābhilāpe pabhedagataṃ ñāṇaṃ niruttippaṭisambhidā. Paṭibhānappabhedassa sallakkhaṇavibhāvanavavatthānakaraṇasamatthaṃ paṭibhānappabhedagataṃ ñāṇaṃ paṭibhānappaṭisambhidā. Vuttañhetaṃ –

Likewise, there are these four analytical knowledges: analytical knowledge of meaning, analytical knowledge of the Dhamma, analytical knowledge of language, and analytical knowledge of ready wit. Therein, the knowledge relating to the diversity of meaning, capable of noting well, analyzing, and determining, is the analytical knowledge of meaning. The knowledge relating to the diversity of the Dhamma, capable of noting well, analyzing, and determining, is the analytical knowledge of the Dhamma. The knowledge relating to the diversity of language, capable of noting well, analyzing, and determining, which is knowledge concerning diversity in expression, is the analytical knowledge of language. The knowledge relating to the diversity of ready wit, capable of noting well, analyzing, and determining, is the analytical knowledge of ready wit. For it has been said:

“Atthe ñāṇaṃ atthappaṭisambhidā, dhamme ñāṇaṃ dhammappaṭisambhidā, tatra dhammaniruttābhilāpe ñāṇaṃ niruttippaṭisambhidā, ñāṇesu ñāṇaṃ paṭibhānappaṭisambhidā”ti (vibha. 718-721).

“Knowledge in the meaning is the analytical knowledge of meaning; knowledge in the Dhamma is the analytical knowledge of the Dhamma; knowledge in the expression of the language of those dhammas is the analytical knowledge of language; knowledge in the knowledges is the analytical knowledge of ready wit.”

Ettha ca hetuanusārena araṇīyato adhigantabbato ca saṅkhepato hetuphalaṃ attho nāma. Pabhedato pana yaṃ kiñci paccayuppannaṃ, nibbānaṃ[P 0.0137], bhāsitattho, vipāko, kiriyāti ime pañca dhammā attho. Taṃ atthaṃ paccavekkhantassa tasmiṃ atthe pabhedagataṃ ñāṇaṃ atthappaṭisambhidā. Dhammoti saṅkhepato paccayo. So hi yasmā taṃ taṃ atthaṃ vidahati pavatteti ceva pāpeti ca, tasmā dhammoti vuccati, pabhedato pana yo koci phalanibbattanako hetu ariyamaggo bhāsitaṃ kusalaṃ akusalanti ime pañca dhammā dhammo, taṃ dhammaṃ paccavekkhantassa tasmiṃ dhamme pabhedagataṃ ñāṇaṃ dhammappaṭisambhidā. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

Here, in brief, 'meaning' is the effect of a cause, since it is to be produced and to be attained by following the cause. In detail, 'meaning' includes these five things: whatever is conditionally arisen, Nibbāna, the meaning of what is spoken, the resultant, and functional consciousness. For one who reviews that meaning, the knowledge concerning its diversity is the analytical knowledge of meaning. 'Dhamma', in brief, is a condition. Since it bears, brings about, and leads to that meaning, it is called 'Dhamma'. In detail, 'Dhamma' includes these five things: any cause that produces a result, the Noble Path, what is spoken, the wholesome, and the unwholesome. For one who reviews that Dhamma, the knowledge concerning its diversity is the analytical knowledge of the Dhamma. And this has also been said:

“Dukkhe [M 0.0121] ñāṇaṃ atthappaṭisambhidā, dukkhasamudaye ñāṇaṃ dhammappaṭisambhidā, dukkhanirodhe ñāṇaṃ atthappaṭisambhidā, dukkhanirodhagāminiyā paṭipadāya ñāṇaṃ dhammappaṭisambhidā”ti (vibha. 719).

“Knowledge of suffering is the analytical knowledge of meaning, knowledge of the origin of suffering is the analytical knowledge of the Dhamma, knowledge of the cessation of suffering is the analytical knowledge of meaning, knowledge of the path leading to the cessation of suffering is the analytical knowledge of the Dhamma.”

Atha vā hetumhi ñāṇaṃ dhammappaṭisambhidā, hetuphale ñāṇaṃ atthappaṭisambhidā. Ye dhammā jātā bhūtā sañjātā nibbattā abhinibbattā pātubhūtā, imesu dhammesu ñāṇaṃ atthappaṭisambhidā. Yamhā dhammā te dhammā jātā bhūtā sañjātā nibbattā abhinibbattā pātubhūtā, tesu dhammesu ñāṇaṃ dhammappaṭisambhidā. Jarāmaraṇe ñāṇaṃ atthappaṭisambhidā, jarāmaraṇasamudaye ñāṇaṃ dhammappaṭisambhidā. Jarāmaraṇanirodhe ñāṇaṃ atthappaṭisambhidā, jarāmaraṇanirodhagāminiyā paṭipadāya ñāṇaṃ dhammappaṭisambhidā. Jātiyā, bhave, upādāne, taṇhāya, vedanāya, phasse, saḷāyatane, nāmarūpe, viññāṇe, saṅkhāresu ñāṇaṃ atthappaṭisambhidā, saṅkhārasamudaye [V 0.0109] ñāṇaṃ dhammappaṭisambhidā. Saṅkhāranirodhe ñāṇaṃ atthappaṭisambhidā, saṅkhāranirodhagāminiyā paṭipadāya ñāṇaṃ dhammappaṭisambhidā.

Or, knowledge of the cause is the analytical knowledge of the Dhamma, and knowledge of the cause's result is the analytical knowledge of meaning. Knowledge regarding those phenomena that are born, have come to be, originated, arisen, been produced, manifested—this is the analytical knowledge of meaning. Knowledge regarding that from which those phenomena are born, have come to be, originated, arisen, been produced, manifested—this is the analytical knowledge of the Dhamma. Knowledge of old age and death is the analytical knowledge of meaning; knowledge of the origin of old age and death is the analytical knowledge of the Dhamma. Knowledge of the cessation of old age and death is the analytical knowledge of meaning; knowledge of the path leading to the cessation of old age and death is the analytical knowledge of the Dhamma. Knowledge of birth, existence, clinging, craving, feeling, contact, the six sense bases, name-and-form, consciousness, and volitional formations is the analytical knowledge of meaning; knowledge of the origin of volitional formations is the analytical knowledge of the Dhamma. Knowledge of the cessation of volitional formations is the analytical knowledge of meaning; knowledge of the path leading to the cessation of volitional formations is the analytical knowledge of the Dhamma.

“Idha bhikkhu dhammaṃ jānāti suttaṃ geyyaṃ…pe… vedallaṃ, ayaṃ vuccati dhammappaṭisambhidā. So tassa tasseva bhāsitassa atthaṃ jānāti ‘ayaṃ imassa bhāsitassa attho, ayaṃ imassa [P 0.0138] bhāsitassa attho’ti, ayaṃ vuccati atthappaṭisambhidā.

“Here, a bhikkhu understands the Dhamma—discourses, mixed prose and verse… up to detailed analyses—this is called the analytical knowledge of the Dhamma. He understands the meaning of each of those statements: ‘This is the meaning of this statement; this is the meaning of that statement’—this is called the analytical knowledge of meaning.”

“Katame dhammā kusalā? Yasmiṃ samaye kāmāvacaraṃ kusalaṃ cittaṃ uppannaṃ hoti somanassasahagataṃ ñāṇasampayuttaṃ rūpārammaṇaṃ vā…pe… dhammārammaṇaṃ vā yaṃ yaṃ vā panārabbha, tasmiṃ samaye phasso hoti…pe… avikkhepo hoti…pe… ime dhammā kusalā. Imesu dhammesu ñāṇaṃ dhammappaṭisambhidā, tesaṃ vipāke ñāṇaṃ atthappaṭisambhidā”tiādi (vibha. 724-725) vitthāro.

“Which states are wholesome? At the time when a wholesome mind pertaining to the sense sphere arises, accompanied by gladness, associated with knowledge, having a form as its object… or… a mental object as its object, or based on whatever it may be, at that time there is contact… there is non-distraction… these states are wholesome. Knowledge in these states is the analytical knowledge of the Dhamma; knowledge of their result is the analytical knowledge of meaning,” and so on in detail.

Yā panetasmiṃ atthe ca dhamme ca sabhāvanirutti abyabhicāravohāro abhilāpo, tasmiṃ sabhāvaniruttābhilāpe māgadhikāya sabbasattānaṃ mūlabhāsāya “ayaṃ sabhāvanirutti, ayaṃ asabhāvaniruttī”ti pabhedagataṃ ñāṇaṃ niruttippaṭisambhidā. Yathāvuttesu tesu ñāṇesu gocarakiccato vitthārato pavattaṃ sabbampi taṃ ñāṇaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā paccavekkhantassa tasmiṃ ñāṇe pabhedagataṃ ñāṇaṃ paṭibhānappaṭisambhidā. Iti imāni cattāri [M 0.0122] paṭisambhidāñāṇāni sayameva bhagavatā adhigatāni atthadhammādike tasmiṃ tasmiṃ attano visaye avisaṃvādanavasena aviparītākārappavattiyā tathāni avitathāni anaññathāni. Evampi bhagavā tathāni āgatoti tathāgato.

Moreover, in this matter of meaning and Dhamma, the natural expression, the unerring communication, the designation—in this natural expression and designation, the knowledge that distinguishes, in Magadhi, the root language of all beings, 'this is natural expression, this is unnatural expression,' is the analytical knowledge of language. As for those knowledges previously mentioned, all that knowledge which operates extensively in terms of object and function—when one reviews it, having made that knowledge itself the object, the knowledge that distinguishes within that knowledge is the analytical knowledge of ready wit. Thus, these four kinds of analytical knowledge were self-attained by the Blessed One. In each of their respective spheres—meaning, Dhamma, and so on—by way of non-contradiction and by proceeding without distortion, they are true, unfailing, and not otherwise. In this way too, the Blessed One is one who has come to what is true—thus, the Tathāgata.

Tathā yaṃkiñci ñeyyaṃ nāma, sabbaṃ taṃ bhagavatā sabbākārena ñātaṃ diṭṭhaṃ adhigataṃ abhisambuddhaṃ. Tathā hissa abhiññeyyā dhammā abhiññeyyato buddhā, pariññeyyā dhammā pariññeyyato, pahātabbā dhammā pahātabbato, sacchikātabbā dhammā sacchikātabbato, bhāvetabbā dhammā bhāvetabbato, yato naṃ koci samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā devo vā māro vā brahmā vā “ime nāma te dhammā anabhisambuddhā”ti saha dhammena anuyuñjituṃ samattho natthi.

Likewise, whatever is knowable, all that has been known, seen, attained, and fully awakened to by the Blessed One in every way. For with respect to him, things to be directly known have been directly known; things to be fully understood have been fully understood; things to be abandoned have been abandoned; things to be realized have been realized; and things to be developed have been developed. Therefore, there is no ascetic, brahmin, deva, Māra, or Brahmā who is able to rightfully challenge him, saying, 'These things have not been fully awakened to by you.'

Yaṃkiñci pahātabbaṃ nāma, sabbaṃ taṃ bhagavato anavasesato bodhimūleyeva pahīnaṃ anuppattidhammaṃ[V 0.0110], na tassa pahānāya uttari karaṇīyaṃ atthi. Tathā hissa lobhadosamohaviparītamanasikāraahirikānottappathinamiddhakodhūpanāha- makkhapalāsaissāmacchariyamāyāsāṭheyyathambhasārambhamānātimānamadappamādatividhā- kusalamūladuccaritavisamaviparītasaññā- [P 0.0139] malavitakkapapañcaesanātaṇhācatubbidhavipariyesaāsavagantha- oghayogāgatitaṇhupādānapañcābhinandananīvaraṇacetokhilacetasovinibandha- chavivādamūlasattānusayaaṭṭhamicchattanavaāghātavatthutaṇhā- mūlakadasaakusalakammapathaekavīsati anesanadvāsaṭṭhidiṭṭhigataaṭṭhasatataṇhāvicaritādippabhedaṃ diyaḍḍhakilesasahassaṃ saha vāsanāya pahīnaṃ samucchinnaṃ samūhataṃ, yato naṃ koci samaṇo vā…pe… brahmā vā “ime nāma te kilesā appahīnā”ti saha dhammena anuyuñjituṃ samattho natthi.

Whatever is to be abandoned, all that has been utterly abandoned by the Blessed One at the very root of enlightenment, leaving no remainder, having a nature of non-arising again. There is nothing further to be done by him for its abandonment. For with respect to him, greed, hatred, delusion, wrong attention, lack of shame and fear of wrongdoing, sloth and torpor, anger, hostility, hypocrisy, malice, envy, stinginess, deceit, fraud, obstinacy, rivalry, conceit, excessive pride, intoxication, heedlessness; the three unwholesome roots; misconduct; distorted and perverted perceptions; defiled thoughts; mental proliferation; seeking and craving; the four perversions; the taints, the bodily ties, the floods, the yokes, the wrong courses, craving and clinging; the five kinds of delight, the hindrances, mental barrenness, mental shackles; the six roots of dispute; the seven latent tendencies; the eight wrongnesses; the nine grounds for ill will; the ten unwholesome courses of action rooted in craving; the twenty-one wrong modes of seeking; the sixty-two kinds of wrong views; the one hundred and eight craving-prompted behaviours, and so on—the one thousand five hundred defilements along with their latent dispositions—have all been abandoned, uprooted, and eradicated. Therefore, there is no ascetic, brahmin, deva, Māra, or Brahmā who is able to rightfully challenge him, saying, 'These defilements have not been abandoned by you.'

Ye cime bhagavatā kammavipākakilesūpavādaāṇāvītikkamappabhedā antarāyikā vuttā, alameva te paṭisevato ekantena antarāyāya. Yato naṃ koci samaṇo vā…pe… brahmā vā “nālaṃ te paṭisevato antarāyāyā”ti saha dhammena anuyuñjituṃ samattho natthi.

And those things declared by the Blessed One to be obstructive—the various kinds of obstacles such as the results of kamma, defilements, accusations, and transgressions of his command—are indeed quite sufficient to be an absolute obstruction for one who engages in them. Therefore, no ascetic, brahmin, deva, Māra, or Brahmā is able to rightfully challenge him, saying, 'For one who engages in them, these are not sufficient to be an obstruction.'

Yo ca bhagavatā niravasesavaṭṭadukkhanissaraṇāya sīlasamādhipaññāya saṅgaho sattakoṭṭhāsiko sattatiṃsappabhedo ariyamaggapubbaṅgamo anuttaro [M 0.0123] niyyāniko dhammo desito, so ekanteneva niyyāti, paṭipannassa vaṭṭadukkhato mokkhāya hoti, yato naṃ koci samaṇo vā…pe… brahmā vā “niyyāniko dhammoti tayā desito na niyyātī”ti saha dhammena anuyuñjituṃ samattho natthīti. Vuttañhetaṃ – “sammāsambuddhassa te paṭijānato ime dhammā anabhisambuddhā”ti (ma. ni. 1.150) vitthāro. Evametāni attano ñāṇappahānadesanāvisesānaṃ avitathabhāvāvabodhanato [P 0.0140] aviparītākārappavattitāni bhagavato catuvesārajjañāṇāni tathāni avitathāni anaññathāni. Evampi bhagavā tathāni āgatoti tathāgato.

And that Dhamma taught by the Blessed One—the unsurpassed, liberating doctrine for the complete escape from the suffering of the round of existence, which is a compendium of morality, concentration, and wisdom, comprising seven sections and thirty-seven divisions, and having the Noble Path as its forerunner—that Dhamma indeed leads out definitively. For one who practices it, it brings about freedom from the suffering of the round. Therefore, no ascetic, brahmin, deva, Māra, or Brahmā is able to rightfully challenge him, saying, 'The Dhamma taught by you as liberating does not liberate.' For it has been said in detail: 'For you, who claim to be a Perfectly Enlightened One, these things are not fully awakened to.' Thus, these four knowledges of self-confidence of the Blessed One, which function without distortion because they realize the true nature of the special qualities of his own knowledge, abandonment, and teaching, are true, not untrue, and not otherwise. In this way too, the Blessed One has arrived at what is true; therefore, he is the Tathāgata.

Tathā nirayagati, tiracchānagati, petagati, manussagati, devagatīti pañca gatiyo, tāsu sañjīvādayo aṭṭha mahānirayā, kukkuḷādayo soḷasa ussadanirayā, lokantarikanirayoti sabbepime ekantadukkhatāya nirassādaṭṭhena nirayā, yathākammunā gantabbato gati cāti nirayagati, tibbandhakārasītanarakāpi etesveva antogadhā. Kimikīṭasarīsapapakkhisoṇasiṅgālādayo tiriyaṃ añchitabhāvena tiracchānā, te eva gatīti tiracchānagati. Khuppipāsitattā paradattūpajīvinijjhāmataṇhikādayo dukkhabahulatāya pākaṭasukhato [V 0.0111] itā vigatāti petā, te eva gatīti petagati, kālakañcikādiasurāpi etesvevantogadhā. Parittadīpavāsīhi saddhiṃ jambudīpādicatumahādīpavāsino manaso ussannatāya manussā, te eva gatīti manussagati. Cātumahārājikato paṭṭhāya yāva nevasaññānāsaññāyatanūpagāti ime chabbīsati devanikāyā dibbanti attano iddhānubhāvena kīḷanti jotanti cāti devā, te eva gatīti devagati.

Likewise, there are five destinations: the hell destination, the animal destination, the ghost destination, the human destination, and the deva destination. Among these, the eight great hells—Sañjīva and so on—the sixteen Ussada hells—Kukkuḷa and so on—and the inter-world hells are all called 'hells' (nirayā) because they are entirely suffering and thus without savor (nirassāda). And because it is a destination (gati) to be gone to according to one's kamma, it is the 'hell destination' (nirayagati). Even the hells of intense darkness and cold are included within these. Creatures like worms, insects, reptiles, winged creatures, dogs, jackals, and so on are called 'animals' (tiracchānā) because they move horizontally (tiriyaṃ); that itself is their destination, thus the 'animal destination' (tiracchānagati). Those tormented by hunger and thirst, those subsisting on what is given by others, the Nijjhamatanhika and others, are called 'ghosts' (petā) because, due to their abundance of suffering, they are departed (itā) from manifest happiness; that itself is their destination, thus the 'ghost destination' (petagati). The Kālakañjika asuras and others are also included within these.
