The inhabitants of the four great continents, such as Jambudīpa, together with the inhabitants of the minor islands, are called 'humans' (manussā) because of the superiority (ussannatāya) of their minds (manaso); that itself is their destination, thus the 'human destination' (manussagati). Beginning from the realm of the Four Great Kings up to the realm of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, these twenty-six classes of devas are called 'devas' because they play (dibbanti), sport (kīḷanti), and shine (jotanti) by their own psychic power and majesty; that itself is their destination, thus the 'deva destination' (devagati).

Tā panetā gatiyo yasmā taṃtaṃkammanibbatto upapattibhavaviseso, tasmā atthato vipākakkhandhā kaṭattā ca rūpaṃ. Tattha “ayaṃ nāma gati iminā nāma kammunā jāyati, tassa ca kammassa paccayavisesehi evaṃ vibhāgabhinnattā visuṃ ete sattanikāyā evaṃ vibhāgabhinnā”ti yathāsakaṃ hetuphalavibhāgaparicchindanavasena ṭhānaso hetuso bhagavato ñāṇaṃ pavattati. Tenāha bhagavā –

Now, since these destinations are particular modes of existence at rebirth produced by their respective kamma, they are, in essence, resultant aggregates and matter produced by kamma. Therein, the Blessed One’s knowledge proceeds by way of discerning and defining the division of cause and effect according to each case, that is, by way of location and by way of cause, as follows: 'This particular destination arises from this particular kamma; and due to the particular conditions of that kamma, these separate classes of beings are thus distinctly divided.' Therefore, the Blessed One said:

“Pañca [M 0.0124] kho imā, sāriputta, gatiyo. Katamā pañca? Nirayo, tiracchānayoni, pettivisayo, manussā, devā. Nirayañcāhaṃ, sāriputta, pajānāmi nirayagāmiñca maggaṃ nirayagāminiñca paṭipadaṃ, yathā paṭipanno ca kāyassa bhedā [P 0.0141] parammaraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjati, tañca pajānāmī”tiādi (ma. ni. 1.153).

“Sāriputta, there are these five destinations. Which five? Hell, the animal womb, the sphere of ghosts, human beings, and devas. I, Sāriputta, know hell, and the path leading to hell, and the practice leading to hell. And I know how one who has practiced in such a way, with the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in the plane of misery, the bad destination, the state of ruin, in hell. That, too, I know,” and so on.

Tāni panetāni bhagavato ñāṇāni tasmiṃ tasmiṃ visaye aviparītākārappavattiyā avisaṃvādanato tathāni avitathāni anaññathāni. Evampi bhagavā tathāni āgatoti tathāgato.

Now, these knowledges of the Blessed One, in their respective domains, function without distortion and are non-deceptive; therefore, they are true, not untrue, and not otherwise. In this way too, the Blessed One has arrived at (āgato) what is true (tathāni); therefore, he is the Tathāgata.

Tathā yaṃ sattānaṃ saddhādiyogavikalāvikalabhāvāvabodhanena apparajakkhamahārajakkhatādivisesavibhāvanaṃ paññāsāya ākārehi pavattaṃ bhagavato indriyaparopariyattañāṇaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ – “saddho puggalo apparajakkho, assaddho puggalo mahārajakkho”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.111) vitthāro.

Likewise, there is the Blessed One's knowledge of the faculties of others, which operates in fifty aspects, discerning the distinctions among beings—such as those with little dust and those with much dust—by understanding their state of being endowed or deficient in faith and other qualities. For this has been said: “A faithful person is one with little dust, a faithless person is one with much dust,” and so on in detail.

Yañca “ayaṃ puggalo apparajakkho, ayaṃ sassatadiṭṭhiko, ayaṃ ucchedadiṭṭhiko, ayaṃ anulomikāyaṃ khantiyaṃ ṭhito, ayaṃ yathābhūtañāṇe ṭhito, ayaṃ kāmāsayo, na nekkhammādiāsayo, ayaṃ nekkhammāsayo, na kāmādiāsayo”tiādinā “imassa kāmarāgo ativiya [V 0.0112] thāmagato, na paṭighādiko, imassa paṭigho ativiya thāmagato, na kāmarāgādiko”tiādinā “imassa puññābhisaṅkhāro adhiko, na apuññābhisaṅkhāro na āneñjābhisaṅkhāro, imassa apuññābhisaṅkhāro adhiko, na puññābhisaṅkhāro na āneñjābhisaṅkhāro, imassa āneñjābhisaṅkhāro adhiko, na puññābhisaṅkhāro na apuññābhisaṅkhāro. Imassa kāyasucaritaṃ adhikaṃ, imassa vacīsucaritaṃ, imassa manosucaritaṃ, ayaṃ hīnādhimuttiko, ayaṃ paṇītādhimuttiko, ayaṃ kammāvaraṇena samannāgato, ayaṃ kilesāvaraṇena samannāgato, ayaṃ vipākāvaraṇena samannāgato, ayaṃ na kammāvaraṇena samannāgato, na kilesāvaraṇena samannāgato, na vipākāvaraṇena samannāgato”tiādinā ca sattānaṃ āsayādīnaṃ yathābhūtaṃ vibhāvanākārappavattaṃ bhagavato āsayānusayañāṇaṃ. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ –

And there is the Blessed One's knowledge of inclinations and underlying tendencies, which proceeds by way of discerning, as it truly is, the inclinations and so on of beings, in such ways as: “This person has little dust; this one holds eternalist views; this one holds annihilationist views; this one is established in conformity-patience; this one is established in knowledge of things as they are; this one is inclined toward sensual pleasures, not toward renunciation and so on; this one is inclined toward renunciation, not toward sensual pleasures and so on”; and in such ways as: “This one's sensual lust is extremely strong, not aversion and so on; this one's aversion is extremely strong, not sensual lust and so on”; and in such ways as: “For this one, meritorious formations are predominant, not demeritorious formations nor imperturbable formations; for this one, demeritorious formations are predominant, not meritorious formations nor imperturbable formations; for this one, imperturbable formations are predominant, not meritorious formations nor demeritorious formations. For this one, bodily good conduct is predominant; for this one, verbal good conduct; for this one, mental good conduct. This one is of inferior disposition; this one is of superior disposition. This one is possessed of the kamma-obstruction; this one is possessed of the defilement-obstruction; this one is possessed of the result-obstruction; this one is not possessed of the kamma-obstruction, not possessed of the defilement-obstruction, not possessed of the result-obstruction,” and so on. Regarding this, it has been said:

“Idha [M 0.0125] tathāgato sattānaṃ āsayaṃ jānāti, anusayaṃ jānāti, caritaṃ jānāti, adhimuttiṃ jānāti, bhabbābhabbe satte jānātī”tiādi (paṭi. ma. 1.113).

“Here, the Tathāgata knows the inclinations of beings, knows their underlying tendencies, knows their conduct, knows their dispositions, knows beings who are capable and those who are incapable,” and so on.

Yañca uparimaheṭṭhimapurimapacchimakāyehi dakkhiṇavāmaakkhikaṇṇasotanāsikasotaaṃsakūṭahatthapādehi aṅguliaṅgulantarehi lomakūpehi ca aggikkhandhūdakadhārāpavattanaṃ anaññasādhāraṇaṃ vividhavikubbaniddhinimmāpanakaṃ [P 0.0142] bhagavato yamakapāṭihāriyañāṇaṃ. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ –

And there is the Blessed One's knowledge of the Twin Miracle, which is not shared by others and produces various kinds of transformations and creations, causing masses of fire and streams of water to issue forth from the upper and lower, front and back parts of the body; from the right and left eyes, ear-orifices, and nostrils; from the shoulders, hands, and feet; from between the fingers and toes; and from the pores of the skin. Regarding this, it has been said:

“Idha tathāgato yamakapāṭihāriyaṃ karoti asādhāraṇaṃ sāvakehi, uparimakāyato aggikkhandho pavattati, heṭṭhimakāyato udakadhārā pavattati. Heṭṭhimakāyato aggikkhandho pavattati, uparimakāyato udakadhārā pavattatī”tiādi (paṭi. ma. 1.116).

“Here, the Tathāgata performs the Twin Miracle, which is not shared with his disciples: from the upper part of his body a mass of fire proceeds, and from the lower part of his body a stream of water proceeds. From the lower part of his body a mass of fire proceeds, and from the upper part of his body a stream of water proceeds,” and so on.

Yañca rāgādīhi jātiādīhi ca anekehi dukkhadhammehi upaddutaṃ sattanikāyaṃ tato nīharitukāmatāvasena nānānayehi pavattassa bhagavato mahākaruṇokkamanassa paccayabhūtaṃ mahākaruṇāsamāpattiñāṇaṃ. Yathāha (paṭi. ma. 1.117-118) –

And there is the Blessed One's knowledge of the attainment of great compassion, which is the cause for the arising of great compassion in the Blessed One, who proceeds in various ways out of a desire to lead the host of beings out from being afflicted by many states of suffering, such as lust and so on, and birth and so on. As it is said:

“Katamaṃ tathāgatassa mahākaruṇāsamāpattiyā ñāṇaṃ? Bahukehi ākārehi passantānaṃ buddhānaṃ bhagavantānaṃ sattesu mahākaruṇā okkamati, āditto lokasannivāsoti passantānaṃ buddhānaṃ bhagavantānaṃ sattesu mahākaruṇā okkamati. Uyyutto, payāto, kummaggappaṭipanno, upanīyati loko addhuvo, atāṇo loko anabhissaro[V 0.0113], assako loko, sabbaṃ pahāya gamanīyaṃ, ūno loko atitto taṇhādāsoti passantānaṃ buddhānaṃ bhagavantānaṃ sattesu mahākaruṇā okkamati.

“What is the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the attainment of great compassion? Seeing in many ways, great compassion arises in the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, for beings. Seeing that the world-dwelling is ablaze, great compassion arises in the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, for beings. The world is striving, journeying, has entered a wrong path, is being led away; the world is impermanent, without protection, without a master, without ownership; all must be left behind in going; the world is deficient, insatiable, a slave to craving—seeing this, great compassion arises in the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, for beings.

“Atāyano lokasannivāso, aleṇo, asaraṇo, asaraṇībhūto. Uddhato loko avūpasanto, sasallo lokasannivāso viddho puthusallehi, avijjandhakārāvaraṇo [M 0.0126] kilesapañjarapakkhitto, avijjāgato lokasannivāso aṇḍabhūto pariyonaddho tantākulakajāto kulaguṇḍikajāto muñjapabbajabhūto apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ saṃsāraṃ nātivattati, avijjāvisadosasaṃlitto, kilesakalalībhūto, rāgadosamohajaṭājaṭito.

“The world-dwelling is without a protector, without shelter, without refuge, and has become no refuge. The world is agitated, unpacified. The world-dwelling is full of darts, pierced by many darts, has the covering of the darkness of ignorance, is enclosed in the cage of defilements. The world-dwelling has gone into ignorance, has become like an egg, is enveloped, has become a tangled skein, has become a tangled ball of thread, has become like muñja grass and bulrushes; it does not transcend the plane of misery, the bad destination, the downfall, the round of rebirths. It is smeared with the poison of ignorance, has become a mire of defilements, is enmeshed in the tangle of lust, hatred, and delusion.

“Taṇhāsaṅghāṭapaṭimukko, taṇhājālena otthaṭo, taṇhāsotena vuyhati, taṇhāsaññojanena saṃyutto, taṇhānusayena [P 0.0143] anusaṭo, taṇhāsantāpena santappati, taṇhāpariḷāhena pariḍayhati.

“It is cloaked in the robe of craving, covered by the net of craving, swept away by the flood of craving, bound by the fetter of craving, pursued by the underlying tendency of craving, tormented by the torment of craving, consumed by the fever of craving.

“Diṭṭhisaṅghāṭapaṭimukko, diṭṭhijālena otthaṭo, diṭṭhisotena vuyhati, diṭṭhisaññojanena saṃyutto, diṭṭhānusayena anusaṭo, diṭṭhisantāpena santappati, diṭṭhipariḷāhena pariḍayhati.

“It is cloaked in the robe of views, covered by the net of views, swept away by the flood of views, bound by the fetter of views, pursued by the underlying tendency of views, tormented by the torment of views, consumed by the fever of views.

“Jātiyā anugato, jarāya anusaṭo, byādhinā abhibhūto, maraṇena abbhāhato, dukkhe patiṭṭhito.

“It is followed by birth, pursued by aging, overwhelmed by sickness, struck down by death, established in suffering.

“Taṇhāya uḍḍito, jarāpākāraparikkhitto, maccupāsena parikkhitto, mahābandhanabaddho, rāgabandhanena dosamohamānadiṭṭhikilesaduccaritabandhanena baddho, mahāsambādhappaṭipanno, mahāpalibodhena palibuddho, mahāpapāte patito, mahākantārappaṭipanno, mahāsaṃsārappaṭipanno, mahāvidugge samparivattati, mahāpalipe palipanno.

“It is driven on by craving, encircled by the wall of aging, surrounded by the snare of death, bound by a great bond, bound by the bond of lust, the bond of hatred, delusion, conceit, views, defilements, and misconduct. It has entered a great jungle, is obstructed by great impediments, has fallen into a great abyss, has entered a great wilderness, has entered the great round of rebirths, revolves in a great impassable place, is stuck in a great mire.

“Abbhāhato lokasannivāso, āditto lokasannivāso rāgagginā dosagginā mohagginā jātiyā jarāya maraṇena sokehi paridevehi dukkhehi domanassehi upāyāsehi, unnītako lokasannivāso haññati niccamatāṇo pattadaṇḍo takkaro, vajjabandhanabaddho [V 0.0114] āghātanapaccupaṭṭhito, anātho lokasannivāso paramakāruññappatto, dukkhābhitunno cirarattaṃ pīḷito, gadhito niccaṃ pipāsito.

The world of beings is afflicted; the world of beings is ablaze with the fire of lust, the fire of aversion, and the fire of delusion; with birth, aging, and death; with sorrows, lamentations, pains, griefs, and despairs. The world of beings is led on, is afflicted, always without protection, subject to punishment, a perpetrator. Bound by the bonds of faults, facing execution, the world of beings is without refuge, deserving of the utmost compassion, pierced by suffering, oppressed for a long time, greedy, and constantly thirsty.

“Andho [M 0.0127] acakkhuko, hatanetto apariṇāyako, vipathapakkhando añjasāparaddho, mahoghapakkhando.

Blind, without eyes, with destroyed eyes, without guidance, gone astray on a wrong path, erred from the straight path, fallen into the great flood.

“Dvīhi diṭṭhigatehi pariyuṭṭhito, tīhi duccaritehi vippaṭipanno, catūhi yogehi yojito, catūhi ganthehi ganthito, catūhi upādānehi upādiyati, pañcagatisamāruḷho, pañcahi kāmaguṇehi rajjati, pañcahi nīvaraṇehi otthaṭo, chahi [P 0.0144] vivādamūlehi vivadati, chahi taṇhākāyehi rajjati, chahi diṭṭhigatehi pariyuṭṭhito, sattahi anusayehi anusaṭo, sattahi saññojanehi saṃyutto, sattahi mānehi unnato, aṭṭhahi lokadhammehi samparivattati, aṭṭhahi micchattehi niyyāto, aṭṭhahi purisadosehi dussati, navahi āghātavatthūhi āghātito, navavidhamānehi unnato, navahi taṇhāmūlakehi dhammehi rajjati, dasahi kilesavatthūhi kilissati, dasahi āghātavatthūhi āghātito, dasahi akusalakammapathehi samannāgato, dasahi saṃyojanehi saṃyutto, dasahi micchattehi niyyāto, dasavatthukāya micchādiṭṭhiyā samannāgato, dasavatthukāya antaggāhikāya diṭṭhiyā samannāgato, aṭṭhasatataṇhāpapañcehi papañcito, dvāsaṭṭhiyā diṭṭhigatehi pariyuṭṭhito, lokasannivāsoti passantānaṃ buddhānaṃ bhagavantānaṃ sattesu mahākaruṇā okkamati.

Obsessed with two kinds of wrong views, engaging in three kinds of misconduct, yoked by four yokes, knotted by four ties, clinging through four kinds of clinging, having ascended to the five destinations, enamored with the five strands of sensual pleasure, overwhelmed by five hindrances, quarreling over six roots of dispute, enamored with six groups of craving, obsessed with six kinds of wrong views, pursued by seven latent tendencies, bound by seven fetters, puffed up with seven kinds of conceit, revolving in eight worldly conditions, led astray by eight wrongnesses, corrupted by eight faults of a person, angered by nine grounds for resentment, inflated with nine kinds of conceit, enamored with nine craving-rooted states, defiled by ten bases of defilement, angered by ten grounds for resentment, endowed with ten unwholesome courses of action, bound by ten fetters, led astray by ten wrongnesses, possessing wrong view based on ten grounds, holding to the ten-factored view that grasps at extremes, entangled in the one hundred and eight proliferations of craving, obsessed with sixty-two kinds of wrong views. Seeing the world’s inhabitants thus, great compassion for beings descends upon the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones.

“Ahañcamhi tiṇṇo, loko ca atiṇṇo. Ahañcamhi mutto, loko ca amutto. Ahañcamhi danto, loko ca adanto. Ahañcamhi santo, loko ca asanto. Ahañcamhi assattho, loko ca anassattho. Ahañcamhi parinibbuto, loko ca aparinibbuto. Pahomi khvāhaṃ tiṇṇo tāretuṃ, mutto mocetuṃ, danto dametuṃ, santo sametuṃ, assattho assāsetuṃ, parinibbuto parinibbāpetunti passantānaṃ buddhānaṃ bhagavantānaṃ sattesu mahākaruṇā okkamatī”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.117-118).

‘I am one who has crossed over, while the world has not crossed over. I am one who is liberated, while the world is not liberated. I am one who is tamed, while the world is not tamed. I am one who is at peace, while the world is not at peace. I am one who is comforted, while the world is not comforted. I am one who is fully extinguished, while the world is not fully extinguished. Being one who has crossed over, I am able to help others cross over; being liberated, I am able to liberate; being tamed, I am able to tame; being at peace, I am able to pacify; being comforted, I am able to comfort; being fully extinguished, I am able to lead to full extinguishment.’ Seeing this, great compassion for beings descends upon the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones.

Evaṃ [M 0.0128] ekūnanavutiyā ākārehi vibhajanaṃ kataṃ.

Thus, the analysis has been made in eighty-nine aspects.

Yaṃ pana yāvatā dhammadhātuyā yattakaṃ ñātabbaṃ saṅkhatāsaṅkhatādikassa sabbassa paropadesanirapekkhaṃ [V 0.0115] sabbākārena paṭivijjhanasamatthaṃ ākaṅkhamattappaṭibaddhavuttianaññasādhāraṇaṃ bhagavato ñāṇaṃ sabbathā anavasesasaṅkhatāsaṅkhatasammutisaccāvabodhato sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ tatthāvaraṇābhāvato nissaṅgappavattimupādāya anāvaraṇañāṇanti vuccati. Ekameva hi taṃ ñāṇaṃ visayappavattimukhena aññehi asādhāraṇabhāvadassanatthaṃ [P 0.0145] duvidhena uddiṭṭhaṃ. Aññathā sabbaññutānāvaraṇañāṇānaṃ sādhāraṇatā sabbavisayatā āpajjeyyuṃ, na ca taṃ yuttaṃ kiñcāpi imāya yuttiyā. Ayañhettha pāḷi –

Now, whatever is to be known within the entire sphere of the Dhamma-element—whether conditioned or unconditioned and so on—all of it is comprehended by the Blessed One’s knowledge independently of others’ instruction, capable of penetrating in every way, its operation connected only with the extent of his wish, unique, not shared by others. This knowledge is called omniscient knowledge because it fully awakens to all conditioned and unconditioned conventional truths without exception, and unobstructed knowledge because, in virtue of its unattached operation, there is no obstruction to it. Indeed, this single knowledge is described in two ways based on the manner of its operation regarding its object, to show that it is unique and not shared by others. Otherwise, for the omniscient and unobstructed knowledges, a state of being common and encompassing all objects would result, and that is not appropriate, whatever the reasoning might be. Here is the Pali text on this:

“Sabbaṃ saṅkhatamasaṅkhataṃ anavasesaṃ jānātīti sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ, tattha āvaraṇaṃ natthīti anāvaraṇañāṇaṃ. Atītaṃ sabbaṃ jānātīti sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ, tattha āvaraṇaṃ natthīti anāvaraṇañāṇaṃ. Anāgataṃ sabbaṃ jānātīti sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ, tattha āvaraṇaṃ natthīti anāvaraṇañāṇaṃ. Paccuppannaṃ sabbaṃ jānātīti sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ, tattha āvaraṇaṃ natthīti anāvaraṇañāṇa”nti (paṭi. ma. 1.119-120) vitthāro.

‘The knowledge that knows all conditioned and unconditioned things without exception is omniscient knowledge; in that, there is no obstruction, so it is unobstructed knowledge. The knowledge that knows all the past is omniscient knowledge; in that, there is no obstruction, so it is unobstructed knowledge. The knowledge that knows all the future is omniscient knowledge; in that, there is no obstruction, so it is unobstructed knowledge. The knowledge that knows all the present is omniscient knowledge; in that, there is no obstruction, so it is unobstructed knowledge.’ This is the detailed explanation.

Evametāni bhagavato chaasādhāraṇañāṇāni aviparītākārappavattiyā yathāsakavisayassa avisaṃvādanato tathāni avitathāni anaññathāni. Evampi bhagavā tathāni āgatoti tathāgato.

Thus, these six unique knowledges of the Blessed One are true, not unreal, and not otherwise, because they operate without distortion and are unerring with respect to their own objects. In this way too, the Blessed One has arrived at what is true; thus he is the Tathāgata.

Tathā –

Likewise—

“Sattime, bhikkhave, bojjhaṅgā – satisambojjhaṅgo, dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgo, vīriyasambojjhaṅgo, pītisambojjhaṅgo, passaddhisambojjhaṅgo, samādhisambojjhaṅgo, upekkhāsambojjhaṅgo”ti (paṭi. ma. 2.17; saṃ. ni. 5.185) evaṃ sarūpato, “yāyaṃ lokuttaramaggakkhaṇe uppajjamānā līnuddhaccapatiṭṭhānāyūhanakāmasukhallikattakilamathānuyogaucchedasassatābhinivesādīnaṃ anekesaṃ upaddavānaṃ paṭipakkhabhūtā satiādibhedā dhammasāmaggī, yāya ariyasāvako bujjhati kilesaniddāya uṭṭhahati, cattāri vā ariyasaccāni paṭivijjhati, nibbānameva vā sacchikarotīti, sā dhammasāmaggī bodhīti vuccati. Tassā ‘bodhiyā aṅgāti bojjhaṅgā, ariyasāvako vā yathāvuttāya dhammasāmaggiyā bujjhatīti [M 0.0129] katvā bodhīti vuccati, tassa bodhissa aṅgātipi bojjhaṅgā”ti evaṃ sāmaññalakkhaṇato. “Upaṭṭhānalakkhaṇo satisambojjhaṅgo, pavicayalakkhaṇo dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgo, paggahalakkhaṇo vīriyasambojjhaṅgo, pharaṇalakkhaṇo pītisambojjhaṅgo, upasamalakkhaṇo [V 0.0116] passaddhisambojjhaṅgo, avikkhepalakkhaṇo samādhisambojjhaṅgo, paṭisaṅkhānalakkhaṇo upekkhāsambojjhaṅgo”ti evaṃ visesalakkhaṇato.

“Monks, there are these seven factors of enlightenment: the mindfulness enlightenment factor, the investigation of phenomena enlightenment factor, the energy enlightenment factor, the rapture enlightenment factor, the tranquility enlightenment factor, the concentration enlightenment factor, and the equanimity enlightenment factor.” This is in terms of their nature. In terms of their general characteristic: “At the moment of the supramundane path, this aggregate of qualities—mindfulness and so forth—arises, counteracting numerous afflictions such as sloth, restlessness, a predisposition to attachment, indulgence in sensual pleasure, indulgence in self-mortification, clinging to annihilationist views, clinging to eternalist views, and so on. Through this aggregate of qualities, the noble disciple awakens from the sleep of defilements, comprehends the Four Noble Truths, or directly realizes Nibbāna. This aggregate of qualities is called ‘enlightenment’ (bodhi). The ‘factors of enlightenment’ (bojjhaṅgā) are the limbs (aṅga) of that enlightenment. Alternatively, since the noble disciple awakens (bujjhati) through the aforementioned aggregate of qualities, he is called ‘enlightened’ (bodhi), and its causes (aṅga) are also the factors of enlightenment.” In terms of their specific characteristics: “The mindfulness enlightenment factor has the characteristic of establishing. The investigation of phenomena enlightenment factor has the characteristic of investigation. The energy enlightenment factor has the characteristic of exertion. The rapture enlightenment factor has the characteristic of suffusing. The tranquility enlightenment factor has the characteristic of calming. The concentration enlightenment factor has the characteristic of non-distraction. The equanimity enlightenment factor has the characteristic of reflection.”

“Tattha katamo satisambojjhaṅgo? Idha, bhikkhu[P 0.0146], satimā hoti paramena satinepakkena samannāgato, cirakatampi cirabhāsitampi saritā hoti anussaritā”tiādinā (vibha. 467) sattannaṃ bojjhaṅgānaṃ aññamaññopakāravasena ekakkhaṇe pavattidassanato, “tattha katamo satisambojjhaṅgo? Atthi ajjhattaṃ, bhikkhave, dhammesu sati, atthi bahiddhā dhammesu satī”tiādinā tesaṃ visayavibhāgena pavattidassanato. “Tattha katamo satisambojjhaṅgo? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu satisambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti vivekanissitaṃ virāganissitaṃ nirodhanissitaṃ vossaggapariṇāmi”ntiādinā (vibha. 471) bhāvanāvidhidassanato. “Tattha katame satta bojjhaṅgā? Idha bhikkhu yasmiṃ samaye lokuttaraṃ jhānaṃ bhāveti…pe… tasmiṃ samaye satta bojjhaṅgā honti satisambojjhaṅgo…pe… upekkhāsambojjhaṅgo. Tattha katamo satisambojjhaṅgo? Yā sati…pe… anussatī”tiādinā (vibha. 478-479) channavutiyā nayasahassavibhāgehīti evaṃ nānākārato pavattāni bhagavato sambojjhaṅgavibhāvanañāṇāni tassa tassa atthassa avisaṃvādanato tathāni avitathāni anaññathāni. Evampi bhagavā tathāni āgatoti tathāgato.

The Blessed One’s knowledges that analyze the enlightenment factors occur in various ways. This is shown by their simultaneous arising through mutual support, as in: “Herein, what is the mindfulness enlightenment factor? Here, a bhikkhu is mindful, endowed with supreme mindfulness and discernment, remembering and recollecting what was done and said long ago.” It is also shown by their occurrence through the division of their objects, as in: “Herein, what is the mindfulness enlightenment factor? There is, bhikkhus, internal mindfulness regarding phenomena, and there is external mindfulness regarding phenomena.” And by the method of cultivation, as in: “Herein, what is the mindfulness enlightenment factor? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu develops the mindfulness enlightenment factor, which is dependent on seclusion, dispassion, cessation, and culminating in relinquishment.” And through ninety-six thousand divisions of methods, as in: “Herein, what are the seven enlightenment factors? Here, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu develops the supramundane jhāna… at that time, the seven enlightenment factors are present—the mindfulness enlightenment factor… the equanimity enlightenment factor. Herein, what is the mindfulness enlightenment factor? It is mindfulness… recollection.” Thus, these knowledges of the Blessed One are true, not untrue, and not otherwise, because they do not deviate from each and every meaning. In this way also, the Blessed One has arrived at what is true (tathāni), thus he is the Tathāgata.

Tathā –

Likewise—

“Tattha katamaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā ariyasaccaṃ? Ayameva ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo. Seyyathidaṃ, sammādiṭṭhi…pe… sammāsamādhī”ti (vibha. 205) evaṃ sarūpato. Sabbakilesehi ārakattā ariyabhāvakarattā ariyaphalappaṭilābhakarattā ca ariyo, aṭṭhavidhattā nibbānādhigamāya ekantakāraṇattā ca aṭṭhaṅgiko. Kilese mārento gacchati, nibbānatthikehi maggīyati, sayaṃ vā nibbānaṃ maggatīti maggoti evaṃ sāmaññalakkhaṇato. “Sammā dassanalakkhaṇā sammādiṭṭhi, sammā abhiniropanalakkhaṇo sammāsaṅkappo, sammā pariggahaṇalakkhaṇā sammāvācā, sammā samuṭṭhānalakkhaṇo [M 0.0130] sammākammanto, sammā vodānalakkhaṇo sammāājīvo, sammā paggahalakkhaṇo sammāvāyāmo, sammā upaṭṭhānalakkhaṇā sammāsati, sammā avikkhepalakkhaṇo sammāsamādhī”ti evaṃ visesalakkhaṇato[P 0.0147]. Sammādiṭṭhi aññehipi attano paccanīkakilesehi saddhiṃ micchādiṭṭhiṃ pajahati, nibbānaṃ ārammaṇaṃ karoti, tappaṭicchādakamohavidhamanena asammohato sampayuttadhamme ca passati. Tathā sammāsaṅkappādayopi micchāsaṅkappādīni [V 0.0117] pajahanti, nibbānañca ārammaṇaṃ karonti, sahajātadhammānaṃ sammāabhiniropanapariggahaṇasamuṭṭhānavodānapaggahaupaṭṭhānasamādahanāni ca karontīti evaṃ kiccavibhāgato. Sammādiṭṭhi pubbabhāge nānakkhaṇā visuṃ visuṃ dukkhādiārammaṇā hutvā maggakāle ekakkhaṇā nibbānameva ārammaṇaṃ katvā kiccato “dukkhe ñāṇa”ntiādīni cattāri nāmāni labhati, sammāsaṅkappādayopi pubbabhāge nānakkhaṇā nānārammaṇā maggakāle ekakkhaṇā ekārammaṇā.

“Now, what is the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering? It is just this noble eightfold path, that is: right view… right concentration.” (vibha. 205) Thus, in terms of its essence. Because it is remote from all defilements, because it creates a noble state, and because it leads to the attainment of noble fruits, it is called noble. Because it consists of eight factors and is the sole cause for reaching Nibbāna, it is called eightfold. It is called the path because it kills defilements while going, because it is sought by those seeking Nibbāna, or because it itself seeks Nibbāna—thus, in terms of its general characteristic. “Right view has the characteristic of right seeing, right intention has the characteristic of right application, right speech has the characteristic of right apprehension, right action has the characteristic of right origination, right livelihood has the characteristic of right cleansing, right effort has the characteristic of right exertion, right mindfulness has the characteristic of right establishing, and right concentration has the characteristic of right non-distraction”—thus, in terms of its specific characteristics. Right view abandons wrong view along with other opposing defilements, makes Nibbāna its object, and sees associated states without delusion by dispelling the delusion that obscures it. Similarly, right intention and the others abandon wrong intention and the rest, make Nibbāna their object, and perform the functions of right application, apprehension, origination, cleansing, exertion, establishing, and concentration for their associated states—thus, in terms of the division of functions. Right view, in the preliminary stages, having different objects such as suffering at different moments, but at the moment of the path, having Nibbāna alone as its object, functionally acquires the four names: “knowledge of suffering,” etc. Right intention and the others, in the preliminary stages, having various objects at different moments, but at the moment of the path, having one object at one moment.

Tesu sammāsaṅkappo kiccato nekkhammasaṅkappotiādīni tīṇi nāmāni labhati, sammāvācādayo tayo pubbabhāge musāvādāveramaṇītiādivibhāgā viratiyopi cetanāyopi hutvā maggakkhaṇe viratiyova, sammāvāyāmasatiyo kiccato sammappadhānasatipaṭṭhānavasena cattāri nāmāni labhanti. Sammāsamādhi pana maggakkhaṇepi paṭhamajjhānādivasena nānā evāti evaṃ pubbabhāgaparabhāgesu pavattivibhāgato, “idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sammādiṭṭhiṃ bhāveti vivekanissita”ntiādinā (vibha. 489) bhāvanāvidhito, “tattha katamo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo? Idha, bhikkhu, yasmiṃ samaye lokuttaraṃ jhānaṃ bhāveti…pe… dukkhāpaṭipadaṃ dandhābhiññaṃ, tasmiṃ samaye aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo hoti sammādiṭṭhi sammāsaṅkappo”tiādinā (vibha. 499) caturāsītiyā nayasahassavibhāgehīti evaṃ anekākārato pavattāni bhagavato ariyamaggavibhāvanañāṇāni atthassa avisaṃvādanato sabbānipi tathāni avitathāni anaññathāni. Evampi bhagavā tathāni āgatoti tathāgato.

Among them, right intention, in terms of its function, obtains three names: the intention of renunciation, and so on. The three—right speech, right action, and right livelihood—in the preliminary stage are classified as ‘abstaining from false speech,’ etc., and are both abstinences and volitions; yet at the moment of the path, they are solely abstinences. Right effort and right mindfulness, in terms of their function, obtain four names each by way of the Right Exertions and the Foundations of Mindfulness. Right concentration, however, even at the moment of the path, is diverse by way of the first jhāna and so on. Thus, from the division of occurrence in the preliminary and subsequent stages; from the method of development, as in, “Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu develops right view based on seclusion,” and so on; and from the divisions into eighty-four thousand methods, as in, “Therein, what is the eightfold path? Here, a bhikkhu, at the time when he develops a supramundane jhāna… a painful practice with slow direct knowledge, at that time the eightfold path exists: right view, right intention,” and so on—in these many ways have the Blessed One’s knowledges that explain the Noble Path arisen. Because they do not deviate from the meaning, all are true, not untrue, and not otherwise. In this way also, the Blessed One has come to what is true; therefore, he is the Tathāgata.

Tathā paṭhamajjhānasamāpatti yā ca nirodhasamāpattīti etāsu anupaṭipāṭiyā viharitabbaṭṭhena samāpajjitabbaṭṭhena ca anupubbavihārasamāpattīsu sampādanapaccavekkhaṇādivasena yathārahaṃ sampayogavasena ca pavattāni bhagavato ñāṇāni tadatthasiddhiyā tathāni avitathāni anaññathāni[P 0.0148]. Tathā [M 0.0131] “idaṃ imassa ṭhānaṃ, idaṃ aṭṭhāna”nti aviparītaṃ tassa tassa phalassa kāraṇākāraṇajānanaṃ, tesaṃ tesaṃ sattānaṃ atītādibhedabhinnassa kammasamādānassa anavasesato yathābhūtaṃ vipākantarajānanaṃ, āyūhanakkhaṇeyeva tassa tassa sattassa “ayaṃ nirayagāminī paṭipadā…pe… ayaṃ nibbānagāminī paṭipadā”ti yāthāvato sāsavānāsavakammavibhāgajānanaṃ, 0.khandhāyatanādīnaṃ upādinnānupādinnādianekasabhāvaṃ nānāsabhāvañca tassa lokassa “imāya nāma dhātuyā ussannattā imasmiṃ dhammappabandhe ayaṃ viseso jāyatī”tiādinā nayena yathābhūtaṃ dhātunānattajānanaṃ, anavasesato sattānaṃ hīnādiajjhāsayādhimuttijānanaṃ, saddhādiindriyānaṃ tikkhamudutājānanaṃ, saṃkilesādīhi saddhiṃ jhānavimokkhādivisesajānanaṃ[V 0.0118], sattānaṃ aparimāṇāsu jātīsu tappaṭibandhena saddhiṃ anavasesato pubbenivutthakkhandhasantatijānanaṃ, hīnādivibhāgehi saddhiṃ cutipaṭisandhijānanaṃ, “idaṃ dukkha”ntiādinā heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva catusaccajānananti imāni bhagavato dasabalañāṇāni avirajjhitvā yathāsakaṃ visayāvagāhanato yathādhippetatthasādhanato ca yathābhūtavuttiyā tathāni avitathāni anaññathāni. Vuttañhetaṃ –

Likewise, the Blessed One’s knowledges that have arisen concerning the successive dwelling attainments—from the attainment of the first jhāna up to the attainment of cessation—in the sense that they are to be dwelled in and attained in due sequence, and which have arisen appropriately by way of accomplishment, reviewing, and so on, and by way of association, are true, not untrue, and not otherwise, due to the accomplishment of that purpose. Likewise, there is the unerring knowledge of the cause and non-cause for each and every result, as in ‘This is the cause for this; this is not the cause’; the knowledge of the specific results, as they really are and without omission, of the past, etc., undertakings of kamma of various beings; the knowledge, just as it is, of the division of kamma with and without taints, at the very moment of exertion for each being, as in ‘This is the path leading to hell… this is the path leading to Nibbāna’; the knowledge of the diversity of elements as they really are, by the method beginning, ‘Due to the prevalence of such-and-such an element in the world, this particular distinction arises in this continuity of phenomena,’ regarding the manifold and various natures of the aggregates, sense bases, etc., whether appropriated or unappropriated; the knowledge, without omission, of the inferior and superior inclinations and dispositions of beings; the knowledge of the sharpness and dullness of the faculties of faith and so on; and the knowledge of the four truths by the method stated below, as in ‘This is suffering,’ and so on. These ten powers of knowledge of the Blessed One, by unerringly grasping their respective objects and by accomplishing their intended purpose, and by their functioning in accordance with reality, are true, not untrue, and not otherwise. For it has been said:

“Idha tathāgato ṭhānañca ṭhānato aṭṭhānañca aṭṭhānato yathābhūtaṃ pajānātī”tiādi (vibha. 809; a. ni. 10.21).

“Here, the Tathāgata understands, as it actually is, the cause as cause and the non-cause as non-cause.”

Evampi bhagavā tathāni āgatoti tathāgato.

In this way also, the Blessed One has come to these true knowledges; therefore, he is the Tathāgata.

Yathā cetesaṃ ñāṇānaṃ vasena, evaṃ yathāvuttānaṃ satipaṭṭhānasammappadhānavibhāvanañāṇādīnaṃ anantāparimeyyabhedānaṃ anaññasādhāraṇānaṃ paññāvisesānaṃ vasena bhagavā tathāni ñāṇāni āgato adhigatoti tathāgato. Evampi tathāni āgatoti tathāgato.

Just as he is the Tathāgata by means of those knowledges, so too, by means of the special kinds of wisdom—which have infinite and immeasurable distinctions, are not shared with others, and consist of the knowledges that explain the aforementioned Foundations of Mindfulness, Right Exertions, and so on—the Blessed One has come to and attained these true knowledges; therefore, he is the Tathāgata. In this way also, having come to what is true, he is the Tathāgata.

Kathaṃ tathā gatoti tathāgato? Yā sā bhagavato abhijāti abhisambodhi dhammavinayapaññāpanā anupādisesanibbānadhātu, sā tathā. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Yadatthaṃ lokanāthena abhisambodhi patthitā pavattitā ca, tadatthassa ekantasiddhiyā avisaṃvādanato aviparītatthavuttiyā tathā avitathā anaññathā. Tathā hi ayaṃ bhagavā bodhisattabhūto samatiṃsapāramiparipūraṇādikaṃ [P 0.0149] vuttappabhedaṃ sabbaṃ buddhattahetuṃ sampādetvā [M 0.0132] tusitapure ṭhitova buddhakolāhalaṃ sutvā dasasahassacakkavāḷadevatāhi ekato sannipatitāhi upasaṅkamitvā –

How is he ‘gone thus,’ a Tathāgata? That supreme birth of the Blessed One, his perfect enlightenment, his promulgation of the Dhamma and Vinaya, and the Nibbāna-element without residue—that is ‘thus.’ What is meant by this? The purpose for which the Lord of the World aspired to and set in motion perfect enlightenment was, due to its certain accomplishment without deviation and its unerring outcome, thus, true, and not otherwise. For indeed, this Blessed One, while a bodhisatta, having fulfilled all the causes for Buddhahood of various kinds as described, such as the thirty perfections, and while dwelling in the Tusita heaven, heard the Buddha-uproar and was approached by the deities of the ten-thousand world-systems who had gathered together—

“Kālo deva mahāvīra, uppajja mātukucchiyaṃ;

Sadevakaṃ tārayanto, bujjhassu amataṃ pada”nti. (bu. vaṃ. 1.67) –

“O Deva, great hero, it is time! Be born in a mother’s womb. Leading the world with its devas across, awaken to the deathless state!”

Āyācito uppannapubbanimitto pañca mahāvilokanāni viloketvā “idānāhaṃ manussayoniyaṃ uppajjitvā abhisambujjhissāmī”ti āsāḷhipuṇṇamāya sakyarājakule mahāmāyāya deviyā kucchimhi paṭisandhiṃ gahetvā dasa māse devamanussehi mahatā parihārena parihariyamāno visākhapuṇṇamāya paccūsasamaye abhijātiṃ pāpuṇi.

Having been requested, with the precursory signs having appeared, he made the five great investigations. Then, considering, “Now I will be born in the human realm and will perfectly awaken,” on the full-moon day of Āsāḷhī, he took conception in the womb of Queen Mahāmāyā in the royal family of the Sakyans. For ten months, he was protected with great care by devas and humans, and on the full-moon day of Visākha, at dawn, he achieved his supreme birth.

Abhijātikkhaṇe [V 0.0119] panassa paṭisandhiggahaṇakkhaṇe viya dvattiṃsapubbanimittāni pāturahesuṃ. Ayañhi dasasahassī lokadhātu kampi saṅkampi sampakampi sampavedhi, dasasu cakkavāḷasahassesu appamāṇo obhāso phari, tassa taṃ siriṃ daṭṭhukāmā viya jaccandhā cakkhūni paṭilabhiṃsu, badhirā saddaṃ suṇiṃsu. Mūgā samālapiṃsu, khujjā ujugattā ahesuṃ, paṅgulā padasā gamanaṃ paṭilabhiṃsu, bandhanagatā sabbasattā andubandhanādīhi mucciṃsu, sabbanirayesu aggi nibbāyi, pettivisaye khuppipāsā vūpasami, tiracchānānaṃ bhayaṃ nāhosi, sabbasattānaṃ rogo vūpasami, sabbasattā piyaṃvadā ahesuṃ, madhurenākārena assā hasiṃsu, vāraṇā gajjiṃsu, sabbatūriyāni sakaṃ sakaṃ ninnādaṃ muñciṃsu, aghaṭṭitāni eva manussānaṃ hatthūpagādīni ābharaṇāni madhurenākārena raviṃsu, sabbadisā vippasannā ahesuṃ, sattānaṃ sukhaṃ uppādayamāno mudusītalavāto vāyi, akālamegho vassi, pathavitopi udakaṃ ubbhijjitvā vissandi, pakkhino ākāsagamanaṃ vijahiṃsu, nadiyo asandamānā aṭṭhaṃsu, mahāsamudde madhuraṃ udakaṃ ahosi, upakkilesavimutte sūriye dissamāne eva ākāsagatā sabbā jotiyo jaliṃsu[P 0.0150], ṭhapetvā arūpāvacare deve avasesā sabbe devā sabbepi nerayikā dissamānarūpā ahesuṃ, tarukuṭṭakavāṭaselādayo anāvaraṇabhūtā ahesuṃ, sattānaṃ cutūpapātā nāhesuṃ, sabbaṃ aniṭṭhagandhaṃ abhibhavitvā dibbagandho vāyi, sabbe phalūpagā rukkhā phaladharā sampajjiṃsu, mahāsamuddo [M 0.0133] sabbatthakameva pañcavaṇṇehi padumehi sañchannatalo ahosi, thalajajalajādīni sabbapupphāni pupphiṃsu, rukkhānaṃ khandhesu khandhapadumāni, sākhāsu sākhapadumāni, latāsu latāpadumāni pupphiṃsu, mahītale silātalāni bhinditvā uparūpari satta satta hutvā daṇḍapadumāni nāma nikkhamiṃsu, ākāse olambakapadumāni nibbattiṃsu, samantato pupphavassaṃ vassi, ākāse dibbatūriyāni vajjiṃsu, sakaladasasahassī lokadhātu vaṭṭetvā vissaṭṭhamālāguḷaṃ viya uppīḷetvā baddhamālākalāpo viya alaṅkatappaṭiyattaṃ mālāsanaṃ viya ca ekamālāmālinī vipphurantavāḷabījanī pupphadhūpagandhaparivāsitā paramasobhaggappattā ahosi, tāni ca pubbanimittāni upari adhigatānaṃ anekesaṃ visesādhigamānaṃ nimittabhūtāni eva ahesuṃ. Evaṃ anekacchariyapātubhāvappaṭimaṇḍitā cāyaṃ abhijāti yadatthaṃ anena abhisambodhi patthitā, tassā abhisambodhiyā ekantasiddhiyā tathāva ahosi avitathā anaññathā.

At the moment of his birth, just as at the moment of his taking rebirth-linking, the thirty-two precursory signs appeared. Indeed, this ten-thousandfold world system quaked, shook, trembled, and vibrated. An immeasurable radiance spread throughout the ten thousand world-spheres. As if desiring to see his glory, those born blind regained their sight. The deaf heard sounds. The mute spoke. The hunchbacked became straight-bodied. The lame gained the ability to walk on foot. All beings in bondage were freed from their fetters, such as ankle-chains. The fires in all hells were extinguished. In the realm of ghosts, hunger and thirst ceased. Fear vanished among animals. The sickness of all beings subsided. All beings spoke kindly to one another. Horses neighed sweetly. Elephants trumpeted. All musical instruments emitted their own sounds. Even when unstruck, the ornaments of humans, such as bracelets, resounded sweetly. All directions became exceptionally clear. A gentle, cool breeze blew, producing happiness in beings. An unseasonal cloud rained. Water sprang up from the earth and flowed forth. Birds abandoned their flight through the sky. Rivers, no longer flowing, stood still. The water in the great ocean became sweet. Even while the sun, free from impurities, was visible, all the lights in the sky blazed. Except for the formless-sphere devas, all other devas and all hell-beings became visible in form. Trees, walls, doors, rocks, and so on became without obstruction. The passing away and arising of beings ceased. Overcoming all unpleasant odors, a divine fragrance wafted. All fruit-bearing trees became laden with fruit. The great ocean everywhere had its surface covered with five-colored lotuses. All flowers—those on land, in water, and elsewhere—bloomed. On the trunks of trees, trunk-lotuses bloomed; on branches, branch-lotuses; on vines, vine-lotuses. Breaking through the earth's surface and stone slabs, stem-lotuses emerged, seven by seven in tiers. Hanging lotuses appeared in the sky. A rain of flowers fell from all around. Divine musical instruments played in the heavens. The entire ten-thousandfold world system—like a rolled-up ball of garlands let loose, like a pressed and bound wreath of flowers, and like a decorated and prepared floral seat—became adorned with a single garland-chain, radiant with waving fans, perfumed with the fragrance of flowers and incense, and attained supreme glory. And those precursory signs were indeed omens of the many superior attainments to be realized later. Thus, this birth, adorned with the manifestation of many marvels, was just so, unfailing, and not otherwise, due to the certain accomplishment of that perfect enlightenment for which he had aspired.

Tathā ye buddhaveneyyā bodhaneyyabandhavā, te sabbepi anavasesato sayameva bhagavatā vinītā. Ye ca sāvakaveneyyā dhammaveneyyā ca, tepi sāvakādīhi vinītā vinayaṃ gacchanti gamissanti cāti yadatthaṃ bhagavatā abhisambodhi abhipatthitā, tadatthassa ekantasiddhiyā abhisambodhi tathā avitathā anaññathā.

Thus, all those who are to be trained by a Buddha, kinsmen who can be awakened, have been personally trained by the Blessed One without remainder. And those who are to be trained by disciples or by the Dhamma are also trained by disciples and others; they are attaining discipline and will attain it. Thus, because of the certain accomplishment of that purpose for which the Blessed One aspired to perfect enlightenment, that perfect enlightenment is true, unfailing, and not otherwise.

Apica [V 0.0120] yassa yassa ñeyyadhammassa yo yo sabhāvo bujjhitabbo, so so hatthatale ṭhapitaāmalakaṃ viya āvajjanamattappaṭibaddhena attano ñāṇena aviparītaṃ anavasesato bhagavatā abhisambuddhoti evampi abhisambodhi tathā avitathā anaññathā.

Moreover, whatever knowable phenomena, whatever their respective natures are to be understood, all these have been perfectly awakened to by the Blessed One with his own knowledge, without error and completely, as a myrobalan fruit placed in the palm of the hand is perceived upon merely directing one's attention. In this way too, perfect enlightenment is true, unfailing, and not otherwise.

Tathā tesaṃ tesaṃ dhammānaṃ tathā tathā desetabbappakāraṃ tesaṃ tesañca sattānaṃ āsayānusayacaritādhimuttiṃ sammadeva oloketvā [P 0.0151] dhammataṃ avijahanteneva paññattinayavohāramaggaṃ anatidhāvanteneva ca dhammataṃ vibhāvantena yathāparādhaṃ yathājjhāsayaṃ yathādhammañca anusāsantena bhagavatā veneyyā vinītā ariyabhūmiṃ sampāpitāti dhammavinayapaññāpanāpissa tadatthasiddhiyā yathābhūtavuttiyā ca tathā avitathā anaññathā.

Thus, the Blessed One, having rightly discerned the various ways the Dhamma should be taught to each of them, and having rightly discerned the inclinations, latent tendencies, characters, and dispositions of each of those beings, without abandoning the nature of the Dhamma, without overstepping the path of conventional expression, and revealing the nature of the Dhamma, while instructing them according to their offenses, their aspirations, and according to the Dhamma, trained those who were to be trained and led them to the noble plane. In this way, his promulgation of the Dhamma and Vinaya, for the accomplishment of that purpose and for its being in accordance with reality, is also true, unfailing, and not otherwise.

Tathā [M 0.0134] yā sā bhagavatā anuppattā pathaviyādiphassavedanādirūpārūpasabhāvavinimuttā lujjanabhāvābhāvato lokasabhāvātītā tamasā visaṃsaṭṭhattā kenaci anobhāsanīyā lokasabhāvābhāvato eva gatiādibhāvarahitā appatiṭṭhā anārammaṇā amatamahānibbānadhātu khandhasaṅkhātānaṃ upādīnaṃ lesamattassapi abhāvato anupādisesāti vuccati, yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ –

Thus, that deathless, great Nibbāna-element which was attained by the Blessed One—free from the nature of earth, etc., sensory impingement, etc., and from the nature of form and formlessness; transcending the nature of the world because it is not subject to disintegration; unmingled with darkness; not illuminated by anything; devoid of the nature of the world itself; free from states such as destination; without foundation; and without object—is called 'Nibbāna with no residue remaining' because of the absence of even a trace of the substrates of existence, which are the aggregates. Concerning this, it was said:

“Atthi, bhikkhave, tadāyatanaṃ, yattha neva pathavī na āpo na tejo na vāyo na ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ na viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ na ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ na nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ nāyaṃ loko na paro loko na ca ubho candimasūriyā, tatrāpāhaṃ, bhikkhave, neva āgatiṃ vadāmi na gatiṃ na ṭhitiṃ na cutiṃ na upapattiṃ, appatiṭṭhaṃ appavattaṃ anārammaṇamevetaṃ, esevanto dukkhassā”ti (udā. 71).

“Monks, there is that dimension where there is no earth, no water, no fire, no wind; no dimension of infinite space, no dimension of infinite consciousness, no dimension of nothingness, no dimension of neither perception nor non-perception; neither this world nor another world nor both sun and moon. There, monks, I say there is no coming, no going, no staying, no passing away, no arising. It is without foundation, without continuation, and without an object. This itself is the end of suffering.”

Sā sabbesampi upādānakkhandhānaṃ atthaṅgamo, sabbasaṅkhārānaṃ samatho, sabbūpadhīnaṃ paṭinissaggo, sabbadukkhānaṃ vūpasamo, sabbālayānaṃ samugghāto, sabbavaṭṭānaṃ upacchedo, accantasantilakkhaṇoti yathāvuttasabhāvassa kadācipi avisaṃvādanato tathā avitathā anaññathā. Evametā abhijātiādikā tathā gato upagato adhigato paṭipanno pattoti tathāgato. Evaṃ bhagavā tathā gatoti tathāgato.

It is the cessation of all clinging-aggregates, the stilling of all fabrications, the relinquishment of all substrata, the pacification of all suffering, the uprooting of all attachments, the cutting off of all rounds of existence, and is characterized by supreme peace; because its nature as described is never discordant, it is thus true, unerring, and not otherwise. Thus, because he has gone (`gato`), approached (`upagato`), attained (`adhigato`), entered upon (`paṭipanno`), and reached (`patto`) these true (`tathā`) things beginning with noble birth, he is a Tathāgata. Thus, the Blessed One has gone to the true; therefore, he is a Tathāgata.

Kathaṃ tathāvidhoti tathāgato? Yathāvidhā purimakā sammāsambuddhā, ayampi bhagavā tathāvidho. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Yathāvidhā te bhagavanto maggasīlena phalasīlena sabbenapi lokiyalokuttarasīlena, maggasamādhinā phalasamādhinā [P 0.0152] sabbenapi lokiyalokuttarasamādhinā, maggapaññāya [V 0.0121] phalapaññāya sabbāyapi lokiyalokuttarapaññāya, devasikaṃ valañjitabbehi catuvīsatikoṭisatasahassasamāpattivihārehi, tadaṅgavimuttiyā, vikkhambhanavimuttiyā, samucchedavimuttiyā, paṭippassaddhivimuttiyā, nissaraṇavimuttiyāti saṅkhepato. Vitthārato pana anantāparimāṇabhedehi acinteyyānubhāvehi sakalasabbaññuguṇehi, ayampi [M 0.0135] amhākaṃ bhagavā tathāvidho. Sabbesañhi sammāsambuddhānaṃ āyuvemattaṃ, sarīrappamāṇavemattaṃ, kulavemattaṃ, dukkaracariyāvemattaṃ, rasmivemattanti, imehi pañcahi vemattehi siyā vemattaṃ, na pana sīlavisuddhiyādīsu visuddhīsu samathavipassanāpaṭipattiyaṃ attanā paṭiladdhaguṇesu ca kiñci nānākaraṇaṃ atthi. Atha kho majjhe bhinnasuvaṇṇaṃ viya aññamaññaṃ nibbisesā te buddhā bhagavanto. Tasmā yathāvidhā purimakā sammāsambuddhā, ayampi bhagavā tathāvidho. Evaṃ tathāvidhoti tathāgato. Vidhattho cettha gatasaddo, tathā hi lokiyā vidhayuttagatasadde pakāratthe vadanti.

How is the Tathāgata 'thus-of-such-a-nature'? Just as the former Perfectly Self-Enlightened Ones were of such a nature, so too is this Blessed One. What is meant by this? Just as those Blessed Ones were endowed with the virtue of the path, the virtue of the fruit, and all mundane and supramundane virtue; with the concentration of the path, the concentration of the fruit, and all mundane and supramundane concentration; with the wisdom of the path, the wisdom of the fruit, and all mundane and supramundane wisdom; with the twenty-four hundred thousand crores of meditative attainments to be resorted to daily, with temporary liberation, liberation by suppression, liberation by eradication, liberation by tranquility, and liberation by deliverance—in brief. In detail, with infinite, immeasurable distinctions, inconceivable potency, and all the qualities of omniscience—so too is our Blessed One of such a nature. For all Perfectly Self-Enlightened Ones may differ in terms of lifespan, bodily measure, clan, difficult practice, and radiance—these five differences—but there is no difference whatsoever in the purities such as purity of virtue, in the practice of serenity and insight, or in the qualities attained by oneself. Rather, like gold broken in the middle, those Blessed Buddhas are indistinguishable from each other. Therefore, just as the former Perfectly Self-Enlightened Ones were of such a nature, so too is this Blessed One. Thus, the Tathāgata is 'thus-of-such-a-nature.' Here, the word 'gata' is used in the sense of 'vidha' (kind/manner), for in worldly usage, they speak of 'vidha-yutta-gata' in the sense of 'kind' or 'manner'.

Kathaṃ tathā pavattitoti tathāgato? Anaññasādhāraṇena iddhānubhāvena samannāgatattā atthappaṭisambhidādīnaṃ ukkaṃsapāramippattiyā anāvaraṇañāṇappaṭilābhena ca bhagavato kāyappavattiyādīnaṃ katthaci paṭighātābhāvato yathā ruci tathā gataṃ gati gamanaṃ kāyavacīcittappavatti etassāti tathāgato. Evaṃ tathā pavattitoti tathāgato.

How is the Tathāgata 'thus-proceeding'? Because he is endowed with uncommon psychic potency, having reached the highest perfection of the analytical knowledges, and through the obtaining of unobstructed knowledge, the Blessed One’s bodily, verbal, and mental activities proceed as he wishes, without obstruction anywhere. Thus, the Tathāgata is 'thus-proceeding'.

Kathaṃ tathehi agatoti tathāgato? Bodhisambhārasambharaṇe tappaṭipakkhappavattisaṅkhātaṃ natthi etassa gatanti agato. So panassa agatabhāvo maccheradānapāramiādīsu aviparītaṃ ādīnavānisaṃsapaccavekkhaṇādinayappavattehi ñāṇehīti tathehi ñāṇehi agatoti tathāgato.

How is the Tathāgata 'thus-not-gone'? Because in accumulating the requisites of enlightenment, there is no going for him into what is reckoned as the arising of opposing forces, he is therefore 'not-gone' (`agato`). And since that state of being 'not-gone' is accomplished by means of true (`tathehi`) knowledges that proceed in an unperverted manner by reflecting on the drawbacks and benefits in the perfections, such as the perfection of generosity free from stinginess, therefore by means of true knowledges he is 'not-gone' (`tathehi agato`), hence Tathāgata.

Atha vā kilesābhisaṅkhārappavattisaṅkhātaṃ khandhappavattisaṅkhātameva vā pañcasupi gatīsu gataṃ gamanaṃ etassa natthīti agato. Saupādisesaanupādisesanibbānappattiyā svāyamassa agatabhāvo tathehi ariyamaggañāṇehīti evampi bhagavā tathehi agatoti tathāgato.

Or, he is 'not-gone' (`agato`) because there is no going for him to the five destinations, which are reckoned as the arising of defilements and volitional formations, or as the arising of the aggregates. This state of being 'not-gone' is due to his attainment of Nibbāna with and without residue by means of true noble path knowledges. Thus, in this way too, the Blessed One, by means of true (knowledges), is 'not-gone' (`tathehi agato`), hence Tathāgata.

Kathaṃ [P 0.0153] tathā gatabhāvena tathāgato? Tathā gatabhāvenāti ca tathāgatassa sabbhāvena atthitāyāti attho. Ko panesa tathāgato, yassa atthitāya bhagavā tathāgatoti vuccatīti? Saddhammo. Saddhammo hi ariyamaggo tāva yathā yuganaddhasamathavipassanābalena anavasesato kilesapakkhaṃ samūhanantena samucchedappahānavasena gantabbaṃ[M 0.0136], tathā gato. Phaladhammo yathā attano maggānurūpaṃ paṭippassaddhipahānavasena gantabbaṃ, tathā gato pavatto. Nibbānadhammo pana yathā gato [V 0.0122] paññāya paṭividdho sakalavaṭṭadukkhavūpasamāya sampajjati, buddhādīhi tathā gato sacchikatoti tathāgato. Pariyattidhammopi yathā purimabuddhehi suttageyyādivasena pavattiādippakāsanavasena ca veneyyānaṃ āsayādianurūpaṃ pavattito, amhākampi bhagavatā tathā gato gadito pavattitoti vā tathāgato. Yathā bhagavatā desito, tathā bhagavato sāvakehi gato avagatoti tathāgato. Evaṃ sabbopi saddhammo tathāgato. Tenāha sakko devānamindo – “tathāgataṃ devamanussapūjitaṃ, dhammaṃ namassāma suvatthi hotū”ti (khu. pā. 6.17; su. ni. 240). Svāssa atthīti bhagavā tathāgato.

How is the Tathāgata 'Tathāgata' by the state of 'thus-gone'? 'By the state of thus-gone' means the existence of the Tathāgata in its true nature—this is the meaning. But what is this Tathāgata, by whose existence the Blessed One is called Tathāgata? It is the True Dhamma. For the noble path, firstly, by the power of serenity and insight yoked together, having utterly eradicated the faction of defilements by way of abandonment through cutting off, is to be gone to in that way—thus it has gone. The fruition Dhamma, as it should be gone to in accordance with its path by way of abandonment through tranquilization, has thus proceeded. The Nibbāna Dhamma, however, as it is penetrated by wisdom for the complete cessation of the suffering of the round, is accomplished—thus gone, realized by the Buddhas and others—thus it is the Tathāgata. The Dhamma of study too, as it was expounded by the former Buddhas by way of suttas, geyyas, etc., and by way of revealing the arising, etc., in accordance with the dispositions of those to be trained, so too has it been spoken and expounded by our Blessed One—thus it is the Tathāgata. As taught by the Blessed One, so it has been gone to and understood by the Blessed One’s disciples—thus it is the Tathāgata. Thus, the entire True Dhamma is the Tathāgata. Therefore, Sakka, king of devas, said: 'We pay homage to the Dhamma, honored by devas and humans; may there be well-being!' And because that (Dhamma) exists for him, the Blessed One is the Tathāgata.

Yathā ca dhammo, evaṃ ariyasaṅghopi yathā attahitāya parahitāya ca paṭipannehi suvisuddhaṃ pubbabhāgasamathavipassanāpaṭipadaṃ purakkhatvā tena tena maggena gantabbaṃ, taṃ taṃ tathā gatoti tathāgato. Yathā vā bhagavatā saccapaṭiccasamuppādādayo desitā, tathāva buddhattā tathā gadanato ca tathāgato. Tenāha sakko devarājā – “tathāgataṃ devamanussapūjitaṃ, saṅghaṃ namassāma suvatthi hotū”ti. Svāssa sāvakabhūto atthīti bhagavā tathāgato. Evaṃ tathāgatabhāvena tathāgatoti.

And just as the Dhamma is, so too is the Noble Sangha a Tathāgata. For by those who practice for their own and others' benefit, having made the well-purified preliminary practice of serenity and insight their foundation, the respective goals are to be reached by the respective paths, and they have thus gone to them; therefore, [the Sangha is] a Tathāgata. Or, as the Blessed One has taught the truths, dependent origination, and so on, he is a Tathāgata because he has understood them thus and because he speaks thus. Therefore, Sakka, the king of devas, said: 'We pay homage to the Sangha, honored by devas and humans; may there be well-being!' And because that Sangha exists for him as his disciples, the Blessed One is a Tathāgata. Thus, by the state of being a Tathāgata, he is a Tathāgata.

Idampi ca tathāgatassa tathāgatabhāvadīpane mukhamattakameva, sabbākārena pana tathāgatova tathāgatassa [P 0.0154] tathāgatabhāvaṃ vaṇṇeyya. Idañhi tathāgatapadaṃ mahatthaṃ mahāgatikaṃ mahāvisayaṃ, tassa appamādapadassa viya tepiṭakampi buddhavacanaṃ yuttito atthabhāvena āharanto “atitthena dhammakathiko pakkhando”ti na vattabboti.

And this, too, is but a mere introduction to explaining the state of a Tathāgata; only a Tathāgata himself could describe the state of a Tathāgata in all its aspects. Indeed, this term 'Tathāgata' is of great meaning, great import, and great scope. Because it has such a great scope, like the term 'heedfulness', a Dhamma preacher who brings forth the Buddha's word, the Tipiṭaka, by way of meaning according to reason, should not be said to be 'one who rushes into an improper place'.

Tatthetaṃ vuccati –

Therein, this is said:

“Yatheva loke purimā mahesino,

Sabbaññubhāvaṃ munayo idhāgatā;

Tathā ayaṃ sakyamunīpi āgato,

Tathāgato vuccati tena cakkhumā.

"Just as the great sages of old in the world,

The sages who attained all-knowingness, have come here;

So too has this Sakyan Sage arrived;

Therefore, the One with Vision is called Tathāgata."

“Pahāya [M 0.0137] kāmādimale asesato,

Samādhiñāṇehi yathā gatā jinā;

Purātanā [V 0.0123] sakyamunī jutindharo,

Tathā gato tena tathāgato mato.

"Just as the ancient Conquerors, having completely abandoned defilements beginning with sensual desire, went by way of concentration and knowledge;

So too has the Sakyan Sage, the bearer of radiance, thus gone;

Therefore, he is considered Tathāgata."

“Tathañca dhātāyatanādilakkhaṇaṃ,

Sabhāvasāmaññavibhāgabhedato;

Sayambhuñāṇena jinoyamāgato,

Tathāgato vuccati sakyapuṅgavo.

"And the true characteristics of elements, sense bases, and so forth,

By way of their specific nature, general nature, and analytical distinctions;

This Conqueror has understood with self-arisen knowledge;

Therefore, the Bull of the Sakyans is called Tathāgata."

“Tathāni saccāni samantacakkhunā,

Tathā idappaccayatā ca sabbaso;

Anaññaneyyā nayato vibhāvitā,

Tathā gato tena jino tathāgato.

"The true Truths, and likewise Dependent Origination in every way,

Have been revealed by the All-Seeing One, through a method not learned from another;

Thus has he gone; therefore the Conqueror is a Tathāgata."

“Anekabhedāsupi lokadhātusu,

Jinassa rūpāyatanādigocare;

Vicittabhede tathameva dassanaṃ,

Tathāgato tena samantalocano.

"Even in the many-fold world-systems,

In the Conqueror's domain of various forms, sense bases, and so forth,

His vision is indeed true;

Therefore, the All-Seeing One is a Tathāgata."

“Yato [P 0.0155] ca dhammaṃ tathameva bhāsati,

Karoti vācāya nurūpamattano;

Guṇehi lokaṃ abhibhuyyirīyati,

Tathāgato tenapi lokanāyako.

"Since he speaks the Dhamma just as it is,

And acts in accordance with his own speech;

He fares, having overcome the world by his virtues;

For that reason too, the World-Leader is a Tathāgata."

“Tathā pariññāya tathāya sabbaso,

Avedi lokaṃ pabhavaṃ atikkami;

Gato ca paccakkhakiriyāya nibbutiṃ,

Arīyamaggañca gato tathāgato.

"Having thus, with true full understanding, in every way known the world and overcome its origin; and having gone to Nibbāna through direct realization and gone to the Noble Path, he is a Tathāgata."

“Tathā paṭiññāya tathāya sabbaso,

Hitāya lokassa yatoyamāgato;

Tathāya [V 0.0124] nātho karuṇāya sabbadā,

Gato ca tenāpi jino tathāgato.

"Since he has come for the welfare of the world, having thus made a true declaration in every way; and since the Protector has always acted with true compassion, for that reason too the Victor is a Tathāgata."

“Tathāni [M 0.0138] ñāṇāni yatoyamāgato,

Yathāsabhāvaṃ visayāvabodhato;

Tathābhijātippabhutī tathāgato,

Tadatthasampādanato tathāgato.

"Since he has attained the true knowledges through understanding objects according to their intrinsic nature; and since he is thus from his super-normal birth onwards, he is a Tathāgata; and from accomplishing that aim, he is a Tathāgata."

“Yathāvidhā te purimā mahesino,

Tathāvidhoyampi tathā yathāruci;

Pavattavācā tanucittabhāvato,

Tathāgato vuccati aggapuggalo.

"Of whatever kind were those great sages of old,

Of that same kind is this one too;

Because his speech, body, and mind proceed thus, as he wishes,

The supreme person is called Tathāgata."

“Sambodhisambhāravipakkhato pure,

Gataṃ na saṃsāragatampi tassa vā;

Na catthi nāthassa bhavantadassino,

Tathehi tasmā agato tathāgato.

"For the Protector who sees the end of becoming, there is no going contrary to the requisites of enlightenment, even before their ripening, nor is there any going to saṃsāra. Therefore, because of those truths, he is one who has not gone, a Tathāgata."

“Tathāgato dhammavaro mahesinā,

Yathā pahātabbamalaṃ pahīyati;

Tathāgato ariyagaṇopi satthuno,

Tathāgato tena samaṅgibhāvato”ti.

"The excellent Dhamma has been realized by the great seer, just as a defilement to be abandoned is abandoned; the noble community of the Teacher has also gone thus; by being endowed with these, he is a Tathāgata."

Mahiddhikatāti [P 0.0156] paramena cittavasībhāvena ca iddhividhayogena dhammānubhāvaññathattanipphādanasamatthatāsaṅkhātāya mahatiyā iddhiyā samannāgamo mahiddhikatā. Cirakālasambhūtena suvidūrappaṭipakkhena icchitatthanipphattihetubhūtena mahājutikena puññatejena samannāgamo mahānubhāvatā. Yatrāti acchariyapasaṃsākotuhalahāsapasādiko paccattatthe nipāto. Tena yuttattā vijāyissatīti anāgatakālavacanaṃ, attho pana atītakāloyeva. Ayañhettha attho – yā hi nāma ayaṃ suppavāsā tathā dukkhanimuggā kicchāpannā bhagavato vacanasamakālameva sukhinī arogā arogaṃ puttaṃ vijāyīti. Attamanoti sakamano, bhagavati pasādena kilesarahitacittoti [V 0.0125] attho. Kilesapariyuṭṭhitañhi cittaṃ vase avattanato attamanoti na sakkā vattunti. Attamanoti vā pītisomanassehi gahitamano. Pamuditoti pāmojjena [M 0.0139] yutto. Pītisomanassajātoti jātabalavapītisomanasso. Athāti pacchā, tato katipāhassa accayena. Sattabhattānīti sattasu divasesu dātabbabhattāni. Svātanāyāti svātanapuññatthaṃ, yaṃ sve buddhappamukhassa saṅghassa dānavasena payirupāsanavasena ca bhavissati puññaṃ tadatthaṃ.

“Greatness of psychic power” (mahiddhikatā) is the possession of great psychic power, defined as the ability to produce various transformations of phenomena through supreme mastery of mind and the application of psychic powers. “Greatness of authority” (mahānubhāvatā) is the possession of great and radiant meritorious power, accumulated over a long time, which overcomes very distant obstacles, and is the causal factor for achieving desired results. “Yatra” is a particle used in the sense of a personal matter, expressing wonder, praise, curiosity, laughter, and serene confidence. Because it is used with it, “she will give birth” is a future tense expression, but the meaning is actually in the past tense. The meaning here is this: that Suppavāsā, who was thus immersed in suffering and difficulty, at the very moment of the Blessed One’s words became happy, healthy, and gave birth to a healthy son. “Delighted” (attamano) means with one's own mind, that is, a mind free from defilements through serene confidence in the Blessed One. Indeed, a mind assailed by defilements cannot be called “delighted” because it is not under one's control. Alternatively, “delighted” means a mind seized by joy and gladness. “Gladdened” (pamudito) means endowed with gladness. “Filled with joy and happiness” (pītisomanassajāto) means one in whom strong joy and gladness have arisen. “Then” (atha) means afterward, after the passing of a few days. “Seven meals” (sattabhattāni) means meals to be given on seven days. “For tomorrow” (svātanāya) means for the sake of tomorrow’s merit, that is, for the merit that will arise tomorrow through giving to the Sangha headed by the Buddha and through attending upon them.

Atha kho bhagavā āyasmantaṃ mahāmoggallānaṃ āmantesīti kasmā āmantesi? Suppavāsāya sāmikassa pasādarakkhaṇatthaṃ. Suppavāsā pana acalappasādāva, upāsakassa pana pasādarakkhaṇaṃ mahāmoggallānattherassa bhāro. Tenāha “tuyheso upaṭṭhāko”ti. Tattha tuyhesoti tuyhaṃ eso. Tiṇṇaṃ dhammānaṃ pāṭibhogoti mama bhogādīnaṃ tiṇṇaṃ dhammānaṃ ahāniyā avināsāya ayyo mahāmoggallāno yadi pāṭibhogo yadi patibhū, ito satta divase atikkamitvā mama sakkā dānaṃ dātunti yadi ayyena ñātanti dīpeti. Theropi tassa tesu divasesu bhogānaṃ jīvitassa ca anupaddavaṃ passitvā āha – “dvinnaṃ kho nesaṃ, āvuso, dhammānaṃ pāṭibhogo bhogānañca jīvitassa cā”ti. Saddhā panassa cittappaṭibaddhāti tasseva bhāraṃ karonto “saddhāya pana tvaññeva pāṭibhogo”ti āha. Api ca so upāsako diṭṭhasacco, tassa saddhāya aññathābhāvo natthīti tathā vuttaṃ. Teneva ca kāraṇena bhagavatā “pacchāpi tvaṃ karissasīti saññāpehī”ti vuttaṃ. Upāsakopi [P 0.0157] satthari there ca gāravena subbacatāya tassā ca puññena vaḍḍhiṃ icchanto “karotu suppavāsā koliyadhītā satta bhattāni, pacchāhaṃ karissāmī”ti anujāni.

Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna. Why did he address him? To preserve the faith of Suppavāsā’s husband. Suppavāsā’s faith was unshakable, but the Blessed One made the preservation of the layman’s faith the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna’s responsibility. Therefore, he said, “He is your attendant.” Here, “tuyheso” means “tuyhaṃ eso” (he is yours). “A guarantor for three things” means: “If the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna is a guarantor or a surety for the non-loss and non-destruction of my three things—possessions and so on—then after seven days have passed, I will be able to give alms.” This is to show if the venerable would agree. The elder, seeing no danger to the layman's possessions or life during those days, said, “Friend, I am a guarantor for two of those things: your possessions and your life.” But since the layman's faith was bound to his mind, placing that responsibility on the layman himself, the elder said, “As for faith, you yourself are the guarantor.” Moreover, that layman had seen the truth, so there could be no change in his faith; thus it was said. And for this very reason, the Blessed One said, “Persuade him by saying, ‘You will do it later.’” The layman, out of reverence for the Teacher and the elder, due to his compliance, and wishing for the growth of her merit, consented, saying, “Let Suppavāsā, the Koliyan daughter, first offer seven meals. I will do it later.”

Tañca dārakanti vijātadivasato paṭṭhāya ekādasamaṃ divasaṃ atikkamitvā tato paraṃ sattāhaṃ buddhappamukhaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ bhojetvā sattame divase taṃ sattavassikaṃ dārakaṃ bhagavantaṃ bhikkhusaṅghañca vandāpesi. Satta me vassānīti satta me saṃvaccharāni, accantasaṃyogavasena cetaṃ upayogavacanaṃ. Lohitakumbhiyaṃ vutthānīti mātukucchiyaṃ attano gabbhavāsadukkhaṃ sandhāya vadati. Aññānipi evarūpāni satta puttānīti “aññepi evarūpe satta putte”ti vattabbe liṅgavipallāsavasena vuttaṃ “evarūpānī”ti. Evaṃ satta vassāni gabbhadhāraṇavasena sattāhaṃ mūḷhagabbhatāya ca mahantaṃ dukkhaṃ [M 0.0140] pāpetvā uppajjanakaputteti attho. Etena mātugāmānaṃ puttalolatāya puttalābhena titti natthīti dasseti.

And 'that boy' refers to this: from the day of his birth, after the eleventh day had passed, for seven days thereafter, the donor fed the community of monks headed by the Buddha. On the seventh day, he made that seven-year-old boy pay homage to the Blessed One and the community of monks. 'Seven years for me' means seven years for me; this is an accusative of duration due to constant connection. 'Having stayed in a blood-filled pot' refers to the suffering of dwelling in the mother’s womb; he speaks with reference to his own gestation. 'Other such seven sons' means: when it should be said 'other such seven sons' (in the masculine), it is said 'such ones' (in the neuter) due to a change of gender. The meaning is: sons who are born after having caused great suffering for seven years by way of gestation and for seven days by way of a confused womb. By this, it is shown that for women, due to their craving for sons, there is no satisfaction from obtaining a son.

Etamatthaṃ viditvāti etaṃ sattadivasādhikāni satta saṃvaccharāni gabbhadhāraṇādivasena pavattaṃ [V 0.0126] mahantaṃ dukkhaṃ ekapade visaritvā puttalolatāvasena tāya vuttamatthaṃ viditvā. Imaṃ udānanti imaṃ cittasukhappamatto viya pamattapuggale iṭṭhākārena vañcetvā taṇhāsinehassa mahānatthakarabhāvadīpakaṃ udānaṃ udānesi.

'Having understood this matter' means: having understood the matter spoken by her out of craving for a son, she having instantly forgotten the great suffering that occurred over seven years and seven days on account of gestation and so on. 'This inspired utterance' means: He uttered this inspired utterance that reveals the great harm of the affection of craving, which deceives heedless individuals in the guise of what is desirable, like a person who is heedless due to mental pleasure.

Tattha asātanti amadhuraṃ asundaraṃ aniṭṭhaṃ. Sātarūpenāti iṭṭhasabhāvena. Piyarūpenāti piyāyitabbabhāvena. Sukhassa rūpenāti sukhasabhāvena. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yasmā asātaṃ appiyaṃ dukkhameva samānaṃ sakalampi vaṭṭagataṃ saṅkhārajātaṃ appahīnavipallāsattā ayonisomanasikārena iṭṭhaṃ viya piyaṃ viya sukhaṃ viya ca hutvā upaṭṭhahamānaṃ sativippavāsena pamattapuggalaṃ ativattati abhibhavati ajjhottharati, tasmā imampi suppavāsaṃ punapi sattakkhattuṃ evarūpaṃ asātaṃ appiyaṃ dukkhaṃ sātādipatirūpakena dukkhena puttasaṅkhātapemavatthusukhena ajjhottharatīti.

Therein, 'unpleasant' means not sweet, not beautiful, not desirable. 'In the form of the agreeable' means with an agreeable nature. 'In the form of the dear' means with a lovable nature. 'In the form of happiness' means with a happy nature. This is what is said: because the entire mass of formations subject to the round of rebirth, while being in fact unpleasant, not dear, and suffering, appears as if it were agreeable, dear, and happy due to unabandoned distortions and unwise attention, it overcomes, overpowers, and overwhelms a heedless person who is lacking in mindfulness. Therefore, this craving also overwhelms this Suppavāsā, who would again seven times undergo such unpleasant, not dear suffering, with suffering disguised as the agreeable, that is, with the happiness related to the object of affection called a son.

Aṭṭhamasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the eighth sutta is concluded.

9. Visākhāsuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Visākhā Sutta

19. Navame [P 0.0158] pubbārāmeti sāvatthiyā pācīnadisābhāge anurādhapurassa uttamadevīvihārasadise ṭhāne kārite ārāme. Migāramātupāsādeti migāramātuyā pāsāde.

19. In the ninth sutta: 'In the Pubbārāma' means in the monastery built in the eastern part of Sāvatthī, in a place resembling the Uttamadevī Vihāra of Anurādhapura. 'In the mansion of Migāramātā' means in the mansion of Migāramātā.

Tatrāyaṃ anupubbikathā – atīte satasahassakappamatthake padumuttaradasabalaṃ ekā upāsikā aññataraṃ upāsikaṃ attano aggupaṭṭhāyikaṭṭhāne ṭhapentaṃ disvā bhagavantaṃ nimantetvā buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusatasahassassa dānaṃ datvā bhagavato nipaccakāraṃ katvā “anāgate tumhādisassa [M 0.0141] buddhassa aggupaṭṭhāyikā bhaveyya”nti patthanaṃ akāsi. Sā kappasatasahassaṃ devesu ca manussesu ca saṃsaritvā amhākaṃ bhagavato kāle bhaddiyanagare meṇḍakaseṭṭhiputtassa dhanañjayaseṭṭhino gehe sumanadeviyā kucchismiṃ paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhi. Jātakāle cassā visākhāti nāmaṃ akaṃsu. Sā yadā bhagavā bhaddiyanagaraṃ agamāsi, tadā pañcahi dārikāsatehi saddhiṃ bhagavato paccuggamanaṃ katvā paṭhamadassaneneva sotāpannā ahosi.

Here is the sequential narrative: In the past, a hundred thousand aeons ago, a certain female lay disciple, seeing the Ten-Powered One, Padumuttara, appointing another female lay disciple to the position of his chief female attendant, invited the Blessed One. Having given alms to a hundred thousand monks headed by the Buddha and having shown reverence to the Blessed One, she made an aspiration: “In the future, may I become the chief female attendant of a Buddha like you.” Having wandered for a hundred thousand aeons among gods and humans, during the time of our Blessed One, she took conception in the womb of Sumanādevī in the house of the merchant Dhanañjaya, son of the merchant Meṇḍaka, in the city of Bhaddiya. At the time of her birth, they gave her the name Visākhā. When the Blessed One came to the city of Bhaddiya, she, together with five hundred maidens, went to meet the Blessed One and became a stream-enterer at the very first sight of him.

Aparabhāge sāvatthiyaṃ migāraseṭṭhiputtassa puṇṇavaḍḍhanakumārassa gehaṃ gatā, tattha naṃ sasuro migāraseṭṭhi [V 0.0127] upakāravasena mātuṭṭhāne ṭhapesi. Tasmā migāramātāti vuccati. Sā attano mahallatāpasādhanaṃ vissajjetvā navakoṭīhi bhagavato bhikkhusaṅghassa ca vasanatthāya karīsamatte bhūmibhāge uparibhūmiyaṃ pañcagabbhasatāni heṭṭhābhūmiyaṃ pañcagabbhasatānīti gabbhasahassehi paṭimaṇḍitaṃ pāsādaṃ kāresi. Tena vuttaṃ “migāramātupāsāde”ti.

Later, in Sāvatthī, she went to the house of the young man Puṇṇavaḍḍhana, son of the merchant Migāra. There, her father-in-law, the merchant Migāra, on account of her great service, placed her in the position of his mother. Therefore, she is called Migāramātā. Having sold her Mahālatā adornment, for ninety million she had a mansion built on a plot of land the size of a karīsa for the Blessed One and the community of monks to reside in. It was adorned with a thousand rooms—five hundred rooms on the upper floor and five hundred rooms on the lower floor. Thus, it is said, 'in the mansion of Migāramātā.'

Kocideva atthoti kiñcideva payojanaṃ. Raññeti rājini. Paṭibaddhoti āyatto. Visākhāya ñātikulato maṇimuttādiracitaṃ tādisaṃ bhaṇḍajātaṃ tassā paṇṇākāratthāya pesitaṃ, taṃ [P 0.0159] nagaradvārappattaṃ suṅkikā tattha suṅkaṃ gaṇhantā tadanurūpaṃ aggahetvā atirekaṃ gaṇhiṃsu. Taṃ sutvā visākhā rañño tamatthaṃ nivedetukāmā patirūpaparivārena rājanivesanaṃ agamāsi, tasmiṃ khaṇe rājā mallikāya deviyā saddhiṃ antepuraṃ gato hoti. Visākhā okāsaṃ alabhamānā “idāni labhissāmi, idāni labhissāmī”ti bhojanavelaṃ atikkamitvā chinnabhattā hutvā pakkāmi. Evaṃ dvīhatīhaṃ gantvāpi okāsaṃ na labhiyeva. Iti rājā aniveditopi tassa atthavinicchayassa okāsākaraṇena “yathādhippāyaṃ na tīretī”ti vutto. Tattha yathādhippāyanti adhippāyānurūpaṃ. Na tīretīti na niṭṭhāpeti. Mahāupāsikāya hi rājāyattasuṅkameva rañño datvā itaraṃ vissajjāpetuṃ adhippāyo, so raññā na diṭṭhattā eva na tīrito. Handāti vossaggatthe nipāto. Divā divassāti divasassa divā, majjhanhike kāleti attho. Kenacideva karaṇīyena dvīhatīhaṃ rājanivesanadvāraṃ gacchantī tassa atthassa aniṭṭhitattā niratthakameva upasaṅkamiṃ[M 0.0142], bhagavati upasaṅkamanameva pana dassanānuttariyādippaṭilābhakāraṇattā sātthakanti evāhaṃ, bhante, imāya velāya idhāgatāti imamatthaṃ dassentī mahāupāsikā “idha me, bhante”tiādimāha.

Here, 'kocideva attho' means 'some purpose or another'. 'Raññe' means 'in the king'. 'Paṭibaddho' means 'dependent'. From Visākhā’s relatives, a collection of goods such as gems and pearls, of such a kind, was sent for her as a gift. When it arrived at the city gate, the tax collectors there, while collecting the tax on it, did not take an amount appropriate to it but took an excess. Hearing this, Visākhā, wishing to inform the king of the matter, went to the royal residence with a suitable retinue. At that moment, the king had gone to the inner quarters with Queen Mallikā. Unable to gain an audience, Visākhā, thinking, 'Now I will get it, now I will get it,' let the mealtime pass, and having missed her meal, she departed. Even after going for two or three days, she still could not get an audience. Thus, though the king was not informed, due to his not providing an opportunity for a decision on the matter, it is said, 'he did not bring it to completion as intended.' Here, 'yathādhippāyaṃ' means 'according to the intention'. 'Na tīretī' means 'he does not bring to completion'. For the great lay devotee's intention was to give only the tax dependent on the king to the king and have the rest released; since this was not seen by the king, it was not brought to completion. 'Handa' is a particle in the sense of relinquishment. 'Divā divassa' means 'by day of the day', that is, at midday. It was as if to say: 'For some business or another, going to the palace gate for two or three days, since that matter was not settled, I approached fruitlessly. However, approaching the Blessed One is indeed fruitful because it is a cause for the attainment of the unsurpassed vision and so forth. Thus, venerable sir, I have come here at this time.' Showing this meaning, the great lay devotee said, 'Here, venerable sir,' and so on.

Etamatthanti etaṃ parāyattatāya adhippāyāsamijjhanasaṅkhātaṃ atthaṃ viditvā. Imaṃ udānanti imaṃ parādhīnāparādhīnavuttīsu ādīnavānisaṃsaparidīpakaṃ udānaṃ udānesi.

Here, 'etam atthaṃ' means 'understanding this matter', that is, the matter defined as the non-fulfillment of intention due to dependence on others. 'Imaṃ udānaṃ' means 'this inspired utterance', that is, he uttered this inspired utterance that illuminates the dangers and benefits in regard to conduct that is dependent on others and not dependent on others.

Tattha sabbaṃ paravasaṃ dukkhanti yaṃ kiñci atthajātaṃ payojanaṃ paravasaṃ parāyattaṃ attano icchāya nipphādetuṃ asakkuṇeyyatāya dukkhaṃ dukkhāvahaṃ hotīti attho. Sabbaṃ issariyaṃ sukhanti duvidhaṃ issariyaṃ lokiyaṃ lokuttarañca. Tattha lokiyaṃ rājissariyādi ceva lokiyajjhānābhiññānibbattaṃ cittissariyañca, lokuttaraṃ maggaphalādhigamanimittaṃ nirodhissariyaṃ. Tesu yaṃ cakkavattibhāvapariyosānaṃ manussesu issariyaṃ, yañca sakkādīnaṃ tasmiṃ tasmiṃ devanikāye ādhipaccabhūtaṃ issariyaṃ, tadubhayaṃ yadipi kammānubhāvena yathicchitanipphattiyā sukhanimittatāya [V 0.0128] sukhaṃ, vipariṇāmadukkhatāya pana sabbathā dukkhameva. Tathā aniccantikatāya [P 0.0160] lokiyajjhānanibbattaṃ cittissariyaṃ, nirodhissariyameva pana lokadhammehi akampanīyato anivattisabhāvattā ca ekantasukhaṃ nāma. Yaṃ panettha sabbattheva aparādhīnatāya labhati cittasukhaṃ, taṃ sandhāya satthā “sabbaṃ issariyaṃ sukha”nti āha.

Here, 'sabbaṃ paravasaṃ dukkhaṃ' means that whatever kind of benefit or purpose is dependent, relying on others, is suffering because it cannot be achieved according to one's own wish; it is suffering-bringing. 'Sabbaṃ issariyaṃ sukhaṃ' means sovereignty is twofold: worldly and supramundane.
