Of these, worldly sovereignty includes royal sovereignty and so forth, as well as the sovereignty of mind produced by worldly jhānas and higher knowledges; supramundane sovereignty is the sovereignty of cessation, which is a cause for the attainment of the supramundane path and fruition. Among these, even though both the sovereignty among humans, which culminates in being a universal monarch, and the sovereignty which is the overlordship of Sakka and others in their respective divine realms, are happiness—in that they arise from the power of kamma and are a cause for happiness by achieving things as wished—they are, however, altogether suffering due to the suffering of change. Likewise, because of its impermanent nature, the sovereignty of mind produced by worldly jhānas is also suffering. But the sovereignty of cessation alone is indeed exclusively happiness, because it is unshaken by worldly conditions and has an irreversible nature. With reference to whatever happiness of mind one obtains here in every way through non-dependence, the Teacher said, 'All sovereignty is happiness.'

Sādhāraṇe vihaññantīti idaṃ “sabbaṃ paravasaṃ dukkha”nti imassa padassa atthavivaraṇaṃ. Ayañhettha attho – sādhāraṇe payojane sādhetabbe sati tassa parādhīnatāya yathādhippāyaṃ anipphādanato ime sattā vihaññanti vighātaṃ āpajjanti kilamanti. Kasmā? Yogā hi duratikkamāti yasmā kāmayogabhavayogadiṭṭhiyogaavijjāyogā anādikālabhāvitā anupacitakusalasambhārehi pajahituṃ asakkuṇeyyatāya duratikkamā. Etesu diṭṭhiyogo paṭhamamaggena atikkamitabbo, kāmayogo tatiyamaggena. Itare aggamaggena. Iti ariyamaggānaṃ duradhigamanīyattā ime yogā duratikkamā. Tasmā kāmayogādivasena icchitālābhahetu sattā vihaññanti, asādhāraṇe pana cittissariye [M 0.0143] nirodhissariye ca sati na kadācipi vighātassa sambhavoti adhippāyo.

The phrase 'sādhāraṇe vihaññanti' is an explanation of the meaning of the phrase 'sabbaṃ paravasaṃ dukkhaṃ'. The meaning here is this: when a shared purpose is to be accomplished, these beings are tormented, fall into distress, and become weary because, due to dependence on others, it is not accomplished as they intend. Why? Because 'the yokes are hard to overcome'. That is, since the yokes of sensual pleasure, existence, views, and ignorance have been developed since beginningless time, they are hard to overcome because those who have not accumulated a store of wholesome qualities are unable to abandon them. Among these, the yoke of views is to be overcome by the first path, and the yoke of sensual pleasure by the third path. The others are to be overcome by the highest path. Thus, because the noble paths are difficult to attain, these yokes are hard to overcome. Therefore, on account of not obtaining what is desired, due to the yokes of sensual pleasure and so forth, beings are tormented. But when there is unshared sovereignty of mind and sovereignty of cessation, there is never any possibility of distress. This is the intended meaning.

Atha vā sabbaṃ paravasanti yaṃ attano aññappaṭibaddhavuttisaṅkhātaṃ, taṃ sabbaṃ aniccasabhāvatāya dukkhaṃ. “Yadaniccaṃ taṃ dukkha”nti hi vuttaṃ. Sabbaṃ issariyanti yaṃ sabbasaṅkhatanissaṭaṃ issariyaṭṭhānatāya issariyanti laddhanāmaṃ nibbānaṃ, taṃ upādisesādivibhāgaṃ sabbaṃ sukhaṃ. “Nibbānaṃ paramaṃ sukha”nti (dha. pa. 203-204) hi vuttaṃ. Sādhāraṇeti evaṃ dukkhasukhe vavatthite ime sattā bahusādhāraṇe dukkhakāraṇe nimuggā hutvā vihaññanti. Kasmā? Yogā hi duratikkamāti yasmā te sabbattha nimujjanassa hetubhūtā kāmayogādayo duratikkamā, tasmā tvampi visākhe parāyattamatthaṃ patthetvā alabhamānā vihaññasīti adhippāyo.

Or else, 'sabbaṃ paravasaṃ' means that whatever is defined as a way of life tied to another is all suffering due to its impermanent nature. For it is said, “What is impermanent is suffering.” 'Sabbaṃ issariyaṃ' means Nibbāna, which has received the name 'sovereignty' because it is the state of sovereignty, escaped from all that is conditioned. That whole, with its divisions of Nibbāna with residue remaining and so forth, is happiness. For it is said, “Nibbāna is the highest happiness” (Dhp. 203–204). 'Sādhāraṇe' means that, when suffering and happiness have been thus determined, these beings, immersed in causes of suffering common to many, are afflicted. Why? Because 'the yokes are hard to overcome'. That is, since those yokes of sensual pleasure and so forth, which are the cause of their immersion everywhere, are hard to overcome, therefore, Visākhā, you too, having sought a matter dependent on another and not obtaining it, are afflicted—this is the intended meaning.

Navamasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the ninth discourse is finished.

10. Bhaddiyasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Bhaddiya Sutta

20. Dasame [V 0.0129][P 0.0161] anupiyāyanti evaṃ nāmake nagare. Ambavaneti tassa nagarassa avidūre mallarājūnaṃ ekaṃ ambavanaṃ ahosi, tattha mallarājūhi bhagavato vihāro kārito, so “ambavana”ntveva vuccati. Anupiyaṃ gocaragāmaṃ katvā tattha bhagavā viharati, tena vuttaṃ “anupiyāyaṃ viharati ambavane”ti. Bhaddiyoti tassa therassa nāmaṃ. Kāḷīgodhāya puttoti kāḷīgodhā nāma sākiyānī sakyarājadevī ariyasāvikā āgataphalā viññātasāsanā, tassā ayaṃ putto. Tassa pabbajjāvidhi khandhake (cūḷava. 330-331) āgatova. So pabbajitvā vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā na cirasseva chaḷabhiñño ahosi, terasapi dhutaṅgāni samādāya vattati. Bhagavatā ca “etadaggaṃ, bhikkhave, mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ uccakulikānaṃ, yadidaṃ bhaddiyo kāḷīgodhāya putto”ti (a. ni. 1.193) uccakulikabhāve etadagge ṭhapito asītiyā sāvakānaṃ abbhantaro.

20. In the tenth [discourse]: in a city named Anupiya. In Ambavana: near that city there was a mango grove belonging to the Malla kings. There, the Malla kings had a monastery built for the Blessed One, and it was simply called “Ambavana.” Having made Anupiya his alms-resort village, the Blessed One dwelled there. Hence it is said, “He dwelled at Ambavana in Anupiya.” Bhaddiya was the name of that elder. Son of Kāḷīgodhā: Kāḷīgodhā was a Sakyan queen of the Sakya royal family, a noble female disciple, an attainer of the fruit, and one who understood the teaching. This was her son. The procedure for his ordination is found in the Khandhaka (Cūḷavagga 330-331). Having gone forth, he established insight and soon became one with the sixfold higher knowledge. He lived undertaking the thirteen ascetic practices. And by the Blessed One he was established as the foremost in terms of high birth with the words, “Monks, among my monastic disciples of high birth, Bhaddiya, the son of Kāḷīgodhā, is the foremost.” He was included among the eighty great disciples.

Suññāgāragatoti “ṭhapetvā gāmañca gāmūpacārañca avasesaṃ arañña”nti vuttaṃ araññaṃ rukkhamūlañca ṭhapetvā aññaṃ pabbatakandarādi pabbajitasāruppaṃ nivāsaṭṭhānaṃ [M 0.0144] janasambādhābhāvato idha suññāgāranti adhippetaṃ. Atha vā jhānakaṇṭakānaṃ saddānaṃ abhāvato vivittaṃ yaṃ kiñci agārampi suññāgāranti veditabbaṃ. Taṃ suññāgāraṃ upagato. Abhikkhaṇanti bahulaṃ. Udānaṃ udānesīti so hi āyasmā araññe divāvihāraṃ upagatopi rattivāsūpagatopi yebhuyyena phalasamāpattisukhena nirodhasukhena ca vītināmeti, tasmā taṃ sukhaṃ sandhāya pubbe attanā anubhūtaṃ sabhayaṃ sapariḷāhaṃ rajjasukhaṃ jigucchitvā “aho sukhaṃ aho sukha”nti somanassasahitaṃ ñāṇasamuṭṭhānaṃ pītisamuṭṭhānaṃ samuggirati.

Gone to an empty dwelling: “Excluding the village and its vicinity, the remainder is the wilderness.” Here, an empty dwelling is intended to mean a suitable dwelling place for one gone forth—such as a mountain cave or the like—excluding the wilderness and the root of a tree, and free from the congestion of people. Alternatively, any secluded dwelling, even a house, devoid of the noises that are thorns to jhāna, should be understood as an empty dwelling. He has gone to such an empty dwelling. Frequently means often. Uttering an inspired utterance: the venerable one, whether having gone to the wilderness for the day-sojourn or for the night-sojourn, mostly passes the time with the bliss of fruition attainment and the bliss of cessation. Therefore, with reference to that happiness, having felt disgust towards the fearful and scorching pleasure of kingship previously experienced by himself, he utters, accompanied by joy, “Ah, happiness! Ah, happiness!”—an exclamation arisen from knowledge and arisen from rapture.

Sutvāna nesaṃ etadahosīti nesaṃ sambahulānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ tassa āyasmato “aho sukhaṃ, aho sukha”nti udānentassa udānaṃ sutvā “nissaṃsayaṃ esa anabhirato brahmacariyaṃ caratī”ti evaṃ parivitakkitaṃ ahosi. Te bhikkhū puthujjanā tassa āyasmato vivekasukhaṃ sandhāya udānaṃ ajānantā [P 0.0162] evaṃ amaññiṃsu, tena vuttaṃ “nissaṃsaya”ntiādi. Tattha nissaṃsayanti asandehena ekantenāti attho. “Yaṃ so pubbe agāriyabhūto samāno”ti pāḷiṃ vatvā “anubhavī”ti vacanasesena keci atthaṃ vaṇṇenti, apare “yaṃ sā”ti paṭhanti, “yaṃsa pubbe agāriyabhūtassā”ti pana pāḷi. Tattha yaṃsāti yaṃ assa, sandhivasena hi akārasakāralopo “evaṃsa te (ma. ni. 1.23; a. ni. 6.58), pupphaṃsā uppajjī”tiādīsu [V 0.0130] (pārā. 36) viya. Tassattho – assa āyasmato bhaddiyassa pabbajitato pubbe agāriyabhūtassa gahaṭṭhassa sato yaṃ rajjasukhaṃ anubhūtaṃ. Sā tamanussaramānoti so taṃ sukhaṃ etarahi ukkaṇṭhanavasena anussaranto.

Having heard this, it occurred to those many monks: when they heard that venerable one uttering the inspired utterance, “Ah, happiness! Ah, happiness!” they thought, “Surely, this one practices the holy life without delight.” Those monks, being worldlings and not knowing that the venerable one uttered this inspired utterance with reference to the happiness of seclusion, thought thus. Hence, it is said, “Surely…” and so on. Here, “surely” means without doubt, certainly. Some explain the meaning by stating the Pāḷi phrase, “That which he, being formerly a householder…” and completing it with the word “experienced.” Others read `yaṃ sā`. The Pāḷi, however, is `yaṃsa pubbe agāriyabhūtassā`. Therein, `yaṃsa` is `yaṃ assa`; for the elision of the vowel ‘a’ occurs by sandhi, as in such phrases as `evaṃsa te` (MN 1.23; AN 6.58) and `pupphaṃsā uppajjī` (Pārā. 36). The meaning of this is: that happiness of kingship which was experienced by this venerable Bhaddiya before he went forth, while he was a householder. Remembering that: this means he now recalls that happiness out of discontent.

Te bhikkhū bhagavantaṃ etadavocunti te sambahulā bhikkhū ullapanasabhāvasaṇṭhitā tassa anuggahaṇādhippāyena bhagavantaṃ etadavocuṃ, na ujjhānavasena. Aññataranti nāmagottena apākaṭaṃ ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ. Āmantesīti āṇāpesi te bhikkhū saññāpetukāmo. Evanti vacanasampaṭiggahe, sādhūti attho. Puna evanti paṭiññāya. Abhikkhaṇaṃ “aho sukhaṃ, aho sukha”nti imaṃ udānaṃ udānesīti yathā te bhikkhū vadanti, taṃ evaṃ tathevāti attano udānaṃ paṭijānāti. Kiṃ pana tvaṃ bhaddiyāti kasmā bhagavā pucchati, kiṃ tassa cittaṃ na jānātīti[M 0.0145]? No na jānāti, teneva pana tamatthaṃ vadāpetvā te bhikkhū saññāpetuṃ pucchati. Vuttañhetaṃ – “jānantāpi tathāgatā pucchanti, jānantāpi na pucchantī”tiādi. Atthavasanti kāraṇaṃ.

Those monks addressed the Blessed One: those several monks, being of a supportive nature and with the intention of helping him, addressed the Blessed One, not out of a desire to complain. A certain one: a single monk, not distinguished by name and clan. Addressed: He commanded [that monk], desiring to make [the other] monks understand. Yes: in acceptance of the statement, meaning “good.” Again, yes: in confirmation. “Repeatedly, ‘Ah, happiness! Ah, happiness!’—this inspired utterance he uttered”; just as those monks say, so he acknowledges his own inspired utterance to be exactly so. “But you, Bhaddiya…”: why does the Blessed One ask? Does he not know his mind? No, it is not that he does not know; rather, he asks in order to have Bhaddiya himself state the reason, and thus to make those monks understand. For it is said: “Even knowing, the Tathāgatas ask; even knowing, they do not ask,” and so on. For a reason: meaning, for a cause.

Antepureti itthāgārassa sañcaraṇaṭṭhānabhūte rājagehassa abbhantare, yattha rājā nhānabhojanasayanādiṃ kappeti. Rakkhā susaṃvihitāti ārakkhādikatapurisehi gutti suṭṭhu samantato vihitā. Bahipi antepureti aḍḍakaraṇaṭṭhānādike antepurato bahibhūte rājagehe. Evaṃ rakkhito gopito santoti evaṃ rājageharājadhānirajjadesesu anto ca bahi ca anekesu ṭhānesu anekasatehi susaṃvihitarakkhāvaraṇaguttiyā mameva nibbhayatthaṃ phāsuvihāratthaṃ rakkhito gopito samāno. Bhītotiādīni padāni aññamaññavevacanāni. Atha [P 0.0163] vā bhītoti pararājūhi bhāyamāno. Ubbiggoti sakarajjepi pakatito uppajjanakabhayubbegena ubbiggo calito. Ussaṅkīti “raññā nāma sabbakālaṃ avissatthena bhavitabba”nti vacanena sabbattha avissāsavasena tesaṃ tesaṃ kiccakaraṇīyānaṃ paccayaparisaṅkāya ca uddhamukhaṃ saṅkamāno. Utrāsīti “santikāvacarehipi ajānantasseva me kadāci anattho bhaveyyā”ti uppannena sarīrakampaṃ uppādanasamatthena tāsena utrāsī. “Utrasto”tipi paṭhanti. Vihāsinti evaṃbhūto hutvā vihariṃ.

“In the inner palace”—the inner part of the royal residence, which is a place of passage for the women's quarters, where the king performs bathing, eating, sleeping, and so on. “Well-guarded”—protection thoroughly well-arranged on all sides by guards and other such men. “And outside the inner palace”—in places such as the law courts and other royal buildings outside the inner palace. “Thus guarded, protected”—being guarded and protected in this way, within the royal residence, the capital, and the kingdom, both inside and outside, in many places, by hundreds of well-arranged guards, barriers, and security, for my own safety and comfort. “Fearful” and so on—these words are synonyms for each other. Alternatively, “fearful”—afraid of other kings. “Terrified”—shaken by fear and anxiety arising naturally even in his own kingdom. “Suspicious”—due to the saying, “A king must always be distrustful,” being distrustful everywhere, and increasingly apprehensive due to suspicion regarding the conditions for their various duties. “Alarmed”—alarmed by the fear that arises from thinking, “Even those who move about near me might someday harm me without my knowledge,” a fear capable of causing the body to tremble. Some also read “utrasto.” “I lived”—having become one in such a state, I dwelt.

Etarahīti idāni pabbajitakālato paṭṭhāya. Ekoti asahāyo, tena vūpakaṭṭhakāyataṃ dasseti. Abhītotiādīnaṃ padānaṃ vuttavipariyāyena attho veditabbo. Bhayādinimittassa pariggahassa taṃ nimittassa ca kilesassa abhāvenevassa abhītāditāti. Etena cittavivekaṃ dasseti[V 0.0131]. Appossukkoti sarīraguttiyaṃ nirussukko. Pannalomoti lomahaṃsuppādakassa chambhitattassa abhāvena anuggatalomo. Padadvayenapi serivihāraṃ dasseti. Paradattavuttoti parehi dinnena cīvarādinā vattamāno, etena sabbaso saṅgābhāvadīpanamukhena anavasesabhayahetuvirahaṃ dasseti. Migabhūtena cetasāti vissatthavihāritāya migassa viya jātena cittena. Migo hi amanussapathe araññe vasamāno [M 0.0146] vissattho tiṭṭhati, nisīdati, nipajjati, yenakāmañca pakkamati appaṭihatacāro, evaṃ ahampi viharāmīti dasseti. Vuttañhetaṃ paccekabuddhena –

“Now”—means from the time of going forth onward. “Alone”—means without a companion; by this, he indicates his seclusion. The meaning of the words “fearless” and so on should be understood as the opposite of what was previously stated. It is due to the absence of possession, which is the cause of fear and so on, and of the defilement that is the cause of that possession, that he is fearless and so on. By this, he shows mental seclusion. “Free from anxiety”—means unconcerned about bodily protection. “With hair lying down”—means having hair that is not standing on end, due to the absence of the trembling that causes hair to bristle. With these two phrases, he also indicates dwelling at ease. “Living on what is given by others”—means subsisting on robes and other requisites provided by others; by this, in showing a complete absence of suspicion, he indicates the lack of any remaining cause for fear. “With a mind that has become like a deer’s”—means with a mind that has become like a deer’s due to dwelling trustingly. For a deer, dwelling in the wilderness on a path not frequented by humans, remains trusting—it stands, sits, lies down, and departs wherever it wishes, its movement unimpeded. He indicates, “Thus I also dwell.” As has been said by a Paccekabuddha:

“Migo araññamhi yathā abaddho,

Yenicchakaṃ gacchati gocarāya;

Viññū naro seritaṃ pekkhamāno,

Eko care khaggavisāṇakappo”ti. (su. ni. 39; apa. thera 1.1.95);

“Just as a deer in the forest, unbound, goes for pasture wherever it wishes; so the wise person, seeing freedom, should wander alone like a rhinoceros horn.”

Imaṃ kho ahaṃ, bhante, atthavasanti, bhante, bhagavā yadidaṃ mama etarahi paramaṃ vivekasukhaṃ phalasamāpattisukhaṃ, idameva kāraṇaṃ sampassamāno “aho sukhaṃ, aho sukha”nti udānaṃ udānesinti.

“Venerable sir, it is for this reason, Blessed One, that seeing this very cause—namely, this supreme bliss of seclusion and bliss of the attainment of fruition that is now mine—I uttered the inspired utterance, ‘Oh, what bliss! Oh, what bliss!’”

Etamatthanti etaṃ bhaddiyattherassa [P 0.0164] puthujjanavisayātītaṃ vivekasukhasaṅkhātamatthaṃ sabbākārato viditvā. Imaṃ udānanti idaṃ sahetukabhayasokavigamānubhāvadīpakaṃ udānaṃ udānesi.

“Having understood this meaning”—means having understood in every way this meaning for Bhaddiya Thera, namely the bliss of seclusion which transcends the sphere of ordinary people. “He uttered this inspired utterance”—he uttered this inspired utterance which reveals the power of the removal of fear and sorrow along with their cause.

Tattha yassantarato na santi kopāti yassa ariyapuggalassa antarato abbhantare attano citte cittakālussiyakaraṇato cittappakopā rāgādayo āghātavatthuādikāraṇabhedato anekabhedā dosakopā eva kopā na santi maggena pahīnattā na vijjanti. Ayañhi antarasaddo kiñcāpi “mañca tvañca kimantara”ntiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 1.228) kāraṇe dissati, “antaraṭṭhake himapātasamaye”tiādīsu (mahāva. 346) vemajjhe, “antarā ca jetavanaṃ antarā ca sāvatthi”ntiādīsu (udā. 13, 44) vivare, “bhayamantarato jāta”ntiādīsu (itivu. 88; mahāni. 5) citte, idhāpi citte eva daṭṭhabbo. Tena vuttaṃ “antarato attano citte”ti.

Herein, “For whom there are no inner corruptions” means: for whichever noble person, within, in their own mind, there are no corruptions. These are corruptions of the mind such as lust, which cause mental turbidity, and the many kinds of corruptions of hatred arising from various causes like grounds for resentment. These corruptions do not exist, are not found, because they have been abandoned by the path. For although this word “antara” is seen to mean “cause” in passages such as “What is the cause between me and you?”; and “in the middle” in passages such as “during the Antaraṭṭhaka, the time of snowfall”; and “interval” in passages such as “between Jetavana and Sāvatthī”; and “mind” in passages such as “fear is born from within”; here too it should be understood as “mind.” Therefore it was said, “within, in their own mind.”

Itibhavābhavatañca vītivattoti yasmā bhavoti sampatti, abhavoti vipatti. Tathā bhavoti [V 0.0132] vuddhi, abhavoti hāni. Bhavoti vā sassataṃ, abhavoti ucchedo. Bhavoti vā puññaṃ, abhavoti pāpaṃ. Bhavoti vā sugati, abhavoti duggati. Bhavoti vā khuddako, abhavoti mahanto. Tasmā yā sā sampattivipattivuḍḍhihānisassatucchedapuññapāpasugatiduggati- khuddakamahantaupapattibhavānaṃ vasena iti anekappakārā bhavābhavatā vuccati. Catūhipi [M 0.0147] ariyamaggehi yathāsambhavaṃ tena tena nayena taṃ itibhavābhavatañca vītivatto atikkanto hoti. Atthavasena vibhatti vipariṇāmetabbā. Taṃ vigatabhayanti taṃ evarūpaṃ yathāvuttaguṇasamannāgataṃ khīṇāsavaṃ cittakopābhāvato itibhavābhavasamatikkamato ca bhayahetuvigamena vigatabhayaṃ, vivekasukhena aggaphalasukhena ca sukhiṃ, vigatabhayattā eva asokaṃ. Devā nānubhavanti dassanāyāti adhigatamagge ṭhapetvā sabbepi upapattidevā vāyamantāpi cittacāradassanavasena dassanāya daṭṭhuṃ nānubhavanti na abhisambhuṇanti na sakkonti, pageva manussā. Sekkhāpi hi puthujjanā viya arahato cittappavattiṃ na jānanti.

“And has overcome this existence and non-existence”—‘existence’ means success, and ‘non-existence’ means failure. Likewise, ‘existence’ is growth, ‘non-existence’ is decline. Or, ‘existence’ is eternalism, ‘non-existence’ is annihilationism. Or, ‘existence’ is merit, ‘non-existence’ is demerit. Or, ‘existence’ is a good destination, ‘non-existence’ is a bad destination. Or, ‘existence’ is the small, ‘non-existence’ is the great. Therefore, this state of ‘existence and non-existence’ is spoken of in its many varieties by way of success and failure, growth and decline, eternalism and annihilationism, merit and demerit, good and bad destinations, the small and the great, and rebirth-existence. By means of the four noble paths, as is appropriate in each case, one has overcome and transcended this state of ‘existence and non-existence.’ The case ending should be changed according to the meaning. “That one, free from fear”—such a person with cankers destroyed, endowed with the qualities as described, is free from fear because the cause of fear has been removed, which is due to the absence of mental corruptions and the transcending of this state of existence and non-existence. They are happy with the bliss of seclusion and the bliss of the highest fruit, and because they are free from fear, they are free from sorrow. “The gods do not experience him for seeing”—setting aside the gods who have attained the path, all the gods by rebirth, even if they strive, do not experience, do not comprehend, are not able to see the movements of his mind; how much less so humans. For even trainees, like ordinary people, do not know the course of an arahant’s mind.

Dasamasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the tenth sutta is concluded.

Niṭṭhitā ca mucalindavaggavaṇṇanā.

And the commentary on the Mucalinda chapter is concluded.

3. Nandavaggo

3. The Chapter on Nanda

1. Kammavipākajasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Discourse on What is Born from the Result of Kamma

21. Nandavaggassa [V 0.0133][M 0.0148][P 0.0165] paṭhame aññataro bhikkhūti nāmagottena apākaṭo eko khīṇāsavabhikkhu. So kira rājagahavāsī kulaputto moggallānattherena saṃvejito saṃsāradosaṃ disvā satthu santike pabbajitvā sīlāni sodhetvā catusaccakammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā na cirasseva vipassanaṃ ussukkāpetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tassa aparabhāge kharo ābādho uppajji, so paccavekkhaṇāya adhivāsento viharati. Khīṇāsavānañhi cetasikadukkhaṃ nāma natthi, kāyikadukkhaṃ pana hotiyeva. So ekadivasaṃ bhagavato dhammaṃ desentassa nātidūre ṭhāne dukkhaṃ adhivāsento pallaṅkena nisīdi. Tena vuttaṃ “bhagavato avidūre nisinno hotī”tiādi.

21. In the first sutta of the Nandavagga: A certain monk means a single arahant monk, not renowned by name and clan. It is said that he was a clansman from Rājagaha who, stirred to urgency by the Elder Moggallāna, saw the fault of saṃsāra and went forth in the presence of the Teacher. After purifying his virtues and taking up the meditation subject on the four truths, not long after, he strove in insight and attained arahantship. Later, a severe illness arose in him; he dwelt enduring it with reflection. For those whose taints are destroyed, there is indeed no such thing as mental suffering, but physical suffering does exist. One day, while the Blessed One was teaching the Dhamma, he sat down cross-legged in a place not too far away, enduring the pain. Therefore, it was said, 'He was sitting not far from the Blessed One,' and so on.

Tattha pallaṅkanti samantato ūrubaddhāsanaṃ. Ābhujitvāti bandhitvā. Ujuṃ kāyaṃ paṇidhāyāti uparimaṃ sarīraṃ ujukaṃ ṭhapetvā aṭṭhārasa piṭṭhikaṇṭake koṭiyā koṭiṃ paṭipādetvā. Evañhi nisinnassa cammamaṃsanhārūni na namanti, tasmā so tathā nisinno hoti. Purāṇakammavipākajanti pubbe katassa kammassa vipākabhāvena jātaṃ, purāṇakammavipāke vā sukhadukkhappakāre vipākavaṭṭasamudāye tadekadesabhāvena jātaṃ. Kiṃ taṃ? Dukkhaṃ. Purāṇakammavipākajanti ca iminā tassa ābādhassa kammasamuṭṭhānataṃ dassento opakkamikautuvipariṇāmajādibhāvaṃ paṭikkhipati. Dukkhanti pacurajanehi khamituṃ asakkuṇeyyaṃ. Tibbanti [P 0.0166] tikhiṇaṃ, abhibhavitvā pavattiyā bahalaṃ vā. Kharanti kakkhaḷaṃ. Kaṭukanti asātaṃ. Adhivāsentoti upari vāsento sahanto khamanto.

Therein, pallaṅka means a cross-legged seat with the thighs bound on all sides. Ābhujitvā means having bound. Ujuṃ kāyaṃ paṇidhāya means having set the upper body straight, having made the eighteen vertebrae touch end to end in sequence. For one seated thus, the skin, flesh, and sinews do not bend; therefore, he is seated in such a manner. Born of the result of old kamma means born as the result of kamma done previously; or, born as a single part of the aggregate of the round of results—which is of the nature of pleasure and pain—that is the result of old kamma. What is that? Suffering. And by stating born of the result of old kamma, in showing that this illness has kamma as its origin, he rejects its nature as being born from assault, change of seasons, and so on. Dukkha means that which cannot be endured by many people. Tibba means sharp; or, because it occurs overwhelmingly, it is severe. Khara means rough. Kaṭuka means unpleasant. Adhivāsento means dwelling above, bearing, enduring.

Sato sampajānoti vedanāpariggāhakānaṃ satisampajaññānaṃ vasena satimā sampajānanto ca. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – “ayaṃ vedanā nāma hutvā abhāvaṭṭhena aniccā, aniṭṭhārammaṇādipaccaye paṭicca uppannattā paṭiccasamuppannā, uppajjitvā ekantena bhijjanasabhāvattā khayadhammā vayadhammā virāgadhammā nirodhadhammā”ti vedanāya aniccatāsallakkhaṇavasena satokāritāya [V 0.0134] sato[M 0.0149], aviparītasabhāvapaṭivijjhanavasena sampajāno ca hutvā. Atha vā sativepullapattiyā sabbattheva kāyavedanācittadhammesu suṭṭhu upaṭṭhitasatitāya sato, tathā paññāvepullappattiyā pariggahitasaṅkhāratāya sampajāno. Avihaññamānoti “assutavā, bhikkhave, puthujjano aññataraññatarena dukkhadhammena phuṭṭho samāno socati kilamati paridevati urattāḷiṃ kandati sammohaṃ āpajjatī”ti vuttanayena andhaputhujjano viya na vihaññamāno maggeneva samugghātitattā cetodukkhaṃ anuppādento kevalaṃ kammavipākajaṃ sarīradukkhaṃ adhivāsento samāpattiṃ samāpanno viya nisinno hoti. Addasāti taṃ āyasmantaṃ adhivāsanakhantiyā tathā nisinnaṃ addakkhi.

Mindful and clearly comprehending means being mindful and clearly comprehending by means of the mindfulness and clear comprehension that comprehend feelings. This is what is said: 'This feeling, being impermanent by way of its non-existence after having been, and dependently arisen because it has arisen in dependence on undesirable objects and other conditions, is, after arising, entirely of a nature to break apart; thus it is subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, subject to cessation.' Thus, one is mindful by the mindful action of noting the characteristic of impermanence in feeling, and one is clearly comprehending by penetrating its undistorted nature. Alternatively, one is mindful due to having reached an abundance of mindfulness, whereby mindfulness is well established in all respects regarding the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena; likewise, one is clearly comprehending due to having reached an abundance of wisdom, whereby conditioned things are comprehended. Without being afflicted means not being afflicted like an unenlightened worldling—in the way it is said: 'An unenlightened worldling, monks, when touched by some painful feeling, sorrows, grieves, and laments, beats his breast and becomes distraught'—and not producing mental suffering since it has been uprooted by the path, he sits enduring only the bodily suffering that is the result of kamma, as if he had entered an attainment. He saw means he saw that venerable one seated thus with the patience of endurance.

Etamatthanti etaṃ tādisassapi rogassa vejjādīhi tikicchanatthaṃ anussukkāpajjanakāraṇaṃ khīṇāsavānaṃ lokadhammehi anupalepitasaṅkhātaṃ atthaṃ sabbākārato viditvā. Imaṃ udānanti imaṃ saṅkhatadhammānaṃ yehi kehici dukkhadhammehi avighātapattivibhāvanaṃ udānaṃ udānesi.

This meaning means: having known in every way that meaning—which is the reason for not striving for treatment by physicians and others even for such a disease, and which is reckoned as the state of being unsullied by worldly conditions for those whose taints are destroyed. This utterance means: he uttered this utterance, which makes manifest the attainment of non-affliction by any painful states whatsoever that belong to conditioned things.

Tattha sabbakammajahassāti pahīnasabbakammassa. Aggamaggassa hi uppannakālato paṭṭhāya arahato sabbāni kusalākusalakammāni pahīnāni nāma honti paṭisandhiṃ dātuṃ asamatthabhāvato, yato ariyamaggañāṇaṃ kammakkhayakaranti vuccati. Bhikkhunoti bhinnakilesatāya bhikkhuno. Dhunamānassa pure kataṃ rajanti arahattappattito pubbe kataṃ rāgarajādimissatāya rajanti laddhanāmaṃ dukkhavedanīyaṃ kammaṃ vipākapaṭisaṃvedanena taṃ [P 0.0167] dhunantassa viddhaṃsentassa, arahattappattiyā parato pana sāvajjakiriyāya sambhavoyeva natthi, anavajjakiriyā ca bhavamūlassa samucchinnattā samucchinnamūlatāya pupphaṃ viya phaladānasamatthatāya abhāvato kiriyamattāva hoti.

Therein, of one who has abandoned all kamma means of one for whom all kamma has been abandoned. For, from the time of the arising of the supreme path, all wholesome and unwholesome kammas of an arahant are said to be abandoned because of their inability to give rebirth, which is why the knowledge of the noble path is called 'that which makes an end of kamma.' Of a monk means of a monk because his defilements are shattered. Shaking off dust previously made refers to the kamma to be experienced painfully that was done before the attainment of arahantship—which received the name 'dust' because it was mixed with the dust of lust and so on—and to one who is shaking off and dispelling that kamma by experiencing its result. After the attainment of arahantship, however, there is no possibility of blameful action arising, and as for blameless action, because the root of existence has been cut off, it is merely functional, like a flower from a plant with its root cut off, which is unable to produce fruit.

Amamassāti rūpādīsu katthaci mamanti gahaṇābhāvato amamassa mamaṅkārarahitassa. Yassa hi mamaṅkāro atthi, so attasinehena vejjādīhi sarīraṃ paṭijaggāpeti. Arahā pana amamo, tasmā so sarīrajagganepi udāsīnadhātukova. Ṭhitassāti catubbidhampi oghaṃ taritvā nibbānathale ṭhitassa, paṭisandhiggahaṇavasena vā sandhāvanassa abhāvena ṭhitassa[M 0.0150]. Sekkhaputhujjanā hi kilesābhisaṅkhārānaṃ appahīnattā cutipaṭisandhivasena saṃsāre dhāvanti nāma, arahā pana tadabhāvato ṭhitoti vuccati. Atha vā dasavidhe khīṇāsavasaṅkhāte ariyadhamme ṭhitassa. Tādinoti “paṭikūle appaṭikūlasaññī viharatī”tiādinā (paṭi. ma. 3.17) nayena [V 0.0135] vuttāya pañcavidhāya ariyiddhiyā aṭṭhahi lokadhammehi akampaniyāya chaḷaṅgupekkhāya ca samannāgatena iṭṭhādīsu ekasadisatāsaṅkhātena tādībhāvena tādino. Attho natthi janaṃ lapetaveti “mama bhesajjādīni karothā”ti janaṃ lapituṃ kathetuṃ payojanaṃ natthi sarīre nirapekkhabhāvato. Paṇḍupalāso viya hi bandhanā pavutto sayamevāyaṃ kāyo bhijjitvā patatūti khīṇāsavānaṃ ajjhāsayo. Vuttañhetaṃ –

"He is without 'mine'"—because there is no grasping of anything as 'mine' in forms, etc., he is without 'mine', devoid of the notion of 'mine.' For whoever has the notion of 'mine' causes his body to be cared for by physicians and others out of self-love. But the arahant is without 'mine,' therefore, even in caring for the body, he remains indifferent by nature. "Standing firm"—having crossed the fourfold flood and standing on the shore of Nibbāna, or because he does not run about through the process of rebirth-linking, he is called 'standing firm.' For trainees and ordinary people, due to not having abandoned the defilements and formations, are said to run through saṃsāra by way of death and rebirth. But the arahant, due to the absence of that, is called 'standing firm.' Alternatively, he stands firm in the noble Dhamma, which is reckoned as the tenfold state of one whose taints are destroyed. "Such"—endowed with the fivefold noble power as stated in the way of "dwelling perceiving the repulsive as non-repulsive" (Paṭisambhidāmagga 3.17), unshaken by the eight worldly conditions, and possessing the sixfold equanimity, he is 'such' by the state of being equal, which is the same in the face of the desirable and undesirable. "There is no need to speak to people"—because he has no concern for the body, there is no purpose in telling people, "Make medicine for me," or in conversing with them. Like a withered leaf released from its stalk, this body will break up and fall of its own accord—such is the resolve of those whose taints are destroyed. For it has been said:

“Nābhikaṅkhāmi maraṇaṃ, nābhikaṅkhāmi jīvitaṃ;

Kālañca paṭikaṅkhāmi, nibbisaṃ bhatako yathā”ti. (theragā. 606);

"I do not desire death, I do not desire life; I await my time, like a worker awaiting his wages."

Atha vā yaṃkiñci nimittaṃ dassetvā “kiṃ ayyassa icchitabba”nti janaṃ lapetave paccayehi nimantanavasena lapāpetuṃ khīṇāsavassa attho natthi tādisassa micchājīvassa maggeneva samugghātitattāti attho. Iti bhagavā “kissāyaṃ thero attano rogaṃ vejjehi atikicchāpetvā bhagavato avidūre nisīdatī”ti cintentānaṃ tassa atikicchāpane kāraṇaṃ pakāsesi.

Or else, for one whose taints are destroyed there is no purpose in showing some sign to cause people to invite him with requisites by asking, 'What does the venerable one desire?'; the meaning is that such wrong livelihood has been uprooted by the path itself. Thus the Blessed One revealed the reason for his non-treatment to those who were thinking, 'Why does this elder, not having his illness treated by physicians, sit not far from the Blessed One?'

Paṭhamasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the first discourse is finished.

2. Nandasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Nanda Sutta

22. Dutiye [P 0.0168] nandoti tassa nāmaṃ. So hi cakkavattilakkhaṇūpetattā mātāpitaro saparijanaṃ sakalañca ñātiparivaṭṭaṃ nandayanto jātoti “nando”ti nāmaṃ labhi. Bhagavato bhātāti bhagavato ekapituputtatāya bhātā. Na hi bhagavato sahodarā uppajjanti, tena vuttaṃ “mātucchāputto”ti, cūḷamātuputtoti attho. Mahāpajāpatigotamiyā hi so putto. Anabhiratoti na abhirato. Brahmacariyanti [M 0.0151] brahmaṃ seṭṭhaṃ uttamaṃ cariyaṃ ekāsanaṃ ekaseyyaṃ methunaviratiṃ. Sandhāretunti paṭhamacittato yāvacarimakacittaṃ sammā paripuṇṇaṃ parisuddhaṃ dhāretuṃ pavattetuṃ. Dutiyena cettha brahmacariyapadena maggabrahmacariyassāpi saṅgaho veditabbo. Sikkhaṃ paccakkhāyāti upasampadakāle bhikkhubhāvena saddhiṃ samādinnaṃ nibbattetabbabhāvena anuṭṭhitaṃ tividhampi sikkhaṃ paṭikkhipitvā, vissajjetvāti attho. Hīnāyāti gihibhāvāya. Āvattissāmīti nivattissāmi.

22. In the second sutta, his name is Nanda. Because he was endowed with the marks of a wheel-turning monarch, his parents together with their retinue and all his relatives were delighted at his birth, so he received the name "Nanda." "The Blessed One’s brother"—he was the Blessed One’s brother by sharing the same father. Indeed, the Blessed One had no full brothers; therefore, it is said "his mother’s sister’s son," meaning the son of his mother’s younger sister. For he was the son of Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī. "Discontent"—not content. "The holy life"—the supreme, excellent practice: a single seat, a single bed, and abstention from sexual intercourse. "To endure"—from the first thought until the last thought, to maintain and develop it correctly, completely, and purely. Here, by the second phrase "the holy life," the path of the holy life should also be understood as included. "Having given up the training"—having rejected the threefold training undertaken at the time of ordination along with the state of a monk, and not brought to fruition, meaning having renounced it. "To the lower life"—to the household life. "I will return"—I will turn back.

Kasmā [V 0.0136] panāyaṃ evamārocesīti? Etthāyaṃ anupubbikathā – bhagavā pavattavaradhammacakko rājagahaṃ gantvā veḷuvane viharanto “puttaṃ me ānetvā dassethā”ti suddhodanamahārājena pesitesu sahassasahassaparivāresu dasasu dūtesu saha parivārena arahattaṃ pattesu sabbapacchā gantvā arahattappattena kāḷudāyittherena gamanakālaṃ ñatvā maggavaṇṇanaṃ vaṇṇetvā jātibhūmigamanāya yācito vīsatisahassakhīṇāsavaparivutto kapilavatthunagaraṃ gantvā ñātisamāgame pokkharavassaṃ aṭṭhuppattiṃ katvā vessantarajātakaṃ (jā. 2.22.1655 ādayo) kathetvā punadivase piṇḍāya paviṭṭho “uttiṭṭhe nappamajjeyyā”ti (dha. pa. 168) gāthāya pitaraṃ sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāpetvā nivesanaṃ gantvā “dhammañcare”ti (dha. pa. 169) gāthāya mahāpajāpatiṃ sotāpattiphale, rājānaṃ sakadāgāmiphale patiṭṭhāpesi.

But why did he announce it thus? Here is the gradual account: The Blessed One, having set in motion the excellent Wheel of Dhamma, went to Rājagaha and stayed in the Bamboo Grove. When King Suddhodana sent ten messengers, each with a retinue of a thousand, saying, "Bring my son to see me," all of whom attained arahantship with their retinues, Kāḷudāyī Thera, who went last and attained arahantship, knowing the time to go, praised the description of the journey and was requested to go to his birthplace. Surrounded by twenty thousand arahants, he went to the city of Kapilavatthu. At the gathering of relatives, he created the incident of the lotus rain and narrated the Vessantara Jātaka (Jā. 2.22.1655 ff.). The next day, having entered for alms, he established his father in the fruit of stream-entry with the verse, "Arise, do not be heedless" (Dhp. 168). Then, going to the palace, he established Mahāpajāpatī in the fruit of stream-entry and the king in the fruit of once-returning with the verse, "Practice the Dhamma" (Dhp. 169).

Bhattakiccāvasāne [P 0.0169] pana rāhulamātuguṇakathaṃ nissāya candakinnarījātakaṃ (jā. 1.14.18 ādayo) kathetvā tatiyadivase nandakumārassa abhisekagehappavesanavivāhamaṅgalesu vattamānesu piṇḍāya pavisitvā nandakumārassa hatthe pattaṃ datvā maṅgalaṃ vatvā uṭṭhāyāsanā pakkamanto kumārassa hatthato pattaṃ na gaṇhi. Sopi tathāgate gāravena “pattaṃ te, bhante, gaṇhathā”ti vattuṃ nāsakkhi. Evaṃ pana cintesi, “sopānasīse pattaṃ gaṇhissatī”ti, satthā tasmiṃ ṭhāne na gaṇhi. Itaro “sopānamūle gaṇhissatī”ti cintesi, satthā tatthapi na gaṇhi. Itaro “rājaṅgaṇe gaṇhissatī”ti cintesi, satthā tatthapi na gaṇhi. Kumāro nivattitukāmo anicchāya gacchanto gāravena “pattaṃ gaṇhathā”ti vattuṃ na sakkoti, “idha gaṇhissati, ettha gaṇhissatī”ti cintento gacchati.

Then, after the meal was finished, based on a talk about the virtues of Rāhula’s mother, the Blessed One spoke the Candakinnarī Jātaka (Jā. 1.14.18, etc.). On the third day, while Prince Nanda’s consecration, house-entry, and marriage ceremonies were proceeding, the Blessed One entered for alms. He placed his bowl in Prince Nanda’s hands, spoke a blessing, and rose from his seat to depart without taking the bowl back from the prince. Out of reverence for the Tathāgata, the prince could not say, "Venerable sir, take your bowl." Instead, he thought, "He will take the bowl at the top of the stairs," but the Teacher did not take it at that place. Then he thought, "He will take it at the foot of the stairs," but the Teacher did not take it there either. Next, he thought, "He will take it in the royal courtyard," but the Teacher did not take it there as well. The prince, wishing to turn back but unwillingly going on, could not, out of reverence, say, "Take your bowl." Thinking, "He will take it here, he will take it there," he continued walking.

Tasmiṃ [M 0.0152] khaṇe janapadakalyāṇiyā ācikkhiṃsu, “ayye bhagavā, nandarājānaṃ gahetvā gacchati, tumhehi vinā karissatī”ti. Sā udakabindūhi paggharantehi aḍḍhullikhitehi kesehi vegena pāsādaṃ āruyha sīhapañjaradvāre ṭhatvā “tuvaṭaṃ kho, ayyaputta, āgaccheyyāsī”ti āha. Taṃ tassā vacanaṃ tassa hadaye tiriyaṃ patitvā viya ṭhitaṃ. Satthāpissa hatthato pattaṃ aggahetvāva taṃ vihāraṃ netvā “pabbajissasi nandā”ti āha. So buddhagāravena “na pabbajissāmī”ti avatvā, “āma, pabbajissāmī”ti āha. Satthā tena hi nandaṃ pabbājethāti kapilavatthupuraṃ gantvā tatiyadivase taṃ pabbājesi. Sattame divase mātarā alaṅkaritvā pesitaṃ “dāyajjaṃ me, samaṇa, dehī”ti vatvā attanā saddhiṃ ārāmāgataṃ rāhulakumāraṃ pabbājesi. Punekadivasaṃ mahādhammapālajātakaṃ (jā. 1.10.92 ādayo) kathetvā rājānaṃ anāgāmiphale patiṭṭhāpesi.

At that moment, they informed Janapadakalyāṇī, 'Noble lady, the Blessed One is taking Prince Nanda away; he will separate you from him.' With water dripping from her half-combed hair, she quickly ascended the palace and, standing at the lion-window, said, 'Noble son, return quickly!' That word of hers remained in his heart as if it had struck it sideways. The Teacher, without taking the bowl from his hand, led him to the monastery and asked, 'Nanda, will you go forth?' Out of reverence for the Buddha, unable to say, 'I will not go forth,' he replied, 'Yes, I will go forth.' The Teacher then said, 'Well then, ordain Nanda.' Having gone to Kapilavatthu, he ordained him on the third day. On the seventh day, he ordained Prince Rāhula—who, having been adorned and sent by his mother, had come to the monastery with him, saying, 'Ascetic, give me my inheritance.' Then one day, after recounting the Mahādhammapāla Jātaka (Jā. 1.10.92, etc.), he established the king in the fruit of non-returning.

Iti [V 0.0137] bhagavā mahāpajāpatiṃ sotāpattiphale, pitaraṃ tīsu phalesu patiṭṭhāpetvā bhikkhusaṅghaparivuto punadeva rājagahaṃ gantvā tato anāthapiṇḍikena sāvatthiṃ āgamanatthāya gahitapaṭiñño niṭṭhite jetavanamahāvihāre tattha gantvā vāsaṃ kappesi. Evaṃ satthari jetavane viharante āyasmā nando attano [P 0.0170] anicchāya pabbajito kāmesu anādīnavadassāvī janapadakalyāṇiyā vuttavacanamanussaranto ukkaṇṭhito hutvā bhikkhūnaṃ attano anabhiratiṃ ārocesi. Tena vuttaṃ “tena kho pana samayena āyasmā nando…pe… hīnāyāvattissāmī”ti.

Thus the Blessed One established Mahāpajāpatī in the fruit of stream-entry and his father in the three fruits. Then, surrounded by the community of monks, he returned to Rājagaha. From there, having accepted Anāthapiṇḍika’s pledge for his visit to Sāvatthī, he went and took up residence in the completed Jetavana Great Monastery. While the Teacher was dwelling at Jetavana, the Venerable Nanda—who had gone forth against his will, not seeing the danger in sensual pleasures—became discontented, recalling the words of the beautiful woman of the countryside, and he declared his lack of delight to the monks. Regarding this, it is said: 'At that time, the Venerable Nanda… I will return to the lower life.'

Kasmā pana naṃ bhagavā evaṃ pabbājesīti? “Puretarameva ādīnavaṃ dassetvā kāmehi naṃ vivecetuṃ na sakkā, pabbājetvā pana upāyena tato vivecetvā uparivisesaṃ nibbattessāmī”ti veneyyadamanakusalo satthā evaṃ naṃ paṭhamaṃ pabbājesi.

But why did the Blessed One ordain him in this way? The Teacher, skilled in taming those to be trained, ordained him first in this way, thinking: 'It is not possible to detach him from sensual pleasures beforehand by showing their drawbacks. But having ordained him first, I will, by a skillful method, detach him from them and bring about a superior attainment.'

Sākiyānīti sakyarājadhītā. Janapadakalyāṇīti janapadamhi kalyāṇī rūpena uttamā chasarīradosarahitā, pañcakalyāṇasamannāgatā. Sā hi yasmā nātidīghā nātirassā nātikisā nātithūlā nātikāḷikā naccodātā atikkantā mānusakavaṇṇaṃ appattā dibbavaṇṇaṃ, tasmā chasarīradosarahitā. Chavikalyāṇaṃ maṃsakalyāṇaṃ nakhakalyāṇaṃ aṭṭhikalyāṇaṃ vayakalyāṇanti imehi pañcahi kalyāṇehi samannāgatā.

"Sākiyānī" means a daughter of the Sakyan king. "Janapadakalyāṇī" means the beautiful one in the country, supreme in form, free from the six bodily defects and possessing the five beauties. For she was neither too tall nor too short, neither too thin nor too fat, neither too dark nor too fair—she surpassed human complexion but had not attained divine complexion. Thus, she was free from the six bodily defects. She possessed these five beauties: beauty of skin, beauty of flesh, beauty of nails, beauty of bones, and beauty of youth.

Tattha [M 0.0153] attano sarīrobhāsena dasadvādasahatthe ṭhāne ālokaṃ karoti, piyaṅgusamā vā suvaṇṇasamā vā hoti, ayamassā chavikalyāṇatā. Cattāro panassā hatthapādā mukhapariyosānañca lākhārasaparikammakataṃ viya rattapavāḷarattakambalena sadisaṃ hoti, ayamassā maṃsakalyāṇatā. Vīsati nakhapattāni maṃsato amuttaṭṭhāne lākhārasaparikitāni viya muttaṭṭhāne khīradhārāsadisāni honti, ayamassā nakhakalyāṇatā. Dvattiṃsadantā suphusitā parisuddhapavāḷapantisadisā vajirapantī viya khāyanti, ayamassā aṭṭhikalyāṇatā. Vīsativassasatikāpi samānā soḷasavassuddesikā viya hoti nippalitā, ayamassā vayakalyāṇatā. Sundarī ca hoti evarūpaguṇasamannāgatā, tena vuttaṃ “janapadakalyāṇī”ti.

Herein, the radiance of her own body illuminates a space of ten or twelve cubits, and her complexion is like the piyaṅgu flower or like gold—this is her beauty of skin. Her four limbs—hands and feet—and the area around her mouth are as if treated with lacquer juice, or similar to red coral or a red woolen cloth—this is her beauty of flesh. Her twenty fingernails, where they are attached to the flesh, are as if bordered with lacquer juice, while in the part that is free, they are like streams of milk—this is her beauty of nails. Her thirty-two teeth are perfectly set and pure, appearing like a row of flawless coral or a row of diamonds—this is her beauty of bones. Even at one hundred and twenty years of age, she appears like a sixteen-year-old, without gray hair—this is her beauty of youth. She was beautiful and endowed with such qualities; hence, she was called "Janapadakalyāṇī."

Gharā nikkhamantassāti anādare sāmivacanaṃ, gharato nikkhamatoti attho. “Gharā nikkhamanta”ntipi paṭhanti. Upaḍḍhullikhitehi [P 0.0171] kesehīti itthambhūtalakkhaṇe karaṇavacanaṃ, vippakatullikhitehi kesehi upalakkhitāti attho. “Aḍḍhullikhitehī”tipi paṭhanti. Ullikhananti [V 0.0138] ca phaṇakādīhi kesasaṇṭhāpanaṃ, “aḍḍhakāravidhāna”ntipi vadanti. Apaloketvāti sineharasavipphārasaṃsūcakena aḍḍhakkhinā ābandhantī viya oloketvā. Maṃ, bhanteti pubbepi “ma”nti vatvā ukkaṇṭhākulacittatāya puna “maṃ etadavocā”ti āha. Tuvaṭanti sīghaṃ. Tamanussaramānoti taṃ tassā vacanaṃ, taṃ vā tassā ākārasahitaṃ vacanaṃ anussaranto.

'Leaving the house' (Gharā nikkhamantassa) is the genitive case used to indicate disregard; the meaning is 'leaving from the house.' Some also read 'gharā nikkhamantaṃ.' 'With half-combed hair' (Upaḍḍhullikhitehi kesehi) is the instrumental case indicating a characteristic; the meaning is 'distinguished by partially arranged hair.' Some also read 'aḍḍhullikhitehi.' Combing (ullikhana) refers to arranging the hair with a comb and so on; some also call it 'a half-done arrangement.' 'Having looked back' (Apaloketvā) means having glanced back as if binding him with a sidelong look indicative of the spreading essence of affection. 'Me, venerable sir' (Maṃ, bhante): having previously said 'me' (maṃ), due to a mind agitated by discontent, he again said, 'she said this to me' (maṃ etadavocā). 'Quickly' (Tuvaṭaṃ) means swiftly. 'Remembering that' (Tamanussaramāno) means remembering that word of hers, or remembering her word together with her demeanor.

Bhagavā tassa vacanaṃ sutvā “upāyenassa rāgaṃ vūpasamessāmī”ti iddhibalena naṃ tāvatiṃsabhavanaṃ nento antarāmagge ekasmiṃ jhāmakhette jhāmakhāṇumatthake nisinnaṃ chinnakaṇṇanāsānaṅguṭṭhaṃ ekaṃ paluṭṭhamakkaṭiṃ dassetvā tāvatiṃsabhavanaṃ nesi. Pāḷiyaṃ pana ekakkhaṇeneva satthārā tāvatiṃsabhavanaṃ gataṃ viya vuttaṃ, taṃ gamanaṃ avatvā tāvatiṃsabhavanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Gacchantoyeva hi bhagavā āyasmato nandassa antarāmagge taṃ paluṭṭhamakkaṭiṃ dasseti. Yadi evaṃ kathaṃ samiñjanādinidassanaṃ? Taṃ antaradhānanidassananti gahetabbaṃ. Evaṃ satthā taṃ tāvatiṃsabhavanaṃ netvā sakkassa devarañño upaṭṭhānaṃ āgatāni kakuṭapādāni pañca accharāsatāni attānaṃ vanditvā ṭhitāni [M 0.0154] dassetvā janapadakalyāṇiyā tāsaṃ pañcannaṃ accharāsatānaṃ rūpasampattiṃ paṭicca visesaṃ pucchi. Tena vuttaṃ – “atha kho bhagavā āyasmantaṃ nandaṃ bāhāyaṃ gahetvā…pe… kakuṭapādānī”ti.

Having heard his words, the Blessed One thought, 'I will subdue his lust through skillful means.' By his psychic power, while leading him to the Tāvatiṃsa realm, along the way, in a charred field, he showed him a scorched female monkey with severed ears, nose, and tail, sitting on a charred tree stump, and then took him to the Tāvatiṃsa realm. In the canonical text, however, it is stated as if the Teacher went to the Tāvatiṃsa realm in an instant; this is said with reference to the Tāvatiṃsa realm, without mentioning the journey. Indeed, it was while traveling that the Blessed One showed Venerable Nanda that scorched female monkey along the way. If so, how is the demonstration of folding and so forth explained? That should be understood as an indication of disappearance. Thus, the Teacher, having led him to the Tāvatiṃsa realm, showed him five hundred celestial nymphs with feet like rooster claws, who had come to attend upon Sakka, king of devas, and who stood paying homage to him. Then, with reference to the perfection of beauty of the country beauty and of those five hundred celestial nymphs, he asked about the difference. Hence it is said: 'Then the Blessed One took Venerable Nanda by the arm... and so forth... with feet like rooster claws.'

Tattha bāhāyaṃ gahetvāti bāhumhi gahetvā viya. Bhagavā hi tadā tādisaṃ iddhābhisaṅkhāraṃ abhisaṅkhāresi, yathā āyasmā nando bhuje gahetvā bhagavatā nīyamāno viya ahosi. Tattha ca bhagavatā sace tassa āyasmato tāvatiṃsadevalokassa dassanaṃ pavesanameva vā icchitaṃ siyā, yathānisinnasseva tassa taṃ devalokaṃ dasseyya lokavivaraṇiddhikāle [P 0.0172] viya, tameva vā iddhiyā tattha peseyya. Yasmā panassa dibbattabhāvato manussattabhāvassa yo nihīnajigucchanīyabhāvo, tassa sukhaggahaṇatthaṃ antarāmagge taṃ makkaṭiṃ dassetukāmo, devalokasirivibhavasampattiyo ca ogāhetvā dassetukāmo ahosi, tasmā taṃ gahetvā tattha nesi. Evañhissa tadatthaṃ brahmacariyavāse visesato abhirati bhavissatīti.

There, 'taking him by the arm' means as if holding him by the arm. For the Blessed One at that time performed such a feat of psychic power that the Venerable Nanda seemed to be led by the Blessed One while being held by the arm. And there, if the Blessed One had wished merely for that venerable one to see or to enter the Tāvatiṃsa deva realm, He could have shown him that deva realm while he was seated right there, as during the display of the world-opening psychic power, or He could have sent him there by psychic power. But because He wished to show him that female monkey along the way, for the sake of easily grasping the inferior and repulsive nature of the human state in comparison to the divine state, and also wished to show him the glory and prosperity of the deva realm after immersing him in it, therefore, He took him and led him there. Thus, his delight in the holy life would become especially strong for that purpose.

Kakuṭapādānīti rattavaṇṇatāya pārāvatasadisapādāni. Tā kira sabbāpi kassapassa bhagavato sāvakānaṃ pādamakkhanateladānena tādisā sukumārapādā ahesuṃ. Passasi noti passasi nu. Abhirūpatarāti visiṭṭharūpatarā. Dassanīyatarāti divasampi passantānaṃ atittikaraṇaṭṭhena passitabbatarā. Pāsādikatarāti sabbāvayavasobhāya samantato pasādāvahatarā.

'Kakuṭapādāni' refers to feet resembling those of a pigeon in their reddish color. It is said that all of them had such delicate feet because they had offered oil for anointing the feet of the disciples of the Blessed One Kassapa. 'Passasi no' means 'Do you see?' 'Abhirūpatarā' means of more distinguished form. 'Dassanīyatarā' means more worthy of being seen, in that they do not satiate those who look at them even for a day. 'Pāsādikatarā' means more delightful in every way, bringing serene joy through the beauty of all their limbs.

Kasmā [V 0.0139] pana bhagavā avassutacittaṃ āyasmantaṃ nandaṃ accharāyo olokāpesi? Sukhenevassa kilese nīharituṃ. Yathā hi kusalo vejjo ussannadosaṃ puggalaṃ tikicchanto sinehapānādinā paṭhamaṃ dose ukkiledetvā pacchā vamanavirecanehi sammadeva nīharāpeti, evaṃ vineyyadamanakusalo bhagavā ussannarāgaṃ āyasmantaṃ nandaṃ devaccharāyo dassetvā ukkiledesi ariyamaggabhesajjena anavasesato nīharitukāmoti veditabbaṃ.

But why did the Blessed One make the Venerable Nanda, whose mind was filled with craving, look at the nymphs? It was to easily draw out his defilements. Just as a skilled physician, treating a person with aggravated humors, first moistens the humors with oily drinks and the like, and then properly expels them with emetics and purgatives, so too the Blessed One, skilled in training those who can be tamed, first moistened the Venerable Nanda, who was filled with lust, by showing him the celestial nymphs, wishing to expel them completely with the medicine of the noble path—this should be understood.

Paluṭṭhamakkaṭīti jhāmaṅgapaccaṅgamakkaṭī. Evameva khoti yathā sā, bhante, tumhehi mayhaṃ dassitā chinnakaṇṇanāsā paluṭṭhamakkaṭī janapadakalyāṇiṃ upādāya[M 0.0155], evameva janapadakalyāṇī imāni pañca accharāsatāni upādāyāti attho. Pañcannaṃ accharāsatānanti upayoge sāmivacanaṃ, pañca accharāsatānīti attho. Avayavasambandhe vā etaṃ sāmivacanaṃ, tena pañcannaṃ accharāsatānaṃ rūpasampattiṃ upanidhāyāti adhippāyo. Upanidhāyāti ca samīpe ṭhapetvā, upādāyāti attho. Saṅkhyanti itthīti gaṇanaṃ. Kalabhāganti kalāyapi bhāgaṃ, ekaṃ soḷasakoṭṭhāse katvā tato ekakoṭṭhāsaṃ gahetvā soḷasadhā gaṇite tattha yo ekeko koṭṭhāso, so kalabhāgoti [P 0.0173] adhippeto, tampi kalabhāgaṃ na upetīti vadati. Upanidhinti “imāya ayaṃ sadisī”ti upamābhāvena gahetvā samīpe ṭhapanampi.

'Paluṭṭhamakkaṭī' means a monkey with burnt major and minor limbs. 'Even so' means: 'Just as, venerable sir, the scorched female monkey with severed ears and nose that you showed me is, when compared to the country beauty, so too is the country beauty when compared to these five hundred celestial nymphs.' The phrase 'pañcannaṃ accharāsatānaṃ' is the genitive case used objectively, meaning 'the five hundred celestial nymphs.' Or, it is the genitive case indicating a relationship to a part, with the intention 'in comparison to the perfection of beauty of the five hundred celestial nymphs.' And 'upanidhāya' means placing near; it has the meaning of 'upādāya' (in comparison to). 'Saṅkhyaṃ' means a count; that is, she does not even enter into the count as a woman. 'Kalabhāga' means a fraction of a kalā (a sixteenth part); when one is divided into sixteen parts, and one of those parts is taken and again divided into sixteen, each single portion is intended as a kalābhāga. It is said that she does not amount even to that kalābhāga. 'Upanidhi' means placing near, taking it as a simile by thinking, 'This one is like that one.'

Yatthāyaṃ anabhirato, taṃ brahmacariyaṃ pubbe vuttaṃ pākaṭañcāti taṃ anāmasitvā tattha abhiratiyaṃ ādarajananatthaṃ abhirama, nanda, abhirama, nandā”ti āmeḍitavasena vuttaṃ. Ahaṃ te pāṭibhogoti kasmā bhagavā tassa brahmacariyavāsaṃ icchanto abrahmacariyavāsassa pāṭibhogaṃ upagañchi? Yatthassa ārammaṇe rāgo daḷhaṃ nipati, taṃ āgantukārammaṇe saṅkāmetvā sukhena sakkā jahāpetunti pāṭibhogaṃ upagañchi. Anupubbikathāyaṃ saggakathā imassa atthassa nidassanaṃ.

That in which he was discontented—that holy life, previously spoken of and well-known—without referring to it, in order to generate delight therein, it was said by way of repetition: 'Delight, Nanda, delight, Nanda!' 'I am your guarantor'—why did the Blessed One, wishing for his dwelling in the holy life, undertake the guarantee for what is not the holy life? Because where his lust was firmly fixed on an object, by transferring that lust to an adventitious object, it could be easily abandoned—thus he undertook the guarantee. In the gradual discourse, the talk on heaven is an illustration of this meaning.

Assosunti kathamassosuṃ? Bhagavā hi tadā āyasmante nande vattaṃ dassetvā attano divāṭṭhānaṃ gate upaṭṭhānaṃ āgatānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ taṃ pavattiṃ kathetvā yathā nāma kusalo puriso anikkhantaṃ āṇiṃ aññāya āṇiyā nīharitvā puna taṃ hatthādīhi sañcāletvā apaneti, evameva āciṇṇavisaye tassa rāgaṃ āgantukavisayena nīharitvā puna tadapi brahmacariyamaggahetuṃ katvā apanetukāmo “etha tumhe, bhikkhave, nandaṃ bhikkhuṃ bhatakavādena ca upakkitakavādena ca samudācarathā”ti āṇāpesi, evaṃ bhikkhū assosuṃ. Keci pana “bhagavā tathārūpaṃ iddhābhisaṅkhāraṃ abhisaṅkhāresi, yathā te bhikkhū tamatthaṃ jāniṃsū”ti vadanti.

'They heard'—how did they hear? For the Blessed One, having shown the duty to Venerable Nanda and gone to his daytime resting place, related that account to the monks who came to attend on him. Just as a skilled man, knowing a peg that has not been extracted, extracts it by means of another peg and then shakes it again with his hand to remove it, so too, having drawn out his attachment from its habitual sphere by means of a newly arrived sphere, he wished to remove even that again by making it a cause for the path of the holy life. 'Come, monks, address the monk Nanda with the terms 'hireling' and 'bought one',' he instructed. Thus the monks heard. Some, however, say, 'The Blessed One performed such a feat of psychic power that those monks understood the matter.'

Bhatakavādenāti [V 0.0140] bhatakoti vādena. Yo hi bhatiyā kammaṃ karoti, so bhatakoti vuccati, ayampi āyasmā accharāsambhoganimittaṃ brahmacariyaṃ caranto bhatako viya hotīti vuttaṃ “bhatakavādenā”ti[M 0.0156]. Upakkitakavādenāti yo kahāpaṇādīhi kiñci kiṇāti, so upakkitakoti vuccati, ayampi āyasmā accharānaṃ hetu attano brahmacariyaṃ kiṇāti, tasmā “upakkitako”ti evaṃ vacanena. Atha vā bhagavato āṇāya accharāsambhogasaṅkhātāya bhatiyā brahmacariyavāsasaṅkhātaṃ jīvitaṃ pavattento tāya bhatiyā yāpane bhagavatā bhariyamāno viya hotīti “bhatako”ti vutto, tathā [P 0.0174] accharāsambhogasaṅkhātaṃ vikkayaṃ ādātabbaṃ katvā bhagavato āṇattiyaṃ tiṭṭhanto tena vikkayena bhagavatā upakkito viya hotīti vuttaṃ “upakkitako”ti.

'Bhatakavādena' (by the term 'hireling') means by the term 'hireling.' Indeed, whoever performs work for wages is called a hireling. This venerable one, too, living the holy life for the sake of the prospect of intercourse with celestial nymphs, is like a hireling—thus it is said, 'by the term 'hireling'.' 'Upakkitakavādena' (by the term 'bought one') means whoever purchases something with coins or the like is called one who is bought. This venerable one, too, for the sake of celestial nymphs, buys his own holy life—therefore, he is called 'one who is bought' by this expression. Or alternatively, by the Blessed One’s command, sustaining a life designated as living the holy life through the wage consisting of intercourse with celestial nymphs, he is like one supported by the Blessed One through that wage—thus he is called a 'hireling.' Similarly, having made the sale, which is designated as intercourse with celestial nymphs, something to be received, he stands by the Blessed One’s command—thus, through that sale, he is like one bought by the Blessed One—hence it is said, 'one who is bought.'

Aṭṭīyamānoti pīḷiyamāno dukkhāpiyamāno. Harāyamānoti lajjamāno. Jigucchamānoti pāṭikulyato dahanto. Ekoti asahāyo. Vūpakaṭṭhoti vatthukāmehi kilesakāmehi ca kāyena ceva cittena ca vūpakaṭṭho. Appamattoti kammaṭṭhāne satiṃ avijahanto. Ātāpīti kāyikacetasikavīriyātāpena ātāpavā, ātāpeti kileseti ātāpo, vīriyaṃ. Pahitattoti kāye ca jīvite ca anapekkhatāya pesitatto vissaṭṭhaattabhāvo, nibbāne vā pesitacitto. Na cirassevāti kammaṭṭhānārambhato na cireneva. Yassatthāyāti yassa atthāya. Kulaputtāti duvidhā kulaputtā jātikulaputtā ca ācārakulaputtā ca, ayaṃ pana ubhayathāpi kulaputto. Sammadevāti hetunā ca kāraṇena ca. Agārasmāti gharato. Anagāriyanti pabbajjaṃ. Kasivaṇijjādikammañhi agārassa hitanti agāriyaṃ nāma, taṃ ettha natthīti pabbajjā anagāriyāti vuccati. Pabbajantīti upagacchanti. Tadanuttaranti taṃ anuttaraṃ. Brahmacariyapariyosānanti maggabrahmacariyassa pariyosānabhūtaṃ arahattaphalaṃ. Tassa hi atthāya kulaputtā idha pabbajanti. Diṭṭheva dhammeti tasmiṃyeva attabhāve. Sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvāti attanāyeva paññāya paccakkhaṃ katvā, aparappaccayena ñatvāti attho. Upasampajja vihāsīti pāpuṇitvā sampādetvā vā vihāsi. Evaṃ viharantova khīṇā jāti…pe… abbhaññāsīti. Iminā assa paccavekkhaṇabhūmi dassitā.

‘Being tormented’ means being oppressed, being afflicted with suffering. ‘Being ashamed’ means feeling embarrassed. ‘Being disgusted’ means burning with revulsion. ‘Alone’ means without a companion. ‘Secluded’ means being withdrawn in body and mind from sensual pleasures related to objects and from sensual pleasures that are defilements. ‘Diligent’ means not abandoning mindfulness in one’s meditation subject. ‘Ardent’ means possessing the ardor of bodily and mental energy; ardor is energy, for it heats and burns up defilements. ‘Resolute’ means having sent forth one’s self, having let go of one’s self, through not caring for body and life, or having a mind directed toward Nibbāna. ‘Not long after’ means not long after beginning the meditation subject. ‘For the sake of which’ means for the sake of which. ‘A clansman’ refers to two kinds of clansmen: those by birth and those by conduct; here, he is a clansman in both respects. ‘Rightly’ means through proper cause and reason. ‘From the household’ means from the house. ‘Into homelessness’ means going forth. For farming, trade, and similar activities are called ‘householder’s activities’ (agariya) because they are beneficial to the household; since these are absent here, the going forth is called ‘homelessness’ (anagariya). ‘They go forth’ means they approach it. ‘That unsurpassed’ means that supreme. ‘The culmination of the holy life’ refers to the fruit of arahantship, which is the culmination of the path of the holy life. It is for this purpose that clansmen go forth here. ‘In this very life’ means in this very existence. ‘Having realized by direct knowledge’ means having directly experienced it for oneself through wisdom; the meaning is, knowing without reliance on others. ‘Having attained and dwelled’ means he dwelled having reached or accomplished it. Dwelling in this way, he understood: ‘Birth is destroyed…’ and so on. By this, his ground for review is shown.

Tattha [M 0.0157] khīṇā jātīti na tāvassa atītā jāti khīṇā pubbeva khīṇattā, na anāgatā anāgatattā eva, na paccuppannā vijjamānattā. Maggassa pana abhāvitattā yā ekacatupañcavokārabhavesu ekacatupañcakkhandhappabhedā [P 0.0175] jāti uppajjeyya, sā maggassa bhāvitattā anuppādadhammataṃ āpajjanena khīṇā. Taṃ so maggabhāvanāya pahīnakilese paccavekkhitvā [V 0.0141] kilesābhāvena vijjamānampi kammaṃ āyatiṃ appaṭisandhikaṃ hotīti jānanena abbhaññāsi. Vusitanti vutthaṃ parivutthaṃ kataṃ caritaṃ, niṭṭhāpitanti attho. Brahmacariyanti maggabrahmacariyaṃ. Puthujjanakalyāṇakena hi saddhiṃ satta sekkhā brahmacariyavāsaṃ vasanti nāma, khīṇāsavo vutthavāso, tasmā so attano brahmacariyavāsaṃ paccavekkhanto “vusitaṃ brahmacariya”nti abbhaññāsi. Kataṃ karaṇīyanti catūsu saccesu catūhi maggehi pariññāpahānasacchikiriyābhāvanāvasena soḷasavidhampi kiccaṃ niṭṭhāpitaṃ. Puthujjanakalyāṇakādayo hi taṃ kiccaṃ karonti nāma, khīṇāsavo katakaraṇīyo, tasmā so attano karaṇīyaṃ paccavekkhanto “kataṃ karaṇīya”nti abbhaññāsi. Nāparaṃ itthattāyāti “idāni puna itthabhāvāya evaṃ soḷasakiccabhāvāya kilesakkhayāya vā maggabhāvanāya kiccaṃ me natthī”ti abbhaññāsi. Nāparaṃ itthattāyāti vā “itthabhāvato imasmā evaṃpakārā vattamānakkhandhasantānā aparaṃ khandhasantānaṃ mayhaṃ natthi, ime pana pañcakkhandhā pariññātā tiṭṭhanti chinnamūlakā viya rukkhā, te carimakacittanirodhena anupādāno viya jātavedo nibbāyissanti, apaṇṇattikabhāvaṃ gamissantī”ti abbhaññāsi. Aññataroti eko. Arahatanti bhagavato sāvakānaṃ arahantānaṃ abbhantaro eko mahāsāvako ahosīti attho.

Here, ‘destroyed is birth’ does not mean that his past birth is destroyed, because it was already destroyed before; nor the future birth, because it is yet to come; nor the present birth, because it exists. However, any birth that might arise in the one-, four-, or five-constituent planes of existence, differentiated into one, four, or five aggregates, due to the non-development of the path, is destroyed by attaining the nature of non-arising through the development of the path. He understood this by reflecting on the defilements abandoned through the cultivation of the path, and by knowing that even existing kamma will not lead to future rebirth due to the absence of defilements. ‘Lived’ means lived, completed, done, practiced; the meaning is, finished. ‘The holy life’ refers to the path-brahmacariya. Indeed, the seven trainees along with the virtuous worldling are said to dwell in the holy life, but one with destroyed taints has completed his dwelling. Therefore, reflecting on his own dwelling in the holy life, he understood, ‘The holy life has been lived.’ ‘What was to be done has been done’ refers to the sixteenfold duty accomplished through full understanding, abandoning, realizing, and developing the four truths by means of the four paths. Indeed, the virtuous worldling and others are said to be performing that duty, but one with destroyed taints has done what was to be done. Therefore, reflecting on his own duty, he understood, ‘What was to be done has been done.’ ‘There is nothing further for this state of being’ means he understood, ‘Now there is no further duty for me for this state of being, for the sixteenfold duty, for the destruction of defilements, or for the cultivation of the path.’ Alternatively, ‘there is nothing further for this state of being’ means he understood, ‘From this state of being, from this kind of present continuum of aggregates, there is no further continuum of aggregates for me. These five aggregates, fully understood, remain like a tree with severed roots; with the cessation of the final consciousness, they will be extinguished without fuel, like a fire, and will reach the state of non-designation.’ `Aññataro` means one. ‘Arahant’ means he was one great disciple among the arahant disciples of the Blessed One.

Aññatarā devatāti adhigatamaggā ekā brahmadevatā. Sā hi sayaṃ asekkhattā asekkhavisayaṃ abbhaññāsi. Sekkhā hi taṃ taṃ sekkhavisayaṃ, puthujjanā ca attano puthujjanavisayameva jānanti. Abhikkantāya rattiyāti parikkhīṇāya rattiyā, majjhimayāmeti attho. Abhikkantavaṇṇāti atiuttamavaṇṇā. Kevalakappanti anavasesena samantato. Obhāsetvāti attano pabhāya cando viya sūriyo viya ca jetavanaṃ ekobhāsaṃ katvā. Tenupasaṅkamīti āyasmato nandassa [M 0.0158] arahattappattiṃ viditvā pītisomanassajātā [P 0.0176] “taṃ bhagavato paṭivedessāmī”ti upasaṅkami.

‘A certain deity’ refers to a Brahma deity who had attained the path. For she herself, being one beyond training, understood the domain of one beyond training. Trainees, indeed, understand their respective domains of training, while ordinary people know only their own ordinary domain. ‘When the night was far advanced’ means when the night was exhausted; the meaning is, in the middle watch of the night. ‘Of surpassing beauty’ means of extremely excellent beauty. ‘The entire Jeta Grove’ means completely, all around. ‘Having illuminated’ means having made the Jeta Grove uniformly bright with her own radiance, like the moon or the sun. ‘She approached him’ means, knowing Venerable Nanda’s attainment of arahantship, she approached the Blessed One, filled with joy and delight, thinking, ‘I shall report this to the Blessed One.’

Āsavānaṃ khayāti ettha āsavantīti āsavā, cakkhudvārādīhi pavattantīti attho. Atha vā āgotrabhuṃ ābhavaggaṃ vā savantīti āsavā, ete dhamme etañca okāsaṃ anto karitvā pavattantīti attho. Cirapārivāsiyaṭṭhena madirādiāsavā viyāti āsavā. “Purimā, bhikkhave, koṭi na paññāyati avijjāyā”tiādivacanehi (a. ni. 10.61) nesaṃ cirapārivāsiyatā veditabbā. Atha vā āyataṃ saṃsāradukkhaṃ savanti pasavantītipi, āsavā. Purimo cettha attho kilesesu yujjati, pacchimo kammepi. Na kevalañca kammakilesā eva āsavā, atha kho nānappakārā upaddavāpi. Tathā hi “nāhaṃ, cunda[V 0.0142], diṭṭhadhammikānaṃyeva āsavānaṃ saṃvarāya dhammaṃ desemī”ti ettha (dī. ni. 3.182) vivādamūlabhūtā kilesā āsavāti āgatā.

Regarding ‘the destruction of the taints,’ here, they flow (āsavanti), therefore they are taints (āsavā); the meaning is, they arise through the eye-door and so on. Alternatively, they flow up to the change-of-lineage knowledge or up to the summit of existence, therefore they are taints; the meaning is, they arise encompassing these states and this sphere. They are taints, like liquor and other intoxicants, in the sense of being long-matured. Their long-matured nature should be understood from such statements as, ‘Monks, the earliest point of ignorance is not discernible’ (AN 10.61). Alternatively, they flow towards and produce long suffering in saṃsāra, therefore they are taints. The first meaning here applies to the defilements; the last, to kamma as well. And not only kamma and defilements are taints, but also various kinds of troubles. Thus, in the passage, ‘Cunda, I do not teach the Dhamma only for the restraint of taints in this very life’ (DN 3.182), the defilements that are the root of disputes are presented as taints.

“Yena devūpapatyassa, gandhabbo vā vihaṅgamo;

Yakkhattaṃ yena gaccheyya, manussattañca abbaje;

Te mayhaṃ āsavā khīṇā, viddhastā vinalīkatā”ti. (a. ni. 4.36) –

‘By which one might be reborn as a deva, or a gandhabba or a bird; by which one might attain the state of a yakkha, and attain human existence—those taints of mine are destroyed, scattered, and eliminated.’ (AN 4.36)

Ettha tebhūmikaṃ kammaṃ avasesā ca akusalā dhammā āsavāti āgatā. “Diṭṭhadhammikānaṃ āsavānaṃ saṃvarāya, samparāyikānaṃ āsavānaṃ paṭighātāyā”ti (pārā. 39) parūpaghātavippaṭisāravadhabandhādayo ceva apāyadukkhabhūtā ca nānappakārā upaddavā.

Here, kamma pertaining to the three realms and the remaining unwholesome states are presented as taints. In the phrase, ‘For the restraint of taints pertaining to the present life, for the warding off of taints pertaining to future lives’ (Pārā. 39), the taints are troubles such as harming others, remorse, killing, and bondage, as well as various troubles that constitute the suffering of the lower realms.

Te panete āsavā vinaye – “diṭṭhadhammikānaṃ āsavānaṃ saṃvarāya samparāyikānaṃ āsavānaṃ paṭighātāyā”ti (pārā. 39) dvidhā āgatā. Saḷāyatane “tayome, āvuso, āsavā – kāmāsavo, bhavāsavo, avijjāsavo”ti (dī. ni. 3.305) tidhā āgatā, tathā aññesu ca suttantesu. Abhidhamme teyeva diṭṭhāsavena saddhiṃ catudhā āgatā. Nibbedhikapariyāye “atthi, bhikkhave, āsavā nirayagāminiyā”tiādinā (a. ni. 6.63) pañcadhā [P 0.0177] āgatā. Chakkanipāte “atthi, bhikkhave, āsavā saṃvarāya pahātabbā”tiādinā (a. ni. 6.58) nayena [M 0.0159] chadhā āgatā. Sabbāsavapariyāye (ma. ni. 1.22) teyeva dassanapahātabbehi saddhiṃ sattadhā āgatā. Idha pana abhidhammanayena cattāro āsavā veditabbā.

These taints are presented in the Vinaya as twofold: ‘for the restraint of taints pertaining to the present life and for the warding off of taints pertaining to future lives’ (Pārā. 39). In the Saḷāyatana, they are presented as threefold: ‘There are, friends, these three taints—the taint of sensuality, the taint of existence, and the taint of ignorance’ (DN 33), and similarly in other discourses. In the Abhidhamma, those same taints are presented as fourfold, together with the taint of views. In the Nibbedhikapariyāya, they are presented as fivefold, beginning with, ‘There are, monks, taints that lead to hell’ (AN 6.63). In the Chakkanipāta, they are presented as sixfold, in the way that begins, ‘There are, monks, taints to be abandoned by restraint’ (AN 6.58). In the Sabbāsavapariyāya (MN 2), those same taints are presented as sevenfold, together with those to be abandoned by seeing. Here, however, the four taints according to the Abhidhamma method should be understood.

Khayāti ettha pana “yo āsavānaṃ khayo bhedo paribhedo”tiādīsu āsavānaṃ sarasabhedo āsavakkhayoti vutto. “Jānato ahaṃ, bhikkhave, passato āsavānaṃ khayaṃ vadāmī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.15) āsavānaṃ āyatiṃ anuppādo āsavakkhayoti vutto.

Here, regarding ‘destruction,’ in passages such as ‘the destruction, breaking, and complete breaking of the taints,’ the breaking of the taints with their essence is called the destruction of the taints. In passages such as ‘Monks, I declare the destruction of the taints for one who knows and sees’ (MN 2), the non-arising of the taints in the future is called the destruction of the taints.

“Sekkhassa sikkhamānassa, ujumaggānusārino;

Khayasmiṃ paṭhamaṃ ñāṇaṃ, tato aññā anantarā”ti. (itivu. 62) –

‘For the learner who is training, following the straight path, first comes the knowledge of destruction, then immediately after, final knowledge.’ (Iti 62)

Ādīsu [V 0.0143] maggo āsavakkhayoti vutto. “Āsavānaṃ khayā samaṇo hotī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.438) phalaṃ.

In such passages, 'the destruction of the taints' is said to be the path. In passages such as 'Through the destruction of the taints one becomes a recluse' (MN 1.438), it refers to the fruit.

“Paravajjānupassissa, niccaṃ ujjhānasaññino;

Āsavā tassa vaḍḍhanti, ārā so āsavakkhayā”ti. –

‘For one who ever looks for others' faults, constantly critical, his taints increase; he is far from the destruction of taints.’

Ādīsu (dha. pa. 253) nibbānaṃ. Idha pana āsavānaṃ accantakhayo anuppādo vā maggo vā “āsavānaṃ khayo”ti vutto.

In such passages (Dhp 253), it refers to Nibbāna. Here, however, 'the destruction of the taints' is said to be the utter destruction of the taints, or their non-arising, or the path.

Anāsavanti paṭipassaddhivasena sabbaso pahīnāsavaṃ. Cetovimuttinti arahattaphalasamādhiṃ. Paññāvimuttinti arahattaphalapaññaṃ. Ubhayavacanaṃ magge viya phalepi samathavipassanānaṃ yuganandhabhāvadassanatthaṃ. Ñāṇanti sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ. Devatāya vacanasamanantarameva “kathaṃ nu kho”ti āvajjentassa bhagavato ñāṇaṃ uppajji “nandena arahattaṃ sacchikata”nti. So hi āyasmā sahāyabhikkhūhi tathā uppaṇḍiyamāno “bhāriyaṃ vata mayā kataṃ, yohaṃ evaṃ svākkhāte dhammavinaye pabbajitvā accharānaṃ paṭilābhāya satthāraṃ pāṭibhogaṃ akāsi”nti uppannasaṃvego hirottappaṃ paccupaṭṭhapetvā ghaṭento vāyamanto arahattaṃ patvā cintesi – “yaṃnūnāhaṃ bhagavantaṃ etasmā paṭissavā moceyya”nti. So bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā attano adhippāyaṃ satthu ārocesi. Tena [P 0.0178] vuttaṃ – “atha kho āyasmā nando…pe… etasmā paṭissavā”ti. Tattha paṭissavāti pāṭibhogappaṭissavā, “accharānaṃ paṭilābhāya ahaṃ paṭibhūto”ti paṭiññāya.

‘Free from taints’ means one whose taints are completely abandoned by way of their subsiding. ‘Liberation of mind’ means the concentration of the fruit of arahantship. ‘Liberation by wisdom’ means the wisdom of the fruit of arahantship. The use of both terms, in relation to the fruit as well as the path, is to show the yoked-together nature of serenity and insight. ‘Knowledge’ means the knowledge of omniscience. Immediately after the devatā’s words, as the Blessed One was reflecting, ‘How now?’, the knowledge arose in him: ‘Nanda has realized arahantship.’ For that venerable one, being thus ridiculed by his fellow monks, felt remorse: ‘Heavy indeed is the deed I have done, that having gone forth in this well-proclaimed Dhamma and Discipline, I made the Teacher a guarantor for obtaining nymphs.’ Arousing a sense of urgency and establishing conscience and fear of wrongdoing, he strove and struggled until he attained arahantship. Then he thought: ‘Suppose I were to release the Blessed One from this promise.’ Approaching the Blessed One, he informed the Teacher of his intention. Hence it is said: ‘Then the venerable Nanda… from this promise.’ Here, ‘promise’ refers to the promise of a guarantee, the declaration made: ‘I am the guarantor for obtaining nymphs.’

Athassa [M 0.0160] bhagavā “yasmā tayā aññā ārādhitāti ñātametaṃ mayā, devatāpi me ārocesi, tasmā nāhaṃ paṭissavā idāni mocetabbo arahattappattiyāva mocitattā”ti āha. Tena vuttaṃ “yadeva kho te nandā”tiādi. Tattha yadevāti yadā eva. Teti tava. Muttoti pamutto. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yasmiṃyeva kāle āsavehi tava cittaṃ vimuttaṃ, atha anantaramevāhaṃ tato pāṭibhogato muttoti.

Then the Blessed One said to him: ‘Since it is known to me that you have attained final knowledge, and a deity also informed me, therefore I am not now to be released from the promise, for I am already released by the very attainment of Arahantship.’ Hence it is said: ‘Just when, O Nanda,’ and so on. Herein, ‘just when’ means precisely when. ‘Te’ means your. ‘Released’ means liberated. This is what is meant: at the very moment your mind was liberated from the taints, then immediately I was released from that guarantee.

Sopi āyasmā vipassanākāleyeva “yadevāhaṃ indriyāsaṃvaraṃ nissāya imaṃ vippakāraṃ patto, tameva suṭṭhu niggahessāmī”ti ussāhajāto balavahirottappo tattha ca katādhikārattā indriyasaṃvare ukkaṭṭhapaṭipadampi agamāsi. Vuttañhetaṃ –

That venerable one, at the very time of insight, thought: ‘It was through lack of sense restraint that I fell into this wrong state; I will firmly control that very thing.’ Thus, becoming energetic, with strong conscience and fear of wrongdoing, and because he had made a resolution in that matter, he attained the supreme practice in the restraint of the senses. For this has been said:

“Sace[V 0.0144], bhikkhave, nandassa puratthimā disā āloketabbā hoti, sabbaṃ cetaso samannāharitvā nando puratthimaṃ disaṃ āloketi ‘evaṃ me puratthimaṃ disaṃ ālokayato na abhijjhādomanassā pāpakā akusalā dhammā anvāssaveyyu’nti, itiha tattha sampajāno hoti.

“Monks, if Nanda needs to look to the eastern direction, he brings his entire mind to bear and looks to the eastern direction, thinking: ‘As I look to the eastern direction, may no covetousness or displeasure, no evil, unwholesome states overwhelm me.’ Thus he is fully aware there.

“Sace, bhikkhave, nandassa pacchimā…pe… uttarā… dakkhiṇā… uddhaṃ… adho… anudisā āloketabbā hoti, sabbaṃ cetaso samannāharitvā nando anudisaṃ āloketi ‘evaṃ me…pe… sampajāno hotī’”ti (a. ni. 8.9).

“Monks, if Nanda needs to look to the west… north… south… upwards… downwards… or to the intermediate directions, he brings his entire mind to bear and looks to the intermediate directions, thinking: ‘As I look… may no evil, unwholesome states overwhelm me.’ Thus he is fully aware there.” (AN 8.9).

Teneva taṃ āyasmantaṃ satthā “etadaggaṃ, bhikkhave, mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ indriyesu guttadvārānaṃ yadidaṃ nando”ti (a. ni. 1.230) etadagge ṭhapesi.

For that very reason, the Teacher established that venerable one in the foremost position, saying: ‘Monks, among my bhikkhu disciples who have guarded sense-doors, the foremost is this one, namely, Nanda.’” (AN 1.230).

Etamatthaṃ viditvāti etaṃ āyasmato nandassa sabbāsave khepetvā sukhādīsu tādibhāvappattisaṅkhātaṃ atthaṃ sabbākārato viditvā. Imaṃ udānanti tadatthavibhāvanaṃ imaṃ udānaṃ udānesi.

‘Having understood this matter’ means having fully understood this meaning in all its aspects, namely, the attainment by the venerable Nanda of a state of being unshaken with respect to pleasant feelings and so on, through the destruction of all taints. ‘This inspired utterance’ means he uttered this inspired utterance to elucidate that meaning.

Tattha yassa nittiṇṇo paṅkoti yena ariyapuggalena ariyamaggasetunā sabbo diṭṭhipaṅko saṃsārapaṅko eva vā nibbānapāragamanena tiṇṇo. Maddito kāmakaṇḍakoti yena sattānaṃ vijjhanato. “Kāmakaṇḍako”ti [M 0.0161] laddhanāmo sabbo kilesakāmo sabbo kāmavisūko aggañāṇadaṇḍena maddito bhaggo anavasesato mathito. Mohakkhayaṃ anuppattoti evaṃbhūto ca dukkhādivisayassa sabbassa sammohassa [P 0.0179] khepanena mohakkhayaṃ patto, arahattaphalaṃ nibbānañca anuppatto.
