Sukhadukkhesu na vedhatī sa bhikkhūti so bhinnakileso bhikkhu iṭṭhārammaṇasamāyogato uppannesu sukhesu aniṭṭhārammaṇasamāyogato uppannesu dukkhesu ca na vedhati na kampati, taṃ nimittaṃ cittavikāraṃ nāpajjati. “Sukhadukkhesū”ti ca desanāmattaṃ, sabbesupi lokadhammesu na vedhatīti veditabbaṃ.

Here, ‘one who has crossed the swamp’ refers to the noble person who, by means of the bridge of the noble path, has crossed over all the swamp of wrong views or the swamp of saṃsāra, by reaching the far shore of Nibbāna. ‘Crushed the thorn of sensual desire’ refers to that which, because it pierces beings, has obtained the name ‘thorn of sensual desire’; it is all the defilements of desire, all the poisonous barbs of sensual pleasure, completely crushed, broken, and utterly destroyed by the staff of supreme knowledge. ‘Attained the destruction of delusion’ means that such a one, by dispelling all delusion regarding the domain of suffering and so on, has reached the destruction of delusion and attained the fruit of arahantship and Nibbāna. ‘That monk does not tremble at pleasure and pain’—that monk, whose defilements are destroyed, does not tremble or waver when pleasure arises from encountering pleasant objects or pain arises from encountering unpleasant objects, nor does he experience any mental disturbance on that account. The phrase ‘at pleasure and pain’ is merely illustrative; it should be understood that he does not tremble at any of the worldly conditions.

Dutiyasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Second Sutta is finished.

3. Yasojasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Yasoja Sutta

23. Tatiye [V 0.0145] yasojappamukhānīti ettha yasojoti tassa therassa nāmaṃ, taṃ pubbaṅgamaṃ katvā pabbajitattā vicaraṇato ca tāni pañca bhikkhusatāni “yasojappamukhānī”ti vuttāni.

23. In the third discourse, regarding the phrase ‘headed by Yasoja’: ‘Yasoja’ is the name of that elder. Because those five hundred monks went forth with him as their leader and because they wandered together, they are called ‘headed by Yasoja.’

Tesaṃ ayaṃ pubbayogo – atīte kira kassapadasabalassa sāsane aññataro bhikkhu āraññako araññe piṭṭhipāsāṇe katapaṇṇakuṭiyaṃ viharati. Tasmiñca samaye pañcasatā corā gāmaghātakādīni katvā corikāya jīvantā corakammaṃ katvā janapadamanussehi anubaddhā palāyamānā araññaṃ pavisitvā tattha kiñci gahaṇaṃ vā paṭisaraṇaṃ vā apassantā avidūre taṃ bhikkhuṃ pāsāṇe nisinnaṃ disvā vanditvā taṃ pavattiṃ ācikkhitvā “amhākaṃ, bhante, paṭisaraṇaṃ hothā”ti yāciṃsu. Thero “tumhākaṃ sīlasadisaṃ paṭisaraṇaṃ natthi, sabbe pañca sīlāni samādiyathā”ti āha. Te “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā sīlāni samādiyiṃsu. Thero “tumhe idāni sīlesu patiṭṭhitā, attano jīvitaṃ vināsayantesupi mā manaṃ padosayitthā”ti kakacūpamavidhiṃ (ma. ni. 1.222 ādayo) ācikkhi. Te “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchiṃsu. Atha te jānapadā taṃ sampattā ito cito ca gavesantā te core disvā sabbeva jīvitā voropesuṃ. Te [M 0.0162] tesu manopadosamattampi akatvā akkhaṇḍasīlā kālaṃ katvā kāmāvacaradevesu nibbattiṃsu. Tesu [P 0.0180] jeṭṭhacoro jeṭṭhadevaputto ahosi, itare tasseva parivārā.

This was their past connection: It is said that in the past, during the dispensation of the Ten-Powered Kassapa, a certain forest-dwelling monk lived in a leaf hut he had made on a flat rock in the wilderness. At that time, five hundred robbers, making their living by banditry—plundering villages and the like—committed their crimes and, being pursued by the people of the countryside, fled into the forest. Not finding any hold or refuge there, they saw that monk sitting on a rock not far away. They paid homage to him, explained their situation, and pleaded, 'Venerable sir, be our refuge!' The elder said, 'There is no refuge for you like virtue. All of you, undertake the five precepts.' They consented, saying, 'Very well,' and undertook the precepts. The elder then instructed them in the method of the simile of the saw, saying, 'Now that you are established in virtue, do not allow your minds to be corrupted even toward those who would destroy your lives.' They consented, saying, 'Very well.' Then those people of the countryside arrived there, and searching here and there, they saw the robbers and deprived them all of life. Without even the slightest corruption of mind toward them, they died with their virtue unbroken and were reborn among the devas of the sensual sphere. The chief robber became the chief deva, and the others became his retinue.

Te aparāparaṃ saṃsarantā ekaṃ buddhantaraṃ devaloke khepetvā amhākaṃ bhagavato kāle devalokato cavitvā jeṭṭhadevaputto sāvatthinagaradvāre kevaṭṭagāme pañcasatakulagāmajeṭṭhakassa kevaṭṭassa putto hutvā nibbatti, yasojotissa nāmaṃ akaṃsu. Itarepi avasesakevaṭṭānaṃ puttā hutvā nibbattiṃsu. Te pubbasannivāsena sabbepi sahāyakā hutvā sahapaṃsukīḷitaṃ kīḷantā anupubbena vayappattā ahesuṃ, yasojo tesaṃ aggo ahosi. Te sabbeva ekato hutvā jālāni gahetvā naditaḷākādīsu macche bandhantā vicaranti.

Wandering from one existence to another, they spent one Buddha-interval in the deva realm. In the time of our Blessed One, the chief deva passed away from the deva realm and was reborn in a fishermen's village near the gate of Sāvatthī as the son of the chief fisherman of the village of five hundred families. They gave him the name Yasojoti. The others were also reborn as sons of the remaining fishermen. Due to their past co-residence, they all became companions, and playing together in the dust, they gradually reached maturity. Yasojo became their leader. They all, acting together, would take their nets and wander about, catching fish in rivers, lakes, and so on.

Athekadivasaṃ aciravatiyā nadiyā jāle khitte suvaṇṇavaṇṇo maccho antojāle pāvisi. Taṃ disvā sabbepi kevaṭṭā “amhākaṃ puttā macche bandhantā suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ macchaṃ bandhiṃsū”ti haṭṭhatuṭṭhā ahesuṃ. Atha te pañcasatāpi sahāyakā macchaṃ nāvāya pakkhipitvā nāvaṃ ukkhipitvā rañño dassesuṃ. Rājā taṃ disvā “bhagavā etassa suvaṇṇavaṇṇakāraṇaṃ jānissatī”ti macchaṃ gāhāpetvā bhagavato dassesi. Satthā “ayaṃ kassapasammāsambuddhassa sāsane [V 0.0146] osakkamāne pabbajitvā micchā paṭipajjanto sāsanaṃ osakkāpetvā niraye nibbatto ekaṃ buddhantaraṃ niraye paccitvā tato cuto aciravatiyaṃ maccho hutvā nibbatto”ti vatvā tassa mātubhaginīnañca niraye nibbattabhāvaṃ, tassa bhātikattherassa parinibbutabhāvañca teneva kathāpetvā imissā aṭṭhuppattiyā kapilasuttaṃ desesi.

Then one day, when a net was cast in the Aciravatī River, a golden-colored fish entered the net. Seeing it, all the fishermen were delighted and joyful, saying, 'Our sons, while catching fish, have caught a golden-colored fish!' Then those five hundred companions placed the fish in a boat, lifted the boat, and presented it to the king. The king, upon seeing it, thought, 'The Blessed One will know the reason for its golden color,' and had the fish taken and presented to the Blessed One. The Teacher said, 'This one, having gone forth when the dispensation of the Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa was in decline, practiced wrongly, causing the dispensation to decline, and was reborn in hell. Having been tormented in hell for one Buddha-interval, he passed away from there and was reborn as a fish in the Aciravatī.' Having said this, he made that very fish relate the fact of its mother and sisters being reborn in hell and the fact of its elder brother, the Thera, having attained Parinibbāna, and in connection with this origin story, he taught the Kapila Sutta.

Satthu desanaṃ sutvā te pañcasatā kevaṭṭaputtā saṃvegajātā hutvā bhagavato santike pabbajitvā, upasampannā hutvā vivekavāsaṃ vasantā bhagavantaṃ dassanāya āgamaṃsu. Tena vuttaṃ – “tena kho pana samayena yasojappamukhāni pañcamattāni bhikkhusatānī”tiādi.

Hearing the Teacher’s discourse, those five hundred sons of fishermen were stirred with spiritual urgency. Having gone forth in the presence of the Blessed One and received the higher ordination, they dwelt in seclusion. Then they came for a sight of the Blessed One. Therefore it is said: 'Now at that time, some five hundred monks headed by Yasojo,' and so on.

Tattha tedhāti te idha. Nevāsikehīti nibaddhavāsaṃ vasamānehi. Paṭisammodamānāti nevāsikabhikkhūhi “kaccāvuso, khamanīya”ntiādinā paṭisanthāravasena sammodanāya katāya “āmāvuso, khamanīya”ntiādinā[M 0.0163], puna sammodamānā tehi saddhiṃ samappavattamodā. Senāsanāni paññāpayamānāti ācariyupajjhāyānaṃ [P 0.0181] attano ca pāpuṇakāni senāsanāni pucchitvā tehi nevāsikehi tesaṃ “idaṃ tumhākaṃ ācariyānaṃ, idaṃ tumhākaṃ upajjhāyānaṃ, idaṃ tumhākaṃ pāpuṇātī”ti senāsanāni saṃvidhāpetvā attanā ca tattha gantvā, dvārakavāṭāni vivaritvā, mañcapīṭhakaṭasārakādīni nīharitvā papphoṭetvā yathāṭhānaṃ ṭhapanādivasena paññāpentā ca.

Therein, `tedhā` is `te idha` (they here). `Nevāsikehi` means: by those dwelling in a fixed residence. `Paṭisammodamānā` means: when the resident monks had exchanged joyful greetings by way of a cordial welcome, saying, 'Friends, I trust you are well?' and so on, they, exchanging joyful greetings in return, saying, 'Yes, friends, we are well,' and so on, shared a mutual joy with them. `Senāsanāni paññāpayamānā` means: having asked for the lodgings that were due to their teachers, their preceptors, and themselves, and having had the lodgings arranged by those resident monks, who said, 'This is for your teachers, this is for your preceptors, this is what is due to you,' they themselves went there, opened the door-panels, brought out the beds, chairs, mats, and rugs, shook them out, and prepared them by placing them in their proper positions, and so on.

Pattacīvarāni paṭisāmayamānāti, “bhante, imaṃ me pattaṃ ṭhapetha, idaṃ cīvaraṃ, idaṃ thālakaṃ, idaṃ udakatumbaṃ, idaṃ me kattarayaṭṭhi”nti evaṃ samaṇaparikkhāraṃ saṃgopayamānā. Uccāsaddā mahāsaddāti uddhaṃ gataṭṭhena ucco saddo yesante uccāsaddā akārassa ākāraṃ katvā. Samantato patthaṭaṭṭhena mahanto saddo yesante mahāsaddā. Kevaṭṭā maññe macchavilopeti kevaṭṭā viya macchavilumpane. Yathā nāma kevaṭṭā udake vaṭṭanato macchaggahaṇatthaṃ pavattanato “kevaṭṭā”ti laddhanāmā macchabandhā macchaggahaṇatthaṃ jale jālaṃ pakkhipitvā “paviṭṭho na paviṭṭho, gahito na gahito”tiādinā uccāsaddamahāsaddā honti. Yathā ca te macchapacchiādīni ṭhapitaṭṭhāne mahājane gantvā “mayhaṃ ekaṃ macchaṃ detha, mayhaṃ ekaṃ macchaphālaṃ detha, amukassa dinno mahanto, mayhaṃ khuddako”tiādīni vatvā vilumpamāne tesaṃ paṭisedhanādivasena uccāsaddamahāsaddā ca honti, evamete bhikkhūti dasseti. Teteti te ete. Kiṃnūti kissa nu, kimatthaṃ nūti attho. Temeti te ime. Paṇāmemīti nīharāmi. Voti tumhe. Na vo mama santike vatthabbanti tumhehi mayhaṃ santike na vasitabbaṃ. Ye tumhe mādisassa buddhassa vasanaṭṭhānaṃ [V 0.0147] āgantvā evaṃ mahāsaddaṃ karotha, attano dhammatāya vasantā kiṃ nāma sāruppaṃ karissatha, tumhādisānaṃ mama santike vasanakiccaṃ natthīti dīpeti. Evaṃ paṇāmitesu ca bhagavatā tesu ekabhikkhupi “bhagavā tumhe mahāsaddamattakena [P 0.0182] amhe paṇāmethā”ti vā aññaṃ vā kiñci paṭivacanaṃ avatvā buddhagāravena sabbe bhagavato vacanaṃ sampaṭicchantā “evaṃ, bhante”ti vatvā nikkhamiṃsu. Evaṃ pana tesaṃ ahosi “mayaṃ satthāraṃ passissāma, dhammaṃ sossāma, satthu santike vasissāmāti āgatā, evarūpassa pana garuno [M 0.0164] satthu santikaṃ āgantvā mahāsaddaṃ karimhā, amhākameva dosoyaṃ, paṇāmitamhā tato, na laddhaṃ satthu santike vatthuṃ, samantapāsādikaṃ suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ sarīraṃ oloketuṃ, madhurassarena desitaṃ dhammaṃ sotu”nti. Te balavadomanassajātā hutvā pakkamiṃsu.

‘While putting away the almsbowl and robes’ means, while safeguarding the requisites of a monastic, saying: ‘Venerable sirs, please put away this bowl for me, this robe, this cup, this water vessel, and this staff.’ ‘Of loud noises, of great noises’: by the meaning of ‘gone upwards,’ their noise is loud, hence they are called ‘of loud noises,’ changing the short ‘a’ to a long ‘ā.’ By the meaning of ‘spread all around,’ their noise is great, hence they are called ‘of great noises.’ ‘It seems like fishermen plundering fish’ means like fishermen plundering fish. Just as fishermen—who are called ‘kevaṭṭā’ because they move about (`vaṭṭanato...pavattanato`) in the water to catch fish—after casting a net into the water to catch fish, make loud and great noises, saying, ‘Has it entered or not? Has it been caught or not?’ And just as when a great crowd goes to the place where they have put the fish, baskets, and so on, and while they are plundering, saying, ‘Give me one fish, give me a piece of fish, the one given to so-and-so was large, mine is small,’ and so on, the fishermen make loud and great noises by way of preventing them and so on—so too, it is shown, do these monks. ‘Those’ means these ones. ‘Why now?’ means for what reason, for what purpose? ‘These’ means these ones. ‘I dismiss’ means I send away. ‘You’ means you. ‘You should not stay near me’ means you should not dwell in my presence. This explains: ‘You who have come to the dwelling place of a Buddha like me and make such a great noise—what proper conduct will you follow while dwelling according to your own nature? There is no need for those like you to stay near me.’ When the Blessed One had dismissed them in this way, not a single monk said, ‘Venerable sir, you dismiss us merely for making a great noise,’ or anything else in reply. Out of reverence for the Buddha, they all accepted the Blessed One's words, saying, ‘Yes, venerable sir,’ and departed. But this thought arose in them: ‘We came with the thought, “We will see the Teacher, we will hear the Dhamma, we will dwell near the Teacher.” Yet after coming into the presence of such a revered Teacher, we made a great noise. The fault is ours alone. We have been dismissed from there. We have not gained the opportunity to dwell near the Teacher, to behold his body, radiant all around with the color of gold, or to hear the Dhamma taught with his sweet voice.’ Having become filled with intense sorrow, they left.

Saṃsāmetvāti suguttaṃ katvā. Vajjīti evaṃnāmako janapado, vajjī nāma jānapadino rājakumārā, tesaṃ nivāso ekopi janapado ruḷhīvasena “vajjī”tveva vuccati. Tena vuttaṃ “vajjīsū”ti. Vaggumudāti evaṃnāma lokassa puññasammatā ekā nadī. “Vaggamudā”tipi pāṭho. Atthakāmenāti kiñci payojanaṃ anapekkhitvā atthameva icchantena. Hitesināti atthaṃ icchantena, “kinti me sāvakā vaṭṭadukkhā parimucceyyu”nti tassa atthasaṅkhātassa atthassa vā hetubhūtassa hitassa esanasīlena. Tato eva attano sarīrakhedaṃ agaṇetvā dūrepi veneyyasantikaṃ gantvā anukampanato anukampakena. Tameva anukampaṃ upādāya mayaṃ paṇāmitā, na attano veyyāvaccādipaccāsīsāya. Yasmā dhammagaruno buddhā bhagavanto sammāpaṭipattiyāva pūjetabbā, ye uccāsaddakaraṇamattepi paṇāmenti, tasmā handa mayaṃ, āvuso, tathā vihāraṃ kappema sabbattha satisampajaññayogena apaṇṇakappaṭipadaṃ pūrentā yathāgahitakammaṭṭhānaṃ matthakaṃ pāpentā catuiriyāpathavihāraṃ kappema viharāma. Yathā no viharatanti yathā amhesu viharantesu, bhagavā attamano assa, sammāpaṭipattiyā pūjāya ārādhito bhaveyyāti attho.

‘Having come to an agreement’ means having made things secure. ‘Vajjī’: there is a country of this name, and the ruling princes of that country are called Vajjīs. Their dwelling, a single country, is also called “Vajjī” by convention. Hence, it is said “among the Vajjīs.” ‘Vaggumudā’ is the name of a river regarded by the world as a place for merit. There is also a variant reading, “Vaggamudā.” ‘By one who desires their welfare’ means by one who desires only their welfare, without regard for any personal benefit. ‘By one who seeks their good’ means by one who desires their benefit, with the disposition of seeking their welfare—which is defined as their good or the cause of that good—thinking, “How might my disciples be freed from the suffering of the cycle of rebirth?” For that very reason, disregarding his own bodily fatigue, he goes even to a distant place to be near those who can be trained, being one who acts out of compassion. It was due to that very compassion that we were dismissed, not out of any expectation for personal service or the like. Since the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, revere the Dhamma and are to be honored only by right practice—they who dismiss others even for the mere making of a loud noise—therefore, friends, come, let us so arrange our dwelling that, while fulfilling the unerring practice everywhere with the application of mindfulness and clear comprehension, and bringing our meditation subject to its culmination, we may perfect our abiding in the four postures. ‘So that as we dwell’ means: in such a way that, as we dwell, the Blessed One would be pleased, that he would be gratified by the offering of right practice. That is the meaning.

Tenevantaravassenāti tasmiṃyeva antaravasse mahāpavāraṇaṃ [P 0.0183] anatikkamitvāva. Sabbeva tisso vijjā sacchākaṃsūti sabbeyeva te pañcasatā bhikkhū pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇaṃ dibbacakkhuñāṇaṃ āsavakkhayañāṇanti imā tisso pubbenivutthakkhandhappaṭicchādakamohakkhandhādīnaṃ vinivijjhanaṭṭhena vijjā attapaccakkhā akaṃsu. Lokiyābhiññāsu imāyeva dve abhiññā āsavakkhayañāṇassa bahūpakārā, na tathā dibbasotacetopariyaiddhividhañāṇānīti dassanatthaṃ vijjattayamevettha tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ adhigamadassanavasena uddhaṭaṃ. Tathā hi verañjasutte (a. ni. 8.11) bhagavā verañjabrāhmaṇassa attano adhigamaṃ dassento vijjattayameva desesi, na dibbasotañāṇādīnaṃ [V 0.0148] abhāvato. Evaṃ tesampi bhikkhūnaṃ vijjamānānipi dibbasotañāṇādīni [M 0.0165] na uddhaṭāni. Chaḷabhiññā hi te bhikkhū. Evañca katvā “vaggumudāya nadiyā tīre antarahitā mahāvane kūṭāgārasālāyaṃ bhagavato sammukhe pāturahesu”nti tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ iddhivaḷañjanaṃ vakkhati.

‘In that very rains retreat’ means in that very rains retreat, without having passed the great Pavāraṇā ceremony. ‘All realized the threefold knowledge’ means all those five hundred monks personally realized the three knowledges: the knowledge of recollecting past lives, the divine eye, and the knowledge of the destruction of the taints. These are called ‘knowledges’ (`vijjā`) because they pierce through the mass of delusion and other things that conceal the aggregates of past lives. Among the worldly higher knowledges, only these two are of great help for the knowledge of the destruction of the taints; the divine ear, knowledge of others’ minds, and the power of psychic feats are not so helpful. To show this, only the threefold knowledge is mentioned here with regard to the monks’ attainment. Indeed, in the Verañja Sutta (AN 8.11), the Blessed One, when showing his own attainment to the brahmin Verañja, taught only the threefold knowledge, not because the divine ear and other knowledges were absent. Similarly, for these monks too, although the divine ear and other knowledges were present, they are not mentioned. For those monks possessed the six higher knowledges. And so, their display of psychic power will be described thus: they “appeared in the presence of the Blessed One in the great forest by the bank of the river Vaggumudā, in the Kūṭāgāra hall, after having vanished.”

Yathābhirantanti yathābhiratiṃ yathājjhāsayaṃ. Buddhānañhi ekasmiṃ ṭhāne vasantānaṃ chāyūdakavipattiṃ vā aphāsukasenāsanaṃ vā manussānaṃ assaddhādibhāvaṃ vā āgamma anabhirati nāma natthi, tesaṃ sampattiyā “phāsuṃ viharāmā”ti ciravihāropi natthi. Yattha pana bhagavati viharante manussā saraṇesu vā patiṭṭhahanti, sīlāni vā samādiyanti pabbajanti, sotāpattimaggādīni vā pāpuṇanti, satthā tāsu sampattīsu tesaṃ patiṭṭhāpanatthaṃ vasati, tadabhāve pakkamati. Tadā hi sāvatthiyaṃ kattabbabuddhakiccaṃ nāhosi. Tena vuttaṃ – “atha kho bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ yathābhirantaṃ viharitvā yena vesālī tena cārikaṃ pakkāmī”ti.

‘As long as he pleased’ means according to his inclination and disposition. For the Buddhas, while dwelling in one place, discontent does not arise from such causes as the failure of shade or water, uncomfortable lodging, or the lack of faith among people. Nor is there any prolonged dwelling because of favorable conditions, with the thought, ‘We dwell at ease.’ But when, in the presence of the Blessed One, people become established in the refuges, undertake the precepts, go forth, or attain the path of stream-entry and so forth, the Teacher remains there to establish them in those attainments. In the absence of such, he departs. At that time, in Sāvatthī, there was no Buddha-duty to be performed. Thus it is said: ‘Then the Blessed One, having dwelt in Sāvatthī as long as he pleased, set out on tour towards Vesālī.’

Cārikaṃ caramānoti addhānagamanaṃ gacchanto. Cārikā ca nāmesā bhagavato duvidhā turitacārikā aturitacārikāti. Tattha dūrepi bodhaneyyapuggalaṃ disvā tassa bodhanatthaṃ sahasā gamanaṃ turitacārikā nāma, sā mahākassapapaccuggamanādīsu daṭṭhabbā. Yā pana gāmanigamarājadhānīpaṭipāṭiyā devasikaṃ yojanaddhayojanavasena piṇḍapātacariyādīhi lokaṃ anuggaṇhanto gacchati, ayaṃ aturitacārikā nāma, ayameva idhādhippetā. Tadavasarīti tena avasari, taṃ vā avasari, tattha avasari[P 0.0184], pāvisīti attho.

‘Journeying’ means going on a journey. This journey of the Blessed One is of two kinds: a swift journey and an unhurried journey. Therein, a swift journey is when, seeing a person capable of being awakened even from afar, he suddenly goes to awaken him, as is to be seen in the case of Mahākassapa’s going forth to meet him and so forth. But when he travels daily from village to market town to capital, in due order, covering half a league or a league, benefiting the world by means of the alms-round and so forth, this is called an unhurried journey, and this is what is intended here. ‘He arrived there’ means he arrived by that, or he arrived at that, or he arrived therein; the meaning is, he entered.

Tatrāti tassaṃ. Sudanti nipātamattaṃ. Vesāliyanti tikkhattuṃ visālībhūtattā “vesālī”ti laddhanāme licchavirājūnaṃ nagare. Mahāvaneti mahāvanaṃ nāma sayaṃjātaṃ aropimaṃ saparicchedaṃ mahantaṃ vanaṃ. Kapilavatthusāmantā pana mahāvanaṃ himavantena saha ekābaddhaṃ aparicchedaṃ hutvā mahāsamuddaṃ āhacca ṭhitaṃ. Idaṃ tādisaṃ na hoti, saparicchedaṃ mahantaṃ vananti mahāvanaṃ. Kūṭāgārasālāyanti tasmiṃ mahāvane bhagavantaṃ uddissa kate ārāme kūṭāgāraṃ anto katvā haṃsavaṭṭakacchannena katā sabbākārasampannā buddhassa bhagavato gandhakuṭi kūṭāgārasālā nāma[M 0.0166], tassaṃ kūṭāgārasālāyaṃ. Vaggumudātīriyānanti vaggumudātīravāsīnaṃ. Cetasā ceto paricca manasi karitvāti attano cittena tesaṃ cittaṃ paricchijja manasi karitvā, cetopariyañāṇena vā sabbaññutaññāṇena vā tehi adhigatavisesaṃ jānitvāti attho.

‘There’ means in that. ‘Sudanti’ is merely a particle. ‘At Vesālī’ means in the city of the Licchavi kings, which obtained the name ‘Vesālī’ because it had been expanded three times. ‘In the Great Wood’ refers to a great wood that is naturally grown, not planted, and has defined boundaries. The Great Wood near Kapilavatthu, however, being connected with the Himalayas, was boundless and extended to the great ocean. This one is not like that; it is a great wood with defined boundaries, hence ‘Great Wood’. ‘In the Hall with the Peaked Roof’ refers to the Blessed One’s perfumed chamber in the monastery built for him in that Great Wood. It is called the Hall with the Peaked Roof because it was constructed with a peaked chamber inside, was roofed with curved tiles, and was endowed with all features. It means in that Hall with the Peaked Roof. ‘Of the Vaggumudātīriyas’ means of those dwelling on the bank of the Vaggumudā River. ‘Having encompassed their minds with his own mind’ means having discerned their minds with his own mind and attended to it; or, it means having known the special attainment reached by them through the knowledge of penetrating minds or through omniscient knowledge.

Ālokajātā [V 0.0149] viyāti sañjātālokā viya. Itaraṃ tasseva vevacanaṃ, candasahassasūriyasahassehi obhāsitā viyāti attho. Yasmā te yasojappamukhā pañcasatā bhikkhū sabbaso avijjandhakāravidhamanena ālokabhūtā obhāsabhūtā hutvā viharanti, tasmā bhagavā tehi ṭhitadisāya “ālokajātā viya me, ānanda, esā disā”tiādinā vaṇṇabhaṇanāpadesena te bhikkhū pasaṃsati. Tena vuttaṃ – “yassaṃ disāyaṃ vaggumudātīriyā bhikkhū viharantī”ti. Appaṭikūlāti na paṭikūlā, manāpā manoharāti attho. Yasmiñhi padese sīlādiguṇasampannā mahesino viharanti, taṃ kiñcāpi ukkūlavikūlavisamaduggākāraṃ, atha kho manuññaṃ ramaṇīyameva. Vuttañhetaṃ –

‘As if light has arisen’ means as if light has come into being. The other term is a synonym for that, meaning ‘as if illuminated by a thousand moons and a thousand suns’. Because those five hundred monks, led by Yasoja, having completely dispelled the darkness of ignorance, dwell as embodiments of light and radiance, therefore the Blessed One praises those monks by way of commendation, describing the direction where they were with words such as, ‘Ānanda, this direction appears to me as if light has arisen.’ Hence it is said: ‘In that direction where the Vaggumudātīriya monks dwell.’ ‘Not disagreeable’ means not disagreeable; the meaning is pleasant and delightful. For in any place where great sages endowed with virtues such as morality dwell, even if it is uneven, rugged, or difficult to traverse, it is still charming and delightful. For it has been said:

“Gāme vā yadi vāraññe, ninne vā yadi vā thale;

Yattha arahanto viharanti, taṃ bhūmirāmaṇeyyaka”nti. (dha. pa. 98);

‘Whether in a village or in the forest, in a valley or on a highland, wherever arahants dwell, that spot of ground is delightful.’ (Dhp. 98)

Pahiṇeyyāsīti [P 0.0185] peseyyāsi. Satthā āyasmantānaṃ dassanakāmoti tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ santike paheṇākāradassanaṃ. Iti bhagavā yadatthaṃ te bhikkhū paṇāmesi, tamatthaṃ matthakappattaṃ disvā āraddhacitto tesaṃ dassanakāmataṃ therassa ārocesi. Evaṃ kirassa ahosi “ahaṃ ime uccāsaddamahāsaddakaraṇe paṇāmessāmi, atha te bhadro assājānīyo viya kasābhighātena, tena coditā saṃvegappattā mamārādhanatthaṃ araññaṃ pavisitvā ghaṭentā vāyamantā khippameva arahattaṃ sacchikarissantī”ti. Idāni te aggaphalappatte disvā tāya arahattappattiyā ārādhitacitto tesaṃ dassanakāmo hutvā evaṃ dhammabhaṇḍāgārikaṃ āṇāpesi.

‘You should send for them’ means you should dispatch a message. ‘The Teacher wishes to see the venerable ones’ shows the reason for sending a message to those monks. Thus the Blessed One, seeing that the purpose for which he had dismissed those monks was accomplished, with an inspired mind, announced to the elder his desire to see them. For it had occurred to him thus: ‘I shall dismiss these monks who are making a loud and great noise. Then, like a fine thoroughbred horse struck by the whip, being urged on by that, they will attain a sense of urgency. Entering the forest to gratify me, striving and making an effort, they will quickly realize arahantship.’ Now, seeing that they had attained the highest fruit, his mind gratified by that attainment of arahantship, he became desirous of seeing them and thus instructed the Treasurer of the Dhamma.

So bhikkhūti ānandattherena tathā āṇatto chaḷabhiñño eko bhikkhu. Pamukheti sammukhe. Āneñjasamādhināti catutthajjhānapādakena aggaphalasamādhinā, “arūpajjhānapādakenā”tipi vadanti. “Āneñjena samādhinā”tipi [M 0.0167] pāṭho. Kasmā pana bhagavā tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ āgamanaṃ jānanto paṭisanthāraṃ akatvā samāpattiṃyeva samāpajji? Tesaṃ attanā samāpannasamāpattiṃ jānitvā samāpajjanatthaṃ, tesaṃ pubbe paṇāmitānaṃ idāni attanā samānasambhogadassanatthaṃ, ānubhāvadīpanatthaṃ, vinā vacībhedena aññabyākaraṇadīpanatthañca. Apare panāhu “pubbe paṇāmitānaṃ idāni attano santikaṃ āgatānaṃ anuttarasukhuppādanena anaññasādhāraṇapaṭisanthārakaraṇattha”nti. Tepi āyasmanto bhagavato ajjhāsayaṃ ñatvā taṃyeva samāpattiṃ samāpajjiṃsu. Tena vuttaṃ – “katamena nu kho bhagavā vihārena etarahi viharatī”tiādi.

‘That monk’ refers to a certain monk possessing the six higher knowledges, who was thus instructed by the Elder Ānanda. ‘In person’ means face to face. ‘With the imperturbable concentration’ means with the concentration of the highest fruition that has the fourth jhāna as its basis; some also say, ‘that has a formless jhāna as its basis.’ There is also the reading, `Āneñjena samādhinā`. But why did the Blessed One, knowing of the arrival of those monks, not offer a greeting but instead enter into an attainment? It was so that they, knowing the attainment he had entered, might enter it themselves; to show those who had previously been dismissed that they now shared the same enjoyment as himself; to display his power; and to demonstrate the declaration of final knowledge without any utterance of speech. Others, however, say it was to provide a welcome not shared by others by producing unsurpassed bliss for those who had previously been dismissed and had now come into his presence. Those venerable ones, too, understanding the Blessed One’s intention, entered that very same attainment. Hence it was said: ‘In what state is the Blessed One dwelling now?’ and so on.

Ettha [V 0.0150] ca rūpāvacaracatutthajjhānaṃ kosajjādīnaṃ pāripantikadhammānaṃ suvidūrabhāvato iddhiyā mūlabhūtehi anoṇamanādīhi soḷasahi vodānadhammehi samannāgamanato āneñjappattaṃ sayaṃ aniñjanaṭṭhena āneñjanti vuccati. Vuttañhetaṃ –

Here, the fourth jhāna of the form realm is called ‘imperturbability’ (āneñja) by reason of its own non-agitation, a state it has reached because it is very far removed from obstructive states such as sloth and so forth, and because it is endowed with sixteen purifying qualities, such as non-bending and others, which are the basis for psychic powers. For it has been said:

“Anoṇataṃ [P 0.0186] cittaṃ kosajje na iñjatīti āneñjaṃ. Anuṇṇataṃ cittaṃ uddhacce na iñjatīti āneñjaṃ. Anabhirataṃ cittaṃ rāge na iñjatīti āneñjaṃ. Anapanataṃ cittaṃ byāpāde na iñjatīti āneñjaṃ. Anissitaṃ cittaṃ diṭṭhiyā na iñjatīti āneñjaṃ. Appaṭibaddhaṃ cittaṃ chandarāge na iñjatīti āneñjaṃ. Vippamuttaṃ cittaṃ kāmarāge na iñjatīti āneñjaṃ. Visaṃyuttaṃ cittaṃ kilese na iñjatīti āneñjaṃ. Vimariyādikataṃ cittaṃ kilesamariyādāya na iñjatīti āneñjaṃ. Ekattagataṃ cittaṃ nānattakilese na iñjatīti āneñjaṃ. Saddhāya pariggahitaṃ cittaṃ assaddhiye na iñjatīti āneñjaṃ. Vīriyena pariggahitaṃ cittaṃ kosajje na iñjatīti āneñjaṃ. Satiyā pariggahitaṃ cittaṃ pamāde na iñjatīti āneñjaṃ. Samādhinā pariggahitaṃ cittaṃ uddhacce na iñjatīti āneñjaṃ. Paññāya pariggahitaṃ cittaṃ avijjāya na iñjatīti āneñjaṃ. Obhāsagataṃ cittaṃ avijjandhakāre na iñjatīti āneñja”nti.

‘The mind not bending in sloth does not stir—this is imperturbability. The mind not elated in restlessness does not stir—this is imperturbability. The mind not delighting in lust does not stir—this is imperturbability. The mind not turning away in ill will does not stir—this is imperturbability. The mind not dependent on views does not stir—this is imperturbability. The mind not bound by desire-lust does not stir—this is imperturbability. The mind liberated from sensual desire does not stir—this is imperturbability. The mind disjoined from defilements does not stir—this is imperturbability. The mind whose boundary is destroyed in regard to the boundary of defilements does not stir—this is imperturbability. The mind gone to oneness does not stir amidst diverse defilements—this is imperturbability. The mind grasped by faith does not stir in faithlessness—this is imperturbability. The mind grasped by energy does not stir in sloth—this is imperturbability. The mind grasped by mindfulness does not stir in heedlessness—this is imperturbability. The mind grasped by concentration does not stir in restlessness—this is imperturbability. The mind grasped by wisdom does not stir in ignorance—this is imperturbability. The mind gone to illumination does not stir in the darkness of ignorance—this is imperturbability.’

Rūpāvacaracatutthajjhānameva ca rūpavirāgabhāvanāvasena pavattitaṃ, ārammaṇavibhāgena catubbidhaṃ arūpāvacarajjhānanti etesaṃ pañcannaṃ jhānānaṃ āneñjavohāro. Tesaṃ yaṃ kiñci pādakaṃ katvā samāpannā arahattaphalasamāpatti āneñjasamādhīti porāṇā.

The fourth jhāna of the form realm, cultivated by way of developing dispassion toward form, and the fourfold formless jhāna, divided by its object—for these five jhānas there is the designation ‘imperturbable.’ The attainment of the fruition of arahantship, entered into by making any one of these jhānas the basis, is the imperturbable concentration, according to the ancients.

Abhikkantāyāti [M 0.0168] atītāya. Nikkhanteti niggate, apagateti attho. Tuṇhī ahosīti bhagavā ariyena tuṇhībhāvena tuṇhī ahosi. Uddhaste aruṇeti uggate aruṇe, aruṇo nāma puratthimadisāya sūriyodayato puretarameva uṭṭhitobhāso. Nandimukhiyāti rattiyā aruṇassa uggatattā eva aruṇappabhāya sūriyālokūpajīvino satte nandāpanamukhiyā viya [P 0.0187] rattiyā jātāya, vibhāyamānāyāti attho.

‘Abhikkantāyā’ means past. ‘Nikkhanteti’ means gone out, departed. ‘Tuṇhī ahosīti’ means the Blessed One remained silent with noble silence. ‘Uddhaste aruṇeti’ means when the dawn had ascended. ‘Aruṇo’ refers to the glow that appears in the eastern direction before sunrise. ‘Nandimukhiyāti’ means that with the rising of the dawn, the night becomes as if joyful-faced for beings who depend on sunlight due to the dawn's light; the meaning is ‘dawning’.

Tamhā samādhimhā vuṭṭhahitvāti yathāparicchedaṃ tato āneñjasamādhito arahattaphalasamāpattito uṭṭhāya. Sace kho tvaṃ, ānanda, jāneyyāsīti bhagavā “ime ca bhikkhū ettakaṃ kālaṃ iminā nāma samāpattisukhena vītināmentī”ti, ānanda, yadi tvaṃ jāneyyāsi. Ettakampi te nappaṭibhāseyyāti lokiyapaṭisammodanaṃ sandhāya yadidaṃ te “abhikkantā, bhante, rattī”tiādinā [V 0.0151] tikkhattuṃ paṭibhānaṃ upaṭṭhitaṃ, tayidaṃ ettakampi te na upaṭṭhaheyya. Yasmā ca kho tvaṃ, ānanda, sekkho asekkhaṃ samāpattivihāraṃ na jānāsi, tasmā maṃ imesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ lokiyapaṭisammodanaṃ kāretuṃ ussukkaṃ āpajji. Ahaṃ pana imehi bhikkhūhi saddhiṃ lokuttarapaṭisammodaneneva tiyāmarattiṃ vītināmesinti dassento bhagavā āha – “ahañca, ānanda, imāni ca pañca bhikkhusatāni sabbeva āneñjasamādhinā nisīdimhā”ti.

‘Tamhā samādhimhā vuṭṭhahitvāti’ means rising from that concentration, that is, from the imperturbable concentration, the attainment of the fruition of arahantship, as defined. ‘Sace kho tvaṃ, ānanda, jāneyyāsīti’ means, Ānanda, if you knew that ‘these monks spent so much time in the bliss of this attainment.’ ‘Ettakampi te nappaṭibhāseyyāti’ refers to worldly greetings. That is, the threefold prompting that arose in you with ‘The night, venerable sir, has passed,’ etc., even this much would not have occurred to you. Because you, Ānanda, being a learner, do not know the attainment-dwelling of the non-learner, therefore you became eager to have me engage in worldly greetings with these monks. But I, showing that I spent the three watches of the night only in supramundane communion with these monks, said, ‘I, Ānanda, and these five hundred monks all were sitting in imperturbable concentration.’

Etamatthaṃ viditvāti etaṃ tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ attanā samaṃ āneñjasamādhisamāpajjanasamatthatāsaṅkhātaṃ vasībhāvatthaṃ sabbākārato viditvā. Imaṃ udānanti imaṃ tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ anavasesarāgādippahānasaṃsiddhitādisabhāvadīpanaṃ udānaṃ udānesi.

‘Etamatthaṃ viditvāti’ means having understood this matter in all its aspects, namely, this state of mastery of those monks, designated as the ability to enter imperturbable concentration equally with himself. ‘Imaṃ udānanti’ means he uttered this inspired utterance, which reveals the nature of the accomplishment of those monks in the complete abandonment of lust and so on.

Tattha yassa jito kāmakaṇḍakoti kusalapakkhavijjhanaṭṭhena kaṇḍakabhūto kilesakāmo yena ariyapuggalena anavasesaṃ jito pahīno, etenassa anunayābhāvaṃ dasseti. “Gāmakaṇṭako”tipi pāṭho. Tassattho – gāme kaṇṭako kaṇṭakaṭṭhāniyo sakalo vatthukāmo yassa jitoti. Jayo cassa tappaṭibaddhachandarāgappahāneneva veditabbo, tena tesaṃ anāgāmimaggo vutto hoti[M 0.0169]. Akkoso ca jitoti sambandho. Vadho ca bandhanañcāti etthāpi eseva nayo. Tesu akkosajayena vacīduccaritābhāvo, itarena kāyaduccaritābhāvo dassito. Tena taṃnimittakassa byāpādassa anavasesappahānena tatiyamaggo vutto hoti. Atha vā akkosādijayavacanena tatiyamaggo vutto hoti, akkosādīnaṃ accantakhamanaṃ tattha pakāsitaṃ hoti, ubhayathāpi nesaṃ virodhābhāvaṃ dasseti. Pabbato [P 0.0188] viya so ṭhito anejoti ejā vuccati calanakilesaparipantho, ejāhetūnaṃ avasesakilesānaṃ abhāvena anejo, anejattāyeva sabbakilesehi paravādavātehi ca akampanīyattā ṭhito ekagghanapabbatasadiso. Sukhadukkhesu na vedhati sa bhikkhūti so bhinnakileso bhikkhu sukhadukkhanimittaṃ na kampatīti heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva attho veditabbo. Iti bhagavā tesaṃ pañcasatānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ arahattādhigamena tādibhāvappattiṃ ekajjhaṃ katvā ekapuggalādhiṭṭhānaṃ udānaṃ udānesīti.

Here, ‘yassa jito kāmakaṇḍako’ means that sensual desire, which is like a thorn due to its piercing of the wholesome side, has been completely conquered and abandoned by that noble person; by this is shown his absence of delight. There is also the reading ‘gāmakaṇṭako.’ Its meaning is: for whom all objective sensuality, which is like a thorn in a village, is conquered. And his victory should be understood as precisely the abandonment of desire and lust connected with that; by that, the path of the non-returner is spoken of for them. The connection is ‘and abuse is conquered.’ Here too, in ‘and killing and bondage,’ this is the method. Among these, by the conquest of abuse, the absence of verbal misconduct is shown; by the other, the absence of bodily misconduct is shown. By that, through the complete abandonment of ill will caused by those things, the third path is spoken of. Alternatively, by the words ‘conquest of abuse, etc.,’ the third path is spoken of; complete forbearance towards abuse, etc., is shown there. In both ways, it shows their absence of opposition. ‘Like a mountain, he stands unshaken’: ‘ejā’ is called the obstacle of agitating defilements. Due to the absence of the remaining defilements which are causes of agitation, he is unshaken (anejo). Precisely because of being unshaken, he stands, unable to be shaken by all defilements and by the winds of others’ doctrines, like a solid mountain. ‘That monk does not tremble in pleasure or pain’: that monk whose defilements are destroyed does not tremble on account of the sign of pleasure and pain; the meaning should be understood in the way stated previously. Thus, the Blessed One, having unified the attainment of the state of ‘suchness’ by those five hundred monks through the realization of arahantship, proclaimed this inspired utterance taking a single person as the basis.

Tatiyasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the third sutta is concluded.

4. Sāriputtasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Sāriputta Sutta

24. Catutthe [V 0.0152] parimukhaṃ satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvāti ārammaṇābhimukhaṃ satiṃ ṭhapayitvā mukhasamīpe katvā. Tathā hi vibhaṅge vuttaṃ –

24. In the fourth sutta, the phrase 'having established mindfulness in front' means having placed mindfulness facing the object, having brought it near the mouth. For thus it is said in the Vibhaṅga:

“Ayaṃ sati upaṭṭhitā hoti supaṭṭhitā nāsikagge vā mukhanimitte vā, tena vuccati parimukhaṃ satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā”ti (vibha. 537).

'This mindfulness is present, well-established at the tip of the nose or at the sign of the face; therefore it is said, "having established mindfulness in front."' (Vibh. 537).

Atha vā “parīti pariggahaṭṭho, mukhanti niyyānaṭṭho, satīti upaṭṭhānaṭṭho, tena vuccati ‘parimukhaṃ sati’”nti. Evaṃ paṭisambhidāyaṃ (paṭi. ma. 1.164) vuttanayenapettha attho veditabbo. Tatrāyaṃ saṅkhepattho – pariggahitaniyyānasatiṃ katvāti. Niyyānanti ca satiyā ogāhitabbaṃ ārammaṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ettha ca purimo pacchimo ca attho sabbasaṅgāhakavasena, itaro samāpattiyā pubbabhāgasamannāhāravasena daṭṭhabbo. Satīti vā satisīsena jhānaṃ vuttaṃ [M 0.0170] “ye kāyagatāsatiṃ paribhuñjantī”tiādīsu (a. ni. 1.600) viya. Katamaṃ pana taṃ jhānanti? Rūpāvacaracatutthajjhānaṃ pādakaṃ katvā samāpannaṃ arahattaphalajjhānaṃ. Kathaṃ panetaṃ jānitabbanti? Āneñjasamādhiyogena therassa savisesaṃ niccalabhāvaṃ kenaci akampanīyatañca [P 0.0189] pabbatopamāya pakāsento bhagavā imaṃ udānaṃ abhāsīti gāthāya eva ayamattho viññāyati. Na cāyaṃ nisajjā therassa saccappaṭivedhāya, atha kho diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārāya. Pubbeyeva hi sūkarakhataleṇe (ma. ni. 2.201) attano bhāgineyyassa dīghanakhaparibbājakassa bhagavati dhammaṃ desente ayaṃ mahāthero saccappaṭivedhakiccaṃ matthakaṃ pāpesīti.

Alternatively, 'pari' has the sense of grasping, 'mukha' has the sense of egress, 'sati' has the sense of establishment; therefore it is called 'parimukhaṃ sati'. Thus, the meaning here should be understood according to the method stated in the Paṭisambhidāmagga (Paṭi. Ma. 1.164). Therein, this is the condensed meaning: having made mindfulness that has grasped the exit. And 'niyyāna' should be seen as the object to be penetrated by mindfulness. Here, the former and the latter meanings should be seen as all-encompassing, while the other should be seen in terms of the preliminary arrangement for attainment. Or, 'sati' refers to jhāna with mindfulness as its chief, as in passages like 'those who cultivate mindfulness directed to the body' (A. Ni. 1.600). But what is that jhāna? It is the jhāna of the fruit of Arahantship, attained having made the fourth fine-material jhāna its basis. How, then, should this be known? The Blessed One, revealing through the simile of a mountain the elder’s special immovability and his state of being unshakeable by anyone—on account of his practice of imperturbable concentration—uttered this inspired utterance, and by this verse alone is this meaning understood. And this sitting of the elder was not for the penetration of the truths, but rather for a pleasant dwelling in this very life. For previously, in the Boar's Cave (Ma. Ni. 2.201), while the Blessed One was teaching the Dhamma to his nephew, the wanderer Dīghanakha, this great elder had already brought the task of penetrating the truths to completion.

Etamatthanti etaṃ therassa āneñjasamādhiyogena tādibhāvappattiyā ca kenaci akampanīyatāsaṅkhātaṃ atthaṃ sabbākārato viditvā tadatthavibhāvanaṃ imaṃ udānaṃ udānesi.

"Knowing this meaning" means: having known in every way this meaning—namely, the elder's state of being unshakeable by anyone, due to his practice of imperturbable concentration and his attainment of a state of 'suchness'—he uttered this inspired utterance which clarifies that meaning.

Tattha yathāpi pabbato seloti yathā silāmayo ekagghanasilāpabbato, na paṃsupabbato na missakapabbatoti attho. Acalo suppatiṭṭhitoti suppatiṭṭhitamūlo pakativātehi acalo akampanīyo hoti. Evaṃ mohakkhayā bhikkhu, pabbatova na vedhatīti mohassa anavasesappahānā mohamūlakattā ca sabbākusalānaṃ pahīnasabbākusalo bhikkhu, yathā so pabbato pakativātehi, evaṃ lokadhammehi na vedhati na kampati. Mohakkhayoti vā yasmā nibbānaṃ arahattañca vuccati, tasmā mohakkhayassa hetu nibbānassa arahattassa vā adhigatattā catūsu ariyasaccesu [V 0.0153] suppatiṭṭhito asamāpannakālepi yathāvuttapabbato viya na kenaci vedhati, pageva samāpannakāleti adhippāyo.

Therein, 'just as a mountain of rock' means a mountain made of stone, a solid mass of rock, not a mountain of dust nor a mixed mountain; this is the meaning. 'Immovable, well-established' means having well-established roots, it is immovable and unshakeable by ordinary winds. 'So, with the destruction of delusion, a bhikkhu, like a mountain, does not tremble' means that because of the remainderless abandoning of delusion, and because delusion is the root of all unwholesome states, a bhikkhu who has abandoned all unwholesome states does not tremble or waver in the face of worldly conditions, just as that mountain does not by ordinary winds. Or, since 'destruction of delusion' is a name for Nibbāna and Arahantship, therefore, because of having attained Nibbāna or Arahantship—the cause for the destruction of delusion—he is well-established in the four noble truths. Even when not in a state of attainment, he is not shaken by anything, just like the aforementioned mountain; how much more so when in a state of attainment. This is the intention.

Catutthasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Fourth Sutta is concluded.

5. Mahāmoggallānasuttavaṇṇanā

5. The Exposition of the Mahāmoggallāna Sutta

25. Pañcame kāyagatāya satiyāti kāyānupassanāvasena kāye gatāya kāyārammaṇāya satiyā, itthambhūtalakkhaṇe idaṃ karaṇavacanaṃ[M 0.0171]. Ajjhattanti idha ajjhattaṃ nāma niyakajjhattaṃ, tasmā attani attasantāneti attho. Atha vā yasmā kammaṭṭhānabhūto kesādiko dvattiṃsakoṭṭhāsasamudāyo idha kāyoti adhippeto, tasmā ajjhattanti padassa gocarajjhattanti [P 0.0190] attho veditabbo. Sūpaṭṭhitāyāti niyakajjhattabhūte gocarajjhattabhūte vā kāye suṭṭhu upaṭṭhitāya. Kā panāyaṃ sati, yā “ajjhattaṃ sūpaṭṭhitā”ti vuttā? Yvāyaṃ bhagavatā “atthi imasmiṃ kāye kesā lomā”tiādinā (dī. ni. 2.377; ma. ni. 1.110; khu. pā. 3.dvattiṃsākāra) ajjhattakesādiko dvattiṃsākāro kāyo vutto, tattha yā paṭikūlamanasikāraṃ pavattentassa upacārappanāvasena kāye upaṭṭhitā sati, sā “kāyagatā satī”ti vuccati. Yathā cāyaṃ, evaṃ ānāpānacatuiriyāpathasatisampajaññānaṃ vasena uddhumātakavinīlakādivasena ca manasikāraṃ pavattentassa yathārahaṃ upacārappanāvasena kāye upaṭṭhitā sati “kāyagatā satī”ti vuccati. Idha pana ajjhattaṃ kāyagatā sati pathavīādikā catasso dhātuyo sasambhārasaṅkhepādīsu catūsu yena kenaci ekenākārena vavatthapetvā tesaṃ aniccādilakkhaṇasallakkhaṇavasena upaṭṭhitā vipassanāsampayuttā sati “kāyagatā satī”ti adhippetā. Thero pana tathā vipassitvā attano phalasamāpattimeva samāpajjitvā nisīdi. Idhāpi gāthāya evaṃ imassa atthassa viññātabbatā “na cāyaṃ nisajjā”tiādinā vuttanayānusārena yojetabbā.

25. In the fifth, 'by mindfulness directed to the body' means by mindfulness that, in the manner of contemplation of the body, has gone to the body and has the body as its object; this is an instrumental case in the sense of indicating a state. 'Internally': here, 'internal' means one's own internal; therefore, the meaning is 'within oneself, within one's own continuum.' Alternatively, since the collection of the thirty-two parts beginning with head-hairs, which is the meditation subject, is here intended as 'the body,' the meaning of the word 'internally' should be understood as 'internal to the domain.' 'Well-established' means well-established in the body that is either one's own internal or internal to the domain. But what is this mindfulness that is said to be 'well-established internally'? The Blessed One has spoken of the body as the thirty-two internal parts beginning with head-hairs, with the words, "There are in this body head-hairs, body-hairs," etc. (Dī. Ni. 2.377; Ma. Ni. 1.110; Khu. Pā. 3.dvattiṃsākāra). In that context, the mindfulness that is established in the body by way of access and absorption for one who cultivates attention to the repulsive is called 'mindfulness directed to the body.' Just as this is, so too, for one who cultivates attention by way of mindfulness of breathing, the four postures, and clear comprehension, or by way of the bloated, the discolored, etc., the mindfulness established in the body by way of access and absorption, as is appropriate, is called 'mindfulness directed to the body.' Here, however, 'mindfulness directed to the body internally' is intended to mean the insight-associated mindfulness that is established by discerning the four elements—earth, etc.—according to any one of the four methods, such as with their components or in brief, and by noting their characteristics of impermanence and so on. The elder, having practiced insight in that way, entered upon his own fruition attainment and sat down. Here too, that this is the meaning should be connected with the verse according to the method stated with the words, "And this sitting was not..." and so on.

Etamatthanti etaṃ therassa catudhātuvavatthānamukhena kāyānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānena vipassanaṃ ogāhetvā phalasamāpattisamāpajjanasaṅkhātaṃ atthaṃ viditvā. Imaṃ udānanti imaṃ satipaṭṭhānabhāvanāya nibbānādhigamadīpakaṃ udānaṃ udānesi.

"Knowing this meaning" means: knowing this meaning, namely, the elder's entering upon fruition attainment, accomplished by plunging into insight through the foundation of mindfulness of contemplation of the body, by way of discerning the four elements. "This inspired utterance" means: he uttered this inspired utterance, which illuminates the attainment of Nibbāna through the development of the foundations of mindfulness.

Tattha [V 0.0154] sati kāyagatā upaṭṭhitāti pubbe vuttalakkhaṇā sati saddhāpubbaṅgamānaṃ samādhivīriyapaññānaṃ yathāsakaṃ kiccanipphādanena sahāyabhāvaṃ āpannattā pahīnappaṭipakkhā tato eva tikkhavisadabhūtā ca yathāvuttakāyasaṃvaraṇavasena ekatthasamosaraṇavasena ca aviparītasabhāvaṃ sallakkhentī upagantvā ṭhitā hoti, etena kāyasaṅkhātānaṃ catunnaṃ dhātūnaṃ tannissitānañca upādārūpānaṃ sallakkhaṇavasena, paccaye vavatthapetvā tato paraṃ tesaṃ aniccādilakkhaṇasallakkhaṇavasena [P 0.0191] ca pavattaṃ ñāṇaparamparāgataṃ [M 0.0172] satiṃ dasseti, satisīsena vā taṃsampayuttaṃ pariññāttayapariyāpannañāṇaparamparameva dasseti. Chasu phassāyatanesu saṃvutoti yathāvuttāya kāye upaṭṭhitāya satiyā samannāgato cakkhādīsu phassassa kāraṇabhūtesu chasu dvāresu kāyānupassanāya abhāvitāya uppajjanārahānaṃ abhijjhādīnaṃ tassā bhāvitattā ñāṇappavattiṃ paṭivedhento te pidahanto “tattha saṃvuto”ti vuccati, etena ñāṇasaṃvaraṃ dasseti.

Therein, 'mindfulness directed to the body is established' means that mindfulness, having the characteristics stated before, having become an assistant to concentration, energy, and wisdom—which are preceded by faith—in accomplishing their respective tasks, has abandoned opposing factors and thus become sharp and clear. Perceiving the undistorted nature by way of restraining the body as described and by way of converging into a single object, it approaches and is established. By this is shown mindfulness that has come from a succession of knowledge, which occurs by way of observing the four elements designated as the body and the derived material forms dependent on them, by way of determining their conditions, and thereafter by way of observing their characteristics of impermanence, etc. Or, with mindfulness as the head, it shows just the succession of knowledge associated with it, which is included in the three kinds of full understanding. 'Restrained in the six sense bases' means that a bhikkhu endowed with mindfulness established in the body as described is called 'restrained therein'; for, in the six doors—the eye, etc., which are the causes of contact—because that contemplation of the body has been developed, he penetrates the occurrence of knowledge and closes off covetousness and the like, which would be liable to arise if it were undeveloped. By this is shown restraint by knowledge.

Satataṃ bhikkhu samāhitoti so bhikkhu evaṃ upaṭṭhitassati sabbattha ca saṃvuto puthuttārammaṇe cittaṃ avissajjetvā aniccādivasena sammasanto vipassanaṃ ussukkāpetvā ñāṇe tikkhe sūre vahante vipassanāsamādhinā tāva satataṃ nirantaraṃ samāhito anulomañāṇānantaraṃ gotrabhuñāṇodayato paṭṭhāya. Jaññā nibbānamattanoti aññesaṃ puthujjanānaṃ supinantepi agocarabhāvato, ariyānaṃ pana tassa tasseva āveṇikattā attasadisattā ca “attā”ti laddhavohārassa maggaphalañāṇassa sātisayavisayabhāvato ekantasukhāvahaṃ nibbānaṃ asaṅkhatadhātu “attano”ti vuttaṃ, taṃ nibbānaṃ jaññā jāneyya, maggaphalañāṇehi paṭivijjheyya, sacchikareyyāti attho. Etena ariyānaṃ nibbāne adhimuttataṃ dasseti. Ariyā hi adhicittappavattikālepi ekanteneva nibbāne ninnapoṇapabbhārabhāvena viharanti. Ettha ca yassa sati kāyagatā upaṭṭhitā, so bhikkhu chasu phassāyatanesu saṃvuto, tato eva satataṃ samāhito attapaccakkhakaraṇena nibbānaṃ attano jāneyyāti evaṃ gāthāpadānaṃ sambandho veditabbo. Evaṃ kāyānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānamukhena yāva arahattā ekassa bhikkhuno niyyānamaggaṃ dasseti dhammarājā.

'The bhikkhu is always concentrated' means that such a bhikkhu, with mindfulness thus established and restrained in all respects, not releasing his mind to diverse objects, contemplating by way of impermanence and so forth, having instigated insight, when knowledge becomes sharp and valiant, is continuously and uninterruptedly concentrated by means of insight-concentration, beginning from the arising of change-of-lineage knowledge, which immediately follows conformity knowledge. 'He should know Nibbāna for himself.' For worldlings, Nibbāna is not an object even in a dream; but for the noble ones, because it is unique to each of them and is like oneself, and because it is the supreme object of the path and fruition knowledge (which has received the designation 'self'), Nibbāna—the unconditioned element that brings certain happiness—is said to be 'one's own.' He should know that Nibbāna, should penetrate it with the path and fruition knowledges, and should realize it. This shows the noble ones' inclination toward Nibbāna. For noble ones, even when the higher mind is occurring, dwell with a state of being entirely inclined, sloping, and tending towards Nibbāna. And here, the connection of the verse-quarters should be understood thus: 'The bhikkhu for whom mindfulness directed to the body is established is restrained in the six sense bases; for that very reason, being always concentrated, he should know Nibbāna for himself by direct realization.' Thus, through the entrance of the foundation of mindfulness of contemplation of the body, the King of Dhamma shows the path of release for a bhikkhu up to Arahantship.

Aparo nayo – sati kāyagatā upaṭṭhitāti etena kāyānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānaṃ dasseti. Chasu phassāyatanesu saṃvutoti phasso āyatanaṃ kāraṇaṃ etesanti phassāyatanāni, tesu phassāyatanesu. Phassahetukesu phassapaccayā nibbattesu [P 0.0192] chasu cakkhusamphassajādivedayitesu taṇhādīnaṃ appavattiyā saṃvuto, etena vedanānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānaṃ [M 0.0173] dasseti. Satataṃ bhikkhu samāhitoti satataṃ niccakālaṃ nirantaraṃ vikkhepābhāvato samāhito bhikkhu. So cāyaṃ avikkhepo [V 0.0155] sabbaso satipaṭṭhānabhāvanāya matthakappattāya hoti. Sammasanto hi atītādibhedabhinnesu pañcupādānakkhandhesu anavasesatova pariggahetvā sammasatīti. Etena sesasatipaṭṭhāne dasseti. Jaññā nibbānamattanoti evaṃ catusatipaṭṭhānabhāvanaṃ matthakaṃ pāpetvā ṭhito bhinnakileso bhikkhu attano kilesanibbānaṃ paccavekkhaṇañāṇena sayameva jāneyyāti attho.

Another method: By 'mindfulness directed to the body is established' is shown the foundation of mindfulness of contemplation of the body. By 'restrained in the six sense bases of contact': 'sense bases of contact' (phassāyatanāni) are so called because contact (phasso) is their basis (āyatanaṃ) and cause (kāraṇaṃ). In those sense bases of contact—that is, in the six feelings born of eye-contact and so on, which are caused by contact and produced from contact as a condition—he is restrained through the non-occurrence of craving and the like. By this is shown the foundation of mindfulness of contemplation of feelings. 'The bhikkhu is always concentrated' means the bhikkhu is concentrated always, constantly, and uninterruptedly, due to the absence of distraction. And this non-distraction occurs when the development of the foundations of mindfulness has, in every way, reached its culmination. For one who contemplates does so by grasping the five aggregates of clinging, divided into past, etc., without remainder, and contemplating them. By this are shown the remaining foundations of mindfulness. 'He should know Nibbāna for himself' means that a bhikkhu who stands having brought the development of the four foundations of mindfulness to its culmination, with his defilements destroyed, should know for himself, with the knowledge of reviewing, the Nibbāna of his own defilements.

Atha vā sati kāyagatā upaṭṭhitāti attano paresañca kāyassa yathāsabhāvapariññādīpanena therassa sativepullappatti dīpitā. Chasu phassāyatanesu saṃvutoti cakkhādīsu chasu dvāresu accantasaṃvaradīpanena satatavihārivasena therassa sampajaññappakāsinī paññāvepullappatti dīpitā. Satataṃ bhikkhu samāhitoti samāpattibahulatādassanena navānupubbavihārasamāpattiyo dassitā. Evaṃbhūto pana bhikkhu jaññā nibbānamattanoti katakiccattā uttari karaṇīyābhāvato kevalaṃ attano anupādisesanibbānameva jāneyya cinteyya, aññampi tassa cintetabbaṃ natthīti adhippāyo.

Or alternatively: by 'mindfulness directed to the body is established', through showing the full understanding of the true nature of one's own and others' bodies, the elder's attainment of an abundance of mindfulness is shown. By 'restrained in the six sense bases', through showing complete restraint in the six doors, such as the eye, and by way of constant abiding, the elder's attainment of an abundance of wisdom that illuminates clear comprehension is shown. By 'The bhikkhu is always concentrated', through showing an abundance of attainments, the nine successive abiding attainments are shown. As for such a bhikkhu, 'he should know Nibbāna for himself' means that because his task is done and there is nothing further to be done, he should know and contemplate only his own Nibbāna-element without residue remaining. There is nothing else for him to contemplate—this is the intention.

Pañcamasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the fifth sutta is finished.

6. Pilindavacchasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Pilindavaccha Sutta.

26. Chaṭṭhe pilindavacchoti pilindātissa nāmaṃ, vacchoti gottavasena theraṃ sañjānanti. Vasalavādena samudācaratīti “ehi, vasala, apehi, vasalā”tiādinā bhikkhū vasalavādena voharati ālapati. Sambahulā bhikkhūti bahū bhikkhū. Te theraṃ tathā samudācarantaṃ disvā “arahāva samāno appahīnavāsanattā [P 0.0193] evaṃ bhaṇatī”ti ajānantā “dosantaro maññe ayaṃ thero evaṃ samudācaratī”ti cintetvā ullapanādhippāyā taṃ tato vuṭṭhāpetuṃ bhagavato ārocesuṃ. Tena [M 0.0174] vuttaṃ – “āyasmā, bhante, pilindavaccho bhikkhū vasalavādena samudācaratī”ti. Keci panāhu – “imaṃ theraṃ bhikkhū ‘arahā’ti sañjānanti, ayañca bhikkhū pharusavacanena evaṃ samudācarati, ‘abhūto eva nu kho imasmiṃ uttarimanussadhammo’ti vāsanāvasena tassa tathā samudācāraṃ ajānantā ariyabhāvañcassa asaddahantā ujjhānasaññino bhagavato tamatthaṃ ārocesu”nti. Bhagavā therassa dosantarābhāvaṃ pakāsetukāmo ekena bhikkhunā taṃ pakkosāpetvā sammukhā tassa “pubbāciṇṇavasenāyaṃ tathā samudācarati, na pharusavacanādhippāyo”ti [V 0.0156] āha. Tena vuttaṃ – “atha kho bhagavā aññataraṃ bhikkhuṃ āmantesī”tiādi.

26. In the sixth discourse: Regarding Pilindavaccha, Pilinda was his name; they recognized the elder as Vaccha on account of his clan. 'He addressed them with the term ‘outcast’' means he would address and speak to the monks with the term ‘outcast,’ saying such things as, “Come, outcast,” and “Go away, outcast.” 'Many monks' means numerous monks. Seeing the elder addressing them in this way, and not knowing that “though he is an Arahant, he speaks thus because his latent tendencies have not been abandoned,” they thought, “I suppose this elder has some inner corruption, addressing others in this way.” With the intention of complaining and to make him cease from that behavior, they reported it to the Blessed One. Therefore it was said: “Venerable sir, the venerable Pilindavaccha addresses the monks with the term ‘outcast.’” Some, however, say: “The monks recognize this elder as an Arahant, yet this monk addresses them with such harsh speech. They wondered, ‘Could it be that the superhuman state in him is indeed non-existent?’ Not knowing that his addressing them in such a way was due to the force of latent tendencies, and not believing in his noble state, they, being disposed to censure, reported the matter to the Blessed One.” The Blessed One, wishing to make clear that the elder had no inner corruption, had him summoned by a certain monk and, in his presence, explained: “He addresses others in this way due to the force of past habit, not from an intention to use harsh speech.” Therefore it was said: “Then the Blessed One addressed a certain monk…” and so on.

Tattha pubbenivāsaṃ manasi karitvāti satthā “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ, vaccha, bhikkhū vasalavādena samudācarasī”ti theraṃ pucchitvā tena “evaṃ, bhante”ti vutte “ayaṃ vaccho kilesavāsanāya vasalavādaṃ na pariccajati, kiṃ nu kho atītesupi attabhāvesu brāhmaṇajātiko ahosī”ti āvajjento pubbenivāsañāṇena sabbaññutaññāṇena vā tassa pubbenivāsaṃ atītāsu jātīsu nivutthakkhandhasantānaṃ manasi karitvā hatthatale ṭhapitaṃ āmalakaṃ viya paccakkhakaraṇavasena attano manasi katvā. Bhikkhū āmantesīti te bhikkhū saññāpetuṃ ālapi, abhāsi. Tena vuttaṃ “mā kho tumhe, bhikkhave”tiādi.

Therein, 'having brought to mind past abodes' means: the Teacher asked the elder, “Is it true, Vaccha, that you address the monks with the term ‘outcast’?” When he replied, “It is so, venerable sir,” the Teacher reflected, “This Vaccha does not abandon the term ‘outcast’ because of the latent tendency of defilements. Could it be that in past existences he was of brahmin birth?” Reflecting thus, with the knowledge of past abodes or with the knowledge of omniscience itself, he brought to mind that elder’s past abodes—the continuum of aggregates he had dwelt in during past lives—making it directly perceptible in his own mind, like a myrobalan fruit placed on the palm of the hand. 'He addressed the monks' means he addressed and spoke to those monks in order to make them understand. Therefore it was said: “Do not, monks…” and so on.

Tattha māti paṭisedhe nipāto, tassa “ujjhāyitthā”ti iminā sambandho. Mā ujjhāyitthāti mā heṭṭhā katvā cintayittha, olokayitthāti attho. Vacchassa bhikkhunoti ca ujjhāyanassa usūyanatthattā sampadānavacanaṃ. Idānissa anujjhāyitabbe kāraṇaṃ dassento “na, bhikkhave, vaccho dosantaro bhikkhū vasalavādena samudācaratī”ti āha. Tassattho – bhikkhave, ayaṃ vaccho dosantaro dosacitto dosena byāpādena dūsitacitto hutvā bhikkhū vasalavādena na samudācarati[P 0.0194], maggeneva cassa byāpādo samugghātito. Evaṃ adosantarattepi tassa tathā samudācārassa purimajātisiddhaṃ kāraṇaṃ dassento “vacchassa, bhikkhave”tiādimāha.

Therein, 'mā' is a particle of prohibition; its connection is with 'ujjhāyittha'. 'Mā ujjhāyittha' means: do not think contemptuously, do not look down upon; this is the meaning. And in 'vacchassa bhikkhuno', because the act of censuring implies envy, the dative case is used. Now, showing the reason why he should not be censured, he said: “Monks, Vaccha does not address the monks with the term ‘outcast’ out of inner corruption.” The meaning of this is: Monks, this Vaccha does not address the monks with the term ‘outcast’ while having a mind with inner corruption, a mind defiled by anger and ill will; for his ill will has been completely uprooted by the path. Thus, even though he is without inner corruption, showing the cause for his addressing them in such a way, a cause established in a former birth, he said: “Monks, for Vaccha…” and so on.

Tattha abbokiṇṇānīti khattiyādijātiantarehi avomissāni anantaritāni. Pañca jātisatāni brāhmaṇakule paccājātānīti sabbāni tāni vacchassa pañca jātisatāni paṭipāṭiyā brāhmaṇakule eva jātāni, ahesunti [M 0.0175] attho. So tassa vasalavādo dīgharattaṃ samudāciṇṇoti yo etarahi khīṇāsavenapi satā pavattiyati, so tassa vacchassa bhikkhuno vasalavādo dīgharattaṃ ito jātito paṭṭhāya uddhaṃ ārohanavasena pañcajātisatamattaṃ kālaṃ brāhmaṇajātikattā samudāciṇṇo samudācarito ahosi. Brāhmaṇā hi jātisiddhena mānena thaddhā aññaṃ vasalavādena samudācaranti. “Ajjhāciṇṇo”tipi paṭhanti, so eva attho. Tenāti tena dīgharattaṃ tathā samudāciṇṇabhāvena, etenassa tathā samudācārassa kāraṇaṃ vāsanāti dasseti. Kā panāyaṃ vāsanā nāma? Yaṃ kilesarahitassāpi santāne appahīnakilesānaṃ samācārasadisasamācārahetubhūtaṃ, anādikālabhāvitehi kilesehi āhitaṃ sāmatthiyamattaṃ, tathārūpā adhimuttīti vadanti. Taṃ panetaṃ abhinīhārasampattiyā ñeyyāvaraṇappahānavasena yattha kilesā [V 0.0157] pahīnā, tattha bhagavato santāne natthi. Yattha pana tathā kilesā na pahīnā, tattha sāvakānaṃ paccekabuddhānañca santāne atthi, tato tathāgatova anāvaraṇañāṇadassano.

Therein, 'unbroken' means unmixed with other castes such as the Khattiya caste; uninterrupted. 'Five hundred births he was reborn in a brahmin family' means all those five hundred births of Vaccha occurred in succession in a brahmin family alone; this is the meaning. 'That term ‘outcast’ of his was long practiced' means: that term ‘outcast’ of that monk Vaccha, which continues to occur even now when he is one whose cankers are destroyed, was habitually practiced for a long time—for a period of five hundred births, counting upwards from this birth—because he was of brahmin birth. For brahmins, stiff with pride established by birth, address others with the term ‘outcast.’ Some also read 'ajjhāciṇṇo' (habitually practiced); the meaning is the same. 'By that' means: by that fact of it having been so practiced for a long time. By this, he shows that the cause of his addressing them in such a way is a latent tendency (vāsanā). What, then, is this so-called latent tendency? It is a mere capacity, established by defilements cultivated since beginningless time, which exists even in the mental continuum of one free from defilements and is the cause of conduct similar to the conduct of those with unabandoned defilements. Such a thing they call a strong inclination (adhimutti). This latent tendency, however, does not exist in the mental continuum of the Blessed One, in whom the defilements have been abandoned through the fulfillment of his aspiration and by means of abandoning the obstruction to knowledge. But it does exist in the mental continuum of disciples and Paccekabuddhas, in whom the defilements have not been abandoned in that way. Therefore, only the Tathāgata possesses unobstructed knowledge and vision.

Etamatthaṃ viditvāti etaṃ āyasmato pilindavacchassa satipi vasalasamudācāre dosantarābhāvasaṅkhātaṃ atthaṃ viditvā. Imaṃ udānanti tassa aggaphalādhigamavibhāvanaṃ imaṃ udānaṃ udānesi.

'Having known this matter' means: having known this matter concerning the venerable Pilindavaccha, designated as the absence of inner corruption even while his addressing with the term ‘outcast’ occurred. 'This inspired utterance' means: he uttered this inspired utterance, which makes plain his attainment of the highest fruit.

Tattha yamhi na māyā vasati na mānoti yasmiṃ ariyapuggale santadosappaṭicchādanalakkhaṇā māyā, “seyyohamasmī”tiādinā sampaggahavasena pavatto uṇṇatilakkhaṇo māno ca na vasati, maggena samugghātitattā na [P 0.0195] pavattati na uppajjati. Yo vītalobho amamo nirāsoti yo ca rāgādipariyāyavasena pavattassa ārammaṇaggahaṇalakkhaṇassa lobhassa sabbathā vigatattā vītalobho, tato eva rūpādīsu katthaci mamāyanābhāvato amamo apariggaho, anāgatānampi bhavādīnaṃ anāsīsanato nirāso. Panuṇṇakodhoti kujjhanalakkhaṇassa kodhassa anāgāmimaggena sabbaso pahīnattā panuṇṇakodho samucchinnāghāto. Abhinibbutattoti yo evaṃ māyāmānalobhakodhānaṃ samugghātena tadekaṭṭhatāya sabbassa saṃkilesapakkhassa suppahīnattā sabbaso kilesaparinibbānena abhinibbutacitto sītibhūto. So brāhmaṇo [M 0.0176] so samaṇo sa bhikkhūti so evarūpo khīṇāsavo sabbaso bāhitapāpattā brāhmaṇo, so eva samitapāpattā samacariyāya ca samaṇo, so eva ca sabbaso bhinnakilesattā bhikkhu nāma. Evaṃbhūto ca, bhikkhave, vaccho so kathaṃ dosantaro kiñci kāyakammādiṃ pavatteyya, kevalaṃ pana vāsanāya appahīnattā vasalavādena samudācaratīti.

In this context, in whom deceit does not dwell, nor conceit means: in that noble person, deceit characterized by concealing existing faults, and conceit, characterized by loftiness, which occurs by way of self-exaltation with such thoughts as “I am superior,” do not dwell; because they have been well uprooted by the path, they do not proceed or arise. He is free from greed, without possessiveness, without longing means: he who, because of being completely devoid of greed—which is characterized by grasping at objects and occurs by way of lust and the like—is free from greed; for that very reason, due to the absence of possessiveness towards forms and so forth anywhere, he is without ‘mine-making,’ without grasping; and due to not longing for future existences and so forth, he is without longing. With anger dispelled means: because anger, characterized by irritation, has been completely abandoned by the non-returner's path, he is one with anger dispelled, with hostility cut off. One who is completely cooled means: he who, in this way, through the uprooting of deceit, conceit, greed, and anger, and their being of a single nature, and because the entire faction of defilements has been well abandoned, is one with a mind completely cooled, become tranquil, through the final quenching of defilements. He is a brahmin, he is an ascetic, he is a monk means: such a one with cankers destroyed is a brahmin because he has entirely cast out evil; he himself is an ascetic because he has pacified evil and because of his tranquil conduct; and he himself is named a bhikkhu because he has entirely broken the defilements. And being such, O monks, how could that Vaccha, with a mind affected by hatred, engage in any bodily action or the like? However, merely because latent tendencies have not been abandoned, he addresses others with the term 'outcaste'.

Chaṭṭhasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the sixth discourse is finished.

7. Sakkudānasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Kassapa Sutta

27. Sattame sattāhaṃ ekapallaṅkena nisinno hoti aññataraṃ samādhiṃ samāpajjitvāti ettha keci tāva āhu “arahattaphalasamādhi idha ‘aññataro samādhī’ti adhippeto”ti. Tañhi so āyasmā [V 0.0158] bahulaṃ samāpajjati diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāratthaṃ, pahoti ca sattāhampi phalasamāpattiyā vītināmetuṃ. Tathā hi bhagavatā –

27. In the seventh sutta: he sat for seven days in one cross-legged posture, having attained a certain concentration. Here, some say: “The concentration of the fruit of arahantship is intended here by ‘a certain concentration.’” For that venerable one frequently enters it for the sake of a pleasant abiding in the here and now, and he is able to spend even seven days in the attainment of fruition. For thus it was said by the Blessed One:

“Ahaṃ, bhikkhave, yāvade ākaṅkhāmi vivicceva kāmehi, vivicca akusalehi dhammehi…pe… viharāmi. Kassapopi, bhikkhave, yāvade ākaṅkhati vivicceva kāmehi…pe… viharatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.152) –

“Monks, for as long as I wish, I dwell secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome qualities… and so on… I dwell. Kassapa, too, monks, for as long as he wishes, dwells secluded from sensual pleasures… and so on… he dwells.” (SN 16.5)

Ādinā navānupubbavihārachaḷabhiññādibhede [P 0.0196] uttarimanussadhamme attanā samasamaṭṭhāne ṭhapito, na cettha “yadi evaṃ thero yamakapāṭihāriyampi kareyyā”ti vattabbaṃ sāvakasādhāraṇānaṃyeva jhānādīnaṃ adhippetattāti.

By this and so on, he was placed on an equal footing with himself in regard to the superhuman states, with their divisions of the nine successive abidings, the six supernormal knowledges, and so forth. And here, it should not be said, “If so, the elder would also perform the twin miracle,” because only the jhānas and so forth, which are common to disciples, are intended.

Porāṇā panāhu – aññataraṃ samādhiṃ samāpajjitvāti nirodhasamāpattiṃ samāpajjitvā. Kathaṃ pana nirodhasamāpatti samādhīti vuttā? Samādhānaṭṭhena. Ko panāyaṃ samādhānaṭṭho? Sammadeva ādhātabbatā. Yā hi esā paccanīkadhammehi akampanīyā balappattiyā samathabalaṃ vipassanābalanti imehi dvīhi balehi, aniccadukkhānattanibbidāvirāganirodhapaṭinissaggavivaṭṭānupassanā cattāri maggañāṇāni cattāri ca phalañāṇānīti imesaṃ [M 0.0177] soḷasannaṃ ñāṇānaṃ vasena soḷasahi ñāṇacariyāhi, paṭhamajjhānasamādhiādayo aṭṭha samādhī ekajjhaṃ katvā gahito tesaṃ upacārasamādhi cāti imesaṃ navannaṃ samādhīnaṃ vasena navahi samādhicariyāhi kāyasaṅkhāro vacīsaṅkhāro cittasaṅkhāroti imesaṃ tiṇṇaṃ saṅkhārānaṃ tattha tattha paṭippassaddhiyā tathā viharitukāmena yathāvuttesu ṭhānesu vasībhāvappattena arahatā anāgāminā vā yathādhippetaṃ kālaṃ cittacetasikasantānassa sammadeva appavatti ādhātabbā, tassā tathā samādhātabbatā idha samādhānaṭṭho, tenāyaṃ vihāro samādhīti vutto, na avikkhepaṭṭhena. Etenassa samāpattiatthopi vuttoti veditabbo. Imañhi nirodhasamāpattiṃ sandhāya paṭisambhidāmagge –

The ancients, however, say that having entered a certain concentration means having entered the attainment of cessation. But how is the attainment of cessation called 'concentration'? By the meaning of 'composing' (samādhāna). And what is this meaning of 'composing'? It is the state of being rightly established. For this attainment is unshaken by opposing states, owing to the strength attained by the power of serenity and the power of insight—these two powers; and by means of the sixteen knowledges (namely, the contemplations of impermanence, suffering, non-self, disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, relinquishment, and turning away, plus the four path knowledges and the four fruition knowledges), through the sixteen courses of knowledge; and by means of the nine concentrations (namely, the eight concentrations beginning with the first jhāna concentration, together with their access concentration), through the nine courses of concentration; and through the pacification of the three formations (bodily formation, verbal formation, and mental formation) here and there. For an arahant or a non-returner, desiring to dwell thus, having attained mastery in the aforementioned states, the non-occurrence of the continuum of consciousness and mental factors must be rightly established for the desired time. This state of being thus established is here the meaning of 'composing'; therefore, this abiding is called 'concentration,' not in the sense of non-distraction. By this, it should be understood that the meaning of 'attainment' is also stated. For in the Paṭisambhidāmagga, referring to this attainment of cessation, it is said:

“Kathaṃ dvīhi balehi samannāgatattā tiṇṇaṃ saṅkhārānaṃ paṭippassaddhiyā soḷasahi ñāṇacariyāhi navahi samādhicariyāhi vasībhāvatāya saññānirodhasamāpattiyā ñāṇa”nti (paṭi. ma. 1.83) –

“How, due to being endowed with two powers, by the pacification of the three formations, by the sixteen courses of knowledge, by the nine courses of concentration, and by means of mastery, is there knowledge of the attainment of the cessation of perception?” (Paṭis I 99)

Pucchitvā “dvīhi balehī”ti dve balāni samathabalaṃ vipassanābalanti vitthāro. Sāyaṃ nirodhasamāpattikathā visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 2.867 ādayo) saṃvaṇṇitāva. Kasmā panāyaṃ thero [V 0.0159] phalasamāpattiṃ asamāpajjitvā nirodhaṃ samāpajji? Sattesu anukampāya. Ayañhi mahāthero sabbāpi samāpattiyo vaḷañjeti, sattānuggahena pana [P 0.0197] yebhuyyena nirodhaṃ samāpajjati. Tañhi samāpajjitvā vuṭṭhitassa kato appakopi sakkāro visesato mahapphalo mahānisaṃso hotīti.

Having asked, the detailed explanation of “with two powers” is that the two powers are the power of serenity and the power of insight. This discourse on the attainment of cessation is indeed explained in the Visuddhimagga. But why did this elder enter cessation without entering the attainment of fruition? Out of compassion for beings. For this great elder makes use of all attainments, but for the benefit of beings, he mostly enters cessation. For even a small offering made to one who has arisen after attaining that is especially of great fruit, of great benefit.

Vuṭṭhāsīti arahattaphalacittuppattiyā vuṭṭhāsi. Nirodhaṃ samāpanno hi arahā ce arahattaphalassa, anāgāmī ce anāgāmiphalassa uppādena vuṭṭhito nāma hoti.

‘He emerged’ means he emerged by the arising of the arahant-fruition-consciousness. For one who has entered cessation is said to have emerged by the arising of the fruition of arahantship if he is an arahant, or by the arising of the fruition of non-returning if he is a non-returner.

Tena kho pana samayena sakko devānamindo āyasmato mahākassapassa piṇḍapātaṃ dātukāmo hotīti kathaṃ tassa dātukāmatā jātā? Yāni “tāni pañcamattāni devatāsatānī”ti vuttāni, tā sakkassa devarañño paricārikā kakuṭapādiniyo pubbe “ayyo mahākassapo rājagahaṃ piṇḍāya pavisati, gacchatha therassa dānaṃ dethā”ti sakkena pesitā upagantvā dibbāhāraṃ dātukāmā ṭhitā therena [M 0.0178] paṭikkhittā devalokameva gatā. Idāni purimappaṭikkhepaṃ cintetvā “kadāci gaṇheyyā”ti samāpattito vuṭṭhitassa therassa dānaṃ dātukāmā sakkassa anārocetvā sayameva āgantvā dibbabhojanāni upanentiyo purimanayeneva therena paṭikkhittā devalokaṃ gantvā sakkena “kahaṃ gatatthā”ti puṭṭhā tamatthaṃ ārocetvā “dinno vo therassa piṇḍapāto”ti sakkena vutte “gaṇhituṃ na icchatī”ti. “Kiṃ kathesī”ti? “‘Duggatānaṃ saṅgahaṃ karissāmī’ti āha, devā”ti. “Tumhe kenākārena gatā”ti? “Imināva, devā”ti. Sakko “tumhādisiyo therassa piṇḍapātaṃ kiṃ dassantī”ti? Sayaṃ dātukāmo, jarājiṇṇo khaṇḍadanto palitakeso obhaggasarīro mahallako tantavāyo hutvā, sujampi asuradhītaraṃ tathārūpimeva mahallikaṃ katvā, ekaṃ pesakāravīthiṃ māpetvā tantaṃ pasārento acchi, sujā tasaraṃ pūreti. Tena vuttaṃ – “tena kho pana samayena sakko devānamindo…pe… tasaraṃ pūretī”ti.

At that time, Sakka, lord of the devas, wished to offer almsfood to the Venerable Mahākassapa. How did this wish arise in him? Those who were spoken of as 'the five hundred devatās' were the attendants of Sakka, king of the devas, known as the Kakuṭapādiniyo. Previously, having been sent by Sakka with the instruction, 'The venerable Mahākassapa is entering Rājagaha for alms; go and give an offering to the elder,' they approached, wishing to give divine food. But they were refused by the elder and returned to the deva world. Now, reflecting on the previous refusal, they thought, 'Perhaps he might accept this time.' When the elder had arisen from meditative attainment, they, wishing to give an offering, came on their own accord without informing Sakka, bringing divine foods. But, being refused by the elder in the same way as before, they went to the deva world. When asked by Sakka, 'Where have you been?' they related the matter. When Sakka said, 'Have you given almsfood to the elder?' they replied, 'He does not wish to accept it.' 'What did he say?' 'He said, "I will render assistance to the destitute," O deva.' 'In what form did you go?' 'In this very form, O deva.' Sakka thought, 'How could beings such as you give almsfood to the elder?' Wishing to give it himself, he took the form of a very old weaver, decrepit, with broken teeth, gray hair, and a stooped body. He also transformed Sujā, daughter of the asuras, into a similarly old woman, conjured a weavers' lane, and sat stretching out the warp, while Sujā filled the shuttle. Therefore it is said: 'At that time, Sakka, lord of the devas… filled the shuttle.'

Tattha tantaṃ vinātīti pasāritatantaṃ vinanto viya hoti. Tasaraṃ pūretīti tasaravaṭṭiṃ vaḍḍhentī viya. Yena sakkassa devānamindassa nivesanaṃ tenupasaṅkamīti thero nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya “duggatajanasaṅgahaṃ karissāmī”ti nagarābhimukho gacchanto [P 0.0198] bahinagare sakkena māpitaṃ pesakāravīthiṃ paṭipajjitvā olokento addasa oluggaviluggajiṇṇasālaṃ tattha ca te jāyampatike yathāvuttarūpe tantavāyakammaṃ karonte disvā cintesi – “ime mahallakakālepi kammaṃ karonti. Imasmiṃ nagare imehi duggatatarā natthi maññe. Imehi dinnaṃ sākamattampi [V 0.0160] gahetvā imesaṃ saṅgahaṃ karissāmī”ti. So tesaṃ gehābhimukho agamāsi. Sakko taṃ āgacchantaṃ disvā sujaṃ āha – “bhadde, mayhaṃ ayyo ito āgacchati, taṃ tvaṃ apassantī viya tuṇhī hutvā nisīda. Khaṇeneva vañcetvā piṇḍapātaṃ dassāmā”ti thero gantvā gehadvāre aṭṭhāsi. Tepi apassantā viya attano kammameva karontā thokaṃ āgamayiṃsu. Atha sakko “gehadvāre ṭhito eko thero viya khāyati, upadhārehi tāvā”ti āha. “Tumhe gantvā upadhāretha, sāmī”ti. So gehā nikkhamitvā theraṃ pañcapatiṭṭhitena vanditvā ubhohi hatthehi jaṇṇukāni olumbitvā nitthunanto uṭṭhāya “kataratthero nu kho ayyo”ti thokaṃ osakkitvā “akkhīni [M 0.0179] me dhūmāyantī”ti vatvā nalāṭe hatthaṃ ṭhapetvā uddhaṃ ulloketvā “aho dukkhaṃ ayyo no mahākassapattherova cirassaṃ me kuṭidvāraṃ āgato. Atthi nu kho kiñci gehe”ti āha. Sujā thokaṃ ākulā viya hutvā “atthi, sāmī”ti paṭivacanaṃ adāsi. Sakko, “bhante, lūkhaṃ vā paṇītaṃ vāti acintetvā saṅgahaṃ no karothā”ti pattaṃ gaṇhi.
