Thero pattaṃ dento “imesaṃ eva duggatānaṃ jarājiṇṇānaṃ mayā saṅgaho kātabbo”ti cintesi. So anto pavisitvā ghaṭiodanaṃ nāma ghaṭito uddharitvā, pattaṃ pūretvā, therassa hatthe ṭhapesi. Tena vuttaṃ – “addasā kho sakko devānamindo…pe… adāsī”ti.

Herein, 'he weaves the thread' means he is like one weaving a stretched thread. 'She fills the shuttle' means she is like one winding the shuttle's spool. The elder, having dressed and taken his bowl and robe, thought, 'I will render assistance to the poor,' and headed toward the city. Proceeding along the weavers' lane created by Sakka outside the city, he looked around and saw a dilapidated, ruined hall, and there he saw the husband and wife, in the form previously described, doing the work of weavers. He thought: 'These people work even in their old age. In this city, I think there are none poorer than they. I will accept even a mere vegetable leaf given by them and thus render them assistance.' So he went towards their house. Sakka, seeing him approaching, said to Sujā: 'My dear, my venerable one is coming this way. You, as if not seeing him, sit in silence. In a moment we shall trick him and give the almsfood.' The elder went and stood at the door of the house. They also, as if not seeing him, carried on with their work and delayed for a short while. Then Sakka said: 'It seems an elder is standing at the door of the house; go and see.' 'You go and see, master,' she said. So he went out of the house, venerated the elder with the five-point prostration, and leaning on his knees with both hands and groaning, he stood up. Drawing back a little, he said: 'Which venerable elder might this be?' Then, saying, 'My eyes are dim,' he placed his hand on his forehead, looked up, and said: 'Oh, what misery! It is our venerable Mahākassapa who has come to my hut after so long. Is there anything in the house?' Sujā, appearing slightly flustered, gave the reply: 'There is, master.' Sakka, saying, 'Venerable sir, without thinking whether it is coarse or fine, please render us assistance,' took the bowl. The elder, while giving the bowl, thought: 'Assistance must be rendered by me to these poor, decrepit old people.' Sakka went inside, and having taken out from the pot what is called 'pot-rice' (ghaṭiodana), he filled the bowl and placed it in the elder's hand. Therefore it is said: 'Sakka, lord of the devas, saw... he gave.'

Tattha ghaṭiyāti bhattaghaṭito. “Ghaṭiodana”ntipi pāṭho, tassa ghaṭiodanaṃ nāma devānaṃ koci āhāravisesoti atthaṃ vadanti. Uddharitvāti kutoci bhājanato uddharitvā. Anekasūpo [P 0.0199] so eva āhāro patte pakkhipitvā therassa hatthe ṭhapanakāle kapaṇānaṃ upakappanakalūkhāhāro viya paññāyittha, hatthe ṭhapitamatte pana attano dibbasabhāveneva aṭṭhāsi. Anekasūpoti muggamāsādisūpehi ceva khajjavikatīhi ca anekavidhasūpo. Anekabyañjanoti nānāvidhauttaribhaṅgo. Anekarasabyañjanoti anekehi sūpehi ceva byañjanehi ca madhurādimūlarasānañceva sambhinnarasānañca abhibyañjako, nānaggarasasūpabyañjanoti attho.

Herein, 'ghaṭiyā' means from a food pot. There is also the reading 'ghaṭiodana,' of which they state the meaning is 'a certain special food of the devas.' 'Uddharitvā' means having taken it out from some vessel. That very food, at the moment of being placed in the elder's hand after being put in the bowl, appeared like coarse food suitable for the destitute. But as soon as it was placed in his hand, it was established in its own divine nature. 'Anekasūpo' (with many soups) means having many kinds of soups, such as those made from green beans and black beans, and also various kinds of hard foods. 'Anekabyañjano' (with many curries) means having various kinds of side dishes. 'Anekarasabyañjano' (with many flavors and curries) means manifesting many soups and curries, and both primary flavors such as sweet, and blended flavors; the meaning is 'having soups and curries of various excellent flavors.'

So kira piṇḍapāto therassa hatthe ṭhapitakāle rājagahanagaraṃ attano dibbagandhena ajjhotthari, tato thero cintesi – “ayaṃ puriso appesakkho, piṇḍapāto ativiya paṇīto sakkassa bhojanasadiso. Ko nu kho eso”ti? Atha naṃ “sakko”ti ñatvā āha – “bhāriyaṃ te, kosiya, kammaṃ kataṃ duggatānaṃ sampattiṃ vilumpantena, ajja mayhaṃ dānaṃ datvā kocideva duggato senāpatiṭṭhānaṃ vā seṭṭhiṭṭhānaṃ vā labheyyā”ti. “Ko mayā duggatataro atthi, bhante”ti? “Kathaṃ tvaṃ duggato devarajjasiriṃ anubhavanto”ti? “Bhante, evaṃ nāmetaṃ, mayā [V 0.0161] pana anuppanne buddhe kalyāṇakammaṃ kataṃ, buddhuppāde pana vattamāne puññakammaṃ katvā cūḷarathadevaputto mahārathadevaputto anekavaṇṇadevaputtoti ime tayo devaputtā [M 0.0180] mamāsannaṭṭhāne nibbattā mahātejavantatarā. Ahaṃ tesu devaputtesu ‘nakkhattaṃ kīḷissāmā’ti paricārikāyo gahetvā antaravīthiṃ otiṇṇesu palāyitvā gehaṃ pavisāmi. Tesañhi sarīrato tejo mama sarīraṃ ottharati, mama sarīrato tejo tesaṃ sarīraṃ na ottharati. Ko mayā duggatataro, bhante”ti? “Evaṃ santepi ito paṭṭhāya mayhaṃ [P 0.0200] mā evaṃ vañcetvā dānamadāsī”ti. “Vañcetvā tumhākaṃ dāne dinne mayhaṃ kusalaṃ atthi natthī”ti? “Atthi, āvuso”ti. “Evaṃ sante kusalakaraṇaṃ nāma mayhaṃ bhāro, bhante”ti vatvā theraṃ vanditvā sujaṃ ādāya theraṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā, vehāsaṃ abbhuggantvā “aho dānaṃ paramadānaṃ, kassape suppatiṭṭhita”nti tikkhattuṃ udānaṃ udānesi. Tena vuttaṃ “atha kho āyasmato mahākassapassa etadahosī”tiādi.

It is said that when the almsfood was placed in the elder’s hand, the city of Rājagaha was pervaded by its divine fragrance. Then the elder thought: “This man is of little power, yet this almsfood is exceedingly excellent, like the food of Sakka. Who could this be?” Then, recognizing him as Sakka, he said: “A heavy deed you have done, Kosiya, by robbing the unfortunate of their prosperity. Today, having given alms to me, some unfortunate person might have gained the position of a general or a great merchant.” “Who is more unfortunate than I, venerable sir?” “How can you be unfortunate while enjoying the glory of the king of gods?” “Venerable sir, it is so. But I performed that wholesome deed when a Buddha had not arisen. Now that a Buddha has arisen, having performed meritorious deeds, these three devaputtas—Cūḷarathadevaputta, Mahārathadevaputta, and Anekavaṇṇadevaputta—have been reborn in my vicinity and are far more powerful. When those devaputtas, thinking, ‘Let us enjoy a festival,’ take their attendants and descend into the main street, I flee and enter my house. For the radiance from their bodies overwhelms my body, but the radiance from my body does not overwhelm theirs. Who is more unfortunate than I, venerable sir?” “Even so, from now on, do not give alms to me by deceiving in this way.” “When a gift is given to you by deception, is there merit for me or not?” “There is, friend.” “If that is so, venerable sir, the making of merit is my responsibility.” Having said this, he paid homage to the elder, took Sujā with him, circumambulated the elder, rose into the air, and three times uttered this inspired utterance: “Oh, the gift, the supreme gift, well-established in Kassapa!” Hence it is said: “Then it occurred to the Venerable Mahākassapa,” and so on.

Tattha kosiyāti sakkaṃ devānamindaṃ gottena ālapati. Puññena atthoti puññena payojanaṃ. Atthīti vacanaseso. Vehāsaṃ abbhuggantvāti pathavito vehāsaṃ abhiuggantvā. Ākāse antalikkheti ākāsameva pariyāyasaddena antalikkheti vadanti. Atha vā antalikkhasaṅkhāte ākāse na kasiṇugghāṭimādiākāseti visesento vadati. Aho dānanti ettha ahoti acchariyatthe nipāto. Sakko hi devānamindo, “yasmā nirodhā vuṭṭhitassa ayyassa mahākassapattherassa sakkaccaṃ sahatthena cittīkatvā anapaviddhaṃ kālena paresaṃ anupahacca, sammādiṭṭhiṃ purakkhatvā idamīdisaṃ mayā dibbabhojanadānaṃ dinnaṃ, tasmā khettasampatti deyyadhammasampatti cittasampattīti, tividhāyapi sampattiyā samannāgatattā sabbaṅgasampannaṃ vata mayā dānaṃ pavattita”nti acchariyabbhutacittajāto tadā attano hadayabbhantaragataṃ pītisomanassaṃ samuggiranto “aho dāna”nti vatvā tassa dānassa vuttanayena uttamadānabhāvaṃ khettaṅgatabhāvañca pakāsento “paramadānaṃ kassape suppatiṭṭhita”nti udānaṃ udānesi.

Therein, Kosiya is an address to Sakka, the lord of the gods, by his clan name. Puññena attho means 'there is a purpose for merit'; the word atthi is to be supplied. Vehāsaṃ abbhuggantvā means having ascended from the earth into the sky. Ākāse antalikkhe ('in the sky, in the atmosphere'): antalikkhe is used as a synonym for ākāse. Alternatively, wishing to specify, it is said: 'in the sky designated as the atmosphere,' not in the space revealed by removing a kasina device, and so on. In Aho dānaṃ ('Oh, the gift!'), aho is a particle in the sense of wonder. For Sakka, the lord of the gods, with a mind of wonder and amazement having arisen, reflected: 'Because to the noble Elder Mahākassapa, who had arisen from cessation, I reverently and respectfully gave with my own hands this kind of divine food-offering—not discarded, at the proper time, without harming others, and having placed right view at the forefront—therefore, because it is endowed with all three perfections (the perfection of the field, the perfection of the gift, and the perfection of the mind), a gift complete in all its aspects has indeed been set in motion by me.' Then, pouring forth the joy and gladness that had arisen within his heart, he exclaimed, “Oh, the gift!” and, proclaiming the supreme nature of that gift and its quality of having reached an excellent field in the aforesaid manner, he uttered the inspired utterance: “The supreme gift, well-established in Kassapa.”

Evaṃ pana sakkassa udānentassa bhagavā vihāre ṭhitoyeva dibbasotena saddaṃ sutvā “passatha, bhikkhave, sakkaṃ devānamindaṃ udānaṃ udānetvā ākāsena gacchanta”nti bhikkhūnaṃ vatvā tehi “kiṃ pana, bhante, tena kata”nti puṭṭho “mama puttassa kassapassa vañcetvā dānaṃ adāsi, tena ca attamano udānesī”ti āha. Tena vuttaṃ “assosi kho bhagavā dibbāya sotadhātuyā”tiādi.

Furthermore, as Sakka was uttering this inspired utterance, the Blessed One, while still in the monastery, heard the sound with his divine ear and said to the monks: “Behold, monks, Sakka, the lord of the gods, uttering an inspired utterance as he goes through the sky.” When asked by them, “But what has he done, venerable sir?” he replied: “He gave alms to my son Kassapa by deceiving him, and, pleased by that, he uttered an inspired utterance.” Hence it is said: “The Blessed One heard with the divine element of hearing,” and so on.

Tattha [V 0.0162][M 0.0181][P 0.0201] dibbāya sotadhātuyāti dibbasadisattā dibbā. Devatānañhi sucaritakammanibbattā pittasemharuhirādīhi apalibuddhā upakkilesavinimuttatāya dūrepi ārammaṇaṃ gahetuṃ samatthā dibbapasādasotadhātu hoti. Ayañcāpi bhagavato vīriyabhāvanābalanibbattā ñāṇamayā sotadhātu tādisā evāti dibbasadisattā dibbā. Api ca dibbavihāravasena paṭiladdhattā attanā ca dibbavihārasannissitattāpi dibbā. Savanaṭṭhena ca sabhāvadhāraṇaṭṭhena ca sotadhātu, sotadhātuyāpi kiccakaraṇena sotadhātu viyāti sotadhātu, tāya dibbāya sotadhātuyā. Visuddhāyāti parisuddhāya nirupakkilesāya. Atikkantamānusikāyāti manussūpacāraṃ atikkamitvā saddassavanena mānusikamaṃsasotadhātuṃ atikkamitvā ṭhitāya.

Herein, dibbāya sotadhātuyā ('with the divine ear-element'): it is dibbā ('divine') because it is like the divine ear. For deities possess a divine sensitive ear-element produced by their good conduct, which is unimpeded by bile, phlegm, blood, and so on; and due to its freedom from defilements, it is capable of grasping objects even at a distance. This ear-element of the Blessed One, too, being knowledge-made and produced by the power of the cultivation of energy, is just like that; hence, it is dibbā because it is like the divine ear. Moreover, it is dibbā because it is attained by means of the divine abiding, and because he himself is supported by the divine abiding. It is a sotadhātu ('ear-element') in the sense of hearing (savana) and in the sense of maintaining its own nature (sabhāva-dhāraṇa). And it is called an ear-element because it acts like an ear-element by performing its function. Thus, 'with that divine ear-element.' Visuddhāya ('purified') means completely pure, free from defilements. Atikkantamānusikāya ('transcending the human') means standing, having surpassed the human fleshly ear-element by hearing sounds beyond the range of humans.

Etamatthaṃ viditvāti “sammāpaṭipattiyā guṇavisese patiṭṭhitaṃ purisātisayaṃ devāpi manussāpi ādarajātā ativiya pihayantī”ti imamatthaṃ viditvā tadatthadīpanaṃ imaṃ udānaṃ udānesi.

Having understood this meaning: “Gods and humans, filled with reverence, greatly cherish a supreme person who is established in the special qualities of right practice,” the Blessed One uttered this inspired utterance to illuminate that meaning.

Tatra piṇḍapātikaṅgasaṅkhātaṃ dhutaṅgaṃ samādāya tassa paripūraṇena piṇḍapātikassa. Nanu cāyaṃ gāthā āyasmantaṃ mahākassapaṃ nimittaṃ katvā bhāsitā, thero ca sabbesaṃ dhutavādānaṃ aggo terasadhutaṅgadharo, so kasmā ekeneva dhutaṅgena kittitoti? Aṭṭhuppattivasenāyaṃ niddeso. Atha vā desanāmattametaṃ, iminā desanāsīsena sabbepissa dhutaṅgā vuttāti veditabbā. Atha vā “yathāpi bhamaro puppha”nti (dha. pa. 49) gāthāya vuttanayena paramappicchatāya kulānuddayatāya cassa sabbaṃ piṇḍapātikavattaṃ akkhaṇḍetvā tattha sātisayaṃ paṭipattiyā pakāsanatthaṃ “piṇḍapātikassā”ti vuttaṃ. Piṇḍapātikassāti ca pihayantīti padaṃ apekkhitvā sampadānavacanaṃ, taṃ upayogatthe daṭṭhabbaṃ. Attabharassāti “appāni ca tāni sulabhāni anavajjānī”ti (a. ni. 4.27; itivu. 101) evaṃ vuttehi appānavajjasulabharūpehi catūhi paccayehi attānameva [P 0.0202] bharantassa. Anaññaposinoti āmisasaṅgaṇhanena aññe sissādike posetuṃ anussukkatāya anaññaposino. Padadvayenassa kāyaparihārikena cīvarena kucchiparihārikena piṇḍapātena vicaraṇato sallahukavuttitaṃ subharataṃ paramañca santuṭṭhiṃ [M 0.0182] dasseti. Atha vā attabharassāti ekavacanicchāya attabhāvasaṅkhātaṃ ekaṃyeva imaṃ attānaṃ bharati, na ito paraṃ aññanti attabharo, tato eva attanā aññassa posetabbassa abhāvato anaññaposī, tassa attabharassa anaññaposino. Padadvayenapi khīṇāsavabhāvena āyatiṃ anādānataṃ dasseti.

Regarding `piṇḍapātikassa` (of the alms-food practitioner): this refers to one who has undertaken the ascetic practice known as the alms-food practice and is fulfilling it. Now, was this verse not spoken with reference to the venerable Mahākassapa? And that elder was the foremost of all who advocate ascetic practices, a holder of the thirteen ascetic practices; so why is he praised for just this one ascetic practice? This designation is made by way of the occasion on which the verse arose. Alternatively, this is merely a manner of teaching, and it should be understood that by this leading topic of the teaching, all of his ascetic practices are spoken of. Or, in accordance with the method stated in the verse, 'Just as a bee from a flower...' (Dhp. 49), it is said 'of the alms-food practitioner' to proclaim his superior practice in that regard, since, due to his supreme fewness of wishes and his compassion for families, he maintained the entire alms-food practice without breaking it. And `piṇḍapātikassa` is a dative case in relation to the word `pihayanti` (they cherish), and it should be understood in the sense of the accusative. `Attabharassa` (of one who supports himself) refers to one who sustains only himself with the four requisites that are of the nature of being few, blameless, and easily obtained, as stated: '...and those are few, easily obtained, and blameless' (AN 4.27; Iti 101). `Anaññaposino` (of one who does not support another) refers to one who does not support another because he is not eager to support other disciples and the like by accumulating material things. By these two terms, his lightness of living, ease of support, and supreme contentment are shown, as he wanders with robes that merely maintain the body and alms-food that merely maintains the belly. Alternatively, `attabharassa`, by the intention of the singular number, means he is an `attabharo` (one who supports himself) because he supports only this single self, his own existence, and not another beyond this. From that very fact, he is an `anaññaposī` (one who does not support another) due to the absence of another to be supported by him. By these two terms, it is also shown that, due to his nature as one whose taints are destroyed, there is no future grasping.

Devā [V 0.0163] pihayanti…pe… satīmatoti taṃ aggaphalādhigamena sabbakilesadarathapariḷāhānaṃ vūpasamena paṭippassaddhiyā upasantaṃ, sativepullappattiyā niccakālaṃ satokāritāya satimantaṃ, tato eva iṭṭhāniṭṭhādīsu tādilakkhaṇappattaṃ khīṇāsavaṃ sakkādayo devā pihayanti patthenti, tassa sīlādiguṇavisesesu bahumānaṃ uppādentā ādaraṃ janenti, pageva manussāti.

The gods cherish... one endowed with mindfulness: he is peaceful through having attained the highest fruit, through the cessation and calming of all defilements, distress, and fevers. He is mindful through having attained an abundance of mindfulness and through always acting with mindfulness. Therefore, that one whose taints are destroyed, who has attained the characteristic of equanimity towards the agreeable and disagreeable, is cherished and longed for by the gods, including Sakka. Generating great respect for his special qualities, such as virtue, they produce reverence. How much more so humans!

Sattamasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Seventh Sutta is completed.

8. Piṇḍapātikasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Alms-food Practitioner Sutta

28. Aṭṭhame pacchābhattanti ekāsanikakhalupacchābhattikānaṃ pātova bhuttānaṃ antomajjhanhikopi pacchābhattameva, idha pana pakatibhattasseva pacchato pacchābhattanti veditabbaṃ. Piṇḍapātapaṭikkantānanti piṇḍapātato paṭikkantānaṃ, piṇḍapātaṃ pariyesitvā bhattakiccassa niṭṭhāpanavasena tato nivattānaṃ. Karerimaṇḍalamāḷeti ettha karerīti varuṇarukkhassa nāmaṃ. So kira gandhakuṭiyā maṇḍapassa sālāya ca antare hoti, tena gandhakuṭīpi [P 0.0203] “karerikuṭikā”ti vuccati, maṇḍapopi sālāpi “karerimaṇḍalamāḷo”ti. Tasmā karerirukkhassa avidūre kate nisīdanasālasaṅkhāte maṇḍalamāḷe. Tiṇapaṇṇacchadanaṃ anovassakaṃ “maṇḍalamāḷo”ti vadanti, atimuttakādilatāmaṇḍapo “maṇḍalamāḷo”ti apare.

28. In the eighth sutta, `pacchābhattaṃ` (after the meal): for one-session-eaters and after-meal-eaters who have eaten in the morning, even the time before midday is 'after the meal.' Here, however, `pacchābhattaṃ` should be understood as after the regular meal. `Piṇḍapātapaṭikkantānaṃ` means 'of those who have returned from the alms round'; that is, of those who have returned from there by way of having finished the business of the meal after seeking alms-food. Regarding `Karerimaṇḍalamāḷe` (in the Kareri circular hall): here, `karerī` is the name of the Varuṇa tree. It is said that this tree stood between the fragrant chamber and the pavilion hall; for that reason, the fragrant chamber is also called `Karerikuṭikā`, and the pavilion or hall is called `Karerimaṇḍalamāḷo`. Therefore, it means in the circular hall, designated as a sitting hall, built not far from the Kareri tree. Some say a `maṇḍalamāḷo` is a rain-proof shelter roofed with grass and leaves; others say a `maṇḍalamāḷo` is a pavilion of creepers such as Atimuttaka.

Kālena kālanti kāle kāle antarantarā, tasmiṃ tasmiṃ samayeti attho. Manāpiketi manavaḍḍhake, piyarūpe iṭṭheti attho. Iṭṭhāniṭṭhabhāvo ca puggalavasena ca dvāravasena ca gahetabbo. Ekaccassa hi iṭṭhābhimato ekaccassa aniṭṭho hoti, ekaccassa aniṭṭhābhimato ekaccassa iṭṭho[M 0.0183]. Tathā ekassa dvārassa iṭṭho aññassa aniṭṭho. Vipākavasena panettha vinicchayo veditabbo. Kusalavipāko hi ekantena iṭṭho, akusalavipāko aniṭṭho evāti. Cakkhunā rūpe passitunti gāmaṃ piṇḍāya paviṭṭho upāsakehi gehaṃ pavesetvā pūjāsakkārakaraṇatthaṃ upanītesu āsanavitānādīsu nānāvirāgasamujjalavaṇṇasaṅkhāte rajanīye aññe ca saviññāṇakarūpe cakkhudvārikaviññāṇehi passituṃ. Saddeti tatheva issarajanānaṃ gehaṃ paviṭṭho tesaṃ payutte gītavāditasadde sotuṃ. Gandheti tathā tehi pūjāsakkāravasena upanīte pupphadhūmādigandhe ghāyituṃ. Raseti tehi dinnāhāraparibhoge nānaggarase sāyituṃ. Phoṭṭhabbeti mahagghapaccattharaṇesu [V 0.0164] āsanesu nisinnakāle sukhasamphasse phoṭṭhabbe phusituṃ. Evañca pañcadvārikaiṭṭhārammaṇappaṭilābhaṃ kittetvā idāni manodvārikaiṭṭhārammaṇappaṭilābhaṃ dassetuṃ “sakkato”tiādi vuttaṃ. Taṃ heṭṭhā vuttatthameva.

`Kālena kālaṃ` means from time to time, at intervals, at this or that time; this is the meaning. `Manāpike` means mind-enhancing, of a pleasing nature, agreeable; this is the meaning. The state of being agreeable or disagreeable should be understood by way of the person and by way of the sense-door. For what is considered agreeable by one person may be disagreeable to another, and what is considered disagreeable by one may be agreeable to another. Similarly, what is agreeable to one sense-door may be disagreeable to another. However, the determination here should be understood in terms of karmic result. For a wholesome result is exclusively agreeable, while an unwholesome result is indeed disagreeable. `Cakkhunā rūpe passituṃ` (to see forms with the eye) means: when one has entered a village for alms and been led into a house by lay devotees, to see with eye-door consciousnesses the various brightly colored and radiant forms, described as enticing, among the seats, canopies, and so on brought forth for the purpose of veneration and honor, as well as other animate forms. `Saddeti` (sounds) means: similarly, when one has entered the house of powerful people, to hear the sounds of singing and music employed by them. `Gandheti` (scents) means: similarly, to smell the scents of flowers, incense, and so on brought forth by them by way of veneration and honor. `Raseti` (tastes) means: to taste the various excellent flavors during the partaking of food given by them. `Phoṭṭhabbeti` (tangibles) means: when seated on seats with valuable coverings, to feel pleasant tangible objects. Having thus declared the attainment of agreeable objects through the five sense-doors, now to show the attainment of agreeable objects through the mind-door, 'honored,' etc., is said. The meaning of that is as stated below.

Kiṃ pana apiṇḍapātikānaṃ ayaṃ nayo na labbhatīti? Labbhati. Tesampi hi nimantanasalākabhattādiatthaṃ gāmaṃ gatakāle uḷāravibhavā upāsakā tathā sakkārasammānaṃ karontiyeva, taṃ pana aniyataṃ. Piṇḍapātikānaṃ pana tadā niccameva tattha pūjāsakkāraṃ kariyamānaṃ disvā, sakkāragarutāya anissaraṇamagge ṭhatvā, ayonisomanasikāravasena te bhikkhū evamāhaṃsu. Tenevāha – “handāvuso, mayampi piṇḍapātikā homā”tiādi.

But is this principle not applicable to those who are not alms-food practitioners? It is applicable. For when they go to a village for the sake of invitation meals, ticket-meals, and so on, lay followers of great wealth indeed offer them honor and respect in the same way. However, that is not certain. But for the alms-food practitioners, it is always so at that time. Seeing the veneration and honor constantly being offered there, and, standing on the path of non-liberation due to esteem for honor and through unwise attention, those bhikkhus said thus. Therefore, He said: 'Come, friends, let us also become alms-food practitioners,' and so on.

Tattha handāti vossaggatthe nipāto. Lacchāmāti labhissāma. Tenupasaṅkamīti tattha surabhigandhakuṭiyaṃ nisinno tesaṃ taṃ kathāsallāpaṃ sutvā [P 0.0204] “ime bhikkhū mādisassa nāma buddhassa sāsane pabbajitvā mayā saddhiṃ ekavihāre vasantāpi evaṃ ayonisomanasikāravasena kathaṃ pavattenti, sallekhe na vattanti, handa te tato nivāretvā sallekhavihāre niyojessāmī”ti maṇḍalamāḷaṃ upasaṅkami. Sesaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayameva.

Here, `handa` is a particle in the sense of exhortation. `Lacchāma` means 'we shall obtain.' `Tenupasaṅkami` means that, while sitting in the fragrant hut, having heard their conversation, he thought: 'These monks, having gone forth in the dispensation of a Buddha like me, and even while dwelling with me in the same monastery, how can they engage in such talk through unwise attention? They do not practice effacement. Come now, I shall turn them away from that and engage them in the abiding of effacement.' And so he approached the circular pavilion. The rest is as explained below.

Etamatthaṃ viditvāti “appicchatāsantuṭṭhitāsallekhānaṃ vasena kilese dhunituṃ taṇhaṃ visosetuṃ paṭipannoti piṇḍapātikassa sato devā pihayanti, tassa paṭipattiyā ādarajātā piyāyanti, na ito aññathā”ti imamatthaṃ viditvā tadatthadīpanaṃ imaṃ udānaṃ udānesi.

Having understood this meaning—'Even the gods long for the alms-goer who is practicing to shake off defilements and dry up craving through fewness of wishes, contentment, and effacement; having developed reverence for his practice, they hold him dear, and not otherwise'—having understood this meaning, he uttered this inspired utterance to illuminate that meaning.

Tattha [M 0.0184] no ce saddasilokanissitoti “aho ayyo appiccho santuṭṭho paramasallekhavuttī”tiādinā parehi kittitabbasaddasaṅkhātaṃ silokaṃ. Taṇhāya nissito na hoti ceti attho. Saddo vā sammukhā vaṇṇabhaṇanathutighoso, siloko parammukhabhūtā pasaṃsā patthaṭayasatā vā. Sesaṃ anantarasutte vuttanayameva.

Here, `no ce saddasilokanissito` means: if one is not dependent on fame—which is reckoned by the sound of being praised by others with such words as, 'Ah, the noble one has few wishes, is content, and leads a life of utmost effacement!'—the meaning is that one is not dependent through craving. `Sadda` (sound) is the noise of spoken praise and eulogy in one's presence; `siloka` (fame) is praise that occurs behind one's back, or widespread renown. The rest is as explained in the preceding discourse.

Aṭṭhamasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the eighth discourse is finished.

9. Sippasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Discourse on Crafts

29. Navame [V 0.0165] ko nu kho, āvuso, sippaṃ jānātīti, āvuso, amhesu idha sannipatitesu ko nu jīvitanimittaṃ sikkhitabbaṭṭhena “sippa”nti laddhanāmaṃ yaṃkiñci ājīvaṃ vijānāti? Ko kiṃ sippaṃ sikkhīti ko dīgharattaṃ sippācariyakulaṃ payirupāsitvā āgamato payogato ca hatthisippādīsu kiṃ sippaṃ sikkhi? Kataraṃ sippaṃ sippānaṃ agganti sabbasippānaṃ agārayhatāya mahapphalatāya akicchasiddhiyā ca kataraṃ sippaṃ aggaṃ uttamaṃ? Yaṃ nissāya sukhena sakkā jīvitunti adhippāyo. Tatthekacceti tesu bhikkhūsu ekacce bhikkhū. Ye hatthācariyakulā pabbajitā te. Evamāhaṃsūti te evaṃ bhaṇiṃsu. Ito parampi “ekacce”ti vuttaṭṭhāne eseva nayo. Hatthisippanti [P 0.0205] yaṃ hatthīnaṃ pariggaṇhanadamanasāraṇarogatikicchādibhedaṃ kattabbaṃ, taṃ uddissa pavattaṃ sabbampi sippaṃ idha “hatthisippa”nti adhippetaṃ. Assasippanti etthāpi eseva nayo. Rathasippaṃ pana rathayoggānaṃ damanasāraṇādividhānavasena ceva rathassa karaṇavasena ca veditabbaṃ. Dhanusippanti issāsasippaṃ, yo dhanubbedhoti vuccati. Tharusippanti sesaāvudhasippaṃ. Muddāsippanti hatthamuddāya gaṇanasippaṃ. Gaṇanasippanti acchiddakagaṇanasippaṃ. Saṅkhānasippanti saṅkalanapaṭuppādanādivasena piṇḍagaṇanasippaṃ. Taṃ yassa paguṇaṃ hoti, so rukkhampi disvā “ettakāni ettha paṇṇānī”ti gaṇituṃ jānāti. Lekhāsippanti nānākārehi akkharalikhanasippaṃ, lipiñāṇaṃ vā. Kāveyyasippanti attano cintāvasena vā parato paṭiladdhasutavasena vā, “imassa ayamattho, evaṃ naṃ yojessāmī”ti evaṃ atthavasena vā, kiñcideva kabbaṃ disvā, “tappaṭibhāgaṃ kabbaṃ karissāmī”ti [M 0.0185] ṭhānuppattikapaṭibhānavasena vā cintākaviādīnaṃ catunnaṃ kavīnaṃ kabbakaraṇasippaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā –

29. In the ninth discourse, `Ko nu kho, āvuso, sippaṃ jānāti` means: 'Friends, among us who are gathered here, who knows any means of livelihood that has received the name "craft" in the sense that it is to be learned for the sake of a living?' `Ko kiṃ sippaṃ sikkhi` means: 'Who, having for a long time attended upon a family of craft-teachers, has learned what craft among the elephant-craft and so on, both from tradition and from practice?' `Kataraṃ sippaṃ sippānaṃ aggaṃ` means: 'Among all crafts, which craft is foremost and best on account of being irreproachable, of great fruit, and accomplished without difficulty? Relying on which, is it possible to live in comfort?' This is the intended meaning. `Tatthekacce` means: among those monks, certain monks—those who had gone forth from families of elephant-trainers. `Evamāhaṃsu` means: they spoke thus. From here on, wherever `ekacce` is stated, this same method applies. `Hatthisippa` (elephant-craft): here, any craft undertaken that is concerned with the various tasks of capturing, taming, guiding, and treating the illnesses of elephants is intended as 'elephant-craft.' `Assasippa` (horse-craft): here too, this same method applies. `Rathasippa` (chariot-craft), however, should be understood both in terms of the methods for taming and guiding draft animals for a chariot and in terms of constructing the chariot. `Dhanusippa` (bow-craft) is the craft of archery, which is called `dhanubbeda` (mastery of the bow). `Tharusippa` (sword-craft) refers to the remaining weapon-crafts. `Muddāsippa` is the craft of counting by hand-signs. `Gaṇanasippa` is the craft of flawless counting. `Saṅkhānasippa` is the craft of counting totals by means of aggregation, production, and so on. One who is skilled in this, upon seeing a tree, knows how to count, 'There are so many leaves on it.' `Lekhāsippa` is the craft of writing letters in various ways, or knowledge of script. `Kāveyyasippa` (poetic craft) is the craft of composing poetry of the four kinds of poets—the poet of thought and so on—either through one's own thought or through what has been learned from another; or by way of meaning, thinking, 'This is the meaning of this; thus I will arrange it'; or upon seeing some composition, thinking, 'I will make a composition corresponding to that,' by way of situational inspiration. For this was said by the Blessed One:

“Cattārome, bhikkhave, kavī – cintākavi, sutakavi, atthakavi, paṭibhānakavī”ti (a. ni. 4.231).

"Monks, there are these four kinds of poets: the poet of thought, the poet of learning, the poet of meaning, and the poet of inspiration." (AN 4.231)

Lokāyatasippanti “kāko seto aṭṭhīnaṃ setattā, balākā rattā lohitassa rattattā”ti evamādinayappavattaṃ paralokanibbānānaṃ paṭisedhakaṃ vitaṇḍasatthasippaṃ. Khattavijjāsippanti abbheyyamāsurakkhādinītisatthasippaṃ. Imāni kira dvādasa mahāsippāni nāma. Tenevāha tattha tattha “sippānaṃ agga”nti.

The craft of Lokāyata is the craft of sophistry which proceeds by such methods as, 'The crow is white because its bones are white; the egret is red because its blood is red,' and which denies the next world and Nibbāna. The craft of royal science (`khattavijjā`) is the craft of statecraft, including policy regarding protection from portents, demons, and so on. These, it is said, are the twelve great crafts. Therefore they said in each case, '...is the foremost of crafts.'

Etamatthaṃ [V 0.0166] viditvāti etaṃ sabbasippāyatanānaṃ jīvikatthatāya vaṭṭadukkhato anissaraṇabhāvaṃ[P 0.0206], sīlādīnaṃyeva pana suparisuddhānaṃ nissaraṇabhāvaṃ, taṃ samaṅginoyeva ca bhikkhubhāvaṃ sabbākārato viditvā tadatthavibhāvanaṃ imaṃ udānaṃ udānesi.

Having understood this meaning in all its aspects—that all bases of craft, being for the sake of a livelihood, are no escape from the suffering of the cycle, but that utterly pure virtue and so on are indeed an escape, and that the state of a bhikkhu belongs only to one endowed with them—he uttered this inspired utterance that clarifies this meaning.

Tattha asippajīvīti catunnaṃ taṇhuppādānaṃ samucchedavikkhambhanena paccayāsāya visositattā yaṃkiñci sippaṃ upanissāya jīvikaṃ na kappetīti asippajīvī, etena ājīvapārisuddhisīlaṃ dasseti. Lahūti appakiccatāya sallahukavuttitāya ca lahu abahulasambhāro, etena catupaccayasantosasiddhaṃ subharataṃ dasseti. Atthakāmoti sadevakassa lokassa atthameva kāmetīti atthakāmo, etena sattānaṃ anatthaparivajjanassa pakāsitattā pātimokkhasaṃvarasīlaṃ dasseti pāṇātipātādianatthaviramaṇaparidīpanato. Yatindriyoti cakkhādīnaṃ channaṃ indriyānaṃ abhijjhādyappavattito saṃyamena yatindriyo, etena indriyasaṃvarasīlaṃ vuttaṃ. Sabbadhi vippamuttoti evaṃ suparisuddhasīlo catupaccayasantose avaṭṭhito sappaccayaṃ nāmarūpaṃ pariggahetvā aniccādivasena saṅkhāre sammasanto vipassanaṃ ussukkāpetvā tato paraṃ paṭipāṭiyā pavattitehi catūhi ariyamaggehi saṃyojanānaṃ pahīnattā sabbadhi sabbattha bhavādīsu vippamutto.

Herein, 'not living by a craft' means that because the desire for requisites has been dried up through the eradication and suppression of the four kinds of craving and clinging, one does not make a living dependent on any craft whatsoever. By this is shown the virtue of purity of livelihood. 'Light' means that due to having few duties and a light way of life, one is unburdened and without many possessions. By this is shown the ease of being supported that is accomplished by contentment with the four requisites. 'Desiring the welfare' means that one desires only the welfare of the world with its devas. By this, as it makes known the avoidance of what is not for the welfare of beings, the virtue of restraint by the Pātimokkha is shown, through its clarification of abstention from what is harmful, such as the destruction of life. 'With senses restrained' means that through restraint of the six senses—the eye and so forth—from the arising of covetousness and the like, one is restrained in the senses. By this, the virtue of sense restraint is stated. 'Freed in every way' means that one who is thus perfectly pure in virtue and established in contentment with the four requisites, having grasped name-and-form together with its causes and contemplating formations by way of impermanence and so forth, strives in insight. Then, through the four noble paths that arise in succession, because the fetters are abandoned, one is freed in every way, in all respects, from existences and so forth.

Anokasārī [M 0.0186] amamo nirāsoti tathā sabbadhi vippamuttattā eva okasaṅkhātesu chasupi āyatanesu taṇhābhisaraṇassa abhāvena anokasārī, rūpādīsu katthaci mamaṅkārābhāvato amamo, sabbena sabbaṃ anāsīsanato nirāso. Hitvā mānaṃ ekacaro sa bhikkhūti evaṃbhūto ca so arahattamaggappattisamakālameva anavasesaṃ mānaṃ hitvā pajahitvā ime bhikkhū viya gaṇasaṅgaṇikaṃ akatvā pavivekakāmatāya taṇhāsahāyavirahena ca sabbiriyāpathesu ekacaro, so sabbaso bhinnakilesattā paramatthato bhikkhu nāma. Ettha ca “asippajīvī”tiādinā lokiyaguṇā kathitā, “sabbadhi vippamutto”tiādinā lokuttaraguṇā kathitā. Tattha asippajīvītiādi “vibhave ṭhitasseva ayaṃ dhammo, na sippaṃ nissāya micchājīvena jīvikaṃ kappentassa, tasmā sippesu sāraggahaṇaṃ vissajjetvā adhisīlādīsuyeva tumhehi sikkhitabba”nti dasseti.

'Not frequenting an abode, without possessiveness, without desire' means: being thus freed in every way, due to the absence of craving's approach in the six sense bases, which are called 'abodes', one is 'not frequenting an abode'. Due to the absence of making anything 'mine' in regard to forms and so forth, one is 'without possessiveness'. Due to being entirely without longing, one is 'without desire'. 'Having abandoned conceit, that bhikkhu wanders alone' means: such a one, at the very moment of attaining the path of Arahantship, having abandoned conceit without remainder, does not engage in socializing in groups like these ordinary monks. Due to a desire for seclusion and being without craving as a companion, one wanders alone in all postures. Because one's defilements are completely destroyed, in the ultimate sense, one is called a 'bhikkhu'. Herein, by 'not living by a craft' and so on, worldly virtues are spoken of; by 'freed in every way' and so on, supramundane virtues are spoken of. Therein, 'not living by a craft' and so on shows that: 'This Dhamma is for one who is established in the state of non-becoming, not for one who makes a living by wrong livelihood depending on a craft. Therefore, having abandoned the taking of substance in crafts, you should train only in higher virtue and so forth.'

Navamasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the ninth discourse is completed.

10. Lokasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Lokasutta

30. Dasame [V 0.0167][P 0.0207] buddhacakkhunāti ettha āsayānusayañāṇaṃ indriyaparopariyattañāṇañca buddhacakkhu nāma. Yathāha –

30. In the tenth sutta, regarding 'with the Buddha-eye': herein, the knowledge of dispositions and underlying tendencies, and the knowledge of the maturity and immaturity of the faculties, are called the Buddha-eye. As it is said:

“Addasā kho bhagavā buddhacakkhunā lokaṃ volokento satte apparajakkhe mahārajakkhe tikkhindriye mudindriye”tiādi (ma. ni. 1.283; 2.339).

“The Blessed One, surveying the world with the Buddha-eye, saw beings with little dust and with much dust, with keen faculties and with dull faculties,” and so on (MN 1.283; 2.339).

Lokanti tayo lokā – okāsaloko, saṅkhāraloko, sattalokoti. Tattha –

Regarding 'the world' (lokaṃ): there are three worlds—the world of space, the world of formations, and the world of beings. Therein:

“Yāvatā candimasūriyā pariharanti,

Disā bhanti virocanā;

Tāva sahassadhā loko,

Ettha te vattatī vaso”ti. –

“As far as the moon and sun revolve, shining, illumining the directions, so far extends the thousandfold world; therein your power prevails.”

Ādīsu (ma. ni. 1.503) okāsaloko. “Eko loko – sabbe sattā āhāraṭṭhitikā, dve lokā – nāmañca rūpañca, tayo lokā – tisso vedanā[M 0.0187], cattāro lokā – cattāro āhārā, pañca lokā – pañcupādānakkhandhā, cha lokā – cha ajjhattikāni āyatanāni, satta lokā – satta viññāṇaṭṭhitiyo, aṭṭha lokā – aṭṭha lokadhammā, nava lokā – nava sattāvāsā, dasa lokā – dasāyatanāni, dvādasa lokā – dvādasāyatanāni, aṭṭhārasa lokā – aṭṭhārasa dhātuyo”tiādīsu (paṭi. ma. 1.112) saṅkhāraloko. “Sassato loko, asassato loko”tiādīsu sattaloko vutto. Idhāpi sattaloko veditabbo.

In such passages (e.g., MN 1.503), the world of space is spoken of. In passages such as, “One world—all beings are sustained by nutriment; two worlds—name-and-form; three worlds—the three feelings; four worlds—the four kinds of nutriment; five worlds—the five aggregates subject to clinging; six worlds—the six internal sense bases; seven worlds—the seven stations of consciousness; eight worlds—the eight worldly conditions; nine worlds—the nine abodes of beings; ten worlds—the ten sense bases; twelve worlds—the twelve sense bases; eighteen worlds—the eighteen elements” (e.g., Paṭis I 112), the world of formations is spoken of. In passages such as, “The world is eternal, the world is not eternal,” the world of beings is spoken of. Here too, the world of beings should be understood.

Tattha lokīyati vicittākārato dissatīti cakkavāḷasaṅkhāto loko okāsaloko, saṅkhāro lujjati palujjatīti loko, lokīyati ettha puññapāpaṃ tabbipāko cāti sattaloko. Tesu bhagavā mahākaruṇāya anukampamāno saṃsāradukkhato mocetukāmo sattalokaṃ olokesi. Katamassa pana sattāhassa accayena olokesi? Paṭhamassa sattāhassa. Bhagavā hi pallaṅkasattāhassa pariyosāne pacchimayāmāvasāne “yadā have pātubhavanti dhammā…pe… sūriyova obhāsayamantalikkha”nti (udā. 1-3; kathā. 321; mahāva. 1-3) imaṃ ariyamaggānubhāvadīpakaṃ [V 0.0168] udānaṃ udānetvā, “ahaṃ tāva evaṃ suduttaraṃ saṃsāramahoghaṃ imāya dhammanāvāya samuttaritvā nibbānapāre ṭhito, handa dāni lokampi tāressāmi, kīdiso nu kho loko”ti lokaṃ volokesi. Taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ – “atha kho bhagavā [P 0.0208] tassa sattāhassa accayena tamhā samādhimhā vuṭṭhahitvā buddhacakkhunā lokaṃ volokesī”ti.

Therein, the world of space, known as the universe-system, is called 'loka' because it is seen (lokīyati) in various forms. A formation is called 'loka' because it breaks up (lujjati) and perishes (palujjati). The world of beings is called 'loka' because herein merit, demerit, and their results are seen (lokīyati). Among these, the Blessed One, out of great compassion, surveyed the world of beings, desiring to free them from the suffering of saṃsāra. After the passing of which week did he survey it? After the first week. For at the end of the week spent in the cross-legged posture, at the end of the last watch of the night, the Blessed One uttered this inspired utterance that illuminates the power of the noble path: 'When phenomena become manifest… like the sun illuminating the sky' (Ud 1-3; etc.). Having uttered this, he thought: 'I, for my part, having crossed over this great flood of saṃsāra, so very hard to cross, by means of this boat of the Dhamma, now stand on the further shore of Nibbāna. Well now, I shall ferry the world across too. Of what kind, I wonder, is the world?' And he surveyed the world. With reference to this it was said: 'Then, after that week had passed, the Blessed One, having emerged from that concentration, surveyed the world with the Buddha-eye.'

Tattha volokesīti vividhehi ākārehi passi, hatthatale ṭhapitaāmalakaṃ viya attano ñāṇena paccakkhaṃ akāsi. Anekehi santāpehītiādi volokitākāradassanaṃ. Anekehi santāpehīti anekehi dukkhehi. Dukkhañhi santāpanapīḷanaṭṭhena santāpoti vuccati. Yathāha – “dukkhassa pīḷanaṭṭho saṅkhataṭṭho santāpaṭṭho vipariṇāmaṭṭho”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.17). Tañca dukkhadukkhādivasena ceva jātiādivasena ca anekappakāraṃ. Tena vuttaṃ “anekehi santāpehī”ti. Anekehi dukkhehi santappamāne pīḷiyamāne bādhiyamāne. Pariḷāhehīti paridāhehi. Pariḍayhamāneti indhanaṃ viya agginā samantato ḍayhamāne. Rāgajehīti rāgasambhūtehi[M 0.0188]. Esa nayo sesesupi. Rāgādayo hi yasmiṃ santāne uppajjanti, taṃ niddahantā viya vibādhenti, tena vuttaṃ – “tayome, bhikkhave, aggī – rāgaggi, dosaggi, mohaggī”ti (itivu. 93). Yato te cittaṃ kāyañca kilesentīti kilesāti vuccanti. Ettha ca pariḍayhamāneti etena bhagavā rāgādikilesānaṃ pavattidukkhataṃ, tena ca sattānaṃ abhibhūtataṃ dasseti. Santappamāneti iminā pana tesaṃ kālantaradukkhataṃ, tena nirantaropaddavatañca dasseti.

Herein, 'he surveyed' means he saw in various ways; he made it directly perceptible through his own knowledge, like an āmalaka fruit placed on the palm of the hand. The phrase 'with many torments,' and so on, indicates the manner of observation. 'With many torments' means with many sufferings. For suffering is called 'torment' because of its meaning of tormenting and oppressing. As it is said: “The meaning of suffering is oppression, the meaning of the conditioned, the meaning of torment, the meaning of change” (Paṭis I 17). And that suffering is of many kinds, by way of suffering-as-suffering, etc., and by way of birth, etc. Therefore it is said, 'with many torments.' Being tormented, oppressed, and afflicted by many sufferings. 'With burnings' means with scorchings. 'Being burned all around' means being burned on all sides by fire, like fuel. 'Born of lust' means arisen from lust. This method applies to the rest as well. For lust and the like, when they arise in a being's continuum, they afflict them as if burning them; hence it is said: “Monks, there are these three fires: the fire of lust, the fire of hatred, and the fire of delusion” (Iti. 93). Because they defile the mind and body, they are called defilements. Here, by 'being burned all around,' the Blessed One shows the suffering of the process of existence of the defilements of lust, etc., and by that, how beings are overwhelmed. By 'being tormented,' however, he shows their suffering at a future time, and by that, their continuous oppression.

Bhagavā hi bodhirukkhamūle aparājitapallaṅke nisinno paṭhamayāme pubbenivāsaṃ anussaritvā majjhimayāme dibbacakkhuṃ visodhetvā pacchimayāme paṭiccasamuppāde ñāṇaṃ otāretvā kilesamūlakaṃ vaṭṭadukkhaṃ abhiññāya saṅkhāre pariggahetvā sammasanto anukkamena vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā ariyamaggādhigamena sayaṃ vigataviddhastakileso abhisambuddho hutvā paccavekkhaṇānantaraṃ anavasesānaṃ kilesānaṃ pahīnattā attano vaṭṭadukkhassa parikkhīṇabhāvadīpakaṃ sabbabuddhānaṃ avijahitaṃ “anekajātisaṃsāra”nti (dha. pa. 153) udānaṃ udānetvā teneva pallaṅkena sattāhaṃ vimuttisukhapaṭisaṃvedī nisinno sattamāya rattiyā tīsu yāmesu vuttanayena tīṇi udānāni udānetvā tatiyaudānānantaraṃ buddhacakkhunā lokaṃ volokento “sakalamidaṃ sattānaṃ vaṭṭadukkhaṃ kilesamūlakaṃ, kilesā nāmete pavattidukkhā āyatimpi dukkhahetubhūtā, tehi [P 0.0209] ime sattā santappanti pariḍayhanti cā”ti passi. Tena vuttaṃ “addasā kho bhagavā…pe… mohajehipī”ti.

Indeed, the Blessed One, seated on the unconquerable seat at the foot of the Bodhi tree, in the first watch recollected his past lives, in the middle watch purified the divine eye, and in the last watch directed his knowledge into dependent origination. Having directly known the suffering of the cycle rooted in defilements, having comprehended and contemplated the formations, having gradually developed insight, and through the attainment of the noble path, having himself become a fully enlightened one with defilements dispelled and destroyed—immediately after the reviewing, because the defilements were abandoned without remainder, he uttered the inspired utterance that is not forsaken by any of the Buddhas, which declares the complete exhaustion of his own suffering of the cycle: “Through many a birth in saṃsāra I wandered” (Dhp. 153). Remaining seated on that very seat for seven days, experiencing the bliss of liberation, on the seventh night he uttered three inspired utterances in the three watches in the manner described. Immediately after the third inspired utterance, while surveying the world with the Buddha-eye, he saw: “All this suffering of the cycle for beings is rooted in defilements. These so-called defilements are the suffering of the process of existence and are a cause of suffering in the future. By these, these beings are tormented and burned.” Therefore, it was said: “The Blessed One saw… and those born of delusion.”

Etamatthaṃ [V 0.0169] viditvāti etaṃ lokassa yathāvuttasantāpapariḷāhehi abhibhuyyamānataṃ sabbākārato viditvā. Imaṃ udānanti imaṃ sabbasantāpapariḷāhato parinibbānavibhāvanaṃ mahāudānaṃ udānesi.

'Having known this meaning' means: having known in all aspects how this world is overwhelmed by the aforesaid torments and burnings. 'This inspired utterance' means: he uttered this great inspired utterance, which makes manifest the complete extinguishment from all torments and burnings.

Tattha ayaṃ loko santāpajātoti ayaṃ sabbopi loko jarārogamaraṇehi ceva nānāvidhabyasanehi ca kilesapariyuṭṭhānehi ca jātasantāpo, uppannakāyikacetasikadukkhābhibhavoti attho. Phassaparetoti tato eva anekehi dukkhasamphassehi parihato upadduto. Atha vā phassaparetoti sukhādisaṅkhātānaṃ tissannaṃ dukkhatānaṃ paccayabhūtehi chahi phassehi abhibhūto, tato tato dvārato tasmiṃ [M 0.0189] tasmiṃ ārammaṇe pavattivasena upassaṭṭho. Rogaṃ vadati attatoti phassapaccayā uppajjamānaṃ vedanāsaṅkhātaṃ rogaṃ dukkhaṃ, khandhapañcakameva vā yathābhūtaṃ ajānanto “aha”nti saññāya diṭṭhigāhavasena “ahaṃ sukhito dukkhito”ti attato vadati. “Attano”tipi paṭhanti. Tassattho – yvāyaṃ loko kenaci dukkhadhammena phuṭṭho abhāvitattatāya adhivāsetuṃ asakkonto “aho dukkhaṃ, īdisaṃ dukkhaṃ mayhaṃ attanopi mā hotū”tiādinā vippalapanto kevalaṃ attano rogaṃ vadati, tassa pana pahānāya na paṭipajjatīti adhippāyo. Atha vā taṃ yathāvuttaṃ dukkhaṃ yathābhūtaṃ ajānanto taṇhāgāhavasena “mama”nti saññāya attato vadati, “mama ida”nti vācaṃ nicchāreti.

Herein, 'this world is born of torment' means that this entire world has arisen torment due to aging, sickness, and death, to various calamities, and to the obsessions of the defilements; the meaning is that it is overwhelmed by arisen physical and mental suffering. 'Beset by contact' means that it is thereby assailed and afflicted by numerous painful contacts. Or alternatively, 'beset by contact' means it is overwhelmed by the six contacts which are the condition for the three kinds of suffering designated as pleasant feeling, etc., and is assailed by their arising in relation to various objects through the various sense doors. 'He speaks of disease as self' means that, not knowing the five aggregates as they truly are, through the perception of 'I' and the grip of wrong view, one speaks of the disease or suffering that arises conditioned by contact—namely, feeling—as 'self,' saying, 'I am happy, I am suffering.' Some also read 'attano' (of one's own). The meaning of that is: this world, when touched by some suffering state, being unable to endure it due to an undeveloped mind, laments, 'Oh, what suffering! May such suffering not befall even me!' and so on, thus merely speaking of its own disease, but not undertaking the practice for its abandonment—this is the intended meaning. Or alternatively, not knowing that aforesaid suffering as it truly is, through the grip of craving and the perception of 'mine,' one speaks of it as 'self,' or utters the words, 'This is mine.'

Yena yena hi maññatīti evamimaṃ rogabhūtaṃ khandhapañcakaṃ attato attano vā vadanto loko yena yena rūpavedanādinā kāraṇabhūtena, yena vā sassatādinā pakārena diṭṭhimānataṇhāmaññanāhi maññati. Tato taṃ hoti aññathāti [P 0.0210] tato attanā parikappitākārato taṃ maññanāya vatthubhūtaṃ khandhapañcakaṃ aññathā anattānattaniyameva hoti. Vase vattetuṃ asakkuṇeyyatāya ahaṅkāramamaṅkārattaṃ na nipphādetīti attho. Atha vā tatoti tasmā maññanāmattabhāvato taṃ khandhapañcakaṃ niccādivasena maññitaṃ aññathā aniccādisabhāvameva hoti. Na hi maññanā bhāvaññathattaṃ vā lakkhaṇaññathattaṃ vā kātuṃ sakkoti.

'For in whatever way one conceives': The world, speaking of this five-aggregate-mass which has become a disease as 'self' or 'belonging to self,' conceives it in one way or another—whether by some causal factor such as form, feeling, and so on, or by some mode such as eternalism—through the conceivings rooted in view, conceit, and craving. 'From that, it becomes otherwise': That five-aggregate-mass, which is the basis for conceiving, becomes other than the mode imagined by oneself; it is merely not-self and does not belong to a self. The meaning is that because it cannot be brought under one's control, it does not establish a state of 'I-making' and 'mine-making.' Or alternatively, 'from that' means: because it is merely conceived as such, that five-aggregate-mass, though conceived as permanent and so on, becomes otherwise, being in its true nature impermanent and so on. For conceiving is unable to effect a change in something's nature or a change in its characteristics.

Aññathābhāvī bhavasattoti asambhave vaḍḍhiyaṃ hitasukhe satto laggo sattaloko maññanāya yathāruci cintiyamānopi viparītappaṭipattiyā tato aññathābhāvī ahitadukkhabhāvī vighātaṃyeva pāpuṇāti. Bhavamevābhinandatīti evaṃ santepi taṃ maññanāparikappitaṃ avijjamānaṃ bhavaṃ vaḍḍhiṃ abhinandati eva abhikaṅkhati eva. Atha vā aññathābhāvīti “nicco me attā”tiādinā maññanāya parikappitākārato sayaṃ aññathābhāvī samāno anicco adhuvoti [V 0.0170] attho. Bhavasattoti kāmādibhavesu bhavataṇhāya satto laggo gadhito. Bhavamevābhinandatīti aniccādisabhāvaṃ bhavameva niccādivasena parāmasitvā, tattha vā adhimuttisaññaṃ taṇhādiṭṭhābhinandanāhi abhinandati, na tattha nibbindati[M 0.0190]. Yadabhinandati taṃ bhayanti yaṃ vaḍḍhisaṅkhātaṃ bhavaṃ kāmādibhavaṃ vā abhinandati, taṃ aniccādivipariṇāmasabhāvattā anekabyasanānubandhattā ca bhavahetubhāvato ativiya bhayānakaṭṭhena bhayaṃ. Yassa bhāyatīti yato jarāmaraṇādito bhāyati, taṃ jarāmaraṇādi dukkhādhiṭṭhānabhāvato dukkhadukkhabhāvato ca dukkhaṃ. Atha vā yassa bhāyatīti bhavābhinandanena yassa vibhavassa bhāyati[P 0.0211], so ucchedasaṅkhāto vibhavo, tato bhāyanañca dukkhavatthubhāvato jātiādidukkhassa anativattanato ca dukkhaṃ dukkhasabhāvamevāti attho. Atha vā yassa bhāyati taṃ dukkhanti yassa aniccādikassa bhāyati taṃ nissaraṇaṃ ajānanto, taṃ bhayaṃ tassa dukkhaṃ hoti, dukkhaṃ āvahatīti attho.

A being attached to existence, prone to change: this refers to the world of beings. Attached and clinging to growth in existence and to welfare and happiness, though it conceives according to its desire, through wrong practice it becomes otherwise—becoming subject to what is not welfare and is suffering—and attains only distress. They delight in existence itself: even so, they delight in and crave that non-existent becoming, that growth, which is imagined by their conceiving. Alternatively, 'prone to change' means this: from the state imagined through conceiving, such as 'my self is permanent,' one is oneself prone to change, being impermanent and unstable; this is the meaning. 'A being attached to existence' means a being attached, clinging, and ensnared by craving for existence in the realms of sensuality and so on. 'They delight in existence itself' means they delight in existence, which is by nature impermanent, having misperceived it as permanent, or having a conviction about it, they delight in it with the delights of craving and views, and do not become disenchanted with it. What they delight in is fear: whatever existence reckoned as growth, or existence in the realm of sensuality and so on, they delight in, that is fear in the sense of being extremely terrifying, because it is by nature subject to change and impermanence, is followed by many misfortunes, and is the cause of existence. That which is feared is suffering: that from which one fears, namely aging, death, and so on, is suffering because it is the basis for suffering and because it is suffering-in-itself. Alternatively, regarding 'that which is feared': through delighting in existence, one fears a certain non-existence. That non-existence is reckoned as annihilation, and the fear of it is suffering because it is a basis for suffering and because one does not overcome the suffering of birth and so on; it is simply the nature of suffering. This is the meaning. Alternatively, regarding 'that which is feared is suffering': for one who fears that which is impermanent and so on but does not know the escape from it, that fear becomes suffering for them; it brings suffering. This is the meaning.

Ettakena vaṭṭaṃ dassetvā idāni vivaṭṭaṃ dassetuṃ, “bhavavippahānāya kho panidaṃ brahmacariyaṃ vussatī”ti āha. Tattha bhavavippahānāyāti kāmādibhavassa pajahanatthāya. Khoti avadhāraṇe, panāti padapūraṇe nipāto. Idanti āsannapaccakkhavacanaṃ. Brahmacariyanti maggabrahmacariyaṃ. Vussatīti pūressati. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – ekanteneva kāmādibhavassa samudayappahānena anavasesapajahanatthāya idaṃ mayā satasahassakappādhikāni cattāri asaṅkhyeyyāni atidukkarāni ācaritvā pāramiyo pūretvā bodhimaṇḍe tiṇṇaṃ mārānaṃ matthakaṃ madditvā adhigataṃ sīlādikkhandhattayasaṅgahaṃ aṭṭhaṅgikamaggabrahmacariyaṃ cariyati bhāviyatīti.

Having thus shown the round of existence, now to show that which is free from the round, it is said: 'This holy life is lived for the abandonment of existence.' Here, 'for the abandonment of existence' means for the purpose of abandoning states of existence such as the realm of desire. 'Kho' is for emphasis; 'pana' is a particle used to fill out the sentence. 'Idaṃ' is a term indicating what is near and directly perceived. 'Brahmacariya' refers to the path as the holy life. 'Vussati' means it is lived. This is what is said: Indeed, solely for the complete abandonment, through the abandoning of its origin, and for the unreserved relinquishment of states of existence such as the realm of desire, this holy life of the eightfold path—comprising the three aggregates beginning with virtue, which was achieved by me after practicing exceedingly difficult perfections for four incalculable ages and a hundred thousand eons, crushing the heads of the three Māras at the Bodhi-maṇḍa—is practiced and developed.

Evaṃ ariyamaggassa ekaṃseneva niyyānikabhāvaṃ dassetvā idāni aññamaggassa tadabhāvaṃ dassento “ye hi kecī”tiādimāha. Tattha yeti aniyamaniddeso. Hīti nipātamattaṃ. Kecīti ekacce. Padadvayenāpi tathāvādino diṭṭhigatike aniyamato pariyādiyati. Samaṇāti pabbajjūpagamanamattena samaṇā, na samitapāpā. Brāhmaṇāti jātimattena brāhmaṇā, na bāhitapāpā. Vāsaddo vikappattho. Bhavena bhavassa vippamokkhamāhaṃsūti ekacce kāmabhavena rūpabhavena vā sabbabhavato vimuttiṃ saṃsārasuddhiṃ kathayiṃsu.

Having thus shown that the Noble Path is exclusively the way of deliverance, now, to show the absence of this quality in any other path, he begins with 'Whatever ascetics or brahmins...' Here, 'whatever' is an indefinite reference. 'Hi' is merely a particle. 'Some' means certain ones. By these two words, those holding such wrong views are indefinitely included. 'Ascetics' refers to those who are ascetics merely by having undertaken the ascetic life, not because they have pacified evil. 'Brahmins' refers to those who are brahmins merely by birth, not because they have banished evil. The word 'or' is used for alternatives. 'They declared liberation from existence by means of existence' means that some declared liberation from all existence and the purification of saṃsāra by means of the sensual-sphere existence or the form-sphere existence.

Ke panevaṃ vadantīti? Diṭṭhadhammanibbānavādino tesu hi keci “uḷārehi pañcahi kāmaguṇehi samappito attā diṭṭheva dhamme paramaṃ nibbutiṃ patto [M 0.0191] hotī”ti vadanti. Keci “rūpāvacarajjhānesu paṭhamajjhānasamaṅgī…pe… keci “dutiyatatiyacatutthajjhānasamaṅgī attā diṭṭheva dhamme paramaṃ nibbutiṃ patto hotī”ti vadanti. Yathāha –

But who speak thus? Advocates of Nibbāna in this very life. For among them some say, 'The self, furnished with the five excellent sense pleasures, attains supreme Nibbāna here and now.' Some say, 'The self, possessing the first jhāna of the form realm... or the self possessing the second, third, or fourth jhāna, attains supreme Nibbāna here and now.' As it is said:

“Idha[V 0.0171], bhikkhave, ekacco samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā evaṃvādī hoti evaṃdiṭṭhi ‘yato kho bho ayaṃ attā pañcahi kāmaguṇehi samappito’”ti [P 0.0212] (dī. ni. 1.94) vitthāro.

‘Here, mendicants, some ascetic or brahmin is one who speaks thus, who has such a view: “When, good sir, this self is replete with the five strands of sensual pleasure...”’ (Dī. Ni. 1.94), and so on in detail.

Te pana yasmā yāvadatthaṃ pītattā suhitāya jalūkāya viya ruhirapipāsā kāmādisukhehi samappitassa tassa attano kāmesanādayo na bhavissanti, tadabhāve ca bhavassa abhāvoyeva, yasmiṃ yasmiñca bhave ṭhitassa ayaṃ nayo labbhati, tena tena bhavena sabbabhavato vimutti hotīti vadanti, tasmā “bhavena bhavassa vippamokkhamāhaṃsū”ti vuttā. Yesañca “ettakaṃ nāma kālaṃ saṃsaritvā bālā ca paṇḍitā ca pariyosānabhave ṭhatvā saṃsārato vimuccantī”ti laddhi, tepi bhavena bhavassa vippamokkhaṃ vadanti nāma. Vuttañhetaṃ –

They argue thus: Just as for a leech that is well-fed, having drunk its fill, there is no thirst for blood, so for a person who is sated with the pleasures of sensuality and so on, the seeking of sensual pleasures and the like will not arise. In the absence of that, there is simply no more existence. And they say that in whatever existence one is established wherein this principle is obtained, by means of that very existence there is liberation from all existence. Therefore, it is said, 'They declared liberation from existence by means of existence.' And those who hold the doctrine that 'after wandering in saṃsāra for a certain period of time, both fools and the wise, being established in a final existence, are liberated from saṃsāra,' they too, indeed, declare liberation from existence by means of existence. For this has been said:

“Cullāsīti mahākappino satasahassāni yāni bāle ca paṇḍite ca sandhāvitvā saṃsaritvā dukkhassantaṃ karissantī”ti (dī. ni. 1.168).

‘For eighty-four thousand great aeons, fools and the wise alike, having run on and transmigrated, will make an end of suffering’ (Dī. Ni. 1.168).

Atha vā bhavenāti bhavadiṭṭhiyā. Bhavati sassataṃ tiṭṭhatīti pavattanato sassatadiṭṭhi bhavadiṭṭhīti vuccati, bhavadiṭṭhi evettha uttarapadalopena bhavataṇhātiādīsu viya bhavoti vutto. Bhavadiṭṭhivasena ca ekacce bhavavisesaṃyeva kilesānaṃ vūpasantavuttiyā āyuno ca dīghāvāsatāya niccādisabhāvaṃ bhavavimokkhaṃ maññanti, seyyathāpi bako brahmā “idaṃ niccaṃ, idaṃ dhuvaṃ, idaṃ sassataṃ, idaṃ avipariṇāmadhamma”nti (ma. ni. 1.501) avoca. Tesamevaṃ viparītagāhīnaṃ anissaraṇe nissaraṇadiṭṭhīnaṃ kuto bhavavimokkho. Tenāha bhagavā – “sabbe te ‘avippamuttā bhavasmā’ti vadāmī”ti.

Alternatively, 'by existence' (bhavena) means by the view of existence (bhavadiṭṭhiyā). Because it occurs thus: 'It exists, it persists eternally,' the eternalist view is called the view of existence. Here, the view of existence itself, by the elision of the latter word, is called 'bhava,' just as in 'bhavataṇhā' and so on. And by means of the view of existence, some consider a particular existence—due to the tranquil state of the defilements and the long duration of life—to have a permanent nature and so on, and they regard it as liberation from existence. Just as Baka Brahmā declared, 'This is permanent, this is stable, this is eternal, this is not subject to change' (Majjhima Nikāya 1.501). For those who thus grasp pervertedly, holding a view of escape in what is not an escape, how can there be liberation from existence? Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'I declare that all of them are not freed from existence.'

Vibhavenāti ucchedena. Bhavassa nissaraṇamāhaṃsūti sabbabhavato niggamanaṃ nikkhantiṃ saṃsārasuddhiṃ vadiṃsu. Te hi “bhavena bhavassa vippamokkho”ti vadantānaṃ vādaṃ ananujānantā bhavūpacchedena nissaraṇaṃ paṭijāniṃsu. Vibhavenāti vā ucchedadiṭṭhiyā. Vibhavati vinassati ucchijjati attā ca loko [M 0.0192] cāti pavattanato ucchedadiṭṭhi vuttanayena “vibhavo”ti [P 0.0213] vuccati. Ucchedadiṭṭhivasena hi sattā adhimuccitvā tattha tattha uppannā ucchijjanti, sā eva saṃsārasuddhīti ucchedavādino. Vuttañhetaṃ –

'By non-existence' (vibhavenā) means by annihilation. They spoke of the escape from existence as the departure, the going out from all existence, the purification of saṃsāra. For they, not approving the doctrine of those who say, 'There is liberation from existence by means of existence,' professed that escape is through the cutting off of existence. Alternatively, 'by non-existence' (vibhavenā) means by the view of annihilation. Because it occurs thus: 'The self and the world cease to exist, perish, are cut off,' the annihilationist view, in the way described, is called 'vibhava.' For by means of the annihilationist view, beings become convinced that beings who have arisen here and there are cut off, and that this itself is the purification of saṃsāra—so say the annihilationists. And it is said:

“Yato kho bho ayaṃ attā rūpī cātumahābhūtiko…pe… nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ [V 0.0172] upasampajja viharati, ettāvatā kho bho ayaṃ attā sammā samucchinno hotī”ti (dī. ni. 1.85).

‘Sirs, when this self, which is possessed of form and composed of the four great elements... having attained the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, abides therein, by this much, sirs, this self is rightly and completely cut off.’

Tathā –

Likewise—

“Natthi, mahārāja, dinnaṃ, natthi yiṭṭhaṃ natthi hutaṃ…pe… bāle ca paṇḍite ca kāyassa bhedā ucchijjanti vinassanti na honti paraṃ maraṇā”ti ca (dī. ni. 1.171).

‘Great king, there is nothing given, nothing offered, nothing sacrificed... fools and wise alike, with the breakup of the body, are cut off, perish, and do not exist after death.’

Tesampi evaṃ viparītagāhīnaṃ kuto bhavanissaraṇaṃ. Tenāha bhagavā – “sabbe te ‘anissaṭā bhavasmā’ti vadāmī”ti. Na hi ariyamaggabhāvanāya anavasesakilesaṃ asamugghātetvā kadācipi bhavato nissaraṇavimutti sambhavati. Tathā hi tesaṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ yathābhūtāvabodhābhāvato “atthi natthī”ti antadvayanipatitānaṃ taṇhādiṭṭhivasena samparitasitavipphanditamattaṃ, yato te diṭṭhigatikā pavattihetūsupi sammūḷhā sakkāyabhūmiyaṃ sunikhāte viparītadassanathambhe taṇhābandhanena baddhā gaddūlabandhanā viya sā na vijahanti bandhanaṭṭhānaṃ, kuto nesaṃ vimokkho?

For them, too, who grasp thus pervertedly, how can there be an escape from existence? Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'I declare that all of them are not released from existence.' For without having uprooted the defilements without remainder through the cultivation of the noble path, escape and liberation from existence is never possible. Indeed, for those ascetics and brahmins, due to their lack of understanding things as they really are, having fallen into the two extremes of 'it is' and 'it is not,' there is merely agitation and trembling all around by the power of craving and views. Since those adherents of views are deluded even about the causes of continued existence, bound by the bond of craving to the pillar of perverted view firmly planted in the ground of identity-view, they are like a dog tied to a post and do not leave the place of bondage. How can there be liberation for them?

Ye pana catusaccavibhāvanena pavattiādīsu asammohato taṃ antadvayaṃ anupagamma majjhimaṃ paṭipadaṃ samāruḷhā, tesaṃyeva bhavavippamokkho nissaraṇañcāti dassento satthā “upadhiṃ hī”tiādimāha. Tattha upadhinti khandhādiupadhiṃ. Hīti nipātamattaṃ. Paṭiccāti nissāya, paccayaṃ katvā. Dukkhanti jātiādi dukkhaṃ. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Yatthime diṭṭhigatikā vimokkhasaññino, tattha khandhakilesābhisaṅkhārūpadhayo adhigatā, kuto tattha dukkhanissaraṇaṃ? Yatra hi kilesā, tatrābhisaṅkhārasambhavato bhavapabandhassa avicchedoyevāti vaṭṭadukkhassa anivatti. Tena vuttaṃ – “upadhiñhi paṭicca dukkhamidaṃ sambhotī”ti.

But as for those who, through the discernment of the four truths, without delusion regarding continued existence and so on, not approaching the two extremes, have ascended the middle path—showing that for them alone there is liberation and escape from existence, the Teacher said, 'For dependent on the substrates...' and so on. Herein, 'substrates' (upadhi) means the substrates of the aggregates and so on. 'For' (hi) is a mere particle. 'Dependent on' (paṭicca) means relying on, having made a condition. 'Suffering' (dukkha) means the suffering of birth and so on. What is meant by this? Where these adherents of views perceive liberation, there the substrates of the aggregates, defilements, and formations are acquired. How can there be an escape from suffering there? For where there are defilements, due to the arising of formations, the continuity of existence is indeed unbroken; thus there is no cessation of the suffering of the cycle. Therefore it is said: 'For dependent on the substrates, this suffering comes to be.'

Idāni [M 0.0193] yaṃ paramatthato dukkhassa nissaraṇaṃ, taṃ dassetuṃ, “sabbupādānakkhayā natthi dukkhassa sambhavo”ti vuttaṃ. Tattha sabbupādānakkhayāti kāmupādānaṃ diṭṭhupādānaṃ sīlabbatupādānaṃ attavādupādānanti sabbesaṃ imesaṃ catunnampi upādānānaṃ ariyamaggādhigamena [P 0.0214] anavasesappahānato. Tattha diṭṭhupādānaṃ sīlabbatupādānaṃ attavādupādānanti imāni tīṇi upādānāni sotāpattimaggena khīyanti, anuppattidhammataṃ āpajjanti. Kāmupādānaṃ apāyagamanīyaṃ [V 0.0173] paṭhamena, kāmarāgabhūtaṃ bahalaṃ dutiyena, sukhumaṃ tatiyena, rūparāgārūparāgappahānaṃ catutthenāti catūhipi maggehi khīyati, anuppattidhammataṃ āpajjatīti veditabbaṃ. Natthi dukkhassa sambhavoti evaṃ sabbaso upādānakkhayā tadekaṭṭhatāya sabbassapi kilesagaṇassa anuppādanato appamattakassapi vaṭṭadukkhassa sambhavo pātubhāvo natthi.

Now, to show what is in the ultimate sense the escape from suffering, it is said, “With the destruction of all clinging, there is no arising of suffering.” Herein, “the destruction of all clinging” means the complete abandonment without remainder of all four kinds of clinging—clinging to sensual pleasures, to views, to rites and rituals, and to the doctrine of self—through the attainment of the noble path. Among these, clinging to views, to rites and rituals, and to the doctrine of self are destroyed by the path of stream-entry; they attain the state of having the nature of non-arising. Clinging to sensual pleasures that leads to the planes of misery is destroyed by the first path; the gross form which is sensual lust by the second path; the subtle form by the third path; and that which pertains to lust for form and the formless is abandoned by the fourth path. Thus it should be understood that it is destroyed by the four paths and attains the state of having the nature of non-arising. “There is no arising of suffering” means that with the complete destruction of clinging, and by the unified nature of that path, due to the non-arising of the entire host of defilements, there is no arising or manifestation of even the slightest suffering of the cycle.

Evaṃ bhagavā hetunā saddhiṃ pavattiṃ nivattiñca dassetvā “imaṃ nayaṃ ajānanto ayaṃ sattaloko vaṭṭatopi sīsaṃ na ukkhipatī”ti dassento “lokamimaṃ passā”tiādimāha. Tattha lokamimaṃ passāti attano buddhacakkhunā paccakkhato visayabhāvassa upagatattā “lokamimaṃ passā”ti bhagavādassanakiriyāya niyojento attānamevālapati. Puthūti bahū, visuṃ visuṃ vā. Avijjāya paretāti “dukkhe aññāṇa”ntiādinā (dha. sa. 1106; vibha. 226) nayena vuttāya catusaccapaṭicchādikāya avijjāya abhibhūtā. Bhūtāti kammakilesehi jātā nibbattā. Bhūtaratāti bhūtesu mātāpituputtadārādisaññāya aññasattesu taṇhāya ratā, bhūte vā khandhapañcake aniccāsubhadukkhānattasabhāve taṃsabhāvānavabodhato itthipurisādiparikappavasena niccādivasena attattaniyagāhavasena ca abhiratā. Bhavā aparimuttāti yathāvuttena taṇhādiṭṭhigāhena bhavato saṃsārato na parimuttā.

Thus, the Blessed One, having shown arising and cessation together with their cause, and demonstrating that “this world of beings, not knowing this method, does not lift its head even from the round of rebirth,” spoke the words beginning with “See this world.” Therein, regarding “See this world”—because it has become the direct object of his own Buddha-eye, the Blessed One, enjoining the act of seeing, addresses himself. ‘Puthū’ means many, or separately. ‘Overcome by ignorance’ means overwhelmed by the ignorance that conceals the Four Truths, as stated in the way of “ignorance concerning suffering,” etc. ‘Beings’ means born or produced by kamma and defilements. ‘Delighting in what has come to be’ means they are attached to other beings through craving, perceiving them as mother, father, son, wife, etc.; or, they greatly delight in the five aggregates, which are by nature impermanent, impure, suffering, and not-self, due to not understanding their true nature, imagining them as permanent, etc., and clinging to them as ‘I’ or ‘mine.’ ‘Not freed from existence’ means they are not liberated from the round of existence due to grasping with craving and wrong view, as described.

Ettha ca “lokamima”nti paṭhamaṃ tāva sakalampi sattanikāyaṃ sāmaññato ekattaṃ upanento ekavacanena anodhiso gahaṇaṃ dīpetvā “svāyaṃ loko bhavayonigatiṭhitisattāvāsādivasena ceva tatthāpi taṃtaṃsattanikāyādivasena ca anekabhedabhinno paccekaṃ mayā volokito”ti attano buddhacakkhuñāṇānubhāvaṃ pakāsento satthā puna vacanabhedaṃ katvā bahuvacanena odhiso gahaṇaṃ dīpeti “puthū [M 0.0194] avijjāya paretā bhūtā”tiādinā. Evañca katvā “lokamima”nti upayogavacanaṃ katvā “avijjāya paretā”tiādinā paccattabahuvacananiddesopi [P 0.0215] aviruddho hoti bhinnavākyattā. Keci pana ekavākyatādhippāyena “avijjāya paretaṃ bhūtaṃ bhūtarataṃ bhavā aparimutta”nti paṭhanti, vibhattibhedavaseneva pana purāṇapāṭho.

And here, with “this world,” first, by bringing the entire collection of beings to a state of oneness in a general sense, the Teacher shows an indiscriminate grasp with the singular number. Then, proclaiming the power of his Buddha-eye-knowledge—that “this world, divided into many kinds by way of existences, origins, destinations, stations, abodes of beings, and so on, and therein also by way of this or that collection of beings, has been individually surveyed by me”—he again makes a distinction in grammatical number and shows a discriminate grasp with the plural number, with the words “many are overcome by ignorance, beings,” and so on. And having done so, by making “this world” a term in the accusative case, the designation in the nominative plural with “overcome by ignorance,” etc., is not contradictory, because they are in separate clauses. Some, however, with the intention of a single sentence, recite it as ‘avijjāya paretaṃ bhūtaṃ bhūtarataṃ bhavā aparimuttaṃ’; but the ancient reading stands precisely because of the difference in case endings.

Idāni yena upāyena bhavavippamokkho hoti, taṃ sabbaṃ titthiyānaṃ avisayabhūtaṃ buddhagocaraṃ vipassanāvīthiṃ dassento “ye hi kecī”tiādimāha. Tattha ye hi keci bhavāti kāmabhavādi saññībhavādi ekavokārabhavādivibhāgena nānābhedabhinnā sātavanto vā asātavanto vā dīghāyukā vā ittarakkhaṇā vā ye hi keci bhavā. Sabbadhīti uddhaṃ adho tiriyanti ādivibhāgena sabbattha. Sabbatthatāyāti saggāpāyamanussādivibhāgena. Sabbe tetiādīsu [V 0.0174] sabbepi te bhavā rūpavedanādidhammā hutvā abhāvaṭṭhena aniccā, udayabbayapaṭipīḷitattā dukkhā, jarāya maraṇena cāti dvidhā vipariṇāmetabbatāya vipariṇāmadhammā. Itisaddo ādiattho pakārattho vā, tena anattalakkhaṇampi saṅgahetvā avasavattanaṭṭhena anattā, vipariṇāmadhammatāya vā avasavattanaṭṭhena anattāti vuttā.

Now, to show the course of insight—the means by which liberation from existence occurs, which is entirely beyond the domain of the sectarians and is the province of a Buddha—the Blessed One spoke the words beginning with, “Whatever existences there may be.” Therein, “whatever existences there may be” refers to any existences whatsoever, divided into various kinds such as sensual existence, existence with perception, and one-constituent existence; whether they are pleasant or unpleasant, long-lived or short-lived. ‘Sabbadhi’ means everywhere, by division into above, below, and across. ‘Sabbatthatāya’ means in all states, by division into heavens, states of deprivation, the human world, and so on. In “all these,” and so on, all those existences, being phenomena such as form and feeling, are impermanent in the sense of non-existence; they are suffering because they are oppressed by arising and passing away; and they are of a nature to change, in two ways: through aging and through death. The word ‘iti’ has the meaning of ‘and so on’ or ‘in this manner.’ By this, the characteristic of not-self is also included: they are called not-self in the sense of being uncontrollable, or they are called not-self because, being of a nature to change, they are in that sense uncontrollable.

Evaṃ lakkhaṇattayapaṭivijjhanākārena etaṃ bhavasaṅkhātaṃ khandhapañcakaṃ yathābhūtaṃ aviparītaṃ sammappaññāya sammā ñāyena vipassanāsahitāya maggapaññāya passato pariññābhisamayādivasena paṭivijjhato “bhavo nicco”ti ādinayappavattā bhavesu taṇhā pahīyati, aggamaggappattisamakālameva anavasesaṃ nirujjhati, ucchedadiṭṭhiyā sabbaso pahīnattā vibhavaṃ vicchedaṃ nābhinandati na pattheti. Evaṃbhūtassa tassa yā kāmataṇhādivasena aṭṭhasatabhedā avatthādivibhāgena anantabhedā ca, tāsaṃ sabbaso sabbappakārena taṇhānaṃ khayā pahānā, tadekaṭṭhatāya sabbassapi saṃkilesapakkhassa [P 0.0216] asesaṃ nissesaṃ virāgena ariyamaggena yo anuppādanirodho, taṃ nibbānanti.

Thus, for one who sees this five-aggregate group called ‘existence’ as it truly is, without distortion, with right wisdom and right method—that is, with path-wisdom accompanied by insight—and who penetrates it in the manner of the three characteristics by means of full understanding, realization, and so on, the craving for existences, which proceeds in the manner of “existence is permanent,” etc., is abandoned. At the very moment of attaining the highest path, it ceases completely without remainder. Because the annihilationist view is completely abandoned, one does not delight in or long for non-existence or cessation. For such a one, whatever cravings there are—the one hundred and eight kinds by way of sensual craving, etc., and the endless kinds by division into states, etc.—through the destruction and abandonment of all those cravings in every way, and synonymous with that, through the complete and utter fading away of the entire faction of defilements by means of the noble path, that which is the non-arising-cessation, that is called Nibbāna.

Evaṃ taṇhāya pahānamukhena saupādisesanibbānaṃ dassetvā idāni anupādisesanibbānaṃ dassento “tassa nibbutassā”tiādimāha. Tassattho [M 0.0195] – yo so sabbaso taṇhānaṃ khayā kilesaparinibbānena nibbuto vuttanayena bhinnakileso khīṇāsavabhikkhu, tassa nibbutassa bhikkhuno anupādā upādānābhāvato kilesābhisaṅkhāramārānaṃ vā aggahaṇato punabbhavo na hoti, āyatiṃ paṭisandhivasena upapattibhavo natthi. Evaṃbhūtena ca tena abhibhūto māro, ariyamaggakkhaṇe kilesamāro abhisaṅkhāramāro devaputtamāro ca carimakacittakkhaṇe khandhamāro maccumāro cāti pañcavidho māro abhibhūto parājito, puna sīsaṃ ukkhipituṃ appadānena nibbisevano kato, yato tena vijito saṅgāmo mārehi tattha tattha pavattito. Evaṃ vijitasaṅgāmo pana iṭṭhādīsu sabbesu vikārābhāvena tādilakkhaṇappattiyā tādī arahā sabbabhavāni yathāvuttabhede sabbepi bhave upaccagā samatikkanto, na yattha katthaci saṅkhaṃ upeti, aññadatthu anupādāno viya jātavedo parinibbānato uddhaṃ apaññattikova hotīti. Iti bhagavā imaṃ mahāudānaṃ anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā kūṭaṃ gahetvā niṭṭhapesi.

Thus, having shown Nibbāna-with-remainder primarily through the abandonment of craving, he now shows Nibbāna-without-remainder, speaking the words beginning with, “For that extinguished one.” The meaning is this: for that monk who is extinguished through the complete destruction of cravings, by the final quenching of defilements—the Arahant whose defilements are shattered and taints destroyed, as described—for that extinguished monk, there is no further becoming, because there is no more clinging, or because he does not grasp the Māras of defilements and formations. In the future, there is no existence through rebirth-linking. And by such a one, Māra has been overcome. At the moment of the noble path, the Māra of defilements, the Māra of formations, and the Māra of the devaputta are overcome; and at the moment of the final consciousness, the Māra of the aggregates and the Māra of death are overcome. Thus the fivefold Māra is overcome and defeated. By giving him no chance to raise his head again, he is rendered powerless. For the war waged by the Māras in various spheres has been won by him. Such a one, a victor in battle, an Arahant who is ‘Such’—having attained the characteristic of one who is imperturbable through the absence of any reaction to all desirable things and so on—has gone beyond, has transcended all existences, all the kinds of becoming as previously described. He does not come into reckoning anywhere. Rather, like a fire without fuel, after final Nibbāna he becomes undesignatable. Thus the Blessed One concluded this great inspired utterance, bringing it to its climax with the Nibbāna-element without remainder.

Dasamasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the tenth sutta is finished.

Niṭṭhitā ca nandavaggavaṇṇanā.

And the commentary on the Nanda chapter is finished.

4. Meghiyavaggo

4. The Meghiya Chapter

1. Meghiyasuttavaṇṇanā

1. The Explanation of the Meghiya Sutta

31. Meghiyavaggassa [V 0.0175][M 0.0196][P 0.0217] paṭhame cālikāyanti evaṃ nāmake nagare. Tassa kira nagarassa dvāraṭṭhānaṃ muñcitvā samantato calapaṅkaṃ hoti, taṃ calapaṅkaṃ nissāya ṭhitattā olokentānaṃ calamānaṃ viya upaṭṭhāti, tasmā “cālikā”ti vuccati. Cālike pabbateti tassa nagarassa avidūre eko pabbato, sopi sabbasetattā kālapakkhauposathe olokentānaṃ calamāno viya upaṭṭhāti, tasmā “cālikapabbato”ti saṅkhaṃ gato. Tattha bhagavato mahantaṃ vihāraṃ kārayiṃsu, bhagavā tadā taṃ nagaraṃ gocaragāmaṃ katvā tasmiṃ cālikapabbatamahāvihāre viharati. Tena vuttaṃ – “cālikāyaṃ viharati cālike pabbate”ti. Meghiyoti tassa therassa nāmaṃ. Upaṭṭhāko hotīti paricārako hoti. Bhagavato hi paṭhamabodhiyaṃ upaṭṭhākā anibaddhā ahesuṃ, ekadā nāgasamālo, ekadā nāgito, ekadā upavāno, ekadā sunakkhatto, tadāpi meghiyattherova upaṭṭhāko. Tenāha – “tena kho pana samayena āyasmā meghiyo bhagavato upaṭṭhāko hotī”ti.

31. In the first sutta of the Meghiya Chapter, there is a city named Cālikā. It is said that, apart from the location of its gate, that city was entirely surrounded by shifting mud.
