Because it was situated by this unstable mud, when people looked at it, it appeared to move; hence it was called 'Cālikā.' Near that city was a mountain, which also appeared to move when viewed on the Uposatha day of the dark fortnight due to its being entirely white. Thus, it came to be known as 'Cālikapabbata.' There, a great monastery was built for the Blessed One. The Blessed One, having made that city his alms-resort village, was then residing in the great monastery on Cālikapabbata. Therefore, it is said: 'He dwells at Cālikā, on the Cālikā Mountain.' Meghiya is the name of that elder. 'He is an attendant' means he was a caretaker. Indeed, in the early period after the Buddha's enlightenment, his attendants were not permanently assigned—sometimes it was Nāgasamāla, sometimes Nāgita, sometimes Upavāna, sometimes Sunakkhatta, and at that time, it was the elder Meghiya who was the attendant. Hence it is said: 'At that time, the Venerable Meghiya was the Blessed One’s attendant.'

Jantugāmanti evaṃ nāmakaṃ tasseva vihārassa aparaṃ gocaragāmaṃ. “Jattugāma”ntipi pāṭho. Kimikāḷāyāti kāḷakimīnaṃ bahulatāya “kimikāḷā”ti laddhanāmāya nadiyā. Jaṅghavihāranti ciranisajjāya jaṅghāsu uppannakilamathavinodanatthaṃ vicaraṇaṃ. Pāsādikanti aviraḷarukkhatāya siniddhapattatāya ca passantānaṃ pasādamāvahatīti pāsādikaṃ. Sandacchāyatāya [P 0.0218] manuññabhūmibhāgatāya ca manuññaṃ. Anto paviṭṭhānaṃ pītisomanassajananaṭṭhena cittaṃ rametīti ramaṇīyaṃ. Alanti pariyattaṃ, yuttantipi attho. Padhānatthikassāti yogena bhāvanāya atthikassa. Padhānāyāti samaṇadhammakaraṇāya. Āgaccheyyāhanti āgaccheyyaṃ ahaṃ. Therena kira pubbe taṃ ṭhānaṃ anupaṭipāṭiyā pañca jātisatāni raññā eva satā anubhūtaṃ uyyānaṃ ahosi, tenassa diṭṭhamatteyeva tattha viharituṃ cittaṃ nami. Āgamehi tāvāti [M 0.0197] satthā therassa vacanaṃ sutvā upadhārento “na tāvassa ñāṇaṃ paripākaṃ gata”nti ñatvā paṭikkhipanto evamāha[V 0.0176]. Ekakamhi tāvāti idaṃ panassa “evamayaṃ gantvāpi kamme anipphajjamāne nirāsaṅko hutvā pemavasena puna āgacchissatī”ti cittamaddavajananatthaṃ āha. Yāva aññopi koci bhikkhu āgacchatīti añño koci bhikkhu mama santikaṃ yāva āgacchati, tāva āgamehīti attho. “Koci bhikkhu dissatī”tipi pāṭho. “Āgacchatū”tipi paṭhanti, tathā “dissatū”ti.

Jantugāma is the name of another alms-resort village for that same monastery. There is also the reading 'Jattugāma.' 'Kimikāḷā' refers to a river that received its name 'Kimikāḷā' due to the abundance of black insects. 'Jaṅghavihāra' means wandering about to relieve the fatigue in the legs caused by prolonged sitting. 'Pāsādika' means it inspires serenity in those who see it due to its dense trees and glossy leaves. 'Manuñña' means charming due to its continuous shade and pleasant stretch of ground. 'Ramaṇīya' means it delights the mind by generating joy and gladness in those who enter. 'Alaṃ' means sufficient; it also means suitable. 'Padhānatthikassa' means for one who has need of exertion and mental development. 'Padhānāya' means for the undertaking of the ascetic's duties. 'Āgaccheyyāhaṃ' means 'I would go.' It is said that this place had previously been a pleasure garden experienced by the elder for five hundred births in succession while he was a king; therefore, as soon as he saw it, his mind inclined to dwell there. 'Āgamehi tāva'—the Teacher, hearing the elder’s words and reflecting, knew, 'His knowledge has not yet reached maturity,' and thus rejecting the request, he said this. 'Ekakamhi tāva'—this he said to generate pliancy in his mind, thinking, 'In this way, even if he goes and his practice is not accomplished, he will become free from anxiety and return again out of affection.' 'Yāva aññopi koci bhikkhu āgacchati' means, 'Wait until some other monk comes to me.' There is also the reading, 'Koci bhikkhu dissati' (some monk is seen). They also read 'Āgacchatu' (let him come), and likewise 'Dissatu' (let him be seen).

Natthi kiñci uttari karaṇīyanti catūsu saccesu catūhi maggehi pariññādīnaṃ soḷasannaṃ kiccānaṃ katattā, abhisambodhiyā vā adhigatattā tato aññaṃ uttari karaṇīyaṃ nāma natthi. Natthi katassa vā paticayoti katassa vā puna paticayopi natthi. Na hi bhāvitamaggo puna bhāvīyati, pahīnakilesānaṃ vā puna pahānena kiccaṃ atthi. Atthi katassa paticayoti mayhaṃ santāne nipphāditassa sīlādidhammassa ariyamaggassa anadhigatattā tadatthaṃ puna vaḍḍhanasaṅkhāto paticayo atthi, icchitabboti attho. Padhānanti kho meghiya vadamānaṃ kinti vadeyyāmāti “samaṇadhammaṃ karomī”ti taṃ vadamānaṃ mayaṃ aññaṃ kiṃ nāma vadeyyāma?

'There is nothing further to be done' means that because the sixteen functions—such as full understanding—regarding the four truths have been accomplished by means of the four paths, or because perfect enlightenment has been attained, there is nothing further to be done beyond that. 'There is no accumulation for what has been done' means there is no further accumulation for what has been done. For the developed path is not developed again, nor is there any task in re-abandoning defilements that have already been abandoned. 'There is accumulation for what has been done' means: because the noble path—the qualities of virtue and so on produced in my mental continuum—has not been attained, there is still an accumulation for that purpose, which is known as further growth. This is what is to be desired; that is the meaning. 'As for striving, Meghiya, what could we say to one who speaks thus?' means: to one who says, 'I will perform the ascetic's duty,' what else could we say?

Divāvihāraṃ [P 0.0219] nisīdīti divāvihāratthāya nisīdi. Nisinno ca yasmiṃ maṅgalasilāpaṭṭe pubbe anupaṭipāṭiyā pañca jātisatāni rājā hutvā uyyānakīḷaṃ kīḷanto vividhanāṭakaparivāro nisinnapubbo, tasmiṃyeva ṭhāne nisīdi. Athassa nisinnakālato paṭṭhāya samaṇabhāvo vigato viya ahosi, rājavesaṃ gahetvā nāṭakaparivāraparivuto setacchattassa heṭṭhā mahārahe pallaṅke nisinno viya jāto. Athassa taṃ sampattiṃ assādayato kāmavitakko udapādi. So tasmiṃyeva khaṇe sahoḍḍhaṃ gahite dve core ānetvā purato ṭhapite viya addasa. Tesu ekassa vadhaṃ āṇāpanavasena byāpādavitakko uppajji, ekassa bandhanaṃ āṇāpanavasena vihiṃsāvitakko, evaṃ so latājālena rukkho viya madhumakkhikāhi madhughātako viya ca akusalavitakkehi parikkhitto samparikiṇṇo ahosi. Taṃ sandhāya “atha kho āyasmato meghiyassā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

'He sat down for the day's abiding' means he sat down for the purpose of the day's abiding. And as he sat there, on that very auspicious stone slab where he had previously sat as a king for five hundred lifetimes in unbroken succession, enjoying the pleasures of the park surrounded by various entertainers, he sat down in that very place. Then, from the moment he sat down, his state as a recluse seemed to vanish. Having taken on royal attire and surrounded by a troupe of performers, he became as if seated beneath a white parasol on a magnificent couch. Then, as he savored that prosperity, a thought of sensual desire arose in him. At that very moment, he saw, as if brought before him, two thieves who had been captured along with their stolen goods. Regarding one, a thought of ill will arose by way of commanding his execution. Regarding the other, a thought of cruelty arose by way of commanding his imprisonment. Thus, like a tree entangled in vines or a honey-destroyer by honeybees, he became enveloped and overwhelmed by unwholesome thoughts. With reference to this, it is said: 'Then, the Venerable Meghiya...' and so on.

Acchariyaṃ [M 0.0198] vata bhoti garahaṇacchariyaṃ nāma kiretaṃ yathā āyasmā ānando bhagavato valiyagattaṃ disvā avoca “acchariyaṃ, bhante, abbhutaṃ, bhante”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.511). Apare pana “tasmiṃ samaye pupphaphalapallavādīsu lobhavasena kāmavitakko, kharassarānaṃ pakkhiādīnaṃ saddassavanena byāpādavitakko, leḍḍuādīhi tesaṃ paṭibāhanādhippāyena vihiṃsāvitakko, ‘idhevāhaṃ vaseyya’nti tattha sāpekkhatāvasena kāmavitakko, vanacarake tattha tattha [V 0.0177] disvā tesu cittadubbhanena byāpādavitakko, tesaṃ viheṭhanādhippāyena vihiṃsāvitakko tassa uppajjī”tipi vadanti. Yathā vā tathā vā tassa micchāvitakkuppattiyeva acchariyakāraṇaṃ. Anvāsattāti anulaggā vokiṇṇā. Attani garumhi ca ekattepi bahuvacanaṃ dissati. “Anusanto”tipi pāṭho.

"Indeed, sirs, it is an astonishment, a blameworthy astonishment, it is said, just as the Venerable Ānanda, upon seeing the Blessed One's wrinkled skin, said: 'It is astonishing, venerable sir, it is marvelous, venerable sir!' (Saṃ. Ni. 5.511). Others, however, say: 'At that time, a thought of sensuality arose in him from greed for flowers, fruits, and young leaves; a thought of ill-will arose from hearing the harsh sounds of birds and other creatures; a thought of harm arose from the intention to drive them away with clods of earth and the like; a thought of sensuality arose from attachment to that place with the thought, "May I live right here!"; a thought of ill-will arose from mental aversion upon seeing forest dwellers here and there; a thought of harm arose from the intention to vex them.' In any case, the very arising of wrong thoughts in him was the reason for astonishment. 'Anvāsattā' means attached to, beset by. The plural is also seen for the singular, with reference to oneself and to a respected person. There is also the reading 'Anusanto.'"

Yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamīti evaṃ micchāvitakkehi samparikiṇṇo kammaṭṭhānasappāyaṃ kātuṃ asakkonto “idaṃ vata disvā dīghadassī bhagavā paṭisedhesī”ti sallakkhetvā “imaṃ kāraṇaṃ dasabalassa ārocessāmī”ti nisinnāsanato [P 0.0220] vuṭṭhāya yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami. Upasaṅkamitvā ca “idha mayhaṃ, bhante”tiādinā attano pavattiṃ ārocesi.

Regarding 'He approached the Blessed One': Thus, beset by wrong thoughts and unable to make his meditation practice suitable, he reflected, 'Indeed, it was having foreseen this that the far-seeing Blessed One forbade it.' Then, thinking, 'I shall report this matter to the One of Ten Powers,' he rose from his seat and approached the Blessed One. Having approached, he reported what had happened to him, beginning with the words, 'Here, venerable sir...'

Tattha yebhuyyenāti bahulaṃ abhikkhaṇaṃ. Pāpakāti lāmakā. Akusalāti akosallasambhūtā. Duggatisampāpanaṭṭhena vā pāpakā, kusalapaṭipakkhatāya akusalā. Vitakketi ūhati ārammaṇaṃ cittaṃ abhiniropetīti vitakko, kāmasahagato vitakko kāmavitakko, kilesakāmasampayutto vatthukāmārammaṇo vitakkoti attho. Byāpādasahagato vitakko byāpādavitakko. Vihiṃsāsahagato vitakko vihiṃsāvitakko. Tesu kāmānaṃ abhinandanavasena pavatto nekkhammapaṭipakkho kāmavitakko, “ime sattā haññantu vā vinassantu vā mā vā ahesu”nti sattesu sampadussanavasena pavatto mettāpaṭipakkho byāpādavitakko, pāṇileḍḍudaṇḍādīhi sattānaṃ viheṭhetukāmatāvasena pavatto karuṇāpaṭipakkho vihiṃsāvitakko.

Herein, 'mostly' means frequently, repeatedly. 'Evil' means base. 'Unwholesome' means arising from unskillfulness. Or, they are 'evil' because they lead to an unhappy destination, and 'unwholesome' because they are the opposite of the wholesome. 'Thought' (vitakka) is so called because it thinks, considers, and applies the mind to an object. A thought accompanied by sensual desire is a sensual thought, meaning a thought conjoined with sensual desire as a defilement and having sensual objects as its resort. A thought accompanied by ill will is a thought of ill will. A thought accompanied by cruelty is a thought of cruelty. Among these, the sensual thought is that which occurs by way of delighting in sensual pleasures and is the opposite of renunciation; the thought of ill will is that which occurs by way of malevolence towards beings, with the thought, 'May these beings be killed or destroyed or cease to exist!', and is the opposite of loving-kindness; the thought of cruelty is that which occurs by way of the desire to vex beings with one's hand, with clods of earth, sticks, and the like, and is the opposite of compassion.

Kasmā panassa bhagavā tattha gamanaṃ anujāni? “Ananuññātopi cāyaṃ maṃ ohāya gacchissateva, ‘paricārakāmatāya maññe bhagavā gantuṃ na detī’ti [M 0.0199] cassa siyā aññathattaṃ. Tadassa dīgharattaṃ ahitāya dukkhāya saṃvatteyyā”ti anujāni.

But why did the Blessed One permit him to go there? (He thought:) 'Even if not permitted, this one will surely leave, abandoning me. And a change of heart might occur in him, thinking, "I suppose the Blessed One does not let me go because he desires an attendant." That would lead to his long-term harm and suffering.' Thus, he permitted it.

Evaṃ tasmiṃ attano pavattiṃ ārocetvā nisinne athassa bhagavā sappāyaṃ dhammaṃ desento “aparipakkāya, meghiya, cetovimuttiyā”tiādimāha. Tattha aparipakkāyāti paripākaṃ appattāya. Cetovimuttiyāti kilesehi cetaso vimuttiyā. Pubbabhāge hi tadaṅgavasena ceva vikkhambhanavasena ca kilesehi cetaso vimutti hoti, aparabhāge samucchedavasena ceva paṭipassaddhivasena ca. Sāyaṃ vimutti heṭṭhā vitthārato kathitāva, tasmā tattha vuttanayena veditabbā. Tattha vimuttiparipācanīyehi dhammehi āsaye paripācite pabodhite vipassanāya maggagabbhaṃ [V 0.0178] gaṇhantiyā paripākaṃ gacchantiyā cetovimutti paripakkā nāma hoti, tadabhāve aparipakkā.

When he had thus informed the Blessed One of what had occurred and had sat down, the Blessed One taught him a suitable teaching, beginning with the words: 'Meghiya, for an immature liberation of mind...' Herein, 'immature' means not having reached maturity. 'Liberation of mind' means the mind's liberation from defilements. For in the preliminary stage, there is liberation of the mind from defilements by way of substitution and by way of suppression; in the later stage, it is by way of eradication and by way of tranquillization. This liberation has already been discussed in detail below, so it should be understood according to the method stated there. In this context, when the underlying disposition has been ripened and awakened by the qualities that bring liberation to maturity, and when insight, by conceiving the embryo of the path, is coming to maturity, the liberation of mind is called 'mature'; in the absence of that, it is 'immature.'

Katame pana vimuttiparipācanīyā dhammā? Saddhindriyādīnaṃ visuddhikaraṇavasena pannarasa dhammā veditabbā. Vuttañhetaṃ –

But what are the qualities that ripen liberation? Fifteen qualities are to be understood as purifying the faculties beginning with the faculty of faith. For it was said:

“Assaddhe puggale parivajjayato, saddhe puggale sevato bhajato payirupāsato, pasādanīye suttante paccavekkhato [P 0.0221] – imehi tīhākārehi saddhindriyaṃ visujjhati.

"By avoiding persons without faith, associating with, cultivating, and attending upon persons with faith, and reflecting on inspiring discourses—through these three means, the faculty of faith is purified."

“Kusīte puggale parivajjayato, āraddhavīriye puggale sevato bhajato payirupāsato, sammappadhāne paccavekkhato – imehi tīhākārehi vīriyindriyaṃ visujjhati.

"By avoiding indolent individuals, associating with, cultivating, and attending upon energetic individuals, and reflecting on right exertions—through these three aspects, the faculty of energy is purified."

“Muṭṭhassatī puggale parivajjayato, upaṭṭhitassatī puggale sevato bhajato payirupāsato, satipaṭṭhāne paccavekkhato – imehi tīhākārehi satindriyaṃ visujjhati.

"By avoiding persons of lost mindfulness, associating with, cultivating, and attending upon persons of established mindfulness, and reflecting on the establishments of mindfulness—by these three ways the faculty of mindfulness is purified."

“Asamāhite puggale parivajjayato, samāhite puggale sevato bhajato payirupāsato, jhānavimokkhe paccavekkhato – imehi tīhākārehi samādhindriyaṃ visujjhati.

"By avoiding persons who are unconcentrated, associating with, cultivating, and attending upon persons who are concentrated, and reflecting on the jhānas and liberations—by these three factors the faculty of concentration is purified."

“Duppaññe puggale parivajjayato, paññavante puggale sevato bhajato payirupāsato, gambhīrañāṇacariyaṃ paccavekkhato – imehi tīhākārehi paññindriyaṃ visujjhati.

"By avoiding unwise persons, associating with, cultivating, and attending upon wise persons, and reflecting on the course of profound knowledge—by these three factors the faculty of wisdom is purified."

“Iti [M 0.0200] ime pañca puggale parivajjayato, pañca puggale sevato bhajato payirupāsato, pañca suttante paccavekkhato – imehi pannarasahi ākārehi, imāni pañcindriyāni visujjhantī”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.185).

"Thus, by avoiding five kinds of persons, by associating with, cultivating, and attending upon five kinds of persons, and by reflecting on five subjects—by these fifteen ways, these five faculties are purified."

Aparepi pannarasa dhammā vimuttiparipācanīyā – saddhāpañcamāni indriyāni, aniccasaññā dukkhasaññā anattasaññā pahānasaññā virāgasaññāti imā pañca nibbedhabhāgiyā [V 0.0179] saññā, kalyāṇamittatā sīlasaṃvaro abhisallekhatā vīriyārambho nibbedhikapaññāti. Tesu vineyyadamanakusalo satthā vineyyassa meghiyattherassa ajjhāsayavasena idha kalyāṇamittatādayo vimuttiparipācanīye dhamme dassento “pañca dhammā paripākāya saṃvattantī”ti vatvā te vitthārento “idha, meghiya, bhikkhu kalyāṇamitto hotī”tiādimāha.

There are also fifteen qualities that ripen liberation: the five faculties beginning with faith; the five perceptions conducive to penetration—impermanence, suffering, non-self, abandonment, and dispassion; and good friendship, restraint in morality, self-effacement, the arousing of energy, and penetrating wisdom. Among these, the Teacher, skilled in taming the trainable, showing the qualities beginning with good friendship that ripen liberation according to the disposition of the venerable Meghiya, said, "Five things lead to maturity," and elaborating on them, he said, "Here, Meghiya, a bhikkhu has good friends..."

Tattha kalyāṇamittoti kalyāṇo bhaddo sundaro mitto etassāti kalyāṇamitto. Yassa sīlādiguṇasampanno “aghassa ghātā, hitassa vidhātā”ti evaṃ sabbākārena upakāro mitto hoti, so puggalo kalyāṇamittova. Yathāvuttehi kalyāṇapuggaleheva sabbiriyāpathesu saha ayati pavattati, na vinā tehīti kalyāṇasahāyo.Kalyāṇapuggalesu eva cittena [P 0.0222] ceva kāyena ca ninnapoṇapabbhārabhāvena pavattatīti kalyāṇasampavaṅko. Padattayena kalyāṇamittasaṃsagge ādaraṃ uppādeti.

Here, "a good friend" means one who has a friend who is good, auspicious, and beautiful. Whoever has a friend endowed with virtues such as morality, a friend who in every way is "a destroyer of harm, a promoter of benefit," that person is indeed a good friend. One who proceeds and fares in all deportments together only with good persons, not without them—thus, a good companion. One who proceeds with good persons with a mind and body inclined, tending, and leaning towards them—thus, a good associate. By these three terms, one generates respect for association with a good friend.

Tatridaṃ kalyāṇamittalakkhaṇaṃ – idha kalyāṇamitto saddhāsampanno hoti sīlasampanno sutasampanno cāgasampanno vīriyasampanno satisampanno samādhisampanno paññāsampanno. Tattha saddhāsampattiyā saddahati tathāgatassa bodhiṃ kammaphalañca, tena sammāsambodhihetubhūtaṃ sattesu hitesitaṃ na pariccajati. Sīlasampattiyā sabrahmacārīnaṃ piyo hoti manāpo garu bhāvanīyo codako pāpagarahī vattā vacanakkhamo, sutasampattiyā saccapaṭiccasamuppādādipaṭisaṃyuttānaṃ gambhīrānaṃ kathānaṃ kattā hoti, cāgasampattiyā appiccho hoti santuṭṭho pavivitto asaṃsaṭṭho, vīriyasampattiyā āraddhavīriyo hoti sattānaṃ hitappaṭipattiyā, satisampattiyā upaṭṭhitassati hoti, samādhisampattiyā avikkhitto [M 0.0201] hoti samāhitacitto, paññāsampattiyā aviparītaṃ jānāti. So satiyā kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ gatiyo samanvesamāno paññāya sattānaṃ hitāhitaṃ yathābhūtaṃ jānitvā, samādhinā tattha ekaggacitto hutvā, vīriyena satte ahitā nisedhetvā hite niyojeti. Tenāha –

Here are the characteristics of a good friend: Here, a good friend is endowed with faith, virtue, learning, generosity, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. In terms of being endowed with faith, they have faith in the enlightenment of the Tathāgata and in kamma and its results; because of this, they do not abandon their desire for the welfare of beings, which is the cause for perfect enlightenment. In terms of being endowed with virtue, they are dear, agreeable, respected, and worthy of cultivation by their fellow practitioners; they are an admonisher, a reprover of evil, one who speaks, and one who is patient in accepting advice. In terms of being endowed with learning, they are a speaker of profound teachings connected with the truths, dependent origination, and the like. In terms of being endowed with generosity, they are of few wants, content, secluded, and unentangled. In terms of being endowed with energy, they have aroused energy for the practice that benefits beings. In terms of being endowed with mindfulness, they have mindfulness established. In terms of being endowed with concentration, they are undistracted and their minds are composed. In terms of being endowed with wisdom, they know things as they are. With mindfulness, they investigate the courses of wholesome qualities; with wisdom, they know what is beneficial and unbeneficial for beings as it is; with concentration, they become one-pointed in mind in that; with energy, they restrain beings from what is unbeneficial and guide them toward what is beneficial. Therefore, it is said:

“Piyo garu bhāvanīyo, vattā ca vacanakkhamo;

Gambhīrañca kathaṃ kattā, no caṭṭhāne niyojaye”ti. (a. ni. 7.37);

"Dear, respected, worthy of cultivation, a speaker, and patient in accepting advice; one who speaks of profound matters, and does not engage one in what is inappropriate."

Ayaṃ paṭhamo dhammo paripākāya saṃvattatīti, ayaṃ kalyāṇamittatāsaṅkhāto brahmacariyavāsassa ādibhāvato, sabbesañca kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ bahukāratāya padhānabhāvato ca imesu pañcasu dhammesu ādito vuttattā paṭhamo anavajjadhammo avisuddhānaṃ saddhādīnaṃ visuddhikaraṇavasena [V 0.0180] cetovimuttiyā paripākāya saṃvattati. Ettha ca kalyāṇamittassa bahukāratā padhānatā ca “upaḍḍhamidaṃ, bhante, brahmacariyassa yadidaṃ kalyāṇamittatā”ti vadantaṃ dhammabhaṇḍāgārikaṃ, “mā hevaṃ, ānandā”ti dvikkhattuṃ paṭisedhetvā, “sakalameva hidaṃ, ānanda, brahmacariyaṃ, yadidaṃ kalyāṇamittatā kalyāṇasahāyatā”tiādisuttapadehi (saṃ. ni. 1.129; 5.2) veditabbā.

This is the first quality that leads to maturity. This, namely good friendship, is the beginning of the holy life, and because it is greatly beneficial for all wholesome qualities and is the principal factor, it is said first among these five qualities as the first blameless quality, conducive to the ripening of the liberation of mind by purifying faith and other qualities that are not yet purified. And here, the great benefit and the principal role of good friendship should be understood through such sutta passages as when the Dhamma-treasurer, saying, "Half of the holy life, venerable sir, is good friendship," was twice refuted, with the words, "Not so, Ānanda! The entire holy life, Ānanda, is good friendship, good companionship," and so forth.

Puna caparanti puna ca aparaṃ dhammajātaṃ. Sīlavāti [P 0.0223] ettha kenaṭṭhena sīlaṃ? Sīlanaṭṭhena sīlaṃ. Kimidaṃ sīlanaṃ nāma? Samādhānaṃ, kāyakammādīnaṃ susīlyavasena avippakiṇṇatāti attho. Atha vā upadhāraṇaṃ, jhānādikusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ patiṭṭhānavasena ādhārabhāvoti attho. Tasmā sīleti sīlatīti vā sīlaṃ. Ayaṃ tāva saddalakkhaṇanayena sīlattho. Apare pana “siraṭṭho sītalaṭṭho sīlaṭṭho saṃvaraṭṭho”ti niruttinayena atthaṃ vaṇṇenti. Tayidaṃ pāripūrito atisayato vā sīlaṃ assa atthīti sīlavā, sīlasampannoti attho.

Furthermore, 'another' (puna caparaṃ) means 'again another' (puna ca aparaṃ) kind of quality. Here, in what sense is it 'virtuous' (sīlavā) or 'virtue' (sīla)? It is virtue in the sense of 'composing' (sīlana). What is this 'composing'? It means composing, the non-scatteredness of bodily actions and so forth by way of good conduct. Or alternatively, it means upholding, the state of being a foundation for wholesome qualities like the jhānas by way of being a support. Therefore, it is virtue because it 'composes' (sīleti) or because it 'upholds' (sīlatī). This, then, is the meaning of virtue according to the method of word analysis. Others, however, explain the meaning by way of etymology as 'the meaning of head (sira), the meaning of coolness (sītala), the meaning of virtue (sīla), the meaning of restraint (saṃvara).' Thus, one who possesses virtue by way of its completeness or its excellence is called 'virtuous' (sīlavā), meaning one endowed with virtue.

Yathā ca sīlavā hoti sīlasampanno, taṃ dassetuṃ “pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvuto”tiādimāha. Tattha pātimokkhanti sikkhāpadasīlaṃ. Tañhi yo naṃ pāti rakkhati, taṃ mokkheti moceti āpāyikādīhi dukkhehīti pātimokkhaṃ. Saṃvaraṇaṃ saṃvaro, kāyavācāhi avītikkamo. Pātimokkhameva [M 0.0202] saṃvaro pātimokkhasaṃvaro, tena saṃvuto pihitakāyavācoti pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvuto, idamassa tasmiṃ sīle patiṭṭhitabhāvaparidīpanaṃ. Viharatīti tadanurūpavihārasamaṅgibhāvaparidīpanaṃ. Ācāragocarasampannoti heṭṭhā pātimokkhasaṃvarassa, upari visesānaṃ yogassa ca upakārakadhammaparidīpanaṃ. Aṇumattesu vajjesu bhayadassāvīti pātimokkhasīlato acavanadhammatāparidīpanaṃ. Samādāyāti sikkhāpadānaṃ anavasesato ādānaparidīpanaṃ. Sikkhatīti sikkhāya samaṅgibhāvaparidīpanaṃ. Sikkhāpadesūti sikkhitabbadhammaparidīpanaṃ.

And to show how one is 'virtuous' (sīlavā) and 'endowed with virtue' (sīlasampanno), he states the passage beginning with 'restrained by the Pātimokkha restraint.' Herein, 'Pātimokkha' means the virtue of the training rules. For that which protects (pāti) one who guards it, and liberates (mokkheti) and frees (moceti) him from sufferings such as those of the lower realms, is called 'Pātimokkha.' Restraining (saṃvaraṇaṃ) is restraint (saṃvaro), meaning non-transgression by body and speech. The Pātimokkha itself is the restraint, hence 'Pātimokkha restraint.' One who is restrained (saṃvuto) by it, with body and speech guarded (pihitakāyavāco), is 'restrained by the Pātimokkha restraint'; this illustrates his established state in that virtue. 'He dwells' (viharati) illustrates his being endowed with a mode of abiding suitable to that. 'Endowed with conduct and resort' (ācāragocarasampanno) illustrates the qualities that are helpful for the Pātimokkha restraint below and for the connection with higher states above. 'Seeing danger in the slightest faults' (aṇumattesu vajjesu bhayadassāvī) illustrates his not falling away from the Pātimokkha virtue. 'Undertaking' (samādāya) illustrates his acceptance of the training rules in their entirety. 'He trains' (sikkhati) illustrates his being endowed with the training. 'In the training rules' (sikkhāpadesu) illustrates the qualities in which he is to be trained.

Aparo nayo – kilesānaṃ balavabhāvato, pāpakiriyāya sukarabhāvato, puññakiriyāya ca dukkarabhāvato bahukkhattuṃ apāyesu patanasīloti pātī, puthujjano. Aniccatāya vā bhavādīsu kammavegakkhitto ghaṭīyantaṃ viya anavaṭṭhānena paribbhamanato gamanasīloti pātī, maraṇavasena vā tamhi tamhi sattanikāye attabhāvassa patanasīloti vā pātī, sattasantāno cittameva vā. Taṃ pātinaṃ saṃsāradukkhato mokkhetīti pātimokkhaṃ. Cittassa [P 0.0224] hi vimokkhena satto “vimutto”ti vuccati. Vuttañhi “cittavodānā sattā visujjhantī”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.100), “anupādāya āsavehi cittaṃ vimutta”nti (mahāva. 28) ca.

Another method: Due to the strength of defilements, the ease of doing evil, and the difficulty of doing good, the ordinary person (puthujjano) tends to fall repeatedly into the lower realms (apāyesu patanasīlo)—hence 'falling' (pātī). Or, due to impermanence, beings tossed by the force of kamma in existences and so forth, wander aimlessly like a potter’s wheel, tending to go (gamanasīlo)—hence 'falling' (pātī). Or, due to death, the individual existence tends to fall (patanasīlo) into various classes of beings—hence 'falling' (pātī); or it is simply the mind, the continuum of beings. That which liberates (mokkheti) those who are liable to fall (pātinaṃ) from the suffering of saṃsāra is called 'Pātimokkha.' For a being is said to be 'liberated' (vimutto) by the liberation of the mind. For it is said: 'Beings are purified by the cleansing of the mind' (SN 3.100), and 'The mind is liberated from the taints through non-clinging' (Mv. 28).

Atha [V 0.0181] vā avijjādihetunā saṃsāre patati gacchati pavattatīti pāti, “avijjānīvaraṇānaṃ sattānaṃ taṇhāsaṃyojanānaṃ sandhāvataṃ saṃsarata”nti (saṃ. ni. 2.124) hi vuttaṃ. Tassa pātino sattassa taṇhādisaṃkilesattayato mokkho etenāti pātimokkho, “kaṇṭhekālo”tiādīnaṃ viya samāsasiddhi veditabbā.

Alternatively, it is 'falling' (pāti) because beings fall (patati), go (gacchati), and continue (pavattati) in saṃsāra due to causes like ignorance. For it is said: 'Beings hindered by ignorance, fettered by craving, run on and transmigrate' (SN 2.124). For such a 'falling' (pāti) being, liberation from the threefold defilements beginning with craving is through this—hence, 'Pātimokkha.' The formation of the compound should be understood like 'kaṇṭhekālo' and similar examples.

Atha vā pāteti vinipāteti dukkhehīti pāti, cittaṃ. Vuttañhi “cittena niyyatī loko, cittena parikassatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 1.62). Tassa pātino mokkho etenāti pātimokkho. Patati vā etena apāyadukkhe saṃsāradukkhe cāti pāti, taṇhādisaṃkilesā. Vuttañhi – “taṇhā janeti purisaṃ (saṃ. ni. 1.55-57), taṇhādutiyo puriso”ti (itivu. 15, 105) cādi. Tato pātito mokkhoti pātimokkho.

Or, 'falling' (pāti) means the mind (cittaṃ), because it causes one to fall (pāteti) and plunge (vinipāteti) into sufferings. For it is said: 'The world is led by the mind, the mind drags it along' (SN 1.62). Liberation from that 'falling' (pāti) is achieved through this—hence, 'Pātimokkha.' Or, 'falling' (pāti) refers to defilements beginning with craving, because through them one falls into the suffering of the lower realms and the suffering of saṃsāra. For it is said: 'Craving gives rise to a person' (SN 1.55-57), 'A person has craving as their companion' (Iti. 15, 105), and so on. Liberation from that 'falling' (pāti) is 'Pātimokkha'.

Atha [M 0.0203] vā patati etthāti pāti, cha ajjhattikabāhirāni āyatanāni. Vuttañhi – “chasu loko samuppanno, chasu kubbati santhava”nti (su. ni. 171). Tato cha ajjhattikabāhirāyatanasaṅkhātapātito mokkhoti pātimokkho. Atha vā pāto vinipāto assa atthīti pātī, saṃsāro. Tato mokkhoti pātimokkho.

Or, 'falling' (pāti) means the six internal and external sense bases (āyatanāni), because one falls therein. For it is said: 'The world arises in the six, in the six it makes connections' (Sn 171). Liberation from that 'falling' (pāti), which is reckoned as the six internal and external sense bases, is 'Pātimokkha.' Or, 'falling' (pātī) means saṃsāra, because falling (pāto) and plunging (vinipāto) exist for it. Liberation from that is 'Pātimokkha'.

Atha vā sabbalokādhipatibhāvato dhammissaro bhagavā patīti vuccati, muccati etenāti mokkho. Patino mokkho tena paññattattāti patimokkho, patimokkho eva pātimokkho. Sabbaguṇānaṃ vā tammūlabhāvato uttamaṭṭhena pati ca, so yathāvuttaṭṭhena mokkho cāti patimokkho, patimokkho eva pātimokkho. Tathā hi vuttaṃ “pātimokkhantiādimetaṃ mukhameta”nti vitthāro.

Alternatively, the Blessed One, being the sovereign of the Dhamma and lord of all the world, is called 'lord' (pati). 'Release' (mokkho) is that by which one is released. Because it is the Lord's release, declared by Him, it is 'patimokkha,' which is indeed 'Pātimokkha.' Or, because it is the root of all virtues, it is 'lord' (pati) in the supreme sense, and it is 'release' (mokkho) in the sense described; hence, 'patimokkha,' which is indeed 'Pātimokkha.' Thus it was said: 'The Pātimokkha is the beginning, this is the principal'—this is the detailed explanation.

Atha vā paiti pakāre, atīti accantatthe nipāto, tasmā pakārehi accantaṃ mokkhetīti pātimokkhaṃ. Idañhi sīlaṃ sayaṃ tadaṅgavasena, samādhisahitaṃ paññāsahitañca vikkhambhanavasena samucchedavasena ca accantaṃ mokkheti mocetīti pātimokkhaṃ. Pati mokkhoti vā patimokkho, tamhā tamhā vītikkamadosato paccekaṃ mokkhoti attho. Patimokkho [P 0.0225] eva pātimokkho. Mokkhoti vā nibbānaṃ, tassa mokkhassa paṭibimbabhūtoti patimokkho. Sīlasaṃvaro hi sūriyassa aruṇuggamanaṃ viya nibbānassa udayabhūto tappaṭibhāgo ca yathārahaṃ saṃkilesanibbāpanato. Patimokkho eva pātimokkho. Pativattati mokkheti [V 0.0182] dukkhanti vā patimokkhaṃ, patimokkhameva pātimokkhanti evaṃ tāvettha pātimokkhasaddassa attho veditabbo.

Or, 'pa' means 'in various ways' (pakāre), and 'ati' is a particle indicating the extreme meaning. Therefore, 'Pātimokkha' means 'it liberates completely in various ways.' For this virtue, by itself by way of its components, and together with concentration and wisdom, liberates completely—either by suppression or by eradication—hence 'Pātimokkha.' Or, 'patimokkha' means 'liberation from each fault' (pati mokkho), meaning liberation individually from each transgression. 'Patimokkha' is indeed 'Pātimokkha.' Or, 'mokkha' means Nibbāna, and 'patimokkha' is its reflection. For restraint in virtue is like the rising of the sun's dawn, being the arising of Nibbāna and its counterpart in extinguishing defilements accordingly. 'Patimokkha' is indeed 'Pātimokkha.' Or, 'patimokkha' means 'it averts (pativattati) and liberates (mokkheti) from suffering.' 'Patimokkha' is indeed 'Pātimokkha.' Thus, the meaning of the term 'Pātimokkha' should be understood in this way.

Saṃvarati pidahati etenāti saṃvaro, pātimokkhameva saṃvaro pātimokkhasaṃvaro. Atthato pana tato tato vītikkamitabbato viratiyo cetanā ca. Tena pātimokkhasaṃvarena upeto samannāgato pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvutoti vutto. Vuttañhetaṃ vibhaṅge –

That by which one restrains (saṃvarati) and closes off (pidahati) is restraint (saṃvaro); the Pātimokkha itself is restraint, hence 'Pātimokkha restraint.' In meaning, however, it refers to abstinences and volition, by way of abstaining from transgressing in various ways. One endowed (upeto) and possessed (samannāgato) of this Pātimokkha restraint is said to be 'restrained by the Pātimokkha restraint.' And this was stated in the Vibhaṅga—

“Iminā [M 0.0204] pātimokkhasaṃvarena upeto hoti samupeto upāgato samupāgato upapanno samupapanno samannāgato, tena vuccati pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvuto”ti (vibha. 511).

'Endowed with this Pātimokkha restraint, fully endowed (samupeto), arrived at (upāgato), fully arrived at (samupāgato), possessed (upapanno), fully possessed (samupapanno), furnished with (samannāgato); therefore, he is called “restrained by the Pātimokkha restraint”' (Vibh. 511).

Viharatīti iriyāpathavihārena viharati irīyati vattati.

'He dwells' (viharati) means he dwells by way of the deportments (iriyāpathavihārena); he moves (irīyati), he proceeds (vattati).

Ācāragocarasampannoti veḷudānādimicchājīvassa kāyapāgabbhiyādīnañca akaraṇena sabbaso anācāraṃ vajjetvā “kāyiko avītikkamo vācasiko avītikkamo kāyikavācasiko avītikkamo”ti evaṃ vuttabhikkhusāruppaācārasampattiyā, vesiyādiagocaraṃ vajjetvā piṇḍapātādiatthaṃ upasaṅkamituṃ yuttaṭṭhānasaṅkhātena gocarena ca sampannattā ācāragocarasampanno.

'Endowed with proper conduct and resort' (ācāragocarasampanno) means that because he entirely avoids improper conduct (anācāraṃ) by not engaging in wrong livelihood beginning with the giving of bamboo, bodily impudence, and so forth, by observing 'no bodily transgression, no verbal transgression, no bodily-verbal transgression' as stated, thus being accomplished in conduct befitting a monk; and because he avoids improper resorts beginning with visiting prostitutes and is accomplished in the proper resort, namely, places suitable for approaching for almsfood and so forth, he is 'endowed with proper conduct and resort'.

Apica yo bhikkhu satthari sagāravo sappatisso sabrahmacārīsu sagāravo sappatisso hirottappasampanno sunivattho supāruto pāsādikena abhikkantena paṭikkantena ālokitena vilokitena samiñjitena pasāritena iriyāpathasampanno indriyesu guttadvāro bhojane mattaññū jāgariyamanuyutto satisampajaññena samannāgato appiccho santuṭṭho pavivitto asaṃsaṭṭho ābhisamācārikesu sakkaccakārī garucittīkārabahulo viharati, ayaṃ vuccati ācārasampanno.

Furthermore, a bhikkhu who is respectful and deferential to the Teacher, respectful and deferential to his fellow monastics, endowed with conscience and shame, well-robed and well-covered, dignified in his going forth and returning, in looking ahead and looking around, in bending and stretching his limbs, perfect in his deportment, guarding the sense doors, moderate in eating, devoted to wakefulness, endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension, of few wants, content, secluded, not mixing closely, diligent in the rules of good conduct, and abounding in reverence and deference—such a one is called 'accomplished in proper conduct.'

Gocaro pana upanissayagocaro ārakkhagocaro upanibandhagocaroti tividho. Tattha yo dasakathāvatthuguṇasamannāgato vuttalakkhaṇo kalyāṇamitto, yaṃ nissāya asutaṃ suṇāti, sutaṃ pariyodāpeti, kaṅkhaṃ vitarati, diṭṭhiṃ ujuṃ karoti, cittaṃ pasādeti, yañca anusikkhanto saddhāya vaḍḍhati[P 0.0226], sīlena, sutena, cāgena, paññāya vaḍḍhati, ayaṃ vuccati upanissayagocaro.

As for a 'domain,' it is threefold: the domain of dependence, the domain of protection, and the domain of being bound to. Here, the good friend endowed with the ten grounds for discourse and the qualities described—relying on whom one hears what has not been heard, clarifies what has been heard, dispels doubt, straightens views, gladdens the mind, and following whose instruction one grows in faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom—this is called the 'domain of dependence.'

Yo [V 0.0183] bhikkhu antaragharaṃ paviṭṭho vīthiṃ paṭipanno okkhittacakkhu yugamattadassāvī cakkhundriyasaṃvutova gacchati, na hatthiṃ olokento, na assaṃ, na rathaṃ, na pattiṃ, na itthiṃ, na purisaṃ olokento, na uddhaṃ olokento, na adho olokento, na disāvidisaṃ pekkhamāno gacchati, ayaṃ ārakkhagocaro.

A bhikkhu who, having entered a village, walks along a street with downcast eyes, seeing only a yoke's length ahead, with his eye faculty restrained, not looking at elephants, horses, chariots, infantry, women, or men, not looking up or down, not gazing around in any direction—this is the domain of protection.

Upanibandhagocaro [M 0.0205] pana cattāro satipaṭṭhānā, yattha bhikkhu attano cittaṃ upanibandhati, vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā –

The 'domain of being bound to,' however, is the four foundations of mindfulness, where a bhikkhu binds his mind. As the Blessed One has said:

“Ko ca, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno gocaro sako pettiko visayo, yadidaṃ cattāro satipaṭṭhānā”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.372).

“And what, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu’s own domain, his ancestral territory? It is the four foundations of mindfulness.” (SN 5.372)

Tattha upanissayagocarassa pubbe vuttattā itaresaṃ vasenettha gocaro veditabbo. Iti yathāvuttāya ācārasampattiyā, imāya ca gocarasampattiyā samannāgatattā ācāragocarasampanno.

Here, since the domain of dependence has been previously stated, the domain in this context should be understood by way of the others. Thus, being endowed with the perfection of conduct as described and with this perfection of domain, he is accomplished in conduct and domain.

Aṇumattesu vajjesu bhayadassāvīti appamattakattā aṇuppamāṇesu assatiyā asañcicca āpannasekhiyaakusalacittuppādādibhedesu vajjesu bhayadassanasīlo. Yo hi bhikkhu paramāṇumattaṃ vajjaṃ aṭṭhasaṭṭhiyojanapamāṇādhikayojanasatasahassubbedhasinerupabbatarājasadisaṃ katvā passati, yopi sabbalahukaṃ dubbhāsitamattaṃ pārājikasadisaṃ katvā passati, ayampi aṇumattesu vajjesu bhayadassāvī nāma. Samādāya sikkhati sikkhāpadesūti yaṃkiñci sikkhāpadesu sikkhitabbaṃ, taṃ sabbena sabbaṃ sabbathā sabbaṃ anavasesaṃ sammā ādiyitvā sikkhati, pavattati paripūretīti attho.

He sees danger in the slightest faults: because he is diligent, he is one whose nature is to see danger in faults of even the slightest measure, such as unintentionally incurring a Sekhiya offense or the arising of unwholesome states of mind from lack of mindfulness. For a bhikkhu who regards even a fault as tiny as an atom to be like Mount Sineru, king of mountains, a hundred thousand and sixty-eight yojanas high, or who sees even the slightest wrong speech to be like a pārājika offense—he too is called one who sees danger in the slightest faults. He trains by undertaking the training rules: this means he properly undertakes and trains in whatever is to be trained in among the training rules, entirely, in every way, completely, without remainder; he practices and fulfills them. This is the meaning.

Abhisallekhikāti ativiya kilesānaṃ sallekhanī, tesaṃ tanubhāvāya pahānāya yuttarūpā. Cetovivaraṇasappāyāti cetaso paṭicchādakānaṃ nīvaraṇānaṃ dūrībhāvakaraṇena cetovivaraṇasaṅkhātānaṃ samathavipassanānaṃ sappāyā, samathavipassanācittasseva vā vivaraṇāya pākaṭīkaraṇāya vā sappāyā upakārikāti cetovivaraṇasappāyā.

Highly conducive to effacement means it effaces defilements to a supreme degree, being the proper means for their attenuation and abandonment. Conducive to mental openness means it is conducive to calm and insight, which are called 'mental openness' because they bring about the removal of the hindrances that cover the mind. Alternatively, it is conducive and helpful to the revealing or making manifest of the mind of calm and insight—thus, it is conducive to mental openness.

Idāni [P 0.0227] yena nibbidādiāvahanena ayaṃ kathā abhisallekhikā cetovivaraṇasappāyā ca nāma hoti, taṃ dassetuṃ “ekantanibbidāyā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha ekantanibbidāyāti ekaṃseneva vaṭṭadukkhato nibbindanatthāya. Virāgāya nirodhāyāti tasseva virajjanatthāya ca nirujjhanatthāya [V 0.0184] ca. Upasamāyāti sabbakilesūpasamāya. Abhiññāyāti sabbassāpi abhiññeyyassa abhijānanāya. Sambodhāyāti catumaggasambodhāya. Nibbānāyāti anupādisesanibbānāya. Etesu hi ādito tīhi padehi vipassanā vuttā, dvīhi maggo, dvīhi nibbānaṃ vuttaṃ. Samathavipassanā ādiṃ [M 0.0206] katvā nibbānapariyosāno ayaṃ sabbo uttarimanussadhammo dasakathāvatthulābhino sijjhatīti dasseti.

Now, to show by what means of bringing about disenchantment and so on this talk is highly conducive to effacement and conducive to mental openness, it is said, "for the sake of complete disenchantment," and so on. Here, "for the sake of complete disenchantment" means solely for the purpose of becoming disenchanted with the suffering of the round of existence. "For the sake of dispassion, for the sake of cessation" means for the purpose of its dispassion and for the purpose of its cessation. "For the sake of peace" means for the pacification of all defilements. "For the sake of direct knowledge" means for the full understanding of all that is to be directly known. "For the sake of enlightenment" means for the enlightenment of the four paths. "For the sake of Nibbāna" means for Nibbāna without remainder of aggregates. Among these, insight is stated by the first three terms, the path by the next two, and Nibbāna by the last two. This shows that all this supramundane Dhamma, beginning with calm and insight and culminating in Nibbāna, is accomplished by one who obtains the ten grounds for discourse.

Idāni taṃ kathaṃ vibhajitvā dassento “appicchakathā”tiādimāha. Tattha appicchoti na iccho, tassa kathā appicchakathā, appicchabhāvappaṭisaṃyuttā kathā vā appicchakathā. Ettha ca atriccho pāpiccho mahiccho appicchoti icchāvasena cattāro puggalā. Tesu attanā yathāladdhena lābhena atitto uparūpari lābhaṃ icchanto atriccho nāma. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ –

Now, analyzing and showing that talk, he begins with "the talk on wanting little." Herein, 'wanting little' means not having wants; talk about that is talk on wanting little, or talk connected with the state of wanting little is talk on wanting little. Here, based on desire, there are four kinds of individuals: the excessively desirous, the evil-desirous, the greatly desirous, and the one who desires little. Among them, one who is not content with the gain he has obtained and desires gain again and again is called the excessively desirous. With reference to this, it is said:

“Catubbhi aṭṭhajjhagamā, aṭṭhabhi cāpi soḷasa;

Soḷasabhi ca dvattiṃsa, atricchaṃ cakkamāsado;

Icchāhatassa posassa, cakkaṃ bhamati matthake”ti. (jā. 1.5.103);

“With four he gained eight, with eight indeed sixteen; with sixteen, thirty-two—he reached the wheel of excessive desire. For a person struck by desire, the wheel spins on his head.” (Jā. 1.5.103)

“Atricchā atilobhena, atilobhamadena cā”ti ca. (jā. 1.2.168);

“Through excessive desire, through excessive greed, and through the intoxication of excessive greed.” (Jā. 1.2.168)

Lābhasakkārasilokanikāmayatāya asantaguṇasambhāvanādhippāyo pāpiccho. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ –

One who, due to desire for gain, honor, and renown, has the intention of being esteemed for non-existent qualities is evil-desirous. With reference to this, it is said:

“Tattha katamā kuhanā? Lābhasakkārasilokasannissitassa pāpicchassa icchāpakatassa paccayappaṭisevanasaṅkhātena vā sāmantajappitena vā iriyāpathassa vā aṭhapanā”tiādi (vibha. 861).

“Here, what is deceit? For one attached to gain, honor, and renown, who is evil-desirous and whose desire is manifest, it is what is known as pretense in the use of requisites, or hinting, or the contriving of deportment.” (Vibh. 861)

Santaguṇasambhāvanādhippāyo [P 0.0228] paṭiggahaṇe amattaññū mahiccho. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ –

One who has the intention of being esteemed for existing qualities and is immoderate in receiving is greatly desirous. With reference to this, it is said:

“Idhekacco saddho samāno ‘saddhoti maṃ jano jānātū’ti icchati, sīlavā samāno ‘sīlavāti maṃ jano jānātū’ti icchatī”tiādi (vibha. 851).

“Here, a certain person, being faithful, desires, ‘Let people know me as faithful.’ Being virtuous, he desires, ‘Let people know me as virtuous,’” and so on (Vibh. 851).

Duttappiyatāya hissa vijātamātāpi cittaṃ gahetuṃ na sakkoti. Tenetaṃ vuccati –

Because of his insatiability, even the mother who bore him cannot capture his mind. Therefore, it is said:

“Aggikkhandho [V 0.0185] samuddo ca, mahiccho cāpi puggalo;

Sakaṭehi paccaye dentu, tayopete atappiyā”ti.

“A mass of fire, the ocean, and a person of great desire; though they be given requisites by the cartload, these three are insatiable.”

Ete [M 0.0207] pana atricchatādayo dose ārakā parivajjetvā santaguṇanigūhanādhippāyo paṭiggahaṇe ca mattaññū appiccho. So attani vijjamānampi guṇaṃ paṭicchādetukāmatāya saddho samāno “saddhoti maṃ jano jānātū”ti na icchati, sīlavā, bahussuto, pavivitto, āraddhavīriyo, upaṭṭhitassati, samāhito, paññavā samāno “paññavāti maṃ jano jānātū”ti na icchati.

But, having from afar avoided these faults such as excessive desire, and with the intention of concealing his own qualities, he is moderate in receiving and of few wants. Being faithful, yet desiring to conceal even the virtue present in himself, he does not wish, “Let people know me as faithful.” Being virtuous, learned, secluded, energetic, with mindfulness established, concentrated, and wise, he does not wish, “Let people know me as wise.”

Svāyaṃ paccayappiccho dhutaṅgappiccho pariyattiappiccho adhigamappicchoti catubbidho. Tattha catūsu paccayesu appiccho paccayadāyakaṃ deyyadhammaṃ attano thāmañca oloketvā sacepi hi deyyadhammo bahu hoti, dāyako appaṃ dātukāmo, dāyakassa vasena appameva gaṇhāti. Deyyadhammo ce appo, dāyako bahuṃ dātukāmo, deyyadhammassa vasena appameva gaṇhāti. Deyyadhammopi ce bahu, dāyakopi bahuṃ dātukāmo, attano thāmaṃ ñatvā pamāṇayuttameva gaṇhāti. Evarūpo hi bhikkhu anuppannaṃ lābhaṃ uppādeti, uppannaṃ lābhaṃ thāvaraṃ karoti, dāyakānaṃ cittaṃ ārādheti. Dhutaṅgasamādānassa pana attani atthibhāvaṃ na jānāpetukāmo dhutaṅgappiccho. Yo attano bahussutabhāvaṃ jānāpetuṃ na icchati, ayaṃ pariyattiappiccho. Yo pana sotāpannādīsu aññataro hutvā sabrahmacārīnampi attano sotāpannādibhāvaṃ jānāpetuṃ na icchati, ayaṃ adhigamappiccho. Evametesaṃ appicchānaṃ yā appicchatā, tassā saddhiṃ sandassanādividhinā anekākāravokāraānisaṃsavibhāvanavasena, tappaṭipakkhassa atricchādibhedassa icchācārassa ādīnavavibhāvanavasena ca pavattā kathā appicchakathā.

This one who has few wishes is fourfold: one who has few wishes regarding requisites, one who has few wishes regarding ascetic practices, one who has few wishes regarding learning, and one who has few wishes regarding attainments. Here, regarding the four requisites, one who has few wishes, having considered the donor, the gift to be given, and his own capacity: even if the gift to be given is abundant, but the giver wishes to give little, he takes only a little out of consideration for the giver. If the gift to be given is little, but the giver wishes to give much, he takes only a little out of consideration for the gift. If both the gift to be given is abundant and the giver wishes to give much, knowing his own capacity, he takes only what is appropriate. Such a bhikkhu generates unarisen gain, makes arisen gain lasting, and pleases the minds of the donors. One who has few wishes regarding ascetic practices, however, does not wish to make known the existence of his undertaking of ascetic practices in himself. One who does not wish to make known his extensive learning has few wishes regarding learning. One who, having become a stream-enterer or the like, does not wish to make known his state as a stream-enterer or the like even to his fellow monastics, has few wishes regarding attainments. Thus, the talk on having few wishes is the discussion that proceeds by explaining the benefits of the quality of having few wishes of those who have few wishes, in various ways, through methods such as showing and so forth, and by explaining the dangers of the conduct of desire, which is its opposite, such as excessive desire and the like.

Santuṭṭhikathāti [P 0.0229] ettha santuṭṭhīti sakena attanā laddhena tuṭṭhi santuṭṭhi. Atha vā visamaṃ paccayicchaṃ pahāya samaṃ tuṭṭhi, santuṭṭhi. Santena vā vijjamānena tuṭṭhi santuṭṭhi. Vuttañcetaṃ –

Here, regarding the talk on contentment, 'contentment' (santuṭṭhi) is satisfaction with what has been obtained by oneself. Alternatively, contentment is even-minded satisfaction, having abandoned the unequal desire for requisites. Or, contentment is satisfaction with what is available. And this was said:

“Atītaṃ nānusocanto, nappajappamanāgataṃ;

Paccuppannena yāpento, santuṭṭhoti pavuccatī”ti.

“Not grieving for the past, not yearning for the future; maintaining himself with the present, he is called contented.”

Sammā vā ñāyena bhagavatā anuññātavidhinā paccayehi tuṭṭhi santuṭṭhi. Atthato itarītarapaccayasantoso[V 0.0186], so dvādasavidho hoti. Kathaṃ[M 0.0208]? Cīvare yathālābhasantoso, yathābalasantoso, yathāsāruppasantosoti tividho, evaṃ piṇḍapātādīsu.

Or, contentment is satisfaction with requisites according to the method rightly permitted by the Blessed One. In essence, it is satisfaction with each and every requisite, which is of twelve kinds. How? Contentment with robes is threefold: contentment according to what is obtained, contentment according to one's strength, and contentment according to suitability. Likewise with almsfood and other requisites.

Tatrāyaṃ pabhedavaṇṇanā – idha bhikkhu cīvaraṃ labhati sundaraṃ vā asundaraṃ vā, so teneva yāpeti, aññaṃ na pattheti, labhantopi na gaṇhāti, ayamassa cīvare yathālābhasantoso. Atha pana pakatidubbalo vā hoti ābādhajarābhibhūto vā, garuṃ cīvaraṃ pārupanto kilamati, so sabhāgena bhikkhunā saddhiṃ taṃ parivattetvā lahukena yāpentopi santuṭṭhova hoti, ayamassa cīvare yathābalasantoso. Aparo paṭṭacīvarādīnaṃ aññataraṃ mahagghacīvaraṃ labhitvā “idaṃ therānaṃ cirapabbajitānaṃ, idaṃ bahussutānaṃ anurūpaṃ, idaṃ gilānānaṃ dubbalānaṃ, idaṃ appalābhīnaṃ vā hotū”ti tesaṃ datvā attanā saṅkārakūṭādito nantakāni uccinitvā saṅghāṭiṃ katvā tesaṃ vā purāṇacīvarāni gahetvā dhārentopi santuṭṭhova hoti, ayamassa cīvare yathāsāruppasantoso.

Herein is the detailed explanation: Here, a bhikkhu obtains a robe, whether beautiful or unattractive, and he maintains himself with just that, not longing for another. Even when obtaining more, he does not take it. This is his contentment with robes according to what is obtained. Then again, if he is naturally weak or afflicted by illness and old age, wearing a heavy robe tires him. He exchanges it with a bhikkhu of similar standing for a lighter one and remains content. This is his contentment with robes according to his strength. Another, upon receiving an expensive robe, such as one of silk or the like, thinks: “This is suitable for elders who have long been ordained, this is appropriate for the learned, this is for the sick or weak, or let this be for those who have little gain.” He gives it to them and instead gathers discarded rags from a refuse heap to make a patched robe, or he takes their old robes and wears them, yet remains content. This is his contentment with robes according to suitability.

Idha pana bhikkhu piṇḍapātaṃ labhati lūkhaṃ vā paṇītaṃ vā, so teneva yāpeti, aññaṃ na pattheti, labhantopi na gaṇhāti, ayamassa piṇḍapāte yathālābhasantoso. Atha pana ābādhiko hoti, lūkhaṃ pakativiruddhaṃ vā byādhiviruddhaṃ vā piṇḍapātaṃ bhuñjitvā gāḷhaṃ rogātaṅkaṃ pāpuṇāti, so sabhāgassa bhikkhuno datvā tassa hatthato sappāyabhojanaṃ bhuñjitvā samaṇadhammaṃ karontopi santuṭṭhova hoti, ayamassa piṇḍapāte yathābalasantoso[P 0.0230]. Aparo bhikkhu paṇītaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ labhati, so “ayaṃ piṇḍapāto cirapabbajitādīnaṃ anurūpo”ti cīvaraṃ viya tesaṃ datvā, tesaṃ vā santakaṃ gahetvā, attanā piṇḍāya caritvā, missakāhāraṃ vā paribhuñjantopi santuṭṭhova hoti. Ayamassa piṇḍapāte yathāsāruppasantoso.

Here, a bhikkhu receives almsfood, whether coarse or fine, and he maintains himself with just that, not longing for anything else. Even when receiving more, he does not take it. This is his contentment with almsfood according to what is received. Then, if he is sick and, having eaten coarse food that is contrary to his constitution or food that is contrary to his illness, he develops a severe affliction of disease, he gives it to a bhikkhu of similar standing, and having eaten suitable food from that bhikkhu's hand, even while practicing the ascetic's duty, he is content. This is his contentment with almsfood according to his strength. Another bhikkhu receives fine almsfood, and thinks, “This almsfood is appropriate for those long gone forth, etc.” So he gives it to them as he would a robe, or takes what belongs to them, and even while wandering for alms himself or eating mixed food, he is content. This is his contentment with almsfood according to suitability.

Idha pana bhikkhuno senāsanaṃ pāpuṇāti manāpaṃ vā amanāpaṃ vā antamaso tiṇakuṭikāpi tiṇasanthārakampi, so teneva santussati, puna aññaṃ sundarataraṃ vā pāpuṇāti, taṃ na gaṇhāti, ayamassa senāsane yathālābhasantoso. Atha pana ābādhiko hoti dubbalo vā, so byādhiviruddhaṃ vā pakativiruddhaṃ vā senāsanaṃ labhati, yatthassa vasato aphāsu hoti, so taṃ sabhāgassa bhikkhuno datvā tassa santake sappāyasenāsane vasitvā samaṇadhammaṃ karontopi santuṭṭhova hoti, ayamassa [M 0.0209] senāsane yathābalasantoso. Aparo sundaraṃ senāsanaṃ pattampi na sampaṭicchati “paṇītasenāsanaṃ pamādaṭṭhāna”nti, mahāpuññatāya vā leṇamaṇḍapakūṭāgārādīni paṇītasenāsanāni labhati, so tāni cīvarādīni viya cirapabbajitādīnaṃ [V 0.0187] datvā yattha katthaci vasantopi santuṭṭhova hoti, ayamassa senāsane yathāsāruppasantoso.

Here, a bhikkhu obtains a dwelling, whether pleasant or unpleasant, even just a grass hut or a grass mat. He is content with that. If he later obtains a more beautiful one, he does not take it. This is his contentment with dwellings according to what is obtained. Then, if he is sick or weak and he receives a dwelling that is unsuitable for his illness or contrary to his constitution—where staying causes him discomfort—he gives it to a bhikkhu of similar standing and stays in a suitable dwelling belonging to that other bhikkhu. Even while practicing the ascetic's duties, he remains content. This is his contentment with dwellings according to his strength. Another, even when obtaining a beautiful dwelling, does not accept it, thinking, “A fine dwelling is a cause for heedlessness.” Or, due to great merit, he may obtain fine dwellings such as caves, pavilions, or gabled halls. But he gives them away, just like robes, to those long-ordained, and remains content wherever he stays. This is his contentment with dwellings according to suitability.

Idha pana bhikkhu bhesajjaṃ labhati lūkhaṃ vā paṇītaṃ vā, so teneva tussati, aññaṃ na pattheti, labhantopi na gaṇhāti, ayamassa gilānapaccaye yathālābhasantoso. Atha pana telena atthiko phāṇitaṃ labhati, so taṃ sabhāgassa bhikkhuno datvā, tassa hatthato telaṃ gahetvā, bhesajjaṃ katvā samaṇadhammaṃ karontopi santuṭṭhova hoti, ayamassa gilānapaccaye yathābalasantoso. Aparo mahāpuñño bahuṃ telamadhuphāṇitādipaṇītabhesajjaṃ labhati, so taṃ cīvarādīni viya cirapabbajitādīnaṃ datvā tesaṃ ābhatena yena kenaci bhesajjaṃ karontopi santuṭṭhova hoti. Yo pana ekasmiṃ bhājane muttaharītakaṃ, ekasmiṃ catumadhuraṃ ṭhapetvā “gaṇhatha, bhante, yadicchasī”ti vuccamāno sacassa tesu aññatarenapi rogo vūpasammati[P 0.0231], “muttaharītakaṃ nāma buddhādīhi vaṇṇitaṃ, pūtimuttabhesajjaṃ nissāya pabbajjā, tattha te yāvajīvaṃ ussāho karaṇīyo”ti (mahāva. 128) vacanamanussaranto catumadhuraṃ paṭikkhipitvā muttaharītakena bhesajjaṃ karonto paramasantuṭṭhova hoti, ayamassa gilānapaccaye yathāsāruppasantoso.

Here, a bhikkhu obtains medicine, whether coarse or refined, and he is content with just that, not desiring anything else. Even when obtaining more, he does not take it. This is his contentment regarding medicinal requisites according to what he receives. Then, one who needs oil obtains molasses. He gives it to a bhikkhu of similar standing, and taking oil from that bhikkhu's hand, preparing the medicine and practicing the renunciate's duty, he remains content. This is his contentment regarding medicinal requisites according to his strength. Another, greatly meritorious, obtains much fine medicine like oil, honey, and molasses. He gives it away just as he would robes, to those long-ordained, and using whatever medicine they bring, he remains content. But one who, when urine-myrobalan is placed in one bowl and the four sweets in another, is told, “Take, venerable sir, whatever you wish,” may find his ailment relieved by either. Remembering the words, “Urine-myrobalan is praised by the Buddhas and others; ordination depends on the medicine of fermented urine—therein, effort should be made throughout one's life,” he rejects the four sweets and prepares the remedy with urine-myrobalan, abiding in supreme contentment. This is his contentment regarding medicinal requisites according to suitability.

So evaṃpabhedo sabbopi santoso santuṭṭhīti pavuccati. Tena vuttaṃ “atthato itarītarapaccayasantoso”ti. Itarītarasantuṭṭhiyā saddhiṃ sandassanādividhinā ānisaṃsavibhāvanavasena, tappaṭipakkhassa atricchatādibhedassa icchāpakatattassa ādīnavavibhāvanavasena ca pavattā kathā santuṭṭhikathā. Ito parāsupi kathāsu eseva nayo, visesamattameva vakkhāma.

Thus, all such distinctions of satisfaction are called contentment. Therefore, it is said, “in essence, satisfaction with each and every requisite.” The talk on contentment is the discussion that proceeds by explaining the benefits of contentment with each and every requisite through methods such as showing and so forth, and by explaining the dangers of the state of being prone to desire, which is its opposite, such as excessive desire and the like. The same method applies to the subsequent discussions as well; we will mention only the differences.

Pavivekakathāti ettha kāyaviveko cittaviveko upadhivivekoti tayo vivekā. Tesu eko gacchati, eko tiṭṭhati, eko nisīdati, eko seyyaṃ kappeti, eko gāmaṃ piṇḍāya pavisati, eko [M 0.0210] paṭikkamati, eko abhikkamati, eko caṅkamaṃ adhiṭṭhāti, eko carati, eko viharatīti evaṃ sabbiriyāpathesu sabbakiccesu gaṇasaṅgaṇikaṃ pahāya vivittavāso kāyaviveko nāma. Aṭṭha samāpattiyo pana cittaviveko nāma. Nibbānaṃ upadhiviveko nāma. Vuttañhetaṃ –

Here, in the talk on seclusion, there are three types of seclusion: bodily seclusion, mental seclusion, and seclusion from the bases of existence. Among these, when one goes, stands, sits, lies down, enters the village for alms, returns, approaches, undertakes walking meditation, walks, or dwells—in all these postures and activities, abandoning the company of a group and dwelling in solitude is called bodily seclusion. The eight attainments are called mental seclusion. Nibbāna is called seclusion from the bases of existence. For it has been said:

“Kāyaviveko ca vivekaṭṭhakāyānaṃ nekkhammābhiratānaṃ, cittaviveko ca parisuddhacittānaṃ paramavodānappattānaṃ, upadhiviveko ca nirupadhīnaṃ puggalānaṃ visaṅkhāragatāna”nti (mahāni. 57).

“Bodily seclusion is for those whose bodies are established in seclusion and who delight in renunciation. Mental seclusion is for those with purified minds, who have attained supreme purification. Seclusion from the bases of existence is for those persons without bases of existence, who have gone to the unconditioned.”

Vivekoyeva [V 0.0188] paviveko, pavivekappaṭisaṃyuttā kathā pavivekakathā.

Seclusion itself is profound seclusion; talk connected with profound seclusion is the talk on seclusion.

Asaṃsaggakathāti ettha savanasaṃsaggo dassanasaṃsaggo samullapanasaṃsaggo sambhogasaṃsaggo kāyasaṃsaggoti pañca saṃsaggā. Tesu idhekacco bhikkhu suṇāti “asukasmiṃ gāme vā nigame vā itthī abhirūpā dassanīyā pāsādikā paramāya vaṇṇapokkharatāya samannāgatā”ti, so taṃ sutvā [P 0.0232] saṃsīdati visīdati, na sakkoti brahmacariyaṃ sandhāretuṃ, sikkhaṃ paccakkhāya hīnāyāvattati, evaṃ visabhāgārammaṇasavanena uppannakilesasanthavo savanasaṃsaggo nāma. Na heva kho bhikkhu suṇāti, apica kho sāmaṃ passati itthiṃ abhirūpaṃ dassanīyaṃ pāsādikaṃ paramāya vaṇṇapokkharatāya samannāgataṃ, so taṃ disvā saṃsīdati visīdati, na sakkoti brahmacariyaṃ sandhāretuṃ, sikkhaṃ paccakkhāya hīnāyāvattati, evaṃ visabhāgārammaṇadassanena uppannakilesasanthavo dassanasaṃsaggo nāma. Disvā pana aññamaññaṃ ālāpasallāpavasena uppanno kilesasanthavo samullapanasaṃsaggo nāma. Sahajagghanādīnipi eteneva saṅgaṇhāti. Attano pana santakaṃ yaṃkiñci mātugāmassa datvā vā adatvā vā tena dinnassa vanabhaṅgiyādino paribhogavasena uppannakilesasanthavo sambhogasaṃsaggo nāma. Mātugāmassa hatthaggāhādivasena uppannakilesasanthavo kāyasaṃsaggo nāma. Yopi cesa –

Here, in the talk on non-association, there are five types of association: association by hearing, association by seeing, association by conversation, association by sharing, and association by bodily contact. Among these, a certain bhikkhu hears: “In such and such village or town, there is a woman who is beautiful, attractive, charming, endowed with the highest beauty and grace.” Having heard that, he becomes disheartened and distressed, unable to maintain the holy life. He abandons the training and reverts to a lower state. The familiarity with defilements that has thus arisen from hearing an unsuitable object is called association by hearing. It is not only that a bhikkhu hears, but he also sees for himself a woman who is beautiful, attractive, charming, endowed with the highest beauty and grace. Having seen her, he becomes disheartened and distressed, unable to maintain the holy life. He abandons the training and reverts to a lower state. The familiarity with defilements that has thus arisen from seeing an unsuitable object is called association by seeing. Furthermore, the familiarity with defilements that arises through mutual talk and conversation after seeing is called association by conversation. This also includes laughing together and so forth. Moreover, the familiarity with defilements that arises through enjoying something given by her—such as a forest twig and so on—whether one has given something of one's own to the woman or not, is called association by sharing. The familiarity with defilements that arises through physical contact with a woman, such as holding her hand and so on, is called association by bodily contact. And also this:

“Gihīhi saṃsaṭṭho viharati ananulomikena saṃsaggena sahasokī sahanandī sukhitesu sukhito, dukkhitesu dukkhito[M 0.0211], uppannesu kiccakaraṇīyesu attanā uyyogaṃ āpajjatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.3; mahāni. 164) –

“He dwells mixed with householders by an inappropriate association, sorrowing with those who sorrow, rejoicing with those who rejoice, happy when they are happy, suffering when they suffer, and personally exerting himself in whatever tasks need to be done when they arise.”

Evaṃ vutto ananulomiko gihisaṃsaggo, yo ca sabrahmacārīhipi kilesuppattihetubhūto saṃsaggo, taṃ sabbaṃ pahāya yvāyaṃ saṃsāre thirataraṃ saṃvegaṃ, saṅkhāresu tibbaṃ bhayasaññaṃ, sarīre paṭikūlasaññaṃ, sabbākusalesu jigucchāpubbaṅgamaṃ hirottappaṃ, sabbakiriyāsu satisampajaññanti sabbaṃ paccupaṭṭhapetvā kamaladale jalabindu viya sabbattha alaggabhāvo, ayaṃ sabbasaṃsaggappaṭipakkhatāya asaṃsaggo. Tappaṭisaṃyuttā kathā asaṃsaggakathā.

Such is the inappropriate association with householders, and any association even with fellow spiritual practitioners that becomes a cause for the arising of defilements. Abandoning all that, and establishing all that which is steadfast urgency regarding this cycle of existence, intense perception of danger in conditioned things, perception of repulsiveness in the body, shame and moral dread preceded by disgust towards all unwholesome things, and mindfulness and clear comprehension in all activities—this unattached state everywhere, like a drop of water on a lotus leaf, is non-association, being the opposite of all associations. The talk connected with this is the talk on non-association.

Vīriyārambhakathāti ettha vīrassa bhāvo, kammanti vā vīriyaṃ, vidhinā īrayitabbaṃ pavattetabbanti vā vīriyaṃ, vīriyañca taṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ pahānāya kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ [P 0.0233] upasampadāya ārambhanaṃ vīriyārambho. Svāyaṃ kāyiko cetasiko cāti duvidho, ārambhadhātu, nikkamadhātu, parakkamadhātu cāti tividho; sammappadhānavasena catubbidho. So sabbopi yo bhikkhu [V 0.0189] gamane uppannaṃ kilesaṃ ṭhānaṃ pāpuṇituṃ na deti; ṭhāne uppannaṃ nisajjaṃ, nisajjāya uppannaṃ sayanaṃ pāpuṇituṃ na deti, tattha tattheva ajapadena daṇḍena kaṇhasappaṃ uppīḷetvā gaṇhanto viya, tikhiṇena asinā amittaṃ gīvāya paharanto viya ca sīsaṃ ukkhipituṃ adatvā vīriyabalena niggaṇhāti, tassevaṃ āraddhavīriyassa vasena veditabbo. Tappaṭisaṃyuttā kathā vīriyārambhakathā.

Here, the talk on the exertion of energy: The state of a hero, or action, is energy; or energy is what should be aroused and maintained by proper means. That energy, which is the undertaking for abandoning unwholesome states and acquiring wholesome states, is the exertion of energy. It is twofold: bodily and mental. It is threefold as the element of initiative, the element of exertion, and the element of striving. It is fourfold according to the four right efforts. All of this should be understood in terms of a bhikkhu who, when walking, does not allow an arisen defilement to reach a standing posture; when standing, does not allow an arisen defilement to reach a sitting posture; when sitting, does not allow an arisen defilement to reach a lying down posture—just as one might press down a black snake with a forked stick and seize it, or as one might strike an enemy on the neck with a sharp sword without letting him raise his head, so too he restrains them right then and there with the power of energy. The talk connected with this is the talk on the exertion of energy.

Sīlakathādīsu duvidhaṃ sīlaṃ lokiyaṃ lokuttarañca. Tattha lokiyaṃ pātimokkhasaṃvarādi catupārisuddhisīlaṃ, lokuttaraṃ maggasīlaṃ phalasīlañca. Tathā vipassanāya pādakabhūtā saha upacārena aṭṭha samāpattiyo lokiyo samādhi, maggasampayutto panettha lokuttaro samādhi nāma. Tathā paññāpi lokiyā sutamayā cintāmayā jhānasampayuttā vipassanāñāṇañca. Visesato panettha vipassanāpaññā gahetabbā, lokuttarā maggapaññā phalapaññā ca. Vimuttīpi ariyaphalavimutti nibbānañca. Apare pana tadaṅgavikkhambhanasamucchedavimuttīnampi vasenettha atthaṃ vaṇṇenti. Vimuttiñāṇadassanampi ekūnavīsatividhaṃ paccavekkhaṇañāṇaṃ. Iti imesaṃ sīlādīnaṃ [M 0.0212] saddhiṃ sandassanādividhinā anekākāravokāraānisaṃsavibhāvanavasena ceva tappaṭipakkhānaṃ dussīlyādīnaṃ ādīnavavibhāvanavasena ca pavattā kathā, tappaṭisaṃyuttā kathā vā sīlādikathā nāma.

In the talk on virtue, etc., virtue is twofold: mundane and supramundane. Herein, mundane virtue is the fourfold purification of virtue, such as the restraint of the monastic code. Supramundane virtue is the virtue of the path and the virtue of the fruit. Similarly, the eight attainments along with access concentration, which serve as the foundation for insight, are mundane concentration; but the concentration associated with the path is supramundane concentration here. Likewise, mundane wisdom is wisdom born of learning, wisdom born of reflection, absorption-related wisdom, and the knowledge of insight. Specifically, here the wisdom of insight should be understood, as well as the supramundane wisdom of the path and the wisdom of the fruit. Liberation, too, is the liberation of the noble fruit and Nibbāna. Others, however, also explain the meaning here in terms of liberation by substitution of opposites, liberation by suppression, and liberation by eradication. The knowledge and vision of liberation is the nineteenfold reviewing knowledge. Thus, the talk that proceeds by explaining the benefits of these virtues, etc., in various ways and aspects, through demonstration and so forth, and by explaining the dangers of their opposites, such as misconduct, or the talk connected with these, is called the talk on virtue, etc.

Ettha ca “attanā ca appiccho hoti, appicchakathañca paresaṃ kattā”ti (ma. ni. 1.252; a. ni. 10.70) “santuṭṭho hoti itarītarena cīvarena, itarītaracīvarasantuṭṭhiyā ca vaṇṇavādī”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.144; cūḷani. khaggavisāṇasuttaniddesa 128) ca ādivacanato sayañca appicchatādiguṇasamannāgatena paresampi tadatthāya hitajjhāsayena pavattetabbā tathārūpī kathā, yā idha abhisallekhikādibhāvena visesetvā vuttā appicchakathādīti veditabbā. Kārakasseva hi kathā visesato adhippetatthasādhinī. Tathā hi vakkhati “kalyāṇamittassetaṃ, meghiya, bhikkhuno pāṭikaṅkhaṃ…pe. [P 0.0234]… akasiralābhī”ti.

Here, from statements such as: “he himself is one of few desires and is a speaker of talk on fewness of desire to others” and “he is content with whatever robes, and is a speaker in praise of contentment with whatever robes,” and the like, it should be understood that such talk, which is specified here as being of an effacing nature, is the talk on fewness of desire, etc. This talk should be initiated by one who is personally endowed with qualities such as having few desires, with a benevolent intention for the benefit of others in that regard. For the talk of one who practices is especially effective in achieving the intended purpose. For instance, it will be said: “This is to be expected of a bhikkhu who has good friends, Meghiya... he obtains without difficulty.”

Evarūpāyāti īdisāya, yathāvuttāya. Nikāmalābhīti yathicchitalābhī yathārucilābhī, sabbakālaṃ imā kathā sotuṃ vicāretuñca yathāsukhaṃ labhanto. Akicchalābhīti niddukkhalābhī. Akasiralābhīti vipulalābhī.

“Of such kind” means of this kind, as was stated. “Gains as he wishes” means he gains what he desires and what pleases him, always being able to hear and reflect on these talks at his leisure. “Gains without trouble” means gains without hardship. “Gains without difficulty” means gains abundantly.

Āraddhavīriyoti paggahitavīriyo. Akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ pahānāyāti akosallasambhūtaṭṭhena akusalānaṃ [V 0.0190] pāpadhammānaṃ pajahanatthāya. Kusalānaṃ dhammānanti kucchitānaṃ salanādiatthena anavajjaṭṭhena ca kusalānaṃ sahavipassanānaṃ maggaphaladhammānaṃ. Upasampadāyāti sampādanāya, attano santāne uppādanāya. Thāmavāti ussoḷhisaṅkhātena vīriyathāmena samannāgato. Daḷhaparakkamoti thiraparakkamo asithilavīriyo. Anikkhittadhuroti anorohitadhuro anosakkitavīriyo.

“With energy aroused” means with energy exerted. “For abandoning unwholesome states” means for the purpose of abandoning unwholesome, evil states, in the sense of their arising from unskillfulness. “Wholesome states” refers to the path and fruition states together with insight, which are wholesome in the sense of shaking off what is contemptible and in the sense of being blameless. “For their attainment” means for accomplishing them, for generating them in one’s own continuum. “Strong” means possessing the strength of energy, defined as exertion. “Persistent in effort” means steadfast in effort, with unremitting energy. “Not shirking the burden” means not laying down the burden, not withdrawing energy.

Paññavāti vipassanāpaññāya paññavā. Udayatthagāminiyāti pañcannaṃ khandhānaṃ udayañca vayañca paṭivijjhantiyā. Ariyāyāti vikkhambhanavasena kilesehi ārakā dūre ṭhitāya niddosāya. Nibbedhikāyāti nibbedhabhāgiyāya. Sammā dukkhakkhayagāminiyāti vaṭṭadukkhassa khepanato “dukkhakkhayo”ti laddhanāmaṃ ariyamaggaṃ sammā hetunā ñāyena gacchantiyā.

“Wise” means wise with the wisdom of insight. “Leading to arising and passing away” refers to that which penetrates the arising and passing away of the five aggregates. “Noble” refers to that which, by way of suppression, stands far from defilements, at a distance, and is blameless. “Penetrative” means pertaining to penetration. “Rightly leading to the cessation of suffering” refers to that which rightly, with cause and method, proceeds to the Noble Path, which has obtained the name “the cessation of suffering” because it eradicates the suffering of the round of existence.

Imesu ca pana pañcasu dhammesu sīlaṃ vīriyaṃ paññā ca yogino ajjhattikaṃ aṅgaṃ, itaradvayaṃ bāhiraṃ aṅgaṃ. Tathāpi kalyāṇamittasannissayeneva sesaṃ [M 0.0213] catubbidhaṃ ijjhati, kalyāṇamittassevettha bahūpakārataṃ dassento satthā “kalyāṇamittassetaṃ, meghiya, bhikkhuno pāṭikaṅkha”ntiādinā desanaṃ vaḍḍheti. Tattha pāṭikaṅkhanti ekaṃsena icchitabbaṃ, avassaṃbhāvīti attho. Yanti kiriyāparāmasanaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – “sīlavā bhavissatī”ti ettha yadetaṃ kalyāṇamittassa bhikkhuno sīlavantatāya bhavanaṃ sīlasampannattaṃ, tassa bhikkhuno sīlasampannattā etaṃ tassa pāṭikaṅkhaṃ, avassaṃbhāvī ekaṃseneva tassa tattha niyojanatoti adhippāyo. Pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvuto viharissatītiādīsupi eseva nayo.

And among these five qualities, virtue, energy, and wisdom are internal factors for a yogi, while the other two are external factors. Nevertheless, the remaining fourfold attainment is achieved solely through reliance on a good friend. To demonstrate the great benefit of a good friend’s support, the Teacher expands the teaching with, “Meghiya, this is to be expected of a monk who has a good friend…” Here, “to be expected” means it should be desired with certainty, meaning it is inevitable. This is what is meant: That a monk with a good friend will be virtuous—this accomplishment of virtue is to be expected of him; it is inevitable, for it is absolutely certain that he will apply himself to it. The same method applies to statements like “He will live restrained by the Pātimokkha restraint…” and so on.

Evaṃ [P 0.0235] bhagavā sadevake loke uttamakalyāṇamittasaṅkhātassa attano vacanaṃ anādiyitvā taṃ vanasaṇḍaṃ pavisitvā tādisaṃ vippakāraṃ pattassa āyasmato meghiyassa kalyāṇamittatādinā sakalaṃ sāsanasampattiṃ dassetvā, idānissa tattha ādarajātassa pubbe yehi kāmavitakkādīhi upaddutattā kammaṭṭhānaṃ na sampajji, tassa tesaṃ ujuvipaccanīkabhūtattā ca bhāvanānayaṃ pakāsetvā, tato paraṃ arahattassa kammaṭṭhānaṃ ācikkhanto, “tena ca pana, meghiya, bhikkhunā imesu pañcasu dhammesu patiṭṭhāya cattāro dhammā uttari bhāvetabbā”tiādimāha. Tattha tenāti evaṃ kalyāṇamittasannissayena yathāvuttasīlādiguṇasamannāgatena. Tenevāha “imesu pañcasu dhammesu patiṭṭhāyā”ti. Uttarīti āraddhataruṇavipassanassa rāgādiparissayā ce uppajjeyyuṃ, tesaṃ visodhanatthaṃ tato uddhaṃ cattāro dhammā bhāvetabbā uppādetabbā vaḍḍhetabbā ca.

Thus the Blessed One, who is reckoned as the ultimate good friend in the world with its gods, showed the entire accomplishment of the teaching, by means of good friendship and so on, to the Venerable Meghiya, who had fallen into such a state of trouble after not heeding His word and entering that grove. Now that eagerness had arisen in Meghiya, whose meditation subject had previously not succeeded because he was troubled by thoughts of sensuality and the like, the Blessed One revealed the method of development which is the direct opposite of those thoughts. Then, instructing further on the meditation subject for arahantship, he said, “And then, Meghiya, a monk, having established himself in these five things, should develop four further things.” Here, “by him” refers to one endowed with the virtues and qualities as described, relying on a good friend in this way. Therefore, he said, “having established himself in these five things.” “Further” means that if disturbances like lust arise for one who has begun the nascent stages of insight, then to purify them, four things should be developed, produced, and increased beyond that.

Asubhāti [V 0.0191] ekādasasu asubhakammaṭṭhānesu yathārahaṃ yattha katthaci asubhabhāvanā. Rāgassa pahānāyāti kāmarāgassa pajahanatthāya. Ayamattho sālilāyakopamāya vibhāvetabbo – eko hi puriso asitaṃ gahetvā koṭito paṭṭhāya sālikhette sāliyo lāyati, athassa vatiṃ bhinditvā gāvo pavisiṃsu. So asitaṃ ṭhapetvā, yaṭṭhiṃ ādāya, teneva maggena gāvo nīharitvā, vatiṃ pākatikaṃ katvā, puna asitaṃ gahetvā sāliyo lāyi. Tattha sālikhettaṃ viya buddhasāsanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, sālilāyako viya yogāvacaro, asitaṃ viya paññā, lāyanakālo viya vipassanāya kammakaraṇakālo, yaṭṭhi viya asubhakammaṭṭhānaṃ, vati viya saṃvaro[M 0.0214], vatiṃ bhinditvā gāvīnaṃ pavisanaṃ viya sahasā appaṭisaṅkhāya pamādaṃ āgamma rāgassa uppajjanaṃ, asitaṃ ṭhapetvā, yaṭṭhiṃ ādāya, paviṭṭhamaggeneva gāvo nīharitvā, vatiṃ paṭipākatikaṃ katvā, puna ṭhitaṭṭhānato paṭṭhāya sālilāyanaṃ viya asubhakammaṭṭhānena rāgaṃ vikkhambhetvā, puna vipassanāya kammakaraṇakāloti idamettha upamāsaṃsandanaṃ. Evaṃbhūtaṃ bhāvanāvidhiṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “asubhā bhāvetabbā rāgassa pahānāyā”ti.

“Foulness” means the development of foulness in any of the eleven foulness meditation subjects, as appropriate. “For the abandoning of lust” means for the purpose of abandoning sensual desire. This meaning should be illustrated by the simile of the rice reaper: A man, having taken his sickle, starts from the edge of the field and cuts the rice. Then, breaking through the fence, cows enter. He sets aside the sickle, takes a stick, drives the cows out by the same path, repairs the fence properly, and again takes the sickle to cut the rice. Here, the rice field should be seen as the Buddha’s dispensation; the rice reaper as the meditator; the sickle as wisdom; the time of cutting rice as the time for practicing insight; the stick as the meditation on foulness; the fence as restraint; the breaking of the fence and the cows entering as the arising of lust due to heedlessness, acting without reflection; setting aside the sickle, taking the stick, driving out the cows by the path they entered, repairing the fence properly, and then resuming the cutting of rice from where he left off—this is like suppressing lust with the meditation on foulness and then returning to the time for practicing insight. This is the connection of the simile here. Referring to such a method of meditation, it is said: “The meditation on foulness should be developed for the abandoning of lust.”

Mettāti [P 0.0236] mettākammaṭṭhānaṃ. Byāpādassa pahānāyāti vuttanayeneva uppannakopassa pajahanatthāya. Ānāpānassatīti soḷasavatthukā ānāpānassati. Vitakkupacchedāyāti vuttanayeneva uppannānaṃ vitakkānaṃ upacchedanatthāya. Asmimānasamugghātāyāti asmīti uppajjanakassa navavidhassa mānassa samucchedanatthāya.
