Aniccasaññinoti hutvā abhāvato udayabbayavantato pabhaṅguto tāvakālikato niccappaṭipakkhato ca “sabbe saṅkhārā aniccā”ti (dha. pa. 277; cūḷani. hemakamāṇavapucchāniddesa 56) pavattaaniccānupassanāvasena aniccasaññino. Anattasaññā saṇṭhātīti asārakato avasavattanato parato rittato tucchato suññato ca “sabbe dhammā anattā”ti (dha. pa. 279; cūḷani. hemakamāṇavapucchāniddesa 56) evaṃ pavattā anattānupassanāsaṅkhātā anattasaññā citte saṇṭhahati, atidaḷhaṃ patiṭṭhāti. Aniccalakkhaṇe hi diṭṭhe anattalakkhaṇaṃ diṭṭhameva hoti. Tīsu hi lakkhaṇesu ekasmiṃ diṭṭhe itaradvayaṃ diṭṭhameva hoti. Tena vuttaṃ – “aniccasaññino hi, meghiya, anattasaññā saṇṭhātī”ti. Anattalakkhaṇe diṭṭhe asmīti uppajjanakamāno suppajahova hotīti āha – “anattasaññī asmimānasamugghātaṃ pāpuṇātī”ti diṭṭheva dhamme nibbānanti diṭṭheyeva dhamme imasmiṃyeva attabhāve apaccayaparinibbānaṃ pāpuṇāti. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthārato pana asubhādibhāvanānayo visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.102) vuttanayena gahetabbo.

“Loving-kindness” refers to the meditation subject of loving-kindness. “For the abandoning of ill will” means, as stated, for the purpose of giving up arisen anger. “Mindfulness of breathing” means the sixteen-fold mindfulness of breathing. “For the cutting off of thoughts” means, as stated, for the purpose of severing arisen thoughts. “For the uprooting of the conceit ‘I am’” means for the purpose of cutting off the ninefold conceit that arises as “I am.” “Perceiving impermanence” means having become one who perceives impermanence through the contemplation of impermanence, which proceeds as “All conditioned things are impermanent” (Dhp. 277; Cūḷaniddesa, Hemakamāṇavapucchā 56), due to their non-existence after having been, being subject to rise and fall, being perishable, temporary, and opposed to permanence. “The perception of non-self becomes established” means the perception of non-self, known as the contemplation of non-self, which proceeds as “All phenomena are non-self” (Dhp. 279; Cūḷaniddesa, Hemakamāṇavapucchā 56), becomes firmly established in the mind, being devoid of essence, uncontrollable, belonging to another, empty, and hollow. For when the characteristic of impermanence is seen, the characteristic of non-self is also seen. Among the three characteristics, when one is seen, the other two are also seen. Therefore, it is said: “For one who perceives impermanence, Meghiya, the perception of non-self becomes established.” When the characteristic of non-self is seen, the conceit “I am” is easily abandoned: thus it is said: “One who perceives non-self attains the uprooting of the conceit ‘I am.’” “Nibbāna in this very life” means that in this very life, in this very existence, one attains final Nibbāna without residue. This is the summary here; for the detailed method, the way of developing foulness and other meditations should be understood as explained in the Visuddhimagga (Visuddhimagga I.102).

Etamatthaṃ [V 0.0192] viditvāti etaṃ āyasmato meghiyassa micchāvitakkacorehi kusalabhaṇḍupacchedasaṅkhātaṃ atthaṃ jānitvā. Imaṃ udānanti imaṃ kāmavitakkādīnaṃ avinodane vinodane ca ādīnavānisaṃsadīpakaṃ udānaṃ udānesi.

“Having understood this matter” means having known this matter of the Venerable Meghiya, which was reckoned as the destruction of the stock of wholesome qualities by the thieves of wrong thoughts. “He uttered this inspired utterance” means he uttered this inspired utterance that reveals the drawbacks of not dispelling and the advantages of dispelling thoughts of sensual desire and the like.

Tattha [M 0.0215] khuddāti hīnā lāmakā. Vitakkāti kāmavitakkādayo tayo pāpavitakkā. Te hi sabbavitakkehi patikiṭṭhatāya idha khuddāti vuttā “na ca khuddamācare”tiādīsu (khu. pā. 9.3; su. ni. 145) viya. Sukhumāti ñātivitakkādayo adhippetā. Ñātivitakko janapadavitakko amarāvitakko parānuddayatāya paṭisaṃyutto vitakko lābhasakkārasilokapaṭisaṃyutto vitakko anavaññattipaṭisaṃyutto vitakkoti ete hi vitakkā kāmavitakkādayo viya [P 0.0237] dāruṇā na hontīti anoḷārikasabhāvatāya sukhumāti vuttā. Anugatāti cittena anuvattitā. Vitakke hi uppajjamāne cittaṃ tadanugatameva hoti tassa ārammaṇābhiniropanato. “Anuggatā”tipi pāḷi, anuuṭṭhitāti attho. Manaso uppilāvāti cetaso uppilāvitattakarā.

Therein, 'petty' (khuddā) means low, inferior. 'Thoughts' (vitakkā) refers to the three unwholesome thoughts beginning with thoughts of sensual desire. Indeed, these are called 'petty' here because they are the most repulsive among all thoughts, as in “one should not engage in petty acts” (Khuddakapāṭha 9.3; Sutta Nipāta 145) and similar passages. 'Subtle' (sukhumā) refers to thoughts concerning relatives and the like. The thought concerning relatives, the thought concerning the district, the thought concerning immortality, the thought connected with compassion for others, the thought connected with gain, honor, and fame, the thought connected with not being despised—these thoughts are not as harsh as thoughts of sensual desire and the like, hence they are called 'subtle' due to their non-gross nature. 'Followed' (anugatā) means being followed by the mind. For when thoughts arise, the mind follows them by focusing on that object. The text also reads 'anuggatā,' meaning 'arisen after.' 'Agitation of the mind' (manaso uppilāvā) means causing the mind to be agitated.

Ete avidvā manaso vitakketi ete kāmavitakkādike manovitakke assādādīnavanissaraṇato ñātatīraṇapahānapariññāhi yathābhūtaṃ ajānanto. Hurā huraṃ dhāvati bhantacittoti appahīnamicchāvitakkattā anavaṭṭhitacitto “kadāci rūpe, kadāci sadde”tiādinā tasmiṃ tasmiṃ ārammaṇe assādādivasena aparāparaṃ dhāvati paribbhamati. Atha vā hurā huraṃ dhāvati bhantacittoti apariññātavitakkattā tannimittānaṃ avijjātaṇhānaṃ vasena paribbhamanamānaso idhalokato paralokaṃ ādānanikkhepehi aparāparaṃ dhāvati saṃsaratīti attho.

‘Not knowing these thoughts of the mind’ means not knowing as they truly are these mental thoughts, such as thoughts of sensual desire, in terms of their gratification, danger, and escape, through the full understanding of knowing, scrutinizing, and abandoning. “Rushing here and there, the mind is restless” means that because wrong thoughts are not abandoned, the unsteady mind runs back and forth, now to forms, now to sounds, and so on, wandering from one object to another in terms of gratification and so forth. Or, “rushing here and there, the mind is restless” means that because the thoughts are not fully understood, the mind, influenced by ignorance and craving for those objects, wanders back and forth from this world to the next, taking up and putting down, thus wandering in saṃsāra.

Ete ca vidvā manaso vitakketi ete yathāvuttappabhede kāmavitakkādike manovitakke assādādito yathābhūtaṃ jānanto. Ātāpiyoti vīriyavā. Saṃvaratīti pidahati. Satimāti satisampanno. Anuggateti dullabhavasena anuppanne. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – ete vuttappakāre kāmavitakkādike manovitakke cittassa uppilāvitahetutāya manaso uppilāve vidvā vipassanāpaññāsahitāya maggapaññāya sammadeva jānanto, tassa sahāyabhūtānaṃ sammāvāyāmasatīnaṃ atthitāya ātāpiyo satimā te ariyamaggabhāvanāya āyatiṃ uppattirahe anuggate anuppanne eva maggakkhaṇe saṃvarati, ñāṇasaṃvaravasena pidahati, āgamanapathaṃ [M 0.0216] pacchindati, evaṃbhūto ca catusaccappabodhena buddho ariyasāvako arahattādhigamena [P 0.0238] asesaṃ, anavasesaṃ [V 0.0193] ete kāmavitakkādike pajahāsi samucchindīti. Etthāpi “anugate”tipi paṭhanti. Tassattho heṭṭhā vuttoyeva.

‘And knowing these thoughts of the mind’ means knowing as they truly are these mental thoughts of the various kinds described, such as thoughts of sensual desire, from their gratification onward. 'Ardent' (ātāpiyo) means possessing energy. 'Restrains' (saṃvarati) means he closes them off. 'Mindful' (satimā) means endowed with mindfulness. 'Not arisen' (anuggate) means not arisen due to difficulty. This is what is meant: The wise one, knowing rightly with the wisdom of insight and the wisdom of the path these mental thoughts of the aforementioned kinds, such as thoughts of sensual desire, as causes of the mind's agitation, being ardent and mindful due to the presence of right effort and mindfulness as his helpers, restrains them by developing the Noble Path at the moment of the path, while they are still unarisen and difficult to arise; he closes them off by means of the restraint of knowledge and cuts off their path of approach. Being thus, an awakened noble disciple, through awakening to the Four Noble Truths and attaining arahantship, entirely and without remainder abandons and uproots these thoughts of sensual desire and the like. Here, some also read 'anugate' (followed). Its meaning has been stated above.

Paṭhamasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the first sutta is concluded.

2. Uddhatasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Uddhata Sutta

32. Dutiye kusinārāyanti kusinārāyaṃ nāma mallarājūnaṃ nagare. Upavattane mallānaṃ sālavaneti yathā hi anurādhapurassa thūpārāmo, evaṃ kusinārāya uyyānaṃ dakkhiṇapacchimadisāya hoti. Yathā thūpārāmato dakkhiṇadvārena nagarapavisanamaggo pācīnamukho gantvā uttarena nivattati, evaṃ uyyānato sālapanti pācīnamukhā gantvā uttarena nivattā, tasmā “upavattana”nti vuccati. Tasmiṃ upavattane mallarājūnaṃ sālavane. Araññakuṭikāyanti sālapantiyā avidūre rukkhagacchasañchannaṭṭhāne katā kuṭikā, taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “araññakuṭikāyaṃ viharatī”ti. Te pana bhikkhū paṭisaṅkhānavirahitā ossaṭṭhavīriyā pamattavihārino, tena vuttaṃ “uddhatā”tiādi.

32. In the second sutta, 'in Kusinārā' means in Kusinārā, the city of the Malla kings. 'In the Upavattana, the Mallas' sal grove'—just as the Thūpārāma is to Anurādhapura, so is the park to Kusinārā, situated in the south-western direction. Just as from the Thūpārāma, the road entering the city through the southern gate goes eastward and then turns north, so from the park, the row of sal trees goes eastward and then turns north—hence it is called “Upavattana.” In that Upavattana, in the Malla kings' sal grove. 'In a forest hut' refers to a hut built not far from the row of sal trees, in a place shaded by trees and shrubs; it is with reference to this that it is said, “dwelling in a forest hut.” Those monks, however, were devoid of reflection, slack in energy, and dwelling negligently; hence it is said “agitated,” etc.

Tattha uddhaccabahulattā avūpasantacittatāya uddhatā. Tucchabhāvena māno naḷo viyāti naḷo, mānasaṅkhāto uggato naḷo etesanti unnaḷā, uggatatucchamānāti attho. Pattacīvaramaṇḍanādicāpallena samannāgatattā bahukatāya vā capalā. Pharusavācatāya mukhena kharāti mukharā. Tiracchānakathābahulatāya vikiṇṇā byākulā vācā etesanti vikiṇṇavācā. Muṭṭhā naṭṭhā sati etesanti muṭṭhassatino, sativirahitā pamādavihārinoti attho. Sabbena sabbaṃ sampajaññābhāvato asampajānā. Gaddūhanamattampi [P 0.0239] kālaṃ cittasamādhānassa abhāvato na samāhitāti asamāhitā. Lolasabhāvattā bhantamigasappaṭibhāgatāya vibbhantacittā. Manacchaṭṭhānaṃ indriyānaṃ asaṃvaraṇato asaññatindriyatāya pākatindriyā.

Therein, 'agitated' (uddhatā) means being abundant in restlessness and having an unpacified mind. 'Arrogant' (unnaḷā) is explained thus: because of its emptiness, conceit is like a reed (naḷa); those for whom this reed of conceit has arisen (uggato naḷo) are 'unnaḷā'; the meaning is having arisen, empty conceit. 'Fickle' (capalā) means being endowed with frivolity regarding the adornment of bowls and robes, etc., or being very fickle due to its abundance. 'Harsh-mouthed' (mukharā) means their mouths are harsh (kharā) due to harsh speech. 'Of scattered speech' (vikiṇṇavācā) means their speech is scattered and confused due to being abundant in animalistic talk. 'Of lapsed mindfulness' (muṭṭhassatino) means their mindfulness (sati) is lost (muṭṭhā) and destroyed; the meaning is that they are devoid of mindfulness, dwelling in heedlessness. 'Without clear comprehension' (asampajānā) means completely lacking in clear comprehension. 'Unconcentrated' (asamāhitā) means there is no mental concentration even for the time it takes to milk a cow. 'Of bewildered mind' (vibbhantacittā) means their minds are bewildered due to a fickle nature, resembling a startled deer. 'With senses exposed' (pākatindriyā) means they are uncontrolled in their senses due to the non-restraint of the six sense faculties, including the mind.

Etamatthaṃ [M 0.0217] viditvāti etaṃ tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ uddhaccādivasena pamādavihāraṃ jānitvā. Imaṃ udānanti imaṃ pamādavihāre appamādavihāre ca yathākkamaṃ ādīnavānisaṃsavibhāvanaṃ udānaṃ udānesi.

‘Having understood this matter’ means knowing this heedless dwelling of those monks, characterized by restlessness and so forth. ‘This inspired utterance’ means he uttered this inspired utterance, which reveals in due order the dangers of heedless dwelling and the benefits of heedful dwelling.

Tattha [V 0.0194] arakkhitenāti satiārakkhābhāvena aguttena. Kāyenāti chaviññāṇakāyena cakkhuviññāṇena hi rūpaṃ disvā tattha nimittānubyañjanaggahaṇavasena abhijjhādipavattito viññāṇadvārassa satiyā arakkhitabhāvato. Sotaviññāṇādīsupi eseva nayo. Evaṃ chaviññāṇakāyassa arakkhitabhāvaṃ sandhāyāha “arakkhitena kāyenā”ti. Keci pana “kāyenā”ti atthaṃ vadanti, tesampi vuttanayeneva atthayojanāya sati yujjeyya. Apare pana “arakkhitena cittenā”ti paṭhanti, tesampi vuttanayo eva attho. Micchādiṭṭhihatenāti sassatādimicchābhinivesadūsitena. Thinamiddhābhibhūtenāti cittassa akalyatālakkhaṇena thinena kāyassa akalyatālakkhaṇena middhena ca ajjhotthaṭena, tena kāyena cittenāti vā sambandho. Vasaṃ mārassa gacchatīti kilesamārādikassa sabbassapi mārassa vasaṃ yathākāmakaraṇīyataṃ upagacchati, tesaṃ visayaṃ nātikkamatīti attho.

Therein, 'unprotected' (arakkhitena) means unguarded due to the absence of mindfulness-protection. 'By body' (kāyena) refers to the body of the six consciousnesses. For when one sees a form with the eye-consciousness, due to grasping at marks and details, the door of consciousness is unprotected due to the absence of mindfulness, leading to the arising of covetousness and so on. The same principle applies to ear-consciousness and the rest. Thus, referring to the unprotected state of the body of the six consciousnesses, it is said, "by an unprotected body." Some, however, explain the meaning of "by body" differently, yet for them too, it would be fitting if the meaning is connected in the manner already stated. Others read it as "by an unprotected mind," but for them too, the meaning is the same as explained. 'Struck down by wrong view' (micchādiṭṭhihatena) means corrupted by adherence to wrong views such as eternalism. 'Overcome by sloth and torpor' (thinamiddhābhibhūtena) means overwhelmed by sloth, which has the characteristic of mental unwieldiness, and torpor, which has the characteristic of bodily unwieldiness; or the connection is with both body and mind. 'Falls under Māra’s control' (vasaṃ mārassa gacchati) means one comes under the control of all Māra, such as the Māra of defilements, becoming subject to his will; meaning, one does not transcend their domain.

Imāya hi gāthāya bhagavā ye satiārakkhābhāvena sabbaso arakkhitacittā, yonisomanasikārassa hetubhūtāya paññāya abhāvato ayoniso ummujjanena niccantiādinā vipariyesagāhino, tato eva kusalakiriyāya vīriyārambhābhāvato kosajjābhibhūtā saṃsāravaṭṭato sīsaṃ na ukkhipissantīti tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ pamādavihāragarahāmukhena vaṭṭaṃ dassetvā idāni vivaṭṭaṃ dassetuṃ, “tasmā rakkhitacittassā”ti dutiyagāthamāha.

For with this verse, the Blessed One, having shown the round of existence by way of censuring the heedless dwelling of those monks whose minds are entirely unprotected due to the absence of mindfulness-protection, who, due to the absence of wisdom which is the cause of wise attention, grasp at perversions such as 'permanence' through unwise attention, and who, therefore, being overcome by sloth due to the absence of the undertaking of energy for wholesome action, will not lift their heads from the round of saṃsāra—now, in order to show the escape from it, he spoke the second verse, 'Therefore, for one with a guarded mind.'

Tattha tasmā rakkhitacittassāti yasmā arakkhitacitto mārassa yathākāmakaraṇīyo hutvā saṃsāreyeva hoti, tasmā satisaṃvarena manacchaṭṭhānaṃ indriyānaṃ rakkhaṇena pidahanena rakkhitacitto assa. Citte hi rakkhite cakkhādiindriyāni [P 0.0240] rakkhitāneva hontīti. Sammāsaṅkappagocaroti yasmā micchāsaṅkappagocaro tathā tathā ayoniso vitakketvā nānāvidhāni micchādassanāni gaṇhanto micchādiṭṭhihatena cittena [M 0.0218] mārassa yathākāmakaraṇīyo hoti, tasmā yonisomanasikārena kammaṃ karonto nekkhammasaṅkappādisammāsaṅkappagocaro assa, jhānādisampayuttaṃ sammāsaṅkappameva attano cittassa pavattiṭṭhānaṃ kareyya. Sammādiṭṭhipurekkhāroti sammāsaṅkappagocaratāya vidhūtamicchādassano puretaraṃyeva kammassakatālakkhaṇaṃ, tato yathābhūtañāṇalakkhaṇañca sammādiṭṭhiṃ purato katvā pubbe vuttanayeneva sīlasamādhīsu yutto payutto vipassanaṃ ārabhitvā saṅkhāre sammasanto ñatvāna udayabbayaṃ pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu samapaññāsāya ākārehi uppādanirodhaṃ vavatthapetvā udayabbayañāṇamadhigantvā tato paraṃ bhaṅgānupassanādivasena vipassanaṃ ussukkāpetvā anukkamena ariyamaggaṃ gaṇhanto aggamaggena, thinamiddhābhibhū bhikkhu sabbā duggatiyo jaheti, evaṃ so heṭṭhimamaggavajjhānaṃ kilesānaṃ paṭhamameva [V 0.0195] pahīnattā diṭṭhivippayuttalobhasahagatacittuppādesu uppajjanakathinamiddhānaṃ adhigatena arahattamaggena samucchindanato tadekaṭṭhānaṃ mānādīnampi pahīnattā sabbaso bhinnakileso khīṇāsavo bhikkhu tividhadukkhatāyogena duggatisaṅkhātā sabbāpi gatiyo ucchinnabhavamūlattā jahe, pajaheyya. Tāsaṃ parabhāge nibbāne patiṭṭheyyāti attho.

Here, 'one with a guarded mind' (rakkhitacittassa) means that since an unguarded mind becomes subject to Māra’s will and remains in saṃsāra, one should be one with a guarded mind through the restraint of mindfulness, by protecting and closing off the sense faculties which have mind as the sixth. For when the mind is guarded, the faculties like the eye are also guarded. 'One whose domain is right intention' (sammāsaṅkappagocaro) means that since one whose domain is wrong intention, thinking unskillfully in various ways and adopting various kinds of wrong views, with a mind afflicted by wrong view, becomes subject to Māra’s will, therefore, by means of wise attention while acting, one should make right intention, such as the intention of renunciation, one's domain. One should establish right intention connected with jhāna and so forth as the place where one's mind moves. 'One who prioritizes right view' (sammādiṭṭhipurekkhāro) means that having dispelled wrong views through the domain of right intention, one should first place before oneself the right view characterized by ownership of kamma, and then the right view characterized by the knowledge of things as they really are. Then, as previously explained, being devoted and applied to virtue and concentration, one should undertake insight meditation, contemplate formations, and know their arising and passing away. Having determined the arising and cessation in the five aggregates of clinging in fifty aspects, one attains the knowledge of arising and passing away. Thereafter, diligently cultivating insight by observing dissolution and so forth, one gradually attains the noble path. By the highest path, 'a bhikkhu who has overcome sloth and torpor abandons all states of woe.' Thus, because the defilements to be abandoned by the lower paths have been abandoned first, and because, through the attainment of the Arahantship path, one has utterly cut off the stubborn sloth and torpor that arise in states of mind associated with greed disconnected from wrong view, and because conceit and so forth, which have the same basis, have also been abandoned, a bhikkhu whose defilements are entirely destroyed, an arahant with exhausted influxes, would abandon all destinations, which are designated as miserable states due to their connection with the three kinds of suffering, because the root of existence has been severed. Subsequently, he is established in Nibbāna—this is the meaning.

Dutiyasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Second Discourse is concluded.

3. Gopālakasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Gopālaka Sutta

33. Tatiye kosalesūti kosalā nāma jānapadino rājakumārā, tesaṃ nivāso ekopi janapado “kosalā”tveva vuccati, tesu kosalesu janapade. Cārikaṃ caratīti aturitacārikāvasena [P 0.0241] janapadacārikaṃ carati. Mahatāti guṇamahattenapi mahatā, aparicchinnasaṅkhyattā saṅkhyāmahattenapi mahatā. Bhikkhusaṅghenāti diṭṭhisīlasāmaññasaṃhatena samaṇagaṇena. Saddhinti ekato. Maggā okkammāti maggato apakkamitvā. Aññataraṃ rukkhamūlanti ghanapattasākhāviṭapasampannassa sandacchāyassa mahato rukkhassa samīpasaṅkhātaṃ mūlaṃ.

33. In the third (sutta), 'among the Kosalans' (kosalesu) means that the Kosalans are country dwellers and princes; even a single territory where they dwell is called 'Kosala'; thus, 'in the Kosalan country.' 'Wandering on tour' (cārikaṃ carati) means traveling through the country on tour without haste. 'With a large' (mahatā) refers to greatness both in terms of virtues and in terms of number, being of an immeasurable number. 'With a community of monks' (bhikkhusaṅghena) means with a group of ascetics united in view and virtue. 'Together with' (saddhiṃ) means unitedly. 'Stepping aside from the road' (maggā okkamma) means deviating from the path. 'To the foot of a certain tree' (aññataraṃ rukkhamūlaṃ) means the vicinity called the root of a large tree abundant with dense leaves, branches, and twigs, possessing thick shade.

Aññataro gopālakoti eko gogaṇarakkhako, nāmena pana nando nāma. So kira aḍḍho mahaddhano mahābhogo, yathā keṇiyo [M 0.0219] jaṭilo pabbajjāvasena, evaṃ anāthapiṇḍikassa goyūthaṃ rakkhanto gopālakattena rājapīḷaṃ apaharanto attano kuṭumbaṃ rakkhati. So kālena kālaṃ pañca gorase gahetvā, mahāseṭṭhissa santikaṃ āgantvā niyyātetvā satthu santikaṃ gantvā, satthāraṃ passati, dhammaṃ suṇāti, attano vasanaṭṭhānaṃ āgamanatthāya satthāraṃ yācati. Satthā tasseva ñāṇaparipākaṃ āgamayamāno agantvā, aparabhāge mahatā bhikkhusaṅghena parivuto janapadacārikaṃ caranto, “idānissa ñāṇaṃ paripakka”nti ñatvā tassa vasanaṭṭhānassa avidūre maggā okkamma aññatarasmiṃ rukkhamūle nisīdi tassa āgamanaṃ āgamayamāno. Nandopi kho “satthā kira janapadacārikaṃ caranto ito āgacchatī”ti sutvā, haṭṭhatuṭṭho vegena gantvā, satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā katapaṭisanthāro ekamantaṃ nisīdi, athassa bhagavā dhammaṃ desesi. So sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahitvā bhagavantaṃ nimantetvā sattāhaṃ pāyāsadānamadāsi, sattame [V 0.0196] divase bhagavā anumodanaṃ katvā pakkāmi. Tena vuttaṃ – “ekamantaṃ nisinnaṃ kho taṃ gopālakaṃ bhagavā dhammiyā kathāya sandassesi…pe… uṭṭhāyāsanā pakkāmī”ti.

'A certain cowherd' refers to a guardian of cattle named Nanda. He was said to be wealthy, with great riches and abundance; just as Keniya the ascetic was wealthy by way of his asceticism, so Nanda, while protecting Anāthapiṇḍika’s herd, protected his family by warding off royal oppression through his status as a cowherd. From time to time, he would take the five dairy products, go to the great merchant, deliver them, and then visit the Teacher. He would see the Teacher, listen to the Dhamma, and request the Teacher to come to his dwelling place. The Teacher, awaiting the ripening of his wisdom, did not go. Later, while traveling through the countryside with a large community of monks, the Teacher, knowing, 'Now his wisdom is ripe,' stepped aside from the road not far from Nanda’s dwelling and sat at the foot of a certain tree, awaiting his arrival. Nanda, hearing that the Teacher was traveling through the countryside and would come this way, was delighted and hurried to approach the Teacher. After paying respects and exchanging courteous greetings, he sat to one side. Then the Blessed One taught him the Dhamma. He became established in the fruit of stream-entry, invited the Blessed One, and for seven days gave a gift of rice porridge. On the seventh day, the Blessed One gave his thanks and departed. Thus it is said: 'The Blessed One instructed... that cowherd seated to one side with a Dhamma talk... then rose from his seat and departed.'

Tattha [P 0.0242] sandassesīti “ime dhammā kusalā, ime dhammā akusalā”tiādinā kusalādidhamme kammavipāke idhalokaparaloke paccakkhato dassento anupubbikathāvasāne cattāri ariyasaccāni sammā dassesi. Samādapesīti “saccādhigamāya ime nāma dhammā attani uppādetabbā”ti sīlādidhamme sammā gaṇhāpetvā tesu taṃ patiṭṭhapesi. Samuttejesīti te dhammā samādinnā anukkamena bhāviyamānā nibbedhabhāgiyā hutvā tikkhavisadā yathā khippaṃ ariyamaggaṃ āvahanti, tathā sammā uttejesi sammadeva tejesi. Sampahaṃsesīti bhāvanāya pubbenāparaṃ visesabhāvadassanena cittassa pamodāpanavasena suṭṭhu pahaṃsesi. Apicettha sāvajjānavajjadhammesu dukkhādīsu ca sammohavinodanena sandassanaṃ, sammāpaṭipattiyaṃ pamādāpanodanena samādapanaṃ, cittassālasiyāpattivinodanena samuttejanaṃ, sammāpaṭipattisiddhiyā sampahaṃsanaṃ veditabbaṃ. Evaṃ so bhagavato sāmukkaṃsikāya dhammadesanāya sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. Adhivāsesīti [M 0.0220] tena diṭṭhasaccena “adhivāsetu me, bhante bhagavā”tiādinā nimantito kāyaṅgavācaṅgaṃ acopento citteneva adhivāsesi sādiyi. Tenevāha “tuṇhībhāvenā”ti.

Therein, 'he instructs' (sandassesi) means that by directly showing wholesome and unwholesome qualities, their karmic results in this world and the next, and so on, he rightly revealed the Four Noble Truths at the conclusion of the gradual talk. 'He exhorted' (samādapesi) means that he had him rightly take up and established him in virtuous and other qualities, saying, 'These qualities should be developed within oneself for the realization of the truths.' 'He roused' (samuttejesi) means that he rightly roused and truly invigorated him so that those qualities, when undertaken and progressively developed, become conducive to penetration, sharp and clear, and quickly lead to the Noble Path. 'He gladdened' (sampahaṃsesi) means that he thoroughly gladdened his mind by showing the successive stages of distinction in the development through meditation. Moreover, here, instruction is to be understood as the dispelling of confusion about blameworthy and blameless states, suffering, and so on; exhortation as the removal of negligence in right practice; rousing as the dispelling of mental laziness; and gladdening through the success of right practice. Thus, he became established in the fruit of stream-entry through the Blessed One's quintessential Dhamma talk. 'He consented' (adhivāsesi) means that, having been invited by him who had seen the truths with words like, 'May the Blessed One consent to me, venerable sir,' he consented and accepted with his mind alone, without moving his body or speech. Hence it is said, 'by remaining silent.'

Appodakapāyāsanti nirudakapāyāsaṃ. Paṭiyādāpetvāti sampādetvā sajjetvā. Navañca sappinti navanītaṃ gahetvā tāvadeva vilīnaṃ maṇḍasappiñca paṭiyādāpetvā. Sahatthāti ādarajāto sahattheneva parivisanto. Santappesīti paṭiyattaṃ bhojanaṃ bhojesi. Sampavāresīti “alaṃ ala”nti vācāya paṭikkhipāpesi. Bhuttāvinti katabhattakiccaṃ. Onītapattapāṇinti pattato apanītapāṇiṃ, “dhotapattapāṇi”ntipi pāṭho, dhotapattahatthanti attho. Nīcanti anuccaṃ āsanaṃ gahetvā āsaneyeva nisīdanaṃ ariyadesavāsīnaṃ cārittaṃ, so pana satthu santike upacāravasena paññattassa dāruphalakāsanassa samīpe nisīdi. Dhammiyā kathāyātiādi sattame divase kataṃ anumodanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ[P 0.0243]. So kira sattāhaṃ bhagavantaṃ bhikkhusaṅghañca tattha vasāpetvā mahādānaṃ pavattesi. Sattame pana divase appodakapāyāsadānaṃ adāsi. Satthā tassa tasmiṃ attabhāve uparimaggatthāya ñāṇaparipākābhāvato anumodanameva katvā pakkāmi.

'Porridge with little water' (Appodakapāyāsaṃ) means a thick porridge. 'Having had it prepared' (Paṭiyādāpetvā) means preparing and arranging it. 'And fresh ghee' (Navañca sappiṃ) refers to taking fresh butter, which melts immediately, and also preparing the cream of ghee. 'With his own hand' (Sahatthā) indicates that out of respect he served with his own hands. 'He satisfied them' (Santappesi) means he served them the prepared food. 'He served them to satisfaction' (Sampavāresi) means causing them to refuse further offerings by saying, 'Enough, enough.' 'When he had finished his meal' (Bhuttāviṃ) refers to having finished the business of the meal. 'With hand withdrawn from the bowl' (Onītapattapāṇiṃ) means having withdrawn the hand from the bowl; another reading is 'dhotapattapāṇiṃ,' meaning having washed the bowl and hands. 'Low' (Nīcaṃ) means taking a low seat; it is the custom of those dwelling in the noble land to sit on a seat that is not high. He, however, sat near the wooden plank seat designated for the Teacher out of respect. 'With a Dhamma talk' (Dhammiyā kathāya) and so forth refers to the talk of appreciation given on the seventh day. It is said that he had the Blessed One and the community of monks stay there for seven days and made a great offering. On the seventh day, he gave the gift of porridge with little water. The Teacher, seeing that the ripening of Nanda's wisdom was not yet sufficient for the higher paths in that very life, merely gave a talk of appreciation and departed.

Sīmantarikāyāti sīmantare, tassa gāmassa antaraṃ. Gāmavāsino kira ekaṃ taḷākaṃ nissāya tena saddhiṃ kalahaṃ akaṃsu. So te abhibhavitvā taṃ taḷākaṃ gaṇhi. Tena baddhāghāto [V 0.0197] eko puriso taṃ satthu pattaṃ gahetvā dūraṃ anugantvā “nivattāhi upāsakā”ti vutte bhagavantaṃ vanditvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā bhikkhusaṅghassa ca añjaliṃ katvā yāva dassanūpacārasamatikkamā dasanakhasamodhānasamujjalaṃ añjaliṃ sirasi paggayha paṭinivattitvā dvinnaṃ gāmānaṃ antare araññappadese ekakaṃ gacchantaṃ sarena vijjhitvā māresi. Tena vuttaṃ acirapakkantassa…pe… voropesī”ti. Kenacideva karaṇīyena ohīyitvā pacchā gacchantā bhikkhū taṃ tathā mataṃ disvā bhagavato tamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ, taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “atha kho sambahulā bhikkhū”tiādi.

'Between the boundaries' (sīmantarikāya) means in the boundary area, the space between villages. It seems the villagers had a dispute with him over a certain pond. He overpowered them and seized that pond. A certain man, bearing a grudge over this, killed him. After Nanda had followed the Teacher for some distance and been told, 'Turn back, lay follower,' he paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him, and made a gesture of reverence to the community of monks. Raising his joined hands—resplendent as the joining of ten fingernails—to his head, he turned back only after the Teacher had passed beyond the range of sight. As he was then walking alone in a wilderness area between two villages, that man shot him with an arrow and killed him. Therefore, it was said: 'Not long after he had departed... deprived him of life.' Some monks, who had been delayed by some business and were coming along behind, saw him lying there dead and reported the matter to the Blessed One. With reference to that, it was said: 'Then, several monks...'

Etamatthaṃ viditvāti yasmā diṭṭhisampannaṃ ariyasāvakaṃ nandaṃ mārentena purisena ānantariyakammaṃ bahulaṃ apuññaṃ pasutaṃ, tasmā yaṃ corehi ca verīhi ca kattabbaṃ, tatopi ghorataraṃ imesaṃ sattānaṃ micchāpaṇihitaṃ cittaṃ karotīti imamatthaṃ jānitvā tadatthadīpanaṃ imaṃ udānaṃ udānesi.

Having understood this meaning—because a man who kills Nanda, a noble disciple accomplished in right view, produces an unwholesome deed with immediate retribution, abundant in demerit, therefore, even more dreadful than what thieves or enemies might do is the wrongly directed mind of these beings—knowing this significance, the Blessed One uttered this inspired utterance to illuminate that meaning.

Tattha [M 0.0221] diso disanti dūsako dūsanīyaṃ coro coraṃ, disvāti vacanaseso. Yaṃ taṃ kayirāti yaṃ tassa anayabyasanaṃ kareyya, dutiyapadepi eseva nayo. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – eko ekassa mittadubbhī coro puttadārakhettavatthugomahiṃsādīsu aparajjhanto yassa aparajjhati, tampi tatheva attani aparajjhantaṃ coraṃ disvā, verī vā pana kenacideva kāraṇena baddhaveraṃ veriṃ disvā attano kakkhaḷatāya dāruṇatāya yaṃ tassa anayabyasanaṃ kareyya, puttadāraṃ vā pīḷeyya, khettādīni vā nāseyya, jīvitā vā voropeyya[P 0.0244], dasasu akusalakammapathesu micchāṭhapitattā micchāpaṇihitaṃ cittaṃ pāpiyo naṃ tato kare, naṃ purisaṃ pāpataraṃ tato kareyya. Vuttappakāro hi diso vā verī vā disassa vā verino vā imasmiṃyeva attabhāve dukkhaṃ vā uppādeyya, jīvitakkhayaṃ vā kareyya. Idaṃ pana akusalakammapathesu micchāṭhapitaṃ cittaṃ diṭṭheva dhamme anayabyasanaṃ pāpeti, attabhāvasatasahassesupi catūsu apāyesu khipitvā sīsamassa ukkhipituṃ na detīti.

Herein, 'diso' (enemy) means a harmer; 'disaṃ' (to an enemy) means that which is to be harmed. 'Coro' (thief) means a thief; 'coraṃ' (to a thief) means a thief. 'Disvāti' is the remainder of the statement. 'Yaṃ taṃ kayirā' means whatever misfortune or ruin he might cause to that person. The same applies to the second phrase. This is what is said: A thief who betrays a friend, offending against someone regarding sons, wives, fields, property, cattle, buffaloes, and so forth, or seeing a thief who offends against himself in the same way; or an enemy who, for some reason, has established enmity, seeing an enemy—due to his own harshness and cruelty, whatever misfortune or ruin he might cause to that person, whether oppressing his sons and wife, destroying his fields and so on, or even depriving him of life—a mind wrongly directed, due to being wrongly established in the ten unwholesome courses of action, would do him a greater evil than that; it would make that person worse off than that. For such a harmer or enemy would cause suffering or the end of life to an enemy or a foe in this very existence. But this mind wrongly established in the unwholesome courses of action leads to misfortune and ruin even in this very life, and for hundreds of thousands of existences, having cast one into the four states of deprivation, it does not allow one to lift one's head.

Tatiyasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the third discourse is concluded.

4. Yakkhapahārasuttavaṇṇanā

4. The Commentary on the Discourse on the Yakkha's Blow

34. Catutthe [V 0.0198] kapotakandarāyanti evaṃnāmake vihāre. Tasmiṃ kira pabbatakandare pubbe bahū kapotā vasiṃsu, tena sā pabbatakandarā “kapotakandarā”ti vuccati. Aparabhāge tattha katavihāropi “kapotakandarā”tveva paññāyittha. Tena vuttaṃ – “kapotakandarāyanti evaṃnāmake vihāre”ti. Juṇhāya rattiyāti sukkapakkharattiyaṃ. Navoropitehi kesehīti aciraohāritehi kesehi, itthambhūtalakkhaṇe cetaṃ karaṇavacanaṃ. Abbhokāseti yattha uparicchadanaṃ parikkhepo vā natthi, tādise ākāsaṅgaṇe.

34. In the fourth, 'at a monastery named Kapotakandara.' It is said that in that mountain cave, many doves had lived in the past, therefore that mountain cave was called 'Kapotakandara' (Dove Cave). Later, a monastery built there also became known as 'Kapotakandara.' Hence it is said: 'at a monastery named Kapotakandara.' 'On a moonlit night' means on a night of the waxing moon. 'With newly shorn hair' means with recently cut hair; this is an instrumental case indicating the state of being. 'In the open air' refers to an open space where there is no roof or enclosure.

Tattha āyasmā sāriputto suvaṇṇavaṇṇo, āyasmā mahāmoggallāno nīluppalavaṇṇo. Ubhopi pana te mahātherā udiccabrāhmaṇajaccā kappānaṃ satasahassādhikaṃ ekaṃ asaṅkhyeyyaṃ abhinīhārasampannā chaḷabhiññāpaṭisambhidāppattā mahākhīṇāsavā samāpattilābhino sattasaṭṭhiyā [M 0.0222] sāvakapāramiñāṇānaṃ matthakappattā etaṃ kapotakandaravihāraṃ upasobhayantā ekaṃ kanakaguhaṃ paviṭṭhā dve sīhā viya, ekaṃ vijambhanabhūmiṃ otiṇṇā dve byagghā viya, ekaṃ supupphitasālavanaṃ paviṭṭhā dve chaddantanāgarājāno viya, ekaṃ simbalivanaṃ paviṭṭhā dve supaṇṇarājāno viya, ekaṃ naravāhanayānaṃ abhiruḷhā dve vessavaṇā viya, ekaṃ paṇḍukambalasilāsanaṃ abhinisinnā dve sakkā [P 0.0245] viya, ekavimānabbhantaragatā dve mahābrahmāno viya, ekasmiṃ gaganaṭṭhāne ṭhitāni dve candamaṇḍalāni viya, dve sūriyamaṇḍalāni viya ca virociṃsu. Tesu āyasmā mahāmoggallāno tuṇhī nisīdi, āyasmā pana sāriputto samāpajji. Tena vuttaṃ – “aññataraṃ samādhiṃ samāpajjitvā”ti.

There, the Venerable Sāriputta was golden in color, and the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna was the color of a blue water lily. Both of those great elders were born into the northern brahmin caste, perfected in resolve for one incalculable aeon and one hundred thousand more, attained to the six higher knowledges and the four analytical knowledges, great ones with destroyed taints, masters of meditative attainments, having reached the pinnacle of the sixty-seven disciples' perfections of knowledge. Adorning this Kapotakandara Monastery, they shone like two lions that have entered a golden cave, like two tigers that have descended upon a place for exercise, like two Chaddanta elephant kings that have entered a fully blossomed sāla grove, like two garuḍa kings that have entered a silk-cotton forest, like two Vessavaṇas that have mounted a palanquin carried by men, like two Sakkas seated upon the Paṇḍukambala stone seat, like two Great Brahmās that have entered a single celestial mansion, like two moon orbs, and like two sun orbs standing in one place in the sky. Among them, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna sat silently, while the Venerable Sāriputta entered meditative absorption. Therefore, it is said: 'Having entered a certain meditative state.'

Tattha aññataraṃ samādhinti upekkhābrahmavihārasamāpattiṃ. Keci “saññāvedayitanirodhasamāpatti”nti vadanti, apare panāhu “āruppapādakaṃ phalasamāpatti”nti. Imā eva hi tisso kāyarakkhaṇasamatthā samāpattiyo. Tattha nirodhasamāpattiyā samādhipariyāyasambhavo heṭṭhā vuttova, pacchimaṃyeva pana ācariyā vaṇṇenti. Uttarāya disāya dakkhiṇaṃ disaṃ gacchantīti uttarāya disāya yakkhasamāgamaṃ gantvā attano bhavanaṃ gantuṃ dakkhiṇaṃ disaṃ gacchanti. Paṭibhāti manti upaṭṭhāti mama. Manti hi paṭisaddayogena sāmiatthe upayogavacanaṃ, imassa sīse pahāraṃ dātuṃ cittaṃ me uppajjatīti attho. So kira purimajātiyaṃ there baddhāghāto, tenassa theraṃ disvā paduṭṭhacittassa evaṃ ahosi. Itaro pana sappaññajātiko, tasmā taṃ paṭisedhento [V 0.0199] “alaṃ sammā”tiādimāha. Tattha mā āsādesīti mā ghaṭṭesi, mā pahāraṃ dehīti vuttaṃ hoti. Uḷāroti uḷārehi uttamehi sīlādiguṇehi samannāgato.

Herein, 'a certain concentration' refers to the attainment of the divine abiding of equanimity. Some say it is the 'attainment of cessation of perception and feeling,' while others say it is the 'fruition attainment which has the formless as its basis.' Indeed, these three attainments are capable of protecting the body. Regarding the attainment of cessation, the possibility of it being a kind of concentration has been mentioned below; but later teachers explain the last-mentioned. 'Going south from the northern direction' means that after attending a gathering of yakkhas in the northern direction, they proceed south to go to their own dwelling. 'It occurs to me' means it presents itself to me. Here, 'maṃ' is a usage in the sense of possession, by grammatical connection; the meaning is, 'the thought arises in me to strike a blow to his head.' It is said that in a past life he harbored resentment towards the elder, and so, seeing the elder, his mind being corrupted, he thought thus. The other, however, was wise by nature, so he restrained him, saying, 'Enough, friend.' Here, 'do not assault' means do not strike, do not deliver a blow—this is what is meant. 'Noble' means endowed with outstanding, supreme qualities such as virtue and so forth.

Anādiyitvāti ādaraṃ akatvā, tassa vacanaṃ aggahetvā. Yasmā pana tassa vacanaṃ aggaṇhanto taṃ anādiyanto nāma hoti, tasmā vuttaṃ – “taṃ yakkhaṃ anādiyitvā”ti. Sīse pahāraṃ adāsīti sabbathāmena ussāhaṃ janetvā ākāse ṭhitova sīse khaṭakaṃ adāsi, muddhani muṭṭhighātaṃ akāsīti attho. Tāva mahāti thāmamahattena tattakaṃ mahanto pahāro ahosi. Tena pahārenāti tena pahārena karaṇabhūtena. Sattaratananti pamāṇamajjhimassa purisassa ratanena sattaratanaṃ. Nāganti hatthināgaṃ. Osādeyyāti pathaviyaṃ [P 0.0246] osīdāpeyya nimujjāpeyya. “Osāreyyā”tipi [M 0.0223] pāṭho, cuṇṇavicuṇṇaṃ kareyyāti attho. Aḍḍhaṭṭhamaratananti aḍḍhena aṭṭhannaṃ pūraṇāni aḍḍhaṭṭhamāni, aḍḍhaṭṭhamāni ratanāni pamāṇaṃ etassāti aḍḍhaṭṭhamaratano, taṃ aḍḍhaṭṭhamaratanaṃ. Mahantaṃ pabbatakūṭanti kelāsakūṭappamāṇaṃ vipulaṃ girikūṭaṃ. Padāleyyāti sakalikākārena bhindeyya. Api osādeyya, api padāleyyāti sambandho.

'Not paying heed' means not showing respect, not accepting his words. Since not accepting his words is called not paying heed, it is therefore said: 'not paying heed to that yakkha.' 'He struck a blow on the head' means, having generated effort with all his strength, and while remaining in the air, he struck a blow on the head; the meaning is that he delivered a fist-blow to the crown. 'So mighty' means the blow was that great due to the greatness of his strength. 'By that blow' means by that very blow which was the instrument. 'Seven ratanas' means seven ratanas as measured by the cubit of a man of average height. 'An elephant' means a great elephant. 'He would sink' means he would cause it to sink into the earth, to submerge. Another reading is 'he would crush,' meaning he would reduce it to powder. 'Seven and a half ratanas' is a term for a measure of that size. 'A great mountain peak' means a vast mountain summit the size of Kelāsa Peak. 'He would split' means he would shatter it into fragments. The connection is: he would either sink it or split it.

Tāvadeva cassa sarīre mahāpariḷāho uppajji, so vedanāturo ākāse ṭhātuṃ asakkonto bhūmiyaṃ pati, taṅkhaṇaññeva aṭṭhasaṭṭhisahassādhikayojanasatasahassubbedhaṃ sinerumpi pabbatarājānaṃ sandhārentī catunahutādhikadviyojanasatasahassabahalā mahāpathavī taṃ pāpasattaṃ dhāretuṃ asakkontī viya vivaramadāsi. Avīcito jālā uṭṭhahitvā kandantaṃyeva taṃ gaṇhiṃsu, so kandanto vippalapanto pati. Tena vuttaṃ – “atha ca pana so yakkho ‘ḍayhāmi ḍayhāmī’ti vatvā tattheva mahānirayaṃ apatāsīti. Tattha apatāsīti apati.

At that very moment, a great burning arose in his body. Overcome by pain and unable to stand in the air, he fell to the ground. Instantly, the great earth—240,000 yojanas thick and supporting even Mount Sineru, the king of mountains, 168,000 yojanas high—as if unable to bear that wicked being, gave an opening. Flames from Avīci rose up and seized him even as he was wailing. Wailing and lamenting, he fell. Therefore it is said: 'Then that yakkha, crying, “I burn! I burn!” fell right there into the great hell.' Here, 'fell' means he plunged.

Kiṃ pana so yakkhattabhāveneva nirayaṃ upagacchīti? Na upagacchi, yañhettha diṭṭhadhammavedanīyaṃ pāpakammaṃ ahosi, tassa balena yakkhattabhāve mahantaṃ dukkhaṃ anubhavi. Yaṃ pana upapajjavedanīyaṃ ānantariyakammaṃ, tena cutianantaraṃ niraye uppajjīti. Therassa pana samāpattibalena upatthambhitasarīrassa na koci vikāro ahosi. Samāpattito avuṭṭhitakāle hi taṃ yakkho pahari, tathā paharantaṃ dibbacakkhunā disvā āyasmā mahāmoggallāno dhammasenāpatiṃ upasaṅkami, upasaṅkamanasamakālameva ca dhammasenāpati samāpattito uṭṭhāsi. Atha naṃ mahāmoggallāno sarīravuttiṃ pucchi, sopissa byākāsi, tena vuttaṃ – “addasā kho āyasmā mahāmoggallāno…pe… api ca me sīsaṃ thokaṃ dukkha”nti.

But did he go to hell in that very yakkha existence? He did not. For here, the evil deed was to be experienced in this very life, and due to its force, he experienced great suffering in his yakkha existence. However, due to the kamma of immediate retribution, which is to be experienced in the next life, he was reborn in hell immediately after passing away. For the Elder, however, whose body was supported by the power of his meditative attainment, there was no alteration. For the yakkha struck him at a time when he had not yet arisen from his attainment. Seeing him striking thus with his divine eye, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna approached the General of the Dhamma. At the very moment of his approach, the General of the Dhamma arose from his attainment. Then Mahāmoggallāna inquired about his physical condition, and he explained it to him. Therefore it is said: 'The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna saw… yet my head aches slightly.'

Tattha [V 0.0200] thokaṃ dukkhanti thokaṃ appamattakaṃ madhurakajātaṃ viya me sīsaṃ dukkhitaṃ, dukkhappattanti [P 0.0247] attho. Dukkhādhiṭṭhānañhi sīsaṃ dukkhanti vuttaṃ. “Sīse thokaṃ dukkha”ntipi pāṭho. Kathaṃ pana samāpattibalena sarīre upatthambhite therassa sīse thokampi dukkhaṃ ahosīti? Acireneva vuṭṭhitattā. Antosamāpattiyaṃ [M 0.0224] apaññāyamānadukkhañhi kāyanissitattā niddaṃ upagatassa makasādijanitaṃ viya paṭibuddhassa thokaṃ paññāyittha.

Herein, 'my head aches slightly' means: my head is pained, afflicted with a minor, insignificant pain, like a mild ache; that is the meaning. For the head, being the basis of the pain, is spoken of as 'pain'. Another reading is, 'There is slight pain in the head.' But how could there be even slight pain in the Elder’s head when his body was supported by the power of meditative attainment? Because he had just emerged from it. For the pain, being dependent on the body, was not perceived while he was within the attainment—just as a pain caused by a mosquito or the like is not felt by one who is asleep, but is slightly perceived upon awakening.

“Mahābalena yakkhena tathā sabbussāhena pahaṭe sarīrepi vikāro nāma natthī”ti acchariyabbhutacittajātena āyasmatā mahāmoggallānena “acchariyaṃ, āvuso sāriputtā”tiādinā dhammasenāpatino mahānubhāvatāya vibhāvitāya sopissa ‘acchariyaṃ, āvuso moggallānā”tiādinā iddhānubhāvamahantatāpakāsanāpadesena attano issāmacchariyāhaṅkārādimalānaṃ suppahīnataṃ dīpeti. Paṃsupisācakampi na passāmāti saṅkārakūṭādīsu vicaraṇakakhuddakapetampi na passāma. Iti adhigamappicchānaṃ aggabhūto mahāthero tasmiṃ kāle anāvajjanena tesaṃ adassanaṃ sandhāya vadati. Tenevāha “etarahī”ti.

When the great power of the General of the Dhamma was revealed by the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna—in whom a mind of wonder and amazement had arisen, thinking, 'Even when struck by a mighty yakkha with all his effort, there is no alteration whatsoever in the body'—with the words, 'It is astonishing, friend Sāriputta,' and so on, he in turn, with the words, 'It is astonishing, friend Moggallāna,' and so on, on the pretext of proclaiming the greatness of his psychic power, reveals the complete abandoning of his own defilements of envy, stinginess, pride, and so on. 'We do not even see a dust-ghoul' means: we do not see even a minor spirit that wanders in garbage heaps and so on. Thus, the great elder, foremost among those with desire for attainment, speaks with reference to not seeing them at that time due to not adverting his mind. Therefore, he says, 'at this time.'

Bhagavā pana veḷuvane ṭhito ubhinnaṃ aggasāvakānaṃ imaṃ kathāsallāpaṃ dibbasotena assosi. Tena vuttaṃ – “assosi kho bhagavā”tiādi, taṃ vuttatthameva.

The Blessed One, while dwelling in the Bamboo Grove, heard this conversation between the two chief disciples with his divine ear. Therefore, it is said: 'The Blessed One heard,' and so on, which has the meaning already stated.

Etamatthaṃ viditvāti etaṃ āyasmato sāriputtassa samāpattibalūpagataṃ iddhānubhāvamahantataṃ viditvā. Imaṃ udānanti tasseva tādibhāvappattidīpakaṃ imaṃ udānaṃ udānesi.

'Having understood this matter' means having understood this greatness of the Venerable Sāriputta's psychic power, which was attained through the power of his meditative attainment. He then uttered this inspired utterance, which illuminates his attainment of such a state.

Tattha yassa selūpamaṃ cittaṃ, ṭhitaṃ nānupakampatīti yassa khīṇāsavassa cittaṃ ekagghanasilāmayapabbatūpamaṃ sabbesaṃ iñjanānaṃ abhāvato vasībhāvappattiyāva ṭhitaṃ sabbehipi lokadhammehi nānupakampati na pavedhati. Idānissa akampanākāraṃ saddhiṃ kāraṇena dassetuṃ “viratta”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha virattaṃ rajanīyesūti virāgasaṅkhātena ariyamaggena rajanīyesu rāguppattihetubhūtesu sabbesu tebhūmakadhammesu virattaṃ, tattha sabbaso samucchinnarāganti attho. Kopaneyyeti paṭighaṭṭhānīye sabbasmimpi āghātavatthusmiṃ na kuppati na dussati na vikāraṃ āpajjati. Yassevaṃ bhāvitaṃ cittanti yassa yathāvuttassa ariyapuggalassa [P 0.0248] cittaṃ evaṃ vuttanayena tādibhāvāvahanabhāvena bhāvitaṃ. Kuto taṃ dukkhamessatīti taṃ uttamapuggalaṃ kuto sattato saṅkhārato vā dukkhaṃ upagamissati, na tādisassa dukkhaṃ atthīti attho.

There, for one whose mind is like a rock, steady and undisturbed—for such a person whose mind, being that of an arahant, is like a solid mountain of stone, firm due to the absence of all agitation, having attained mastery, it is not disturbed or shaken by any worldly conditions. Now, to show the nature of its unshakenness along with the reason, it is said: 'detached' and so on. Herein, 'detached from the enticing'—detached from all things in the three realms that are causes for the arising of lust, by means of the noble path called dispassion; the meaning here is that lust is completely uprooted therein. 'Not angered by what is provoking'—in all grounds for resentment, it does not get angry, does not become hostile, and does not undergo change. 'For one whose mind is thus developed'—for that noble person whose mind, as described, is developed in such a way as to bring about such a state. 'How can suffering touch him?'—how can suffering approach such an excellent person, whether from a being or from conditioned phenomena? It means that there is no suffering for such a one.

Catutthasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the fourth discourse is completed.

5. Nāgasuttavaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Nāga Sutta

35. Pañcame [M 0.0225][V 0.0201] kosambiyanti kusumbena nāma isinā vasitaṭṭhāne māpitattā “kosambī”ti evaṃladdhanāmake nagare. Ghositārāmeti ghositaseṭṭhinā kārite ārāme. Bhagavā ākiṇṇo viharatīti bhagavā sambādhappatto viharati. Kiṃ pana bhagavato sambādho atthi, saṃsaggo vāti? Natthi. Na hi koci bhagavantaṃ anicchāya upasaṅkamituṃ sakkoti. Durāsadā hi buddhā bhagavanto sabbattha ca anupalittattā. Hitesitāya pana sattesu anukampaṃ upādāya “mutto mocessāmī”ti paṭiññānurūpaṃ caturoghanittharaṇatthaṃ aṭṭhannaṃ parisānaṃ attano santikaṃ kālena kālaṃ upasaṅkamanaṃ adhivāseti, sayañca mahākaruṇāsamussāhito kālaññū hutvā tattha upasaṅkamati, idaṃ sabbabuddhānaṃ āciṇṇaṃ, ayamidha ākiṇṇavihāroti adhippeto.

35. In the fifth, at Kosambi—a city named 'Kosambi' because it was built at the place inhabited by the sage named Kusumba. At Ghositarama—in the monastery built by the merchant Ghosita. The Blessed One dwelt amidst a throng—this means the Blessed One dwelt having attained to a state of being crowded. But does the Blessed One experience crowding or association? No. For no one is able to approach the Blessed One against his will. For the Blessed Buddhas are difficult to approach, being untainted in all things. Yet out of compassion for beings, desiring their welfare, thinking, 'Being liberated, I shall liberate others,' in accordance with his vow, for the sake of crossing the four floods, he approves the eight assemblies approaching him from time to time. And he himself, aroused by great compassion, knowing the right time, approaches there. This is the habitual practice of all Buddhas; this is the meaning of dwelling amidst a throng here.

Idha pana kosambikānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ kalahajātānaṃ satthā dīghītissa kosalarañño vatthuṃ āharitvā, “na hi verena verāni, sammantīdha kudācana”ntiādinā (dha. pa. 5; ma. ni. 3.237; mahāva. 464) ovādaṃ adāsi, taṃ divasaṃ tesaṃ kalahaṃ karontānaṃyeva ratti vibhātā. Dutiyadivasepi bhagavā tameva vatthuṃ kathesi, taṃ divasampi tesaṃ kalahaṃ karontānaṃyeva ratti vibhātā. Tatiyadivasepi bhagavā tameva vatthuṃ kathesi, athaññataro bhikkhu bhagavantaṃ evamāha – “appossukko, bhante bhagavā, diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāramanuyutto viharatu, mayametena bhaṇḍanena kalahena viggahena vivādena [P 0.0249] paññāyissāmā”ti. Satthā “pariyādinnacittā kho ime moghapurisā na dānime sakkā saññāpetuṃ, natthi cettha saññāpetabbā, yaṃnūnāhaṃ ekacārikavāsaṃ vaseyyaṃ, evaṃ ime bhikkhū kalahato oramissantī”ti cintesi. Evaṃ tehi kalahakārakehi bhikkhūhi saddhiṃ ekavihāre vāsaṃ vinetabbābhāvato upāsakādīhi upasaṅkamanañca ākiṇṇavihāraṃ katvā vuttaṃ – “tena kho pana samayena bhagavā ākiṇṇo viharatī”tiādi.

Here, when the Kosambī monks had become quarrelsome, the Teacher brought up the story of King Dīghīti of Kosala and advised them with, 'Never indeed is hatred appeased by hatred here,' and so on. But that very night dawned while they were still quarreling. On the second day, the Blessed One again related the same story, but that night too dawned while they were still quarreling. On the third day, the Blessed One once more told the same story, then a certain monk said to the Blessed One: 'Let the Blessed One be without concern, devoted to dwelling in the bliss of the present life. We will become known through this bickering, quarreling, contention, and disputation.' The Teacher thought: 'These foolish men are overwhelmed in mind. It is no longer possible to persuade them; there is no one here who can be persuaded. Suppose I were to live in solitary retreat; perhaps these monks would then desist from quarreling.' Thus, because those quarrelsome monks could not be disciplined, and because the visits of lay followers and others made for a crowded dwelling, it was said: 'At that time, the Blessed One was dwelling amidst a throng,' and so on.

Tattha dukkhanti na sukhaṃ, anārādhitacittatāya na iṭṭhanti attho. Tenevāha “na phāsu viharāmī”ti. Vūpakaṭṭhoti pavivekaṭṭho dūrībhūto. Tathā cintetvāva bhagavā pātova sarīrappaṭijagganaṃ katvā kosambiyaṃ piṇḍāya [M 0.0226] caritvā kañci anāmantetvā eko adutiyo gantvā kosalaraṭṭhe pālileyyake vanasaṇḍe bhaddasālamūle vihāsi. Tena vuttaṃ – “atha kho bhagavā pubbaṇhasamayaṃ…pe… bhaddasālamūle”ti. Tattha sāmanti sayaṃ. Saṃsāmetvāti paṭisāmetvā. Pattacīvaramādāyāti [V 0.0202] etthāpi sāmanti padaṃ ānetvā yojetabbaṃ. Upaṭṭhāketi kosambinagaravāsino ghositaseṭṭhiādike upaṭṭhāke, vihāre ca aggupaṭṭhākaṃ āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ anāmantetvā.

Here, 'dukkha' means not happiness; the meaning is 'not pleasing' because of an unsatisfied mind. Therefore, he said, 'I do not dwell at ease.' 'Vūpakaṭṭha' means secluded, being far removed. Having reflected thus, the Blessed One, after attending to his body early in the morning, having wandered for alms in Kosambī, without addressing anyone, went alone, without a second, and dwelled in the Pārileyyaka forest in the Kosala country, at the foot of a noble sal tree. Hence it is said: 'Then the Blessed One, in the morning... at the foot of the noble sal tree.' Here, 'sāmaṃ' means by himself. 'Saṃsāmetvā' means having packed away. 'Pattacīvaramādāya'—here too, the word 'sāmaṃ' should be supplied and connected. 'Upaṭṭhāke' refers to the attendants of Kosambī city, such as the merchant Ghosita and others, and the chief attendant in the monastery, the Venerable Ānanda, without addressing them.

Evaṃ gate satthari pañcasatā bhikkhū āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ āhaṃsu – “āvuso ānanda, satthā ekakova gato, mayaṃ anubandhissāmā”ti. “Āvuso, yadā bhagavā sāmaṃ senāsanaṃ saṃsāmetvā pattacīvaramādāya anāmantetvā upaṭṭhāke ca anapaloketvā bhikkhusaṅghaṃ adutiyo gacchati, tadā ekacāraṃ carituṃ bhagavato ajjhāsayo, sāvakena nāma satthu ajjhāsayānurūpaṃ paṭipajjitabbaṃ, tasmā na imesu divasesu bhagavā anugantabbo”ti nivāresi, sayampi nānugacchi.

When the Teacher had thus departed, five hundred monks said to Venerable Ānanda: 'Friend Ānanda, the Teacher has gone alone; we will follow him.' 'Friends, when the Blessed One himself puts his lodging in order, takes his bowl and robe, and departs without informing his attendants or taking leave of the Sangha of monks, going without a second—then it is the Blessed One's inclination to wander alone. A disciple should act in accordance with the Teacher's inclination. Therefore, the Blessed One should not be followed during these days.' Thus he restrained them, and he himself did not follow.

Anupubbenāti anukkamena, gāmanigamapaṭipāṭiyā cārikaṃ caramāno “ekacāravāsaṃ tāva vasamānaṃ bhikkhuṃ passissāmī”ti bālakaloṇakāragāmaṃ gantvā tattha bhaguttherassa sakalaṃ pacchābhattañceva tiyāmañca rattiṃ ekacāravāse ānisaṃsaṃ kathetvā punadivase tena pacchāsamaṇena piṇḍāya caritvā taṃ tattheva nivattetvā “samaggavāsaṃ vasamāne tayo kulaputte passissāmī”ti [P 0.0250] pācīnavaṃsamigadāyaṃ gantvā tesampi sakalarattiṃ samaggavāse ānisaṃsaṃ kathetvā tepi tattheva nivattetvā ekakova pālileyyagāmaṃ sampatto. Pālileyyagāmavāsino paccuggantvā bhagavato dānaṃ datvā pālileyyagāmassa avidūre rakkhitavanasaṇḍo nāma atthi, tattha bhagavato paṇṇasālaṃ katvā “ettha bhagavā vasatū”ti yācitvā vāsayiṃsu. Bhaddasāloti pana tattheko manāpo bhaddako sālarukkho, bhagavā taṃ gāmaṃ upanissāya vanasaṇḍe paṇṇasālasamīpe tasmiṃ rukkhamūle vihāsi. Tena vuttaṃ – “pālileyyake viharati rakkhitavanasaṇḍe bhaddasālamūle”ti.

"Gradually" means in sequence, traveling from village to market town in order. Thinking, "I will see a monk who stays in solitary dwelling for a while," he went to the village of Bālakaloṇakāra and there, for the entire post-meal period and the three watches of the night, he explained the benefits of solitary dwelling to the elder Bhagu. The next day, after going for alms with that attendant monk, he sent him back right there. Thinking, "I will see three sons of good family living in harmony," he went to the Pācīnavaṃsa deer park and explained the benefits of harmonious living to them all night. He sent them back right there as well, and he alone arrived at the village of Pālileyya. The residents of Pālileyya came out to meet him, offered alms to the Blessed One, and not far from the village was a protected grove called Rakkhitavanasaṇḍa. There, they built a leaf hut for the Blessed One and, having requested, "May the Blessed One stay here," they had him stay. Now, in that place, there was a beautiful and auspicious sāl tree called Bhaddasāla. The Blessed One, relying on that village, dwelled in the grove near the leaf hut at the foot of that tree. Therefore, it is said: "He dwelled at Pālileyyaka, in the Rakkhita forest grove, at the foot of the Bhaddasāla tree."

Hatthināgoti mahāhatthī yūthapati. Hatthikalabhehīti hatthipotakehi. Hatthicchāpehīti khīrūpagehi daharahatthipotakehi, ye “bhiṅkā”tipi [M 0.0227] vuccanti. Chinnaggānīti purato purato gacchantehi tehi hatthiādīhi chinnaggāni khāditāvasesāni khāṇusadisāni khādati. Obhaggobhagganti tena hatthināgena uccaṭṭhānato bhañjitvā bhañjitvā pātitaṃ. Assa sākhābhaṅganti etassa santakaṃ sākhābhaṅgaṃ te khādanti. Āvilānīti tehi paṭhamataraṃ otaritvā pivantehi āluḷitattā āvilāni kaddamamissāni pānīyāni pivati. Ogāhāti titthato. “Ogāha”ntipi pāḷi. Assāti hatthināgassa. Upanighaṃsantiyoti ghaṭṭentiyo, upanighaṃsiyamānopi [V 0.0203] attano uḷārabhāvena na kujjhati, tena tā taṃ ghaṃsantiyeva. Yūthāti hatthighaṭā.

A "great elephant" is a great elephant, a leader of the herd. "Young elephants" refers to elephant calves. "Elephant infants" means young, milk-fed elephant calves, who are also called "bhiṅkā." "With broken tips" means he eats the remnants, like stumps, with their tips broken off and eaten by those elephants and others as they go ahead. "Broken and shattered" refers to what has been broken again and again and felled from a high place by that great elephant. "His broken branch" means they eat the broken branch belonging to him. "Muddied" means he drinks turbid water mixed with mud because it has been stirred up by those who descended to drink first. "From the bathing place" means from the ford. `Ogāha` is also the reading in the text. "His" refers to the great elephant. "Rubbing against" means jostling. Although he is being jostled, due to his noble nature, he does not become angry; therefore, they continue to jostle him. "Herd" refers to a group of elephants.

Yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamīti so kira hatthināgo yūthavāse ukkaṇṭhito taṃ vanasaṇḍaṃ paviṭṭho tattha bhagavantaṃ disvā ghaṭasahassena nibbāpitasantāpo viya nibbuto hutvā pasannacitto bhagavato santike aṭṭhāsi, tato paṭṭhāya vattasīse ṭhatvā bhaddasālassa paṇṇasālāya ca samantato appaharitakaṃ katvā sākhābhaṅgehi sammajjati, bhagavato mukhadhovanaṃ deti, nhānodakaṃ āharati, dantakaṭṭhaṃ deti, araññato madhurāni phalāni āharitvā satthu upaneti, satthā tāni paribhuñjati[P 0.0251]. Tena vuttaṃ – “tatra sudaṃ so hatthināgo yasmiṃ padese bhagavā viharati, taṃ padesaṃ appaharitañca karoti, soṇḍāya bhagavato pānīyaṃ paribhojanīyaṃ upaṭṭhāpetī”ti. Soṇḍāya dārūni āharitvā aññamaññaṃ ghaṃsitvā aggiṃ uṭṭhāpetvā dārūni jālāpetvā tattha pāsāṇakhaṇḍāni tāpetvā tāni daṇḍakehi pavaṭṭetvā soṇḍiyaṃ khipitvā udakassa tattabhāvaṃ ñatvā bhagavato santikaṃ upagantvā tiṭṭhati, bhagavā “hatthināgo mama nhānaṃ icchatī”ti tattha gantvā nhānakiccaṃ karoti, pānīyepi eseva nayo. Tasmiṃ pana sītale sañjāte upasaṅkamati, taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ – “soṇḍāya bhagavato pānīyaṃ paribhojanīyaṃ upaṭṭhāpetī”ti.

"He approached the Blessed One" means that the great elephant, it is said, being discontented with life in the herd, entered that forest grove. There, upon seeing the Blessed One, he stood near him with a serene mind, his torment extinguished as if by a thousand pots of water. From then on, standing in attendance, he kept the area all around the Bhaddasāla tree and the leaf hut free of green growth, swept it with broken branches, provided water for the Blessed One to wash his face, brought bathing water, offered a tooth-stick, gathered sweet fruits from the forest, and presented them to the Teacher, who partook of them. Thus it is said: "There, indeed, that great elephant kept the place where the Blessed One was dwelling free of green growth, and with his trunk he provided drinking water and water for use for the Blessed One." With his trunk, he would gather firewood, rub the pieces together to produce a fire, light the wood, heat stones in it, roll them with sticks, and toss them with his trunk into a hollow of water. Knowing the water was heated, he would approach the Blessed One and stand by. The Blessed One, understanding, "The great elephant wishes me to bathe," would go there and perform his bathing. The same method applied to drinking water. When it became cold, he would approach him in this way. It is with reference to this that it was said: "With his trunk he provided drinking water and water for use for the Blessed One."

Atha kho bhagavato rahogatassātiādi ubhinnaṃ mahānāgānaṃ vivekasukhapaccavekkhaṇadassanaṃ, taṃ vuttatthameva. Attano ca pavivekaṃ viditvāti kehici anākiṇṇabhāvaladdhaṃ kāyavivekaṃ jānitvā, itare pana vivekā bhagavato sabbakālaṃ vijjantiyeva.

"Then, the Blessed One, being in seclusion…" and so on, shows the two great beings' vision in reflecting on the bliss of seclusion; the meaning of this has already been stated. "And knowing his own seclusion" means knowing the physical seclusion attained by not being crowded by anyone; as for the other kinds of seclusion, they are always present for the Blessed One.

Imaṃ [M 0.0228] udānanti imaṃ attano hatthināgassa ca pavivekābhiratiyā samānajjhāsayabhāvadīpanaṃ udānaṃ udānesi.

"This inspired utterance" means he uttered this inspired utterance illustrating the state of having a shared inclination for the delight in seclusion, both for himself and for the great elephant.

Tatthāyaṃ saṅkhepattho – etaṃ īsādantassa rathaīsāsadisadantassa hatthināgassa cittaṃ nāgena buddhanāgassa cittena sameti saṃsandati. Kathaṃ sameti ce? Yadeko ramatī vane yasmā buddhanāgo “ahaṃ kho pubbe ākiṇṇo vihāsi”nti purimaṃ ākiṇṇavihāraṃ jigucchitvā vivekaṃ upabrūhayamāno idāni yathā eko adutiyo vane araññe ramati abhiramati, evaṃ ayampi hatthināgo pubbe attano hatthiādīhi ākiṇṇavihāraṃ jigucchitvā vivekaṃ upabrūhayamāno idāni [V 0.0204] eko asahāyo vane araññe ramati abhiramati. Tasmāssa cittaṃ nāgena sameti tassa cittena sametīti katvā ekībhāvaratiyā ekasadisaṃ hotīti attho.

Here is the concise meaning: The mind of this great elephant, whose tusks are like chariot poles, aligns and corresponds with the mind of the Nāga, the Buddha-Nāga. How does it align? Because just as the Buddha-Nāga, detesting his former crowded dwelling with the thought, "Formerly, I lived crowded," and cultivating seclusion, now delights in the forest alone, without a second; so too this great elephant, detesting his former crowded dwelling with other elephants, and cultivating seclusion, now delights in the forest alone, without a companion. Therefore, his mind aligns with the Nāga, it corresponds with his mind; the meaning is that it becomes one and the same in the delight of being alone.

Pañcamasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the fifth sutta is finished.

6. Piṇḍolasuttavaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Piṇḍola Sutta

36. Chaṭṭhe [P 0.0252] piṇḍolabhāradvājoti piṇḍaṃ ulamāno pariyesamāno pabbajitoti piṇḍolo. So kira parijiṇṇabhogo brāhmaṇo hutvā mahantaṃ bhikkhusaṅghassa lābhasakkāraṃ disvā piṇḍatthāya nikkhamitvā pabbajito. So mahantaṃ kapallaṃ “patta”nti gahetvā carati, kapallapūraṃ yāguṃ pivati, bhattaṃ bhuñjati, pūvakhajjakañca khādati. Athassa mahagghasabhāvaṃ satthu ārocesuṃ. Satthā tassa pattatthavikaṃ nānujāni, heṭṭhāmañce pattaṃ nikkujjitvā ṭhapeti, so ṭhapentopi ghaṃsentova paṇāmetvā ṭhapeti, gaṇhantopi ghaṃsentova ākaḍḍhitvā gaṇhāti. Taṃ gacchante gacchante kāle ghaṃsanena parikkhīṇaṃ, nāḷikodanamattasseva gaṇhanakaṃ jātaṃ. Tato satthu ārocesuṃ, athassa satthā pattatthavikaṃ anujāni. Thero aparena samayena indriyabhāvanaṃ bhāvento aggaphale arahatte patiṭṭhāsi. Iti so pubbe savisesaṃ piṇḍatthāya ulatīti piṇḍolo, gottena pana bhāradvājoti ubhayaṃ ekato katvā “piṇḍolabhāradvājo”ti vuccati.

36. Sixth is Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja. 'Piṇḍola' means one who, having gone forth, wanders seeking alms-food. It is said that he was a brahmin whose wealth had decayed, who, upon seeing the great gains and honors of the community of monks, went forth for the sake of alms. He carried a large potsherd, calling it a 'bowl,' and wandered about. He would drink gruel that filled the potsherd, eat rice, and consume cakes and sweets. Then his gluttonous nature was reported to the Teacher. The Teacher did not permit him a bowl-bag. He would place the bowl overturned under his bed. When placing it, he would set it down with a scraping sound, and when taking it, he would drag it out with a scraping sound. As time went on, it wore down from the scraping until it could hold only a nāḷi measure of rice. This was reported to the Teacher, who then permitted him a bowl-bag. Later, the elder, developing his faculties, became established in arahantship, the highest fruit. Thus, because he previously wandered especially for alms-food, he was called 'Piṇḍola,' and as his clan name was Bhāradvāja, the two were combined, and he was called 'Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja.'

Āraññakoti [M 0.0229] gāmantasenāsanapaṭikkhipanena araññe nivāso assāti āraññako, āraññakadhutaṅgaṃ samādāya vattantassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Tathā bhikkhāsaṅkhātānaṃ āmisapiṇḍānaṃ pāto piṇḍapāto, parehi dinnānaṃ piṇḍānaṃ patte nipatananti attho. Piṇḍapātaṃ uñchati taṃ taṃ kulaṃ upasaṅkamanto gavesatīti piṇḍapātiko, piṇḍāya vā patituṃ carituṃ vatametassāti piṇḍapātī, piṇḍapātīyeva piṇḍapātiko. Saṅkārakūṭādīsu paṃsūnaṃ upari ṭhitattā abbhuggataṭṭhena paṃsukūlaṃ viyāti paṃsukūlaṃ, paṃsu viya vā kucchitabhāvaṃ ulati gacchatīti paṃsukūlaṃ, paṃsukūlassa dhāraṇaṃ paṃsukūlaṃ, taṃ sīlaṃ etassāti paṃsukūliko. Saṅghāṭiuttarāsaṅgaantaravāsakasaṅkhātāni tīṇi cīvarāni ticīvaraṃ, ticīvarassa dhāraṇaṃ ticīvaraṃ, taṃ sīlaṃ etassāti tecīvariko. Appicchotiādīnaṃ padānaṃ attho heṭṭhā vuttoyeva.

'Forest-dweller' (āraññaka) means one whose dwelling is in the forest, by way of rejecting lodgings near a village; this is the name for one who undertakes the forest-dweller's ascetic practice. Similarly, 'alms-food' (piṇḍapāta) is the 'falling' (pāta) of lumps (piṇḍa) of material food, known as alms; the meaning is the falling of lumps of food given by others into the bowl. One who gleans alms-food, approaching various families and seeking it, is an 'alms-food-goer' (piṇḍapātika). Or, one whose observance it is to go or wander for alms is an 'alms-goer' (piṇḍapātī); an alms-goer is indeed an alms-food-goer. 'Rag-robes' (paṃsukūla) are so called because, being found on dust heaps and the like, they are taken up from there; or, because they go (ulati) to a despised state like dust (paṃsu), they are called paṃsukūla. The wearing of rag-robes is the rag-robe practice; one for whom this is a practice is a 'rag-robe-wearer' (paṃsukūlika). The three robes—the outer cloak (saṅghāṭi), upper robe (uttarāsaṅga), and inner robe (antaravāsaka)—are the 'triple robe' (ticīvara). The wearing of the triple robe is the triple-robe practice; one for whom this is a practice is a 'triple-robe-wearer' (tecīvarika). The meaning of terms such as 'of few wishes' has been explained previously.

Dhutavādoti [V 0.0205][P 0.0253] dhuto vuccati dhutakileso puggalo, kilesadhunanakadhammo vā. Tattha atthi dhuto, na dhutavādo, atthi na dhuto, dhutavādo, atthi neva dhuto, na dhutavādo, atthi dhuto ceva, dhutavādo cāti idaṃ catukkaṃ veditabbaṃ. Tesu yo sayaṃ dhutadhamme samādāya vattati, na paraṃ tadatthāya samādapeti, ayaṃ paṭhamo. Yo pana sayaṃ na dhutadhamme samādāya vattati, paraṃ samādapeti, ayaṃ dutiyo. Yo ubhayarahito, ayaṃ tatiyo. Yo pana ubhayasampanno, ayaṃ catuttho. Evarūpo ca āyasmā piṇḍolabhāradvājoti. Tena vuttaṃ “dhutavādo”ti. Ekadesasarūpekasesavasena hi ayaṃ niddeso yathā taṃ “nāmarūpa”nti.

'Proclaimer of asceticism' (dhutavāda): 'Dhuta' refers to a person whose defilements are shaken off, or to a practice that shakes off defilements. In this regard, this fourfold distinction should be understood: there is one who is dhuta but not a proclaimer of dhuta; there is one who is not dhuta but is a proclaimer of dhuta; there is one who is neither dhuta nor a proclaimer of dhuta; and there is one who is both dhuta and a proclaimer of dhuta. Among these, the first is one who himself undertakes the dhuta practices, but does not encourage others to do so. The second is one who does not himself undertake the dhuta practices, but encourages others to do so. The third is devoid of both. The fourth is endowed with both. The Venerable Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja was of this last kind. Therefore, he is called a 'proclaimer of asceticism.' For this exposition is made by way of partial inclusion, as in the case of 'name-and-form.'

Adhicittamanuyuttoti ettha aṭṭhasamāpattisampayogato arahattaphalasamāpattisampayogato vā cittassa adhicittabhāvo veditabbo, idha pana “arahattaphalacitta”nti vadanti. Taṃtaṃsamāpattīsu samādhi eva adhicittaṃ, idha pana arahattaphalasamādhi veditabbo. Keci pana “adhicittamanuyuttena, bhikkhave, bhikkhunā kālena kālaṃ tīṇi nimittāni manasi kātabbānīti etasmiṃ adhicittasutte (a. ni. 3.103) viya samathavipassanācittaṃ adhicittanti idhādhippeta”nti vadanti, taṃ na sundaraṃ. Purimoyevattho gahetabbo.

'One devoted to higher mind': Here, the state of higher mind should be understood as the mind's association with the eight attainments or with the attainment of the fruit of arahantship. In this context, however, they speak of 'the mind of the fruit of arahantship.' In those attainments, concentration itself is the higher mind; here, it should be understood as the concentration of the fruit of arahantship. Some, however, say: "In this context, 'higher mind' refers to the mind of serenity and insight, as in the Higher Mind Sutta (Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.103), where it is said: 'Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu devoted to higher mind should from time to time attend to three signs.'" That is not well-stated; the former explanation should be adopted.

Etamatthaṃ [M 0.0230] viditvāti etaṃ āyasmato piṇḍolabhāradvājassa adhiṭṭhānaparikkhārasampadāsampannaṃ adhicittānuyogasaṅkhātaṃ atthaṃ sabbākārato viditvā. Evaṃ “adhicittānuyogo mama sāsanānuṭṭhāna”nti dīpento imaṃ udānaṃ udānesi.

'Having understood this matter' means having understood in all its aspects this matter concerning the Venerable Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja—namely, his being endowed with the accomplishment of the requisites of resolve, which is known as devotion to the higher mind. Thus, illuminating that 'Devotion to the higher mind is the practice of my teaching,' he uttered this inspired utterance.

Tattha anūpavādoti vācāya kassacipi anupavadanaṃ. Anūpaghātoti kāyena kassaci upaghātākaraṇaṃ. Pātimokkheti ettha pātimokkhapadassa attho heṭṭhā nānappakārehi vutto, tasmiṃ pātimokkhe. Sattannaṃ āpattikkhandhānaṃ avītikkamalakkhaṇo saṃvaro. Mattaññutāti [P 0.0254] paṭiggahaṇaparibhogavasena pamāṇaññutā. Pantañca sayanāsananti vivittaṃ saṅghaṭṭanavirahitaṃ senāsanaṃ. Adhicitte ca āyogoti aṭṭhannaṃ samāpattīnaṃ adhigamāya bhāvanānuyogo.

Here, 'not reproaching' means not reproaching anyone with speech. 'Not harming' means not doing harm to anyone with the body. As for 'in the Pātimokkha,' the meaning of the word 'Pātimokkha' has been explained previously in various ways. In that Pātimokkha, restraint is characterized by the non-transgression of the seven classes of offenses. 'Knowing moderation' means knowing the proper measure with regard to receiving and using. 'And a secluded lodging' means a dwelling that is remote and free from crowding. 'And application to the higher mind' means the practice of development for the attainment of the eight attainments.

Aparo nayo – anūpavādoti kassacipi uparujjhanavacanassa avadanaṃ. Tena sabbampi vācasikaṃ sīlaṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Anūpaghātoti kāyena kassaci upaghātassa paraviheṭhanassa akaraṇaṃ. Tena sabbampi kāyikaṃ sīlaṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Yādisaṃ panidaṃ ubhayaṃ buddhānaṃ sāsanantogadhaṃ hoti, taṃ dassetuṃ – “pātimokkhe ca saṃvaro”ti vuttaṃ. Casaddo nipātamattaṃ. Pātimokkhe ca saṃvaroti pātimokkhasaṃvarabhūto anūpavādo anūpaghāto cāti attho.

Another method of interpretation: 'non-reproach' means not uttering speech that is obstructive to anyone. By this, all verbal virtue is included. 'Non-harming' means not causing physical harm or vexation to anyone. By this, all bodily virtue is included. To show how both of these are included in the teaching of the Buddhas, it is said: 'and restraint in the Pātimokkha.' The word 'ca' is a mere particle. The meaning is: non-reproach and non-harming, which constitute the Pātimokkha restraint.

Atha [V 0.0206] vā pātimokkheti adhikaraṇe bhummaṃ. Pātimokkhe nissayabhūte saṃvaro. Ko pana soti? Anūpavādo anūpaghāto. Upasampadavelāyañhi avisesena pātimokkhasīlaṃ samādinnaṃ nāma hoti, tasmiṃ pātimokkhe ṭhitassa tato paraṃ upavādūpaghātānaṃ akaraṇavasena saṃvaro, so anūpavādo anūpaghāto cāti vutto.

Alternatively, 'Pātimokkha' here is in the locative case, indicating a basis. Restraint is based on the Pātimokkha. What, then, is it? Non-reviling and non-harming. For at the time of ordination, the Pātimokkha precepts are undertaken in a comprehensive manner. For one established in that Pātimokkha, restraint thereafter consists of not reviling and not harming—hence, it is called non-reviling and non-harming.

Atha vā pātimokkheti nipphādetabbe bhummaṃ yathā “cetaso avūpasamo ayonisomanasikārapadaṭṭhāna”nti (saṃ. ni. 5.232). Tena pātimokkhena sādhetabbo anūpavādo anūpaghāto, pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṅgahito anūpavādo anūpaghātoicceva attho. Saṃvaroti iminā pana satisaṃvaro[M 0.0231], ñāṇasaṃvaro, khantisaṃvaro, vīriyasaṃvaroti imesaṃ catunnaṃ saṃvarānaṃ gahaṇaṃ, pātimokkhasādhanaṃ idaṃ saṃvaracatukkaṃ.

Alternatively, 'Pātimokkha' here is in the locative case in the sense of 'that which is to be accomplished', as in: 'Non-calmness of mind has unwise attention as its proximate cause' (SN 5.232). By means of that Pātimokkha, non-reviling and non-harming are to be accomplished; the meaning is simply non-reviling and non-harming as included in the restraint of the Pātimokkha. Furthermore, by this 'restraint,' the taking up of these four restraints is meant: restraint by mindfulness, restraint by knowledge, restraint by patience, and restraint by effort; this fourfold restraint is the means for accomplishing the Pātimokkha.

Mattaññutā ca bhattasminti pariyesanapaṭiggahaṇaparibhogavissajjanānaṃ vasena bhojane pamāṇaññutā. Pantañca sayanāsananti bhāvanānukūlaṃ araññarukkhamūlādivivittasenāsanaṃ. Adhicitte ca āyogoti sabbacittānaṃ adhikattā uttamattā adhicittasaṅkhāte arahattaphalacitte sādhetabbe tassa nipphādanatthaṃ samathavipassanābhāvanāvasena āyogo. Etaṃ buddhāna sāsananti etaṃ parassa anūpavadanaṃ, anūpaghātanaṃ, pātimokkhasaṃvaro[P 0.0255], pariyesanapaṭiggahaṇādīsu mattaññutā, vivittavāso, yathāvuttaadhicittānuyogo ca buddhānaṃ sāsanaṃ ovādo anusiṭṭhīti attho. Evaṃ imāya gāthāya tisso sikkhā kathitāti veditabbā.

'And moderation in food' means knowing the proper measure in food with regard to seeking, receiving, consuming, and disposing. 'And a secluded lodging' means a solitary abode conducive to meditation, such as in a forest or at the root of a tree. 'And application to the higher mind' means the application, by way of developing serenity and insight, for the purpose of realizing the fruition-consciousness of Arahantship, which is to be accomplished and is designated as the 'higher mind' because it is superior to and the highest of all minds. 'This is the teaching of the Buddhas' means that this—not reviling another, not harming, restraint in the Pātimokkha, moderation in seeking, receiving, and so on, a secluded dwelling, and application to the higher mind as described—is the teaching, the advice, and the instruction of the Buddhas. Thus, it should be understood that by this verse the three trainings are explained.

Chaṭṭhasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the sixth sutta is finished.

7. Sāriputtasuttavaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Sāriputta Sutta

37. Sattame apubbaṃ natthi. Gāthāya adhicetasoti adhicittavato, sabbacittānaṃ adhikena arahattaphalacittena samannāgatassāti attho. Appamajjatoti na pamajjato, appamādena anavajjadhammesu sātaccakiriyāya samannāgatassāti vuttaṃ hoti. Muninoti “yo munāti ubho loke, muni tena pavuccatī”ti (dha. pa. 269; cūḷani. mettagūmāṇavapucchāniddesa 21) evaṃ ubhayalokamunanena monaṃ vuccati ñāṇaṃ, tena arahattaphalañāṇasaṅkhātena ñāṇena samannāgatattā [V 0.0207] vā khīṇāsavo muni nāma, tassa munino. Monapathesu sikkhatoti arahattañāṇasaṅkhātassa monassa pathesu sattatiṃsabodhipakkhiyadhammesu tīsu vā sikkhāsu sikkhato. Idañca pubbabhāgappaṭipadaṃ gahetvā vuttaṃ. Pariniṭṭhitasikkho hi arahā, tasmā evaṃ sikkhato, imāya sikkhāya munibhāvaṃ pattassa muninoti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Yasmā ca etadeva, tasmā heṭṭhimamaggaphalacittānaṃ vasena adhicetaso, catusaccasambodhapaṭipattiyaṃ appamādavasena appamajjato, maggañāṇasamannāgamena muninoti evametesaṃ tiṇṇaṃ padānaṃ attho yujjatiyeva. Atha vā “appamajjato sikkhato”ti [M 0.0232] padānaṃ hetuatthatā daṭṭhabbā appamajjanahetu sikkhanahetu ca adhicetasoti.

37. In the seventh sutta, there is nothing new. In the verse, 'adhicetaso' means 'of one with a higher mind'; the meaning is 'of one endowed with the fruition-consciousness of Arahantship, which is superior to all minds.' 'Appamajjato' means 'of one who is not negligent'; it is said to mean 'of one endowed with diligence, which is the constant practice regarding blameless states.' 'Munino' means 'of the sage': 'One who understands both worlds is thereby called a sage (muni)' (Dhp 269; Cnd 21). Thus, by means of understanding both worlds, wisdom (ñāṇa) is called 'mona'; and because he is endowed with that wisdom designated as the knowledge of the fruition of Arahantship, the one whose taints are destroyed is called a 'muni'—it is of that sage. 'Monapathesu sikkhato' means 'of one training in the paths to wisdom (mona),' that is, in the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment or in the three trainings. This is said with reference to the preliminary practice. For an Arahant is one who has completed the training; therefore, the meaning here should be understood thus: 'of one training' refers to the sage who has attained the state of a sage through this training.
