And since this is so, the meaning of these three terms is indeed fitting as follows: 'adhicetaso' by way of the lower path and fruition consciousnesses; 'appamajjato' by way of diligence in the practice for awakening to the Four Noble Truths; and 'munino' by being endowed with path-knowledge. Alternatively, the words 'appamajjato' and 'sikkhato' should be understood as having the meaning of cause: one is 'adhicetaso' because of the cause of diligence and the cause of training.

Sokā na bhavanti tādinoti tādisassa khīṇāsavamunino abbhantare iṭṭhaviyogādivatthukā sokā cittasantāpā na honti. Atha vā tādinoti tādilakkhaṇasamannāgatassa evarūpassa munino sokā na bhavantīti [P 0.0256] ayamettha attho. Upasantassāti rāgādīnaṃ accantūpasamena upasantassa. Sadā satīmatoti sativepullappattiyā niccakālaṃ satiyā avirahitassa.

'Sorrows do not exist for such a one' means that for such a sage whose taints are destroyed, there are no sorrows or mental distresses within, founded on things such as separation from what is dear. Alternatively, 'of such a one' means that for a sage of such a kind, endowed with the characteristic of being 'such,' sorrows do not exist—this is the meaning here. 'Of one who is at peace' means of one who is at peace through the utter pacification of lust and so on. 'Of one who is always mindful' means of one who is never without mindfulness at any time, due to having attained the fullness of mindfulness.

Ettha ca “adhicetaso”ti iminā adhicittasikkhā, “appamajjato”ti etena adhisīlasikkhā, “munino monapathesu sikkhato”ti etehi adhipaññāsikkhā. “Munino”ti vā etena adhipaññāsikkhā, “monapathesu sikkhato”ti etena tāsaṃ lokuttarasikkhānaṃ pubbabhāgapaṭipadā, “sokā na bhavantī”tiādīhi sikkhāpāripūriyā ānisaṃso pakāsitoti veditabbaṃ. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva.

Here, by 'of one with a higher mind' is meant the training in the higher mind (adhicittasikkhā); by 'of one who is diligent,' the training in higher virtue (adhisīlasikkhā); and by 'of the sage training in the paths of wisdom,' the training in higher wisdom (adhipaññāsikkhā). Alternatively, by 'of the sage' is meant the training in higher wisdom, and by 'training in the paths of wisdom' is meant the preliminary practice for those supramundane trainings. It should be understood that by 'sorrows do not exist,' and so on, the benefit of the complete fulfillment of the trainings is proclaimed. The rest is just as has been explained.

Sattamasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the seventh sutta is finished.

8. Sundarīsuttavaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Sundarī Sutta

38. Aṭṭhame sakkatotiādīnaṃ padānaṃ attho heṭṭhā vaṇṇitoyeva. Asahamānāti na sahamānā, usūyantāti attho. Bhikkhusaṅghassa ca sakkāraṃ asahamānāti sambandho.

38. In the eighth sutta, the meaning of the words beginning with 'sakkata' has already been explained above. 'Asahamānā' means not enduring; the meaning is 'being envious.' The connection is: 'not enduring the honor shown to the community of monks.'

Sundarīti [V 0.0208] tassā nāmaṃ. Sā kira tasmiṃ kāle sabbaparibbājikāsu abhirūpā dassanīyā pāsādikā paramāya vaṇṇapokkharatāya samannāgatā, teneva sā “sundarī”ti paññāyittha. Sā ca anatītayobbanā asaṃyatasamācārāva hoti, tasmā te sundariṃ paribbājikaṃ pāpakamme uyyojesuṃ. Te hi aññatitthiyā buddhuppādato paṭṭhāya sayaṃ hatalābhasakkārā heṭṭhā akkosasuttavaṇṇanāyaṃ āgatanayena bhagavato bhikkhusaṅghassa ca uḷāraṃ aparimitaṃ lābhasakkāraṃ pavattamānaṃ disvā issāpakatā ekato hutvā sammantayiṃsu – mayaṃ samaṇassa gotamassa uppannakālato paṭṭhāya naṭṭhā hatalābhasakkārā, na no koci [M 0.0233] atthibhāvampi jānāti, kiṃ nissāya nu kho loko samaṇe gotame abhippasanno uḷāraṃ sakkārasammānaṃ upanetīti? Tattheko āha – “uccākulappasuto asambhinnāya mahāsammatappaveṇiyā jāto”ti, aparo “abhijātiyaṃ tassa anekāni [P 0.0257] acchariyāni pātubhūtānī”ti, añño “kāladevilaṃ vandāpetuṃ upanītassa pādā parivattitvā tassa jaṭāsu patiṭṭhitā”ti, aparo “vappamaṅgalakāle jambucchāyāya sayāpitassa vītikkantepi majjhanhike jambucchāyā aparivattitvā ṭhitā”ti, añño “abhirūpo dassanīyo pāsādiko rūpasampattiyā”ti, aparo “jiṇṇāturamatapabbajitasaṅkhātanimitte disvā saṃvegajāto āgāminaṃ cakkavattirajjaṃ pahāya pabbajito”ti. Evaṃ aparimāṇakāle sambhataṃ anaññasādhāraṇaṃ bhagavato puññañāṇasambhāraṃ ukkaṃsapāramippattaṃ nirupamaṃ sallekhappaṭipadaṃ anuttarañca ñāṇapahānasampadādibuddhānubhāvaṃ ajānantā attanā yathādiṭṭhaṃ yathāsutaṃ dharamānaṃ taṃ taṃ bhagavato bahumānakāraṇaṃ kittetvā abahumānakāraṇaṃ pariyesitvā apassantā “kena nu kho kāraṇena mayaṃ samaṇassa gotamassa ayasaṃ uppādetvā lābhasakkāraṃ nāseyyāmā”ti. Tesu eko tikhiṇamantī evamāha – “ambho imasmiṃ sattaloke mātugāmasukhe asattasattā nāma natthi, ayañca samaṇo gotamo abhirūpo devasamo taruṇo, attano samarūpaṃ mātugāmaṃ labhitvā sajjeyya. Athāpi na sajjeyya, janassa pana saṅkiyo bhaveyya, handa mayaṃ sundariṃ paribbājikaṃ tathā uyyojema, yathā samaṇassa gotamassa ayaso pathaviyaṃ patthareyyā”ti.

Her name was Sundarī. It is said that at that time, she was the most beautiful, lovely, and graceful among all the female wanderers, endowed with supreme beauty and complexion. Hence, she was known as “Sundarī.” And she was not past her youth, and of unrestrained conduct. Therefore, they incited the female wanderer Sundarī to a wicked deed. For those of other sects, from the time of the Buddha’s appearance, had lost their gains and honors. As described in the commentary on the Akkosa Sutta, seeing the vast and immeasurable gains and honors bestowed upon the Blessed One and his community of monks, they became envious. Gathering together, they deliberated: “Since the ascetic Gotama appeared, we have been ruined, deprived of gains and honors. No one even acknowledges our existence. On what grounds has the world placed such great faith in the ascetic Gotama, offering him supreme reverence?” Then one said: “He is born of a high family, of the unbroken lineage of the great King Mahāsammata.” Another said: “Many marvels appeared at his birth.” Another said: “When brought to pay homage to Kāḷadevila, his feet turned around and rested on the ascetic’s matted locks.” Another said: “At the time of the plowing festival, though he lay in the shade of the rose-apple tree, the shadow did not move past noon.” Another said: “He is handsome, pleasing, and radiant, endowed with perfection of form.” Another said: “Seeing the signs of old age, sickness, death, and a renunciant, he was stirred with urgency, renounced the future universal kingship, and went forth.” Thus, not knowing the Blessed One’s unparalleled store of merit and knowledge accumulated over an immeasurable time, his supreme perfection in ascetic practices, and his unsurpassed power of Buddhahood, including the perfection of knowledge and relinquishment—holding to their own views and hearsay—praising whatever they considered grounds for honoring the Buddha and seeking grounds for dishonor, but finding none, they asked: “By what means can we bring dishonor upon the ascetic Gotama and deprive him of gains and honors?” Among them, one with sharp intellect said: “Friends, in this world of beings, there is no being not attached to the pleasures of women. And this ascetic Gotama is handsome, like a god, and young. If he obtained a woman suitable for him, he would become attached. Even if he did not, people would suspect him. Come, let us incite the female wanderer Sundarī in such a way that the ascetic Gotama’s disgrace spreads across the earth.”

Taṃ sutvā itare “idaṃ suṭṭhu tayā cintitaṃ, evañhi kate samaṇo gotamo ayasakena upadduto sīsaṃ ukkhipituṃ asakkonto yena vā tena vā palāyissatī”ti sabbeva ekajjhāsayā hutvā tathā uyyojetuṃ sundariyā santikaṃ agamaṃsu. Sā te disvā “kiṃ tumhe ekato āgatatthā”ti āha. Titthiyā anālapantā ārāmapariyante paṭicchanne ṭhāne nisīdiṃsu. Sā tattha gantvā punappunaṃ ālapantī paṭivacanaṃ alabhitvā kiṃ tumhākaṃ aparajjhaṃ? Kasmā me paṭivacanaṃ na dethāti? Tathā hi pana tvaṃ amhe [P 0.0258] viheṭhiyamāne ajjhupekkhasīti[V 0.0209]. Ko [M 0.0234] tumhe viheṭhetīti? “Kiṃ pana tvaṃ na passasi, samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ amhe viheṭhetvā hatalābhasakkāre katvā vicaranta”nti vatvā “tattha mayā kiṃ kātabba”nti vutte “tena hi tvaṃ abhikkhaṇaṃ jetavanasamīpaṃ gantvā mahājanassa evañcevañca vadeyyāsī”ti āhaṃsu. Sāpi “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchi. Tena vuttaṃ – “aññatitthiyā paribbājakā bhagavato sakkāraṃ asahamānā”tiādi.

Hearing this, the others said, “Well thought out by you! For if this is done, the ascetic Gotama, harassed by disgrace, unable to lift his head, will flee in some direction.” All being of one accord, they went to Sundarī to persuade her thus. Seeing them, she asked, “Why have you all come together?” The sectarians, without replying, sat down in a secluded spot at the edge of the monastery. Going there and repeatedly addressing them without receiving a reply, she asked, “What wrong have I done to you? Why do you not answer me?” They replied, “Because you remain indifferent while we are being harassed.” “Who harasses you?” she asked. “Do you not see?” they said, “The ascetic Gotama, having harassed us, roams about, having destroyed our gains and honors.” When she asked, “What then should I do about it?” they replied, “Then you should frequently go near Jetavana and speak thus and thus to the crowd.” She agreed, saying, “Good.” Hence it is said, “The wandering ascetics of other sects, unable to bear the honor shown to the Blessed One,” etc.

Tattha ussahasīti sakkosi. Atthanti hitaṃ kiccaṃ vā. Kyāhanti kiṃ ahaṃ. Yasmā te titthiyā tassā aññātakāpi samānā pabbajjasambandhamattena saṅgaṇhituṃ ñātakā viya hutvā “ussahasi tvaṃ bhagini ñātīnaṃ atthaṃ kātu”nti āhaṃsu. Tasmā sāpi migaṃ valli viya pāde laggā jīvitampi me pariccattaṃ ñātīnaṃ atthāyāti āha.

Here, ‘ussahasīti’ means ‘you are able.’ ‘Atthanti’ means benefit or task. ‘Kyāhanti’ means ‘what I.’ Because those sectarians, though strangers to her, treated her like a relative merely due to their shared connection of having gone forth, saying, “Sister, are you able to act for the benefit of your relatives?” Therefore she too, like a deer entangled by a creeper at its feet, said, “Even my life is given up for the sake of my relatives.”

Tena hīti “yasmā tvaṃ ‘jīvitampi me tumhākaṃ atthāya pariccatta’nti vadasi, tvañca paṭhamavaye ṭhitā abhirūpā sobhaggappattā ca, tasmā yathā taṃ nissāya samaṇassa gotamassa ayaso uppajjissati, tathā kareyyāsī”ti vatvā “abhikkhaṇaṃ jetavanaṃ gacchāhī”ti uyyojesuṃ. Sāpi kho bālā kakacadantapantiyā pupphāvalikīḷaṃ kīḷitukāmā viya, pabhinnamadaṃ caṇḍahatthiṃ soṇḍāya parāmasantī viya, nalāṭena maccuṃ gaṇhantī viya titthiyānaṃ vacanaṃ sampaṭicchitvā mālāgandhavilepanatambūlamukhavāsādīni gahetvā mahājanassa satthu dhammadesanaṃ sutvā nagaraṃ pavisanakāle jetavanābhimukhī gacchantī “kahaṃ gacchasī”ti ca puṭṭhā “samaṇassa gotamassa santikaṃ, ahañhi tena saddhiṃ ekagandhakuṭiyaṃ vasāmī”ti vatvā aññatarasmiṃ titthiyārāme vasitvā pātova jetavanamaggaṃ otaritvā nagarābhimukhī āgacchantī [P 0.0259] “kiṃ sundari kahaṃ gatāsī”ti ca puṭṭhā “samaṇena gotamena saddhiṃ ekagandhakuṭiyaṃ vasitvā taṃ kilesaratiyā ramāpetvā āgatāmhī”ti vadati. Tena vuttaṃ – “evaṃ ayyāti kho sundarī paribbājikā tesaṃ aññatitthiyānaṃ paribbājakānaṃ paṭissutvā abhikkhaṇaṃ jetavanaṃ agamāsī”ti.

Then they said, “Since you say, ‘I have even given my life for your sake,’ and you are in your youth, beautiful, and fortunate, therefore, act in such a way that, on your account, disgrace will arise for the ascetic Gotama.” Having said this, they urged her, “Go frequently to Jetavana.” And that foolish woman, like one desiring to play a flower-garland game with a row of saw-teeth, like one stroking the trunk of a fierce, rutting elephant, like one seizing death by the forehead, accepted the words of the sectarians. Taking garlands, perfumes, ointments, betel, mouth fresheners, and so forth, she went towards Jetavana when the great crowd was entering the city after hearing the Teacher’s Dhamma discourse. When asked, “Where are you going?” she would say, “To the ascetic Gotama’s presence, for I live with him in a single perfumed chamber.” Then, staying in a certain sectarian monastery, she would descend onto the path to Jetavana early in the morning and return towards the city. When asked, “O Sundarī, where have you been?” she would reply, “I have been living with the ascetic Gotama in a single perfumed chamber, delighting him with sensual pleasures, and have now returned.” Thus it is said: “Having assented to those other sectarian wanderers with ‘Yes, sirs,’ the wanderer Sundarī went frequently to Jetavana.”

Titthiyā katipāhassa accayena dhuttānaṃ kahāpaṇe datvā “gacchatha, sundariṃ māretvā samaṇassa gotamassa gandhakuṭiyā avidūre mālākacavarantare nikkhipitvā ethā”ti vadiṃsu. Te tathā akaṃsu. Tato titthiyā “sundariṃ na passāmā”ti kolāhalaṃ katvā rañño ārocetvā [M 0.0235] “kattha pana tumhe parisaṅkathā”ti raññā vuttā imesu divasesu jetavane vasati, tatthassā pavattiṃ na jānāmāti. “Tena hi gacchatha, naṃ tattha vicinathā”ti raññā anuññātā attano upaṭṭhāke gahetvā jetavanaṃ gantvā vicinantā viya hutvā mālākacavaraṃ byūhitvā tassā [V 0.0210] sarīraṃ mañcakaṃ āropetvā nagaraṃ pavesetvā “samaṇassa gotamassa sāvakā ‘satthunā kataṃ pāpakammaṃ paṭicchādessāmā’ti sundariṃ māretvā mālākacavarantare nikkhipiṃsū”ti rañño ārocesuṃ. Rājāpi anupaparikkhitvā “tena hi gacchatha, nagaraṃ āhiṇḍathā”ti āha. Te nagaravīthīsu “passatha samaṇānaṃ sakyaputtiyānaṃ kamma”ntiādīni vadantā vicaritvā puna rañño nivesanadvāraṃ agamaṃsu. Rājā sundariyā sarīraṃ āmakasusāne aṭṭakaṃ āropetvā rakkhāpesi. Sāvatthivāsino ṭhapetvā ariyasāvake yebhuyyena “passatha samaṇānaṃ sakyaputtiyānaṃ kamma”ntiādīni vatvā antonagare bahinagare ca bhikkhū akkosantā vicariṃsu. Tena vuttaṃ – “yadā te aññiṃsu titthiyā paribbājakā ‘vodiṭṭhā kho sundarī’”tiādi.

After a few days, the sectarians gave money to some scoundrels and said, “Go, kill Sundarī, place her body near the Gandhakuṭī of the ascetic Gotama, not too far away, among the flower-refuse, and then return.” They did as instructed. Then the sectarians, making a commotion, said, “We do not see Sundarī,” and reported it to the king. When the king asked, “Where do you suspect she might be?” they replied, “These days, she is staying at Jetavana, but we do not know what happened to her there.” The king permitted them, saying, “Then go and search for her there.” Taking their attendants, they went to Jetavana and pretended to search. They cleared away the flower-refuse, placed her body on a stretcher, and brought it into the city, reporting to the king, “The disciples of the ascetic Gotama, thinking, ‘We will conceal the evil deed done by our teacher,’ killed Sundarī and hid her among the flower-refuse.” Without investigating, the king said, “Then go and parade her through the city.” They wandered through the city streets, saying, “See the deeds of the Sakyan ascetics!” and so on, and then returned to the king’s palace gate. The king had Sundarī’s body placed on a scaffold in the charnel ground and set guards over it. The residents of Sāvatthī, except for the noble disciples, for the most part went around inside and outside the city, reviling the monks, saying, “See the deeds of the Sakyan ascetics!” and so on. Hence it was said: “When those sectarian wanderers knew, ‘Sundarī has been seen,’ ” and so on.

Tattha aññiṃsūti jāniṃsu. Vodiṭṭhāti byapadiṭṭhā, jetavanaṃ āgacchantī ca gacchantī ca visesato diṭṭhā, bahulaṃ diṭṭhāti attho. Parikhākūpeti dīghikāvāṭe[P 0.0260]. Yā sā, mahārāja, sundarīti, mahārāja, yā sā imasmiṃ nagare rūpasundaratāya “sundarī”ti pākaṭā abhiññātā paribbājikā. Sā no na dissatīti sā amhākaṃ cakkhu viya jīvitaṃ viya ca piyāyitabbā, idāni na dissati. Yathānikkhittanti purise āṇāpetvā mālākacavarantare attanā yathāṭhapitaṃ. “Yathānikhāta”ntipi pāṭho, pathaviyaṃ nikhātappakāranti attho.

Therein, `aññiṃsu` means they knew. `Vodiṭṭhā` means designated, specifically seen; she was especially seen coming and going to Jetavana, frequently seen—that is the meaning. `Parikhākūpe` refers to a moat or a pit. The phrase `Yā sā, mahārāja, sundarī` means: ‘O great king, that wandering ascetic in this city, renowned and well-known as “Sundarī” on account of her beauty.’ The phrase `Sā no na dissati` means: ‘She, who was to be cherished by us like our own eyes and life, is now not seen.’ `Yathānikkhittaṃ` means as it was placed by themselves among the flower-refuse, after having commanded their men. `Yathānikhāta` is also a reading, meaning ‘as buried in the ground.’

Rathiyāya rathiyanti vīthito vīthiṃ. Vīthīti hi vinivijjhanakaracchā. Siṅghāṭakanti tikoṇaracchā. Alajjinoti na lajjino, pāpajigucchāvirahitāti attho. Dussīlāti nissīlā. Pāpadhammāti lāmakasabhāvā nihīnācārā. Musāvādinoti dussīlā samānā “sīlavanto maya”nti alikavāditāya musāvādino. Abrahmacārinoti “methunappaṭisevitāya aseṭṭhacārino ime hi nāmā”ti hīḷentā vadanti. Dhammacārinoti kusaladhammacārino. Samacārinoti kāyakammādisamacārino. Kalyāṇadhammāti [M 0.0236] sundarasabhāvā, paṭijānissanti nāmāti sambandho. Nāmasaddayogena hi ettha paṭijānissantīti anāgatakālavacanaṃ. Sāmaññanti samaṇabhāvo samitapāpatā. Brahmaññanti seṭṭhabhāvo bāhitapāpatā. Kutoti kena kāraṇena. Apagatāti apetā paribhaṭṭhā. Purisakiccanti methunappaṭisevanaṃ sandhāya vadanti.

From street to street means from lane to lane. A street is a road for passing through. A crossroads is a three-cornered road. Shameless means not ashamed, that is, devoid of abhorrence for evil. Immoral means without virtue. Of evil nature means of base character, of inferior conduct. Liars: being immoral, they speak falsely by claiming, ‘We are virtuous.’ Unchaste: they speak scornfully, saying, ‘These are indeed of ignoble conduct for they indulge in sexual intercourse.’ Practicing the Dhamma means practicing wholesome states. Practicing evenly means practicing evenness in bodily action and so on. Of good nature means of beautiful nature; the connection is with the phrase `paṭijānissanti nāma` (they will indeed claim), for here, due to its connection with the word `nāma`, `paṭijānissanti` is a future tense verb. Asceticism means the state of an ascetic, the calming of evil. The holy life means the supreme state, the expulsion of evil. Whence means for what reason. Gone means departed, fallen away. A man’s duty: this is said in reference to engaging in sexual intercourse.

Atha bhikkhū taṃ pavattiṃ bhagavato ārocesuṃ. Satthā “tena hi, bhikkhave, tumhepi te manusse imāya gāthāya paṭicodethā”ti vatvā “abhūtavādī”ti gāthamāha. Taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ – “atha kho sambahulā…pe… nihīnakammā manujā paratthā”ti. Tattha neso, bhikkhave, saddo ciraṃ [V 0.0211] bhavissatīti idaṃ satthā tassa ayasassa nipphattiṃ sabbaññutaññāṇena jānitvā bhikkhū samassāsento āha.

Then the monks reported that incident to the Blessed One. The Teacher said, “Well then, monks, you too should reprove those people with this verse,” and he spoke the verse beginning, “An utterer of untruth.” In reference to this, it was said: “Then many… of low deeds, these people in another world.” Therein, the Teacher, knowing with his omniscient knowledge the outcome of that disgrace, consoled the monks, saying: “This noise, monks, will not last long.”

Gāthāyaṃ abhūtavādīti parassa dosaṃ adisvāva musāvādaṃ katvā abhūtena atacchena paraṃ abbhācikkhanto. Yo vāpi katvāti yo vā pana pāpakammaṃ katvā “nāhaṃ etaṃ karomī”ti āha. Pecca samā bhavantīti te ubhopi janā ito paralokaṃ gantvā [P 0.0261] nirayūpagamanena gatiyā samā bhavanti. Gatiyeva hi nesaṃ paricchinnā, āyū pana aparicchinnā. Bahukañhi pāpaṃ katvā ciraṃ niraye paccati, parittakaṃ katvā appamattakameva kālaṃ paccati. Yasmā pana nesaṃ ubhinnampi lāmakameva kammaṃ, tena vuttaṃ – nihīnakammā manujā paratthāti. “Paratthā”ti imassa pana padassa purato “peccā”tipadena sambandho, pecca parattha ito gantvā te nihīnakammā paraloke samā bhavantīti attho.

In the verse, 'speaker of falsehood' means one who, without having seen another's fault, speaks falsely and accuses another with what is untrue, with what is not so. Or, 'having done' means one who, having done an evil deed, says, 'I did not do this.' 'After death, they become equal' means both these people, having gone from here to the other world, become equal in destiny by going to hell. For their destiny is indeed determined, but their lifespan is undetermined. Having done much evil, one is tormented in hell for a long time; having done little, one is tormented for only a short while. But because the deeds of both are base, therefore it is said: 'people of low deeds in the other world.' The word 'in the other world' here connects with the preceding word 'after death'; the meaning is that after death, having gone from here, those of low deeds become equal in the other world.

Pariyāpuṇitvāti uggahetvā. Akārakāti aparādhassa na kārakā. Nayimehi katanti evaṃ kira nesamahosi – imehi samaṇehi sakyaputtiyehi addhā taṃ pāpakammaṃ na kataṃ, yaṃ aññatitthiyā ugghositvā sakalanagaraṃ āhiṇḍiṃsu, yasmā ime amhesu evaṃ asabbhāhi pharusāhi vācāhi abbhācikkhantesupi na kiñci vikāraṃ dassenti, khantisoraccañca na vijahanti, kevalaṃ pana “abhūtavādī nirayaṃ upetī”ti dhammaṃyeva vadantā sapantiyeva, ime samaṇā sakyaputtiyā amhe anupadhāretvā abbhācikkhante sapanti, sapathaṃ karontā viya vadanti[M 0.0237]. Atha vā “yo vāpi katvā ‘na karomi’ cāhā”ti vadantā sapanti, attano akārakabhāvaṃ bodhetuṃ amhākaṃ sapathaṃ karonti imeti attho.

'Having mastered it' means having learned it. 'Not the doers' means not being the doers of the offense. 'Surely these did not do it'—thus, it seems, they thought: 'Certainly, those ascetics, the Sakyan disciples, did not commit that evil deed which the other sectarians proclaimed as they wandered about the whole city. For even when we revile them with such unseemly and harsh words, they show no sign of agitation, nor do they abandon patience and gentleness. They simply declare the Dhamma, saying, "A liar goes to hell," and thus they seem to be swearing an oath. These Sakyan ascetics, when we accuse them without proper investigation, are swearing an oath; they speak as if making an oath.' Or, by saying, 'Or one who, having done it, says, "I did not do it,"' they swear an oath, making known their own non-involvement. The meaning is that they are making an oath to us to make us understand they are not the doers.

Tesañhi manussānaṃ bhagavatā bhāsitagāthāya savanasamanantarameva buddhānubhāvena sārajjaṃ okkami, saṃvego uppajji “nayidaṃ amhehi paccakkhato diṭṭhaṃ, sutaṃ nāma tathāpi hoti, aññathāpi hoti, ete ca aññatitthiyā imesaṃ anatthakāmā ahitakāmā, tasmā te saddhāya nayidaṃ amhehi vattabbaṃ, dujjānā hi samaṇā”ti. Te tato paṭṭhāya tato oramiṃsu.

For those people, immediately after hearing the verse spoken by the Blessed One, through the Buddha's power, embarrassment arose and a sense of spiritual urgency was born: 'This was not seen by us directly; what is heard may be so or otherwise. And those other sectarians are ill-wishers, desiring harm for these ascetics. Therefore, we should not speak of this based on mere faith, for ascetics are hard to know.' From that point onward, they desisted from it.

Rājāpi yehi sundarī māritā, tesaṃ jānanatthaṃ purise āṇāpesi. Atha te dhuttā tehi kahāpaṇehi suraṃ pivantā aññamaññaṃ kalahaṃ kariṃsu. Tesu hi eko ekaṃ āha – “tvaṃ sundariṃ ekappahārena māretvā mālākacavarantare khipitvā tato laddhakahāpaṇehi suraṃ pivasi, hotu hotū”ti. Rājapurisā taṃ sutvā te dhutte gahetvā rañño dassesuṃ. Rājā [P 0.0262] “tumhehi sā [V 0.0212] māritā”ti te dhutte pucchi. “Āma, devā”ti. “Kehi mārāpitā”ti? “Aññatitthiyehi, devā”ti. Rājā titthiye pakkosāpetvā tamatthaṃ paṭijānāpetvā, “ayaṃ sundarī tassa samaṇassa gotamassa avaṇṇaṃ āropetukāmehi amhehi mārāpitā, neva gotamassa, na gotamasāvakānaṃ doso atthi, amhākameva dosoti evaṃ vadantā nagaraṃ āhiṇḍathā”ti āṇāpesi. Te tathā akaṃsu. Mahājano sammadeva saddahi. Titthiyānaṃ dhikkāraṃ akāsi, titthiyā manussavadhadaṇḍaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu. Tato paṭṭhāya buddhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa ca bhiyyosomattāya sakkārasammāno mahā ahosi. Bhikkhū acchariyabbhutacittajātā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā attamanā paṭivedesuṃ. Tena vuttaṃ – “atha kho sambahulā bhikkhū…pe… antarahito so, bhante, saddo”ti.

The king, too, ordered his men to find out by whom Sundarī had been killed. Then those scoundrels, drinking liquor with the money they had received, began quarreling among themselves. Among them, one said to another, 'You killed Sundarī with a single blow, threw her into a rubbish heap of flowers, and now you drink liquor with the money you got—so be it, so be it!' Hearing this, the king's men seized those scoundrels and brought them before the king. The king asked them, 'Did you kill her?' 'Yes, lord.' 'Who ordered you to kill her?' 'The other sectarians, lord.' The king summoned the sectarians, made them confess to the deed, and then commanded: 'This Sundarī was killed by us, wishing to cast aspersion on the ascetic Gotama. There is no fault in Gotama or his disciples—the fault is ours alone. Go and proclaim this throughout the city.' They did so. The great multitude truly believed. They reviled the sectarians, and the sectarians received the punishment for killing a human. From then on, the honor and respect for the Buddha and his monastic community greatly increased even more. The monks, with minds filled with wonder and amazement, paid homage to the Blessed One and joyfully reported the matter. Thus it was said: 'Then a number of monks... that sound, venerable sir, has vanished.'

Kasmā pana bhagavā “titthiyānaṃ idaṃ kamma”nti bhikkhūnaṃ nārocesi? Ariyānaṃ tāva ārocanena payojanaṃ natthi, puthujjanesu pana “ye na saddaheyyuṃ, tesaṃ taṃ dīgharattaṃ ahitāya dukkhāya saṃvatteyyā”ti nārocesi. Apicetaṃ buddhānaṃ anāciṇṇaṃ, yaṃ anāgatassa īdisassa vatthussa ācikkhanaṃ. Parānuddesikameva hi bhagavā saṃkilesapakkhaṃ vibhāveti[M 0.0238], kammañca katokāsaṃ na sakkā nivattetunti abbhakkhānaṃ tannimittañca bhagavā ajjhupekkhanto nisīdi. Vuttañhetaṃ –

But why did the Blessed One not announce to the monks, 'This was the deed of the sectarians'? For the noble ones, there was no purpose in such an announcement. But for ordinary people, those who would not believe it, it would lead to their harm and suffering for a long time—thus, he did not announce it. Moreover, it is not the custom of the Buddhas to reveal such a future event. Indeed, the Blessed One only explains the side of defilement when prompted by others. And a deed, having found its opportunity, cannot be turned back. Thus, the Blessed One sat, indifferent to the false accusation and its cause. For it was said:

“Na antalikkhe na samuddamajjhe,

Na pabbatānaṃ vivaraṃ pavissa;

Na vijjatī so jagatippadeso,

Yatthaṭṭhito mucceyya pāpakammā”ti. (dha. pa. 127; mi. pa. 4.2.4);

'Not in the sky, nor in the midst of the sea,

Nor by entering a mountain cave;

No place on earth exists

Where standing, one can be freed from an evil deed.'

Etamatthaṃ viditvāti mammacchedanavasenāpi bālajanehi pavattitaṃ duruttavacanaṃ khantibalasamannāgatassa dhīrassa duttitikkhā nāma natthīti imamatthaṃ sabbākārato viditvā. Imaṃ udānanti imaṃ adhivāsanakhantibalavibhāvanaṃ udānaṃ udānesi.

'Understanding this meaning' means knowing in every way this meaning: that even harsh words uttered by foolish people, which are like cutting into one's vital organs, are not something unbearable to the wise one endowed with the strength of patience. 'This inspired utterance' means he uttered this inspired utterance, which reveals the power of forbearance and patience.

Tattha tudanti vācāya janā asaññatā, sarehi saṅgāmagataṃva [P 0.0263] kuñjaranti kāyikasaṃvarādīsu kassacipi saṃvarassa abhāvena asaṃyatā avinītā bālajanā sarehi sāyakehi saṅgāmagataṃ yuddhagataṃ kuñjaraṃva hatthināgaṃ paṭiyodhā viya vācāsattīhi tudanti vijjhanti, ayaṃ tesaṃ sabhāvo[V 0.0213]. Sutvāna vākyaṃ pharusaṃ udīritaṃ, adhivāsaye bhikkhu aduṭṭhacittoti taṃ pana tehi bālajanehi udīritaṃ bhāsitaṃ mammaghaṭṭanavasena pavattitaṃ pharusaṃ vākyaṃ vacanaṃ abhūtaṃ bhūtato nibbeṭhento mama kakacūpamaovādaṃ (ma. ni. 1.222 ādayo) anussaranto īsakampi aduṭṭhacitto hutvā “saṃsārasabhāvo eso”ti saṃsāre bhayaṃ ikkhaṇasīlo bhikkhu adhivāsaye, adhivāsanakhantiyaṃ ṭhatvā khameyyāti attho.

Therein, 'unrestrained people pierce with speech, like an elephant gone to battle with arrows' means that those unrestrained, undisciplined fools, lacking any restraint in bodily conduct and so forth, pierce and wound with the spears of speech, like opposing warriors piercing an elephant-king gone to battle with arrows. Such is their nature. 'Having heard a harsh word spoken, a bhikkhu should endure with a mind without ill will' means that a bhikkhu, recalling my advice in the Kakacūpama Sutta (MN 21, etc.), refuting the harsh and untrue words uttered by those foolish people, which are spoken to wound one's vitals, and becoming not even slightly malevolent in mind, thinking, 'Such is the nature of saṃsāra,' and being accustomed to seeing danger in saṃsāra, should endure. Established in the patience of endurance, he should forbear—that is the meaning.

Etthāha – kiṃ pana taṃ kammaṃ, yaṃ aparimāṇakālaṃ sakkaccaṃ upacitavipulapuññasambhāro satthā evaṃ dāruṇaṃ abhūtabbhakkhānaṃ pāpuṇīti? Vuccate – ayaṃ so bhagavā bodhisattabhūto atītajātiyaṃ munāḷi nāma dhutto hutvā pāpajanasevī ayonisomanasikārabahulo vicarati. So ekadivasaṃ surabhiṃ nāma paccekasambuddhaṃ nagaraṃ piṇḍāya pavisituṃ cīvaraṃ pārupantaṃ passi. Tasmiñca samaye aññatarā itthī tassa avidūrena gacchati. Dhutto “abrahmacārī ayaṃ samaṇo”ti abbhācikkhi. So tena kammena bahūni vassasatasahassāni niraye paccitvā tasseva kammassa vipākāvasesena idāni buddho hutvāpi sundariyā kāraṇā abhūtabbhakkhānaṃ [M 0.0239] pāpuṇi. Yathā cetaṃ, evaṃ ciñcamāṇavikādīnaṃ vikārakitthīnaṃ bhagavato abbhakkhānādīni dukkhāni pattāni, sabbāni pubbe katassa kammassa vipākāvasesāni, yāni “kammapilotikānī”ti vuccanti. Vuttañhetaṃ apadāne (apa. thera 1.39.64-96) –

Here it is said: "But what sort of deed is it, that the Teacher, having accumulated a vast store of merit with great care for an immeasurable time, should come to such a cruel false accusation?" It is said: "This Blessed One, when he was a Bodhisatta in a past life, having been a rogue named Munāḷi, associating with evil people, indulging much in unwise attention, went about. One day he saw a Solitary Buddha named Surabhi putting on his robe to enter the city for alms. At that time, a certain woman was walking not far from him. The rogue falsely accused him, saying, 'This ascetic is not practicing celibacy.' By that deed, having been cooked in hell for many hundreds of thousands of years, by the remaining result of that very deed, even now, having become a Buddha, he came to false accusation on account of Sundarī. And just as this happened, so the sufferings that were attained by Ciñcamāṇavikā and other deceitful women, such as false accusations against the Blessed One, all are the remaining results of deeds done in the past, which are called 'karma-remnants.'" For it was said in the Apadāna (Apa. Thera 1.39.64-96):

“Anotattasarāsanne, ramaṇīye silātale;

Nānāratanapajjote, nānāgandhavanantare.

"Near Lake Anotatta, on a delightful rocky plateau, resplendent with various jewels, amidst forests filled with diverse fragrances.

“Mahatā bhikkhusaṅghena, pareto lokanāyako;

Āsīno byākarī tattha, pubbakammāni attano.

Surrounded by a large community of bhikkhus, the Leader of the World, seated there, declared his own past deeds.

“Suṇātha bhikkhavo mayhaṃ, yaṃ kammaṃ pakataṃ mayā;

Pilotikassa kammassa, buddhattepi vipaccati.

Listen, bhikkhus, to this deed done by me; the result of this remnant of karma ripens even in Buddhahood.

1.

1.

“Munāḷi [P 0.0264] nāmahaṃ dhutto, pubbe aññāsu jātisu;

Paccekabuddhaṃ surabhiṃ, abbhācikkhiṃ adūsakaṃ.

I was a rogue named Munāḷi in former lives; I falsely accused the innocent Paccekabuddha Surabhi.

“Tena [V 0.0214] kammavipākena, niraye saṃsariṃ ciraṃ;

Bahū vassasahassāni, dukkhaṃ vedemi vedanaṃ.

Due to that karmic result, I wandered long in hell, experiencing painful feeling for many thousands of years.

“Tena kammāvasesena, idha pacchimake bhave;

Abbhakkhānaṃ mayā laddhaṃ, sundarikāya kāraṇā.

By the remnant of that karma, in this final existence, I received a false accusation because of Sundarikā.

2.

2.

“Sabbābhibhussa buddhassa, nando nāmāsi sāvako;

Taṃ abbhakkhāya niraye, ciraṃ saṃsaritaṃ mayā.

Of the Buddha Sabbābhibhū, there was a disciple named Nanda; having falsely accused him, I wandered long in hell.

“Dasa vassasahassāni, niraye saṃsariṃ ciraṃ;

Manussabhāvaṃ laddhāhaṃ, abbhakkhānaṃ bahuṃ labhiṃ.

For ten thousand years, I wandered long in hell. Having obtained human existence, I received much false accusation.

“Tena kammāvasesena, ciñcamāṇavikā mamaṃ;

Abbhācikkhi abhūtena, janakāyassa aggato.

By the remaining effect of that karma, Ciñcamāṇavikā falsely accused me with what was untrue before a great assembly.

3.

3.

“Brāhmaṇo sutavā āsiṃ, ahaṃ sakkatapūjito;

Mahāvane pañcasate, mante vācemi māṇave.

I was a learned brahmin, revered and honored. In the great forest, I recited mantras to five hundred young men.

“Tatthāgato [M 0.0240] isī bhīmo, pañcābhiñño mahiddhiko;

Tañcāhaṃ āgataṃ disvā, abbhācikkhiṃ adūsakaṃ.

There came a formidable sage, possessed of the five supernormal knowledges and great psychic power; seeing him coming, I falsely accused the blameless one.

“Tatohaṃ avacaṃ sisse, kāmabhogī ayaṃ isi;

Mayhampi bhāsamānassa, anumodiṃsu māṇavā.

Then I said to my students, ‘This sage is an enjoyer of sensual pleasures.’ As I was speaking, the young men approved.

“Tato māṇavakā sabbe, bhikkhamānaṃ kule kule;

Mahājanassa āhaṃsu, kāmabhogī ayaṃ isi.

Then, as that sage was going for alms from house to house, all those young men declared to the great crowd: ‘This sage is an enjoyer of sensual pleasures.’

“Tena kammavipākena, pañca bhikkhusatā ime;

Abbhakkhānaṃ labhuṃ sabbe, sundarikāya kāraṇā.

By the result of that karma, these five hundred bhikkhus all received a false accusation on account of Sundarikā.

4.

4.

“Vemātubhātikaṃ pubbe, dhanahetu haniṃ ahaṃ;

Pakkhipiṃgiriduggasmiṃ, silāya ca apiṃsayiṃ.

Formerly, for the sake of wealth, I killed my half-brother, threw him into a mountain chasm, and crushed him with a rock.

“Tena [V 0.0215] kammavipākena, devadatto silaṃ khipi;

Aṅguṭṭhaṃ piṃsayī pāde, mama pāsāṇasakkharā.

By the result of that karma, Devadatta hurled a rock; a rock fragment crushed the big toe of my foot.

5.

5.

“Purehaṃ dārako hutvā, kīḷamāno mahāpathe;

Paccekabuddhaṃ disvāna, magge sakalikaṃ khipiṃ.

Formerly, as a boy playing on the highway, I saw a Paccekabuddha and threw a potsherd in his path.

“Tena [P 0.0265] kammavipākena, idha pacchimake bhave;

Vadhatthaṃ maṃ devadatto, abhimāre payojayi.

By the result of that karma, here in my final existence, Devadatta employed assassins to kill me.

6.

6.

“Hatthāroho pure āsiṃ, paccekamunimuttamaṃ;

Piṇḍāya vicarantaṃ taṃ, āsādesiṃ gajenahaṃ.

Formerly, I was an elephant driver, and I set an elephant on a supreme solitary sage who was wandering for alms.

“Tena kammavipākena, bhanto nāḷāgirī gajo;

Giribbaje puravare, dāruṇo samupāgami.

By the result of that karma, the raging elephant Nāḷāgiri fiercely approached me in the excellent city of Giribbaja.

7.

7.

“Rājāhaṃ patthivo āsiṃ, sattiyā purise haniṃ;

Tena kammavipākena, niraye paccisaṃ bhusaṃ.

I was a king, a ruler of the earth, and I killed men with a spear. By the result of that karma, I suffered intensely in hell.

“Kammuno tassa sesena, sodāni sakalaṃ mama;

Pāde chaviṃ pakappesi, na hi kammaṃ vinassati.

By the remnant of that karma, a splinter has now pierced the skin of my foot; for karma is never destroyed.

8.

8.

“Ahaṃ [M 0.0241] kevaṭṭagāmasmiṃ, ahuṃ kevaṭṭadārako;

Macchake ghātite disvā, janayiṃ somanassakaṃ.

In a fishing village, I was a fisherman's son. Seeing fish being killed, I felt a sense of gladness.

“Tena kammavipākena, sīsadukkhaṃ ahū mama;

Sakkā ca sabbe haññiṃsu, yadā hani viṭaṭūbho.

By the result of that karma, I suffered from a headache; and all the Sakyans were slain when Viḍūḍabha slaughtered them.

9.

9.

“Phussassāhaṃ pāvacane, sāvake paribhāsayiṃ;

Yavaṃ khādatha bhuñjatha, mā ca bhuñjatha sālayo.

During the dispensation of the Buddha Phussa, I reviled his disciples, saying: ‘Eat barley, consume it, but do not eat fine rice.’

“Tena [V 0.0216] kammavipākena, temāsaṃ khāditaṃ yavaṃ;

Nimantito brāhmaṇena, verañjāyaṃ vasiṃ tadā.

By the result of that karma, for three months I ate barley. Invited by a brahmin, I was then dwelling in Verañjā.

10.

10.

“Nibbuddhe vattamānamhi, mallaputtaṃ niheṭhayiṃ;

Tena kammavipākena, piṭṭhidukkhaṃ ahū mama.

At a time when there was no Buddha, I harassed the son of a wrestler. By the result of that karma, I have suffered from pain in the back.

11.

11.

“Tikicchako ahaṃ āsiṃ, seṭṭhiputtaṃ virecayiṃ;

Tena kammavipākena, hoti pakkhandikā mama.

I was a physician and I purged a wealthy merchant’s son; by the result of that karma, I suffer from dysentery.

12.

12.

“Avacāhaṃ jotipālo, kassapaṃ sugataṃ tadā;

Kuto nu bodhi muṇḍassa, bodhi paramadullabhā.

I, as Jotipāla, then said of Kassapa, the Fortunate One: ‘How could there be enlightenment for this shaveling? Enlightenment is supremely difficult to attain.’

“Tena kammavipākena, acariṃ dukkaraṃ bahuṃ;

Chabbassānuruvelāyaṃ, tato bodhiṃ apāpuṇiṃ.

By the result of that kamma, I undertook many difficult austerities for six years at Uruvelā, and only then did I attain enlightenment.

“Nāhaṃ [P 0.0266] etena maggena, pāpuṇiṃ bodhimuttamaṃ;

Kummaggena gavesissaṃ, pubbakammena vārito.

It was not by that path that I attained supreme enlightenment; hindered by my past kamma, I had been searching along a wrong path.

“Puññapāpaparikkhīṇo, sabbasantāpavajjito;

Asoko anupāyāso, nibbāyissamanāsavo.

With merit and demerit exhausted, devoid of all anguish, sorrowless and free from despair, I shall attain final Nibbāna, free from taints.

“Evaṃ jino viyākāsi, bhikkhusaṅghassa aggato;

Sabbābhiññābalappatto, anotattamahāsare”ti. (apa. thera 1.39.64-96);

Thus the Conqueror, who had attained the power of all the direct knowledges, made this declaration in front of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus at the great lake Anotatta.

Aṭṭhamasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Eighth Sutta is concluded.

9. Upasenasuttavaṇṇanā

9. The Commentary on the Upasena Sutta

39. Navame [V 0.0217][M 0.0242] upasenassāti ettha upasenoti tassa therassa nāmaṃ, vaṅgantabrāhmaṇassa pana puttattā “vaṅgantaputto”ti ca naṃ voharanti.

39. In the ninth sutta, regarding ‘Upasena’s’: Here, ‘Upasena’ is the name of that elder. However, because he was the son of the brahmin Vaṅganta, they also refer to him as ‘Vaṅgantaputta.’

Ayañhi thero āyasmato sāriputtassa kaniṭṭhabhātā, sāsane pabbajitvā apaññatte sikkhāpade upasampadāya dvivasso upajjhāyo hutvā ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ upasampādetvā tena saddhiṃ bhagavato upaṭṭhānaṃ gato, tassa bhikkhuno bhagavatā tassa saddhivihārikabhāvaṃ pucchitvā khandhake āgatanayena “atilahuṃ kho tvaṃ, moghapurisa, āvatto bāhullāya, yadidaṃ gaṇabandhiya”nti (mahāva. 75) vigarahito patodābhitunno viya ājānīyo saṃviggamānaso “yadipāhaṃ idāni parisaṃ nissāya bhagavatā vigarahito, parisaṃyeva pana nissāya pāsaṃsiyo bhaveyya”nti ussāhajāto sabbe dhutadhamme samādāya vattamāno vipassanaṃ ārabhitvā na cirasseva chaḷabhiñño paṭisambhidāppatto mahākhīṇāsavo hutvā attano nissitake dhutaṅgadhare eva katvā tehi saddhiṃ bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā santhatasikkhāpade (pārā. 565 ādayo) āgatanayena “pāsādikā kho tyāyaṃ, upasena, parisā”ti parisavasena bhagavato santikā laddhapasaṃso “etadaggaṃ, bhikkhave, mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ samantapāsādikānaṃ yadidaṃ upaseno [P 0.0267] vaṅgantaputto”ti (a. ni. 1.213) etadagge ṭhapito asītiyā mahāsāvakesu abbhantaro.

This elder was the younger brother of the Venerable Sāriputta. Having gone forth in the Dispensation, when the training rule had not yet been laid down, he acted as a preceptor after only two years in the order and gave the higher ordination to a bhikkhu. He then went with him to attend upon the Blessed One. When the Blessed One questioned him about that bhikkhu being his pupil, he rebuked him in the manner recorded in the Khandhaka, saying: “Too quickly, you foolish man, you have resorted to worldliness, that is, to forming a following.” Like a thoroughbred struck by a goad, he felt a sense of urgency and thought: “If I have now been rebuked by the Blessed One on account of my following, then it is on account of my following that I might become praiseworthy.” Arousing his energy, he undertook all the ascetic practices, began insight meditation, and before long became a great arahant whose taints were destroyed, having attained the six supernormal knowledges and the analytical knowledges. Having made his own dependents also upholders of the ascetic practices, he approached the Blessed One with them. As recorded in connection with the training rule on spreading mats, he received praise from the Blessed One on account of his following: “This following of yours is inspiring, Upasena.” He was then placed in the foremost position: “Bhikkhus, among my bhikkhu disciples who are inspiring in every respect, the foremost is Upasena Vaṅgantaputta.” He was thus included among the eighty great disciples.

So ekadivasaṃ pacchābhattaṃ piṇḍapātappaṭikkanto antevāsikesu attano attano divāṭṭhānaṃ gatesu udakakumbhato udakaṃ gahetvā pāde pakkhāletvā gattāni sītiṃ katvā cammakkhaṇḍaṃ attharitvā divāṭṭhāne divāvihāraṃ nisinno attano guṇe āvajjesi. Tassa te anekasatā anekasahassā poṅkhānupoṅkhaṃ upaṭṭhahiṃsu. So “mayhaṃ tāva sāvakassa sato ime evarūpā guṇā, kīdisā nu kho mayhaṃ satthu guṇā”ti bhagavato guṇābhimukhaṃ manasikāraṃ pesesi. Te tassa ñāṇabalānurūpaṃ anekakoṭisahassā upaṭṭhahiṃsu. So “evaṃsīlo me satthā evaṃdhammo evaṃpañño evaṃvimuttī”tiādinā ca “itipi so bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho”tiādinā ca āvibhāvānurūpaṃ satthu guṇe anussaritvā[M 0.0243], tato “svākkhāto”tiādinā dhammassa, “suppaṭipanno”tiādinā ariyasaṅghassa ca guṇe anussari. Evaṃ mahāthero anekākāravokāraṃ ratanattayaguṇesu āvibhūtesu attamano pamudito uḷārapītisomanassaṃ [V 0.0218] paṭisaṃvedento nisīdi. Tamatthaṃ dassetuṃ “āyasmato upasenassa vaṅgantaputtassa rahogatassā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

One day, after his meal, having returned from his almsround, when his resident pupils had each gone to their own daytime resting places, he took water from a water pot, washed his feet, cooled his limbs, spread out a piece of leather, and sat down in his resting place for the day’s abiding. He then reflected on his own virtues. Hundreds and thousands of them occurred to him in succession. He thought: “If I, a mere disciple, possess such virtues, what must the virtues of my Teacher be like?” He then directed his mind toward the virtues of the Blessed One. In accordance with the power of his knowledge, many hundred thousands of millions of them occurred to him. He then recollected the Teacher’s virtues in a way that made them manifest, beginning with “My Teacher is of such virtue, such a nature, such wisdom, such liberation,” and “Thus is the Blessed One an arahant, a perfectly enlightened one.” Then he recollected the virtues of the Dhamma, beginning with “The Dhamma is well expounded,” and the virtues of the noble Saṅgha, beginning with “The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way.” Thus the great elder sat there, gratified and joyful, experiencing sublime rapture and gladness as the qualities of the Triple Gem became manifest to him in their manifold aspects. To show this, the words “of the Venerable Upasena Vaṅgantaputta, when he had gone into seclusion…” were stated.

Tattha rahogatassāti rahasi gatassa. Paṭisallīnassāti ekībhūtassa. Evaṃ cetaso parivitakko udapādīti evaṃ idāni vuccamānākāro cittassa vitakko uppajji. Lābhā vata meti ye ime manussattabuddhuppādasaddhāsamadhigamādayo, aho vata me ete lābhā. Suladdhaṃ vata meti yañcidaṃ mayā bhagavato sāsane pabbajjūpasampadāratanattayapayirupāsanādi paṭiladdhaṃ, taṃ me aho vata suṭṭhu laddhaṃ. Tattha kāraṇamāha “satthā ca me”tiādinā.

Herein, ‘having gone into seclusion’ means having gone to a solitary place. ‘Withdrawn’ means having become solitary. ‘Thus a reflection arose in his mind’ means a thought of the kind about to be described arose in his mind. ‘Ah, what a gain for me!’ refers to such gains as the attainment of a human state, the arising of a Buddha, the acquisition of faith, and so on: ‘Ah, what a gain these are for me!’ ‘Ah, what a good gain for me!’ refers to what has been gained by me in the Blessed One’s Dispensation—the going forth, the higher ordination, attendance upon the Triple Gem, etc.: ‘Ah, this has been so well gained by me!’ The reason for this is stated in the words beginning: ‘My Teacher is…’

Tattha diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikaparamatthehi yathārahaṃ satte anusāsatīti satthā. Bhāgyavantatādīhi kāraṇehi bhagavā. Ārakattā kilesehi, kilesārīnaṃ hatattā, saṃsāracakkassa vā arānaṃ hatattā, paccayādīnaṃ arahattā, pāpakaraṇe rahābhāvā arahaṃ[P 0.0268]. Sammā sāmañca sabbadhammānaṃ buddhattā sammāsambuddhoti ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthāro pana visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.123 ādayo) buddhānussatiniddesato gahetabbo.

Herein, he is the Teacher (Satthā) because he instructs beings according to what is proper with respect to their welfare in this life, their welfare in the lives to come, and the ultimate good. He is the Blessed One (Bhagavā) for such reasons as his being fortunate. He is an Arahant because he is far (āraka) from the defilements, because he has destroyed (hata) the enemies (ari) which are the defilements, because he has destroyed the spokes (ara) of the wheel of saṃsāra, because he is worthy (araha) of requisites, and because he has no secret place (raha) for doing evil. He is the Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha) because he has awakened to all dhammas rightly (sammā) and by himself (sāmaṃ). This is the summary here; the detailed explanation, however, should be understood from the exposition on the recollection of the Buddha in the Visuddhimagga.

Svākkhāteti suṭṭhu akkhāte, ekantaniyyānikaṃ katvā bhāsite. Dhammavinayeti pāvacane. Tañhi yathānusiṭṭhaṃ paṭipajjamānānaṃ saṃsāradukkhapātato dhāraṇena, rāgādikilese vinayanena ca dhammavinayoti vuccati. Sabrahmacārinoti seṭṭhaṭṭhena brahmasaṅkhātaṃ bhagavato sāsanaṃ ariyamaggaṃ saha caranti paṭipajjantīti sabrahmacārino. Sīlavantoti maggaphalasīlavasena sīlavanto. Kalyāṇadhammāti samādhipaññāvimuttivimuttiñāṇadassanādayo kalyāṇā sundarā dhammā etesaṃ atthīti kalyāṇadhammā. Etena saṅghassa suppaṭipattiṃ dasseti. Sīlesu camhi paripūrakārīti “ahampi pabbajitvā na tiracchānakathākathiko kāyadaḷhibahulo hutvā vihāsiṃ, atha kho pātimokkhasaṃvarādiṃ catubbidhampi sīlaṃ akhaṇḍaṃ achiddaṃ asabalaṃ akammāsaṃ [M 0.0244] bhujissaṃ viññuppasatthaṃ aparāmaṭṭhaṃ katvā paripūrento ariyamaggaṃyeva pāpesi”nti vadati. Etena heṭṭhimaphaladvayasampattimattano dīpeti. Sotāpannasakadāgāmino hi sīlesu paripūrakārino. Susamāhito camhi ekaggacittoti upacārappanābhedena samādhinā sabbathāpi samāhito ca amhi avikkhittacitto. Iminā samādhismiṃ paripūrakāritāvacanena tatiyaphalasampattimattano dīpeti. Anāgāmino hi samādhismiṃ paripūrakārino. Arahā camhi khīṇāsavoti kāmāsavādīnaṃ sabbaso khīṇattā khīṇāsavo, tato eva parikkhīṇabhavasaṃyojano sadevake loke aggadakkhiṇeyyatāya arahā camhi. Etena attano katakaraṇīyataṃ dasseti. Mahiddhiko [V 0.0219] camhi mahānubhāvoti adhiṭṭhānavikubbanādiiddhīsu mahatā vasībhāvena samannāgatattā mahiddhiko uḷārassa puññānubhāvassa [P 0.0269] guṇānubhāvassa ca sampattiyā mahānubhāvo ca asmi. Etena lokiyābhiññānavānupubbavihārasamāpattiyogamattano dīpeti. Abhiññāsu vasībhāvena hi ariyā yathicchitanipphādanena mahiddhikā, pubbūpanissayasampattiyā nānāvihārasamāpattīhi ca visodhitasantānattā mahānubhāvā ca hontīti.

'Well-expounded' means well proclaimed, spoken having made it exclusively leading out. 'Dhamma and Discipline' refers to the teaching. For it is called 'Dhamma and Discipline' because for those who practice in accordance with its instructions, it holds them back from falling into the suffering of saṃsāra and disciplines defilements such as lust. 'Fellow practitioners of the holy life' are those who fare together, that is, who practice the noble path, the teaching of the Blessed One, which is called 'holy' in the sense of being supreme. 'Virtuous' means those who are virtuous by way of the virtue of the path and the virtue of the fruit. 'Of good qualities' means they possess good, beautiful qualities such as concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation. By this he shows the good practice of the Sangha. 'And I am one who fulfills the virtues' means he is saying: 'Having gone forth, I did not dwell as one who engages in animal talk and is devoted to strengthening the body. Rather, while fulfilling the fourfold virtue—that connected with the Pātimokkha restraint, etc.—making it unbroken, unblemished, unspotted, unmottled, liberating, praised by the wise, and ungrasped, I attained the noble path itself.' By this he reveals his own attainment of the two lower fruits. For stream-enterers and once-returners are fulfillers in the virtues. 'And I am well concentrated, with a one-pointed mind' means: I am well concentrated by means of concentration of the access and absorption stages, with a mind that is in every way undistracted. By this statement of his fulfillment in concentration, he reveals his own attainment of the third fruit. For non-returners are fulfillers in concentration. 'And I am an arahant, with taints destroyed' means: because the taints—such as the taint of sensual desire—are all destroyed, I am one with taints destroyed; for that very reason, with the fetter of existence utterly eradicated, I am an arahant, worthy of the highest offerings in the world with its gods. By this he shows that for him what had to be done has been done. 'And I am of great spiritual power and great might' means: because I am endowed with great mastery over the spiritual powers of determination, transformation, etc., I am of great spiritual power; and because of my attainment of the great might of merit and the great might of virtue, I am of great might. By this he reveals his own practice of the mundane direct knowledges and the successive dwellings and attainments. For noble ones are of great spiritual power because of their mastery over the direct knowledges and their ability to produce whatever they wish; and they are of great might because of their accomplishment of previous supporting conditions and because their mental continuums have been purified by the various dwellings and meditative attainments.

Bhaddakaṃ me jīvitanti evaṃvidhasīlādiguṇasamannāgatassa me yāvāyaṃ kāyo dharati, tāva sattānaṃ hitasukhameva vaḍḍhati, puññakkhettabhāvato jīvitampi me bhaddakaṃ sundaraṃ. Bhaddakaṃ maraṇanti sace panidaṃ khandhapañcakaṃ ajja vā imasmiṃyeva vā khaṇe anupādāno viya jātavedo nibbāyati, taṃ appaṭisandhikaṃ parinibbānasaṅkhātaṃ maraṇampi me bhaddakanti ubhayattha tādibhāvaṃ dīpeti. Evaṃ mahāthero appahīnasomanassuppilāvitavāsanussannattā uḷārasomanassito dhammabahumānena dhammapītipaṭisaṃvedanena parivitakkesi.

'Blessed is my life': for me, who am endowed with such qualities as virtue, as long as this body is sustained, the welfare and happiness of beings only increases; because my life is a field of merit, it is blessed and beautiful. 'Blessed is my death': but if this pentad of aggregates were to be extinguished today or at this very moment, like a fire without fuel, that death, which is final Nibbāna involving no further relinking, would also be blessed for me. Thus he shows his equanimous state in both cases. In this way the great elder, because his latent tendencies that surge up as gladness had not been abandoned, being filled with lofty gladness, with great esteem for the Dhamma, and experiencing joy in the Dhamma, reflected thus.

Taṃ satthā gandhakuṭiyaṃ nisinnova sabbaññutaññāṇena jānitvā jīvite maraṇe ca tassa tādibhāvavibhāvanaṃ imaṃ udānaṃ udānesi. Tena vuttaṃ – “atha kho bhagavā…pe… udānesī”ti.

The Teacher, while seated in the fragrant chamber, knew this with his knowledge of omniscience and uttered this inspired utterance to make manifest that elder's state of 'suchness' in regard to life and death. Therefore it was said: 'Then the Blessed One …pe… uttered this inspired utterance.'

Tattha yaṃ jīvitaṃ na tapatīti yaṃ khīṇāsavapuggalaṃ jīvitaṃ āyatiṃ khandhappavattiyā sabbena sabbaṃ abhāvato na tapati na bādhati, vattamānameva vā [M 0.0245] jīvitaṃ sabbaso saṅkhatadhammattā satipaññāvepullappattiyā sabbattha satisampajaññasamāyogato na bādhati. Yo hi andhaputhujjano pāpajanasevī ayonisomanasikārabahulo akatakusalo akatapuñño, so “akataṃ vata me kalyāṇa”ntiādinā vippaṭisārena tapatīti tassa jīvitaṃ taṃ tapati nāma. Itare pana akatapāpā katapuññā kalyāṇaputhujjanena saddhiṃ satta sekhā tapanīyadhammaparivajjanena atapanīyadhammasamannāgamena ca pacchānutāpena na tapantīti na tesaṃ jīvitaṃ tapati. Khīṇāsave pana vattabbameva natthīti pavattidukkhavasena atthavaṇṇanā katā.

Herein, 'life does not torment him': life does not torment, does not oppress, the person whose taints are destroyed because in the future there is the complete non-occurrence of the aggregates. Or else, his present life does not oppress him because all things are conditioned, because he has attained fullness of mindfulness and wisdom, and because he is endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension everywhere. For the blind worldling who associates with evil people, is given to unwise attention, has done no wholesome deeds, and has made no merit, is tormented by remorse, thinking, 'Alas, I have not done what is good!' Thus his life torments him. But others who have done no evil and have made merit—the seven trainees along with virtuous worldlings—are not tormented by subsequent regret because they have avoided tormenting things and possess things that do not torment; therefore their life does not torment them. As for one whose taints are destroyed, however, there is nothing at all to be said. This explanation of the meaning has been made in terms of the suffering of the round of existence.

Maraṇante na socatīti maraṇasaṅkhāte ante pariyosāne, maraṇasamīpe vā na socati anāgāmimaggeneva sokassa samugghātitattā. Sa ve diṭṭhapado dhīro, sokamajjhe na socatīti so anabhijjhādīnaṃ [P 0.0270] catunnaṃ dhammapadānaṃ nibbānasseva vā diṭṭhattā diṭṭhapado, dhitisampannattā dhīro [V 0.0220] khīṇāsavo socanadhammattā “sokā”ti laddhanāmānaṃ avītarāgānaṃ sattānaṃ, sokahetūnaṃ vā lokadhammānaṃ majjhe ṭhatvāpi na socati.

'At death's end he does not grieve': at the end, the conclusion, called death, or at the approach of death, he does not grieve because grief has been uprooted by the path of non-returning. 'Having seen the state, that steadfast one does not grieve amid grief': he has seen the state because he has seen the four states of the Dhamma—non-covetousness, etc.—or Nibbāna itself; he is steadfast because he is endowed with fortitude; he is one with taints destroyed. Even though he stands amidst beings who are not devoid of lust and have thus acquired the name 'grievers' because it is their nature to grieve, or amidst worldly conditions that are causes for grief, he does not grieve.

Idānissa sabbaso sokahetūnaṃ abhāvaṃ dīpetuṃ “ucchinnabhavataṇhassā”tiādimāha. Tattha yassa aggamaggena sabbaso ucchinnā bhavataṇhā, so ucchinnabhavataṇho. Tassa avasesakilesānaṃ anavasesavūpasamena santacittassa khīṇāsavabhikkhuno. Vikkhīṇo jātisaṃsāroti jātiādiko –

Now, to show the complete absence of causes for grief, he says, 'For one whose craving for existence is cut off,' etc. Herein, one for whom craving for existence has been entirely cut off by the supreme path is 'one whose craving for existence is cut off.' For that bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, whose mind is peaceful through the complete appeasement of the remaining defilements, the round of births is exhausted. The round of births is that which begins with birth:

“Khandhānañca paṭipāṭi, dhātuāyatanāna ca;

Abbocchinnaṃ vattamānā, ‘saṃsāro’ti pavuccatī”ti. –

The succession of aggregates, elements, and sense bases, proceeding on without a break, is called 'saṃsāra.'

Vuttalakkhaṇo saṃsāro visesato khīṇo. Tasmā natthi tassa punabbhavoti yasmā tassa evarūpassa ariyapuggalassa āyatiṃ punabbhavo natthi, tasmā tassa jātisaṃsāro khīṇo. Kasmā panassa punabbhavo natthi? Yasmā ucchinnabhavataṇho santacitto ca hoti, tasmāti āvattetvā vattabbaṃ. Atha vā vikkhīṇo jātisaṃsāro, tato eva natthi tassa punabbhavoti attho yojetabbo.

The saṃsāra with the characteristic just stated is especially exhausted. Therefore, 'there is no further becoming for him': since for such a noble person there is no future new becoming, his round of births is exhausted. But why is there no new becoming for him? Because his craving for existence is cut off and his mind is peaceful. Thus it should be stated, linking it back. Alternatively, the meaning should be construed thus: the round of births is exhausted, and for that very reason there is no new becoming for him.

Navamasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Ninth Sutta is finished.

10. Sāriputtaupasamasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Sutta on Sāriputta's Peace

40. Dasame [M 0.0246] attano upasamanti sāvakapāramīmatthakappattiyā hetubhūtaṃ aggamaggena attano anavasesakilesavūpasamaṃ.

40. In the tenth sutta, 'his own peace' refers to the pacification of his own defilements without remainder by means of the supreme path, which is the cause for attaining the summit of a disciple's perfections.

Āyasmā hi sāriputto anupasantakilesānaṃ sattānaṃ rāgādikilesajanitasantāpadarathapariḷāhadukkhañceva kilesābhisaṅkhāranimittaṃ jātijarābyādhimaraṇasokaparidevādidukkhañca paccakkhato disvā [P 0.0271] atītānāgatepi nesaṃ vaṭṭamūlakadukkhaṃ parituletvā karuṇāyamāno attanāpi puthujjanakāle anubhūtaṃ kilesanimittaṃ vā anappakaṃ dukkhaṃ anussaritvā “īdisassa [V 0.0221] nāma mahādukkhassa hetubhūtā kilesā idāni me suppahīnā”ti attano kilesavūpasamaṃ abhiṇhaṃ paccavekkhati. Paccavekkhanto ca “ime ettakā kilesā sotāpattimaggena upasamitā, ettakā sakadāgāmimaggena, ettakā anāgāmimaggena, ettakā arahattamaggena upasamitā”ti taṃtaṃmaggañāṇehi odhiso kilesānaṃ upasamitabhāvaṃ paccavekkhati, tena vuttaṃ – “attano upasamaṃ paccavekkhamāno”ti.

For the Venerable Sāriputta, having directly seen the suffering—the fever, agitation, and burning born of lust and other defilements in beings whose defilements are unpacified, and the suffering of birth, aging, illness, death, sorrow, lamentation, and so on, which is the mark of volitional formations rooted in defilements; and having considered the suffering at the root of the round for them in the past and future; being compassionate, and having recollected the not insignificant suffering that he himself had experienced on account of the mark of the defilements when he was a worldling, reflects: 'Indeed, such defilements that were the cause of such great suffering have now been well abandoned by me,' and thus he frequently reviews the pacification of his own defilements. While reviewing, he considers: 'This many defilements were pacified by the path of stream-entry, this many by the path of the once-returner, this many by the path of the non-returner, and this many by the path of arahantship.' Thus he reviews the state of the pacified defilements, making distinctions according to the knowledge of each respective path. Therefore it was said: 'reviewing his own peace.'

Apare “thero arahattaphalasamāpattiṃ samāpajjitvā taṃ paccavekkhitvā ‘imassa vatāyaṃ santapaṇītabhāvo accantasantāya asaṅkhatāya dhātuyā ārammaṇato, sayañca sammadeva kilesavūpasamato’ti evaṃ abhiṇhaṃ upasamaṃ paccavekkhatī”ti vadanti. Aññe pana “anavasesakilesānaṃ upasamapariyosāne jātaṃ aggaphalamevettha upasamo nāma, taṃ paccavekkhamāno nisinno”ti.

Others say: “The elder, having entered the attainment of the fruit of arahantship and reviewed it, frequently reflects on that peace, thinking: ‘Indeed, this peaceful and sublime state is due to taking the utterly peaceful, unconditioned element as its object, and to the right pacification of the defilements in oneself.’” Still others say: “Peace here is just the supreme fruit that arises at the final pacification of all defilements without remainder. He is seated, reviewing that.”

Etamatthaṃ viditvāti yadidaṃ āyasmato sāriputtassa mahāpaññatādihetubhūtaṃ sāvakesu anaññasādhāraṇaṃ kilesappahānaṃ aggaphalaṃ vā upasamapariyāyena vuttaṃ, tassa paccavekkhaṇasaṅkhātaṃ atthaṃ sabbākārato viditvā tadanubhāvadīpakaṃ imaṃ udānaṃ udānesi.

Having understood this matter—that is, having understood in all its aspects the meaning connected with his reviewing of that which was spoken of by way of 'peace,' namely, the abandonment of defilements or the supreme fruit, which is unique to him among the disciples and the cause for the Venerable Sāriputta's great wisdom and other qualities—the Blessed One uttered this inspired utterance illuminating its power.

Tattha upasantasantacittassāti upasantameva hutvā santaṃ cittaṃ etassāti upasantasantacitto. Samāpattiyā vikkhambhanena hi upasantakilesattā upasantacittaṃ na sabbathā “upasantasanta”nti vuccati tassa upasamassa anaccantikabhāvato, na tathā aggamaggena. Tena pana accantameva kilesānaṃ samucchinnattā arahato cittaṃ puna kilesānaṃ anupasametabbatāya samathavipassanāheṭṭhimamaggehi upasantakilesaṃ hutvā accantasantabhāvatova [M 0.0247] “upasantasanta”nti vuccati. Tena vuttaṃ – “upasantameva hutvā santaṃ cittaṃ etassāti upasantasantacitto”ti. Upasantanti vā upasamo vuccati, tasmā “upasantasantacittassā”ti accantūpasamena santacittassāti attho.

Herein, 'of one with a calmed and peaceful mind' means one whose mind, having become calmed, is peaceful. For through suppression by means of an attainment, the mind with its defilements calmed is called a 'calmed mind,' but it is not called 'calmed and peaceful' in every way because that calming is not final, as it is with the supreme path. But since by that path the defilements are utterly extirpated, the mind of an arahant—no longer needing to have its defilements pacified again, its defilements having been pacified by the lower paths of serenity and insight—is called 'calmed and peaceful' precisely because of its state of ultimate peace. Therefore it was said: 'One whose mind, having become calmed, is peaceful is one with a calmed and peaceful mind.' Alternatively, 'calmed' (upasanta) means peace (upasama); therefore, 'of one with a calmed and peaceful mind' means 'one whose mind is peaceful through ultimate peace.'

Atha vā satipi sabbesaṃ khīṇāsavānaṃ anavasesakilesavūpasame sāvakapāramīñāṇassa pana matthakappattihetubhūto sāvakesu anaññasādhāraṇo saviseso dhammasenāpatino [P 0.0272] kilesavūpasamoti dassetuṃ satthā upasantasaddena visesetvā āha “upasantasantacittassā”ti.

Or, although there is a pacification of defilements without remainder in all who have destroyed the taints, in order to show that the pacification of defilements of the General of the Dhamma is special, unique among the disciples, and the cause for attaining the summit of the knowledge of a disciple's perfections, the Teacher, making a distinction with the word 'pacified,' said: 'of one with a pacified, peaceful mind.'

Tatrāyamattho – bhusaṃ daḷhaṃ vā santaṃ upasantaṃ, tena upasantena upasantameva hutvā santaṃ upasantasantaṃ[V 0.0222], tādisaṃ cittaṃ etassāti sabbaṃ purimasadisameva. Tathā hesa bhagavatā – “sāriputto, bhikkhave, mahāpañño puthupañño hāsapañño javanapañño tikkhapañño nibbedhikapañño”tiādinā (ma. ni. 3.93) anekapariyāyena vaṇṇito thomito. Netticchinnassāti netti vuccati bhavataṇhā saṃsārassa nayanato, sā netti chinnā etassāti netticchinno. Tassa netticchinnassa, pahīnataṇhassāti attho. Mutto so mārabandhanāti so evaṃvidho parikkhīṇabhavasaṃyojano sabbasmā mārabandhanato mutto, na tassa mārabandhanamocanāya karaṇīyaṃ atthi, tasmā dhammasenāpati attano upasamaṃ paccavekkhatīti. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva.

Herein, this is the meaning: `Upasanta` means exceedingly or firmly peaceful. `Upasantasanta` means peaceful by having become pacified through that pacification; such is the mind of this one. All this is similar to the previous explanation. Likewise, he has been praised and lauded by the Blessed One in many ways: 'Monks, Sāriputta is of great wisdom, expansive wisdom, joyful wisdom, swift wisdom, sharp wisdom, penetrating wisdom,' etc. (MN 111). 'Of one whose guide-rope is cut' (netticchinnassa): The guide-rope (netti) is said to be craving for existence because it leads one through saṃsāra. He for whom that guide-rope is cut is netticchinno. Thus, 'of one whose guide-rope is cut' means 'of one whose craving is abandoned'. 'Freed from the bonds of Māra': One such as this, whose fetter of existence is destroyed, is freed from all Māra's bonds. There is nothing further for him to do for release from Māra's bonds. Therefore the General of the Dhamma reviews his own peace. The rest is as was already explained.

Dasamasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the tenth sutta is finished.

Niṭṭhitā ca meghiyavaggavaṇṇanā.

And the commentary on the Meghiya Chapter is finished.

5. Soṇavaggo

5. The Soṇa Chapter

1. Piyatarasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Discourse on What Is Dearer

41. Mahāvaggassa [V 0.0223][M 0.0248][P 0.0273] paṭhame mallikāya deviyā saddhinti mallikāya nāma attano mahesiyā saha. Uparipāsādavaragatoti pāsādavarassa upari gato. Kocañño attanā piyataroti koci añño attanā piyāyitabbataro. Atthi nu kho teti “kiṃ te atthī”ti deviṃ pucchati.

41. In the first sutta of the Mahāvagga, 'with Queen Mallikā' means with his own chief queen named Mallikā. 'Gone to the top of the excellent palace' means gone to the upper story of the excellent palace. 'Is there anyone else dearer than oneself?' means is there anyone else who should be held dearer than oneself. 'Is there for you?' means he asks the queen: 'Is there for you...?'

Kasmā pucchati? Ayañhi sāvatthiyaṃ duggatamālākārassa dhītā. Ekadivasaṃ āpaṇato pūvaṃ gahetvā mālārāmaṃ gantvā “khādissāmī”ti gacchantī paṭipathe bhikkhusaṅghaparivutaṃ bhagavantaṃ bhikkhācāraṃ pavisantaṃ disvā pasannacittā taṃ bhagavato adāsi. Satthā tathārūpe ṭhāne nisīdanākāraṃ dassesi. Ānandatthero cīvaraṃ paññāpetvā adāsi. Bhagavā tattha nisīditvā taṃ pūvaṃ paribhuñjitvā mukhaṃ vikkhāletvā sitaṃ pātvākāsi. Thero “ko imissā, bhante, dānassa vipāko bhavissatī”ti pucchi. “Ajjesā, ānanda, tathāgatassa paṭhamaṃ bhojanaṃ adāsi, ajjeva kosalarañño aggamahesī bhavissati piyā manāpā”ti. Taṃ divasameva ca rājā kāsigāme bhāgineyyena saddhiṃ yujjhitvā parājito palāyitvā āgato nagaraṃ pavisanto “balakāyassa āgamanaṃ āgamessāmī”ti taṃ mālārāmaṃ pāvisi. Sā rājānaṃ āgataṃ passitvā tassa vattamakāsi. Rājā tassā vatte pasīditvā pitaraṃ pakkosāpetvā mahantaṃ issariyaṃ datvā [P 0.0274] taṃ antepuraṃ paṭiharāpetvā aggamahesiṭṭhāne ṭhapesi. Athekadivasaṃ rājā cintesi – “mayā imissā mahantaṃ issariyaṃ dinnaṃ, yaṃnūnāhaṃ imaṃ puccheyyaṃ ‘ko te piyo’ti? Sā ‘tvaṃ me, mahārāja, piyo’ti vatvā, puna maṃ pucchissati, athassāhaṃ ‘mayhampi tvaṃyeva piyā’ti vakkhāmī”ti. Iti so aññamaññaṃ vissāsajananatthaṃ sammodanīyaṃ karonto pucchi.

Why did he ask? She was the daughter of a poor garland-maker in Sāvatthī. One day, having taken a cake from a shop, she was going to a garland park intending to eat it. On the way, she saw the Blessed One surrounded by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus entering for the almsround. With a confident mind, she gave it to the Blessed One. The Teacher indicated a place to sit. The Venerable Ānanda spread out a robe and offered it. The Blessed One sat there, partook of the cake, rinsed his mouth, and smiled. The Elder asked: “Venerable Sir, what will be the result of this gift?” “Today, Ānanda, she has given the first food offering to the Tathāgata; this very day she will become the chief queen of the king of Kosala, dear and agreeable.” On that very day, the king, having fought with his nephew in a village of Kāsi and been defeated, was fleeing. As he was entering the city, he entered that garland park, thinking: “I will await the arrival of my forces.” She saw the king arriving and rendered service to him. Pleased with her service, the king had her father summoned, gave him great wealth, had her brought into the inner quarters, and established her in the position of chief queen. Then one day the king thought: “I have given her great wealth. What if I were to ask her, ‘Who is dear to you?’ She will say, ‘You are dear to me, great king,’ and then she will ask me in return. Then I will say to her, ‘You alone are dear to me.’” Thus, in order to generate mutual trust, he engaged in pleasantries and asked.

Devī pana paṇḍitā buddhupaṭṭhāyikā saṅghupaṭṭhāyikā “nāyaṃ pañho rañño mukhaṃ ulloketvā [V 0.0224] kathetabbo”ti cintetvā yathābhūtameva vadantī “natthi kho me, mahārāja, kocañño attanā piyataro”ti [M 0.0249] āha. Vatvāpi attanā byākatamatthaṃ upāyena rañño paccakkhaṃ kātukāmā “tuyhaṃ pana, mahārāja, atthañño koci attanā piyataro”ti tatheva rājānaṃ pucchi yathā raññā sayaṃ puṭṭhā. Rājāpi tāya sarasalakkhaṇena kathitattā nivattituṃ asakkonto sayampi sarasalakkhaṇeneva kathento tatheva byākāsi yathā deviyā byākataṃ.

But the queen, being wise, an attendant of the Buddha and the Saṅgha, thought, “This question should not be answered by looking at the king’s face,” and speaking in accordance with reality, she said: “Indeed, great king, there is no one else dearer to me than myself.” Having spoken, and wishing to make the meaning she had declared directly evident to the king by a skillful means, she asked the king just as she herself had been asked: “But for you, great king, is there anyone else dearer than yourself?” The king, unable to refuse because she had spoken in a pleasing manner, also spoke in a pleasing manner and declared just as the queen had declared.

Byākaritvā ca mandadhātukatāya evaṃ cintesi – “ahaṃ rājā pathavissaro mahantaṃ pathavimaṇḍalaṃ abhivijiya ajjhāvasāmi, mayhaṃ tāva yuttaṃ ‘attanā piyataraṃ aññaṃ na passāmī’ti, ayaṃ pana vasalī hīnajaccā samānā mayā ucce ṭhāne ṭhapitā sāmibhūtaṃ maṃ na tathā piyāyati, ‘attāva piyataro’ti mama sammukhā vadati, yāva kakkhaḷā vatāya”nti anattamano hutvā “nanu te tīṇi ratanāni piyatarānī”ti codesi. Devī ‘ratanattayaṃpāhaṃ deva attano saggasukhaṃ mokkhasukhañca patthayantī sampiyāyāmi, tasmā attāva me piyataro”ti āha. Sabbo cāyaṃ loko attadatthameva paraṃ piyāyati, puttaṃ patthentopi “ayaṃ maṃ jiṇṇakāle posessatī”ti pattheti, dhītaraṃ “mama kulaṃ vaḍḍhissatī”ti, bhariyaṃ “mayhaṃ pāde paricarissatī”ti, aññepi ñātimittabandhave taṃtaṃkiccavasena, iti attadatthameva [P 0.0275] sampassanto loko paraṃ piyāyatīti. Ayañhi deviyā adhippāyo.

And having declared this, due to his dull-wittedness, he thought: “I am a king, lord of the earth; having conquered the great circle of the earth, I dwell as sovereign. For me it is fitting to say, ‘I see no one dearer than myself.’ But this low-born woman, though placed by me in a high position, does not love me, her master, so much, but says in my presence, ‘Oneself is dearer.’ How harsh she is!” Being displeased, he pressed her: “Are not the Three Jewels dearer to you?” The queen replied: “Your Majesty, I hold the Three Jewels dear while aspiring for my own heavenly happiness and the happiness of liberation. Therefore, myself is indeed dearer to me.” This whole world holds others dear only for its own benefit. When desiring a son, one desires him thinking: “He will support me in my old age.” When desiring a daughter, one desires her thinking: “She will increase my family line.” When desiring a wife, one desires her thinking: “She will attend to my feet.” And so too with other relatives, friends, and companions, for this or that task. Thus it is by seeing one’s own benefit that the world holds another dear. This was the queen’s intention.

Atha rājā cintesi – “ayaṃ mallikā kusalā paṇḍitā nipuṇā ‘attāva me piyataro’ti vadati, mayhampi attāva piyataro hutvā upaṭṭhāti, handāhaṃ imamatthaṃ satthu ārocessāmi, yathā ca me satthā byākarissati, tathā naṃ dhāressāmī”ti. Evaṃ pana cintetvā satthu santikaṃ upasaṅkamitvā tamatthaṃ ārocesi. Tena vuttaṃ – “atha kho rājā pasenadi kosalo…pe… piyataro”ti.

Then the king thought: “This Mallikā is skilled, wise, and astute. She says, ‘Oneself is dearer to me.’ To me too, it occurs that oneself is dearer. Well now, I will report this matter to the Teacher, and as the Teacher explains it to me, so I will bear it in mind.” Having thought thus, he approached the Teacher and reported the matter. Therefore it is said: “Then King Pasenadi of Kosala … dearer.”

Etamatthaṃ viditvāti etaṃ “loke sabbasattānaṃ attāva attano piyataro”ti raññā vuttamatthaṃ sabbaso jānitvā tadatthaparidīpanaṃ imaṃ udānaṃ udānesi.

Having understood this matter: this means, having completely understood this meaning spoken by the king—“In the world, for all beings, oneself is dearer to oneself”—and illuminating that meaning, he uttered this inspired utterance.

Tattha sabbā disā anuparigamma cetasāti sabbā anavasesā dasapi disā pariyesanavasena cittena anugantvā. Nevajjhagā piyataramattanā kvacīti attanā atisayena piyaṃ aññaṃ koci puriso sabbussāhena pariyesanto [M 0.0250] kvaci katthaci sabbadisāsu neva adhigaccheyya na passeyya. Evaṃ piyo puthu attā paresanti evaṃ kassaci attanā piyatarassa anupalabbhanavasena [V 0.0225] puthu visuṃ visuṃ tesaṃ tesaṃ sattānaṃ attāva piyo. Tasmā na hiṃse paramattakāmoti yasmā evaṃ sabbopi satto attānaṃ piyāyati attano sukhakāmo dukkhappaṭikūlo, tasmā attakāmo attano hitasukhaṃ icchanto paraṃ sattaṃ antamaso kunthakipillikaṃ upādāya na hiṃse na haneyya na pāṇileḍḍudaṇḍādīhipi viheṭheyya. Parassa hi attanā kate dukkhe taṃ tato saṅkamantaṃ viya kālantare attani sandissati. Ayañhi kammānaṃ dhammatāti.

Therein, having traversed all directions with the mind means having gone over all ten directions without remainder by way of investigation with the mind. Nowhere did one find anyone dearer than oneself means that a person, searching with all effort anywhere at all in all directions, would never find or see another who is more exceedingly dear than oneself. So too for others, the separate self is dear means that, because no one dearer than oneself is found, for each and every separate being, oneself is dear. Therefore one who loves himself should not harm another means that since every being loves itself, desires its own happiness, and is averse to suffering, therefore one who loves oneself, desiring one's own welfare and happiness, should not harm another being—not even down to an insect or an ant—should not kill it, should not harass it with hand, clod, or stick. For the suffering inflicted by oneself on another will, at a later time, be seen in oneself, as if it were transferred from that other. For this is the nature of kamma.

Paṭhamasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the first sutta is concluded.

2. Appāyukasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Appāyuka Sutta

42. Dutiye [P 0.0276] acchariyaṃ, bhanteti idampi meghiyasutte viya garahaṇacchariyavasena veditabbaṃ. Yāva appāyukāti yattakaṃ parittāyukā, atiittarajīvitāti attho. Sattāhajāteti sattāhena jāto sattāhajāto. Tasmiṃ sattāhajāte, jātassa sattame ahanīti attho. Tusitaṃ kāyaṃ upapajjīti tusitaṃ devanikāyaṃ paṭisandhiggahaṇavasena upapajji.

42. In the second sutta, 'It is astonishing, venerable sir': this, as in the Meghiya Sutta, should be understood in the sense of astonishment mixed with reproach. 'So short-lived' means having such a limited lifespan, that is, a very fleeting life. 'Born for seven days' means born seven days ago; in that phrase, the meaning is 'on the seventh day after being born.' 'Was reborn into the Tusita realm' means she was reborn into the host of Tusita devas by way of rebirth-linking.

Ekadivasaṃ kira thero pacchābhattaṃ divāṭṭhāne nisinno lakkhaṇānubyañjanappaṭimaṇḍitaṃ sobhaggappattaṃ dassanānuttariyabhūtaṃ bhagavato rūpakāyasiriṃ manasi karitvā, “aho buddhānaṃ rūpakāyasampatti dassanīyā samantapāsādikā manoharā”ti uḷāraṃ pītisomanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedento evaṃ cintesi – “vijātamātuyā nāma virūpopi putto surūpo viya manāpo hoti, sace pana buddhānaṃ mātā mahāmāyā devī dhareyya, kīdisaṃ nu kho tassā bhagavato rūpadassane pītisomanassaṃ uppajjeyya, mahājāni kho mayhaṃ mahāmātu deviyā, yā sattāhajāte bhagavati kālakatā”ti. Evaṃ pana cintetvā bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā attano parivitakkitaṃ ārocento tassā kālakiriyaṃ garahanto “acchariyaṃ, bhante”tiādimāha.

It is said that one day the elder, while sitting in his daytime resting place after the meal, brought to mind the splendor of the Blessed One’s physical form, adorned with the major and minor marks, possessed of beauty, and unsurpassed for vision. Experiencing sublime joy and happiness, he thought: 'Ah, how lovely to see, inspiring confidence all around, and enchanting is the perfection of the physical form of the Buddhas! To a mother who has given birth, even an ugly son is dear as if he were handsome. If the Buddha’s mother, Queen Mahāmāyā, had lived, what kind of joy and happiness would have arisen in her on seeing the Blessed One’s form? Great was the loss of Queen Mahāmāyā, who passed away when the Blessed One was seven days old!' Having thought thus, he approached the Blessed One and, reporting his reflection and lamenting her death, said: 'It is astonishing, venerable sir,' and so on.

Keci [M 0.0251] panāhu – “mahāpajāpati gotamī bhagavantaṃ mahatā āyāsena pabbajjaṃ yācitvāpi paṭikkhittā, mayā pana upāyena yācito bhagavā aṭṭhagarudhammappaṭiggahaṇavasena tassā pabbajjaṃ upasampadañca anujāni, sā te dhamme paṭiggahetvā laddhapabbajjūpasampadā bhagavato dutiyaṃ parisaṃ uppādetvā catutthāya parisāya paccayo ahosi. Sace pana bhagavato janetti [V 0.0226] mahāmāyā devī dhareyya, evametā cubhopi khattiyabhaginiyo ekato hutvā imaṃ sāsanaṃ sobheyyuṃ, bhagavā ca mātari bahumānena mātugāmassa sāsane pabbajjaṃ upasampadañca sukheneva anujāneyya, appāyukatāya panassā kasirena nipphannamidanti iminā adhippāyena thero bhagavato santike ‘acchariyaṃ, bhante’tiādimāhā”ti. Taṃ akāraṇaṃ. Bhagavā hi mātuyā vā aññassa vā mātugāmassa attano sāsane [P 0.0277] pabbajjaṃ anujānanto garukaṃyeva katvā anujānāti, na lahukaṃ ciraṭṭhitikāmatāyāti.

Some, however, say: 'Although Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī requested the going forth from the Blessed One with great effort, she was refused. But when the Blessed One was asked by me with a stratagem, he permitted her going forth and higher ordination by way of her accepting the eight weighty rules. Having accepted those rules and obtained the going forth and higher ordination, she established the second assembly for the Blessed One and became a condition for the fourth assembly. But if the Blessed One’s birth mother, Queen Mahāmāyā, had lived, then both these royal sisters, having come together, would have adorned this dispensation. And the Blessed One, out of great respect for his mother, would have easily permitted the going forth and higher ordination for women in the dispensation. But because her life was short, this was accomplished with difficulty.' It was with this intention that the elder said to the Blessed One, 'It is astonishing, venerable sir,' and so on. But that is without reason. For the Blessed One, when permitting his mother or any other woman to go forth in his dispensation, permits it only after making it a weighty matter, not lightly, out of a desire for the long duration of the teaching.

Apare panāhu – “dasabalacatuvesārajjādike anaññasādhāraṇe anantāparimāṇe buddhaguṇe thero manasi karitvā yā evaṃ mahānubhāvaṃ nāma loke aggapuggalaṃ satthāraṃ kucchinā dasa māse parihari, sā buddhamātā kassaci paricārikā bhavissatīti ayuttamidaṃ. Kasmā?
