Satthu guṇānucchavikamevetaṃ, yadidaṃ sattāhajāte bhagavati janetti kālaṃ karoti, kālakatā ca tusitesu uppajjatīti acchariyabbhutacittajāto hutvā taṃ attano vitakkuppādanaṃ bhagavato ārocento ‘acchariyaṃ, bhante’tiādivacanaṃ avocā”ti.

Still others say: 'The elder, reflecting on the infinite and immeasurable qualities of a Buddha, not shared by others—such as the ten powers and the four kinds of fearlessness—thought: “That she who carried in her womb for ten months such a one of great power, the foremost person in the world, the Teacher—that this mother of a Buddha would become an attendant to someone is unfitting. Why? Because it is in accordance with the Teacher’s qualities that the mother passes away seven days after the Blessed One’s birth, and having passed away, is reborn among the Tusita devas.” His mind filled with wonder and amazement at such thoughts, he reported the arising of his thought to the Blessed One, saying: “It is astonishing, venerable sir,” and so on.'

Satthā pana yasmā sattāhajātesu bodhisattesu bodhisattamātu kālakiriyā dhammatā siddhā, tasmā taṃ dhammataṃ paridīpento “evametaṃ, ānandā”tiādimāha. Sā panāyaṃ dhammatā yasmā yathā sabbe bodhisattā pāramiyo pūretvā tusitapure nibbattitvā tattha yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā āyupariyosāne dasasahassacakkavāḷadevatāhi sannipatitvā abhisambodhiṃ pattuṃ manussaloke paṭisandhiggahaṇāya ajjhesitā kāladīpadesakulāni viya janettiyā āyuparimāṇampi oloketvā paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhanti, ayampi bhagavā bodhisattabhūto tatheva tusitapure ṭhito pañca mahāvilokanāni vilokento sattadivasādhikadasamāsaparimāṇaṃ [M 0.0252] mātuyā āyuparimāṇaṃ paricchinditvā “ayaṃ mama paṭisandhiggahaṇassa kālo, idāni uppajjituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti ñatvāva paṭisandhiṃ aggahesi, tasmā sabbabodhisattānaṃ āciṇṇasamāciṇṇavaseneva veditabbaṃ. Tenāha bhagavā – “appāyukā hi, ānanda, bodhisattamātaro hontī”tiādi.

The Teacher, since it is an established norm that a Bodhisatta’s mother passes away seven days after the Bodhisatta is born, said, 'So it is, Ānanda,' and so on, in order to illuminate that norm. For this is the norm: just as all Bodhisattas, having fulfilled the perfections, are reborn in the Tusita heaven and dwell there for their full lifespan, and at the end of their life the devas from the ten thousand world-systems assemble and invite them to take rebirth in the human world to attain perfect enlightenment—and they take rebirth only after investigating the time, continent, country, and clan, as well as the lifespan of the mother—so too this Blessed One, when he was a Bodhisatta dwelling in the Tusita heaven, made the five great investigations. He determined that his mother’s lifespan would be ten months and seven days, and only after knowing, 'This is the time for my rebirth; it is now fitting to be born,' did he take rebirth. Therefore, this should be understood as the constant practice of all Bodhisattas. Thus the Blessed One said: 'Bodhisatta-mothers are short-lived, Ānanda,' and so on.

Tattha kālaṃ karontīti yathāvuttaāyuparikkhayeneva kālaṃ karonti, na vijātapaccayā. Carimattabhāvehi bodhisattehi vasitaṭṭhānaṃ cetiyagharasadisaṃ hoti, na aññesaṃ paribhogārahaṃ, na ca sakkā bodhisattamātaraṃ apanetvā aññaṃ aggamahesiṭṭhāne ṭhapetunti tattakaṃ eva bodhisattamātu āyuppamāṇaṃ hoti, tasmā tadā kālaṃ karonti. Imameva hi atthaṃ sandhāya mahābodhisattā pañcamaṃ mahāvilokanaṃ karonti.

Here, 'they pass away' means they die due to the exhaustion of their lifespan as stated, not on account of childbirth. The womb in which a Bodhisatta has dwelt in his final existence becomes like a shrine, not fit for the use of others. Nor is it possible to set aside the Bodhisatta’s mother and establish another in the position of chief queen. Therefore, the lifespan of a Bodhisatta’s mother is just that long, and thus she passes away at that time. It is with this very meaning in mind that Great Bodhisattas make the fifth great investigation.

Katarasmiṃ [V 0.0227] pana vaye kālaṃ [P 0.0278] karontīti? Majjhimavaye. Paṭhamavayasmiñhi sattānaṃ attabhāve chandarāgo balavā hoti, tena tadā sañjātagabbhā itthiyo yebhuyyena gabbhaṃ anurakkhituṃ na sakkonti. Gaṇheyyuṃ ce, gabbho bahvābādho hoti. Majjhimavayassa pana dve koṭṭhāse atikkamitvā tatiyakoṭṭhāse vatthu visadaṃ hoti, visade vatthumhi nibbattadārakā arogā honti, tasmā bodhisattamātaro paṭhamavaye sampattiṃ anubhavitvā majjhimavayassa tatiyakoṭṭhāse vijāyitvā kālaṃ karontīti.

At what age, then, do they pass away? In middle age. For in the first stage of life, beings’ sensual passion for their bodies is strong, and thus women who conceive then are for the most part unable to protect the embryo. If they should conceive, the embryo would have many afflictions. But after two parts of middle age have passed, in the third part the womb becomes clear. Children born from a clear womb are healthy. Therefore, the mothers of Bodhisattas, having enjoyed prosperity in the first stage of life, give birth in the third part of middle age and then pass away.

Etamatthaṃ viditvāti etaṃ bodhisattamātu aññesañca sabbasattānaṃ attabhāve āyussa maraṇapariyosānataṃ viditvā tadatthavibhāvanamukhena anavajjappaṭipattiyaṃ ussāhadīpakaṃ imaṃ udānaṃ udānesi.

Having understood this meaning—that is, having known that the lifespan of the Bodhisatta’s mother and of all other beings in their individual existences culminates in death—he uttered this inspired utterance as a means of clarifying that meaning and inspiring effort in the blameless practice.

Tattha ye kecīti aniyamaniddeso. Bhūtāti nibbattā. Bhavissantīti anāgate nibbattissanti. Vāsaddo vikappattho, apisaddo sampiṇḍanattho. Tena nibbattamānepi saṅgaṇhāti. Ettāvatā atītādivasena tiyaddhapariyāpanne satte anavasesato pariyādiyati. Apica gabbhaseyyakasattā gabbhato nikkhantakālato paṭṭhāya bhūtā nāma, tato pubbe bhavissanti nāma. Saṃsedajūpapātikā paṭisandhicittato parato bhūtā [M 0.0253] nāma, tato pubbe uppajjitabbabhavavasena bhavissanti nāma. Sabbepi vā paccuppannabhavavasena bhūtā nāma, āyatiṃ punabbhavavasena bhavissanti nāma. Khīṇāsavā bhūtā nāma. Te hi bhūtā eva, na puna bhavissantīti, tadaññe bhavissanti nāma.

Here, 'whatever beings' is an indefinite specification. 'Have been' means have come to be. 'Will be' means will come to be in the future. The word 'vā' has the sense of alternation; the word 'api' has the sense of inclusion. Thus it also includes those who are in the process of coming to be. In this way, it comprehensively encompasses without remainder all beings comprised within the three periods of time. Further, womb-born beings are called 'have been' from the time they emerge from the womb; before that, they are called 'will be.' Moisture-born and spontaneously born beings are called 'have been' from the moment after the rebirth-linking consciousness; before that, they are called 'will be' in the sense of a future existence to be born. Alternatively, all beings are called 'have been' in the sense of their present existence, and 'will be' in the sense of future rebirth. Arahants are called 'have been,' for they have indeed been, but they will not be again; those other than them are called 'will be.'

Sabbe gamissanti pahāya dehanti sabbe yathāvuttabhedā sabbabhavayonigativiññāṇaṭṭhitisattāvāsādivasena anekabhedabhinnā sattā dehaṃ attano sarīraṃ pahāya nikkhipitvā paralokaṃ gamissanti, asekkhā pana nibbānaṃ. Ettha koci acavanadhammo nāma natthīti dasseti. Taṃ sabbajāniṃ kusalo viditvāti tadetaṃ sabbassa sattassa jāniṃ hāniṃ maraṇaṃ, sabbassa vā sattassa jāniṃ vināsaṃ pabhaṅgutaṃ kusalo paṇḍitajātiko maraṇānussativasena aniccatāmanasikāravasena vā jānitvā. Ātāpiyo brahmacariyaṃ careyyāti vipassanāya kammaṃ karonto ātāpiyasaṅkhātena [P 0.0279] vīriyena samannāgatattā ātāpiyo catubbidhasammappadhānavasena āraddhavīriyo anavasesamaraṇasamatikkamanūpāyaṃ maggabrahmacariyaṃ careyya, paṭipajjeyyāti attho.

All will depart, leaving behind the body: All beings, differentiated in many ways through the various kinds of existence, birth, destination, stations of consciousness, abodes of beings, and so on, will go to the next world, having abandoned and laid down the body, their own frame; but those beyond training go to Nibbāna. This shows that there is nothing here that is not subject to passing away. Having wisely understood this total loss: that is, having known this loss, decline, and death of every being—or this loss, destruction, and fragility of every being—a wise and skillful person, by way of the recollection of death or attention to impermanence, should lead the holy life with ardor. One is ardent because, while doing the work of insight, one is endowed with the energy called ardor; with energy aroused by way of the four right strivings, one should practice the holy life of the path, the means for completely transcending death without residue. This is the meaning.

Dutiyasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Second Sutta is finished.

3. Suppabuddhakuṭṭhisuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Discourse on Suppabuddha the Leper

43. Tatiye [V 0.0228] rājagahe suppabuddho nāma kuṭṭhī ahosīti suppabuddhanāmako eko puriso rājagahe ahosi. So ca kuṭṭhī kuṭṭharogena bāḷhavidūsitagatto. Manussadaliddoti yattakā rājagahe manussā tesu sabbaduggato. So hi saṅkārakūṭavatiādīsu manussehi chaḍḍitapilotikakhaṇḍāni sibbitvā paridahati, kapālaṃ gahetvā gharā gharaṃ gantvā laddhaācāmaucchiṭṭhabhattāni nissāya jīvati, tampi pubbe katakammapaccayā na yāvadatthaṃ labhati. Tena vuttaṃ “manussadaliddo”ti. Manussakapaṇoti manussesu paramakapaṇataṃ patto. Manussavarākoti manussānaṃ hīḷitaparibhūtatāya ativiya dīno. Mahatiyā parisāyāti mahatiyā bhikkhuparisāya ceva upāsakaparisāya ca.

43. In the third sutta: In Rājagaha there was a leper named Suppabuddha. This means a man named Suppabuddha was in Rājagaha. He was a leper, his body severely afflicted by the disease of leprosy. A human pauper—among all the people in Rājagaha, he was the most destitute. For he would sew together and wear discarded pieces of cloth from rubbish heaps and such places; and, carrying a bowl, he would go from house to house, surviving on the gruel and leftover rice he received. Even that, on account of past kamma, he did not obtain in sufficient measure. Hence it is said, 'a human pauper.' A human wretch—he had reached the ultimate wretchedness among people. A human pariah—due to being scorned and despised by people, he was exceedingly miserable. In a great assembly—in a large assembly of both bhikkhus and lay followers.

Ekadivasaṃ [M 0.0254] kira bhagavā mahābhikkhusaṅghaparivāro rājagahaṃ piṇḍāya pavisitvā bhikkhūnaṃ sulabhapiṇḍapātaṃ katvā pacchābhattaṃ piṇḍapātappaṭikkanto katipayabhikkhuparivāro nikkhanto yehi dānaṃ dinnaṃ, tesaṃ upāsakānaṃ avasesabhikkhūnañca āgamanaṃ āgamayamāno antonagareyeva aññatarasmiṃ ramaṇīye padese aṭṭhāsi. Tāvadeva bhikkhū tato tato āgantvā bhagavantaṃ parivāresuṃ, upāsakāpi “anumodanaṃ sutvā vanditvā nivattissāmā”ti bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamiṃsu, mahāsannipāto ahosi. Bhagavā nisīdanākāraṃ dassesi. Tāvadeva buddhārahaṃ āsanaṃ paññāpesuṃ. Atha bhagavā asītianubyañjanappaṭimaṇḍitehi [P 0.0280] dvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇehi virocamānāya byāmappabhāparikkhepasamujjalāya nīlapītalohitodātamañjeṭṭhapabhassarānaṃ vasena chabbaṇṇabuddharaṃsiyo vissajjentiyā anupamāya rūpakāyasiriyā sakalameva taṃ padesaṃ obhāsento tārāgaṇaparivuto viya puṇṇacando bhikkhugaṇaparivuto paññattavarabuddhāsane nisīditvā manosilātale kesarasīho viya sīhanādaṃ nadanto karavīkarutamañjunā brahmassarena dhammaṃ deseti.

One day, it is said, the Blessed One, surrounded by a great assembly of bhikkhus, entered Rājagaha for alms. Having made almsfood easily obtainable for the bhikkhus, after the meal, on his return from the almsround, he left with a few bhikkhus and stood in a certain delightful spot inside the city, awaiting the arrival of those lay followers who had given alms and of the remaining bhikkhus. Soon, bhikkhus arrived from various directions and surrounded the Blessed One. The lay followers also approached the Blessed One, thinking, 'After hearing the words of appreciation and paying homage, we will depart.' A great assembly gathered. The Blessed One indicated that they should sit. Immediately, they prepared a seat worthy of the Buddha. Then the Blessed One, radiant with the eighty minor characteristics and adorned with the thirty-two major marks of a great man, resplendent with a surrounding fathom-long halo, emitting the six-colored Buddha-rays—blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, and brilliant—and with the incomparable splendor of his physical body illuminating the entire area like the full moon encircled by a host of stars, sat on the prepared supreme Buddha-seat, surrounded by the assembly of bhikkhus. Like a maned lion on a plateau of red arsenic roaring its lion's roar, he began to teach the Dhamma with a voice as lovely as the call of the karavīka bird and as deep as Brahmā's.

Bhikkhūpi kho appicchā santuṭṭhā pavivittā asaṃsaṭṭhā āraddhavīriyā pahitattā codakā pāpagarahino vattāro vacanakkhamā sīlasampannā samādhisampannā paññāsampannā vimuttisampannā vimuttiñāṇadassanasampannā meghavaṇṇaṃ paṃsukūlacīvaraṃ pārupitvā suvammitā viya gandhahatthino bhagavantaṃ parivāretvā ohitasotā dhammaṃ suṇanti. Upāsakāpi suddhavatthanivatthā suddhuttarāsaṅgā pubbaṇhasamayaṃ mahādānāni pavattetvā gandhamālādīhi bhagavantaṃ pūjetvā vanditvā bhikkhusaṅghassa nipaccakāraṃ dassetvā bhagavantaṃ bhikkhusaṅghañca parivāretvā saṃyatahatthapādā ohitasotā sakkaccaṃ [V 0.0229] dhammaṃ suṇanti. Tena vuttaṃ – “tena kho pana samayena bhagavā mahatiyā parisāya parivuto dhammaṃ desento nisinno hotī”ti.

The bhikkhus too—being of few desires, content, secluded, unentangled, energetic, resolute, admonishers, censurers of evil, able speakers, tolerant of speech, accomplished in virtue, accomplished in concentration, accomplished in wisdom, accomplished in liberation, and accomplished in the knowledge and vision of liberation—having put on cloud-colored rag-robes, surround the Blessed One like well-armored noble elephants and listen to the Dhamma with attentive ears. The lay followers too—clad in clean lower garments and clean upper robes, having provided great alms in the morning, having honored the Blessed One with perfumes, garlands, and so on, having paid homage, having shown respectful service to the Sangha of bhikkhus—surround the Blessed One and the Sangha of bhikkhus and, with restrained hands and feet, listen attentively and respectfully to the Dhamma. Therefore it is said: 'At that time, the Blessed One was seated, teaching the Dhamma, surrounded by a great assembly.'

Suppabuddho pana jighacchādubbalyapareto ghāsapariyesanaṃ caramāno antaravīthiṃ otiṇṇo dūratova taṃ mahājanasannipātaṃ disvā, “kiṃ nu kho ayaṃ mahājanakāyo sannipatito, addhā ettha bhojanaṃ dīyati maññe, appeva nāmettha gatena kiñci khādanīyaṃ vā bhojanīyaṃ vā laddhuṃ sakkā”ti sañjātābhilāso tattha gantvā addasa bhagavantaṃ pāsādikaṃ dassanīyaṃ [M 0.0255] pasādanīyaṃ uttamadamathasamathamanuppattaṃ dantaṃ guttaṃ santindriyaṃ susamāhitaṃ tāya parisāya parivutaṃ dhammaṃ desentaṃ, disvāna purimajātisambhatāya paripakkāya upanissayasampattiyā codiyamāno “yaṃnūnāhampi dhammaṃ suṇeyya”nti parisapariyante nisīdi. Taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ – “addasā kho suppabuddho kuṭṭhī…pe… tattheva ekamantaṃ nisīdi [P 0.0281] ‘ahampi dhammaṃ sossāmī’”ti.

Now Suppabuddha, overcome by weakness from hunger and searching for food, had entered an inner street. Seeing from afar that great gathering of people, he thought: 'Why has this great crowd gathered? Surely, I think, food is being given here. Perhaps if I go there I might be able to get some food to eat.' Filled with desire, he went there and saw the Blessed One—gracious, beautiful to see, inspiring confidence, one who had attained the supreme taming and calming, tamed, guarded, with tranquil senses, and well-composed—surrounded by that assembly and teaching the Dhamma. Upon seeing him, impelled by the maturity of his supporting conditions accumulated in past lives, he thought, 'Why don't I too listen to the Dhamma?' and sat down at the edge of the assembly. In reference to this it was said: 'Suppabuddha the leper saw ... and sat down to one side, thinking, "I too will listen to the Dhamma."

Sabbāvantanti sabbāvatiṃ hīnādisabbapuggalavataṃ, tattha kiñcipi anavasesetvāti attho. “Sabbavanta”ntipi paṭhanti. Cetasāti buddhacakkhusampayuttacittena. Cittasīsena hi ñāṇaṃ niddiṭṭhaṃ, tasmā āsayānusayañāṇena indriyaparopariyattañāṇena cāti attho. Ceto paricca manasākāsīti tassā parisāya cittaṃ paccekaṃ paricchinditvā manasi akāsi te volokesi. Bhabbo dhammaṃ viññātunti maggaphaladhammaṃ adhigantuṃ samattho, upanissayasampannoti attho. Etadahosīti ayaṃ suppabuddho kiñcāpi tagarasikhimhi paccekabuddhe aparajjhitvā īdiso jāto, maggaphalūpanissayo panassa paṃsupaṭicchannasuvaṇṇanikkhaṃ viya antohadayeyeva vijjotati, tasmā suviññāpiyoti idaṃ ahosi. Tenāha – “ayaṃ kho idha bhabbo dhammaṃ viññātu”nti.

All-encompassing: this means encompassing the vows of all individuals, inferior and so on, without leaving anything out. Some also read it as sabbavanta. With the mind: with a mind associated with the Buddha-eye. For knowledge is indicated by the 'head of the mind'; therefore, it means with the knowledge of dispositions and underlying tendencies and with the knowledge of the maturity of others' faculties. Having encompassed with mind, he attended: he individually discerned the minds of that assembly, attended to them, and surveyed them. Capable of understanding the Dhamma: capable of attaining the Dhamma of the path and fruit; that is, endowed with supporting conditions. This occurred to him: this is what occurred to him: 'Although this Suppabuddha has become like this for having wronged the Paccekabuddha Tagarasikhī, still the supporting condition for the path and fruit shines within his heart like a gold coin covered by dust. Therefore, he is easy to instruct.' Thus he said: 'This one here is capable of understanding the Dhamma.'

Anupubbiṃ kathanti dānānantaraṃ sīlaṃ, sīlānantaraṃ saggaṃ, saggānantaraṃ magganti evaṃ anupaṭipāṭikathaṃ. Bhagavā hi paṭhamaṃ hetunā saddhiṃ assādaṃ dassetvā tato satte vivecetuṃ nānānayehi ādīnavaṃ pakāsetvā ādīnavasavanena saṃviggahadayānaṃ nekkhammaguṇavibhāvanamukhena ca vivaṭṭaṃ dasseti.

A gradual talk means a talk in sequential order: after giving, morality; after morality, heaven; and after heaven, the path—thus, a talk in due course. For the Blessed One first shows the gratification along with its cause; then, in order to detach beings, he explains the danger in various ways; and for those whose hearts are stirred by hearing of the danger, he reveals the turning away by way of explaining the quality of renunciation.

Dānakathanti idaṃ nāma sukhānaṃ nidānaṃ, sampattīnaṃ mūlaṃ, bhogānaṃ patiṭṭhā, visamagatassa tāṇaṃ leṇaṃ gati parāyaṇaṃ, idhalokaparalokesu dānasadiso avassayo patiṭṭhā ālambanaṃ tāṇaṃ leṇaṃ gati parāyaṇaṃ natthi. Idañhi avassayaṭṭhena ratanamayasīhāsanasadisaṃ, patiṭṭhānaṭṭhena mahāpathavisadisaṃ[V 0.0230], ālambanaṭṭhena ālambanarajjusadisaṃ, dukkhanittharaṇaṭṭhena nāvāsadisaṃ, samassāsanaṭṭhena saṅgāmasūro, bhayaparittāṇaṭṭhena suparikhāparikkhittanagaraṃ, maccheramalādīhi anupalittaṭṭhena padumaṃ, tesaṃ nidahanaṭṭhena jātavedo, durāsadaṭṭhena āsīviso, asantāsaṭṭhena sīho, balavantaṭṭhena [M 0.0256] hatthī, abhimaṅgalasammataṭṭhena setausabho, khemantabhūmisampāpanaṭṭhena valāhako assarājā. Dānañhi loke rajjasiriṃ deti, cakkavattisampattiṃ sakkasampattiṃ mārasampattiṃ brahmasampattiṃ sāvakapāramīñāṇaṃ [P 0.0282] paccekabodhiñāṇaṃ sammāsambodhiñāṇaṃ detīti evamādidānaguṇappaṭisaṃyuttakathaṃ.

A talk on giving means this: giving is the source of happiness, the root of accomplishments, the foundation of wealth, a protection, shelter, destination, and final resort for one in a difficult situation. In this world and the next there is no support, foundation, foothold, protection, shelter, destination, or final resort like giving. Indeed, in the sense of being a support, it is like a jeweled lion-throne; in the sense of being a foundation, it is like the great earth; in the sense of being a foothold, it is like a supporting rope; in the sense of crossing over suffering, it is like a boat; in the sense of giving comfort, it is like a hero in battle; in the sense of protection from fear, it is like a city surrounded by a good moat; in the sense of being unsullied by the stain of stinginess and so on, it is like a lotus; in the sense of burning these up, it is like fire; in the sense of being difficult to approach, it is like a venomous snake; in the sense of being fearless, it is like a lion; in the sense of being strong, it is like an elephant; in the sense of being considered a high blessing, it is like a white bull; in the sense of bringing one to a land of safety, it is like the cloud-horse king Valāhaka. For giving in the world bestows royal splendor, the attainment of a wheel-turning monarch, the attainment of Sakka, the attainment of Māra, the attainment of Brahmā, the knowledge of a disciple’s perfections, the knowledge of a Paccekabuddha, and the knowledge of a Perfectly Self-Enlightened Buddha. Such is the talk connected with the qualities of giving.

Yasmā pana dānaṃ dento sīlaṃ samādātuṃ sakkoti, tasmā dānakathānantaraṃ sīlakathaṃ kathesi. Sīlakathanti sīlaṃ nāmetaṃ sattānaṃ avassayo patiṭṭhā ālambanaṃ tāṇaṃ leṇaṃ gati parāyaṇaṃ. Idhalokaparalokasampattīnañhi sīlasadiso avassayo patiṭṭhā ālambanaṃ tāṇaṃ leṇaṃ gati parāyaṇaṃ natthi, sīlālaṅkārasadiso alaṅkāro, sīlapupphasadisaṃ pupphaṃ, sīlagandhasadiso gandho natthi, sīlālaṅkārena hi alaṅkataṃ sīlakusumapiḷandhitaṃ sīlagandhānulittaṃ sadevako loko olokento tittiṃ na gacchatīti evamādīhi sīlaguṇappaṭisaṃyuttakathaṃ.

But since one who gives is able to undertake morality, he therefore spoke a talk on morality after the talk on giving. A talk on morality means that morality is the support, foundation, foothold, protection, shelter, destination, and final resort of beings. For in regard to the accomplishments of this world and the next, there is no support, foundation, foothold, protection, shelter, destination, or final resort like morality; there is no ornament like the adornment of morality, no flower like the flower of morality, no fragrance like the fragrance of morality. Indeed, the world with its devas, looking upon one adorned with the ornament of morality, wearing the garland of morality-flowers, and anointed with the fragrance of morality, does not become satiated. Such is the talk connected with the qualities of morality.

Idaṃ pana sīlaṃ nissāya ayaṃ saggo labbhatīti dassetuṃ sīlānantaraṃ saggakathaṃ kathesi. Saggakathanti saggo nāma iṭṭho kanto manāpo, niccamettha kīḷā niccasampattiyo labbhanti, cātumahārājikā devā navutivassasatasahassāni dibbasukhaṃ dibbasampattiṃ paṭilabhanti, tāvatiṃsā tisso vassakoṭiyo saṭṭhi ca vassasatasahassānīti evamādisaggaguṇappaṭisaṃyuttakathaṃ. Saggasampattiṃ kathentānañhi buddhānaṃ mukhaṃ nappahoti. Vuttampi cetaṃ “anekapariyāyena kho ahaṃ, bhikkhave, saggakathaṃ katheyya”ntiādi.

To show that 'by relying on this morality, this heaven is attained,' he spoke a talk on heaven after the talk on morality. A talk on heaven means that heaven is desirable, lovely, and pleasing; there, constant sport and constant accomplishments are obtained. The Cātumahārājika devas obtain divine happiness and divine accomplishment for nine million years; the Tāvatiṃsa devas, for thirty-six million years. Thus he spoke a talk connected with the qualities of heaven. Indeed, the mouths of the Buddhas are not adequate to describe the heavenly accomplishments. And this was said: 'In many ways, bhikkhus, I could speak of heaven,' etc.

Evaṃ hetunā saddhiṃ saggakathāya palobhetvā puna hatthiṃ alaṅkaritvā tassa soṇḍaṃ chindanto viya “ayampi saggo anicco adhuvo, na ettha chandarāgo kātabbo”ti dassanatthaṃ “appassādā kāmā bahudukkhā bahupāyāsā, ādīnavo ettha bhiyyo”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.177; 2.42) nayena kāmānaṃ ādīnavaṃ okāraṃ saṃkilesaṃ kathesi. Tattha ādīnavanti dosaṃ. Okāranti lāmakasabhāvaṃ, aseṭṭhehi sevitabbaṃ seṭṭhehi na sevitabbaṃ nihīnasabhāvanti attho. Saṃkilesanti tehi sattānaṃ saṃsāre saṃkilissanaṃ. Tenāha – “kilissanti vata bho sattā”ti (ma. ni. 2.351).

Having thus lured them with the discourse on heaven along with its reasons, then—like one who, having adorned an elephant, would cut off its trunk—in order to show that “this heaven, too, is impermanent, unstable; desire and lust should not be aroused for it,” he spoke of the danger, degradation, and defilement of sensual pleasures by way of the passage beginning: “Sensual pleasures give little gratification, much suffering, much despair; the danger in them is greater.” Here, danger means fault. Degradation means a base nature; that is, a low nature to be pursued by the ignoble, not to be pursued by the noble. Defilement means the defiling of beings in saṃsāra by them. Thus it is said: “Alas, beings are defiled!”

Evaṃ [M 0.0257][V 0.0231] kāmādīnavena tajjetvā nekkhamme ānisaṃsaṃ pakāsesi pabbajjāya jhānādīsu ca guṇaṃ dīpesi vaṇṇesi. Kallacittantiādīsu kallacittanti kammaniyacittaṃ, heṭṭhā pavattitadesanāya assaddhiyādīnaṃ cittadosānaṃ [P 0.0283] vigatattā uparidesanāya bhājanabhāvūpagamanena kammaniyacittaṃ, kammakkhamacittanti attho. Diṭṭhimānādisaṃkilesavigamena muducittaṃ. Kāmacchandādivigamena vinīvaraṇacittaṃ. Sammāpaṭipattiyaṃ uḷārapītipāmojjayogena udaggacittaṃ. Tattha saddhāsampattiyā pasannacittaṃ, yadā bhagavā aññāsīti sambandho.

Having thus frightened them with the danger of sensual pleasures, he declared the benefit of renunciation, and he showed and praised the quality in the going forth, in the jhānas, and so on. In the passage beginning 'a ready mind': A ready mind means a workable mind. Because the mental faults such as lack of faith have departed on account of the teaching given earlier, the mind becomes workable by having approached the state of being a vessel for the higher teaching; the meaning is a mind fit for the task. With the departure of defilements such as views and conceit, the mind becomes pliant. With the departure of sensual desire and other hindrances, the mind becomes without hindrances. Through connection with lofty joy and gladness in right practice, the mind becomes uplifted. Therein, through the accomplishment of faith, the mind is confident. The connection is with: “When the Blessed One knew….”

Atha vā kallacittanti kāmacchandavigamena arogacittaṃ. Muducittanti byāpādavigamena mettāvasena akathinacittaṃ. Vinīvaraṇacittanti uddhaccakukkuccavigamena avikkhipanato na pihitacittaṃ. Udaggacittanti thinamiddhavigamena sampaggahavasena alīnacittaṃ. Pasannacittanti vicikicchāvigamena sammāpaṭipattiyā adhimuttacittaṃ.

Alternatively: a ready mind is a healthy mind through the departure of sensual desire. A pliant mind is a mind that is not stiff by way of loving-kindness through the departure of ill will. A mind without hindrances is a mind that is not covered because it is undistracted through the departure of restlessness and remorse. An uplifted mind is a mind that is not sluggish by way of exertion through the departure of sloth and torpor. A confident mind is a mind resolved on right practice through the departure of doubt.

Athāti pacchā. Sāmukkaṃsikāti sāmaṃ ukkaṃsikā attanāva uddharitvā gahitā, sayambhūñāṇena sāmaṃ diṭṭhā, aññesaṃ asādhāraṇāti attho. Kā ca pana sāti? Ariyasaccadesanā. Tenevāha – “dukkhaṃ samudayaṃ nirodhaṃ magga”nti. Idañhi saccānaṃ sarūpadassanaṃ, tasmā imasmiṃ ṭhāne ariyasaccāni kathetabbāni, tāni sabbākārato vitthārena visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 2.529) vuttānīti tattha vuttanayena veditabbāni.

Atha means afterwards. Sāmukkaṃsikā means that which is exalted by himself, taken up by having lifted it up himself, seen by himself with self-originated knowledge; the meaning is that it is not common to others. And what is that? The teaching of the Noble Truths. Therefore he said: “suffering, origin, cessation, and path.” For this is the showing of the nature of the truths. Therefore, at this point, the Noble Truths should be spoken of. They are stated in detail in all their aspects in the Visuddhimagga, so they should be understood according to the method stated there.

Seyyathāpītiādinā upamāvasena suppabuddhassa kilesappahānaṃ ariyamagguppādañca dasseti. Apagatakāḷakanti vigatakāḷakaṃ. Sammadevāti suṭṭhuyeva. Rajananti nīlapītalohitamañjeṭṭhādiraṅgajātaṃ. Paṭiggaṇheyyāti gaṇheyya, pabhassaraṃ bhaveyya. Tasmiṃyeva āsaneti tassaṃyeva nisajjāyaṃ. Etenassa lahuvipassanakatā tikkhapaññatā sukhāpaṭipadā khippābhiññatā ca dassitā honti. Virajaṃ vītamalanti apāyagamanīyarāgarajādīnaṃ abhāvena virajaṃ, anavasesadiṭṭhivicikicchāmalāpagamena vītamalaṃ. Paṭhamamaggavajjhakilesarajābhāvena vā virajaṃ, pañcavidhadussīlamalāpagamena vītamalaṃ. Dhammacakkhunti sotāpattimaggo adhippeto. Tassa uppattiākāradassanatthaṃ “yaṃkiñci samudayadhammaṃ, sabbaṃ taṃ nirodhadhamma”nti vuttaṃ. Tañhi nirodhaṃ ārammaṇaṃ [P 0.0284] katvā kiccavasena eva saṅkhatadhamme paṭivijjhantaṃ uppajjati.

By the passage beginning “Just as…,” he shows by way of a simile the abandoning of defilements and the arising of the noble path for Suppabuddha. Free from black specks means with black specks departed. Properly means very well. Dye means the kinds of dye such as blue, yellow, red, and madder. Would take means would accept, would become radiant. On that very seat means in that very sitting. By this are shown his swiftness of insight, sharpness of wisdom, pleasant practice, and quick direct knowledge. Stainless and dustless: it is stainless because of the absence of the dust of lust, etc., which leads to the plane of misery; it is dustless because of the removal of the stains of views and doubt without remainder. Or, it is stainless because of the absence of the dust of the defilements to be abandoned by the first path; it is dustless because of the removal of the five kinds of stains of bad moral conduct. The Dhamma-eye means the path of stream-entry is intended. To show the mode of its arising, it is said: “Whatever is subject to origination is all subject to cessation.” For it arises penetrating conditioned phenomena by way of their function, having made cessation its object.

Tatridaṃ [M 0.0258] upamāsaṃsandanaṃ – vatthaṃ viya cittaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, vatthassa āgantukamalehi kiliṭṭhabhāvo viya cittassa rāgādimalehi saṃkiliṭṭhabhāvo, dhovanaphalakaṃ viya anupubbikathā, udakaṃ [V 0.0232] viya saddhā, udakena temetvā temetvā gomayakhārehi kāḷake sammadditvā vatthassa dhovanappayogo viya saddhāsalilena temetvā satisamādhipaññāhi dose sithile katvā saddhādividhinā cittassa sodhane vīriyārambho, tena payogena vatthe kāḷakāpagamo viya vīriyārambhena kilesavikkhambhanaṃ, raṅgajātaṃ viya ariyamaggo, tena suddhassa vatthassa pabhassarabhāvo viya vikkhambhitakilesassa cittassa maggena pariyodāpananti.

Here is the application of the simile: The mind should be seen as the cloth. The mind’s being defiled by the stains of lust, etc., is like the cloth’s being soiled by adventitious stains. The gradual discourse is like the washing board. Faith is like the water. The undertaking of energy in purifying the mind by the method of faith, etc.—having moistened it with the water of faith and having loosened the faults with mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom—is like the application of washing the cloth by repeatedly moistening it with water and scrubbing out the black specks with cow-dung and lye. The suppression of the defilements by the undertaking of energy is like the removal of the black specks from the cloth by that application. The noble path is like the dye. The cleansing of the mind with its defilements suppressed by means of the path is like the cleansed cloth’s becoming radiant by means of the dye.

Evaṃ pana suppabuddho parisapariyante nisinno dhammadesanaṃ sutvā sotāpattiphalaṃ patvā attanā paṭiladdhaguṇaṃ satthu ārocetukāmo parisamajjhaṃ ogāhituṃ avisahanto mahājanassa satthāraṃ vanditvā anugantvā nivattakāle bhagavati vihāraṃ gate sayampi vihāraṃ agamāsi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe sakko devarājā “ayaṃ suppabuddho kuṭṭhī attanā satthu sāsane paṭiladdhaguṇaṃ pākaṭaṃ kātukāmo”ti ñatvā “vīmaṃsissāmi na”nti gantvā ākāse ṭhito etadavoca – “suppabuddha tvaṃ manussadaliddo manussakapaṇo manussavarāko, ahaṃ te aparimitaṃ dhanaṃ dassāmi, ‘buddho na buddho, dhammo na dhammo, saṅgho na saṅgho, alaṃ me buddhena, alaṃ me dhammena, alaṃ me saṅghenā’ti vadehī”ti. Atha naṃ so āha “kosi tva”nti? “Ahaṃ sakko devarājā”ti. “Andhabāla ahirika, tvaṃ mayā saddhiṃ kathetuṃ na yuttarūpo, yo tvaṃ evaṃ avattabbaṃ vadesi, apica maṃ tvaṃ ‘duggato daliddo kapaṇo’ti kasmā vadesi, nanu ahaṃ lokanāthassa orasaputto, nevāhaṃ duggato na daliddo na kapaṇo, atha kho sukhappatto paramena sukhena apāhamasmi mahaddhano”ti vatvā āha –

Now Suppabuddha, having heard the Dhamma teaching while sitting at the fringe of the assembly, attained the fruit of stream-entry. Desiring to announce to the Teacher the quality he had attained, but being unable to plunge into the middle of the assembly, he paid homage to the Teacher and followed him as the great crowd was departing. When the Blessed One had gone to the monastery, he himself also went to the monastery. At that moment Sakka, ruler of the devas, knowing, “This leper Suppabuddha wishes to make manifest the quality he has attained in the Teacher’s Dispensation,” thought, “I will test him.” He went and, standing in the air, said this: “Suppabuddha, you are a poor human, a miserable human, a wretched human. I will give you immeasurable wealth. Just say: ‘The Buddha is no Buddha, the Dhamma is no Dhamma, the Sangha is no Sangha. Enough with the Buddha for me, enough with the Dhamma for me, enough with the Sangha for me!’” Then Suppabuddha said to him: “Who are you?” “I am Sakka, ruler of the devas.” “You blind fool, you shameless one! You are not a suitable person to speak with me, you who say what should not be said. Moreover, why do you call me ‘poor, destitute, and miserable’? Am I not the legitimate son of the Protector of the World? I am not poor, not destitute, not miserable. Rather, I have attained happiness, the supreme happiness. I am indeed very wealthy!” Having said this, he continued:

“Saddhādhanaṃ [P 0.0285] sīladhanaṃ, hiriottappiyaṃ dhanaṃ;

Sutadhanañca cāgo ca, paññā ve sattamaṃ dhanaṃ.

“The treasure of faith, the treasure of virtuous behavior, the treasure of conscience and fear of wrongdoing; the treasure of learning and also generosity, and wisdom as the seventh treasure.

“Yassa ete dhanā atthi, itthiyā purisassa vā;

‘Adaliddo’ti taṃ āhu, amoghaṃ tassa jīvita”nti. (a. ni. 7.5) –

“Whatever woman or man possesses these treasures, they call that one ‘not poor’; their life is not fruitless.”

Tassimāni [M 0.0259] me satta ariyadhanāni santi. Yesañhi imāni dhanāni santi, na tveva te buddhehi vā paccekabuddhehi vā ‘daliddā’ti vuccantī”ti.

“I possess these seven noble treasures. For those who possess these treasures are not called ‘poor’ by the Buddhas or by the Paccekabuddhas.”

Sakko tassa kathaṃ sutvā taṃ antarāmagge ohāya satthu santikaṃ gantvā sabbaṃ taṃ vacanaṃ paṭivacanañca ārocesi. Atha naṃ bhagavā āha – “na kho sakka sakkā tādisānaṃ satenapi [V 0.0233] sahassenapi suppabuddhaṃ kuṭṭhiṃ ‘buddho na buddho, dhammo na dhammo, saṅgho na saṅgho’ti kathāpetu”nti. Suppabuddhopi kho kuṭṭhī satthu santikaṃ gantvā satthārā katapaṭisanthāro attanā paṭiladdhaguṇaṃ ārocesi. Tena vuttaṃ – “atha kho suppabuddho kuṭṭhī diṭṭhadhammo”tiādi.

Having heard his speech, Sakka left him on the path and went to the Teacher’s presence, where he related the entire conversation and reply. Then the Blessed One said to him: “Indeed, Sakka, it is not possible even for a hundred or a thousand such as you to make the leper Suppabuddha say: ‘The Buddha is no Buddha, the Dhamma is no Dhamma, the Sangha is no Sangha.’” The leper Suppabuddha also went to the Teacher’s presence and, after exchanging courteous greetings with the Teacher, announced the quality he had attained. Therefore it was said: “Then the leper Suppabuddha, one who has seen the Dhamma…” and so on.

Tattha diṭṭhadhammoti diṭṭho ariyasaccadhammo etenāti diṭṭhadhammo. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Tattha “diṭṭhadhammo”ti cettha sāmaññavacano dhammasaddo. Dassanaṃ nāma ñāṇadassanato aññampi atthīti taṃ nivattanatthaṃ “pattadhammo”ti vuttaṃ. Patti ca ñāṇasampattito aññāpi vijjatīti tato visesanatthaṃ “viditadhammo”ti vuttaṃ. Sā panāyaṃ viditadhammatā dhammesu ekadesenāpi hotīti nippadesato viditabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ “pariyogāḷhadhammo”ti vuttaṃ. Tenassa yathāvuttaṃ saccābhisambodhaṃyeva dīpeti. Maggañāṇañhi ekābhisamayavasena pariññādikiccaṃ sādhentaṃ nippadesenapi pariññeyyadhammaṃ samantato ogāḷhaṃ nāma hoti, na tadaññañāṇaṃ. Tena vuttaṃ – “diṭṭho ariyasaccadhammo etenāti diṭṭhadhammo”ti. Tenevāha “tiṇṇavicikiccho”tiādi.

Here, one who has seen the Dhamma means: the Dhamma of the Noble Truths has been seen by him, thus he is one who has seen the Dhamma. This same method applies to the other terms as well. Herein, in the expression one who has seen the Dhamma, the word “dhamma” is a general term. Since there is also seeing other than seeing with knowledge, to exclude that, it is said one who has attained the Dhamma. And since there is also attainment other than the attainment of knowledge, to specify it further, it is said one who has understood the Dhamma. But since that state of having understood the Dhamma can be partial in regard to the dhammas, to show the state of having understood it without remainder, it is said one who has fully penetrated the Dhamma. This indicates for him precisely the awakening to the truths as stated. For the knowledge of the path, while accomplishing the functions of full understanding, etc., by way of a single penetration, is called “one that has thoroughly penetrated the knowable Dhamma all around without remainder”; no other knowledge is like that. Therefore it was said: “The Dhamma of the Noble Truths has been seen by him, thus he is one who has seen the Dhamma.” For that reason he said: one who has crossed over doubt, and so on.

Tattha paṭibhayakantārasadisā soḷasavatthukā ca aṭṭhavatthukā ca tiṇṇā vicikicchā etenāti tiṇṇavicikiccho. Tato eva pavattiādīsu “evaṃ nu kho, na nu kho”ti evaṃ pavattitā vigatā samucchinnā kathaṃkathā etassāti [P 0.0286] vigatakathaṃkatho. Sārajjakarānaṃ pāpadhammānaṃ pahīnattā tappaṭipakkhesu ca sīlādiguṇesu suppatiṭṭhitattā vesārajjaṃ visāradabhāvaṃ veyyattiyaṃ pattoti vesārajjappatto. Nāssa paro paccayo, na parassa saddhāya ettha vattatīti aparappaccayo. Katthāti āha “satthusāsane”ti.

Here, one who has crossed over doubt is so called because the doubt, which has sixteen and eight bases and is like a fearful wilderness, has been crossed by him. From that very reason, the wavering that arose as 'Is it so? Is it not so?' is removed and cut off for him; thus, he is one whose wavering is gone. Because unwholesome qualities that cause timidity have been abandoned, and because he is well-established in virtues such as morality, which counteract them, he has attained fearlessness, confidence, and proficiency; thus, he is one who has attained fearlessness. He does not rely on another, nor does he proceed herein by another's faith; thus, he is independent. To the question 'Where?', the reply is 'in the Teacher's Dispensation.'

Abhikkantantiādīsu [M 0.0260] kiñcāpi ayaṃ abhikkantasaddo khayasundarābhirūpabbhanumodanādīsu anekesu atthesu dissati, idha pana abbhanumodane daṭṭhabbo. Teneva so pasādavasena pasaṃsāvasena ca dvikkhattuṃ vutto, sādhu sādhu, bhanteti vuttaṃ hoti. Abhikkantanti vā atikantaṃ atiiṭṭhaṃ atimanāpaṃ, atisundaranti attho. Tattha ekena abhikkantasaddena bhagavato desanaṃ thometi, ekena attano pasādaṃ.

In phrases such as 'Abhikkanta,' although this word 'abhikkanta' is seen in many meanings such as decay, beauty, pleasing appearance, and approval, here it should be understood as expressing approval. Therefore, it is stated twice, both as an expression of confidence and as praise, meaning 'Excellent, excellent, venerable sir.' Or, 'Abhikkanta' means surpassing, exceedingly agreeable, most delightful, extremely beautiful—such is the meaning. Therein, with one use of the word 'abhikkanta,' he praises the Blessed One's teaching; with the other, his own confidence.

Ayañhettha adhippāyo – abhikkantaṃ, bhante, yadidaṃ bhagavato dhammadesanā, abhikkantaṃ, bhante, yadidaṃ bhagavato dhammadesanaṃ āgamma mama pasādoti. Bhagavato eva vā vacanaṃ abhikkantaṃ dosanāsanato, abhikkantaṃ guṇādhigamanato, tathā saddhāvaḍḍhanato, paññājananato, sātthato[V 0.0234], sabyañjanato, uttānapadato, gambhīratthato, kaṇṇasukhato, hadayaṅgamato, anattukkaṃsanato, aparavambhanato, karuṇāsītalato, paññāvadātato, āpātharamaṇīyato, vimaddakkhamato, suyyamānasukhato, vīmaṃsiyamānahitatoti evamādinayehi thomento padadvayaṃ āha.

Here is the intended meaning: 'Excellent, venerable sir, is this teaching of the Dhamma by the Blessed One; excellent, venerable sir, is my confidence that has arisen in dependence on this teaching of the Dhamma by the Blessed One.' Or, the Blessed One's words are excellent because they dispel faults, excellent because they lead to the attainment of virtues, and likewise because they increase faith, generate wisdom, are meaningful, well-phrased, straightforward in expression, profound in meaning, pleasing to the ear, touching the heart, not self-praising, not disparaging others, cool with compassion, radiant with wisdom, delightful in their presentation, withstanding scrutiny, joyful to hear, and beneficial when investigated—thus, praising in such ways, he speaks these two words.

Tato parampi catūhi upamāhi desanaṃyeva thometi. Tattha nikkujjitanti adhomukhaṭṭhapitaṃ, heṭṭhāmukhajātaṃ vā. Ukkujjeyyāti upari mukhaṃ kareyya. Paṭicchannanti tiṇapaṇṇādinā chāditaṃ. Vivareyyāti ugghāṭeyya. Mūḷhassāti disāmūḷhassa. Maggaṃ ācikkheyyāti hatthe gahetvā “esa maggo”ti maggaṃ upadiseyya. Andhakāreti caturaṅgasamannāgate. Ayaṃ tāva padattho.

Furthermore, he praises the teaching itself with four similes. Herein, 'overturned' means placed face-down or turned face downwards. 'Set upright' means to turn the face upwards. 'Covered' means concealed by grass, leaves, and so forth. 'Uncover' means to open. 'Lost' means one who is lost and confused regarding directions. 'Show the path' means taking them by the hand and saying, 'This is the path,' thus pointing out the way. 'Darkness' refers to a darkness endowed with four characteristics. This, indeed, is the meaning of the words.

Ayaṃ pana adhippāyayojanā [P 0.0287] – yathā koci nikkujjitaṃ ukkujjeyya, evaṃ saddhammavimukhaṃ asaddhamme patiṭṭhitaṃ maṃ asaddhammā vuṭṭhāpentena, yathā paṭicchannaṃ vivareyya, evaṃ kassapassa bhagavato sāsanantaradhānato paṭṭhāya micchādiṭṭhigahanapaṭicchannaṃ sāsanaṃ vivarantena, yathā mūḷhassa maggaṃ ācikkheyya, evaṃ kummaggamicchāmaggappaṭipannassa me saggamokkhamaggaṃ āvikarontena, yathā andhakāre telapajjotaṃ dhāreyya, evaṃ mohandhakāre nimuggassa me buddhādiratanarūpāni apassato tappaṭicchādakamohandhakāraviddhaṃsanadesanāpajjotadhāraṇena bhagavatā nānānayehi pakāsitattā anekapariyāyena dhammo pakāsito.

Now, this is the intended application: Just as one might set upright what is overturned, so the Blessed One raised me up—I who was turned away from the true Dhamma and established in the false Dhamma. Just as one might uncover what is hidden, so he revealed the Dispensation, which had been concealed by the thicket of wrong views since the disappearance of the Dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa. Just as one might show the path to one who is lost, so he revealed the path to heaven and liberation to me, who was practicing the wrong path, the false path. Just as one might hold up an oil lamp in the darkness, so for me, who was submerged in the darkness of delusion and unable to see the treasures of the Buddha and so forth, he held up the lamp of the teaching which dispels the obscuring darkness of delusion. Thus, because it has been proclaimed by the Blessed One through various methods, the Dhamma has been illuminated in many ways.

Evaṃ [M 0.0261] desanaṃ thometvā tāya desanāya ratanattaye pasannacitto pasannākāraṃ karonto “esāha”ntiādimāha. Tattha esāhanti eso ahaṃ. Bhagavantaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmīti bhagavā me saraṇaṃ parāyaṇaṃ aghassa ghātā, hitassa vidhātāti iminā adhippāyena bhagavantaṃ gacchāmi bhajāmi, evaṃ vā jānāmi bujjhāmīti. Yesañhi dhātūnaṃ gatiattho, buddhipi tesaṃ atthoti. Dhammanti adhigatamagge sacchikatanirodhe yathānusiṭṭhaṃ paṭipajjamāne catūsu apāyesu apatamāne dhāretīti dhammo. So atthato ariyamaggo ceva nibbānañca. Vuttañhetaṃ –

Having praised the teaching in this way, with a mind confident in the Triple Gem because of that teaching, and showing signs of confidence, he said, 'Here I am,' and so forth. Here, 'Here I am' means 'This is I.' 'I go to the Blessed One for refuge'—meaning, 'The Blessed One is my refuge, my final resort, the destroyer of evil, the provider of welfare'—with this intention, I go to the Blessed One, I attend upon Him. Or, I know, I understand thus. For those roots that have the meaning of going, they also have the meaning of understanding. 'Dhamma'—that which, for one practicing as instructed on the path attained and the cessation realized, holds them back from falling into the four states of loss. Thus, it is called Dhamma. In meaning, it is both the Noble Path and Nibbāna. For it has been said—

“Yāvatā, bhikkhave, dhammā saṅkhatā, ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo tesaṃ aggamakkhāyatī”ti (a. ni. 4.34; itivu. 90).

'Bhikkhus, among all conditioned phenomena, the Noble Eightfold Path is declared the foremost.' (AN 4.34; Itiv 90)

“Yāvatā, bhikkhave, dhammā saṅkhatā vā asaṅkhatā vā, virāgo tesaṃ aggamakkhāyatī”ti (itivu. 90) ca –

'Bhikkhus, among all phenomena, conditioned or unconditioned, dispassion is declared the foremost.' (Itiv 90)

Na [V 0.0235] kevalaṃ ariyamaggo [P 0.0288] ceva nibbānañca, apica kho ariyaphalehi saddhiṃ pariyattidhammopi. Vuttañhetaṃ –

Not only the Noble Path and Nibbāna, but also the scriptural Dhamma together with the Noble Fruits. For it has been said:

“Rāgavirāgamanejamasokaṃ, dhammamasaṅkhatamappaṭikūlaṃ;

Madhuramimaṃ paguṇaṃ suvibhattaṃ, dhammamimaṃ saraṇatthamupehī”ti. (vi. va. 887);

'To this Dhamma—the fading of passion, unshakable, sorrowless, unconditioned, not repulsive, sweet, proper, and well-expounded—come for refuge.' (Vv 887)

Ettha hi rāgavirāganti maggo vutto. Anejamasokanti phalaṃ. Asaṅkhatanti nibbānaṃ. Appaṭikūlaṃ madhuramimaṃ paguṇaṃ suvibhattanti pariyattidhammo vuttoti.

Here, indeed, 'the fading of passion' refers to the path. 'Unshakable and sorrowless' refers to the fruit. 'The unconditioned' refers to Nibbāna. 'Not repulsive, sweet, proper, and well-differentiated' refers to the scriptural Dhamma.

Bhikkhusaṅghanti diṭṭhisīlasāmaññena saṃhataṃ aṭṭhaariyapuggalasamūhaṃ. Ettāvatā suppabuddho tīṇi saraṇagamanāni paṭivedesi. Upāsakaṃ maṃ bhagavā dhāretu ajjatagge pāṇupetaṃ saraṇaṃ gatanti ajjataggeti ajjataṃ ādiṃ katvā. “Ajjadagge”tipi pāṭho, tattha dakāro padasandhikaro, ajja agge ajja ādiṃ katvāti attho. Pāṇupetanti pāṇehi upetaṃ, yāva me jīvitaṃ pavattati, tāva upetaṃ anaññasatthukaṃ tīhi saraṇagamanehi saraṇaṃ gataṃ ratanattayassa upāsanato upāsakaṃ kappiyakārakaṃ maṃ bhagavā upadhāretu jānātūti attho. Imassa ca saraṇagamanaṃ ariyamaggādhigameneva nipphannaṃ, ajjhāsayaṃ pana āvikaronto evamāha.

The community of monks (bhikkhusaṅgha) is an assembly of eight noble individuals united by commonality of view and virtue. Thus, Suppabuddha declared the three refuges. 'May the Blessed One remember me as a lay follower who, from this day forward, has gone for refuge for as long as life lasts.' 'From this day forward' (ajjatagge) means making today the beginning. There is also the reading 'ajjadagge,' where the letter 'd' is a euphonic consonant, meaning 'today onwards,' having made today the beginning. 'For as long as life lasts' (pāṇupetaṃ) means endowed with life; that is, for as long as my life continues. The meaning of the whole utterance is: 'May the Blessed One acknowledge me, know me, as a lay follower (upāsaka) who attends upon the Triple Gem, one who has gone for refuge for life by the three refuges, having no other teacher, a maker of what is suitable.' This going for refuge of his was accomplished only with the attainment of the noble path; however, revealing his disposition, he spoke thus.

Bhagavato [M 0.0262] bhāsitaṃ abhinanditvā anumoditvāti bhagavato vacanaṃ cittena abhinanditvā tameva abhinanditabhāvaṃ pakāsento vuttanayena vācāya anumoditvā. Abhivādetvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā pakkāmīti taṃ bhagavantaṃ pañcapatiṭṭhitena vanditvā tikkhattuṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā satthu guṇaninnacitto yāva dassanavisayasamatikkamā bhagavantaṃyeva pekkhamāno pañjaliko namassamāno pakkāmi.

Having rejoiced and approved of the Blessed One’s words, meaning, having delighted in the Blessed One’s speech with his mind, and manifesting that delighted state, having approved with words in the manner described. Having paid homage and circumambulated, he departed—meaning, having venerated that Blessed One with the five-point prostration, having circumambulated him three times, his mind inclined toward the Teacher’s virtues, gazing upon the Blessed One until he passed out of sight, with hands reverently joined in añjali, paying homage, he departed.

Pakkanto ca kuṭṭharogābhibhavena chinnahatthapādaṅguli ukkāragatto samantato vissandamānāsavo kaṇḍūtipatipīḷito [P 0.0289] asuci duggandho jegucchatamo paramakāruññataṃ patto “nāyaṃ kāyo imassa accantasantassa paṇītatamassa ariyadhammassa ādhāro bhavituṃ yutto”ti uppannābhisandhinā viya saggasaṃvattaniyena puññakammena okāse kate appāyukasaṃvattaniyena upacchedakena pāpakammena katūpacitena codiyamāno taruṇavacchāya dhenuyā āpatitvā mārito. Tena vuttaṃ – “atha kho acirapakkantaṃ suppabuddhaṃ kuṭṭhiṃ gāvī taruṇavacchā adhipatitvā jīvitā voropesī”ti.

After departing, overwhelmed by leprosy, his hands, feet, and fingers cut off, his body a cesspool oozing pus all around, tormented by itching and pain, impure, foul-smelling, and utterly repulsive, he reached a state of extreme wretchedness. Thinking, 'This body is not fit to be the vessel for such a supreme and excellent noble Dhamma,' as if with an intention arisen from meritorious deeds leading to heaven, when the opportunity was made, he, being impelled by destructive evil kamma accumulated that leads to a short life, was charged at and killed by a cow with a young calf. Thus it is said: 'Then, not long after Suppabuddha the leper had departed, a cow with a young calf charged at him and deprived him of life.'

So [V 0.0236] kira atīte eko seṭṭhiputto hutvā attano sahāyehi tīhi seṭṭhiputtehi saddhiṃ kīḷanto ekaṃ nagarasobhiniṃ gaṇikaṃ uyyānaṃ netvā divasaṃ sampattiṃ anubhavitvā atthaṅgate sūriye sahāye etadavoca – “imissā hatthe kahāpaṇasahassaṃ bahukañca suvaṇṇaṃ mahagghāni ca pasādhanāni saṃvijjanti, imasmiṃ vane añño koci natthi, ratti ca jātā, handa imaṃ mayaṃ māretvā sabbaṃ dhanaṃ gahetvā gacchāmā”ti. Te cattāropi janā ekajjhāsayā hutvā taṃ māretuṃ upakkamiṃsu. Sā tehi māriyamānā “ime nillajjā nikkaruṇā mayā saddhiṃ kilesasanthavaṃ katvā niraparādhaṃ maṃ kevalaṃ dhanalobhena mārenti, ekavāraṃ tāva maṃ ime mārentu, ahaṃ pana yakkhinī hutvā anekavāraṃ ime māretuṃ samatthā bhaveyya”nti patthanaṃ katvā kālamakāsi. Tesu kira eko pakkusāti kulaputto ahosi, eko bāhiyo dārucīriyo, eko tambadāṭhiko coraghātako, eko suppabuddho kuṭṭhī, iti imesaṃ catunnaṃ janānaṃ anekasate attabhāve sā yakkhayoniyaṃ nibbattā gāvī hutvā jīvitā voropesi. Te tassa kammassa nissandena tattha [M 0.0263] tattha antarāmaraṇaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu. Evaṃ suppabuddhassa kuṭṭhissa sahasā maraṇaṃ jātaṃ, tena vuttaṃ – “atha kho acirapakkantaṃ…pe… voropesī”ti.

It is said that in the past a certain merchant's son, while playing with three other merchant's sons, took a beautiful courtesan to a park. After enjoying a day of pleasure, when the sun had set, he said to his companions: 'In her possession are a thousand coins, much gold, and many valuable ornaments. There is no one else in this forest, and night has fallen. Come, let us kill her, take all the wealth, and go.' All four men, united in their intent, proceeded to kill her. As she was being killed by them, she made an aspiration: 'These shameless, merciless men, after having formed a defiled intimacy with me, now kill me, who am innocent, merely out of greed for wealth. Let them kill me just this once—but may I, having become a yakkhinī, be able to kill them many times over!' Having made this aspiration, she passed away. Among them, it is said, one was the young man of the Pakkusāti clan, one was Bāhiya Dārucīriya, one was Tambadāṭhika the executioner of thieves, and one was Suppabuddha the leper. Thus, for many hundreds of existences, she, having been reborn in the womb of a yakkhinī, deprived them of life by becoming a cow. As a result of that kamma, they met untimely deaths here and there. Thus Suppabuddha the leper met a sudden death, which is why it was said: 'Then, not long after he had departed... she deprived him of life.'

Atha sambahulā bhikkhū tassa kālakiriyaṃ bhagavato ārocetvā abhisamparāyaṃ pucchiṃsu. Bhagavā byākāsi. Tena vuttaṃ – “atha kho sambahulā bhikkhū”tiādi.

Then a number of monks, having informed the Blessed One of his death, asked about his destiny in the next life. The Blessed One declared it. Therefore it is said: 'Then a number of monks…' and so on.

Tattha tiṇṇaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ parikkhayāti sakkāyadiṭṭhi vicikicchā sīlabbataparāmāsoti imesaṃ tiṇṇaṃ bhavabandhanānaṃ samucchedavasena [P 0.0290] pahānā. Sotāpannoti sotasaṅkhātaṃ ariyamaggaṃ ādito panno. Vuttañhetaṃ –

Here, 'with the destruction of the three fetters' means the abandoning of these three fetters of existence by way of their eradication: identity view, doubt, and clinging to rules and observances. 'A stream-enterer' is one who has initially entered the noble path, which is designated as the stream. For it was said:

“Soto sototi idaṃ, āvuso sāriputta, vuccati. Katamo nu kho, āvuso, sototi? Ayameva ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo”tiādi (saṃ. ni. 5.1001).

'Friend Sāriputta, this is called “stream, stream.” But what, friend, is the stream? It is just this Noble Eightfold Path…' (SN 55.5).

Avinipātadhammoti vinipatanaṃ vinipāto, nāssa vinipāto dhammoti avinipātadhammo, catūsu apāyesu upapajjanavasena apatanasabhāvoti attho. Niyatoti dhammaniyāmena sammattaniyāmena niyato. Sambodhiparāyaṇoti uparimaggattayasaṅkhātā sambodhi paraṃ ayanaṃ assa gati paṭisaraṇaṃ avassaṃ pattabbanti sambodhiparāyaṇo. Etena “tassa kā gati, ko abhisamparāyo”ti pucchāya bhaddikā eva suppabuddhassa gati, na pāpikāti ayamattho dassito. Na pana tena sampattā gati, taṃ pana pucchānusandhivasena pakāsetukāmo dhammarājā ettakameva [V 0.0237] abhāsi. Passati hi bhagavā “mayā ettake kathite imissaṃyeva parisati anusandhikusalo eko bhikkhu suppabuddhassa kuṭṭhibhāvadāliddiyakapaṇabhāvānaṃ kāraṇaṃ pucchissati, athāhaṃ tassa taṃ kāraṇaṃ tena pucchānusandhinā pakāsetvā desanaṃ niṭṭhāpessāmī”ti. Tenevāha – “evaṃ vutte aññataro bhikkhū”tiādi. Tattha hetūti asādhāraṇakāraṇaṃ, sādhāraṇakāraṇaṃ pana paccayoti, ayametesaṃ viseso. Yenāti yena hetunā yena paccayena ca.

'Not subject to perdition' means falling is vinipāta; one whose nature is not to fall is avinipātadhammo. The meaning is that one's nature is not to fall into the four planes of misery. 'Fixed in destiny' means one is fixed by the fixed order of the Dhamma, by the fixed order of rightness. 'Bound for enlightenment' means that enlightenment, designated as the three higher paths, is one's supreme goal, refuge, and inevitable destination. By this, the question, 'What is his destination, what is his future state?' is answered: 'The destination of Suppabuddha is indeed excellent, not a bad one.' However, the destination he attained was not yet stated; the King of Dhamma, wishing to reveal it in connection with the sequence of the question, spoke only this much. Indeed, the Blessed One foresaw: 'When I have spoken this much, a certain monk in this very assembly, skilled in connecting questions, will ask about the cause of Suppabuddha’s leprosy, poverty, and wretchedness. Then, I will explain the reason in connection with that question and conclude the discourse.' Therefore, it is said: 'When this was said, a certain monk…' and so on. Here, hetu (cause) refers to the specific cause, while paccaya (condition) refers to the general condition—this is the distinction between them. 'Because of which' means by that cause and by that condition.

Bhūtapubbanti jātapubbaṃ. Atīte kāle nibbattaṃ taṃ dassetuṃ “suppabuddho”tiādi vuttaṃ. Kadā pana bhūtanti? Atīte kira anuppanne tathāgate [M 0.0264] bārāṇasiyā sāmantā ekasmiṃ gāme ekā kuladhītā khettaṃ rakkhati. Sā ekaṃ paccekabuddhaṃ disvā pasannacittā tassa pañcahi lājāsatehi saddhiṃ ekaṃ padumapupphaṃ datvā pañca puttasatāni patthesi. Tasmiṃyeva khaṇe pañcasatā migaluddakā paccekabuddhassa madhuramaṃsaṃ datvā “etissā puttā bhaveyyāma, tumhehi pattavisesaṃ labheyyāmā”ti ca patthayiṃsu. Sā yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā devaloke nibbattā. Tato cutā ekasmiṃ jātassare padumagabbhe nibbatti. Tameko tāpaso disvā paṭijaggi. Tassā vicarantiyā pāduddhāre pāduddhāre [P 0.0291] bhūmito padumāni uṭṭhahanti. Eko vanacarako disvā bārāṇasirañño ārocesi. Rājā taṃ ānetvā aggamahesiṃ akāsi. Tassā kucchiyaṃ gabbho saṇṭhāsi. Mahāpadumakumāro tassā kucchiyaṃ vasi, sesā gabbhamalaṃ nissāya nibbattā, te vayappattā uyyāne padumasare kīḷantā ekekasmiṃ padume nisīditvā paripakkañāṇā saṅkhāresu khayavayaṃ paṭṭhapetvā paccekabodhiṃ pāpuṇiṃsu. Tesaṃ byākaraṇagāthā ahosi –

'Once upon a time' means having come into being previously. The words 'Suppabuddha…' and so on are said to show that this occurred in a past time. But when did this happen? It is said that in the past, before the Tathāgata had arisen, a clansman's daughter was guarding a field in a certain village near Bārāṇasī. Seeing a paccekabuddha, with a confident mind, she gave him a lotus flower along with five hundred grains of roasted rice and aspired to have five hundred sons. At that very moment, five hundred deer hunters gave sweet meat to the paccekabuddha and made an aspiration: 'May we become her sons, and may we obtain a special attainment through you.' Having lived out her lifespan, she was reborn in a world of the devas. Passing away from there, she was reborn in the calyx of a lotus in a natural lake. A certain ascetic saw her and raised her. As she walked, lotuses sprang up from the ground at every footstep. A forest-dweller saw this and reported it to the king of Bārāṇasī. The king had her brought to him and made her his chief queen. A conception took place in her womb. Prince Mahāpaduma dwelt in her womb, while the rest were born depending on the impurities of the womb. When they came of age, while playing in a lotus pond in the park, they each sat on a lotus and, their knowledge having matured, they discerned the destruction and vanishing of conditioned formations and attained the enlightenment of a paccekabuddha. Their verse of declaration was:

“Saroruhaṃ padumapalāsapatrajaṃ,

Supupphitaṃ bhamaragaṇānukiṇṇaṃ;

Aniccataṃ khayavayataṃ viditvā,

Eko care khaggavisāṇakappo”ti.

“A lotus grown in a lake, sprung from a lotus petal, well-blossomed and swarmed by a host of bees—seeing its impermanence, its nature of destruction and passing away, one should wander alone like a rhinoceros horn.”

Evaṃ paccekabodhiṃ abhisambuddhesu tesu pañcasu paccekabuddhasatesu abbhantaro tagarasikhī nāma paccekasambuddho gandhamādanapabbate nandamūlapabbhāre sattāhaṃ nirodhasamāpattiṃ samāpajjitvā sattāhassa accayena nirodhā vuṭṭhito ākāsena āgantvā isigilipabbate otaritvā pubbaṇhasamayaṃ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya rājagahaṃ piṇḍāya pāvisi. Tasmiñca samaye rājagahe eko seṭṭhiputto mahatā parivārena uyyānakīḷanatthaṃ nagarato nikkhamanto tagarasikhipaccekabuddhaṃ [V 0.0238] disvā “ko ayaṃ bhaṇḍukāsāvavasano, kuṭṭhī bhavissati, tathā hi kuṭṭhicīvarena sarīraṃ pārupitvā gacchatī”ti niṭṭhubhitvā apasabyaṃ katvā pakkāmi. Taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ – “suppabuddho kuṭṭhī imasmiṃyeva rājagahe…pe… pakkāmī”ti.

When those five hundred had thus become fully enlightened as paccekabuddhas, one among them, the paccekabuddha named Tagarasikhī, entered the attainment of cessation for seven days in the Nandamūla Cave on Mount Gandhamādana. At the end of seven days, he emerged from cessation, came through the sky, and descended on Mount Isigili. In the forenoon, having dressed and taken his bowl and robe, he entered Rājagaha for alms. At that time in Rājagaha, a certain merchant’s son with a large retinue was leaving the city to play in the park. Seeing the paccekabuddha Tagarasikhī, he spat, turned his left side toward him, and departed, saying: 'Who is this contemptible fellow in a saffron robe? He must be a leper, for he goes about with his body wrapped in a leper’s robe.' In reference to this it was said: 'Suppabuddha the leper, in this very Rājagaha… departed.'

Tattha [M 0.0265] kvāyanti ko ayaṃ. Khuṃsanavasena vadati. “Kovāya”ntipi pāḷi. Kuṭṭhīti akuṭṭhiṃyeva taṃ seṭṭhi kuṭṭharogaṃ akkosavatthuṃ pāpento vadati. Kuṭṭhicīvarenāti kuṭṭhīnaṃ cīvarena. Yebhuyyena hi kuṭṭhino ḍaṃsamakasasarīsapapaṭibāhanatthaṃ rogapaṭicchādanatthañca [P 0.0292] yaṃ vā taṃ vā pilotikakhaṇḍaṃ gahetvā pārupati, evamayampīti dasseti. Paṃsukūlacīvaradharattā vā aggaḷānaṃ anekavaṇṇabhāvena kuṭṭhasarīrasadisoti hīḷento “kuṭṭhicīvarenā”ti āha. Niṭṭhubhitvāti kheḷaṃ pātetvā. Apasabyato karitvāti paṇḍitā tādisaṃ paccekabuddhaṃ disvā vanditvā padakkhiṇaṃ karonti, ayaṃ pana aviññutāya paribhavena taṃ apasabyaṃ katvā attano apasabyaṃ apadakkhiṇaṃ katvā gato. “Apasabyāmato”tipi pāṭho. Tassa kammassāti tagarasikhimhi paccekabuddhe “kvāyaṃ kuṭṭhī”ti hīḷetvā niṭṭhubhanaapasabyakaraṇavasena pavattapāpakammassa. Niraye paccitthāti niraye nirayagginā dayhittha. “Paccitvā nirayagginā”tipi paṭhanti. Tasseva kammassa vipākāvasesenāti yena kammena so niraye paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhi, na taṃ kammaṃ manussaloke vipākaṃ deti. Yā panassa nānakkhaṇikā cetanā tadā paccekabuddhe vippaṭipajjanavasena pavattā aparāpariyavedanīyabhūtā, sā aparāpariyavedanīyeneva puññakammena manussesu tihetukapaṭisandhiyā dinnāya pavattiyaṃ kuṭṭhibhāvaṃ dāliddiyaṃ paramakāruññataṃ āpādesi. Taṃ sandhāya kammasabhāgatāvasena “tasseva kammassa vipākavasesenā”ti vuttaṃ. Sadisepi hi loke tabbohāro diṭṭho yathā taṃ “sā eva tittirī, tāniyeva osadhānī”ti.

Here, kvāyaṃ means 'Who is this?' He speaks contemptuously. The reading is also kovāyaṃ. Kuṭṭhīti: The merchant's son calls him a leper, though he was not a leper, thus making the disease of leprosy a basis for abuse. Kuṭṭhicīvarena means with the robe of lepers. For lepers usually take any old piece of cloth and wrap themselves in it, both to ward off biting flies, mosquitoes, and reptiles, and to conceal their disease; this implies that this one too is like that. Or, because he was a wearer of rag-robes, he reviled him saying 'with a leper's robe,' since its patches of many colors resembled a leper's body. Niṭṭhubhitvā means having spat, having expelled phlegm. Apasabyato karitvā means that while the wise, on seeing such a paccekabuddha, pay homage and circumambulate him keeping their right side toward him, this one, out of ignorance and contempt, turned his left side toward him and departed without circumambulating him. The reading is also apasabyāmato. Tassa kammassāti refers to the evil kamma that occurred by way of reviling the paccekabuddha Tagarasikhī with the words, 'Who is this leper?', spitting, and turning his left side toward him. Niraye paccitthāti means he was roasted in hell, burned by the fire of hell. Some read paccitvā nirayagginā, 'having been roasted by the fire of hell.' Tasseva kammassa vipākāvasesenāti: By the residual result of that same kamma by which he took rebirth in hell; that kamma does not give its result in the human world. But those diverse momentary volitions that arose in him then by way of misconduct towards the paccekabuddha, which were to be experienced in a subsequent life, produced in the course of that life his state of leprosy, poverty, and extreme wretchedness, after a three-rooted rebirth among humans had been given by wholesome kamma that was also to be experienced in a subsequent life. It is with reference to this, on account of the similarity of the kamma, that the phrase 'by the residual result of that same kamma' was said. For a similar usage is seen in the world, as in 'That very partridge, those very herbs.'

Ettāvatā “ko nu kho, bhante, hetū”ti tena bhikkhunā puṭṭhapañhaṃ vissajjetvā idāni yo “tassa kā gati, ko abhisamparāyo”ti pubbe bhikkhūhi puṭṭhapañho, taṃ vissajjetuṃ “so tathāgatappavedita”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha tathāgatappaveditanti tathāgatena bhagavatā desitaṃ akkhātaṃ pakāsitanti tathāgatappaveditaṃ. Āgammāti adhigantvā, nissāya ñatvā vā. “Tathāgatappavedite dhammavinaye”tipi pāṭho. Saddhaṃ samādiyīti sammāsambuddho bhagavā, svākkhāto bhagavatā dhammo, suppaṭipanno [M 0.0266] bhagavato sāvakasaṅghoti ratanattayasannissayaṃ pubbabhāgasaddhañceva lokuttarasaddhañcāti duvidhampi [P 0.0293] saddhaṃ sammā ādiyi. Yathā na puna ādātabbā hoti, evaṃ yāva bhavakkhayā gaṇhi, attano cittasantāne uppādesīti attho. Sīlaṃ samādiyītiādīsupi eseva nayo. Sīlanti pubbabhāgasīlena saddhiṃ maggasīlaṃ phalasīlañca[V 0.0239]. Sutanti pariyattibāhusaccaṃ paṭivedhabāhusaccañcāti duvidhampi sutaṃ. Pariyattidhammāpi hi tena dhammassavanakāle saccappaṭivedhāya sāvakehi yathāladdhappakāraṃ sutā paricitā manasānupekkhitā diṭṭhiyā suppaṭividdhā cāti. Cāganti paṭhamamaggavajjhakilesābhisaṅkhārānaṃ vossaggasaṅkhātaṃ cāgaṃ, yena ariyasāvakā deyyadhammesu muttacāgā ca honti payatapāṇī vossaggaratā. Paññanti saddhiṃ vipassanāpaññāya maggapaññañceva phalapaññañca.

At this point, having answered the question, 'What, venerable sir, is the cause?' posed by that monk, now, to answer the question previously asked by the monks, 'What is his destination, what is his future state?' it is said, 'He, in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata,' etc. Here, 'proclaimed by the Tathāgata' means taught, declared, and revealed by the Blessed One, the Tathāgata. 'Having approached' means having attained or having known through reliance. There is also the reading, 'In the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.' 'He undertook faith rightly' means he rightly undertook two kinds of faith, preliminary faith and supramundane faith, relying on the Triple Gem: the Blessed One, the perfectly enlightened Buddha; the Dhamma well-expounded by the Blessed One; and the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples practicing well. He held it in such a way that it need not be taken up again; this means he grasped it until the destruction of existence, arousing it in the continuum of his own mind. The same method applies to 'he undertook virtue,' etc. Here, 'virtue' includes preliminary virtue along with the virtue of the path and the virtue of the fruit. 'Learning' refers to two kinds of learning: extensive learning of the scriptures and learning through penetration. For at the time of hearing the Dhamma, the scriptural teachings were also heard by him for the penetration of the truths—in whatever way they are received by disciples—and were familiarized, mentally examined, and thoroughly penetrated by vision. 'Generosity' refers to the relinquishment of the defilements and formations to be abandoned by the first path, by which noble disciples become freely generous, open-handed, and delighting in relinquishment. 'Wisdom' includes the wisdom of insight along with the wisdom of the path and the wisdom of the fruit.

Kāyassa bhedāti upādinnakkhandhapariccāgā. Paraṃ maraṇāti tadanantaraṃ abhinibbattakkhandhagahaṇā. Atha vā kāyassa bhedāti jīvitindriyassa upacchedā. Paraṃ maraṇāti cutito uddhaṃ. Sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokanti padattayenāpi devalokameva vadati. So hi sampattīnaṃ sobhanattā sundarā gatīti sugati, rūpādīhi visesehi suṭṭhu aggoti saggo, sabbakālaṃ sukhamevettha lokiyati, lujjatīti vā lokoti vuccati. Upapannoti paṭisandhiggahaṇavasena upagato. Sahabyatanti sahabhāvaṃ. Vacanattho pana saha byati pavattati, vasatīti vā sahabyo, sahaṭhāyī sahavāyī vā. Tassa bhāvo sahabyatā. Atirocatīti atikkamma abhibhavitvā rocati virocati. Vaṇṇenāti rūpasampattiyā. Yasasāti parivārena. So hi asucimakkhitaṃ jajjaraṃ mattikābhājanaṃ chaḍḍetvā anekaratanavicittaṃ pabhassararaṃsijālavinaddhasuddhajambunadabhājanaṃ gaṇhanto viya vuttappakāraṃ kaḷevaraṃ idha nikkhipitvā ekacittakkhaṇena yathāvuttaṃ dibbattabhāvaṃ mahatā parivārena saddhiṃ paṭilabhīti.

With the breakup of the body means the relinquishment of the aggregates clung to. After death means the taking up of newly arisen aggregates immediately following. Alternatively, with the breakup of the body means the cutting off of the life faculty. After death means onward from passing away. A good destination, a heavenly realm, a world—by these three terms it refers only to the world of the devas. For because it is a beautiful state of attainment, it is called a 'good destination' (sugati); because it is thoroughly excellent with distinctions such as form, it is 'heavenly' (sagga); and because happiness is always experienced (lokīyati) there, or because it decays (lujjati), it is called a 'world' (loka). Reborn means having arrived by taking up rebirth-linking. Companionship means co-existence. The verbal meaning, however, is: one who fares on together or dwells together is a companion (sahabyo), one who stays together or lives together. The state of that is companionship (sahabyatā). He outshines means he shines, surpassing and overpowering. With beauty means with the accomplishment of beautiful form. With glory means with a retinue. For just as one might discard a dirty, smeared, worn-out clay pot and take up a pot made of pure Jambu-river gold, variegated with many jewels and entwined with a net of radiant rays, so too, having laid aside here the kind of body described, in a single mind-moment he attains the divine state as described, along with a great retinue.

Etamatthaṃ viditvāti etaṃ pāpānaṃ aparivajjane ādīnavaṃ, parivajjane ca ānisaṃsaṃ sabbākārato viditvā tadatthavibhāvanaṃ imaṃ udānaṃ udānesi.

Having understood this meaning, that is, having fully understood in every way the danger in not avoiding evil and the benefit in avoiding it, he uttered this inspired utterance to clarify that meaning.

Tassāyaṃ [P 0.0294] saṅkhepattho – yathā cakkhumā puriso parakkame kāyikavīriye vijjamāne sarīre vahante visamāni papātādiṭṭhānāni caṇḍabhāvena vā visamāni hatthiassaahikukkuragorūpādīni parivajjaye, evaṃ [M 0.0267] jīvalokasmiṃ imasmiṃ sattaloke paṇḍito sappañño puriso tāya sappaññatāya attano hitaṃ jānanto pāpāni lāmakāni duccaritāni parivajjeyya. Evañhi yathāyaṃ suppabuddho tagarasikhimhi paccekabuddhe pāpaṃ aparivajjetvā mahantaṃ anayabyasanaṃ āpajji, evaṃ āpajjeyyāti adhippāyo. Yathā vā suppabuddho kuṭṭhī mama dhammadesanaṃ āgamma idāni saṃvegappatto pāpāni parivajjento uḷāraṃ visesaṃ adhigañchi, evaṃ aññopi uḷāraṃ visesādhigamaṃ icchanto pāpāni parivajjeyyāti adhippāyo.

This is the concise meaning: Just as a clear-sighted person, when physical energy is present and the body is capable, would avoid dangerous places like cliffs and precipices, or would avoid what is dangerous due to fierceness, such as elephants, horses, snakes, dogs, and cattle, so too in this world of living beings, in this realm of beings, a wise and discerning person, knowing their own good through that discernment, should avoid evil, inferior, and unwholesome deeds. For just as Suppabuddha met with great calamity and ruin by not avoiding an evil deed towards the paccekabuddha Tagarasikhi, so too one might meet with such—this is the intention. Or just as Suppabuddha the leper, having come to my teaching and now being filled with a sense of urgency, attained a sublime distinction by avoiding evil, so too another who desires to attain a sublime distinction should avoid evil—this is the intention.

Tatiyasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the third discourse is concluded.

4. Kumārakasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Discourse to the Young Boys

44. Catutthe [V 0.0240] kumārakāti taruṇapuggalā. Ye subhāsitadubbhāsitassa atthaṃ jānanti, te idha kumārakāti adhippetā. Ime hi sattā jātadivasato paṭṭhāya yāva pañcadasavassakā, tāva “kumārakā, bālā”ti ca vuccanti, tato paraṃ vīsativassāni “yuvāno”ti. Macchake bādhentīti maggasamīpe ekasmiṃ taḷāke nidāghakāle udake parikkhīṇe ninnaṭṭhāne ṭhitaṃ udakaṃ ussiñcitvā khuddakamacche gaṇhanti ceva hananti ca “pacitvā khādissāmā”ti. Tenupasaṅkamīti maggato thokaṃ taḷākaṃ atikkamitvā ṭhito, tasmā “upasaṅkamī”ti vadati. Kasmā pana upasaṅkami? Te kumārake attani vissāsaṃ janetuṃ upasaṅkami. Bhāyatha voti ettha voti nipātamattaṃ. Dukkhassāti nissakke sāmivacanaṃ, dukkhasmāti attho. Appiyaṃ vo dukkhanti “kiṃ tumhākaṃ sarīre uppajjanakadukkhaṃ appiyaṃ aniṭṭha”nti pucchati.

44. In the fourth, `kumārakā` means young persons. Those who understand the meaning of what is well spoken and badly spoken are meant here by `kumārakā`. For these beings, from the day of their birth up to the age of fifteen years, are called 'young boys' and 'fools'; after that, for twenty years, they are called 'youths.' `Tormenting fish` means that near a road, in a certain pond, during the hot season when the water had diminished, they were bailing out the water that remained in a low-lying spot, catching small fish, and killing them, thinking, 'We will cook and eat them.' `He approached` means that having gone a little way from the road past the pond, he stood there; therefore it says `he approached`. But why did he approach? He approached to inspire confidence in those young boys. `Are you afraid?`: here `vo` is just a particle. `Of suffering`: this is the genitive case with the sense of the ablative; it means 'from suffering.' `Is suffering disagreeable to you?`: he asks, 'Is the suffering that arises in your body disagreeable and undesirable to you?'

Etamatthaṃ viditvāti ime sattā [P 0.0295] attano dukkhaṃ anicchantā eva hutvā dukkhahetuṃ paṭipajjantā attano taṃ icchantā eva nāma hontīti etamatthaṃ sabbākārato viditvā. Imaṃ udānanti imaṃ pāpakiriyāya nisedhanaṃ ādīnavavibhāvanañca udānaṃ udānesi.

Having understood this matter in all its aspects—that these beings, not wishing for their own suffering, nevertheless engage in the cause of suffering and thus, it seems, desire their own suffering—he uttered this inspired utterance. He uttered this inspired utterance, which is a prohibition of evil actions and an explanation of the danger.

Tassattho – yadi tumhākaṃ sakalamāpāyikaṃ, sugatiyañca appāyukatāmanussadobhaggiyādibhedaṃ dukkhaṃ appiyaṃ aniṭṭhaṃ, yadi tumhe tato bhāyatha, āvi vā paresaṃ pākaṭabhāvavasena appaṭicchannaṃ katvā kāyena [M 0.0268] vā vācāya vā pāṇātipātādippabhedaṃ yadi vā raho apākaṭabhāvavasena paṭicchannaṃ katvā manodvāre eva abhijjhādippabhedaṃ aṇumattampi pāpakaṃ lāmakadhammaṃ mākattha mā karittha, atha pana taṃ pāpakammaṃ etarahi karotha, āyatiṃ vā karissatha, nirayādīsu catūsu apāyesu manussesu ca tassa phalabhūtaṃ dukkhaṃ ito vā etto vā palāyante amhe nānubandhissatīti adhippāyena upecca apecca palāyatampi tumhākaṃ tato mutti mokkho natthi. Gatikālādipaccayantarasamavāye vipaccissatiyevāti dasseti. “Palāyane”tipi paṭhanti, vuttanayena yattha katthaci gamane pakkamane satīti attho. Ayañca attho “na antalikkhe na samuddamajjhe…pe… pāpakammā”ti (dha. pa. 127; mi. pa. 4.2.4) imāya gāthāya dīpetabbo.

The meaning is this: If all the suffering of the lower realms, and in the happy destinies the suffering distinguished as short life, human misfortune, and so on, is displeasing and undesirable to you; if you fear it—then do not commit even the slightest evil, lowly deed, do not do it, whether openly, making it evident to others through body or speech in forms like killing living beings, or secretly, concealing it from others through the mind-door in forms like covetousness. But if you do that evil deed now or will do it in the future, thinking, 'The suffering that is its result in the four woeful states, such as hell, and among humans will not pursue us whether we flee here or there,' then even if you flee away from it, there is no escape or liberation for you from it. This shows that it will inevitably ripen when there is a conjunction of conditions such as destination and time. Some also read it as `palāyane` (in fleeing), meaning 'when one goes or departs anywhere at all.' This meaning should be illustrated by the verse: 'Not in the sky, nor in the ocean’s midst… from evil kamma' (Dhp. 127; Mil. 4.2.4).

Catutthasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the fourth discourse is finished.

5. Uposathasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Uposatha Sutta

45. Pañcame [V 0.0241][P 0.0296] tadahūti tasmiṃ ahani tasmiṃ divase. Uposatheti ettha upavasanti etthāti uposatho, upavasantīti sīlena vā anasanena vā upetā hutvā vasantīti attho. Ayañhi uposathasaddo “aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgataṃ uposathaṃ upavasāmī”tiādīsu (a. ni. 3.71; 10.46) sīle āgato. “Uposatho vā pavāraṇā vā”tiādīsu (mahāva. 155) pātimokkhuddesādivinayakamme. “Gopālakūposatho nigaṇṭhūposatho”tiādīsu (a. ni. 3.71) upavāse. “Uposatho nāma nāgarājā”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 2.246) paññattiyaṃ. “Ajjuposatho pannaraso”tiādīsu (mahāva. 168) divase. Idhāpi divaseyeva daṭṭhabbo, tasmā “tadahuposathe”ti tasmiṃ uposathadivasabhūte ahanīti attho. Nisinno hotīti mahābhikkhusaṅghaparivuto ovādapātimokkhaṃ uddisituṃ nisinno hoti. Nisajja pana bhikkhūnaṃ cittāni olokento ekaṃ dussīlapuggalaṃ disvā, “sacāhaṃ imasmiṃ puggale idha nisinneyeva pātimokkhaṃ uddisissāmi, sattadhāssa muddhā phalissatī”ti tasmiṃ anukampāya tuṇhīyeva ahosi.

45. In the fifth, `on that day` means on that particular day. `Uposatha`: they observe on it, thus it is the Uposatha; the meaning is that they dwell endowed with virtue or with fasting. This word 'Uposatha' appears in the sense of virtue in passages such as, 'I undertake the Uposatha with eight factors.' In passages such as, 'Uposatha or Pavāraṇā,' it refers to Vinaya acts such as the recitation of the Pātimokkha. In passages such as, 'The cowherd's Uposatha, the Nigaṇṭha's Uposatha,' it refers to fasting. In passages such as, 'Uposatha is the name of a Nāga king,' it refers to a designation. In passages such as, 'Today is the fifteenth, the Uposatha,' it refers to the day. Here too, it should be understood as referring to the day; therefore, `on that Uposatha day` means on that day which was the Uposatha day. `He was seated`: He was seated surrounded by the great Saṅgha of monks in order to recite the Ovāda-pātimokkha. While seated, however, surveying the minds of the monks, he saw one immoral person. Thinking, 'If I recite the Pātimokkha while this person is seated here, his head will split into seven pieces,' out of compassion for him, he remained silent.

Ettha [M 0.0269] ca uddhastaṃ aruṇanti aruṇuggamanaṃ vatvāpi “uddisatu, bhante bhagavā, bhikkhūnaṃ pātimokkha”nti thero bhagavantaṃ pātimokkhuddesaṃ yāci tasmiṃ kāle “na, bhikkhave, anuposathe uposatho kātabbo”tisikkhāpadassa (mahāva. 183) apaññattattā. Aparisuddhā, ānanda, parisāti tikkhattuṃ therena pātimokkhuddesassa yācitattā anuddesassa kāraṇaṃ kathento “asukapuggalo aparisuddho”ti avatvā “aparisuddhā, ānanda, parisā”ti āha. Kasmā pana bhagavā tiyāmarattiṃ tathā vītināmesi? Tato paṭṭhāya ovādapātimokkhaṃ anuddisitukāmo tassa vatthuṃ pākaṭaṃ kātuṃ.

Here, even though it was said that dawn had arisen—that is, the sun had risen—the elder requested the Blessed One to recite the Pātimokkha, saying, 'Venerable sir, may the Blessed One recite the Pātimokkha for the monks.'
