This was because at that time the training rule, 'Monks, the Uposatha should not be performed on a non-Uposatha day,' had not yet been laid down. `The assembly is impure, Ānanda`: when the elder had requested the recitation of the Pātimokkha for a third time, the Blessed One, explaining the reason for not reciting it, said, 'The assembly is impure, Ānanda,' without saying, 'Such and such a person is impure.' But why did the Blessed One spend the three watches of the night in that way? In order to make the reason clear for his intention not to recite the Ovāda-pātimokkha from that time onwards.

Addasāti kathaṃ addasa. Attano cetopariyañāṇena tassaṃ parisati bhikkhūnaṃ cittāni parijānanto tassa moghapurisassa dussīlyacittaṃ passi. Yasmā pana citte diṭṭhe taṃsamaṅgīpuggalo diṭṭho nāma hoti, tasmā “addasā kho āyasmā mahāmoggallāno taṃ puggalaṃ dussīla”ntiādi vuttaṃ[P 0.0297]. Yatheva hi anāgate sattasu divasesu pavattamānaṃ paresaṃ cittaṃ cetopariyañāṇalābhī jānāti, evaṃ atītepīti. Dussīlanti nissīlaṃ, sīlavirahitanti attho. Pāpadhammanti dussīlattā eva hīnajjhāsayatāya lāmakasabhāvaṃ. Asucinti aparisuddhehi kāyakammādīhi samannāgatattā na suciṃ. Saṅkassarasamācāranti kiñcideva asāruppaṃ disvā “idaṃ [V 0.0242] iminā kataṃ bhavissatī”ti evaṃ paresaṃ āsaṅkanīyatāya saṅkāya saritabbasamācāraṃ, atha vā kenacideva karaṇīyena mantayante bhikkhū disvā “kacci nu kho ime mayā katakammaṃ jānitvā mantentī”ti attanoyeva saṅkāya saritabbasamācāraṃ.

How did he see? With his own knowledge of encompassing minds, discerning the minds of the monks in that assembly, he saw the immoral mind of that worthless man. Since when the mind is seen, the person endowed with it is said to be seen, it is therefore said, 'Indeed, Venerable Mahāmoggallāna saw that immoral person,' and so on. Just as one who has attained the knowledge of encompassing minds knows the minds of others that will occur in the future over seven days, so too does one know the past. `Immoral` means without virtue, lacking moral conduct. `Of evil nature` means of a base nature on account of his immorality and low inclination. `Impure` means not clean, because he is endowed with impure bodily actions and so forth. `Of suspicious conduct` means that upon seeing some impropriety, others suspect, 'This must have been done by him,' thus his conduct is to be suspected by others. Or, upon seeing monks discussing some matter, he himself suspects, 'Could they be discussing some deed I have done?'—thus his conduct is to be suspected by himself.

Lajjitabbatāya paṭicchādetabbakāraṇato paṭicchannaṃ kammantaṃ etassāti paṭicchannakammantaṃ. Kucchitasamaṇavesadhāritāya na samaṇanti assamaṇaṃ. Salākaggahaṇādīsu “kittakā samaṇā”ti ca gaṇanāya “ahampi samaṇomhī”ti micchāpaṭiññāya samaṇapaṭiññaṃ. Aseṭṭhacāritāya abrahmacāriṃ. Aññe brahmacārino sunivatthe supārute supattadhare gāmanigamādīsu piṇḍāya caritvā jīvikaṃ kappente disvā abrahmacārī samāno sayampi tādisena ākārena paṭipajjanto uposathādīsu sandissanto “ahampi [M 0.0270] brahmacārī”ti paṭiññaṃ dento viya hotīti brahmacāripaṭiññaṃ. Pūtinā kammena sīlavipattiyā anto anupaviṭṭhattā antopūtiṃ. Chahi dvārehi rāgādikilesavassanena tintattā avassutaṃ. Sañjātarāgādikacavarattā sīlavantehi chaḍḍetabbattā ca kasambujātaṃ. Majjhe bhikkhusaṅghassa nisinnanti saṅghapariyāpanno viya bhikkhusaṅghassa anto nisinnaṃ. Diṭṭhosīti ayaṃ pana na pakatattoti bhagavatā diṭṭho asi. Yasmā ca evaṃ diṭṭho, tasmā natthi te tava bhikkhūhi saddhiṃ ekakammādisaṃvāso. Yasmā pana so saṃvāso tava natthi, tasmā uṭṭhehi, āvusoti evamettha padayojanā veditabbā.

His work is concealed because it is a cause for shame and needs to be hidden. He is a non-recluse because, wearing the guise of a contemptible recluse, he is not a recluse. He claims to be a recluse by falsely professing, 'I too am a recluse,' during a count of recluses for matters like taking tickets. He is not a celibate on account of his ignoble conduct. He claims to be a celibate because, though not a celibate himself, on seeing other celibates—well-dressed, well-robed, holding their bowls properly, sustaining their lives by wandering for alms in villages and towns—he too conducts himself in a similar manner and appears at the Uposatha and so on, as if making the claim, 'I too am a celibate.' He is inwardly rotten because he is putrid within due to corrupt kamma and the collapse of virtue. He is drenched because he is soaked by the rain of defilements such as lust through the six doors. He has become like rubbish because defilements such as lust have arisen in him like rubbish, and because he should be discarded by the virtuous. 'Seated in the midst of the Saṅgha of monks' means seated inside the Saṅgha of monks as if included in it. 'You have been seen': this was not an ordinary seeing; you were seen by the Blessed One. And because you have been seen thus, there is no communion for you with the monks in single acts and so on. Since you have no such communion, 'Rise up, friend!'—this is how the connection of words here should be understood.

Tatiyampi kho so puggalo tuṇhī ahosīti anekavāraṃ vatvāpi thero “sayameva nibbinno oramissatī”ti vā, “idāni imesaṃ paṭipattiṃ jānissāmī”ti vā adhippāyena tuṇhī ahosi. Bāhāyaṃ gahetvāti bhagavatā mayā ca yāthāvato diṭṭho, yāvatatiyaṃ uṭṭhehīti vutto na uṭṭhāti, “idānissa nikkaḍḍhanakālo [P 0.0298] mā saṅghassa uposathantarāyo ahosī”ti taṃ bāhāyaṃ aggahesi, tathā gahetvā. Bahidvārakoṭṭhakā nikkhāmetvāti dvārakoṭṭhakasālato bahi nikkhāmetvā. Bahīti pana nikkhāmitaṭṭhānadassanaṃ, atha vā bahidvārakoṭṭhakāti bahidvārakoṭṭhakatopi nikkhāmetvā, na antodvārakoṭṭhakato, evaṃ ubhayathāpi vihārato bahi katvāti attho. Sūcighaṭikaṃ datvāti aggaḷasūciñca uparighaṭikañca ādahitvā, suṭṭhutaraṃ kavāṭaṃ thaketvāti attho. Yāva bāhāgahaṇāpi nāmāti iminā “aparisuddhā, ānanda, parisā”ti vacanaṃ sutvā eva hi tena pakkamitabbaṃ siyā, evaṃ apakkamitvā yāva bāhāgahaṇāpi nāma so moghapuriso āgamessatīti acchariyamidanti dasseti. Idampi garahaṇacchariyamevāti veditabbaṃ.

For a third time that person remained silent. Even after being spoken to repeatedly, the elder remained silent with the thought: 'He will become disenchanted and leave on his own,' or, 'Now I will learn his practice.' Taking him by the arm: He has been seen as he really is by the Blessed One and by me, and though told up to the third time, 'Get up!' he does not get up. Thinking, 'Now is the time to expel him, lest he become an obstacle to the Sangha’s Uposatha,' he took him by the arm. Having taken him thus, he led him out from the outer gatehouse: he led him out from the hall of the gatehouse. 'Outside' here indicates the place to which he was expelled. Or else, 'from the outer gatehouse' means from the outer gatehouse itself, not from the inner gatehouse. In either case, the meaning is that he was put outside the monastery. He applied the bolt: he inserted the bolt-pin and the upper latch; the meaning is that he fastened the door very securely. Even up to being taken by the arm!: this shows the astonishment that, 'Indeed, upon hearing the words, “Ānanda, the assembly is impure,” he should have departed. Not having departed thus, that foolish man would wait even up to being taken by the arm!' This, too, should be understood as an astonishment connected with censure.

Atha [V 0.0243] bhagavā cintesi – “idāni bhikkhusaṅgho abbudajāto, aparisuddhā puggalā uposathaṃ āgacchanti, na ca tathāgatā aparisuddhāya parisāya uposathaṃ karonti, pātimokkhaṃ uddisanti, anuddisante ca bhikkhusaṅghassa uposatho pacchijjati, yaṃnūnāhaṃ ito paṭṭhāya bhikkhūnaṃyeva pātimokkhuddesaṃ anujāneyya”nti. Evaṃ pana cintetvā bhikkhūnaṃyeva pātimokkhuddesaṃ anujāni. Tena vuttaṃ – “atha kho bhagavā…pe… pātimokkhaṃ uddiseyyāthā”ti.

Then the Blessed One thought: 'Now a boil has arisen in the Sangha of monks; impure persons come to the Uposatha, and Tathāgatas do not perform the Uposatha or recite the Pātimokkha with an impure assembly. When it is not recited, the Uposatha of the Sangha of monks is interrupted. What if, from now on, I were to authorize the monks themselves to recite the Pātimokkha?' Having thought thus, he authorized the monks themselves to recite the Pātimokkha. Therefore it was said: 'Then the Blessed One ... you should recite the Pātimokkha.'

Tattha [M 0.0271] na dānāhanti idāni ahaṃ uposathaṃ na karissāmi, pātimokkhaṃ na uddisissāmīti paccekaṃ na-kārena sambandho. Duvidhañhi pātimokkhaṃ āṇāpātimokkhaṃ ovādapātimokkhanti. Tesu “suṇātu me, bhante”tiādikaṃ (mahāva. 134) āṇāpātimokkhaṃ, taṃ sāvakāva uddisanti, na buddhā, ayaṃ anvaddhamāsaṃ uddisiyati. “Khantī paramaṃ…pe… sabbapāpassa akaraṇaṃ…pe… anūpavādo anūpaghāto…pe… etaṃ buddhāna sāsana”nti (dī. ni. 2.90; dha. pa. 183-185) imā pana tisso gāthā ovādapātimokkhaṃ nāma, taṃ buddhāva uddisanti, na sāvakā, channampi vassānaṃ accayena uddisanti. Dīghāyukabuddhānañhi dharamānakāle ayameva pātimokkhuddeso[P 0.0299], appāyukabuddhānaṃ pana paṭhamabodhiyaṃyeva. Tato paraṃ itaro, tañca kho bhikkhū eva uddisanti, na buddhā, tasmā amhākampi bhagavā vīsativassamattaṃ ovādapātimokkhaṃ uddisitvā imaṃ antarāyaṃ disvā tato paraṃ na uddisi. Aṭṭhānanti akāraṇaṃ. Anavakāsoti tasseva vevacanaṃ. Kāraṇañhi yathā tiṭṭhati ettha phalaṃ tadāyattavuttitāyāti ṭhānanti vuccati, evaṃ anavakāsotipi vuccatīti. Yanti kiriyāparāmasanaṃ, taṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayena yojetabbaṃ.

Herein, in the phrase 'From now on I will not,' the word 'not' is connected with each part: 'I will not perform the Uposatha' and 'I will not recite the Pātimokkha.' For the Pātimokkha is twofold: the Pātimokkha of command and the Pātimokkha of exhortation. Of these, the Pātimokkha of command, beginning 'Venerable sirs, let the Sangha listen to me…' (Mahāvagga 134), is recited only by disciples, not by Buddhas; this is recited every half-month. But these three verses—'Forbearance is the supreme austerity… the non-doing of any evil… non-reviling, non-harming… this is the teaching of the Buddhas' (DN 2:90; Dhp 183–185)—are called the Pātimokkha of exhortation. This is recited only by Buddhas, not by disciples; they recite it after a lapse of six years. For long-lived Buddhas, this is the recitation of the Pātimokkha for as long as they are alive, but for short-lived Buddhas, it is only at their first enlightenment. After that, the other one is recited, and that is recited only by the monks, not by the Buddhas. Therefore our Blessed One, too, recited the Pātimokkha of exhortation for about twenty years, but after seeing this obstacle, he did not recite it thereafter. It is impossible: it is without cause. There is no opportunity: this is a synonym for that. For a cause is called a 'basis' (ṭhāna) because the result 'stands' (tiṭṭhati) on it, its occurrence being dependent on that; thus 'no opportunity' (anavakāsa) is also said. That: this is a reference to the action. It should be connected in the way stated above.

Aṭṭhime, bhikkhave, mahāsamuddeti ko anusandhi? Yvāyaṃ aparisuddhāya parisāya pātimokkhassa anuddeso vutto, so imasmiṃ dhammavinaye acchariyo abbhuto dhammoti taṃ aparehi sattahi acchariyabbhutadhammehi saddhiṃ vibhajitvā dassetukāmo paṭhamaṃ tāva tesaṃ upamābhāvena mahāsamudde aṭṭha acchariyabbhutadhamme dassento satthā “aṭṭhime, bhikkhave, mahāsamudde”tiādimāha.

What is the connection with the passage beginning, 'Monks, in the great ocean there are these eight...'? The non-recitation of the Pātimokkha to an impure assembly that has been mentioned is a wonderful and marvellous quality in this Dhamma and Vinaya. Wishing to show this by analyzing it together with seven other wonderful and marvellous qualities, the Teacher, first showing the eight wonderful and marvellous qualities in the great ocean that serve as their similes, spoke the words beginning: 'Monks, in the great ocean there are these eight...'

Pakatidevā viya na suranti na isanti na virocantīti asurā, surā nāma devā, tesaṃ paṭipakkhāti vā asurā, vepacittipahārādādayo. Tesaṃ bhavanaṃ sinerussa heṭṭhābhāge, te tattha pavisantā nikkhamantā sinerupāde maṇḍapādiṃ nimminitvā kīḷantāva abhiramanti. Tattha tesaṃ [V 0.0244] abhirati ime guṇe disvāti āha – “ye disvā disvā asurā mahāsamudde abhiramantī”ti. Tattha abhiramantīti ratiṃ vindanti, anukkaṇṭhamānā vasantīti attho.

They are asuras because, unlike ordinary devas, they do not revel (na suranti), are not masters (na isanti), and do not shine (na virocanti). Or, the devas are called suras, and the asuras are their opponents, such as Vepacitti, Pahārāda, and others. Their abode is in the region below Mount Sineru. When entering and leaving there, they create pavilions and so on at the foot of Sineru and delight in playing. It is said that their delight there is from seeing these qualities: 'Seeing which again and again, the asuras delight in the great ocean.' Here, 'they delight' means they find pleasure; the meaning is that they dwell without longing.

Anupubbaninnotiādīni sabbāni anupaṭipāṭiyā ninnabhāvasseva vevacanāni. Na āyatakeneva papātoti na chinnataṭo mahāsobbho viya [M 0.0272] ādito eva papāto. So hi tīradesato paṭṭhāya ekaṅguladvaṅgulavidatthiratanayaṭṭhiusabhaaḍḍhagāvutagāvutaḍḍhayojanādivasena gambhīro hutvā gacchanto gacchanto sinerupādamūle caturāsītiyojanasahassagambhīro hutvā ṭhitoti dasseti.

Gradually shelving and so on are all synonyms for being sloped in sequence. Not an abrupt precipice means it is not a precipice right from the start, like a great chasm with a sheer bank. For it is shown that, starting from the shore region, it becomes progressively deeper by increments of one finger, two fingers, a span, a cubit, a pole, a bullock-measure, half a gāvuta, a gāvuta, half a yojana, and so on, until at the foot of Mount Sineru it stands at a depth of eighty-four thousand yojanas.

Ṭhitadhammoti ṭhitasabhāvo avaṭṭhitasabhāvo. Na matena kuṇapena saṃvasatīti yena kenaci hatthiassādīnaṃ kaḷevarena saddhiṃ na saṃvasati. Tīraṃ vāhetīti tīraṃ apaneti. Thalaṃ ussāretīti [P 0.0300] hatthena gahetvā viya vīcippahāreneva thale khipati. Gaṅgā yamunāti anotattadahassa dakkhiṇamukhato nikkhantanadī pañca dhārā hutvā pavattaṭṭhāne gaṅgātiādinā pañcadhā saṅkhaṃ gatā.

Of a stable nature means of a fixed nature, of an established nature. It does not co-exist with a dead corpse means it does not co-exist with the carcass of any creature whatsoever, such as an elephant or a horse. It washes it to the shore means it carries it to the shore. It casts it up on high ground means it throws it onto dry land by the striking of a wave as if seizing it with a hand. The Ganges, the Yamunā...: this refers to the river that issues from the southern mouth of Lake Anotatta. At the place where it flows on, having become five streams, it comes to be designated in five ways, beginning with 'Ganges'.

Tatrāyaṃ imāsaṃ nadīnaṃ ādito paṭṭhāya uppattikathā – ayañhi jambudīpo dasasahassayojanaparimāṇo, tattha catusahassayojanappamāṇo padeso udakena ajjhotthaṭo samuddoti saṅkhaṃ gato, tisahassayojanappamāṇe manussā vasanti, tisahassayojanappamāṇe himavā patiṭṭhito ubbedhena pañcayojanasatiko caturāsītikūṭasahassapaṭimaṇḍito samantato sandamānapañcasatanadīvicitto, yattha āyāmena vitthārena gambhīratāya ca paṇṇāsayojanappamāṇo diyaḍḍhayojanasataparimaṇḍalo anotattadaho kaṇṇamuṇḍadaho rathakāradaho chaddantadaho kuṇāladaho mandākinidaho sīhapapātadahoti satta mahāsarā patiṭṭhitā.

Here is the story of the origin of these rivers from the beginning. This Jambudīpa is ten thousand yojanas in extent. Of this, a region of four thousand yojanas is submerged by water and is reckoned as the ocean; in a region of three thousand yojanas humans dwell; and in a region of three thousand yojanas the Himālaya is established. It is five hundred yojanas in height, adorned with eighty-four thousand peaks, and variegated with five hundred rivers flowing all around. There, seven great lakes are established: Lake Anotatta, which is fifty yojanas in length, breadth, and depth, and one hundred and fifty yojanas in circumference; Lake Kaṇṇamuṇḍa; Lake Rathakāra; Lake Chaddanta; Lake Kuṇāla; Lake Mandākinī; and Lake Sīhapapāta.

Tesu anotattadaho sudassanakūṭaṃ cittakūṭaṃ kāḷakūṭaṃ gandhamādanakūṭaṃ kelāsakūṭanti imehi pañcahi pabbatakūṭehi parikkhitto. Tattha sudassanakūṭaṃ sovaṇṇamayaṃ tiyojanasatubbedhaṃ antovaṅkaṃ kākamukhasaṇṭhānaṃ tameva saraṃ paṭicchādetvā ṭhitaṃ, cittakūṭaṃ sattaratanamayaṃ. Kāḷakūṭaṃ añjanamayaṃ. Gandhamādanakūṭaṃ masāragallamayaṃ abbhantare muggavaṇṇaṃ; mūlagandho, sāragandho, pheggugandho, tacagandho, papaṭikāgandho, khandhagandho, rasagandho, pupphagandho, phalagandho, pattagandhoti imehi dasahi gandhehi ussannaṃ, nānappakāraosadhasañchannaṃ, kāḷapakkhuposathadivase ādittaṃ viya aṅgāraṃ pajjalantaṃ tiṭṭhati. Kelāsakūṭaṃ rajatamayaṃ. Sabbāni cetāni sudassanena [M 0.0273] samānubbedhasaṇṭhānāni [V 0.0245] tameva saraṃ paṭicchādetvā ṭhitāni. Tattha devānubhāvena nāgānubhāvena ca devo vassati, nadiyo ca sandanti, taṃ sabbampi udakaṃ anotattameva pavisati, candimasūriyā dakkhiṇena [P 0.0301] vā uttarena vā gacchantā pabbatantarena tattha obhāsaṃ karonti, ujukaṃ gacchantā na karonti, tenevassa “anotatta”nti saṅkhā udapādi.

Of these, Lake Anotatta is surrounded by five mountain peaks: Sudassanakūṭa, Cittakūṭa, Kāḷakūṭa, Gandhamādanakūṭa, and Kelāsakūṭa. Of these, Sudassanakūṭa is made of gold, three hundred yojanas high, curved inward, shaped like a crow’s beak, and stands covering that very lake. Cittakūṭa is made of the seven kinds of gems. Kāḷakūṭa is made of collyrium. Gandhamādanakūṭa is made of masāragalla stone, the color of mung beans inside; it is replete with ten kinds of fragrances—root, heartwood, sapwood, bark, outer bark, trunk, sap, flower, fruit, and leaf fragrance—and is covered with various kinds of medicinal herbs; on the Uposatha day of the dark fortnight, it stands blazing like a burning ember. Kelāsakūṭa is made of silver. All these peaks are equal in height and shape to Sudassana and stand covering that very lake. There, by the power of devas and nāgas, the god sends rain and the rivers flow. All that water enters Lake Anotatta itself. The moon and sun, when travelling to the south or to the north, cast their light there through the space between the mountains, but they do not do so when travelling directly overhead. For that reason the designation ‘Anotatta’ (Unheated) arose for it.

Tattha ratanamayamanuññasopānasilātalāni nimmacchakacchapāni phalikasadisāni nimmalūdakāni tadupabhogasattānaṃ kammanibbattāneva nahānatitthāni ca honti, yattha buddhapaccekabuddhā iddhimanto sāvakā isayo ca nahānādīni karonti, devayakkhādayo udakakīḷaṃ kīḷanti.

There, there are also bathing places—produced by the kamma of the beings who make use of them—with delightful stairways and stone terraces made of gems, free from fish and turtles, and with water as clear and pure as crystal. It is there that Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, disciples possessed of psychic power, and seers perform bathing and other activities, while devas, yakkhas, and others engage in water sports.

Tassa catūsu passesu sīhamukhaṃ, hatthimukhaṃ, assamukhaṃ, usabhamukhanti cattāri udakanikkhamanamukhāni honti, yehi catasso nadiyo sandanti. Sīhamukhena nikkhantanadītīre kesarasīhā bahutarā honti, tathā hatthimukhādīhi hatthiassausabhā. Puratthimadisato nikkhantanadī anotattaṃ tikkhattuṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā itarā tisso nadiyo anupagamma pācīnahimavanteneva amanussapathaṃ gantvā mahāsamuddaṃ pavisati. Pacchimadisato uttaradisato ca nikkhantanadiyopi tatheva padakkhiṇaṃ katvā pacchimahimavanteneva uttarahimavanteneva ca amanussapathaṃ gantvā mahāsamuddaṃ pavisanti.

On its four sides, there are four water-outlet mouths: a lion's mouth, an elephant's mouth, a horse's mouth, and a bull's mouth. Through these, four rivers flow forth. On the bank of the river that flows forth from the lion's mouth, lions with manes are most abundant. Similarly, elephants, horses, and bulls are found near the elephant's, horse's, and bull's mouths. The river flowing forth from the eastern direction circles Lake Anotatta three times clockwise and, without approaching the other three rivers, travels along the eastern Himalayas through a path of non-humans before entering the great ocean. Likewise, the rivers flowing forth from the western and northern directions also circle clockwise and travel along the western Himalayas and the northern Himalayas, respectively, through a path of non-humans before entering the great ocean.

Dakkhiṇadisato nikkhantanadī pana taṃ tikkhattuṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā dakkhiṇena ujukaṃ pāsāṇapiṭṭheneva saṭṭhiyojanāni gantvā pabbataṃ paharitvā uṭṭhāya parikkhepena tigāvutappamāṇaudakadhārā hutvā ākāsena saṭṭhiyojanāni gantvā tiyaggaḷe nāma pāsāṇe patitā, pāsāṇo udakadhārāvegena bhinno. Tattha paññāsayojanappamāṇā tiyaggaḷā nāma pokkharaṇī jātā, pokkharaṇiyā kūlaṃ bhinditvā pāsāṇaṃ pavisitvā saṭṭhiyojanāni gantvā tato ghanapathaviṃ bhinditvā umaṅgena saṭṭhiyojanāni gantvā viñjhaṃ nāma tiracchānapabbataṃ paharitvā hatthatale pañcaṅgulisadisā [P 0.0302] pañcadhārā hutvā pavattanti.

The river flowing from the southern side, however, having circled it three times to the right, then went straight south along a rocky surface for sixty yojanas, struck a mountain, rose up, and as a torrential stream three gāvutas in circumference, traveled sixty yojanas through the sky before falling onto a rock called Tiyaggaḷa. The rock was shattered by the force of the water. There, a pond named Tiyaggaḷa, fifty yojanas in size, was formed. Breaking the bank of the pond, the water entered the rock and traveled sixty yojanas, then broke through the solid earth and traveled another sixty yojanas through a tunnel before striking a transverse mountain named Viñjha. There, it split into five streams resembling the five fingers of a hand and flowed onward.

Sā tikkhattuṃ anotattaṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā gataṭṭhāne “āvaṭṭagaṅgā”ti vuccati, ujukaṃ pāsāṇapiṭṭhena saṭṭhiyojanāni gataṭṭhāne “kaṇhagaṅgā”ti, ākāsena [M 0.0274] saṭṭhiyojanāni gataṭṭhāne “ākāsagaṅgā”ti, tiyaggaḷapāsāṇe paññāsayojanokāse ṭhitā “tiyaggaḷapokkharaṇī”ti, kūlaṃ bhinditvā pāsāṇaṃ pavisitvā saṭṭhiyojanāni [V 0.0246] gataṭṭhāne “bahalagaṅgā”ti, umaṅgena saṭṭhiyojanāni gataṭṭhāne “umaṅgagaṅgā”ti vuccati, viñjhaṃ nāma tiracchānapabbataṃ paharitvā pañcadhārā hutvā pavattaṭṭhāne gaṅgā, yamunā, aciravatī, sarabhū, mahīti pañcadhā saṅkhaṃ gatā. Evametā pañca mahānadiyo himavantato pavattantīti veditabbā.

Where it went after circling Lake Anotatta three times to the right, it is called ‘Āvaṭṭagaṅgā.’ Where it flowed straight along the rocky surface for sixty yojanas, it is called ‘Kaṇhagaṅgā.’ Where it traveled sixty yojanas through the sky, it is called ‘Ākāsagaṅgā.’ Where it stood as a pool covering fifty yojanas on the Tiyaggaḷa rock, it is called ‘Tiyaggaḷapokkharaṇī.’ Where it went for sixty yojanas after breaking the bank and entering the rock, it is called ‘Bahalagaṅgā.’ Where it went for sixty yojanas through a tunnel, it is called ‘Umaṅgagaṅgā.’ At the place where it flowed on after striking the transverse mountain named Viñjha and splitting into five streams, it became known as the five rivers: Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Aciravatī, Sarabhū, and Mahī. Thus it should be understood that these five great rivers flow from the Himalayas.

Tattha nadī ninnagātiādikaṃ gottaṃ, gaṅgā yamunātiādikaṃ nāmaṃ. Savantiyoti yā kāci savamānā sandamānā gacchantiyo mahānadiyo vā kunnadiyo vā. Appentīti allīyanti osaranti. Dhārāti vuṭṭhidhārā. Pūrattanti puṇṇabhāvo. Mahāsamuddassa hi ayaṃ dhammatā – “imasmiṃ kāle devo mando jāto, jālakkhipādīni ādāya macchakacchape gaṇhissāmā”ti vā “imasmiṃ kāle atimahantī vuṭṭhi, na labhissāma nu kho piṭṭhipasāraṇaṭṭhāna”nti vā taṃ na sakkā vattuṃ. Paṭhamakappikakālato paṭṭhāya hi yaṃ vassitvā sinerumekhalaṃ āhacca udakaṃ ṭhitaṃ, taṃ tato ekaṅgulamattampi udakaṃ neva heṭṭhā otarati, na uddhaṃ uttarati.

Here, 'river' (nadī) is the general class, such as 'flowing downward' (ninnagā), while 'Gaṅgā' and 'Yamunā' are names. 'Flowing' means whatever great or small rivers that flow, stream, or go. 'Enter' means they adhere and descend. 'Stream' refers to a stream of rain. 'Fullness' denotes the state of being full. For this is the nature of the great ocean: it is not possible to say of it, "At this time, the rain is weak, so we will take nets and so on and catch fish and turtles," or "At this time, the rain is extremely heavy—surely we won't find a place to stretch our backs?" For from the time of the first aeon onward, the water that has rained and stands having struck the girdle of Mount Sineru does not go down below nor rise up above that level even by a finger's breadth.

Ekarasoti asambhinnaraso. Muttāti khuddakamahantavaṭṭadīghādibhedā anekavidhā muttā. Maṇīti rattanīlādibhedo anekavidho maṇi. Veḷuriyoti vaṃsavaṇṇasirīsapupphavaṇṇādisaṇṭhānato anekavidho. Saṅkhoti dakkhiṇāvattatambakucchikadhamanasaṅkhādibhedo anekavidho. Silāti setakāḷamuggavaṇṇādibhedā anekavidhā. Pavāḷanti khuddakamahantamandarattaghanarattādibhedaṃ anekavidhaṃ. Lohitaṅgoti padumarāgādibhedo anekavidho masāragallanti kabaramaṇi. “Cittaphalika”ntipi vadanti.

'Single taste' means unmixed taste. Pearls are of many kinds, differentiated as small, large, round, long, and so on. Gems are of many varieties, differentiated as ruby, sapphire, and others. Beryl is of many types, differentiated by shape as bamboo-colored, acacia-flower-colored, and so on. Conch shells are of many kinds, differentiated as right-spiraled, tambakucchika, dhamana, and so on. Stones are of many varieties, differentiated as white, black, mung-bean-colored, and so on. Coral is of many types, differentiated as small, large, pale red, deep red, and so on. Lohitaṅga is of many kinds, differentiated as lotus-red (padumarāga) and so on. Masāragalla is a variegated gem; it is also called 'cittaphalika'.

Mahataṃ [P 0.0303] bhūtānanti mahantānaṃ sattānaṃ. Timitimiṅgalādikā tisso macchajātiyo. Timiṃ gilanasamatthā timiṅgalā, timiñca timiṅgalañca gilanasamatthā “timitimiṅgalā”ti vadanti. Nāgāti ūmipiṭṭhivāsinopi vimānaṭṭhakanāgāpi.

'Of great beings' means of large beings. The three kinds of fish are the timi, timiṅgala, and timitimiṅgala. The timiṅgalas are those capable of swallowing timis; those capable of swallowing both timis and timiṅgalas are called 'timitimiṅgalas.' 'Nāgas' means both nāgas dwelling on the surface of the waves and nāgas residing in celestial palaces.

Evameva [M 0.0275] khoti kiñcāpi satthā imasmiṃ dhammavinaye soḷasapi bāttiṃsapi tato bhiyyopi acchariyabbhutadhamme vibhajitvā dassetuṃ sakkoti, tadā upamābhāvena pana gahitānaṃ aṭṭhannaṃ anurūpavasena aṭṭheva te upametabbadhamme vibhajitvā dassento “evameva kho, bhikkhave, imasmiṃ dhammavinaye aṭṭha acchariyā abbhutā dhammā”tiādimāha.

Similarly, although the Teacher could analyze and explain sixteen, thirty-two, or even more marvelous and wonderful things in this Dhamma and Discipline, since eight things were taken for the simile, in accordance with them he analyzed and explained just those eight things to be compared, saying: "Just so, bhikkhus, in this Dhamma and Discipline there are eight marvelous and wonderful things," and so on.

Tattha anupubbasikkhāya tisso bhikkhā gahitā, anupubbakiriyāya terasa dhutaṅgadhammā, anupubbapaṭipadāya [V 0.0247] satta anupassanā aṭṭhārasa mahāvipassanā aṭṭhatiṃsa ārammaṇavibhattiyo sattatiṃsa bodhipakkhiyadhammā ca gahitā. Na āyatakeneva aññāpaṭivedhoti maṇḍūkassa uppatitvā gamanaṃ viya āditova sīlapūraṇādīni akatvā arahattapaṭivedho nāma natthi, paṭipāṭiyā pana sīlasamādhipaññāyo pūretvāva arahattappattīti attho.

Here, by 'gradual training' the three trainings are meant; by 'gradual performance,' the thirteen ascetic practices; and by 'gradual practice,' the seven contemplations, the eighteen great insights, the thirty-eight classifications of objects, and the thirty-seven constituents of enlightenment are meant. The penetration to final knowledge is not abrupt, like a frog's leap. Without having fulfilled morality and so on from the very beginning, there is no such thing as the realization of arahantship. The meaning is that arahantship is attained only by fulfilling morality, concentration, and wisdom in sequence.

Mama sāvakāti sotāpannādike ariyapuggale sandhāya vadati. Na saṃvasatīti uposathakammādivasena saṃvāsaṃ na karoti. Ukkhipatīti apaneti. Ārakāvāti dūreyeva. Na tena nibbānadhātuyā ūnattaṃ vā pūrattaṃ vāti asaṅkhyeyyepi mahākappe buddhesu anuppajjantesu ekasattopi parinibbātuṃ na sakkoti, tadāpi “tucchā nibbānadhātū”ti na sakkā vattuṃ, buddhakāle pana ekekasmiṃ samāgame asaṅkhyeyyāpi sattā amataṃ ārādhenti, tadāpi na sakkā vattuṃ “pūrā nibbānadhātū”ti. Vimuttirasoti kilesehi vimuccanaraso. Sabbā hi sāsanassa sampatti yāvadeva anupādāya āsavehi cittassa vimuttiyā hoti.

'My disciples' refers to noble persons, such as stream-enterers and others. 'Does not associate with' means does not engage in communion by way of the Uposatha ceremony and so on. 'Removes' means eliminates. 'At a distance' means very far away. There is neither deficiency nor fullness in the Nibbāna element on that account. Even in countless great aeons when Buddhas do not arise, not a single being can attain final Nibbāna; even then, one cannot say, "The Nibbāna element is empty." But during the time of a Buddha, at a single gathering, countless beings realize the Deathless; even then, one cannot say, "The Nibbāna element is full." 'The taste of liberation' is the taste of being liberated from the defilements. For the entire accomplishment of the teaching is just for the sake of the mind's liberation from the taints through non-clinging.

Ratanānīti ratijananaṭṭhena ratanāni. Satipaṭṭhānādayo hi bhāviyamānā pubbabhāgepi anappakaṃ pītipāmojjaṃ nibbattenti, pageva aparabhāge. Vuttañhetaṃ –

'Jewels' are so called because they produce delight. For the foundations of mindfulness and so on, when developed, generate no small amount of joy and gladness even in the preliminary stage, how much more so in the later stage. This has been said:

“Yato [P 0.0304] yato sammasati, khandhānaṃ udayabbayaṃ;

Labhatī pītipāmojjaṃ, amataṃ taṃ vijānata”nti. (dha. pa. 374) –

"Whenever one comprehends the rise and fall of the aggregates, one obtains joy and gladness; that is the Deathless for those who know."

Lokiyaratananimittaṃ pana pītipāmojjaṃ na tassa kalabhāgampi agghatīti ayamattho heṭṭhā dassito eva. Apica –

But the joy and gladness caused by worldly treasures is not worth even a fraction of that spiritual joy—this meaning has been shown below. Moreover:

“Cittīkataṃ [M 0.0276] mahagghañca, atulaṃ dullabhadassanaṃ;

Anomasattaparibhogaṃ, ‘ratana’nti pavuccatī”ti.

"Esteemed, of great price, unequalled, and rare to see; used by the most eminent beings, it is called a 'jewel'."

Yadi ca cittīkatādibhāvena ratanaṃ nāma hoti, satipaṭṭhānādīnaṃyeva bhūtato ratanabhāvo. Bodhipakkhiyadhammānañhi so ānubhāvo, yaṃ sāvakā sāvakapāramīñāṇaṃ, paccekabuddhā paccekabodhiñāṇaṃ, sammāsambuddhā sammāsambodhiṃ adhigacchantīti āsannakāraṇattā. Paramparakāraṇañhi dānādiupanissayoti evaṃ ratijananaṭṭhena cittīkatādiatthena ca ratanabhāvo bodhipakkhiyadhammānaṃ [V 0.0248] sātisayo. Tena vuttaṃ – “tatrimāni ratanāni, seyyathidaṃ, cattāro satipaṭṭhānā”tiādi.

And if something is called a jewel because it is esteemed and so on, then the true state of being a jewel belongs only to the foundations of mindfulness and the like. For such is the power of the constituents of enlightenment that disciples attain the knowledge of a disciple, paccekabuddhas attain the knowledge of a paccekabuddha, and perfectly enlightened ones attain perfect enlightenment—because these are the proximate cause. For the remote cause is the supporting condition of generosity and so on. Thus, in the sense of generating delight and in the sense of being esteemed and so on, the state of being a jewel is pre-eminent for the constituents of enlightenment. Therefore it is said: "Herein are these jewels, that is to say, the four foundations of mindfulness," and so on.

Tattha ārammaṇe pakkhanditvā upaṭṭhānaṭṭhena paṭṭhānaṃ, satiyeva paṭṭhānaṃ satipaṭṭhānaṃ. Ārammaṇassa pana kāyādivasena catubbidhattā vuttaṃ “cattāro satipaṭṭhānā”ti. Tathā hi kāyavedanācittadhammesu subhasukhaniccaattasaññānaṃ pahānato asubhadukkhāniccānattatāgahaṇato ca nesaṃ kāyānupassanādibhāvo vibhatto.

Here, 'foundation' (paṭṭhāna) is so called in the sense of establishing (upaṭṭhāna) by plunging into the object; mindfulness itself is the foundation, hence 'foundation of mindfulness' (satipaṭṭhāna). But because the object is fourfold—body, and so on—it is said, 'the four foundations of mindfulness.' For by abandoning perceptions of beauty, pleasure, permanence, and self in regard to body, feelings, mind, and phenomena, and by grasping ugliness, suffering, impermanence, and non-self, their nature as contemplation of the body and so on is distinguished.

Sammā padahanti etena, sayaṃ vā sammā padahati, pasatthaṃ, sundaraṃ vā padahanti sammappadhānaṃ. Puggalassa vā sammadeva padhānabhāvakaraṇato sammappadhānaṃ. Vīriyassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tampi anuppannuppannānaṃ akusalānaṃ anuppādanapahānavasena anuppannuppannānaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ uppādanabhāvanavasena ca catukiccaṃ katvā vuttaṃ “cattāro sammappadhānā”ti.

It is 'right striving' (sammappadhāna) because one strives rightly (sammā padahati) with it, or it itself strives rightly; or because the striving is praiseworthy and beautiful. Or it is 'right striving' because it rightly brings about a state of exertion for a person. This is a synonym for energy. And that too, having been made into a fourfold task—in terms of the non-arising of unarisen unwholesome states and the abandoning of arisen ones, and in terms of the arising of unarisen wholesome states and the development of arisen ones—is called 'the four right strivings.'

Ijjhatīti iddhi, samijjhati nipphajjatīti attho. Ijjhanti vā etāya sattā iddhā vuddhā ukkaṃsagatā hontīti iddhi. Iti paṭhamena atthena iddhi eva pādo iddhipādo, iddhikoṭṭhāsoti attho[P 0.0305]. Dutiyena atthena iddhiyā pādo patiṭṭhā adhigamūpāyoti iddhipādo. Tena hi uparūparivisesasaṅkhātaṃ iddhiṃ pajjanti pāpuṇanti, svāyaṃ iddhipādo yasmā chandādike cattāro adhipatidhamme dhure jeṭṭhake katvā nibbattiyati, tasmā vuttaṃ “cattāro iddhipādā”ti.

It succeeds, thus it is 'spiritual power' (iddhi); the meaning is that it prospers and is accomplished. Or, by means of this, beings succeed, prosper, and attain eminence, thus it is 'spiritual power.' In the first sense, spiritual power itself is the base (pāda), hence 'base of spiritual power' (iddhipāda); the meaning is a constituent of spiritual power. In the second sense, the base for spiritual power is the foundation, the means for its attainment, hence 'base of spiritual power.' For by this one proceeds to and attains the spiritual power described as progressively higher distinctions. Since this base for spiritual power is generated by placing the four dominant phenomena beginning with desire at the forefront as the chief factors, it is therefore said: 'the four bases for spiritual power.'

Pañcindriyānīti saddhādīni pañca indriyāni. Tattha assaddhiyaṃ abhibhavitvā adhimokkhalakkhaṇe indaṭṭhaṃ kāretīti saddhindriyaṃ, kosajjaṃ abhibhavitvā paggahalakkhaṇe[M 0.0277], pamādaṃ abhibhavitvā upaṭṭhānalakkhaṇe, vikkhepaṃ abhibhavitvā avikkhepalakkhaṇe, aññāṇaṃ abhibhavitvā dassanalakkhaṇe indaṭṭhaṃ kāretīti paññindriyaṃ.

The five faculties are the five faculties beginning with faith. Herein, the faculty of faith, by overcoming lack of faith, exercises sovereignty in the characteristic of resolution. The faculty of energy, by overcoming laziness, exercises sovereignty in the characteristic of exertion. The faculty of mindfulness, by overcoming heedlessness, exercises sovereignty in the characteristic of establishment. The faculty of concentration, by overcoming distraction, exercises sovereignty in the characteristic of non-distraction. The faculty of wisdom, by overcoming ignorance, exercises sovereignty in the characteristic of seeing.

Tāniyeva assaddhiyādīhi anabhibhavanīyato akampiyaṭṭhena sampayuttadhammesu thirabhāvena “balānī”ti veditabbāni.

These same faculties should be understood as 'powers' because they are unshakable, in that they cannot be overcome by lack of faith and the other opposing states, and because of their stability among the states with which they are associated.

Satta bojjhaṅgāti bodhiyā, bodhissa vā aṅgāti bojjhaṅgā. Yā hi esā dhammasāmaggī yāya lokuttaramaggakkhaṇe uppajjamānāya līnuddhaccapatiṭṭhānāyūhanakāmasukhattakilamathānuyoga- ucchedasassatābhinivesādīnaṃ anekesaṃ upaddavānaṃ paṭipakkhabhūtāya satidhammavicayavīriyapītipassaddhisamādhiupekkhāsaṅkhātāya [V 0.0249] dhammasāmaggiyā ariyasāvako bujjhati, kilesaniddāya vuṭṭhahati, cattāri vā ariyasaccāni paṭivijjhati, nibbānameva vā sacchikarotīti “bodhī”ti vuccati, tassā dhammasāmaggisaṅkhātāya bodhiyā aṅgātipi bojjhaṅgā jhānaṅgamaggaṅgādayo viya. Yopesa vuttappakārāya dhammasāmaggiyā bujjhatīti katvā ariyasāvako “bodhī”ti vuccati, tassa bodhissa aṅgātipi bojjhaṅgā senaṅgarathaṅgādayo viya. Tenāhu porāṇā – “bujjhanakassa puggalassa aṅgāti bojjhaṅgā”ti. “Bodhiyā saṃvattantīti bojjhaṅgā”tiādinā nayenapi bojjhaṅgānaṃ bojjhaṅgattho veditabbo.

The seven enlightenment factors (bojjhaṅgā) are so called because they are factors (aṅgā) of enlightenment (bodhi), or of one who is enlightened (bodhissa). For there is this harmony of phenomena, which, arising at the moment of the supramundane path, is the opponent of numerous troubles such as sinking and restlessness, striving for a footing, indulgence in sensual pleasures and self-mortification, and adherence to annihilationism and eternalism. By means of this harmony of phenomena—comprising mindfulness, investigation of phenomena, energy, rapture, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity—the noble disciple awakens, rises from the sleep of the defilements, penetrates the Four Noble Truths, or directly realizes Nibbāna. This is called 'enlightenment' (bodhi). The factors of this enlightenment, which is described as a harmony of phenomena, are the enlightenment factors, just like the jhāna factors and path factors. And since the noble disciple who awakens by means of this harmony of phenomena is called 'enlightened' (bodhi), the factors of this enlightened one are also the enlightenment factors, just like the constituents of an army or a chariot. Therefore the ancients said: 'They are the factors of the person who awakens, thus they are enlightenment factors.' The meaning of 'enlightenment factors' should also be understood by the method beginning with: 'They conduce to enlightenment, thus they are enlightenment factors.'

Ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggoti taṃtaṃmaggavajjhakilesehi ārakattā ariyabhāvakarattā ariyaphalapaṭilābhakarattā ca ariyo. Sammādiṭṭhiādīni aṭṭhaṅgāni assa atthi, aṭṭha aṅgāniyeva vā aṭṭhaṅgiko. Kilese mārento gacchati, nibbānatthikehi [P 0.0306] maggiyati, sayaṃ vā nibbānaṃ maggatīti maggoti. Evametesaṃ satipaṭṭhānādīnaṃ atthavibhāgo veditabbo.

The Noble Eightfold Path is called 'noble' because it is far from the defilements to be abandoned by the respective paths, because it produces the state of a noble one, and because it brings about the attainment of the noble fruit. It is 'eightfold' because it has eight factors beginning with right view, or because it is simply eight factors. It is called a 'path' because it proceeds while destroying the defilements, or because it is sought by those who seek Nibbāna, or because it itself seeks Nibbāna. In this way, the analysis of the meaning of these factors, beginning with the foundations of mindfulness, should be understood.

Sotāpannoti maggasaṅkhātaṃ sotaṃ āpajjitvā pāpuṇitvā ṭhito, sotāpattiphalaṭṭhoti attho. Sotāpattiphalasacchikiriyāya paṭipannoti sotāpattiphalassa attapaccakkhakaraṇāya paṭipajjamāno paṭhamamaggaṭṭho, yo aṭṭhamakotipi vuccati. Sakadāgāmīti sakideva imaṃ lokaṃ paṭisandhiggahaṇavasena āgamanasīlo dutiyaphalaṭṭho. Anāgāmīti paṭisandhiggahaṇavasena kāmalokaṃ anāgamanasīlo tatiyaphalaṭṭho[M 0.0278]. Yo pana saddhānusārī dhammānusārī ekabījīti evamādiko ariyapuggalavibhāgo, so etesaṃyeva pabhedoti. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva.

A stream-enterer is one who, having entered and attained the stream called the path, is established therein; the meaning is one established in the fruit of stream-entry. One practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry is one established on the first path, practicing for the personal realization of the fruit of stream-entry; this person is also called the eighth person. A once-returner is one established in the second fruit, who is of a nature to return to this world only once more by way of rebirth. A non-returner is one established in the third fruit, who is of a nature not to return to the sense-sphere world by way of rebirth. As for the classification of noble persons such as the faith-follower, the Dhamma-follower, the one-seeder, and so on, this is a subdivision of these same persons. The rest is in the way already stated.

Etamatthaṃ viditvāti etaṃ attano dhammavinaye matakuṇapasadisena dussīlapuggalena saddhiṃ saṃvāsābhāvasaṅkhātaṃ atthaṃ viditvā. Imaṃ udānanti imaṃ asaṃvāsārahasaṃvāsārahavibhāgakāraṇaparidīpanaṃ udānaṃ udānesi.

Having known this meaning: this means, having known this matter in his own Dhamma and Discipline, namely, the absence of communion with an immoral person who is like a dead corpse. He uttered this inspired utterance: this means, he uttered this inspired utterance that illuminates the reason for the distinction between one fit and one unfit for communion.

Tattha channamativassatīti āpattiṃ āpajjitvā paṭicchādento aññaṃ navaṃ āpattiṃ āpajjati, tato paraṃ tato paranti evaṃ āpattivassaṃ kilesavassaṃ ativiya vassati. Vivaṭaṃ nātivassatīti āpattiṃ āpanno taṃ appaṭicchādetvā vivaranto sabrahmacārīnaṃ pakāsento yathādhammaṃ yathāvinayaṃ paṭikaronto desento vuṭṭhahanto aññaṃ navaṃ āpattiṃ na āpajjati, tenassa vivaṭaṃ puna āpattivassaṃ kilesavassaṃ na vassati. Yasmā ca etadevaṃ, tasmā channaṃ chāditaṃ āpattiṃ vivaretha pakāsetha. Evaṃ taṃ nātivassatīti evaṃ sante taṃ āpattiāpajjanakaṃ āpannapuggalaṃ [V 0.0250] attabhāvaṃ ativijjhitvā kilesavassaṃ na vassati na temeti. Evaṃ so kilesehi anavassuto parisuddhasīlo samāhito hutvā vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā sammasanto anukkamena nibbānaṃ pāpuṇātīti adhippāyo.

Herein, 'what is concealed rains excessively' means: one who, having fallen into an offense, conceals it, falls into another new offense. Thereafter, again and again, the rain of offenses, the rain of defilements, rains down excessively. 'What is open does not rain excessively' means: one who has fallen into an offense, by not concealing it but opening it up, making it known to his fellows in the holy life, making amends according to the Dhamma and Discipline, confessing it, and rising up from it, does not fall into another new offense. For him, what is open does not rain again with the rain of offenses, the rain of defilements. Since this is so, therefore, 'you should open up, you should make known, the concealed offense.' 'Thus it does not rain on him excessively' means: this being so, the rain of defilements does not rain upon and drench the individual existence of that person who has fallen into an offense. Thus, not being drenched by the defilements, having become pure in virtue and concentrated in mind, he establishes insight and, by exploring, gradually attains Nibbāna. This is the intended meaning.

Pañcamasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the fifth sutta is finished.

6. Soṇasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Soṇa Sutta

46. Chaṭṭhe [P 0.0307] avantīsūti avantiraṭṭhe. Kuraraghareti evaṃnāmake nagare. Pavatte pabbateti pavattanāmake pabbate. “Papāte pabbate”tipi paṭhanti. Soṇo upāsako kuṭikaṇṇoti nāmena soṇo nāma, tīhi saraṇagamanehi upāsakabhāvappaṭivedanena upāsako, koṭiagghanakassa kaṇṇapiḷandhanassa dhāraṇena “koṭikaṇṇo”ti vattabbe “kuṭikaṇṇo”ti evaṃ abhiññāto, na sukhumālasoṇoti adhippāyo[M 0.0279]. Ayañhi āyasmato mahākaccāyanassa santike dhammaṃ sutvā sāsane abhippasanno, saraṇesu ca sīlesu ca patiṭṭhito pavatte pabbate chāyūdakasampanne ṭhāne vihāraṃ kāretvā theraṃ tattha vasāpetvā catūhi paccayehi upaṭṭhāti. Tena vuttaṃ – “āyasmato mahākaccānassa upaṭṭhāko hotī”ti.

46. In the sixth, 'in Avantī' means in the country of Avantī. 'In Kuraraghara' means in the city of that name. 'On the Pavatta mountain' means on the mountain named Pavatta. Some also read it as 'on the Papāta mountain'. The lay disciple Soṇa Kuṭikaṇṇa: he was Soṇa by name; a lay disciple by his declaration of having gone to the three refuges; and he was known as 'Kuṭikaṇṇa'—though he should have been called 'Koṭikaṇṇa' because he wore an ear-ornament worth a koṭi—the meaning is that he was not the delicate Soṇa. For he, having heard the Dhamma from the Venerable Mahākaccāyana, gained faith in the Dispensation and became established in the refuges and the virtues. He had a monastery built in a place on the Pavatta mountain endowed with shade and water, had the elder reside there, and attended to him with the four requisites. Therefore it is said: 'He was the attendant of the Venerable Mahākaccāyana'.

So kālena kālaṃ therassa upaṭṭhānaṃ gacchati. Thero cassa dhammaṃ deseti. Tena saṃvegabahulo dhammacariyāya ussāhajāto viharati. So ekadā satthena saddhiṃ vāṇijjatthāya ujjeniṃ gacchanto antarāmagge aṭaviyaṃ satthe niviṭṭhe rattiyaṃ janasambādhabhayena ekamantaṃ apakkamma niddaṃ upagañchi. Sattho paccūsavelāyaṃ uṭṭhāya gato, na ekopi soṇaṃ pabodhesi, sabbepi visaritvā agamaṃsu. So pabhātāya rattiyā pabujjhitvā uṭṭhāya kañci apassanto sattheneva gatamaggaṃ gahetvā sīghaṃ sīghaṃ gacchanto ekaṃ vaṭarukkhaṃ upagañchi. Tattha addasa ekaṃ mahākāyaṃ virūpadassanaṃ gacchantaṃ purisaṃ aṭṭhito muttāni attano maṃsāni sayameva khādantaṃ, disvāna “kosi tva”nti pucchi. “Petomhi, bhante”ti. “Kasmā evaṃ karosī”ti. “Attano pubbakammenā”ti. “Kiṃ pana taṃ kamma”nti. “Ahaṃ pubbe bhārukacchanagaravāsī kūṭavāṇijo hutvā paresaṃ santakaṃ vañcetvā khādiṃ, samaṇe ca bhikkhāya upagate ‘tumhākaṃ maṃsaṃ [V 0.0251] khādathā’ti akkosiṃ, tena kammena etarahi imaṃ dukkhaṃ anubhavāmī”ti. Taṃ [P 0.0308] sutvā soṇo ativiya saṃvegaṃ paṭilabhi.

From time to time, he would go to attend on the elder, and the elder would teach him the Dhamma. Filled with a sense of spiritual urgency, he lived diligently in the practice of the Dhamma. One day, while traveling with a caravan to Ujjeni for trade, the caravan stopped in a forest along the way. At night, fearing the crowd, he went aside and fell asleep. At dawn, the caravan set off. No one woke Soṇa; they all forgot him and departed. When he awoke at daybreak and got up, seeing no one, he followed the path taken by the caravan, walking quickly. He came upon a banyan tree. There he saw a large, frightful-looking man walking about and eating his own flesh that had fallen from his limbs. Seeing this, he asked, 'Who are you?' 'I am a peta, sir,' he replied. 'Why do you do this?' 'Because of my past kamma.' 'What was that kamma?' 'Formerly, I lived in the city of Bhārukaccha and was a deceitful merchant who cheated others of their belongings. When recluses came for alms, I insulted them, saying, “Eat your own flesh!” Because of that kamma, I now experience this suffering.' Hearing this, Soṇa was overcome with a profound sense of spiritual urgency.

Tato paraṃ gacchanto mukhato paggharitakāḷalohite dve petadārake passitvā tatheva pucchi. Tepissa attano kammaṃ kathesuṃ. Te kira bhārukacchanagare dārakakāle gandhavāṇijjāya jīvikaṃ kappentā attano mātari khīṇāsave nimantetvā bhojentiyā gehaṃ gantvā “amhākaṃ santakaṃ kasmā samaṇānaṃ desi, tayā dinnaṃ bhojanaṃ bhuñjanakasamaṇānaṃ mukhato kāḷalohitaṃ paggharatū”ti akkosiṃsu. Te tena kammena niraye paccitvā tassa vipākāvasesena petayoniyaṃ nibbattitvā tadā imaṃ dukkhaṃ anubhavanti. Tampi sutvā soṇo ativiya saṃvegajāto ahosi.

Then, going further, he saw two young petas with blackish-red blood oozing from their mouths and asked them the same question. They too recounted their own kamma. It seems that in the city of Bhārukaccha, when they were boys, they made a living by trading in perfumes. Once, when their mother, who was one whose taints were destroyed, had invited recluses and was feeding them, they went to her house and scolded her, saying: 'Why do you give what belongs to us to the recluses? May blackish-red blood ooze from the mouths of the recluses who eat the food you give!' Because of that kamma, they were boiled in hell, and due to the residue of its result, they were reborn in the realm of petas, where they now experience this suffering. Hearing this too, Soṇa became extremely stirred with spiritual urgency.

So [M 0.0280] ujjeniṃ gantvā taṃ karaṇīyaṃ tīretvā kulagharaṃ paccāgato theraṃ upasaṅkamitvā katapaṭisanthāro therassa tamatthaṃ ārocesi. Theropissa pavattinivattīsu ādīnavānisaṃse vibhāvento dhammaṃ desesi. So theraṃ vanditvā gehaṃ gato sāyamāsaṃ bhuñjitvā sayanaṃ upagato thokaṃyeva niddāyitvā pabujjhitvā sayanatale nisajja yathāsutaṃ dhammaṃ paccavekkhituṃ āraddho. Tassa taṃ dhammaṃ paccavekkhato, te ca petattabhāve anussarato saṃsāradukkhaṃ ativiya bhayānakaṃ hutvā upaṭṭhāsi, pabbajjāya cittaṃ nami. So vibhātāya rattiyā sarīrapaṭijagganaṃ katvā theraṃ upasaṅkamitvā attano ajjhāsayaṃ ārocetvā pabbajjaṃ yāci. Tena vuttaṃ – “atha kho soṇassa upāsakassa kuṭikaṇṇassa rahogatassa…pe… pabbājetu maṃ, bhante, ayyo mahākaccāno”ti.

Having gone to Ujjeni and completed his business, he returned to his family's home and approached the elder. After an exchange of courteous greetings, he informed the elder of the matter. The elder taught him the Dhamma, explaining the danger and the benefit in occurrence and cessation. He paid homage to the elder, went home, ate his evening meal, and went to bed. After sleeping a little, he awoke and sat on his bed and began to review the Dhamma as he had heard it. As he was reviewing the Dhamma and recollecting that peta-existence, the suffering of saṃsāra appeared extremely terrifying to him, and his mind inclined toward the going forth. At the break of dawn, having attended to his bodily needs, he approached the elder, revealed his intention, and requested the going forth. Therefore it is said: 'Then, when the lay follower Soṇa Kuṭikaṇṇa had gone into seclusion… he said: “Venerable sir, let the Venerable Mahākaccāna give me the going forth.”'

Tattha yathā yathātiādīnaṃ padānaṃ ayaṃ saṅkhepattho – yena yena ākārena ayyo mahākaccāno dhammaṃ deseti ācikkhati paññapeti paṭṭhapeti vivarati vibhajati uttānīkaroti pakāseti, tena tena me upaparikkhato evaṃ hoti, yadetaṃ sikkhattayabrahmacariyaṃ ekampi divasaṃ akkhaṇḍaṃ katvā carimakacittaṃ pāpetabbatāya ekantaparipuṇṇaṃ. Ekadivasampi kilesamalena amalinaṃ katvā carimakacittaṃ pāpetabbatāya ekantaparisuddhaṃ. Saṅkhalikhitanti likhitasaṅkhasadisaṃ dhotasaṅkhasappaṭibhāgaṃ caritabbaṃ. Idaṃ na [P 0.0309] sukaraṃ agāraṃ ajjhāvasatā agāramajjhe vasantena ekanta paripuṇṇaṃ…pe… carituṃ yaṃnūnāhaṃ kese ceva massūni ca ohāretvā voropetvā kāsāyarasapītatāya kāsāyāni brahmacariyaṃ carantānaṃ anucchavikāni vatthāni acchādetvā nivāsetvā ceva pārupitvā ca agārasmā nikkhamitvā anagāriyaṃ pabbajeyyaṃ[V 0.0252]. Yasmā agārassa hitaṃ kasivāṇijjādikammaṃ agāriyanti vuccati, tañca pabbajjāya natthi, tasmā pabbajjā anagāriyā nāma. Taṃ anagāriyaṃ pabbajjaṃ pabbajeyyaṃ upagaccheyyaṃ, paṭipajjeyyanti attho.

Here, the concise meaning of the phrases 'in whatever way' and so on is this: In whatever manner the Venerable Mahākaccāna teaches, explains, promulgates, establishes, reveals, analyzes, clarifies, and makes plain the Dhamma, in that very way, as I examine it, it occurs to me that this holy life of the threefold training should be lived perfectly even for a single day, unbroken, to attain the final consciousness. Even for a single day, it should be lived utterly pure, free from the stain of the defilements, to attain the final consciousness. It should be lived as something polished like a conch shell, comparable to a washed conch shell. This is not easy for one living at home, dwelling in the midst of household life, to live perfectly... It would be better if I, having shaved off my hair and beard, donned the saffron-dyed robes—the proper attire for those living the holy life—and, having dressed and wrapped myself in them, went forth from the household life into homelessness. Since activities beneficial to the household, such as farming and trade, are called ‘household activities,’ and that is absent in the going forth, therefore the going forth is called ‘homelessness.’ That homelessness—I should go forth into that homelessness, undertake it, and practice it—this is the meaning.

Evaṃ attanā rahovitakkitaṃ soṇo upāsako therassa ārocetvā taṃ paṭipajjitukāmo “pabbājetu maṃ, bhante, ayyo mahākaccāno”ti āha. Thero pana “tāvassa ñāṇaparipākaṃ katha”nti upadhāretvā [M 0.0281] ñāṇaparipākaṃ āgamayamāno “dukkaraṃ kho”tiādinā pabbajjāchandaṃ nivāresi.

Thus, having reported to the elder the thought that had occurred to him in seclusion, the lay follower Soṇa, desiring to undertake that, said: 'Venerable sir, let the Venerable Mahākaccāna give me the going forth.' But the elder, considering, 'What is the state of his maturity of knowledge?' and awaiting the maturing of his knowledge, discouraged his desire for the going forth with the words, 'It is difficult…' and so on.

Tattha ekabhattanti “ekabhattiko hoti rattūparato virato vikālabhojanā”ti (dī. ni. 1.194; a. ni. 3.71) evaṃ vuttaṃ vikālabhojanaviratiṃ sandhāya vadati. Ekaseyyanti adutiyaseyyaṃ. Ettha ca seyyāsīsena “eko tiṭṭhati, eko gacchati, eko nisīdatī”tiādinā (mahāni. 7; 49) nayena vuttesu catūsu iriyāpathesu kāyavivekaṃ dīpeti, na ekākinā hutvā sayanamattaṃ. Brahmacariyanti methunaviratibrahmacariyaṃ, sikkhattayānuyogasaṅkhātaṃ sāsanabrahmacariyaṃ vā. Iṅghāti codanatthe nipāto. Tatthevāti geheyeva. Buddhānaṃ sāsanaṃ anuyuñjāti niccasīlauposathasīlādibhedaṃ pañcaṅgaaṭṭhaṅgadasaṅgasīlaṃ, tadanurūpañca samādhipaññābhāvanaṃ anuyuñja. Etañhi upāsakena pubbabhāge anuyuñjitabbaṃ buddhasāsanaṃ nāma. Tenāha – “kālayuttaṃ ekabhattaṃ ekaseyyaṃ brahmariya”nti.

Here, 'one meal a day' refers to abstinence from eating at the wrong time, as stated: 'He takes one meal a day, refrains at night, abstains from eating at the wrong time.' 'Sleeping alone' means sleeping without a second person. Here, with 'sleeping' as the heading, it indicates bodily seclusion in the four postures mentioned in the way of 'one stands, one walks, one sits,' etc., not merely lying down alone. 'The holy life' refers to the holy life of celibacy, abstaining from sexual intercourse, or the holy life of the Dispensation, reckoned as devotion to the threefold training. Iṅgha is a particle used for exhortation. 'Right there' means right there in the home. 'You should apply yourself to the Buddha's Dispensation' means you should apply yourself to the virtues of five, eight, and ten training rules, distinguished as the regular virtues, the Uposatha virtues, etc., and to the corresponding development of concentration and wisdom. For this is called the Buddha's Dispensation to which a lay follower should apply himself in the preliminary stage. Therefore he said: 'At the proper time, one meal a day, sleeping alone, and the holy life.'

Tattha kālayuttanti cātuddasīpañcadasīaṭṭhamīpāṭihāriyapakkhasaṅkhātena kālena yuttaṃ, yathāvuttakāle vā tuyhaṃ anuyuñjantassa yuttaṃ patirūpaṃ sakkuṇeyyaṃ, na sabbakālaṃ pabbajjāti adhippāyo. Sabbametaṃ ñāṇassa aparipakkattā tassa kāmānaṃ [P 0.0310] duppahānatāya sammāpaṭipattiyaṃ yogyaṃ kārāpetuṃ vadati, na pabbajjāchandaṃ nivāretuṃ. Pabbajjābhisaṅkhāroti pabbajituṃ ārambho ussāho. Paṭipassambhīti indriyānaṃ aparipakkattā, saṃvegassa ca nātitikkhabhāvato vūpasami. Kiñcāpi paṭipassambhi, therena vuttavidhiṃ pana anutiṭṭhanto kālena kālaṃ theraṃ upasaṅkamitvā payirupāsanto dhammaṃ suṇāti. Tassa vuttanayeneva dutiyaṃ pabbajjāya cittaṃ uppajji, therassa ca ārocesi. Dutiyampi thero paṭikkhipi. Tatiyavāre pana ñāṇassa paripakkabhāvaṃ ñatvā “idāni naṃ pabbājetuṃ kālo”ti thero pabbājesi, pabbajitañca taṃ tīṇi saṃvaccharāni atikkamitvā gaṇaṃ pariyesitvā upasampādesi. Taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ – “dutiyampi kho soṇo…pe… upasampādesī”ti.

There, 'at the proper time' means what is suitable at the time reckoned as the fourteenth, fifteenth, and eighth days, and the special fortnight; or, at the time mentioned, it would be suitable, fitting, and possible for you to practice. The meaning is that the going forth is not for all times. All this was said to get him to practice correctly, because his knowledge was immature and because of the difficulty of abandoning sensual pleasures; it was not said to discourage his desire for the going forth. 'Volitional formation for the going forth' means the undertaking and effort to go forth. 'It subsided' means it calmed down because his faculties were immature and his sense of spiritual urgency was not very sharp. Although it had subsided, by following the method instructed by the elder, he from time to time approached the elder, attended on him, and listened to the Dhamma. In the same way as described, the thought of the going forth arose in him a second time, and he informed the elder. The elder rejected him a second time. But on the third occasion, having understood that his knowledge had matured, the elder gave him the going forth, thinking, 'Now is the time to give him the going forth.' And after he had passed three years as one who had gone forth, the elder sought a chapter of bhikkhus and gave him the higher ordination. With reference to this it is said: 'A second time, Soṇa… he gave him the higher ordination.'

Tattha [V 0.0253] appabhikkhukoti katipayabhikkhuko. Tadā kira bhikkhū yebhuyyena majjhimadese eva vasiṃsu. Tasmā tattha katipayā eva ahesuṃ[M 0.0282], te ca ekasmiṃ nigame eko, ekasmiṃ dveti evaṃ visuṃ visuṃ vasiṃsu. Kicchenāti dukkhena. Kasirenāti āyāsena. Tato tatoti tasmā tasmā gāmanigamādito. Therena hi katipaye bhikkhū ānetvā aññesu ānīyamānesu pubbe ānītā kenacideva karaṇīyena pakkamiṃsu, kiñci kālaṃ āgametvā puna tesu ānīyamānesu itare pakkamiṃsu. Evaṃ punappunaṃ ānayanena sannipāto cireneva ahosi, thero ca tadā ekavihārī ahosi. Dasavaggaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ sannipātetvāti tadā bhagavatā paccantadesepi dasavaggeneva saṅghena upasampadā anuññātā. Itonidānañhi therena yācito pañcavaggena saṅghena paccantadese upasampadaṃ anujāni. Tena vuttaṃ – “tiṇṇaṃ vassānaṃ…pe… sannipātetvā”ti.

Here, 'few monks' means a few monks. At that time, it seems, monks lived for the most part only in the Middle Country. Therefore, there were only a few there, and they lived separately: one in one town, two in another. 'With difficulty' means with suffering. 'With trouble' means with exertion. 'From here and there' means from this and that village, town, etc. For when the Elder had brought a few monks, while others were being brought, those who had been brought earlier departed on some business. After waiting for some time, when they were being brought again, the others departed. Thus, by bringing them again and again, the assembly came together only after a long time, and at that time the Elder was dwelling alone. 'Having assembled a Saṅgha of ten monks': at that time the Blessed One had allowed higher ordination in the border regions with a Saṅgha of ten monks. For on account of this, when requested by the Elder, He permitted higher ordination in the border regions with a Saṅgha of five monks. Therefore it is said: 'After three years … having assembled.'

Vassaṃvuṭṭhassāti upasampajjitvā paṭhamavassaṃ upagantvā vusitavato. Īdiso ca īdiso cāti evarūpo ca evarūpo ca, evarūpāya nāmakāyarūpakāyasampattiyā samannāgato, evarūpāya dhammakāyasampattiyā samannāgatoti sutoyeva me so bhagavā. Na kho me so bhagavā sammukhā diṭṭhoti etena puthujjanasaddhāya evaṃ āyasmā soṇo bhagavantaṃ daṭṭhukāmo ahosi. Aparabhāge pana satthārā saddhiṃ ekagandhakuṭiyaṃ vasitvā paccūsasamayaṃ ajjhiṭṭho soḷasa aṭṭhakavaggikāni satthu [P 0.0311] sammukhā aṭṭhiṃ katvā manasi katvā sabbaṃ cetaso samannāharitvā atthadhammappaṭisaṃvedī hutvā bhaṇanto dhammūpasañhitapāmojjādimukhena samāhito sarabhaññapariyosāne vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā saṅkhāre sammasanto anupubbena arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Etadatthameva hissa bhagavatā attanā saddhiṃ ekagandhakuṭiyaṃ vāso āṇattoti vadanti.

'One who has spent the rains-residence' means one who, having received the higher ordination, has entered upon and completed the first rains-residence. 'Such and such' means of such a kind and such a kind, endowed with such an attainment of the name-body and form-body, endowed with such an attainment of the Dhamma-body—thus have I only heard of that Blessed One. 'But I have not seen that Blessed One face to face': by this it is shown that the Venerable Soṇa desired to see the Blessed One with the faith of an ordinary person. But later, having dwelt in the same fragrant chamber with the Teacher, having been requested at dawn, he recited the sixteen discourses of the Aṭṭhakavagga in the Teacher's presence, having learned them by heart, attended to them, and brought them all together in his mind. Becoming one who experienced the meaning and the Dhamma, speaking with joy connected to the Dhamma, concentrated, at the conclusion of the recitation he established insight. Contemplating the formations, he gradually attained arahantship. They say that it was for this very purpose that the Blessed One instructed him to dwell with him in the same fragrant chamber.

Keci panāhu – “na kho me so bhagavā sammukhā diṭṭho”ti idaṃ rūpakāyadassanameva sandhāya vuttanti. Āyasmā hi soṇo pabbajitvāva therassa santike kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā ghaṭento vāyamanto anupasampannova sotāpanno hutvā upasampajjitvā “upāsakāpi sotāpannā honti, ahampi sotāpanno, kimettha citta”nti uparimaggatthāya vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā antovasseyeva chaḷabhiñño hutvā visuddhipavāraṇāya pavāresi[M 0.0283]. Ariyasaccadassanena hi bhagavato dhammakāyo diṭṭho nāma hoti. Vuttañhetaṃ –

But some say that this statement, 'I have not seen the Blessed One face to face,' was said referring only to seeing the physical body. For the Venerable Soṇa, right after going forth, took a meditation subject from the elder and, by striving and making an effort, became a stream-enterer even before his higher ordination. After receiving higher ordination, he thought: 'Lay followers, too, become stream-enterers, and I am a stream-enterer. What is so special about this?' Developing insight for the sake of the higher paths, within that very rains-residence he attained the six direct knowledges and performed the Pavāraṇā with the purity invitation. For the Blessed One's Dhamma-body is said to be seen through the vision of the Noble Truths. As it is said:

“Yo kho, vakkali, dhammaṃ passati, so maṃ passati. Yo maṃ passati, so dhammaṃ passatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.87).

“Vakkali, one who sees the Dhamma sees me; one who sees me sees the Dhamma.” (SN 22.87)

Tasmāssa [V 0.0254] dhammakāyadassanaṃ pageva siddhaṃ, pavāretvā pana rūpakāyaṃ daṭṭhukāmo ahosīti.

Therefore, his seeing of the Dhamma-body was already accomplished; but after performing the Pavāraṇā, he wished to see the physical body.

“Sace maṃ upajjhāyo anujānātī”tipi pāṭho. “Bhante”ti pana likhanti. Tathā “sādhu sādhu, āvuso soṇa, gaccha tvaṃ, āvuso soṇā”tipi pāṭho. “Āvuso”ti pana kesuci potthakesu natthi. Tathā “evamāvusoti kho āyasmā soṇo”tipi pāṭho. Āvusovādoyeva hi aññamaññaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ bhagavato dharamānakāle āciṇṇo. Bhagavantaṃ pāsādikantiādīnaṃ padānaṃ attho heṭṭhā vuttoyeva.

There is also the reading: “If my preceptor permits me.” Some texts, however, write “Venerable sir.” Similarly, there is the reading: “Good, good, friend Soṇa, go, friend Soṇa.” But in some books, “friend” is not found. Likewise, there is the reading: “'So be it, friend,' said the Venerable Soṇa.” For addressing one another as 'friend' was indeed the custom among monks while the Blessed One was alive. The meaning of the terms beginning with “the Blessed One is inspiring” has already been stated below.

Kacci bhikkhu khamanīyanti bhikkhu idaṃ tuyhaṃ catucakkaṃ navadvāraṃ sarīrayantaṃ kacci khamanīyaṃ, kiṃ sakkā khamituṃ sahituṃ pariharituṃ, kiṃ dukkhabhāro nābhibhavati. Kacci yāpanīyanti kiṃ taṃtaṃkiccesu yāpetuṃ gametuṃ sakkā, na kañci antarāyanti dasseti. Kaccisi appakilamathenāti anāyāsena imaṃ ettakaṃ addhānaṃ kacci āgatosi.

“I hope, monk, you are keeping well”: this means, “Monk, is this four-wheeled, nine-gated body-machine of yours bearable? Is it possible to endure it, to bear with it, to manage it? Does the burden of suffering not overwhelm you?” “I hope you are getting by”: this means, “Is it possible to carry on and proceed with your various duties?” This shows that he is asking if there is any obstacle. “I hope you have come with little fatigue”: this means, “Have you come this long way without exertion?”

Etadahosīti buddhāciṇṇaṃ anussarantassa āyasmato ānandassa [P 0.0312] etaṃ “yassa kho maṃ bhagavā”tiādinā idāni vuccamānaṃ citte āciṇṇaṃ ahosi. Ekavihāreti ekagandhakuṭiyaṃ. Gandhakuṭi hi idha vihāroti adhippetā. Vatthunti vasituṃ.

“This occurred to him”: this thought, now being expressed, beginning with “For whomever the Blessed One…,” became customary in the mind of the Venerable Ānanda as he recollected the Buddha’s customary behavior. “In a single dwelling” means in a single fragrant chamber. For here “fragrant chamber” is intended by “dwelling.” “To dwell” means to reside.

Nisajjāya vītināmetvāti ettha yasmā bhagavā āyasmato soṇassa samāpattisamāpajjane paṭisanthāraṃ karonto sāvakasādhāraṇā sabbā samāpattiyo anulomapaṭilomaṃ samāpajjanto bahudeva rattiṃ…pe… vihāraṃ pāvisi, tasmā āyasmāpi soṇo bhagavato adhippāyaṃ ñatvā tadanurūpaṃ sabbā tā samāpattiyo samāpajjanto “bahudeva rattiṃ…pe… vihāraṃ pāvisī”ti keci vadanti. Pavisitvā ca bhagavatā [M 0.0284] anuññāto cīvaraṃ tirokaraṇīyaṃ katvāpi bhagavato pādapasse nisajjāya vītināmesi. Ajjhesīti āṇāpesi. Paṭibhātu taṃ bhikkhu dhammo bhāsitunti bhikkhu tuyhaṃ dhammo bhāsituṃ upaṭṭhātu ñāṇamukhe āgacchatu, yathāsutaṃ yathāpariyattaṃ dhammaṃ bhaṇāhīti attho.

“Having spent it in sitting”: Here, some say that because the Blessed One, while making provision for the Venerable Soṇa's entering into attainment, himself entered and emerged from all the attainments common to disciples in forward and reverse order and spent much of the night … and entered the dwelling, therefore the Venerable Soṇa, too, understanding the Blessed One's intention, accordingly entered all those attainments and “spent much of the night … and entered the dwelling.” And having entered, being permitted by the Blessed One, after making his robe into a screen, he spent the time sitting at the Blessed One's feet. “He requested” means he instructed. “Let the Dhamma occur to you, monk, for recitation”: this means, “Monk, let the Dhamma to be spoken present itself to you, let it come to the door of your knowledge; speak the Dhamma as you have heard it, as you have mastered it.”

Soḷasa aṭṭhakavaggikānīti aṭṭhakavaggabhūtāni kāmasuttādīni soḷasa suttāni. Sarena abhaṇīti suttussāraṇasarena abhāsi, sarabhaññavasena kathesīti attho. Sarabhaññapariyosāneti ussāraṇāvasāne. Suggahitānīti sammā uggahitāni. Sumanasikatānīti suṭṭhu manasi katāni. Ekacco uggahaṇakāle sammā uggahetvāpi pacchā sajjhāyādivasena manasi karaṇakāle [V 0.0255] byañjanāni vā micchā ropeti, padapacchābhaṭṭhaṃ vā karoti, na evamayaṃ. Iminā pana sammadeva yathuggahitaṃ manasi katāni. Tena vuttaṃ – “sumanasikatānīti suṭṭhu manasi katānī”ti. Sūpadhāritānīti atthatopi suṭṭhu upadhāritāni. Atthe hi suṭṭu upadhārite sakkā pāḷiṃ sammā ussāretuṃ. Kalyāṇiyāsi vācāya samannāgatoti sithiladhanitādīnaṃ yathāvidhānavacanena parimaṇḍalapadabyañjanaparipuṇṇāya poriyā vācāya samannāgato āsi. Vissaṭṭhāyāti vimuttāya. Etenassa vimuttavāditaṃ [P 0.0313] dasseti. Anelagaḷāyāti elā vuccati doso, taṃ na paggharatīti anelagaḷā, tāya niddosāyāti attho. Atha vā anelagaḷāyāti anelāya ca agaḷāya ca niddosāya agaḷitapadabyañjanāya, aparihīnapadabyañjanāyāti attho. Tathā hi naṃ bhagavā “etadaggaṃ, bhikkhave, mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ kalyāṇavākkaraṇānaṃ yadidaṃ soṇo kuṭikaṇṇo”ti (a. ni. 1.206) etadagge ṭhapesi. Atthassa viññāpaniyāti yathādhippetaṃ atthaṃ viññāpetuṃ samatthāya.

“The sixteen discourses of the Aṭṭhakavagga” means the sixteen suttas that constitute the Aṭṭhakavagga, such as the Kāma Sutta. “He chanted them” means he spoke with the voice for chanting suttas; the meaning is that he recited them in the style of chanting. “At the end of the chanting” means at the conclusion of the recitation. “Well-grasped” means well-learned. “Well-attended to” means properly attended to in the mind. Someone might learn correctly at the time of learning but later, at the time of attending to it through recitation and so on, might misplace the phrases or get the words out of order; but this one was not so. By this it is shown that he attended to them in his mind exactly as he had learned them. Hence it is said: “'Well-attended to' means properly attended to in the mind.” “Well-considered” means well-considered as to the meaning. For when the meaning is well-considered, it is possible to chant the Pāli correctly. “You are endowed with a lovely voice” means he was endowed with urbane speech that was well-rounded, with full words and phrases, spoken according to the rules for soft and hard consonants. “Clear” means articulate. This shows he spoke articulately. “Without a stammer”: eḷā is a fault; “it does not ooze” (na paggharati) is aneḷagaḷā; the meaning is “faultless.” Or else, aneḷagaḷā means both aneḷā (faultless) and agaḷā (unimpeded), that is, with phrases that are not slurred or deficient. For the Blessed One placed him at the head of his disciples, saying: “Bhikkhus, the foremost of my bhikkhu disciples with lovely voices is Soṇa Kuṭikaṇṇa” (AN 1.24). “For making the meaning known” means capable of making the intended meaning known.

Kativassoti so kira majjhimavayassa tatiyakoṭṭhāse ṭhito ākappasampanno ca paresaṃ ciratarapabbajito viya khāyati. Taṃ sandhāya bhagavā pucchatīti keci, taṃ akāraṇaṃ. Evaṃ sante samādhisukhaṃ anubhavituṃ yutto, ettakaṃ kālaṃ kasmā pamādamāpannoti puna anuyuñjituṃ satthā “kativassosī”ti taṃ pucchati. Tenevāha – “kissa pana tvaṃ bhikkhu evaṃ ciraṃ akāsī”ti.

“How old are you in rains?”: It is said that he was in the third stage of middle age and, being possessed of good deportment, he appeared to others as if he had been ordained for a very long time. Some say that the Blessed One asked with reference to this, but that is without reason. This being so, he was fit to experience the bliss of concentration; to question him further as to why he had been heedless for so long, the Teacher asked him, “How old are you in rains?” For that very reason he said: “But why, monk, did you delay for so long?”

Tattha [M 0.0285] kissāti kiṃ kāraṇā. Evaṃ ciraṃ akāsīti evaṃ cirāyi, kena kāraṇena evaṃ cirakālaṃ pabbajjaṃ anupagantvā agāramajjhe vasīti attho. Ciraṃ diṭṭho meti cirena cirakālena mayā diṭṭho. Kāmesūti kilesakāmesu ca vatthukāmesu ca. Ādīnavoti doso. Api cāti kāmesu ādīnave kenaci pakārena diṭṭhepi na tāvāhaṃ gharāvāsato nikkhamituṃ asakkhiṃ. Kasmā? Sambādho gharāvāso uccāvacehi kiccakaraṇīyehi samupabyūḷho agāriyabhāvo. Tenevāha – “bahukicco bahukaraṇīyo”ti.

Here, “Why?” means for what reason. “Did you delay so long?” means you have delayed; the meaning is: for what reason did you live in a house for such a long time without going forth? “The danger has been seen by me for a long time” means seen by me over a long period. “In sensual pleasures” means in both the defilements of sensual pleasure and the objects of sensual pleasure. “Danger” means fault. “And yet”: even though the danger in sensual pleasures was seen by me in some way, I was not able to go forth from the household life. Why? The household life is confining; the state of a householder is hemmed in by various high and low tasks and duties. Hence he said: “full of duties, full of things to do.”

Etamatthaṃ viditvāti kāmesu yathābhūtaṃ ādīnavadassino cittaṃ cirāyitvāpi na patiṭṭhāti, aññadatthu padumapalāse udakabindu viya vinivattatiyevāti etamatthaṃ sabbākārato viditvā. Imaṃ udānanti pavattiṃ nivattiñca sammadeva jānanto pavattiyaṃ tannimitte ca na kadācipi ramatīti idamatthadīpakaṃ imaṃ udānaṃ udānesi.

Having understood this matter: The mind of one who sees the danger in sensual pleasures as they actually are does not become established, even after lingering for a time; on the contrary, it turns away like a drop of water on a lotus leaf. Having understood this matter in every way. This inspired utterance: Knowing rightly both arising and cessation, one does not delight at any time in arising or its sign. He uttered this inspired utterance, which illuminates this meaning.

Tattha [V 0.0256] disvā ādīnavaṃ loketi sabbasmiṃ saṅkhāraloke “anicco dukkho vipariṇāmadhammo”tiādinā ādīnavaṃ dosaṃ paññāya passitvā. Etena vipassanāvāro kathito[P 0.0314]. Ñatvā dhammaṃ nirupadhinti sabbūpadhipaṭinissaggattā nirupadhiṃ nibbānadhammaṃ yathābhūtaṃ ñatvā nissaraṇavivekāsaṅkhatāmatasabhāvato maggañāṇena paṭivijjhitvā. “Disvā ñatvā”ti imesaṃ padānaṃ “sappiṃ pivitvā balaṃ hoti, sīhaṃ disvā bhayaṃ hoti, paññāya disvā āsavā parikkhīṇā hontī”tiādīsu (pu. pa. 208; a. ni. 9.42-43) viya hetuatthatā daṭṭhabbā. Ariyo na ramatī pāpeti kilesehi ārakattā ariyo sappuriso aṇumattepi pāpe na ramati. Kasmā? Pāpe na ramatī sucīti suvisuddhakāyasamācārāditāya visuddhapuggalo rājahaṃso viya ukkāraṭṭhāne pāpe saṃkiliṭṭhadhamme na ramati nābhinandati. “Pāpo na ramatī suci”ntipi pāṭho. Tassattho – pāpo pāpapuggalo suciṃ anavajjaṃ vodānadhammaṃ na ramati, aññadatthu gāmasūkarādayo viya ukkāraṭṭhānaṃ asuciṃ saṃkilesadhammaṃyeva ramatīti paṭipakkhato desanaṃ parivatteti.

Herein, having seen the danger in the world: having seen with wisdom the fault and danger in the entire world of formations as 'impermanent, suffering, and subject to change,' etc. By this the section on insight is stated. Having known the Dhamma without acquisitions: having known the Dhamma of Nibbāna as it truly is—which is without acquisitions because of the relinquishment of all acquisitions—one penetrates it with the knowledge of the path, which has the nature of escape, seclusion, the unconditioned, and the deathless. The meaning of the phrases 'having seen' and 'having known' should be understood in terms of their causal significance, as in examples like 'drinking ghee brings strength,' 'seeing a lion causes fear,' or 'seeing with wisdom destroys the taints.' The noble one does not delight in evil: being far removed from defilements, the noble and virtuous person does not take even the slightest pleasure in wrongdoing. Why? Because the pure one does not delight in evil: being utterly purified in body, conduct, and so on, the purified individual, like a royal swan, does not delight in or approve of the foul and defiled things found in a refuse heap. Alternatively, the reading may be: 'The wicked do not delight in purity.' Its meaning is this: the wicked person does not take pleasure in what is pure and blameless, the cleansed Dhamma. On the contrary, like village pigs and such, they delight only in the impure, the defiled Dhamma. Thus, the teaching is presented from the opposite perspective.

Evaṃ bhagavatā udāne udānite āyasmā soṇo uṭṭhāyāsanā bhagavantaṃ vanditvā attano upajjhāyassa vacanena paccantadese pañcavaggena [M 0.0286] upasampadādipañcavatthūni yāci. Bhagavāpi tāni anujānīti taṃ sabbaṃ khandhake (mahāva. 242 ādayo) āgatanayena veditabbaṃ.

Thus, when the Blessed One had uttered this inspired utterance, the Venerable Soṇa rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and, at the behest of his preceptor, requested the five matters, beginning with higher ordination by a group of five in the border regions. The Blessed One also granted these. All this should be understood according to the method found in the Khandhaka (Mahāvagga 242ff.).

Chaṭṭhasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the sixth discourse is finished.

7. Kaṅkhārevatasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Kaṅkhārevata Sutta

47. Sattame kaṅkhārevatoti tassa therassa nāmaṃ. So hi sāsane pabbajitvā laddhūpasampado sīlavā kalyāṇadhammo viharati, “akappiyā muggā, na kappanti muggā paribhuñjituṃ, akappiyo guḷo”ti (mahāva. 272) ca ādinā vinayakukkuccasaṅkhātakaṅkhābahulo pana hoti. Tena kaṅkhārevatoti paññāyittha. So aparabhāge satthu santike kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā ghaṭento vāyamanto chaḷabhiññā sacchikatvā jhānasukhena [P 0.0315] phalasukhena vītināmeti, yebhuyyena pana attanā adhigataṃ ariyamaggaṃ garuṃ katvā paccavekkhati. Tena vuttaṃ – “attano kaṅkhāvitaraṇavisuddhiṃ paccavekkhamāno”ti. Maggapaññā hi “ahosiṃ [V 0.0257] nu kho ahaṃ atītamaddhāna”ntiādinayapavattāya (ma. ni. 1.18; saṃ. ni. 2.20) soḷasavatthukāya, “buddhe kaṅkhati…pe… paṭiccasamuppannesu dhammesu kaṅkhatī”ti (dha. sa. 1008) evaṃ vuttāya aṭṭhavatthukāya, pageva itarāsanti anavasesato sabbakaṅkhānaṃ vitaraṇato samatikkamanato, aññehi ca attanā pahātabbakilesehi accantavisujjhanato “kaṅkhāvitaraṇavisuddhī”ti idhādhippetā. Tañhi ayamāyasmā dīgharattaṃ kaṅkhāpakatattā “imaṃ maggadhammaṃ adhigamma imā me kaṅkhā anavasesā pahīnā”ti garuṃ katvā paccavekkhamāno nisīdi, na sappaccayanāmarūpadassanaṃ aniccantikattā tassa kaṅkhāvitaraṇassa.

47. In the seventh sutta, Kaṅkhārevata is the elder's name. This elder, having gone forth in the Dispensation and received higher ordination, lived virtuously with good qualities. However, he was greatly troubled by doubt in the form of scrupulousness concerning the Vinaya, such as, 'Are mung beans allowable? Are mung beans not allowable to eat? Is jaggery allowable?' and so on. Thus, he became known as Kaṅkhārevata. Later, having received a meditation subject from the Teacher, he strove and exerted himself, realized the six higher knowledges, and passed his time in the bliss of jhāna and the bliss of fruition. Mostly, however, he reflected with reverence on the noble path he had attained. Therefore, it is said: 'reflecting on the purification by overcoming doubt.' For here 'purification by overcoming doubt' refers to the wisdom of the path, because it overcomes and transcends without remainder all doubts—the sixteen-fold doubt concerning existence such as, 'Did I exist in the past?' and the eight-fold doubt stated as, 'He doubts the Buddha... he doubts dependently arisen phenomena'—and because it is utterly purified from the other defilements to be abandoned by oneself. This venerable one, having long been afflicted by doubt, sat reflecting with reverence, thinking: 'Having attained this path-Dhamma, my doubts have been completely abandoned.' He was reflecting on that overcoming of doubt, not on the seeing of conditioned name-and-form, on account of the latter's impermanence.

Etamatthaṃ viditvāti etaṃ ariyamaggassa anavasesakaṅkhāvitaraṇasaṅkhātaṃ atthaṃ viditvā tadatthadīpakaṃ imaṃ udānaṃ udānesi.

Having understood this matter: Having understood this meaning, namely, the noble path’s complete overcoming of doubt, the Blessed One uttered this inspired utterance, which illuminates that meaning.

Tattha yā kāci kaṅkhā idha vā huraṃ vāti idha imasmiṃ paccuppanne attabhāve “ahaṃ nu khosmi no nu khosmī”tiādinā huraṃ vā, atītānāgatesu attabhāvesu “ahosiṃ nu kho ahaṃ atītamaddhāna”ntiādinā uppajjanakā kaṅkhā. Sakavediyā vā paravediyā vāti tā evaṃ vuttanayeneva [M 0.0287] sakaattabhāve ārammaṇavasena paṭilabhitabbāya pavattiyā sakavediyā vā parassa attabhāve paṭilabhitabbāya “buddho nu kho, no nu kho”tiādinā vā parasmiṃ padhāne uttame paṭilabhitabbāya pavattiyā paravediyā vā yā kāci kaṅkhā vicikicchā.
