pañca vimuttāyatanañāṇāni, pañca vimuttiparipācanīyā saññā, cha anussatiṭṭhānāni, cha gāravā, cha nissāraṇīyā dhātuyo, cha satatavihārā, cha anuttariyāni, cha nibbedhabhāgiyā paññā, cha abhiññā, cha asādhāraṇañāṇāni, satta aparihāniyā dhammā, satta ariyadhanāni, satta bojjhaṅgā, satta [M 0.0305] sappurisadhammā, satta nijjaravatthūni, satta [P 0.0336] saññā, satta dakkhiṇeyyapuggaladesanā, satta khīṇāsavabaladesanā, aṭṭha paññāpaṭilābhahetudesanā, aṭṭha sammattāni, aṭṭha lokadhammātikkamā, aṭṭha ārambhavatthūni, aṭṭha akkhaṇadesanā, aṭṭha mahāpurisavitakkā, aṭṭha abhibhāyatanadesanā, aṭṭha vimokkhā, nava yonisomanasikāramūlakā dhammā, nava pārisuddhipadhāniyaṅgāni, nava sattāvāsadesanā, nava āghātappaṭivinayā, nava saññā, nava nānattāni, nava anupubbavihārā, dasa nāthakaraṇā dhammā, dasa kasiṇāyatanāni, dasa kusalakammapathā, dasa sammattāni, dasa ariyavāsā, dasa asekkhā dhammā, dasa tathāgatabalāni, ekādasa mettānisaṃsā, dvādasa dhammacakkākārā, terasa dhutaṅgaguṇā, cuddasa buddhañāṇāni, pannarasa vimuttiparipācanīyā dhammā, soḷasavidhā ānāpānassati, soḷasa aparantapanīyā dhammā, aṭṭhārasa mahāvipassanā, aṭṭhārasa buddhadhammā, ekūnavīsati paccavekkhaṇañāṇāni, catucattālīsa ñāṇavatthūni, paññāsa udayabbayañāṇāni, paropaññāsa kusalā dhammā, sattasattati ñāṇavatthūni, catuvīsatikoṭisatasahassasamāpattisañcārimahāvajirañāṇaṃ, anantanayasamantapaṭṭhānapavicayapaccavekkhaṇadesanāñāṇāni, tathā anantāsu lokadhātūsu anantānaṃ sattānaṃ āsayādivibhāvanañāṇāni cāti evamādike aneke attano kusale anavajjadhamme anantakālaṃ pāramiparibhāvanāya maggabhāvanāya ca pāripūriṃ vuddhiṃ gate “imepi anavajjadhammā mayi saṃvijjanti, imepi anavajjadhammā mayi saṃvijjantī”ti rucivasena manasikārābhimukhe buddhaguṇe vaggavagge puñjapuñje katvā paccavekkhamāno nisinno hoti. Te ca [V 0.0274] kho sapadesato eva, na nippadesato. Sabbe buddhaguṇe bhagavatāpi anupadaṃ anavasesato manasi kātuṃ na sakkā anantāparimeyyabhāvato.

'And numerous wholesome qualities'—such as virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation; the four establishments of mindfulness, the four right strivings, the four bases for spiritual power, the four noble paths, the four fruits, the four analytical knowledges, the knowledge that defines the four kinds of generation, the four noble traditions, the four kinds of intrepidity; the five factors of striving, the five-factored right concentration, the right concentration with its five knowledges, the five faculties, the five powers, the five elements of escape, the knowledges of the five occasions for liberation, the five perceptions that ripen into liberation; the six bases for recollection, the six kinds of respect, the six elements of escape, the six constant abidings, the six unsurpassed things, the six kinds of wisdom pertaining to penetration, the six direct knowledges, the six uncommon knowledges; the seven conditions for non-decline, the seven noble treasures, the seven factors of enlightenment, the seven qualities of a good person, the seven items for wearing away defilements, the seven perceptions, the discourse on the seven persons worthy of offerings, the discourse on the seven powers of one whose taints are destroyed; the discourse on the eight causes for the acquisition of wisdom, the eight rightnesses, the eight transcendences of worldly states, the eight grounds for undertaking, the discourse on the eight inopportune moments, the eight thoughts of a great man, the eight bases of mastery, the eight liberations; the nine states rooted in wise attention, the nine factors of striving for purity, the discourse on the nine abodes of beings, the nine ways of subduing resentment, the nine perceptions, the nine kinds of diversity, the nine successive abodes; the ten qualities that make a protector, the ten kasiṇa bases, the ten wholesome courses of action, the ten rightnesses, the ten abodes of the noble ones, the ten qualities of one beyond training, the ten powers of a Tathāgata; the eleven benefits of loving-kindness; the twelve aspects of the Wheel of the Dhamma; the thirteen ascetic qualities; the fourteen Buddha-knowledges; the fifteen qualities that ripen into liberation; the sixteenfold mindfulness of breathing, the sixteen qualities that cause no future remorse; the eighteen great insights, the eighteen distinct qualities of a Buddha; the nineteen reviewing knowledges; the forty-four bases of knowledge; the fifty knowledges of arising and passing away; more than fifty wholesome states; the seventy-seven bases of knowledge; the great diamond-like knowledge that ranges through twenty-four hundred thousand crores of attainments; the knowledges for teaching, which involve reviewing and investigating the Conditional Relations with its infinite methods; and also the knowledges that make plain the dispositions of infinite beings in infinite world-systems—and other such numerous blameless qualities of his that had reached fulfillment and growth through the age-long cultivation of the perfections and the cultivation of the path. He was seated reviewing them, making the Buddha-qualities, toward which his mind was directed with delight, into groups and heaps, thinking: 'These blameless qualities, too, are present in me; these blameless qualities, too, are present in me.' And this, indeed, is only in part, not completely. For all the Buddha-qualities cannot be brought to mind step-by-step and without remainder even by the Blessed One, because of their infinite and immeasurable nature.

Vuttañhetaṃ –

For this has been said:

“Buddhopi buddhassa bhaṇeyya vaṇṇaṃ,

Kappampi ce aññamabhāsamāno;

Khīyetha kappo ciradīghamantare,

Vaṇṇo na khīyetha tathāgatassā”ti.

Even if a Buddha were to speak the praise of another Buddha for an entire eon without speaking of anything else, that eon would be spent and exhausted in the long interval, but the praise of the Tathāgata would not be exhausted.

Aparampi [M 0.0306][P 0.0337] vuttaṃ –

Furthermore, it has been said:

“Asaṅkhyeyyāni nāmāni, saguṇena mahesino;

Guṇena nāmamuddheyyaṃ, api nāma sahassato”ti.

Innumerable are the names of the great sage, corresponding to his qualities; by each quality a name might be designated, even a thousand names.

Tadā hi bhagavā pacchābhattaṃ piṇḍapātappaṭikkanto vihāraṃ pavisitvā gandhakuṭippamukhe ṭhatvā bhikkhūsu vattaṃ dassetvā gatesu mahāgandhakuṭiṃ pavisitvā paññattavarabuddhāsane nisinno attano atītajātivisayaṃ ñāṇaṃ pesesi. Athassa tāni nirantaraṃ poṅkhānupoṅkhaṃ anantāparimāṇappabhedā upaṭṭhahiṃsu. So “evaṃ mahantassa nāma dukkhakkhandhassa mūlabhūtā ime kilesā”ti kilesavisayaṃ ñāṇācāraṃ pesetvā te pahānamukhena anupadaṃ paccavekkhitvā “ime vata kilesā anavasesato mayhaṃ suṭṭhu pahīnā”ti puna tesaṃ pahānakaraṃ sākāraṃ saparivāraṃ sauddesaṃ ariyamaggaṃ paccavekkhanto anantāparimāṇabhede attano sīlādianavajjadhamme manasākāsi. Tena vuttaṃ –

For at that time, the Blessed One, after the meal, having returned from his alms round, entered the monastery. Having stood at the entrance to the fragrant chamber and shown the bhikkhus their duties, after they had gone, he entered the great fragrant chamber, sat down on the excellent Buddha-seat that had been prepared, and sent forth his knowledge into the domain of his past births. Then they appeared to him continuously, in uninterrupted succession, of endless and immeasurable variety. Reflecting, 'These defilements are the root of such a great mass of suffering,' he sent forth the range of his knowledge into the domain of the defilements. Having reviewed them step by step by way of their abandonment, he thought: 'Indeed, these defilements have been well and completely abandoned by me.' Then, again reviewing the noble path that brings about their abandonment—with its aspects, its retinue, and its summary points—he attended to his own blameless qualities beginning with virtue, in their endless and immeasurable variety. Therefore it was said:

“Tena kho pana samayena bhagavā attano aneke pāpake akusale dhamme pahīne paccavekkhamāno nisinno hoti, aneke ca kusale dhamme bhāvanāpāripūriṃ gate”ti.

At that time, the Blessed One was seated, reviewing the many evil, unwholesome qualities that he had abandoned, and the many wholesome qualities that had reached full development through cultivation.

Evaṃ paccavekkhitvā uppannapītisomanassuddesabhūtaṃ imaṃ udānaṃ udānesi.

Having reviewed thus, he uttered this inspired utterance, which was the source of the joy and gladness that had arisen:

Tattha ahu pubbeti arahattamaggañāṇuppattito pubbe sabbopi cāyaṃ rāgādiko kilesagaṇo [V 0.0275] mayhaṃ santāne ahu āsi, na imasmiṃ kilesagaṇe kocipi kileso nāhosi. Tadā nāhūti tadā tasmiṃ kāle ariyamaggakkhaṇe so kilesagaṇo na ahu na āsi, tattha aṇumattopi kileso aggamaggakkhaṇe appahīno nāma natthi. “Tato nāhū”tipi paṭhanti, tato arahattamaggakkhaṇato paraṃ nāsīti attho. Nāhu pubbeti yo cāyaṃ mama aparimāṇo anavajjadhammo etarahi bhāvanāpāripūriṃ gato upalabbhati, sopi ariyamaggakkhaṇato pubbe na ahu na āsi. Tadā ahūti yadā pana me aggamaggañāṇaṃ uppannaṃ, tadā sabbopi me anavajjadhammo āsi. Aggamaggādhigamena hi saddhiṃ sabbepi sabbaññuguṇā buddhānaṃ hatthagatā eva honti.

Here, 'there was before' means: before the arising of the knowledge of the path to arahantship, this entire mass of defilements, such as lust, existed in my continuum; in this mass of defilements, there was no defilement that was not present. 'Then there was not' means: at that time, at the moment of the noble path, that mass of defilements was not, did not exist. At the moment of the supreme path, there is not even a minute defilement that remains unabandoned. Some also read this as 'From then, there was not,' meaning that after the moment of the path to arahantship, it was no more. 'There was not before' means: this immeasurable blameless state of mine, which is now found having reached fulfillment through development, also was not, did not exist, before the moment of the noble path. 'Then there was' means: but when the knowledge of the supreme path arose in me, then all my blameless states existed. For with the attainment of the supreme path, all the qualities of an omniscient one come into the hands of the Buddhas.

Na [M 0.0307] cāhu na ca bhavissati, na cetarahi vijjatīti yo pana so anavajjadhammo ariyamaggo [P 0.0338] mayhaṃ bodhimaṇḍe uppanno, yena sabbo kilesagaṇo anavasesaṃ pahīno, so yathā mayhaṃ maggakkhaṇato pubbe na cāhu na ca ahosi, evaṃ attanā pahātabbakilesābhāvato te kilesā viya ayampi na ca bhavissati anāgate na uppajjissati, etarahi paccuppannakālepi na vijjati na upalabbhati attanā kattabbakiccābhāvato. Na hi ariyamaggo anekavāraṃ pavattati. Tenevāha – “na pāraṃ diguṇaṃ yantī”ti.

'It was not, it will not be, and it does not exist now' means: that blameless state, the noble path that arose for me at the seat of enlightenment, by which the entire mass of defilements was abandoned without remainder—just as it was not and did not exist before the moment of my path, so too, because there are no more defilements to be abandoned by it, this path, like those defilements, will not be in the future, it will not arise. Even now, in the present, it does not exist, it is not found, because it has no task to perform. For the noble path does not occur repeatedly. Therefore it is said: 'They do not go to the far shore a second time.'

Iti bhagavā ariyamaggena attano santāne anavasesaṃ pahīne akusale dhamme bhāvanāpāripūriṃ gate aparimāṇe anavajjadhamme ca paccavekkhamāno attupanāyikapītivegavissaṭṭhaṃ udānaṃ udānesi. Purimāya kathāya purimavesārajjadvayameva kathitaṃ, pacchimadvayaṃ sammāsambodhiyā pakāsitattā pakāsitameva hotīti.

Thus the Blessed One, reflecting on the unwholesome states in his own continuum that had been abandoned without remainder by the noble path, and on the immeasurable blameless states that had reached fulfillment through development, uttered an inspired utterance released by the force of joy directed toward himself. By the former statement, the first pair of grounds of confidence is explained; the latter pair is also explained, as it is clarified by the attainment of perfect self-enlightenment.

Tatiyasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Third Sutta is finished.

4. Paṭhamanānātitthiyasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the First Sutta concerning Various Sectarians

54. Catutthe nānātitthiyasamaṇabrāhmaṇaparibbājakāti ettha taranti etena saṃsāroghanti titthaṃ, nibbānamaggo. Idha pana viparītavipallāsavasena diṭṭhigatikehi tathā gahitadiṭṭhidassanaṃ “tittha”nti adhippetaṃ. Tasmiṃ sassatādinānākāre titthe niyuttāti nānātitthiyā, nagganigaṇṭhādisamaṇā [V 0.0276] ceva kaṭhakalāpādibrāhmaṇā ca pokkharasātādiparibbājakā ca samaṇabrāhmaṇaparibbājakā. Nānātitthiyā ca te samaṇabrāhmaṇaparibbājakā cāti nānātitthiyasamaṇabrāhmaṇaparibbājakā.

54. In the fourth sutta: Regarding 'various sectarians, ascetics, brahmins, and wanderers': here, a 'ford' (tittha) is that by which one crosses the flood of saṃsāra, that is, the path to Nibbāna. Here, however, a 'ford' or 'sect' is intended as a view and a doctrine grasped in a certain way by those holding views, on account of their perversion and distortion. Those engaged in a sect of various kinds, such as eternalism, are 'various sectarians' (nānātitthiyā). The ascetics are the naked ascetics (Nigaṇṭhas) and others; the brahmins are the Kaṭhakas and Kalāpas and others; and the wanderers are Pokkharasāti and others. These are the ascetics, brahmins, and wanderers. They are both various sectarians and ascetics, brahmins, and wanderers; hence 'various sectarians, ascetics, brahmins, and wanderers'.

“Sassato attā ca loko cā”tiādinā passanti etāya, sayaṃ vā passati, tathā dassanamattameva vāti diṭṭhi, micchābhinivesassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Sassatādivasena nānā anekavidhā diṭṭhiyo etesanti nānādiṭṭhikā. Sassatādivaseneva khamanaṃ khanti, rocanaṃ ruci, atthato “sassato [M 0.0308] attā ca loko cā”tiādinā (udā. 55) pavatto cittavipallāso saññāvipallāso [P 0.0339] ca. Tathā nānā khantiyo etesanti nānākhantikā, nānā ruciyo etesanti nānārucikā. Diṭṭhigatikā hi pubbabhāge tathā tathā cittaṃ rocetvā khamāpetvā ca pacchā “idameva saccaṃ moghamañña”nti abhinivisanti. Atha vā “aniccaṃ nicca”ntiādinā tathā tathā dassanavasena diṭṭhi, khamanavasena khanti, ruccanavasena rucīti evaṃ tīhipi padehi diṭṭhi eva vuttāti veditabbā. Nānādiṭṭhinissayanissitāti sassatādiparikappavasena nānāvidhaṃ diṭṭhiyā nissayaṃ vatthuṃ kāraṇaṃ, diṭṭhisaṅkhātameva vā nissayaṃ nissitā allīnā upagatā, taṃ anissajjitvā ṭhitāti attho. Diṭṭhiyopi hi diṭṭhigatikānaṃ abhinivesākārānaṃ nissayā honti.

A 'view' (diṭṭhi) is that by which they see such things as 'the self and the world are eternal,' or one sees for oneself, or it is mere seeing in such a way; this is a designation for wrong adherence. They have various and manifold views based on eternalism and so on; thus they are 'those of diverse views' (nānādiṭṭhikā). Similarly, in terms of eternalism, forbearance is khanti and preference is ruci; in meaning, this is the distortion of mind and distortion of perception that proceeds as 'the self and the world are eternal,' etc. Thus, they have diverse forbearances, so they are 'those of diverse forbearances' (nānākhantikā); they have diverse preferences, so they are 'those of diverse preferences' (nānārucikā). For those who have gone to views, having first made the mind approve and accept in such and such a way, afterwards adhere, thinking, 'This alone is true, anything else is futile.' Alternatively, it should be understood that view arises from seeing in such ways as 'the impermanent as permanent,' forbearance from forbearing, and preference from approving; thus view alone is spoken of by all three terms. 'Dependent on the support of diverse views' means: they are dependent on, have clung to, and have resorted to the support for views—that is, the object and cause of various kinds of views based on speculations about eternalism, etc., or the support that is simply the view itself—and they stand without relinquishing it. For views themselves are also supports for the modes of adherence of those who have gone to views.

Santīti atthi saṃvijjanti upalabbhanti. Eketi ekacce. Samaṇabrāhmaṇāti pabbajjūpagamena samaṇā, jātiyā brāhmaṇā, lokena vā samaṇāti ca brāhmaṇāti ca evaṃ gahitā. Evaṃvādinoti evaṃ idāni vattabbākārena vadantīti evaṃvādino. Evaṃ idāni vattabbākārena pavattā diṭṭhi etesanti evaṃdiṭṭhino. Tattha dutiyena diṭṭhigatikānaṃ micchābhiniveso dassito, paṭhamena tesaṃ yathābhinivesaṃ paresaṃ tattha patiṭṭhāpanavasena vohāro.

'There are' (santi) means they exist, are found, are met with. 'Some' (eke) means certain ones. 'Ascetics and brahmins' means: ascetics by having gone forth into homelessness, brahmins by birth, or those regarded by the world as ascetics and brahmins. 'Those who speak thus' (evaṃvādino) means they speak in the way that will now be stated. 'Those who hold such views' (evaṃdiṭṭhino) means they have a view that proceeds in the way that will now be stated. Therein, the second term shows the wrong adherence of those who have gone to views, while the first shows their verbal expression, by which, in accordance with their own adherence, they seek to establish others in that view.

Sassato loko, idameva saccaṃ moghamaññanti ettha lokoti attā. So hi diṭṭhigatikehi lokiyanti ettha puññaṃ pāpaṃ tabbipākā, sayaṃ vā kārakādibhāvena abhiyuttehi lokiyatīti lokoti adhippeto. Svāyaṃ sassato amaro nicco dhuvoti yadidaṃ amhākaṃ dassanaṃ idameva saccaṃ aviparītaṃ, aññaṃ pana asassatotiādi paresaṃ dassanaṃ moghaṃ micchāti attho. Etena cattāropi sassatavādā dassitā honti. Asassatoti na sassato, anicco adhuvo cavanadhammoti attho. “Asassato”ti sassatabhāvappaṭikkhepeneva ucchedo dīpitoti sattapi ucchedavādā dīpitā honti.

In the statement 'The world is eternal; this alone is true, anything else is futile,' here 'world' means the self. For by those who have gone to views, it is intended as 'world' (loka) because merit, demerit, and their results are 'seen' (lokiyanti) in it, or because it is 'seen' by those who are engaged as agents and so on. The meaning is: 'This view of ours—that this self is eternal, deathless, permanent, and stable—this alone is true and not mistaken. But the view of others, that it is non-eternal and so on, is futile and wrong.' By this, the four kinds of eternalism are shown. 'Non-eternal' means not eternal, that is, impermanent, unstable, and subject to passing away. By 'non-eternal,' through the very rejection of an eternal nature, annihilationism is indicated; thus the seven kinds of annihilationism are indicated.

Antavāti [V 0.0277] sapariyanto parivaṭumo paricchinnappamāṇo, na sabbagatoti attho. Etena sarīraparimāṇo aṅguṭṭhaparimāṇo avayavaparimāṇo paramāṇuparimāṇo [M 0.0309] attāti evamādivādā dassitā honti. Anantavāti apariyanto, sabbagatoti attho. Etena kapilakaṇādādivādā dīpitā honti.

'Finite' means having a limit, having a circumference, of circumscribed measure; the meaning is that it is not all-pervading. By this are shown such doctrines as that the self has the measure of the body, the measure of a thumb, the measure of a limb, or the measure of an atom. 'Infinite' means without a limit; the meaning is that it is all-pervading. By this are indicated the doctrines of Kapila, Kaṇāda, and others.

Taṃ jīvaṃ taṃ [P 0.0340] sarīranti yaṃ sarīraṃ, tadeva jīvasaṅkhātaṃ vatthu, yañca jīvasaṅkhātaṃ vatthu, tadeva sarīranti jīvañca sarīrañca advayaṃ samanupassati. Etena ājīvakānaṃ viya “rūpī attā”ti ayaṃ vādo dassito hoti. Aññaṃ jīvaṃ aññaṃ sarīranti iminā pana “arūpī attā”ti ayaṃ vādo dassito.

Regarding 'the life principle is the same as the body': one sees that what the body is, that is the thing called the life principle; and what the thing called the life principle is, that is the body. Thus one sees the life principle and the body as non-dual. By this is shown the doctrine, 'the self is corporeal,' similar to that of the Ājīvakas. But by 'the life principle is one thing, the body another,' the doctrine 'the self is incorporeal' is shown.

Hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇāti ettha tathāgatoti satto. Tañhi diṭṭhigatiko kārakavedakādisaṅkhātaṃ, niccadhuvādisaṅkhātaṃ vā tathābhāvaṃ gatoti tathāgatoti voharati, so maraṇato idhakāyassa bhedato paraṃ uddhaṃ hoti, atthi saṃvijjatīti attho. Etena sassataggāhamukhena soḷasa saññīvādā aṭṭha asaññīvādā aṭṭha ca nevasaññīnāsaññīvādā dassitā honti. Na hotīti natthi na upalabbhati. Etena ucchedavādo dassito. Hoti ca na ca hotīti atthi ca natthi cāti. Etena ekaccasassatavādā satta saññīvādā ca dassitā. Neva hoti na na hotīti iminā pana amarāvikkhepavādo dassitoti veditabbaṃ.

Here, in 'a Tathāgata exists after death,' 'Tathāgata' means a being. For one who has gone to a view speaks of it as 'Tathāgata' because it has 'gone to such a state' (tathābhāvaṃ gato), being designated as an agent, an experiencer, etc., or as eternal, permanent, etc. The meaning is that after death, after the breakup of this body, it exists beyond; that is, it is, it is found. By this, by way of grasping at eternalism, are shown the sixteen doctrines of a percipient self, the eight doctrines of a non-percipient self, and the eight doctrines of a neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient self. 'Does not exist' means it is not, it is not found. By this, annihilationism is shown. 'Both exists and does not exist' means it is and it is not. By this are shown the doctrines of partial eternalism and the seven doctrines of a percipient self. But by 'neither exists nor does not exist,' it should be understood that the doctrine of evasive wriggling is shown.

Ime kira diṭṭhigatikā nānādesato āgantvā sāvatthiyaṃ paṭivasantā ekadā samayappavādake sannipatitvā attano attano vādaṃ paggayha aññavāde khuṃsentā vivādāpannā ahesuṃ. Tena vuttaṃ “te bhaṇḍanajātā”tiādi.

It is said that these adherents of views, having come from various regions and while dwelling in Sāvatthī, once gathered at the Hall for Debates. Each extolled their own doctrine while disparaging the doctrines of others, and they fell into dispute. Therefore it was said: 'They became quarrelsome,' etc.

Tattha bhaṇḍanaṃ nāma kalahassa pubbabhāgo. Bhaṇḍanajātāti jātabhaṇḍanā. Kalahoti kalaho eva, kalassa vā hananato kalaho daṭṭhabbo. Aññamaññassa viruddhavādaṃ āpannāti vivādāpannā. Mammaghaṭṭanato mukhameva sattīti mukhasatti, pharusavācā. Phalūpacārena viya hi kāraṇaṃ kāraṇūpacārena phalampi vohariyati yathā taṃ “sukho buddhuppādo, pāpakammaṃ paccanubhotī”ti ca. Tāhi mukhasattīhi vitudantā vijjhantā viharanti. Ediso dhammoti dhammo aviparītasabhāvo ediso evarūpo, yathā mayā vuttaṃ “sassato loko”ti. Nediso dhammoti na ediso dhammo[M 0.0310], yathā tayā vuttaṃ “asassato loko”ti, evaṃ sesapadehipi yojetabbaṃ. So ca titthiyānaṃ vivādo sakalanagare pākaṭo jāto. Atha bhikkhū sāvatthiṃ piṇḍāya [V 0.0278] paviṭṭhā taṃ sutvā “atthi no idaṃ kathāpābhataṃ, yaṃ nūna mayaṃ imaṃ pavattiṃ [P 0.0341] bhagavato āroceyyāma, appeva nāma taṃ nissāya satthu saṇhasukhumaṃ dhammadesanaṃ labheyyāmā”ti te pacchābhattaṃ dhammadesanākāle bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ. Tena vuttaṃ – “atha kho sambahulā bhikkhū”tiādi.

Herein, 'bhaṇḍanaṃ' is the preliminary stage of a quarrel. 'Bhaṇḍanajātā' means those who have become quarrelsome. 'Kalaho' is a quarrel itself, or 'kalaho' should be understood as that which destroys (hanana) what is good (kala). 'Vivādāpannā' means they have fallen into mutual dispute. 'Mukhasatti' (mouth-spear) is harsh speech, so called because it strikes the vital spots (mammaghaṭṭanato). For just as a cause is designated metaphorically by its effect, so too an effect is designated metaphorically by its cause, as in the examples: 'The arising of a Buddha is happiness,' and 'One experiences an evil deed.' With such mouth-spears they dwell, piercing and stabbing one another. 'The Dhamma is like this' means the Dhamma is of such a nature, not of a contrary nature, just as I have said: 'The world is eternal.' 'The Dhamma is not like this' means the Dhamma is not like that, as you have said: 'The world is not eternal.' The same should be applied to the remaining terms. This dispute among the sectarians became widely known throughout the entire city. Then, a number of monks who had entered Sāvatthī for alms heard about it and thought, 'Here we have a topic for a report. Why don’t we report this matter to the Blessed One? It is possible that, with this as a basis, we might get to hear a subtle and refined Dhamma discourse from the Teacher.' So after their meal, during the time for the Dhamma discourse, they reported this matter to the Blessed One. Hence it is said: 'Then a number of monks...' and so on.

Taṃ sutvā bhagavā aññatitthiyānaṃ dhammassa ayathābhūtapajānanaṃ pakāsento “aññatitthiyā, bhikkhave”tiādimāha. Tattha andhāti paññācakkhuvirahena andhā. Tenāha “acakkhukā”ti. Paññā hi idha “cakkhū”ti adhippetā. Tathā hi vuttaṃ “atthaṃ na jānantī”tiādi. Tattha atthaṃ na jānantīti idhalokatthaṃ paralokatthaṃ na jānanti, idhalokaparalokesu vuddhiṃ abbhudayaṃ nāvabujjhanti, paramatthe pana nibbāne kathāvakā. Ye hi nāma pavattimattepi sammūḷhā, te kathaṃ nivattiṃ jānissantīti. Anatthaṃ na jānantīti yadaggena te atthaṃ na jānanti, tadaggena anatthampi na jānanti. Yasmā dhammaṃ na jānanti, tasmā adhammampi na jānanti. Te hi vipariyesaggāhitāya dhammaṃ kusalampi akusalaṃ karonti, adhammampi akusalaṃ kusalaṃ karonti. Na kevalañca dhammādhammesu eva, atha kho tassa vipākesupi sammūḷhā. Tathā hi te kammampi vipākaṃ katvā voharanti, vipākampi kammaṃ katvā. Tathā dhammaṃ sabhāvadhammampi na jānanti, adhammaṃ asabhāvadhammampi na jānanti. Evaṃbhūtā ca sabhāvadhammaṃ asabhāvadhammañca, asabhāvadhammaṃ sabhāvadhammañca katvā pavedenti.

Having heard that, the Blessed One, in order to show how those of other sects do not understand the Dhamma as it really is, said: 'Monks, those of other sects…' and so on. Herein, 'blind' means blind due to the absence of the eye of wisdom. Hence he said, 'they are without eyes.' For here wisdom is intended by the word 'eye.' Thus it is said: 'They do not know the goal,' and so on. Herein, 'they do not know the goal' means they do not know the goal in this world and the goal in the next world; they do not understand growth and progress in this world and the next. As for the ultimate goal, Nibbāna, what is there to say? For how can those who are deluded about the mere process of existence know its cessation? 'They do not know what is not the goal' means that to the extent they do not know the goal, to that same extent they do not know what is not the goal. Because they do not know the Dhamma, they also do not know the non-Dhamma. For, due to perverse grasping, they make the Dhamma, which is wholesome, into something unwholesome, and the non-Dhamma, which is unwholesome, into something wholesome. And they are deluded not only about the Dhamma and non-Dhamma, but also about their results. Thus they speak of kamma as result and of result as kamma. Similarly, they do not know the Dhamma as what has a real nature, nor the non-Dhamma as what does not have a real nature. Being such, they declare what has a real nature to be what does not have a real nature, and what does not have a real nature to be what has a real nature.

Iti bhagavā titthiyānaṃ mohadiṭṭhipaṭilābhabhāvena paññācakkhuvekallato andhabhāvaṃ dassetvā idāni tamatthaṃ jaccandhūpamāya pakāsetuṃ “bhūtapubbaṃ, bhikkhave”tiādimāha. Tattha bhūtapubbanti pubbe bhūtaṃ, atītakāle nibbattaṃ. Aññataro rājā ahosīti purātano nāmagottehi loke apākaṭo eko rājā ahosi. So rājā aññataraṃ purisaṃ āmantesīti tassa kira rañño sobhaggappattaṃ sabbaṅgasampannaṃ attano opavayhaṃ hatthiṃ upaṭṭhānaṃ āgataṃ disvā etadahosi – “bhaddakaṃ vata, bho, hatthiyānaṃ dassanīya”nti. Tena ca samayena eko jaccandho rājaṅgaṇena gacchati. Taṃ disvā rājā [M 0.0311] cintesi – “mahājāniyā [P 0.0342] kho ime andhā ye evarūpaṃ dassanīyaṃ na labhanti daṭṭhuṃ. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ imissā sāvatthiyā yattakā jaccandhā sabbe te sannipātāpetvā ekadesaṃ ekadesaṃ hatthena phusāpetvā tesaṃ vacanaṃ suṇeyya”nti. Keḷisīlo rājā ekena purisena sāvatthiyā sabbe jaccandhe sannipātāpetvā tassa purisassa saññaṃ adāsi “yathā ekeko jaccandho sīsādikaṃ ekekaṃyeva hatthissa aṅgaṃ phusitvā ‘hatthī mayā diṭṭho’ti saññaṃ uppādesi, tathā karohī”ti. So puriso tathā akāsi. Atha rājā te jaccandhe [V 0.0279] paccekaṃ pucchi “kīdiso, bhaṇe, hatthī”ti. Te attanā diṭṭhadiṭṭhāvayavameva hatthiṃ katvā vadantā “ediso hatthī, nediso hatthī”ti aññamaññaṃ kalahaṃ karontā hatthādīhi upakkamitvā rājaṅgaṇe mahantaṃ kolāhalaṃ akaṃsu. Rājā saparijano tesaṃ taṃ vippakāraṃ disvā phāsukehi bhijjamānehi hadayena uggatena mahāhasitaṃ hasi. Tena vuttaṃ – “atha kho, bhikkhave, so rājā…pe… attamano ahosī”ti.

Thus the Blessed One, having shown that the sectarians are blind due to a lack of the wisdom-eye, which results from their acquisition of deluded views, now, in order to illustrate that point with the simile of the men born blind, said: 'Once upon a time, monks,' and so on. Herein, 'once upon a time' means it happened previously, it occurred in a past time. 'There was a certain king' means there was a certain ancient king who was not famous in the world by name or clan. 'That king addressed a certain man': it is said that when that king saw his own magnificent, perfectly proportioned royal elephant arrive for service, this occurred to him: 'Oh, what a fine and lovely sight this elephant is!' At that time, a man born blind was passing through the royal courtyard. Seeing him, the king thought: 'These blind people are greatly deprived, in that they do not get to see such a lovely sight. Why don't I have all the men born blind in this Sāvatthī assembled, have them touch the elephant part by part, and then listen to what they say?' The king, being of a playful nature, had a man assemble all the men born blind in Sāvatthī and gave him this instruction: 'Have each man born blind touch just one part of the elephant, such as its head, and then make him form the perception, "I have seen the elephant." Do it in this way.' That man did so. Then the king asked each of the men born blind: 'Well, my man, what is an elephant like?' Each of them, taking the part he had 'seen' to be the entire elephant, said, 'An elephant is like this; it is not like that.' Quarreling with one another, they came to blows with their fists and caused a great uproar in the royal courtyard. The king and his retinue, seeing their misbehavior, laughed a great laugh, with his heart uplifted as if it would break his ribs. Hence it is said: 'Then, monks, that king … was delighted.'

Tattha ambhoti ālapanaṃ. Yāvatakāti yattakā. Jaccandhāti jātiyā andhā, jātito paṭṭhāya acakkhukā. Ekajjhanti ekato. Bhaṇeti abahumānālāpo. Hatthiṃ dassehīti yathāvuttaṃ hatthiṃ sayāpetvā dassehi. So ca susikkhitattā aparipphandanto nipajji. Diṭṭho no hatthīti hatthena parāmasanaṃ dassanaṃ katvā āhaṃsu. Tena purisena sīsaṃ parāmasāpetvā “ediso hatthī”ti saññāpitattā tādisaṃyeva naṃ hatthiṃ sañjānantā jaccandhā “ediso deva hatthī seyyathāpi kumbho”ti vadiṃsu. Kumbhoti ca ghaṭoti attho. Khīloti nāgadantakhīlo. Soṇḍoti hattho. Naṅgalīsāti naṅgalassa sirassa īsā. Kāyoti sarīraṃ. Koṭṭhoti kusūlo. Pādoti jaṅgho. Thūṇoti thambho. Naṅguṭṭhanti vāḷassa urimappadeso. Vāladhīti vālassa aggappadeso. Muṭṭhīhi saṃsumbhiṃsūti muṭṭhiyo bandhitvā pahariṃsu, muṭṭhighātaṃ akaṃsu. Attamano ahosīti keḷisīlattā so rājā tena jaccandhānaṃ kalahena attamano pahāsena gahitamano ahosi.

Herein, 'ambho' is a form of address. 'Yāvatakā' means however many. 'Jaccandhā' means blind by birth, without eyes from birth onwards. 'Ekajjhaṃ' means in one place. 'Bhaṇe' is a disrespectful form of address. 'Show the elephant' means: 'Having made the elephant lie down as described, show it.' And because it was well-trained, it lay down without moving. 'We have seen the elephant': they said this, taking the touching with the hand to be a 'seeing.' Because that man had them touch the head and gave them the perception, 'An elephant is like this,' those men born blind, perceiving the elephant to be just like that, said: 'Your Majesty, an elephant is like this, just like a pot.' 'Kumbho' means a water pot. 'Khīlo' means an elephant-post. 'Soṇḍo' means the trunk. 'Naṅgalīsā' means the pole of a plow. 'Kāyo' means the body. 'Koṭṭho' means a granary. 'Pādo' means the leg. 'Thūṇo' means a pillar. 'Naṅguṭṭhaṃ' means the base of the tail. 'Vāladhī' means the tuft of the tail. 'They pummeled with fists' means they clenched their fists and struck; they delivered blows with their fists. 'He was delighted' means that the king, being of a playful nature, was delighted by the quarrel of the men born blind, his mind captivated by the amusement.

Evameva khoti upamāsaṃsandanaṃ. Tassattho – bhikkhave, yathā te jaccandhā acakkhukā ekaṅgadassino anavasesato hatthiṃ apassitvā attanā [M 0.0312] diṭṭhāvayavamattaṃ hatthisaññāya [P 0.0343] itarehi diṭṭhaṃ ananujānantā aññamaññaṃ vivādaṃ āpannā kalahaṃ akaṃsu, evameva ime aññatitthiyā sakkāyassa ekadesaṃ rūpavedanādiṃ attano diṭṭhidassanena yathādiṭṭhaṃ “attā”ti maññamānā tassa sassatādibhāvaṃ āropetvā “idameva saccaṃ moghamañña”nti abhinivisitvā aññamaññaṃ vivadanti, yathābhūtaṃ pana atthānatthaṃ dhammādhammañca na jānanti. Tasmā andhā acakkhukā jaccandhapaṭibhāgāti.

This is the application of the simile. Its meaning is this: 'Monks, just as those men born blind, being without eyes, saw only a single part and did not see the elephant completely, and taking the part they had seen to be the elephant, they did not acknowledge what the others had seen and thus fell into dispute and quarreled with one another; even so, these sectarians, with the seeing of their own views, regard a single part of the personal identity—such as form or feeling—as it was seen by them, to be the 'self.' Having superimposed on it such states as permanence, and having adhered to the conviction, 'This alone is true, anything else is futile,' they dispute with one another. But they do not know the goal and what is not the goal, the Dhamma and the non-Dhamma, as they really are. Therefore, they are blind, without eyes, counterparts of the men born blind.'

Etamatthaṃ viditvāti etaṃ titthiyānaṃ dhammasabhāvaṃ yathābhūtaṃ ajānantānaṃ apassantānaṃ jaccandhānaṃ viya hatthimhi yathādassanaṃ micchābhinivesaṃ, tattha ca vivādāpattiṃ sabbākārato viditvā tadatthadīpakaṃ imaṃ udānaṃ udānesi.

'Having understood this matter': Having understood in all its aspects this wrong adherence of the sectarians—who, not knowing and not seeing the real nature of things, cling to their own particular view just as the men born blind did to their particular sight of the elephant—and having understood the disputes that arise from that, the Blessed One uttered this inspired utterance to illuminate that meaning.

Tattha [V 0.0280] imesu kira sajjanti, eke samaṇabrāhmaṇāti idhekacce pabbajjūpagamanena samaṇā, jātimattena brāhmaṇā “sassato loko”tiādinayappavattesu imesu eva asāresu diṭṭhigatesu diṭṭhābhinandanavasena, imesu vā rūpādīsu upādānakkhandhesu evaṃ aniccesu dukkhesu vipariṇāmadhammesu taṇhābhinandanadiṭṭhābhinandanānaṃ vasena “etaṃ mamā”tiādinā sajjanti kira. Aho nesaṃ sammohoti dasseti. Kirasaddo cettha arucisūcanattho. Tena tattha saṅgakāraṇābhāvameva dīpeti. Na kevalaṃ sajjanti eva, atha kho viggayha naṃ vivadanti “na tvaṃ imaṃ dhammavinayaṃ ājānāsi, ahaṃ imaṃ dhammavinayaṃ ājānāmī”tiādinā viggāhikakathānuyogavasena viggayha vivadanti vivādaṃ āpajjanti. Nanti cettha nipātamattaṃ. Atha vā viggayha nanti naṃ diṭṭhinissayaṃ sakkāyadiṭṭhimeva vā viparītadassanattā sassatādivasena aññamaññaṃ viruddhaṃ gahetvā vivadanti visesato vadanti, attano eva vādaṃ visiṭṭhaṃ aviparītaṃ katvā abhinivissa voharanti. Yathā kiṃ? Janā ekaṅgadassino yatheva jaccandhajanā hatthissa ekekaṅgadassino “yaṃ yaṃ attanā phusitvā ñātaṃ, taṃ tadeva hatthī”ti gahetvā aññamaññaṃ viggayha vivadiṃsu, evaṃsampadamidanti attho. Ivasaddo cettha luttaniddiṭṭhoti veditabbo.

Herein, it is said, some ascetics and brahmins cling. That is, some who are ascetics by having gone forth and some who are brahmins by birth alone cling to these very same worthless views, such as 'the world is eternal,' by way of delighting in views. Or, by way of delight in craving and delight in views, they cling to these very aggregates subject to clinging—form and so on—which are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, thinking, 'This is mine,' and so on. This shows, alas, their delusion! The word 'kira' (it is said) here indicates displeasure. It thereby reveals that there is no reason for clinging. Not only do they cling, but they also dispute and argue about it. By engaging in contentious talk such as, 'You do not know this Dhamma and Discipline, I know this Dhamma and Discipline,' they dispute and fall into argument. Here 'naṃ' is a mere particle. Or, 'viggayha naṃ' means: having contentiously grasped that basis for views—or even personality view itself—which, because of their distorted perception, they hold in mutually contradictory ways such as eternalism, etc., they dispute. That is, they speak with distinction; having made their own doctrine out to be superior and unerring, they adhere to it and proclaim it. To what is this comparable? To people who see only one part. Just as people blind from birth, each seeing only one part of an elephant, having grasped, 'Whatever I have touched and known, that alone is the elephant,' disputed and argued with one another—such is the meaning here. The word 'iva' (just as) should be understood as elided here.

Catutthasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Fourth Sutta is finished.

5. Dutiyanānātitthiyasuttavaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Second Sutta on Various Sectarians

55. Pañcame [M 0.0313][P 0.0344] sassato attā ca loko cāti rūpādīsu aññataraṃ attāti ca lokoti ca gahetvā taṃ sassataṃ niccanti aññepi ca tathā gāhentā voharanti. Yathāha –

55. In the fifth, holding that 'the self and the world are eternal,' they take one or another among form, etc., as the self and as the world, and they declare it to be eternal and permanent. Others too, grasping in the same way, proclaim this. As it is said:

“Rūpaṃ attā ceva loko ca sassato cāti attānañca lokañca paññapenti. Vedanaṃ… saññaṃ… saṅkhāre… viññāṇaṃ attā ca loko ca sassato cāti attānañca lokañca paññapentī”ti.

'Form is the self and the world, and it is eternal'; thus they posit the self and the world. 'Feeling… perception… formations… consciousness is the self and the world, and it is eternal'; thus they posit the self and the world.

Atha vā attāti ahaṅkāravatthu, lokoti mamaṅkāravatthu, yaṃ “attaniya”nti vuccati. Attāti vā sayaṃ, lokoti paro. Attāti vā pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu eko khandho, itaro loko[V 0.0281]. Attāti vā saviññāṇako khandhasantāno, aviññāṇako loko. Evaṃ taṃ taṃ attāti ca lokoti ca yathādassanaṃ dvidhā gahetvā tadubhayaṃ “nicco dhuvo sassato”ti abhinivissa voharanti. Etena cattāro sassatavādā dassitā. Asassatoti sattapi ucchedavādā dassitā. Sassato ca asassato cāti ekacco attā ca loko ca sassato, ekacco asassatoti evaṃ sassato ca asassato cāti attho. Atha vā sveva attā ca loko ca attagatidiṭṭhikānaṃ viya sassato ca asassato ca, siyā sassatoti evamettha attho veditabbo. Sabbathāpi iminā ekaccasassatavādo dassito. Neva sassato nāsassatoti iminā amarāvikkhepavādo dassito. Te hi sassatavāde asassatavāde ca dosaṃ disvā “neva sassato nāsassato attā ca loko cā”ti vikkhepaṃ karontā vivadanti.

Or, 'self' is the basis for I-making, and 'world' is the basis for mine-making, which is called 'what pertains to the self.' Or, 'self' is oneself, and 'world' is another. Or, 'self' is one of the five aggregates subject to clinging, and 'world' is the others. Or, 'self' is the stream of aggregates with consciousness, and 'world' is what is without consciousness. Thus, having taken 'self' and 'world' in these two ways according to their respective views, they adhere to and proclaim both to be 'permanent, stable, eternal.' By this, the four eternalist doctrines are shown. By 'non-eternal,' the seven annihilationist doctrines are shown. 'Both eternal and non-eternal' means that one part of the self and world is eternal and another part is non-eternal; this is the meaning of 'both eternal and non-eternal.' Or, that very self and world is for them both eternal and non-eternal, just as for those who hold views about the self; the meaning here should be understood as 'it might be eternal.' In every way, this shows the partial-eternalist doctrine. By 'neither eternal nor non-eternal,' the doctrine of the eel-wrigglers is shown. For they, seeing the fault in both eternalism and annihilationism, equivocate and dispute, saying, 'The self and the world are neither eternal nor non-eternal.'

Sayaṃkatoti attanā kato. Yathā hi tesaṃ tesaṃ sattānaṃ attā ca attano dhammānudhammaṃ katvā sukhadukkhāni paṭisaṃvedeti, evaṃ attāva attānaṃ tassa ca upabhogabhūtaṃ kiñcanaṃ palibodhasaṅkhātaṃ lokañca karoti, abhinimminātīti attaladdhi viya ayampi tesaṃ laddhi. Paraṃkatoti parena kato, attato parena issarena vā purisena vā pajāpatinā vā kālena vā pakatiyā vā attā ca loko ca kato[M 0.0314], nimmitoti attho. Sayaṃkato ca paraṃkato cāti yasmā attānañca lokañca nimminantā issarādayo na kevalaṃ sayameva nimminanti, atha kho tesaṃ tesaṃ sattānaṃ dhammādhammānaṃ sahakārīkāraṇaṃ labhitvāva, tasmā sayaṃkato ca paraṃkato [P 0.0345] ca attā ca loko cāti ekaccānaṃ laddhi. Asayaṃkāro aparaṃkāroti natthi etassa sayaṃkāroti asayaṃkāro, natthi etassa parakāroti aparakāro. Anunāsikāgamaṃ katvā vuttaṃ “aparaṃkāro”ti. Ayaṃ ubhayattha dosaṃ disvā ubhayaṃ paṭikkhipati. Atha kathaṃ uppannoti āha – adhiccasamuppannoti yadicchāya samuppanno kenaci kāraṇena vinā uppannoti adhiccasamuppannavādo dassito. Tena ca ahetukavādopi saṅgahito hoti.

‘Self-made’ means made by oneself. Just as the self of each being experiences pleasure and pain by acting in accordance with its nature, so the self creates itself and the world—which is the basis of its enjoyment and is called an impediment. It fashions them. This is their doctrine, similar to the doctrine of a self. ‘Other-made’ means made by another: the self and the world are made, that is, created, by another different from the self, such as a supreme lord, a primal person, Pajāpati, time, or nature. ‘Both self-made and other-made’: since creators of the self and the world, such as a supreme lord, do not create them solely by themselves but only after obtaining the co-operating cause of the righteous and unrighteous deeds of those various beings, therefore some hold the doctrine that the self and the world are both self-made and other-made. ‘Neither self-made nor other-made’ (asayaṃkāro aparaṃkāro): ‘there is no self-maker of this’ (asayaṃkāro); ‘there is no other-maker of this’ (aparakāro). The form aparaṃkāro is stated with the insertion of a nasal. This view rejects both, seeing the fault in each. Then how has it arisen? It is said: ‘arisen spontaneously,’ meaning it has arisen by chance, without any cause. Thus the doctrine of spontaneous arising is shown, and by this the doctrine of causelessness is also included.

Idāni ye diṭṭhigatikā attānaṃ viya sukhadukkhampi tassa guṇabhūtaṃ kiñcanabhūtaṃ vā sassatādivasena abhinivissa voharanti, tesaṃ taṃ vādaṃ dassetuṃ “santeke samaṇabrāhmaṇā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Taṃ vuttanayameva.

Now, to show the doctrine of those who go by views, who, like they do with the self, also adhere to and proclaim that happiness and suffering are its quality or its possession in terms of eternalism and so on, the passage beginning 'There are some ascetics and brahmins...' was stated. The meaning of that is just as was explained.

Etamatthaṃ viditvāti ettha pana idha jaccandhūpamāya anāgatattā taṃ hitvā heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva attho yojetabbo, tathā gāthāya.

Regarding the phrase 'Having known this meaning': here, however, since the simile of the man blind from birth has not been given, that should be omitted, and the meaning should be construed only by the method stated below; and so too for the verse.

Tattha [V 0.0282] antarāva visīdanti, apatvāva tamogadhanti ayaṃ viseso. Tassattho – evaṃ diṭṭhigatesu diṭṭhinissayesu āsajjamānā diṭṭhigatikā kāmoghādīnaṃ catunnaṃ oghānaṃ, saṃsāramahoghasseva vā antarāva vemajjhe eva yaṃ tesaṃ pārabhāvena patiṭṭhaṭṭhena vā ogadhasaṅkhātaṃ nibbānaṃ tadadhigamūpāyo vā ariyamaggo taṃ appatvāva anadhigantvāva visīdanti saṃsīdanti. Ogādhanti patiṭṭhahanti etena, ettha vāti ogādho, ariyamaggo nibbānañca. Ogādhamevettha rassattaṃ katvā ogadhanti vuttaṃ. Taṃ ogadhaṃ tamogadhanti padavibhāgo.

Here, the distinction is 'they sink right in the middle' and 'without reaching that foundation.' The meaning is this: those who go by views, clinging to views as their support, sink down and come to ruin right in the middle of the four floods—the flood of sensual pleasure, the flood of existence, the flood of views, and the flood of ignorance—or in the great flood of saṃsāra itself, without having reached and attained Nibbāna, which is called a 'foundation' (ogadha) because it is the further shore and a firm standing place, or the noble path which is the means to its attainment. An 'ogādha' is that by which or wherein one plunges or gets a footing; it is the noble path and Nibbāna. Here 'ogādha' itself, having been shortened, is stated as 'ogadha.' The word division of 'tamogadhaṃ' is 'taṃ' + 'ogadhaṃ' (that foundation).

Pañcamasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Fifth Sutta is finished.

6. Tatiyanānātitthiyasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Third Discourse on Various Sectarians

56. Chaṭṭhe sabbaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayameva. Imaṃ udānanti ettha pana diṭṭhitaṇhāmānesu dosaṃ disvā te dūrato vajjetvā saṅkhāre yathābhūtaṃ passato ca tattha anādīnavadassitāya [P 0.0346] micchābhiniviṭṭhassa yathābhūtaṃ apassato [M 0.0315] ca yathākkamaṃ saṃsārato ativattanānativattanadīpakaṃ imaṃ udānaṃ udānesīti attho yojetabbo.

56. In the sixth, everything is just as was explained before. But here, regarding 'this utterance,' the meaning should be construed thus: He uttered this utterance which illuminates, in due order, the transcending of saṃsāra for one who sees formations as they really are—having seen the danger in views, craving, and conceit and avoided them from afar—and the non-transcending of saṃsāra for one who does not see them as they really are because he is wrongly attached and does not see the danger in them.

Tattha ahaṅkārapasutāyaṃ pajāti “sayaṃkato attā ca loko cā”ti evaṃ vuttasayaṃkārasaṅkhātaṃ ahaṅkāraṃ tathāpavattaṃ diṭṭhiṃ pasutā anuyuttā ayaṃ pajā micchābhiniviṭṭho sattakāyo. Paraṃkārūpasaṃhitāti paro añño issarādiko sabbaṃ karotīti evaṃ pavattaparaṃkāradiṭṭhisannissitā tāya upasaṃhitāti paraṃkārūpasaṃhitā. Etadeke nābbhaññaṃsūti etaṃ diṭṭhidvayaṃ eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā tattha dosadassino hutvā nānujāniṃsu. Kathaṃ? Sati hi sayaṃkāre kāmakārato sattānaṃ iṭṭheneva bhavitabbaṃ, na aniṭṭhena. Na hi koci attano dukkhaṃ icchati, bhavati ca aniṭṭhaṃ, tasmā na sayaṃkāro. Paraṃkāropi yadi issarahetuko, svāyaṃ issaro attatthaṃ vā kareyya paratthaṃ vā. Tattha yadi attatthaṃ, attanā akatakicco siyā asiddhassa sādhanato. Atha vā paratthaṃ sabbesaṃ hitasukhameva nipphajjeyya, na ahitaṃ dukkhaṃ nipphajjati, tasmā issaravasena na paraṃkāro sijjhati. Yadi ca issarasaṅkhātaṃ aññanirapekkhaṃ niccamekakāraṇaṃ pavattiyā siyā, kammena uppatti na siyā, sabbeheva ekajjhaṃ uppajjitabbaṃ kāraṇassa sannihitattā. Athassa aññampi sahakārīkāraṇaṃ icchitaṃ, taññeva [V 0.0283] hetu, kiṃ issarena apariniṭṭhitasāmatthiyena parikappitena. Yathā ca issarahetuko paraṃkāro na sijjhati, evaṃ pajāpatipurisapakatibrahmakālādihetutopi na sijjhateva tesampi asiddhattā vuttadosānativattanato ca. Tena vuttaṃ “etadeke nābbhaññaṃsū”ti. Ye pana yathāvutte sayaṃkāraparaṃkāre nānujānantāpi adhiccasamuppannaṃ attānañca lokañca paññapenti, tepi na naṃ sallanti addasuṃ adhiccasamuppannantivādinopi micchābhinivesaṃ anatikkamanato yathābhūtaṃ ajānantānaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ tattha tattha dukkhuppādanato vijjhanaṭṭhena “salla”nti na passiṃsu.

Herein, 'this generation is intent on I-making' means this generation, this wrongly adhering body of beings, is intent on and devoted to the view of I-making, which is called 'self-making' and expressed as 'the self and the world are self-made.' 'Connected with another's making' means reliant on and associated with the view of another's making, which holds that another, such as a lord (Isvara), makes everything; thus they are 'connected with another's making.' 'Some did not approve of this' means some ascetics and brahmins did not assent to this twofold view, seeing fault in them. How so? If there were self-making, beings would act according to their will and should experience only what is desirable, not the undesirable. For no one wishes suffering for themselves, yet the undesirable occurs. Therefore, there is no self-making. If another's making were due to a lord, that lord would act either for his own benefit or for the benefit of others. If for his own benefit, he would be one with an unaccomplished task, since he would be achieving what is not yet achieved. If for the benefit of others, only the welfare and happiness of all would be produced, not harm and suffering. Thus, another's making dependent on a lord is not established. Furthermore, if a single, constant, independent cause called a 'lord' were the source of existence, then things would not arise from kamma; all would have to arise at once, as the cause is always present. But if another cooperating cause is required for him, then that is the actual cause; what need is there for an imagined lord whose power is incomplete? Just as another's making dependent on a lord is not established, so too it cannot be established when attributed to a Pajāpati, a Purisa, Pakati, Brahmā, Time, etc., for these too are unproven and do not escape the faults already mentioned. Therefore, it is said, 'Some did not approve of this.' But those who, while not assenting to the aforementioned views of self-making and other-making, still postulate that the self and the world have arisen spontaneously, they too did not see it as a dart. Even the advocates of spontaneous origination, because they do not transcend wrong adherence and do not know things as they really are, did not see the view they have adopted as a 'dart'—in the sense of piercing because it produces suffering here and there.

Etañca sallaṃ paṭikacca passatoti [P 0.0347] yo pana āraddhavipassako pañcapi upādānakkhandhe aniccato dukkhato anattato samanupassati, so etañca tividhaṃ viparītadassanaṃ aññañca sakalaṃ micchābhinivesaṃ tesañca nissayabhūte pañcupādānakkhandhepi tujjanato duruddhārato ca “salla”nti paṭikacca pubbeyeva [M 0.0316] vipassanāpaññāya passati. Evaṃ passato ariyamaggakkhaṇe ekanteneva ahaṃ karomīti na tassa hoti. Yathā ca attano kārakabhāvo tassa na upaṭṭhāti, evaṃ paro karotīti na tassa hoti, kevalaṃ pana aniccasaṅkhātaṃ paṭiccasamuppannadhammamattameva hoti. Ettāvatā sammāpaṭipannassa sabbathāpi diṭṭhimānābhāvova dassito. Tena ca arahattappattiyā saṃsārasamatikkamo pakāsito hoti.

'He sees this dart, having comprehended it': One who has undertaken insight meditation repeatedly sees the five aggregates subject to clinging as impermanent, suffering, and non-self. With the wisdom of insight, he sees beforehand and comprehends this threefold perverted view and all other wrong adherence—and also the five aggregates subject to clinging that are their basis—as a 'dart' because of its piercing nature and its being difficult to extract. For one seeing in this way, at the moment of the noble path, the thought 'I am doing' does not occur at all. Just as the notion of being a doer does not occur to him, so the thought 'another is doing' does not occur. There is merely the bare phenomenon that has arisen dependently, designated as impermanent. To this extent, for one who has practiced rightly, the complete absence of views and conceit is shown. And through this, the attainment of arahantship and the transcendence of saṃsāra are declared.

Idāni yo diṭṭhigate allīno, na so saṃsārato sīsaṃ ukkhipituṃ sakkoti, taṃ dassetuṃ “mānupetā”ti gāthamāha. Tattha mānupetā ayaṃ pajāti ayaṃ sabbāpi diṭṭhigatikasaṅkhātā pajā sattakāyo “mayhaṃ diṭṭhi sundarā, mayhaṃ ādāno sundaro”ti attano gāhassa saṃpaggahalakkhaṇena mānena upetā samannāgatā. Mānaganthā mānavinibaddhāti tato eva tena aparāparaṃ uppajjamānena yathā taṃ diṭṭhiṃ na paṭinissajjati, evaṃ attano santānassa ganthitattā vinibaddhattā ca mānaganthā mānavinibaddhā. Diṭṭhīsu sārambhakathā, saṃsāraṃ nātivattatīti “idameva saccaṃ moghamañña”nti attukkaṃsanaparavambhanavasena attano diṭṭhābhinivesena paresaṃ diṭṭhīsu sārambhakathā virodhakathā saṃsāranāyikānaṃ avijjātaṇhānaṃ appahānato saṃsāraṃ nātivattati, na atikkamatīti attho.

Now, whoever is attached to what has become a view cannot lift their head from saṃsāra. To show this, he spoke the verse beginning 'Endowed with conceit.' Here, 'this generation is endowed with conceit' means this entire generation, this body of beings characterized by what has become a view, is possessed of conceit, which has the characteristic of firmly grasping one's own position, thinking, 'My view is fine, my grasping is fine.' 'Knotted by conceit, bound by conceit': because that conceit arises again and again, one does not relinquish that view; thus, because one's own mental continuity is knotted and bound, one is 'knotted by conceit, bound by conceit.' 'Contentious talk about views, does not transcend saṃsāra' means: due to one's own adherence to a view, by way of exalting oneself and disparaging others with the thought, 'This alone is true, the other is futile,' one engages in contentious and contradictory talk regarding the views of others. Because of not abandoning ignorance and craving, which lead one through saṃsāra, one does not transcend saṃsāra; that is, one does not overcome it. This is the meaning.

Chaṭṭhasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the sixth discourse is concluded.

7. Subhūtisuttavaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Subhūti Sutta

57. Sattame [V 0.0284][P 0.0348] subhūtīti tassa therassa nāmaṃ. So hi āyasmā padumuttarassa bhagavato pādamūle katābhinīhāro kappasatasahassaṃ upacitapuññasambhāro imasmiṃ buddhuppāde uḷāravibhave gahapatikule uppanno bhagavato dhammadesanaṃ sutvā saṃvegajāto gharā nikkhamma pabbajitvā katādhikārattā ghaṭento vāyamanto na cirasseva chaḷabhiñño jāto, brahmavihārabhāvanāya pana ukkaṃsapāramippattiyā “etadaggaṃ, bhikkhave, mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ araṇavihārīnaṃ yadidaṃ subhūtī”ti (a. ni. 1.201) araṇavihāre bhagavatā etadagge ṭhapito. So ekadivasaṃ sāyanhasamayaṃ divāṭṭhānato vihāraṅgaṇaṃ otiṇṇo catuparisamajjhe bhagavantaṃ dhammaṃ [M 0.0317] desentaṃ disvā “desanāpariyosāne vuṭṭhahitvā vandissāmī”ti kālaparicchedaṃ katvā bhagavato avidūre aññatarasmiṃ rukkhamūle nisinno phalasamāpattiṃ samāpajji. Tena vuttaṃ – “tena kho pana samayena āyasmā subhūti…pe… samāpajjitvā”ti.

57. In the seventh sutta, 'Subhūti' is the name of that elder. That venerable one had made his aspiration at the feet of the Blessed One Padumuttara and for a hundred thousand eons had accumulated a store of merit. In this Buddha-era he was born into a householder family of great wealth. Having heard the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma, he was stirred with a sense of urgency, went forth from the household life, and because he had the requisite conditions, by striving and making an effort, before long he attained the six higher knowledges. Moreover, through the cultivation of the divine abidings he reached the peak of perfection, and he was placed by the Blessed One at the head of his monk disciples who are dwellers in non-conflict with the words: “Monks, this is the foremost of my monk disciples who are dwellers in non-conflict, that is, Subhūti.” One day, in the evening, having descended from his day-abode to the monastery courtyard, he saw the Blessed One teaching the Dhamma in the midst of the fourfold assembly. Thinking, “I will rise and pay homage at the conclusion of the discourse,” he decided on the time, sat down at the foot of a certain tree not far from the Blessed One, and entered the attainment of fruition. Therefore it was said: “Now at that time the Venerable Subhūti … having entered….”

Tattha dutiyajjhānato paṭṭhāya rūpāvacarasamādhi sabbopi arūpāvacarasamādhi avitakkasamādhi eva. Idha pana catutthajjhānapādako arahattaphalasamādhi “avitakkasamādhī”ti adhippeto. Dutiyajjhānādīhi pahīnā micchāvitakkā na tāva suppahīnā accantapahānābhāvato, ariyamaggena pana pahīnā eva puna pahānakiccābhāvato. Tasmā aggamaggapariyosānabhūto arahattaphalasamādhi sabbesaṃ micchāvitakkānaṃ pahānante uppannattā visesato “avitakkasamādhī”ti vattabbataṃ arahati, pageva catutthajjhānapādako. Tena vuttaṃ – “idha pana catutthajjhānapādako arahattaphalasamādhi ‘avitakkasamādhī’ti adhippeto”ti.

Therein, from the second jhāna onwards, all form-sphere concentration and all formless-sphere concentration are indeed concentration without thought-conception. Here, however, the concentration of the fruit of arahantship that has the fourth jhāna as its basis is intended by ‘concentration without thought-conception.’ The wrong thoughts abandoned by the second jhāna and so on are not yet well abandoned, since they have not been abandoned for good; but those abandoned by the noble path are truly abandoned, since there is no further task of abandoning them. Therefore the concentration of the fruit of arahantship, which is the culmination of the highest path, deserves to be specially called ‘concentration without thought-conception’ because it arises at the end of the abandonment of all wrong thoughts—how much more so when it has the fourth jhāna as its basis. Hence it was said: ‘Here, however, the concentration of the fruit of arahantship that has the fourth jhāna as its basis is intended by “concentration without thought-conception.”’

Etamatthaṃ viditvāti etaṃ āyasmato subhūtissa sabbamicchāvitakkasabbasaṃkilesapahānasaṅkhātaṃ atthaṃ sabbākārato jānitvā tadatthadīpakaṃ imaṃ udānaṃ udānesi.

Having understood this matter—that is, having known in all its aspects this matter concerning the Venerable Subhūti, designated as the abandonment of all wrong thoughts and all defilements—the Blessed One uttered this inspired utterance that illuminates that matter.

Tattha yassa vitakkā vidhūpitāti yena ariyapuggalena, yassa vā [P 0.0349] ariyapuggalassa kāmavitakkādayo sabbepi micchāvitakkā vidhūpitā ariyamaggañāṇena santāpitā samucchinnā. Ajjhattaṃ suvikappitā asesāti niyakajjhattasaṅkhāte attano santāne uppajjanārahā suvikappitā suṭṭhu vikappitā asesato, kiñcipi asesetvā susamucchinnāti attho. Taṃ saṅgamaticca arūpasaññīti ettha nti nipātamattaṃ. Atha vā hetuattho taṃsaddo. Yasmā anavasesena micchāvitakkā samucchinnā, tasmā rāgasaṅgādikaṃ pañcavidhaṃ saṅgaṃ, sabbampi vā kilesasaṅgaṃ [V 0.0285] aticca atikkamitvā atikkamanahetu rūpasabhāvābhāvato ruppanasaṅkhātassa ca vikārassa tattha abhāvato nibbikārahetubhāvato vā “arūpa”nti laddhanāmaṃ nibbānaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā pavattāhi maggaphalasaññāhi arūpasaññī. Catuyogātigatoti kāmayogo bhavayogo diṭṭhiyogo avijjāyogoti cattāro yoge yathārahaṃ catūhipi maggehi atikkamitvā gato. Na jātu metīti makāro padasandhikaro, jātu ekaṃseneva punabbhavāya na eti, āyatiṃ punabbhavābhinibbatti tassa natthīti attho. “Na [M 0.0318] jāti metī”tipi paṭhanti, so evattho. Iti bhagavā āyasmato subhūtissa arahattaphalasamāpattivihāraṃ anupādisesanibbānañca ārabbha pītivegavissaṭṭhaṃ udānaṃ udānesi.

Herein, yassa vitakkā vidhūpitā (‘for whom thoughts are dispelled’) refers to the noble person by whom, or of whom, all wrong thoughts such as sensual thoughts have been dispelled, scorched, and cut off by the knowledge of the noble path. Ajjhattaṃ suvikappitā asesā (‘internally well disposed of without remainder’) means that those thoughts that could arise in one's own continuity, designated as one's own internal sphere, are well disposed of, thoroughly disposed of, without remainder, utterly cut off leaving nothing behind. Taṃ saṅgam aticca arūpasaññī (‘having overcome attachment, he is a perceiver of the formless’): here the ‘ti’ is just a particle. Alternatively, the word taṃ has a causal sense. Because the wrong thoughts are cut off without remainder, therefore, having overcome and transcended the fivefold attachment beginning with the attachment of lust, or all attachments of the defilements, he is a ‘perceiver of the formless.’ He is so called because of the perceptions of path and fruit that proceed by taking as their object Nibbāna, which has obtained the name ‘formless’ (arūpa) by reason of transcending, because of the absence of the nature of form, because of the absence there of the alteration designated as ‘being afflicted’ (ruppana), or because it is the cause of the unalterable. Catuyogātigato (‘gone beyond the four yokes’) means he has gone beyond by transcending the four yokes—the yoke of sensuality, the yoke of existence, the yoke of views, and the yoke of ignorance—as is appropriate, by means of the four paths. Na jātu m-eti (‘he never comes’): the ‘m’ is for euphonic conjunction. Jātu means ‘certainly.’ He does not come to renewed existence; the meaning is that for him there is no generation of renewed existence in the future. Some also read na jāti m-eti (‘he does not come to birth’); the meaning is the same. Thus the Blessed One, with reference to the Venerable Subhūti’s abiding in the attainment of the fruit of arahantship and his final Nibbāna without residue remaining, uttered this inspired utterance impelled by a surge of joy.

Sattamasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Seventh Sutta is finished.

8. Gaṇikāsuttavaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Courtesan Sutta

58. Aṭṭhame dve pūgāti dve gaṇā. Aññatarissā gaṇikāyāti aññatarāya nagarasobhiniyā. Sārattāti suṭṭhu rattā. Paṭibaddhacittāti kilesavasena baddhacittā. Rājagahe kira ekasmiṃ chaṇadivase bahū dhuttapurisā gaṇabandhanena vicarantā ekamekassa ekamekaṃ vesiṃ ānetvā uyyānaṃ pavisitvā chaṇakīḷaṃ kīḷiṃsu. Tato parampi dve tayo chaṇadivase taṃ taṃyeva vesiṃ ānetvā chaṇakīḷaṃ kīḷiṃsu. Athāparasmiṃ [P 0.0350] chaṇadivase aññepi dhuttā tatheva chaṇakīḷaṃ kīḷitukāmā vesiyo ānentā purimadhuttehi pubbe ānītaṃ ekaṃ vesiṃ ānenti. Itare taṃ disvā “ayaṃ amhākaṃ pariggaho”ti āhaṃsu. Tepi tatheva āhaṃsu. “Evaṃ amhākaṃ pariggaho, amhākaṃ pariggaho”ti kalahaṃ vaḍḍhetvā pāṇippahārādīni akaṃsu. Tena vuttaṃ – “tena kho pana samayena rājagahe dve pūgā”tiādi. Tattha upakkamantīti paharanti. Maraṇampi nigacchantīti balavūpakkamehi maraṇaṃ upagacchanti, itarepi maraṇamattaṃ maraṇappamāṇadukkhaṃ pāpuṇanti.

58. In the eighth sutta, dve pūgā (two groups) means two factions. Aññatarissā gaṇikāya (of a certain courtesan) means of a certain city-beautifying woman. Sārattā (infatuated) means deeply attached. Paṭibaddhacittā (with mind bound) means with mind bound by way of the defilements. It seems that in Rājagaha, on a certain festival day, many roguish men wandering about in a band brought one courtesan for each, entered a park, and played festival games. Then for two or three more festival days they brought those very same courtesans and played festival games. Then on another festival day, other rogues, also wishing to play festival games in the same way, were bringing courtesans, and they brought one courtesan who had previously been brought by the former rogues. The others, seeing her, said, ‘She is our possession.’ These ones also said the same. Saying, ‘She is our possession! Our possession!’ they escalated the quarrel and came to blows and the like. Therefore it was said: ‘Now at that time in Rājagaha there were two groups,’ and so on. Therein, upakkamanti (they attack) means they strike. Maraṇam pi nigacchanti (they even come to death) means that through violent attacks some meet death, while others reach a measure of suffering equivalent to death.

Etamatthaṃ viditvāti etaṃ kāmesu gedhaṃ vivādamūlaṃ sabbānatthamūlanti sabbākārato viditvā. Imaṃ udānanti antadvaye ca majjhimāya paṭipattiyā ādīnavānisaṃsavibhāvanaṃ imaṃ udānaṃ udānesi.

Having understood this matter—that is, having understood in all its aspects this greed for sensual pleasures to be the root of conflict and the root of all calamity—the Blessed One uttered this inspired utterance, which makes plain the dangers and benefits concerning the two extremes and the middle practice.

Tattha [V 0.0286] yañca pattanti yaṃ rūpādipañcakāmaguṇajātaṃ pattaṃ “natthi kāmesu doso”ti diṭṭhiṃ purakkhatvā vā apurakkhatvā vā etarahi laddhaṃ anubhuyyamānaṃ. Yañca pattabbanti yañca kāmaguṇajātameva “bhuñjitabbā kāmā, paribhuñjitabbā kāmā, āsevitabbā kāmā, paṭisevitabbā kāmā, yo kāme paribhuñjati, so lokaṃ vaḍḍheti, yo lokaṃ vaḍḍheti, so bahuṃ puññaṃ pasavatī”ti diṭṭhiṃ upanissāya taṃ anissajjitvā katena kammunā anāgate pattabbaṃ anubhavitabbañca. Ubhayametaṃ rajānukiṇṇanti etaṃ ubhayaṃ [M 0.0319] pattaṃ pattabbañca rāgarajādīhi anukiṇṇaṃ. Sampatte hi vatthukāme anubhavanto rāgarajena vokiṇṇo hoti, tattha pana saṃkiliṭṭhacittassa phale āyatiṃ āpanne domanassuppattiyā dosarajena vokiṇṇo hoti, ubhayatthāpi moharajena vokiṇṇo hoti. Kassa panetaṃ rajānukiṇṇanti āha – “āturassānusikkhato”ti kāmapatthanāvasena kilesāturassa, tassa ca phalena dukkhāturassa ca ubhayatthāpi paṭikārābhilāsāya kilesaphale anusikkhato.

Therein, yañca pattam (and what has been attained) means the set of five strands of sensual pleasure—forms, etc.—that has been attained, obtained, and is now being experienced, whether or not one has placed at the forefront the view, ‘There is no fault in sensual pleasures.’ And yañca pattabbam (and what is to be attained) means that same set of sensual pleasures that is to be attained and experienced in the future through kamma done without relinquishing them, based on the view: ‘Sensual pleasures should be enjoyed, indulged in, frequented, and pursued; whoever indulges in sensual pleasures enhances the world, and whoever enhances the world generates much merit.’ Ubhayam etaṃ rajānukiṇṇam (both these are strewn with dust) means that both what has been attained and what is to be attained are strewn with the dust of lust and so on. For when one experiences available sensual objects, one is strewn with the dust of lust. Then, when the fruit ripens in the future for one with a defiled mind, with the arising of sorrow one is strewn with the dust of aversion. In both cases, one is strewn with the dust of delusion. But for whom are these strewn with dust? He said: āturassānusikkhato (of one who is sick and trains accordingly). This refers to one who is sick with defilements by way of craving for sensual pleasures, and sick with suffering by way of their fruit; and who, in both cases, trains in accordance with the defilements and their fruit out of a desire for a remedy.

Tathā yañca pattanti yaṃ acelakavatādivasena pattaṃ attaparitāpanaṃ[P 0.0351]. Yañca pattabbanti yaṃ micchādiṭṭhikammasamādānahetu apāyesu pattabbaṃ phalaṃ. Ubhayametaṃ rajānukiṇṇanti tadubhayaṃ dukkharajānukiṇṇaṃ. Āturassāti kāyakilamathena dukkhāturassa. Anusikkhatoti micchādiṭṭhiṃ, tassā samādāyake puggale ca anusikkhato.

Similarly, yañca pattam (and what has been attained) means the self-torment that has been attained by way of such vows as naked asceticism. And yañca pattabbam (and what is to be attained) means the fruit to be attained in the planes of misery because of undertaking action based on wrong view. Ubhayam etaṃ rajānukiṇṇam (both these are strewn with dust) means that both are strewn with the dust of suffering. Āturassa (of one who is sick) means of one who is sick with suffering through bodily fatigue. Anusikkhato (who trains accordingly) means of one who trains in accordance with wrong view and the person who undertakes it.

Ye ca sikkhāsārāti yehi yathāsamādinnaṃ sīlabbatādisaṅkhātaṃ sikkhaṃ sārato gahetvā “iminā saṃsārasuddhī”ti kathitā. Tenāha – sīlabbataṃ jīvitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ upaṭṭhānasārāti. Tattha yaṃ “na karomī”ti oramati, taṃ sīlaṃ, visabhojanakicchācaraṇādikaṃ vataṃ, sākabhakkhatādijīvikā jīvitaṃ, methunavirati brahmacariyaṃ, etesaṃ anutiṭṭhanaṃ upaṭṭhānaṃ, bhūtapiṇḍakaparibhaṇḍādivasena khandhadevasivādiparicaraṇaṃ vā upaṭṭhānaṃ, evametehi yathāvuttehi sīlādīhi saṃsārasuddhi hotīti tāni sārato gahetvā ṭhitā samaṇabrāhmaṇā sikkhāsārā sīlabbataṃ jīvitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ “upaṭṭhānasārā”ti veditabbā. Ayameko antoti ayaṃ sīlabbataparāmāsavasena attakilamathānuyogasaṅkhāto majjhimāya paṭipattiyā uppathabhūto lāmakaṭṭhena ca eko anto. Ayaṃ dutiyo antoti ayaṃ kāmasukhallikānuyogo kāmesu pātabyatāpattisaṅkhāto dutiyo vuttanayena anto.

Ye ca sikkhāsārā (and those for whom training is the essence) refers to those who have taken as the essence the training—designated as precepts, vows, etc., as undertaken by them—and have declared: ‘By this there is purification from saṃsāra.’ Therefore he said: sīlabbataṃ jīvitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ upaṭṭhānasārā (for whom precepts and vows, livelihood, and the holy life are the essence of their observance). Therein, sīla (precepts) is when one refrains, thinking, ‘I will not do this.’ Vata (vows) are such things as painful practices like eating unevenly. Jīvita (livelihood) is a way of life such as eating greens. Brahmacariya (holy life) is abstinence from sexual intercourse. Upaṭṭhāna (observance) is the undertaking of these, or it is the serving of deities such as Khandha and Siva, and spirits, by way of food-offerings, utensils, etc. Thus, those ascetics and brahmins who stand firm, having taken these aforesaid precepts and so on as the essence, thinking that by these there is purification from saṃsāra, are to be known as sikkhāsārā and sīlabbataṃ jīvitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ upaṭṭhānasārā. Ayam eko anto (this is one extreme) means this devotion to self-mortification by way of clinging to precepts and vows, which has become a wrong path in relation to the middle practice, and is one extreme because of its inferiority. Ayaṃ dutiyo anto (this is the second extreme) means this devotion to indulgence in sensual pleasure, designated as the state of being given to sensual pleasures, which is the second extreme in the way explained.

Iccete ubho antāti kāmasukhallikānuyogo attakilamathānuyogo ca iti ete ubho antā. Te ca kho etarahi patte, āyatiṃ pattabbe ca kilesadukkharajānukiṇṇe kāmaguṇe attaparitāpane [V 0.0287] ca allīnehi kilesadukkhāturānaṃ anusikkhantehi, sayañca [M 0.0320] kilesadukkhāturehi paṭipajjitabbattā lāmakā uppathabhūtā cāti antā. Kaṭasivaḍḍhanāti andhaputhujjanehi abhikaṅkhitabbaṭṭhena kaṭasisaṅkhātānaṃ taṇhāavijjānaṃ abhivaḍḍhanā. Kaṭasiyo diṭṭhiṃ vaḍḍhentīti tā pana [P 0.0352] kaṭasiyo nānappakāradiṭṭhiṃ vaḍḍhenti. Vatthukāmesu assādānupassino hi te pajahituṃ asakkontassa taṇhāavijjāsahakārīkāraṇaṃ labhitvā “natthi dinna”ntiādinā (dha. sa. 1221; vibha. 938) natthikadiṭṭhiṃ akiriyadiṭṭhiṃ ahetukadiṭṭhiñca gaṇhāpenti, attaparitāpanaṃ anuyuttassa pana avijjātaṇhāsahakārīkāraṇaṃ labhitvā “sīlena suddhi vatena suddhī”tiādinā attasuddhiabhilāsena sīlabbataparāmāsadiṭṭhiṃ gaṇhāpenti. Sakkāyadiṭṭhiyā pana tesaṃ paccayabhāvo pākaṭoyeva. Evaṃ antadvayūpanissayena taṇhāavijjānaṃ diṭṭhivaḍḍhakatā veditabbā. Keci pana “kaṭasīti pañcannaṃ khandhānaṃ adhivacana”nti vadanti. Tesaṃ yadaggena tato antadvayato saṃsārasuddhi na hoti, tadaggena te upādānakkhandhe abhivaḍḍhetīti adhippāyo. Apare pana “kaṭasivaḍḍhanā”ti padassa “aparāparaṃ jarāmaraṇehi sivathikavaḍḍhanā”ti atthaṃ vadanti. Tehipi antadvayassa saṃsārasuddhihetubhāvābhāvoyeva vutto, kaṭasiyā pana diṭṭhivaḍḍhanakāraṇabhāvo vattabbo.

Thus these are the two extremes: the pursuit of indulgence in sensual pleasures and the pursuit of self-mortification. These are the two extremes. And these are extremes because they are inferior and have become a wrong path, for they are to be practiced by those who are themselves afflicted with defilements and suffering, and by those who follow the afflicted, clinging to sensual pleasures and self-torment—which are attained now and to be attained in the future, and are strewn with the dust of defilements and suffering. 'Increase of the charnel ground' means the increase of craving and ignorance, designated as 'the charnel ground' because they are longed for by blind worldlings. 'The charnel grounds increase views' means that these charnel grounds increase various kinds of views. For one who dwells contemplating gratification in sensual objects, being unable to abandon them, having obtained the cooperative cause of craving and ignorance, they cause him to adopt the nihilistic view, the view of inaction, and the view of non-causality, with such thoughts as, 'There is nothing given,' etc. But for one devoted to self-torment, having obtained the cooperative cause of ignorance and craving, out of a desire for self-purification, they cause him to adopt the view of clinging to rules and observances with such thoughts as, 'Purity comes through virtue, purity comes through an observance.' Their being a condition for identity view is indeed evident. Thus it should be understood how craving and ignorance, with the two extremes as their support, increase views. Some, however, say that 'charnel ground' is a designation for the five aggregates. Their intention is that since there is no purification from saṃsāra by means of those two extremes, they thereby increase the aggregates subject to clinging. Still others say that the meaning of the term 'increase of the charnel ground' is 'the repeated increase of the cemetery through aging and death.' They too have stated that the two extremes are not a cause for purification from saṃsāra; but it should be said that the charnel ground is a cause for the increase of views.

Ete te ubho ante anabhiññāyāti te ete yathāvutte ubhopi ante ajānitvā “ime antā te ca evaṃgahitā evaṃanuṭṭhitā evaṃgatikā evaṃabhisamparāyā”ti evaṃ ajānanahetu ajānanakāraṇā. “Paññāya cassa disvā āsavā parikkhīṇā”tiādīsu (pu. pa. 208; a. ni. 9.43) viyassa hetuatthatā daṭṭhabbā. Olīyanti eketi eke kāmasukhānuyogavasena saṅkocaṃ āpajjanti. Atidhāvanti eketi eke attakilamathānuyogavasena atikkamanti. Kāmasukhamanuyuttā hi vīriyassa akaraṇato kosajjavasena sammāpaṭipattito saṅkocamāpannatā olīyanti nāma, attaparitāpanamanuyuttā pana kosajjaṃ pahāya anupāyena vīriyārambhaṃ karontā sammāpaṭipattiyā atikkamanato atidhāvanti nāma, tadubhayaṃ pana tattha ādīnavādassanato. Tena vuttaṃ – “ubho ante anabhiññāya olīyanti eke atidhāvanti eke”ti. Tattha taṇhābhinandanavasena olīyanti, diṭṭhābhinandanavasena atidhāvantīti veditabbaṃ.

“Not having directly known these two extremes”: not having known both these extremes as described—“These are the extremes, and they are thus grasped, thus practiced, have such a destination, such a future course”—thus, because of not knowing, for the reason of not knowing. The causal meaning of the instrumental case should be seen here as in such passages as: “And having seen with wisdom, his taints are destroyed.” “Some fall short”: some shrink back by way of the pursuit of indulgence in sensual pleasures. “Some overshoot”: some go too far by way of the pursuit of self-mortification. For those devoted to sensual pleasure, by not making an effort, through laziness they shrink back from the right practice; thus they are said to “fall short.” But those devoted to self-torment, having abandoned laziness, make an effort by a wrong method and thus go beyond the right practice; thus they are said to “overshoot,” since both are spoken of as disadvantageous in this context. Therefore it is said: “Not having directly known the two extremes, some fall short, some overshoot.” Herein, it should be understood that they fall short by way of delighting in craving, and they overshoot by way of delighting in views.

Atha [M 0.0321] vā sassatābhinivesavasena olīyanti eke, ucchedābhinivesavasena atidhāvanti eke. Gosīlādivasena hi attaparitāpanamanuyuttā ekacce “imināhaṃ sīlena vā vatena vā tapena vā brahmacariyena vā [P 0.0353] devo vā bhavissāmi devaññataro vā, tattha nicco dhuvo sassato [V 0.0288] avipariṇāmadhammo sassatisamaṃ tatheva ṭhassāmī”ti sassatadassanaṃ abhinivisantā saṃsāre olīyanti nāma, kāmasukhamanuyuttā pana ekacce yaṃkiñci katvā indriyāni santappetukāmā lokāyatikā viya tadanuguṇaṃ ucchedadassanaṃ abhinivisantā anupāyena vaṭṭupacchedassa pariyesanato atidhāvanti nāma. Evaṃ sassatucchedavasenapi olīyanātidhāvanāni veditabbāni.

Alternatively, some fall short through adherence to eternalism, while others overshoot through adherence to annihilationism. For some who are devoted to self-mortification, such as those who practice the cow-vow, adhering to the eternalist view, think: “By this virtue or observance or austerity or holy life I will become a deva or a certain kind of deva. There I will be permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change; I will stand fast like the eternal.” Thus they are said to fall short in saṃsāra. But some who are devoted to sensual pleasures, wishing to gratify their faculties by any means, like the Lokāyatikas, adhere to the corresponding annihilationist view and are said to overshoot by seeking the cutting off of the round by a wrong method. Thus falling short and overshooting should be understood as being due to eternalism and annihilationism.

Ye ca kho te abhiññāyāti ye ca kho pana ariyapuggalā te yathāvutte ubho ante “ime antā evaṃgahitā evaṃanuṭṭhitā evaṃgatikā evaṃabhisamparāyā”ti abhivisiṭṭhena ñāṇena vipassanāsahitāya maggapaññāya jānitvā majjhimapaṭipadaṃ sammāpaṭipannā, tāya sammāpaṭipattiyā. Tatra ca nāhesunti tatra tasmiṃ antadvaye patitā na ahesuṃ, taṃ antadvayaṃ pajahiṃsūti attho. Tena ca nāmaññiṃsūti tena antadvayapahānena “mama idaṃ antadvayapahānaṃ, ahaṃ antadvayaṃ pahāsiṃ, iminā antadvayapahānena seyyo”tiādinā taṇhādiṭṭhimānamaññanāvasena na amaññiṃsu sabbamaññanānaṃ sammadeva pahīnattā. Ettha ca aggaphale ṭhite ariyapuggale sandhāya “tatra ca nāhesuṃ, tena ca nāmaññiṃsū”ti atītakālavasena ayaṃ desanā pavattā, maggakkhaṇe pana adhippete vattamānakālavaseneva vattabbaṃ siyā. Vaṭṭaṃ tesaṃ natthi paññāpanāyāti ye evaṃ pahīnasabbamaññanā uttamapurisā, tesaṃ anupādāparinibbutānaṃ kammavipākakilesavasena tividhampi vaṭṭaṃ natthi paññāpanāya, vattamānakkhandhabhedato uddhaṃ anupādāno viya jātavedo apaññattikabhāvameva gacchatīti attho.

“But those who have directly known them”: those noble persons who, having known the two extremes as described—“These are the extremes, they are thus grasped, thus practiced, have such a destination, such a future course”—with superior knowledge, that is, with the path-wisdom accompanied by insight, have rightly entered upon the middle path; by that right practice. “And they were not therein”: they were not fallen into those two extremes; the meaning is that they abandoned the two extremes. “And by that they did not conceive”: by that abandonment of the two extremes, they did not conceive by way of the conceivings of craving, view, and conceit, such as “This abandonment of the two extremes is mine,” “I have abandoned the two extremes,” “By this abandonment of the two extremes I am superior,” etc., because all conceivings have been rightly abandoned. Here, this teaching, “they were not therein, and by that they did not conceive,” is stated in the past tense with reference to the noble person established in the highest fruit. But if the path-moment is intended, it should be stated in the present tense. “For them there is no round for designation”: for those supreme persons who have thus abandoned all conceivings, who are fully extinguished without clinging, the threefold round—of kamma, its result, and defilements—does not exist for designation. The meaning is that after the breakup of the present aggregates, like a fire without fuel, they reach a state that cannot be designated.

Aṭṭhamasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Eighth Sutta is concluded.

9. Upātidhāvantisuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Upātidhāvanti Sutta
