59. Navame [M 0.0322][P 0.0354] rattandhakāratimisāyanti rattiyaṃ andhakāre mahātimisāyaṃ. Rattīpi hi andhakāravirahitā hoti, yā puṇṇamāya ratti juṇhobhāsitā. Andhakāropi “timisā”ti na vattabbo hoti abbhamahikādiupakkilesavirahite deve. Mahandhakāro hi “timisā”ti vuccati. Ayaṃ pana amāvasī ratti devo ca meghapaṭalasañchanno. Tena vuttaṃ – “rattandhakāratimisāyanti [V 0.0289] rattiyā andhakāre mahātimisāya”nti. Abbhokāseti appaṭicchanne okāse vihāraṅgaṇe. Telappadīpesu jhāyamānesūti telapajjotesu jalamānesu.

59. In the ninth: “In the darkness and gloom of the night” means at night, in the darkness, in the great gloom. For a night may be without darkness, as when a full-moon night is illuminated by moonlight. And darkness is not called “gloom” when the sky is free from such defilements as clouds and mist, for it is great darkness that is called “gloom.” But this was a new-moon night and the sky was covered by a blanket of clouds. Therefore it was said, “in the darkness and gloom of the night,” meaning, “at night, in the darkness, in the great gloom.” “In the open” means in an uncovered space, in the monastery courtyard. “While the oil lamps were burning” means while the oil flames were blazing.

Nanu ca bhagavato byāmappabhā pakatiyā byāmamattappadesaṃ abhibyāpetvā candimasūriyālokaṃ abhibhavitvā ghanabahalaṃ buddhālokaṃ vissajjentī andhakāraṃ vidhamitvā tiṭṭhati, kāyappabhāpi nīlapītādivasena chabbaṇṇaghanabuddharasmiyo vissajjetvā pakatiyāva samantato asītihatthappadesaṃ obhāsentī tiṭṭhati, evaṃ buddhālokeneva ekobhāsabhūte bhagavato nisinnokāse padīpakaraṇe kiccaṃ natthīti? Saccaṃ natthi, tathāpi puññatthikā upāsakā bhagavato bhikkhusaṅghassa ca pūjākaraṇatthaṃ devasikaṃ telappadīpaṃ upaṭṭhapenti. Tathā hi vuttaṃ – sāmaññaphalepi “ete maṇḍalamāle dīpā jhāyantī”ti (dī. ni. 1.159). “Rattandhakāratimisāya”nti idampi tassā rattiyā sabhāvakittanatthaṃ vuttaṃ, na pana bhagavato nisinnokāsassa andhakārabhāvato. Pūjākaraṇatthameva hi tadāpi upāsakehi padīpā kāritā.

But does not the Blessed One’s fathom-wide aura, by its nature, pervade an area of a fathom, overpower the light of the moon and sun, and stand dispelling the darkness while emitting a dense, thick Buddha-light? And does not his bodily radiance, by its nature, emit dense Buddha-rays of six colors—blue, yellow, and so on—and stand illuminating an area of eighty cubits all around? Thus, since the place where the Blessed One was sitting had become a single mass of light from the Buddha-light, was there any need to provide lamps? Truly, there was no need. Nevertheless, lay followers desirous of merit provide a daily oil lamp for the purpose of honoring the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. For so it is said in the Sāmaññaphala Sutta: “These lamps are burning in the assembly hall.” The phrase “in the darkness and gloom of the night” was stated to describe the natural condition of that night, not because the place where the Blessed One sat was dark. For on that occasion too, lamps were provided by the lay followers solely for the purpose of making an offering.

Tasmiñhi divase sāvatthivāsino bahū upāsakā pātova sarīrapaṭijagganaṃ katvā vihāraṃ gantvā uposathaṅgāni samādiyitvā buddhappamukhaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ nimantetvā nagaraṃ pavisitvā mahādānāni pavattetvā bhagavantaṃ bhikkhusaṅghañca anugantvā nivattitvā attano attano gehāni gantvā sayampi paribhuñjitvā suddhavatthanivatthā suddhuttarāsaṅgā gandhamālādihatthā vihāraṃ gantvā bhagavantaṃ pūjetvā keci manobhāvanīye bhikkhū payirupāsantā keci yonisomanasikarontā divasabhāgaṃ vītināmesuṃ. Te sāyanhasamaye bhagavato santike [P 0.0355] dhammaṃ sutvā satthari dhammasabhāmaṇḍapato paṭṭhāya [M 0.0323] gandhakuṭisamīpe ajjhokāse paññattavarabuddhāsane nisinne, bhikkhusaṅghe ca bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā payirupāsante uposathavisodhanatthañceva yonisomanasikāraparibrūhanatthañca nagaraṃ agantvā vihāreyeva vasitukāmā ohīyiṃsu. Atha te bhagavato bhikkhusaṅghassa ca pūjākaraṇatthaṃ bahū telappadīpe āropetvā satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā bhikkhusaṅghassa ca añjaliṃ katvā bhikkhūnaṃ pariyante nisinnā kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ, “bhante, ime titthiyā nānāvidhāni diṭṭhigatāni abhinivissa voharanti, tathā voharantā ca kadāci sassataṃ, kadāci asassataṃ, ucchedādīsu aññataranti ekasmiṃyeva aṭṭhatvā navanavāni diṭṭhigatāni ‘idameva saccaṃ moghamañña’nti paggayha tiṭṭhanti ummattakasadisā, tesaṃ tathā abhiniviṭṭhānaṃ kā gati, ko abhisamparāyo”ti. Tena ca samayena bahū paṭaṅgapāṇakā patantā patantā tesu telappadīpesu nipatanti. Tena vuttaṃ – “tena kho pana samayena sambahulā adhipātakā”tiādi.

On that day, many lay followers from Sāvatthī, having attended to their bodily needs early in the morning, went to the monastery, undertook the Uposatha observances, invited the Saṅgha of bhikkhus with the Buddha at its head, entered the city, arranged a great distribution of alms, and after accompanying the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, they turned back, went to their respective homes, and ate their meal. Then, dressed in clean lower and upper robes, with perfumes and garlands in hand, they went to the monastery and honored the Blessed One. Some spent the day attending on bhikkhus who inspire confidence, while others practiced wise attention. In the evening, after they had heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, when the Teacher had gone from the Dhamma-hall pavilion and was sitting on the excellent Buddha-seat prepared in the open near the fragrant chamber, and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus had approached and was attending on him, they remained behind in the monastery, not wishing to go to the city, both to purify the Uposatha and to cultivate wise attention. Then, for the purpose of honoring the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, they lit many oil lamps, approached the Teacher, paid homage, and, having made the añjali gesture to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, they sat down at the edge of the bhikkhus and initiated a discussion: 'Venerable sir, these sectarians, adhering to various views, declare them. In so doing, they sometimes declare eternalism, sometimes non-eternalism, or one of the other views such as annihilationism. Yet, having become stuck on one view, they keep upholding ever new views, asserting, "This alone is true, anything else is wrong," like madmen. What is their destination, what is their future course?' And at that time, many moths, fluttering about, were falling into those oil lamps. Therefore it was said: 'Now at that time, numerous moths…' and so on.

Tattha [V 0.0290] adhipātakāti paṭaṅgapāṇakā, ye “salabhā”tipi vuccanti. Te hi dīpasikhaṃ adhipatanato “adhipātakā”ti adhippetā. Āpātaparipātanti āpātaṃ paripātaṃ, āpatitvā āpatitvā paripatitvā paripatitvā, abhimukhapātañceva paribbhamitvā pātañca katvāti attho. “Āpāthe paripāta”nti keci paṭhanti, āpāthe padīpassa attano āpāthagamane sati paripatitvā paripatitvāti attho. Anayanti avaḍḍhiṃ dukkhaṃ. Byasananti vināsaṃ. Purimapadena hi maraṇamattaṃ dukkhaṃ, pacchimapadena maraṇaṃ tesaṃ dīpeti. Tattha keci pāṇakā saha patanena mariṃsu, keci maraṇamattaṃ dukkhaṃ āpajjiṃsu.

Herein, 'moths' (adhipātakā) are winged insects, which are also called 'salabhā.' They are intended by the term 'adhipātakā' because they fall upon (adhipatanti) the lamp flame. 'Plunging and falling all around' (āpātaparipātaṃ) means plunging and falling, falling upon again and again, falling all around again and again; the meaning is that they made both a headlong fall and a fall after circling around. Some read 'āpāthe paripātaṃ,' meaning, 'when it comes into their path, into the range of the lamp, they fall all around again and again.' 'They come to misfortune' (anayaṃ) means decline and suffering. 'And calamity' (byasanaṃ) means destruction. By the former term, mortal suffering is indicated; by the latter, their death is shown. Among them, some insects died as soon as they fell; others met with mortal suffering.

Etamatthaṃ viditvāti etaṃ adhipātakapāṇakānaṃ attahitaṃ ajānantānaṃ attupakkamavasena niratthakabyasanāpattiṃ viditvā tesaṃ viya diṭṭhigatikānaṃ diṭṭhābhinivesena anayabyasanāpattidīpakaṃ imaṃ udānaṃ udānesi.

Having understood this matter: having understood that these moths, not knowing their own welfare, met with a pointless calamity through their own endeavor, the Blessed One uttered this inspired utterance to illuminate how those who fare according to views, like them, meet with misfortune and calamity through their adherence to views.

Tattha upātidhāvanti na sāramentīti sīlasamādhipaññāvimuttiādibhedaṃ [P 0.0356] sāraṃ na enti, catusaccābhisamayavasena na adhigacchanti. Tasmiṃ pana saupāye sāre tiṭṭhanteyeva vimuttābhilāsāya taṃ upentā viya hutvāpi diṭṭhivipallāsena atidhāvanti atikkamitvā gacchanti, pañcupādānakkhandhe “niccaṃ [M 0.0324] subhaṃ sukhaṃ attā”ti abhinivisitvā gaṇhantāti attho. Navaṃ navaṃ bandhanaṃ brūhayantīti tathā gaṇhantā ca taṇhādiṭṭhisaṅkhātaṃ navaṃ navaṃ bandhanaṃ brūhayanti vaḍḍhayanti. Patanti pajjotamivādhipātakā, diṭṭhe sute itiheke niviṭṭhāti evaṃ taṇhādiṭṭhibandhanehi baddhattā eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā diṭṭhe attanā cakkhuviññāṇena diṭṭhidassaneneva vā diṭṭhe anussavūpalabbhamatteneva ca sute “itiha ekantato evameta”nti niviṭṭhā diṭṭhābhinivesena “sassata”ntiādinā abhiniviṭṭhā, ekantahitaṃ vā nissaraṇaṃ ajānantā rāgādīhi ekādasahi aggīhi ādittaṃ bhavattayasaṅkhātaṃ aṅgārakāsuṃyeva ime viya adhipātakā imaṃ pajjotaṃ patanti, na tato sīsaṃ ukkhipituṃ sakkontīti attho.

Herein, 'They run past and do not take as essence': they do not go to the essence, that is, they do not attain by way of the direct realization of the Four Truths the essence comprising such things as virtue, concentration, wisdom, and liberation. Though, while standing right in the essence together with its means, they seem to be approaching it with a desire for liberation, they run past it—they pass it by—due to the perversion of view. The meaning is that they grasp the five aggregates subject to clinging, adhering to them as 'permanent, beautiful, pleasant, self.' 'They build up a new bondage ever anew': by grasping in this way, they build up, they augment, a new bondage ever anew, which is called craving and views. 'They fall into the flame like moths; some are settled on the seen and the heard': Thus, being bound by the bonds of craving and views, some ascetics and brahmins are settled on what is seen—seen by themselves with eye-consciousness or just by the seeing of a view—and on what is heard, which is merely obtained by oral tradition, convinced that 'it is just so, absolutely.' Adhering to views such as eternalism, and not knowing the escape which is the ultimate good, they fall into the pit of embers called the triple existence, which is ablaze with the eleven fires of lust and so on, just as these moths fall into this flame. The meaning is that they are unable to lift their heads out of it.

Navamasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the ninth sutta is finished.

10. Uppajjantisuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Uppajjanti Sutta

60. Dasame yāvakīvanti yattakaṃ kālaṃ. Yatoti yadā, yato paṭṭhāya, yasmiṃ kāleti vā [V 0.0291] attho. Evametaṃ, ānandāti, ānanda, tathāgate uppanne tathāgatassa tathāgatasāvakānaṃyeva ca lābhasakkāro abhivaḍḍhati, titthiyā pana nittejā vihatappabhā pahīnalābhasakkārā hontīti yaṃ tayā vuttaṃ, etaṃ evaṃ, na etassa aññathābhāvo. Cakkavattino hi cakkaratanassa pātubhāvena loko cakkaratanaṃ muñcitvā aññattha pūjāsakkārasammānaṃ na pavatteti, cakkaratanameva pana sabbo loko sabbabhāvehi sakkaroti garuṃ karoti māneti pūjeti. Iti vaṭṭānusāripuññamattanissandassapi tāva mahanto ānubhāvo, kimaṅgaṃ [P 0.0357] pana vivaṭṭānusāripuññaphalūpatthambhassa anantāparimeyyaguṇagaṇādhārassa buddharatanassa dhammaratanassa saṅgharatanassa cāti dasseti.

60. In the tenth sutta, 'as long as' (yāvakīvaṃ) means for whatever length of time. 'From when' (yato) means when, from when, or at what time. 'So it is, Ānanda': Ānanda, what you have said is indeed so—that when a Tathāgata arises, the gain and honor of the Tathāgata and the Tathāgata's disciples increase, while the sectarians become powerless, their radiance destroyed, deprived of gain and honor. It is not otherwise. For when the Wheel-Treasure of a Wheel-Turning Monarch appears, the world does not, abandoning the Wheel-Treasure, offer worship, honor, or respect elsewhere. Instead, the entire world in every way honors, reveres, esteems, and worships the Wheel-Treasure. Thus, if even the mere result of merit that follows the round of existence has such great power, how much more so the Buddha Jewel, the Dhamma Jewel, and the Saṅgha Jewel—the receptacle for a collection of infinite and immeasurable virtues, supported by the fruit of merit that leads beyond the round? This is shown.

Bhagavā hi sammāsambodhiṃ patvā pavattavaradhammacakko anukkamena loke ekasaṭṭhiyā arahantesu jātesu saṭṭhi arahante janapadacārikāya vissajjetvā uruvelaṃ patvā uruvelakassapappamukhe sahassajaṭile arahatte patiṭṭhāpetvā tehi parivuto laṭṭhivanuyyāne nisīditvā bimbisārappamukhānaṃ aṅgamagadhavāsīnaṃ dvādasa nahutāni sāsane otāretvā yadā rājagahe vihāsi, tato paṭṭhāya bhagavato bhikkhusaṅghassa [M 0.0325] ca yathā yathā uparūpari uḷāralābhasakkāro abhivaḍḍhati, tathā tathā sabbatitthiyānaṃ lābhasakkāro parihāyi eva.

For the Blessed One, having attained perfect enlightenment and set in motion the excellent Wheel of the Dhamma, proceeded gradually. When sixty-one arahants had arisen in the world, he sent forth sixty arahants on a journey through the countryside. Then, arriving at Uruvelā, he established the thousand matted-hair ascetics headed by Uruvelā Kassapa in arahantship. Surrounded by them, he sat down in the Laṭṭhivana grove and led twelve myriads of the inhabitants of Aṅga and Magadha, headed by King Bimbisāra, into the Dispensation. When he was dwelling at Rājagaha, from that time onward, just as the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus received increasingly abundant gain and honor, so did the gain and honor of all the sectarians decline.

Athekadivasaṃ āyasmā ānando divāṭṭhāne nisinno bhagavato ca ariyasaṅghassa ca sammāpaṭipattiṃ paccavekkhitvā pītisomanassajāto “kathaṃ nu kho titthiyāna”nti tesaṃ paṭipattiṃ āvajjesi. Athassa nesaṃ sabbathāpi duppaṭipattiyeva upaṭṭhāsi. So “evaṃmahānubhāve nāma puññūpanissayassa dhammānudhammappaṭipattiyā ca ukkaṃsapāramippatte bhagavati, ariyasaṅghe ca dharante kathaṃ ime aññatitthiyā evaṃ duppaṭipannā akatapuññā varākā lābhino sakkatā bhavissantī”ti titthiyānaṃ lābhasakkārahāniṃ nissāya kāruññaṃ uppādetvā atha attano parivitakkaṃ “yāvakīvañca, bhante”tiādinā bhagavato ārocesi. Bhagavā ca taṃ, “ānanda, tayā micchā parivitakkita”nti avatvā suvaṇṇāliṅgasadisaṃ gīvaṃ unnāmetvā supupphitasatapattasassirikaṃ mahāmukhaṃ abhippasannataraṃ katvā “evametaṃ, ānandā”ti sampahaṃsitvā “yāvakīvañcā”tiādinā tassa vacanaṃ paccanumodi. Tena vuttaṃ – “atha kho āyasmā ānando…pe… bhikkhusaṅgho cā”ti. Atha bhagavā tassaṃ aṭṭhuppattiyaṃ atītepi mayi anuppanne ekacce nīcajanā sammānaṃ labhitvā mama uppādato paṭṭhāya hatalābhasakkārā ahesunti bāverujātakaṃ (jā. 1.4.153 ādayo) kathesi.

Then one day, the Venerable Ānanda, seated in his daytime dwelling, reflected on the right practice of the Blessed One and the noble Saṅgha. Filled with rapture and happiness, he considered the practice of the sectarians, thinking: "How is it with them?" It then became clear to him that their practice was entirely wrong. He thought: "While the Blessed One—of such great power, supported by merit, practicing the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma, and having reached the highest perfection—and the noble Saṅgha are present, how can these other sectarians, so wrongly practiced, without merit, so wretched, become recipients of gain and honor?" Arousing compassion for the sectarians on account of their loss of gain and honor, he then reported his thought to the Blessed One, beginning with, "For as long as, venerable sir…." The Blessed One, without saying, "Ānanda, you have thought wrongly," raised his neck, which was like a golden drum, made his great face—splendid as a fully bloomed hundred-petaled lotus—even more radiant, and joyfully affirmed: "So it is, Ānanda," approving his words with, "For as long as…." Thus it was said: "Then the Venerable Ānanda… and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus…." Then the Blessed One, on that occasion, recounted the Bāveru Jātaka (Jā 1.4.153ff), explaining that even in the past, before his arising, some lowly people gained honor, but from the time of his arising, they were deprived of gain and honor.

Etamatthaṃ [V 0.0292] viditvāti diṭṭhigatikānaṃ tāva sakkārasammāno yāva na [P 0.0358] sammāsambuddhā loke uppajjanti, tesaṃ pana uppādato paṭṭhāya te hatalābhasakkārā nippabhā nittejāva honti, duppaṭipattiyā dukkhato ca na muccantīti etamatthaṃ sabbākārato viditvā tadatthadīpanaṃ imaṃ udānaṃ udānesi.

Having understood this matter—"Those who hold speculative views receive honor and respect only so long as Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas do not arise in the world. But from the time of their arising, they are deprived of gain and honor, becoming lusterless and powerless; and because of their wrong practice, they are not freed from suffering"—having understood this matter in all its aspects, he uttered this inspired utterance to illuminate its meaning.

Tattha obhāsati tāva so kimīti so khajjūpanakakimi tāvadeva obhāsati jotati dibbati. Yāva na unnamate pabhaṅkaroti tīsupi mahādīpesu ekakkhaṇe ālokakaraṇena “pabhaṅkaro”ti laddhanāmo sūriyo yāva na uggamati na udeti. Anuggate hi sūriye laddhokāsā khajjūpanakā viparivattamānāpi kaṇṭakaphalasadisā tamasi vijjotanti. Sa verocanamhi uggate, hatappabho hoti na cāpi bhāsatīti samantato [M 0.0326] andhakāraṃ vidhamitvā kiraṇasahassena virocanasabhāvatāya verocananāmake ādicce uṭṭhite so khajjūpanako hatappabho nittejo kāḷako hoti, rattandhakāre viya na bhāsati na dibbati.

Herein, “the worm shines only so long” means that the glow-worm shines, gleams, and radiates only for that long. “Until the Light-maker rises” means: until the sun—which has received the name “Light-maker” (pabhaṅkara) because it illuminates the three great continents in a single moment—rises and comes up. For when the sun has not yet risen, the glow-worms, having found their opportunity, gleam in the darkness like thorn-fruits even while moving about. “But when the Illuminator has risen, its splendor is lost and it shines no more” means: when the sun named “the Illuminator” (Verocana)—so-called because its nature is to shine with a thousand rays, having dispelled the darkness all around—has risen, that glow-worm's splendor is lost. It becomes powerless and dark; it does not shine or gleam as it did in the darkness of night.

Evaṃ obhāsitameva takkikānanti yathā tena khajjūpanakena sūriyuggamanato pureyeva obhāsitaṃ hoti, evaṃ takketvā vitakketvā parikappanamattena diṭṭhīnaṃ gahaṇato “takkikā”ti laddhanāmehi titthiyehi obhāsitaṃ attano samayatejena dīpetvā adhiṭṭhitaṃ tāva, yāva sammāsambuddhā loke nuppajjanti. Na takkikā sujjhanti na cāpi sāvakāti yadā pana sammāsambuddhā loke uppajjanti, tadā diṭṭhigatikā na sujjhanti na sobhanti, na cāpi tesaṃ sāvakā sobhanti, aññadatthu vihatasobhā rattikhittā viya sarā na paññāyanteva. Atha vā yāva sammāsambuddhā loke nuppajjanti, tāvadeva takkikānaṃ obhāsitaṃ attano samayena jotanaṃ bālalāpanaṃ, na tato paraṃ. Kasmā? Yasmā na takkikā sujjhanti, na cāpi sāvakā. Te hi durakkhātadhammavinayā sammāpaṭipattirahitā na saṃsārato sujjhanti aniyyānikasāsanattā. Tenāha “duddiṭṭhī na dukkhā pamuccare”ti. Takkikā hi ayāthāvaladdhikatāya [P 0.0359] duddiṭṭhino micchābhiniviṭṭhadiṭṭhikā viparītadassanā taṃ diṭṭhiṃ anissajjitvā saṃsāradukkhato na kadācipi muccantīti.

“So do the speculators shine” means: just as that glow-worm shines only before the sun rises, so the shining of the sectarians—who get the name “speculators” (takkikā) because they grasp views merely by reasoning, thinking, and imagining—illuminating and establishing with the power of their own doctrine, lasts only as long as Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas do not arise in the world. “The speculators are not purified, nor their disciples” means: when Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas arise in the world, then the speculative theorists do not shine, nor do their disciples shine. On the contrary, their splendor destroyed, like arrows shot at night, they are not even perceived. Or alternatively: as long as Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas do not arise in the world, for just so long is the shining of the speculators, their illuminating with their own doctrine, a childish prattle, and nothing more. Why? Because the speculators are not purified, nor are their disciples. For they, with a Dhamma and Discipline that is poorly proclaimed and being devoid of right practice, are not purified from saṃsāra because their teaching is not emancipating. Therefore he said: “Those of wrong view are not freed from suffering.” For the speculators, being of wrong view because of their unauthentic attainment, holding to their views with wrong adherence, having a distorted vision, do not ever escape from the suffering of saṃsāra without having abandoned that view.

Dasamasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the tenth discourse is finished.

Niṭṭhitā ca jaccandhavaggavaṇṇanā.

The commentary on the Jaccandha Vagga is finished.

7. Cūḷavaggo

7. The Lesser Chapter

1. Paṭhamalakuṇḍakabhaddiyasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the First Discourse on Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya

61. Cūḷavaggassa [M 0.0327][V 0.0293][P 0.0360] paṭhame lakuṇḍakabhaddiyanti ettha bhaddiyoti tassa āyasmato nāmaṃ, kāyassa pana rassattā “lakuṇḍakabhaddiyo”ti naṃ sañjānanti. So kira sāvatthivāsī kulaputto mahaddhano mahābhogo rūpena apāsādiko dubbaṇṇo duddasiko okoṭimako. So ekadivasaṃ satthari jetavane viharante upāsakehi saddhiṃ vihāraṃ gantvā dhammadesanaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā laddhūpasampado satthu santike kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā vipassanāya kammaṃ karonto sotāpattiphalaṃ pāpuṇi. Tadā sekkhā bhikkhū yebhuyyena āyasmantaṃ sāriputtaṃ upasaṅkamitvā uparimaggatthāya kammaṭṭhānaṃ yācanti, dhammadesanaṃ yācanti, pañhaṃ pucchanti. So tesaṃ adhippāyaṃ pūrento kammaṭṭhānaṃ ācikkhati, dhammaṃ deseti, pañhaṃ vissajjeti. Te ghaṭentā vāyamantā appekacce sakadāgāmiphalaṃ, appekacce anāgāmiphalaṃ, appekacce arahattaṃ, appekacce tisso vijjā, appekacce chaḷabhiññā, appekacce catasso paṭisambhidā adhigacchanti. Te disvā lakuṇḍakabhaddiyopi sekho samāno kālaṃ ñatvā attano cittakallatañca sallekhañca paccavekkhitvā dhammasenāpatiṃ upasaṅkamitvā katapaṭisanthāro sammodamāno dhammadesanaṃ yāci. Sopissa ajjhāsayassa anurūpaṃ kathaṃ kathesi. Tena vuttaṃ – “tena kho pana samayena āyasmā sāriputto āyasmantaṃ lakuṇḍakabhaddiyaṃ anekapariyāyena dhammiyā kathāya sandassetī”tiādi.

61. In the first [sutta] of the Lesser Chapter, concerning Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya: here, 'Bhaddiya' is that venerable one’s name, but because of the shortness of his body, they knew him as 'Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya.' It is said that he was a clansman from Sāvatthī, very wealthy and prosperous, but unpleasing in appearance, of bad complexion, unpleasant to see, and dwarfish. One day, while the Teacher was dwelling in the Jeta Grove, he went to the monastery with lay followers, heard a Dhamma discourse, and having gained faith, went forth. Having received the higher ordination, he took a meditation subject from the Teacher and, by working at insight, he attained the fruit of stream-entry. At that time, monks in higher training would for the most part approach the Venerable Sāriputta to request a meditation subject for the higher paths, ask for a Dhamma discourse, or pose questions. Fulfilling their wishes, he would explain the meditation subject, teach the Dhamma, and answer their questions. Striving and exerting themselves, some attained the fruit of once-returning, some the fruit of non-returning, some arahantship, some the three true knowledges, some the six higher knowledges, and some the four analytical knowledges. Seeing this, Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya, who was also a trainee, recognizing the right time and reflecting on his own mental readiness and effacement, approached the General of the Dhamma, exchanged courteous greetings, and requested a Dhamma discourse. He spoke to him in a manner suited to his disposition. Thus it is said: 'On that occasion the Venerable Sāriputta was instructing, encouraging, inspiring, and gladdening the Venerable Lakuṇḍakabhaddiya in various ways with a Dhamma talk,' and so on.

Tattha [P 0.0361] anekapariyāyenāti “itipi pañcakkhandhā aniccā, itipi dukkhā, itipi anattā”ti evaṃ anekehi kāraṇehi. Dhammiyā kathāyāti pañcannaṃ upādānakkhandhānaṃ udayabbayādipakāsaniyā dhammiyā kathāya. Sandassetīti tāniyeva aniccādilakkhaṇāni udayabbayādike ca sammā dasseti, hatthena gahetvā viya paccakkhato dasseti. Samādapetīti tattha [M 0.0328] lakkhaṇārammaṇikaṃ vipassanaṃ sammā ādapeti, yathā vīthipaṭipannā hutvā pavattati, evaṃ gaṇhāpeti. Samuttejetīti vipassanāya āraddhāya saṅkhārānaṃ udayabbayādīsu upaṭṭhahantesu yathākālaṃ [V 0.0294] paggahaniggahasamupekkhaṇehi bojjhaṅgānaṃ anupavattanena bhāvanaṃ majjhimaṃ vīthiṃ otāretvā yathā vipassanāñāṇaṃ sūraṃ pasannaṃ hutvā vahati, evaṃ indriyānaṃ visadabhāvakaraṇena vipassanācittaṃ sammā uttejeti, visadāpanavasena vodapeti. Sampahaṃsetīti tathā pavattiyamānāya vipassanāya samappavattabhāvanāvasena ceva upariladdhabbabhāvanābalena ca cittaṃ sammā pahaṃseti, laddhassādavasena vā suṭṭhu toseti. Anupādāya āsavehi cittaṃ vimuccīti yathā yathā dhammasenāpati dhammaṃ deseti, tathā tathā tathalakkhaṇaṃ vipassantassa therassa ca desanānubhāvena, attano ca upanissayasampattiyā ñāṇassa paripākaṃ gatattā desanānusārena ñāṇe anupavattante kāmāsavādīsu kañci āsavaṃ aggahetvā maggapaṭipāṭiyāva anavasesato cittaṃ vimucci, arahattaphalaṃ sacchākāsīti attho.

Herein, 'in many ways' means for various reasons, such as: 'Thus the five aggregates are impermanent; thus they are suffering; thus they are non-self.' 'With a Dhamma talk' refers to a discourse that illuminates the arising and passing away, and so forth, of the five aggregates subject to clinging. 'He instructs' means he correctly points out those very characteristics of impermanence, etc., and the arising and passing away, making them directly perceptible as if holding them in his hand. 'He encourages' means he makes one properly undertake insight meditation focused on those characteristics, ensuring it proceeds along the path. 'He inspires' means that when insight has been undertaken and the arising and passing away of formations become apparent, by applying the factors of enlightenment with timely balancing of energy, restraint, and equanimity, he steers the meditation along the middle path so that insight knowledge flows strong and lucid; by clarifying the faculties, he properly inspires the mind of insight. 'He gladdens' means that as insight thus progresses, he gladdens the mind through the balanced development of meditation and the power of the development yet to be attained, or he thoroughly delights it with the taste that has been obtained. 'His mind was liberated from the taints without clinging' means that as the General of the Dhamma taught the Dhamma, the elder was contemplating those characteristics accordingly. Then, through the power of the discourse and because the perfection of his own supporting condition had brought his knowledge to maturity, as his knowledge followed along with the discourse, his mind was liberated from the taints without remainder—without grasping any taint such as the taint of sensual desire—in the very sequence of the path. The meaning is that he realized the fruit of arahantship.

Etamatthaṃ viditvāti etaṃ āyasmato lakuṇḍakabhaddiyassa aññārādhanasaṅkhātaṃ atthaṃ sabbākārato viditvā tadatthadīpanaṃ imaṃ udānaṃ udānesi.

Having understood this matter: Having known in all its aspects this matter concerning the Venerable Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya, designated as the attainment of final knowledge, the Blessed One uttered this inspired utterance to illuminate that meaning.

Tattha uddhanti rūpadhātuyā arūpadhātuyā ca. Adhoti kāmadhātuyā. Sabbadhīti sabbasmimpi saṅkhāragate. Vippamuttoti pubbabhāge vikkhambhanavimuttiyā aparabhāge samucchedapaṭipassaddhivimuttīhi sabbappakārena vimutto. Ettha ca uddhaṃ vippamuttoti etena pañcuddhambhāgiyasaṃyojanapahānaṃ dasseti. Adho vippamuttoti etena pañcorambhāgiyasaṃyojanapahānaṃ. Sabbadhi [P 0.0362] vippamuttoti etena avasiṭṭhasabbākusalapahānaṃ dasseti. Atha vā uddhanti anāgatakālaggahaṇaṃ. Adhoti atītakālaggahaṇaṃ. Ubhayaggahaṇeneva tadubhayapaṭisaṃyuttattā paccuppanno addhā gahito hoti, tattha anāgatakālaggahaṇena anāgatakkhandhāyatanadhātuyo gahitā. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Sabbadhīti kāmabhedādike sabbasmiṃ bhave. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – anāgato atīto paccuppannoti evaṃ tiyaddhasaṅgahite sabbasmiṃ bhave vippamuttoti.

Herein, 'above' refers to the form realm and the formless realm. 'Below' refers to the sensual sphere. 'Everywhere' means in all conditioned existence. 'Fully liberated' indicates liberation in the preliminary stage through suppression, and in the later stage through eradication and tranquillization, being completely free in every way. Herein, 'liberated above' signifies the abandonment of the five higher fetters. 'Liberated below' signifies the abandonment of the five lower fetters. 'Liberated everywhere' signifies the abandonment of all remaining unwholesome states. Alternatively, 'above' refers to grasping future time. 'Below' refers to grasping past time. By grasping both, the present time is included, as it is connected to both. Therein, grasping future time includes the future aggregates, bases, and elements. The same method applies to the remaining terms. 'Everywhere' means in all existence, such as the divisions of the sensual sphere. This is said to mean: liberated in all existence, encompassed by the three times—future, past, and present.

Ayaṃhamasmīti [M 0.0329] anānupassīti yo evaṃ vippamutto, so rūpavedanādīsu “ayaṃ nāma dhammo ahamasmī”ti diṭṭhimānamaññanāvasena evaṃ nānupassati. Tassa tathā dassane kāraṇaṃ natthīti adhippāyo. Atha vā ayaṃhamasmīti anānupassīti idaṃ yathāvuttāya vimuttiyā adhigamupāyadīpanaṃ. Tiyaddhasaṅgahite tebhūmake saṅkhāre “etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā”ti pavattanasabhāvāya maññanāya anadhiṭṭhānaṃ katvā “netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na me so attā”ti evaṃ uppajjamānā yā pubbabhāgavuṭṭhānagāminī vipassanā, sā vimuttiyā padaṭṭhānaṃ. Evaṃ vimutto udatāri oghaṃ, atiṇṇapubbaṃ apunabbhavāyāti evaṃ dasahi saṃyojanehi sabbākusalehi [V 0.0295] ca sabbathā vimutto arahā ariyamaggādhigamanato pubbe supinantepi atiṇṇapubbaṃ kāmogho bhavogho diṭṭhogho avijjoghoti imaṃ catubbidhaṃ oghaṃ, saṃsāramahoghameva vā apunabbhavāya anupādisesāya nibbānāya udatāri uttiṇṇo, uttaritvā pāre ṭhitoti attho.

'He does not regard, ‘I am this’': One who is thus fully liberated does not, by way of view, conceit, and 'I'-making, regard form, feeling, etc., thus: 'This is such a thing; I am this.' The intention is that there is no reason for him to see in such a way. Alternatively, 'he does not regard, ‘I am this’' illuminates the means for attaining the aforementioned liberation. By not being grounded in the 'I'-making that proceeds as 'This is mine, this I am, this is my self' with regard to the conditioned phenomena in the three planes encompassed by the three times, but instead seeing, 'This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self,' the preliminary insight that leads to emergence becomes the proximate cause for liberation. 'Thus liberated, he has crossed the flood, never crossed before, for no renewed existence': Thus the arahant, fully liberated in every way from the ten fetters and all unwholesome states through the attainment of the noble path, has crossed the fourfold flood—the flood of sensuality, the flood of existence, the flood of views, and the flood of ignorance—or the great flood of saṃsāra, which he had never crossed before, not even in a dream. He crossed it for the sake of no renewed existence, for Nibbāna without remainder. Having crossed, he stands on the far shore—this is the meaning.

Paṭhamasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the first sutta is finished.

2. Dutiyalakuṇḍakabhaddiyasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Second Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya Discourse

62. Dutiye [P 0.0363] sekhaṃ maññamānoti “sekho aya”nti maññamāno. Tatrāyaṃ vacanattho – sikkhatīti sekho. Kiṃ sikkhati? Adhisīlaṃ adhicittaṃ adhipaññañca. Atha vā sikkhanaṃ sikkhā, sā etassa sīlanti sekho. So hi apariyositasikkhattā tadadhimuttattā ca ekantena sikkhanasīlo, na pariniṭṭhitasikkho asekho viya tattha paṭippassaddhussukko, nāpi vissaṭṭhasikkho pacurajano viya tattha anadhimutto. Atha vā ariyāya jātiyā tīsu sikkhāsu jāto, tattha vā bhavoti sekho. Bhiyyosomattāyāti pamāṇato uttari, pamāṇaṃ atikkamitvā adhikataranti attho. Āyasmā hi lakuṇḍakabhaddiyo paṭhamasutte vuttena vidhinā paṭhamovādena yathānisinnova āsavakkhayappatto. Dhammasenāpati pana tassa taṃ arahattappattiṃ anāvajjanena ajānitvā “sekhoyevā”ti maññamāno appaṃ yācito bahuṃ [M 0.0330] dadamāno uḷārapuriso viya bhiyyo bhiyyo anekapariyāyena āsavakkhayāya dhammaṃ kathetiyeva. Āyasmāpi lakuṇḍakabhaddiyo “katakicco dānāhaṃ, kiṃ iminā ovādenā”ti acintetvā saddhammagāravena pubbe viya sakkaccaṃ suṇātiyeva. Taṃ disvā bhagavā gandhakuṭiyaṃ nisinnoyeva buddhānubhāvena yathā dhammasenāpati tassa kilesakkhayaṃ jānāti, tathā katvā imaṃ udānaṃ udānesi. Tena vuttaṃ “tena kho pana samayenā”tiādi. Tattha yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ anantarasutte vuttameva.

62. In the second discourse, thinking him a trainee means thinking, 'This is a trainee.' The meaning of the word is this: one who trains is a trainee. What does he train in? In the higher virtue, the higher mind, and the higher wisdom. Alternatively, training is the training; since that is his nature, he is a trainee. For since his training is unfinished and he is intent on it, he is exclusively devoted to training; he has not completed the training like one beyond training, who is at ease in that regard, nor has he abandoned the training like an ordinary person, who is not intent on it. Or, one born by the noble birth into the three trainings, or one who abides therein, is a trainee. Exceedingly means further in measure; the meaning is 'surpassing the measure, more abundantly.' For the Venerable Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya, by the method stated in the first discourse, attained the destruction of the taints through the first instruction just as he was sitting. But the General of the Dhamma, not having adverted to it, did not know of his attainment of arahantship and, thinking, 'He is still just a trainee,' like a magnanimous person who gives much when asked for little, he spoke on the Dhamma again and again in many ways for the destruction of the taints. The Venerable Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya, too, without thinking, 'I have done what had to be done, what is the use of this instruction?' listened attentively as before out of reverence for the good Dhamma. Seeing this, the Blessed One, while sitting in the fragrant chamber, by his Buddha-power acted in such a way that the General of the Dhamma would know about the destruction of his defilements, and then he uttered this inspired utterance. Therefore it was said: 'Now at that time,' and so on. Whatever needs to be said on this has already been said in the preceding discourse.

Gāthāyaṃ pana acchecchi vaṭṭanti anavasesato kilesavaṭṭaṃ samucchindi, chinne ca kilesavaṭṭe kammavaṭṭampi chinnameva. Byagā nirāsanti āsā vuccati taṇhā, natthi ettha āsāti nirāsaṃ, nibbānaṃ. Taṃ nirāsaṃ visesena agā adhigatoti byagā, aggamaggassa adhigatattā puna adhigamakāraṇena vinā adhigatoti attho. Yasmā taṇhā dukkhasamudayabhūtā, tāya [V 0.0296] pahīnāya appahīno nāma kileso natthi, tasmāssa [P 0.0364] taṇhāpahānaṃ savisesaṃ katvā dassento “visukkhā saritā na sandatī”ti āha. Tassattho – catutthasūriyapātubhāvena viya mahānadiyo catutthamaggañāṇuppādena anavasesato visukkhā visositā taṇhāsaritā nadī na sandati, ito paṭṭhāya na pavattati. Taṇhā hi “saritā”ti vuccati. Yathāha – “saritāni sinehitāni ca, somanassāni bhavanti jantuno”ti (dha. pa. 341), “saritā visattikā”ti (dha. sa. 1065; mahāni. 3) ca. Chinnaṃ vaṭṭaṃ na vattatīti evaṃ kilesavaṭṭasamucchedena chinnaṃ vaṭṭaṃ anuppādadhammataṃ avipākadhammatañca āpādanena upacchinnaṃ kammavaṭṭaṃ na vattati na pavattati. Esevanto dukkhassāti yadetaṃ sabbaso kilesavaṭṭābhāvato kammavaṭṭassa appavattanaṃ, so āyatiṃ vipākavaṭṭassa ekaṃseneva anuppādo eva sakalassāpi saṃsāradukkhassa anto paricchedo parivaṭumabhāvoti.

But in the verse: He has cut off the cycle means he has uprooted the cycle of defilements without remainder. And when the cycle of defilements is cut off, the cycle of kamma is also cut off. He has gone beyond to the desireless: 'desire' (āsā) is a term for craving. Where there is no desire, that is the desireless, Nibbāna. He has gone beyond (byagā) means he has especially gone to, has attained, that desireless state. The meaning is that because he has attained the highest path, he has attained it without any cause for further attainment. Since craving is the origin of suffering, when it is abandoned there is no defilement that remains unabandoned. Therefore, showing the abandonment of craving with special emphasis, he said: The dried-up stream does not flow. The meaning of this is: just as great rivers are completely dried up by the appearance of the fourth sun, so with the arising of the knowledge of the fourth path, the river of craving is completely dried up and does not flow; from this point on, it does not proceed. For craving is called a 'stream' (saritā), as it is said: 'Streams and affections and pleasant feelings arise for a person' (Dhp 341), and 'the stream of attachments' (Dhs 1065; Mahāni 3). The cut-off cycle does not turn: in this way, with the uprooting of the cycle of defilements, the cycle of kamma is cut off by being brought to a state of non-arising and non-ripening; it does not turn, does not proceed. This is the end of suffering: this non-operation of the cycle of kamma due to the complete absence of the cycle of defilements, this definite non-arising in the future of the cycle of results, is itself the end, the termination, the cessation of revolving, of all the suffering of saṃsāra.

Dutiyasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Second Discourse is finished.

3. Paṭhamasattasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the First Discourse on the Seven

63. Tatiye kāmesūti vatthukāmesu. Ativelanti velaṃ atikkamitvā. Sattāti ayonisomanasikārabahulatāya vijjamānampi ādīnavaṃ [M 0.0331] anoloketvā assādameva saritvā sajjanavasena sattā, āsattā laggāti attho. Rattāti vatthaṃ viya raṅgajātena cittassa vipariṇāmakaraṇena chandarāgena rattā sārattā. Giddhāti abhikaṅkhanasabhāvena abhijjhanena giddhā gedhaṃ āpannā. Gadhitāti rāgamucchitā viya dummocanīyabhāvena tattha paṭibaddhā. Mucchitāti kilesavasena [P 0.0365] visaññībhūtā viya anaññakiccā mucchaṃ mohaṃ āpannā. Ajjhopannāti anaññasādhāraṇe viya katvā gilitvā pariniṭṭhapetvā ṭhitā. Sammattakajātāti kāmesu pātabyataṃ āpajjantā appasukhavedanāya sammattakā suṭṭhu mattakā jātā. “Sammodakajātā”tipi pāṭho, jātasammodanā uppannapahaṃsāti attho. Sabbehipi padehi tesaṃ taṇhādhipannataṃyeva vadati. Ettha ca paṭhamaṃ “kāmesū”ti vatvā punapi “kāmesū”ti vacanaṃ tesaṃ sattānaṃ tadadhimuttidīpanatthaṃ. Tena sabbiriyāpathesu kāmaguṇasamaṅgino hutvā tadā vihariṃsūti dasseti.

63. In the third: in sensual pleasures means in the objects of sensual pleasure. Exceedingly means having exceeded the limit. Attached: because of an abundance of unwise attention, they do not see the existing danger but only recall the gratification, and thus by way of attachment they are attached, clinging, stuck; this is the meaning. Infatuated: they are infatuated, impassioned, by sensual lust, which transforms the mind like a coloring agent on cloth. Greedy: they are greedy, have fallen into greed, through covetousness, which has the nature of strong desire. Captivated: as if besotted by lust, they are bound to them in a way that is difficult to escape. Infatuated: as if rendered unconscious by the defilements, they are unable to do anything else, having fallen into infatuation and delusion. Engrossed: they abide as if having made them their own, having swallowed and consumed them. Become intoxicated: falling into indulgence in sensual pleasures, they have become intoxicated, thoroughly intoxicated, by a slight pleasant feeling. There is also the reading sammodakajātā, which means they have become joyful, with delight arisen. All these terms speak of their being overcome by craving. Here, having first said 'in sensual pleasures' and then saying it again is for the purpose of showing the inclination of those beings towards them. Thereby he shows that at that time they dwelt endowed with sensual qualities in all postures.

Tasmiñhi [V 0.0297] samaye ṭhapetvā ariyasāvake sabbe sāvatthivāsino ussavaṃ ghosetvā yathāvibhavaṃ āpānabhūmiṃ sajjetvā bhuñjantā pivantā āvi ceva raho ca kāme paribhuñjantā indriyāni paricārentā kāmesu pātabyataṃ āpajjiṃsu. Bhikkhū sāvatthiyaṃ piṇḍāya carantā tattha tattha gehe ārāmuyyānādīsu ca manusse ussavaṃ ghosetvā kāmaninne tathā paṭipajjante disvā “vihāraṃ gantvā saṇhasukhumaṃ dhammaṃ labhissāmā”ti bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ. Tena vuttaṃ – “atha kho sambahulā bhikkhū…pe… kāmesu viharantī”ti.

For at that time, with the exception of the noble disciples, all the residents of Sāvatthī had proclaimed a festival and, having prepared drinking halls according to their means, were eating, drinking, and enjoying sensual pleasures both openly and in secret. Indulging their faculties, they fell into indulgence in sensual pleasures. The bhikkhus, while wandering for alms in Sāvatthī, saw people in houses, parks, gardens, and so on, who had proclaimed a festival and were behaving in a way inclined toward sensual pleasures. Thinking, 'Having gone to the monastery, we will obtain the subtle and refined Dhamma,' they reported this matter to the Blessed One. Therefore it was said: 'Then a number of bhikkhus...pe... dwelling in sensual pleasures.'

Etamatthaṃ viditvāti etaṃ tesaṃ manussānaṃ āpānabhūmiramaṇīyesu mahāpariḷāhesu anekānatthānubandhesu ghorāsayhakaṭukaphalesu kāmesu anādīnavadassitaṃ sabbākārato viditvā kāmānañceva kilesānañca ādīnavavibhāvanaṃ imaṃ udānaṃ udānesi.

Having understood this matter: that is, having in every way understood this lack of perception of danger in sensual pleasures—which are the delightful drinking halls of those people, which involve great burning, are followed by many troubles, and have terrible, unbearable, and bitter results—he uttered this inspired utterance clarifying the danger of sensual pleasures and defilements.

Tattha kāmesu sattāti vatthukāmesu kilesakāmena rattā mattā [P 0.0366] sattā visattā laggā laggitā saṃyuttā. Kāmasaṅgasattāti tāyeva kāmasattiyā vatthukāmesu rāgasaṅgena ceva diṭṭhimānadosaavijjāsaṅgehi ca sattā āsattā. Saṃyojane vajjamapassamānāti kammavaṭṭaṃ [M 0.0332] vipākavaṭṭena, bhavādike vā bhavantarādīhi, satte vā dukkhehi saṃyojanato bandhanato saṃyojananāmake kāmarāgādikilesajāte saṃyojanīyesu dhammesu assādānupassitāya vaṭṭadukkhamūlabhāvādikaṃ vajjaṃ dosaṃ ādīnavaṃ apassantā. Na hi jātu saṃyojanasaṅgasattā, oghaṃ tareyyuṃ vipulaṃ mahantanti evaṃ ādīnavadassanābhāvena saṃyojanasabhāvesu saṅgesu, saṃyojanasaṅkhātehi vā saṅgehi tesaṃ visayesu tebhūmakadhammesu sattā vipulavisayatāya anādikālatāya ca vipulaṃ vitthiṇṇaṃ mahantañca kāmādioghaṃ, saṃsāroghameva vā na kadāci tareyyuṃ, ekaṃseneva tassa oghassa pāraṃ na gaccheyyunti attho.

Therein, attached to sensual pleasures means infatuated, intoxicated, attached, clinging, stuck, bound, and fettered to the objects of sensual pleasure by sensual desire as a defilement. Attached to the bond of sensuality means attached and clinging by that same attachment to sensuality, by the bond of lust for the objects of sensual pleasure, and also by the bonds of views, conceit, aversion, and ignorance. Not seeing the fault in the fetter: not seeing the fault, the defect, the danger—such as its being the root of the suffering of the cycle—in the things subject to fetters, that is, in the mass of defilements such as sensual lust, which are called 'fetters' (saṃyojana) because they fetter (saṃyojanato) or bind (bandhanato) the cycle of kamma to the cycle of results, or one existence to another, or beings to suffering. This is because they contemplate gratification in them. For those attached to the fetter-bond would never cross the vast, great flood: because they do not see the danger, those who are attached to the bonds that have the nature of fetters, or by the bonds called fetters, are attached to their objects, the things of the three planes. Because its domain is vast and because it is beginningless, they would never cross the vast and great flood of sensuality and so on, or the flood of saṃsāra itself; the meaning is that they would definitely never get to the far shore of that flood.

Tatiyasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Third Sutta is finished.

4. Dutiyasattasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Second Sutta on Beings

64. Catutthe andhīkatāti kāmā nāma anandhampi andhaṃ karonti.

64. In the fourth, blinded means that sensual pleasures make blind even one who can see.

Yathāha [V 0.0298] –

As was said:

“Luddho atthaṃ na jānāti, luddho dhammaṃ na passati;

Andhatamaṃ tadā hoti, yaṃ lobho sahate nara”nti. (itivu. 88; mahāni. 5; cūḷani. khaggavisāṇasuttaniddesa 128) –

“The greedy person does not know the goal; the greedy person does not see the Dhamma. There is blinding darkness then, when greed overcomes a person.”

Tasmā kāmena anandhāpi andhā katāti andhīkatā. Sesaṃ anantarasutte vuttanayameva. Tattha hi manussānaṃ pavatti bhikkhūhi disvā bhagavato ārocitā, idha bhagavatā sāmaṃyeva diṭṭhāti ayameva viseso. Satthā sāvatthito nikkhamitvā jetavanaṃ gacchanto antarāmagge aciravatiyaṃ nadiyaṃ macchabandhehi oḍḍitaṃ kuminaṃ pavisitvā nikkhantuṃ asakkonte bahū macche passi, tato aparabhāge [P 0.0367] ekaṃ khīrapakaṃ vacchaṃ goravaṃ katvā anubandhitvā thaññapipāsāya gīvaṃ pasāretvā mātu antarasatthiyaṃ mukhaṃ upanentaṃ passi. Atha bhagavā vihāraṃ pavisitvā pāde pakkhāletvā paññattavarabuddhāsane nisinno pacchimaṃ vatthudvayaṃ purimassa upamānabhāvena gahetvā imaṃ udānaṃ udānesi.

Therefore, by sensual desire, even those who are not blind are made blind; thus they are called “blinded.” The rest is just as explained in the preceding sutta. For in that case the behavior of people was seen by the bhikkhus and reported to the Blessed One, but here it was seen by the Blessed One himself—this is the only difference. The Teacher, having departed from Sāvatthī and while on his way to Jetavana, saw on the road many fish in the Aciravatī River that had entered a fish-trap set by fishermen and were unable to get out. Then, further on, he saw a suckling calf following its mother respectfully, stretching out its neck out of thirst for milk, and putting its mouth between its mother’s thighs. Then the Blessed One entered the monastery, washed his feet, and sat down on the excellent Buddha-seat that had been prepared. Taking these last two stories as a simile for the first, he uttered this inspired utterance.

Tattha [M 0.0333] kāmandhāti vatthukāmesu kilesakāmena andhā vicakkhukā katā. Jālasañchannāti sakattabhāvaparattabhāvesu ajjhattikabāhirāyatanesu, tannissitesu ca dhammesu atītādivasena anekabhedabhinnesu heṭṭhupariyavasena aparāparaṃ uppattiyā antogadhānaṃ anatthāvahato ca jālabhūtāya taṇhāya sukhumacchiddena jālena parivuto viya udakarahado sañchannā paliguṇṭhitā ajjhotthaṭā. Taṇhāchadanachāditāti taṇhāsaṅkhātena chadanena sevālapaṇakena viya udakaṃ chāditā, paṭicchannā pihitāti attho. Padadvayenāpi kāmacchandanīvaraṇanivāritakusalacittācārataṃ dasseti.

Therein, “blinded by sensual desire” means made blind, bereft of vision, by the defilement of sensual desire in regard to sensual objects. “Covered by a net” means covered, enmeshed, and overwhelmed by the net of craving—like a lake enveloped by a fine-meshed net—which brings what is unbeneficial, being included in the successive arising, high and low, of one’s own and others’ states of existence, the internal and external sense bases, and the phenomena dependent on them, which are differentiated in many ways as past, etc. “Shrouded by the covering of craving” means covered, concealed, and hidden by the covering called craving, as water is by moss and duckweed; this is the meaning. By this pair of phrases it also shows that wholesome conduct of mind is prevented by the hindrance of sensual desire.

Pamattabandhunā baddhāti kilesamārena devaputtamārena ca baddhā. Yadaggena hi kilesamārena baddhā, tadaggena devaputtamārenapi baddhā nāma honti. Vuttañhetaṃ –

“Bound by the Kinsman of the Negligent” means bound by Māra as the defilements and by Māra the deva’s son. For to the extent that they are bound by Māra as the defilements, to that extent they are also said to be bound by Māra the deva’s son. For this was said:

“Antalikkhacaro pāso, yvāyaṃ carati mānaso;

Tena taṃ bādhayissāmi, na me samaṇa mokkhasī”ti. (saṃ. ni. 1.151; mahāva. 33);

“The snare that roams in the sky, the mental one—with that I will fetter you; you will not escape me, recluse.”

Namuci [V 0.0299] kaṇho pamattabandhūti tīṇi mārassa nāmāni. Devaputtamāropi hi kilesamāro viya anatthena pamatte satte bandhatīti pamattabandhu. “Pamattā bandhane baddhā”tipi paṭhanti. Tattha bandhaneti kāmaguṇabandhaneti attho. Baddhāti niyamitā. Yathā kiṃ? Macchāva kumināmukhe yathā nāma macchabandhakena oḍḍitassa kuminassa mukhe paviṭṭhā macchā tena baddhā hutvā maraṇamanventi [P 0.0368] pāpuṇanti, evameva mārena oḍḍitena kāmaguṇabandhanena baddhā ime sattā jarāmaraṇamanventi. Vaccho khīrapakova mātaraṃ yathā khīrapāyī taruṇavaccho attano mātaraṃ anveti anugacchati, na aññaṃ evaṃ mārabandhanabaddhā sattā saṃsāre paribbhamantā maraṇameva anventi anugacchanti, na ajaraṃ amaraṇaṃ nibbānanti adhippāyo.

“Namuci,” “Kaṇha” (the Dark One), and “Pamattabandhu” (Kinsman of the Negligent) are three names for Māra. For Māra the deva’s son, like Māra as the defilements, binds negligent beings with what is unbeneficial, thus he is the “Kinsman of the Negligent.” Some also read: “The negligent are bound in the bond.” Here, “in the bond” means in the bond of the cords of sensual pleasure. “Bound” means confined. Like what? Just as fish that have entered the mouth of a fish-trap set by a fisherman are bound by it and meet with death, so these beings, bound by the bond of the cords of sensual pleasure set by Māra, meet with aging and death. “Like a suckling calf its mother”: just as a young suckling calf follows its own mother and no other, so these beings, bound by the bond of Māra, wandering in saṃsāra, follow only death; they do not follow the unaging, deathless Nibbāna. This is the intention.

Catutthasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Fourth Sutta is finished.

5. Aparalakuṇḍakabhaddiyasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Other Sutta on Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya

65. Pañcame [M 0.0334] sambahulānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ piṭṭhito piṭṭhitoti āyasmā lakuṇḍakabhaddiyo ekadivasaṃ sambahulehi bhikkhūhi saddhiṃ gāmantarena piṇḍāya caritvā katabhattakicco pattaṃ vodakaṃ katvā thavikāya pakkhipitvā aṃse laggetvā cīvaraṃ saṅgharitvā tampi vāmaṃse ṭhapetvā pāsādikena abhikkantena paṭikkantena ālokitena vilokitena samiñjitena pasāritena okkhittacakkhu iriyāpathasampanno attano satipaññāvepullaṃ pakāsento viya satisampajaññaṃ sūpaṭṭhitaṃ katvā samāhitena cittena pade padaṃ nikkhipanto gacchati, gacchanto ca bhikkhūnaṃ pacchato pacchato gacchati tehi bhikkhūhi asaṃmisso. Kasmā? Asaṃsaṭṭhavihāritāya. Apica tassāyasmato rūpaṃ paribhūtaṃ paribhavaṭṭhānīyaṃ puthujjanā ohīḷenti. Thero taṃ jānitvā piṭṭhito piṭṭhito gacchati “mā ime maṃ nissāya apuññaṃ pasaviṃsū”ti. Evaṃ te bhikkhū ca thero ca sāvatthiṃ patvā vihāraṃ pavisitvā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamanti. Tena vuttaṃ – “tena kho pana samayena āyasmā lakuṇḍakabhaddiyo”tiādi.

65. In the fifth sutta: “Behind a number of bhikkhus.” One day, the Venerable Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya, having gone for alms in a village with a number of bhikkhus and finished his meal, rinsed his bowl, put it in its bag, slung it over his shoulder, folded his outer robe and placed it on his left shoulder. Perfect in deportment—in his advancing and returning, his looking ahead and looking aside, his bending and stretching, with eyes downcast—as if displaying the fullness of his own mindfulness and wisdom, with mindfulness and clear comprehension well established, with a concentrated mind, he walked placing one foot after another. And as he walked, he went right at the back of the bhikkhus, not mixing with them. Why? Because he was one who dwelt unassociated. Moreover, the venerable one’s physical form was despised, a cause for contempt, and worldlings looked down on him. The elder, knowing this, walked right at the back, thinking, “May they not produce demerit on account of me.” Thus those bhikkhus and the elder reached Sāvatthī, entered the monastery, and approached the Blessed One. Therefore it was said: “Now at that time the Venerable Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya…” and so on.

Tattha dubbaṇṇanti virūpaṃ. Tenassa vaṇṇasampattiyā saṇṭhānasampattiyā ca abhāvaṃ dasseti. Duddasikanti [P 0.0369] apāsādikadassanaṃ. Tenassa anubyañjanasampattiyā ākārasampattiyā ca abhāvaṃ dasseti. Okoṭimakanti rassaṃ. Iminā ārohasampattiyā abhāvaṃ dasseti. Yebhuyyena [V 0.0300] bhikkhūnaṃ paribhūtarūpanti puthujjanabhikkhūhi ohīḷitarūpaṃ. Puthujjanā ekacce chabbaggiyādayo tassāyasmato guṇaṃ ajānantā hatthakaṇṇacūḷikādīsu gaṇhantā parāmasantā kīḷantā paribhavanti, na ariyā, kalyāṇaputhujjanā vā.

Therein, “of poor complexion” means deformed. By this it shows his lack of accomplishment in complexion and form. “Unpleasant to see” means of uninspiring appearance. By this it shows his lack of accomplishment in the minor characteristics and deportment. “Dwarfish” means short. By this it shows his lack of accomplishment in stature. “Despised by the bhikkhus for the most part” means his form was looked down upon by the worldling bhikkhus. Certain worldlings, such as the Group of Six Bhikkhus, not knowing the venerable one’s virtue, would treat him with contempt, grabbing and touching his hands, ears, topknot, and so on, and playing with them; but not the noble ones or virtuous worldlings.

Bhikkhū āmantesīti kasmā āmantesi? Therassa guṇaṃ pakāsetuṃ. Evaṃ kira bhagavato ahosi “ime bhikkhū mama puttassa mahānubhāvataṃ na jānanti, tena taṃ paribhavanti, taṃ nesaṃ dīgharattaṃ ahitāya dukkhāya bhavissati, handāhaṃ imassa guṇe bhikkhūnaṃ pakāsetvā paribhavato naṃ mocessāmī”ti.

“He addressed the bhikkhus”: why did he address them? To declare the elder’s virtue. It is said that the Blessed One thought: “These bhikkhus do not know the great power of my son, and so they treat him with contempt. This will be for their harm and suffering for a long time. Well now, I will declare his virtues to the bhikkhus and thereby release him from their contempt.”

Passatha noti passatha nu. Na ca sā samāpatti sulabharūpā, yā tena bhikkhunā asamāpannapubbāti rūpasamāpatti arūpasamāpatti brahmavihārasamāpatti nirodhasamāpatti phalasamāpattīti evaṃ pabhedā sāvakasādhāraṇā yā kāci samāpattiyo nāma, tāsu ekāpi samāpatti na [M 0.0335] sulabharūpā, dullabhā, natthiyeva sā tena lakuṇḍakabhaddiyena bhikkhunā asamāpannapubbā. Etenassa yaṃ vuttaṃ. “Mahiddhiko mahānubhāvo”ti, tattha mahiddhikataṃ pakāsetvā idāni mahānubhāvataṃ dassetuṃ “yassa catthāyā”tiādimāha. Taṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayameva. Ettha ca bhagavā “eso, bhikkhave, bhikkhū”tiādinā, “bhikkhave, ayaṃ bhikkhu na yo vā so vā dubbaṇṇo duddasiko okoṭimakoti bhikkhūnaṃ piṭṭhito piṭṭhito āgacchatīti ca ettakena na oññātabbo, atha kho mahiddhiko mahānubhāvo, yaṃkiñci sāvakena pattabbaṃ, sabbaṃ taṃ tena anuppattaṃ, tasmā taṃ pāsāṇacchattaṃ viya garuṃ katvā oloketha, taṃ vo dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāya bhavissatī”ti dasseti.

“Do you not see?” means “Do you see?” “And there is no attainment easy to gain that has not been previously attained by that bhikkhu”: of the various kinds of attainments common to disciples—such as the form attainments, the formless attainments, the attainments of the divine abidings, the attainment of cessation, and the attainment of fruition—among these, not a single attainment is easy to gain; they are difficult to gain. There is indeed no such attainment that has not been previously attained by that bhikkhu Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya. By this, what was said of him, “of great spiritual power and great might,” is clarified. Having declared his great spiritual power, now to show his great might, he said, “For the sake of which…,” and so on. This is in the way explained below. And here the Blessed One shows: by saying, “This, bhikkhus, is that bhikkhu,” etc., he means: “Bhikkhus, this bhikkhu is not to be disdained just because he is of poor complexion, unpleasant to see, a dwarf, and comes right at the back of the bhikkhus. Rather, he is of great spiritual power and great might. Whatever is to be attained by a disciple, all that has been attained by him. Therefore, you should look upon him with respect, as upon a stone canopy. This will be for your welfare and happiness for a long time.”

Etamatthaṃ viditvāti etaṃ āyasmato lakuṇḍakabhaddiyassa mahiddhikatāmahānubhāvatādibhedaṃ guṇarāsiṃ sabbākārato jānitvā tadatthadīpanaṃ imaṃ udānaṃ udānesi.

“Having understood this matter”: having known in all its aspects this mass of virtues of the Venerable Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya, differentiated as great spiritual power, great might, and so on, he uttered this inspired utterance that illuminates that meaning.

Tattha nelaṅgoti elaṃ vuccati doso, nāssa elanti nelaṃ[P 0.0370]. Kiṃ pana taṃ? Suparisuddhasīlaṃ. Tañhi niddosaṭṭhena idha “nela”nti adhippetaṃ. Taṃ nelaṃ padhānabhūtaṃ aṅgaṃ etassāti nelaṅgo. So yaṃ “ratho”ti vakkhati, tena sambandho, tasmā suparisuddhasīlaṅgoti attho. Arahattaphalasīlañhi idhādhippetaṃ. Seto pacchādo etassāti setapacchādo. Pacchādoti rathassa upari attharitabbakambalādi. So pana suparisuddhadhavalabhāvena seto vā hoti rattanīlādīsu vā aññataro. Idha pana arahattaphalavimuttiyā adhippetattā suparisuddhabhāvaṃ upādāya [V 0.0301] “setapacchādo”ti vuttaṃ yathā aññatrāpi “ratho sīlaparikkhāro”ti. Eko satisaṅkhāto aro etassāti ekāro. Vattatīti pavattati. Rathoti therassa attabhāvaṃ sandhāya vadati.

Therein, “with stainless parts” (nelaṅgo): “stain” (ela) is a term for a fault; “stainless” (nela) is that which has no stain. What is that? Supremely pure virtue. For here “stainless” is intended in the sense of being faultless. “One for whom that stainlessness is the chief part” is nelaṅgo. This is connected with what will be called a “chariot”; therefore the meaning is “having the part of supremely pure virtue.” For here the virtue of the fruit of arahantship is intended. “With a white canopy” (setapacchādo): “a white canopy is its.” “Canopy” is a blanket or the like to be spread over the chariot. This is either white because of its supremely pure, bright nature, or it is one of another color such as red or blue. Here, however, since the liberation of the fruit of arahantship is intended, it is called “with a white canopy” with reference to its supremely pure nature, just as elsewhere it is said: “The chariot is the equipment of virtue.” “With one spoke” (ekāro): “one spoke, called mindfulness, is its.” “Goes on” (vattati) means it proceeds. “Chariot” is said with reference to the elder’s personal existence.

Anīghanti niddukkhaṃ, khobhavirahitaṃ yānaṃ viya kilesaparikhobhavirahitanti attho. Āyantanti sambahulānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ piṭṭhito piṭṭhito āgacchantaṃ. Chinnasotanti pacchinnasotaṃ. Pakatirathassa hi sukhapavattanatthaṃ akkhasīsesu [M 0.0336] nābhiyañca upalittānaṃ sappitelādīnaṃ soto savanaṃ sandanaṃ hoti, tena so acchinnasoto nāma hoti. Ayaṃ pana chattiṃsatiyā sotānaṃ anavasesato pahīnattā chinnasoto nāma hoti, taṃ chinnasotaṃ. Natthi etassa bandhananti abandhano. Rathūpattharassa hi akkhena saddhiṃ niccalabhāvakaraṇatthaṃ bahūni bandhanāni honti, tena so sabandhano. Ayaṃ pana sabbasaṃyojanabandhanānaṃ anavasesato parikkhīṇattā abandhano, taṃ abandhanaṃ. Passāti bhagavā therassa guṇehi somanassappatto hutvā attānaṃ vadati.

Free from affliction means free from suffering; like a vehicle free from agitation, it is free from the agitation of defilements—this is the meaning. Coming means coming behind many bhikkhus, one after another. With stream cut off means with the stream severed. For a regular chariot, for the purpose of smooth running, there is a flow, a dripping, a seepage of ghee, oil, and the like applied to the axle-ends and the hub; therefore it is called 'with stream not cut off.' But this one, because the thirty-six streams have been abandoned without remainder, is called 'with stream cut off'; thus, 'with stream cut off.' There is no bond for him means unbound. For a chariot's frame, there are many bonds to make it steady with the axle; therefore it is 'with bonds.' But this one, because all the fetter-bonds have been completely exhausted, is 'unbound'; thus, 'unbound.' The Blessed One says 'See,' having become filled with mental joy on account of the elder's virtues.

Iti satthā āyasmantaṃ lakuṇḍakabhaddiyaṃ arahattaphalasīsena sucakkaṃ, arahattaphalavimuttiyā suuttaracchadaṃ, sūpaṭṭhitāya satiyā svāraṃ, kilesaparikhobhābhāvena [P 0.0371] aparikhobhaṃ, taṇhūpalepābhāvena anupalepaṃ, saṃyojanādīnaṃ abhāvena abandhanaṃ suparikkhittaṃ suyuttaṃ ājaññarathaṃ katvā dasseti.

Thus the Teacher shows the Venerable Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya as a thoroughbred chariot, well-protected and well-yoked: with good wheels by means of the virtue of the fruit of arahantship; with an excellent canopy by means of the liberation of the fruit of arahantship; with a good charioteer in well-established mindfulness; unagitated due to the absence of the agitation of defilements; unstained due to the absence of the stain of craving; and unbound due to the absence of fetters and so on.

Pañcamasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Fifth Discourse is finished.

6. Taṇhāsaṅkhayasuttavaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Discourse on the Destruction of Craving

66. Chaṭṭhe aññāsikoṇḍaññoti ettha koṇḍaññoti tassāyasmato gottato āgatanāmaṃ. Sāvakesu pana sabbapaṭhamaṃ ariyasaccāni paṭivijjhīti bhagavatā “aññāsi vata, bho, koṇḍañño”ti (mahāva. 17; saṃ. ni. 5.1081) vuttaudānavasena thero sāsane “aññāsikoṇḍañño”tveva paññāyittha. Taṇhāsaṅkhayavimuttinti taṇhā saṅkhīyati pahīyati etthāti taṇhāsaṅkhayo, nibbānaṃ. Tasmiṃ taṇhāsaṅkhaye vimutti. Taṇhā vā saṅkhīyati pahīyati etenāti taṇhāsaṅkhayo, ariyamaggo. Tassa phalabhūtā, pariyosānabhūtā vā vimuttīti taṇhāsaṅkhayavimutti[V 0.0302], nippariyāyena arahattaphalasamāpatti. Taṃ paccavekkhamāno nisinno hoti. Ayañhi āyasmā bahulaṃ phalasamāpattiṃ samāpajjati, tasmā idhāpi evamakāsi.

66. In the sixth discourse, regarding Aññāsikoṇḍañña: Here, 'Koṇḍañña' is the name derived from that venerable one's clan name. Since among the disciples he was the very first to penetrate the Noble Truths, on account of the inspired utterance spoken by the Blessed One, 'Indeed, friend, Koṇḍañña has understood!' (Vin Mv 1:6.17; SN 56.11), the elder became renowned in the Dispensation as 'Aññāsikoṇḍañña.' 'Liberated through the destruction of craving' means: craving is destroyed and abandoned in this—hence, 'the destruction of craving' is Nibbāna. Liberation is in that destruction of craving. Alternatively: craving is destroyed and abandoned by this—hence, 'the destruction of craving' is the Noble Path. The liberation that is its fruit or culmination is called 'liberation through the destruction of craving,' which, in the definitive sense, is the fruition-attainment of Arahantship. He was seated, reflecting upon that. For this venerable one frequently entered fruition-attainment, and so here too he did likewise.

Etamatthaṃ [M 0.0337] viditvāti etaṃ aññāsikoṇḍaññattherassa aggaphalapaccavekkhaṇaṃ viditvā tadatthadīpanaṃ imaṃ udānaṃ udānesi.

Having understood this matter—that is, having understood this reflection on the ultimate fruit by the Elder Aññāsikoṇḍañña—the Blessed One uttered this inspired utterance that illuminates that meaning.

Tattha yassa mūlaṃ chamā natthīti yassa ariyapuggalassa attabhāvarukkhamūlabhūtā avijjā, tassāva patiṭṭhā hetubhūtā āsavanīvaraṇaayonisomanasikārasaṅkhātā chamā pathavī ca natthi aggamaggena samugghātitattā. Paṇṇā natthi kuto latāti natthi latā kuto paṇṇāti padasambandho. Mānātimānādipabhedā sākhāpasākhādisaṅkhātā latāpi natthi, kuto eva madappamādamāyāsāṭheyyādipaṇṇānīti attho. Atha vā paṇṇā natthi kuto latāti rukkhaṅkurassa vaḍḍhamānassa paṭhamaṃ paṇṇāni nibbattanti. Pacchā sākhāpasākhāsaṅkhātā latāti katvā vuttaṃ. Tattha [P 0.0372] yassa ariyamaggabhāvanāya asati uppajjanārahassa attabhāvarukkhassa ariyamaggassa bhāvitattā yaṃ avijjāsaṅkhātaṃ mūlaṃ, tassa patiṭṭhānabhūtaṃ āsavādi ca natthi. Mūlaggahaṇeneva cettha mūlakāraṇattā bījaṭṭhāniyaṃ kammaṃ tadabhāvopi gahitoyevāti veditabbo. Asati ca kammabīje taṃnimitto viññāṇaṅkuro, viññāṇaṅkuranimittā ca nāmarūpasaḷāyatanapattasākhādayo na nibbattissantiyeva. Tena vuttaṃ – “yassa mūlaṃ chamā natthi, paṇṇā natthi kuto latā”ti.

Therein, 'for whom there is no root in the earth' means: for that noble person, since ignorance—the root of the tree of individual existence—and the 'earth,' its foundation and cause, consisting of the taints, hindrances, and unwise attention, have been uprooted by the highest path, they do not exist. 'There are no leaves, from where a creeper?' The connection of the words is: 'There is no creeper, from where leaves?' The meaning is: the creeper, reckoned as branches and twigs of various kinds such as pride and conceit, does not exist; how then could there be leaves of intoxication, negligence, deceit, and fraudulence? Alternatively, it is said 'there are no leaves, from where a creeper?' because for a growing tree-sprout, leaves arise first, and afterwards the creeper, reckoned as branches and twigs. Therein, for that person, because the noble path has been developed, the root called ignorance of the tree of existence—which is liable to arise when the path is absent—does not exist, nor does its foundation, the taints, etc. By the mention of 'root' alone, it should be understood that the absence of kamma, which is the seed-place and the root cause, is also included. And when the seed of kamma is absent, the sprout of consciousness caused by it, and consequently the leaves and branches of name-and-form, the six sense bases, and so on, will not arise at all. Therefore it is said: 'For whom there is no root in the earth, there are no leaves, from where a creeper?'

Taṃ dhīraṃ bandhanā muttanti taṃ catubbidhasammappadhānavīriyayogena vijitamārattā dhīraṃ, tato eva sabbakilesābhisaṅkhārabandhanato muttaṃ. Ko taṃ ninditumarahatīti ettha nti nipātamattaṃ. Evaṃ sabbakilesavippamuttaṃ sīlādianuttaraguṇasamannāgataṃ ko nāma viññujātiko nindituṃ garahituṃ arahati nindānimittasseva abhāvato. Devāpi naṃ pasaṃsantīti aññadatthu devā sakkādayo guṇavisesavidū, apisaddena manussāpi khattiyapaṇḍitādayo pasaṃsanti. Kiñca bhiyyo brahmunāpi pasaṃsito mahābrahmunāpi aññehipi brahmanāgayakkhagandhabbādīhipi pasaṃsito thomitoyevāti.

'That resolute one freed from bonds' means: that one is resolute because he has conquered Māra through the application of energy in the four right strivings; for that very reason he is freed from all the bonds of defilements and formations. In 'Who is worthy to blame him?,' the 'nti' is merely a particle. Thus, who among the wise is worthy to blame or censure one so freed from all defilements and endowed with unsurpassed virtues such as morality, since there is no cause at all for blame? 'Even the devas praise him' means: on the contrary, the devas, such as Sakka and others who know his special virtues, praise him; and by the particle 'api,' humans too, such as noble warriors and learned men, praise him. What is more, he is praised by Brahmā, by a Mahābrahmā, and also praised and extolled by other brahmās, nāgas, yakkhas, gandhabbas, and so on.

Chaṭṭhasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Sixth Sutta is finished.

7. Papañcakhayasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Sutta on the Destruction of Proliferation

67. Sattame [V 0.0303][M 0.0338] papañcasaññāsaṅkhāpahānanti papañcenti yattha sayaṃ uppannā, taṃ santānaṃ vitthārenti ciraṃ ṭhapentīti papañcā, kilesā. Visesato rāgadosamohataṇhādiṭṭhimānā. Tathā hi vuttaṃ –

67. In the seventh sutta, 'the abandoning of the categories of perception rooted in proliferation': 'They proliferate' (papañcenti) means that where they have arisen, they extend that continuity and make it last long; thus they are called 'proliferations' (papañcā). These are the defilements, specifically, lust, hatred, delusion, craving, views, and conceit. For so it has been said:

“Rāgo papañco, doso papañco, moho papañco, taṇhā papañco, diṭṭhi papañco, māno papañco”ti. –

“Lust is a proliferation, hatred is a proliferation, delusion is a proliferation, craving is a proliferation, views are a proliferation, conceit is a proliferation.”

Apica saṃkilesaṭṭho papañcaṭṭho, kacavaraṭṭho papañcaṭṭho. Tattha rāgapapañcassa subhasaññā nimittaṃ, dosapapañcassa āghātavatthu, mohapapañcassa āsavā, taṇhāpapañcassa [P 0.0373] vedanā, diṭṭhipapañcassa saññā, mānapapañcassa vitakko nimittaṃ. Tehi papañcehi sahagatā saññā papañcasaññā. Papañcasaññānaṃ saṅkhā bhāgā koṭṭhāsā papañcasaññāsaṅkhā. Atthato saddhiṃ nimittehi taṃtaṃpapañcassa pakkhiyo kilesagaṇo. Saññāgahaṇañcettha tassa nesaṃ sādhāraṇahetubhāvena. Vuttañhetaṃ – “saññānidānā hi papañcasaṅkhā”ti (su. ni. 880). Tesaṃ pahānaṃ, tena tena maggena rāgādikilesānaṃ samucchedananti attho.

Moreover, the meaning of proliferation is defilement, and the meaning of proliferation is rubbish. Therein, the sign for the proliferation of lust is the perception of the beautiful; for the proliferation of hatred, the basis for resentment; for the proliferation of delusion, the taints; for the proliferation of craving, feeling; for the proliferation of views, perception; for the proliferation of conceit, thought is the sign. Perceptions associated with those proliferations are perceptions of proliferation. The categories, portions, and divisions of perceptions of proliferation are the categories of perception rooted in proliferation. In meaning, this is the group of defilements, together with their signs, that is allied with this or that proliferation. And perception is mentioned here because it is a common cause for them. For it has been said: “For the categories of proliferation are rooted in perception” (Snp 880). Their abandonment means the eradication of defilements such as lust by the respective path.

Tadā hi bhagavā atītāsu anekakoṭisatasahassasaṅkhāsu attano jātīsu anatthassa nimittabhūte kilese imasmiṃ carimabhave ariyamaggena bodhimaṇḍe savāsane pahīne paccavekkhitvā sattasantānañca kilesacaritaṃ rāgādikilesasaṃkiliṭṭhaṃ kañjiyapuṇṇalābuṃ viya takkabharitacāṭiṃ viya vasāpītapilotikaṃ viya ca dubbinimociyaṃ disvā “evaṃ gahanaṃ nāmidaṃ kilesavaṭṭaṃ anādikālabhāvitaṃ mayhaṃ anavasesaṃ pahīnaṃ, aho suppahīna”nti uppannapītipāmojjo udānaṃ udānesi. Tena vuttaṃ – “atha kho bhagavā attano papañcasaññāsaṅkhāpahānaṃ viditvā tāyaṃ velāyaṃ imaṃ udānaṃ udānesī”ti.

For at that time the Blessed One, having reflected that the defilements—which had been the cause of harm in his countless hundreds of thousands of crores of past lives—had now been abandoned with their latent tendencies by the noble path at the seat of awakening in this final existence; and having seen that the continuity of beings, with their defiled conduct, was sullied by defilements such as lust and was as difficult to be freed from as a gourd full of sour gruel, a pot full of buttermilk, or a cloth soaked in grease, he was filled with joy and gladness and uttered this inspired utterance: “So dense, indeed, is this round of defilements, developed since beginningless time, which has been abandoned by me without remainder. Ah, how well it has been abandoned!” Therefore it was said: “Then the Blessed One, having understood the abandonment of the categories of perception rooted in proliferation, on that occasion uttered this inspired utterance.”

Tattha yassa papañcā ṭhiti ca natthīti yasmā bhagavā attānameva paraṃ viya katvā niddisati tasmā yassa aggapuggalassa vuttalakkhaṇā papañcā, tehi katā saṃsāre ṭhiti ca natthi. Nettiyaṃ pana “ṭhiti nāma anusayo”ti (netti. 27) vuttaṃ. Anusayo hi bhavapavattiyā mūlanti. Satte saṃsāre papañcentīti [M 0.0339] papañcā. “Papañcaṭṭhitī”ti ca pāṭho. Tassattho – papañcānaṃ ṭhiti vijjamānatā maggena asamucchedo papañcaṭṭhiti, papañcā eva vā avasiṭṭhakusalākusalavipākānaṃ [V 0.0304] pavattiyā hetubhāvato vaṭṭassa ṭhiti papañcaṭṭhiti, sā yassa aggapuggalassa natthi. Sandānaṃ palighañca vītivattoti yo bandhanaṭṭhena santānasadisattā [P 0.0374] “sandāna”nti laddhanāmā taṇhādiṭṭhiyo, nibbānanagarapavesanisedhanato palighasadisattā palighasaṅkhātaṃ avijjañca vītivatto savāsanapahānena visesato atikkanto. Apare pana kodhaṃ “sandāna”nti vadanti, taṃ na gahetabbaṃ. So hi “parābhisajjanī”ti vuttoti.

Herein, 'for whom proliferations and persistence exist not': since the Blessed One indicates himself as if he were another, this means: for which supreme individual the above-described proliferations and the persistence in saṃsāra created by them do not exist. In the Nettipakaraṇa, however, it is said: “Persistence means the underlying tendency” (Neti 27). For the underlying tendency is the root for the continuation of existence. They proliferate beings in saṃsāra, thus they are called “proliferations.” There is also the reading “the persistence of proliferation.” Its meaning is this: the persistence of proliferations—their existence, their non-eradication by the path—is the persistence of proliferation. Or, the proliferations themselves are the persistence of the round, being a cause for the continuation of the remaining wholesome and unwholesome results; this is the persistence of proliferation. For that supreme individual, this does not exist. 'Having crossed beyond the tether and the bar': he has crossed beyond—especially transcended by abandoning their latent tendencies—craving and views, which are called the “tether” because they are like a continuous chain in the sense of binding, and ignorance, which is designated as the “bar” because it is like a cross-bar obstructing entry into the city of Nibbāna. Others, however, say that anger is the “tether,” but that should not be accepted, for it has been called “hostile clinging.”

Taṃ nittaṇhaṃ muniṃ carantanti taṃ sabbathāpi taṇhābhāvena nittaṇhaṃ, ubhayalokamunanato attahitaparahitamunanato ca muniṃ, ekanteneva sabbasattahitatthaṃ catūhi iriyāpathehi nānāsamāpatticārehi anaññasādhāraṇena ñāṇacārena ca carantaṃ. Nāvajānāti sadevakopi lokoti sabbo sapaññajātiko sattaloko sadevakopi sabrahmakopi na kadācipi avajānāti na paribhoti, atha kho ayameva loke aggo seṭṭho uttamo pavaroti garuṃ karonto sakkaccaṃ pūjāsakkāranirato hotīti.

That craving-free sage who wanders means: him, who is craving-free in all ways due to the absence of craving; a sage because of knowing both worlds and knowing his own welfare and the welfare of others; who wanders entirely for the welfare of all beings in the four postures, with the conduct of various attainments, and with the conduct of knowledge unshared by others. The world with its devas does not despise him means: the entire world of beings endowed with wisdom, including its devas and its brahmās, never despises or scorns him. Rather, holding him in esteem as, ‘This one is the highest in the world, the best, the supreme, the most excellent,’ it becomes devoted to paying him homage and veneration respectfully.

Sattamasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Seventh Sutta is finished.

8. Kaccānasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Kaccāna Sutta

68. Aṭṭhame ajjhattanti ettha ayaṃ ajjhattasaddo “cha ajjhattikāni āyatanānī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 3.304) ajjhattajjhatte āgato. “Ajjhattā dhammā (dha. sa. tikamātikā 20), ajjhattaṃ vā kāye kāyānupassī”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 2.373-374) niyakajjhatte. “Sabbanimittānaṃ amanasikārā ajjhattaṃ suññataṃ upasampajja viharatī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 3.187) visayajjhatte, issariyaṭṭhāneti attho. Phalasamāpatti hi buddhānaṃ issariyaṭṭhānaṃ nāma. “Tenānanda, bhikkhunā tasmiṃyeva purimasmiṃ samādhinimitte ajjhattameva cittaṃ saṇṭhapetabba”ntiādīsu (ma. ni. 3.188) gocarajjhatte. Idhāpi gocarajjhatteyeva [M 0.0340] daṭṭhabbo. Tasmā ajjhattanti gocarajjhattabhūte kammaṭṭhānārammaṇeti vuttaṃ hoti. Parimukhanti [P 0.0375] abhimukhaṃ. Sūpaṭṭhitāyāti suṭṭhu upaṭṭhitāya kāyagatāya satiyā. Satisīsena cettha jhānaṃ vuttaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti “ajjhattaṃ kāyānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānavasena paṭiladdhaṃ uḷāraṃ jhānaṃ samāpajjitvā”ti.

68. In the eighth sutta, internally: here this word ‘internal’ (ajjhatta) occurs in the sense of ‘internal proper’ in such passages as “the six internal sense bases” (MN 148); in the sense of ‘one’s own internal’ in such passages as “internal states” (Dhs, Tika-mātikā 20) and “contemplating the body internally in the body” (DN 22); in the sense of ‘internal as object’—meaning, in the state of mastery, for the attainment of fruition is indeed a state of mastery for the Buddhas—in such passages as “by not attending to any signs, he enters and dwells in the internal emptiness” (MN 121); and in the sense of ‘internal as range’ in such passages as “Therefore, Ānanda, the bhikkhu should establish his mind right there internally on that same earlier sign of concentration” (MN 122). Here too it should be understood as ‘internal as range.’ Therefore, internally means: in the meditation subject that has become the internal range. Around the mouth means in front. Well established means: with mindfulness directed to the body well established. And here jhāna is spoken of as headed by mindfulness. This is said to mean: ‘having attained the sublime jhāna acquired by way of the foundation of mindfulness involving the contemplation of the body internally.’”

Ayañhi [V 0.0305] thero bhagavati sāvatthiyaṃ viharante ekadivasaṃ sāvatthiyaṃ piṇḍāya caritvā pacchābhattaṃ piṇḍapātappaṭikkanto vihāraṃ pavisitvā bhagavato vattaṃ dassetvā divāṭṭhāne divāvihāraṃ nisinno nānāsamāpattīhi divasabhāgaṃ vītināmetvā sāyanhasamayaṃ vihāramajjhaṃ otaritvā bhagavati gandhakuṭiyaṃ nisinne “akālo tāva bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitu”nti gandhakuṭiyā avidūre, aññatarasmiṃ rukkhamūle kālaparicchedaṃ katvā yathāvuttaṃ samāpattiṃ samāpajjitvā nisīdi. Satthā taṃ tathānisinnaṃ gandhakuṭiyaṃ nisinnoyeva passi. Tena vuttaṃ – “tena kho pana samayena āyasmā mahākaccāno…pe… sūpaṭṭhitāyā”ti.

For while the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī, this elder, having wandered for alms in Sāvatthī one day and returned from his alms round after the meal, entered the monastery. Having performed his duties to the Blessed One, he sat down in his day-dwelling for the day’s abiding. Having passed the daytime with various attainments, in the evening he came down into the central part of the monastery. As the Blessed One was seated in the fragrant chamber, the elder thought, “It is not yet the time to approach the Blessed One.” Having set a time limit, he sat down at the foot of a certain tree not far from the fragrant chamber and entered the aforesaid attainment. The Teacher, while himself seated in the fragrant chamber, saw him seated thus. Therefore it was said: “Now at that time the Venerable Mahākaccāna … well established.”

Etamatthaṃ viditvāti etaṃ āyasmato mahākaccānattherassa satipaṭṭhānabhāvanāvasena adhigataṃ jhānaṃ pādakaṃ katvā samāpajjanaṃ sabbākārato viditvā tadatthadīpanaṃ imaṃ udānaṃ udānesi.
