Having understood this matter means: having known in all its aspects how the Venerable Mahākaccāna had entered an attainment by making the jhāna he had reached through the development of the foundations of mindfulness his basis, the Blessed One uttered this inspired utterance to illuminate that meaning.

Tattha yassa siyā sabbadā sati, satataṃ kāyagatā upaṭṭhitāti yassa āraddhavipassakassa ekadivasaṃ cha koṭṭhāse katvā sabbasmimpi kāle nāmarūpabhedena duvidhepi kāye gatā kāyārammaṇā pañcannaṃ upādānakkhandhānaṃ aniccādisammasanavasena satataṃ nirantaraṃ sātaccābhiyogavasena sati upaṭṭhitā siyā.

Herein, For whom there might always be mindfulness, constantly established, directed to the body means: for whichever meditator who has begun insight practice, mindfulness might be established—constantly, uninterruptedly, through persistent application—by way of comprehending the impermanence, etc., of the five aggregates subject to clinging. This mindfulness is directed to the body, which is twofold by the distinction of mentality-materiality, and has the body as its object; and it is established at all times, having divided the day into six portions.

Ayaṃ kirāyasmā paṭhamaṃ kāyagatāsatikammaṭṭhānavasena jhānaṃ nibbattetvā taṃ pādakaṃ katvā kāyānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānamukhena vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā arahattaṃ patto. So aparabhāgepi yebhuyyena tameva jhānaṃ samāpajjitvā vuṭṭhāya tatheva ca vipassitvā phalasamāpattiṃ samāpajjati. Svāyaṃ yena vidhinā arahattaṃ patto, taṃ vidhiṃ dassento satthā “yassa siyā sabbadā sati, satataṃ kāyagatā upaṭṭhitā”ti vatvā tassā upaṭṭhānākāraṃ vibhāvetuṃ “no [P 0.0376] cassa no ca me siyā, na bhavissati na ca me bhavissatī”ti āha.

It is said that this venerable one first produced jhāna by way of the meditation subject of mindfulness directed to the body. Having made that a basis, he established insight through the approach of the foundation of mindfulness of contemplating the body and attained arahantship. Later on, too, he would for the most part enter that same jhāna, and having emerged, he would contemplate in the same way and enter the attainment of fruition. In order to show the method by which he attained arahantship, the Teacher said: “For whom there might always be mindfulness, constantly established, directed to the body.” And in order to explain the mode of that establishment, he added: “It was not, and it would not be for me; it will not be, and it will not be for me.”

Tassattho [M 0.0341] dvidhā veditabbo sammasanato pubbabhāgavasena sammasanakālavasena cāti. Tesu pubbabhāgavasena tāva no cassa no ca me siyāti atītakāle mama kilesakammaṃ no cassa na bhaveyya ce, imasmiṃ paccuppannakāle ayaṃ attabhāvo no ca me siyā na me uppajjeyya. Yasmā pana me atīte kammakilesā ahesuṃ, tasmā taṃnimitto etarahi ayaṃ me attabhāvo pavattati. Na bhavissati na ca me bhavissatīti imasmiṃ attabhāve paṭipakkhādhigamena kilesakammaṃ na bhavissati na uppajjissati me, āyatiṃ vipākavaṭṭaṃ na ca me bhavissati na me pavattissatīti. Evaṃ kālattaye kammakilesahetukaṃ idaṃ mayhaṃ attabhāvasaṅkhātaṃ khandhapañcakaṃ[V 0.0306], na issarādihetukaṃ, yathā ca mayhaṃ, evaṃ sabbasattānanti sappaccayanāmarūpadassanaṃ pakāsitaṃ hoti.

Its meaning should be understood in two ways: by way of the preliminary stage of contemplation and by way of the time of contemplation. First, by way of the preliminary stage: 'It was not, and it would not be for me' means: if in the past my defilements and kamma had not existed, then in this present time this self-existence would not be for me, would not arise for me. But because in the past my kamma and defilements did exist, this self-existence of mine now continues on account of that. 'It will not be, and it will not be for me' means that, by attaining the antidote in regard to this self-existence, defilements and kamma will not be, will not arise for me; and in the future the round of results will not be, will not continue for me. Thus, in the three periods of time, this pentad of aggregates called my self-existence is caused by kamma and defilements, not by a creator or other such causes. And just as for me, so for all beings. In this way, the seeing of name-and-form with its conditions is clarified.

Sammasanakālavasena pana no cassa no ca me siyāti yasmā idaṃ khandhapañcakaṃ hutvā abhāvaṭṭhena aniccaṃ, abhiṇhapaṭipīḷanaṭṭhena dukkhaṃ, avasavattanaṭṭhena anattā, evaṃ yadi ayaṃ attā nāma nāpi khandhapañcakavinimutto koci no cassa no ca siyā na bhaveyya, evaṃ, bhante, no ca me siyā mama santakaṃ nāma kiñci na bhaveyya. Na bhavissatīti attani attaniye bhavitabbaṃ yathā cidaṃ nāmarūpaṃ etarahi ca atīte ca attattaniyaṃ suññaṃ, evaṃ na bhavissati na me bhavissati, anāgatepi khandhavinimutto attā nāma na koci na me bhavissati na pavattissati, tato eva kiñci palibodhaṭṭhāniyaṃ na me bhavissati āyatimpi attaniyaṃ nāma na me kiñci bhavissatīti. Iminā tīsu kālesu “aha”nti gahetabbassa abhāvato “mama”nti gahetabbassa ca abhāvaṃ dasseti. Tena catukkoṭikā suññatā pakāsitā hoti.

However, by way of the time of contemplation: 'It might not be, and it might not be mine.' Since this pentad of aggregates, having come to be, is impermanent in the sense of becoming non-existent, suffering in the sense of constant oppression, and not-self in the sense of being uncontrollable, thus, if this so-called self is not something apart from the pentad of aggregates, it would not be, it would not exist. Thus, venerable sir, 'it might not be mine' means there would be nothing at all called 'mine.' 'It will not be': this should be understood regarding the self and what belongs to the self. Just as this name-and-form, now and in the past, is void of self and what belongs to a self, so 'it will not be, it will not be mine.' In the future, too, there will be no self apart from the aggregates; it will not be mine, it will not continue. Therefore, there will be no basis for attachment for me; in the future, too, there will be nothing at all called 'mine.' By this is shown the absence in the three periods of time of anything to be grasped as 'I' and of anything to be grasped as 'mine.' Thereby the four-limbed emptiness is clarified.

Anupubbavihāri tattha soti evaṃ tīsupi kālesu attattaniyaṃ suññataṃ tattha saṅkhāragate anupassanto anukkamena udayabbayañāṇādivipassanāñāṇesu uppajjamānesu anupubbavipassanāvihāravasena anupubbavihārī samāno. Kāleneva [P 0.0377] tare visattikanti so evaṃ vipassanaṃ matthakaṃ pāpetvā ṭhito yogāvacaro indriyānaṃ paripākagatakālena vuṭṭhānagāminiyā vipassanāya maggena ghaṭitakālena ariyamaggassa uppattikālena [M 0.0342] sakalassa bhavattayassa saṃtananato visattikāsaṅkhātaṃ taṇhaṃ tareyya, vitaritvā tassā paratīre tiṭṭheyyāti adhippāyo.

'He dwells gradually there': thus, contemplating the voidness of self and what belongs to a self in the three periods of time there in the conditioned phenomena, as the insight knowledges beginning with the knowledge of arising and passing away arise in sequence, by way of the dwelling in gradual insight, he becomes one who dwells gradually. 'In due time he would cross over clinging': that yogi, having brought insight to its culmination and being established therein, at the time when his faculties have reached maturity, at the time when the insight leading to emergence is connected with the path, at the time of the arising of the noble path, would cross over craving—called 'clinging' because it stretches across the entire triple existence. Having crossed over, he would stand on its further shore—this is the intended meaning.

Iti bhagavā aññāpadesena āyasmato mahākaccānassa arahattuppattidīpanaṃ udānaṃ udānesi.

Thus the Blessed One, by way of an indirect indication, uttered this inspired utterance illuminating the Venerable Mahākaccāna's attainment of arahantship.

Aṭṭhamasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Eighth Sutta is finished.

9. Udapānasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Udapāna Sutta

69. Navame mallesūti mallā nāma jānapadino rājakumārā, tesaṃ nivāso ekopi janapado [V 0.0307] ruḷhīvasena “mallā”ti vuccati, tesu mallesu, yaṃ loke “mallo”ti vuccati. Keci pana “mālesū”ti paṭhanti. Cāriyaṃ caramānoti aturitacārikāvasena mahāmaṇḍalajanapadacārikaṃ caramāno. Mahatā bhikkhusaṅghenāti aparicchedaguṇena mahantena samaṇagaṇena. Tadā hi bhagavato mahābhikkhuparivāro ahosi. Thūṇaṃ nāma mallānaṃ brāhmaṇagāmoti puratthimadakkhiṇāya disāya majjhimadesassa avadhiṭṭhāne malladese thūṇanāmako brāhmaṇabahulatāya brāhmaṇagāmo. Tadavasarīti taṃ avasari, thūṇagāmamaggaṃ pāpuṇīti attho. Assosunti suṇiṃsu, sotadvārasampattavacananigghosānusārena jāniṃsūti attho. Khoti padapūraṇe, avadhāraṇatthe vā nipāto. Tattha avadhāraṇatthena assosuṃyeva, na tesaṃ savanantarāyo ahosīti vuttaṃ hoti. Padapūraṇena padabyañjanasiliṭṭhattamattameva. Thūṇeyyakāti thūṇagāmavāsino. Brāhmaṇagahapatikāti ettha brahmaṃ aṇantīti brāhmaṇā, mante sajjhāyantīti attho. Idameva hi jātibrāhmaṇānaṃ nibbacanaṃ, ariyā [P 0.0378] pana bāhitapāpattā “brāhmaṇā”ti vuccanti. Gahapatikāti khattiyabrāhmaṇe vajjetvā ye keci agāraṃ ajjhāvasantā vuccanti, visesato vessā. Brāhmaṇā ca gahapatikā ca brāhmaṇagahapatikā.

69. In the ninth sutta: 'Among the Mallas': the Mallas are a people, royal princes. Their dwelling is a single country, but by convention it is called 'the Mallas'; that is, among those who in the world are called 'Mallas.' Some, however, read it as 'Mālesu.' 'Wandering on tour': wandering on a great tour of the country by way of an unhurried journey. 'With a great Saṅgha of bhikkhus': with a great community of ascetics, great in its immeasurable virtue. For at that time the Blessed One had a large retinue of bhikkhus. 'Thūṇa, a brahmin village of the Mallas': in the southeastern direction, at the border of the Middle Country, in the land of the Mallas, there was a brahmin village named Thūṇa, so called because of its abundance of brahmins. 'He approached it': he approached it, meaning he reached the road to the village of Thūṇa. 'They heard': they listened; that is, they came to know in accordance with the sound of speech that reached the ear-door. 'Kho' is a particle used for filling out a line or for emphasis. Here, in the sense of emphasis, it means they indeed heard; there was no obstacle to their hearing. As a filler, it merely serves to smooth the words and syllables. 'The Thūṇeyyakas': the inhabitants of the village of Thūṇa. 'Brahmin householders': here, those who utter the sacred word (brahma) are called brahmins, meaning they recite the hymns. This, indeed, is the etymology for brahmins by birth. But the noble ones are called 'brahmins' because they have cast out evil. 'Householders': excluding khattiyas and brahmins, all who dwell in a household are called this, especially Vessas. 'Brahmin householders': brahmins and householders.

Idāni yamatthaṃ te assosuṃ, taṃ dassetuṃ “samaṇo khalu, bho, gotamo”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha samitapāpattā “samaṇo”ti veditabbo. Vuttañhetaṃ [M 0.0343] – “samitāssa honti pāpakā akusalā dhammā”tiādi (ma. ni. 1.434). Bhagavā ca anuttarena ariyamaggena sabbaso samitapāpo. Tenassa yathābhuccaguṇādhigatametaṃ nāmaṃ, yadidaṃ samaṇoti. Khalūti anussavatthe nipāto. Bhoti brāhmaṇajātikānaṃ jātisamudāgataṃ ālapanamattaṃ. Vuttampi cetaṃ “bhovādi nāma so hoti, sace hoti sakiñcano”ti (dha. pa. 396). Gotamoti gottavasena bhagavato parikittanaṃ. Tasmā “samaṇo khalu, bho, gotamo”ti samaṇo kira, bho, gotamagottoti ayamettha attho. Sakyaputtoti idaṃ pana bhagavato uccākulaparidīpanaṃ. Sakyakulā pabbajitoti saddhāpabbajitabhāvaparidīpanaṃ. Kenaci pārijuññena anabhibhūto aparikkhīṇaṃyeva taṃ kulaṃ pahāya nekkhammādhigamasaddhāya pabbajitoti vuttaṃ hoti. Udapānaṃ tiṇassa ca bhusassa ca yāva mukhato pūresunti pānīyakūpaṃ tiṇena ca bhusena ca mukhappamāṇena vaḍḍhesuṃ, tiṇādīni pakkhipitvā kūpaṃ pidahiṃsūti attho.

Now, to show what it was that they heard, the words 'The ascetic Gotama, good sirs...' were said. Here, he should be understood as an 'ascetic' (samaṇa) because his evils have been stilled (samita). For it is said: 'His evil, unwholesome states have been stilled,' etc. (MN I 434). And the Blessed One has completely stilled all evil by the unsurpassed noble path. Therefore this name, 'ascetic,' has been acquired by him in accordance with his true qualities. 'Khalu' is a particle in the sense of hearsay. 'Bho' is merely a term of address that comes from the birth of those of the brahmin caste. And this is said: 'He is called a "bho-sayer" if he has some possessions' (Dhp 396). 'Gotama' is a proclamation of the Blessed One by way of his clan name. Therefore, 'The ascetic Gotama, good sirs' means 'The ascetic of the Gotama clan, it seems, good sirs'—this is the meaning here. 'Son of the Sakyans' clarifies the Blessed One's high birth. 'Gone forth from the Sakyan clan' clarifies the fact that he went forth out of faith. This means that he went forth out of faith for attaining renunciation, having left that clan which was unconquered by any decline and was undiminished. 'They filled the well with grass and chaff up to its mouth': this means they filled the water-well with grass and chaff up to the level of its opening; the meaning is that they covered the well by throwing in grass and other things.

Tassa kira gāmassa bahi bhagavato āgamanamagge brāhmaṇānaṃ paribhogabhūto eko udapāno ahosi. Taṃ ṭhapetvā tattha sabbāni kūpataḷākādīni udakaṭṭhānāni tadā visukkhāni nirudakāni ahesuṃ. Atha thūṇeyyakā ratanattaye appasannā maccherapakatā bhagavato āgamanaṃ [V 0.0308] sutvā “sace samaṇo gotamo sasāvako imaṃ gāmaṃ pavisitvā dvīhatīhaṃ vaseyya, sabbaṃ imaṃ janaṃ attano vacane ṭhapeyya, tato brāhmaṇadhammo patiṭṭhaṃ na labheyyā”ti tattha bhagavato avāsāya parisakkantā “imasmiṃ gāme aññattha udakaṃ natthi, amuṃ udapānaṃ aparibhogaṃ karissāma, evaṃ samaṇo gotamo sasāvako imaṃ gāmaṃ na pavisissatī”ti sammantayitvā sabbe gāmavāsino sattāhassa [P 0.0379] udakaṃ gahetvā cāṭiādīni pūretvā udapānaṃ tiṇena ca bhusena ca pidahiṃsu. Tena vuttaṃ – “udapānaṃ tiṇassa ca bhusassa ca yāva mukhato pūresuṃ, ‘mā te muṇḍakā samaṇakā pānīyaṃ apaṃsū’”ti.

It seems that outside that village, on the road of the Blessed One's approach, there was a well for the use of the brahmins. Except for that one, all the other water-places there—wells, ponds, and so on—were at that time dried up and without water. Then the people of Thūṇā, who were without confidence in the Triple Gem and were of a stingy nature, having heard of the Blessed One's arrival, thought: 'If the ascetic Gotama with his disciples enters this village and stays for two or three days, he will establish all these people in his teaching, and then the brahmin doctrine will find no footing.' Scheming to prevent the Blessed One from dwelling there, they thought: 'There is no other water in this village. We will make that well unusable. In that way, the ascetic Gotama with his disciples will not enter this village.' Having consulted together, all the villagers took a seven-day supply of water, filled their jars and other containers, and covered the well with grass and chaff. Therefore it was said: 'They filled the well with grass and chaff up to its mouth, thinking, "Let not those shaveling ascetics drink the water!"'

Tattha muṇḍakā samaṇakāti muṇḍe “muṇḍā”ti samaṇe “samaṇā”ti vattuṃ vaṭṭeyya, te pana khuṃsanādhippāyena hīḷentā evamāhaṃsu. Māti paṭisedhe, mā apaṃsu mā piviṃsūti attho. Maggā okkammāti [M 0.0344] maggato apasakkitvā. Etamhāti yo udapāno tehi tathā kato, tameva niddisanto āha. Kiṃ pana bhagavā tesaṃ brāhmaṇānaṃ vippakāraṃ anāvajjitvā evamāha – “etamhā udapānā pānīyaṃ āharā”ti, udāhu āvajjitvā jānantoti? Jānanto eva bhagavā attano buddhānubhāvaṃ pakāsetvā te dametvā nibbisevane kātuṃ evamāha, na pānīyaṃ pātukāmo. Tenevettha mahāparinibbānasutte viya “pipāsitosmī”ti (dī. ni. 2.191) na vuttaṃ. Dhammabhaṇḍāgāriko pana satthu ajjhāsayaṃ ajānanto thūṇeyyakehi kataṃ vippakāraṃ ācikkhanto “idāni so, bhante”tiādimāha.

Here, 'shaveling ascetics' (muṇḍakā samaṇakā): it would be proper to say 'shaven ones' (muṇḍā) and 'ascetics' (samaṇā), but they spoke thus disparagingly with the intention of reviling. 'Mā' is in the sense of prohibition; the meaning is 'let them not drink, let them not imbibe.' 'Having turned aside from the road' (maggā okkamma): having moved away from the road. 'From this' (etamhā): he said this indicating that very well that had been treated thus by them. But did the Blessed One say, 'Bring drinking water from this well,' without adverting to the mischief of those brahmins, or did he say it knowing it after having adverted to it? The Blessed One spoke thus knowing it full well, in order to display his Buddha-power, to tame them, and to render them harmless, not because he wanted to drink water. For that reason, it is not said here, 'I am thirsty,' as in the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta. But the Treasurer of the Dhamma, not knowing the Teacher's intention, pointed out the mischief done by the people of Thūṇā, saying, 'Now, venerable sir...'

Tattha idānīti adhunā, amhākaṃ āgamanavelāyamevāti attho. Eso, bhante, udapānoti paṭhanti. Thero dvikkhattuṃ paṭikkhipitvā tatiyavāre “na kho tathāgatā tikkhattuṃ paccanīkā kātabbā, kāraṇaṃ diṭṭhaṃ bhavissati dīghadassinā”ti mahārājadattiyaṃ bhagavato pattaṃ gahetvā udapānaṃ agamāsi. Gacchante there udapāne udakaṃ paripuṇṇaṃ hutvā uttaritvā samantato sandati, sabbaṃ tiṇaṃ bhusañca uplavitvā sayameva apagacchi. Tena ca sandamānena salilena uparūpari vaḍḍhantena tasmiṃ gāme sabbeva pokkharaṇīādayo jalāsayā visukkhā paripūriṃsu, tathā parikhākusubbhaninnādīni ca. Sabbo gāmappadeso mahoghena ajjhotthaṭo mahāvassakāle viya ahosi. Kumuduppalapadumapuṇḍarīkādīni jalajapupphāni tattha tattha ubbhijjitvā vikasamānāni udakaṃ sañchādiṃsu. Saresu haṃsakoñcacakkavākakāraṇḍavabakādayā [P 0.0380]e udakasakuṇikā vassamānā tattha tattha vicariṃsu. Thūṇeyyakā taṃ mahoghaṃ tathā uttarantaṃ samantato vīcitaraṅgasamākulaṃ pariyantato samuṭṭhahamānaṃ ruciraṃ pheṇabubbuḷakaṃ disvā acchariyabbhutacittajātā evaṃ sammantesuṃ “mayaṃ samaṇassa gotamassa udakupacchedaṃ kātuṃ vāyamimhā, ayaṃ pana [V 0.0309] mahogho tassa āgamanakālato paṭṭhāya evaṃ abhivaḍḍhati, nissaṃsayaṃ kho ayaṃ tassa iddhānubhāvo. Mahiddhiko hi so mahānubhāvo. Ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ vijjati, yathā yaṃ mahogho uṭṭhahitvā amhākaṃ gāmampi otthareyya. Handa mayaṃ samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ upasaṅkamitvā payirupāsitvā accayaṃ desentā khamāpeyyāmā”ti.

Herein, idāni means 'now,' that is, 'at the very time of our arrival.' They recite: 'Venerable sir, this is the well.' The elder declined twice, but on the third occasion, thinking, 'The Tathāgatas should not be opposed three times; the far-seeing one must have seen a reason,' he took the Blessed One’s bowl, the gift of the great king, and went to the well. As the elder was going, the water in the well became full, overflowed, and flowed all around. All the grass and chaff floated up and went away on their own. And as that water flowed and rose higher and higher, all the dried-up ponds and other reservoirs in that village became full, as did the moats, pits, and low-lying areas. The entire village region was inundated by a great flood, as if during a great rain. Water lilies, lotuses, white lotuses, and other aquatic flowers sprang up here and there, blooming and covering the water. Geese, herons, ruddy shelducks, coots, cranes, and other water birds, calling out, roamed about here and there. When the people of Thūṇā saw that great flood rising up, agitated all around with rippling waves, with beautiful foam and bubbles rising from its edge, their minds were struck with wonder and amazement, and they conferred thus: 'We tried to cut off the ascetic Gotama's water, but this great flood has been rising ever since his arrival. Without a doubt, this is the power of his spiritual might. For he is of great spiritual power, of great might. It is possible that this great flood could rise and inundate our village. Come, let us approach the ascetic Gotama, attend upon him, confess our transgression, and ask for his forgiveness.'

Te [M 0.0345] sabbeva ekajjhāsayā hutvā saṅghasaṅghī gaṇībhūtā gāmato nikkhamitvā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṃsu. Upasaṅkamitvā appekacce bhagavato pāde sirasā vandiṃsu, appekacce añjaliṃ paṇāmesuṃ, appekacce bhagavatā saddhiṃ sammodiṃsu, appekacce tuṇhībhūtā nisīdiṃsu, appekacce nāmagottaṃ sāvesuṃ. Evaṃ pana katvā sabbeva ekamantaṃ nisīditvā “idha mayaṃ, bho gotama, bhoto ceva gotamassa gotamasāvakānañca udakappaṭisedhaṃ kārayimha, amukasmiṃ udapāne tiṇañca bhusañca pakkhipimha. So pana udapāno acetanopi samāno sacetano viya bhoto guṇaṃ jānanto viya sayameva sabbaṃ tiṇaṃ bhusaṃ apanetvā suvisuddho jāto, sabbopi cettha ninnappadeso mahatā udakoghena paripuṇṇo ramaṇīyova jāto, udakūpajīvino sattā parituṭṭhā. Mayaṃ pana manussāpi samānā bhoto guṇe na jānimha, ye mayaṃ evaṃ akarimha, sādhu no bhavaṃ gotamo tathā karotu, yathāyaṃ mahogho imaṃ gāmaṃ na otthareyya, accayo no accagamā yathābālaṃ, taṃ no bhavaṃ gotamo accayaṃ paṭiggaṇhātu anukampaṃ upādāyā”ti accayaṃ desesuṃ. Bhagavāpi “taggha tumhe accayo accagamā yathābālaṃ, taṃ vo mayaṃ paṭiggaṇhāma āyatiṃ saṃvarāyā”ti tesaṃ accayaṃ [P 0.0381] paṭiggahetvā pasannacittataṃ ñatvā uttari ajjhāsayānurūpaṃ dhammaṃ desesi. Te bhagavato dhammadesanaṃ sutvā pasannacittā saraṇādīsu patiṭṭhitā bhagavantaṃ vanditvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā pakkamiṃsu. Tesaṃ pana āgamanato puretaraṃyeva āyasmā ānando taṃ pāṭihāriyaṃ disvā acchariyabbhutacittajāto pattena pānīyaṃ ādāya bhagavato upanāmetvā taṃ pavattiṃ ārocesi. Tena vuttaṃ – “evaṃ, bhanteti kho āyasmā ānando”tiādi.

All of them, having come to a single resolve, forming groups and crowds, left the village and approached the Blessed One. Having approached, some paid homage by placing their heads at the Blessed One’s feet; some raised their hands in reverential salutation; some exchanged friendly greetings with the Blessed One; some sat down silently; and some announced their name and clan. Having done so, they all sat down to one side and said: 'Here, Master Gotama, we caused the water to be withheld from Master Gotama and his disciples, and we threw grass and chaff into a certain well. But that well, though insentient, as if it were sentient, as if it knew your virtue, on its own removed all the grass and chaff and became perfectly clear. And this entire low-lying area has become filled with a great flood of water and is delightful, and the creatures that live in water are satisfied. But we, though we are human beings, did not know your virtue, we who acted in such a way. It would be good, Master Gotama, if you would act in such a way that this great flood does not inundate this village. A transgression overcame us, as we were foolish. May Master Gotama accept this transgression of ours out of compassion.' They confessed their transgression. The Blessed One said: 'Indeed, a transgression overcame you, as you were foolish. We accept this from you for the sake of future restraint.' Having accepted their transgression and recognizing that their minds were confident, he taught them the Dhamma further, in accordance with their dispositions. Having heard the Blessed One’s discourse on the Dhamma, with confident minds they became established in the refuges and so on. Then, having paid homage to the Blessed One and circumambulated him, they departed. But even before their arrival, the Venerable Ānanda, having seen that miracle, his mind struck with wonder and amazement, took drinking water in the bowl, brought it to the Blessed One, and reported the event. Therefore it was said: '“So be it, venerable sir,” the Venerable Ānanda replied,' and so on.

Tattha mukhato ovamitvāti sabbaṃ taṃ tiṇādiṃ mukhena chaḍḍetvā. Vissandanto maññeti pubbe dīgharajjukena udapānena ussiñcitvā gahetabbaudakogho bhagavato pattaṃ gahetvā therassa gatakāle mukhena vissandanto viya samatittiko kākapeyyo hutvā aṭṭhāsi. Idañca therassa gatakāle udakappavattiṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tato paraṃ pana pubbe vuttanayena tasmiṃ gāme sakalaṃ ninnaṭṭhānaṃ udakena paripuṇṇaṃ ahosīti. Ayaṃ paniddhi na buddhānaṃ adhiṭṭhānena, nāpi devānubhāvena, atha kho bhagavato [M 0.0346] puññānubhāvena parittadesanatthaṃ rājagahato vesāligamane viya. Keci [V 0.0310] pana “thūṇeyyakānaṃ bhagavati pasādajananatthaṃ tesaṃ atthakāmāhi devatāhi kata”nti. Apare “udapānassa heṭṭhā vasanakanāgarājā evamakāsī”ti. Sabbaṃ taṃ akāraṇaṃ, yathā bhagavato puññānubhāvenayeva tathā udakuppattiyā paridīpitattā.

Herein, 'having vomited from its mouth' means having discarded all that grass and so on with its mouth. 'It stood, it seems, overflowing': The mass of water that previously had to be drawn up and taken from the well with a long rope, at the time when the elder went there having taken the Blessed One's bowl, stood level with the brim, so full that a crow could drink from it, as if it were overflowing from its mouth. And this was said with reference to the flowing of the water at the time the elder went. Thereafter, in the way previously stated, the entire low-lying area in that village became filled with water. This spiritual power, however, was not by the determination of the Buddhas, nor by the power of devas, but rather by the power of the Blessed One's merit, just as when he went from Rājagaha to Vesālī for the purpose of teaching the Paritta. Some, however, say: 'It was done by deities wishing for their welfare, in order to generate confidence in the Blessed One among the people of Thūṇā.' Others say: 'The nāga king dwelling beneath the well did this.' All that is without basis, because the arising of the water has been explained as being due solely to the power of the Blessed One's merit.

Etamatthaṃ viditvāti etaṃ adhiṭṭhānena vinā attanā icchitanipphattisaṅkhātaṃ atthaṃ sabbākārato viditvā tadatthadīpanaṃ imaṃ udānaṃ udānesi.

'Having understood this matter': having understood in all its aspects this matter—namely, the accomplishment of what is wished for without an act of determination—he uttered this inspired utterance that illuminates that matter.

Tattha kiṃ kayirā udapānena, āpā ce sabbadā siyunti yassa sabbakālaṃ sabbattha ca āpā ce yadi siyuṃ yadi upalabbheyyuṃ yadi ākaṅkhāmattapaṭibaddho, tesaṃ lābho, tena udapānena kiṃ kayirā kiṃ kareyya, kiṃ payojananti attho. Taṇhāya mūlato chetvā, kissa pariyesanaṃ careti yāya taṇhāya [P 0.0382] vinibaddhā sattā akatapuññā hutvā icchitālābhadukkhena vihaññanti, tassā taṇhāya mūlaṃ, mūle vā chinditvā ṭhito mādiso sabbaññubuddho kissa kena kāraṇena pānīyapariyesanaṃ, aññaṃ vā paccayapariyesanaṃ careyya. “Mūlato chettā”tipi paṭhanti, taṇhāya mūlaṃ mūleyeva vā chedakoti attho. Atha vā mūlato chettāti mūlato paṭṭhāya taṇhāya chedako. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yo bodhiyā mūlabhūtamahāpaṇidhānato paṭṭhāya aparimitaṃ sakalaṃ puññasambhāraṃ attano acintetvā lokahitatthameva pariṇāmanavasena paripūrento mūlato pabhuti taṇhāya chettā, so taṇhāhetukassa icchitālābhassa abhāvato kissa kena kāraṇena udakapariyesanaṃ careyya, ime pana thūṇeyyakā andhabālā imaṃ kāraṇaṃ ajānantā evamakaṃsūti.

Herein, 'What would one do with a well, if there were water always?' The meaning is: for one for whom there would be water always and everywhere, if its acquisition were dependent merely on wishing for it, what would he do with a well? What would be its purpose? 'Having cut off craving by the root, for what would he search?' Beings bound by that craving, having made no merit, are afflicted by the suffering of not obtaining what they wish for. Having cut the root of that craving, or standing having cut it at the root, for what reason would an all-knowing Buddha like myself go in search of water or in search of any other requisite? They also recite 'mūlato chettā' (a cutter from the root), meaning a cutter of the root of craving, or at the very root. Or, 'a cutter from the root' means a cutter of craving starting from the root. This is what is said: He who, starting from the great aspiration that is the root of enlightenment, while fulfilling the entire immeasurable accumulation of merit—not for his own sake but dedicating it solely for the welfare of the world—is a cutter of craving from the root onwards, for what reason would he go in search of water, since for him there is no non-acquisition of what is wished for, which is caused by craving? But these people of Thūṇā, blind fools, not knowing this reason, acted thus.

Navamasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Ninth Sutta is finished.

10. Utenasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Utena Sutta

70. Dasame rañño utenassāti utenassa nāma rañño, yo “vajjirājā”tipi vuccati. Uyyānagatassāti uyyānakīḷanatthaṃ uyyānaṃ gatassa[M 0.0347]. Anādare hi idaṃ sāmivacanaṃ, “antepura”nti pana padaṃ apekkhitvā sambandhepetaṃ sāmivacanaṃ hoti. Kālaṅkatānīti aggidaḍḍhāni hutvā matāni honti. Sāmāvatīpamukhānīti ettha kā panāyaṃ sāmāvatī, kathañca daḍḍhāti? Vuccate, bhaddavatiyaṃ seṭṭhino dhītā ghosakaseṭṭhinā dhītuṭṭhāne ṭhapitā pañcasataitthiparivārā [V 0.0311] rañño utenassa aggamahesī mettāvihārabahulā ariyasāvikā sāmāvatī nāma. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthārato pana ādito paṭṭhāya sāmāvatiyā uppattikathā dhammapadavatthumhi (dha. pa. aṭṭha. 1.20 sāmāvatīvatthu) vuttanayena veditabbā. Māgaṇḍiyassa nāma brāhmaṇassa dhītā attano mātāpitūnaṃ –

70. In the tenth, of King Utena means of the king named Utena, who is also called 'the Vajjī king.' Gone to the park means gone to the park for amusement. This is a genitive of disrespect; however, in connection with the word 'harem,' it is a genitive of relation. They had passed away means they died, having been burned by fire. With Sāmāvatī at their head: who is this Sāmāvatī, and how was she burned? It is said: She was Sāmāvatī, the daughter of a wealthy merchant in Bhaddavatī. Established in the position of a daughter by the wealthy merchant Ghosaka, with a retinue of five hundred women, she became the chief queen of King Utena. She was a noble female disciple who abounded in the abiding in loving-kindness. This is the brief account here. In detail, the story of Sāmāvatī’s origin from the beginning should be understood in the way it is told in the Dhammapada Commentary (Dhp-A 1.20, the Story of Sāmāvatī). The daughter of the brahmin named Māgaṇḍiya said to her mother and father:—

“Disvāna [P 0.0383] taṇhaṃ aratiṃ ragañca,

Nāhosi chando api methunasmiṃ;

Kimevidaṃ muttakarīsapuṇṇaṃ,

Pādāpi naṃ samphusituṃ na icche”ti. (su. ni. 841) –

“Having seen Craving, Discontent, and Passion, I had no desire even for sexual intercourse. What is this body, full of urine and feces? I would not want to touch it even with my foot.”

Bhagavatā desitaṃ imaṃ gāthaṃ sutvā satthari baddhāghātā māgaṇḍiyā aparabhāge raññā utenena mahesiṭṭhāne ṭhapitā bhagavato kosambiṃ upagatabhāvaṃ, sāmāvatīpamukhānañca pañcannaṃ itthisatānaṃ upāsikābhāvaṃ ñatvā “āgato nāma samaṇo gotamo imaṃ nagaraṃ, dānissa kattabbaṃ jānissāmi, imāpi tassa upaṭṭhāyikā, imāsampi sāmāvatīpamukhānañca kattabbaṃ jānissāmī”ti anekapariyāyehi tathāgatassa tāsañca anatthaṃ kātuṃ vāyamitvāpi asakkontī punekadivasaṃ raññā saddhiṃ uyyānakīḷaṃ gacchantī cūḷapitu sāsanaṃ pahiṇi “sāmāvatiyā pāsādaṃ gantvā dussakoṭṭhāgāratelakoṭṭhāgārāni vivarāpetvā dussāni telacāṭīsu temetvā thambhe veṭhetvā tā sabbā ekato katvā dvāraṃ pidahitvā bahi yantaṃ datvā daṇḍadīpikāhi gehe aggiṃ dadamāno otaritvā gacchatū”ti.

Māgaṇḍiyā, having heard this verse spoken by the Blessed One, conceived a hatred for the Teacher. Later, after she had been made chief queen by King Utena, she learned that the Blessed One had come to Kosambī and that Sāmāvatī and her five hundred women had become lay disciples. She thought: 'So the ascetic Gotama has come to this city. Now I will see what can be done to him. And these women are his attendants; I will see what can be done to them, with Sāmāvatī at their head, too.' Though she tried in many ways to bring harm to the Tathāgata and to them, she was unable. Then one day, while going to the park with the king for amusement, she sent a message to her paternal uncle: 'Go to Sāmāvatī’s palace, have the storerooms for cloth and oil opened, soak the cloths in jars of oil, wrap them around the pillars, gather all those women together, close the door, bolt it from the outside, set the house on fire with torches, and then come down and go away.'

Taṃ sutvā so pāsādaṃ abhiruyha koṭṭhāgārāni vivaritvā vatthāni telacāṭīsu temetvā thambhe veṭhetuṃ ārabhi. Atha naṃ sāmāvatīpamukhā itthiyo “kiṃ etaṃ cūḷapitā”ti vadantiyo upasaṅkamiṃsu. “Ammā, rājā daḷhikammatthāya ime thambhe telapilotikāhi bandhāpeti[M 0.0348], rājagehe nāma suyuttaduyuttaṃ dujjānaṃ, mā me santike hothā”ti vatvā tā āgatā gabbhesu pavesetvā dvārāni pidahitvā bahi yantakaṃ datvā ādito paṭṭhāya aggiṃ dento otari. Sāmāvatī tāsaṃ ovādaṃ adāsi, “ammā, anamatagge saṃsāre vicarantīnaṃ evameva agginā jhāmattabhāvānaṃ buddhañāṇenapi paricchedo na sukaro, appamattā hothā”ti. Tā satthu santike dhammaṃ sutvā adhigataphalāya viññātasāsanāya [P 0.0384] khujjuttarāya ariyasāvikāya sekkhapaṭisambhidāpattāya satthārā desitaniyāmeneva dhammaṃ desentiyā santike sotāpattiphalassa adhigatā antarantarā kammaṭṭhānamanasikārena yuttappayuttā gehe jhāyante vedanāpariggahakammaṭṭhānaṃ manasi [V 0.0312] karontiyo kāci dutiyaphalaṃ, kāci tatiyaphalaṃ pāpuṇitvā kālamakaṃsu. Atha bhikkhū kosambiyaṃ piṇḍāya carantā taṃ pavattiṃ ñatvā pacchābhattaṃ bhagavato ārocetvā tāsaṃ abhisamparāyaṃ pucchiṃsu. Bhagavā ca tāsaṃ ariyaphalādhigamaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ abhāsi. Tena vuttaṃ – “tena kho pana samayena rañño utenassa…pe… anipphalā kālaṅkatā”ti.

Hearing this, he went up into the palace, opened the storerooms, soaked cloths in jars of oil, and began to wrap them around the pillars. Then the women, with Sāmāvatī at their head, approached him, saying, 'Uncle, what is this?' He replied: 'My ladies, the king is having these pillars wrapped with oil-soaked rags to strengthen them. In a king's house, it is hard to know what is proper and what is not. Do not stay near me.' Having said this, he ushered them into the inner chambers, closed the doors, bolted them from the outside, set fire to the house all around, and descended. Sāmāvatī gave them this advice: 'My ladies, for those wandering in beginningless saṃsāra, the number of times one has been burned by fire just like this is not easy to determine even with a Buddha's knowledge. Be heedful!' These women had already attained the fruit of stream-entry from the noble female disciple Khujjuttarā, who had herself realized the fruit, understood the teaching, attained the analytical knowledges of a trainee, and taught the Dhamma exactly as it was set forth by the Teacher. They had been diligently applying themselves to meditation from time to time. As the house was burning, they attended to the meditation subject of the full understanding of feeling, and some attained the second fruit and some the third fruit before they passed away. Then some bhikkhus who were walking for alms in Kosambī learned of the incident. After their meal, they reported it to the Blessed One and asked about the future destiny of those women. The Blessed One told the bhikkhus of their attainment of the noble fruits. Therefore it was said: 'At that time King Utena’s … passed away not without fruit.'

Tattha anipphalāti na nipphalā, sampattasāmaññaphalā eva kālaṅkatā. Tā pana phalāni paṭilabhantiyo sāmāvatiyā –

Herein, not without fruit means they were not fruitless; they passed away having attained the fruits of recluseship. They obtained those fruits as Sāmāvatī admonished them with the verses:—

“Ārambhatha nikkamatha, yuñjatha buddhasāsane;

Dhunātha maccuno senaṃ, naḷāgāraṃva kuñjaro.

“Bestir yourselves, go forth, apply yourselves to the Buddha’s teaching. Shake off the army of Death as an elephant a hut of reeds.

“Yo imasmiṃ dhammavinaye, appamatto vihassati;

Pahāya jātisaṃsāraṃ, dukkhassantaṃ karissatī”ti. (saṃ. ni. 1.185; netti. 29) –

“Whoever will live diligently in this Dhamma and Discipline, abandoning the round of births, will make an end of suffering.”

Gāthāhi ovadiyamānā vedanāpariggahakammaṭṭhānaṃ manasi karontiyo vipassitvā dutiyatatiyaphalāni paṭilabhiṃsu. Khujjuttarā pana āyusesassa atthitāya, pubbe tādisassa kammassa akatattā ca tato pāsādato bahi ahosi. “Dasayojanantare pakkāmī”ti ca vadanti. Atha bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ, “āvuso, ananucchavikaṃ vata ariyasāvikānaṃ evarūpaṃ maraṇa”nti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte[M 0.0349], “bhikkhave, yadipi tāsaṃ imasmiṃ attabhāve ayuttaṃ, pubbe katakammassa pana yuttameva tāhi laddha”nti vatvā tehi yācito atītaṃ āhari.

Being admonished with these verses, they attended to the meditation subject of the full understanding of feeling, and having developed insight, they attained the second and third fruits. But Khujjuttarā, because her life-span was not yet exhausted and because she had not done such a kamma in the past, was outside the palace. Some say she had gone ten yojanas away. Then the bhikkhus raised a topic of discussion in the Dhamma hall: 'Friends, it is truly unfitting for noble female disciples to meet such a death.' The Teacher came and asked: 'Bhikkhus, for what topic of discussion are you now gathered together?' When they told him what it was, he said: 'Bhikkhus, although this was unfitting for them in this present life, what they received was indeed fitting for the kamma they had done in the past.' Then, at their request, he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente aṭṭha paccekabuddhā rañño nivesane nibaddhaṃ bhuñjanti. Pañcasatā [P 0.0385] itthiyo te upaṭṭhahanti. Tesu satta janā himavantaṃ gacchanti, eko nadītīrasamīpe ekasmiṃ tiṇagahane samāpattiyā nisīdati. Athekadivasaṃ rājā paccekabuddhesu gatesu tāhi itthīhi saddhiṃ udakakīḷaṃ kīḷitukāmo tattha gato. Tā itthiyo divasabhāgaṃ udake kīḷitvā sītapīḷitā visibbitukāmā taṃ tiṇagahanaṃ upari visukkhatiṇasañchannaṃ “tiṇarāsī”ti saññāya parivāretvā aggiṃ datvā tiṇesu jhāyitvā patantesu paccekabuddhaṃ disvā [V 0.0313] “rañño paccekabuddho jhāyati, taṃ rājā ñatvā amhe nāsessati, sudaḍḍhaṃ naṃ karissāmā”ti sabbā ito cito ca dāruādīni āharitvā tassa upari rāsiṃ katvā ālimpetvā “idāni jhāyissatī”ti pakkamiṃsu. Tā paṭhamaṃ asañcetanikā hutvā idāni kammunā bajjhiṃsu. Paccekabuddhaṃ pana antosamāpattiyaṃ sace dārūnaṃ sakaṭasahassampi āharitvā ālimpentā usumākāramattampi gāhetuṃ na sakkonti, tasmā so sattame divase uṭṭhāya yathāsukhaṃ agamāsi. Tā tassa kammassa katattā bahūni vassasahassāni bahūni vassasatasahassāni niraye paccitvā tasseva kammassa vipākāvasesena attabhāvasate imināva niyāmena gehe jhāyamāne jhāyiṃsu. Idaṃ tāsaṃ pubbakammaṃ.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, eight paccekabuddhas regularly ate their meal in the king's palace. Five hundred women attended on them. Seven of them would go to the Himalayas, but one would sit in attainment in a grass thicket near the river bank. One day, after the paccekabuddhas had gone, the king went there, wishing to play in the water with those women. The women played in the water for part of the day and then, feeling cold and wanting to warm themselves, they approached the grass thicket, which was covered with dry grass. Perceiving it to be a heap of grass, they surrounded it and set it on fire. As the grass burned and fell away, they saw the paccekabuddha. They thought: 'The king's paccekabuddha is burning! If the king finds out, he will have us destroyed. Let us burn him thoroughly.' So they all gathered firewood and other things from here and there, made a pile on top of him, and set it on fire. Saying, 'Now he will be burned,' they departed. At first they had acted without intention, but now they were bound by their kamma. However, when a paccekabuddha is in attainment, even if one were to bring a thousand cartloads of firewood and set it ablaze, one could not cause him to feel even a trace of heat. Therefore, on the seventh day, he rose and went on his way as he pleased. Because they had done that kamma, those women were tormented in hell for many thousands of years, for many hundreds of thousands of years. Then, as a residual result of that same kamma, for a hundred existences they were burned to death in this very manner as their houses burned. This was their past kamma.

Yasmā pana te imasmiṃ attabhāve ariyaphalāni sacchākaṃsu, ratanattayaṃ payirupāsiṃsu, tasmā tattha anāgāminiyo suddhāvāsesu upapannā, itarā kāci tāvatiṃsesu, kāci yāmesu, kāci tusitesu, kāci nimmānaratīsu, kāci paranimmitavasavattīsu upapannā.

However, since in this very life they realized the noble fruits and attended upon the Three Jewels, the non-returners among them were reborn in the Pure Abodes. Of the others, some were reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, some in the Yāma heaven, some in the Tusita heaven, some in the heaven of the Devas Who Delight in Creating, and some in the heaven of the Devas Who Wield Power over Others' Creations.

Rājāpi kho uteno “sāmāvatiyā gehaṃ kira jhāyatī”ti sutvā vegena āgacchantopi taṃ padesaṃ tāsu daḍḍhāsuyeva sampāpuṇi. Āgantvā pana gehaṃ nibbāpetvā uppannabalavadomanasso māgaṇḍiyāya tathā kāritabhāvaṃ upāyena ñatvā ariyasāvikāsu katāparādhakammunā codiyamāno tassā rājāṇaṃ kāresi saddhiṃ ñātakehi. Evaṃ sā saparijanā samittabandhavā anayabyasanaṃ pāpuṇi.

When King Utena heard, 'They say Sāmāvatī’s quarters are on fire,' he rushed there with all speed but reached the place only after they had been burned to death. After he arrived and had the fire extinguished, he was overcome with intense grief. By means of a stratagem he discovered that Māgaṇḍiyā had instigated the deed. Impelled by the kamma of the offense he had committed against the noble female disciples, he had the royal punishment inflicted upon her along with her relatives. Thus she, together with her retinue, friends, and relatives, met with misfortune and disaster.

Etamatthaṃ [M 0.0350] viditvāti etaṃ sāmāvatīpamukhānaṃ tāsaṃ itthīnaṃ aggimhi anayabyasanāpattihetuṃ, māgaṇḍiyāya ca [P 0.0386] samittabandhavāya rājāṇāya anayabyasanāpattinimittaṃ sabbākārato viditvā tadatthadīpanaṃ imaṃ udānaṃ udānesi.

Having understood this matter: having understood in all its aspects this cause of the misfortune and disaster in the fire for those women headed by Sāmāvatī, and the reason for the misfortune and disaster by the king's punishment for Māgaṇḍiyā along with her friends and relatives, the Blessed One uttered this inspired utterance to illuminate that meaning.

Tattha mohasambandhano loko, bhabbarūpova dissatīti yo idha sattaloko bhabbarūpova hetusampanno viya hutvā dissati, sopi mohasambandhano mohena paliguṇṭhito attahitāhitaṃ ajānanto hite na paṭipajjati, ahitaṃ dukkhāvahaṃ bahuñca apuññaṃ ācināti. “Bhavarūpova dissatī”tipi pāṭho. Tassattho – ayaṃ loko mohasambandhano mohena paliguṇṭhito, tato eva bhavarūpova sassatasabhāvo viyassa attā dissati, ajarāmaro viya upaṭṭhāti, yena pāṇātipātādīni akattabbāni karoti.

Herein, 'the world is bound by delusion and appears to be capable' means that this world of beings, which appears as if it were capable, as if endowed with a cause, is in fact bound by delusion, enveloped by delusion. Not knowing what is for its own welfare and what is not, it does not practice what is for its welfare but accumulates much demerit that brings suffering. There is also the reading, 'It appears to be becoming.' The meaning of this is: this world is bound by delusion, enveloped by it. For that very reason, it appears to be becoming, as if its self had an eternal nature, presenting itself as if ageless and deathless. Because of this, one does things that should not be done, such as destroying life.

Upadhibandhano [V 0.0314] bālo, tamasā parivārito. Sassatoriva khāyatīti na kevalañca mohasambandhano eva, apica kho upadhibandhanopi ayaṃ andhabālaloko avijjātamasā parivārito. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yena ñāṇena aviparītaṃ kāme ca khandhe ca “aniccā dukkhā vipariṇāmadhammā”ti passeyya, tassa abhāvato yasmā bālo andhaputhujjano aññāṇatamasā samantato parivārito nivuto, tasmā so kāmūpadhi kilesūpadhi khandhūpadhīti imesaṃ upadhīnaṃ vasena ca upadhibandhano, tato eva cassa sopadhissa passato sassato viya nicco sabbakālabhāvī viya khāyati. “Asassatiriva khāyatī”tipi pāṭho. Tassattho – attā sabbakālaṃ vijjati upalabbhatīti añño asassati aniccoti lokassa so upadhi micchābhinivesavasena ekadeso viya khāyati, upaṭṭhahatīti attho. Rakāro hi padasandhikaro. Passato natthi kiñcananti yo pana saṅkhāre pariggahetvā aniccādivasena vipassati, tasseva vipassanāpaññāsahitāya maggapaññāya yathābhūtaṃ passato jānato paṭivijjhato rāgādikiñcanaṃ [P 0.0387] natthi, yena saṃsāre bajjheyya. Tathā apassanto eva hi avijjātaṇhādiṭṭhiādibandhanehi saṃsāre baddho siyāti adhippāyo.

'The fool is bound by acquisitions, enveloped in darkness. It appears as if eternal.' This means that this blind, foolish world is not only bound by delusion, but it is also bound by acquisitions, enveloped by the darkness of ignorance. This is what is said: because of the absence of the knowledge by which one would see without distortion that sensual pleasures and the aggregates are 'impermanent, suffering, and subject to change,' the blind worldling, the fool, is completely enveloped and shrouded by the darkness of ignorance. Therefore, he is bound by acquisitions, that is, by the acquisitions of sensual pleasures, the acquisition of defilements, and the acquisition of the aggregates. For that very reason, to him who possesses acquisitions and sees, it appears as if eternal, as if permanent, as if existing for all time. There is also the reading, 'It appears as if non-eternal.' The meaning is this: while the self is held to exist and be found at all times, the other view—that it is non-eternal and impermanent—appears as a partial aspect of that worldly acquisition through wrong adherence; 'it presents itself' is the meaning. The 'r' is a euphonic consonant. 'For one who sees, there is no impediment' means that for one who, having comprehended the formations, contemplates them as impermanent, etc., for him who sees, knows, and penetrates things as they really are with insight wisdom accompanied by path wisdom, there is no impediment of lust and so on by which he would be bound in saṃsāra. The intention is that it is one who does not see thus who would be bound in saṃsāra by the fetters of ignorance, craving, views, and so on.

Dasamasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Tenth Sutta is finished.

Niṭṭhitā ca cūḷavaggavaṇṇanā.

And the commentary on the Cūḷavagga is completed.

8. Pāṭaligāmiyavaggo

8. The Pāṭaligāmiya Chapter

1. Paṭhamanibbānapaṭisaṃyuttasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the First Discourse Connected with Nibbāna

71. Pāṭaligāmiyavaggassa [V 0.0315][P 0.0388][M 0.0351] paṭhame nibbānapaṭisaṃyuttāyāti amatadhātusannissitāya asaṅkhatadhātuyā pavedanavasena pavattāya. Dhammiyā kathāyāti dhammadesanāya. Sandassetīti sabhāvasarasalakkhaṇato nibbānaṃ dasseti. Samādapetīti tameva atthaṃ te bhikkhū gaṇhāpeti. Samuttejetīti tadatthagahaṇe ussāhaṃ janento tejeti joteti. Sampahaṃsetīti nibbānaguṇehi sammadeva sabbappakārehi toseti.

71. In the first [sutta] of the Pāṭaligāmiya Chapter: 'Connected with Nibbāna' means based on the deathless element, grounded in the unconditioned element, proceeding by way of declaration. 'A talk on the Dhamma' means a Dhamma discourse. 'He shows clearly' means he shows Nibbāna in terms of its intrinsic nature, its flavor, and its characteristic. 'He encourages' means he makes those bhikkhus grasp that very meaning. 'He incites' means, generating enthusiasm for grasping that meaning, he fires them up and illuminates them. 'He gladdens' means he satisfies them rightly and in all ways with the qualities of Nibbāna.

Atha vā sandassetīti “so sabbasaṅkhārasamatho sabbūpadhipaṭinissaggā taṇhakkhayo virāgo nirodho”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.281; 2.337; mahāva. 8) nayeneva sabbathā tena tena pariyāyena tesaṃ tesaṃ ajjhāsayānurūpaṃ sammā dasseti. Samādapetīti “iminā ariyamaggena taṃ adhigantabba”nti adhigamapaṭipadāya saddhiṃ tattha bhikkhū ninnapoṇapabbhāre karonto sammā ādapeti gaṇhāpeti. Samuttejetīti etaṃ dukkaraṃ durabhisambhavanti “mā sammāpaṭipattiyaṃ pamādaṃ antarāvosānaṃ āpajjatha, upanissayasampannassa vīriyavato nayidaṃ dukkaraṃ, tasmā sīlavisuddhiādivisuddhipaṭipadāya uṭṭhahatha ghaṭayatha vāyameyyāthā”ti nibbānādhigamāya ussāheti, tattha vā cittaṃ vodapeti. Sampahaṃsetīti “madanimmadano pipāsavinayo ālayasamugghāto”ti (a. ni. 4.34; itivu. 90), rāgakkhayo dosakkhayo mohakkhayoti (saṃ. ni. 4.367; itivu. 44), asaṅkhatanti (saṃ. ni. 4.367), amatañca santantiādinā ca anekapariyāyena (saṃ. ni. 4.409) nibbānānisaṃsappakāsanena tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ cittaṃ tosento hāsento sampahaṃseti samassāseti.

Or alternatively, 'he shows clearly' means that by the method beginning, 'It is the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation' (MN 1.281; 2.337; Mahāva. 8), he shows it rightly in all ways, by this and that means, in conformity with their respective dispositions. 'He encourages' means, along with the path to its attainment, he makes the bhikkhus rightly undertake and grasp it, saying, 'It is to be attained by this noble path,' thus making them slope, incline, and tend towards it. 'He incites' means, thinking, 'This is difficult, hard to attain,' he exhorts them to attain Nibbāna, saying: 'Do not be negligent in the right practice or come to a premature end. For one endowed with supporting conditions and possessed of energy, this is not difficult. Therefore, in the path of the purifications beginning with the purification of virtue, you should arise, strive, and endeavor.' Or, he purifies their minds for it. 'He gladdens' means that by declaring the benefits of Nibbāna in many ways, such as 'the subduing of intoxication, the removal of thirst, the uprooting of clinging' (AN 4.34; Itiv. 90), 'the destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, the destruction of delusion' (SN 4.367; Itiv. 44), 'the unconditioned' (SN 4.367), and 'the deathless and peaceful' (SN 4.409), he gladdens, delights, and reassures the minds of those bhikkhus.

Tedhāti [P 0.0389] te idha. Aṭṭhiṃ katvāti “atthi kiñci ayaṃ no attho adhigantabbo”ti evaṃ sallakkhetvā tāya desanāya atthikā hutvā. Manasi katvāti citte ṭhapetvā anaññavihitā taṃ desanaṃ attano cittagatameva [M 0.0352] katvā. Sabbaṃ cetaso samannāharitvāti sabbena kārakacittena [V 0.0316] ādito paṭṭhāya yāva pariyosānā desanaṃ āvajjetvā, taggatameva ābhogaṃ katvāti attho. Atha vā sabbaṃ cetaso samannāharitvāti sabbasmā cittato desanaṃ sammā anu anu āharitvā. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – desentassa yehi cittehi desanā katā, sabbasmā cittato pavattaṃ desanaṃ bahi gantuṃ adento sammā aviparītaṃ anu anu āharitvā attano cittasantānaṃ āharitvā yathādesitadesitaṃ desanaṃ suṭṭhu upadhāretvā. Ohitasotāti avahitasotā, suṭṭhu upitasotā. Ohitasotāti vā avikkhittasotā. Tameva upalabbhamānopi hi savane avikkhepo satisaṃvaro viya cakkhundriyādīsu sotindriyepi vattumarahatīti. Ettha ca “aṭṭhiṃ katvā”tiādīhi catūhipi padehi tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ tapparabhāvato savane ādaradīpanena sakkaccasavanaṃ dasseti.

'Those here' means those bhikkhus here. 'Having made it a matter of substance' means, having considered, 'There is some goal here for us to attain,' they became desirous of that teaching. 'Having applied the mind' means, having placed it in the mind, not distracted by anything else, they made that teaching the sole resort of their minds. 'Having brought it to bear with the whole mind' means having adverted to the teaching with the entire active mind from beginning to end; the meaning is that they made it the sole object of their attention. Or alternatively, 'having brought it to bear with the whole mind' means having properly drawn in the teaching bit by bit from the entire mind. This is what is said: not allowing the teaching that proceeded from the entire mind of the teacher to go outside, having properly and without distortion drawn it in bit by bit, having brought it into their own mental continuums, they thoroughly retained the teaching just as it was taught. 'With ears lent' means with attentive ears, with ears well-applied. Or, 'with ears lent' means with undistracted ears. For although it is found in the impulsions, non-distraction in hearing is as appropriate to be called the ear faculty as mindfulness and restraint are for the eye faculty and so on. And here, by these four phrases beginning with 'having made it a matter of substance,' their respectful listening is shown by indicating their respect in hearing, which stems from their dedication to it.

Etamatthaṃ viditvāti etaṃ tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ tassā nibbānapaṭisaṃyuttāya dhammakathāya savane ādarakāritaṃ sabbākārato viditvā. Imaṃ udānanti imaṃ nibbānassa tabbidhuradhammadesanāmukhena paramatthato vijjamānabhāvavibhāvanaṃ udānaṃ udānesi.

'Having understood this matter' means, having understood in all its aspects this respect shown by those bhikkhus in listening to that Dhamma talk connected with Nibbāna. 'This inspired utterance' means he uttered this inspired utterance which clarifies the existence of Nibbāna in an ultimate sense by way of an exposition of the Dhamma that is its opposite.

Tattha atthīti vijjati, paramatthato upalabbhatīti attho. Bhikkhaveti tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ ālapanaṃ. Nanu ca udānaṃ nāma pītisomanassasamuṭṭhāpito vā dhammasaṃvegasamuṭṭhāpito vā dhammapaṭiggāhakanirapekkho udāhāro, tathā ceva ettakesu suttesu āgataṃ, idha kasmā bhagavā udānento te bhikkhū āmantesīti? Tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ saññāpanatthaṃ. Nibbānapaṭisaṃyuttañhi bhagavā tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ dhammaṃ desetvā nibbānaguṇānussaraṇena uppannapītisomanassā udānaṃ udānesi. Idha [P 0.0390] nibbānavajjo sabbo sabhāvadhammo paccayāyattavuttikova upalabbhati, na paccayanirapekkho. Ayaṃ pana nibbānadhammo katamapaccaye upalabbhatīti tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ cetoparivitakkamaññāya te ca saññāpetukāmo “atthi, bhikkhave, tadāyatana”ntiādimāha, na ekantatova te paṭiggāhake katvāti veditabbaṃ. Tadāyatananti taṃ kāraṇaṃ. Dakāro padasandhikaro. Nibbānañhi [M 0.0353] maggaphalañāṇādīnaṃ ārammaṇapaccayabhāvato rūpādīni viya cakkhuviññāṇādīnaṃ ārammaṇapaccayabhūtānīti kāraṇaṭṭhena “āyatana”nti vuccati. Ettāvatā ca bhagavā tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ asaṅkhatāya dhātuyā paramatthato atthibhāvaṃ pavedesi.

Therein, 'there is' means it exists, it is found in an ultimate sense; that is the meaning. 'Bhikkhus' is an address to those bhikkhus. Now, is not an inspired utterance an exclamation independent of any recipient of the teaching, aroused either by joy and gladness or by a sense of spiritual urgency? And it is found as such in so many suttas. Why then, while uttering an inspired utterance here, did the Blessed One address those bhikkhus? To make them understand. For having taught those bhikkhus the Dhamma connected with Nibbāna, the Blessed One uttered the inspired utterance out of the joy and gladness that arose from recollecting the qualities of Nibbāna. Here, apart from Nibbāna, every real phenomenon is found to be dependent on conditions for its occurrence, not independent of conditions. But on what condition is this phenomenon of Nibbāna found? Having known the thought in the minds of those bhikkhus and wishing to make them understand, he said, 'There is, bhikkhus, that sphere,' and so on. It should be understood that he did not do so exclusively to make them the recipients. 'That sphere': that cause. The 'd' is a euphonic consonant. For Nibbāna, because it is the object-condition for the path, fruition, knowledge, etc.—just as forms, etc., are the object-condition for eye-consciousness, etc.—is called a 'sphere' in the sense of a cause. By this much the Blessed One declared to those bhikkhus the existence in an ultimate sense of the unconditioned element.

Tatrāyaṃ dhammanvayo – idha saṅkhatadhammānaṃ vijjamānattā asaṅkhatāyapi dhātuyā bhavitabbaṃ tappaṭipakkhattā sabhāvadhammānaṃ. Yathā hi dukkhe vijjamāne tappaṭipakkhabhūtaṃ sukhampi vijjatiyeva[V 0.0317], tathā uṇhe vijjamāne sītampi vijjati, pāpadhammesu vijjamānesu kalyāṇadhammāpi vijjanti eva. Vuttañcetaṃ –

Herein, this is the textual connection in the Dhamma: since conditioned phenomena exist, the unconditioned element must also exist, because real phenomena have their opposites. For just as when suffering exists, its opposite, happiness, also exists; so when heat exists, cold also exists; and when evil qualities exist, wholesome qualities also exist. And this has been said:

“Yathāpi dukkhe vijjante, sukhaṃ nāmapi vijjati;

Evaṃ bhave vijjamāne, vibhavopi icchitabbako.

"Just as when suffering is present, happiness is also found; so when existence is present, non-existence too should be sought."

“Yathāpi uṇhe vijjante, aparaṃ vijjati sītalaṃ;

Evaṃ tividhaggi vijjante, nibbānaṃ icchitabbakaṃ.

"Just as when heat is present, the other, coolness, is found; so when the threefold fire is present, Nibbāna should be sought."

“Yathāpi pāpe vijjante, kalyāṇamapi vijjati;

Evameva jāti vijjante, ajātimapi icchitabbaka”ntiādi. (bu. vaṃ. 2.10-12) –

"Just as when evil is present, the good is also found; so too when birth is present, the unborn should be sought," and so on (Bv 2:10–12).

Apica nibbānassa paramatthato atthibhāvavicāraṇaṃ parato āvibhavissati.

Moreover, the investigation into the existence of Nibbāna in an ultimate sense will become clear later on.

Evaṃ bhagavā asaṅkhatāya dhātuyā paramatthato atthibhāvaṃ sammukhena dassetvā idāni tabbidhuradhammāpohanamukhenassa sabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ, “yattha neva pathavī na āpo”tiādimāha. Tattha yasmā nibbānaṃ sabbasaṅkhāravidhurasabhāvaṃ yathā saṅkhatadhammesu katthaci natthi, tathā tatthapi sabbe saṅkhatadhammā. Na hi saṅkhatāsaṅkhatadhammānaṃ samodhānaṃ sambhavati. Tatrāyaṃ atthavibhāvanā [P 0.0391] – yattha yasmiṃ nibbāne yassaṃ asaṅkhatadhātuyaṃ neva kakkhaḷalakkhaṇā pathavīdhātu atthi, na paggharaṇalakkhaṇā āpodhātu, na uṇhalakkhaṇā tejodhātu, na vitthambhanalakkhaṇā vāyodhātu atthi. Iti catumahābhūtābhāvavacanena yathā sabbassapi upādārūpassa abhāvo vutto hoti tannissitattā. Evaṃ anavasesato kāmarūpabhavassa [M 0.0354] tattha abhāvo vutto hoti tadāyattavuttibhāvato. Na hi mahābhūtanissayena vinā pañcavokārabhavo ekavokārabhavo vā sambhavatīti.

Thus, the Blessed One, having directly shown the ultimate existence of the unconditioned element, now, in order to show its nature by way of rejecting phenomena distinct from it, spoke the words beginning with, 'Where there is neither earth nor water.' Herein, because Nibbāna has a nature remote from all conditioned phenomena, just as it is not found anywhere among conditioned phenomena, so too, all conditioned phenomena are not found there. For the intermingling of conditioned and unconditioned phenomena is not possible. Here is the explanation of the meaning: In that Nibbāna, in that unconditioned element, there is neither the earth element with its characteristic of hardness, nor the water element with its characteristic of fluidity, nor the fire element with its characteristic of heat, nor the air element with its characteristic of support. Thus, by stating the absence of the four great elements, the absence of all derived materiality is also stated, because it is dependent on them. In this way, the complete absence of the realms of sensual and form existence is stated to be there, because their occurrence is dependent on these. For without the support of the great elements, neither the five-aggregate existence nor the one-aggregate existence is possible.

Idāni arūpasabhāvattepi nibbānassa arūpabhavapariyāpannānaṃ dhammānaṃ tattha abhāvaṃ dassetuṃ, “na ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ…pe… na nevasaññānāsaññāyatana”nti vuttaṃ. Tattha na ākāsānañcāyatananti saddhiṃ ārammaṇena kusalavipākakiriyabhedo tividhopi ākāsānañcāyatanacittuppādo natthīti attho. Sesesupi eseva nayo. Yadaggena ca nibbāne kāmalokādīnaṃ [V 0.0318] abhāvo hoti, tadaggena tattha idhalokaparalokānampi abhāvoti āha – “nāyaṃ loko na paraloko”ti. Tassattho – yvāyaṃ “itthattaṃ diṭṭhadhammo idhaloko”ti ca laddhavohāro khandhādiloko, yo ca “tato aññathā paro abhisamparāyo”ti ca laddhavohāro khandhādiloko, tadubhayampi tattha natthīti. Na ubho candimasūriyāti yasmā rūpagate sati tamo nāma siyā, tamassa ca vidhamanatthaṃ candimasūriyehi vattitabbaṃ. Sabbena sabbaṃ pana yattha rūpagatameva natthi, kuto tattha tamo. Tamassa vā vidhamanā candimasūriyā, tasmā candimā sūriyo cāti ubhopi tattha nibbāne natthīti attho. Iminā ālokasabhāvataṃyeva nibbānassa dasseti.

Now, to show that even though Nibbāna has a formless nature, the phenomena included in the formless existence are absent there, it is said, 'neither the base of infinite space… nor the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.' Here, 'neither the base of infinite space' means that the arising of consciousness of the base of infinite space of all three kinds—wholesome, resultant, and functional—together with its object, does not exist. The same method applies to the remaining phrases. And by the same token that there is an absence of the sense-sphere world and so on in Nibbāna, by that same token there is also an absence of this world and the next world; thus he said, 'neither this world nor the other world.' The meaning of this is: that which is designated as 'this present state, the seen Dhamma, this world'—that world of aggregates—and that which is designated as 'other than that, the future state'—that world of aggregates—both of these are absent there. 'Neither both sun and moon': because where there is materiality, there could be what is called darkness, and to dispel darkness, the sun and moon would be required to revolve. But where there is no materiality whatsoever, how could there be darkness? Or how could there be the sun and moon, the dispellers of darkness? Therefore, the meaning is that both the moon and the sun are not present there in Nibbāna. By this, he shows the very nature of Nibbāna as luminosity.

Ettāvatā ca anabhisametāvīnaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ anādimatisaṃsāre supinantepi ananubhūtapubbaṃ paramagambhīraṃ atiduddasaṃ saṇhasukhumaṃ atakkāvacaraṃ accantasantaṃ paṇḍitavedanīyaṃ atipaṇītaṃ amataṃ nibbānaṃ vibhāvento paṭhamaṃ tāva “atthi, bhikkhave, tadāyatana”nti tassa atthibhāvā tesaṃ aññāṇādīni apanetvā “yattha neva pathavī [P 0.0392] …pe… na ubho candimasūriyā”ti tadaññadhammāpohanamukhena taṃ vibhāveti dhammarājā. Tena pathavīādisabbasaṅkhatadhammavidhurasabhāvā yā asaṅkhatā dhātu, taṃ nibbānanti dīpitaṃ hoti. Tenevāha, “tatrāpāhaṃ, bhikkhave, neva āgatiṃ vadāmī”ti.

By this much, the Dhamma-king makes clear to the monks who have not yet realized it the deathless Nibbāna—which is supremely profound, exceedingly difficult to see, subtle and delicate, beyond the sphere of reasoning, utterly peaceful, to be experienced by the wise, most sublime, and never before experienced even in a dream in this beginningless saṃsāra. First, having removed their ignorance and so on concerning its existence by stating, 'Monks, there is that base,' he then makes it clear by way of rejecting other phenomena, saying: 'Where there is neither earth… nor both sun and moon.' By this, it is shown that Nibbāna is that unconditioned element which has a nature remote from all conditioned phenomena such as earth. It is for this reason that he said, 'There, monks, I say there is no coming.'

Tattha tatrāti tasmiṃ. Apisaddo samuccaye. Ahaṃ, bhikkhave, yattha saṅkhārapavatte kutoci kassaci āgatiṃ na vadāmi yathāpaccayaṃ tattha dhammamattassa [M 0.0355] uppajjanato. Evaṃ tasmimpi āyatane nibbāne kutoci āgatiṃ āgamanaṃ neva vadāmi āgantabbaṭṭhānatāya abhāvato. Na gatinti katthaci gamanaṃ na vadāmi gantabbaṭṭhānatāya abhāvato. Na hi tattha sattānaṃ ṭhapetvā ñāṇena ārammaṇakaraṇaṃ āgatigatiyo sambhavanti, nāpi ṭhiticutūpapattiyo vadāmi. “Tadāpaha”ntipi pāḷi. Tassattho – tampi āyatanaṃ gāmantarato gāmantaraṃ viya na āgantabbatāya na āgati, na gantabbatāya na gati, pathavīpabbatādi viya apatiṭṭhānatāya na ṭhiti, apaccayattā vā uppādābhāvo, tato amatasabhāvattā cavanābhāvo, uppādanirodhābhāvato ceva tadubhayaparicchinnāya ṭhitiyā ca abhāvato na ṭhitiṃ na cutiṃ na upapattiṃ vadāmi. Kevalaṃ pana taṃ arūpasabhāvattā apaccayattā ca na katthaci patiṭṭhitanti appatiṭṭhaṃ. Tattha pavattābhāvato pavattappaṭipakkhato ca appavattaṃ. Arūpasabhāvattepi vedanādayo viya kassacipi ārammaṇassa anālambanato upatthambhanirapekkhato ca anārammaṇameva taṃ “āyatana”nti vuttaṃ nibbānaṃ. Ayañca evasaddo appatiṭṭhameva appavattamevāti padadvayenapi yojetabbo[V 0.0319]. Esevanto dukkhassāti yadidaṃ “appatiṭṭha”ntiādīhi vacanehi vaṇṇitaṃ thomitaṃ yathāvuttalakkhaṇaṃ nibbānaṃ, eso eva sakalassa vaṭṭadukkhassa anto pariyosānaṃ tadadhigame sati sabbadukkhābhāvato. Tasmā “dukkhassa anto”ti ayameva tassa sabhāvoti dasseti.

Therein, 'there' means 'in that'; the particle 'api' is for conjunction. Monks, just as I do not speak of a 'coming' from anywhere in the process of conditioned phenomena—because a phenomenon there merely arises dependent on conditions—so too, in that base, in Nibbāna, I do not speak of any coming from anywhere, because of the absence of a place to be come to. I do not speak of 'going,' meaning going anywhere, because of the absence of a place to be gone to. For there, apart from making it an object by means of knowledge, no comings or goings of beings are possible; nor do I speak of standing, passing away, or rebirth. There is also the Pāli reading 'Tadāpahaṃ.' Its meaning is: that base, not being a place to be come to like one village from another, is not a 'coming'; not being a place to be gone to, is not a 'going'; not being a place of standing like the earth, mountains, and so on, is not a 'standing.' Or, because it is unconditioned, there is an absence of arising; because of its deathless nature, there is an absence of passing away from it; and because of the absence of arising and ceasing, and thus the absence of a duration defined by those two, I do not speak of 'standing,' 'passing away,' or 'rebirth.' But simply, because it has a formless nature and is unconditioned, it is not established anywhere; thus it is 'unestablished.' Because there is no occurrence there and because it is the opposite of occurrence, it is 'non-occurring.' Although it has a formless nature, unlike feelings and so on, because it does not take any object as an object and is independent of support, that Nibbāna, being indeed objectless, is called a 'base' (āyatana). And this particle 'eva' should also be connected with the two words: 'unestablished indeed' and 'non-occurring indeed.' 'This is the end of suffering' means: this Nibbāna, which is described and praised with words such as 'unestablished' and possesses the aforementioned characteristics, this itself is the end, the final conclusion, of all the suffering of the cycle of rebirth, because with its attainment there is the absence of all suffering. Therefore, this shows that 'the end of suffering' is its very nature.

Paṭhamasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the first sutta is finished.

2. Dutiyanibbānapaṭisaṃyuttasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Second Discourse Connected with Nibbāna

72. Dutiye [P 0.0393] imaṃ udānanti imaṃ nibbānassa pakatiyā gambhīrabhāvato duddasabhāvadīpanaṃ udānaṃ udānesi. Tattha duddasanti sabhāvagambhīrattā atisukhumasaṇhasabhāvattā ca anupacitañāṇasambhārehi passituṃ na sakkāti duddasaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ – “tañhi te, māgaṇḍiya, ariyaṃ paññācakkhu natthi, yena tvaṃ ārogyaṃ jāneyyāsi, nibbānampi passeyyāsī”ti (ma. ni. 2.218). Aparampi vuttaṃ – “idampi kho ṭhānaṃ duddasaṃ, yadidaṃ sabbasaṅkhārasamatho”tiādi (mahāva. 8; ma. ni. 1.281; 2.337). Anatanti [M 0.0356] rūpādiārammaṇesu, kāmādīsu ca bhavesu namanato tanninnabhāvena pavattito sattānañca tattha namanato taṇhā natā nāma, natthi ettha natāti anataṃ, nibbānanti attho. “Ananta”ntipi paṭhanti, niccasabhāvattā antavirahitaṃ, acavanadhammaṃ nirodhaṃ amatanti attho. Keci pana “ananta”nti padassa “appamāṇa”nti atthaṃ vadanti. Ettha ca “duddasa”nti iminā paññāya dubbalīkaraṇehi rāgādikilesehi cirakālabhāvitattā sattānaṃ apaccayabhāvanā na sukarāti nibbānassa kicchena adhigamanīyataṃ dasseti. Na hi saccaṃ sudassananti imināpi tamevatthaṃ pākaṭaṃ karoti. Tattha saccanti nibbānaṃ. Tañhi kenaci pariyāyena asantasabhāvābhāvato ekanteneva santattā aviparītaṭṭhena saccaṃ. Na hi taṃ sudassanaṃ na sukhena passitabbaṃ, sucirampi kālaṃ puññañāṇasambhāre samānentehipi kasireneva samadhigantabbato. Tathā hi vuttaṃ bhagavatā – “kicchena me adhigata”nti (mahāva. 8; ma. ni. 1.281; 2.337).

72. In the second sutta, regarding the words 'this inspired utterance,' he uttered this inspired utterance to illuminate the difficult-to-see nature of Nibbāna, which is due to its natural profundity. Herein, 'difficult to see' (duddasa) means it cannot be seen by those whose accumulation of knowledge is insufficient, due to its inherently profound nature and extremely subtle quality. As it is said: 'For you, Māgaṇḍiya, lack the noble eye of wisdom by which you might know health or even see Nibbāna.' Furthermore, it is stated: 'This state, too, is difficult to see—namely, the stilling of all formations,' and so on. 'Without craving' (anata) means that because craving (taṇhā) inclines towards objects such as form and towards sensual and other kinds of existence, proceeds with an inclination towards them, and makes beings incline towards them, it is called 'inclination' (natā); but in this state, there is no inclination—thus, it is 'without craving,' meaning Nibbāna. Some read it as 'boundless' (ananta), meaning it is without end due to its permanent nature, a state that does not pass away, is without cessation, and is deathless. Others, however, say the meaning of the word 'ananta' is 'immeasurable.' Here, by the word 'difficult to see,' it shows that Nibbāna is attainable only with difficulty because it is not easy for beings to develop the unconditioned, since they have long been imbued with defilements such as lust which weaken wisdom. By the words 'For the truth is not easily seen,' it also makes that same meaning clear. Herein, 'truth' (sacca) refers to Nibbāna. For it is truth in the sense of being unperverted, since it is absolutely real, having no unreal nature in any way. It is not easily seen, not to be perceived with ease, being attainable only with difficulty even by those who have been accumulating the provisions of merit and knowledge for a very long time. For so it was said by the Blessed One: 'With difficulty have I attained it.'

Paṭividdhā taṇhā jānato passato natthi kiñcananti tañca nirodhasaccaṃ sacchikiriyābhisamayavasena abhisamentena visayato kiccato ca ārammaṇato ca ārammaṇappaṭivedhena asammohappaṭivedhena ca paṭividdhaṃ, yathāpariññābhisamayavasena dukkhasaccaṃ, bhāvanābhisamayavasena [V 0.0320] maggasaccañca [P 0.0394] asammohato paṭividdhaṃ hoti, evaṃ pahānābhisamayavasena asammohato ca paṭividdhā taṇhā hoti. Evañca cattāri saccāni yathābhūtaṃ ariyamaggapaññāya jānato passato bhavādīsu natabhūtā taṇhā natthi, tadabhāve sabbassapi kilesavaṭṭassa abhāvo, tatova kammavipākavaṭṭānaṃ asambhavoyevāti evaṃ bhagavā tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ anavasesavaṭṭadukkhavūpasamahetubhūtaṃ amatamahānibbānassa ānubhāvaṃ pakāsesi. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva.

Regarding the words, 'For one who knows and sees, craving is penetrated; there is nothing': Just as the truth of suffering is penetrated without delusion through realization by way of full understanding, and the truth of the path is penetrated without delusion through realization by way of development, so too craving is penetrated through realization by way of abandonment and without delusion. And that truth of cessation is also penetrated by one who realizes it through the realization of direct experience in terms of its object, function, and basis, by the penetration of the object and by the penetration of non-delusion. And so, for one who knows and sees the four truths as they really are with the wisdom of the noble path, there is no craving, which is what inclines one toward states of being and so on. In its absence, there is an absence of the entire cycle of defilements, and from that, the cycles of kamma and its results are simply impossible. In this way, the Blessed One declared to those monks the power of the deathless, great Nibbāna, which is the cause for the appeasement of the suffering of the round without remainder. The rest is as previously stated.

Dutiyasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Second Sutta is finished.

3. Tatiyanibbānapaṭisaṃyuttasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Third Sutta Connected with Nibbāna

73. Tatiye atha kho bhagavā etamatthaṃ viditvāti tadā kira bhagavatā anekapariyāyena saṃsārassa ādīnavaṃ pakāsetvā sandassanādivasena [M 0.0357] nibbānapaṭisaṃyuttāya dhammadesanāya katāya tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ etadahosi – “ayaṃ saṃsāro bhagavatā avijjādīhi kāraṇehi sahetuko pakāsito, nibbānassa pana tadupasamassa na kiñci kāraṇaṃ vuttaṃ, tayidaṃ ahetukaṃ, kathaṃ saccikaṭṭhaparamatthena upalabbhatī”ti. Atha bhagavā tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ etaṃ yathāvuttaṃ parivitakkasaṅkhātaṃ atthaṃ viditvā. Imaṃ udānanti tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ vimatividhamanatthañceva idha samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ “nibbānaṃ nibbānanti vācāvatthumattameva, natthi hi paramatthato nibbānaṃ nāma anupalabbhamānasabhāvattā”ti lokāyatikādayo viya vippaṭipannānaṃ bahiddhā ca puthudiṭṭhigatikānaṃ micchāvādabhañjanatthañca imaṃ amatamahānibbānassa paramatthato atthibhāvadīpanaṃ udānaṃ udānesi.

73. In the third sutta, regarding the words 'Then the Blessed One, having understood this matter': at that time, it seems, when the Blessed One had expounded in many ways the dangers of saṃsāra and had given a teaching connected with Nibbāna by way of instruction and so on, this thought occurred to those monks: 'This saṃsāra has been shown by the Blessed One to have causes, such as ignorance; but of Nibbāna, its appeasement, no cause has been stated. So this is causeless—how then can it be apprehended in the ultimate sense as a reality to be realized?' Then the Blessed One, having understood this matter, which was as stated and is called a deliberation, uttered this inspired utterance—both to dispel the doubt of those monks and to shatter the wrong view of those outside the teaching who have gone astray, like the Materialists and others with various wrong views, who claim, 'Nibbāna is merely a basis for speech; for in an ultimate sense, there is no such thing as Nibbāna, because its nature cannot be found.' Thus, he proclaimed this inspired utterance, which illuminates the existence in an ultimate sense of the deathless, great Nibbāna.

Tattha ajātaṃ abhūtaṃ akataṃ asaṅkhatanti sabbānipi padāni [P 0.0395] aññamaññavevacanāni. Atha vā vedanādayo viya hetupaccayasamavāyasaṅkhātāya kāraṇasāmaggiyā na jātaṃ na nibbattanti ajātaṃ, kāraṇena vinā, sayameva vā na bhūtaṃ na pātubhūtaṃ na uppannanti abhūtaṃ, evaṃ ajātattā abhūtattā ca yena kenaci kāraṇena na katanti akataṃ, jātabhūtakatasabhāvo ca nāmarūpānaṃ saṅkhatadhammānaṃ hoti, na asaṅkhatasabhāvassa nibbānassāti dassanatthaṃ asaṅkhatanti vuttaṃ. Paṭilomato vā samecca sambhūya paccayehi katanti saṅkhataṃ, tathā na saṅkhataṃ saṅkhatalakkhaṇarahitanti asaṅkhatanti. Evaṃ anekehi kāraṇehi nibbattitabhāve paṭisiddhe “siyā [V 0.0321] nu kho ekeneva kāraṇena kata”nti āsaṅkāya “na yena kenaci kata”nti dassanatthaṃ “akata”nti vuttaṃ. Evaṃ apaccayampi samānaṃ “sayameva nu kho idaṃ bhūtaṃ pātubhūta”nti āsaṅkāya tannivattanatthaṃ “abhūta”nti vuttaṃ. “Ayañcetassa asaṅkhatākatābhūtabhāvo sabbena sabbaṃ ajātidhammattā”ti dassetuṃ “ajāta”nti vuttaṃ. Evametesaṃ catunnampi padānaṃ sātthakabhāvaṃ viditvā “tayidaṃ nibbānaṃ atthi, bhikkhave”ti paramatthato nibbānassa atthibhāvo pakāsitoti veditabbo. Ettha udānentena bhagavatā, “bhikkhave”ti ālapane kāraṇaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

Herein, 'unborn,' 'unbecome,' 'unmade,' and 'unconditioned'—all these terms are synonyms. Alternatively, it is 'unborn' because it is not born, not produced by the assemblage of causes and conditions, like feelings and other phenomena. Without a cause, it does not come to be by itself, does not appear, does not arise—thus it is 'unbecome.' Because it is unborn and unbecome, it is 'unmade' by any cause whatsoever. The nature of name-and-form, which are conditioned phenomena, is to be born, become, and made—but this is not so for the unconditioned nature of Nibbāna. To show this, it is called 'unconditioned.' Or, conversely, what is produced by combining and assembling causes is 'conditioned.' That which is not so produced, being devoid of the characteristics of the conditioned, is 'unconditioned.' Thus, having refuted that it is produced by multiple causes, the doubt arises: 'Could it be made by a single cause?' To show that 'it is not made by any cause whatsoever,' it is called 'unmade.' Similarly, even being without a cause, the doubt arises: 'Does this come to be or appear by itself?' To negate this, it is called 'unbecome.' To demonstrate that 'this unconditioned, unmade, unbecome state is entirely due to its nature of non-arising,' it is called 'unborn.' Thus, having understood the meaningfulness of these four terms, it should be known that the existence of Nibbāna in an ultimate sense was declared thus: 'Monks, this Nibbāna exists.' Herein, the reason for the address 'Monks' by the Blessed One, who uttered this inspired utterance, should be understood in the manner previously explained.

Iti satthā “atthi, bhikkhave, ajātaṃ abhūtaṃ akataṃ asaṅkhata”nti vatvā tattha hetuṃ dassento “no cetaṃ, bhikkhave”tiādimāha. Tassāyaṃ [M 0.0358] saṅkhepattho – bhikkhave, yadi ajātādisabhāvā asaṅkhatā dhātu na abhavissa na siyā, idha loke jātādisabhāvassa rūpādikkhandhapañcakasaṅkhātassa saṅkhatassa nissaraṇaṃ anavasesavūpasamo na paññāyeyya na upalabbheyya na sambhaveyya. Nibbānañhi ārammaṇaṃ katvā pavattamānā sammādiṭṭhiādayo ariyamaggadhammā anavasesakilese samucchindanti. Tenettha sabbassapi vaṭṭadukkhassa appavatti apagamo nissaraṇaṃ paññāyati.

Thus, the Teacher said, 'There is, monks, the unborn, unbecome, unmade, unconditioned,' and then, showing the reason for this, he spoke the words beginning, 'If, monks, this were not...' The concise meaning of this is as follows: Monks, if there were not that unconditioned element with the nature of the unborn and so forth, no escape, no complete pacification, would be discerned, found, or possible in this world from the conditioned—that is, the five aggregates of form and so forth, which have the nature of being born and so on. For, having Nibbāna as their object, the noble path factors such as right view arise and utterly cut off all defilements without remainder. Therefore, herein, the non-occurrence, departure, and escape from all suffering of the round of existence is discerned.

Evaṃ byatirekavasena nibbānassa atthibhāvaṃ dassetvā idāni anvayavasenapi taṃ dassetuṃ, “yasmā ca kho”tiādi vuttaṃ. Taṃ vuttatthameva. Ettha [P 0.0396] ca yasmā “apaccayā dhammā, asaṅkhatā dhammā (dha. sa. dukamātikā 7, 8), atthi, bhikkhave, tadāyatanaṃ, yattha neva pathavī (udā. 71), idampi kho ṭhānaṃ duddasaṃ, yadidaṃ sabbasaṅkhārasamatho sabbūpadhipaṭinissaggo (mahāva. 8; ma. ni. 1.281; 2.337), asaṅkhatañca vo, bhikkhave, dhammaṃ desessāmi asaṅkhatagāminiñca paṭipada”ntiādīhi (saṃ. ni. 4.366-367) anekehi suttapadehi, “atthi, bhikkhave, ajāta”nti imināpi ca suttena nibbānadhātuyā paramatthato sambhavo sabbalokaṃ anukampamānena sammāsambuddhena desito, tasmā yadipi tattha apaccakkhakārīnampi viññūnaṃ kaṅkhā vā vimati vā natthiyeva. Ye pana paraneyyabuddhino puggalā, tesaṃ vimativinodanatthaṃ ayamettha adhippāyaniddhāraṇamukhena yuttivicāraṇā – yathā pariññeyyatāya sauttarānaṃ kāmānaṃ rūpādīnañca paṭipakkhabhūtaṃ tabbidhurasabhāvaṃ nissaraṇaṃ paññāyati, evaṃ taṃsabhāvānaṃ sabbesampi saṅkhatadhammānaṃ paṭipakkhabhūtena tabbidhurasabhāvena nissaraṇena bhavitabbaṃ. Yañcetaṃ nissaraṇaṃ, sā asaṅkhatā dhātu. Kiñca bhiyyo saṅkhatadhammārammaṇaṃ vipassanāñāṇaṃ api anulomañāṇaṃ kilese samucchedavasena pajahituṃ na [V 0.0322] sakkoti. Tathā sammutisaccārammaṇaṃ paṭhamajjhānādīsu ñāṇaṃ vikkhambhanavaseneva kilese pajahati, na samucchedavasena.
