Iti saṅkhatadhammārammaṇassa sammutisaccārammaṇassa ca ñāṇassa kilesānaṃ samucchedappahāne asamatthabhāvato tesaṃ samucchedappahānakarassa ariyamaggañāṇassa tadubhayaviparītasabhāvena ārammaṇena bhavitabbaṃ[M 0.0359], sā asaṅkhatā dhātu. Tathā “atthi, bhikkhave, ajātaṃ abhūtaṃ akataṃ asaṅkhata”nti idaṃ nibbānapadassa paramatthato atthibhāvajotakaṃ vacanaṃ aviparītatthaṃ bhagavatā bhāsitattā. Yañhi bhagavatā bhāsitaṃ, taṃ aviparītatthaṃ paramatthaṃ yathā taṃ “sabbe saṅkhārā aniccā, sabbe saṅkhārā dukkhā, sabbe dhammā [P 0.0397] anattā”ti (a. ni. 3.137; mahāni. 27), tathā nibbānasaddo katthaci visaye yathābhūtaparamatthavisayo upacāramattavuttisabbhāvato seyyathāpi sīhasaddo. Atha vā attheva paramatthato asaṅkhatā dhātu, itaratabbiparītavinimuttasabhāvattā seyyathāpi pathavīdhātu vedanāti. Evamādīhi nayehi yuttitopi asaṅkhatāya dhātuyā paramatthato atthibhāvo veditabbo.

Having thus shown the existence of Nibbāna by way of exclusion, now to demonstrate it also by way of inclusion, the passage beginning 'And because…' was stated. It has the meaning as already stated. And here, because the ultimate existence of the Nibbāna-element has been taught by the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One out of compassion for the whole world through numerous sutta passages—such as: 'There are conditioned phenomena, unconditioned phenomena'; 'There is, monks, that base where there is neither earth…'; 'This state, too, is hard to see, namely, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions…'; 'And I will teach you, monks, the unconditioned and the path leading to the unconditioned'; as well as by this sutta, 'There is, monks, the unborn…'—therefore, even for those wise ones who have not directly realized it, there is no doubt or uncertainty about it. However, for those persons whose understanding is to be guided by others, this examination of reasoning by way of determining the intended meaning is presented here to dispel their uncertainty. Just as, with respect to what is to be fully understood, an escape from sensual pleasures, forms, and so on, which have a superior, is discerned as their counterpart, a state far from them, so too there must be an escape from all conditioned phenomena, which are of the same nature, by means of a counterpart that is a state far from them. And that escape is the unconditioned element. Furthermore, insight knowledge that takes conditioned phenomena as its object, and even conformity knowledge, cannot abandon the defilements by way of eradication. Similarly, knowledge in the first jhāna and so forth, which takes conventional truth as its object, abandons the defilements only by way of suppression, not by way of eradication. Thus, because knowledge that takes conditioned phenomena as its object and knowledge that takes conventional truth as its object are incapable of abandoning the defilements by way of eradication, the noble path-knowledge, which accomplishes their eradication, must have an object with a nature contrary to both. That is the unconditioned element. Moreover, the statement 'There is, monks, the unborn, unbecome, unmade, unconditioned'—this utterance which illuminates the ultimate existence of the state of Nibbāna—has an undistorted meaning because it was spoken by the Blessed One. For whatever is spoken by the Blessed One is of undistorted meaning and ultimate truth, as in the statements: 'All formations are impermanent, all formations are suffering, all phenomena are not-self.' Similarly, the term 'Nibbāna' in certain contexts refers to the ultimate reality as it truly is, because of the existence of merely figurative usage, just like the term 'lion.' Alternatively, the unconditioned element does indeed exist in an ultimate sense, because its nature is free from its other, its opposite, just as the earth element and feeling are. By such methods of reasoning, the ultimate existence of the unconditioned element should be understood.

Tatiyasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Third Sutta is concluded.

4. Catutthanibbānapaṭisaṃyuttasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Fourth Sutta Connected with Nibbāna

74. Catutthe atha kho bhagavā etamatthaṃ viditvāti tadā kira bhagavatā anekapariyāyena sandassanādivasena nibbānapaṭisaṃyuttāya dhammadesanāya katāya tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ etadahosi – “ayaṃ tāva bhagavatā amatamahānibbānadhātuyā anekākāravokāraṃ ānisaṃsaṃ dassentena anaññasādhāraṇo ānubhāvo pakāsito, adhigamūpāyo panassā na bhāsito, kathaṃ nu kho paṭipajjantehi amhehi ayaṃ adhigantabbā”ti. Atha bhagavā tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ etaṃ yathāvuttaparivitakkasaṅkhātaṃ atthaṃ sabbākārato viditvā. Imaṃ udānanti taṇhāvasena katthaci anissitassa passaddhakāyacittassa vīthipaṭipannavipassanassa ariyamaggena anavasesato taṇhāpahānena nibbānādhigamavibhāvanaṃ imaṃ udānaṃ udānesi.

74. In the fourth sutta: Then the Blessed One, having understood this matter… At that time, after the Blessed One had given a discourse on the Dhamma connected with Nibbāna in many ways—by way of instruction, etc.—it occurred to those monks: “The Blessed One, by showing the manifold benefits of the deathless great Nibbāna-element, has revealed its unique power, but the means to its attainment has not been stated. How should we who are practicing attain this?” Then the Blessed One, having understood in all its aspects this matter, that is, the thought that had arisen in those monks as described, uttered this inspired utterance, which clarifies the attainment of Nibbāna through the complete abandonment of craving by the noble path for one who has entered upon the path of insight, whose body and mind are tranquil, and who is not dependent on anything on account of craving.

Tattha nissitassa calitanti rūpādisaṅkhāre taṇhādiṭṭhīhi nissitassa calitaṃ “etaṃ mama, eso me attā”ti taṇhādiṭṭhivipphanditaṃ hoti. Appahīnataṇhādiṭṭhikassa hi puggalassa sukhādīsu uppannesu tāni abhibhuyya viharituṃ asakkontassa [P 0.0398] “mama vedanā, ahaṃ vediyāmī”tiādinā [V 0.0323] taṇhādiṭṭhigāhavasena kusalappavattito cittasantānassa calanaṃ kampanaṃ, avakkhalitaṃ vā [M 0.0360] hotīti attho. Anissitassa calitaṃ natthīti yo pana visuddhipaṭipadaṃ paṭipajjanto samathavipassanāhi taṇhādiṭṭhiyo vikkhambhetvā aniccādivasena saṅkhāre sammasanto viharati, tassa taṃ anissitassa yathāvuttaṃ calitaṃ avakkhalitaṃ, vipphanditaṃ vā natthi kāraṇassa suvikkhambhitattā.

Therein, regarding the phrase for one who is dependent there is agitation: for one who is dependent on formations such as form by way of craving and views, there is agitation, which is the throbbing of craving and views expressed as “This is mine, this is my self.” For a person who has not abandoned craving and views, when pleasant feelings and so on arise, being unable to overcome them and live mindfully, there is agitation, trembling, or faltering of the mental continuum due to the grip of craving and views, thinking, “My feeling, I feel,” and so on. This is the meaning. For one who is not dependent, there is no agitation: for one who, practicing the path of purification, has suppressed craving and views by means of serenity and insight and dwells contemplating formations as impermanent, etc.—for such a one who is not dependent, there is no such agitation, faltering, or throbbing as described, because the cause has been thoroughly suppressed.

Calite asatīti yathāvutte calite asati yathā taṇhādiṭṭhigāhā nappavattanti, tathā vīthipaṭipannāya vipassanāya taṃ ussukkantassa. Passaddhīti vipassanācittasahajātānaṃ kāyacittānaṃ sārambhakarakilesavūpasaminī duvidhāpi passaddhi hoti. Passaddhiyā sati nati na hotīti pubbenāparaṃ visesayuttāya passaddhiyā sati anavajjasukhādhiṭṭhānaṃ samādhiṃ vaḍḍhetvā taṃ paññāya samavāyakaraṇena samathavipassanaṃ yuganaddhaṃ yojetvā maggaparamparāya kilese khepentassa kāmabhavādīsu namanato “natī”ti laddhanāmā taṇhā arahattamaggakkhaṇe anavasesato na hoti, anuppattidhammataṃ āpāditattā na uppajjatīti attho.

When there is no agitation: When there is no agitation as described for one who is striving with insight that has entered the path, so that the grips of craving and views do not operate. Tranquility: This is the twofold tranquility—of body and of mind—conascent with the insight-consciousness, which pacifies the defilements that cause agitation. When there is tranquility, there is no inclination: When there is tranquility endowed with successive distinctions, one develops concentration which is the basis for blameless happiness. By making them concordant by means of wisdom, one yokes serenity and insight in unison. For one who is destroying the defilements through the sequence of the paths, craving—which is called “inclination” (nati) because it inclines (namati) toward sensual existence, other kinds of existence, etc.—does not exist at the moment of the path of arahantship; it is without remainder. The meaning is that it does not arise because it has been brought to a state of non-arising.

Natiyā asatīti arahattamaggena taṇhāya suppahīnattā bhavādiatthāya ālayanikanti pariyuṭṭhāne asati. Āgatigati na hotīti paṭisandhivasena idha āgati āgamanaṃ cutivasena gati ito paralokagamanaṃ peccabhāvo na hoti na pavattati. Āgatigatiyā asatīti vuttanayena āgatiyā ca gatiyā ca asati. Cutūpapāto na hotīti aparāparaṃ cavanupapajjanaṃ na hoti na pavattati. Asati hi kilesavaṭṭe kammavaṭṭaṃ pacchinnameva, pacchinne ca tasmiṃ kuto vipākavaṭṭassa sambhavo. Tenāha – “cutūpapāte asati nevidha na hura”ntiādi. Tattha yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ heṭṭhā bāhiyasutte vitthārato vuttameva. Tasmā tattha vuttanayeneva attho veditabbo.

When there is no inclination: Since craving has been thoroughly abandoned by the path of arahantship, there is no obsession, which is longing and attachment for existence and so on. There is no coming and going: There is no coming, an arrival here by way of rebirth-linking, and no going, a departure from here to the next world by way of death; no future existence occurs. When there is no coming and going: When there is no arrival and departure in the way stated. There is no passing away and rebirth: There is no subsequent passing away and reappearing. For when the round of defilements is absent, the round of kamma is cut off; and when that is cut off, how can the round of results arise? Hence he said: When there is no passing away and rebirth, there is neither here nor beyond… and so on. Whatever needs to be said about this has already been stated in detail in the Bāhiya Sutta. Therefore the meaning should be understood in the way stated there.

Iti [P 0.0399] bhagavā idhāpi tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ anavasesato vaṭṭadukkhavūpasamahetubhūtaṃ amatamahānibbānassa ānubhāvaṃ sammāpaṭipattiyā pakāseti.

Thus here too the Blessed One fully reveals to those monks, through right practice, the power of the deathless great Nibbāna, which is the cause for the complete pacification of the suffering of the round of existence.

Catutthasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Fourth Sutta is finished.

5. Cundasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Cunda Sutta

75. Pañcame [V 0.0324][M 0.0361] mallesūti evaṃnāmake janapade. Mahatā bhikkhusaṅghenāti guṇamahattasaṅkhyāmahattehi mahatā. So hi bhikkhusaṅgho sīlādiguṇavisesayogenapi mahā tattha sabbapacchimakassa sotāpannabhāvato, saṅkhyāmahattenapi mahā aparicchinnagaṇanattā. Āyusaṅkhārossajjanato paṭṭhāya hi āgatāgatā bhikkhū na pakkamiṃsu. Cundassāti evaṃnāmakassa. Kammāraputtassāti suvaṇṇakāraputtassa. So kira aḍḍho mahākuṭumbiko bhagavato paṭhamadassaneneva sotāpanno hutvā attano ambavane satthuvasanānucchavikaṃ gandhakuṭiṃ, bhikkhusaṅghassa ca rattiṭṭhānadivāṭṭhānaupaṭṭhānasālākuṭimaṇḍapacaṅkamanādike ca sampādetvā pākāraparikkhittaṃ dvārakoṭṭhakayuttaṃ vihāraṃ katvā buddhappamukhassa saṅghassa niyyādesi. Taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ – “tatra sudaṃ bhagavā pāvāyaṃ viharati cundassa kammāraputtassa ambavane”ti.

75. In the fifth sutta, “in the land of the Mallas” means in the country thus named. “With a great assembly of bhikkhus” means great due to the greatness of their virtues and great in number. For that bhikkhu Saṅgha was great due to the excellence of virtues such as morality, because even the very last among them was a stream-enterer; and also great in number due to their incalculable count. From the time of the determination to relinquish the life-span onwards, the bhikkhus who arrived did not depart. “Of Cunda” means of one named thus. “The metalworker’s son” means the son of a goldsmith. He, it is said, was wealthy and a great householder, and became a stream-enterer upon first seeing the Blessed One. Having prepared a fragrant hut suitable for the Teacher’s dwelling in his mango grove, as well as halls, huts, pavilions, walking paths, and other facilities suitable for the bhikkhu Saṅgha’s night and day residence and attendance, he built a monastery enclosed by walls and equipped with gatehouses and offered it to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha. Referring to this, it is said: “There the Blessed One was dwelling at Pāvā in the mango grove of Cunda, the metalworker’s son.”

Paṭiyādāpetvāti sampādetvā. “Sūkaramaddavanti sūkarassa mudusiniddhaṃ pavattamaṃsa”nti mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ. Keci pana “sūkaramaddavanti na sūkaramaṃsaṃ, sūkarehi madditavaṃsakaḷīro”ti vadanti. Aññe “sūkarehi madditappadese jātaṃ ahichattaka”nti. Apare pana “sūkaramaddavaṃ nāma ekaṃ rasāyana”nti bhaṇiṃsu[P 0.0400]. Tañhi cundo kammāraputto “ajja bhagavā parinibbāyissatī”ti sutvā “appeva nāma naṃ paribhuñjitvā cirataraṃ tiṭṭheyyā”ti satthu cirajīvitukamyatāya adāsīti vadanti.

Paṭiyādāpetvā means having made ready. “Sūkaramaddava” means “the soft and tender meat of a pig,” as stated in the Great Commentary. Some, however, say, “Sūkaramaddava” is not pig’s meat, but a bamboo shoot trampled by pigs. Others say, “It is a mushroom that grows in a place trampled by pigs.” Still others said, “Sūkaramaddava” is a certain elixir. For it is said that Cunda the metalworker, upon hearing, “Today the Blessed One will attain final Nibbāna,” gave it out of a wish for the Teacher to live longer, thinking, “Perhaps after consuming this, he might remain for a longer time.”

Tena maṃ parivisāti tena mamaṃ bhojehi. Kasmā bhagavā evamāha? Parānuddayatāya. Tañca kāraṇaṃ pāḷiyaṃ vuttameva. Tena abhihaṭabhikkhāya paresaṃ aparibhogārahato ca tathā vattuṃ vaṭṭatīti dassitaṃ hoti. Tasmiṃ kira sūkaramaddave dvisahassadīpaparivāresu catūsu mahādīpesu devatā ojaṃ pakkhipiṃsu. Tasmā taṃ añño koci sammā jīrāpetuṃ na sakkoti, tamatthaṃ pakāsento satthā parūpavādamocanatthaṃ “nāhaṃ taṃ, cunda, passāmī”tiādinā sīhanādaṃ nadi. Ye hi pare upavadeyyuṃ “attanā paribhuttāvasesaṃ neva bhikkhūnaṃ, na aññesaṃ manussānaṃ adāsi, āvāṭe nikhaṇāpetvā vināsesī”ti, “tesaṃ vacanokāso mā hotū”ti parūpavādamocanatthaṃ sīhanādaṃ nadi.

Tena maṃ parivisa means “serve me with that,” that is, “feed me with that.” Why did the Blessed One say so? Out of compassion for others. And that reason is indeed stated in the Pāli. It is shown that it was fitting to speak thus, because the alms brought by him were unfit for others to consume. It is said that, into that sūkaramaddava, deities from the four great continents surrounded by two thousand islands infused nutritive essence. Therefore, no one else could properly digest it. To reveal that meaning, and to prevent the criticism of others, the Teacher roared the lion’s roar with the words, “I do not see, Cunda…” and so on. For if others were to criticize, saying, “He did not give the remainder of what he himself consumed to the monks, nor to other humans, but had it buried in a pit and destroyed,” then to prevent any opportunity for their words, he roared the lion’s roar to prevent the criticism of others.

Tattha [M 0.0362] sadevaketiādīsu saha devehīti sadevako, saha mārenāti samārako, saha brahmunāti sabrahmako, saha samaṇabrāhmaṇehīti sassamaṇabrāhmaṇī, pajātattā pajā, saha devamanussehīti [V 0.0325] sadevamanussā. Tasmiṃ sadevake loke…pe… sadevamanussāya. Tattha sadevakavacanena pañcakāmāvacaradevaggahaṇaṃ, samārakavacanena chaṭṭhakāmāvacaradevaggahaṇaṃ, sabrahmakavacanena brahmakāyikādibrahmaggahaṇaṃ, sassamaṇabrāhmaṇīvacanena sāsanassa paccatthikapaccāmittasamaṇabrāhmaṇaggahaṇaṃ samitapāpabāhitapāpasamaṇabrāhmaṇaggahaṇañca, pajāvacanena sattalokaggahaṇaṃ, sadevamanussavacanena sammutidevaavasesamanussaggahaṇaṃ. Evamettha tīhi padehi okāsalokavasena, dvīhi pajāvasena sattaloko gahitoti veditabbo. Aparo [P 0.0401] nayo – sadevakavacanena arūpāvacaraloko gahito, samārakavacanena chakāmāvacaradevaloko, sabrahmakavacanena rūpī brahmaloko, sassamaṇabrāhmaṇavacanena catuparisavasena sammutidevehi saha manussaloko, avasesasattaloko vā gahitoti veditabbo.

In the phrase “sadevake” and so on: `sadevako` is `saha devehi`, “with the devas”; `samārako` is `saha mārena`, “with Māra”; `sabrahmako` is `saha brahmunā`, “with Brahmā”; `sassamaṇabrāhmaṇī` is `saha samaṇabrāhmaṇehi`, “with ascetics and brahmins”; `pajā` is so called because of being born (`pajātattā`); `sadevamanussā` is `saha devamanussehi`, “with devas and humans.” In that world “with the devas”… and so on… “with devas and humans.” Here, by the term `sadevaka`, the five sense-sphere deva realms are to be understood; by the term `samāraka`, the sixth sense-sphere deva realm; by the term `sabrahmaka`, the Brahmā realms such as the Brahmākāyika; by the term `sassamaṇabrāhmaṇī`, the ascetics and brahmins who are opponents and adversaries of the Dispensation, as well as the ascetics and brahmins who have pacified and abandoned evil; by the term `pajā`, the world of beings; and by the term `sadevamanussa`, conventional devas and the remaining humans. Thus it should be understood here that by three terms the world is taken as a plane of existence, and by two terms the world of beings is taken by way of 'beings'. Another method: by the term `sadevaka`, the formless realm is taken; by the term `samāraka`, the six sense-sphere deva realms; by the term `sabrahmaka`, the form-Brahmā realm; by the term `sassamaṇabrāhmaṇa`, the human world together with conventional devas in the fourfold assembly is taken, or else the remaining world of beings.

Bhuttāvissāti bhuttavato. Kharoti pharuso. Ābādhoti visabhāgarogo. Pabāḷhāti balavatiyo. Māraṇantikāti maraṇantā maraṇasamīpapāpanasamatthā. Sato sampajāno adhivāsesīti satiṃ upaṭṭhitaṃ katvā ñāṇena paricchinditvā adhivāsesi. Avihaññamānoti vedanānuvattanavasena asallakkhitadhammo viya aparāparaṃ parivattanaṃ akaronto apīḷiyamāno adukkhiyamāno viya adhivāsesi. Bhagavato hi veḷuvagāmakeyeva tā vedanā uppannā, samāpattibalena pana vikkhambhitā yāva parinibbānadivasā na uppajjiṃsu divase divase samāpattīhi paṭipaṇāmanato. Taṃ divasaṃ pana parinibbāyitukāmo “koṭisahassahatthīnaṃ balaṃ dhārentānaṃ vajirasaṅghātasamānakāyānaṃ aparimitakālaṃ upacitapuññasambhārānampi bhave sati evarūpā vedanā pavattanti, kimaṅgaṃ pana aññesa”nti sattānaṃ saṃvegajananatthaṃ samāpattiṃ na samāpajji, tena vedanā kharā vattiṃsu. Āyāmāti ehi yāma.

`Bhuttāvī` means `bhuttavato`, 'one who has eaten'. `Khara` means `pharuso`, 'harsh'. `Ābādho` means `visabhāgarogo`, 'a disease of discordant elements'. `Pabāḷhā` means `balavatiyo`, 'powerful'. `Māraṇantikā` means `maraṇantā`, 'ending in death', and `maraṇasamīpapāpanasamatthā`, 'capable of bringing one to the proximity of death'. `Sato sampajāno adhivāsesi` means he endured by establishing mindfulness and discerning with wisdom. `Avihaññamāno` means he endured without being afflicted, without being pained, and without tossing and turning back and forth in accordance with the feeling, like an unconditioned element. For those feelings had arisen for the Blessed One in the village of Veḷuva itself, but having been suppressed by the power of meditative attainment, they did not arise again until the day of his final Nibbāna, due to his warding them off day by day with meditative attainments. On that day, however, wishing to attain final Nibbāna, and in order to generate a sense of spiritual urgency in beings, he did not enter meditative attainment, thinking: “For those who possess the strength of a thousand million elephants, whose bodies are like a mass of diamond, and who have accumulated a store of merit over an immeasurable time, such feelings still arise when existence remains. What then to say of others?” Therefore, the feelings became harsh. `Āyāma` means `ehi yāma`: 'Come, let us go'.

Cundassa bhattaṃ bhuñjitvātiādikā aparabhāge dhammasaṅgāhakehi ṭhapitā gāthā. Tattha bhuttassa ca sūkaramaddavenāti bhuttassa udapādi, na pana bhuttapaccayā. Yadi hi abhuttassa uppajjissā, atikharo abhavissā, siniddhabhojanaṃ [M 0.0363] pana bhuttattā tanukā vedanā ahosi, teneva padasā gantuṃ asakkhi. Etena yvāyaṃ “yassa taṃ paribhuttaṃ sammā pariṇāmaṃ gaccheyya aññatra tathāgatassā”ti sīhanādo nadito, tassa sātthakatā dassitā. Buddhānañhi aṭṭhāne gajjitaṃ nāma natthi. Yasmā taṃ paribhuttaṃ bhagavato na kiñci vikāraṃ uppādesi, kammena pana laddhokāsena uppādiyamānaṃ vikāraṃ appamattatāya upasamento [P 0.0402] sarīre balaṃ uppādesi, yena yathā vakkhamānaṃ tividhaṃ payojanaṃ sampādesi, tasmā sammadeva taṃ pariṇāmaṃ gataṃ, māraṇantikattā [V 0.0326] pana vedanānaṃ aviññātaṃ apākaṭaṃ ahosīti. Viriccamānoti abhiṇhaṃ pavattalohitavirecanova samāno. Avocāti attanā icchitaṭṭhāne parinibbānatthāya evamāha.

The verses beginning `Cundassa bhattaṃ bhuñjitvā` were placed in the latter part by the compilers of the Dhamma. Therein, `bhuttassa ca sūkaramaddavena` means that the illness arose for him who had eaten, but not as a result of having eaten. For if it had arisen without his having eaten, it would have been extremely harsh; but because he had eaten a rich meal, the feeling was slight, and for that very reason he was able to proceed on foot. By this, the meaningfulness of the lion’s roar that was roared—namely, “Other than the Tathāgata, there is no one for whom that which was eaten could be properly digested”—is shown. For there is no such thing as a baseless roar for the Buddhas. Since that which was eaten did not produce any affliction for the Blessed One, but rather, by pacifying and making slight the affliction that was being produced by kamma which had found its opportunity, it generated strength in the body, by which, as will be stated, it accomplished a threefold purpose—therefore, it was indeed properly digested. However, because the feelings were fatal, they were not unknown or unmanifest. `Viriccamāno` means having continuous bloody dysentery. `Avoca` means he spoke thus in order to attain final Nibbāna in a place he himself desired.

Kasmā pana bhagavā evaṃ roge uppanne kusināraṃ agamāsi, kiṃ aññattha na sakkā parinibbāyitunti? Parinibbāyituṃ nāma na katthaci na sakkā, evaṃ pana cintesi – mayi kusināraṃ gate mahāsudassanasuttadesanāya (dī. ni. 2.241) aṭṭhuppatti bhavissati, tāya yā devaloke anubhavitabbasadisā sampatti manussaloke mayā anubhūtā, taṃ dvīhi bhāṇavārehi paṭimaṇḍetvā desessāmi, taṃ sutvā bahū janā kusalaṃ kattabbaṃ maññissanti. Subhaddopi kattha maṃ upasaṅkamitvā pañhaṃ pucchitvā vissajjanapariyosāne saraṇesu patiṭṭhāya pabbajitvā laddhūpasampado kammaṭṭhānaṃ bhāvetvā mayi dharanteyeva arahattaṃ patvā pacchimasāvako nāma bhavissati. Aññattha mayi parinibbute dhātunimittaṃ mahākalaho bhavissati, lohitaṃ nadī viya sandissati. Kusinārāyaṃ pana parinibbute doṇabrāhmaṇo taṃ vivādaṃ vūpasametvā dhātuyo vibhajitvā dassatīti imāni tīṇi kāraṇāni passanto bhagavā mahatā ussāhena kusināraṃ agamāsi.

But why did the Blessed One go to Kusinārā when this illness arose? Was it not possible for him to attain Parinibbāna elsewhere? It is not that it was impossible to attain Parinibbāna anywhere, but he thought thus: 'When I have gone to Kusinārā, the occasion for the teaching of the Mahāsudassana Sutta will arise. Through it, I will teach, adorning it with two recitations, about the prosperity I experienced in the human world, which is comparable to that to be experienced in the deva world. Having heard it, many people will consider that wholesome deeds ought to be done. Subhadda, too, will approach me, ask a question, and at the conclusion of the answer, having been established in the refuges, he will go forth, receive the higher ordination, develop a meditation subject, and attain Arahantship while I am still living, becoming the last disciple. If I attain Parinibbāna elsewhere, a great conflict will arise on account of the relics, and blood will flow like a river. But in Kusinārā, when I have attained Parinibbāna, the brahmin Doṇa will quell that dispute and distribute the relics.' Seeing these three reasons, the Blessed One went to Kusinārā with great effort.

Iṅghāti codanatthe nipāto. Kilantosmīti parissanto asmi. Tena yathāvuttavedanānaṃ balavabhāvaṃ eva dasseti. Bhagavā hi attano ānubhāvena tadā padasā agamāsi, aññesaṃ pana yathā paduddhārampi kātuṃ na sakkā, tathā vedanā tikhiṇā kharā kaṭukā vattiṃsu. Tenevāha “nisīdissāmī”ti.

The word `iṅgha` is a particle in the sense of urging. `Kilantosmi` means 'I am weary.' By this, he shows the very powerful nature of the aforesaid feelings. For the Blessed One, by his own spiritual power, went on foot at that time; but for others, the feelings that arose were so sharp, harsh, and bitter that they would not have been able to even lift a foot. For that very reason, he said, 'I will sit down.'

Idānīti adhunā. Luḷitanti madditaṃ viya ākulaṃ. Āvilanti ālulaṃ. Acchodakāti tanupasannasalilā. Sātodakāti madhuratoyā. Sītodakāti [M 0.0364] sītalajalā. Setodakāti nikkaddamā[P 0.0403]. Udakañhi sabhāvato setavaṇṇaṃ, bhūmivasena kaddamāvilatāya ca aññādisaṃ hoti, kakudhāpi nadī vimalavālikā samokiṇṇā setavaṇṇā sandati. Tena vuttaṃ “setodakā”ti. Supatitthāti sundaratitthā. Ramaṇīyāti manoharabhūmibhāgatāya ramitabbā yathāvuttaudakasampattiyā ca manoramā.

`Idāni` means 'now.' `Luḷitaṃ` means agitated, as if trampled. `Āvilaṃ` means stirred up. `Acchodakā` means having clear, settled water. `Sātodakā` means having sweet-tasting water. `Sītodakā` means having cool water. `Setodakā` means free from mud. For water is by nature of a clear color, but due to the influence of the earth and turbidity from mud, it becomes otherwise. The Kakudhā river, too, flows with spotless sand, suffused with a clear color. Therefore, it was called `setodakā`. `Supatiṭṭhā` means having good fords. `Ramaṇīyā` means delightful on account of its charming terrain and to be delighted in because of the aforesaid excellence of its water.

Kilantosmi cundaka, nipajjissāmīti tathāgatassa hi –

“I am weary, Cunda, I will lie down.” For the Tathāgata—

“Kāḷāvakañca [V 0.0327] gaṅgeyyaṃ, paṇḍaraṃ tambapiṅgalaṃ;

Gandhamaṅgalahemañca, uposathachaddantime dasā”ti. –

“Kāḷāvaka and Gaṅgeyya, Paṇḍara, Tamba, and Piṅgala; Gandha, Maṅgala, and Hema, Uposatha and Chaddanta—these are the ten.”

Evaṃ vuttesu dasasu hatthikulesu kāḷāvakasaṅkhātānaṃ yaṃ dasannaṃ pakatihatthīnaṃ balaṃ, taṃ ekassa gaṅgeyyassāti evaṃ dasaguṇitāya gaṇanāya pakatihatthīnaṃ koṭisahassabalappamāṇaṃ sarīrabalaṃ. Taṃ sabbampi tasmiṃ divase pacchābhattato paṭṭhāya caṅgavāre pakkhittaudakaṃ viya parikkhayaṃ gataṃ. Pāvāya tigāvute kusinārā. Etasmiṃ antare pañcavīsatiyā ṭhānesu nisīditvā mahantaṃ ussāhaṃ katvā āgacchanto sūriyatthaṅgamanavelāya bhagavā kusināraṃ pāpuṇīti evaṃ “rogo nāma sabbaṃ ārogyaṃ maddanto āgacchatī”ti imamatthaṃ dassento sadevakassa lokassa saṃvegakaraṃ vācaṃ bhāsanto “kilantosmi, cundaka, nipajjissāmī”ti āha.

Among these ten elephant lineages thus mentioned, the strength of ten ordinary elephants of the Kāḷāvaka lineage is equal to that of one Gaṅgeyya. Thus, by a tenfold progressive calculation, the Tathāgata's bodily strength amounts to the strength of ten billion ordinary elephants. Yet all of that strength, from after the meal on that day, was exhausted, like water poured into a filter. Kusinārā is three gāvutas from Pāvā. In that interval, having sat down in twenty-five places and made a great effort, the Blessed One arrived in Kusinārā at the time of sunset. Thus, to show the meaning, 'Indeed, sickness comes crushing all health,' and to utter words that inspire a sense of spiritual urgency in the world with its devas, he said: 'I am weary, Cunda, I will lie down.'

Sīhaseyyanti ettha kāmabhogīseyyā petaseyyā tathāgataseyyā sīhaseyyāti catasso seyyā. Tattha “yebhuyyena, bhikkhave, kāmabhogī vāmena passena seyyaṃ kappentī”ti (a. ni. 4.246) ayaṃ kāmabhogīseyyā. “Yebhuyyena[P 0.0404], bhikkhave, petā uttānā sentī”ti (a. ni. 4.246) ayaṃ petaseyyā. Catutthajjhānaṃ tathāgataseyyā. “Sīho, bhikkhave, migarājā dakkhiṇena passena seyyaṃ kappetī”ti (a. ni. 4.246) ayaṃ sīhaseyyā. Ayañhi tejussadairiyāpathattā uttamaseyyā nāma. Tena vuttaṃ – “dakkhiṇena passena sīhaseyyaṃ kappesī”ti. Pāde pādanti dakkhiṇapāde vāmapādaṃ. Accādhāyāti atiādhāya, gopphakaṃ atikkamma ṭhapetvā. Gopphakena hi gopphake, jāṇunā jāṇumhi saṅghaṭṭiyamāne abhiṇhaṃ vedanā uppajjanti[M 0.0365], seyyā phāsukā na hoti. Yathā pana na saṅghaṭṭeti, evaṃ atikkamma ṭhapite vedanā nuppajjanti, seyyā phāsukā hoti. Tasmā evaṃ nipajji.

Regarding 'the lion's posture,' there are four postures: the posture of sensual pleasure-seekers, the posture of hungry ghosts, the posture of the Tathāgata, and the lion's posture. Among these, 'For the most part, monks, those who indulge in sensual pleasures adopt a lying position on their left side'—this is the posture of sensual pleasure-seekers. 'For the most part, monks, hungry ghosts lie on their backs'—this is the posture of hungry ghosts. The fourth jhāna is the Tathāgata's posture. 'The lion, monks, the king of beasts, adopts a lying position on his right side'—this is the lion's posture. Indeed, because it is a posture of great majesty, it is called the supreme posture. Therefore, it is said: 'He adopted the lion's posture, lying on his right side.' 'Foot upon foot' means placing the left foot on the right foot. 'Placing one over the other' means placing it slightly overlapping, beyond the ankle. For when ankle is pressed against ankle, or knee against knee, pains frequently arise, and the posture is not comfortable. But when they are placed so they do not press against each other, pains do not arise, and the posture is comfortable. Therefore, he lay down in this manner.

Gantvāna buddhoti imā gāthā aparabhāge dhammasaṅgāhakehi ṭhapitā. Tattha nadikanti nadiṃ. Appaṭimodha loketi appaṭimo idha imasmiṃ sadevake loke. Nhatvā ca pivitvā cudatārīti gattānaṃ sītikaraṇavasena nhatvā ca pānīyaṃ pivitvā ca nadito uttari. Tadā kira bhagavati nhāyante antonadiyaṃ macchakacchapā, udakaṃ, ubhosu tīresu vanasaṇḍo, sabbo ca so bhūmibhāgoti sabbaṃ suvaṇṇavaṇṇameva ahosi. Purakkhatoti guṇavisiṭṭhasattuttamagarubhāvato sadevakena lokena pūjāsammānavasena purakkhato. Bhikkhugaṇassa majjheti bhikkhusaṅghassa majjhe. Tadā bhikkhū bhagavato vedanānaṃ adhimattabhāvaṃ viditvā āsannā hutvā samantato parivāretvāva gacchanti. Satthāti diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikaparamatthehi sattānaṃ anusāsanato satthā. Pavattā bhagavā idha [V 0.0328] dhammeti bhāgyavantatādīhi bhagavā idha sīlādisāsanadhamme pavattā, dhamme vā caturāsītidhammakkhandhasahassāni pavattā pavattetā. Ambavananti tassā eva nadiyā tīre ambavanaṃ. Āmantayi cundakanti tasmiṃ kira khaṇe āyasmā ānando udakasāṭikaṃ pīḷento ohīyi, cundakatthero samīpe ahosi. Tasmā [P 0.0405] taṃ bhagavā āmantayi. Pamukhe nisīdīti vattasīsena satthu purato nisīdi “kiṃ nu kho satthā āṇāpetī”ti. Ettāvatā dhammabhaṇḍāgāriko anuppatto. Evaṃ anuppattaṃ atha kho bhagavā āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ āmantesi.

The verses beginning 'Gantvāna buddho' were later established by the compilers of the Dhamma. Therein, “nadikaṃ” means the river. “Appaṭimo dha loke” means incomparable here in this world with its devas. “Having bathed and drunk, he crossed over” means having bathed to cool his body and drunk water, he crossed over the river. At that time, it is said, while the Blessed One was bathing in the river, the fish and turtles in the river, the water, the forests on both banks, and all that portion of the earth became golden in color. “Purakkhato” means placed foremost by the world with its devas through honor and reverence due to his venerable state as the supreme being, preeminent in virtues. “In the midst of the community of monks” means in the midst of the community of bhikkhus. At that time, the bhikkhus, knowing the excessive severity of the Blessed One’s feelings, stayed close and surrounded him on all sides as they went. “Teacher” means the teacher who instructs beings with the welfare in this life, the next, and the ultimate goal. “The Blessed One set in motion the Dhamma here” means the Blessed One, by virtue of his blessedness and so forth, set in motion the teaching of virtue and so forth here, or he set in motion the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dhamma. “Mango grove” means a mango grove on the bank of that very river. “He addressed Cunda” means at that moment, it is said, Venerable Ānanda, while wringing out the water-cloth, had remained behind, and the elder Cunda was nearby. Therefore, the Blessed One addressed him. “Sat in front” means he sat in front of the Teacher with his head bowed, thinking, “What might the Teacher command?” At this point, the treasurer of the Dhamma had arrived. Having thus arrived, then the Blessed One addressed Venerable Ānanda.

Upadaheyyāti uppādeyya, vippaṭisārassa uppādako koci puriso siyā api bhaveyya. Alābhāti ye aññesaṃ dānaṃ dadantānaṃ dānānisaṃsasaṅkhātā lābhā honti, te alābhā. Dulladdhanti puññavisesena laddhampi manussattaṃ dulladdhaṃ. Yassa teti yassa tava. Uttaṇḍulaṃ vā atikilinnaṃ vā ko taṃ jānāti, kīdisampi pacchimaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ bhuñjitvā tathāgato parinibbuto, addhā tena yaṃ vā taṃ vā dinnaṃ bhavissatīti. Lābhāti diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikā dānānisaṃsasaṅkhātā lābhā. Suladdhanti tuyhaṃ manussattaṃ suladdhaṃ. Sammukhāti sammukhato, na anussavena na paramparāyāti attho. Metanti me etaṃ mayā etaṃ. Dvemeti dve ime. Samasamaphalāti sabbākārena samānaphalā.

‘Would cause remorse’ means would produce; some person who causes remorse might arise. ‘It is a loss’ means for you it is a loss of those gains, known as the benefits of giving, that other donors receive. ‘Ill-gotten’ means even the human state, though obtained through special merit, is ill-gotten for you. ‘Of you whose...’ means of you. ‘Whether it was undercooked or too soggy, who knows? Having eaten your final almsfood, whatever it was like, the Tathāgata attained final Nibbāna. Surely, something or other must have been given by you.’ ‘It is a gain’ means the gains known as the benefits of giving, both in this life and the next. ‘Well-gotten’ means your human state is well-gotten. ‘Face to face’ means from his very presence; the meaning is not by hearsay, not by tradition. ‘Me’taṃ’ is to be divided as ‘me etaṃ,’ meaning ‘by me, this was heard.’ ‘Dve’me’ is to be divided as ‘dve ime,’ meaning ‘these two.’ ‘Equal in fruit’ means equal in fruit in every way.

Nanu [M 0.0366] ca yaṃ sujātāya dinnaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ bhuñjitvā tathāgato abhisambuddho, taṃ kilesānaṃ appahīnakāle dānaṃ, idaṃ pana cundassa dānaṃ khīṇāsavakāle, kasmā etāni samaphalānīti? Parinibbānasamatāya samāpattisamatāya anussaraṇasamatāya ca. Bhagavā hi sujātāya dinnaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ bhuñjitvā saupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā parinibbuto, cundena dinnaṃ bhuñjitvā anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā parinibbutoti evaṃ parinibbānasamatāyapi samaphalāni. Abhisambujjhanadivase ca aggamaggassa hetubhūtā catuvīsatikoṭisatasahassasaṅkhā samāpattiyo samāpajji, parinibbānadivasepi sabbā tā samāpajji. Evaṃ samāpattisamatāyapi samaphalāni. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā –

But wasn’t the almsfood given by Sujātā, which the Tathāgata ate before his supreme enlightenment, given when the defilements were not yet abandoned? And this gift of Cunda was given when the taints were destroyed. Why then are these of equal fruit? Because of the equality of final Nibbāna, the equality of attainment, and the equality of recollection. For the Blessed One, having eaten the almsfood given by Sujātā, attained final Nibbāna with the Nibbāna-element with residue remaining. Having eaten the almsfood given by Cunda, he attained final Nibbāna with the Nibbāna-element without residue remaining. Thus, they are of equal fruit due to the equality of final Nibbāna. Moreover, on the day of his supreme enlightenment, he entered into twenty-four hundred thousand crores of attainments. On the day of his final Nibbāna, he entered into all those attainments again. Thus, they are of equal fruit due to the equality of attainment. For this was said by the Blessed One—

“Yassa cetaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ [P 0.0406] paribhuñjitvā anuttaraṃ appamāṇaṃ cetosamādhiṃ upasampajja viharati, appamāṇo tassa puññābhisando kusalābhisando”tiādi. –

‘Of whomever one partakes of this almsfood and then abides having attained the unsurpassed, immeasurable concentration of mind, for that person the outpouring of merit is immeasurable, the outpouring of wholesomeness is immeasurable,’ and so on.

Sujātā ca aparabhāge assosi “na kira sā rukkhadevatā, bodhisatto kiresa, taṃ kira piṇḍapātaṃ paribhuñjitvā anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ abhisambuddho, sattasattāhaṃ kirassa tena yāpanā [V 0.0329] ahosī”ti. Tassā idaṃ sutvā “lābhā vata me”ti anussarantiyā balavapītisomanassaṃ udapādi. Cundassapi aparabhāge “avasānapiṇḍapāto kira mayā dinno, dhammasīsaṃ kira mayā gahitaṃ, mayhaṃ kira piṇḍapātaṃ paribhuñjitvā satthā attanā cirakālābhipatthitāya anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā parinibbuto”ti sutvā “lābhā vata me”ti anussarato balavapītisomanassaṃ udapādi. Evaṃ anussaraṇasamatāyapi samaphalāni dvepi piṇḍapātadānānīti veditabbāni.

Later, Sujātā heard, “It was not a tree deity, but the Bodhisatta. Having partaken of that almsfood, he attained unsurpassed perfect enlightenment. For seven weeks, he sustained himself on that.” Upon hearing this, intense joy and happiness arose in her as she reflected, “What a gain for me!” Similarly, Cunda later heard, “Indeed, the final alms offering was given by me. I have, as it were, grasped the pinnacle of the Dhamma. Having partaken of my almsfood, the Teacher attained the Nibbāna-element without residue remaining, which he had long desired.” Reflecting on this, intense joy and happiness arose in him, thinking, “What a gain for me!” Thus, it should be understood that both alms offerings have equal fruit due to the equality of recollection.

Āyusaṃvattanikanti dīghāyukasaṃvattanikaṃ. Upacitanti pasutaṃ uppāditaṃ. Yasasaṃvattanikanti parivārasaṃvattanikaṃ. Ādhipateyyasaṃvattanikanti seṭṭhabhāvasaṃvattanikaṃ.

‘Conducive to life-span’ means conducive to longevity. ‘Accumulated’ means acquired or produced. ‘Conducive to fame’ means conducive to having an entourage. ‘Conducive to sovereignty’ means conducive to a state of supremacy.

Etamatthaṃ viditvāti etaṃ dānassa mahapphalatañceva sīlādiguṇehi attano ca anuttaradakkhiṇeyyabhāvaṃ anupādāparinibbānañcāti tividhampi atthaṃ sabbākārato viditvā tadatthadīpanaṃ imaṃ udānaṃ udānesi.

“Having understood this matter”—that is, the great fruitfulness of generosity, one’s own unsurpassed worthiness as a recipient of offerings due to the qualities of virtue and so forth, and also Nibbāna without clinging—having fully comprehended this threefold meaning in all its aspects, the Blessed One uttered this inspired utterance to illuminate that meaning.

Tattha [M 0.0367] dadato puññaṃ pavaḍḍhatīti dānaṃ dentassa cittasampattiyā ca dakkhiṇeyyasampattiyā ca dānamayaṃ puññaṃ upacīyati, mahapphalatarañca mahānisaṃsatarañca hotīti attho. Atha vā dadato puññaṃ pavaḍḍhatīti deyyadhammaṃ pariccajanto pariccāgacetanāya bahulīkatāya anukkamena sabbattha anāpattibahulo suvisuddhasīlaṃ rakkhitvā samathavipassanañca bhāvetuṃ sakkotīti tassa dānādivasena tividhampi puññaṃ abhivaḍḍhatīti evamettha attho veditabbo. Saṃyamatoti [P 0.0407] sīlasaṃyamena saṃyamantassa, saṃvare ṭhitassāti attho. Veraṃ na cīyatīti pañcavidhaveraṃ na pavaḍḍhati, adosapadhānattā vā adhisīlassa kāyavācācittehi sayaṃmanto suvisuddhasīlo khantibahulatāya kenaci veraṃ na karoti, kuto tassa upacayo. Tasmā tassa saṃyamato saṃyamantassa, saṃyamahetu vā veraṃ na cīyati. Kusalo ca jahāti pāpakanti kusalo pana ñāṇasampanno suvisuddhasīle patiṭṭhito aṭṭhatiṃsāya ārammaṇesu attano anurūpaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā upacārappanābhedaṃ jhānaṃ sampādento pāpakaṃ lāmakaṃ kāmacchandādiakusalaṃ vikkhambhanavasena jahāti pariccajati. So tameva jhānaṃ pādakaṃ katvā saṅkhāresu khayavayaṃ paṭṭhapetvā vipassanāya kammaṃ karonto vipassanaṃ ussukkāpetvā ariyamaggena anavasesaṃ pāpakaṃ lāmakaṃ akusalaṃ samucchedavasena jahāti. Rāgadosamohakkhayā sa nibbutoti so evaṃ pāpakaṃ pajahitvā rāgādīnaṃ khayā anavasesakilesanibbānena, tato paraṃ khandhanibbānena ca nibbuto [V 0.0330] hotīti evaṃ bhagavā cundassa ca dakkhiṇasampattiṃ, attano ca dakkhiṇeyyasampattiṃ nissāya pītivegavissaṭṭhaṃ udānaṃ udānesi.

There, “for the giver, merit increases”—this means that for one who gives a gift, merit consisting of giving is accumulated through the excellence of the mind and the excellence of the recipient; it becomes more fruitful and of greater benefit—this is the meaning. Alternatively, “for the giver, merit increases” means that by relinquishing the gift, through the repeated cultivation of the intention to renounce, one gradually becomes largely free from offenses in all respects. Maintaining perfectly pure virtue, one becomes capable of developing serenity and insight. Thus, through giving and other virtuous deeds, threefold merit grows—this is the meaning to be understood here. “Restrained” means one who restrains through moral restraint, established in restraint—this is the meaning. “Hostility does not accumulate”—the fivefold hostility does not increase. Or, because non-aversion is the basis of higher virtue, one who restrains body, speech, and mind, being perfectly pure in virtue and abundant in patience, does not create hostility toward anyone—how could it accumulate? Therefore, for one who is restrained or restraining, hostility does not accumulate because of restraint. “Moreover, the skillful abandon evil”—the skillful one, endowed with knowledge, established in perfectly pure virtue, takes up a meditation subject suitable for oneself among the thirty-eight objects. Developing absorption with its stages of access and attainment, one abandons and relinquishes evil, inferior unwholesome states such as sensual desire and so forth through suppression. Having made that absorption a foundation, one establishes the destruction and passing away of formations, engages in insight work, and arouses insight. Through the noble path, one abandons all remaining evil, inferior unwholesome states by eradication. “With the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, one is at peace”—thus, having abandoned evil in this way, through the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, one is at peace with the complete extinction of defilements, and thereafter, one is at peace with the extinction of the aggregates. In this way, the Blessed One, relying on the excellence of Cunda's offering and his own excellence as one worthy of offerings, uttered this inspired utterance, overflowing with joy.

Pañcamasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the fifth sutta is finished.

6. Pāṭaligāmiyasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Sutta on the Pāṭaligāmiyans

76. Chaṭṭhe magadhesūti magadharaṭṭhe. Mahatāti idhāpi guṇamahattenapi aparicchinnasaṅkhyattā gaṇanamahattenapi mahatā bhikkhusaṅghena. Pāṭaligāmoti evaṃnāmako magadharaṭṭhe eko gāmo. Tassa kira gāmassa māpanadivase [P 0.0408] gāmaggahaṇaṭṭhāne dve tayo pāṭalaṅkurā pathavito ubbhijjitvā [M 0.0368] nikkhamiṃsu. Tena taṃ “pāṭaligāmo”tveva vohariṃsu. Tadavasarīti taṃ pāṭaligāmaṃ avasari anupāpuṇi. Kadā pana bhagavā pāṭaligāmaṃ anupāpuṇi? Heṭṭhā vuttanayena sāvatthiyaṃ dhammasenāpatino cetiyaṃ kārāpetvā tato nikkhamitvā rājagahe vasanto tattha āyasmato mahāmoggallānassa ca cetiyaṃ kārāpetvā tato nikkhamitvā ambalaṭṭhikāyaṃ vasitvā aturitacārikāvasena janapadacārikaṃ caranto tattha tattha ekarattivāsena vasitvā lokaṃ anuggaṇhanto anukkamena pāṭaligāmaṃ anupāpuṇi.

76. In the sixth sutta: “in Magadha” means in the country of Magadha. “With a great” means here too, with a great Saṅgha of bhikkhus, great due to the greatness of their virtues and also great in number due to their immeasurable count. Pāṭaligāma: a village of that name in the country of Magadha. It is said that on the day that village was founded, at the site for the village, two or three pāṭala shoots sprouted from the earth and came forth. Therefore, they called it “Pāṭaligāma.” “He arrived there” means he arrived at, he reached, that Pāṭaligāma. But when did the Blessed One reach Pāṭaligāma? According to the method described before, after having the Dhammasenāpati’s shrine built in Sāvatthī, he left there and stayed in Rājagaha. There, having had the shrine of the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna built, he left there and stayed in Ambalaṭṭhikā. Traveling through the country on an unhurried tour, staying overnight in various places while benefiting the world, he gradually reached Pāṭaligāma.

Pāṭaligāmiyāti pāṭaligāmavāsino upāsakā. Te kira bhagavato paṭhamadassanena keci saraṇesu, keci sīlesu, keci saraṇesu ca sīlesu ca patiṭṭhitā. Tena vuttaṃ “upāsakā”ti. Yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṃsūti pāṭaligāme kira ajātasattuno licchavirājūnañca manussā kālena kālaṃ gantvā gehasāmike gehato nīharitvā māsampi aḍḍhamāsampi vasanti. Tena pāṭaligāmavāsino manussā niccupaddutā “etesañceva āgatakāle vasanaṭṭhānaṃ bhavissatī”ti ekapasse issarānaṃ bhaṇḍappaṭisāmanaṭṭhānaṃ, ekapasse vasanaṭṭhānaṃ, ekapasse āgantukānaṃ addhikamanussānaṃ, ekapasse daliddānaṃ kapaṇamanussānaṃ, ekapasse gilānānaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ bhavissatīti sabbesaṃ aññamaññaṃ aghaṭṭetvā vasanappahonakaṃ nagaramajjhe mahāsālaṃ kāresuṃ, tassā nāmaṃ āvasathāgāranti. Taṃ divasañca niṭṭhānaṃ agamāsi. Te tattha gantvā hatthakammasudhākammacittakammādivasena supariniṭṭhitaṃ susajjitaṃ devavimānasadisaṃ taṃ dvārakoṭṭhakato paṭṭhāya oloketvā “idaṃ āvasathāgāraṃ ativiya manoramaṃ sassirikaṃ, kena nu [V 0.0331] kho paṭhamaṃ paribhuttaṃ amhākaṃ dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāya assā”ti cintesuṃ, tasmiṃyeva ca khaṇe “bhagavā taṃ gāmaṃ anuppatto”ti assosuṃ. Tena te uppannapītisomanassā “amhehi bhagavā gantvāpi [P 0.0409] ānetabbo siyā, so pana sayameva amhākaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ sampatto, ajja mayaṃ bhagavantaṃ idha vasāpetvā paṭhamaṃ paribhuñjāpessāma tathā bhikkhusaṅghaṃ, bhikkhusaṅghe āgate tepiṭakaṃ buddhavacanaṃ āgatameva bhavissati, satthāraṃ maṅgalaṃ vadāpessāma, dhammaṃ kathāpessāma. Iti tīhi ratanehi paribhutte pacchā amhākañca paresañca paribhogo bhavissati, evaṃ no dīgharattaṃ [M 0.0369] hitāya sukhāya bhavissatī”ti sanniṭṭhānaṃ katvā etadatthameva bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamiṃsu. Tasmā evamāhaṃsu – “adhivāsetu no, bhante bhagavā, āvasathāgāra”nti.

“The Pāṭaligāmiyans” means the lay followers residing in Pāṭaligāma. It is said that at their first sight of the Blessed One, some became established in the refuges, some in the precepts, and some in both the refuges and the precepts. Therefore, it is said, “lay followers.” “They approached where the Blessed One was”: it is said that in Pāṭaligāma, men of King Ajātasattu and of the Licchavi rulers would come from time to time, remove the householders from their homes, and stay for a month or half a month. Therefore, the people of Pāṭaligāma, being constantly troubled, thought, “There must be a place for these people to stay when they come.” Thus, they had a great hall built in the middle of the town, sufficient for everyone to stay without inconveniencing one another. On one side would be a place to store the goods of the rulers, on another side a place to stay, on another for guests and travelers, on another for the poor and destitute, and on another a place for the sick to stay. Its name was Āvasathāgāra, or Lodging Hall. And on that very day, it was completed. They went there and, gazing at it from the gatehouse onward, saw that it was exquisitely finished and well-adorned like a celestial mansion with handiwork, plasterwork, and painted designs, and they thought: “This lodging hall is exceedingly delightful and splendid. Who, having been the first to use it, would bring about our long-term welfare and happiness?” At that very moment, they heard, “The Blessed One has arrived in the village.” At this, with joy and gladness arisen, they thought: “We would have had to go and bring the Blessed One ourselves, but he has come to our dwelling place on his own. Today, we will have the Blessed One stay here and have him be the first to use it, and likewise the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. When the Saṅgha of bhikkhus has come, the Tipiṭaka, the word of the Buddha, will have come as well. We will have the Teacher speak on what is auspicious and teach the Dhamma. Thus, after it has been used by the Three Jewels, it will afterward be for our use and that of others. In this way, it will be for our long-term welfare and happiness.” Having made this resolution, they approached the Blessed One for this very purpose. Therefore, they spoke thus: “Venerable sir, may the Blessed One consent to the lodging hall.”

Yena āvasathāgāraṃ tenupasaṅkamiṃsūti kiñcāpi taṃ taṃ divasameva pariniṭṭhitattā devavimānaṃ viya susajjitaṃ supaṭijaggitaṃ, buddhārahaṃ pana katvā na paññattaṃ, “buddhā nāma araññajjhāsayā araññārāmā, antogāme vaseyyuṃ vā no vā, tasmā bhagavato ruciṃ jānitvāva paññāpessāmā”ti cintetvā te bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamiṃsu, idāni bhagavato ruciṃ jānitvā tathā paññāpetukāmā yena āvasathāgāraṃ tenupasaṅkamiṃsu. Sabbasanthariṃ āvasathāgāraṃ santharitvāti yathā sabbameva santhataṃ hoti, evaṃ taṃ santharitvā sabbapaṭhamaṃ tāva “gomayaṃ nāma sabbamaṅgalesu vattatī”ti sudhāparikammakatampi bhūmiṃ allagomayena opuñjāpetvā parisukkhabhāvaṃ ñatvā yathā akkantaṭṭhāne padaṃ na paññāyati, evaṃ catujjātiyagandhehi limpetvā upari nānāvaṇṇakaṭasārake santharitvā tesaṃ upari mahāpiṭṭhikakojavādiṃ katvā hatthattharaṇādīhi nānāvaṇṇehi attharaṇehi santharitabbayuttakaṃ sabbokāsaṃ santharāpesuṃ. Tena vuttaṃ – “sabbasanthariṃ āvasathāgāraṃ santharitvā”ti.

Regarding 'they approached the place where the rest house was': although on that very day it was finished, well-adorned, and well-maintained like a celestial mansion, it had not yet been prepared as suitable for the Buddha. Thinking, 'Buddhas, indeed, are inclined to the wilderness and delight in the wilderness. They may or may not stay within a village. Therefore, we shall prepare it only after knowing the Blessed One’s preference,' they approached the Blessed One. Now, wishing to prepare it accordingly after having learned the Blessed One’s preference, they went to the place where the rest house was. Regarding 'having spread the rest house with all kinds of coverings': having spread it so that it was completely covered, they first, thinking, 'Cow dung is suitable for all auspicious occasions,' had the floor, though it was finished with plaster, smeared with fresh cow dung. Knowing it to be completely dry, so that a footprint would not be visible where one stepped, they anointed it with perfumes of four kinds. Above that, they spread mats of various colors, and over them, they placed large woolen carpets and so on, having the entire space suitable for spreading covered with spreads of various colors, such as elephant-saddle cloths. Therefore, it was said: 'having spread the rest house with all kinds of coverings.'

Āsanānañhi majjhaṭṭhāne tāva maṅgalathambhaṃ nissāya mahārahaṃ buddhāsanaṃ paññāpetvā tattha yaṃ yaṃ mudukañca manoramañca paccattharaṇaṃ, taṃ taṃ paccattharitvā ubhatolohitakaṃ manuññadassanaṃ upadhānaṃ [P 0.0410] upadahitvā upari suvaṇṇarajatatārakāvicittaṃ vitānaṃ bandhitvā gandhadāmapupphadāmādīhi alaṅkaritvā samantā dvādasahatthe ṭhāne pupphajālaṃ kāretvā tiṃsahatthamattaṭṭhānaṃ paṭasāṇiyā parikkhipāpetvā pacchimabhittiṃ nissāya bhikkhusaṅghassa pallaṅkaapassayamañcapīṭhādīni paññāpetvā upari setapaccattharaṇehi paccattharāpetvā sālāya pācīnapassaṃ attano nisajjāyoggaṃ kāresuṃ. Taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “āsanāni paññāpetvā”ti.

Regarding 'seats': first, in the central place, against the auspicious pillar, they prepared a valuable seat for the Buddha. Having spread there whatever covering was soft and pleasing, they placed a pillow, red at both ends and pleasing to see. Above, they fastened a canopy variegated with gold and silver stars and decorated it with garlands of perfumes, garlands of flowers, and so on. All around, in a space of twelve cubits, they had a net of flowers made, and had a space of about thirty cubits enclosed with a cloth curtain. Against the western wall, they prepared for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus couches, chairs with leaning boards, beds, stools, and so on, and had them covered with white spreads. On the eastern side of the hall, they made a place suitable for their own seating. In reference to this, it was said: 'having prepared the seats.'

Udakamaṇikanti mahākucchikaṃ udakacāṭiṃ. Evaṃ bhagavā bhikkhusaṅgho ca yathāruciyā hatthapāde [V 0.0332] dhovissanti, mukhaṃ vikkhālessantīti tesu tesu ṭhānesu maṇivaṇṇassa udakassa pūretvā vāsatthāya nānāpupphāni ceva udakavāsacuṇṇāni ca pakkhipitvā kadalipaṇṇehi pidahitvā patiṭṭhapesuṃ. Tena vuttaṃ “udakamaṇikaṃ patiṭṭhāpetvā”ti.

Regarding 'a water-pot': this means a large-bellied water jar. Thinking, 'Thus the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus will wash their hands and feet as they wish, and rinse their mouths,' in various places they filled jars with water the color of a jewel, and for fragrance, they put in various flowers and perfumed powders for water. Having covered them with banana leaves, they set them in place. Therefore, it was said: 'having set up a water-pot.'

Telappadīpaṃ [M 0.0370] āropetvāti rajatasuvaṇṇādimayadaṇḍadīpikāsu yodhakarūpavilāsakhacitarūpakādīnaṃ hatthe ṭhapitasuvaṇṇarajatādimayakapallikāsu telappadīpaṃ jālayitvā. Yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṃsūti ettha pana te pāṭaligāmiyā upāsakā na kevalaṃ āvasathāgārameva, atha kho sakalasmimpi gāme vīthiyo sajjāpetvā dhaje ussāpetvā gehadvāresu puṇṇaghaṭe kadaliyo ca ṭhapāpetvā sakalagāmaṃ dīpamālāhi vippakiṇṇatārakaṃ viya katvā “khīrapake dārake khīraṃ pāyetha, daharakumāre lahuṃ lahuṃ bhojetvā sayāpetha, uccāsaddaṃ mā karittha, ajja ekarattiṃ satthā antogāme vasissati, buddhā nāma appasaddakāmā hontī”ti bheriṃ carāpetvā sayaṃ [P 0.0411] daṇḍadīpikā ādāya yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṃsu.

Regarding 'having lit oil lamps': this means having lit oil lamps on lampstands made of silver, gold, and so on, and in small bowls made of gold, silver, and so on, placed in the hands of figures of warriors, figures inlaid with graceful designs, and the like. Regarding 'they approached the place where the Blessed One was': here, those lay followers of Pāṭaligāma did not only prepare the rest house. Rather, having had the streets in the entire village decorated, having raised banners, and having had full water pots and banana trees placed at the doors of the houses, they made the whole village seem like scattered stars with its rows of lamps. They had a drum beaten to announce: 'Give milk to the suckling infants, feed the young children quickly and put them to sleep, and do not make loud noises. Tonight, for one night, the Teacher will stay within the village. Buddhas, indeed, desire quiet.' Then, taking up lampstands themselves, they approached the place where the Blessed One was.

Atha kho bhagavā nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya saddhiṃ bhikkhusaṅghena yena āvasathāgāraṃ tenupasaṅkamīti “yassa dāni, bhante, bhagavā kālaṃ maññatī”ti evaṃ kira tehi kāle ārocite bhagavā lākhārasena tintarattakoviḷārapupphavaṇṇaṃ rattadupaṭṭaṃ kattariyā padumaṃ kantento viya, saṃvidhāya timaṇḍalaṃ paṭicchādento nivāsetvā suvaṇṇapāmaṅgena padumakalāpaṃ parikkhipanto viya, vijjulatāsassirikaṃ kāyabandhanaṃ bandhitvā rattakambalena gajakumbhaṃ pariyonandhanto viya, ratanasatubbedhe suvaṇṇagghike pavāḷajālaṃ khipamāno viya, mahati suvaṇṇacetiye rattakambalakañcukaṃ paṭimuñcanto viya, gacchantaṃ puṇṇacandaṃ rattavalāhakena paṭicchādento viya, kañcanagirimatthake supakkalākhārasaṃ parisiñcanto viya, cittakūṭapabbatamatthakaṃ vijjulatājālena parikkhipanto viya, sakalacakkavāḷasineruyugandharamahāpathaviṃ cāletvā gahitanigrodhapallavasamānavaṇṇaṃ surattavarapaṃsukūlaṃ pārupitvā vanagahanato nikkhantakesarasīho viya, samantato udayapabbatakūṭato puṇṇacando viya, bālasūriyo viya ca attanā nisinnacārumaṇḍapato nikkhami.

Regarding the passage, 'Then the Blessed One, having dressed, taking his bowl and robe, together with the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, approached the place where the rest house was': It is said that when they had announced the time, saying, 'Venerable sir, the Blessed One may now do as he sees fit,' the Blessed One dressed. He wore his lower robe—a red double-robe the color of a coral tree flower, dyed with lac-resin—arranging it to cover the three circles, like one cutting a lotus with scissors. He tied his waistband, which was as splendid as a flash of lightning, like one encircling a bunch of lotuses with a golden band. He then donned his excellent, deep-red rag-robe, which was the color of a banyan sprout and had been taken up causing the entire cosmos with Sineru, Yugandhara, and the great earth to tremble. This was like one wrapping an elephant’s frontal globes with a red woolen blanket; like casting a coral net over a golden pillar one hundred ratanas high; like putting a red woolen cloak on a great golden cetiya; like covering the moving full moon with a red cloud; like sprinkling well-cooked lac-resin on the peak of a golden mountain; or like encircling the peak of Mount Cittakūṭa with a net of lightning. He then emerged from the beautiful pavilion where he had been sitting, like a maned lion emerging from a forest thicket, like the full moon from the peak of the sunrise mountain, and like the morning sun.

Athassa kāyato meghamukhato vijjukalāpā viya rasmiyo nikkhamitvā suvaṇṇarasadhārāparisekapiñjarapattapupphaphalasākhāviṭape viya samantato rukkhe kariṃsu. Tāvadeva attano attano pattacīvaramādāya mahābhikkhusaṅgho bhagavantaṃ parivāresi. Te ca naṃ parivāretvā ṭhitā bhikkhū [M 0.0371] evarūpā ahesuṃ appicchā santuṭṭhā pavivittā asaṃsaṭṭhā āraddhavīriyā vattāro vacanakkhamā [V 0.0333] codakā pāpagarahino sīlasampannā samādhisampannā paññāsampannā vimuttisampannā vimuttiñāṇadassanasampannā. Tehi parivuto bhagavā rattakambalaparikkhitto viya suvaṇṇakkhandho, nakkhattaparivārito viya puṇṇacando, rattapadumavanasaṇḍamajjhagatā [P 0.0412] viya suvaṇṇanāvā, pavāḷavedikaparikkhitto viya suvaṇṇapāsādo virocittha. Mahākassapappamukhā pana mahātherā meghavaṇṇaṃ paṃsukūlacīvaraṃ pārupitvā maṇivammavammitā viya mahānāgā parivārayiṃsu vantarāgā bhinnakilesā vijaṭitajaṭā chinnabandhanā kule vā gaṇe vā alaggā.

Then, from his body, like flashes of lightning from a rain cloud, rays emerged and made the surrounding trees, with their leaves, flowers, fruits, branches, and twigs, appear as if sprinkled with streams of liquid gold, rendering them golden-hued. At that very moment, the great Saṅgha of bhikkhus, taking their own bowls and robes, surrounded the Blessed One. And those bhikkhus who stood surrounding him were of such a nature: of few wishes, content, secluded, unassociated, of aroused energy, able speakers, patient of speech, admonishers, censurers of evil, accomplished in virtue, accomplished in concentration, accomplished in wisdom, accomplished in liberation, and accomplished in the knowledge and vision of liberation. Surrounded by them, the Blessed One shone like a mass of gold wrapped in a red blanket, like a golden boat in the midst of a thicket of red lotuses, and like a golden palace enclosed by a coral balustrade. The great elders, led by Mahākassapa, wearing dust-heap robes the color of clouds, surrounded him like great elephants adorned with jeweled armor—they who had abandoned passion, whose defilements were shattered, whose tangles were unraveled, whose fetters were severed, and who were unattached to family or to a group.

Iti bhagavā sayaṃ vītarāgo vītarāgehi, vītadoso vītadosehi, vītamoho vītamohehi, nittaṇho nittaṇhehi, nikkileso nikkilesehi, sayaṃ buddho anubuddhehi parivārito pattaparivāritaṃ viya kesaraṃ, kesaraparivāritā viya kaṇṇikā, aṭṭhanāgasahassaparivārito viya chaddanto nāgarājā, navutihaṃsasahassaparivārito viya dhataraṭṭho haṃsarājā, senaṅgaparivārito viya cakkavattirājā, marugaṇaparivārito viya sakko devarājā, brahmagaṇaparivārito viya hāritamahābrahmā, tārāgaṇaparivārito viya puṇṇacando, anupamena buddhavesena aparimāṇena buddhavilāsena pāṭaligāminaṃ maggaṃ paṭipajji.

Thus the Blessed One—himself free from passion, surrounded by those free from passion; himself free from hatred, surrounded by those free from hatred; himself free from delusion, surrounded by those free from delusion; himself free from craving, surrounded by those free from craving; himself free from defilements, surrounded by those free from defilements; himself a Buddha, surrounded by those who had awakened after him—was like the stamen surrounded by petals, like the pericarp surrounded by stamens, like the elephant king Chaddanta surrounded by eight thousand elephants, like the goose king Dhataraṭṭha surrounded by ninety thousand geese, like a wheel-turning monarch surrounded by his army, like Sakka, king of the gods, surrounded by the host of Maruts, like the Great Brahmā Hārita surrounded by the host of Brahmās, and like the full moon surrounded by the host of stars. With incomparable Buddha-guise and immeasurable Buddha-grace, he set out on the road to Pāṭaligāma.

Athassa puratthimakāyato suvaṇṇavaṇṇā ghanabuddharasmiyo uṭṭhahitvā asītihatthaṭṭhānaṃ aggahesuṃ, tathā pacchimakāyato dakkhiṇapassato vāmapassato suvaṇṇavaṇṇā ghanabuddharasmiyo uṭṭhahitvā asītihatthaṭṭhānaṃ aggahesuṃ, uparikesantato paṭṭhāya sabbakesāvaṭṭehi moragīvarājavaṇṇā asitā ghanabuddharasmiyo uṭṭhahitvā gaganatale asītihatthaṭṭhānaṃ aggahesuṃ, heṭṭhāpādatalehi pavāḷavaṇṇā rasmiyo uṭṭhahitvā ghanapathaviyaṃ asītihatthaṭṭhānaṃ aggahesuṃ, dantato akkhīnaṃ setaṭṭhānato, nakhānaṃ maṃsavimuttaṭṭhānato odātā ghanabuddharasmiyo uṭṭhahitvā asītihatthaṭṭhānaṃ aggahesuṃ, rattapītavaṇṇānaṃ sambhinnaṭṭhānato mañjeṭṭhavaṇṇā rasmiyo uṭṭhahitvā asītihatthaṭṭhānaṃ aggahesuṃ, sabbatthakameva pabhassarā rasmiyo uṭṭhahiṃsu. Evaṃ samantā asītihatthaṭṭhānaṃ chabbaṇṇā buddharasmiyo vijjotamānā vipphandamānā vidhāvamānā kañcanadaṇḍadīpikādīhi [P 0.0413] niccharitvā ākāsaṃ pakkhandamānā mahāpadīpajālā viya, cātuddīpikamahāmeghato nikkhantavijjulatā [M 0.0372] viya ca disodisaṃ pakkhandiṃsu. Yāhi sabbe disābhāgā suvaṇṇacampakapupphehi vikiriyamānā viya, suvaṇṇaghaṭato suvaṇṇarasadhārāhi āsiñciyamānā viya, pasāritasuvaṇṇapaṭaparikkhittā viya, verambhavātena samuddhatakiṃsukakaṇikārakoviḷārapupphacuṇṇasamokiṇṇā viya, cīnapiṭṭhacuṇṇasamparirañjitā viya ca virociṃsu.

Then, from the front of his body, golden-hued, dense Buddha-rays arose and occupied a space of eighty cubits. Likewise, from the back of his body, from his right side, and from his left side, golden-hued, dense Buddha-rays arose and occupied a space of eighty cubits. From above, starting from the ends of his hair, from all the hair-whorls, dark blue, dense Buddha-rays the color of a peacock’s neck arose and occupied a space of eighty cubits in the sky. From below, from the soles of his feet, coral-colored rays arose and occupied a space of eighty cubits in the solid earth. From his teeth, from the white parts of his eyes, and from the parts of his nails free of flesh, pure white, dense Buddha-rays arose and occupied a space of eighty cubits. From the places where the red and yellow colors mingled, madder-colored rays arose and occupied a space of eighty cubits. From every single part, brilliant rays arose. Thus, all around for a space of eighty cubits, the six-colored Buddha-rays, blazing, shimmering, and darting about, spread in all directions, like great flames from a lamp leaping into the sky from golden lampstands, and like flashes of lightning issuing from a great cloud covering the four continents. By these rays, all regions of space shone brilliantly, as if strewn with golden campaka flowers, as if sprinkled with streams of golden essence from golden pitchers, as if draped with outstretched golden cloths, as if thoroughly scattered with the pollen of kiṃsuka, kaṇikāra, and koviḷāra flowers tossed by the Verambha wind, and as if thoroughly dyed with fine Chinese powder.

Bhagavatopi [V 0.0334] asītianubyañjanabyāmappabhāparikkhepasamujjalaṃ dvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇappaṭimaṇḍitaṃ sarīraṃ abbhamahikādiupakkilesavimuttaṃ samujjalantatārakāvabhāsitaṃ viya, gaganatalaṃ vikasitaṃ viya padumavanaṃ, sabbapāliphullo viya yojanasatiko pāricchattako, paṭipāṭiyā ṭhapitānaṃ dvattiṃsasūriyānaṃ dvattiṃsacandimānaṃ dvattiṃsacakkavattīnaṃ dvattiṃsadevarājānaṃ dvattiṃsamahābrahmānaṃ siriyā siriṃ abhibhavamānaṃ viya virocittha, yathā taṃ dasahi pāramīhi dasahi upapāramīhi dasahi paramatthapāramīhīti sammadeva paripūritāhi samatiṃsapāramitāhi alaṅkataṃ kappasatasahassādhikāni cattāri asaṅkhyeyyāni dinnena dānena rakkhitena sīlena katena kalyāṇakammena ekasmiṃ attabhāve samosaritvā vipākaṃ dātuṃ okāsaṃ alabhamānena sambādhappattaṃ viya nibbattitaṃ nāvāsahassabhaṇḍaṃ ekaṃ nāvaṃ āropanakālo viya, sakaṭasahassabhaṇḍaṃ ekaṃ sakaṭaṃ āropanakālo viya, pañcavīsatiyā gaṅgānaṃ sambhinnamukhadvāre ekato rāsibhūtakālo viya ahosi.

The body of the Blessed One, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man and radiant with the surrounding splendor of the eighty minor characteristics and the fathom-wide aura, was free from impurities such as clouds and mist. It shone brilliantly, like the vault of the sky illuminated by shining stars, like a lotus grove in full bloom, like a Pāricchattaka tree a hundred yojanas in extent, bursting into bloom all over. It shone as if surpassing with its own glory the splendor of thirty-two suns, thirty-two moons, thirty-two wheel-turning monarchs, thirty-two kings of the gods, and thirty-two Great Brahmās, all placed in a row. It was as if the merit, adorned by the thirty perfections—ten perfections, ten secondary perfections, and ten ultimate perfections—which had been perfectly fulfilled through giving, guarding morality, and performing wholesome deeds for four incalculable aeons and a hundred thousand more kappas, had come together in a single existence and, being unable to find an opportunity to yield its fruit, had been brought to completion in a compressed state. This was like the time of loading the cargo of a thousand ships onto a single ship, or loading the cargo of a thousand carts onto a single cart, or like the time when twenty-five Ganges rivers become a single mass at their confluence.

Imāya buddhasiriyā obhāsamānassapi bhagavato purato anekāni daṇḍadīpikāsahassāni ukkhipiṃsu. Tathā pacchato vāmapasse dakkhiṇapasse jātikusumacampakavanamālikārattuppalanīluppalabakulasinduvārādipupphāni ceva nīlapītādivaṇṇasugandhacuṇṇāni ca cātuddīpikamahāmeghavissaṭṭhā salilavuṭṭhiyo viya vippakiriṃsu[P 0.0414]. Pañcaṅgikatūriyanigghosā ca buddhadhammasaṅghaguṇāsaṃyuttā thutighosā ca sabbā disā pūrayamānā mukhasambhāsā viya ahesuṃ. Devasupaṇṇanāgayakkhagandhabbamanussānaṃ akkhīni amatapānaṃ viya labhiṃsu. Imasmiṃ pana ṭhāne ṭhatvā padasahassehi gamanavaṇṇanaṃ vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Tatriyaṃ mukhamattaṃ –

As if to outshine the very splendor of the Blessed One, many thousands of torch-bearers raised their torches before him. Likewise, from behind, from the left, and from the right, they scattered flowers such as jasmine, champak, forest jasmine, red and blue lotuses, bakula, and sinduvāra, as well as fragrant powders of blue, yellow, and other colors, like a shower of water released by a great cloud over the four continents. The sounds of the fivefold musical instruments and the sounds of praise connected with the virtues of the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Sangha, filling all directions, were as if spoken aloud. The eyes of devas, supaṇṇas, nāgas, yakkhas, gandhabbas, and humans received a drink of the deathless, as it were. Now, standing in this place, it is fitting to describe the procession in a thousand verses. Of that, this is but a foretaste:

“Evaṃ [M 0.0373] sabbaṅgasampanno, kampayanto vasundharaṃ;

Aheṭhayanto pāṇāni, yāti lokavināyako.

Thus endowed with all excellent characteristics, causing the earth to tremble, not harming living beings, the Guide of the world proceeds.

“Dakkhiṇaṃ paṭhamaṃ pādaṃ, uddharanto narāsabho;

Gacchanto sirisampanno, sobhate dvipaduttamo.

Lifting his right foot first, the bull among men, endowed with splendor, the supreme among bipeds, shines as he proceeds.

“Gacchato buddhaseṭṭhassa, heṭṭhā pādatalaṃ mudu;

Samaṃ samphusate bhūmiṃ, rajasānupalimpati.

As the foremost Buddha proceeds, the soft soles of his feet touch the ground evenly and are not smeared with dust.

“Ninnaṃ [V 0.0335] ṭhānaṃ unnamati, gacchante lokanāyake;

Unnatañca samaṃ hoti, pathavī ca acetanā.

When the Guide of the world proceeds, low places rise up and high places become level, though the earth itself is without consciousness.

“Pāsāṇā sakkharā ceva, kathalā khāṇukaṇṭakā;

Sabbe maggā vivajjanti, gacchante lokanāyake.

When the Guide of the world proceeds, all stones, gravel, potsherds, stumps, and thorns clear themselves from the path.

“Nātidūre uddharati, naccāsanne ca nikkhipaṃ;

Aghaṭṭayanto niyyāti, ubho jāṇū ca gopphake.

He lifts his foot not too far, nor does he place it down too near; he proceeds without his knees and ankles knocking against each other.

“Nātisīghaṃ pakkamati, sampannacaraṇo muni;

Na cāpi saṇikaṃ yāti, gacchamāno samāhito.

The sage, perfect in conduct and composed in mind, does not proceed too quickly as he goes, nor does he go too slowly.

“Uddhaṃ adho ca tiriyaṃ, disañca vidisaṃ tathā;

Na pekkhamāno so yāti, yugamattaṃvapekkhati.

He proceeds without looking up, down, or across, nor to the cardinal and intermediate directions; he looks only a yoke's length ahead.

“Nāgavikkantacāro so, gamane sobhate jino;

Cāruṃ gacchati lokaggo, hāsayanto sadevake.

With the bold stride of a great elephant, the Conqueror is glorious in his gait; the Foremost in the World proceeds gracefully, delighting devas and humans.

“Usabharājāva sobhanto, cārucārīva kesarī;

Tosayanto bahū satte, gāmaṃ seṭṭho upāgamī”ti. –

Shining like a kingly bull, moving gracefully like a lion, delighting many beings, the Supreme One approached the village.

Vaṇṇakālo [P 0.0415] nāma kiresa. Evaṃvidhesu kālesu bhagavato sarīravaṇṇe vā guṇavaṇṇe vā dhammakathikassa thāmoyeva pamāṇaṃ, cuṇṇiyapadehi gāthābandhehi yattakaṃ sakkoti, tattakaṃ vattabbaṃ. “Dukkathita”nti vā “atitthena pakkhando”ti vā na vattabbo. Aparimāṇavaṇṇā hi buddhā bhagavanto, tesaṃ buddhāpi anavasesato vaṇṇaṃ vattuṃ asamatthā. Sakalampi hi kappaṃ vaṇṇentā pariyosāpetuṃ na sakkonti, pageva itarā pajāti. Iminā sirivilāsena alaṅkatappaṭiyattaṃ pāṭaligāmaṃ pāvisi[M 0.0374], pavisitvā bhagavā pasannacittena janena pupphagandhadhūmavāsacuṇṇādīhi pūjiyamāno āvasathāgāraṃ pāvisi. Tena vuttaṃ – “atha kho bhagavā nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya saddhiṃ bhikkhusaṅghena yena āvasathāgāraṃ tenupasaṅkamī”ti.

This, it is said, is called the time for praise. At such times, in praising the Blessed One’s physical form or his virtues, the measure is simply the Dhamma-preacher's own ability. As much as one is able to say, whether in prose or in verse, that much should be said. One should not be criticized by saying, 'It was poorly spoken,' or 'He rushed on without satisfying the audience.' For the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are of immeasurable virtue; even Buddhas are unable to describe their virtues without remainder. Indeed, praising them for an entire eon, they would not be able to bring it to an end—how much less so other beings. With this majestic splendor, he entered the adorned and prepared village of Pāṭali. Having entered, the Blessed One, being honored by the people of devoted heart with flowers, fragrances, incense, aromatic powders, and the like, entered the rest house. Therefore it was said: 'Then the Blessed One, having adjusted his robe, taking his bowl and outer robe, together with the Sangha of bhikkhus, approached the rest house where it was.'

Pāde [V 0.0336] pakkhāletvāti yadipi bhagavato pāde rajojallaṃ na upalimpati, tesaṃ pana upāsakānaṃ kusalābhivuddhiṃ ākaṅkhanto paresaṃ diṭṭhānugatiṃ āpajjanatthañca bhagavā pāde pakkhāleti. Apica upādinnakasarīraṃ nāma sītaṃ kātabbampi hotīti etadatthampi bhagavā nhānapādadhovanādīni karotiyeva. Bhagavantaṃyeva purakkhatvāti bhagavantaṃ purato katvā. Tattha bhagavā bhikkhūnañceva upāsakānañca majjhe nisinno gandhodakena nhāpetvā dukūlacumbaṭakena vodakaṃ katvā jātihiṅgulakena majjitvā rattakambalena paliveṭhetvā pīṭhe ṭhapitā rattasuvaṇṇaghanapaṭimā viya ativirocittha.

Regarding 'having washed his feet': although dust and dirt never clung to the Blessed One's feet, he nevertheless washed his feet, desiring an increase in merit for those lay followers and so that others might follow the example they had seen. Moreover, a body produced by grasping sometimes needs to be cooled, and for this purpose as well, the Blessed One would indeed bathe, wash his feet, and so on. Regarding 'having placed the Blessed One at the forefront': this means making the Blessed One foremost. There, the Blessed One, seated in the midst of the bhikkhus and the lay followers, having been bathed with fragrant water, dried with a fine linen towel, polished with natural vermilion, and wrapped in a red woolen blanket, shone exceedingly, like a solid statue of red gold placed upon a seat.

Ayaṃ panettha porāṇānaṃ vaṇṇabhaṇanamaggo –

Herein, this is the ancient teachers' way of reciting praise:

“Gantvāna maṇḍalamāḷaṃ, nāgavikkantacāraṇo;

Obhāsayanto lokaggo, nisīdi varamāsane.

Having gone to the pavilion hall, he of the elephant's majestic stride, the Foremost in the World, sat upon the excellent seat, illuminating all.

“Tahiṃ [P 0.0416] nisinno naradammasārathi,

Devātidevo satapuññalakkhaṇo;

Buddhāsane majjhagato virocati,

Suvaṇṇanikkhaṃ viya paṇḍukambale.

Seated there, the Tamer of persons to be tamed, the Deva beyond devas, endowed with the marks of a hundred merits, having come to the center, shines upon the Buddha-seat like a golden figure on a pale woolen cloth.

“Nekkhaṃ jambonadasseva, nikkhittaṃ paṇḍukambale;

Virocati vītamalo, maṇiverocano yathā.

Like an ornament of Jambu-river gold placed upon a pale woolen cloth, so he shines, the stainless one, like a radiant Verocana gem.

“Mahāsālova samphullo, merurājāvalaṅkato;

Suvaṇṇayūpasaṅkāso, padumo kokanado yathā.

Like a great Sāla tree in full bloom, adorned like Meru, king of mountains; like a golden sacrificial post, like a red lotus.

“Jalanto dīparukkhova, pabbatagge yathā sikhī;

Devānaṃ pārichattova, sabbaphullo virocatī”ti.

Like a blazing lamp-tree, like a fire on a mountain peak, like the Pāricchattaka tree of the devas in full bloom, so does he shine.

Pāṭaligāmiye [M 0.0375] upāsake āmantesīti yasmā tesu upāsakesu bahū janā sīlesu patiṭṭhitā, tasmā paṭhamaṃ tāva sīlavipattiyā ādīnavaṃ pakāsetvā pacchā sīlasampadāya ānisaṃsaṃ dassetuṃ, “pañcime gahapatayo”tiādinā dhammadesanatthaṃ āmantesi.

Regarding 'he addressed the lay followers of Pāṭaligāma': because many people among those lay followers were established in virtue, he addressed them for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma, first explaining the danger in the corruption of virtue and then showing the benefit in the accomplishment of virtue, beginning with the words, 'Householders, these five...'

Tattha [V 0.0337] dussīloti nissīlo. Sīlavipannoti vipannasīlo bhinnasaṃvaro. Ettha ca “dussīlo”ti padena puggalassa sīlābhāvo vutto. So panassa sīlābhāvo duvidho asamādānena vā samādinnassa bhedena vāti. Tesu purimo na tathā sāvajjo, yathā dutiyo sāvajjataro. Yathādhippetādīnavanimittaṃ sīlābhāvaṃ puggalādhiṭṭhānāya desanāya dassetuṃ, “sīlavipanno”ti vuttaṃ. Tena “dussīlo”ti padassa atthaṃ dasseti. Pamādādhikaraṇanti pamādakāraṇā. Idañca suttaṃ gahaṭṭhānaṃ vasena āgataṃ, pabbajitānampi pana labbhateva. Gahaṭṭho hi yena sippaṭṭhānena jīvikaṃ kappeti yadi kasiyā yadi vāṇijjāya yadi gorakkhena, pāṇātipātādivasena pamatto taṃ taṃ yathākālaṃ sampādetuṃ na sakkoti, athassa kammaṃ vinassati. Māghātakāle [P 0.0417] pana pāṇātipātādīni karonto daṇḍavasena mahatiṃ bhogajāniṃ nigacchati. Pabbajito dussīlo pamādakāraṇā sīlato buddhavacanato jhānato sattaariyadhanato ca jāniṃ nigacchati.

Herein, ‘immoral’ (dussīla) means one who is without virtue (nissīla). ‘Corrupt in virtue’ (sīlavipanna) means one whose virtue is corrupted, one with broken restraint. And here, by the term ‘immoral,’ a person’s lack of virtue is stated. This lack of virtue is twofold: either through not undertaking the precepts or through breaking what has been undertaken. Among these, the former is not as blameworthy as the latter, which is more blameworthy. To show the lack of virtue which is the cause of the intended dangers, by means of a discourse based on the individual, it is said, ‘corrupt in virtue.’ Thereby, the meaning of the term ‘immoral’ is shown. ‘On account of negligence’ (pamādādhikaraṇa) means due to the cause of negligence. And this discourse is given in connection with householders, but it is also applicable to monastics. For a householder who makes a living by some craft—be it farming, trade, or cattle-herding—if he is negligent by way of killing living beings and so on, he is unable to accomplish his various tasks at the proper time, and thus his work is ruined. Furthermore, when engaging in the killing of living beings and so on, at a time when he is forbidden to kill, he incurs a great loss of wealth by way of punishment. An immoral monastic, due to the cause of negligence, incurs loss with respect to virtue, the Buddha’s word, meditative absorption, and the seven noble treasures.

Pāpako kittisaddoti gahaṭṭhassa “asuko amukakule jāto dussīlo pāpadhammo pariccattaidhalokaparaloko salākabhattamattampi na detī”ti parisamajjhe pāpako kittisaddo abbhuggacchati. Pabbajitassa “asuko nāma thero satthu sāsane pabbajitvā nāsakkhi sīlāni rakkhituṃ, na buddhavacanaṃ gahetuṃ, vejjakammādīhi jīvati, chahi agāravehi samannāgato”ti evaṃ pāpako kittisaddo abbhuggacchati.

Regarding ‘an evil report arises’: For a householder, an evil report arises in the midst of an assembly, saying: ‘So-and-so, born in such-and-such a family, is immoral, of evil character, one who has abandoned this world and the next; he does not give even so much as a meal distributed by ticket.’ For a monastic, an evil report arises, saying: ‘The elder named so-and-so, having gone forth in the Teacher’s dispensation, was unable to keep the precepts and unable to grasp the Buddha’s word; he makes a living by medical practice and the like, and is possessed of the six kinds of irreverence.’

Avisāradoti gahaṭṭho tāva avassaṃ bahūnaṃ sannipātaṭṭhāne “koci mama kammaṃ jānissati, atha maṃ nindissati, rājakulassa vā dassessatī”ti sabhayo upasaṅkamati, maṅkubhūto pattakkhandho adhomukho nisīdati, visārado hutvā kathetuṃ na sakkoti. Pabbajitopi bahubhikkhusaṅghe sannipatite “avassaṃ koci mama kammaṃ jānissati, atha me uposathampi pavāraṇampi ṭhapetvā sāmaññato cāvetvā nikkaḍḍhissatī”ti sabhayo upasaṅkamati, visārado hutvā kathetuṃ [M 0.0376] na sakkoti. Ekacco pana dussīlopi samāno susīlo viya carati, sopi ajjhāsayena maṅku hotiyeva.

Regarding ‘not confident’: A householder, for his part, approaches a place where many have assembled, full of fear, thinking: ‘Someone will know of my deed, and then they will blame me or report me to the royal court.’ He sits abashed, with drooping shoulders and downcast face, unable to speak with confidence. A monastic, too, when a large community of monks has assembled, approaches full of fear, thinking: ‘Someone will surely know of my deed, and then, having suspended my Uposatha and Pavāraṇā, they will depose me from the state of a recluse and expel me.’ He is unable to speak with confidence.
