A certain one, however, though immoral, may behave as if he were virtuous; yet he too, in his heart, is indeed abashed.

Sammūḷho kālaṃ karotīti dussīlassa hi maraṇamañce nipannassa dussīlakammāni samādāya pavattitaṭṭhānāni āpāthaṃ āgacchanti. So ummīletvā idhalokaṃ, nimīletvā paralokaṃ passati. Tassa cattāro apāyā kammānurūpaṃ upaṭṭhahanti, sattisatena pahariyamāno viya aggijālābhighātena [V 0.0338] jhāyamāno viya ca hoti. So “vāretha, vārethā”ti viravantova marati. Tena vuttaṃ – “sammūḷho kālaṃ karotī”ti.

Regarding ‘he dies bewildered’: Indeed, for an immoral person lying on his deathbed, the instances of immoral deeds he has undertaken and performed come into the range of his mind. Opening his eyes, he sees this world; closing his eyes, he sees the next world. The four states of deprivation appear to him in accordance with his kamma, and he feels as if he were being struck by a hundred spears or being consumed by the assault of a mass of flames. He dies wailing, ‘Ward them off! Ward them off!’ Therefore it is said: ‘He dies bewildered.’

Kāyassa [P 0.0418] bhedāti upādinnakkhandhapariccāgā. Paraṃ maraṇāti tadanantaraṃ abhinibbattakkhandhaggahaṇā. Atha vā kāyassa bhedāti jīvitindriyassa upacchedā. Paraṃ maraṇāti cutito uddhaṃ. Apāyantiādi sabbaṃ nirayavevacanaṃ. Nirayo hi saggamokkhahetubhūtā puññasaṅkhātā ayā apetattā, sukhānaṃ vā ayassa, āgamanassa vā abhāvā apāyo. Dukkhassa gati paṭisaraṇanti duggati, dosabahulatāya vā duṭṭhena kammunā nibbattā gatīti duggati. Vivasā nipatanti ettha dukkatakārinoti vinipāto, vinassantā vā ettha nipatanti sambhijjamānaṅgapaccaṅgāti vinipāto. Natthi ettha assādasaññito ayoti nirayo.

‘With the breakup of the body’ means with the relinquishing of the appropriated aggregates. ‘After death’ means at the grasping of newly arisen aggregates immediately after that. Alternatively, ‘with the breakup of the body’ means with the cutting off of the life faculty. ‘After death’ means subsequent to passing away. The terms ‘state of deprivation,’ and so on, are all synonyms for hell. Indeed, it is a ‘state of deprivation’ (apāya) because it is devoid of the good fortune (aya) called merit, which is the cause of heaven and liberation; or because of the absence of the arrival (aya or āgamana) of happiness. It is a ‘woeful destination’ (duggati) because it is a destination and resort for suffering; or it is a destination produced by a corrupt deed due to an abundance of hatred. It is a ‘place of ruin’ (vinipāta) because evildoers fall (nipatanti) here helplessly (vivasā); or because they fall here while being destroyed, with their major and minor limbs breaking apart. It is ‘hell’ (niraya) because there is no (natthi) delight (aya), known as enjoyment, here.

Atha vā apāyaggahaṇena tiracchānayoniṃ dīpeti. Tiracchānayoni hi apāyo sugatito apetattā, na duggati mahesakkhānaṃ nāgarājādīnaṃ sambhavato. Duggatiggahaṇena pettivisayaṃ dīpeti. So hi apāyo ceva duggati ca sugatito apetattā, dukkhassa ca gatibhūtattā, na tu vinipāto asurasadisaṃ avinipatitattā petamahiddhikānampi vijjamānattā. Vinipātaggahaṇena asurakāyaṃ dīpeti. So hi yathāvuttenaṭṭhena “apāyo” ceva “duggati” ca sabbasampattisamussayehi vinipatitattā “vinipāto”ti ca vuccati. Nirayaggahaṇena avīciādikaṃ anekappakāraṃ nirayameva dīpeti. Upapajjatīti nibbattati.

Alternatively, by the term ‘state of deprivation’ (apāya), the animal womb is indicated. For the animal womb is a state of deprivation because it is devoid of a happy destination, but it is not a woeful destination, due to the existence of powerful beings such as nāga kings. By the term ‘woeful destination’ (duggati), the sphere of ghosts is indicated. For that is both a state of deprivation and a woeful destination—because it is devoid of a happy destination and because it is a destination of suffering—but it is not a place of ruin, because they have not fallen into ruin like the asuras, and because powerful ghosts also exist. By the term ‘place of ruin’ (vinipāta), the host of asuras is indicated. For that, by the meaning already stated, is both a ‘state of deprivation’ and a ‘woeful destination,’ and it is also called a ‘place of ruin’ because they have fallen away from the whole mass of all accomplishments. By the term ‘hell’ (niraya), the many kinds of hells, beginning with Avīci, are indicated. ‘Is reborn’ (upapajjati) means arises.

Ānisaṃsakathā vuttavipariyāyena veditabbā. Ayaṃ pana viseso – sīlavāti samādānavasena sīlavā. Sīlasampannoti parisuddhaṃ paripuṇṇañca katvā [M 0.0377] sīlassa samādānena sīlasampanno. Bhogakkhandhanti bhogarāsiṃ. Sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokanti ettha sugatiggahaṇena manussagatipi saṅgayhati, saggaggahaṇena devagati eva. Tattha sundarā gati sugati, rūpādīhi visayehi suṭṭhu aggoti saggo, so sabbopi lujjanapalujjanaṭṭhena lokoti.

The discourse on the benefits should be understood in the opposite way to what has been said. This, however, is a specific point: ‘virtuous’ (sīlavā) means one is virtuous by way of undertaking the precepts. ‘Endowed with virtue’ (sīlasampanna) means one is endowed with virtue by undertaking it, having made it pure and complete. ‘A mass of wealth’ (bhogakkhandha) means a heap of wealth. In the phrase ‘a happy destination, a heavenly world,’ by the term ‘happy destination’ the human destination is also included; by the term ‘heavenly’ only the deva destination is included. Therein, a ‘happy destination’ (sugati) is a beautiful destination. ‘Heaven’ (sagga) is so called because it is truly supreme (suṭṭhu agga) with respect to sense objects such as forms. All of this is called a ‘world’ (loka) in the sense of crumbling and breaking up.

Pāṭaligāmiye [P 0.0419] upāsake bahudeva rattiṃ dhammiyā kathāyāti aññāyapi pāḷimuttāya dhammakathāya ceva āvasathānumodanakathāya ca. Tadā hi bhagavā yasmā ajātasattunā tattha pāṭaliputtanagaraṃ māpentena aññesu gāmanigamajanapadarājadhānīsu ye sīlācārasampannā kuṭumbikā, te ānetvā dhanadhaññagharavatthukhettavatthādīni ceva parihārañca dāpetvā nivesiyanti. Tasmā pāṭaligāmiyā upāsakā ānisaṃsadassāvitāya visesato sīlagarukā sabbaguṇānañca sīlassa [V 0.0339] adhiṭṭhānabhāvato tesaṃ paṭhamaṃ sīlānisaṃse pakāsetvā tato paraṃ ākāsagaṅgaṃ otārento viya, pathavojaṃ ākaḍḍhanto viya, mahājambuṃ matthake gahetvā cālento viya, yojanikamadhukaṇḍaṃ cakkayantena pīḷetvā madhurasaṃ pāyamāno viya pāṭaligāmikānaṃ upāsakānaṃ hitasukhāvahaṃ pakiṇṇakakathaṃ kathento “āvāsadānaṃ nāmetaṃ gahapatayo mahantaṃ puññaṃ, tumhākaṃ āvāso mayā paribhutto, bhikkhusaṅghena ca paribhutto, mayā ca bhikkhusaṅghena ca paribhutte pana dhammaratanenapi paribhuttoyeva hoti. Evaṃ tīhi ratanehi paribhutte aparimeyyo ca vipāko, apica āvāsadānasmiṃ dinne sabbadānaṃ dinnameva hoti, bhūmaṭṭhakapaṇṇasālāya vā sākhāmaṇḍapassa vā saṅghaṃ uddissa katassa ānisaṃso paricchindituṃ na sakkā. Āvāsadānānubhāvena hi bhave nibbattamānassapi sampīḷitagabbhavāso nāma na hoti, dvādasahattho ovarako viyassa mātukucchi asambādhova hotī”ti evaṃ nānānayehi vicittaṃ bahuṃ dhammakathaṃ kathetvā –

Regarding the phrase 'with a talk on the Dhamma for much of the night to the lay followers of Pāṭaligāma': this refers to another Dhamma talk apart from the Pāḷi canon, and also a talk of appreciation for the lodging. For at that time, King Ajātasattu, while establishing the city of Pāṭaliputta there, brought householders endowed with virtue and good conduct from other villages, towns, provinces, and royal capitals, and had them settled there, having had them given wealth, grain, houses, land, fields, goods, and so forth, as well as protection. Therefore, because the benefits had been shown to them, the lay followers of Pāṭaligāma were especially reverent towards virtue, and because virtue is the foundation of all good qualities, the Blessed One first declared to them the benefits of virtue. Then, like one causing the celestial Ganges to descend, like one drawing up the nutritive essence of the earth, like one grasping the great Jambu tree by its top and shaking it, or like one pressing a yojana-sized honeycomb with a machine and causing the sweet juice to be drunk, he delivered a miscellaneous discourse for the welfare and happiness of the lay followers of Pāṭaligāma, saying: 'Householders, this gift of lodging is a great merit. Your lodging has been used by me and by the Saṅgha of monks. And when it is used by me and the Saṅgha of monks, it is also used by the Jewel of the Dhamma. Thus, when used by the Three Jewels, the result is immeasurable. Moreover, when the gift of lodging is given, all gifts are given. The benefit of a leaf-hut on the ground or a branch-pavilion made for the Saṅgha cannot be measured. Indeed, by the power of the gift of lodging, even for one being reborn in a future existence, there is no such thing as a constricted stay in the womb; their mother’s womb is as unconfined as a twelve-cubit chamber.' Having thus delivered a diverse and manifold Dhamma talk in many ways—

“Sītaṃ uṇhaṃ paṭihanti, tato vāḷamigāni ca;

Sarīsape ca makase, sisire cāpi vuṭṭhiyo.

“It wards off cold and heat, and also beasts of prey; and serpents and mosquitoes, and the rains in the cold season.

“Tato vātātapo ghoro, sañjāto paṭihaññati;

Leṇatthañca sukhatthañca, jhāyituñca vipassituṃ.

“Furthermore, the fierce wind and heat that has arisen is warded off; it is for the sake of refuge and for happiness, for meditating and for developing insight.

“Vihāradānaṃ [M 0.0378] saṅghassa, aggaṃ buddhena vaṇṇitaṃ;

Tasmā [P 0.0420] hi paṇḍito poso, sampassaṃ atthamattano.

“The gift of a dwelling to the Saṅgha has been praised by the Buddha as foremost; therefore, a wise person, seeing their own welfare,

“Vihāre kāraye ramme, vāsayettha bahussute;

Tesaṃ annañca pānañca, vatthasenāsanāni ca.

“Should have delightful monasteries built, and have the learned dwell therein.

“Dadeyya ujubhūtesu, vippasannena cetasā;

Te tassa dhammaṃ desenti, sabbadukkhāpanūdanaṃ;

Yaṃ so dhammaṃ idhaññāya, parinibbāti anāsavo”ti. (cūḷava. 295) –

“To them, being upright, one should give with a confident mind food, drink, clothing, and lodgings. They teach that person the Dhamma that removes all suffering; having understood that Dhamma here, taintless, one attains final Nibbāna.”

Evaṃ ayampi āvāsadāne ānisaṃsoti bahudeva rattiṃ atirekataraṃ diyaḍḍhayāmaṃ āvāsadānānisaṃsakathaṃ [V 0.0340] kathesi. Tattha imā gāthā tāva saṅgahaṃ āruḷhā, pakiṇṇakadhammadesanā pana saṅgahaṃ nārohati. Sandassetvātiādīni vuttatthāneva.

Thus, this too is a benefit of giving lodging. For much of the night, for more than one and a half watches, he spoke on the benefits of giving lodging. Therein, these verses are included in the collection, but the miscellaneous Dhamma discourse is not included in the collection. The meaning of 'having instructed,' and so on, is as already stated.

Abhikkantāti atikkantā dve yāmā gatā. Yassa dāni kālaṃ maññathāti yassa gamanassa tumhe kālaṃ maññatha, gamanakālo tumhākaṃ, gacchathāti vuttaṃ hoti. Kasmā pana bhagavā te uyyojesīti? Anukampāya. Tiyāmarattiñhi tattha nisīditvā vītināmentānaṃ tesaṃ sarīre ābādho uppajjeyyāti, bhikkhusaṅghepi ca vippabhātasayananisajjāya okāso laddhuṃ vaṭṭati, iti ubhayānukampāya uyyojesīti. Suññāgāranti pāṭiyekkaṃ suññāgāraṃ nāma tattha natthi. Tena kira gahapatayo tasseva āvasathāgārassa ekapasse paṭasāṇiyā parikkhipāpetvā kappiyamañcaṃ paññāpetvā tattha kappiyapaccattharaṇaṃ attharitvā upari suvaṇṇarajatatārakāgandhamālādipaṭimaṇḍitaṃ vitānaṃ bandhitvā telappadīpaṃ āropesuṃ “appeva nāma satthā dhammāsanato vuṭṭhāya thokaṃ vissamitukāmo idha nipajjeyya, evaṃ no idaṃ āvasathāgāraṃ bhagavatā catūhi iriyāpathehi paribhuttaṃ dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāya bhavissatī”ti. Satthāpi tadeva sandhāya tattha saṅghāṭiṃ paññāpetvā sīhaseyyaṃ kappesi. Taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “suññāgāraṃ pāvisī”ti. Tattha pādadhovanaṭṭhānato paṭṭhāya yāva dhammāsanā agamāsi, ettake ṭhāne gamanaṃ nipphannaṃ. Dhammāsanaṃ patvā [P 0.0421] thokaṃ aṭṭhāsi, idaṃ tattha ṭhānaṃ. Bhagavā dve yāme dhammāsane nisīdi, ettake ṭhāne nisajjā nipphannā. Upāsake uyyojetvā dhammāsanato [M 0.0379] oruyha yathāvutte ṭhāne sīhaseyyaṃ kappesi. Evaṃ taṃ ṭhānaṃ bhagavatā catūhi iriyāpathehi paribhuttaṃ ahosīti.

“Abhikkantā” means “passed”; two watches of the night have gone by. “Yassa dāni kālaṃ maññatha” means “Whatever time you now consider right for departure, it is your time for departure; go”—this is what was said. But why did the Blessed One dismiss them? Out of compassion. For if they were to spend the three watches of the night sitting there, an illness might arise in their bodies; moreover, it is fitting for the Saṅgha of monks to have an opportunity for lying down and sitting at dawn. Thus, out of compassion for both, he dismissed them. “Suññāgāra” (empty dwelling) does not mean there was a separate empty dwelling there. It is said that those householders had a cloth screen set up on one side of that very rest-house, prepared a suitable couch, spread a suitable covering on it, and above it they tied a canopy adorned with gold and silver stars, perfumes, garlands, and so on, and lit an oil lamp, thinking: “Perhaps the Teacher, after rising from the Dhamma-seat and wishing to rest for a while, might lie down here. In this way, this rest-house of ours, having been used by the Blessed One in the four postures, will be for our long-term welfare and happiness.” The Teacher, too, with reference to that, had his outer robe spread there and adopted the lion’s posture. It is with reference to this that it was said, “He entered the empty dwelling.” Therein, from the place for washing the feet up to the Dhamma-seat he walked; in that much space, the act of walking was accomplished. Having reached the Dhamma-seat, he stood for a short while; this was the act of standing there. The Blessed One sat on the Dhamma-seat for two watches; in that much space, the act of sitting was accomplished. Having dismissed the lay followers and descended from the Dhamma-seat, he adopted the lion’s posture in the aforementioned place. Thus, that place was used by the Blessed One in the four postures.

Sunidhavassakārāti sunidho ca vassakāro ca dve brāhmaṇā. Magadhamahāmattāti magadharañño mahāamaccā, magadharaṭṭhe vā mahāmattā mahatiyā issariyamattāya samannāgatāti mahāmattā. Pāṭaligāme nagaraṃ māpentīti pāṭaligāmasaṅkhāte bhūmipadese nagaraṃ māpenti. Vajjīnaṃ paṭibāhāyāti licchavirājūnaṃ āyamukhappacchindanatthaṃ. Sahassasahassevāti ekekavaggavasena sahassaṃ sahassaṃ hutvā. Vatthūnīti gharavatthūni. Cittāni namanti nivesanāni māpetunti rañño rājamahāmattānañca nivesanāni māpetuṃ vatthuvijjāpāṭhakānaṃ cittāni namanti. Te kira attano sippānubhāvena heṭṭhāpathaviyaṃ tiṃsahatthamatte ṭhāne “idha nāgaggāho, idha yakkhaggāho, idha bhūtaggāho, idha pāsāṇo vā khāṇuko vā atthī”ti jānanti. Te tadā sippaṃ jappetvā devatāhi saddhiṃ sammantayamānā viya māpenti.

Sunidha and Vassakāra were two brahmins. 'Ministers of Magadha' means the great ministers of the king of Magadha, or great ministers in the kingdom of Magadha, endowed with great authority. 'They were building a city at Pāṭaligāma' means they were constructing a city in the region known as Pāṭaligāma. 'To obstruct the Vajjis' means for the purpose of cutting off the sources of income of the Licchavi kings. 'A thousand each' means in individual groups of a thousand. 'Sites' means house sites. 'Their minds inclined to planning and constructing residences' means the minds of those who knew the science of sites inclined to planning and constructing residences for the king and his great ministers. It is said that by the power of their own skill, they knew what was at a depth of thirty cubits below the ground: 'Here is a nāga-haunt, here a yakkha-haunt, here a spirit-haunt; here is a rock or a stump.' At that time, reciting their spells, they would build as if consulting with deities.

Atha [V 0.0341] vā nesaṃ sarīre devatā adhimuccitvā tattha tattha nivesanāni māpetuṃ cittaṃ nāmenti. Tā catūsu koṇesu khāṇuke koṭṭetvā vatthumhi gahitamatte paṭivigacchanti. Saddhakulānaṃ saddhā devatā tathā karonti, assaddhakulānaṃ assaddhā devatā. Kiṃkāraṇā? Saddhānañhi evaṃ hoti “idha manussā nivesanaṃ māpentā paṭhamaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ nisīdāpetvā maṅgalaṃ vadāpessanti, atha mayaṃ sīlavantānaṃ dassanaṃ dhammakathaṃ pañhavissajjanaṃ anumodanaṃ sotuṃ labhissāma, manussā ca dānaṃ datvā amhākaṃ pattiṃ dassantī”ti. Assaddhā devatāpi “attano icchānurūpaṃ tesaṃ paṭipattiṃ passituṃ, kathañca sotuṃ labhissāmā”ti tathā karonti.

Alternatively, deities, having possessed their bodies, would incline their minds to build residences in those various places. Having driven stakes into the four corners, those deities withdraw as soon as the site is laid out. For faithful families, faithful deities act thus; for faithless families, faithless deities do so. For what reason? For faithful deities have this thought: 'Here, when people build a residence, they will first have the community of monks take their seats and have them recite auspicious verses. Then we will get to see the virtuous ones, and to hear a Dhamma talk, the answering of questions, and the blessing. And the people, having given alms, will share the merit with us.' The faithless deities also act thus, thinking: 'We will get to see their conduct, which is in accordance with our own wishes, and to hear their talk.'

Tāvatiṃsehīti [P 0.0422] yathā hi ekasmiṃ kule ekaṃ paṇḍitamanussaṃ, ekasmiñca vihāre ekaṃ bahussutaṃ bhikkhuṃ upādāya “asukakule manussā paṇḍitā, asukavihāre bhikkhū bahussutā”ti saddo abbhuggacchati, evameva sakkaṃ devarājānaṃ, vissakammañca devaputtaṃ upādāya “tāvatiṃsā paṇḍitā”ti saddo abbhuggato. Tenāha “tāvatiṃsehī”ti. Seyyathāpītiādinā [M 0.0380] devehi tāvatiṃsehi saddhiṃ mantetvā viya sunidhavassakārā nagaraṃ māpentīti dasseti.

'By the Tāvatiṃsa': For just as, on account of one wise person in a family, or one learned monk in a monastery, the reputation spreads, 'The people in such-and-such a family are wise,' or 'The monks in such-and-such a monastery are learned'; even so, on account of Sakka, king of the devas, and the deva Vissakamma, the reputation has spread, 'The Tāvatiṃsa are wise.' Therefore, He said, 'by the Tāvatiṃsa.' By the words beginning with 'Just as,' He shows that Sunidha and Vassakāra built the city as if consulting with the Tāvatiṃsa devas.

Yāvatā, ānanda, ariyaṃ āyatananti yattakaṃ ariyamanussānaṃ osaraṇaṭṭhānaṃ nāma atthi. Yāvatā vaṇippathoti yattakaṃ vāṇijānaṃ āhaṭabhaṇḍassa rāsivasena kayavikkayaṭṭhānaṃ nāma, vāṇijānaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ vā atthi. Idaṃ agganagaranti tesaṃ ariyāyatanavaṇippathānaṃ idaṃ nagaraṃ aggaṃ bhavissati jeṭṭhakaṃ pāmokkhaṃ. Puṭabhedananti bhaṇḍapuṭabhedanaṭṭhānaṃ, bhaṇḍabhaṇḍikānaṃ mocanaṭṭhānanti vuttaṃ hoti. Sakalajambudīpe aladdhabhaṇḍampi hi idheva labhissanti, aññattha vikkayaṃ agacchantāpi idheva vikkayaṃ gacchissanti, tasmā idheva puṭaṃ bhindissantīti attho. Āyānampi hi catūsu dvāresu cattāri, sabhāyaṃ ekanti evaṃ divase divase pañcasatasahassāni tattha uṭṭhahissanti. Tāni sabhāvāni āyānīti dasseti.

'As far, Ānanda, as the noble domain extends' means whatever place there is that is a resort for noble people. 'As far as the trade route extends' means whatever place there is for the buying and selling of merchants' goods brought in heaps, or a dwelling place for merchants. 'This will be the foremost city' means that among these noble domains and trade routes, this city will be the best, the chief, the most prominent. 'A place for the opening of bundles' means a place for breaking open bundles of merchandise; it is said to be a place for untying packages of goods. For even goods not found in all of Jambudīpa will be found right here. Even those who sell elsewhere will come right here to sell. Therefore, it is right here that they will break open their bundles; this is the meaning. As for revenues, four hundred thousand will arise at the four gates and one hundred thousand in the assembly hall; thus, five hundred thousand will arise there daily. He shows that these will be its future revenues.

Aggito vātiādīsu samuccayattho vāsaddo, agginā ca udakena ca mithubhedena ca nassissatīti attho. Tassa hi eko koṭṭhāso agginā nassissati, nibbāpetuṃ na sakkhissanti, ekaṃ koṭṭhāsaṃ gaṅgā gahetvā gamissati, eko iminā akathitaṃ amussa, amunā akathitaṃ imassa vadantānaṃ pisuṇavācānaṃ vasena bhinnānaṃ manussānaṃ aññamaññabhedena vinassissati. Evaṃ vatvā bhagavā paccūsakāle gaṅgātīraṃ gantvā katamukhadhovano bhikkhācāravelaṃ āgamayamāno nisīdi.

In the phrase beginning 'From fire, or...,' the particle 'or' is used in the sense of conjunction; the meaning is that it will be destroyed by fire, and by water, and by internal dissension. For one part of it will be destroyed by fire, which they will not be able to extinguish; one part the Ganges will carry away; and one part will be destroyed by the mutual division of people who have been split apart by the slanderous speech of those who tell one person what another has not said, and tell that other person what the first has not said. Having said this, the Blessed One, having gone to the bank of the Ganges at dawn and washed his face, sat down awaiting the time for the alms-round.

Sunidhavassakārāpi [V 0.0342] “amhākaṃ rājā samaṇassa gotamassa upaṭṭhāko[P 0.0423], so amhe upagate pucchissati ‘satthā kira pāṭaligāmaṃ agamāsi, kiṃ tassa santikaṃ upasaṅkamittha, na upasaṅkamitthā’ti. ‘Upasaṅkamimhā’ti ca vutte ‘nimantayittha, na nimantayitthā’ti pucchissati. ‘Na nimantayimhā’ti ca vutte amhākaṃ dosaṃ āropetvā niggaṇhissati, idañcāpi mayaṃ akataṭṭhāne nagaraṃ māpema, samaṇassa kho pana gotamassa gatagataṭṭhāne kāḷakaṇṇisattā paṭikkamanti, taṃ mayaṃ nagaramaṅgalaṃ vācāpessāmā”ti cintetvā satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā nimantayiṃsu. Tena vuttaṃ – “atha kho sunidhavassakārā”tiādi.

Sunidha and Vassakāra also thought: 'Our king is a supporter of the ascetic Gotama. When we go to him, he will ask us: “The Teacher, I hear, has gone to Pāṭaligāma; did you approach him or not?” And when we say, “We did approach him,” he will ask, “Did you invite him or not?” And when we say, “We did not invite him,” he will find fault with us and punish us. Moreover, we are building this city in an unestablished place, and wherever the ascetic Gotama goes, inauspicious beings retreat. Let us have him pronounce a blessing for the city.' Having thought thus, they approached the Teacher and invited him. Therefore it is said: 'Then Sunidha and Vassakāra…' and so on.

Pubbaṇhasamayanti [M 0.0381] pubbaṇhe kāle. Nivāsetvāti gāmapavesananīhārena nivāsanaṃ nivāsetvā kāyabandhanaṃ bandhitvā. Pattacīvaramādāyāti cīvaraṃ pārupitvā pattaṃ hatthena gahetvā.

'In the forenoon' means in the morning time. 'Having dressed' means having put on his lower robe in the manner for entering a village and having tied his waistband. 'Taking his bowl and robe' means having draped his outer robe and taken his bowl in hand.

Sīlavantetthāti sīlavanto ettha attano vasanaṭṭhāne. Saññateti kāyavācācittehi saññate. Tāsaṃ dakkhiṇamādiseti saṅghassa dinne cattāro paccaye tāsaṃ gharadevatānaṃ ādiseyya pattiṃ dadeyya. Pūjitā pūjayantīti “ime manussā amhākaṃ ñātakāpi na honti, evampi no pattiṃ dentī”ti ārakkhaṃ susaṃvihitaṃ karonti suṭṭhu ārakkhaṃ karonti. Mānitā mānayantīti kālānukālaṃ balikammakaraṇena mānitā “ete manussā amhākaṃ ñātakāpi na honti, tathāpi catupañcachamāsantaraṃ no balikammaṃ karontī”ti mānenti uppannaparissayaṃ haranti. Tato nanti tato taṃ paṇḍitajātikaṃ purisaṃ. Orasanti ure ṭhapetvā vaḍḍhitaṃ, yathā mātā orasaṃ puttaṃ anukampati, uppannaparissayaharaṇatthamevassa yathā vāyamati, evaṃ anukampantīti attho. Bhadrāni passatīti sundarāni passati.

'Sīlavantettha' means virtuous ones here, in their dwelling place. 'Saññate' means restrained in body, speech, and mind. 'Tāsaṃ dakkhiṇamādise' means he should assign the merit of the four requisites given to the Saṅgha to those household deities; he should give them a share. 'Pūjitā pūjayanti' signifies that 'these humans are not even our relatives, yet they give us a share,' thus they provide well-arranged protection, they protect well. 'Mānitā mānayanti' means honored by making offering rites from time to time, thinking, 'Though these humans are not our relatives, they still make offering rites to us every four, five, or six months,' and they honor them and remove arisen dangers. 'Tato nanti' refers to that man of wise nature. 'Orasanti' means raised holding on the breast; just as a mother has compassion for her own breast-born child and strives to remove arisen dangers for him, in the same way they show compassion—this is the meaning. 'Bhadrāni passati' means he sees beautiful things.

Anumoditvāti tehi tadā pasutapuññassa anumodanavasena [P 0.0424] tesaṃ dhammakathaṃ katvā. Sunidhavassakārāpi “yā tattha devatā āsuṃ, tāsaṃ dakkhiṇamādise”ti bhagavato vacanaṃ sutvā devatānaṃ pattiṃ adaṃsu. Taṃ gotamadvāraṃ nāma ahosīti tassa nagarassa yena dvārena bhagavā nikkhami, taṃ gotamadvāraṃ nāma ahosi. Gaṅgāya pana uttaraṇatthaṃ anotiṇṇattā gotamatitthaṃ nāma nāhosi. Pūrāti puṇṇā. Samatittikāti taṭasamaṃ udakassa tittā bharitā. Kākapeyyāti tīre ṭhitakākehi pātuṃ sakkuṇeyyaudakā. Dvīhipi padehi ubhatokūlasamaṃ paripuṇṇabhāvameva dasseti. Uḷumpanti pāragamanatthāya dārūni saṅghāṭetvā āṇiyo koṭṭetvā kataṃ. Kullanti veḷudaṇḍādike valliādīhi bandhitvā kataṃ.

'Anumoditvā' means having given a Dhamma talk to them by way of rejoicing in the merit produced by them at that time. Sunidha and Vassakāra also, hearing the Blessed One's words, 'Assign a share to the deities there,' gave a share to the deities. 'That was called the Gotama Gate' means the gate of that city through which the Blessed One departed was called the Gotama Gate. However, since he did not enter the Ganges for the purpose of crossing, it was not called the Gotama Ford. 'Pūrā' means full. 'Samatittikā' means filled with water, level with the bank. 'Kākapeyyā' means water that crows standing on the bank could drink. By both words, it shows only the state of being completely full, level on both banks. 'Uḷumpa' refers to a raft made by joining pieces of wood and hammering in nails for the purpose of crossing over. 'Kulla' means a raft made by binding bamboo poles and so forth with vines and so forth.

Etamatthaṃ [V 0.0343] viditvāti etaṃ mahājanassa gaṅgodakamattassapi kevalaṃ tarituṃ asamatthataṃ, attano pana bhikkhusaṅghassa ca atigambhīravitthataṃ saṃsāramahaṇṇavaṃ [M 0.0382] taritvā ṭhitabhāvañca sabbākārato viditvā tadatthaparidīpanaṃ imaṃ udānaṃ udānesi.

'Etamatthaṃ viditvā' means understanding the inability of the great populace to cross even the mere waters of the Ganges, while he himself, along with the community of monks, had crossed the exceedingly deep and vast great ocean of saṃsāra and were established. Having fully comprehended this in every way, he uttered this inspired utterance to illuminate its meaning.

Tattha aṇṇavanti sabbantimena paricchedena yojanamattaṃ gambhīrassa ca vitthatassa ca udakaṭṭhānassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Saranti saritvā gamanato idha nadī adhippetā. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – ye gambhīravitthataṃ saṃsāraṇṇavaṃ taṇhāsaritañca taranti, te ariyamaggasaṅkhātaṃ setuṃ katvāna visajja pallalāni anāmasitvāva udakabharitāni ninnaṭṭhānāni, ayaṃ pana idaṃ appamattakaṃ udakaṃ taritukāmo kullañhi jano pabandhati kullaṃ bandhituṃ āyāsaṃ āpajjati. Tiṇṇā medhāvino janāti ariyamaggañāṇasaṅkhātāya medhāya samannāgatattā medhāvino buddhā ca buddhasāvakā ca vinā eva kullena tiṇṇā paratīre patiṭṭhitāti.

There, 'aṇṇava' is a designation for a body of water that is, by the lowest measure, a yojana in depth and breadth. 'Saranti' means flowing; hence here a river is intended. This is what is said: those who cross the deep and vast ocean of saṃsāra and the river of craving, having made the bridge known as the Noble Path, abandoning puddles and low-lying places filled with water without even touching them; but this populace, wishing to cross this small amount of water, indeed fashions a raft; a person undergoes effort to bind a raft. 'The wise have crossed' means those endowed with wisdom, namely the wisdom known as the knowledge of the Noble Path—the Buddhas and the disciples of the Buddha—have crossed without a raft and are established on the far shore.

Chaṭṭhasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the sixth sutta is finished.

7. Dvidhāpathasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Dvidhāpatha Sutta

77. Sattame [P 0.0425] addhānamaggapaṭipannoti addhānasaṅkhātaṃ dīghamaggaṃ paṭipanno gacchanto hoti. Nāgasamālenāti evaṃnāmakena therena. Pacchāsamaṇenāti ayaṃ tadā bhagavato upaṭṭhāko ahosi. Tena naṃ pacchāsamaṇaṃ katvā maggaṃ paṭipajji. Bhagavato hi paṭhamabodhiyaṃ vīsativassāni anibaddhā upaṭṭhākā ahesuṃ, tato paraṃ yāva parinibbānā pañcavīsativassāni āyasmā ānando chāyāva upaṭṭhāsi. Ayaṃ pana anibaddhupaṭṭhākakālo. Tena vuttaṃ – “āyasmatā nāgasamālena pacchāsamaṇenā”ti. Dvidhāpathanti dvidhābhūtaṃ maggaṃ. “Dvedhāpatha”ntipi paṭhanti āyasmā nāgasamālo attanā pubbe tattha kataparicayattā ujubhāvañcassa sandhāya vadati “ayaṃ, bhante bhagavā, pantho”ti.

77. In the seventh sutta, 'addhānamaggapaṭipanno' means one who has entered upon a long path, designated as a journey, and is proceeding. 'Nāgasamālena' refers to the elder of that name. 'Pacchāsamaṇena' means he was then an attendant of the Blessed One. Therefore, having made him his follower, he proceeded on the path. Indeed, for the Blessed One, for twenty years in the first period after his enlightenment, there were unassigned attendants; thereafter, for twenty-five years until his final Nibbāna, the Venerable Ānanda attended him like a shadow. This, however, was the period of unassigned attendants. Hence it is said: 'by the Venerable Nāgasamāla, his follower.' 'Dvidhāpatha' means a path that has become twofold. Some also read 'dvedhāpatha.' The Venerable Nāgasamāla, having previously gained familiarity with that place himself and referring to its directness, says: 'This, Venerable Sir, O Blessed One, is the path.'

Bhagavā pana tadā tassa saparissayabhāvaṃ ñatvā tato aññaṃ maggaṃ gantukāmo “ayaṃ, nāgasamāla, pantho”ti āha. “Saparissayo”ti ca vutte asaddahitvā “bhagavā na tattha parissayo”ti vadeyya, tadassa dīgharattaṃ ahitāya dukkhāyāti “saparissayo”ti na kathesi. Tikkhattuṃ [V 0.0344] “ayaṃ [M 0.0383] pantho, iminā gacchāmā”ti vatvā catutthavāre “na bhagavā iminā maggena gantuṃ icchati, ayameva ca ujumaggo, handāhaṃ bhagavato pattacīvaraṃ datvā iminā maggena gamissāmī”ti cintetvā satthu pattacīvaraṃ dātuṃ asakkonto bhūmiyaṃ ṭhapetvā paccupaṭṭhitena dukkhasaṃvattanikena kammunā codiyamāno bhagavato vacanaṃ anādiyitvāva pakkāmi. Tena vuttaṃ – “atha kho āyasmā nāgasamālo bhagavato pattacīvaraṃ tattheva chamāyaṃ nikkhipitvā pakkāmī”ti. Tattha bhagavato pattacīvaranti attano hatthagataṃ bhagavato pattacīvaraṃ. Tatthevāti tasmiṃyeva magge chamāyaṃ pathaviyaṃ nikkhipitvā pakkāmi. Idaṃ vo bhagavā pattacīvaraṃ, sace icchatha, gaṇhatha, yadi attanā icchitamaggaṃyeva gantukāmatthāti adhippāyo. Bhagavāpi attano pattacīvaraṃ sayameva gahetvā yathādhippetaṃ maggaṃ paṭipajji.

The Blessed One, however, knowing at that time that the path was perilous and wishing to go by another, said: 'Nāgasamāla, this is the path.' For if, when it was said, 'It is perilous,' he were not to believe it and were to say, 'Venerable Sir, there is no peril there,' that would be for his harm and suffering for a long time. Therefore, the Blessed One did not say, 'It is perilous.' After he had said three times, 'This is the path, let us go by this way,' on the fourth occasion, Nāgasamāla thought: 'The Blessed One does not wish to go by this path, yet this is the direct path. Come now, I will give the Blessed One his bowl and robe and go by this path.' But being unable to give the Teacher his bowl and robe, he placed them on the ground. Then, urged on by a kamma that had presented itself and was productive of suffering, he departed, disregarding the Blessed One's word. Therefore it is said: 'Then the Venerable Nāgasamāla placed the Blessed One's bowl and robe right there on the ground and departed.' Herein, 'the Blessed One's bowl and robe' refers to the Blessed One's bowl and robe that was in his own hand. 'Right there' means on that very path, on the ground. The meaning was: 'Venerable Sir, here is your bowl and robe; if you wish, take them, since you are intent on going only by the path you desire.' The Blessed One, for his part, took his own bowl and robe himself and proceeded along the path he intended.

Antarāmagge corā nikkhamitvāti tadā kira pañcasatā purisā [P 0.0426] luddā lohitapāṇino rājāparādhino hutvā araññaṃ pavisitvā corikāya jīvikaṃ kappentā “pāripanthikabhāvena rañño āyapathaṃ pacchindissāmā”ti maggasamīpe araññe tiṭṭhanti. Te theraṃ tena maggena gacchantaṃ disvā “ayaṃ samaṇo iminā maggena āgacchati, avaḷañjitabbaṃ maggaṃ vaḷañjeti, amhākaṃ atthibhāvaṃ na jānāti, handa naṃ jānāpessāmā”ti kujjhitvā gahanaṭṭhānato vegena nikkhamitvā sahasā theraṃ bhūmiyaṃ pātetvā hatthapādehi koṭṭetvā mattikāpattañcassa bhinditvā cīvaraṃ khaṇḍākhaṇḍikaṃ chinditvā pabbajitattā “taṃ na hanāma, ito paṭṭhāya imassa maggassa parissayabhāvaṃ jānāhī”ti vissajjesuṃ. Tena vuttaṃ – “atha kho āyasmato…pe… vipphālesu”nti.

On the road, robbers emerged: it is said that at that time, five hundred fierce men with blood-stained hands, having offended the king, had entered the forest and were making a living by robbery. Thinking, 'As highwaymen, we will cut off the king’s revenue path,' they were waiting in the forest near the road. Seeing the elder traveling along that path, they thought, 'This ascetic is coming along this path, taking a path that should not be taken. He does not know of our presence—come, let us make him know!' Angered, they swiftly emerged from their hiding place in the thicket, suddenly threw the elder to the ground, beat him with their hands and feet, shattered his earthenware bowl, and tore his robe to shreds. But because he was a renunciant, they said, 'We will not kill you, but from now on, know the perilous nature of this path,' and released him. Therefore it is said: 'Then... of the Venerable One... they tore to pieces.'

Bhagavāpi “ayaṃ tena maggena gato corehi bādhito maṃ pariyesitvā idāneva āgamissatī”ti ñatvā thokaṃ gantvā maggā okkamma aññatarasmiṃ rukkhamūle nisīdi. Āyasmāpi kho nāgasamālo paccāgantvā satthārā gatamaggameva gahetvā gacchanto tasmiṃ rukkhamūle bhagavantaṃ passitvā upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā taṃ pavattiṃ sabbaṃ ārocesi. Tena vuttaṃ – “atha kho āyasmā nāgasamālo…pe… saṅghāṭiñca vipphālesu”nti.

The Blessed One, knowing, 'He has gone by that path, been harassed by thieves, and searching for me, will now return,' walked a short distance, left the path, and sat down at the foot of a certain tree. The Venerable Nāgasamāla, returning and taking the same path the Teacher had gone, saw the Blessed One at the foot of that tree, approached, paid homage, and reported the entire incident. Therefore, it is said: 'Then the Venerable Nāgasamāla... and tore his outer robe to pieces.'

Etamatthaṃ viditvāti etaṃ āyasmato nāgasamālassa attano vacanaṃ anādiyitvā akhemantamaggagamanaṃ, attano ca khemantamaggagamanaṃ viditvā tadatthadīpanaṃ imaṃ udānaṃ udānesi.

Understanding this matter: knowing that the Venerable Nāgasamāla had disregarded his words and had gone by the unsafe path, and knowing his own going by the safe path, the Blessed One uttered this inspired utterance to illustrate that point.

Tattha [M 0.0384] saddhiṃ caranti saha caranto. Ekato vasanti idaṃ tasseva vevacanaṃ, saha vasantoti attho[V 0.0345]. Misso aññajanena vedagūti veditabbaṭṭhena vedasaṅkhātena catusaccaariyamaggañāṇena gatattā adhigatattā, vedassa vā sakalassa ñeyyassa pāraṃ gatattā vedagū. Attano hitāhitaṃ na jānātīti añño, avidvā bāloti attho. Tena aññena janena misso sahacaraṇamattena misso. Vidvā pajahāti pāpakanti tena vedagūbhāvena vidvā jānanto pāpakaṃ abhaddakaṃ attano dukkhāvahaṃ pajahāti, pāpakaṃ vā akalyāṇapuggalaṃ pajahāti. Yathā kiṃ? Koñco khīrapakova ninnaganti [P 0.0427] yathā koñcasakuṇo udakamissite khīre upanīte vinā toyaṃ khīramattasseva pivanato khīrapako ninnaṭṭhānagamanena ninnagasaṅkhātaṃ udakaṃ pajahāti vajjeti, evaṃ paṇḍito kira duppaññapuggalehi ṭhānanisajjādīsu sahabhūtopi ācārena te pajahāti, na kadācipi sammisso hoti.

Here, 'saddhiṃ caranti' means 'traveling together.' 'Ekato vasanti' is a synonym for that; the meaning is 'living together.' 'Vedagū' (Veda-knower) means one who is a 'Veda-knower' because, through the knowledge of the Noble Path regarding the Four Truths—called 'veda' in the sense of what is to be known—one has gone to or attained them; or because one has gone to the further shore of the entirety of what is knowable, the 'veda.' 'Añño' (another) means one who does not know what is for one's own welfare or harm; the meaning is an ignorant fool. 'Mixed with such a person' means mixed merely by way of traveling together. 'The wise one abandons the bad' means that, being wise through that quality of being a Veda-knower, one knows and abandons what is bad, unwholesome, and brings suffering to oneself; or one abandons a bad person, one who is not a good friend. Like what? As in the saying: 'The heron, a milk-drinker, leaves what goes downwards.' Just as a heron, when milk mixed with water is brought, is a 'milk-drinker' because it drinks only the milk, apart from the water, and it abandons the water, which is called 'what goes downwards' (ninnaga) because it goes to a low place, so too, it is said, a wise person, even when together with foolish individuals in standing, sitting, and so on, abandons them by way of conduct and is never mixed with them.

Sattamasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Seventh Sutta is concluded.

8. Visākhāsuttavaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Visākha Sutta

78. Aṭṭhame visākhāya migāramātuyā nattā kālaṅkatā hotīti visākhāya mahāupāsikāya puttassa dhītā kumārikā kālaṅkatā hoti. Sā kira vattasampannā sāsane abhippasannā mahāupāsikāya gehaṃ paviṭṭhānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ bhikkhunīnañca attanā kātabbaveyyāvaccaṃ purebhattaṃ pacchābhattañca appamattā akāsi, attano pitāmahiyā cittānukūlaṃ paṭipajji. Tena visākhā gehato bahi gacchantī sabbaṃ tassāyeva bhāraṃ katvā gacchati, rūpena ca dassanīyā pāsādikā, iti sā tassā visesato piyā manāpā ahosi. Sā rogābhibhūtā kālamakāsi. Tena vuttaṃ – “tena kho pana samayena visākhāya migāramātuyā nattā kālaṅkatā hoti piyā manāpā”ti. Atha mahāupāsikā tassā maraṇena sokaṃ sandhāretuṃ asakkontī dukkhī dummanā sarīranikkhepaṃ kāretvā “api nāma satthu santikaṃ gatakāle cittassādaṃ labheyya”nti bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkami. Tena vuttaṃ – “atha kho visākhā migāramātā”tiādi. Tattha divā divassāti divasassāpi divā, majjhanhike kāleti attho.

78. In the eighth discourse, it is said that Visākhā Migāramātā’s granddaughter had passed away. This means that the young daughter of the great female lay disciple Visākhā’s son had died. She, it is said, was accomplished in virtue and deeply devoted to the Teaching. Whenever monks and nuns entered the great female lay disciple's house, she diligently and personally attended to the services that were to be done for them, both before and after the meal. She acted in accordance with her grandmother's wishes. For that reason, whenever Visākhā went out of the house, she would leave all responsibilities in her charge. She was also pleasing to see and graceful in appearance; thus, she was especially dear and beloved to her. Afflicted by illness, she passed away. Therefore it was said: “At that time, Visākhā Migāramātā’s granddaughter, who was dear and beloved, had passed away.” Then the great female lay disciple, unable to contain her grief at the girl's death, sorrowful and dejected, had the funeral rites performed and approached the Blessed One, thinking, “Perhaps I might find peace of mind when I go into the Teacher’s presence.” Therefore it was said: “Then Visākhā Migāramātā…” and so on. Therein, “in broad daylight” means during the day, that is, at midday.

Bhagavā [M 0.0385] visākhāya vaṭṭābhiratiṃ jānanto upāyena sokatanukaraṇatthaṃ “iccheyyāsi tvaṃ visākhe”tiādimāha. Tattha yāvatikāti yattakā. Tadā kira satta janakoṭiyo sāvatthiyaṃ paṭivasanti[V 0.0346]. Taṃ sandhāya bhagavā “kīvabahukā pana visākhe sāvatthiyā manussā devasikaṃ kālaṃ karontī”ti pucchi. Visākhā “dasapi, bhante”tiādimāha. Tattha tīṇīti tayo. Ayameva vā pāṭho. Avivittāti asuññā.

The Blessed One, knowing Visākhā's delight in the round of existence, wishing to lessen her sorrow by a skillful means, said, “Would you wish, Visākhā…” and so on. Therein, “as many as” means however many. At that time, it is said, seven crores of people were living in Sāvatthī. With reference to this, the Blessed One asked, “But how many people in Sāvatthī, Visākhā, die each day?” Visākhā replied, “Ten, venerable sir,” and so on. Therein, “three” means three persons. Or this is the reading itself. “Not empty” means not devoid.

Atha [P 0.0428] bhagavā attano adhippāyaṃ pakāsento “api nu tvaṃ kadāci karahaci anallavatthā vā bhaveyyāsi anallakesā vā”ti āha. Nanu evaṃ sante tayā sabbakālaṃ sokābhibhūtāya matānaṃ puttādīnaṃ amaṅgalūpacāravasena udakorohaṇena allavatthāya allakesāya eva bhavitabbanti dasseti. Taṃ sutvā upāsikā saṃvegajātā “no hetaṃ, bhante”ti paṭikkhipitvā piyavatthuṃ vippaṭisārato attano cittassa nivattabhāvaṃ satthu ārocentī “alaṃ me, bhante, tāvabahukehi puttehi ca nattārehi cā”ti āha.

Then the Blessed One, revealing his own intention, said, “Would you then, at any time, ever have clothes that are not wet, or hair that is not wet?” By this he shows: “Is it not so that, this being the case, you, constantly overwhelmed by grief, on account of performing inauspicious rites for your dead sons and others by descending into water, would always have wet clothes and wet hair?” Hearing this, the female lay disciple was struck with a sense of urgency. Rejecting his words, saying, “Certainly not, venerable sir,” she informed the Teacher of her mind’s turning away from beloved things, saying, “Enough for me, venerable sir, with so many sons and grandsons.”

Athassā bhagavā “dukkhaṃ nāmetaṃ piyavatthunimittaṃ, yattakāni piyavatthūni, tattakāni dukkhāni. Tasmā sukhakāmena dukkhappaṭikūlena sabbaso piyavatthuto cittaṃ vivecetabba”nti dhammaṃ desento “yesaṃ kho visākhe sataṃ piyāni, sataṃ tesaṃ dukkhānī”tiādimāha. Tattha sataṃ piyānīti sataṃ piyāyitabbavatthūni. “Sataṃ piya”ntipi keci paṭhanti. Ettha ca yasmā ekato paṭṭhāya yāva dasa, tāva saṅkhyā saṅkhyeyyappadhānā, tasmā “yesaṃ dasa piyāni, dasa tesaṃ dukkhānī”tiādinā pāḷi āgatā. Keci pana “yesaṃ dasa piyānaṃ, dasa nesaṃ dukkhāna”ntiādinā paṭhanti, taṃ na sundaraṃ. Yasmā pana vīsatito paṭṭhāya yāva sataṃ, tāva saṅkhyā saṅkhyeyyappadhānāva, tasmā tatthāpi saṅkhyeyyappadhānataṃyeva gahetvā “yesaṃ kho visākhe sataṃ piyāni, sataṃ tesaṃ dukkhānī”tiādinā pāḷi āgatā. Sabbesampi ca “yesaṃ ekaṃ piyaṃ, ekaṃ tesaṃ dukkha”nti pāṭho, na pana dukkhassāti. Etasmiñhi pakkhe ekarasā ekajjhāsayā ca bhagavato desanā hoti. Tasmā yathāvuttanayāva pāḷi veditabbā.

Then the Blessed One, teaching her the Dhamma, said, “This suffering, by name, is caused by beloved objects; as many beloved objects as there are, so many are the sufferings. Therefore, one who desires happiness and is averse to suffering should completely detach the mind from all beloved objects.” Thus he spoke, beginning with, “Visākhā, for those who have a hundred beloved things, they have a hundred sufferings.” Therein, “a hundred beloved things” means a hundred objects to be cherished. Some also recite “a hundred beloved.” And here, since from one up to ten the number-word has the enumerated as primary, the Pāli text proceeds with the nominative case: “for whom there are ten beloved things, for them there are ten sufferings,” and so on. Some, however, recite with the genitive case: “for whom there are ten of beloved things, for them there are ten of sufferings,” but this is not elegant. Moreover, since from twenty up to a hundred, the number also emphasizes the enumerated, therefore there too, having taken it as emphasizing the enumerated, the Pāli text proceeds: “Visākhā, for those who have a hundred beloved things, a hundred are their sufferings,” and so on.

Etamatthaṃ [M 0.0386] viditvā sokaparidevādikaṃ cetasikaṃ kāyikañca dukkhaṃ piyavatthunimittaṃ piyavatthumhi sati hoti, asati na hotīti etamatthaṃ sabbākārato jānitvā tadatthaparidīpanaṃ imaṃ udānaṃ udānesi.

Having understood this matter—that suffering, both mental and physical, such as sorrow and lamentation, is caused by a beloved object, arising when a beloved object exists and not arising when it does not—and knowing this matter in all its aspects, he uttered this inspired utterance that illuminates its meaning.

Tassattho – ñātibhogarogasīladiṭṭhibyasanehi phuṭṭhassa anto nijjhāyantassa bālassa cittasantāpalakkhaṇā ye keci mudumajjhādibhedena yādisā tādisā sokā vā tehiyeva phuṭṭhassa [P 0.0429] sokuddehakasamuṭṭhāpitavacīvippalāpalakkhaṇā paridevitā vā aniṭṭhaphoṭṭhabbapaṭihatakāyassa [V 0.0347] kāyapīḷanalakkhaṇā dukkhā vā tathā avuttatthassa vikappanatthena vāsaddena gahitā domanassūpāyāsādayo vā nissayabhedena ca anekarūpā nānāvidhā imasmiṃ sattaloke dissanti upalabbhanti, sabbepi ete piyaṃ piyajātikaṃ sattaṃ saṅkhārañca paṭicca nissāya āgamma paccayaṃ katvā pabhavanti nibbattanti. Tasmiṃ pana yathāvutte piyavatthumhi piye asante piyabhāvakare chandarāge pahīne na kadācipi ete bhavanti. Vuttañhetaṃ – “piyato jāyatī soko…pe… pemato jāyatī soko”ti ca ādi (dha. pa. 212-213). Tathā “piyappabhūtā kalahā vivādā, paridevasokā sahamaccharehī”ti ca ādi (su. ni. 869). Ettha ca “paridevitā vā dukkhā vā”ti liṅgavipallāsena vuttaṃ, “paridevitāni vā dukkhāni vā”ti vattabbe vibhattilopo vā katoti veditabbo.

Its meaning is this: For a fool, burning internally, afflicted by the loss of relatives, wealth, health, virtue, or right view, whatever sorrows there may be—mild, moderate, or otherwise; or lamentations characterized by verbal raving instigated by the burning of sorrow for one afflicted by those same losses; or sufferings characterized by bodily affliction for one whose body is struck by unpleasant tangible objects; or, similarly, displeasure, despair, and so on, which are included by the word 'or' to suggest what has not been stated—all these, in many and various forms due to different bases, are seen and found in this world of beings. All of them arise and are generated depending on, relying on, resorting to, and conditioned by a beloved being and beloved conditioned phenomena. But when that aforementioned beloved object, that beloved one, is absent, when desire and lust, which create the state of being beloved, are abandoned, these states never come to be. For this has been said: “From what is dear, sorrow is born… from affection, sorrow is born,” and so on. And also: “From what is dear arise quarrels, disputes, lamentation and sorrow, together with avarice,” and so on. And here, “lamentation or suffering” is stated with a gender inversion; it should be understood that where “lamentations or sufferings” should be said, an elision of the case-ending has been made.

Tasmā hi te sukhino vītasokāti yasmā piyappabhūtā sokādayo yesaṃ natthi, tasmā te eva sukhino vītasokā nāma. Ke pana te? Yesaṃ piyaṃ natthi kuhiñci loke yesaṃ ariyānaṃ sabbaso vītarāgattā katthacipi sattaloke saṅkhāraloke ca piyaṃ piyabhāvo “putto”ti vā “bhātā”ti vā “bhaginī”ti vā “bhariyā”ti vā piyaṃ piyāyanaṃ piyabhāvo natthi, saṅkhāralokepi “etaṃ mama santakaṃ, imināhaṃ imaṃ nāma sukhaṃ labhāmi labhissāmī”ti piyaṃ piyāyanaṃ piyabhāvo natthi. Tasmā asokaṃ virajaṃ patthayāno, piyaṃ na kayirātha kuhiñci loketi yasmā ca sukhino nāma vītasokā, vītasokattāva katthacipi visaye piyabhāvo natthi, tasmā attano yathāvuttasokābhāvena ca asokaṃ asokabhāvaṃ rāgarajādivigamanena virajaṃ [M 0.0387] virajabhāvaṃ arahattaṃ, sokassa rāgarajādīnañca abhāvahetubhāvato vā “asokaṃ viraja”nti laddhanāmaṃ nibbānaṃ patthayāno kattukamyatākusalacchandassa vasena chandajāto katthaci loke rūpādidhamme [P 0.0430] antamaso samathavipassanādhammepi piyaṃ piyabhāvaṃ viyāyanaṃ na kayirātha na uppādeyya. Vuttañhetaṃ – “dhammāpi vo, bhikkhave, pahātabbā, pageva adhammā”ti (ma. ni. 1.240).

Therefore, they are happy and free from sorrow. Since sorrows and so forth originate from what is dear, and since they do not exist for those for whom nothing is dear, such persons are indeed called 'happy' and 'free from sorrow.' Who, then, are they? They are those for whom there is nothing dear anywhere in the world. For those noble ones who are entirely free from lust, there is no dear thing or state of dearness anywhere in the world of beings or the world of formations—no affection for a 'son,' 'brother,' 'sister,' or 'wife.' In the world of formations, too, there is no affection in thinking, 'This is my possession; through this I obtain or will obtain such-and-such happiness.' Therefore, one aspiring to the sorrowless and the dustless—that is, Arahantship, which is sorrowless through the aforementioned absence of sorrow and dustless through the removal of the dust of lust and so on; or aspiring to Nibbāna, which is named 'sorrowless and dustless' because it is the cause for their absence—should not, through wholesome desire born of a wish to act, create affection for any phenomena in the world, not even, at the very least, for the phenomena of serenity and insight. For this has been said: 'Monks, even dhammas are to be abandoned, how much more so non-dhammas?' (Majjhima Nikāya 1.240).

Aṭṭhamasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the eighth discourse is finished.

9. Paṭhamadabbasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the First Dabba Sutta

79. Navame [V 0.0348] āyasmāti piyavacanaṃ. Dabboti tassa therassa nāmaṃ. Mallaputtoti mallarājassa putto. So hi āyasmā padumuttarassa bhagavato pādamūle katābhinīhāro kappasatasahassaṃ upacitapuññasañcayo amhākaṃ bhagavato kāle mallarājassa devikā kucchiyaṃ nibbatto katādhikārattā jātiyā sattavassikakāleyeva mātāpitaro upasaṅkamitvā pabbajjaṃ yāci. Te ca “pabbajitvāpi ācāraṃ tāva sikkhatu, sace taṃ nābhiramissati, idheva āgamissatī”ti anujāniṃsu. So satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā pabbajjaṃ yāci. Satthāpissa upanissayasampattiṃ oloketvā pabbajjaṃ anujāni. Tassa pabbajjāsamaye dinnaovādena bhavattayaṃ ādittaṃ viya upaṭṭhāsi. So vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā khuraggeyeva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Yaṃkiñci sāvakena pattabbaṃ, “tisso vijjā catasso paṭisambhidā chaḷabhiññā nava lokuttaradhammā”ti evamādikaṃ sabbaṃ adhigantvā asītiyā mahāsāvakesu abbhantaro ahosi. Vuttañhetaṃ tena āyasmatā –

79. In the ninth sutta, 'venerable' is a term of affection. 'Dabba' was that elder's name. 'Son of the Mallians' means he was the son of a Mallian king. This venerable one, having made an aspiration at the feet of the Blessed One Padumuttara and accumulated a store of merit for a hundred thousand eons, was, in the time of our Blessed One, born from the womb of a queen of the Mallians. Because he had made the requisite aspiration, at the age of only seven years he approached his parents and requested the going forth. They permitted it, thinking: 'Having gone forth, let him first learn the conduct. If he does not delight in it, he can return here.' He then approached the Teacher and requested the going forth. The Teacher, seeing his endowment with supporting conditions, permitted him to go forth. At the time of his going forth, through the instruction that was given, the three kinds of existence appeared to him as if on fire. Establishing insight, he attained Arahantship at the very tip of the razor. He attained everything that can be attained by a disciple—such as the three true knowledges, the four analytical knowledges, the six direct knowledges, and the nine supramundane states—and was included among the eighty great disciples. This was stated by that venerable one:

“Mayā kho jātiyā sattavassena arahattaṃ sacchikataṃ, yaṃkiñci sāvakena pattabbaṃ, sabbaṃ taṃ anuppattaṃ mayā”tiādi (pārā. 380).

“At the age of seven years I realized Arahantship. Whatever is to be attained by a disciple, all that has been attained by me,” and so on (Pārā. 380).

Yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamīti so kirāyasmā ekadivasaṃ rājagahe piṇḍāya caritvā pacchābhattaṃ piṇḍapātappaṭikkanto bhagavato vattaṃ dassetvā divāṭṭhānaṃ gantvā [P 0.0431] udakakumbhato udakaṃ gahetvā pāde pakkhāletvā gattāni [M 0.0388] sītiṃ katvā cammakkhaṇḍaṃ paññāpetvā nisinno kālaparicchedaṃ katvā samāpattiṃ samāpajji. Athāyasmā yathākālaparicchedaṃ samāpattito vuṭṭhahitvā attano āyusaṅkhāre olokesi. Tassa te parikkhīṇā katipayamuhuttikā upaṭṭhahiṃsu. So cintesi – “na kho metaṃ patirūpaṃ, yamahaṃ satthu anārocetvā sabrahmacārīhi ca avidito idha yathānisinnova parinibbāyissāmi. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā parinibbānaṃ anujānāpetvā satthu vattaṃ dassetvā sāsanassa niyyānikabhāvadassanatthaṃ mayhaṃ iddhānubhāvaṃ vibhāvento ākāse nisīditvā tejodhātuṃ samāpajjitvā parinibbāyeyyaṃ. Evaṃ sante ye mayi assaddhā appasannā, tesampi pasādo uppajjissati, tadassa tesaṃ dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāyā”ti. Evañca so āyasmā cintetvā bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā sabbaṃ taṃ tatheva akāsi. Tena vuttaṃ – “atha kho āyasmā dabbo mallaputto yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamī”tiādi.

Regarding the words, 'Then the venerable Dabba Mallaputta approached the Blessed One...': It is said that one day, after wandering for alms in Rājagaha, having returned from the alms round and finished his meal, the venerable one performed his duties toward the Blessed One, went to his daytime resting place, took water from a water pot, washed his feet, cooled his limbs, spread out a piece of leather, sat down, determined a period of time, and entered a meditative attainment. Then, emerging from the attainment at the determined time, the venerable one examined his life-formations. They appeared to him as exhausted, with only a few moments remaining. He thought: 'It is not proper for me to attain final Nibbāna right here as I am sitting, without informing the Teacher and unknown to my companions in the holy life. Let me approach the Teacher, obtain his permission for my final Nibbāna, perform my duties toward the Teacher, and then, to demonstrate the liberating nature of the teaching, I will display my psychic power, sit in the air, enter the fire element, and attain final Nibbāna. When this is done, confidence will arise even in those who lack faith and trust in me, and that will be for their long-term welfare and happiness.' Having reflected thus, the venerable one approached the Blessed One and did exactly so. Therefore it is said: 'Then the venerable Dabba Mallaputta approached the Blessed One,' and so on.

Tattha [V 0.0349] parinibbānakālo meti “bhagavā mayhaṃ anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā parinibbānakālo upaṭṭhito, tamahaṃ bhagavato ārocetvā parinibbāyitukāmomhī”ti dasseti. Keci panāhu “na tāva thero jiṇṇo, na ca gilāno, parinibbānāya ca satthāraṃ āpucchati, kiṃ tattha kāraṇaṃ? ‘Mettiyabhūmajakā bhikkhū pubbe maṃ amūlakena pārājikena anuddhaṃsesuṃ, tasmiṃ adhikaraṇe vūpasantepi akkosantiyeva. Tesaṃ saddahitvā aññepi puthujjanā mayi agāravaṃ paribhavañca karonti. Imañca dukkhabhāraṃ niratthakaṃ vahitvā kiṃ payojanaṃ, tasmāhaṃ idāneva parinibbāyissāmī’ti sanniṭṭhānaṃ katvā satthāraṃ āpucchī”ti. Taṃ akāraṇaṃ. Na hi khīṇāsavā aparikkhīṇe āyusaṅkhāre paresaṃ upavādādibhayena parinibbānāya cetenti ghaṭayanti vāyamanti, na ca paresaṃ [P 0.0432] pasaṃsādihetu ciraṃ tiṭṭhanti, atha kho saraseneva attano āyusaṅkhārassa parikkhayaṃ āgamenti. Yathāha –

Herein, the words 'the time for my final Nibbāna has come' show that he is saying: 'Blessed One, the time for my final Nibbāna by means of the Nibbāna element with no residue remaining has arrived. Having informed the Blessed One, I wish to attain final Nibbāna.' Some, however, say: 'The elder is not yet old, nor is he ill, yet he asks the Teacher for leave to attain final Nibbāna. What is the reason? “The bhikkhus Mettiya and Bhūmajaka previously accused me with a groundless charge of a pārājika offense. Even though that legal issue has been settled, they still revile me. Believing them, other worldlings also show me disrespect and contempt. What is the use of carrying this useless burden of suffering? Therefore I will attain final Nibbāna right now.” Having made this resolution, he asked the Teacher for leave.' That is not the reason. For those whose taints are destroyed do not intend, strive, or exert themselves for final Nibbāna out of fear of the blame of others and so on when their life-formations are unexhausted, nor do they remain long for the sake of others' praise and so on. Rather, they await the natural exhaustion of their own life-formations. As it is said:

“Nābhikaṅkhāmi maraṇaṃ, nābhikaṅkhāmi jīvitaṃ;

Kālañca paṭikaṅkhāmi, nibbisaṃ bhatako yathā”ti. (theragā. 196, 606; mi. pa. 2.2.4) –

“I do not long for death, I do not long for life; I await the time, like a hireling for his wages.”

Bhagavāpissa āyusaṅkhāraṃ oloketvā parikkhīṇabhāvaṃ ñatvā “yassadāni tvaṃ, dabba, kālaṃ maññasī”ti āha.

The Blessed One, having surveyed his life-formations and knowing they were exhausted, said: “Now, Dabba, is the time for that which you are thinking.”

Vehāsaṃ [M 0.0389] abbhuggantvāti ākāsaṃ abhiuggantvā, vehāsaṃ gantvāti attho. Abhisaddayogena hi idaṃ upayogavacanaṃ, attho pana bhummavasena veditabbo. Vehāsaṃ abbhuggantvā kiṃ akāsīti āha – “ākāse antalikkhe pallaṅkena nisīditvā”tiādi. Tattha tejodhātuṃ samāpajjitvāti tejokasiṇacatutthajjhānasamāpattiṃ samāpajjitvā. Thero hi tadā bhagavantaṃ vanditvā tikkhattuṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā ekamantaṃ ṭhito “bhagavā kappasatasahassaṃ tumhehi saddhiṃ tattha tattha vasanto puññāni karonto imamevatthaṃ sandhāya akāsiṃ, svāyamattho ajja matthakaṃ patto, idaṃ pacchimadassana”nti āha. Ye tattha puthujjanabhikkhū sotāpannasakadāgāmino ca, tesu ekaccānaṃ mahantaṃ kāruññaṃ ahosi, ekacce ārodanappattā ahesuṃ. Athassa bhagavā cittācāraṃ ñatvā “tena hi, dabba, mayhaṃ bhikkhusaṅghassa ca iddhipāṭihāriyaṃ dassehī”ti āha. Tāvadeva sabbo bhikkhusaṅgho sannipati. Athāyasmā dabbo “ekopi hutvā bahudhā hotī”tiādinā (paṭi. ma. 1.102; dī. ni. 1.484) nayena āgatāni sāvakasādhāraṇāni sabbāni pāṭihāriyāni dassetvā puna ca bhagavantaṃ vanditvā ākāsaṃ abbhuggantvā [V 0.0350] ākāse pathaviṃ nimminitvā tattha pallaṅkena nisinno tejokasiṇasamāpattiyā parikammaṃ katvā samāpattiṃ samāpajjitvā vuṭṭhāya sarīraṃ āvajjitvā puna samāpattiṃ samāpajjitvā sarīrajhāpanatejodhātuṃ adhiṭṭhahitvā parinibbāyi. Saha adhiṭṭhānena sabbo kāyo agginā āditto ahosi. Khaṇeneva ca so aggi kappavuṭṭhānaggi viya aṇumattampi saṅkhāragataṃ masimattampi tattha kiñci anavasesento adhiṭṭhānabalena jhāpetvā nibbāyi. Tena vuttaṃ – “atha kho āyasmā dabbo mallaputto”tiādi. Tattha vuṭṭhahitvā parinibbāyīti iddhicittato vuṭṭhahitvā bhavaṅgacittena [P 0.0433] parinibbāyi.

“Having risen into the air” means having ascended into the sky; “having gone into the air” is the meaning. This is an accusative of motion used with the prefix abhi, but the meaning should be understood in the sense of the locative. “Having risen into the air, what did he do?” It is said: “in the sky, in the mid-air, having sat down cross-legged,” and so on. Therein, “having attained the fire element” means having attained the attainment of the fourth jhāna based on the fire kasiṇa. For at that time the elder, having paid homage to the Blessed One and circumambulated him three times, stood to one side and said: “Blessed One, for a hundred thousand eons I dwelt with you in various places, performing meritorious deeds with this very purpose in mind. Today that purpose has reached its culmination. This is the final sight of you.” Among the worldling bhikkhus, stream-enterers, and once-returners who were there, great compassion arose in some, while others were moved to lamentation. Then the Blessed One, knowing the disposition of his mind, said: “Well then, Dabba, display a psychic marvel to me and to the Bhikkhu Saṅgha.” Immediately, the entire Bhikkhu Saṅgha assembled. Then the venerable Dabba, having displayed all the marvels common to disciples that are described in the way beginning “Being one, he becomes many…,” again paid homage to the Blessed One, rose into the air, created an earth-disk in the sky, sat there cross-legged, did the preliminary work for the fire-kasiṇa attainment, entered the attainment, emerged and adverted to his body, entered the attainment again, made a determination on the fire element for the cremation of his body, and attained final Nibbāna. Simultaneously with his determination, his whole body was set ablaze. In an instant that fire, like the fire at the dissolution of the eon, burned up everything by the power of his determination without leaving the slightest conditioned thing, not even a speck of soot, and was then extinguished. Therefore it is said: “Then the venerable Dabba the Mallian…,” and so on. Therein, “having emerged and attained final Nibbāna” means having emerged from the mind of psychic power and attained final Nibbāna with the life-continuum consciousness.

Jhāyamānassāti jāliyamānassa. Ḍayhamānassāti tasseva vevacanaṃ. Atha vā jhāyamānassāti jālāpavattikkhaṇaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, ḍayhamānassāti vītaccitaṅgārakkhaṇaṃ. Chārikāti bhasmaṃ. Masīti kajjalaṃ. Na paññāyitthāti na passittha, adhiṭṭhānabalena sabbaṃ khaṇeneva antaradhāyitthāti attho. Kasmā pana thero uttarimanussadhammaṃ iddhipāṭihāriyaṃ dassesi, nanu bhagavatā iddhipāṭihāriyakaraṇaṃ paṭikkhittanti[M 0.0390]? Na codetabbametaṃ gihīnaṃ sammukhā pāṭihāriyakaraṇassa paṭikkhittattā. Tañca kho vikubbanavasena, na panevaṃ adhiṭṭhānavasena. Ayaṃ panāyasmā dhammasāminā āṇattova pāṭihāriyaṃ dassesi.

“Of him burning” means of him blazing. “Of him being burnt” is a synonym for that. Or alternatively, “of him burning” is said with reference to the moment the flame arises, while “of him being burnt” refers to the moment of glowing embers. “Ash” means cinders. “Soot” means lampblack. “Was not perceived” means it was not seen; the meaning is that it all vanished in an instant by the power of his determination. But why did the elder display a superhuman state, a psychic marvel? Did not the Blessed One prohibit the performance of psychic marvels? This should not be raised as an objection, for what was prohibited was the performance of marvels in the presence of householders. And that, moreover, was with respect to the marvel of transformation, not one based on determination. This venerable one, however, displayed the marvel only after being commanded by the Lord of the Dhamma.

Etamatthaṃ viditvāti etaṃ āyasmato dabbassa mallaputtassa anupādāparinibbānaṃ sabbākārato viditvā tadatthaparidīpanaṃ imaṃ udānaṃ udānesi.

“Having understood this matter” means: having understood in all its aspects this final Nibbāna without clinging of the venerable Dabba Mallaputta, the Blessed One uttered this inspired utterance to illuminate that meaning.

Tattha abhedi kāyoti sabbo bhūtupādāyapabhedo catusantatirūpakāyo bhijji, anavasesato ḍayhi, antaradhāyi, anuppattidhammataṃ āpajji. Nirodhi saññāti rūpāyatanādigocaratāya rūpasaññādibhedā sabbāpi saññā appaṭisandhikena nirodhena nirujjhi. Vedanā sītibhaviṃsu sabbāti vipākavedanā kiriyavedanāti sabbāpi vedanā appaṭisandhikanirodhena niruddhattā aṇumattampi vedanādarathassa abhāvato sītibhūtā ahesuṃ, kusalākusalavedanā pana arahattaphalakkhaṇeyeva nirodhaṃ gatā. “Sītirahiṃsū”tipi paṭhanti, santā niruddhā ahesunti attho. Vūpasamiṃsu saṅkhārāti vipākakiriyappabhedā sabbepi phassādayo saṅkhārakkhandhadhammā appaṭisandhikanirodheneva niruddhattā visesena upasamiṃsu. Viññāṇaṃ atthamāgamāti viññāṇampi vipākakiriyappabhedaṃ sabbaṃ appaṭisandhikanirodheneva atthaṃ vināsaṃ upacchedaṃ agamā agacchi.

Therein, “the body was shattered”: the entire physical body, differentiated into primary elements and derived matter, the continuity of form arising from four causes, was broken, burnt up without remainder, disappeared, and reached a state of non-arising. “Perception ceased”: all perceptions, differentiated as perception of form and so on, having the form base and so on as their sphere, ceased with the cessation that involves no relinking. “All feelings grew cold”: all feelings, both resultant and functional, became cool because they ceased with the cessation that involves no relinking, due to the absence of even a particle of the fever of feeling. Wholesome and unwholesome feelings, however, had already gone to cessation at the very moment of the fruit of arahantship. Some also recite “sītirahiṃsū,” meaning they became tranquil and ceased. “Formations were pacified”: all states of the formations aggregate, such as contact and so on, both resultant and functional, were especially pacified by the very cessation that involves no relinking. “Consciousness went to its setting”: all consciousness, both resultant and functional, went to its setting, to destruction, to termination, by the very cessation that involves no relinking.

Iti [V 0.0351] bhagavā āyasmato dabbassa mallaputtassa pañcannampi khandhānaṃ pubbeyeva kilesābhisaṅkhārupādānassa anavasesato niruddhattā anupādāno [P 0.0434] viya jātavedo appaṭisandhikanirodhena niruddhabhāvaṃ nissāya pītivegavissaṭṭhaṃ udānaṃ udānesīti.

Thus the Blessed One, impelled by a surge of joy, uttered this inspired utterance concerning the Venerable Dabba the Mallian, relying on his state of having ceased with the cessation that involves no relinking—like a fire without fuel—because the clinging related to the five aggregates, which consists of defilements and formations, had already previously ceased without remainder.

Navamasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the ninth sutta is completed.

10. Dutiyadabbasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Second Dabba Sutta

80. Dasame tatra kho bhagavā bhikkhū āmantesīti bhagavā rājagahe yathābhirantaṃ viharitvā janapadacārikaṃ caranto anukkamena sāvatthiṃ patvā jetavane viharantoyeva yesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ āyasmato dabbassa mallaputtassa parinibbānaṃ apaccakkhaṃ, tesaṃ taṃ paccakkhaṃ katvā dassetuṃ, yepi [M 0.0391] ca mettiyabhūmajakehi katena abhūtena abbhācikkhaṇena there gāravarahitā puthujjanā, tesaṃ there bahumānuppādanatthañca āmantesi. Tattha tatrāti vacanasaññāpane nipātamattaṃ. Khoti avadhāraṇe. Tesu “tatrā”ti iminā “bhagavā bhikkhū āmantesī”ti etesaṃ padānaṃ vuccamānataṃyeva joteti. “Kho”ti pana iminā āmantesiyeva, nāssa āmantane koci antarāyo ahosīti imamatthaṃ dasseti. Atha vā tatrāti tasmiṃ ārāme. Khoti vacanālaṅkāre nipāto. Āmantesīti abhāsi. Kasmā pana bhagavā bhikkhūyeva āmantesīti? Jeṭṭhattā seṭṭhattā āsannattā sabbakālaṃ sannihitattā dhammadesanāya visesato bhājanabhūtattā ca.

80. In the tenth sutta: There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus. The Blessed One, having dwelt in Rājagaha for as long as he wished, was wandering on tour through the country and in due course arrived at Sāvatthī, where he was dwelling in Jeta’s Grove. He addressed the bhikkhus in order to make the final Nibbāna of the Venerable Dabba the Mallian directly perceptible to those bhikkhus for whom it had not been directly perceptible, and also to generate great esteem for the elder among those ordinary monks who, on account of the baseless accusation made by Mettiya and Bhūmajaka, were devoid of respect for him. Therein, tatra is just a particle for indicating a statement. Kho is for emphasis. Among these, by tatra, it illuminates the fact that the words 'the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus' are being spoken. But by kho, it shows this meaning: he did indeed address them; there was no obstacle to his addressing them. Alternatively, tatra means 'in that monastery.' Kho is a particle for embellishing speech. Addressed means he spoke. But why did the Blessed One address only the bhikkhus? Because of their seniority, their excellence, their closeness, their constant presence, and because they are an especially suitable vessel for the teaching of the Dhamma.

Bhikkhavoti tesaṃ āmantanākāradassanaṃ. Bhadanteti āmantitānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ gāravena satthu paṭivacanadānaṃ. Tattha “bhikkhavo”ti vadanto bhagavā te bhikkhū ālapati. “Bhadante”ti vadantā te paccālapanti. Apica “bhikkhavo”ti iminā karuṇāvipphārasommahadayanissitapubbaṅgamena vacanena te bhikkhū kammaṭṭhānamanasikāradhammapaccavekkhaṇādito nivattetvā attano mukhābhimukhe karoti. “Bhadante”ti iminā satthari ādarabahumānagāravadīpanavacanena te bhikkhū attano sussūsataṃ ovādappaṭiggahagāravabhāvañca paṭivedenti. Bhagavato paccassosunti te bhikkhū bhagavato vacanaṃ patiassosuṃ sotukāmataṃ janesuṃ[P 0.0435]. Etadavocāti bhagavā etaṃ idāni vakkhamānaṃ sakalaṃ suttaṃ abhāsi. Dabbassa, bhikkhave, mallaputtassātiādi [V 0.0352] anantarasutte vuttatthameva. Etamatthantiādīsupi apubbaṃ natthi, anantarasutte vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

Bhikkhus shows the mode of addressing them. Venerable Sir is the respectful reply given to the Teacher by the bhikkhus who have been addressed. Therein, when the Blessed One says, 'Bhikkhus,' he is addressing those bhikkhus. When they say, 'Venerable Sir,' they are replying to him. Furthermore, with this word 'Bhikkhus,' a word preceded by and based on a compassionate, expansive, and gentle heart, the Blessed One turns those bhikkhus from their attention to their meditation subject, their reflection on the Dhamma, and so on, and makes them face him. With this word 'Venerable Sir,' a word that expresses regard, great esteem, and respect for the Teacher, those bhikkhus indicate their readiness to listen and their attitude of respectfully accepting his advice. They attended to the Blessed One means they listened to the Blessed One’s words; they generated a desire to hear. He said this means the Blessed One spoke this entire sutta that is now about to be spoken. Of Dabba the Mallian, O bhikkhus... and so on has the same meaning as stated in the immediately preceding sutta. In This is the meaning... and so on, there is also nothing new; it should be understood in the same way as explained in the immediately preceding sutta.

Gāthāsu pana ayoghanahatassāti ayo haññati etenāti ayoghanaṃ, kammārānaṃ ayokūṭaṃ ayomuṭṭhi ca. Tena ayoghanena hatassa pahatassa. Keci pana “ayoghanahatassāti ghanaayopiṇḍaṃ hatassā”ti atthaṃ vadanti. Eva-saddo cettha nipātamattaṃ. Jalato jātavedasoti jhāyamānassa aggissa. Anādare etaṃ sāmivacanaṃ. Anupubbūpasantassāti anukkamena upasantassa vijjhātassa niruddhassa. Yathā na ñāyate gatīti yathā tassa gati na ñāyati. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – ayomuṭṭhikūṭādinā mahatā ayoghanena hatassa saṃhatassa, kaṃsabhājanādigatassa vā jalamānassa aggissa, tathā uppannassa [M 0.0392] vā saddassa anukkamena upasantassa suvūpasantassa dasasu disāsu na katthaci gati paññāyati paccayanirodhena appaṭisandhikaniruddhattā.

In the verses: Of one struck by an iron hammer: iron is struck with this, thus it is an 'iron-striker' (ayoghana), that is, a blacksmith's iron hammer or iron mallet. Struck means beaten by that iron hammer. Some, however, say the meaning is 'of a solid iron ball that has been struck.' Here the word eva is just a particle. Of a blazing fire means of a burning fire. This is a genitive of disregard. Of one gradually pacified means of one sequentially pacified, extinguished, ceased. Just as its destination is not known means just as its destination is not discerned. This is what is said: of a fire in an iron ball struck and beaten by an iron hammer, or of a blazing fire in a bronze vessel or the like, or of a sound that has arisen—when it has been sequentially pacified, well pacified, its destination is not discerned anywhere in the ten directions, because of its having ceased without relinking through the cessation of conditions.

Evaṃ sammāvimuttānanti evaṃ sammā hetunā ñāyena tadaṅgavikkhambhanavimuttipubbaṅgamena ariyamaggena catūhipi upādānehi āsavehi ca vimuttattā sammā vimuttānaṃ, tato eva kāmapabandhasaṅkhātaṃ kāmoghaṃ bhavoghādibhedaṃ avasiṭṭhaṃ oghañca taritvā ṭhitattā kāmabandhoghatārinaṃ suṭṭhu paṭipassambhitasabbakilesavipphanditattā kilesābhisaṅkhāravātehi ca akampanīyatāya acalaṃ anupādisesanibbānasaṅkhātaṃ sabbasaṅkhārūpasamaṃ sukhaṃ pattānaṃ adhigatānaṃ khīṇāsavānaṃ gati devamanussādibhedāsu gatīsu ayaṃ nāmāti paññapetabbatāya abhāvattā paññāpetuṃ natthi na upalabbhati, yathāvuttajātavedo viya apaññattikabhāvameva hi so gatoti attho.

Thus for the rightly liberated: this means for those who are rightly liberated—because they have been liberated from the four kinds of clinging and from the taints by the noble path, which is preceded by momentary liberation and liberation by suppression—thus they are liberated rightly, by cause, by method. Of those who have crossed the flood of sensual bonds: because they have crossed over the flood of sensuality (called the bond of sensuality) and the remaining floods (distinguished as the flood of existence, etc.) and stand firm. For those canker-destroyed ones who have attained and realized the unshakable happiness which is the stilling of all formations, called the Nibbāna-element with no residue remaining—because all stirring of the defilements has been well calmed and because they are unshakable by the winds of defilements and formations—their destination among the various destinations of gods and humans cannot be designated as 'such-and-such,' for there is no way to designate it; it is not found. The meaning is that, like the aforementioned fire, he has indeed gone to a state beyond designation.

Dasamasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the tenth sutta is completed.

Niṭṭhitā ca pāṭaligāmiyavaggavaṇṇanā.

And the commentary on the Pāṭaligāmiya Vagga is completed.

Nigamanakathā

Concluding Remarks

Ettāvatā [V 0.0353][M 0.0393][P 0.0436] ca –

And thus far—

Suvimuttabhavādāno, devadānavamānito;

Pacchinnataṇhāsantāno, pītisaṃvegadīpano.

Well-liberated from grasping at existence, honored by gods and asuras; whose stream of craving is cut off, who illuminates joy and spiritual urgency.

Saddhammadānanirato, upādānakkhayāvaho;

Tattha tattha udāne ye, udānesi vināyako.

Delighting in the gift of the true Dhamma, bringing about the destruction of clinging; whatever exclamations the Leader uttered in various situations,

Te sabbe ekato katvā, āropentehi saṅgahaṃ;

Udānamiti saṅgītaṃ, dhammasaṅgāhakehi yaṃ.

all those, having been gathered together and included in the collection, were recited as the 'Udāna' by the compilers of the Dhamma.

Tassa atthaṃ pakāsetuṃ, porāṇaṭṭhakathānayaṃ;

Nissāya yā samāraddhā, atthasaṃvaṇṇanā mayā.

To explain its meaning, relying on the method of the ancient commentaries, this exposition of the meaning has been undertaken by me.

Sā tattha paramatthānaṃ, suttantesu yathārahaṃ;

Pakāsanā paramatthadīpanī nāma nāmato.

That exposition, because it clarifies the ultimate meanings in the discourses as is appropriate, is named the Paramatthadīpanī.

Sampattā pariniṭṭhānaṃ, anākulavinicchayā;

Catuttiṃsappamāṇāya, pāḷiyā bhāṇavārato.

With its unconfused ascertainment, it has reached completion for the Pāli text measuring thirty-four recitation sections.

Iti taṃ saṅkharontena, yaṃ taṃ adhigataṃ mayā;

Puññaṃ tassānubhāvena, lokanāthassa sāsanaṃ.

By the power of whatever merit has been attained by me in thus composing this,

Ogāhitvā visuddhāya, sīlādipaṭipattiyā;

Sabbepi dehino hontu, vimuttirasabhāgino.

may all beings, having plunged into the pure practice of virtue and so forth, become partakers of the taste of liberation.

Ciraṃ tiṭṭhatu lokasmiṃ, sammāsambuddhasāsanaṃ;

Tasmiṃ sagāravā niccaṃ, hontu sabbepi pāṇino.

Long may the Teaching of the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One endure in the world; may all living beings constantly be respectful towards it.

Sammā [V 0.0354] vassatu kālena, devopi jagatīpati;

Saddhammanirato lokaṃ, dhammeneva pasāsatūti.

May the god of rain shower properly in due season; and may the ruler of the world, delighting in the true Dhamma, govern the world by Dhamma alone.

Badaratitthavihāravāsinā ācariyadhammapālattherena

By the Venerable Ācariya Dhammapāla, resident at the Badaratittha Monastery.

Katāudānassa aṭṭhakathā samattā.

The composed commentary on the Udāna is complete.
